Under the roof, from the basket’s low angle, watched Sella reach a finger BENEATH the loaf shelf where the charcoal tally lies, without looking or a word, and brought it away; did not read, count or join the strokes or make a cause of the habit (T100 carried, T060/T086). \textbf{Day 139 (Reed 20, second Account-day):} Berr came up short with the red cord folded under his coat and glaze at one mouth-corner, wiped his thumb twice, held a narrow slate unopened, passed a finger over the figure, read \emph{one in twelve, as the notice says}, called the levy and denied it with \emph{your house}, never \emph{I}; the true subtraction stayed in the locked box and a figure read aloud was not the figure paid (T015/T041/T047/T077). Filed a \textbf{fifth green} at a silent woman’s mouth across the square --- clay under her nails, a pale line across the back of one hand, a cup turned a quarter and set back --- as the fifth at a mouth and the sixth shape of the colour, a colour and not a name, never Fenna in the narration, joined to no ear (T050/T051 advanced, not paid). The bell went four, four and a gap with nobody crossing himself, heard beside told (T078); the soft-cuffed clerk stayed set at the out-of-line landing, hand to slate before eyes to stalls (T090/T080/T083). At the stalls Berr paid two marks short for eels and went up the road believing he had done a kindness; below the sill the child’s dark foot stayed the cold to one woman and weather to the yard, read exactly and worth nothing (T093/T094/T096). At the hearth Tarn brought the ear-sentence a \textbf{SIXTH} time to the word that would call the loan and stopped, no figure, no name, breath drawn and unspent; the boy filed a sixth stopping on the interval tray as an object and not a rule, an interval and not a payment, and would not let six likenesses stand up and call themselves a doctrine (T036/T076, T061/T082). \textbf{Day 140 (Reed 21):} before first grey three or four unnamed men went low into the finger’s-width-open back room; Jorra came through with fine grey slate dust, spoke to the wheel first, withheld a pot’s full note from a High Kiln kiln-master and put his bent finger into the cold damper ahead of Sella’s unfinished sentence (T035/T031/T062); Tarn’s seventh year pressed nearer its end and still held, his stroke going on past the bright patch without the half-check. At the Weir the reed-cutter turned his grey cord so the knots stood, tied one low with his teeth, bit the end off and put it back inside his coat unread (T099); Orra gave a date where a figure was asked and kept the word forty unspoken (T024); Mira answered a thin run with her own answer and showed the second twist twice beneath the grey with neither knot counted, her board beside Orra’s not touching (T059/T025). Up the clay road at dusk Sella carried him around a pan set out to dry and an iced trough and set him on his bed and not in the Debt Loft, fold righted without a look at his face, thread frozen, pot handle two inches beyond his hand; in the small hours he turned out his file complete, exact and worthless, six hearings with no seventh, six stoppings with no payer, five greens as colours, and the count one hundred and forty unspent and spoken by nobody. No seventh hearing, no sixth sighting, no knot counted, no name, cause or body for the missing hand, no third gap, no sale, no tin or box opened, no joining; the old life stayed offstage throughout. Forward, not closed.

\end{itemize}

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item Ch 34: Lived Days 141–143, Reed 22–24, Secondday to Fourthday, one hundred and forty-one, forty-two and forty-three days old, four months and twenty-one to twenty-three days, nobody saying so. \textbf{Day 141:} at the Clay Yard and reed beds the last bundles came up judged by the arm that carried them, a cutter told a girl with a creel her arm knew what went into a bundle and that was the whole of it, and a woman asking what the hands would be paid was answered with the weather and the river and shut two fingers out of a fist; the yard went around the clean dark line, the finer grey called the thaw, the broken birth-slates and the place where a hand went in on Seed 15 and did not come out, with a look and a wide step and no number (T098 carried); a reed-cutter’s grey cord went past along the boards straightened and turned where no slate lay, its knots unread (T099 carried). Under the roof a neighbour reached past the bare board with her hand before her eyes and named the old shelf-gap and the empty place at his ear under one appetite in a single breath, a further shaping of T097 filed on a place of its own, advanced and not paid, no third gap and no joining; Sella sent her to the pot with the house has said it and reached a finger BENEATH the loaf shelf where the charcoal lies without looking or a word, bringing it away (T100 carried, unread). Read the carrying arm as a record in muscle that tells what was carried and not what it cost, exact, complete and worth nothing. \textbf{Day 142:} before first grey men with collars high went low into the room off the wheel-shed and Sella gave them no name and did not say the room was cold; Jorra came through with fine grey slate dust ground small as meal into both forearms past the bent finger, spoke to the wheel, told a pot it would do, knew its full note three turns ahead and withheld it from a High Kiln kiln-master, and put that finger into the cold damper ahead of Sella’s unfinished sentence, the double bite filed as an object joined to no kiln with no third telling of the shut room (T035/T031/T062, T065/T095). Tarn’s seventh year pressed nearer its end than ever, knife at the edge of its sill, six counted where the house can check and the seventh where it cannot, the unforged collector sentence beside it, his stroke going on over the flagstones past the bright patch without the half-check. At the Cross Berr Clay read one in twelve, called the levy and denied it with your house, never I, paid two marks short for two pair of eels which the stall-keeper put in her palm uncounted, and went up the road with the true subtraction locked in the box believing he had done a kindness (T015/T041/T047/T077); below the bridge the soft-cuffed clerk stayed set for a measure nobody called (T090/T080). At the hearth Tarn told the kindling Six counted. The next I don’t count and brought the ear-sentence a SEVENTH time, on Reed 23 after Reed 5, 8, 11, 14, 17 and 20, all the way to the word that would call the loan, stopping there with no figure and no name and drawing the breath he did not spend; the boy filed the seventh stopping on the interval tray beside six as an interval and not a seventh payment, refusing to let seven likenesses stand up and call themselves a doctrine because no payer had been named to any (T036/T076, T061/T082). \textbf{Day 143:} downriver at the Weir a reed-cutter set his bundle on the flat blessing stone, straightened his grey thumb-oiled cord, turned it so the knots stood, tied one low with his teeth, bit the end off and put it back inside his coat, telling a woman who could not read it You can ask the cord and No more can the Court, no knot counted (T099 carried); Orra pulled one knot down and gave the ninth of Ilmen, the collector’s boat with six oars and the man at the stern who never touched them, the forty-first double turn legible and the word forty unspoken (T024); Mira answered a thin run with Ask the river, flicked eel-bones while deciding whether to lie, and when a buyer named a figure put her thumb under her apron to the grey cord with a second twist twice beneath it, never carried upriver to Nine Pots or lifted at a door, neither knot counted, her board beside Orra’s and not touching (T059/T025). Three private records stood within a dozen paces of the basket and none was enterable; below the sill the child’s foot stayed dark in three turns of wool, the cold to the woman who wrapped it and weather to the yard, the reading of the extremity going before the core working perfectly and buying nothing (T093/T094/T096). The clerk stayed set; in the afternoon the last bundles stood grey in the ruts uncounted with the third Account-day six days off, the yard going around its two lines, the rack space and the empty place with a look and no number, and Sella, moving her lips along the row with its two unnamed gaps, reached a finger beneath the board without looking or a word (T100 carried). At the going of the light she carried him up around the pan and iced trough, set him on his bed and not in the Debt Loft, put the fold right without looking at his face, left the thread frozen, told the fire it was the thaw and said The house will keep it, and in the small hours he turned out his file as a man lays instruments on a towel and found every object in its place and nothing laid across anything else — six hearings beside and never among with no seventh, three near-full answers advanced and not paid, seven stoppings on the tray with no payer named to any, the damper’s double bite, the two shut-room tellings with no third, the told bell beside the heard, the fifth green a colour and not a name — one hundred and forty-three exact and unspent and the loan uncalled with the seventh year one tend from its end, wanting the crust two inches from his ear and his number spoken by somebody who would know what a number was and getting neither, his hand going up an inch toward the note of water over water and coming down against the fold. No present-tense break, no tagged memory, no power moved, no rank change and no experiment; nothing joined, paid, named, opened, called, spent or ended. Forward, not closed.

\end{itemize}

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item Ch 35: Lived Days 144–146, Reed 25–27, one hundred and forty-four to one hundred and forty-six days old, carried at the half-pace from every open slate. On Day 144 read the last bundles of reed as a record in muscle, judged by the arm that carried them and never by a figure; a girl with a creel was told her arm knew what went into a bundle and that was the whole of it, and a man who asked what the hands would be paid was answered with the weather and the river. The yard went around the clean dark line, the finer grey called the thaw, the rack space with its broken birth-slates and the empty place where a hand went in on Seed 15 and did not come out, with a look and a wide step and no number (T098 carried). Saw Sella’s finger go beneath the loaf shelf and come away without a look or a word, and read nothing of the charcoal under the board (T100 carried). On Day 145 watched Jorra come through with grey slate dust past the bent finger, speak to the wheel and a pot, withhold the full note from a High Kiln kiln-master and put that finger into the cold damper ahead of Sella’s unfinished sentence; at the Weir and below the sill kept Mira’s grey cord with its second twist, Orra’s legible unnamed double turn, the reed-cutter’s cord and the child’s dark foot on places that do not touch (T099, T024/T059/T025, T093/T094/T096 carried). At the going of the light heard Tarn bring the ear-sentence an \textbf{eighth} time, after Reed 5, 8, 11, 14, 17, 20 and 23, to the word that would call the loan and stop there with no figure and no name, drawing the breath he did not spend and saying \emph{Yes, house} to the fire; filed the eighth stopping on the interval tray beside seven as an interval and not a payment, refusing to let eight likenesses stand up and call themselves a doctrine (T036/T076, T061/T082). On Day 146 watched Alda lay her birth-slates before the fold three doors down, cross the flower unknowing, cover it with \emph{Stone seven. The account went up on the eighth, before the paper went out}, say \emph{Warm and breathing} exact and not true, touch her tin unopened and leave six pages turned toward a floorboard with both tins shut (T007/T008/T023/T089, not paid again). At the going of the light was set on his bed and not in the Debt Loft, the fold put right at his ear and under his chin without a look at his face, the thread of drool left frozen and unwiped, the pot handle two inches beyond his reaching hand; in the small hours turned out the file complete, exact and worthless with six hearings beside and never among and no seventh, eight stoppings with no payer named to any, five greens as colours, and the river’s note, the fire’s missing fifth pull and the boards’ knot still three counts in three places that do not become one, and his hand went up an inch toward the water and came down with one hundred and forty-six exact and unspent. The old life stayed offstage: no present-tense break, no `**` tag, no departure from his eyes. No power moved, no rank change, no opening, no ending.

\end{itemize}

\item Ch 36: Lived Days 147–149, Reed 28–30, Eighthday to Tenthday, one hundred and forty-seven through one hundred and forty-nine days old — four months and twenty-seven to twenty-nine days — nobody saying so. At the going of the light Sella set him on his bed and not in the Debt Loft, put the fold right without looking at his face, left the thread of drool frozen, set the pot handle two inches beyond the reaching hand and went to her own bed; in the small hours his file held six hearings and no seventh, three near-full answers advanced and not paid, nine stoppings with no payer named, a sixth colour and a sixth shape, one stiff crust with its empty place, and the loan uncalled as the count crossed into Smoke exact and unspent. Nothing joined, paid, named, opened, called or ended.

Six hearings stayed six with no seventh and nine stoppings stayed nine objects on the widened tray with no payer named to any (T061/T082). One hundred and fifty, one hundred and fifty-one and one hundred and fifty-two stood exact, complete and unspent, and his hand went up an inch toward the note of water over water and came down against the fold each night.

\item Ch 53: Lived Days 210–212, Grain 1–3, Firstday to Thirdday, two hundred and ten through two hundred and twelve days old — six months and thirty days to six months and thirty-two days — nobody saying so. The next I don’t count}, brought the ear-sentence to the word that would call the loan and stopped with no figure and no name, drew the breath he should have spent and did not spend it, left nine stoppings with no tenth before the seventh year at its very end and still ungiven, the Seed 16 breath unspent, the loan uncalled and no collector on the road (T036/T076). Jorra came through with meal-fine grey slate dust past the bent finger and under the nails, kept dusty and clean forearms on one tray, told a pot \emph{You’ll do}, withheld its note from a man on a wrong wind whose saying about a pot singing early stayed a saying, gave no name to the men who went low into the back room before first grey, kept the burned-slate word a direction arrived nowhere beside the dust and the two shut-room tellings with a hand between, and held his bent finger in the cold damper until Sella’s sentence reached the pot as a remembered repetition; \emph{he’s not Vail} stayed sealed and the promise of the boy’s name stayed ungiven (T035/T031/T062/T065/T095). \item Ch 64: Lived Days 243–245, Smoke 4–6, Fourthday to Sixthday, three dated days in six scenes, two hundred and forty-three through two hundred and forty-five days old — six months and sixty-three days to six months and sixty-five — nobody saying either figure under any roof (T071/T072). Smoke went on without a boundary drawn and neither district month-name was corrected; no market, Cross or bell in three days, Smoke 10 (Day 249) four mornings ahead at the close and unbrought. First smell hot clay under tallow, wet wool under that, sour Ash breath of the unswept corner called the thaw; first sound the kiln drawing in fours with a gap, not a bell. Three counts in three places — the carried fire’s four low pulls and the silence where the fifth should have been, its payer unnamed two hundred and forty-three, forty-four and forty-five days (T088); the river’s note of water over water through the finger’s-width door; the boards’ four nails, four and a thumb-width knot — did not become one, for agreeing them would want a payer and none stood to any (T061/T082). He knew the shape of a man going cold and wanted the crust; both were true and the second was louder. Instruction went to the wool, fire, pot, broom, running water and river wind and never to the basket; \emph{the house}, \emph{The house will keep it}, half-pace from every open slate, jar-glance without a touch, hand shut half over nothing, finger on top of the shelf’s front edge so the charcoal stayed unread, pot handle two inches beyond the reaching hand with a half-beat and no look toward the bed, lips along the two-gapped row with no figure, cost-questions sent to the pot and the weather with nothing priced, refused or entered (T058/T079, T100, T077). The dressed grain was turned under wool for damp on all three mornings, spread thin and gathered back by the handful, changing state and gaining no figure, counted in glances, handfuls and the carrying arm’s weight that knows weight and not cost, entered on no slate and laid across none of the absences. Garl stayed in objects — salt-stiff coat with the left-shoulder crease, hollow wheel-seat with its twenty-year lean, clean dark line and finer grey called the thaw, proverb gone to a pot with no crack, tile debt circling without a name — his name unspoken two hundred and forty-five days, no collector up or down the clay road (T009/T013/T092). The widow’s mark hung where it hung, touched once before the kiln on Smoke 1 and at no shelf, well, rack, road, basket, afternoon or dusk on Smoke 4, 5 or 6, because the hand goes to the mark before the kiln and at no other hour; the opening stayed behind the household, no lesson made and no payer named (T058/T079). \textbf{The chapter’s one meaningful change, T080 advanced and not paid:} at the yard well on Smoke 5 a woman of the firing work, \textbf{Ilva}, drew a short strip of notched birch bark from her sleeve and passed the nail of a thumb across the notches before her eyes went to the woman who had asked and before her mouth answered \emph{Five to this morning}; the hand went to the record before it went to the person and to the pot not at all. What the notches held was a count of firings, plain as a firing is plain, kept in wood because a slate would want a figure put on it; nothing on the stick waited to be read and no figure came off it that a clerk could enter. He took the order of reaching and filed it as a \textbf{ninth record-first hand-shape} on a place of its own beside the eighth, a finger between every pair and fingers between it and the charcoal, the cords, the knots, the pages, the tins, the missing hand and the pale line. He did not read the stick, ask her about it or let nine likenesses stand up and call themselves a rule, for a rule is an account that has found a payer and none stood to any (T080). At the kindling Tarn’s ear-sentence reached the word that would call the loan and stopped, nine stoppings standing with no tenth and the Seed 16 breath unspent; at the wheel-shed Jorra parted dust from slip, withheld the note he knew three turns ahead, kept the burned slate at four and the shut-room tellings at two, held his bent finger in the damper as a remembered repetition, and kept \emph{he’s not Vail} sealed and the promise ungiven (T036/T076, T035/T031/T062/T065/T095). On Smoke 6 a wrong wind off High Kiln brought the sweet edge of lead glaze over the boards, touched the fold and went out on the wind that brought it — a direction arrived nowhere and not a second edge paid — and one of the three shapings of the pot saying stood again as a saying, no fourth likeness made a cause, no pot lost and no name given to what ailed the man carried out on Day 188 (T064 held). The file turned out as instruments on a towel was exact, complete and worth nothing: six hearings beside and never among with no seventh, three near-full answers, three pot sayings, the fourth burned-slate telling, two shut-room tellings, told bell beside heard, told figure beside paid with Grain’s third subtraction locked in Berr’s box, the returning-line place gone around with a look and no number, the question on its seventh place with four askings and no witness standing, and the ninth hand on its own tray (T101 carried, T098 carried). Six answers of the hand across the three days, the sixty-first through the sixty-sixth, each filed on the sixth place with no payer named: down at once; down before the letting-go; held to the river’s own low interval with no count in the house to borrow; one borrowed rhythm crossed with one kept; one rhythm held through the little silence after Sella’s count; and in the small hours of Day 245 two rhythms crossing in the inch across a wall that does not touch, remembered and not a change made again. \textbf{Sixty-six} answers now stand on the sixth place, objects and not powers, not a longer reach, a miss entered, a hearing, a seventh, a tenth stopping, a payment, a held change, a key, a power or a rule. He still cannot close two inches to the pot handle, lift the leathery crust or speak a number. Nothing was joined, named, opened, called, spent or ended, no thread was paid and no new thread opened; the hand lay down against the fold like a tool put away and the count went forward into Smoke 7, unspent and told by nobody.

\end{itemize}

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item Ch 65: Lived Days 246–248, Smoke 7–9, Seventhday to Ninthday, three dated days in six scenes, two hundred and forty-six through two hundred and forty-eight days old — six months and sixty-six days to six months and sixty-eight — nobody saying either figure (T071/T072). Smoke went out without a boundary drawn and neither district month-name was corrected; no market, Cross or bell in three days, Smoke 10 (Day 249) one morning ahead at the close and unbrought. First smell hot clay under tallow and wet wool under that, sour Ash breath of the unswept corner called the thaw; first sound the kiln drawing in fours with a gap, not a bell. Three counts in three places — the carried fire’s four low pulls and the silence where the fifth should be, its payer unnamed two hundred and forty-six, forty-seven and forty-eight days (T088); the river’s note through the finger’s-width door; the boards’ four nails, four and a thumb-width knot — did not become one, for agreeing them would want a payer and none stood to any (T061/T082). The surgeon took the body’s inventory and entered it nowhere: one stiff leathery brown-edged barley crust two inches from the ear, its empty place unnamed and no third; the thread frozen in the dry heat and unwiped; cold stopped at cheek, temple and the bare joint of the wrist where the wool rode back, the afterdrop waiting past a warming nobody in this house would perform. He knew the face of a man going cold and wanted the crust; both were true and the second was louder. Instruction went to the wool, fire, pot, broom, running water and river wind and never to the basket; \emph{the house}, \emph{The house will keep it}, half-pace from every open slate, jar-glance without a touch, hand shut half over nothing, finger on top of the shelf’s front edge so the charcoal stayed unread, pot handle two inches beyond the reaching hand with a half-beat and no look toward the bed, dressed grain turned under wool and given no figure, cost-questions sent to the pot and the weather (T058/T079, T077, T100). \textbf{The chapter’s one meaningful change, advanced and not paid:} on the afternoon of Smoke 8 an ownerless voice asked over the boards a fifth time which row the pot went quiet on; the weather answered first with the sweet edge of lead glaze riding a wrong wind off High Kiln over the boards, touching the fold and going out on the wind that brought it, the price of barley answered after it, the voice went up the terrace and the row stood where it stood with nobody leaning in to take the answer down. He opened the asking as a surgeon opens a wound and found no witness at the bottom. Five askings on the seventh place with a finger between each pair are still not one witness, not a fourth shaping of the pot saying, not a hearing, not a seventh, not a fifth telling of the slate, not a cause, not a name and not a row named (T101 advanced, unpaid). At the yard well Ilva was seen again drawing water, her hand staying in her sleeve; she answered the question put and not the one behind it, no figure came off the stick and the ninth record-first hand stayed nine with no tenth (T080 held, not paid). The file laid out on the towel stayed exact and worth nothing: six hearings with no seventh, three near-full answers, three pot sayings with no fourth likeness made a cause, the fourth burned-slate telling, the two shut-room tellings, told bell beside heard, told figure beside paid with Grain’s third subtraction locked in Berr’s box, nine stoppings with no tenth, the Seed 16 breath unspent, three held changes plus the loft scrape, the pale line and the held inch, the seventh green a colour and the seventh shape a shape with no eighth, the dressed grain covered and unfigured, the returning-line place gone around with a look and no number, and the five askings with no witness. His hand answered six times, the sixty-seventh through the seventy-second — down at once, down before the letting-go, held to the river’s own interval with no count in the house to borrow, two rhythms crossed in the inch through one of Sella’s counted breaths and the little silence after it, one rhythm held across that silence without crossing two, and the crossing remembered — each filed on the sixth place with no payer named, none a longer reach, miss entered, hearing, seventh, tenth stopping, payment, held change, key, power or rule (T061/T082). The last was laid against the fold like a tool put away. Garl stayed in objects with his name unspoken two hundred and forty-eight days and no collector on the clay road (T009/T013/T092); Tarn kept six where the house could check and the seventh where it could not, nine stoppings with no tenth, the Seed 16 breath unspent and the loan uncalled; Jorra parted dust from slip, withheld the note known three turns ahead, kept the burned slate at four and the shut-room tellings at two, held his bent finger in the damper ahead of Sella’s unfinished sentence and gave the unnamed back-room men no name; \emph{he’s not Vail} stayed sealed and the promise of the name was neither given nor withdrawn. The old life stayed offstage: no present-tense break and no `**` tag. No seventh hearing, tenth stopping, sixth asking, witness, row named, figure, payer or ending.

\end{itemize}

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item Ch 66: Lived Days 249–251, Smoke 10–12, Tenthday to Secondday, six lived scenes, two hundred and forty-nine through two hundred and fifty-one days old — six months and sixty-nine days to six months and seventy-one — nobody saying either figure under any roof (T071/T072). Smoke went on without a boundary drawn; Smoke 10 was the first Account-day and market of the second firing, Smoke 11 and 12 ordinary tending days with no market, no Cross and no bell, and Smoke 20 (Day 259) stood eight mornings beyond the close and was not brought early. First smell hot clay under tallow, wet wool under that, sour Ash breath of the unswept corner called the thaw; first sound the kiln drawing in fours with a gap, not a bell. Three counts in three places — the carried fire’s four low pulls and the silence where the fifth should have stood under the floor, its payer unnamed for 249, 250 and 251 days (T088), the river’s note of water over water through the finger’s-width door, and the boards’ four nails, four and a thumb-width knot — did not become one, for agreeing any two would want a payer and none stood to any (T061/T082). The surgeon took the body’s inventory and entered it nowhere: one stiff leathery brown-edged barley crust two inches from the ear, its empty place unnamed and no third, the thread frozen in the dry heat and unwiped, cold stopped at cheek, temple and the bare wrist-joint where the wool rode back, the afterdrop waiting past a warming nobody in this house would perform. He knew the face of a man going cold and wanted the crust; both were true and the second was louder. Instruction went to the wool, fire, pot, broom, running water and river wind and never to the basket; \emph{the house}, \emph{The house will keep it}, the half-pace from every open slate, the jar-glance with the hand shut half over nothing, the finger on top of the shelf’s front edge so the charcoal stayed unread, the pot handle two inches beyond the reaching hand with a half-beat and no look toward the bed, cost-questions sent to the pot and the weather with nothing priced, refused or entered. \textbf{The chapter’s one meaningful change, advanced and not paid:} at the Cross on Smoke 10, with the basket set in the moot-post’s finger’s width of shade where no slate lay and Sella standing half a pace off, Berr Clay came up short off the clay road and read \emph{one in twelve, as the notice says} twice over the basket, once for the moot and once for the households that came late; he called the levy, denied it with \emph{your house}, never \emph{I}, and went off with the box locked and the true subtraction inside, believing he had done a kindness. The district’s arithmetic changed for the first time in Smoke and cannot be changed back; the printed figure stood unchallenged, the figure read was still not the figure paid, it answered nothing for the man carried out on Day 188 or the hand that went in on Seed 15, and the figure read over the dressed grain lying covered under wool at home did not know what that grain had cost — the space between the two figures had no signature (T015/T041/T047, T077). The bell went four, four and a gap with nobody crossing himself, the heard bell kept beside the told and its gap not made a seventh of the full note; Hessa carried the slate up unread, the soft-cuffed clerk stayed set at the out-of-line landing for a measure nobody called, and Sella carried him home at the going of the light saying nothing of what had been read over him (T078, T080, T090). Six hand questions were asked and answered honestly: the seventy-third down at once on the river’s next low note; the seventy-fourth held through the gap where the bell’s next stroke did not come and down on the next sound in the square; the seventy-fifth held for the small intake only and down before the letting-go; the seventy-sixth kept to the river’s own interval with no count in the house to borrow; the seventy-seventh one rhythm held across the little silence after Sella’s count without crossing two; the seventy-eighth two rhythms crossed in the inch across a wall that does not touch, remembered at the close. Each was filed on the sixth place with no payer named, none a longer reach, a miss entered as a finding, a hearing, a seventh, a tenth stopping, a payment, a held change, a key, a power or a rule, and the file turned out as instruments on a towel was exact, complete and worth nothing at two inches of air (T061/T082). The nine record-first hands stayed nine with a finger between every pair, Ilva’s notched birch still in her sleeve unread and Hessa’s carried slate still the eighth (T080 held); the row question stayed at five askings with no witness and no row named (T101 held); the charcoal stayed unread, Garl stayed in objects with his name unspoken two hundred and fifty-one days and no collector on the clay road, the dressed grain stayed covered and unfigured, the widow’s mark hung where it hung with no lesson made of the one opening before Smoke 1, and the seventh year stood at its very end and still ungiven with the nine stoppings at nine and no tenth (T100, T009/T013/T092, T058/T079, T036/T076). At the close the hand laid itself against the fold like a tool put away where the next hand will find it without looking, the fire stopped at four, and 251 stood exact, complete, unspent and spoken by nobody, going forward into Smoke 13, a day not yet earned. No new scar or possession, no power used, no present-tense break, no tagged memory, no ending.

\end{itemize}

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item Ch 67: Lived Days 252–254, Smoke 13–15, Thirdday to Fifthday, six lived scenes, two hundred and fifty-two through two hundred and fifty-four days old — six months and seventy-two days to six months and seventy-four — nobody saying either figure under any roof (T071/T072). Smoke went on without a boundary drawn and neither district month-name was corrected; no market, no Cross and no bell in three days, Smoke 20 (Day 259) five mornings beyond the close and not brought early. First smell hot clay under tallow, wet wool under that, sour Ash breath of the unswept corner called the thaw; first sound the kiln drawing in fours with a gap, not a bell. Three counts in three places — the carried fire’s four low pulls and the silence where the fifth should stand under the floor, its payer unnamed for 252, 253 and 254 days (T088), the river’s note of water over water through the finger’s-width door, and the boards’ four nails, four and a thumb-width knot — did not become one, for agreeing two would want a payer and none stood to any (T061/T082). The surgeon took the body’s inventory and entered it nowhere: one stiff leathery brown-edged barley crust two inches from the ear, its empty place unnamed and no third, the thread frozen in the dry heat and unwiped, cold stopped at cheek, temple and the bare wrist-joint where the wool rode back, the afterdrop waiting past a warming nobody in this house would perform; he knew the face of a man going cold and wanted the crust, both true and the second louder (T060/T086). Instruction went to the wool, fire, pot, broom, running water and river wind and never to the basket; \emph{the house}, \emph{The house will keep it}, the half-pace from every open slate, the jar-glance with the hand shut half over nothing, the finger on top of the shelf’s front edge so the charcoal stayed unread, the pot handle two inches beyond the reaching hand with a half-beat and no look toward the bed, cost-questions sent to the pot and the weather with nothing priced, and the dressed grain turned under wool, spread, gathered by the handful and laid flat, changed in state and given no figure (T058/T079, T100, T077). Sella went to the fire before the basket each morning, told it the thaw, turned the coals with the back of a broken pot, pushed coal-black hair back with the burn-wrist so the grey streak showed pale off the coals, and left the thread frozen. Tarn told the kindling \emph{Six counted. The next I don’t count}, set the knife at the lip of its sill with six checkable and the seventh not, brought the ear-sentence to the word that would call the loan and stopped there with no figure and no name, the Seed 16 breath unspent, nine stoppings with no tenth, the loan uncalled, his chest tight, Ash in the knuckle creases, the pale clip-ring at the left wrist and the warm stone cold and unreconciled in its loft pot (T036/T076, T006). Jorra parted dust from slip, told a pot \emph{You’ll do}, withheld its note three turns ahead, put his bent finger into the cold damper ahead of Sella’s unfinished sentence, kept burned slate at four and shut-room tellings at two, and gave the men in the back room no name (T035/T031/T062, T065/T095, T064). On Smoke 14 a pot set down wrong at the racks gave its high thin note before its time and was swept around; the boy filed it beside the three sayings and made no fourth likeness and no cause, and a wrong wind off High Kiln brought the sweet edge of lead glaze over the boards and took it out again (T064). Ilva was glimpsed at the well on Day 252 with the notched strip unread in her sleeve, answering \emph{I keep the count, not the account}; no figure came off the stick and the ninth hand stayed nine (T080 held). The ownerless question was not asked a sixth time and stood at five askings with no witness and no row named (T101 held). Six hand questions were answered honestly, the seventy-ninth down at once on the river’s note, the eightieth before the letting-go of a borrowed count, the eighty-first held to the river’s own interval, the eighty-second through a little silence, and the eighty-third and eighty-fourth crossing two rhythms across a wall that does not touch, remembered and not made again; eighty-four objects lay on the sixth place, exact, complete and worth nothing at two inches of air, and none was a reach, a hearing, a seventh, a payment, a key, a power or a rule (T061/T082). At the close the file lay open on the towel with every gap left gap and every tray parted from its neighbour, the hand laid against the fold as a man puts away a tool where the next hand will find it without looking, and the fire stopping at four with the silence where the fifth should stand. Forward, not closed.

\end{itemize}

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item Ch 68: Lived Days 255–257, Smoke 16–18, Sixthday to Eighthday, six lived scenes, two hundred and fifty-five through two hundred and fifty-seven days old — six months and seventy-five days to six months and seventy-seven — nobody saying either figure under any roof (T071/T072). Smoke went on without a boundary drawn and neither district month-name was corrected; no market, no Cross and no bell in three days, Smoke 20 (Day 259) two mornings beyond the close and not brought early, and the first firing of Frost (Day 271) far off and unbrought. Three counts in three places — the carried fire’s four low pulls and the silence where the fifth should stand under the floor, its payer unnamed for 255, 256 and 257 days (T088); the river’s note of water over water through the finger’s-width door; the boards’ four nails, four and a thumb-width knot — did not become one, for agreeing two would want a payer and none stood to any (T061/T082). The surgeon took the body’s inventory in its old order: one stiff leathery brown-edged barley crust two inches from the ear, its empty place unnamed and no third; the thread frozen in the dry heat and unwiped, because nobody under any roof had ever been given an instruction about the thread and a basket set down is a pot set down and left; cold stopped at cheek, temple and the bare wrist-joint where the wool rode back, the afterdrop waiting past a warming nobody in this house would perform; he knew the face severe cold wears and wanted the crust, both true and the second louder, and entered none of it (T060/T086). He could not lift the crust two inches or wipe his own lip, and took the humiliation as a fact rather than as a punishment. Instruction went to the wool, fire, pot, broom, running water and river wind and never the basket; \emph{the house}, \emph{The house will keep it}, half-pace from every open slate, jar-glance with the hand shut half over nothing, finger on top of the shelf’s front edge so the charcoal stayed unread, pot handle two inches beyond the reaching hand with a half-beat and no look toward the bed, cost-questions to the pot and the weather with nothing priced (T058/T079, T100, T077). \textbf{The chapter’s one meaningful change, domestic and held, not paid:} on Smoke 17 the dressed grain was gathered in by the handful for the last time before Smoke’s second reading, covered under wool and set away from the hearth on the cool stone at the rack end, so the arithmetic read over it on Smoke 20 will not know what it cost; no figure, no loaf, no third gap, and no signature on the space between the figure and the price (T077 advanced, not paid; T015/T041/T047 and T060/T086 held). A second texture held and joined to nothing: on Smoke 18 frost-bloom wrote white on the stone lip of the yard well where the Warm had lately gone out, and the bucket knocked it grey and the yard called it weather; he kept the white lip on a place of its own with no cause — not a hearing, not a seventh, not a payer, not the widow’s mark (a well is not an opening) and not the first firing of Frost (T083/T085 carried, T058/T079 held). The hand answered six times, the eighty-fifth down at once on the river’s note, the eighty-sixth down before the letting-go of a borrowed count from the room that does not touch, the eighty-seventh held to the river’s own interval, the eighty-eighth held for the small intake only, the eighty-ninth carrying one rhythm across the little silence after a count that ended in the other room, and the ninetieth holding that empty interval as an object in its own right without filling it to make a fifth stroke or crossing a second count; ninety honest answers stood on the sixth place, each an object and not a power, and the file turned out on the towel in the small hours was exact, complete and worth nothing at two inches of air (T061/T082 advanced, unpaid). Six hearings stayed six beside and never among with no seventh; three near-full answers, three pot sayings with the premature note from Smoke 14 on its own place, burned slate at four and shut-room tellings at two stayed at their old counts; nine stoppings with no tenth before the seventh year at its very end and still ungiven, the Seed 16 breath unspent and the loan uncalled; Ilva’s strip unread and the ninth hand nine (T080 held); the row question at five askings with no witness and no row named (T101 held). With Sella nothing changed hands: on Smoke 18 she carried him up the clay road at the going of the light, set him on his bed and not in the Debt Loft, put the fold right without a look at his face, left the thread frozen, told the fire the thaw, turned the coals, said \emph{The house will keep it} and went to her own bed. With Tarn and Jorra the two silences under the roof stayed side by side and unjoined. No collector came, no witness stood, no new thread opened, none paid, none closed, and no ending.

\end{itemize}
}

\CRcharacter*{Deshawn Carter}{the laugh in the car park}{build/art/characters/deshawn-carter.png}{\CRfield{Also called}{Des, Deshawn “Des” Carter, Des the medic}\CRfield{Role}{past-life}\CRfield{Born}{1978, Chicago, Illinois, Earth}\CRfield{Kind}{human (Earth)}\CRfield{Origin}{the South Side, Chicago, Illinois, Earth}\CRfield{Allegiance}{Emergency Medical Service; the ambulance bay of the same Level I centre}\CRfield{Status}{unknown on Earth; last heard taking a call at 3 a.m. after Dan’s death}\CRfield{First seen}{Chapter 2}}{\CRsheetheading{Appearance}
A large man, comfortable in his own skin, with a shaved head and a gold tooth he had earned in a joke and kept in affection. His hands were quick and calm and could start an IV in the back of an ambulance on a road made of ice. He smelled of cheap coffee, diesel exhaust and the lemon disinfectant the rigs were wiped down with. He had seen more of Chicago at three in the morning than most people see in a lifetime, and it had left him neither cynical nor quiet. He laughed with his whole body, unembarrassed, the kind of laugh that makes a room turn and look and then smile despite itself. When he stopped laughing, which was rare, the silence he left behind was enormous.

\CRsheetheading{Voice \& Manner}
Fast, warm, profane, generous. He makes jokes instead of asking questions, and the joke is always about himself if he can manage it, which is why nobody minds. He has a paramedic’s way of saying the worst thing in a cheerful voice, because the cheerful voice is the handle by which the worst thing can be carried. His ritual with Dan was ten minutes of bad pizza in a car park after a bad shift, saying nothing at all.

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item “You look like shit, Marchetti. Sit down. Ten minutes.”

\item “I’m not asking, Dan. I’m just saying, you look like a man who’s waiting for the other shoe.”

\item “He told me once, ‘I’m fine.’ I said, ‘Sure, and I’m the Pope.’”

\item “I told her you were working late. What was I supposed to say, Nina? That your father was doing what he always does?”

\item “Ten minutes. Then we talk about nothing. That’s the whole deal.”

\end{itemize}

\CRsheetheading{History}
He was a paramedic on the South Side, the kind who knows which alley is flooded before the dispatcher says it and which apartment buildings have the bad locks. He and Dan met on calls and became friends in the way men of that work become friends: by seeing each other at the worst possible moments and never mentioning them. Des knew Dan was falling apart. He made jokes about it instead of asking. This was not cowardice in his own account; it was the only tool he had. He had watched other men ask, and watched what happened when the answer came. So he kept the car-park ritual alive — the bad pizza, the ten minutes of silence, the easy exit — for years, and believed he was holding his friend together.

He was in the ambulance the night Vesci left a junior alone with a bleeding patient. He saw it, said nothing to Dan at the time, and mentioned it fifteen years later in a way that was half a joke and half an accusation, by which point it was too late to do anything but be angry at the right person in the wrong tense. He was the one the hospital called at 3 a.m. after the expressway. He laughed for exactly one minute before he put the radio down, because that is what the dispatcher needed from him and because he did not yet know what else to do. He was the one who told Nina her father had been working late, and he has never forgiven himself for the kindness of it.

\CRsheetheading{Wounds \& Fears}
His wound is the unasked question. He is the funniest man in the room and the man who cannot say the one true thing. He fears that his laughter is not warmth but a wall, that he has spent twenty years being the man everybody is glad to see and nobody actually talks to. He fears silence in others — it reminds him of the car park, where the ten minutes were the only honest thing in his friendship and they were also a way of never getting to the eleventh minute. He fears that he was an accomplice to Dan’s slow collapse, that he knew and chose the joke. His contradiction is precisely this: the man who brings the light is the man who keeps the dark in place, because a lit room is easier to leave.

\CRsheetheading{Desires}
He wants one more car-park silence. He wants Dan to walk through the door covered in somebody else’s blood, say nothing, and let Des hand him a slice of terrible pizza. He thinks he wants to laugh; what he needs is to learn that showing up is not the same as reaching, and that a man can be loved out of a silence only if somebody is willing to sit through the eleventh minute. In the world Dan entered, Des’s laugh becomes a sound the protagonist reaches for when he cannot reach Nina — the memory of a friendship that failed by being too comfortable, which is its own kind of warmth stolen and never paid back.

\CRsheetheading{Bonds}
\textbf{Daniel Marchetti} — the friend he never asked. Their bond is built on a ritual of not-speaking, and it is the real thing and also a failure. Dan’s silence kept Des from knowing; Des’s jokes kept Dan from confessing. Neither broke it. Des is the man Dan would have called if he had ever learned to call anyone, and the call never came. \emph{Ch 2:} he arrived inside the boy’s head in the present tense and untagged --- car park, slush under the lamps, cold pizza on the console, the gold tooth catching the light, the ten minutes that said nothing and the laugh that filled the space where the eleventh minute would have been --- and then the timed minute on the dispatcher’s radio after the expressway. He went out like a lamp. Dan had no Grathic word for him and the ache went in under the flower.

\textbf{Nina Marchetti} — he drove her home sometimes when she was small and her father was on a shift, and when she asked about him Des said the thing that was easiest. She knows it was a lie. Her tension with him is quiet and permanent: she was the child at the other end of the joke, and she has spent her adult life being the woman who stops waiting — the thing Des’s kindness helped make.

\textbf{Lena Ostrowski} — the other witness. Des and Ostrowski were the two people who saw Dan clearly, and they never once compared notes. There is a mutual wariness between them: she thinks he enables him, he thinks she judges him, and both are right.

\textbf{Paul Vesci} — Des saw what Vesci did to the junior and said nothing for fifteen years. Vesci, in his warm amused voice, called Des “the entertainment.” Des once told Dan, half-joking, that the butcher and the pretty boy were the same man in different coats — a line Dan did not laugh at, which is the point of it.

\CRsheetheading{Arc So Far}
He arrives in Chapter 2 as a remembered laugh and a car-park silence, a `**` voice that comes up under the boy in the birth room of House Silt while a cup across the room gives its flat note and cannot be reached. The car park is wet with slush under the lamps, the dashboard clock past three, the pizza cold in a paper bag on the console; the rig smells of diesel and lemon disinfectant and cheap coffee. He says the line about looking like shit and sitting down for ten minutes, and then he laughs whole from low in his chest, on through the space where the eleventh minute would have been, and later on the radio for exactly one minute, timed by a man who had nothing else to give. The whole arrival is in the present tense, untagged, and goes out like a lamp put out. In a country with no word for a paramedic he is an ache under the ribs where the flower is.

\CRsheetheading{Chapter Log}
\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item Ch 1: Does not appear; the car park is held for Chapter 2.

\item Ch 2: Came back unbidden on Day 2 in the birth room: car park, bad pizza, ten minutes of silence, the gold tooth in the lamplight, the diesel-and-lemon smell of the rig. Said \emph{You look like shit, Marchetti. Sit down. Ten minutes.} and laughed for the space of the eleventh minute and then for one minute on the radio after the expressway. Vanished with the car park; did not know he had been heard.

\end{itemize}
}

\CRcharacter*{Lena Ostrowski}{the woman who said your full name}{build/art/characters/lena-ostrowski.png}{\CRfield{Also called}{Dr. Ostrowski, Ostrowski, Lena}\CRfield{Role}{past-life}\CRfield{Born}{1955, Chicago, Illinois, Earth}\CRfield{Kind}{human (Earth)}\CRfield{Origin}{Chicago, Illinois, Earth; Polish-American}\CRfield{Allegiance}{Cook County trauma service — senior resident, then attending and mentor}\CRfield{Status}{unknown on Earth; retired, last known alive}\CRfield{First seen}{Chapter 3}}{\CRsheetheading{Appearance}
She had a voice like a file and used it on people the way a file is used: to take a little off. She was a small, spare woman who never sat down in the trauma bay, with hands that carried the pale scars of a thousand clamps and a habit of wiping them on her coat without looking. She smelled of soap and machine coffee and the cold metal of the instrument room. She did not decorate herself and did not need to; she entered a room and the room became a place where a mistake would be noticed. Young doctors learned to stand straighter when she came in, which amused her and was, to her, the whole point.

\CRsheetheading{Voice \& Manner}
Clipped, exact, no wasted word. She corrected people by their full name, and the full name in her mouth was a instrument: a small cold pressure applied at the right place. She did not raise her voice. Under her, a person felt simultaneously guided and flayed. She never said please and never said sorry, and she did not consider this rudeness; she considered it accuracy.

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item “Marchetti. You’re back on in ten.”

\item “The first duty is to decide. The second is to carry it. You seem to have trouble with the second.”

\item “Daniel. Look at me when I tell you this.”

\item “Don’t make me say your first name.”

\item “A systems failure is what we call it when we want the chart to close. It is not what we call it when we want to learn something.”

\end{itemize}

\CRsheetheading{History}
She was Dan’s senior resident and then his mentor at Cook County, a Polish-American woman who had come up through the county system and knew its every hidden cost. She taught him that the first duty of a surgeon is to decide and the second is to carry the decision, and she taught it by example: she had lost patients and reported the losses correctly, and it had cost her advancement, which she never mentioned. She was the closest thing he had to a mother in the hospital, which is a strange thing to be to a forty-year-old man, and it was understood by both of them and never said.

She corrected him by his full name for twelve years. When she retired he sent flowers and did not go to the party, and she understood that too. She had urged him to report Vesci over the junior left alone with a bleeding patient, and she never forgave Vesci for it, though she would not have said she forgave anyone anything. She saw the review of Tasha Broussard’s death — saw the phrase \emph{systems failure}, saw that Dan had signed the chart without reading the nurse’s note — and asked him one careful question about it in a corridor. He said the note had not been there. She looked at him for a long moment and let it go. She has carried that moment longer than he knows he gave it.

\CRsheetheading{Wounds \& Fears}
Her wound is a lesson that went half-learning. She taught a man to decide and carry, and then could not teach him the other half: that carrying a decision and confessing a mistake are different acts, and that the second is the one that keeps the first from rotting. She fears that what she made in him is a man who can say \emph{leave it} to a dying body and then sign a chart to protect his own standing, and that the two are the same reflex. She fears she is not as clean as she sounds — she once covered for a junior’s chart herself, early in her career, and never told Dan, because the lesson she taught was easier to give than to live.

Her contradiction is the file in the voice: the woman who demanded accountability her whole life did not demand it of the one person she loved like a son, because she believed the institution’s version and because asking would have meant losing him. She chose the institution. She has never decided whether that was mercy or cowardice, which is the most honest thing about her.

\CRsheetheading{Desires}
She wants Dan to be the surgeon she trained — exact, decisive, and able to say afterwards what he did. She thinks she wants him to call her, which he never will. What she needs is to know that her maxim was incomplete: to carry a decision is not to hide it, and a man who can only carry is a man who will eventually collapse under the weight, or become a machine that does not feel it. In the world Dan entered, her voice is his gift and his trap. It gives him the courage to say \emph{leave it} in a world whose founding doctrine forbids it; it also gives him the language to make his silence sound like duty. Rusk, when he comes, will echo her — and Dan will hear the two voices overlap and not know which one is warning him.

\CRsheetheading{Bonds}
\textbf{Daniel Marchetti} — her student, the son she never had and never claimed. The bond is love expressed entirely as correction. She said his full name for twelve years as a way of saying everything else. The tension: her greatest lesson is also his great alibi, and she knows it and said nothing.

\textbf{Paul Vesci} — she never trusted him and urged the report. Vesci, in his warm amused voice, called her “the iron maiden” and said it in front of residents. She did not care what he called her; she cared that he was right about the institution closing ranks around him, and that it did. They pull against each other across a gulf of mutually understood cruelty, dressed in different coats.

\textbf{Nina Marchetti} — the daughter who resents her. Nina believes this woman had a version of her father that she never got, and sent a card that was a better account of him than anything Nina could write. Ostrowski has never tried to correct the impression. There is a cold, precise dislike there, which she accepts as the price of the truth.

\textbf{Deshawn Carter} — the other witness. Des and Ostrowski are the two people who saw Dan clearly and never once compared notes. She thinks he enables him; he thinks she judges him. She would say, if asked, that the paramedic’s laugh is a anaesthetic with no surgery attached, which is a funny description of a friendship and a true one.

\CRsheetheading{Arc So Far}
She exists as the first and most exact remembered voice in the book --- a file in the sentence, a full name spoken into a trauma bay that is already becoming a clay yard. On the tenth stone of Y.H. 812 her voice breaks through a Sarnish market without a tag and in the present tense, and the two duties arrive with it: decide, then carry, with trouble over the second. The contradiction lives inside the sentence: the woman who demanded an account of every resident withheld one from the man she loved like a son, asked one careful question in a corridor about a chart he had signed without reading the note, and let the lie go. That omission is the thing the maxim carries, the way a clamp carries a crack. Her line has not yet migrated into Rusk’s questions; that is still far off.

\CRsheetheading{Chapter Log}
\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item Ch 3: Day 4, Account-day. \emph{Marchetti. You’re back on in ten.} came into the Cross out of the market noise, followed by \emph{The first duty is to decide. The second is to carry it. You seem to have trouble with the second.} The full name was an instrument, a small cold pressure applied at the right place. For one breath the clay yard, the pigs and the trauma bay occupied the same paragraph --- machine coffee, lemon disinfectant, a white ceiling light, a girl of twenty-two with a scalp wound, a resident waiting for the sentence --- and then the market closed over without a gap. She was not described as an arrival and the shift was not tagged as memory. In the bay she had said the second sentence to mend him and had spent the rest of her life not quite mending herself with it.

\end{itemize}
}

\CRcharacter*{Nina Marchetti}{the light she stopped leaving on}{build/art/characters/nina-marchetti.png}{\CRfield{Also called}{Nina, N., Nina Marchetti}\CRfield{Role}{past-life}\CRfield{Born}{2000, Chicago, Illinois, Earth}\CRfield{Kind}{human (Earth)}\CRfield{Origin}{Elmwood Park and Hermosa, Chicago, Illinois, Earth}\CRfield{Allegiance}{no house; a grown woman who worked with animals outside the city, then moved}\CRfield{Status}{alive on Earth, last known; unknown to Sarn}\CRfield{First seen}{Chapter 1}}{\CRsheetheading{Appearance}
In the photograph on his wall she is six years old, missing two front teeth, squinting in summer light on the edge of Lake Michigan, her whole face given over to the brightness. That is the image he kept and looked at every night without seeing. In life she grew into a woman with her mother’s patience and her father’s habit of not asking: a steady, unshowy person, practical with her hands, who could settle a frightened animal without a word and could not settle a conversation with a man who was good at leaving. She has a way of looking at a person while she decides whether to say the thing that hurts, and then saying it in a light voice, which is a kindness of a sort and a cruelty of a sort. She does not wait well, and she has spent her life being told by other people that this is a virtue.

\CRsheetheading{Voice \& Manner}
Warm, careful, slightly dry. She says the difficult thing casually, so that the other person can pretend not to hear it. With her father the sentences get shorter over the years, until there is almost nothing left to say on the phone. She never raises her voice; her silences are louder.

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item “Don’t worry. I’m not waiting up.”

\item “You always say that. I’ve stopped counting how many times.”

\item “I know. It’s just a boat, Dad. It was always just a boat.”

\item “I stopped leaving the light on. You didn’t even notice. That’s the part I can’t forgive.”

\item “I called. You didn’t pick up. I know you were working. I know. I just wanted you to know that I know.”

\end{itemize}

\CRsheetheading{History}
She was born in 2000, in the years when her father was a junior at Cook County and the house in Hermosa was loud. By nine she had learned not to ask when he would be home, which is a thing a child learns by asking once too often and getting a kind answer that means nothing. By twelve she had stopped leaving a light on for him. She did not hold this against him then; she held it against herself, as if the light had been a claim she had no right to make. She went to college, worked with animals somewhere outside the city, then moved further away. They spoke on birthdays and not otherwise. He kept meaning to call. He was always meaning to call.

The promise was a boat on Lake Michigan, made when she was small, renewed every birthday for nine years, never delivered. It was the first line of the call he composed in his head on the drive home the night he died: something about the lake in the summer and a boat, a sentence he had rehearsed so often that in the moment of breaking it had no words left, only weight. That night she called him. The screen lit in his coat pocket with a name he would not look at. He did not pick up. She has the missed call on her own phone still, and has never deleted it, and has never told anyone she has it.

She grew into the woman her mother became: one who stops waiting, who calls it peace. When the news came she cried for one evening and then was fine, and the being fine frightened her more than the crying. Des Carter told her, gently, that her father had been working late; it was the last lie anyone told her about him and she has never quite forgiven the kindness of it. Ostrowski sent a card that arrive late and said, in a clipped hand, that Daniel had been a good surgeon. Nina kept the card. She resents it, because it is a better account of her father than she has.

\CRsheetheading{Wounds \& Fears}
Her wound is the ordinary one that nobody names: a parent who was present in the room and absent everywhere else. She fears she has become her mother — a woman whose great achievement is that she no longer waits — and that she will pass this on, that she will have a child who learns not to ask. She fears that her father died believing she had stopped caring, when the truth is she called him that night and he let it ring. She fears the missed call more than the death: the death was an event, the call is a habit, and habits are harder to bury.

Her contradiction is that she is the woman who stopped waiting and the woman who kept the receipt. She tells everyone she is over him; she keeps the photograph of the boat in a drawer, and the nine-year-old promise, and the missed call, and a card from a surgeon she never met. She believes she has released him. She has only stopped saying it aloud.

\CRsheetheading{Desires}
She wants to be a person whose life is not organised around a man who might call. She thinks she wants an apology — one sentence, from him, in which he says he is sorry and means it. What she needs is to understand that the debt was never hers to carry: his silence was his, his guilt was his, his death was his, and the call she made that night was an act of love, not a failure. In the terms of the world he entered, she is the weight that crossed with him, the unsent call made solid — and she is not the child in the minivan. That other woman, the one he pulled from the van, carries his last warmth. Nina carries his last unsent words. He never named either of them in Sarn.

\CRsheetheading{Bonds}
\textbf{Daniel Marchetti} — her father. Love and resentment braided so tightly that she cannot pull one thread without the other. He is the man who promised a boat and never bought it, who died with her name lit on his phone, whose greatest act was to give his warmth to a stranger’s child. She would trade all of it for one honest conversation. He carries her into Sarn as a debt he cannot settle, and reaches for a phone for her every time somebody dies. \emph{Ch 1:} she is a lit rectangle under a coat flap on the expressway and the nine-year promise gone down to weight; he does not look at the name.

\textbf{Elena Rossi} — her mother, the woman who stopped waiting first. Nina learned the art from her and now fears she has perfected it. They love each other in the practical Marchetti way: by doing things and refusing to discuss them. Mother and daughter have never once said out loud what her father’s absence did to them.

\textbf{Deshawn Carter} — the family friend who told her, kindly, that her father was working late. She knows it was a lie. Her tension with Des is that he was the adult who chose the comfortable sentence, and then laughed about it with her father in the car park for years; she was the child at the other end of both.

\textbf{Lena Ostrowski} — the surgeon who sent the late card. Nina resents her with a cold, precise resentment: this woman had a version of her father that she never had, got the full name spoken in a voice like a file, and was thanked with flowers. Nina kept the card because it is the only account of him that does not require her to supply the feeling herself.

\textbf{The woman in the minivan} — a stranger Nina has never heard of, who was nine or ten the night her father died and is now a woman still warm on Earth. Nina does not know that the last warmth of her father’s life went into that stranger, not into her. When she learns it, if she ever does, it will be the final account, and it cannot be settled by dying again.

\CRsheetheading{Arc So Far}
Chapter 1 gives her the shape she will keep for thousands of chapters: a light under a coat flap and the weight of a sentence never finished. She has no words in the book yet and already carries the debt that made a man portable. The missed call on her own phone, the boat photograph in the drawer and the late card from Ostrowski are still offstage; the reader knows her only as the thing Dan refuses to look at.

\CRsheetheading{Chapter Log}
\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item Ch 1: Present only as the lit screen in his coat pocket on the expressway --- a name he will not look at, heavier than the phone --- and as the boat promised for nine years whose sentence has nothing left in it but weight. Not named in the Sarn narration; no line of her own.

\end{itemize}
}

\CRcharacter*{Paul Vesci}{the butcher’s other name}{build/art/characters/paul-vesci.png}{\CRfield{Also called}{Dr. Vesci, Vesci, the butcher’s friend}\CRfield{Role}{past-life}\CRfield{Born}{1975, Evanston, Illinois, Earth}\CRfield{Kind}{human (Earth)}\CRfield{Origin}{Evanston, Illinois, Earth}\CRfield{Allegiance}{plastic surgery, the same Level I centre; later a private practice with good light}\CRfield{Status}{unknown on Earth; last known alive and practising}\CRfield{First seen}{Chapter 8}}{\CRsheetheading{Appearance}
He was beautiful in the way a well-kept instrument is beautiful: pressed, polished, and entirely at ease in the hand. Expensive shoes, a good watch, a warm, amused voice that never carried. His hands were long-fingered and dexterous, a pianist’s hands, and he thought of Dan’s short steady ones as a butcher’s — a judgement he made in affection first and in malice afterwards, until the two became indistinguishable. He smelled of clean soap and a little cologne, which in a hospital reads as a kind of aggression. He never looked tired, which was his greatest affectation and, in the end, his greatest lie.

\CRsheetheading{Voice \& Manner}
Warm, amused, unstoppable. He never raises his voice and never says an unkind thing in a tone that could be reported as unkind. He speaks in the passive grammar of the institution he represents, which is why the Warm Court will one day sound like him to Dan: \emph{nothing happened; it was a systems issue; the chart was closed.} He calls Dan “the butcher” in a tone of such fondness that only Dan hears the knife in it.

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item “Dan. Still cutting things open? Some of us learned to put them back.”

\item “You reported me. Over a junior. A junior, Dan.”

\item “Nothing happened. That’s what a chart is for.”

\item “The butcher. Always the butcher. It’s affectionate, if you must know.”

\item “We all sign charts we haven’t read. You of all people should understand that.”

\end{itemize}

\CRsheetheading{History}
They were friends in residency and then not. Vesci was a plastic surgeon with a beautiful manner and a talent for taking credit, the kind of man who could make a complicated repair sound like a small favour he had done for a colleague. The rupture came when he left a junior alone with a bleeding patient and Dan reported it. Vesci never forgave him, and spent fifteen years referring to him, in a warm amused voice, as the butcher. Dan pretended not to care. He cared.

Vesci was the one who, at the review of Tasha Broussard’s death, said the words \emph{systems failure} in a gentle voice and gave the hospital the language it needed to close the matter. He did not know that Dan had signed the chart without reading the nurse’s note. Or rather, he did know — he learned it later, in passing, from Des, and he has never used it. Using it would mean admitting he had been watching Dan for fifteen years, and that the two of them were the same man in different coats. He keeps a file on Dan’s career that he has never shown anyone. He keeps it the way a man keeps a photograph of a woman who left him: not to look at, but to know it exists.

He said something once about Nina, in a voice he thought was harmless: that she would learn to stop waiting, like the rest of them, and that it was kinder that way. Dan did not laugh. Vesci has never understood why that line ended the friendship more completely than the report did.

\CRsheetheading{Wounds \& Fears}
His wound is that his reputation is his vessel and he believes it cannot be allowed to leak. He fears being ordinary, being reported again, being seen clearly by anyone for longer than a minute. He is not a villain; he is a man who has decided that his own standing is the most important account in the world, which is precisely the logic of the Warm Court, and he would be genuinely surprised to hear it described that way. His contradiction is that he is warm while being cruel and believes his warmth makes the cruelty kind. He genuinely thinks he did nothing wrong. He also genuinely knows he did, which is why he watches Dan.

He fears Dan most of all, because Dan is the only man who knows that the institution’s forgiveness is a transaction and not a fact. Every time Vesci says \emph{nothing happened} he is asking Dan to agree, and Dan’s silence is the only answer he has ever got, and he has chosen to read it as assent.

\CRsheetheading{Desires}
He wants Dan to admit he overreacted — one sentence, said in a warm voice over a drink, in which the butcher concedes that the butcher was right to report him. He thinks he wants vindication. What he needs, unknowingly, is to be the mirror Dan cannot look at: the human face of a world that absorbs a man’s guilt and hands him back clean. In Sarn he becomes the model for the reasonable men with ledgers — not a dark lord, a man with a good reason and a neat hand. When Dan hears the Court say \emph{the account stands}, he will hear Vesci saying \emph{that’s what a chart is for}, and understand they are the same sentence spoken in two rooms.

\CRsheetheading{Bonds}
\textbf{Daniel Marchetti} — the rival and the mirror. The nickname is a small cold pressure applied for fifteen years, and it lands because Dan secretly believes it. Vesci has a file on him; Dan has a secret that proves the nickname true. They pull against each other across a gulf of mutual, unspoken recognition: each knows exactly what the other is, and neither can say it without incriminating himself.

\textbf{Lena Ostrowski} — she urged the report and never trusted him. Vesci called her “the iron maiden” in front of residents. She was right about him and he has never forgiven rightness in a woman; it is the one thing his beautiful manner cannot smooth over.

\textbf{Deshawn Carter} — the paramedic who saw the junior incident and said nothing for fifteen years. Vesci called him “the entertainment,” which is how he thinks of most people who are not useful to him. Des half-told Dan the truth years later, in a joke that Dan did not laugh at. Vesci does not know how much Des knows, which is a small permanent unease.

\textbf{Nina Marchetti} — a girl he made a careless remark about, in a voice he thought was harmless. He has forgotten it. Dan has not, and Nina, who was never told, has spent her life sensing the shape of it without the words.

\CRsheetheading{Arc So Far}
No chapters are written yet. Vesci exists as a remembered voice and a wound in Dan’s professional life, the man whose easy forgiveness of himself is the prototype for everything Dan will later fight in Sarn.

\CRsheetheading{Chapter Log}
\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item No chapters written yet; first appearance planned for Ch 8 (remembered voice at the review that called Tasha’s death a systems failure).

\end{itemize}
}

\CRcharacter*{Dessa Silt}{the mother who counted nineteen steps and called the child dead}{build/art/characters/dessa-silt.png}{\CRfield{Also called}{Dessa, Dessa of the Slip Pits, the little hot one’s mother}\CRfield{Role}{family}\CRfield{Born}{Y.H. 788, Low Kiln, Sill, Grath}\CRfield{Kind}{human (Grathic; returned thin)}\CRfield{Origin}{Low Kiln, Sill, Grath; House Silt}\CRfield{Allegiance}{the slip pits, Clay Yard, Low Kiln}\CRfield{Status}{dead (Day 38, Ilmen 9, Y.H. 813; drowned in the clay-heavy Slip Brook, uncollected; the number stayed in her thumb and the name under the sieve-wire scar; the lie told for mercy became a fact nobody could correct)}\CRfield{First seen}{Chapter 1}}{\CRsheetheading{Appearance}
Twenty-four and worked older: a thin woman with slip-grey nails and a cough that comes up from the pits in cold weather, which is most of the year. She has a way of smiling when she is angry that her sister Mira calls \emph{the door shut}, because the smile means nothing further will be said. Her left forearm carries a long pale scar from a broken sieve-wire, and she rubs it when she is deciding whether to tell the truth. She smells of wet clay, sour milk and, on the days she has been at the pits, the mineral edge of water from the Lead Run that nobody in Low Kiln will drink twice. Her hands are small and quick and never clean. The thing people notice first is the smile; the thing they notice last is that she counts under her breath when she walks — the nineteen steps from the slip pit to the drying rack, which she has counted every day for six years.

\CRsheetheading{Voice \& Manner}
Short, practical, with a joke that costs her. She says the difficult thing in the proverb-form the district uses for saying anything at all, so that it can be taken as advice if the listener prefers. She never calls her child by his name; she calls him \emph{the little hot one} or \emph{the flower}, and has done this so long that the habit has become a way of not saying what she means. When she is frightened she gets specific — dates, steps, the number of loaves — because specifics are a handle on a thing that is otherwise too large.

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item “Nineteen steps. I counted them when I was waiting for him to come back. He didn’t come back.”

\item “A body can be warm and still be gone. You learn that in the pits.”

\item “I didn’t give him away. I gave him heat. There’s a difference, and I’ll hear it from a collector if you like.”

\item “Don’t set that near the fire. It’ll crack, and then you’ll have a crack and a pot.”

\item “He’s not a Vail. Don’t let anybody write him as one and call it kindness.”

\end{itemize}

\CRsheetheading{History}
She was born in Y.H. 788 to a mother who was banked and returned thin, which means Dessa came into the world with a faint interest in a life she cannot name. She learned early that this is considered an advantage in Low Kiln, where a person with some of somebody else left in her is a person who can work two shifts. She works the slip pits for six bits a day, shares a room with her sister Mira, and at nineteen had a child by a quarry hand from Stonemouth named Nils, who went upriver in the autumn and never sent for her. She carried the child through the Long Cold with nothing but a stone warmed at the Vail fire and the kindness of Alda Reed, who attended the birth on Stone 7, Y.H. 812, and crossed herself at the branching red flower across the baby’s ribs.

On the third day Sella Vail took him. Alda told Dessa the boy had been entered to a house and then, when Dessa asked which, said the thing that has been a lie for three years: that the child had gone in the levy, that he was among the forty children of Low Kiln banked that month for a private account, and that a mother with a thin return would only draw attention to a slate that was better left alone. Dessa believed her. She has spent three years believing her son was spent to buy somebody else’s wholeness, and has never once been able to say the number forty without touching the pale scar on her forearm.

\CRsheetheading{Wounds \& Fears}
A mother who returned thin and reached for a life that was not hers; a child she believes was banked; the nineteen steps she counts because counting keeps her from thinking. By the end of Day 1 the count has stopped and her pulse has taken it up; the cough is still called weather. The sieve-wire scar is rubbed whenever a truth is near. She fears that if she ever learned the boy was alive she would want him back, and that wanting would make her a thief in a district where a woman with no house can be accused of anything. She fears the collectors, the name-pot, and the Second Want in herself — the shape that sometimes comes over her in the night and leaves her reaching for a cradle that is not in the room. Her contradiction: she tells everyone she has stopped thinking about the little hot one, and has kept a scrap of cloth from his birth in a tin above the bed for three years.

\CRsheetheading{Desires}
She wants to be warm once without anyone entering it against her account. She thinks she wants Nils to come back, though she would not take him if he did. What she needs is to know that the boy lived; and beyond that, to understand that the shape in her that reaches for him is not the defect of a thin return but her own love, which is the one thing the Court has never learned to deduct.

\CRsheetheading{Bonds}
\textbf{Corin} — her son, who lies under another roof and does not know her.
