\CRcharacter*{Mira Silt}{the aunt who knows and will not say}{build/art/characters/mira-silt.png}{\CRfield{Also called}{Mira, Mira of the Fishstairs, Dessa’s sister}\CRfield{Role}{family}\CRfield{Born}{Y.H. 785, Low Kiln, Sill, Grath}\CRfield{Kind}{human (Grathic; returned thin)}\CRfield{Origin}{Low Kiln, Sill, Grath; House Silt}\CRfield{Allegiance}{the Fishstairs, Sill; eel trade; House Silt}\CRfield{Status}{alive — the secret kept out of love still unsaid at the close of Day 169, Tallow 20; on stage on Day 167 at the Weir’s lower boards and below the sill; her board beside Orra Weir’s and not touching it, the second cord twisted twice beneath the creel with neither knot counted}\CRfield{First seen}{Chapter 1}}{\CRsheetheading{Appearance}
Twenty-seven, broad-hipped, with eel slime dried on her sleeves and a small smile she keeps on her face the way another woman keeps a door on the latch: it can be shut without anybody noticing the movement. The top half of her left ear is missing, taken by a knife in a Fishstairs quarrel when she was nineteen; she says a hook did it, and the scar says otherwise, and nobody has ever made anything of it. She smells of river silt, salted perch, tallow smoke and the cold off the water. She carries a string of eel-bones in her pocket and flicks them against her thumb when she is deciding whether to lie, which is often. The thing people notice first is the smile; the thing they notice last is that she never sits down at a table where a slate is open.

\CRsheetheading{Voice \& Manner}
Fast, low, with the proverb turned sideways. She answers a question with a question and then answers it herself, which gives her the room to choose which answer the listener gets. She never tells a story with a beginning; she starts at the part where somebody is already in trouble. She has learned from Fen traders to mark accounts in knots rather than on slate, and will not write a name down if a knot will hold it. When she is being kind she becomes brisk, because kindness in her house is a thing done quickly before anyone can make a speech about it.

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item “You want to know. You don’t want to know. I can see which one’s winning.”

\item “The secret’s in what happens to it after. I didn’t tell anybody anything. There’s nothing to tell. That’s the whole of it.”

\item “It came from a warm house, that’s all. There’s barley in it and a little smoke and it’s a crust, not a sermon.”

\item “Nineteen steps. Your sister counts them. I count the ones she doesn’t take.”

\item “Don’t ask a Fishstairs woman what she saw. She’ll sell it to you and then it’s yours and you’ll have to carry it.”

\item “He’s warm. That’s all I’ll say on a slate, and I’m saying it off the slate.”

\item “I kept your secret for three years, Dessa. Don’t make it a fourth.”

\item “Thin? Who’s to say thin? It comes when it comes. Ask the river.” --- the answer she gives to her own question on Reed 18.

\item “Two marks the pair and two short. You’ve said it twice and I’ve counted it twice. There’s nothing in the sentence that wants an answer.” --- to a buyer at the fish-trade shade on Reed 18.

\end{itemize}

\CRsheetheading{History}
Born in Low Kiln to the same thin-returned mother as Dessa, Mira learned the eel trade at the Fishstairs at twelve and has worked the dawn market there ever since. She knows which households pay and which owe, which collectors take their ale before a collection and which after, and which boats on the Ilm are carrying something other than fish. She has been the district’s informal ledger of who is warm and who is cooling for fifteen years, and has never once put a name on paper.

She was in the room on Stone 7, Y.H. 812, when her sister bore the child with the branching red flower. She saw Sella Vail carry a covered bundle up the Clay Yard three days later, and she understood what had been done without being told. Alda Reed told Dessa the boy was among the Forty; Mira let her believe it. She has let her believe it for three years, and has taken a share of the barley Sella pays every winter, which she spends on Dessa, who does not know where the barley comes from. She has a child of her own, returned thin in Y.H. 802 to a household in Nine Pots, who does not recognize her; she has walked to Nine Pots twice and never knocked.

\CRsheetheading{Wounds \& Fears}
Her sister’s lie is hers too, and she has begun to feel the weight of it in the hand that holds the eel knife. She fears that telling Dessa the truth will put the boy on a slate that someone can use against him; she fears more that if she waits much longer the truth will come out in a quarrel, which is the worst way for a thing like that to be said. She fears she has become a woman who trades in other people’s warmth and calls it looking after them. Her contradiction: she gossips all day at the Fishstairs and has kept the one secret that matters for three years without a single slip.

\CRsheetheading{Desires}
She wants Dessa to stop reaching for a child she believes is dead, and she wants to be believed once about something that is not a rumour. She thinks she wants the truth to come out, and has arranged her life so that it never has to. What she needs is to understand that a secret kept out of love is still a debt, and that it gathers Ash like any other debt, and that the only way to stop paying interest on it is to say the thing.

\CRsheetheading{Bonds}
\textbf{Dessa Silt} — her sister, her room-mate, the woman whose child she has hidden for three years. Dessa suspects; Mira has begun to be afraid of the moment Dessa stops suspecting and knows. Everything between them is said in the language of barley, coughs and the nineteen steps. \emph{Ch 1:} she crossed the room and pressed a crust of Vail-smoked barley into Dessa’s hand in two brisk movements, stopping short of the slate to do it.

\textbf{Corin} — the nephew she watches from a distance at the market and once followed as far as the Clay Yard. She has never called him anything, not even in her head, because a name is a thing that can be overheard. \emph{Ch 1:} she would not hold him and would not sit where the slate lay open, but pushed the wool back under him briskly with two movements before anyone could make a speech about it. \emph{Ch 3:} a background figure at the eel stall in the afternoon, eel slime dried pale on her sleeves and the top of her left ear gone; she flicked an eel-bone against her thumb and never once looked at the basket. When she turned to go she shoved a loose board clear of the barrow men’s path with the side of her hand, brisk, her face still toward the eels. She had not looked at him once all day. He put her not-looking beside the man on the block’s: one priced him, the other kept him, and he had no word in Grathic for either.

\textbf{Sella Vail} — they have an arrangement: barley and silence. Mira has begun to resent the barley and has never once refused it, which is the precise shape of her complicity. \emph{Ch 1:} she watched the hand in the door without moving, her thumb quiet in her pocket and the eel-bone put away.

\textbf{Alda Reed} — they trade small facts and never the large one. Alda knows more about the birth; Mira knows more about what happened after it. Neither will sit at a table with a slate on it, and they have built a friendship entirely out of things said standing up. \emph{Ch 1:} they worked the same room standing, each with her back to the writing.

\textbf{Orra Weir} — her supplier at the Weir and her oldest friend, who wants the secret out and has said so twice. Mira has answered both times with the weather.

\textbf{Berr Clay, the Thane of Clay} — buys her eels for the levy feast and pays in marks that are short by two. She short-weights him by two eels. This small war has been going on for six years and neither has acknowledged it. \emph{Ch 3:} at the eel stall she asked him the price and answered it herself --- \emph{two marks the pair or two marks the pair and two short? Don’t trouble yourself. It’s two marks the pair and two short, and I’ve counted them twice, and I’ll count them again after I’ve eaten.} He did not answer, because she had left him nothing in the sentence that wanted an answer. She moved an eel-bone from hand to hand and said a figure under her breath. The knot-string is still not shown; only the counting is.

\textbf{Tarn} — the Vail’s clay-bound hand. She has suspected for a year that he is more than the debt he says he is, and has not asked, because she recognizes a person who keeps a secret and knows better than to open him.

\textbf{Ch 5.} At the Fishstairs on Stone 14 and the market’s edge on Stone 15 she worked with pale slime on her sleeves and silt in her neck, head held a little to the right against the cold where the ear had been. She flicked three eel-bones against her thumb while deciding whether to lie and put one away when the deciding was done; she gave Berr four eels where six should go against his two marks short of six years, and neither acknowledged the war. Asked whose the basket was, she answered with a question and then her own: \emph{he’s warm} --- all she would say on a slate, and she was saying it off the slate. Her grey wool cord at the waist was touched three times in two mornings when a number was spoken, and the second cord twisted twice beneath it has never gone up the river to Nine Pots and has never been lifted at a door; the thumb goes always to the first. She put a brown-edged crust into the fold briskly, called it a crust and not a sermon, and went back to the eels without looking in.

\textbf{Ch 7.} On Stone 28 she came up the Clay Yard from the fish-trade with pale eel slime dried on her sleeves and the top of her left ear gone, head held to the right against the cold. Asked whose basket was going past, she answered with a question and her own answer --- \emph{Whose do you think? A basket’s a basket. It came from a warm house, that’s all, and it’s going back to one} --- and flicked an eel-bone against her thumb and put it away. When a woman at the well said a figure for the Five, her thumb went under her apron to the grey cord and stayed there while she decided, and came out with another bone between finger and thumb. She crossed three paces and put a fresh brown-edged barley crust into the fold beside the spent one, saying \emph{It’s a crust, not a sermon}, and went back to the eels without looking in; the old crust lay stiff where it had lain since Stone 15 and neither woman named either. Shifting the basket’s weight showed the second cord twisted twice beneath the grey, the one never taken upriver to Nine Pots or lifted at a door; the knots on neither were counted. Three doors down Dessa coughed from the pits and called it weather, and Mira’s smile did not move. She has not said she knows the child is Dessa’s.

\textbf{Ch 8.} On the Last Day she came up from the eels with pale slime dried on her sleeves and the top of her left ear gone, brisk, answering a question with a question and her own answer --- a basket came from a warm house and goes back to one --- and flicked an eel-bone against her thumb before putting it away. When a figure was spoken her thumb went under her apron to the grey wool cord and stayed while she decided, and shifting the weight showed the second cord twisted twice beneath it, never taken upriver to Nine Pots and never lifted at a door; the knots were not counted. She put nothing into the fold this chapter --- no third crust came --- and went back down the yard without once looking in or saying she knew the child.

\textbf{Ch 9.} On Ilmen 2 she came up from the eels with pale slime dried on her sleeves and silt in the hollow of her neck, head held to the right where the top of her left ear had been, and answered a question about the eels with a question and her own answer. When a figure was spoken at the well her thumb went under her apron to the grey wool cord and stayed while she decided; shifting the basket showed the second cord twisted twice beneath it, never taken upriver to Nine Pots and never lifted at a door, and neither was counted. On Ilmen 8 she came up again and passed her sister at the end of nineteen steps without looking at her, brought no crust and put nothing into the fold, and went back down the yard toward the eels without once looking in. Two not-lookings of the same shape were opposite things and the boy kept them apart. She has not said she knows the child is Dessa’s.

\textbf{Ch 10.} She comes up from the eels at the brook’s edge on Ilmen 9 with pale slime dried on her sleeves and her head held to the right where the top of her left ear had been, answers a neighbour’s question about the water with her own answer, brings no crust and does not look into the basket on the bank where her sister lies dead. At the Fishstairs on Ilmen 12 she answers a question about the run with a question and then her own --- \emph{It comes when it comes. Ask the river} --- and shifting the weight of a basket shows the second cord twisted twice beneath the grey, never carried upriver to Nine Pots and never lifted at a door, the knots on neither counted. On the river road on Ilmen 14 she tells Sella to ask Orra what night the boat came and not what she is owed, because Orra will tell her the oars; on Ilmen 15, at the blessing, she gives the same answer in the same form and keeps her grey wool on its own board beside Orra’s knot-string without letting the two touch. She has not said she knows the child is Dessa’s, and her small smile stays on the latch.

\textbf{Ch 11.} On Day 45 she worked the eels at the far racks with pale slime dried on her sleeves, silt in the hollow of her neck and her head held right where the top of her left ear had been. Asked whether the run would come with the blessing done she answered the question and then her own --- \emph{Does it come now the stone’s blessed? It comes when it comes. Ask the river} --- and flicked an eel-bone against her thumb while deciding whether to lie, putting one away when the deciding was done. When a buyer said a figure her thumb went under her apron to the grey cord and shifting a basket showed the second twisted twice beneath it, never carried to Nine Pots or lifted at a door, neither knot counted. Her board stood beside Orra’s and did not touch it. The smoky crust she put in the fold on Stone 28 is gone by the afternoon of Day 46, taken quietly and never named; the boy set her hand on a tray with two other hands and made no cause of it. She has not said she knows the child is Dessa’s.

\textbf{Ch 12.} On Day 53 she answered a question about the run with a question and her own answer and moved eel-bones while deciding whether to lie; when a buyer said a figure her thumb went under her apron to the grey cord and stayed. The second cord twisted twice beneath it showed and was not carried upriver to Nine Pots or lifted at a door, and her board lay beside Orra’s without touching it. Dessa has been dead sixteen mornings and she has not said she knows the child is Dessa’s; the barley and the silence between her and Sella went on unentered, as did the small war with Berr over two marks short and two eels short.

\textbf{Ch 13.} At the last market before Silt she worked the eels with pale slime dried on her sleeves, silt in the hollow of her neck and her head held right where the top of her left ear had been. Asked about the run she answered a question with a question and her own answer, and moved eel-bones against her thumb while deciding whether to lie, putting one away when the deciding was done. A figure was spoken; her thumb went under her apron to the grey cord and stayed, and shifting a basket showed the second cord twisted twice beneath it, never carried upriver to Nine Pots, never lifted at a door, the knots on neither counted. Her board lay beside Orra’s knot-string and did not touch it. She brought no crust and did not look into the basket. Her not-looking was a keeping; the man at the block’s not-looking had been a pricing, and she had no word in Grathic for either. Dessa has been dead twenty-two mornings and she has not said she knows the child is Dessa’s.

\textbf{Ch 14.} On Silt 2 she worked the eels at the outer boards of the Fishstairs with pale slime dried on her sleeves, river silt in the hollow of her neck and her head held right where the top of her left ear had been, the small smile kept on its face the way a door is kept on the latch. Asked whether the run would come now the month had turned, she answered the question and her own — \emph{Does it come now? It comes when it comes. Ask the river} — and moved eel-bones against her thumb while deciding whether to lie, putting one away when the deciding was done. When a buyer said a figure her thumb went under her apron to the grey cord and stayed, and shifting a creel showed the second cord twisted twice beneath it, never carried upriver to Nine Pots, never lifted at a door, the knots on neither counted by any thumb but her own. Her board lay beside Orra’s knot-string and did not touch it. She brought no crust and did not look into the basket; her not-looking was a keeping where Berr’s not-looking at the same shade was a pricing, and the boy set the two in places that did not touch. She has not said she knows the child is Dessa’s, and Dessa is twenty-nine mornings dead.

\textbf{Ch 15.} On Silt 13, the day the water fell, she worked the eels at the Fishstairs with pale slime dried on her sleeves, silt in the hollow of her neck and her head held right where the top of her left ear had been, the small smile kept on the latch. A woman come down the steps with salt white at her wrists asked whether the run would be thin now the water had gone down; Mira flicked an eel-bone against her thumb, answered the question and her own --- \emph{Thin? Who’s to say thin? It comes when it comes. Ask the river} --- moved two bones hand to hand while deciding whether to lie and put one away when the deciding was done. A buyer in a wet coat named a figure; her thumb went under her apron to the grey cord and stayed while she decided, and shifting a creel showed the second cord twisted twice beneath it, never carried upriver to Nine Pots or lifted at a door, the knots on neither counted by any thumb but her own and the knot for the thin child upriver not touched. Her board stood beside Orra’s knot-string and did not touch it. She brought no crust and did not look into the basket; her not-looking was a keeping where the man at the block’s was a pricing, and the boy set the two in places that did not touch. She has not said she knows the child is Dessa’s, and Dessa is thirty-six mornings dead.

\textbf{Ch 16.} On Day 76, Silt 17, she works the eels below the north bridge at the Fishstairs with pale slime dried on her sleeves, silt in the hollow of her neck and her head held right where the top of her left ear had been, the small smile kept on her face the way a door is kept on the latch. Asked whether the run will be thin she answers her own answer --- \emph{Thin? Who’s to say thin? It comes when it comes. Ask the river} --- moves eel-bones against her thumb while deciding whether to lie and puts one away when the deciding is done. When a buyer names a figure she says \emph{Two marks the pair and two short --- you’ve said it twice and I’ve counted it twice ... there’s nothing in the sentence that wants an answer}, and her thumb goes under her apron to the grey cord and stays there while she decides. Shifting a creel shows the second cord twisted twice beneath it, never carried upriver to Nine Pots, never lifted at a door, neither knot counted by any thumb but her own and the knot for the thin child upriver untouched. Her board lies beside Orra Weir’s knot-string and does not touch it; Orra is present only as the board, not on stage. She brings no crust and does not look into the basket. The steps have come back four, four and a landing a hand’s breadth out of line that a whole market walks over carefully without making a fall of it, and the soft-cuffed clerk still sits for a measure nobody called, hand to slate before eyes to stalls; the boy files the order apart from Marra, the Drawing collector and the Court-table clerk, with no sixth sighting of the neat dark hand. Her not-speaking, her not-looking and Berr’s taking-himself-out-of-his-sentence stand as three omissions of one shape that do not touch. She has not said she knows the child is Dessa’s, thirty-eight mornings dead now.

\textbf{Ch 17.} On Silt 20 and Silt 24 she works the eels at the boards below the north bridge with pale slime dried on her sleeves, silt in the hollow of her neck and her head held right where the top of her left ear had been, the small smile kept on her face the way a door is kept on the latch. Asked about the run she answers a question with her own answer and moves eel-bones while deciding whether to lie. When a figure is named her thumb goes under her apron to the grey cord and stays while she decides, and shifting a creel shows the second cord twisted twice beneath it, never carried upriver to Nine Pots or lifted at a door, neither knot counted by any thumb but her own and the knot for the thin child upriver untouched. Her board lies beside Orra Weir’s knot-string and does not touch it. She brings no crust and does not look into the basket; her not-looking is a keeping where Berr’s not-looking at the same shade is a pricing, and the boy sets the two in places that do not touch. She has not said she knows the child is Dessa’s, forty mornings dead and uncollected.

\textbf{Ch 20 (bonds).} With Corin nothing is said and nothing is looked at: she answered a question about the run from the side of her mouth and never once looked into the basket, and that not-looking is a keeping, the opposite of Berr’s pricing at the Cross. With Dessa nothing can be said at all; her sister is more mornings dead than any living person keeps count of and Mira has not said she knows the child is Dessa’s. The barley and silence with Sella hold unentered, as does the small war with Berr over two marks short and two eels short; Orra watches from where she watches and gets no answer, her knot-string beside Mira’s board and not touching it. No knot was counted, no cord carried to Nine Pots or lifted at a door, and the secret kept out of love went on gathering interest in a record no Court thumb will look at.

No knot was counted, no cord carried to Nine Pots or lifted at a door, and the secret kept out of love went on gathering interest in a record no Court thumb will look at.

\textbf{Ch 24 (bonds).} On Seed 23, dawn, at the very end of the fish-trade shade below the north bridge, offstage for the other two days. Sella set the basket where no slate lay and gave the instruction to the wool and the running water and never to the basket; Mira worked the eels with pale slime dried on her sleeves in long grey strokes, silt dried pale in the hollow of her neck and her head held a little to the right where the top of her left ear had been, the small smile kept like a door on the latch. Asked whether the run would be thin she answered her own answer — \emph{Thin? Who’s to say thin? It comes when it comes. Ask the river} — and moved eel-bones against her thumb while deciding whether to lie, putting one away when the deciding was done. When a buyer in a coat with the river in its hem named a figure her thumb went under her apron to the grey cord and stayed longer than the figure required; shifting a creel showed the second cord twisted twice beneath it, never carried upriver to Nine Pots or lifted at a door, neither knot counted by any thumb but her own and the knot for the thin child upriver untouched. Her board lay beside Orra Weir’s knot-string and did not touch it; Orra was upriver and present only as the board. \CRsheetheading{Arc So Far}
She is in the birth room from the first hours of Day 1 and is already arranged: the smile kept on the face like a door on the latch, the back turned to the slate, the eel-bones flicked and put away. She says the one true thing in the room --- that the secret is in what happens to a child after it is born --- in a form that can be taken as nothing, and follows it with \emph{there’s nothing to tell}. In Chapter 3 she is seen for the first time in her own element, the eel stall at the Cross, and the arrangement holds: dried slime, the missing top of her left ear, a question asked and answered by herself, a board shoved clear for the barrow men, and not one look into the basket all afternoon. The knot-string and the barley account are still offstage; the woman who knows and will not say is not. Her marker is reconciled to Chapter 1: she is on stage here, not first seen at the Fishstairs in Chapter 5.

On Days 8 and 9 the woman who knows is seen in her own element for two mornings, and the keeping becomes a craft with tools: eel-bones moved while an answer is chosen, a cord touched when a figure is spoken, a second cord kept apart and never taken to the door it belongs to. The little war with Berr is given its exact arithmetic --- four eels for six, two marks short for six years --- and neither will name it. She answers the question about the basket without letting the sentence want a reply, and gives the warmth briskly before anyone can make a speech about it, which is how kindness is done in her house. The knot-string itself is still not shown plainly and the knots are not counted; what the boy sees is the hand, the movement and the difference between two cords, and he has no word for any of it.

On Days 15 through 24 the two records stand side by side in the fold and the yard. On Stone 28 she answers a question about the basket with a lie in the form of a proverb, touches the grey cord when a figure is spoken, and gives the boy a fresh crust briskly, the second warmth in the fold beside the spent one from Stone 15. Both are entered nowhere and neither is named; a gift done quickly is a gift no one can make a speech about. The separate cord twisted twice below the grey shows again as she shifts the basket, still unknotted by any hand but her own and still not taken to the thin child upriver. Dessa’s cough comes up from the pits three doors down and is called weather, and the sister who knows keeps the knowing under the same small smile. The boy sees the hand and the twist and counts neither, and cannot thank either woman for the bread.

On the Last Day the woman who knows comes up from the eels for a question about a basket and gives the same answer in the same form --- a question, then her own answer, with room to choose which answer the listener gets. The grey cord is touched under the apron when a figure is spoken, the second cord twisted twice shows beneath it, and neither is counted or carried to the door it belongs to; the knot-string itself stays unshown. She puts no crust in the fold this chapter and the two already there are neither eaten nor named; three doors down the house is quiet and she says nothing about knowing the child. The smile stays on the latch, the eel-bone goes away, and the secret she keeps out of love goes on gathering interest in a record no Court’s thumb will look at.

On Days 31 through 37 the woman who knows comes up twice from the eels and keeps the knowing under the same small smile. On Ilmen 2 she answers a question with a question and her own answer, flicks an eel-bone, touches the grey cord under her apron when a figure is spoken and shows the second cord twisted twice beneath it with the knots uncounted; on Ilmen 8 she passes her sister at the end of nineteen steps without looking at her, brings no crust and says nothing. The smile stays on the latch. The secret she keeps out of love goes on gathering interest in a record no Court’s thumb will look at, and her sister goes on going thin three doors down and calling it weather.

On Days 38 through 44 the woman who knows keeps the knowing under the same small smile while her sister goes into the brook and stays there. On Ilmen 9 she came up from the eels with slime dried pale on her sleeves, silt in the hollow of her neck and her head held to the right where the top of her left ear had been, answered a neighbour’s question about the water with a silence and her own answer, brought no crust and did not look into the basket held on the bank above her sister’s body. On Ilmen 12 she came up from the eels at the Fishstairs, answered a question about the run with \emph{Does it come when you bless it? It comes when it comes. Ask the river}, flicked an eel-bone and put it away; when a figure was spoken her thumb went under her apron to the grey cord and stayed, and shifting the basket showed the second cord twisted twice beneath it, never carried upriver to Nine Pots and never lifted at a door, neither knot counted. She brought no third crust and did not look in. On Ilmen 14 she met Sella on the river road with eel-bones at her hip and said \emph{Ask her what night the boat came. Don’t ask her what she’s owed. She’ll tell you the oars.} On Ilmen 15 she answered a weir woman about the blessing with a question and her own answer, kept the grey cord and the second cord side by side with the knots uncounted, put her board beside Orra’s knot-string without letting the two touch, and did not look into the boy’s basket. She has not said she knows the child is Dessa’s.

On Days 45 through 47 the woman who knows keeps the knowing under the same small smile while the record she keeps in wool stands beside another woman’s on a board that does not touch it. On Day 45 she answers a weir woman about the run with a question and her own answer, moves eel-bones while deciding whether to lie, touches the grey cord when a figure is spoken and shows the second twisted twice beneath it with neither knot counted. The smoky crust she gave on Stone 28 --- the warmth the boy most wanted and could never reach --- goes quietly out of the fold on Day 46 and nobody says it is gone, who took it or what became of it. The boy sets her hand on a tray with Sella’s and Alda’s and refuses to make a cause, and she is offstage for the rest of the chapter. She has not said she knows the child is Dessa’s; the secret kept out of love goes on gathering interest in a record no Court’s thumb will look at.

On Days 48 through 54 the woman who knows keeps the knowing under the same small smile while the record she keeps in wool stands beside another woman’s on a board that does not touch it. On Day 53 at the Fishstairs she works the eels with pale slime dried on her sleeves, silt in the hollow of her neck and her head held right where the top of her left ear had been; she answers a question about the run with a question and her own answer and flicks eel-bones against her thumb while deciding whether to lie, putting one away when the deciding is done. When a buyer says a figure her thumb goes under her apron to the grey cord and stays there while she decides, and shifting a basket shows the second cord twisted twice beneath the grey, never carried upriver to Nine Pots or lifted at a door, the knots on neither counted by any thumb but her own. Her board lies beside Orra’s knot-string and does not touch it; the shape of the forty-first knot is legible to the boy without its name and the word is not spoken. She has not said she knows the child is Dessa’s; the secret kept out of love goes on gathering interest in a record no Court’s thumb will look at.

On Days 55 through 60 the woman who knows keeps the knowing under the same small smile while the month of mud arrives and the river begins to move. On Ilmen 30, the last Account-day and market before Silt, she works the eels at the Fishstairs with pale slime dried pale on her sleeves, silt in the hollow of her neck and her head held right where the top of her left ear had been. She answers a question about the run with a question and her own answer, moves eel-bones against her thumb while deciding whether to lie and puts one away when the deciding is done. When a figure is spoken her thumb goes under her apron to the grey cord and stays; shifting a basket shows the second cord twisted twice beneath it, never taken upriver to Nine Pots or lifted at a door, the knots on neither counted by any thumb but her own. She brings no crust and does not look into the basket; her not-looking is a keeping where the man at the block’s is a pricing, and she has no Grathic word for either. Dessa is twenty-two mornings dead and uncollected and Mira has not said she knows the child is Dessa’s; the secret kept out of love goes on gathering interest in a record no Court’s thumb will look at.

On Days 113 through 115 the woman who knows keeps the knowing under the same small smile while the planting holds its last tend and then gives up its seed. When a buyer names a figure her thumb goes under her apron to the grey cord and stays longer than the figure required; shifting a creel shows the second cord twisted twice beneath it, never carried upriver to Nine Pots or lifted at a door, neither knot counted and the knot for the thin child upriver untouched. On Days 116 through 119 the woman who knows keeps the knowing under the same small smile while the planting hands come out of the strips one short and the month turns into Reed. She works the eels with pale slime dried in long grey strokes on her sleeves, silt dried pale in the hollow of her neck and her head held a little to the right where the top of her left ear had been, the small smile kept like a door on the latch; a string of eel-bones in her apron pocket moves against her thumb under the talk the way a second pulse goes on under a fever. A weir woman with salt dried white at her wrists asks whether the run will be thin now the hands are out of the strips; Mira answers the question and then her own — \emph{Thin? Who’s to say thin? It comes when it comes. Ask the river} — moves three bones from hand to hand while deciding whether to lie and puts one away when the deciding is done. She says something low about a boat that came up on the flood and not a word about the hand that did not come out of the strips, so that a direction with no figure at the foot of it stands edge to edge with a saying in the dark part under the bridge and the two do not touch. A buyer in a coat with the river in its hem names a figure for two pair; her thumb goes under her apron to the grey wool cord and stays several breaths longer than the figure requires, and shifting a creel shows the second cord twisted twice beneath it, never carried upriver to Nine Pots or lifted at a door, neither knot counted by any thumb but her own and the knot for the thin child upriver untouched. Her board lies beside Orra Weir’s knot-string and does not touch it; Orra is upriver and present only as the board. She brings no crust and does not look into the basket; her not-looking is a keeping set on a place of its own and joined to no pricing, while the man who priced the district in the strips looked away from the same basket for a different reason. Two faces turned the same way mean opposite things, and there is no word in Grathic for the difference. She has not said she knows the child is Dessa’s; the secret kept out of love goes on gathering interest in a record no Court thumb will look at.

Orra stood at the lower boards and got no answer. The steps below the bridge came back four, four and a landing a hand’s breadth out of line that a whole market walked over carefully without a fall, and the soft-cuffed clerk still sat for a measure nobody called. She says \emph{Two marks the pair and two short ... there’s nothing in the sentence that wants an answer}, and does not look into the basket. Her board lies beside Orra’s and does not touch it; the reed-cutter’s grey cord goes past inside a man’s coat with its knots unread, and she does not join it to her keeping or to the empty place in the strip. The secret kept out of love goes on gathering interest in a record no Court thumb will look at.

On Days 126 through 128 she keeps the two cords and the secret out of love where they have always been, and the reed month goes on around her without a figure entering any record. She is offstage on Reed 7 and 8 and appears once at the outer boards of the Weir on Reed 9. There’s nothing in the sentence that wants an answer.} She does not look into the basket, and the keeping of that not-looking is set on a place of its own beside the pricing faces she has watched all her life. Her board lies beside Orra’s knot-string and does not touch it; the reed-cutter’s grey cord goes past unread and the soft-cuffed clerk holds his slate for an uncalled measure. The second cord stays twisted twice beneath the grey, never carried upriver to Nine Pots or lifted at a door; neither knot is counted and the thin child’s knot is untouched. The child’s foot stays dark inside three turns of wool below the sill and she does not make the cold into a cause. Nothing is counted, named, opened or joined and no secret changes hands.

Nothing has been counted, joined or said.

Asked whether the run would be thin she answered her own question and her own answer — \emph{Thin? Who’s to say thin? It comes when it comes. When a buyer named a figure her thumb went under her apron to the grey wool cord and stayed longer than the figure required; shifting a creel showed the second cord twisted twice beneath it, never carried upriver to Nine Pots or lifted at a door, neither knot counted by any thumb but hers and the knot for the thin child upriver untouched. To the buyer who said the figure twice she said \emph{Two marks the pair and two short. You’ve said it twice and I’ve counted it twice. There’s nothing in the sentence that wants an answer.} She said something low about a boat that had come up on the flood and nothing about the hand that had not come out of the strips. Her board lay beside Orra Weir’s knot-string and did not touch it (T024/T059/T025); the reed-cutter came along the same boards and turned his grey cord on the flat blessing stone, tied one low with his teeth, bit the end off and put it back inside his coat with its knots unread (T099 carried). Below the sill the child’s foot stayed dark inside three turns of wool, the cold to the woman who wound it and weather to the yard, uncured, uncaused and unnamed (T093/T094/T096 carried). She did not look into the basket and did not lay the foot beside any of the figures at the boards. Nothing has been counted, joined or said.

On Day 148, with the reed month in its last two days, the keeping at the Weir stays in knots and questions rather than figures. The reed-cutter straightens his thumb-oiled grey cord on the flat blessing stone, ties one knot low with his teeth and puts it back inside his coat, answering the woman who cannot read it with \emph{You can ask the cord} and \emph{No more can the Court}; Mira works the eels with pale slime dried in long grey strokes on her sleeves and silt pale in the hollow of her neck, her head held a little right where the top of her left ear had been, answers a thin run with her own question and answer (\emph{Thin? Who’s to say thin? It comes when it comes. Ask the river}), flicks eel-bones against her thumb while deciding whether to lie and puts one away. When a buyer names a figure her thumb goes under her apron to the grey cord and stays longer than the figure required; a shifting creel shows the second cord twisted twice beneath it, never carried upriver to Nine Pots or lifted at a door, neither knot counted and the thin child’s knot untouched. Her board lies beside Orra’s and does not touch it; the child’s foot below the sill stays dark in three turns of wool, the cold to the woman who wound it and weather to a neighbour with a pail, uncured, uncaused and unnamed. Nothing is joined, paid or spoken, and she has still not said she knows whose child he is.

\textbf{Ch 37.} On Day 151, Tallow 2, at the lower boards of the Weir and below the sill at the fish-trade shade; offstage on Days 150 and 152. Worked the eels with pale slime dried in long grey strokes on her sleeves and silt pale in the hollow of her neck, her head held a little to the right where the top of her left ear had been, her small smile kept like a door on the latch. Ask the river} --- flicked an eel-bone against her thumb while deciding whether to lie, moved two from hand to hand and put one away. When a buyer named a figure for two pair she said \emph{Two marks the pair and two short. You’ve said it twice and I’ve counted it twice. There’s nothing in the sentence that wants an answer}, and her thumb went under her apron to the grey cord and stayed longer than the figure required; a shifting creel showed the second cord twisted twice beneath it, never carried upriver to Nine Pots or lifted at a door, neither knot counted by any thumb but her own and the knot for the thin child upriver untouched. Her board lay beside Orra Weir’s and did not touch it; the reed-cutter’s cord went past along the same boards with its knots unread, a fourth private record within a dozen paces of the basket that the boy could not enter. She brought no crust and did not look into the basket; her not-looking was a keeping set on a place of its own and joined to no pricing face. Still had not said she knows the child is Dessa’s. No new scar or possession, no knot counted, nothing joined.

\textbf{Ch 39.} On Day 162, Tallow 13, at the Weir’s lower boards and below the fish-trade shade (offstage on Days 160 and 161), the reed work was finished and had become a direction counted in the arm that carries it, which knows the weight and not the cost; a cost asked as a direction was answered with the river and the weather and left no entry. She worked the eels with slime dried in long grey strokes on her sleeves and silt pale in the hollow of her neck, her head held a little right where the top of her left ear had been, her small smile kept like a door on the latch. Asked whether the run would be thin she answered her own question and her own answer — \emph{Thin? Who’s to say thin? It comes when it comes. Ask the river} — and flicked eel-bones against her thumb while deciding whether to lie. When a buyer named a figure she said \emph{Two marks the pair and two short. You’ve said it twice and I’ve counted it twice. There’s nothing in the sentence that wants an answer}, and her thumb went under her apron to the grey cord and stayed longer than the figure required; shifting a creel showed the second twist twice beneath it, never carried upriver to Nine Pots or lifted at a door, neither knot counted by any thumb but hers and the knot for the thin child upriver untouched (T024/T059/T025). Her board lay beside Orra Weir’s and did not touch it; the reed-cutter straightened his grey cord on the blessing stone, tied one knot low with his teeth and put it back inside his coat with the knots unread (T099 carried). Below the sill a child’s foot stayed dark inside three turns of wool, the cold to one woman and weather to a neighbour with a pail, and the boy’s reading of the extremity going before the core and the afterdrop waiting past a warming nobody would perform worked perfectly and bought nothing; no silt-leach, cause or cure was spoken (T093/T094/T096 carried). She brought no crust and did not look into the basket. Nothing was counted, joined or paid.

Into the firing month’s third week the eel work goes on below the sill with the reeds finished and counted in the carrying arm, and the woman who knows keeps the knowing under the same small smile. The thin run is answered with the river, the buyer’s figure is answered twice and counted twice, and the second cord stays twisted twice beneath the grey with the knots uncounted and the knot for the thin child upriver untouched. Her board lies beside Orra’s without touching it and the reed-cutter’s tally goes past unread, three private records in wool and teeth and thumb that the boy can see and cannot enter. The child’s dark foot stays the cold to one woman and weather to another below the shade, with no silt-leach, cause or cure spoken, and the perfect surgical reading buys nothing at two paces.

\CRsheetheading{Chapter Log}
\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item Ch 1: Came in from the yard with eel slime dried on her sleeves and the cold on them; stood in the one patch of floor the slate did not reach, back to the writing and face to the door. Answered a question with a question and then her own answer: the secret is in what happens to a child after. Said she had told nobody and there was nothing to tell. Flicked an eel-bone against her thumb and put it away when the hand came; kept the small smile on the latch all night. Crossed the room to press a crust of brown-edged Vail-smoked barley bread into Dessa’s hand, briskly, stopping short of the slate. The top of her left ear is missing --- a hook, she says; the scar says a knife.

\item Ch 3: Day 4, Account-day. Background figure at the eel stall at the edge of the Cross in the afternoon, with the top of her left ear gone and eel slime dried pale on her sleeves; kept her head a little to the right against the cold in the place where the ear had been. Flicked eel-bones against her thumb, asked Berr the eel price and answered it herself with \emph{two marks the pair and two short}, said a figure under her breath and moved another bone. Shoved a loose board clear of the barrow men’s path with the side of her hand and went on talking as if she had moved nothing. Never looked at the basket once all day.

\end{itemize}

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item Ch 5: Days 8 and 9. At the eel board below the north bridge with slime dried pale on her sleeves, silt in her neck and the top of her left ear gone; head held to the right against the cold. Flicked three eel-bones against her thumb while deciding whether to lie and put one away when the deciding was done; gave Berr four eels where six should go against his two marks short for six years, and did not acknowledge it. Answered a question about the basket with a question and her own answer --- \emph{he’s warm}, off the slate --- and shifted her back to the corner of his open slate rather than look at it. Her hand went to the grey cord at her waist three times in two mornings when a figure was spoken, never to the second cord twisted twice beneath it, which has never been carried up the river to Nine Pots. On Stone 15 put a brown-edged barley crust into the fold at the boy’s side in two brisk movements, called it a crust and not a sermon, and went back to the eels. Never said she knew him.

\end{itemize}

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item Ch 7: Day 22, Stone 28, came up the Clay Yard from the fish-trade with eel slime dried pale on her sleeves and the top of her left ear gone, head held a little to the right against the cold. Asked whose basket was going past, answered \emph{Whose do you think? A basket’s a basket. It came from a warm house, that’s all, and it’s going back to one}, flicked an eel-bone against her thumb and put it away. When a woman at the well said a figure for the Five, her thumb went under her apron to the grey wool cord and stayed while she decided, then came out with another bone. Crossed three paces and put a fresh brown-edged barley crust into the fold at the boy’s side --- \emph{It’s a crust, not a sermon} --- and went back to the eels without looking in; the spent crust of Stone 15 lay stiff beside it and neither was named. Shifting the basket’s weight showed the second cord twisted twice under the grey, never taken upriver to Nine Pots and never lifted at a door; the knots were not counted. Three doors down she heard Dessa call the cough from the pits weather and went on with the eels.

\end{itemize}

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

Asked whose basket was going past, answered with a question and her own answer --- \emph{Whose do you think? A basket’s a basket. It came from a warm house, that’s all, and it’s going back to one} --- and flicked an eel-bone against her thumb and put it away. When a figure was spoken her thumb went under her apron to the grey wool cord and stayed while she decided; shifting the weight showed the second cord twisted twice beneath it, never taken upriver to Nine Pots and never lifted at a door, and the knots were not counted. Put no third crust into the fold and went back down the yard without looking in or saying she knew the child.

On Ilmen 2 came up from the eels with pale slime dried on her sleeves, river silt in the hollow of her neck and her head held to the right where the top of her left ear had been; asked whether the eels ran early, answered \emph{Do they run early? When a woman at the well said a figure, her thumb went under her apron to the grey wool cord and stayed while she decided; shifting the basket’s weight showed the second cord twisted twice beneath it, never taken upriver to Nine Pots and never lifted at a door, and neither was counted. The soft-cuffed clerk stayed set for an uncalled measure (T090/T080). She did not look into the basket, brought no crust and has still not said she knows the child is Dessa’s. No new scar or possession, no knot counted, nothing joined.

\end{itemize}

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item Ch 40: Day 167, Tallow 18, at the Weir’s lower boards and below the fish-trade shade; offstage on the other six days. Worked the eels with eel slime dried grey in long strokes on her sleeves and silt pale in the hollow of her neck, her head held a little right where the top of her left ear had been, her small smile kept like a door on the latch. To the weir woman who asked whether the run was thin she gave her own question and her own answer, \emph{Thin? Who’s to say thin? It comes when it comes. Ask the river}, flicked eel-bones against her thumb while deciding whether to lie, and to the buyer who named a figure said \emph{Two marks the pair and two short. You’ve said it twice and I’ve counted it twice. There’s nothing in the sentence that wants an answer}. Her thumb went under her apron to the grey cord and stayed longer than the figure required, and the second twist showed twice beneath a shifting creel, never carried upriver to Nine Pots or lifted at a door, neither knot counted and the knot for the thin child untouched (T059/T025). Her board lay beside Orra’s and did not touch it; the reed-cutter straightened his grey cord on the flat blessing stone, tied one knot low with his teeth and put it back inside his coat with the flat of his hand, answering \emph{You can ask the cord} and \emph{No more can the Court}, its knots unread and not joined to hers (T099 carried). Below the shade the child’s foot stayed dark inside three turns of wool, the cold to the woman who wound it and weather to the neighbour with a pail, the afterdrop waiting past a warming nobody would perform and the perfect reading worth nothing; no silt-leach, cause or cure was spoken (T093/T094/T096 carried). The soft-cuffed clerk stayed set at the out-of-line landing for a measure nobody called (T090/T080 carried). She did not look into the basket, brought no crust and has still not said she knows the child is Dessa’s; no new scar or possession, no knot counted, nothing joined.

\end{itemize}
}

set him on his bed under the roof, left the thread frozen and unwiped, and went to her own bed before the small hours; no new scar, possession or change of voice}\CRfield{First seen}{Chapter 1}}{\CRsheetheading{Appearance}
A broad woman of thirty-three with forearms the colour of dried slip and a burn across the back of her left hand shaped like a little door --- two straight sides, a lintel and a threshold, the skin inside it puckered and pale --- which she keeps half-closed when she carries a cup, and which closes on nothing when her hand has nothing to hold. She is not tall and she does not make herself tall; she takes up room by being impossible to move. Her hair is coal-black with one grey streak at the temple that she says came from the winter Garl died and will not discuss further. She smells of woodsmoke, wet wool, and under it the faint sour mineral tang of the Ash ridge along the skirting board, which she has not swept in two years and does not intend to sweep. Her hands are never still. When they have nothing to do they count: spoons, nails, the breaths of a sleeping child. She wears her widow’s mark on a cord at her throat, a thumb-length of lead-glazed clay with the Vail kiln scratched into it, and she touches it before she opens the kiln and never at any other time. People notice the burn first and the mark last, which is the order she prefers.

\CRsheetheading{Voice \& Manner}
Grathic proverbs and half-sentences, practical instruction addressed to the pot or the fire before it is addressed to a person. She says \emph{the house} where another woman would say \emph{I}, and \emph{the boy} where another would say \emph{my son}. She never finishes a sentence that would require her to say what she feels, and she is not unaware of this; she has simply decided that a thing said aloud becomes a thing the Court can enter. Her humour is dry and costs her something. When she is angry she gets quieter, and the quieter she gets the more the household straightens up.

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item “The fire doesn’t know you’re sorry. Feed it.” --- said to the fire on Ilmen 25, Y.H. 814, at the going of the light; never to the basket, never as a rebuke and never with a name under it.

\item “Don’t set that near the door. You’ll pay for it in the thaw.”

\item “He’s a boy. He’s warm. That’s the whole of what I know.”

\item “You can ask me what you like. I won’t answer it. Ask the pot instead; it’s more use.”

\item “A slate-name with no house is a coat anybody can wear. I’ve seen it before.”

\item “The boy comes under the roof on the morrow. The house will keep him.” --- the taking announced without an \emph{I} in it, and never explained.

\item “Don’t set that near the door. You’ll pay for it in the thaw.” --- instruction to the pot, not to a person, given with the kiln already open.

\item “The house will keep it.” --- said to the fire at the going of the light on Reed 18 where another woman would have said \emph{I}; the instruction always goes to the wool, the pot, the broom and the fire and never to the basket.

\end{itemize}

\CRsheetheading{History}
She was born in Low Kiln to slip-mixers, married Garl Vail at seventeen, and kept the Vail fire ever since in the way a widow keeps a wound clean: daily, without comment, with a hand that knows exactly how much pressure the thing will bear. She bore two children. Jorra, who lived, and Enna, who died at nine months of the second chill in Y.H. 804, after Alda Reed had warmed the stone and done everything the craft knew. Sella sat up with that child for three nights and learned what the midwives already knew: that a vessel can cool while everybody is being kind to it. In Y.H. 811, in the Long Cold, Garl died with the river iced and no collector able to cross, and his warmth went where unkept warmth goes. The Ash in the Vail corner is thicker than in any other house in the district. Sella has never swept it and has never said why.

On Stone 7, Y.H. 812, a woman in the district bore a child with a branching red flower across his ribs, and Sella took him in on the third day. She gave as her reason the one she has given ever since: a foundling with no house-name can be used by anyone, and a boy entered under a roof is a boy nobody can take for a levy without answering to that roof. This is true. It is not the whole of it. Alda Reed, who delivered him, crossed herself at the birth-flower and told nobody what she had seen, and Sella, who saw the same look on the midwife’s face, asked her nothing at all. She has kept the boy close for three years and has never once asked where his memory came from. She is waiting to see what he will become.

\CRsheetheading{Wounds \& Fears}
Enna’s second chill; Garl going uncollected; the Ash ridge that has grown an inch since. She fears another Long Cold, and fears more than that the day somebody from Slate Row notices that one child in her house listens to the fire before he looks at it. She fears Jorra, who has begun to disappear into the back rooms with men whose names are not spoken, and she fears that she has already lost the wheel to him while he still stands at it. Her contradiction is the whole of her: the woman who feeds every hungry child in the yard has never once said she loves one. She would sooner swallow the widow’s mark.

\CRsheetheading{Desires}
She wants the fire to hold, the wheel to stay in the house, and a Vail name written on the birth-slate of every child born under her roof. She thinks she wants a whole return for Garl, so that he might come back as himself and sit where he used to sit and say nothing in his own voice. What she needs is to admit that she did not take Corin in for the house at all. She took him because he was the only warm thing in a room full of people pretending not to be cold, and because she had already lost one child to the second chill and could not bear to lose another to an explanation.

\CRsheetheading{Bonds}
\textbf{Ch 128 (bonds).} With Corin nothing crossed under the roof, out of the yard or up the clay road across Silt 11, 12 and 13 as sign, lesson, mending, cause, payment or payer, and neither the second asking at the well on the twelfth nor the Slate Row face at the yard’s edge on the thirteenth was brought under the roof as a teaching or told on an unearned day. She came to the hearth before the basket at both ends of every day, told the coals it was the thaw and turned them with the back of a broken pot, gave the small intake, hold and letting-go toward no opening with neither gap figured, kept her finger along the top of the loaf shelf so the charcoal stayed unread, moved her lips on a two-gapped row, glanced once at the cold clay jar with the hand shut half over nothing and the little-door burn closing on air, lifted the twice-mended pot thumb-first where the wire crossed the crack with the hairline showing and both proverbs to pot and fire and never to a person, turned the dressed grain under wool unfigured and set the pot rim two inches beyond the reaching hand with a half-beat and no look toward the bed. Her hands counted spoons and nails when they had nothing to do and came back to the hairline at the wire. She carried him down and up the nineteen steps at the half-pace, went wide around the seven walked-around places once and not twice, set him under the roof and never in the Debt Loft, put the fold right without a look at his face and added no second fold, and found the keeping where it had been put. \textbf{The widow’s mark hung where it hangs on all three days} — a tending day is not an opening, seven openings in seven months are seven and not a rule and no eighth came due. On Silt 12 she was at the well with him while a second neighbour asked whether a count kept in wood would be taken at the next reading; Ilva answered the question put and Sella said nothing to the basket of it, carrying him home at the going of the light saying nothing of the asking. On Silt 13 she carried him home saying nothing of the man from Slate Row at the yard’s edge. No new scar or possession, no change of voice, nothing paid, opened or ended; forward, not closed.

\textbf{Ch 127 (bonds).} With Corin nothing crossed under the roof, out of the yard or up the clay road across Silt 8, 9 and 10 as sign, lesson, mending, cause, payment or payer, and nothing from the reported second slate at the well or the hair-thin thaw at the corner was brought under the roof on a later day as a teaching or a custom. She came to the hearth before the basket at both ends of every day, told the coals it was the thaw in the voice another woman would use for a child who could not hear her, turned them with the back of a broken pot, gave the small intake, the hold and the letting-go toward no opening with neither gap figured, kept her finger along the top of the loaf shelf so the charcoal tally beneath stayed unread, moved her lips on a two-gapped row, glanced once at the cold clay jar beyond the pot board with the hand shut half over nothing and the little-door burn on the back of her left hand closing on air. She lifted the twice-mended pot thumb-first where the tighter wire crossed the crack, left the hairline showing between the older brass staple and the wire, gave both proverbs to the pot and the fire and never to a person, kept repair apart from restoration, turned the dressed grain under wool with a touch lighter than a woman would use on a sleeping child and with no figure or handful, and set the pot rim two inches beyond the reaching hand with a half-beat and no look toward the bed. Her hands were never still; when they had nothing to do they counted spoons, nails and the breaths of a child nobody numbers and came back to the hairline at the wire. She carried him down and up the nineteen steps at the half-pace from every open slate, gave the instruction to the wool, the river wind, the pot, the fire and the banked fire and never to the basket, went wide around the seven walked-around places once and not twice, widest around the returning-line place where a hand went in on Seed 15 and did not come back, set him under the roof and never in the Debt Loft, put the fold right at his ear and under his chin without a look at his face and added no second fold; the keeping at the fold was found where put and stayed a finding. \textbf{The widow’s mark hung where it hangs on all three days} — a morning, a shelf, a pot, a yard, a market, a reading, a basket, a bed and a going of the light are not openings, seven openings in seven months are seven and not a rule, and an Account-day did not make an eighth come due. On Silt 10, before first grey, she set the basket in the moot-post’s finger’s width of shade where no slate lay and stood half a pace off with his cheek to the cold iron, so the reading came sideways and nobody looked into the wicker; she gave no instruction and no reason to the basket, carried him home at the going of the light saying nothing of the fourth reading, the bell’s gap, the runner’s slate going up unread, the clerk’s figure, the two sightings or the fourth subtraction gone up the road in a locked box. She said nothing of what the market had left standing on the turnip heap and found the keeping where put at the close. No new scar or possession, no change of voice, nothing opened, named, paid or ended.

\textbf{Ch 126 (bonds).} With Corin nothing crossed under the roof, out of the yard or up the clay road across Silt 5, 6 and 7 as sign, lesson, mending, cause, payment or payer, and nothing from the reported second slate at the well or the hair-thin thaw at the corner was brought under the roof on the morning after as a teaching or a custom. She came to the hearth before the basket at both ends of every day, told the coals it was the thaw in the voice another woman would use for a child who could not hear her, turned them with the back of a broken pot, gave the small intake, the hold and the letting-go toward no opening with neither gap figured, kept her finger along the top of the loaf shelf so the charcoal tally beneath stayed unread, moved her lips on a two-gapped row, glanced once at the cold clay jar beyond the pot board with the hand shut half over nothing and the little-door burn on the back of her left hand closing on air. She lifted the twice-mended pot thumb-first where the tighter wire crossed the crack, left the hairline showing between the older brass staple and the wire, gave both proverbs to the pot and the fire and never to a person, kept repair apart from restoration, turned the dressed grain under wool with a touch lighter than a woman would use on a sleeping child and with no figure or handful, and set the pot rim two inches beyond the reaching hand with a half-beat and no look toward the bed. She carried him down and up the nineteen steps at the half-pace from every open slate, gave the instruction to the wool, the river wind, the pot, the fire and the banked fire and never to the basket, went wide around the seven walked-around places once and not twice, widest around the returning-line place where a hand went in on Seed 15 and did not come back, set him under the roof and never in the Debt Loft, put the fold right at his ear and under his chin without a look at his face and added no second fold; the keeping at the fold was found where put and stayed a finding. \textbf{The widow’s mark hung where it hangs on all three days} — a tending day, a shelf, a hearth, a well, a yard, a basket and a going of the light are not openings, seven openings in seven months are seven and not a rule and no eighth came due. On Silt 7 she told the fire it was the thaw and did not tell the basket, and she asked nothing of either slate or of the softer air off the river. With Tarn six stood where the house could check and the seventh at the lip beside Garl’s unforged collector sentence, his sentence found where put on all three days and not made a habit, the loan uncalled in a term already ended; with Jorra her unfinished sentence went to the pot through his bent finger in the cold damper and came out without the extra holding of Ash 26 a second time, \emph{he’s not Vail} sealed and the promise under the shed neither given nor withdrawn. She said \emph{the house} where another woman would say \emph{I} and \emph{the boy} where another would say \emph{my son}, because a thing said aloud becomes a thing the Court can enter; the one grey streak at her temple said winter and she said nothing about the winter. No new scar or possession and no change of voice.

\textbf{Ch 125 (bonds).} With Corin nothing crossed under the roof, out of the yard or up the clay road across Silt 2, 3 and 4 as sign, lesson, mending, cause, payment or payer, and nothing that happened at the loaf shelf on Silt 3 was brought under the roof on the morning after as a teaching. She came to the hearth before the basket at both ends of every day, told the coals it was the thaw in the voice another woman would use for a child who could not hear her, turned them with the back of a broken pot, gave the small intake, the hold and the letting-go toward no opening with neither gap figured, kept her finger along the top of the loaf shelf so the charcoal tally beneath stayed unread, moved her lips on a two-gapped row, glanced once at the cold clay jar beyond the pot board with the hand shut half over nothing and the little-door burn on the back of her left hand closing on air. She lifted the twice-mended pot thumb-first where the tighter wire crossed the crack, left the hairline showing between the older brass staple and the wire, gave both proverbs to the pot and the fire and never to a person, kept repair apart from restoration, turned the dressed grain under wool with a touch lighter than a woman would use on a sleeping child and with no figure or handful, and set the pot rim two inches beyond the reaching hand with a half-beat and no look toward the bed. On the third morning she weighed a fist of barley in her hand and set it back, saying no number. She carried him down and up the nineteen steps at the half-pace from every open slate, gave the instruction to the wool, the river wind, the pot, the fire and the banked fire and never to the basket, went wide around the seven walked-around places once and not twice, widest around the returning-line place, set him under the roof and never in the Debt Loft, put the fold right at his ear and under his chin without a look at his face and added no second fold; the keeping at the fold was found where put and stayed a finding. \textbf{The widow’s mark hung where it hangs on all three days} — a morning, a hearth, a shelf, a pot, a yard, a basket, an afternoon and a going of the light are not openings, seven openings in seven months are seven and not a rule, and no eighth came due. On Silt 3, when the neighbour’s finger went along the shelf’s top and then toward the empty place at the boy’s ear, Sella’s own finger stayed where it had always gone and went no further; she did not go beneath the board, did not ask what had been said and did not look at the boy’s face to see whether he had heard, and the house took up its grammar as though nothing had turned. She told the fire it was the thaw and said nothing to the basket of the near-reaching, the softening at the river’s skin, the count or the three readings. What she said low went to the pot and the fire; she said \emph{the house} where another woman would say \emph{I} and \emph{the boy} where another would say \emph{my son}, because a thing said aloud becomes a thing the Court can enter. She did not speak of the one grey streak at her temple. No new scar or possession, no change of voice.

\textbf{Ch 124 (bonds).} With Corin nothing crossed under the roof, out of the yard or up the clay road across Ilmen 29, Ilmen 30 and Silt 1 as sign, lesson, mending, cause, payment or payer, and neither the third reading nor the two market sightings were brought under the roof as a teaching or told on an unearned day. She came to the hearth before the basket at both ends of every day, told the coals it was the thaw in the voice another woman would use for a child who could not hear her, turned them with the back of a broken pot, gave the small intake, the hold and the letting-go toward no opening with neither gap figured, kept her finger along the top of the loaf shelf so the charcoal stayed unread, lips on a two-gapped row, one glance at the cold clay jar beyond the pot board with the hand shut half over nothing and the little-door burn closing on air. She lifted the twice-mended pot thumb-first where the tighter wire crossed the crack, left the hairline showing between old-brass staple and wire, gave both proverbs to the pot and the fire and never to a person, kept repair apart from restoration, turned the dressed grain under wool with a touch lighter than a woman would use on a sleeping child and with no figure or handful, and set the pot rim two inches beyond the reaching hand with a half-beat and no look toward the bed. On Ilmen 30, the month’s third and last Account-day and market, she set the basket in the moot-post’s finger’s width of shade where no slate lay and stood half a pace off through Berr Clay’s twice-read figure and the bell, giving no instruction and no reason to the basket, and carried him home at the going of the light saying nothing of what had been read over him, of the bell’s gap, of Hessa’s slate or of the clerk’s figure. She said \emph{the house} where another woman would say \emph{I} and \emph{the boy} where another would say \emph{my son}, because a thing said aloud becomes a thing the Court can enter; one grey streak at her temple said winter and she said nothing about the winter. With Tarn the six and the seventh held at the kindling and the loan stayed uncalled; with Jorra her unfinished sentence still arrived at the pot through his bent finger in the cold damper. No new scar or possession, no change of voice.

\textbf{Ch 123 (bonds).} With Corin nothing crossed under the roof, out of the yard or up the clay road across Ilmen 26, 27 and 28 as sign, lesson, mending, cause, payment or payer, and the figure offered at the well was not brought under the roof as a teaching or told a second time on a day that had earned only its twenty-seventh or twenty-eighth. She came to the hearth before the basket at both ends of every day, told the coals it was the thaw in the voice another woman would use for a child who could not hear her, turned them with the back of a broken pot, gave the small intake, the hold and the letting-go toward no opening with neither gap figured, kept her finger above the unread charcoal, lips on a two-gapped row, one glance at the clay jar standing cold under lead glaze beyond the pot board with the hand half over nothing and the little-door burn on the back of her left hand closing on air. She lifted the twice-mended pot thumb-first where the tighter wire crossed the crack, left the hairline showing between old-brass staple and wire, gave both proverbs to the pot and the fire and never to a person, kept repair apart from restoration, turned the dressed grain under wool with a touch lighter than a woman would use on a sleeping child and with no figure or handful, and set the pot rim two inches beyond the reaching hand with a half-beat and no look toward the bed. She carried him down and up the nineteen steps at the half-pace, gave the instruction to the wool, the river wind, the pot, the fire and the banked fire and never to the basket, went wide around the seven walked-around places once and not twice, widest at the returning-line place, set him under the roof and never in the Debt Loft, put the fold right at his ear and under his chin without a look at his face and added no second fold; the keeping at the fold was found where put and stayed a finding. \textbf{The widow’s mark hung where it hangs on all three days} — a morning, a hearth, a shelf, a pot, a yard, a well, a basket and a going of the light are not openings, seven openings in seven months are seven and not a rule and no eighth came due. She did not make the offered figure a price, a reader, a witness or a payment, and did not join it to the asking that came up at the well on the twenty-third or to the softening under the river’s skin. With Tarn six stood where the house could check and the seventh at the lip with \emph{Six counted. The next I don’t count} found where put and not made a habit; with Jorra her unfinished sentence still arrived at the pot through the bent finger in the cold damper, taken out without the extra holding of Ash 26 a second time, and \emph{he’s not Vail} stayed sealed. Garl stayed in objects with his name unspoken 420, 421 and 422 days and his tile debt uncalled, his coat on the peg, his hollow seat and the twice-mended pot’s hairline keeping the house in his shape. No bond changed hands, no new scar or possession and no change of voice.

\textbf{Ch 122 (bonds).} With Corin nothing crossed under the roof, out of the yard or up the clay road across Ilmen 23, 24 and 25 as sign, lesson, mending, cause, payment or payer, and the asking that came up at the well was not made a teaching under the roof or told a second time on an unearned day. She came to the hearth before the basket at both ends of every day, told the coals it was the thaw in the voice another woman would use for a child who could not hear her, turned them with the back of a broken pot, gave the small intake, the hold and the letting-go toward no opening with neither gap figured, kept her finger above the unread charcoal, lips on a two-gapped row, one glance at the clay jar with the hand half over nothing and the little-door burn closing on air, lifted the twice-mended pot thumb-first where the tighter wire crossed the crack with the hairline showing between old-brass staple and wire and both proverbs to pot and fire and never to a person, kept repair apart from restoration, turned the dressed grain under wool with no figure or handful and set the pot rim two inches beyond the reaching hand with a half-beat and no look toward the bed. She carried him down and up the nineteen steps at the half-pace, gave the instruction to the wool, the river wind, the pot, the fire and the banked fire and never to the basket, went wide around the seven walked-around places once and not twice, widest at the returning-line place, set him under the roof and never in the Debt Loft, put the fold right at his ear and under his chin without a look at his face and added no second fold; the keeping was found where put and stayed a finding. \textbf{The widow’s mark hung where it hangs on all three days} — a morning, a hearth, a shelf, a pot, a yard, a basket and a going of the light are not openings, seven openings in seven months are seven and not a rule and no eighth came due. She said nothing of the figure gone twice over a basket, of the man whose slate had gone down the road with the writing turned away, of the asking that came up at the well on the twenty-third or of the softening nobody owned; the well gave back the weather and she gave it no teaching. On Ilmen 25 she said \emph{The fire doesn’t know you’re sorry. Feed it} to the fire and to no basket, with no name and no payer standing under it. With Tarn six stood where the house could check and the seventh at the lip beside Garl’s unforged collector sentence, his hand over blade and sill and away; the sentence was found where put and not made a habit, the loan uncalled in an ended term. With Jorra her unfinished sentence still reached the pot through the bent finger in the cold damper and came out without the extra holding of Ash 26. Garl stayed in the hairline of the pot and the hollow wheel-seat, his name unspoken 417, 418 and 419 days while the fire’s fifth went unpaid the same number. No new scar or possession, no change of voice, nothing paid, forgiven, named or ended; forward, not closed.

\textbf{Ch 121 (bonds).} With Corin nothing crossed under the roof, out of the yard or up the clay road across Ilmen 20, 21 and 22 as sign, lesson, mending, cause, payment or payer, and neither the second reading nor the second man’s passing was made a teaching under the roof. She carried him down and up the nineteen steps at the half-pace, gave the instruction to the wool, the river wind, the pot, the fire and the banked fire and never to the basket, went wide around the seven walked-around places once and not twice, widest at the returning-line place, set him under the roof and never in the Debt Loft, put the fold right at his ear and under his chin without a look at his face and added no second fold; the keeping was found where put and stayed a finding. \textbf{The widow’s mark was not touched on any of the three days} — a morning, a hearth, a shelf, a basket, a well, a yard, a market, a road and a going of the light are not openings, seven openings in seven months are seven and not a rule and no eighth came due. On Ilmen 20, the month’s second Account-day and market, she set the basket in the moot-post’s finger’s width of shade where no slate lay, stood half a pace off through Berr Clay’s twice-read figure and the bell, and carried him home at the going of the light saying nothing of what had been read over him or of the kindness Berr believed he had done. With Tarn the sixth piece stood where the house could check and the seventh at the lip, the sentence found where put and not made a habit, the loan uncalled at the end of an ended term; with Jorra her unfinished sentence still arrived at the pot through his bent finger in the damper and came out without the extra holding of Ash 26. She said nothing of the second man’s turned slate going down the bridge road, of the clerk’s entered figure, of the softening at the river’s skin or of the two readings gone up the road in a box with no key; what she put down in the room was a pot in its place and a fire kept. No new scar or possession, no change of voice.
