With Tarn the thumb he laid on the uncut seventh on Bone 26 got no question from her, and the late thaw he kept because it puts off the paying got no instruction; with Jorra the grey dust, the bent finger standing in the cold damper ahead of her unfinished sentence and the men unnamed before first grey went unasked about and \emph{he’s not Vail} stayed sealed; Ilva at the well on the twenty-sixth kept her count in wood and answered the question put, and nothing from that well crossed under the roof; Garl’s name was unspoken three hundred and twenty-four, twenty-five and twenty-six days and his tile debt stayed uncalled. No bond changed hands, no tin or box was opened, no new scar or possession and no change of voice.

\textbf{Ch 90 (bonds).} With Corin nothing changed hands across Bone 22–24, and the one movement was hers. She came to the hearth before the basket at both ends of every day, told the coals it was the thaw and \emph{The house will keep it}, turned them with the back of a broken pot, stood a moment counting small intake, hold and letting-go toward no opening with neither gap figured, kept her finger on top of the loaf shelf so the charcoal stayed unread, moved her lips along a two-gapped row with neither gap figured, glanced once at the clay jar cold under lead glaze with her hand half over nothing, lifted the twice-mended pot with the thumb first where the wire crossed the crack and both proverbs to the pot and the fire with the crack showing, turned the dressed grain under wool with a lighter touch and no figure, set the pot rim two inches beyond the reaching hand with a half-beat and no look toward the bed, righted the fold without looking at his face and left the thread. On Bone 22 at the rack end she lifted the wool from the dressed grain, took a small handful, let it fall back through her fingers onto the heap instead of spreading it, said nothing, gave no figure and never did it again on the twenty-third or twenty-fourth; on those two mornings her fingers went in and came out without closing and she made no show of not repeating it. She carried him down and up at the half-pace from every open slate, gave the instruction to the wool and the river wind and never to the basket, and went wide around the seven walked-around places with a look and a wide step and no number. The three coverings stayed weather entered nowhere, the hunts and repairs stayed directions judged by the arm and the weather, and the widow’s mark hung where it hung at every morning, rack, well, yard, hearth and bed, because none was an opening and five openings in five months are five and not a rule. With Tarn the exact account of six and the seventh went unremarked and his stroke over the bright patch without the half-check asked no question from her; with Jorra the men unnamed before first grey, the dust and the bent finger standing in the cold damper ahead of her unfinished sentence went unasked about, and his quieter silence at the burned-slate saying got no instruction from her. Ilva at the well on Bone 23 kept her count in wood and answered the question put; nothing came from that well under the roof as lesson, figure, mending, cause or payment. Garl’s name was unspoken three hundred and twenty-three days and his tile debt stayed uncalled. The handful stayed one object nobody under the roof saw as a meaning, and the boy’s staying and early letting-go stayed two objects neither made again. No tin or box was opened, no bond changed hands, no new scar or possession and no change of voice.

\textbf{Ch 89 (bonds).} With Corin nothing changed hands across Bone 19–21. She came to the hearth before the basket at both ends of every day, told the coals it was the thaw and \emph{The house will keep it} where another woman would say \emph{I}, turned them with the back of a broken pot, counted small intake, hold and letting-go toward no opening with neither gap figured, kept her finger on top of the loaf shelf so the charcoal stayed unread, glanced once at the clay jar cold under lead glaze with her hand half over nothing, lifted the twice-mended pot with the thumb first where the wire crossed the crack with both proverbs to pot and fire and the crack showing, turned the dressed grain under wool with a lighter touch and no figure, set the pot rim two inches beyond the reaching hand with a half-beat and no look toward the bed, righted the fold without looking and left the thread. On Bone 20 she set the basket in the moot-post’s finger’s width of shade where no slate lay, stood half a pace off through the reading and the bell, and carried him home at the going of the light saying nothing of what had been read over him. Berr’s reading went up the road and back without changing any grammar under the roof. Garl’s name was unspoken three hundred and twenty days and his tile debt stayed uncalled. The boy’s staying at the inch and his early letting-go were two objects nobody under the roof saw and neither was made into a habit. No bond changed hands, no tin or box opened, no secret entered, no new scar or possession and no change of voice.

\textbf{Ch 88 (bonds).} With Corin nothing changed hands across Bone 16–18. She came to the hearth before the basket at both ends of every day, gave the instruction to the wool, the wind, the pot, the broom and the running water and never to the basket, said \emph{The house will keep it}, counted intake, hold and letting-go toward no opening with neither gap figured, kept the charcoal unread beneath her finger on top of the shelf, glanced once at the clay jar cold under lead glaze with her hand half over nothing, lifted the twice-mended pot with the thumb first where the wire crossed the crack and left the crack showing, turned the dressed grain beneath the wool with a lighter touch and no figure, set the pot rim two inches beyond his reach with a half-beat and no look toward his face, righted the fold without looking and left the thread. She carried him down and up at the half-pace from every open slate and went wide around the seven walked-around places with a look and a wide step and no number, and touched the widow’s mark at no hour because a morning, a hearth, a going of the light and a bed are not openings; five openings in five months are five and not a rule. With Tarn the exact account of six and the seventh went unremarked and his stroke over the bright patch without the half-check asked no question from her; with Jorra the men unnamed before first grey, the dust and the bent finger in the cold damper went unasked about and his quieter silence at the burned-slate saying got no instruction from her. Ilva at the well on Bone 17 kept her count in wood and answered the question put; nothing came from that well under the roof as lesson, figure, mending, cause or payment. Garl’s name was unspoken three hundred and seventeen days and his tile debt stayed uncalled. The boy’s staying at the inch and his early letting-go were two objects nobody under the roof saw and neither was made into a habit. No bond changed hands, no tin or box was opened, no new scar or possession and no secret was entered.

\textbf{Ch 87 (bonds).} With Corin nothing changed hands across Bone 13–15. She came to the hearth before the basket at both ends of every day, told the coals it was the thaw and \emph{The house will keep it} where another woman would say \emph{I}, turned them with the back of a broken pot, counted small intake, hold and letting-go under her breath toward no opening, kept her finger on top of the shelf so the charcoal stayed unread and her lips along the two-gapped row with neither gap figured, glanced once at the clay jar cold under its glaze, lifted the twice-mended pot with her thumb first where the wire crossed the crack and left the crack showing, turned the dressed grain under wool with a progressively lighter touch and no figure, and set the pot rim two inches beyond the reaching hand with a half-beat and no look toward the bed. She carried him down and up at the half-pace from every open slate, gave the instruction to the wool and the river wind and never to the basket, went wide around the seven walked-around places with a look and a wide step and no number, and left the thread where it lay; the widow’s mark hung where it hung at every morning, yard, afternoon and going of the light, because none was an opening and five openings in five months are five and not a rule. With Tarn the exact account of six and the seventh went unremarked and his stroke over the bright patch without the half-check asked no question from her; with Jorra the men unnamed before first grey, the dust and the bent finger in the cold damper went unasked about and his quieter silence at the burned-slate saying got no instruction from her. Ilva at the well on the fourteenth kept her count in wood and answered the question put; nothing came from that well under the roof as lesson, figure, mending, cause or payment. Garl’s name was unspoken three hundred and fourteen days and his tile debt stayed uncalled. No bond changed hands, no tin or box was opened and no secret was entered.

\textbf{Jorra Vail} — her son, the keeper of the wheel. He believes she took the foundling in to replace Enna and to keep the house’s standing while he did the work. She has never told him otherwise, which is how he has come to believe it. They speak about the kiln, the levy, the weather; they do not speak about Garl, or Enna, or the boy. \emph{Ch 2:} he said \emph{he’s not Vail} when she announced the taking, and she did not answer him; she grew quieter and the house straightened up around it. He went on turning the wheel without looking at her and obeyed her before she had finished. The sentence stands and the boy is under the roof and still unwritten.

\textbf{Corin} — the foundling she took in and has never questioned. She watches him with a hearth-maid’s attention and a widow’s refusal to name what she sees. Her silence is its own kind of Court: kindness that does not want an answer, and that therefore cannot be refused. \emph{Ch 1:} her hand came in ahead of her, felt for the heat at his belly, found none, opened and shut once over the covered bundle, and withdrew. She did not look at him, or at any of the women, and said nothing. \emph{Ch 2:} the hand that hovered now takes. She crossed to the bench first and put her hand near the slate as near a sleeping animal, then lifted him, the little-door burn closing first on nothing and then on his weight. She said \emph{the boy} and \emph{the house}, carried him up the yard without looking back, laid him on fresh straw, and gave instruction to the pot and the fire. She has not written him as Vail and has said nothing of payment or purpose. \emph{Ch 3:} she carried him out under the Vail roof for the first time, in a basket under a fold of wool, like a pot filled that must not be slopped. She kept a half-pace from every open slate, put the fold back without looking, answered a question about whose house with \emph{the house}, and answered a question about the mother with \emph{Account-day}. All morning she spoke to the wool and the wind: \emph{Keep it off his ears. It’s the river wind.} She did not look into the basket on the walk home and said nothing of what had been read over him.

\textbf{Alda Reed} — delivered Enna and Corin both, and crossed herself at the second birth. They have traded one silence for three years. Alda has the fuller notes; Sella has the fuller knowledge of what a silence costs when a household must eat. \emph{Ch 1:} Alda laid the slate flat on the bench as Sella’s hand went back out the door; the trade of silences begins in that room. \emph{Ch 2:} Sella put her hand near the writing on the bench as she took the child and did not touch it, and Alda did not look at her. The arrangement holds without a word passing between them.

\textbf{Dessa Silt} — the woman who bore the boy. Sella knows it and has paid her in barley and slip-clay to stay away, and has never entered the payment in any account, not even the private one she keeps in her head. \emph{Ch 1:} Dessa’s pulse rose under her \emph{door shut} smile while the hand hung above her child; neither looked at the other. \emph{Ch 2:} Sella took the boy up the yard without once looking at the woman standing at the end of the nineteen steps, and Dessa did not follow.

\textbf{Berr Clay, the Thane of Clay} — confirmed her widow’s mark and has never called in the debt Garl left against a shipment of tiles. The uncalled debt is worse than a called one, because she cannot pay it and cannot settle it and cannot stop owing it. \emph{Ch 3:} at the Slate Row end of the Cross he told her the mark was confirmed by the factor at Greybank, that it was a kindness, and that kindness is entered. She did not answer him about the mark; she pulled the wool up over the boy’s ear and said it was the river wind. He stood a moment with his mouth open on the next part, then left the debt where it lay as carefully as he had found it. She has never asked and has never thanked him, which he has decided means she knows.

\textbf{Garl Vail} — her husband, uncollected in the Long Cold. She decided he would not be collected; he did not ask her to decide. The Ash in the corner is the shape of that decision and she has lived beside it for a year. \emph{Ch 2:} she keeps his seat empty and his coat on its peg, will not let anyone sweep the ridge, and touches the widow’s mark only before she opens the kiln. The house keeps a roll of its own in which he is entered, and does not show it to a man from Slate Row.

\textbf{Ch 4.} The boy was carried to the Drawing and back like a pot filled that must not be slopped; she placed him where he could see and not join and stood a half-pace off, her burn shut on nothing, and would not be the one to tell him what the room was doing. She did not answer Jorra’s \emph{the back room’s cold}; she shifted the damper. With Alda, a half-pace and a turned slate stood in for the arrangement, and neither asked what the other had written. Dessa at her threshold got no look from her and no word, and the barley between the two houses went on being unentered. Garl’s mark was touched before the kiln and not at the bank, and his coat, seat, ridge and proverb kept the house in his shape while the debt stayed uncalled.

\textbf{Ch 5.} The rule of the mark held exactly: touched before the opening on Stone 13 and at no other time, not at the bank that night or on Stone 15. She fed him barley gruel from the house’s own dish, holding his head with two fingers behind the ear, and gave every instruction to the fire, the pot and the wool --- \emph{keep it off his ears; it’s the river wind} --- never to the basket. She carried him down to the Fishstairs twice and to the market’s edge once, kept her half-pace from every open slate, laid marks for two pair of eels and counted them with her eyes, and said nothing about the collector’s cuff, the cord or where they had been. At dusk on Stone 15 her hand did not go to the mark; she counted loaves and bits with her lips and came back to the same place twice, keeping the shape of the days to Kindling without giving the number. She neither saw nor refused the crust Mira put in the fold, and where she is concerned these are the same thing.

\textbf{Ch 6.} On Stone 16 she touched the mark before the lid and at no other hour, moved her lips along the loaf shelf so the days to Kindling stood as a shape, and told the neighbour at the threshold to ask the pot. She carried him down to the Cross on Stone 20 and back, kept her half-pace from every open slate, set the basket in the moot-post’s shade and did not look into it; at dusk she put the fold right without his face, banked the coals with the back of a broken pot and did not touch the mark, because a reading is not an opening. On Stone 19 she slid the basket a hand’s breadth out of the draught and would not have called it love, measured the ridge with her thumb --- near two thumbs here, a finger more two doors down --- and said leave it until the Last Day. The crust Mira put in the fold went from warm to cold and she neither took it out nor named it. With Alda a half-pace and a turned slate stood in for the arrangement again; Berr read his figure over the basket and went around Garl’s uncalled debt another year; Jorra moved the damper before she had finished and did not say the back room was cold.

\textbf{Ch 7.} Through Days 15--24 she went to the fire before anything else and touched the widow’s mark before each opening and at no other hour --- not when she banked with the back of a broken pot, not at the reading on Stone 30. She counted fuel and bread into the last tend in loaves, glances and the space where a loaf should have stood, and answered the man who came back from the ice with a number in his fist by saying it was a cold and feeding the fire. She sent Tarn for a collector for a neighbour, carried the basket two doors down and set it at the edge of the light with her burn shut on nothing. On Stone 29 she laid her thumb in the Vail Ash ridge and then in the death-house ridge, near two thumbs here and a finger thicker there, and walked back without saying which was which. At the last market she kept her half-pace from every open slate, set the basket in the moot-post’s shade and gave instruction to the wool, and at dusk put the fold right without looking at his face, set him on his bed under the roof and not in the Debt Loft, and banked the coals. She neither took out nor named either crust. With Alda a half-pace and a slate turned writing-down stood in for the arrangement again; she did not answer Jorra’s silence about the back room, let Berr go around Garl’s debt, and carried the keeping into Kindling without explaining any of it.

\textbf{Ch 8.} On Kindling she took the clay dish of fire up from the yard before first light, put her hand to the widow’s mark for one breath before she opened the kiln and tipped the coal in, and did not touch it again; nobody said where the flame came from or what it cost, and she gave the instruction to the fire and the wool and fed him from the house’s own dish, saying \emph{the house}. Through the Five the mark was touched before openings and at no other hour, never at the bank. At the Weighing she kept her half-pace from every open slate and did not repeat the name the officer read; the clean voice and the Court’s room reached the basket only as a sound through a doorway, and she did not turn toward it. On the Long Night she let the fire go out at dusk and sat with the others telling the Return in the dark, saying \emph{the house} where another woman would have said \emph{I} and going around Garl’s name as she went around Ash. On the Remembering she did not say Garl’s name and let Alda put dates where it should have stood. On the Last Day she would not let anyone sweep the Ash early, laid her thumb flat in the Vail ridge and then the neighbour’s, near two thumbs here and a finger’s width thicker two doors down, and left both where they lay. On Ilmen 1, with the grey burned in the morning and called dealt with by a neighbour and not by her, the coals were still banked under ash so there was no opening and she did not touch the mark; she put the fold right without looking at his face, fed him from the house’s own dish, and said nothing about where any of the warmth came from or who had paid for it.

\textbf{Ch 9.} Through Days 31–37 the keeping went on without an entry. At the well she drew with her free hand, the little-door burn closing on the rope and then on nothing, spoke \emph{the house} where another woman would say \emph{I}, and gave the instruction to the bucket, the fire and the wool and never to the basket; she did not say where the warmth in the household dish came from. On Ilmen 3 she fed him from the house’s own dish with two fingers behind his ear and sat with the mark untouched at the bank, because a dusk is not an opening. On Ilmen 5 she stood a half-pace off while Alda laid dates and wrote what she turned down, and did not ask. On Ilmen 6 she touched the mark before the opening, held it one breath and let go, and did not touch it for a pot, a note or a nearly full sound. On Ilmen 8 she set him in the shade of the nineteen steps three doors down, carried him up the yard at dusk, turned the coals with the back of a broken pot and did not touch the mark, because a bank was not an opening. She has said nothing about the payer of any warmth.

\textbf{Ch 10.} On Day 38 she holds the basket on the higher ground at the Slip Brook and turns the boy’s face toward the bank, as she would turn a pot so the light fell where she wanted it; she does not set him down. She goes to the fire, not down the road for a collector, and sends nobody; the omission is not entered and she does not name it. On Day 42 she fetches a clay jar from House Silt and sets it on the shelf by the wall, without turning the errand into a walk to a bank or opening a slate. On Day 43 and Day 44 she leaves the boy in shade at the Weir and carries him home at dusk, setting him on his bed and not in the Debt Loft, putting the fold right without looking at his face. She still says \emph{the house}, gives every instruction to the wool, the fire and the pot, touches the mark only before openings, and has named neither the payer of the warmth nor the woman in the brook.

\textbf{Ch 11.} She carried him down to the Fishstairs before light and set him below the north bridge where a pot would be set, out of the draught, then up the Clay Yard and onto his bed at dusk, never into the Debt Loft; the fold went right at his ear without a look at his face. Every instruction went to the fire, the pot and the wool, and she said the house where another woman would have said I. She touched the widow’s mark once before the opening on Day 45 and not at any bank or on any other day. She fed him gruel thinned with milk from the house’s own dish, two fingers behind his ear, spoon wiped on her sleeve and his mouth not wiped. At the well she went at a half-pace from every open slate, went wide around a slate propped at the rack end and gave the instruction to the bucket. She said nothing about the payer of any warmth, did not name Dessa, and did not say that the smoky crust was gone. Her hand is one of the three the boy set on a tray as possible takers.

\textbf{Ch 12.} Through seven more days she gave every instruction to the fire, the wool and the bucket and none to the basket, and said the house where another woman would say I. With Alda a half-pace and a turned slate stood in for the arrangement again while the fifth note went under a floorboard and she did not ask; with Berr the debt against the tiles lay where it lay and one in twelve went over the basket unchallenged; with Jorra the dust out of the back room went unasked about and the damper went ahead of her sentence. She did not look toward the bed or into the basket, did not touch the mark at a well or a bank, and said nothing about the payer of the milk, the coal that went up with the bird or the crust that went out of the fold on Day 46.

\textbf{Ch 13.} She carried him three doors down into House Silt on Ilmen 27 and set the basket just inside the finger’s-width-open door at the edge of the light and away from every open slate; she opened no slate and turned the errand into no walk to Slate Row. Alda came and she stood a half-pace off with her burn shut on nothing and asked no question about the birth-slates or the fold pressed too long. At the well and at the last market she gave every instruction to the fire, the wool and the bucket and never to the basket, and said the house where another woman would say I. She fed the fire and told it the thaw when a man from Greybank spoke of a counting room shut in the war; if she connected any of it to her own roof she put the connection in the private roll nobody is shown, but she did not connect it. On Ilmen 29 she laid one thumb in the clean dark line where the Ash ridge turned and the same thumb in the ridge two doors down, and fetched no broom for either. On Silt 1 she stood over a new hairline of grey in the corner with a broom in her hand and did not sweep, telling the fire it was the thaw and would go when it goes; she touched the widow’s mark before the opening and at no other hour, not for the new grey, not for a basket, not at a bank.

\textbf{Ch 14.} Through Silt 2–8 she kept the house the way she kept the fire: instruction to the fire, the wool and the bucket and never to the basket, \emph{the house} where another woman would say \emph{I}, and a half-pace kept from every open slate at the racks, the Fishstairs, House Silt and the well. She told the fire it was the thaw when the brook came up clay-heavy behind the racks and again when the ice was called honeyed all through, and stood over the new grey in the corner without sweeping it, finer than the old clean dark line beside it. No opening came in seven days and the widow’s mark hung where it hung, untouched at a rack, a basket, a well, a door and a bed. On Silt 5 she carried him three doors down, set the basket inside the finger’s-width-open door away from any open slate, stood a half-pace off while Alda wrote, and asked nothing about the writing or the tin; the little-door burn shut on nothing. At dusk each day she set him on his bed under the roof and not in the Debt Loft and put the fold right without looking at his face, carrying one crust and an empty place through seven days without a name.

\textbf{Ch 15.} Through Silt 9–15 she kept the house the way she kept the fire: every instruction to the fire, the wool and the bucket and never to the basket, \emph{the house} where another woman would say \emph{I}, a half-pace kept from every open slate at the Fishstairs, the Cross, the racks and three doors down in House Silt. She carried him to the edge of the thin brown sheet and back, and when the water went around the clean dark line she stood over it and the new finer grey beside it with a broom in her hand and swept neither, telling the fire it was the thaw and would go when it went. A neighbour said the house had been saved and she did not. On Silt 14 she gave the broom its instruction before anybody (\emph{Round it / Go around}), went wide around the space under the lowest rack, and did not answer Jorra’s silence about the room off the shed. No opening came in seven days and the widow’s mark was not touched once, not at a rack, a shore, a step or a bed. It is told of her that she once sat up three nights with a child of her own who cooled while everybody was kind; she did not go toward the child in the yard whose foot stayed cold, and the boy did not lay the two together. At dusk of the last day she carried him up at the half-pace, set him on his bed under the roof and not in the Debt Loft, put the fold right without looking at his face, and left the thread at his mouth frozen and unwiped. One brown-edged crust lay stiff in the fold with the empty place beside it unnamed. The private roll stayed unshown.

\textbf{Ch 16.} Through Days 75–77 she keeps the house the way she keeps the fire: every instruction to the fire, the wool, the bucket and the broom and never to the basket, and \emph{the house} where another woman would say \emph{I}. The flood has gone out of the yard and left mud, and the sweeping goes around the clean dark line at the Vail corner, the new finer grey beside it and the space under the lowest rack; she gives the broom its instruction before she gives it to anybody (\emph{Go around. It cost enough to come in. It’ll cost more to take out.}), stands over the two lines with a broom in her hand and sweeps neither, and tells the fire it is the thaw. The yard counts what the water took in loaves, glances and a space at the row’s end that nobody calls a number, and when a woman asks for a figure she tells her to ask the pot what a wet thing costs set down there. She keeps the half-pace from every open slate, goes wide around a slate set out to dry at the well’s edge and does not touch the widow’s mark, because a well is not an opening and a basket is not a door. At the well she does not look at the quick child in cast-offs or at the warm loaf in his pocket and does not connect the man from Slate Row with either; if she saw the passing she put it where she puts the other things she does not enter, in the private roll nobody is shown. No opening came in three days and the mark hung where it hung. At dusk each day she sets him on his bed under the roof and not in the Debt Loft, puts the fold right without looking at his face and leaves the thread at his mouth frozen and unwiped; one brown-edged crust lies stiff in the fold with the empty place beside it unnamed and no third comes. The wall has acquired no door: it keeps out the mud, the half-beat, the loaf, the man from Slate Row, the two unswept lines and the empty place, and keeps the boy warm without ever entering the warmth.

\textbf{Ch 17.} Through the lean week the keeping goes on in the same grammar: every instruction to the fire, the wool, the bucket and the broom and never to the basket, \emph{the house} where another woman would say \emph{I}, a half-pace from every open slate at the well, the Cross, House Silt and the racks. She gives the broom its instruction before anybody — go around what the water left, it cost enough to come in and will cost more to take out — and sweeps neither the clean dark line nor the new finer grey. Three doors down she sets the basket just inside the finger’s-width-open door at the edge of the light, opens no slate and turns no errand into a walk to Slate Row, and stands a half-pace off while Alda writes what she will not show. When the second man from Greybank repeats the story of the counting room at the well she tells the fire it is the thaw, makes nothing of it and does not connect it to her own roof; she has lost a husband to that danger and has never described it that way herself. Jorra’s dust and the damper ahead of her sentence go unasked about, Tarn’s knife and his seventh year go unremarked, Alda’s tin and Berr’s box stay shut. The widow’s mark is untouched in seven days, because a well, a reading, a story over a bucket, a basket and a bed are not openings. The private roll stays unshown and the empty place at the row’s end stays unnamed.

\textbf{Ch 20 (bonds).} Jorra still comes through the finger’s-width-open shed door with dust he does not name and puts his bent finger into the damper ahead of her unfinished sentence; he did not look toward the bed or the basket and \emph{he’s not Vail} stays sealed. Corin was carried up the yard at the half-pace from every open slate and set on his bed under the roof, not in the Debt Loft, with the fold put right without a look at his face and the thread left frozen; she has still not said whose fire, whose child or whose hundred. With Alda a half-pace and a turned slate stood in for the arrangement again on Seed 8; she asked nothing about the sign, the date, the tin or the sixth page. Dessa stays dead and uncollected, more mornings gone than any living person keeps count of, and her name and number were not spoken. Berr’s box stayed locked and Garl’s debt against the tiles neither paid nor settled; the salt coat, hollow seat and clean dark line kept their places. No bond changed hands this chapter and no secret was entered.

\textbf{Ch 21 (bonds).} With Corin nothing was said and nothing was joined: she carried him at the half-pace from every open slate, gave the instruction to the pot, the fire, the broom and the wool and never to the basket, set the fold right without looking at his face each dusk and left the thread frozen, and has still not said whose child he is. When a neighbour named the shelf’s old space and the boy’s empty place in one breath she moved her lips along the loaf row and left both gaps unfigured, hearing two sayings and not one absence. With Jorra the household kept its old shape on Seed 13: men unnamed came before first grey, his bent finger went into the damper ahead of her unfinished sentence so the end of it arrived at the pot, and the household straightened around his silence; he did not look toward the bed and \emph{he’s not Vail} stayed sealed. With Tarn the exact account held: six counted, the seventh nearly gone and still held, the broom over the collector’s road without turning, the loan uncalled. With Alda a half-pace and a turned slate stood in for the arrangement again on Seed 14; she asked nothing about the sign, the date, the tin or the sixth page. Berr went off toward High Kiln with the box locked and the debt against the tiles neither paid nor settled; Mira’s cords and Orra’s board stayed unread. Dessa stayed dead and uncollected and her name and number were not spoken. No bond changed hands, no tin or box was opened and no secret was entered.

\textbf{Ch 22 (bonds).} With Corin nothing changed hands across three lived days: the half-pace from every open slate, every instruction to the bucket, the broom, the pot, the wool, the water and the fire and never to the basket, \emph{the house} where another woman would say \emph{I}, the fold put right without a look at his face and the thread left frozen; she has still not said whose child he is, and the private roll stays unshown. On Seed 15 she gave the broom its instruction before anybody (\emph{Go around. It cost enough to come in. It’ll cost more to take out}) and went around the clean dark line, the new finer grey called the thaw and the space under the lowest rack without sweeping any of them; at the loaf shelf she moved her lips along a row standing with two gaps, glanced at the clay jar and gave nobody a figure while a neighbour named the old gap as a thing the planting brought in, and she did not join the two tellings or touch the widow’s mark, because a strip, a shelf, a rack and a yard are not openings. She told the fire it was the thaw, turned the coals with the back of a broken pot and let the fire answer four low pulls and the silence where the fifth should have been, its payer unnamed for a hundred and four days. On Seed 16 she stood a half-pace off while men unnamed came before first grey and Jorra’s bent finger went into the damper ahead of her unfinished sentence; the end of her instruction arrived at the pot and the household straightened around his silence, and she gave the house no name for the men. At the well she said \emph{Yes, house} to the early thaw and the late and kept wanting the late because it puts off the paying, though the paying had stood in the ruts since the water went. On Seed 17 she set the basket at the very end of the fish-trade shade where no slate lay and told the wool and the water and never the basket, and midday set it just inside the finger’s-width-open door three doors down away from every open slate, opening none and turning no errand into a walk to Slate Row; she said nothing about the writing, the tin or the fold pressed too long. At dusk each day she set him on his bed under the roof and not in the Debt Loft. The two shelf gaps and the fold’s one crust stayed in rooms that do not touch, no third came, no tin or box was opened and no bond changed hands; no new scar, possession or change of voice.

\textbf{Ch 23 (bonds).} With Corin nothing changed hands across Seed 18–20: the half-pace from every open slate, every instruction to the broom, bucket, wool, water, pot and fire and never to the basket, \emph{the house} where another woman would say \emph{I}, the fold put right without a look at his face and the thread left frozen, and she has still not said whose child he is. At the fire she told it the thaw, turned the coals with the back of a broken pot and stood a moment with the back of the pot in her hand counting something under her breath toward no opening; she pushed a strand of coal-black hair back with the wrist that carries the burn and did not look toward the bed. With Jorra the household kept its old shape on Seed 19: men unnamed came before first grey, his bent finger went into the damper ahead of her unfinished sentence and she gave the end of it to the pot, and he did not look at her or answer with a word. Three doors down on Seed 18 she set the basket just inside the finger’s-width-open door away from every open slate, opened none, turned no errand into a walk to Slate Row and stood a half-pace off while Alda pressed the fold too long; she said nothing of the writing, the tin or the date over the sign. \textbf{Ch 24 (bonds).} With Corin nothing changed hands across Seed 21–23: the half-pace from every open slate, every instruction to the bucket, broom, wool, water, pot and fire and never to the basket, \emph{the house} where another woman would say \emph{I}, the fold put right without a look at his face and the thread left frozen; she has still not said whose child he is. \textbf{Ch 63 (bonds).} With Corin nothing was said and nothing was joined across Smoke 1–3: the half-pace from every open slate, every instruction to the wool, fire, pot, broom, running water and river wind and never to the basket, \emph{the house} where another woman would say \emph{I}, the bed under the roof and not the Debt Loft, the fold put right without a look at his face and the thread left frozen. \textbf{Her act of the chapter, and the chapter’s one meaningful change, advanced and not paid:} before the first firing of Smoke she went to the kiln mouth first, put her hand to the widow’s mark, held it one breath, let go, lifted the clay lid with the back of a hand and tipped the carried coal under the back of a broken pot; the fire took, still answering four low pulls with the fifth missing and no payer, and nobody praised the opening or saw what it mended. She kept the fire before the basket, the instruction to the tools and never the basket, \emph{the house} and \emph{The house will keep it}, the half-pace from every open slate, the finger on top of the shelf with the charcoal unread, the two-gapped row unfigured, the one glance at the clay jar with the hand half over nothing, the pot rim two inches beyond the reaching hand with a half-beat and no look toward the bed, and the widow’s mark untouched because none of these hours was an opening. On Bone 10 she set the basket in the moot-post’s thin shade where no slate lay, stood half a pace off through Berr’s reading and the bell and carried him home at the going of the light saying nothing; the printed figure stood unchallenged and the true subtractions went up the road in the locked box. Her twice-mended pot kept its crack showing and both proverbs went to the pot and the fire; the dressed grain lay covered and unfigured under wool; the three coverings at the well were weather entered nowhere; Garl’s name was unspoken three hundred and eleven days and his tile debt uncalled. Tarn’s loan stayed uncalled and his ear-sentence stopped at the calling word; Jorra’s promise stayed ungiven and \emph{he’s not Vail} sealed; Hessa carried Berr’s slate up the road unread and was no reader for any shaping. No name given, no debt paid, no bond paid, sold, named or spoken.

\CRsheetheading{Arc So Far}
\textbf{Ch 128 (Days 435–437, Silt 11–13).} The kiln-house kept three tending days lived one at a time under the old grammar as though nothing had turned, with no lesson made of the fourth reading behind. Fire before basket at both ends of every day; coals told the thaw and turned with the back of a broken pot; the small intake, hold and letting-go toward no opening with neither gap figured; her finger along the top of the loaf shelf so the charcoal stayed unread; lips on a two-gapped row; one glance at the cold clay jar with the hand shut half over nothing and the little-door burn closing on air; the twice-mended pot lifted thumb-first where the wire crossed the crack with the hairline showing and both proverbs given to pot and fire, never to a person; dressed grain turned under wool unfigured; pot rim two inches beyond the reaching hand with a half-beat and no look toward the bed; the nineteen steps at the half-pace; the seven walked-around places once and not twice; the fold righted without a look at his face and no second fold. Her hands counted spoons and nails and came back to the hairline at the wire. The widow’s mark hung where it hangs on all three days — a tending day is not an opening, seven openings in seven months are seven and not a rule and no eighth came due. On Silt 12 she was at the well with him while a second neighbour asked whether a count kept in wood would be taken at the next reading; Ilva answered and Sella said nothing to the basket and carried him home at the going of the light saying nothing of it. On Silt 13 she carried him home saying nothing of the man from Slate Row at the yard’s edge. The keeping at the fold was found where put; no name, figure, payment or payer came to any of it. No new scar or possession, no change of voice, nothing paid, opened or ended; forward, not closed.

\textbf{Ch 127 (Days 432–434, Silt 8–10).} The kiln-house kept three days lived one at a time under the old grammar as though nothing had turned: two ordinary tending days and then Silt’s first Account-day and market and the year’s fourth reading, earned by its own morning and not made a threshold, a signing or an eighth opening. Fire before basket at both ends of every day; coals told the thaw and turned with the back of a broken pot; the small intake, hold and letting-go toward no opening with neither gap figured; her finger along the top of the loaf shelf so the charcoal stayed unread; lips on a two-gapped row; one glance at the cold clay jar with the hand shut half over nothing and the little-door burn closing on air; the twice-mended pot lifted thumb-first where the wire crossed the crack with the hairline showing between old-brass staple and tighter wire and both proverbs given to pot and fire, never to a person; dressed grain turned under wool with no figure or handful; pot rim two inches beyond the reaching hand with a half-beat and no look toward the bed; the basket carried down and up the nineteen steps at the half-pace from every open slate; the seven walked-around places gone around once and not twice; the fold righted without a look at his face or a second fold. Her hands counted spoons and nails when they had nothing to do and came back to the hairline at the wire. The widow’s mark hung where it hangs on all three days — a morning, a hearth, a shelf, a pot, a yard, a market, a reading, a basket, a bed and a going of the light are not openings, seven openings in seven months are seven and not a rule and no eighth came due. Before first grey on Silt 10 she carried him down, set the basket in the moot-post’s finger’s width of shade where no slate lay and stood half a pace off through Berr Clay’s twice-read figure and the bell, giving the wicker no instruction and no reason, and carried him home at the going of the light saying nothing of the reading, the bell’s gap, the unread slate going up the road or the fourth subtraction in the locked box. She told the fire it was the thaw and did not tell the basket, and neither the reported second slate nor the hair-thin thaw was brought under the roof as a lesson on a later day. The keeping at the fold was found where put and stayed a finding; the grain lay covered and unfigured and the fourth figure read over it did not know what it cost. No new scar or possession, no change of voice, nothing paid, opened or ended; forward, not closed.

\textbf{Ch 126 (Days 429–431, Silt 5–7).} The kiln-house kept its three tending days under the old grammar as though nothing had turned. Fire before basket at both ends of every day; coals told the thaw and turned with the back of a broken pot; the small intake, hold and letting-go toward no opening with neither gap figured; her finger along the top of the loaf shelf so the charcoal stayed unread; lips on a two-gapped row; one glance at the cold clay jar with the hand shut half over nothing and the little-door burn closing on air; the twice-mended pot lifted thumb-first where the wire crossed the crack with the hairline showing between old-brass staple and tighter wire and both proverbs given to pot and fire, never to a person; dressed grain turned under wool with no figure or handful; pot rim two inches beyond the reaching hand with a half-beat and no look toward the bed; the basket carried down and up the nineteen steps at the half-pace from every open slate; the fold righted without a look at his face or a second fold. Her hands were never still when they had nothing to do: they counted spoons, nails and the breaths of a child nobody numbers and came back to the hairline at the wire. The widow’s mark hung where it hangs on all three days — a morning, a hearth, a shelf, a pot, a yard, a basket, a bed and a going of the light are not openings, seven openings in seven months are seven and not a rule and no eighth came due. The keeping at the fold was found where put and stayed a finding; the grain lay covered and unfigured and the figure that would be read over it on a later morning did not know what it cost. The one change was not hers: a word at the well on Silt 6 about a second, narrower slate carried edge-on under the arm, which she did not bring under the roof or ask about; and on Silt 7 the grey called the thaw lying a hair less distinct along one unswept stretch at the Vail corner and the air off the river less cold at one edge, which she told the fire was the thaw and did not tell the basket. With Tarn and Jorra the two silences stayed maintenance under one roof and not a compact, and her unfinished sentence still arrived at the pot through Jorra’s bent finger in the cold damper. No new scar or possession, no change of voice, nothing paid, opened or ended; forward, not closed.

\textbf{Ch 125 (Days 426–428, Silt 2–4).} The kiln-house kept its three tending days under the old grammar as though nothing had turned. Fire before basket at both ends of every day; coals told the thaw and turned with the back of a broken pot; the small intake, hold and letting-go toward no opening with neither gap figured; her finger along the top of the loaf shelf so the charcoal stayed unread; lips on a two-gapped row; one glance at the cold clay jar with the hand shut half over nothing and the little-door burn closing on air; the twice-mended pot lifted thumb-first where the wire crossed the crack with the hairline showing and both proverbs given to pot and fire, never to a person; dressed grain turned under wool with no figure or handful; pot rim two inches beyond the reaching hand with a half-beat and no look toward the bed; the widow’s mark untouched because none of these hours was an opening and seven openings in seven months are seven and not a rule. On the third morning she weighed a fist of barley and set it back, saying no number. The one change was not hers: a neighbour’s near-reaching at the shelf on Silt 3, a finger’s width short of the fold. Her own finger stayed on the shelf’s top where it had always gone; she did not go beneath the board, did not ask and did not look at the boy’s face, and the grammar resumed on Silt 4 unchanged. The keeping at the fold was found where put and stayed a finding; no second fold, third crust, name, gift, payment or payer. No new scar or possession, no change of voice, nothing paid, opened or ended; forward, not closed.

\textbf{Ch 124 (Days 423–425, Ilmen 29–30, Silt 1).} The keeper of the fire held the whole grammar at both ends of an ordinary Ninthday, the month’s third and last Account-day and market, and the first day of Silt come on without a boundary drawn: fire before basket, coals told the thaw and turned with the back of a broken pot, intake/hold/letting-go with neither gap figured, finger above the unread charcoal, lips on a two-gapped row, one glance at the cold clay jar with the hand half over nothing and the little-door burn closing on air, the twice-mended pot lifted thumb-first with the hairline showing and both proverbs to pot and fire, dressed grain turned under wool with no figure or handful, pot rim two inches beyond the reaching hand, nineteen steps at the half-pace, seven walked-around places once and not twice, fold righted without a second fold, widow’s mark untouched at every hour that was not an opening. On Ilmen 30 she carried the basket down and set it in the moot-post’s finger’s width of shade where no slate lay and stood half a pace off through Berr Clay’s twice-read figure and the bell, giving the basket no instruction and no reason, and carried him home at the going of the light saying nothing of the reading, the bell’s gap, the unread slate or the clerk’s figure. She said \emph{the house} where another woman would say \emph{I} and \emph{the boy} where another would say \emph{my son}, because a thing said aloud becomes a thing the Court can enter; the one grey streak at her temple said winter and she did not discuss the winter. The third reading changed the district’s arithmetic and nothing under her roof; three readings stood behind one unsigned figure and she made no lesson, mending or payment of it. No new scar or possession, no change of voice; forward, not closed.

\textbf{Ch 123 (Days 420–422, Ilmen 26–28).} Keeper of the fire through three ordinary tending days lived one dated day at a time, with the old grammar unbroken at both ends of each: fire before basket, coals told the thaw and turned with the back of a broken pot, intake/hold/letting-go with neither gap figured, charcoal unread, lips on a two-gapped row, clay jar glanced at with the hand half over nothing, twice-mended pot thumb-first with its hairline showing and both proverbs to pot and fire, dressed grain turned under wool with no figure or handful, pot rim two inches beyond the reaching hand, nineteen steps at the half-pace, seven walked-around places once and not twice, fold righted without a second fold, widow’s mark untouched because none of these days was an opening and seven openings in seven months are seven and not a rule. Repair stayed apart from restoration: the second mending was the true one because it was done by a hand that had already handled the break, and the hairline was left showing. She said nothing of the figure offered at the well and gone back into the fist, of the woman who said \emph{Then it’s a stick} and went back to the round, of a note that was not a price or of the softening nobody owned, and did not repeat a previous day’s sentence to the fire on a day that had not earned it. Tarn’s sentence was found where put and not made a habit, the loan uncalled in an ended term; Jorra’s unfinished sentence still arrived at the pot through the bent finger in the damper without a second holding. The keeping at the fold was found where put and stayed a finding; no second fold, third crust, name or payment. No new scar or possession, no change of voice, nothing paid, forgiven, named or ended; forward, not closed.

\textbf{Ch 122 (Days 417–419, Ilmen 23–25).} Keeper of the fire through three ordinary tending days lived one dated day at a time, with the old grammar unbroken at both ends of each: fire before basket, coals told the thaw and turned with the back of a broken pot, intake/hold/letting-go with neither gap figured, charcoal unread, lips on a two-gapped row, clay jar glanced at with the hand half over nothing, twice-mended pot thumb-first with its hairline showing and both proverbs to pot and fire, dressed grain turned under wool with no figure or handful, pot rim two inches beyond the reaching hand, nineteen steps at the half-pace, seven walked-around places once and not twice, fold righted without a second fold, widow’s mark untouched because none of these days was an opening and no eighth came due. She said nothing of the asking that came up at the well, of the softened air, of the two readings gone up the road or of the man who had gone down it with his writing turned away; on Ilmen 25 she said \emph{The fire doesn’t know you’re sorry. Feed it} to the fire and to no basket. Tarn’s sentence was found where put and not made a habit, the loan uncalled in an ended term; Jorra’s unfinished sentence still arrived at the pot through the bent finger in the damper without a second holding. The keeping at the fold was found where put and stayed a finding; no second fold, third crust, name or payment. No new scar or possession, no change of voice, nothing paid, forgiven, named or ended; forward, not closed.

\textbf{Ch 121 (Days 414–416, Ilmen 20–22).} Keeper of the fire through the month’s second Account-day and market and two ordinary tending days lived one dated day at a time, with the old grammar unbroken at both ends of each: fire before basket, coals told the thaw and turned with a broken pot’s back, the twice-mended pot thumb-first with its hairline showing between staple and wire and both proverbs to pot and fire, dressed grain turned under wool with no figure or handful, pot rim two inches beyond the reaching hand, charcoal unread, widow’s mark untouched, seven openings in seven months and not a rule. She carried him down and up the nineteen steps at the half-pace, went wide around the seven walked-around places once and not twice, righted the fold without a second fold, and said nothing of the reading, the second man’s passing, the clerk’s entered figure, the two readings up the road or the softening under the river’s skin. On Ilmen 20 she set the basket in the moot-post’s finger’s width of shade where no slate lay, stood half a pace off through the reading and the bell and carried him home at the going of the light saying nothing. The keeping at the fold was found where put and stayed a finding; no second fold, third crust, name or payment. No new scar or possession, no change of voice, nothing paid, forgiven, named or ended; forward, not closed.

\textbf{Ch 120 (Days 411–413, Ilmen 17–19).} Keeper of the fire through three more ordinary tending days lived one dated day at a time, with the old grammar unbroken at both ends of each: fire before basket, coals told the thaw and turned with a broken pot’s back, the twice-mended pot thumb-first with its hairline showing between staple and wire and both proverbs to pot and fire, dressed grain turned under wool with no figure or handful, pot rim two inches beyond the reaching hand, charcoal unread, widow’s mark untouched, seven openings in seven months and not a rule. She carried him down and up the nineteen steps at the half-pace, went wide around the seven walked-around places once and not twice, righted the fold without a second fold, and said nothing of the air that had turned on the nineteenth — she told the fire it was the thaw and did not tell the basket. Tarn spoke his sentence on the seventeenth, withheld it on the eighteenth and spoke it again on the nineteenth, and the loan stayed uncalled at the end of an ended term; Jorra’s unfinished sentence still arrived at the pot through the bent finger in the damper. No new scar or possession, no change of voice, nothing paid, forgiven, named or ended; forward, not closed.

\textbf{Ch 119 (Days 408–410, Ilmen 14–16).} Keeper of the fire and the house through three more ordinary tending days lived one dated day at a time, with the old grammar unbroken at both ends of each: fire before basket, coals told it was the thaw and turned with a broken pot’s back, the twice-mended pot thumb-first with its hairline showing between old-brass staple and tighter wire and both proverbs to pot and fire, dressed grain turned under wool with no figure or handful, the pot rim two inches beyond the reaching hand, the charcoal unread, the widow’s mark untouched, seven openings in seven months and not a rule. \textbf{Ch 118 (Days 405–407, Ilmen 11–13).} Keeper of the fire through three ordinary tending days lived one dated day at a time, with the old grammar unbroken at both ends of each: fire before basket, coals told the thaw and turned with the back of a broken pot, the twice-mended pot thumb-first with its hairline showing and both proverbs to pot and fire, dressed grain turned under wool with no figure or handful, the pot rim two inches beyond the reaching hand, the charcoal unread, the widow’s mark untouched, seven opened in seven months and not a rule. She carried him down and up the nineteen steps at the half-pace, went wide around the seven walked-around places once and not twice, righted the fold without a second fold, and said nothing of the word that came up at the well on Ilmen 12. The keeping at the fold was found where put and stayed a finding; no second fold, third crust, name or payment. Forward, not closed. \textbf{Ch 117 (Days 402–404, Ilmen 8–10).} Keeper of the fire through two ordinary tending days and the year’s first Account-day, three dated days lived one at a time with the old grammar unbroken: fire before basket, coals told the thaw, the twice-mended pot thumb-first with its hairline showing and both proverbs to pot and fire, grain covered and unfigured, the half-beat at setting, the charcoal unread, the widow’s mark untouched, seven opened in seven months and not a rule. On Ilmen 10 she set the basket in the moot-post’s thin shade where no slate lay, stood half a pace off through the reading and the bell and carried him home saying nothing; the arithmetic that began again up the road did not come under the roof as sign, lesson, mending, cause, payment or payer. The keeping at the fold was found where put and stayed a finding; no second fold, third crust, name or payment. Forward, not closed. \textbf{Ch 116 (Days 399–401, Ilmen 5–7).} Keeper of the fire through the new year’s first working week, three dated days lived one at a time with the old grammar unbroken: fire before basket at both ends, coals told the thaw and turned with a broken pot’s back, the twice-mended pot lifted thumb-first with the hairline showing and both proverbs to pot and fire, the dressed grain turned under wool with a touch lighter than a woman would use on a sleeping child and \emph{Lie down. You’ll keep better there}, the pot rim set two inches beyond the reaching hand with a half-beat and no look toward the bed, the charcoal unread, the widow’s mark untouched, the seven walked-around places once and not twice. She carried the boy down and up at the half-pace and set him under the roof and never in the Debt Loft, put the fold right at his ear and under his chin without a look at his face and added no second fold; the wool was found where put on all three mornings and goings of the light and stayed a finding (T097/T060/T086 advanced, not paid). On Ilmen 6 she gave the men unnamed in the back room no name and the man from Slate Row at the yard’s edge no word, no loaf passing, no slate shown; her silence left the promise under the shed ungiven and Tarn’s ended term uncalled, and the boy filed the waiting on its own tray and made no cause of it (T035/T031/T080, T036/T076/T006 advanced, not paid). Garl stayed in his objects with his name unspoken 399, 400 and 401 days, the fire’s fifth unpaid the same number. No new scar or possession, no change of voice, nothing paid, forgiven, named or ended; forward, not closed.

\textbf{Ch 115 (Days 396–398, Ilmen 2–4).} The turned year is taken up as an ordinary week: the house goes back to its grammar, the fire is fed before the basket, the coals are told it is the thaw, and the pot rim is set two inches beyond the reaching hand with a half-beat and no look toward the bed. A wrong wind off High Kiln brings the sweet edge of lead glaze over the boards on Ilmen 3 and takes it out again; a fist opens toward the pail and closes empty; word comes up of a runner going up the clay road with the writing turned to her sleeve and unread, and of the soft-cuffed clerk still set below the north bridge at the out-of-line landing with his slate turned inward for a measure nobody called. She does not go near the landing or make a door of it, and no slate is opened within reach of the basket. Count \textbf{398 exact}, six months and two hundred and eighteen days told by nobody, \textbf{372 honest answers} on the sixth place; twelve arithmetics of Y.H. 813 remain behind one unsigned figure and Ilmen 10’s first arithmetic waits six mornings off as a reset and not a signing. The keeping at the fold is found where put and stays a finding; Tarn’s term ends with the loan uncalled and Jorra’s promise is neither given nor withdrawn; Garl stays in objects with her kept ridge unswept, his name unspoken 396, 397 and 398 days and the carried fire’s fifth unpaid the same number. No rank, power, growth or ending. Forward, not closed.

\textbf{Ch 114 (Days 393–395, the Remembering–Ilmen 1).} The keeper of the Vail fire carries the last two of the Five and the turn of a year in the same grammar in which she kept all that went before: fire before basket, coals told the thaw and turned with a broken pot’s back, \emph{The house will keep it}, the half-pace from every open slate, the pot lifted thumb-first with the crack showing, the grain covered and unfigured, the pot rim two inches beyond the reaching hand with a half-beat, the charcoal unread and the widow’s mark untouched. On the Remembering she carries him to House Silt on an errand and neither opens the tin above the empty bed nor names the woman who lay there; the names of the dead go up the yard and she does not say the one that matters. On the Last Day she bakes bread, leaves the grey in the corners and will not say \emph{dealt with} after a neighbour calls the burning of it dealt with; on Ilmen 1 the yard burns its grey and she still says nothing, keeping the called-gone on its own place beside the left-in-place ridge. Her hand puts the fold right at his ear and under his chin at each going of the light and adds no second fold; the wool is found where she put it on the three mornings and goings and stays a finding, not a habit, way or payment. Twelve arithmetics of Y.H. 813 stand behind one unsigned figure and the year turns with nothing signed, and neither buys a teaching under this roof; the carried fire’s fifth stays unpaid and Garl’s name unspoken 393, 394 and 395 days. No change of voice, no new scar or possession; she has still not said whose child he is, and the house goes on as a house goes when a pot is set down in its place and the fire kept.

\textbf{Ch 113 (Days 390–392, Kindling–the Long Night).} The keeper of the Vail fire keeps the first three of the Five in the same grammar in which she kept the year: fire before basket, coals told the thaw and turned with a broken pot’s back, \emph{The house will keep it}, the half-pace from every open slate, the pot lifted thumb-first with the crack showing, the grain covered and unfigured, the pot rim two inches beyond the reaching hand with a half-beat, the charcoal unread and the widow’s mark untouched because a holy day is not an opening and seven openings in seven months are seven and not a rule with no eighth made due. On Kindling she sets the basket at the edge of the light two doors down while a collector takes the year’s first measure and says nothing of it afterward; on Weighing she carries him past the clean voice’s name in the yard without repeating it; on the Long Night she banks the coals early, turns them with the broken pot’s back, leaves no fire after dusk and sits in the dark with her hands in her lap and not still. Her hand puts the fold right at his ear and under his chin at each going of the light and adds no second fold; the wool is found where she put it on the three mornings and goings and stays a finding, not a habit, way or payment. The year’s fire comes up the Clay Yard from a source nobody names or prices; twelve arithmetics stand behind one unsigned figure and buy no teaching under this roof; the carried fire’s fifth stays unpaid and Garl’s name unspoken 390, 391 and 392 days. No change of voice, no new scar or possession; she has still not said whose child he is and the Five are not over.

\textbf{Ch 112 (Days 387–389, Stone 28–30).} The keeper of the Vail fire carries the year out in the same grammar in which she kept it: fire before basket, coals told the thaw and turned with a broken pot’s back, \emph{The house will keep it}, the half-pace from every open slate, the pot lifted thumb-first with the crack showing, the grain covered and unfigured, the pot rim two inches beyond the reaching hand, the charcoal unread and the widow’s mark untouched because seven openings in seven months are seven and not a rule and no eighth is made due. On the last Account-day she sets the basket in the moot-post’s finger’s width of shade and stands half a pace off through Berr’s twice-read figure and the bell, and carries him home saying nothing of what was read over the wicker. Her hand puts the fold right at his ear and under his chin at each going of the light and adds no second fold; the wool is found where she put it on the three mornings and goings and stays a finding, not a habit, way or payment. Twelve arithmetics stand behind one unsigned figure and buy no teaching under this roof; the carried fire’s fifth stays unpaid and Garl’s name unspoken 387, 388 and 389 days. No change of voice, no new scar or possession; she has still not said whose child he is, and the year ends without a boundary drawn.

\textbf{Ch 111.} Through Stone 25, 26 and 27 she keeps the Vail fire and the Vail house in the old grammar, and the year’s last working week brings no lesson under the roof. Fire before basket at both ends of every day, coals told the thaw and turned with the broken pot’s back, \emph{The house will keep it}, intake, hold and letting-go toward no opening with neither gap figured, finger on the shelf with the charcoal unread, lips on a two-gapped row, one glance at the clay jar with the hand half over nothing and the little-door burn closing on air, the twice-mended pot lifted thumb-first where the wire crosses the crack with both proverbs to pot and fire, dressed grain turned under wool with no figure or handful, pot rim two inches beyond the reaching hand with a half-beat and no look toward the bed. She carries him down and up the nineteen steps at the half-pace, gives the instruction to the wool, the river wind and the fire and never to the basket, goes wide around the seven walked-around places, and at each going of the light sets him on his bed under the roof and never in the Debt Loft. \textbf{The keeping, advanced and NOT paid (T097/T060/T086):} at each setting she puts the fold right at his ear and under his chin without a look at his face and adds no second fold; the wool is found folded once where she put it on the fifteenth on the tenth, eleventh and twelfth mornings and at the tenth, eleventh and twelfth goings of the light, with no third crust, no name, no gift, no payment and no payer, and twelve findings add no twelfth placing. \textbf{The widow’s mark was not touched on any of the three days} — seven openings in seven months are seven and not a rule and no eighth is made due. Eleven arithmetics stand behind one unsigned figure with no doctrine out of eleven; Garl’s name is unspoken 384, 385 and 386 days with the carried fire’s fifth unpaid the same number; her hand rests the half-beat longer than the setting needed and she says nothing of where they have been. Forward, not closed.

\textbf{Ch 110.} Through Stone 22, 23 and 24 she keeps the Vail fire and the Vail house in the old grammar, and the last full working week of the year brings no lesson under the roof. Fire before basket at both ends of every day; coals told the thaw and turned with the back of a broken pot; \emph{The house will keep it}; a small intake, a hold and a letting-go toward no opening with neither gap figured; charcoal unread beneath her finger on top of the shelf; lips on a two-gapped row figuring neither gap; one glance at the clay jar under lead glaze with the hand half over nothing and the little-door burn closing on air; the twice-mended pot lifted thumb-first at the wire with the hairline showing and both proverbs to pot and fire; dressed grain turned under wool with no figure and no handful; pot rim two inches beyond the reaching hand with a half-beat and no look toward the bed. She carries him down and up the nineteen steps at the half-pace from every open slate, gives the instruction to the wool, the river wind and the fire and never to the basket, goes wide around the seven walked-around places with a look and no number, widest around the returning-line place and once and not twice, and at each going of the light sets him on his bed under the roof and never in the Debt Loft. \textbf{The keeping, advanced and NOT paid (T097/T060/T086):} at each setting she puts the fold right at his ear and under his chin without a look at his face and adds no second fold; the wool is found folded once where she put it on the fifteenth on the seventh, eighth and ninth mornings and at the seventh, eighth and ninth goings of the light, with no third crust, no name, no gift, no payment and no payer, not a joining of rooms, not a sixth held object, not a habit, way, sign, hearing, mending, cause or rule; nine findings add no ninth placing. \textbf{The widow’s mark was not touched on any of the three days} — a morning, a hearth, a shelf, a well, a rack, a yard, a going of the light and a bed are no openings — seven openings in seven months are seven and not a rule and no eighth is made due. Eleven arithmetics stand behind one unsigned figure with no doctrine out of eleven; the fourth ownerless direction over the boards on Stone 23 brought no teaching under this roof; the carried fire’s fifth is unpaid and Garl’s name unspoken 381, 382 and 383 days. In Chapter 1 she is a hand in a doorway and a shadow, not a speaking part. Woodsmoke and wet wool arrive ahead of her; then the burn shaped like a little door reaches for the heat at the child’s belly, finds none, hovers over the bundle and withdraws. In Chapter 2 she is inside the house for the first time on the page and is known by its objects before she is known by her words: the hollow seat, the salt coat, the Ash ridge a thumb and then two thumbs wide, the charred edge of a slate nobody picks up, the roll the house keeps and does not show. She announces the taking, is answered by her son, refuses the answer by getting quieter, and on the third day performs the taking with a hand that knows how much a thing will bear. She lays the boy on a bed and tells the fire what to do. In Chapter 3 she takes that keeping out of the house for the first time and into a market that explains him as a figure. She carries him in a basket, keeps her half-pace from every open slate, refuses to say whose house he is beyond \emph{the house}, refuses to answer Berr about the mark, and walks him home without a word about where they have been. The private roll and the Court’s slate are seen to be the same shape of account, both entering a child who has not agreed to either, and her little-door hand is at one end of it. She has not explained any of it. Her silence has stopped being a pause and become a wall, and the wall has acquired a second face in the district’s grammar of entered kindness. Through the middle tend of Grain she took the year’s first grain at the yard’s edge and set it near the hearth under wool with no figure, and went around the returning-line place with a look and no number, while the widow’s mark stayed untouched and the private roll unshown (T058/T079, T098 advanced and unpaid).

On Days 5 and 6 the keeping goes on without an entry. She touches the widow’s mark before the kiln on Stone 11 and at no other time, banks the coals with the back of a broken pot at dusk on Stone 12 and does not touch the mark then; she feeds the boy from her own dish and puts the fold right without looking at his face. She carries him to the Drawing and places the basket where he can see the work and cannot be part of it, never where a slate lies open, and stands a half-pace off with her little-door burn shut on nothing, refusing by her stillness to tell him what is being done. She says nothing about where they went, what was taken or from whom; when Jorra says \emph{the back room’s cold} she shifts the damper instead of answering. The wall has acquired a door she will not open and a room she will not enter, and the fire inside the rule of the mark goes on holding.

On Days 7, 8 and 9 the keeping goes on without an entry and adds no explanation. She opens the kiln under a hand that touches the mark and lets it go, feeds the foundling from the house’s dish and says \emph{the house} where another woman would say \emph{I}, and puts the fold right without looking at his face. She carries him down twice through the cold off the Slip Brook and sets him in the bridge’s shade on a patch no slate has reached, the same care she used at the edge of the light at the Drawing; she stands a half-pace from every open slate and buys eels without counting them with her fingers. At the bank she does not touch the mark, and at the end of Stone 15 she goes around the days to Kindling in the arrangement of loaves and bits and comes back to the same place twice, so that the number need never be said. The wall has grown a second face: it keeps out the woman at the eels, the crust in the fold, the cuff on the bridge and the count her son will not speak, and it keeps the boy warm without ever entering the warmth.

On Days 10 through 14 the keeping goes on without an entry and the shape of the number becomes a household’s whole arithmetic. The wall has acquired no door: it keeps out the neighbour with the slate, the clerk’s soft sentence, the figure at the moot and the number her son will not speak, and keeps the boy warm without ever entering the warmth.

On Days 15 through 24 the keeping takes the measure of a tend and a year. On Ilmen 11 she measures the clean dark line where the Vail Ash turned its corner against the ridge two doors down, lays one thumb in each and carries the knowledge back without saying which was which; she does not fetch a broom. On Days 48 through 54 the keeping takes the measure of seven more days of thaw and adds no explanation.
