Each dusk she sets him on his bed under the roof and not in the Debt Loft and puts the fold right without looking at his face. She stands a half-pace off while Alda writes and does not ask what was written, and says nothing about the payer of any warmth or about the woman dead sixteen mornings with no collector called. The wall has acquired no door: it keeps out the slack frame, the silence where an argument stood, the fifth note under a floorboard, the number that went from fist to mouth to shoulder, and the omission nobody will name.

On Days 55 through 60 the keeping takes the measure of the approach to Silt and the month named for what the river does, and adds no explanation. She tells the fire it is the thaw when a stranger at the well speaks of a sealed counting room and men dead of the breath, and she does not join the story to the kiln under her own roof; whatever she would put away she puts in the private roll nobody is shown, and there is nothing to put away. On Ilmen 27 she carries the basket three doors down into House Silt, sets it just inside the finger’s-width-open door at the edge of the light and away from any open slate, straightens a chipped cup and does nothing else; she stands a half-pace from Alda and the birth-slates and asks nothing. Her instruction goes to the fire, the wool and the bucket and never to the basket, and she says the house where another woman would say I. The stores go around in loaves and glances and a space at the row’s end that she does not call a number; the days to Silt are three, two, whatever the moot will say, and she gives the boy no figure. On Ilmen 29 she lays one thumb flat in the clean dark line where the Ash ridge turned and the same thumb in the ridge two doors down, a finger’s width wider, and fetches no broom for either, while the yard prepares a sweeping done a month ago. At the last market she keeps the half-pace, sets the basket in the moot-post’s shade and carries him home at dusk. On Silt 1 she stands over a fresh hairline of grey beside the clean dark line with a broom in her hand and does not sweep, saying it is the thaw; the mark is touched before the kiln is opened and not for the grey, a basket or a bank, and the carried fire keeps four, four and a gap under blind ash. The wall has acquired no door: it keeps out the Greybank story, the new grey, the withheld number, the sixth note that was not written and the woman dead twenty-two mornings with no collector called.

On Days 61 through 67 the keeping takes the measure of a week in which the river rises and the district calls it weather, and adds no explanation. She gives every instruction to the fire, the wool and the bucket and never to the basket, says \emph{the house} where another woman would say \emph{I}, and keeps the half-pace from every open slate at the racks, the Fishstairs, three doors down in House Silt and at the well. She tells the fire it is the thaw when the brook comes up clay-heavy and when the ice is honeyed all through, and the new hairline of grey in the Vail corner lies finer than the old clean dark line and is not swept because the house says it is the thaw. There is no opening in any of the seven days, so the widow’s mark is not touched once, not at a rack, a well, a door or a basket. In House Silt she stands a half-pace off while Alda lays the slates writing-down and writes what she will not leave lying, and asks nothing; the arrangement between the two women holds without a word, a wall with a door neither opens. Each dusk she carries him up at a half-pace, sets him on his bed under the roof and not in the Debt Loft, and puts the fold right without looking at his face. The private roll stays unshown, she has not written him as Vail, and the higher water has given her nobody to answer. The wall has acquired no door: it keeps out the sixth page, the gone stone, the second cord, the clerk’s slate and the rising river, and keeps the boy warm without ever entering the warmth.

On Days 68 through 74 the keeping takes the measure of a flood that comes up around everything the house has left where it lies and then goes down again, and adds no explanation. She carries him to the edge of the thin brown sheet and back at the half-pace, says \emph{the house}, gives every instruction to the fire, the wool and the bucket and never to the basket, and tells the fire it is the thaw when a neighbour says the house was saved. The Ilm comes up over the Fishstairs, stands on the second step at the Cross on Account-day, and goes around both the clean dark line at the Vail corner and the burned line two doors down; she stands over the standing line and the new finer grey with a broom and sweeps neither, and gives the broom its instruction before anybody. No opening comes in seven days and the widow’s mark is not touched once. On Silt 13 she carries him three doors down and back with the door a finger’s width open and no slate opened, and asks nothing about the sixth page or the tin; the arrangement with Alda holds without a word. She does not go down to the child in the yard whose foot stays cold, though it is told of her that she once sat three nights with a child of her own who cooled while everyone was kind, and the boy does not lay the two together. At dusk of the last day she sets him on his bed under the roof and not in the Debt Loft, puts the fold right without looking at his face, and leaves the thread at his mouth frozen and unwiped. The wall has acquired no door: it keeps out the flood, the cold foot, the two lines and the empty place beside the one crust, and keeps the boy warm without ever entering the warmth.

On Days 75 through 77 the keeping takes the measure of a recovery that is another kind of avoidance. The yard sweeps around what the water left and calls the new grey thaw, and she stands over both lines with a broom and sweeps neither; a figure goes from fist to mouth to shoulder and arrives nowhere, and she answers a woman who wants it by sending her to the pot. A warm loaf passes from a man from Slate Row into a foundling’s pocket with no slate between them, and she neither looks nor connects the two. The half-pace, the unentered basket, the untouched mark and the private roll all hold exactly as they held before the flood; the wall has acquired no door, and the boy is still not written as Vail.

On Days 78 through 84 the keeping takes the measure of a lean week that changes nothing and adds no explanation. The flood has gone into mud that sets into a brown skin over the ruts, and she gives the broom its instruction before she gives it to anybody: go around what the water left, the clean dark line at the Vail corner, the new finer grey beside it and the space under the lowest rack, because it cost enough to come in and will cost more to take out. She sweeps none of them. The house keeps its number in loaves moved along a shelf, glances at the clay jar and a space at the row’s end nobody calls a figure, while she says \emph{the house}, sends every instruction to the fire, the wool, the bucket and the broom, and never to the basket. Three doors down she sets the basket at the edge of the light away from any open slate and stands a half-pace from Alda’s writing; at the well she goes wide around a slate set out to dry and does not touch the mark. When a second man come downriver from Greybank tells the bucket-round of a counting room shut in the war with the men inside dead of the breath, she tells the fire it is the thaw and lets it lie, joining nothing to her roof. No opening comes in seven days and the mark hangs where it hangs. The wall has acquired no door: it keeps out the second telling, the thinner crowd, the gone board, the cold foot and the empty place, and keeps the boy warm without ever entering the warmth.

On Days 85 through 90 the keeping takes the measure of a month turning on the same mud it came in on, and adds no explanation. The boy is eighty-five through ninety days old, three months at the close, and she carries him at the half-pace from every open slate to the yard, the well, the racks, House Silt, the Fishstairs, the Cross and the moot-post’s shade, setting him on his bed under the roof each dusk and never in the Debt Loft. On Silt 26 and Seed 1 she gives the broom its instruction before she gives it to anybody --- go around what the water left, it cost enough to come in, it will cost more to take out --- stands over the clean dark line, the new finer grey and the space under the lowest rack, and sweeps none of them; when a woman asks what the month will cost she moves her lips along the loaf shelf, glances at the clay jar and tells her to ask the pot. Every instruction goes to the fire, the wool, the bucket and the broom and never to the basket; she says the house where another woman would say I. When the second telling of the shut counting room goes over the bucket she tells the fire it is the thaw and joins nothing to her roof, though she lost a husband to that danger and has never once described it that way herself. Three doors down she sets the basket just inside the finger’s-width-open door at the edge of the light away from every open slate, stands a half-pace off while Alda presses the fold too long and writes what she will not show, and asks nothing. On Silt 30 she sets him in the moot-post’s thin shade with cold iron at his cheek while Berr reads one in twelve over fewer bodies and takes himself out of his own sentence, and carries him home saying nothing about what was read over him. No opening came in six days and a month’s turning is not an opening, so the widow’s mark hung where it hung; the private roll stayed unshown and she has not said whose child he is. At the turn into Seed the first work is sweeping and the work after it lies east of Low Kiln in strips she has not gone to see. The wall has acquired no door: it keeps out the second telling, the thinner crowd, the out-of-line landing, the foundling’s half-beat, the turned slate, the cold foot and the unnamed empty place, and keeps the boy warm without ever entering the warmth.

Through Days 91–93 the keeping takes the measure of the first planting week and adds no explanation. The house’s work moves east of Low Kiln into strips she goes around with a broom and a look, and her rule holds exactly: every instruction to the fire, the wool, the bucket and the broom and never to the basket, \emph{the house} where another woman would say \emph{I}, the half-pace from every open slate at the well, the strips, House Silt and the Fishstairs. On Seed 2 she gives the broom its instruction before anybody, goes around the clean dark line, the new finer grey called thaw and the space under the lowest rack, sweeps none of them, and at the well sends a woman asking the planting cost to the pot with \emph{the house has said it}, leaving the empty place at the row’s end with no figure. She tells the fire it is the thaw each day and turns the coals with the back of a broken pot; its payer has gone unnamed for ninety-three days. No opening came in three days --- not a strip, a broom, a basket, a well, a market, a door or a bed --- so the widow’s mark hung where it hangs; she has lost a husband to that danger and has never described it that way herself. Three doors down she sets the basket just inside the finger’s-width-open door at the edge of the light, away from every open slate, opens none and turns no errand into a walk to Slate Row, standing a half-pace off while Alda presses the fold too long and writes what she will not show. Jorra’s dust and the damper ahead of her sentence, Tarn’s six counted and seventh held, Mira’s cords, Berr’s box and Alda’s tin all stay as they were. At dusk she sets him on his bed under the roof and not in the Debt Loft, puts the fold right without looking at his face and leaves the thread frozen; the private roll stays unshown and she has not said whose child he is. The wall has acquired no door.

Through Days 94 through 100 the keeping takes the measure of a planting month that has become waiting and adds no explanation. The house’s arithmetic is now two empty places on the loaf shelf --- the old space at the row’s end nobody calls a number and a new gap that came in the night of Seed 5 --- and she moves her lips along the row, glances at the clay jar, gives the instruction to the pot, the fire, the wool, the bucket and the broom and never to the basket, and says \emph{the house} where another woman would say \emph{I}. To a woman at the well she says ask the pot what a wet thing costs set down there, because \emph{the house has said it}, and leaves the space at the row’s end with no figure. She goes around the brown skin holding a boot-print, the clean dark line, the new finer grey called thaw and the space under the lowest rack with a broom and a glance and sweeps none of them, telling the fire it is the thaw each day and turning the coals with the back of a broken pot. The carried fire’s payer has gone unnamed for a hundred days and the coal the gull took is entered in no slate. No opening came in seven days --- a strip, a shelf, a basket, a well, a market, a door and a bed are not openings --- so the widow’s mark stayed where it hung; she lost a husband to that danger and has never described it that way herself. Three doors down she set the basket just inside the finger’s-width-open door at the edge of the light, away from every open slate, opened none and stood a half-pace off while Alda pressed the fold too long. At the going of the light on Day 100 she set the boy on his bed under the roof and not in the Debt Loft, put the fold right at his ear and under his chin without looking at his face and left the thread frozen and unwiped; the river’s note came through the finger’s-width-open door and the fire’s four, four and a gap through the floor, in two separate places as for a hundred days. The private roll stayed unshown, she has not written him as Vail, and nothing was joined, paid, explained or ended. No new scar, possession or change of voice.

Through Days 101 through 103 the keeping takes the measure of a planting month that has become three ordinary days of two absences nobody joins. A neighbour at the loaf shelf reaches past the bare board, names the row’s old space as a thing the planting brought in and the empty place at the boy’s ear as a child’s appetite in one breath, takes her loaf and goes with her pot; Sella moves her lips along the row, glances at the clay jar and leaves both gaps with no figure, and does not hear the two places as one. On Seed 13 she agrees with the early thaw and the late and keeps wanting the late because it puts off the paying; Jorra’s bent finger goes into the damper ahead of her unfinished sentence and the household straightens around his silence, and a neighbour at the bucket-round only mentions a room shut in the war with men dead of the breath, which she answers by telling the fire it is the thaw and joining nothing to her roof. On Seed 14 she sets the basket at the end of the fish-trade shade where no slate lies and then three doors down just inside a finger’s-width-open door, opens no slate and turns no errand into a walk to Slate Row, and asks nothing about the writing, the tin or the fold pressed too long. Every instruction goes to the fire, the wool, the water, the pot and the broom and never to the basket; she says \emph{the house} where another woman would say \emph{I}, tells the fire the thaw each day and turns the coals with the back of a broken pot. No opening came in three days, so the widow’s mark hung where it hung; the carried fire’s payer has gone unnamed for a hundred and three days and the two lines in the corner stayed unswept. At dusk each day she set him on his bed under the roof and not in the Debt Loft, put the fold right without looking at his face and left the thread frozen, carrying one crust and its unnamed empty place and two shelf gaps in another room that does not touch it. The private roll stayed unshown, she has not written him as Vail, and the wall has acquired no door.

On Days 104 through 106 the keeping takes the measure of the hands going into the strips and adds no explanation. The boy is one hundred and four, then one hundred and five, then one hundred and six days old and nobody under the roof says so. She gives the instruction to the broom and the bucket before anybody and never to the basket, says \emph{the house}, keeps the half-pace from every open slate at the strips, the loaf shelf, the wheel-shed, the well, the Fishstairs and three doors down in House Silt, and goes around the clean dark line, the new finer grey called the thaw and the space under the lowest rack without sweeping any of them. At the loaf shelf she hears a neighbour name the old gap and the boy’s empty place in one breath and leaves both gaps unfigured, hearing two sayings and not one absence; the T097 witness is advanced, not paid. She hears the yard want the thaw early and late, agrees with both and wants the late because it puts off the paying. Jorra’s dust and the damper ahead of her unfinished sentence and Tarn’s knife and seventh year go unremarked: the household still straightens around a silence the way cloth straightens when a weight is lifted. She tells the fire it is the thaw through all three days and turns the coals with the back of a broken pot, its payer unnamed for a hundred and six days; the fire keeps its four low pulls and the missing fifth, and the carried fire stays under blind ash and the back of a broken pot. No opening comes in three days --- a strip, a shelf, a rack, a well, a market, a door and a bed are not openings --- so the widow’s mark hangs where it hangs. Each dusk she sets the boy on his bed under the roof and not in the Debt Loft, puts the fold right without looking at his face and leaves the thread frozen. The wall has acquired no door: it keeps out the neighbour’s one-breath joining, the near-spoken number of hands, the men in the back room, the seventh year at the edge of the sill and the two empty places in rooms that do not touch, and keeps the boy warm without ever entering the warmth.

On Days 107 through 109 the keeping takes the measure of the planting month entering its last tend and an Account-day read over the worked strips, and adds no explanation. The boy is one hundred and seven, then one hundred and eight, then one hundred and nine days old and nobody under the roof says so. Every instruction goes to the broom, the bucket, the wool, the water, the pot and the fire and never to the basket; she says \emph{the house} where another woman would say \emph{I}, keeps the half-pace from every open slate at the well, the wheel-shed, the loaf shelf, the Fishstairs, the Cross, the moot-post’s shade and three doors down, and goes around the clean dark line, the new finer grey called thaw and the space under the lowest rack without sweeping any of them. At the loaf shelf she hears a neighbour name the row’s old gap as a thing the planting brought in and go off with her pot without seeing the empty place at his ear, and hears a second say it two days later; she leaves both gaps unfigured, hearing two sayings and not one absence, and the T097 witness advances toward the far-off finger without being paid. She gives the instruction to the broom before she gives it to anybody, and Tarn takes it only then and sweeps the collector’s road without turning along it while his seventh year lies at the very edge of the sill and his breath stays unspent. On Seed 19 men unnamed come before first grey and Jorra’s bent finger goes into the damper ahead of her unfinished sentence; she gives the end of it to the pot and the household straightens around his silence, and she gives the house no name for the men. She tells the fire it is the thaw on all three days and turns the coals with the back of a broken pot, its payer unnamed for a hundred and nine days; at the fire she counts something under her breath and pushes a strand of coal-black hair back with the burn-wrist, and the grey streak at her temple shows pale. No opening comes in three days — a strip, a shelf, a rack, a wheel-shed, a market, a reading, a door and a bed are not openings — so the widow’s mark hangs where it hangs and the private roll stays unshown. Each dusk she sets him on his bed under the roof and not in the Debt Loft, puts the fold right without looking at his face and leaves the thread frozen; one brown-edged crust lies stiff in the fold with its empty place unnamed and the shelf keeps two gaps in a room that does not touch it. The wall has acquired no door: it keeps out the neighbour’s one-breath joinings, the men in the back room, the seventh year at the edge of the sill and the two empty places in rooms that do not touch.

On Days 110 through 112 the keeping takes the measure of the planting month’s last tend and adds no explanation. She carries him at the half-pace from every open slate to the worked strips, the loaf shelf, the wheel-shed, the yard well, the Fishstairs and three doors down, setting him on his bed under the roof each dusk and never in the Debt Loft. Every instruction goes to the bucket, the broom, the wool, the water, the pot and the fire and never to the basket; she says \emph{the house}, moves her lips along a loaf row standing with two gaps, glances at the clay jar and gives nobody a figure, and leaves a neighbour’s one-breath joining unjoined and the widow’s mark untouched, because a shelf, a strip, a rack, a well, a market, a post, a road, a door, a basket and a bed are not openings. At the well she sends a woman asking the planting’s cost to the pot with \emph{the house has said it}; at the fire she tells it the thaw, turns the coals with the back of a broken pot and feeds them, says \emph{The house will keep it} where another woman would say \emph{I}, and stands a moment counting under her breath toward no opening with the grey streak pale at her temple, pushing a strand of coal-black hair back with the burn-wrist and not looking toward the bed. On Seed 22 men unnamed come before first grey and Jorra’s bent finger goes into the damper ahead of her unfinished sentence, the household straightening around his silence; the debt’s broom checks half a beat behind the wheel-keeper’s finger and goes on, and she asks nothing about either. Three doors down she stands a half-pace off while Alda writes what she will not show and asks nothing about the writing, the tin or the date over a dead woman’s sign. No opening came in three days, the private roll stayed unshown, she has not written him as Vail, and the wall has acquired no door: it keeps out the third shaping of the shelf’s absence, the first small change in the two silences under the roof, the fist that would not give its number and the two empty places in rooms that do not touch, and keeps the boy warm without ever entering the warmth.

Through Days 113 through 115 the keeping takes the measure of the planting’s last tend and adds no explanation. She carries him at the half-pace from every open slate to the loaf shelf, the worked strips, the wheel-shed, the yard well, the Fishstairs, the Cross and three doors down in House Silt, setting him on his bed under the roof and not in the Debt Loft at the going of the light and leaving the thread frozen and unwiped. Every instruction goes to the bucket, the broom, the pot, the wool, the water and the fire and never to the basket; she says \emph{the house}, moves her lips along a loaf row standing with two gaps, glances at the clay jar cold under its glaze and gives nobody a figure, and sends a woman with wet sleeves to the pot with \emph{the house has said it}. She hears a neighbour lay the shelf’s old space and the empty place at his ear under one cause in a single breath and does not make the joining either, and the witness advances unpaid. At the fire she tells it the thaw, turns the coals with the back of a broken pot, feeds them and says \emph{The house will keep it}, standing a moment with the back of the pot in her hand counting under her breath toward no opening, her grey streak pale in the dying light, and not looking toward the bed. On Seed 25 men unnamed come before first grey and Jorra’s bent finger goes into the damper ahead of her unfinished sentence; the household straightens around his silence and the debt’s broom goes on over the flagstones without the check it made the day before, the stones keeping the stopped place, and she asks nothing about either. No opening comes in three days, the widow’s mark hangs untouched, the private roll stays unshown, and she has not said whose child he is. The wall has acquired no door: it keeps out the neighbour’s one-breath joining, the fist that would not give its figure, the moved equality under the roof, the two shelf gaps and the empty place in the fold, and keeps the boy warm without ever entering the warmth.

On Days 116 through 119 the keeping takes the measure of the planting’s end and crosses into Reed without an entry. She carried him to the very edge of the worked strips and stood a half-pace from every open slate with the basket held level, giving the instruction to the wool and the river wind and never to the basket, saying \emph{the house} where another woman would say \emph{I}; the last hands came out of the strips and one place in the line was gone around with a look and no figure, and she went around it as wide as a pail of hot water set where a child might knock it, entering nothing. Back under the roof she gave the bucket, broom, pot and fire their instructions before anybody and never the basket, moved her lips along a loaf row standing with two gaps and gave nobody a figure, glanced once at the clay jar cold under its glaze and did not touch the widow’s mark, because a shelf is not an opening. At the well and in the yard she sent women asking the planting’s cost to the pot with \emph{Ask the pot what a wet thing costs set down there. The house has said it.} On all four days she told the fire it was the thaw, turned the coals with the back of a broken pot, fed them and said \emph{The house will keep it}; she stood a moment counting under her breath toward no opening, pushed a strand of coal-black hair back with the burn-wrist, the grey streak pale in the dying light, and did not look toward the bed. She carried him to the wheel-shed’s edge of light, the stalls beyond the Cross, the Fishstairs, House Silt and the moot-post’s shade, setting the basket where no slate lay and opening none. With Jorra men unnamed came before first grey and his bent finger went into the damper ahead of her unfinished sentence; she gave the end of it to the pot and asked nothing. With Tarn the exact account held and she did not ask about his seventh year or his ear. No opening came in four days, the mark hung where it hung, the private roll stayed unshown and the two shelf gaps and the fold’s gap stayed apart and unnamed. The wall has acquired no door: it keeps out the missing hand, the neighbours’ joinings, the green at a mouth, the clerk’s uncalled measure and a count nobody will say, and keeps the boy warm without ever entering the warmth.

Through Reed 1–3, Y.H. 813 the keeping takes the measure of a month turning toward the reed beds and adds no explanation. She carried him at the half-pace from every open slate to the Clay Yard, the worked strips’ edge, the stalls beyond the Cross, the road downriver, the Weir and under the roof, setting him on his bed under the roof and not in the Debt Loft each going of the light and putting the fold right without a look at his face, the thread left frozen and unwiped, her hand resting a half-beat longer than the setting needed. Every instruction went to the bucket, the broom, the pot, the fire, the wool and the river wind and never to the basket; she said \emph{the house} where another woman would say \emph{I}, sent a woman who asked what the reeds would cost to the pot with \emph{Ask the pot what a wet thing costs set down there. The house has said it}, and told a man who asked what the work would want to ask the river. She went around the clean dark line, the new finer grey called the thaw, the space beneath the lowest rack and the missing hand’s place in the strip as wide as a pail of hot water set where a child might knock it, entering none of them. At the loaf shelf she moved her lips along a row standing with two gaps, glanced once at the clay jar cold under its glaze and gave nobody a figure, and did not touch the widow’s mark, because a shelf, a strip, a rack, a market and a bed are not openings. On all three days she told the fire it was the thaw, turned the coals with the back of a broken pot, fed them and said \emph{The house will keep it}, standing a moment counting under her breath toward no opening, pushing a strand of coal-black hair back with the burn-wrist, the grey streak pale in the dying light, and not looking toward the bed. On Reed 2 men unnamed before first grey went low-voiced into the back room and Jorra’s bent finger went into the cold damper ahead of her unfinished sentence; she gave the end of it to the pot and asked nothing, and Tarn’s stroke went on without the half-check while the stones kept the place where it had stopped. No opening came in three days, the private roll stayed unshown and she has not said whose child he is; the fire’s missing fifth breath went unnamed for a hundred and twenty-two days and the two shelf gaps and the fold’s one crust stayed in rooms that do not touch. The wall has acquired no door.

On Days 123 through 125 the keeping takes the measure of the reed month’s first days and adds no explanation. She carries him at the half-pace from every open slate to the Clay Yard, the worked strips’ edge, the Weir and the stalls beyond the Cross, and each going of the light up the clay road and under the roof, setting him on his bed and not in the Debt Loft, putting the fold right without looking at his face and leaving the thread frozen. The instruction goes to the wool, the river wind, the bucket, the broom, the pot and the fire, and never to the basket; she says \emph{the house} where another woman would say \emph{I}, goes wide around the space beneath the lowest rack and the empty place in the strip, and sends a woman asking the reeds’ cost to the pot with \emph{the house has said it}. At the loaf shelf her lips move along a row standing with two gaps and she glances once at the clay jar cold under its glaze and gives nobody a figure; the two rooms do not touch and no neighbour names the gaps in these three days. On all three days she tells the fire it was the thaw, turns the coals with the back of a broken pot, feeds them and says \emph{The house will keep it}, standing a moment counting under her breath toward no opening and pushing a strand of coal-black hair back with the burn-wrist, the grey streak pale in the dying light. On Reed 5 men unnamed come before first grey and Jorra’s bent finger goes into the cold damper ahead of her unfinished sentence, so the end of it arrives at the pot and the household straightens around his silence; she asks nothing. She is within hearing on Reed 5 when Tarn’s sentence comes to the threshold of the word and goes back, and asks nothing, because a question said aloud becomes a thing a house must answer. Through all three days the carried fire keeps four, four and a gap with its payer unnamed for a hundred and twenty-five days, the river’s note comes through the finger’s-width-open door, the boards keep four nails, four and a knot, and the three counts do not become one. No opening came, the widow’s mark was not touched, and she has still not said whose child he is.

On Days 126 through 128 the keeping takes the measure of the first counted bundles of Reed and adds no explanation. She carries him at the half-pace from every open slate to the Clay Yard, the stalls beyond the Cross, the Weir, House Silt three doors down and back under the roof each going of the light, sets him on his bed and not in the Debt Loft, puts the fold right without a look at his face and leaves the thread frozen, her hand resting a half-beat longer than the setting before it goes away. At the yard the reeds stand green at the broken ends and pale at the tips; a woman who asks what they cost is sent to the pot with \emph{the house has said it}, a man who asks what the beds will want is given the weather, and the question arrives nowhere held level. She goes around the clean dark line, the new finer grey called the thaw, the space beneath the lowest rack and the place in the strip where a hand did not come back, entering none of them, and does not touch the widow’s mark at a rack, a strip, a well, a yard, a market, a road, a basket, a bed or a dusk. At the Cross she sets the basket in the moot-post’s shade and keeps a half-pace from every slate; at the Weir she goes around a propped slate and sets him at the edge of the work; three doors down she stands a half-pace off while Alda writes and asks nothing about the slates, the tin or the date. At the fire she tells it the thaw on all three days, turns the coals with the back of a broken pot, says \emph{The house will keep it}, counts under her breath toward no opening, pushes the coal-black hair back with the burn-wrist, the grey streak pale, sets the pot rim out and handle toward the reaching hand and does not look toward the bed. She hears Tarn’s sentence come a second time to the word that would call the loan and stop there, and asks nothing within hearing; Jorra’s dust, the unnamed men and the damper ahead of her unfinished sentence go unasked about. The wall has acquired no door: it keeps out the cost asked as a direction, the second stopping, the third green, the four unread records downriver and the lie curdling three doors down, and keeps the boy warm without ever entering the warmth.

The house has said it}, and the woman carried it away level with nothing slopped, priced, refused or entered (T077). \textbf{The chapter’s one meaningful change, paid small and non-fatally:} on Day 188, after a rack-worker’s pot gave its note before its time and sang itself out early with the woman going on with her hands and making no lesson of it, two men carried a glaze-room hand out of the kiln and across the yard toward the clay road, one with a thumb hooked under his arm to keep the head from lopping. She set the basket down at the yard’s edge, turned the boy’s face as she would turn a pot so the light fell where she wanted it, went wide around the place the carriers crossed, and gave the yard no name for what ailed him; nobody called a collector, gave a figure or opened a slate, and the cost stayed entered nowhere (T077 advanced, not paid). At the going of the light each day she carried him home up the clay road, woodsmoke before her in long low bars and river wind behind, and set him on his bed and not in the Debt Loft, base first and the weight settled as a woman sets a vessel that must not rock, the fold right at his ear and under his chin without a look at his face, the thread left frozen and unwiped. Her finger did not go beneath the front edge of the loaf shelf on any of the three days; the charcoal tally stayed unread, uncounted and uncopied (T100 carried). Her end of the instruction waited at the hearth on all three days while Jorra’s bent finger stood in the cold damper and the sentence reached the pot, the fraction a remembered holding and not a new change, not paired with the Day 166 shelf beat or the Day 171 flagstone half-check into a rule with a payer (T062). The wall has acquired no door: it keeps out the pale line at the gum, the sweet breath on the wrong wind, the cost carried up the road unentered, the two men’s passage across the yard and the number nobody says, and keeps the boy warm without ever entering the warmth.

On Days 189 through 191 she carries him at the half-pace from every open slate, gives the instruction to the wool, the fire, the pot, the broom, the running water and the river wind and never to the basket, says \emph{the house}, sets the pot handle two inches beyond the reaching hand, and leaves the widow’s mark where it hangs, because the one opening was before the kiln on Ember 1. On the first Account-day of Ember she sets the basket in the moot-post’s shade where no slate lies and stands half a pace off through the reading and the bell, giving no reason to the basket; on the two mornings after she sends women’s cost-questions to the pot and the weather and goes wide around the unswept places and the place the carriers crossed with a look and a wide step and no number. Her finger stays from beneath the loaf shelf and the charcoal stays unread. The fire’s payer goes unnamed for a hundred and eighty-nine, ninety and ninety-one days, and the cost of the man carried out on Day 188 is entered nowhere.

Through Days 192 through 194, Ember 13–15, Thirdday to Fifthday, the keeping takes the measure of three quiet days after the reading and adds no explanation. The boy is one hundred and ninety-two, then ninety-three, then ninety-four days old and nobody says so; the district keeps calling Tallow the firing month and Ember the kiln month and neither usage is corrected. Every instruction goes to the wool, the fire, the pot, the broom and the running water and never to the basket; she says \emph{the house} where another woman would say \emph{I}, keeps her half-pace from every open slate, glances once at the clay jar cold under its glaze without touching it, sets the pot handle two inches beyond the reaching hand with her hand resting a half-beat longer at the setting, feeds him barley gruel from the house’s own dish with two fingers behind his ear, wipes the spoon on her sleeve and does not wipe his mouth, tells the fire it was the thaw, turns the coals with the back of a broken pot, says \emph{The house will keep it}, stands with the back of the pot in her hand counting under her breath toward no opening — the small intake, the hold, the letting go — pushes coal-black hair back with the burn-wrist so the grey streak shows pale, and does not look toward the bed. The fire under the broken pot answers four low pulls and the silence where the fifth should have been, its payer unnamed for a hundred and ninety-two, ninety-three and ninety-four days. The widow’s mark hangs where it hung, untouched at every morning, shelf, well, rack, road, basket, yard, afternoon and dusk, because a quiet morning after a reading is not an opening and there has been no opening since before the kiln on Ember 1; nobody praised what it mended and nobody saw it broken. On all three days a cost-question goes to the pot and the weather with \emph{Ask the pot what a wet thing costs set down there. The house has said it}, and goes away level with nothing slopped, priced, refused or entered (T077). She goes wide around the clean dark line, the new finer grey called the thaw, the space beneath the lowest rack with its broken birth-slates, the pan’s gone round ring, the bare dark trough whose water is called weather, the field’s empty place where a hand went in on Seed 15 and the place the carriers crossed, each with a look and a wide step and no number (T009/T013/T092/T098). When her instruction goes low and unfinished at the hearth, Jorra’s bent finger stands in the cold damper until the sentence reaches the pot, then moves the tongue a hair’s breadth and is left standing — a remembered repetition and not a change made again (T062). Men unnamed go low into the back room before first grey and she gives them no name and does not say the room is cold, and the two shut-room tellings stay two with no third (T035/T031/T065/T095). Her finger stays from beneath the front edge of the loaf shelf on all three days, so the charcoal tally stays unread, uncounted and uncopied (T100), and the stone in its pot in the loft stays cold and unreconciled without her speaking of it (T006). At the going of each light she carries him home up the clay road, woodsmoke before her in long low bars and river wind behind with the taste of water over water, sets him on his bed under the roof and not in the Debt Loft, base first and the weight settled the way a woman sets a vessel that must not rock, puts the fold right at his ear and under his chin without once looking at his face, leaves the thread frozen and unwiped, tells the fire it was the thaw, banks the coals with the back of a broken pot and does not touch the mark, because a dusk is not an opening; the two rooms do not touch — hers holds a pot, a fire and a woman counting toward nothing entered, and his holds a crust two inches from an ear and an empty place beside it with no name. The counting under her breath at the fire, held as she sets down the pot and as she banks the coals, becomes the measure by which the boy holds his own inch in the small hours, though no word passes between the rooms and she is asleep when he does it. The private roll stays unshown and she has still not said whose child he is. No new scar or possession, no change of voice, no opening and no bond paid.

Through Days 195–197 (Ember 16–18) the keeping takes the measure of three more days of the kiln month’s second working week and adds no explanation. She gives every instruction to the wool, the fire, the pot, the broom and the running water and never to the basket, says \emph{the house}, keeps her half-pace from every open slate, glances once at the clay jar cold under its glaze without touching it, pushes coal-black hair back with the burn-wrist so the grey streak shows pale off the coals, sets the pot handle two inches beyond the reaching hand with her hand resting a half-beat longer at the setting, feeds him gruel from the house’s own dish with the spoon on her sleeve and his mouth not wiped, tells the fire it was the thaw, turns the coals with the back of a broken pot, says \emph{The house will keep it}, stands a moment counting under her breath toward no opening — small intake, hold, letting go — and does not look toward the bed. Cost-questions go to the pot and the weather on all three days and arrive level with nothing priced, refused or entered. The widow’s mark hangs where it hung, untouched at a morning, a shelf, a well, a rack, a road, a basket, an afternoon and a dusk, because there has been no opening since before the kiln on Ember 1; nobody praises what it mended and nobody sees it broken. Her finger stays from beneath the loaf shelf and the charcoal remains unread; at the hearth her unfinished sentence is allowed to finish at the pot behind Jorra’s standing finger as a remembered repetition, not a new change. She carries him home up the clay road at each going of the light, going wide around the unswept places and the carriers’ place, sets him on his bed and not in the Debt Loft, puts the fold right without a look at his face and leaves the thread frozen; the fire’s payer is unnamed for a hundred and ninety-five, ninety-six and ninety-seven days.

Through Days 198–203 (Ember 19–24) the keeping takes the measure of the second reading and the kiln month’s last tend and adds no explanation. On Day 199 she carried him to the Cross at the half-pace, set the basket in the moot-post’s shade where no slate lay and stood half a pace off through Berr’s twice-read figure and the bell, giving no instruction or reason to the basket and keeping her hand off the mark because a reading is not an opening; the box went up the locked road with the true subtraction inside and the printed figure standing. Through Days 201–203 she gave every instruction to the wool, fire, pot, broom, running water and river wind and never the basket, said \emph{the house}, kept her half-pace, glanced once at the clay jar without a touch, pushed coal-black hair back with the burn-wrist so the grey streak showed pale, set the pot handle two inches beyond his hand with the half-beat at setting, fed him from the house’s own dish with the spoon on her sleeve and his mouth unwiped, moved her lips along a row with two unnamed gaps and gave nobody a figure, kept her finger from beneath the charcoal, told the fire it was the thaw, turned the coals with the back of a broken pot, said \emph{The house will keep it}, and counted under her breath toward no opening — small intake, hold, letting go. Cost-questions went to the pot and the weather on all three days and went away level. The widow’s mark hung where it hung, touched once before the kiln on Ember 1 and at no other hour, because no morning, shelf, market, road, yard, basket, afternoon or dusk was an opening. She carried him home around the pan’s gone ring with a wide step and no number, set him on his bed and not in the Debt Loft, put the fold right without a look at his face, left the thread frozen and went to her own bed. The fire’s payer was unnamed for two hundred and one, two and three days; at the hearth her unfinished sentence was allowed to finish at the pot behind Jorra’s remembered finger and she asked nothing of the men who went low into the back room.

Through Days 204–206 (Ember 25–27) the keeping takes the measure of the kiln month’s last working week and turns nothing into a story. She comes to the fire before the basket on all three mornings and gives the instruction to the wool, the fire, the pot, the broom, the running water and the river wind and never to the basket; she says \emph{the house} and \emph{The house will keep it}, keeps her half-pace from every open slate, glances once at the clay jar cold under its glaze without touching it, shuts her hand half over nothing without a touch, feeds him from the house’s own dish with the spoon on her sleeve and his mouth unwiped, moves her lips along a row standing with two unnamed gaps and gives nobody a figure, keeps her finger from beneath the loaf shelf so the charcoal stays unread, tells the fire it was the thaw, turns the coals with the back of a broken pot, stands counting under her breath toward no opening — small intake, hold, letting go — pushes coal-black hair back with the burn-wrist so the grey streak shows pale, sets the pot handle two inches beyond the reaching hand with a half-beat at the setting and does not look toward the bed. The fire answers four low pulls with the fifth missing under the floor, its payer unnamed for two hundred and four, five and six days; the river keeps its note through the finger’s-width door and the boards keep four nails, four and a knot, three counts in three places that do not become one. Cost-questions go to the pot and the weather and away level, nothing priced, refused or entered. The widow’s mark hangs where it hung, touched once before the kiln on Ember 1 and at no hour since, because no morning, shelf, yard or dusk is an opening and there has been no opening in twenty-six days. She hears the burned-slate word go around the boards and makes nothing of it; her unfinished sentence still finishes at the pot behind Jorra’s remembered finger. She carries him home around the absences with a wide step and no number, sets him on his bed and not in the Debt Loft, puts the fold right without looking at his face, leaves the thread frozen and goes to her own bed before the last small hours. The house keeps Garl in objects, not in a story, and no collector is called. Forward, not closed.

\textbf{Ch 52.} Through Days 207–209, the last working week of the kiln month, the house is kept in the same grammar: instruction to the fire, the wool, the pot, the broom and the river wind and never to the basket, \emph{the house} where another woman would say \emph{I}, the half-pace from every open slate, the pot handle set two inches beyond the reaching hand with a half-beat and no look toward the bed, her lips moving along a row with two unnamed gaps and nobody given a figure, her finger kept on top of the shelf’s front edge so the charcoal stays unread, and the widow’s mark hanging where it hung since the opening before the kiln on Ember 1 — no opening in twenty-nine days, at a shelf, a well, a market, a road, a basket, an afternoon or a dusk. She tells the fire the thaw, turns the coals with the back of a broken pot, says \emph{The house will keep it}, counts under her breath toward no opening, pushes coal-black hair back with the burn-wrist so the grey streak shows pale, sends cost-questions to the pot and the weather with nothing priced, refused or entered, and goes wide around the pan’s gone ring, the bare dark trough, the rack space, the field’s empty place and the place the carriers crossed with a look and no number. Garl is kept to the very last day in objects and not in a story — salt coat holding a broader man’s shape, hollow seat with its leftward lean, clean dark line and finer grey unswept, proverb gone to the pot, debt against the tiles uncalled and worse for being uncalled — no lesson made, no collector called, his name unspoken for two hundred and nine days. On Day 209 she carries him down to the Cross, sets the basket in the moot-post’s finger’s width of shade where no slate lay, stands half a pace off through Berr’s third reading and the bell’s four, four and a gap, gives no instruction or reason to the basket and carries him home at the going of the light saying nothing of what was read over him. The fire answers four low pulls with the fifth missing and its payer unnamed for two hundred and seven, eight and nine days while the river keeps its note through the door and the boards keep their knot — three counts in three places that do not become one. Her unfinished sentence at the hearth is allowed to finish at the pot behind Jorra’s bent finger as a remembered repetition; the two silences stay unjoined and Ember goes out without a boundary drawn.

\textbf{Ch 53.} Through Days 210–212, Grain 1–3, the house keeps the turning of the month the way it keeps the fire: without a boundary drawn, without a figure spoken and without correcting either of the district’s two names for the months. Ember thins into the ordinary tending of a year begun and the yard goes around its left places — the clean dark line and the finer grey called the thaw, the rack space under the lowest rack with its broken birth-slates, the pan’s gone round ring, the bare trough whose water is called weather, the field’s empty place and the place the carriers crossed — with a look and a wide step and no number. Garl is kept in objects and not in a story: the salt coat holds a broader man’s shape, the seat its hollow and leftward lean, the proverb has gone to the pot and the debt against the tiles is circled without a name, worse for being uncalled, with no lesson made and no collector called and his name unspoken for two hundred and twelve days. Sella gives the instruction to everything but the basket, says \emph{the house}, keeps the half-pace and the two inches, moves her lips along a row standing with two unnamed gaps and gives nobody a figure, keeps her finger on top of the shelf’s front edge so the charcoal stays unread, glances once at the cold clay jar and shuts her hand half over nothing without a touch, tells the fire it is the thaw and says \emph{The house will keep it}, and does not look toward the bed at the setting. The widow’s mark hangs where it hung at a shelf, a well, a yard, a basket and a dusk, because none is an opening and there has been no opening since before the kiln on Ember 1. Cost-questions go to the pot and the weather and arrive nowhere; a number in a fist goes back into a coat with nothing paid. The fire answers four low pulls with the silence where the fifth should have been, its payer unnamed for two hundred and ten, eleven and twelve days. Forward, not closed.

\textbf{Ch 54.} Through Days 213–215, Grain 4–6, the house keeps the first working week of Grain the way it keeps the fire: without an entry, without correcting either of the district’s two month-names, and with no market and no Account-day until Grain 10 (Day 219). She comes to the fire before the basket on all three mornings, gives every instruction to the wool, the fire, the pot, the broom, the running water and the river wind and never to the basket, says \emph{the house} and \emph{The house will keep it}, keeps her half-pace from every open slate, glances once at the clay jar cold under its glaze and shuts her hand half over nothing without a touch, pushes coal-black hair back with the burn-wrist so the grey streak shows pale, moves her lips along a row standing with two gaps and gives nobody a figure, keeps her finger on top of the shelf’s front edge so the charcoal stays unread, tells the fire it is the thaw, turns the coals with the back of a broken pot and stands counting under her breath toward no opening (small intake, hold, letting go). The pot rim goes out with its handle two inches beyond the reaching hand and her hand rests a half-beat longer at the setting; on the last day she does not look toward the bed. The fire answers four low pulls with the fifth missing under the floor, its payer unnamed for two hundred and thirteen, fourteen and fifteen days, while the river’s note comes through the finger’s-width door and the boards keep their knot: three counts in three places that do not become one. The widow’s mark hangs where it hung, touched once before the kiln on Ember 1 and at no hour since — no opening in thirty-five days — and the private roll stays unshown while Dessa’s cost stays unentered. Cost-questions at the door and the well go to the pot and the weather and away level, nothing priced, refused or entered; a number in a fist goes nowhere and pays nothing. Garl is kept to every day in objects and not in a story: the salt-stiff coat with its crease at the left shoulder, the seat’s twenty-year hollow and leftward lean, the clean dark line and the finer grey called the thaw unswept, the proverb gone to a pot with no crack, and the debt against the tiles neither paid, settled nor named, worse for being uncalled, with no lesson made and no collector. When the burned-slate word goes around the boards a third time she makes nothing of it; when Jorra grows quieter the household straightens around the quiet without an order from her, and her unfinished sentence at the hearth still finishes at the pot behind his remembered finger (T058/T079, T100, T077, T009/T013/T092/T098, T035/T031/T062, T065/T095, T088). Forward, not closed.

\textbf{Ch 55.} Through Days 216–218, Grain 7–9, the house keeps the second working week the way it keeps the fire: without an entry, with no market until Grain 10, and with the same grammar of instruction to the wool, fire, pot, broom, running water and river wind and never to the basket. She comes to the fire before the basket, says \emph{the house} and \emph{The house will keep it}, keeps her half-pace and her two inches, holds her finger on top of the shelf’s front edge so the charcoal stays unread, and leaves the widow’s mark untouched for thirty-six, thirty-seven and thirty-eight days. The fire misses its fifth with its payer unnamed for two hundred and sixteen, seventeen and eighteen days; the river’s note and the boards’ knot keep three counts in three places that do not become one. A pot saying takes a third shaping and the burned-slate word a fourth telling, both directions arrived nowhere, and she joins neither to the house. Jorra’s quiet goes before him into the shed and the household straightens around it without an order; her unfinished sentence still finishes at the pot behind his remembered finger. Tarn’s ninth stopping stands with no tenth and no collector; Garl stays in objects with the tile debt uncalled. The boy is carried home at the half-pace each dusk, set on his bed under the roof and not in the Debt Loft, with the fold put right without a look at his face and the thread left frozen; the two rooms do not touch. Forward, not closed.

Through Grain 10–12 she keeps the house the way she keeps the fire: the boy carried up and down the clay road at the half-pace, set in the moot-post’s thin shade where no slate lay at Grain’s first market, and set on his bed and not in the Debt Loft each night with the fold put right without a look at his face and the thread left frozen. She gives every instruction to the wool, the fire, the pot, the broom, the running water and the river wind and never to the basket, says \emph{the house} and \emph{The house will keep it}, keeps her finger on top of the shelf’s front edge so the charcoal stays unread, moves her lips along the two-gapped row without a figure, and leaves the widow’s mark hanging where it hung through thirty-nine, forty and forty-one days without an opening. The seventh green and the seventh shape come and go across the square without reaching under her roof; nothing is explained, entered, paid or named.

Through Grain 13–18 she brings the year’s harvest under the roof in two steps and keeps both by covering: the first cut grain comes in off the strips and is set near the hearth under wool, then across Grain 16–18 it is taken out, beaten with a flail on the flagstones, winnowed on the river wind, spread thin to finish drying and poured back under the fold --- dressed and stored, counted in glances and handfuls and by the carrying arm’s weight, with no slate opened and no figure given. Every cost-question goes to the pot and the weather and arrives nowhere; a number comes up out of a fist and goes back into its sleeve. She goes around the clean dark line, the finer grey called the thaw, the rack space with its broken birth-slates, the pan’s gone ring, the bare trough, the field’s empty place and the place in the returning line where a hand went in on Seed 15 and did not come out, each with a look and a wide step and no number. Her pot handle stands two inches beyond the reaching hand, her hand resting a half-beat longer at the setting and never looking toward the bed; her finger lies on top of the shelf’s front edge while her lips move along a row with two gaps, and the charcoal is not read. The widow’s mark is untouched since before the kiln on Ember 1, no opening in forty-two through forty-seven days; her private roll stays unshown, Dessa’s cost unentered, and Garl kept in objects with the tile debt uncalled. She carries him home at each going of the light without looking at his face, sets him on his bed under the roof and not in the Debt Loft, and leaves the thread frozen. Forward into Grain 19, not closed.

Through Grain 19–21 she keeps the house in the same grammar with one more tend behind her and Grain’s second Account-day read over the basket on Day 229: she changes nothing under the roof in answer to the figure, sends cost-questions to the pot and the weather, goes wide around the yard’s places with a look and no number, and carries him home at the going of the light saying nothing of what was read over him. The dressed grain stays dressed and covered with no figure, and the returning-line place stays gone around with a look and no number; T098 advances and is not paid. The widow’s mark has now gone fifty days untouched since the opening before the kiln on Ember 1, and the rule still holds that the hand goes to the mark before the kiln and at no other hour. On Grain 21 she goes to her own bed before the small hours and leaves the coals to keep themselves; in the room that does not touch his her breaths go small intake, hold, letting go — a count kept toward no opening and never offered to any ear under this roof — and the wall stands between that count and his ear. She has taken in a foundling, kept a fire, held a wheel in the house through a son’s silence and a husband’s uncollected debt, and has never once said what any of it cost or asked where the boy’s memory came from. Nothing joined, named, opened, spent or ended.

Through Grain 22–24 (Days 231–233) she keeps the last tend of the harvest the way she keeps the fire: by instruction given to the tool and never to the basket, by a figure sent to the pot and the weather, and by a wide step around every place the yard has left where it lies.
