The second ownerless asking goes over the boards in the afternoon of Day 232 and is answered with the pot and the weather as the first was, the weather first and the price of barley after it, and the row stands where it stood. She goes around the clean dark line, the finer grey called the thaw, the rack space with its broken birth-slates, the pan’s gone ring, the bare trough, the field’s empty place and the returning-line place, each with a look and a wide step and no number. She sets him on his bed under the roof and not in the Debt Loft, goes to her own bed before the small hours and leaves the coals to keep themselves; in the room that does not touch his her breaths go small intake, hold, letting go, a count kept toward no opening and never offered to any ear under this roof. She has taken in a foundling, kept a fire, held a wheel in the house through a son’s silence and a husband’s uncollected debt, and has never once said what any of it cost or asked where the boy’s memory came from. Nothing joined, named, opened, spent or ended.

Through Grain 25–27 (Days 234–236) she keeps the last tend of the harvest the way she keeps the fire: by instruction given to the tool and never to the basket, by a figure sent to the pot and the weather, and by a wide step around every place the yard has left where it lies. She comes to the fire before the basket on all three mornings, turns the coals with the back of a broken pot, tells it the thaw, says \emph{The house will keep it} where another woman would say \emph{I}, counts under her breath toward no opening, pushes coal-black hair back with the burn-wrist so the grey streak shows pale, sets the pot handle two inches beyond the reaching hand with a half-beat and no look toward the bed, moves her lips along the two-gapped row with no figure, keeps her finger on top of the shelf’s front edge so the charcoal stays unread, and does not touch the widow’s mark — now fifty-four, fifty-five and fifty-six days since the opening before the kiln on Ember 1. She turns the dressed grain under wool for damp, spreads it thin and gathers it back by the handful, counted in glances and the carrying arm’s weight, entered on no slate and given no figure. The third ownerless asking goes over the boards on the afternoon of Day 235 and is answered with the pot and the weather as the first two were, the weather first and the price of barley after it, and the voice goes off up the terrace with the row standing where it stood and nobody leaning in to take the answer down. She goes around the seven walked-around places with a look and a wide step and no number, sets him on his bed under the roof and not in the Debt Loft, goes to her own bed before the small hours of Day 236 and leaves the coals to keep themselves; in the room that does not touch his her breaths go small intake, hold, letting go, a count kept toward no opening and never offered to any ear under this roof. She has taken in a foundling, kept a fire, held a wheel in the house through a son’s silence and a husband’s uncollected debt, and has never once said what any of it cost or asked where the boy’s memory came from. Nothing joined, named, opened, spent or ended.

Through Smoke 1–3 (Days 240–242) she keeps the house the way she keeps the fire: instruction to the wool, fire, pot, broom, running water and river wind and never to the basket, \emph{the house} and \emph{The house will keep it}, the half-pace from every open slate, the jar-glance without a touch, the hand shut half over nothing, the burn-wrist pushing coal-black hair back so the grey streak shows pale, the finger on top of the shelf’s front edge so the charcoal stays unread, the pot handle two inches beyond the reaching hand with a half-beat and no look toward the bed, lips along the two-gapped row with no figure, cost-questions to the pot and the weather. \textbf{The one change in these days was hers:} before the first firing of Smoke she went to the kiln mouth, put her hand to the widow’s mark, held it one breath, let go, lifted the clay lid with the back of a hand and tipped the carried coal under a broken pot; the fire took with its fifth still missing and no payer named, nobody praised what it mended and nobody saw it, and she put it behind the household without a word. She did not touch the mark again at any shelf, well, rack, road, basket, afternoon or dusk in three days, because the hand goes to the mark before the kiln and at no other hour, as on Tallow 1 and Ember 1. The dressed grain was turned under wool for damp, spread thin and gathered back by the handful, changed in state and given no figure, entered on no slate and laid across none of the absences. A wrong wind off High Kiln on Smoke 3 brought the sweet edge of glaze over the boards, touched the fold and went out on it, and she let one of the three sayings stand as a saying with no fourth likeness made a cause. She carried him home each evening around the seven walked-around places with a look and a wide step and no number, set him on his bed under the roof, left the thread frozen and went to her own bed before the small hours. No new scar or possession, no bond changed hands, and the private roll stayed unshown.

Through Smoke 4–6 (Days 243–245) she keeps the house the way she keeps the fire: instruction to the tool and never to the basket, \emph{the house}, the half-pace, the jar-glance, the hand shut half over nothing, the unread charcoal under the shelf’s front edge, the pot handle two inches beyond the reaching hand, and cost-questions sent to the pot and the weather. The widow’s mark has not been touched since the opening before Smoke 1; the hand goes to it before the kiln and at no other hour. The dressed grain is turned under wool and given no figure; the fire answers four low pulls with a missing fifth whose payer is unnamed for two hundred and forty-five days. On Smoke 6 a wrong wind off High Kiln brings the sweet edge of lead glaze over the boards and takes it out again. She goes wide around the walked-around places, sets him on his bed under the roof, leaves the thread frozen and goes to her own bed before the small hours. No new scar or possession, no bond changed hands.

Through Smoke 7–9 (Days 246–248) she keeps the house the way she keeps the fire: instruction to the tool and never to the basket, \emph{the house}, the half-pace, the jar-glance, the hand shut half over nothing, the unread charcoal under the shelf’s front edge, the pot handle two inches beyond the reaching hand, and cost-questions sent to the pot and the weather. She goes to the fire before the basket on all three mornings, tells it the thaw, turns the coals with the back of a broken pot, says \emph{The house will keep it} where another woman would say \emph{I}, counts under her breath toward no opening, pushes coal-black hair back with the burn-wrist so the grey streak shows pale, lips along the two-gapped row with no figure, and sets him on his bed under the roof at the going of each light, leaving the thread frozen and going to her own bed before the small hours. The widow’s mark has not been touched since the opening before Smoke 1; the hand goes to it before the kiln and at no other hour, and a shelf, a well, a rack, a road, a basket, an afternoon and a dusk are not openings. The dressed grain is turned under wool, spread thin and gathered back by the handful on all three mornings, changed in state and given no figure. On the afternoon of Smoke 8 the ownerless question comes over the boards a fifth time and she answers it with the weather first and the price of barley after it; the row stands where it stood, nobody leans in to take the answer down and no witness stands. A wrong wind off High Kiln brings the sweet edge of lead glaze over the boards, touches the fold and goes out on it, and she makes no lesson of it. The fire answers four low pulls with a missing fifth whose payer is unnamed for two hundred and forty-six, forty-seven and forty-eight days. No new scar or possession, no bond changed hands, no opening made after the first.

Through Smoke 10–12 (Days 249–251) she keeps the house the way she keeps the fire: instruction to the wool, fire, pot, broom, running water and river wind and never the basket, \emph{the house} and \emph{The house will keep it} where another woman would say \emph{I}, the half-pace from every open slate, the jar-glance without a touch, the hand shut half over nothing, the finger on top of the shelf’s front edge so the charcoal stays unread, the pot handle two inches beyond the reaching hand with a half-beat and no look toward the bed, and cost-questions sent to the pot and the weather with nothing priced. She comes to the fire before the basket on all three mornings, tells it the thaw, turns the coals with the back of a broken pot, counts under her breath toward no opening, pushes coal-black hair back with the burn-wrist so the grey streak shows pale, lips along the two-gapped row without a figure, and sets him on his bed under the roof at the going of each light with the thread frozen and unwiped, going to her own bed before the small hours. The dressed grain is turned under wool, spread thin and gathered by the handful on all three mornings, changed in state and given no figure. On Smoke 10 she carries him down to the Cross, sets the basket in the moot-post’s finger’s width of shade where no slate lies and stands half a pace off through Berr’s twice-read figure and the bell, giving no instruction and no reason to the basket, and carries him home at the going of the light saying nothing of what was read over him and going wide around the walked-around places with a look and no number. The widow’s mark has not been touched since the opening before Smoke 1; the hand goes to it before the kiln and at no other hour, and no lesson is made of the one opening behind the household. The fire answers four low pulls with a missing fifth, its payer unnamed for two hundred and forty-nine, fifty and fifty-one days. No new scar or possession, no bond changed hands, no opening made after the first.

Through Smoke 13–15 (Days 252–254) she keeps the house the way she keeps the fire: instruction to the wool, fire, pot, broom, running water and river wind and never to the basket, \emph{the house} and \emph{The house will keep it} where another woman would say \emph{I}, the half-pace from every open slate, the jar-glance with the hand shut half over nothing, the finger on top of the shelf’s front edge so the charcoal stays unread, the pot handle two inches beyond the reaching hand with a half-beat and no look toward the bed, and cost-questions sent to the pot and the weather with nothing priced. She comes to the fire before the basket on all three mornings, tells it the thaw, turns the coals with the back of a broken pot, counts under her breath toward no opening, pushes coal-black hair back with the burn-wrist so the grey streak shows pale, lips along the two-gapped row without a figure, and sets him on his bed under the roof at the going of each light with the thread frozen and unwiped, going to her own bed before the small hours. The dressed grain is turned under wool, spread, gathered by the handful and laid flat on all three mornings, changed in state and given no figure. The widow’s mark has not been touched since the opening before Smoke 1; the hand goes to it before the kiln and at no other hour, and no lesson is made of the one opening behind the household. On Smoke 14 a pot set down wrong at the racks gives its high thin note before its time and a woman sweeps around it with a practical word about the slip, making no cause of the sound; a wrong wind off High Kiln brings the sweet edge of lead glaze over the boards and takes it out again. The fire answers four low pulls with a missing fifth, its payer unnamed for two hundred and fifty-two, fifty-three and fifty-four days. No new scar or possession, no bond changed hands, no opening made after the first.

Through Smoke 16–18, Days 255–257, the keeping goes on in the same grammar and makes one small domestic change she does not name. She comes to the fire before the basket on all three mornings, gives every instruction to the wool, fire, pot, broom, running water and river wind and never to the basket, says \emph{the house} and \emph{The house will keep it}, turns the coals with the back of a broken pot, counts under her breath toward no opening, and keeps her finger on top of the shelf’s front edge so the charcoal stays unread. On Smoke 17 she gathers the dressed grain in by the handful for the last time before Smoke’s second reading, draws the wool over it and sets it away from the hearth on the cool stone at the rack end, giving the heap no figure and saying nothing that the work has ended; the arithmetic that will be read over it on Smoke 20 will not know what it cost. On Smoke 18 she gives the instruction to the bucket and the fire and never the basket, goes around the trough with a look and a wide step, and lets the yard call the white frost on the well lip weather, because a well is not an opening. The widow’s mark hangs where it hung, touched once before the kiln on Smoke 1 and at no hour since; the one opening stays behind the household with no lesson and no payer, and the next real opening is the first firing of Frost, far off and unbrought. At the going of the light on Smoke 18 she sets him on his bed and not in the Debt Loft, puts the fold right without a look at his face, leaves the thread frozen and goes to her own bed. The wall has acquired no door.

Through Smoke 19–21 she keeps the house the way she keeps the fire: to the fire before the basket on all three mornings, instruction to the wool, fire, pot, broom and river wind and never to the basket, \emph{the house} where another woman would say \emph{I}, the half-pace from every open slate, the jar-glance with the hand shut half over nothing, coal-black hair pushed back with the burn-wrist so the grey streak shows pale, her finger on top of the shelf’s front edge so the charcoal stays unread, the pot handle two inches beyond the reaching hand with a half-beat and no look toward the bed. The dressed grain is lifted for damp and laid back on the 19th, turned under wool and laid back on the 21st, and given no figure on either day; on the 20th the district’s arithmetic changes a second time up the road and nothing under this roof is settled by it. On Smoke 20 she sets the basket in the moot-post’s thin shade where no slate lies and stands half a pace off through Berr’s twice-read figure and the bell, carrying him home at the going of the light and saying nothing of what was read over him. At each dusk she sets him on the bed under the roof and not in the Debt Loft, puts the fold right without a look at his face and leaves the thread frozen. The widow’s mark hangs where it hangs, touched once before the kiln on Smoke 1 and at no shelf, well, rack, road, basket, market, morning, afternoon, dusk or going of the light on these three days, because a market and a reading are not openings (T058/T079, T077, T100).

Through Smoke 22–24, Days 261–263, she keeps the house the way she keeps the fire, and the keeping is made as much of what she leaves undone as of what she does. She comes to the fire before the basket on all three mornings, tells the coals it is the thaw, turns them with the back of a broken pot, says \emph{The house will keep it} where another woman would say \emph{I}, counts under her breath toward no opening, pushes coal-black hair back with the burn-wrist so the grey streak shows pale, keeps her finger on top of the shelf’s front edge so the charcoal stays unread, moves her lips along a two-gapped row without giving either gap a figure, glances once at the clay jar and shuts her hand half over nothing, and sets the pot handle two inches beyond the reaching hand with a half-beat and no look toward the bed. She lifts a corner of the wool over the dressed grain for damp on the 22nd and 23rd and turns it under the wool on the 24th, each with no figure, so the arithmetic on Smoke 30 will not know what it cost. She carries him about the yard and up at the going of the light at the half-pace from every open slate, goes wide around the seven walked-around places, sets him on his bed under the roof and not in the Debt Loft, puts the fold right without a look at his face and leaves the thread frozen. The widow’s mark hangs where it hangs, touched once before the kiln on Smoke 1 and at no shelf, well, rack, road, basket, yard, morning, afternoon, dusk or going of the light in these three days, because none is an opening; the one opening stays behind the household with no lesson, sign, mending or payer, and the next real opening is the first firing of Frost, far off and unbrought (T058/T079, T077, T100). Nothing is priced, named or entered, and the wall has acquired no door.

Through Smoke 25–27, Days 264–266, she keeps the house through the third working week’s going out: fire before basket, the thaw told to the coals, the back of a broken pot, \emph{The house will keep it}, the count under her breath toward no opening, the finger on top of the shelf’s front edge with the charcoal unread, the two-gapped row without a figure, the glance at the clay jar and the hand shut half over nothing, the pot handle two inches out with a half-beat and no look toward the bed. On Smoke 26 she draws the wool wholly back from the dressed grain and turns it piece by piece in her flat hand for damp and rot, setting each piece where it lay, then covers it and carries the dish from the hearth; on Smoke 27 she turns it once with a lighter touch. No figure on any day, so the arithmetic on Smoke 30 will not know what it cost. She carries him at the half-pace, goes wide around the seven places, sets him on his bed under the roof and not in the Debt Loft, puts the fold right without a look at his face and leaves the thread frozen. The widow’s mark hangs where it hangs, touched once before the kiln on Smoke 1 and at no hour in these three days, because none is an opening; the one opening before Smoke 1 stays behind the household with no lesson, mending, sign or payer. Nothing is settled by the week’s going out and the count goes into Smoke 28 unspent.

Through Frost 1–3, Days 270–272, she keeps the house the way she keeps the fire, and in the first light of Frost 2 she performs the month’s one real opening. She comes to the kiln mouth before the basket and before any word, holds the widow’s mark one breath, lets go, lifts the clay lid with the back of a hand and tips the carried coal under the back of a broken pot; the fire takes, still answering four low pulls with the silence where the fifth should have stood, its payer unnamed two hundred and seventy-one days. Nobody praises the opening and nobody names what it mended; no slate is entered, no lesson made, no bond changed hands, no payer named and no sign made. She does not touch the mark again at a shelf, well, rack, road, basket, yard, morning, hearth, afternoon, dusk or going of the light on Frost 1, 2 or 3, because the hand goes to the mark before the kiln and at no other hour; four openings in four months are four and not a rule, and the next opening stands in a later month’s first firing, far off. On the other mornings she tells the coals it was the thaw, turns them with the back of a broken pot, says \emph{The house will keep it}, counts under her breath toward no opening, keeps her finger above the charcoal, sets the pot handle two inches beyond the reaching hand with a half-beat and no look toward the bed, turns the dressed grain beneath the wool for damp with a progressively lighter touch and gives it no figure, carries him at the half-pace, goes wide around the seven places and sets him on his bed under the roof with the thread frozen. Nothing is settled by the firing and the count goes into Frost 4 unspent.

Through Frost 4–6, Days 273–275, she keeps the house through the week of going around, and in the middle of it makes the chapter’s one change without a word. She comes to the fire before the basket each morning, tells the coals it was the thaw, turns them with the back of a broken pot, says \emph{The house will keep it} where another woman would say \emph{I}, counts under her breath toward no opening, pushes coal-black hair back with the burn-wrist so the grey streak shows pale, keeps her finger on top of the shelf’s front edge, moves her lips along a two-gapped row without giving either gap a figure, glances once at the clay jar and shuts her hand half over nothing, and sets the pot rim out with its handle two inches beyond the reaching hand, a half-beat at the setting and no look toward the bed. On Frost 5 her finger goes beneath the shelf’s front edge and stays for two counted breaths where on Day 166 it stayed for one, and comes away without a look, a word or a going back — a change a house can make and say nothing about (T100 advanced, not paid). She turns the dressed grain under wool for damp on all three mornings with a progressively lighter touch and gives it no figure; she goes wide around the seven walked-around places and sets him on his bed under the roof with the thread frozen. The widow’s mark hangs where it hangs, touched once before the kiln on Frost 2 and at no shelf, well, rack, road, basket, yard, morning, hearth, afternoon, dusk or going of the light on Frost 4, 5 or 6; the first firing of Frost stays behind the household with no lesson or payer and four openings remain four. Nothing is settled by the week’s going out and the count goes into Frost 7 unspent.

Through Frost 7–9, Days 276–278, she keeps the house through the week’s going out, and on the last morning makes the chapter’s one change as maintenance and gives nobody a figure. She comes to the fire before the basket each morning, tells the coals it was the thaw, turns them with the back of a broken pot, says \emph{The house will keep it} where another woman would say \emph{I}, counts under her breath toward no opening, keeps her finger on top of the shelf’s front edge with the charcoal unread, moves her lips along a two-gapped row without giving either gap a figure, glances once at the clay jar and shuts her hand half over nothing, and sets the pot rim two inches beyond the reaching hand with a half-beat and no look toward the bed. The white the frost wrote on the well lip on Frost 8 does not go with the sun as it went on Frost 4, and stays past noon, past the going of the light and onto Frost 9; the rope stiffens, the trough takes a skin and she banks the coals an hour earlier at the going of the light, and the yard calls all of it weather. On Frost 9 she goes to the trough with the back of the broken pot, presses the skin until it gives with a thin dry sound, lifts a plate of ice clouded with silt, sets it on a flat stone out of the path of feet and draws what the yard calls weather, telling the weather where to stand and giving nobody a figure (T083/T085 advanced, not paid). She turns the dressed grain a second time that morning because the stone has gone cold, lifts the wool with a lighter touch and gives no figure, so the arithmetic that will read over it tomorrow will not know what it cost (T077). She goes wide around the seven walked-around places with a look and a wide step and no number, sets him on his bed under the roof each dusk and not in the Debt Loft, puts the fold right without a look at his face and leaves the thread frozen. The widow’s mark hangs where it hangs, touched once before the kiln on Frost 2 and at no shelf, well, rack, road, basket, yard, morning, hearth, afternoon, dusk or going of the light on Frost 7, 8 or 9, because none is an opening; the first firing of Frost stays behind the household with no lesson or payer and four openings remain four. Nothing is settled by the week’s going out and the count goes into Frost 10 unspent.

Through Frost 10–12, Days 279–281, she keeps the house the way she keeps the fire, and the month’s first reading passes the roof without leaving a figure behind. On Frost 10 she carries him to the Cross, sets the basket in the moot-post’s finger’s width of shade where no slate lay and stands half a pace off through the reading and the bell, giving no instruction or reason to the basket, and carries him home at the going of the light saying nothing. The arithmetic changed for the month up the road in Berr’s locked box and cannot be changed back, while the printed one in twelve stands unchallenged and the figure read is still not the figure paid; nothing of it comes back under the roof as a lesson, a mending, a figure or a payment. On Frost 11 and 12 she turns the dressed grain under wool for damp with a lighter touch and gives it no figure, so the number that read over it does not know what it cost, and the space between figure and price stays unsigned (T077). The grammar holds exactly — fire before basket, instruction to the tools and never the basket, \emph{the house}, \emph{The house will keep it}, half-pace, pot rim two inches out, fold righted without a look, finger above the charcoal, lips along a two-gapped row, one glance at the clay jar and the hand shut half over nothing, the widow’s mark untouched because no hour among these days is an opening. The stayed frost, the plate of ice and the week’s small goings-around are called weather and entered nowhere (T083/T085 held), the fire’s fifth stays unsupplied with its payer unnamed for three more days (T088), and Frost 20 stands eight mornings ahead and unbrought. Nothing is opened, named, called, paid or ended.

Through Frost 13–15, Days 282–284, she keeps the house the way she keeps the fire, and the second working week settles nothing. She comes to the hearth before the basket each morning, tells the coals it was the thaw, turns them with the back of a broken pot, says \emph{The house will keep it} where another woman would say \emph{I}, keeps her finger above the charcoal so the tally beneath stays unread, moves her lips along a two-gapped row without a figure, glances once at the clay jar and shuts her hand half over nothing, and sets the pot rim two inches beyond the reaching hand with a half-beat and no look toward the bed. She goes wide around the seven walked-around places with a look and a wide step and no number, turns the dressed grain under wool for damp and gives it no figure, carries him at the half-pace and sets him on his bed under the roof with the fold righted and the thread frozen. The widow’s mark hangs where it hangs at every morning, afternoon and going of the light, because none is an opening; the first firing of Frost stays behind the household with no lesson or payer and four openings remain four. The stayed frost, the skinned trough and the plate of ice are called weather and entered nowhere, and the fire’s fifth stays unsupplied with its payer unnamed for two hundred and eighty-four days. Frost 20 stands five mornings ahead and unbrought, and nothing is opened, named, called, paid or ended.

Through Bone 10–12, Days 309–311, she keeps the house the way she keeps the fire, and the month’s first reading passes the roof without leaving a figure behind. On the tenth she carries him to the Cross, sets the basket in the moot-post’s finger’s width of shade where no slate lay and stands half a pace off through the twice-read figure and the bell, and carries him home at the going of the light saying nothing. The arithmetic changed for the month up the road in Berr’s locked box and cannot be changed back, while the printed one in twelve stands unchallenged, the figure read is still not the figure paid, four readings are four and not one account, and a rule made from them would want a payer where none stood. Through the eleventh and twelfth her grammar holds exactly: fire before basket, instruction to the wool, the wind, the pot, the broom and the running water and never to the basket, the charcoal unread, the two gaps unfigured, the twice-mended pot lifted with the thumb on the wire and the crack showing, the pot rim two inches out, the dressed grain turned under wool with a lighter touch and no figure, and the widow’s mark touched at no hour. Five openings in five months are five and not a rule; the seven walked-around places go around with a look and no number, and the skinned trough and silt-clouded plate stay weather entered nowhere. The carried fire’s fifth is unpaid three hundred and eleven days with its payer unnamed. Bone 20 stands five mornings ahead and is not brought early. Nothing is joined, named, opened, called, paid or ended, and no lesson is made of the reading.

Through Bone 22–24, Days 321–323, she keeps the house the way she keeps the fire, and the chapter’s one movement is a domestic testing that says nothing and is not repeated. She comes to the hearth before the basket at both ends of every day, tells the coals it was the thaw, turns them with the back of a broken pot, says \emph{The house will keep it}, counts small intake, hold and letting-go toward no opening with neither gap figured, keeps her finger on top of the loaf shelf so the charcoal stays unread, moves her lips along a two-gapped row with neither gap figured, glances once at the clay jar cold under lead glaze with her hand half over nothing, lifts the twice-mended pot with the thumb first where the wire crosses the crack and both proverbs to the pot and the fire with the crack showing, turns the dressed grain under wool with a lighter touch and no figure, sets the pot rim two inches beyond the reaching hand with a half-beat and no look toward the bed, righted the fold without looking at his face and leaves the thread. On Bone 22 at the rack end she lifts the wool from the dressed grain, takes a small handful and lets it fall back through her fingers onto the heap instead of spreading it — a hand testing dryness — with no word, no figure and no repetition; on Bone 23 and 24 her fingers go in and come out without closing and she makes no show of not repeating it. She carries him down and up at the half-pace from every open slate, gives the instruction to the wool and the river wind and never to the basket, and goes wide around the seven walked-around places with a look and a wide step and no number. The three coverings stay weather entered nowhere, the month’s hunts and repairs stay directions judged by the carrying arm and the weather, and the widow’s mark hangs where it hangs at every morning, rack, well, yard, hearth and bed, because none is an opening and five openings in five months are five and not a rule. With Tarn the exact account of six and the seventh goes unremarked and his stroke over the bright patch without the half-check asks no question from her; with Jorra the men unnamed before first grey, the dust and the bent finger standing in the cold damper ahead of her unfinished sentence go unasked about. Ilva at the well on Bone 23 keeps her count in wood and answers the question put; nothing comes from that well under the roof as lesson, figure, mending, cause or payment. Garl’s name is unspoken three hundred and twenty-three days and his tile debt uncalled. Nothing is opened, joined, named, called, paid or ended.

\CRsheetheading{Chapter Log}
\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item Ch 128: Through Silt 11, 12 and 13 nothing crossed under the roof, out of the yard or up the clay road as sign, lesson, mending, cause, payment or payer, and neither the second asking at the well on the twelfth nor the Slate Row face at the yard’s edge on the thirteenth was made a teaching under the roof or told on an unearned day. She came to the hearth before the basket at both ends of all three days, told the coals it was the thaw and turned them with the back of a broken pot, gave the intake, hold and letting-go toward no opening with neither gap figured, kept her finger along the top of the loaf shelf so the charcoal stayed unread, lips on a two-gapped row, one glance at the cold clay jar with the hand shut half over nothing and the little-door burn closing on air. She lifted the twice-mended pot thumb-first with the hairline showing and both proverbs to pot and fire and never to a person, kept repair apart from restoration, turned the dressed grain under wool with no figure or handful and set the pot rim two inches beyond the reaching hand with a half-beat and no look toward the bed. Her hands counted spoons and nails when they had nothing to do and came back to the hairline at the wire. She carried him down and up the nineteen steps at the half-pace, went wide around the seven walked-around places once and not twice, set him under the roof and never in the Debt Loft, put the fold right without a look at his face and added no second fold, and found the keeping where it had been put. \textbf{The widow’s mark hung where it hangs on all three days} — seven openings in seven months are seven and not a rule and a tending day did not make an eighth come due. On Silt 12 she was at the well with him while a second neighbour asked whether a count kept in wood would be taken at the next reading; Ilva answered and Sella said nothing to the basket, carrying him home at the going of the light saying nothing of the asking. On Silt 13 she carried him home saying nothing of the man from Slate Row at the yard’s edge. No new scar or possession, no change of voice, nothing paid, opened or ended; forward, not closed.

\end{itemize}

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item Ch 127: Through Silt 8, 9 and 10 nothing crossed under the roof, out of the yard or up the clay road as sign, lesson, mending, cause, payment or payer, and neither the reported second slate of Silt 6 nor the hair-thin thaw of Silt 7 was made a teaching under the roof on a later day. She came to the hearth before the basket at both ends of all three days, told the coals it was the thaw and turned them with the back of a broken pot, gave the intake, hold and letting-go toward no opening with neither gap figured, kept her finger along the top of the loaf shelf so the charcoal stayed unread, lips on a two-gapped row, one glance at the cold clay jar with the hand shut half over nothing and the little-door burn closing on air. She lifted the twice-mended pot thumb-first with the hairline showing and both proverbs to pot and fire and never to a person, kept repair apart from restoration, turned the dressed grain under wool with no figure or handful and set the pot rim two inches beyond the reaching hand with a half-beat and no look toward the bed. Her hands counted spoons, nails and the breaths of a child nobody numbers when they had nothing to do and came back to the hairline at the wire. She carried him down and up the nineteen steps at the half-pace, went wide around the seven walked-around places once and not twice, set him under the roof and never in the Debt Loft, put the fold right without a look at his face or a second fold, and found the keeping where it had been put on each morning and going of the light. \textbf{The widow’s mark hung where it hangs on all three days} — seven openings in seven months are seven and not a rule and an Account-day did not make an eighth come due. On Silt 10, before first grey, she set the basket in the moot-post’s finger’s width of shade where no slate lay and stood half a pace off through Berr Clay’s fourth reading and the bell, giving the wicker no instruction or reason, never looking into it, and carried him home at the going of the light saying nothing of the reading, the bell’s gap, the runner’s slate going up unread, the clerk’s figure, the two sightings or the fourth subtraction gone up the road in a locked box. On the market afternoon the figures left standing on the turnip heap and the woman sent for a pot’s cost who got a note and not a price brought no teaching under the roof; Sella told the fire it was the thaw. She said \emph{the house} where another woman would say \emph{I} and \emph{the boy} where another would say \emph{my son}, and did not discuss the one grey streak winter had put at her temple. No new scar or possession, no change of voice.

\end{itemize}

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item Ch 126: Through Silt 5, 6 and 7 nothing crossed under the roof, out of the yard or up the clay road as sign, lesson, mending, cause, payment or payer, and neither the reported second slate of Silt 6 nor the hair-thin thaw of Silt 7 was made a teaching under the roof on the day after. She came to the hearth before the basket at both ends of all three days, told the coals it was the thaw and turned them with the back of a broken pot, gave the small intake, hold and letting-go toward no opening with neither gap figured, kept her finger along the top of the loaf shelf so the charcoal stayed unread, moved her lips on a two-gapped row, glanced once at the cold clay jar with the hand shut half over nothing and the little-door burn closing on air, lifted the twice-mended pot thumb-first with the hairline showing and both proverbs to pot and fire and never to a person, turned the dressed grain under wool with no figure or handful and set the pot rim two inches beyond the reaching hand with a half-beat and no look toward the bed. Her hands were never still when they had nothing to do, counting spoons, nails and the breaths of a child nobody numbers and coming back to the hairline at the wire. She carried him down and up the nineteen steps at the half-pace, went wide around the seven walked-around places once and not twice, set him under the roof and never in the Debt Loft, put the fold right without a look at his face or a second fold, and found the keeping where it had been put on each morning and going of the light. \textbf{The widow’s mark hung where it hangs on all three days} — seven openings in seven months are seven and not a rule and no eighth came due. On Silt 7 she told the fire it was the thaw and did not tell the basket, and she asked nothing about the word at the well of the day before or the softer air off the river. With Tarn the sixth piece stood where the house could check and the seventh at the lip beside Garl’s unforged collector sentence, his sentence found where put and not made a habit, the loan uncalled in a term already ended; with Jorra the dusty forearms were parted from clean as clot from vessel, the wheel and a pot spoken to before any person, the full note withheld from a High Kiln master, and the bent finger taken from the cold damper without the extra holding of Ash 26 a second time, \emph{he’s not Vail} sealed and the promise neither given nor withdrawn. She said \emph{the house} where another woman would say \emph{I} and \emph{the boy} where another would say \emph{my son}; the one grey streak at her temple said winter and she did not discuss the winter. No new scar or possession, no change of voice, nothing opened, paid or ended.

\end{itemize}

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item Ch 125: Through Silt 2, 3 and 4 nothing crossed under the roof, out of the yard or up the clay road as sign, lesson, mending, cause, payment or payer, and the neighbour’s near-reaching at the loaf shelf was not brought under the roof as a teaching or told on an unearned morning. She came to the hearth before the basket at both ends of every day, told the coals it was the thaw and turned them with the back of a broken pot, gave the intake, hold and letting-go toward no opening with neither gap figured, kept her finger along the top of the loaf shelf so the charcoal tally stayed unread, lips on a two-gapped row, one glance at the cold clay jar with the hand shut half over nothing and the little-door burn closing on air. She lifted the twice-mended pot thumb-first where the wire crossed the crack, left the hairline showing, gave both proverbs to pot and fire and never to a person, kept repair apart from restoration, turned the dressed grain under wool with no figure or handful and set the pot rim two inches beyond the reaching hand with a half-beat and no look toward the bed; on the third morning she weighed a fist of barley and set it back, saying no number. She carried him down and up the nineteen steps at the half-pace, went wide around the seven walked-around places once and not twice, set him under the roof and never in the Debt Loft, put the fold right without a look at his face and added no second fold; the keeping at the fold was found where put. \textbf{The widow’s mark hung where it hangs on all three days} — seven openings in seven months are seven and not a rule and no eighth came due. On Silt 3 her finger stayed along the shelf’s top where it had always gone and went no further after the neighbour’s reaching; she did not go beneath the board, did not ask what had been said and did not look at the boy’s face, and on Silt 4 the house took up its grammar as though nothing had turned. She said \emph{the house} where another woman would say \emph{I} and \emph{the boy} where another would say \emph{my son}, and said nothing of the grey streak winter had put at her temple. No new scar or possession, no change of voice.

\end{itemize}

On Ilmen 30, the month’s third and last Account-day and market, she set the basket in the moot-post’s finger’s width of shade where no slate lay and stood half a pace off through Berr Clay’s twice-read figure and the bell, giving no instruction or reason to the basket, and carried him home at the going of the light saying nothing of the reading, the bell’s gap, the unread slate or the clerk’s figure. \textbf{The widow’s mark hung where it hangs on all three days} — a morning, a hearth, a shelf, a pot, a yard, a basket, a market, a reading and a going of the light are not openings, seven openings in seven months are seven and not a rule and no eighth came due. She said \emph{the house} and \emph{the boy} where another woman would say \emph{I} and \emph{my son}; one grey streak at her temple said winter and she said nothing about the winter. She came to the hearth before the basket at both ends of every day, told the coals it was the thaw in the voice another woman would use for a child who could not hear her, turned them with the back of a broken pot, gave the small intake, the hold and the letting-go toward no opening with neither gap figured, kept her finger above the unread charcoal, lips on a two-gapped row, one glance at the clay jar standing cold under lead glaze beyond the pot board with the hand half over nothing and the little-door burn on the back of her left hand closing on air. She carried him down and up the nineteen steps at the half-pace, gave the instruction to the wool, the river wind, the pot, the fire and the banked fire and never to the basket, went wide around the seven walked-around places once and not twice, widest at the returning-line place, set him under the roof and never in the Debt Loft, put the fold right at his ear and under his chin without a look at his face and added no second fold. \textbf{The widow’s mark hung where it hangs on all three days} — a morning, a hearth, a shelf, a pot, a yard, a well, a basket and a going of the light are not openings, seven openings in seven months are seven and not a rule and no eighth came due. At the yard well on Ilmen 26 a woman waiting her turn offered a figure to Ilva’s strip and took it back into her sleeve; Sella was not there to see it and no figure came under this roof, no reader was made of the count in wood and nothing was paid, priced or joined. She said nothing of it at either end of any day, and nothing of the softening under the river’s skin that the yard called weather. With Tarn six stood where the house could check and the seventh at the lip, \emph{Six counted. Garl stayed in objects with his name unspoken 420, 421 and 422 days and his tile debt uncalled. No new scar or possession, no change of voice; forward, not closed.

Before first grey on Ilmen 6 three or more men unnamed went low into the back room off the wheel-shed and she gave them no name and did not say the room was cold; Jorra came out with meal-fine grey dust white in a fist-crease. When a man from Slate Row whose name was on no roll stood at the yard’s edge with his hands loose she carried the basket down at the half-pace and went wide around the seven places and spoke no word to him; no loaf passed, no slate was shown and the waiting was never called a sale (T035/T031/T080 advanced, not paid). With Tarn the six and the seventh held at the kindling, \emph{Six counted. The next I don’t count}, the loan uncalled at the end of a term already ended and no turn of the head toward the landing; with Jorra her unfinished sentence arrived at the pot through his bent finger standing in the cold damper and the promise under the shed was neither given nor withdrawn. With Jorra her unfinished sentence still arrived at the pot through the bent finger in the cold damper, out without a second holding of Ash 26, \emph{he’s not Vail} sealed and the promise neither given nor withdrawn; Garl stayed in objects, his name unspoken 396, 397 and 398 days and the carried fire’s fifth unpaid the same number. On the Remembering she carried him to House Silt on an errand, set the basket just inside the finger’s-width door away from every open slate, took what she came for and went without opening the tin above the empty bed or naming the woman. On the Last Day she baked bread and left the grey in the corners; a neighbour called it dealt with because it would be burnt in the morning and she did not say it. On Ilmen 1 the yard burnt its grey and called it gone and she still said nothing, keeping the called-gone beside the left-in-place ridge. \textbf{The keeping, advanced and NOT paid (T097/T060/T086):} found where put on the three mornings and at the three goings of the light, no second fold, third crust, name, gift, payment or payer. \textbf{The widow’s mark was not touched on any of the three days} — a holy day, a baking and a burning are not openings, seven openings in seven months seven and not a rule, no eighth due. The carried fire’s fifth stayed unpaid and Garl’s name unspoken 393, 394 and 395 days; no new scar or possession and no change of voice.

On Kindling she took the basket to the room two doors down, set him at the edge of the light where he could see and not join, stood half a pace off through the taking of the year’s first measure and carried him home saying nothing of the room, the tube, the slate or the woman. On the Long Night she banked the fire early, told the coals it was the thaw, lifted the twice-mended pot thumb-first with the hairline showing, turned the dressed grain under wool with no figure and set the pot rim two inches beyond his reach, then sat in the dark near the hearth with her hands in her lap and not still, counting the spoons, the nails and the breaths of a child nobody has numbered; her fingers stayed on the pot’s hairline a breath longer than any check required and came away without a sixth held object or a cause written across it, and she said low to the banked coals something about the thaw in the voice another woman would use for a child who could not hear her. No fire was lit after dusk and no eighth opening was made due. The year’s fire came up the Clay Yard from a source nobody under the roof names or prices; twelve arithmetics stood behind one unsigned figure; the carried fire’s fifth stayed unpaid with Garl’s name unspoken 390, 391 and 392 days. No new scar or possession and no change of voice; the Five are not over.

The empty place beside the crust was left on the thirteenth, the fourteenth and the morning of the fifteenth exactly as it had been, no hand at it, no third, no name, so that the evening’s keeping would be a change and not a habit. \textbf{The chapter’s one meaningful change, advanced and NOT paid (T097/T060/T086):} at the going of the light on the fifteenth she carried him up the nineteen steps under the Vail kiln-house roof and never into the Debt Loft, set him on the bed at the low angle of the loaf shelf, put the fold right at his ear and under his chin without a look at his face, righting the wool where the cold had ridden it back — and her hand tucked the wool into the empty place beside the crust. The wool went in as a hand goes in where a thing used to be and is not, not to fill the place, which kept its shape and its emptiness both, but to leave the warmth of a hand where the cold had been. It was a small keeping: no word with it, no third crust put there, no name spoken over the place, no look toward his face, no instruction to the basket; the little-door burn on the back of her left hand closed on nothing, her hand rested the half-beat longer than the setting needed before it went away, and the thread of drool at his mouth was left frozen in the dry kiln heat and unwiped where it lay. She said nothing of where they had been. The boy took the interval apart by what was there and by what was not and filed the keeping on a place of its own beside the crust’s gap, the shelf’s two gaps, the gone pan’s round ring and the field’s empty place, expressly not a joining of rooms, not a third crust, not a gift, not a payment, no payer, not a sixth held object, not a habit or a rule, gathered once and not made again, gathering interest toward the far-off finger that is not his. \textbf{The widow’s mark was not touched on Stone 13, 14 or 15} — a morning, a hearth, a shelf, a well, a yard, a road, a going of the light and a bed are no openings — and seven openings in seven months are seven and not a rule with no eighth made due. With Tarn the exact account held at six counted and the seventh at the lip beside Garl’s unforged sentence, the Ash 14 breath and Bone 26 thumb’s resting found where put and not made again, the loan uncalled; with Jorra her unfinished sentence still arrived at the pot through his bent finger in the cold damper, one iron with two bites, and the extra holding of Ash 26 was not left a second time. Ilva stood once at the well on the thirteenth with her strip unread and her ninth hand nine; Hessa came down the clay road on the fourteenth with the writing turned to her sleeve and gave no figure; Garl stayed in his objects with his name unspoken 372, 373 and 374 days and the carried fire’s fifth unpaid the same. Grey streak at the temple pale, coal-black hair pushed back with the burn-wrist. No new scar or possession, no change of voice, no bond paid. Forward, not closed.

Sella said nothing of the room, the tube, the child or the cup on the carry home, and that was not a refusal to tell him, for nobody under any roof tells a basket what a keeping is worth. \textbf{The widow’s mark was not touched on any of the three days} — a market, a well, a yard, a Drawing, a hearth and a bed are not openings, seven openings in seven months are seven and not a rule and no eighth is made due. The river’s winter skin was found where put and not spent on the reading or the Drawing; the three coverings stayed weather entered nowhere with a finger between every pair; the fire’s fifth stayed unpaid and Garl’s name unspoken 369, 370 and 371 days; the four rooms with the same gap stayed apart with a finger between every pair and the Drawing’s flat knock stayed on its own place outside the six hearings. Tarn kept six in the worn thumb-mark and the seventh at the lip, found the Ash 14 breath and Bone 26 thumb’s resting where put and not made again, brought the ear-sentence to the calling word and stopped as a remembered ninth stopping with no tenth, Seed 16 breath unspent and loan uncalled; Jorra parted dusty forearms from clean as clot from vessel, spoke to the wheel before any person, withheld the full note three turns ahead and put his bent finger into the cold damper with its two bites without leaving Ash 26’s extra holding a second time, \emph{he’s not Vail} sealed and the promise under the wheel-shed neither given nor withdrawn. No new scar or possession, no change of voice, no bond paid or spoken, no lesson, payment or ending. Forward, not closed.

The fire took, answering four low pulls with the silence where the fifth should have stood, its payer unnamed three hundred and thirty-one days; nobody praised the opening, named what it mended, entered a slate or made a lesson, sign, mending, cause or payer of it, the five behind were not looked at again as signs or payments, and no seventh was made due. She did not touch the mark again at shelf, well, rack, road, basket, yard, morning, afternoon, dusk or going of the light on any of the three days, because the hand goes to the mark before the kiln and at no other hour. The grey streak at her temple showed pale and she pushed coal-black hair back with the burn-wrist without looking toward the bed. On all three days her fingers at the rack end went in and came out and did not close on the grain; the handful of Bone 22 stayed one object and was not made again. She carried him down and up at the half-pace from every open slate, gave the instruction to the wool, the fire, the pot and the river wind and never to the basket, and went wide around the seven walked-around places with a look and a wide step and no number — the clean dark line and its finer grey called the thaw, the space beneath the lowest rack with its broken birth-slates, the gone pan’s round ring, the trough’s skin of ice, the field’s empty place and the returning-line place where a hand went in on Seed 15 and did not come out. The three coverings — the frost gone off the well’s north lip on Bone 3, the skin on the trough breaking and closing under a pail’s knock, the silt-clouded plate of ice on the flat stone out of the path of feet — stayed weather entered nowhere with a finger between every pair and no fourth likeness made a cause. The month’s hunts and repairs stayed directions judged by the carrying arm and the weather: the Cold Acre hare answered with the weather and gone toward the clay road with nobody weighing it or opening a slate, the cracked jar in a rope sling sent to the pot, and the pot said nothing. On Ash 2 at the well Ilva drew with the pail against her knee and answered a woman’s question about the firings with \emph{Ask the pot what it cost. I keep the count, not the account}, her strip unread and her ninth hand nine; nothing from that well crossed under the roof as sign, lesson, mending, cause or payment. With Tarn the exact account of six and the seventh went unremarked; with Jorra the men unnamed before first grey, the dust and the bent finger in the cold damper went unasked about and he gave the house no name for the men. On Ash 3 at the going of the light she carried him up at the half-pace, went wide around the seven places, set him on the bed under the roof and never in the Debt Loft, put the fold right at his ear and under his chin without a look at his face, let her hand rest the half-beat longer than the setting needed before it went away, left the thread where it lay and said nothing of where they had been; the small dry scrape of the loft came from above and behind earlier, with no interior entered. Garl’s name was unspoken three hundred and thirty, thirty-one and thirty-two days, his tile debt uncalled, his twice-mended pot’s crack showing and repair kept apart from restoration. Six arithmetics of the year stood behind one printed figure in Berr’s locked box, one in twelve printed and unchallenged and the figure read still not the figure paid. She wants the house kept as it is kept, with no figure spoken over what it does. No bond changed hands, no new scar or possession and no change of voice.

The widow’s mark hung where it hung at every morning, rack, well, yard, hearth and bed, because none was an opening; five openings in five months are five and not a rule. Garl’s name was unspoken three hundred and twenty-one, twenty-two and twenty-three days and his tile debt stayed uncalled; five arithmetics rode up the road in his locked box under one unsigned figure and no collector came. No tin or box was opened, no bond changed hands, no new scar or possession and no change of voice.

On the pot board the handle stood mended twice with the hairline of the crack dark between the staples; she put her thumb first where the wire crossed the crack, felt what the thumb had to feel and only then let the weight come on the handle, saying both proverbs to the pot and to the fire and never to a person, and left the crack showing. She set the pot rim two inches beyond the reaching hand with a half-beat and no look toward the bed, put the fold right at his ear and under his chin without a look at his face, and left the thread where it lay. In the yard she went wide around the seven walked-around places with a look and a wide step and no number: the clean dark line and its finer grey called the thaw, the space under the lowest rack with its broken birth-slates, the round ring where the shallow pan had stood, the water in the trough, the field’s empty place and the returning-line place where a hand went in on Seed 15 and did not come out. The carried fire answered four low pulls with the silence where the fifth should have stood, its payer unnamed three hundred and nine, ten and eleven days. No new scar, possession or change of voice, no lesson made of the reading, no bond paid or spoken.

The fire’s fifth went unsupplied for two hundred and eighty-two, eighty-three and eighty-four days with its payer unnamed (T088), and Frost’s first arithmetic stayed locked in Berr’s box up the clay road with the printed one in twelve unchallenged and the figure read still not the figure paid (T015/T041/T047). On the afternoon of Frost 14 she carried him down at the half-pace and up again at the going of the light while the yard well went about its small commerce; she heard nothing that made an opening and gave no instruction at any hour to the basket, and the saying that passed between two women at the well was not brought under the roof as a lesson, a joining, a cause or a figure (T080 advanced, not paid). No new scar or possession, no change of voice, no bond changed hands, no opening made and nothing paid.

The widow’s mark hung where it hung, touched once before the kiln on Frost 2 and at no shelf, well, rack, road, basket, yard, morning, hearth, afternoon, dusk or going of the light on Frost 10, 11 or 12, because none was an opening; the first firing of Frost stood behind the household with no lesson or payer and four openings remained four (T058/T079). She drew what the yard calls weather with the pail against her knee, told the weather where to stand, gave nobody a figure and said nothing to the basket. \item Ch 62: Days 237, 238 and 239, Grain 28–30, Eighthday to Tenthday, on stage on all three days at the fire, the loaf shelf, the hearth, the drying racks, the yard well, the terrace, the Cross, the moot-post’s thin shade, the clay road at the going of the light and the bed; offstage on none of the three.
