\CRsheetheading{Arc So Far}
The two gestures that will define her are on the page in Chapter 1: the crossed sign she does not know she makes in front of strangers, and the exact, unasked-for dates with which she covers it. In Chapter 2 both gestures repeat and a third is added. She reaches for the slate before the child again, touches the little tin on its cord twice more, crosses the sign over the flower in front of the boy without knowing it, and answers every unasked question with an exact history --- a cooper’s seventh in Mud End, the account going up on the eighth before the paper went out --- until the dates arrive faster than dates have any business arriving. Then she tells Dessa the boy went in the levy. The lie is told as mercy and cannot be undone. In Chapter 3 she keeps the birth-slates at the edge of the market, touches the tin a third time and makes the sign a third time in front of witnesses, and the date she uses to cover it is the same one she gave Dessa: the account up on the eighth, before the paper went out. The market goes on around the sign and the date and the red edge at a wrist, arranging itself around the things it does not read. The tin under the floorboard is years away from being read.

On Days 5 and 6 the tin is touched twice more and the second notes acquire a second hiding place. She comes under the Vail roof to look at the child she delivered, reaches for the slate before him, presses the fold at his shoulder too long, crosses the sign at the red edge of his wrist without knowing she does it in front of him, and answers a mother’s three questions with exact dates and a graft settling. In the death-house she sets her own slate writing-down on the bench and then writes a second note that she turns down and slides under a milk cup, where no mother and no officer will think to pick it up. She crosses her fingers again at a red mark at a rekindled child’s hairline without knowing it. The Court’s struck word is still not spoken in the room; the kindest voice in it is closing a question nobody opened, and the boy knows the shape of the gesture and has no sentence for it.

On Days 10 through 14 the lie and the writing go on together. She comes under the Vail roof on Stone 16 and reaches for the slate before the child, presses the fold flat too long, touches the tin once, crosses the sign at the red edge of his wrist without knowing it and covers it with the same unasked-for date she gave Dessa, then with more dates after the question has stopped. On a narrow slate she writes a second note of what she will not leave lying about and turns it face-down into her shawl, toward a floorboard in her house the boy cannot name; the note and the warmth of the fold are one gesture. The tin stays inside her bodice, unopened; neither this note nor the one under the milk cup in the death-house has been read. \emph{Warm and breathing} is said exactly and is a lie, and the sign is made a further time in front of a child who cannot hand it back.

On Days 15 through 24 the lie and the writing go on together and the hidden record grows another page. On Stone 24 she reaches for the slate before the child, touches the unopened tin, presses the fold too long, crosses the sign at the red edge of the flower without knowing it and covers it with the date she gave Dessa, then pours out dates after the question has stopped. She writes a further note that she does not leave lying and turns it face-down toward the floorboard, so that a third hidden record goes where no officer’s thumb will look. The boy cannot read Grathic, cannot ask which house holds the floorboard, cannot hand the gesture back; he keeps the sign and the turned slate beside the dust from the back room as two truths arranged in one morning by women who are kind. Dessa coughs from the pits three doors down and calls it weather, and the lie told for mercy is still a fact in her face. The tin stays shut and none of the notes has been read.

On Days 25 through 30 the lie and the gestures go on without the writing. On the Long Night she gives dates where wonder should stand in a story told in the dark, and the boy files the gap after the question with the intervals; on the Remembering she comes under the Vail roof with the birth-slates, lays a date where a name should stand, touches the tin once unopened and crosses two fingers at the red edge of the birth-flower without knowing it, covering the sign with the same date she gave Dessa. She is offstage on the Last Day and Ilmen 1. The boy cannot read Grathic, cannot ask which house holds the floorboard and cannot hand the gesture back; he keeps the sign and the date beside the unspoken name as truths arranged by a woman who is kind. The tin stays shut, no further note is written, and the lie told to Dessa for mercy is still a fact in her face.

On Days 31 through 37 the lie and the writing go on together and the hidden record grows a fourth page. On Ilmen 5 she reaches for the slate before the child, touches the unopened tin, presses the fold too long, crosses the sign at the red edge of the flower without knowing it and covers it with the date she gave Dessa, then pours out dates after the question has stopped. She writes a fourth note that she does not leave lying and turns it face-down toward the floorboard, so that another page goes where no officer’s thumb will look. Three doors down Dessa’s cough is worse and is called weather, and the note under the milk cup, the notes under the floorboard and the tin inside the bodice stay shut. The boy cannot read Grathic, cannot ask which house holds the floorboard and cannot hand the gesture back; he keeps the sign and the turned slate as two truths arranged in one morning by a woman who is kind.

On Days 38 through 44 the lie curdles against the death it was told to hide, and the writing goes on without the writing-down. On Ilmen 9 she came down from the road after the vessel had given, with lye and wet wool and the mineral edge of river water instead of soap and warm milk, and went to a narrow slate before she went to the body, laying it writing-down on a flat stone at the bank; her hand went once inside her bodice and touched the tin without opening it, and she did not say the woman’s name. She laid dates where a wonder should have stood and went on after there was no question left to answer; the boy lay in the basket on the bank and watched the order of reaching. On Ilmen 14 she came up the river road with soap-and-milk still on her and stood with Orra Weir in the lee of the Eel House, saying the date of the last high water where Orra said the river was up. Her hand went into her bodice once and came out empty; when a figure came near, she said the weather had turned and Orra said the river would do what the river did, and the subject changed so neatly nobody could have said it had been there. Nothing was said of the third day, no note was written, and the tin stayed shut while the lie she told for mercy became a fact nobody could correct.

On Days 45 through 47 the lie curdles and the gestures go on without the writing-down. On Day 46 she comes under the Vail roof with the birth-slates and reaches for them before she reaches for the child, presses the fold too long, touches the tin once and does not open it, makes the two-finger sign at the red edge of the flower without knowing it and covers it with the date she gave Dessa. The dates go on arriving after the question has stopped because dates are a handle on a thing too large to carry; \emph{warm and breathing} is exact and not true, and the death it can no longer be corrected against is six days old. She writes no new note and the tin stays shut. Three doors down the woman who believed the lie has been in the ground nine mornings, and the boy lies in a fold from which the smoky crust has quietly gone; she is one of the three hands he sets on a tray and refuses to turn into a cause.

On Days 48 through 54 the lie curdles and the gestures go on without the writing-down until a fifth page is added. On Day 51 she comes short under the Vail roof with soap-and-milk gone cold under river silt and lye under the soap, lays the birth-slates writing-down on the bench before she turns to the fold, presses the fold flat at his shoulder a breath too long, touches the tin once inside her bodice without opening it, and makes the two-finger sign at the flower’s red edge before she knows she has done it, covering it with the date she gave Dessa. The dates go on arriving after the question has stopped --- a cooper’s seventh in Mud End, a potter’s third child in Stonemouth, the last high water --- because dates are a handle on a thing too large to carry. She says \emph{Warm and breathing}, exact and not true, does not say the woman’s name or the third day, and writes a fifth note in the second hand which she turns face-down toward a floorboard in a house the boy cannot name. The lie told for mercy is eleven days old and has curdled all the way through to a death nobody entered that no living person can correct.

On Days 55 through 60 the lie curdles and the gestures go on without the writing-down. On Ilmen 27 she comes short under the roof three doors down with soap-and-milk gone cold under river silt and lye under the soap, lays the birth-slates writing-down on the bench before she turns to the fold, presses the fold flat at his shoulder a breath too long, crosses two fingers at the red edge of the flower before she knows she has done it and covers the sign with the date she gave Dessa, then goes on with the cooper’s seventh in Mud End and a potter’s third child in Stonemouth after there is no question left to answer. \emph{Warm and breathing} is said exactly and is not true; she touches the little tin inside her bodice without opening it, does not say the woman’s name or the third day, and writes no sixth note, so the hidden record stays at five and the sixth page waits for another week. Above the empty bed the pewter tin with its pale fold and thumb-bright lid keeps its place and neither tin is opened; two private records in two materials stand in one room on separate trays and are read by nobody. The lie told for mercy is now curdled all the way through to a death twenty-two mornings old that nobody entered and no living person can correct. Her hand is one of the three the boy keeps on a tray and does not turn into a cause.

On Days 61 through 67 the lie curdles and the hidden record gains its sixth page. On Silt 5 she comes short into the death-house room three doors down with soap-and-milk gone cold under river silt and lye sour under the soap, lays the birth-slates writing-down on the bench before she turns to the fold, presses the fold too long, touches the tin inside her bodice without opening it, crosses two fingers at the flower’s red edge without knowing it and covers the sign with the date she gave Dessa. \emph{Warm and breathing} is said exactly and is not true, and no living person can correct it against a woman twenty-six mornings dead. She goes on with her exact dates after the question has stopped, because dates are a handle on a thing too large to carry. Then, on the narrow slate, she writes in the second hand what she will not leave lying and turns it face-down into her shawl toward a floorboard in a house the boy cannot name: the sixth page, paid on Day 64 and read by nobody. Above the board-bed the pewter tin keeps its pale fold and thumb-bright lid, and in the fold of grey wool where the small pale river stone once lay there is only the hollow, which neither the house nor the boy mentions. Two private records in two materials stand in one room on separate trays, and she goes home to a house he cannot enter, with the date still laid over the sign and the number and the third day still unsaid.

On Days 68 through 74 the lie curdles against a death thirty-six mornings old and the writing stays where it is. She is offstage through the flood, and the sixth page written on Silt 5 lies turned face-down toward a floorboard in a house the boy cannot name, unread, while the little tin stays shut inside her bodice; three doors down the pewter tin above the empty bed keeps its pale fold and thumb-bright lid and nobody opens it. Two private records in two materials stand unread while the water rises and falls, and neither is carried to a door. The narrow page is not written again, the tin is not opened, and no living person can correct the mercy-lie told for a child who was never among the Forty. The number stays in Dessa’s thumb and the name under the sieve-wire scar and the third day is still unsaid, and her hand is one of three on the tray the boy refuses to turn into a cause.

On Days 75 through 77 the lie curdles against a death thirty-nine mornings old and the writing stays where it is. She comes short on Silt 17, lays the slates down before the fold, presses the fold too long, crosses the sign unknowing and covers it with the date given to Dessa; \emph{warm and breathing} is exact and not true, and she goes on with dates after the question stops because dates are a handle on a thing too large to carry. The sixth page written on Day 64 is not written again and is not paid again; the little tin and the pewter tin above the empty bed stay shut. Two private records in two materials stand unread in one room and are carried to no door, and the boy cannot enter either. Her hand stays on the tray with Sella’s and Mira’s and does not become a cause.

On Days 78 through 84 the lie curdles against a death forty mornings old and the writing stays where it is. On Silt 21 she comes short three doors down with soap-and-milk gone cold under river silt and lye sour under the soap, lays the writing-down on the bench before turning to the fold, presses the fold a breath too long, touches the tin inside her bodice without opening it, crosses two fingers at the flower’s red edge unaware and covers the sign with the exact date she gave Dessa. \emph{Warm and breathing} is said exactly and is not true, and she goes on with dates after the question has stopped because dates are a handle on a thing too large to carry. The date she laid over the sign now stands over a woman forty mornings dead and uncollected and cannot be taken off by any living person; the number stays in Dessa’s thumb, the name under the sieve-wire scar, the third day unsaid. The narrow sixth page written on Day 64 lies turned face-down toward a floorboard in a house the boy cannot name, unread, and no seventh is written. Above the empty bed the pewter tin keeps its pale fold and thumb-bright rub, unopened. Two private records in two materials stand apart in one room and are carried to no door. Her hand stays on the tray with Sella’s and Mira’s and does not become a cause.

On Days 85 through 90 the lie curdles against a death more mornings gone than any living person keeps count of, and the writing stays where it is. On Silt 28 she comes short three doors down in House Silt with soap-and-milk gone cold under river silt and lye sour under the soap, nails scrubbed to the quick with clay still under them, the birth-slates under her arm; she lays the writing-down on the bench before she turns to the fold, in the order of a hand that reaches for the record before the person, presses the fold flat at his shoulder a breath longer than a fold requires, crosses two fingers at the red edge of the birth-flower before she knows it and covers the sign with the exact date she gave Dessa --- the seventh of Stone, the account up on the eighth --- which now stands over a woman nobody alive can correct. To Sella’s \emph{he lies quiet} she says \emph{Warm and breathing, that’s all I’ve set down}, exact and not true, and goes on with dates after the question has stopped, because dates are a handle on a thing too large to carry. Her hand goes once to the little tin inside her bodice and comes away without opening it; her sixth narrow slate, written in the second hand on Day 64, stays face-down toward a floorboard in a house the boy cannot name, six pages all unread, no seventh written and T023 not paid again. Above the abandoned board-bed the round pewter tin keeps its pale fold at the seam and thumb-bright rub on the lid, unopened, and the grey wool below holds only the hollow where the small pale river stone lay; nobody says either is gone. Two private records in two materials stand apart in one room, read by nobody and carried to no door, and she sets them on separate places without a cause written across them. The month turns into Seed with the date still over the sign and the number still in a thumb gone into the water; her hand stays on the tray with Sella’s and Mira’s and does not become a cause.

\CRsheetheading{Chapter Log}
\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item Ch 1: Delivered Corin in the front room of House Silt and worked with steady hands, clay under her nails. Reached for the slate before the child. Put her two fingers to the branching flower, noticed she had done it before witnesses, and covered the act with \emph{birth-flower} plus an unasked-for history from Nine Pots: Y.H. 806, fourth day of Stone, a potter’s third child, now a carter in Stonemouth. Touched the tin at her bodice twice. Gave a date and a weather report for the unasked question and said warm and breathing was all she had set down. Closed the slate flat on the bench while Sella Vail’s hand hovered in the door.

\item Ch 2: On Day 2 washed the child in her order, reached for the slate first, touched the tin a further time, made the crossed sign over the flower before witnesses without knowing it, and gave a date and weather where comfort was expected. On Day 3 stood behind Dessa at the end of the Clay Yard and told her the boy was entered in the levy among the children taken for the account that month, that the account went up on the eighth before the paper went out, and that a woman with a thin return who goes asking draws a hand down on a slate better left where it lay. Said warm and breathing was all she had set down. The number was never spoken; she went on giving dates after the question had stopped.

\item Ch 3: Day 4, Account-day. Kept the birth-slates under her arm and in a row on a bench at the fringe of the market, turning the writing down when a mother came near. Touched the tin inside her bodice once, the third sighting of it, when there was no question in the air to answer. Saw the edge of the birth-flower at the boy’s wrist, crossed two fingers at the corner of it without knowing she had done it in front of a market full of people, and covered the sign with an exact, unasked-for date: \emph{Stone seven; the account went up on the eighth, before the paper went out.} Nobody commented on the sign or the date or the red edge; the two women bargaining over short weight went on standing side by side without making their figures agree.

\end{itemize}

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item Ch 4: Days 5 and 6. Came under the Vail roof on Stone 11 to see the child she delivered, reached for the slate before him, pressed the fold flat at his shoulder longer than a fold required, touched the tin inside her bodice, crossed two fingers at the red edge of the flower at his wrist without knowing he saw it, and gave exact dates where the neighbour mother asked for comfort: \emph{Stone seven; the account went up on the eighth, before the paper went out.} Called the rekindled child’s second chill a graft settling and wrote on her own slate what she then turned writing-down on the bench. On Stone 12, in the death-house, touched the tin again, wrote a second note, turned it down and slid it under a milk cup, crossed the sign at a red mark at the child’s hairline, and went on giving dates after the questions had stopped. Neither note was read and the tin was not opened.

\end{itemize}

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item Ch 6: Day 10, Stone 16. Came under the Vail roof at mid-morning with soap and warm milk on her and the birth-slates under her arm; reached for the slate before the child and laid it writing-down on the bench. Pressed the fold flat at his shoulder too long, touched the little tin once inside her bodice, and crossed two fingers at the red edge of the branching mark at his wrist without knowing she did it in front of him. Covered the sign with \emph{Stone seven; the account went up on the eighth, before the paper went out}, then with the cooper’s seventh in Mud End and a potter’s third child in Stonemouth, going on after there was no question to stop. Took up a narrow slate and wrote on it what she did not leave lying about, then turned it writing-down into her shawl toward a floorboard in her house he does not know. Said \emph{Warm and breathing --- that’s all I’ve set down} to Sella’s \emph{he lies quiet}. The tin was touched once and never opened; the note was not read.

\end{itemize}

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item Ch 7: Day 18, Stone 24, came under the Vail roof at mid-morning with soap and warm milk and the smell of lye on her, the birth-slates under her arm; laid them writing-down on the bench before she turned to the fold and pressed the fold flat at his shoulder longer than a fold required. Reached once to the little tin inside her bodice and came away without opening it. Saw the red edge of the birth-flower where the wool had ridden back, crossed two fingers at the corner of it before she knew she had done it, and covered the sign with \emph{Stone seven; the account went up on the eighth, before the paper went out}, then with the cooper’s seventh in Mud End and a potter’s third child in Stonemouth, going on after there was no question left. Said \emph{Warm and breathing --- that’s all I’ve set down} to Sella’s \emph{he lies quiet}, which was exact and not true. Took up a narrow slate, wrote what she did not leave lying about in a second hand, and turned it writing-down into her shawl toward a floorboard in a house the boy could not name, where a further note would go into the tin still unread. Three doors down Dessa’s cough went on being weather.

\end{itemize}

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item Ch 8: Days 27 and 28. On the Long Night sat in the dark under the Vail roof with the fire out and told the hearth-maid’s account in which dates stand where wonder should be, going on after the question had stopped; made the two-finger sign at the red edge of his wrist without knowing it. On the Remembering came under the roof with the birth-slates and the smell of soap and warm milk, laid an exact date where a name should stand, touched the tin once inside her bodice without opening it, pressed the fold flat too long at his shoulder, crossed two fingers at the red edge of the birth-flower before she knew she had done it, and covered the sign with the same unasked-for date she had given Dessa. Wrote no new note and went home to a house the boy cannot name; offstage on the Last Day and Ilmen 1, and the lie went on standing.

\end{itemize}

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item Ch 9: Day 34, Ilmen 5, came under the Vail roof smelling of soap and warm milk with the birth-slates under her arm; laid them writing-down on the bench before she turned to the fold, pressed the fold flat at his shoulder too long, reached once to the little tin inside her bodice and came away without opening it. Saw the red edge of the birth-flower where the wool had ridden back, crossed two fingers at it before she knew she had done it, and covered the sign with \emph{Stone seven; the account went up on the eighth, before the paper went out}, then with the cooper’s seventh in Mud End and a potter’s third child in Stonemouth, going on after there was no question left. To Sella’s \emph{he lies quiet} said \emph{Warm and breathing --- that’s all I’ve set down}, exact and not true. Took up a narrow slate, wrote what she would not leave lying in a second hand no Court physician had seen, and turned it writing-down into her shawl toward a floorboard in a house the boy could not name: a fourth note for the tin, still unread. Three doors down Dessa’s cough went on being weather.

\end{itemize}

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item Ch 10: Days 38 and 43. On Ilmen 9 came down to the Slip Brook after Dessa Silt had given, with lye and wet wool and the mineral edge of the water in place of soap and warm milk; reached for the narrow slate before the body and laid it writing-down on a flat stone at the bank, touched the tin once inside her bodice without opening it, did not say the woman’s name, and laid dates --- Stone seven, the account up on the eighth, a cooper’s seventh, a potter’s third child --- over the body as she would have laid them over a cradle, going on after there was no question left. On Ilmen 14 stood with Orra Weir in the lee of the Eel House, gave the date of the last high water, touched the tin once and came away empty, and let a figure for the traps change into weather; nothing was said of the third day. No new note was written and the tin stayed shut. The lie told to Dessa is now a fact in a dead woman’s face that nobody can correct.

\end{itemize}

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item Ch 11: Day 46, Ilmen 17. Came short under the Vail roof at mid-morning with soap-and-warm-milk gone cold under river silt, lye under the soap, the birth-slates under her arm; laid them writing-down on the bench before she turned to the fold, pressed the fold flat at his shoulder a breath too long, touched the tin once inside her bodice without opening it, and crossed two fingers at the red edge of the birth-flower before she knew she had done it. Covered the sign with the date she gave Dessa --- Stone seven, the account up on the eighth --- and went on with the cooper’s seventh in Mud End, a potter’s third child in Stonemouth and the last high water after there was no question left. Said \emph{Warm and breathing --- that’s all I’ve set down}, exact and not true; did not say the woman’s name or the third day, wrote no new note and went away with the tin still shut. Offstage on Days 45 and 47. One of the three hands on the boy’s tray of possible takers of the crust.

\end{itemize}

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item Ch 12: Day 51, Ilmen 22. Came short under the Vail roof with soap-and-milk gone cold under river silt and lye under the soap, the birth-slates under her arm; laid them writing-down on the bench before she turned to the fold, pressed the fold flat at his shoulder a breath too long, touched the tin once inside her bodice without opening it, and crossed two fingers at the red edge of the birth-flower before she knew she had done it, covering the sign with the date she gave Dessa. Went on with the cooper’s seventh in Mud End, a potter’s third child in Stonemouth and the last high water after there was no question left. Said \emph{Warm and breathing}, exact and not true; did not say the woman’s name or the third day. Wrote a fifth note in the second hand and turned it face-down toward a floorboard in a house the boy cannot name. The lie told for mercy is eleven days old and curdles against a death nobody entered.

\end{itemize}

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item Ch 13: Day 56, Ilmen 27. Came short into House Silt with soap-and-milk gone cold under river silt and lye under the soap, the birth-slates under her arm; laid them writing-down on the bench before she turned to the fold, pressed the fold flat at his shoulder a breath too long, made the two-finger sign at the flower’s red edge before she knew it and covered it with the date she gave Dessa (T007). Went on giving dates after there was no question left --- a cooper’s seventh in Mud End, a potter’s third child in Stonemouth --- and said \emph{Warm and breathing}, exact and not true (T008, T073). Touched the tin inside her bodice without opening it and wrote no sixth note; the hidden record stays at five and the sixth page waits for Day 64 (T023). Did not say the woman’s name or the third day; above the empty bed the pewter tin kept its pale fold and thumb-bright lid unopened (T089). The lie told for mercy has curdled through to a death twenty-two mornings old that no living person can correct. Her hand is one of three on the boy’s tray of possible takers of the crust.

\end{itemize}

Said \emph{warm and breathing}, exact and not true, and went on with dates after the question stopped. \textbf{Wrote the withheld sixth note in the second hand and turned it face-down into her shawl toward a floorboard in a house the boy could not name; the hidden record grew from five pages to six, unread, and bought no recognition (T023 paid here and nowhere earlier).} Did not say the woman’s name or the third day; the pewter tin above the bed stayed unopened. \CRcharacter{Orra Weir}{the woman who keeps the traps and counts the names}{build/portraits/orra-weir.pdf}{\CRfield{Also called}{Orra, Orra of the Weir, the trap-keeper}\CRfield{Role}{ally}\CRfield{Born}{Y.H. 778, the Weir, Grath}\CRfield{Kind}{human (Grathic)}\CRfield{Origin}{the Weir, one league upriver of Sill, Grath}\CRfield{Allegiance}{the eel traps at the Weir; the Fish Blessing; House Weir}\CRfield{Status}{alive — the long vigil held at the Weir through Tallow 20 (Day 169), the word forty still unspoken and the forty-first double turn still legible and unnamed; gave the ninth of Ilmen, the boat of six oars and the man at the stern where a figure was asked on Day 167, her thumb’s return still undecided}\CRfield{First seen}{Chapter 10}}{\CRsheetheading{Appearance}
Thirty-four, with hands like old rope and a grey streak through black hair from a winter she spent on the weir when she was twenty and would do again. Eel scars lie across both forearms in pale arcs, and she never covers them, because a trap-keeper without scars is a trap-keeper who does not work. She smells of river silt, cold fish and tallow smoke, and in the spring of wet mud so strongly that people at the Cross know she has come before they see her. She keeps her accounts in knots on a cord of grey wool and will not sit at a table where a slate is open; she learned the habit from a Fen woman who sold her reed and taught her that a written name is a name somebody else can read. The thing people notice first is the grey streak; the thing they notice last is the cord, which she touches when a number is spoken.

\CRsheetheading{Voice \& Manner}
Slow, and when she is tired the nasal half-song of the Fen comes into it, which she has never entirely lost. She tells a story sideways and gives a date where another person would give an opinion. She never answers a question about the levy directly, but she will tell you which night the collector’s boat came and how many oars it had. When she is lying she ties a knot, which is invisible to anyone who does not know the cord.

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item “I don’t keep names on slate. Slates burn. Knots don’t.”

\item “Forty. I tied forty knots in the year of the flower. I tied one more and I don’t know what to call it.”

\item “The river takes what the Court doesn’t. You can shout at either one. I’ve tried.”

\item “A trap works because the eel can’t see the way out. That’s all a trap is. Don’t make it more than that.”

\item “You’re the Vail boy. You’ve got her eyes and somebody else’s listening.”

\item “The ninth of Ilmen. The collector’s boat came round the bend on the flood and had six oars. One man stood at the stern and never touched them.” --- given on Reed 18 where a levy figure was asked; to \emph{That isn’t the levy}, \emph{It’s a date. The river takes what the Court doesn’t. You can shout at either one. I’ve tried.}

\end{itemize}

\CRsheetheading{History}
She was born at the Weir, one league upriver of Sill, where the eel traps stand on a plank walk and the Fish Blessing is held on Ilmen 15. She has kept the traps since she was eighteen, knows the river’s moods better than the weather, and can tell a collector’s boat by its oars before it comes round the bend. She married a man who went downriver with a cart of pots and never came back, and has not looked for him, which she calls \emph{not being a fool about it}. Her son Kess was one of the forty children of Low Kiln banked in the first weeks of Stone, Y.H. 812. No return has been announced for him. She tied forty knots that year and then tied a forty-first, because on the night the children were taken she saw Sella Vail carry a covered bundle up the Clay Yard, and the bundle was small and warm and had a flower on it, and she could not account for it.

She was in the room on Stone 7 when the child with the branching red flower was born, and she saw the collector’s slate that night, and saw a name written on it before anyone had seen the infant’s face. She cannot spell the name; she remembers its shape, which is a thing no Court clerk can take away.

\CRsheetheading{Wounds \& Fears}
A son spent for a return that never came. She has gone to the Bone Orchard twice looking for a shallow grave with his name on it and found none, which is worse than finding one, because it means his warmth was banked and not wasted and is somewhere in an account she will never see. She fears the Weighing, where whole returns are announced in a clean voice to people whose children are not coming back. She fears that the forty-first knot is a thing she has made into a mystery because a plain answer would be too ordinary: the boy she saw carried was simply another child, and she has needed him not to be. Her contradiction: she sells eels to the Court’s clerk and hates the Court, and has learned the collector’s schedule in order to avoid him and also in order to be there when he comes.

\CRsheetheading{Desires}
She wants her son returned whole, which she knows will not happen, and she wants somebody else to say his name who is not herself. She thinks she wants to know what happened to the boy in the covered bundle. What she needs is to understand that a mother’s account is never settled by a return, whole or thin, and that the knot cord is not a ledger but a way of continuing to hold on to something the Court has already booked.

\CRsheetheading{Bonds}
\textbf{Kess} — her son, one of the Forty. She has a knot for him and no return, and has begun to speak to the knot in the evening, which she knows is not sensible and does not stop.

\textbf{Corin} — the Vail boy. She sees something in him that belongs to the year of the flower and cannot place it: the way he turns his head, the mark under his sleeve, the attention of a person much older than his body. She has never said this to anyone except the cord.

\textbf{Sella Vail} — she blames Sella for taking a child at the very moment forty others were taken, and has never said why she blames her, which leaves the blame floating free and available for anything.

\textbf{Dessa Silt} — they were both in the room on Stone 7. Dessa believes her baby died; Orra knows she is lying and has not said. It is the one thing she has never sold at the Fishstairs.

\textbf{Alda Reed} — the only person with whom she has ever discussed the third day. They do not discuss the birth-flower. They discuss the weather and the river and occasionally the number forty, and then one of them touches something and the subject changes.

\textbf{Mira Silt} — her eel buyer, her friend, and the one person she lets near the knots. Mira wants the secret out; Orra wants it kept, which is the only disagreement in a friendship of fifteen years.

\textbf{Berr Clay, the Thane of Clay} — bought her eels for the levy feast and paid two marks short. She has never forgiven the arithmetic, and has served him the same short measure ever since.

\textbf{Ch 10.} Her first appearance is moved forward from the planned Chapter 12 to Chapter 10 so that the word \emph{forty} can land in the boy’s hearing at the Fish Blessing. She comes onstage on Ilmen 14, rope-handed and eel-scarred, smelling of silt, cold fish and tallow, telling a story sideways and giving a date where another woman would give an opinion, with the collector’s boat and its oars where a direct answer should be; her knot-accounts are in the Eel House and she will not sit at a table where a slate lies open. On Ilmen 15 she keeps the accounts in knots on grey wool, tells the boy that an eel goes into a trap and cannot find the way out, ties a forty-first knot she cannot account for over the story of a small warm covered bundle with a flower carried up the Clay Yard in the year of the flower, says \emph{forty} low into the basket and watches what he does with it. He is too young to answer. She does not know that he is the child in the bundle, and she keeps the watching. Alda stands with her in the lee of the Eel House and the third day is not spoken of; Mira keeps her own grey wool beside the knot-string without either woman saying what she knows.

\textbf{Ch 11.} She came down from the Weir on Day 45 with eels, with silt and cold fish and tallow smoke going ahead of her, pale eel scars uncovered and the grey knot-string at her waist worrying under her thumb. The boy could now read the shape of the forty-first knot --- double turn, tail tucked, tied left over right, the small extra weight of a thumb --- but not its name, and she watched him watching without saying the word a second time or asking what he had made of it. Once she tied a knot, pulled it down with her thumb and set it among the others; at the end of the morning the cord went back upriver to the Eel House, where no clerk could spell it and no boy could read it. She gave a date where another woman would have given an opinion and kept the watching, which has had no answer.

\textbf{Ch 15.} She is offstage through the flood except for one morning. On Silt 13, as the water fell, she came down from the Weir before light with silt on her boots and the smell of cold fish and tallow going ahead of her, the grey streak showing first through the black hair, the pale eel scars uncovered across both forearms and her hands like old rope. She stood at the edge where the water had gone down to the last wrinkle with her board and her cord and nothing else, set the board on its side and turned it with her wrist, the turn of a person who has done it ten thousand times, and did not speak. Once she pulled a knot down with her thumb and set it among the others and did not look into the basket. She gave a date where another woman would have given an opinion, and here there was not even a date, only the standing and the cord and the board turned on its side. The boy watched her watching him and the watching got no answer; the cord went back upriver to the Eel House where no clerk could spell it and no boy could read it, and the word was not spoken. Her board lay beside Mira’s on the Fishstairs boards and did not touch it.

\textbf{Ch 27 (bonds).} On Reed 3 she stood at the lower boards of the Weir with her board on its side and a cord at her waist, pulling one knot down with her thumb and setting it among the others. When a weir woman asked her a question about the levy she gave a date instead of an answer and went back to the knots; when the reed-cutter lifted his bundle she watched what there was to watch at the edge of the shade and got no answer from the basket. She did not ask and nobody asked her. The shape of the last knot on her cord was legible to the boy without its name and he did not spend it; the word forty stayed unspoken. Her cord lay beside Mira’s board and did not touch it, and a third private record — the reed-cutter’s tally in wool gone grey with handling — passed along the same boards unread, not joined to hers and not carried to any door. The long vigil holds: she has set a thing down in front of him and is waiting to see whether it will be picked up, and a baby with no hand that can reach a league upriver cannot pick it up. No new scar, possession or change of voice.

\textbf{Ch 28 (bonds).} On Reed 6 she stood at the lower boards of the Weir with her board on its side and a cord at her waist, pulling one knot down with her thumb and setting it among the others; her hands were like old rope and the pale eel scars lay uncovered across both forearms, and the nasal half-song of the Fen came into her voice where she was tired, as it had at the blessing and every morning since. When the weir woman with salt white at her wrists asked what the levy would take now the hands were out of the reeds, Orra gave a date instead of a figure: \emph{The ninth of Ilmen. The collector’s boat came round the bend on the flood and had six oars. One man stood at the stern and never touched them.} To \emph{That isn’t the levy} she said \emph{It’s a date. The river takes what the Court doesn’t. You can shout at either one. I’ve tried}, and pulled another knot down. Her thumb went to the cord again as the sentence ended, and the boy could not tell whether that was a lie or only the habit of counting and did not make a cause of it. When the reed-cutter lifted his bundle off the stone she watched what there was to watch at the edge of the shade and got no answer from the basket; nobody asked her and she did not ask. The shape of the last knot on her cord was legible without its name — double turn, tail tucked, left over right, the small extra weight of a thumb — and the boy did not spend it. Her board lay beside Mira’s eel board and did not touch it; the reed-cutter’s tally went past unread, a third private record not joined to hers. The word forty stayed unspoken and the long vigil held: she has set a thing down in front of him and is waiting to see whether it will be picked up, and a baby with no hand that can reach a league upriver cannot pick it up. No new scar, possession or change of voice.

\textbf{Ch 29 (bonds).} On Reed 9 she stood at the lower boards of the Weir with her board on its side and a cord at her waist, turning the board with the wrist that had turned it ten thousand times. Her hands were like old rope and the pale eel scars lay uncovered across both forearms; the grey streak showed first through the black hair when she moved her head, and the nasal half-song she had never lost came into her voice where she was tired. She pulled one knot down with her thumb and set it among the others. When a woman at the rails asked what the levy would take now the hands were out of the reeds, she gave a date instead of a figure: \emph{The ninth of Ilmen. The collector’s boat came round the bend on the flood and had six oars. One man stood at the stern and never touched them.} To \emph{That isn’t the levy} she said \emph{It’s a date. The river takes what the Court doesn’t. You can shout at either one. I’ve tried}, and went back to the knots. Her thumb went to the cord again as the sentence ended, and the boy could not tell whether that was a lie or only the habit of counting and did not make a cause of it. A date given where a figure was asked was an answer with the question taken out of it, a chart closed over a note nobody had opened, and he set it where it belonged; the man at the stern who kept his hands off the oars was set on a place of its own, apart from the midwife’s reaching hand and the thane’s twice-wiped thumb, and no cause written across the three. She watched what there was to watch at the edge of the shade when the reed-cutter lifted his bundle and got no answer from the basket; she did not ask and nobody asked her. The shape of the last knot on her cord was legible without its name — double turn, tail tucked, left over right, the small extra weight of a thumb — and the boy did not spend it. The word forty stayed unspoken and the long vigil held: she has set a thing down in front of him and is waiting to see whether it will be picked up, and a baby with no hand that can reach a league upriver cannot pick it up. No new scar, possession or change of voice.

The reed-cutter tied one knot low with his teeth on the flat blessing stone, bit the end off and put his grey cord back inside his coat; she watched what there was to watch and got no answer from the basket, and did not ask and was not asked. The long vigil held.

\CRsheetheading{Arc So Far}
She enters in Chapter 10, two chapters ahead of the planting marker on her sheet, at the Weir one league upriver of Sill. On Ilmen 14 the boy is carried up the river road past the Cross where she has just been spoken of as a roof that has stood in a storm; she lifts a trap with a turn of the wrist that has done it ten thousand times and looks at the basket only after the trap is set on its side. On Ilmen 15, with the hearth-maids blessing the traps from the flat stone and the eels running as they always run, she ties the forty-first knot over a story told sideways and says the word into the basket. She watches. He cannot answer, and does not forget the shape of the cord. Her cord and Mira’s two cords stand side by side in the boy’s private file and do not join, and he has no standing to ask either woman what she keeps. The long vigil begins here, with a word a baby cannot spend.

Three more days pass with the cord upriver and the word unspoken. On Day 45 she comes down with eels and works among them while the boy, who could only hold the shape of the forty-first knot the night before, reads it now as a double turn with a tucked tail and the weight of a thumb, without a name for it in any tongue he has. She watches him watching, ties a knot and pulls it down with her thumb, does not say the word again and takes the cord back to the Eel House. The long vigil continues: she has set a thing down in front of him and is waiting to see whether it will be picked up, and a baby with no hand that can reach a league upriver cannot pick it up. The shape is on its own tray beside an unspoken saying and the weight of the thumb is apart from both.

Through Days 68 to 74 the long vigil holds through a flood and is not answered. She is offstage for all but Silt 13, when she comes down from the Weir before light with silt on her boots and cold fish and tallow going ahead of her, the grey streak showing first and the pale eel scars uncovered, and stands at the edge where the water has gone down with her board and her cord and nothing else. She turns the board on its side with her wrist, pulls a knot down with her thumb and sets it among the others, gives a date where another woman would give an opinion and here gives not even a date, and does not look into the basket or say the word. The boy watches her watching him and the watching gets no answer; the cord goes back upriver to the Eel House where no clerk can spell it and no boy can read it, and her board lies beside Mira’s without touching it. She has set a thing down in front of him and is waiting to see whether it will be picked up, and a baby with no hand that can reach a league upriver cannot pick it up.

Through Reed 1–3 the long vigil holds at the Weir and is not answered. On Reed 3 she came to the lower boards with her board on its side and a cord at her waist, and pulled one knot down with her thumb and set it among the others. The shape of the last knot was legible to the boy without its name and he did not spend it; the word forty stayed unspoken. She gave a date where the weir woman asked for a figure about the levy and went back to the knots, and when a reed-cutter came along the boards with a bundle on his shoulder and a short length of grey cord looped inside his coat, she watched what there was to watch at the edge of the shade and got no answer from the basket. She did not ask and nobody asked her. Her board lay beside Mira’s and did not touch it, and the reed-cutter’s tally — knots at arm’s length with one tied low by teeth and thumb — went past along the same boards unread, a third private record in a material no Court thumb would read, not joined to her cord and not carried away from the Weir. The cord went back upriver to the Eel House where no clerk could spell it and no boy could read it, and she keeps the count, which in Sarn is the most subversive act available to a person with no slate.

On Day 125 the long vigil holds at the lower boards and the date takes the place of the figure once more. She comes to the boards with her board on its side and a cord at her waist, pulls one knot down with her thumb and sets it among the others, her hands like old rope and the pale eel scars uncovered across both forearms; the grey streak shows first through the black hair when she turns her head, and the half-sung nasal of the Fen comes into her voice where she is tired. To the weir woman who asks what the levy will take now the hands are out of the reeds she answers with the ninth of Ilmen and a collector’s boat that came round the bend on the flood with six oars and one man at the stern who never touched them; when the woman says that is not the levy she says it is a date, that the river takes what the Court does not, that a person can shout at either one, and that she has tried. A date given where a figure was asked is an answer with the question taken out of it, a chart with the finding left off and the neat margin left in, and the boy sets it where it belongs and makes no cause of it. Her thumb goes to the cord as the sentence ends and he cannot tell lie from habit. When the reed-cutter lifts his bundle she watches what there is to watch at the edge of the shade and gets no answer from the basket; the shape of the last knot is legible without its name and she does not spend it. The word forty stays where it has stayed since the year of the flower, unspoken in a morning that has a great many figures in it and not one he can enter, and her board lies beside Mira’s and does not touch it.

On Days 126 through 128 the long vigil holds and the word forty stays unspoken. She is offstage on Reed 7 and 8 and stands at the lower boards of the Weir on Reed 9 with her board on its side and a cord at her waist, turning it with the wrist that has turned it ten thousand times; her hands are like old rope, the pale eel scars lie uncovered across both forearms and the nasal half-song of the Fen comes into her voice where she is tired. She pulls one knot down with her thumb and sets it among the others. Asked what the levy will take now the hands are out of the reeds she gives a date where another woman would give an opinion — \emph{The ninth of Ilmen. The collector’s boat came round the bend on the flood and had six oars. One man stood at the stern and never touched them} — and to the answer that it is not the levy she says \emph{It’s a date. The river takes what the Court doesn’t. You can shout at either one. I’ve tried}. Her thumb goes to the cord again as the sentence ends, and the boy cannot tell whether it is a lie or the habit of counting and makes no cause of it. The man who stands at the stern keeping his hands off the oars is the man whose work is the counting of other men’s pulling, and the boy sets the untouched hand on a place of its own apart from the midwife’s reaching hand and the thane’s twice-wiped thumb. Her knot-string lies beside Mira Silt’s board and does not touch it; the last knot shows its shape — double turn, tail tucked, left over right, the small extra weight of a thumb pressed in — and she does not spend it. Three accounts of the district stand on the boards in wool and teeth and thumb, and the Court’s neat slate stands ready a league downriver for a measure nobody called; the boy can see every one and enter none. The reed-cutter’s tally goes past unread, a third private record not joined to hers. She watches at the edge of the shade and gets no answer from the basket, and the vigil goes on.

The ninth of Ilmen, the boat of six oars and the man at the stern who never touched them stand on her place beside the told bell and the twice-wiped thumb, joined to no account. The forty-first double turn is legible without its name; the word forty is unspoken and the long vigil holds. Her board lies beside Mira’s and does not touch it, and the reed-cutter’s cord goes past unread.

Through the third week of Tallow the long vigil keeps its shape at the lower boards and the count stays in the cord where no clerk can read it. The reed work is a direction judged by the arm that carried it; a cost asked as a direction is answered with the river and the weather and leaves no entry. She gives a date where a figure is asked and keeps the question out of the answer; her thumb returns to the cord at the end of the sentence and the boy reads neither lie nor habit into it. The small flat knock of a knot laid where it belongs stays apart from the small flat knock of a vessel cracked all the way through. Her forty-first double turn is still legible without its name, the word forty is still unspoken, and the cord goes back upriver to the Eel House. She has set a thing down in front of him and is waiting to see whether it will be picked up, and a league of river still lies between her cord and the small hand outside the wool.

\CRsheetheading{Chapter Log}
\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item Ch 10: Days 43 and 44. On Ilmen 14 she was spoken of at the Cross as a roof a woman had stood under in a storm, and came onstage at the top of the rise with her sleeves wet to the elbow, lifting a trap with a turn of the wrist and setting it on its side before she looked at the basket. The grey streak showed first through the black hair, the pale eel scars lay uncovered across both forearms, her hands were like old rope, and the knot-string at her waist was the thing people noticed last. She told the pot that an eel goes in and cannot find the way out, and said not to make more of a trap than that. On Ilmen 15, with the hearth-maids blessing the traps from the flat stone, she took a fresh length of grey wool and tied a forty-first knot while telling sideways the story of a small warm bundle carried up the Clay Yard in the year of the flower, tied a knot when a lie went into it, said \emph{forty} low into the basket and watched what the boy did with the word. He was too young to answer. She stood with Alda Reed in the lee of the Eel House, gave a date where the other woman gave the weather, touched her cord when a figure came near and let the subject change; nothing was said of the third day. Mira’s grey wool kept its own board beside hers and the two did not touch.

\end{itemize}

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item Ch 11: Day 45. Came down from the Weir with eels, rope-hands wet and dried thirty years, pale eel scars uncovered, the grey streak showing first and the knot-string at her waist worrying under her thumb; silt, cold fish and tallow smoke arrived ahead of her. Worked among the eels while the boy watched, and he could now read the shape of the forty-first knot she had tied at the blessing --- a double turn with the tail tucked, tied left over right, the small extra weight of a thumb --- though he had no name for it. She did not say the word again and did not ask what he had made of it; once she tied a knot and pulled it down with her thumb and set it among the others, and at the end of the morning the cord went back upriver to the Eel House. She watched him watching and got no answer. Offstage on Days 46 and 47.

\end{itemize}

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item Ch 15: Days 68–74, Silt 9–15. Offstage through the flood except on Silt 13, when she came down from the Weir before light as the water fell, with silt on her boots and the smell of cold fish and tallow going ahead of her, the grey streak showing first through the black hair, the pale eel scars uncovered across both forearms and her hands like old rope. Stood at the edge where the water had gone down to the last wrinkle with her board and her cord and nothing else, set the board on its side and turned it with her wrist, pulled one knot down with her thumb and set it among the others, and did not look into the basket. Gave a date where another woman would have given an opinion and here gave not even a date, only the standing and the cord and the board turned on its side. The boy watched her watching him and the watching got no answer; the cord went back upriver to the Eel House where no clerk could spell it and no boy could read it, and the word was not spoken. Her board lay beside Mira’s without touching it.

\end{itemize}

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item Ch 23: Day 108, Seed 19, at the dawn market below the north bridge. Came down from the Weir before light with silt on her boots and the grey streak showing first through her black hair, and stood at the edge of the fish-trade shade where Mira worked the eels. The shape of the last knot on her cord was legible to the boy without its name, but he did not count it and the word forty stayed unspoken in a market where a great many figures went past him and none had his number in them. She stood where she stood, watched what there was to watch and got no answer; her board lay beside Mira Silt’s and did not touch it, and the knot-string went back upriver to the Eel House unread. The boy’s two tellings of the shelf and the watcher’s late turn were kept on three places apart, and no finger was laid across them. Offstage on Seed 18 and 20.

\end{itemize}

Her board lay beside Mira’s and did not touch it; the reed-cutter’s tally went past unread, a third private record in a material no Court thumb would read, not joined to her cord. The cord went back upriver to the Eel House where no clerk could spell it and no boy could read it. No new scar, possession or change of voice.

\CRcharacter{Siv of the First Seam}{the man who kept the page that was crossed out}{build/portraits/siv-first-seam.pdf}{\CRfield{Also called}{Siv of the First Seam, Siv, the surveyor, the hunter of the deep seam}\CRfield{Role}{ally}\CRfield{Born}{Y.H. 770, Keld Keep, the Rim}\CRfield{Kind}{human (Keldish)}\CRfield{Origin}{Keld Keep, the First Seam, the Rim}\CRfield{Allegiance}{the Keldish survey of the rim-seam; the Order of the Tenth Clamp; hunter of seam-serpents}\CRfield{Status}{alive}\CRfield{First seen}{Chapter 200}}{\CRsheetheading{Appearance}
Forty-two, with the stillness of a man who has spent twenty years sitting in a shaft listening to stone, which makes him seem slower than he is and much harder to interrupt. He is tall for Keldish and slightly stooped from the low roof of the survey, with a thin grey scar across the bridge of his nose from a Warm-flood he did not get out of fast enough, and eyes that have adjusted to dark seams and therefore look vaguely at people in daylight. His measure-number is tattooed on his forearm in hard Keldish numerals and has never been cut out, which in the First Seam is a statement of confidence or stubbornness. He carries a bone tally on a cord and makes marks on it with a nail when a number changes, and he does not carry a clamp, which is unusual for a man of the Order and is the first thing Hald Iron notices about him. He smells of cold stone, hot lead, coal smoke and the particular mineral sweetness that comes just before the Sweating. The thing people notice first is the scar; the thing they notice last is that he listens to walls before he listens to the person standing next to one.

\CRsheetheading{Voice \& Manner}
Slow, clipped, numerical, with the Keldish habit of putting the number before the noun — \emph{two seams, one passing, no name for it}. He gives dates where another man would give a judgement and has never in his life offered an opinion about a thing he has not measured. When the Vorr say \emph{the numbers are correct}, he writes it down and does not ask them to expand, because he has learned that a one-sentence answer from a Vorr is a complete answer and that asking for more is a way of losing the number. He is the only Keldish man Hald Iron will allow near the crossed-out file, which is a compliment neither man has ever spoken. When he is frightened he starts counting under his breath, which sounds like the seam itself.

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item “Five repairs in this wall. Four of stone. One of something the translation says is Ash and the Court’s copy says is language. Both translations are guesses. I have entered them both.”

\item “The serpent passed at the third hour. The numbers changed by two. I did not see it whole. Nobody does.”

\item “Y.H. 588. A man with a mark. The entry is crossed out because a surveyor wrote the shape of it and then thought better of it. I have kept the shape. I do not know what it means. That is not the same as not keeping it.”

\item “You ask what holds the world together. I can tell you how many repairs I have counted. I cannot tell you what they were made of. Nobody can. The Vorr will only say the numbers are correct.”

\item “I don’t hunt the thing because it’s a monster. It drinks through the stone where a man can’t reach. So I reach where it does. That’s the whole of it.”

\end{itemize}

\CRsheetheading{History}
He went down the First Seam at thirteen, as every Keldish child does, and his number changed from thirty-four to forty-one on the day of his Descent, which is unusual and made the mine-reeve look at him twice. He became a surveyor of the rim-seam, a hunter of seam-serpents when a passing was measured in the deep shafts, and a man who has spent twenty years entering the repairs of the world in a bone tally that no officer below the rank of assessor is allowed to read. He has survived two Sweatings by being further down than the men who died and by knowing, from the smell of hot lead, that there were minutes and not hours. He has sat with Vorr at the Listening Stones for a season and come away with three sentences, all of them \emph{the numbers are correct}, and has entered all three.

In Y.H. 806 the First Seam survey was sealed and the crossed-out entry of Y.H. 588 was copied into the sealed file at the Hearthseat. Siv made the copy. He is the clerk who could not have known why he was asked, and he has known ever since. He copied the shape of the branching red mark onto the back of his own tally, under the numbers, and has carried it for six years without showing it to anyone except Hald Iron, who copied it onto the back of his own and has not spoken of it since. In Y.H. 811 he recorded a repair in the rim-seam as \emph{words that hold} and was not removed from the shaft, which he attributes to the death of the man who would have removed him and not to luck. He has entered both explanations and kept the slate.

When a lowlander boy arrives in Keld with a branching red flower across his ribs and an ear that hears a faulty vessel through a wall, Siv will not know what the mark means. He will know that the same shape was crossed out in Y.H. 588 and written in the margin of a Low Kiln slate in Y.H. 803, and that the world has an unlucky habit of producing the same man in different vessels. He will tell the boy the numbers, which is all he has, and the boy will hear something in them that Siv has never heard, because the boy knows what a spiral is.

\CRsheetheading{Wounds \& Fears}
The scar, and the twenty years of numbers that do not resolve into anything a Court will print. He fears the Sweating, which he has smelled twice and dreamt of a hundred times, and fears more than that the day the Vorr finally translate the oldest repairs and the translation turns out to be a thing the Keeping has already entered under another name. He fears that he has spent his life measuring a wound and will die without having said what it is, which is the fate of a surveyor and, in Keld, an honourable one. His contradiction: the man who enters everything has kept one thing — the shape of the mark — outside all his tallies, on the back, where only another surveyor would think to look.

\CRsheetheading{Desires}
He wants the numbers to be right and the shaft to keep its record after he is gone, which in Keld is a form of immortality available to a man with no house. He thinks he wants the translation. What he needs is to understand that a repair made of unkept promises is still a repair, and that the world has been held together by the very thing the Court’s economy produces, which is a thought a surveyor can enter but cannot act on without becoming something other than a surveyor. He will one day give the boy the crossed-out page, and it will be the first thing in his life he has given away rather than entered.

\CRsheetheading{Bonds}
\textbf{Hald Iron} — master of the floor, who respects the man’s patience and distrusts what he finds. They have shared the shape of the mark in silence, each copying it onto the back of a tally, and neither has said what they think, which is how Keldish men show that a thing is too large for speech.

\textbf{Corin} — the lowlander with the flower. Siv will not tell him what the mark means because he does not know, and will show him the crossed-out page because the boy is the first person who might. The tension is a gift given by a man who has spent his life keeping, to a boy who will read it with an ear the surveyor does not have.

\textbf{The Vorr} — Ao of the Third Seam and Iyn of the Listening Stone, who sit against the stones and come away with numbers. Siv is patient with them in a way no other Keldish man is, because he has learned that a one-sentence answer can be a whole answer if you write it down exactly.

\textbf{Karric VII, Warden of the Rim} — the ruler who keeps the true-Hearth claim for reasons of trade. Siv serves the claim without believing it, which in Keld is not hypocrisy but a way of keeping the shaft open.

\textbf{Rusk of the Weir} — a lowlander who asked him once, twenty years ago, whether the oldest repairs were made of language. Siv said the numbers were correct and told him nothing else, and has wondered ever since whether the man asked the same question of the stones.

\textbf{Marra} — whose name appears in the margin of a Low Kiln slate in Y.H. 803 beside a shape Siv recognises. He has never shown that slate to anyone and has copied the shape into his tally, which is the closest thing to a friendship the Hearthseat will ever have with the First Seam.

\CRsheetheading{Arc So Far}
No chapters are written yet. He enters in the survey shaft, listening to a wall before he looks at the visitor, and gives a lowlander boy a number where the boy expected an answer.

\CRsheetheading{Chapter Log}
\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item No chapters written yet; first appearance planned for Ch 200 (the First Seam, the crossed-out page).

\end{itemize}
}

\CRcharacter{Rennick}{the assessor who can add}{build/portraits/rennick.pdf}{\CRfield{Also called}{Assessor Rennick, Rennick, the young man with the good hand}\CRfield{Role}{rival}\CRfield{Born}{Y.H. 786, the Hearthseat, on the Keel}\CRfield{Kind}{human (Grathic; officer of the Keeping)}\CRfield{Origin}{the Hearthseat; slate-name entered on the rolls, no house and no kin}\CRfield{Allegiance}{the College of Assessors; posted to Slate Row, Sill, in Y.H. 810}\CRfield{Status}{alive}\CRfield{First seen}{Chapter 300}}{\CRsheetheading{Appearance}
Twenty-six, narrow, with the pressed, maintained look of a man who irons his cuffs before he goes to a district where there is no ironing. His hands are good hands — quick, clean, certain on a slate — and he has the student’s habit of tapping the chalk once against the frame before he writes, which the hearth-maids of Low Kiln have learned to read as a signal that a number is about to be entered against somebody. He wears the College’s black wool even in Silt, when a sensible man would wear clay-stained linen, and it marks him as a visitor from the Hearthseat in a way he is unaware of or has decided not to mind. His face is open and slightly eager, which is the least threatening expression in Sarn and, on him, the most dangerous, because it disarms people a moment before the figure lands. He smells of new chalk, clean paper and, when he has been in the Weighing Hall, the Hearth-fire, which he has never mentioned to anyone in Sill.

\CRsheetheading{Voice \& Manner}
Fast, precise, quietly delighted by his own accuracy. He says \emph{the figure} where another man would say \emph{the truth}, and he has a way of offering a correct number as if it were a gift, which it is, to the person who asked for it and not to the person it is about. He does not sneer. He does not need to; his certainty does the work. When he is beaten — and he will be beaten — he becomes curious rather than angry, which is worse for the victor, because curiosity is a hand that keeps hold. He has one verbal tic: he repeats the last figure of another person’s statement back to them, quietly, as a way of checking both the figure and the person.

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item “One in twelve. I’ve checked the notice, the roll and the factor’s copy. They agree. Three copies agreeing is a kind of truth in my trade.”

\item “Forty. I keep coming back to forty. Why forty unspent measures for one intact one? I’ve asked the provost. He said the account stands.”

\item “You heard the flat note before I tapped it. That’s a good trick. I’d like to know how you did it. Not to take it. I want to know whether it’s a method.”

\item “I’m not your enemy. That’s the thing nobody understands about me. I’m a man with a slate. The slate is the enemy, if there has to be one, and even the slate is only following the figure.”

\item “Seven. Six. Five — you’ve lost count, haven’t you? I counted for both of us. That’s my gift, I suppose.”

\end{itemize}

\CRsheetheading{History}
He was born in the Hearthseat and entered on the rolls at nineteen, which in the College means he has never had a house-name to be proud of or ashamed of. He proved early that he could add, which in the College of Assessors is the rarest of gifts: most officers memorise the figures, a few compute them, and almost none check the printed ones against the rolls. Rennick checked, at twenty-one, and found that one in twelve on the notice did not agree with the deduction on a Fen household’s slate, and that the difference was not an error but a method. He asked Provost Wessen about it. Wessen said the account stands and gave him a figure for his trouble, which Rennick has entered in his private tally as the first kindness shown to him by the institution.

He was posted to Slate Row in Sill in Y.H. 810, at twenty-four, to value the lives of a district whose households he cannot pronunciation-proof and whose children he cannot keep track of. He has kept his own count of the Forty of Low Kiln, which is forty-one, because on the night of the levy he saw a covered bundle carried up the Clay Yard that did not appear on any list, and a collector’s slate with a name written before a face. He cannot spell the name but he remembers the shape of it, and he has begun to look for that shape in every document that passes across his table. He has not told anyone about the forty-first. He has told Wessen about the forty, who told him to enter it as an irregularity and forget it, which he entered and did not forget.

He is good at his work and he likes being good at it, which is his great disqualification. He will meet the foundling Corin as a boy with an ear and no ledger, and will recognise in him a rival in the only sense Rennick understands: a person whose method produces correct answers by a route the College cannot teach. He will try to learn the route, honestly, by asking, and will be refused, and will keep asking, because a refusal is a thing with a shape and he wants to know what it is.

\CRsheetheading{Wounds \& Fears}
He can add, and nobody in his institution wants him to. His wound is a gift that his teachers have spent six years trying to correct out of him, and his fear is that he will succeed at last and become an ordinary officer who prints one in twelve and never asks why. He fears a person who can hear a vessel without a tool, because such a person makes his arithmetic look like a slow, clumsy way of doing the same thing. He fears the grey fingers of Collector Marra, whose reports are more exact than his and whose exactness he has begun to suspect is a kind of concealment. His contradiction: the young man who believes figures are a form of honesty has learned to hide the one figure he cannot explain, and calls the hiding \emph{an irregularity entered in the proper form}.

\CRsheetheading{Desires}
He wants to be right in a room where being right is noticed. He thinks he wants the foundling’s method, because a method that hears a cracked vessel through a wall would make the College’s work faster and truer, and perhaps make the true deduction public without anyone having to say who took it. What he needs is to learn that a figure is not a person and that adding a district correctly is not the same as being kind to it, which is the lesson the Warm Court has built eight hundred years on not learning. He will learn it late, and will become more dangerous when he does, because he will then be an assessor who can add and knows who pays.

\CRsheetheading{Bonds}
\textbf{Corin} — the rival. Rennick admires the boy’s ear without understanding it and has begun to suspect that the boy hears things he is not supposed to hear, which makes him want to check him the way one checks a slate. The tension is admiration curdling into a need to verify: Rennick will not be able to leave the boy’s method alone, and the boy will not be able to explain it without lying.

\textbf{Wessen} — his teacher, who corrected the verb out of him and refused to correct the arithmetic, which Rennick has decided means the provost wants him to keep adding. He is right about this and wrong about why.

\textbf{Marra} — the collector whose reports are the standard he measures himself against and whose fingers are going grey. He has begun to watch her hands when she writes, which she has noticed and pretended not to.

\textbf{Berr Clay, the Thane of Clay} — who tells him one in twelve in a moot and shakes hands afterwards. Rennick has checked the Thane’s figures three times and found them correct in the way a printed notice is correct, which is to say: agreeable and wrong.

\textbf{Alda Reed} — who answers his questions about births with the weather. He has begun to suspect the weather is an answer and has entered the suspicion nowhere, because an assessor who writes down what a hearth-maid means is an assessor who has started to add in the wrong direction.

\textbf{Steward Derren} — whom he has never met and whose signature he recognises on the private-authorisation of a whole return with no purchaser named. Forty. One. He keeps coming back to it.

\CRsheetheading{Arc So Far}
No chapters are written yet. He enters at a table in Slate Row, tapping chalk against the frame, offering a correct figure as a gift to a household that will pay for it.

\CRsheetheading{Chapter Log}
\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item No chapters written yet; first appearance planned for Ch 300 (Slate Row, the account-day after the boy’s first refusal).

\end{itemize}
}
