Forty-eight, heavy in the way a wagoner is heavy, with a back that has carried clay and a grey stubble he trims with a knife before market-day. He has a ring of lead-glaze green at the corner of his mouth from the old kiln-master’s habit of tasting glaze, and he cannot stop doing it in front of people, which the masters read as thoroughness and Sella reads as nerves. He wears a cord of red wool across his chest when he sits as Thane and takes it off before he goes home, folding it into a drawer. His hands are large and clean; he wipes his thumb on his apron before he touches a slate so that the slate will stay clean. He smells of hot clay, lead and, on Court business, nothing at all, which is the most expensive smell in Grath.

\CRsheetheading{Voice \& Manner}
The kiln-master’s proverb braided with the Court’s passive grammar. He never says \emph{I} when he can say \emph{the district} or \emph{the account}, and he never raises his voice, which in a moot is more frightening than shouting because the crowd has to lean in to hear him. He apologises in the form of an instruction. He uses the phrase \emph{as the notice says} the way another man might cross himself.

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item “The levy is called. It is not called by me.”

\item “One in twelve, as the notice says. If your household has heard otherwise, your household has heard wrong.”

\item “You can bring the slate to the moot. The moot will shout. The slate will not change.”

\item “Sella. Your widow’s mark is confirmed by the factor at Greybank. That is a kindness, and kindness is entered.”

\item “I signed for the Hearth. I did not sign for a name. There’s a difference, and you can take it to the Cross if you like.”

\item “The figure stands as read. There’ll be a slate at the watch if the house wants it again.”

\item “A number goes into a slate, not a bundle. If your house wants it again, there’ll be a slate at the watch.” --- at the eel stall on Reed 18, with the red cord folded under his coat and the true subtraction in the locked box.

\end{itemize}

\CRsheetheading{History}
He was born in High Kiln, the son of a glaze-mixer, and worked up through the yards until the masters chose him Thane of Clay and the Court’s factor at Greybank confirmed it, which is the only way a Thane is confirmed. He has kept the Sill kilns firing through two bad winters and a war of deductions that he describes, when pressed, as \emph{a disagreement about arithmetic}. In Y.H. 811, when the Long Cold had the district calling itself walking thin, he raised the levy to one in three on the factor’s instruction and announced it as one in twelve, because the printed notices say one in twelve and the notices are what a man can be seen reading. He has read the difference in a locked box in his own house. He has never destroyed the box.

In the first weeks of Stone, Y.H. 812, he signed the slate that took forty children of Low Kiln for a private account. The factor at Greybank showed him the purchaser’s name and Berr has forgotten it on purpose, which is a thing a man can do if he is sufficiently determined and sufficiently afraid. He told the district the warmth was for the Hearth, and to a mother named Dessa Silt he said one in twelve and meant one in three. His daughter came back thin in Y.H. 800 and does not remember him; he has kept her name on a slate at home and has never corrected the deduction on her return, because the return is what the household was given and a household does not look a gift in the mouth.

\CRsheetheading{Wounds \& Fears}
A daughter who calls him by another man’s name when she is feverish. He fears being seen clearly by Sella, who knew his wife and knows the difference between a levy and a theft. He fears that the locked box will outlive him and that his son will open it. He fears, most of all, that the district will one day ask him why forty children were necessary when one intact measure should have served, because he has an answer ready and knows it will not balance. His contradiction: the man who counts warmth as a public good has privately bought a whole return for his granddaughter and paid for it with the deduction from Low Kiln, and calls the purchase \emph{a gift from the Hearth}.

\CRsheetheading{Desires}
He wants the kilns firing, his name on the roll, and the factor at Greybank to write back in the same hand next year. He thinks he wants the Court’s confirmation. What he needs is to learn that he is the most frightening thing in Sarn — not a dark lord, but a reasonable man with a ledger and a good reason — and that the reason is the part that will be remembered against him.

\CRsheetheading{Bonds}
\textbf{Ch 127 (bonds).} On Silt 10 (Day 434), Silt’s first Account-day and market and the year’s fourth reading, he came up short off the clay road to the reading block under the moot-post with the red wool cord of his office folded square under his coat instead of worn across it and the sweetish green of tasted lead glaze at one mouth-corner; under the hot clay of him was the smell of nothing at all, which is the most expensive smell in Grath, and his hands were large and clean. He wiped the thumb twice on his apron before touching nothing, once for the slate and once for the figure that would be on it, held a narrow slate unopened against his forearm with the writing inward, passed a finger over the figure through the cloth of his own sleeve, and let his eyes rest on the writing a breath longer than the writing required, the way a man checks that a number is still where he put it. Then he read low into the goers-by, \emph{One in twelve, as the notice says}, and sent the figure twice over the basket, once for the moot and once for the households that came late, never looking into it. He called the levy and denied it: \emph{The levy is called. It is not called by me}; \emph{Your house wants it again, there’ll be a slate at the watch}; \emph{If your household has heard otherwise, your household has heard wrong} — \emph{your house}, never \emph{I} — taking himself out of his own sentence as a surgeon draws a hand from a field before the dressing goes on, leaving the work clean and the hand that did it nowhere in it. To a man who had brought a number up out of a shut fist he did not give the number back; the man was sent to a slate at the watch, and the number went from the fist to a mouth to a shoulder going up the road and arrived nowhere. Something low he said to the block about kindness being entered, in the tone of a man setting a cup where a cup belongs, and the block answered nothing; there was no anger in it and no triumph and no payer stood under it. He went off up the clay road toward High Kiln with the cord folded, the narrow slate under his arm and its writing turned to his sleeve, the box locked and Silt’s fourth true subtraction riding inside, believing he had done a kindness. The key went up in a coat pocket that never comes back down and there was no key under any roof. \textbf{This is T015/T041/T047 advanced and NOT paid:} four readings of the year now stand behind one unsigned figure — four are four and not one account, the first is not made a thirteenth by the three that follow, the second supplies no signature, the third no doctrine, the fourth no payer — the twelve arithmetics of Y.H. 813 are not laid across the four to make a row come out even, the figure read is still not the figure paid and no signature stands on the space. The boy took the order of his reaching apart as a surgeon takes a field apart and filed it on a tray of its own with a finger between it and the face of the man from Slate Row and another between it and the runner’s eighth that would come up the road before noon; no tenth stood up in the empty place and he made no doctrine of the twice-wiped thumb and no payer of the man who had wiped it. His kindness and his \emph{your house} stand each on a place of its own, believed and not owed, gathering toward the far-off accounting. No new scar or possession, no change of voice.

\textbf{Ch 124 (bonds).} On Ilmen 30 (Day 424), the month’s third and last Account-day and market, he came up short off the clay road to the reading block under the moot-post with the red wool cord of his office folded square under his coat and the sweetish green of tasted lead glaze at one mouth-corner, under the hot clay of him the smell of nothing at all. His large clean hands wiped the thumb twice before touching nothing, once for the slate and once for the figure that would be on it; he held a narrow slate unopened to his forearm with the writing inward, passed a finger over the figure through the cloth of his sleeve, let his eyes rest on the writing a breath longer than the writing required, and read \emph{One in twelve, as the notice says} low into the goers-by, sending the figure twice over the basket, once for the moot and once for the households that came late, never looking into it. He called the levy and denied it — \emph{The levy is called. It is not called by me}; \emph{your house}, never \emph{I} — taking himself out of his own sentence as a surgeon draws a hand from a field before the dressing goes on; to the man with the number in a shut fist he sent the number into a slate at the watch, and it went fist to mouth to shoulder and arrived nowhere. Something low he said to the block about kindness being entered, in the tone of a man setting a cup where a cup belongs, and the block answered nothing; there was no anger in it and no triumph and no payer standing under it. He went off up the clay road toward High Kiln with the cord folded, the narrow slate under his arm and the box locked, Ilmen’s third true subtraction riding inside, believing he had done a kindness. \textbf{This is T015/T041/T047 advanced and NOT paid:} three readings of the year now stand behind one unsigned figure — three are three and not one account, the first is not made a thirteenth by the second or the third, the figure read is still not the figure paid, no signature stands on the space and no doctrine comes out of three — and the twelve old arithmetics were not laid across the three to make a row come out even, for paper is not a payer and the key went up in a coat pocket that never comes back down. The boy filed the order of his reaching on its own tray and kept his low saying about kindness on a place of its own with a finger between it and his \emph{your house}; his self-removal gathers toward the day a hand that was in a field must be found to have gone away before the dressing went on, and his kindness toward the day it is remembered against him. Hessa carried the slate up the road before noon unread and was not made a reader by a third figure; Sella set the basket in the moot-post’s finger’s width of shade and stood half a pace off through the reading and the bell; the bell went four, four and a gap with nobody crossing himself. He was offstage on Ilmen 29 and Silt 1. No new scar or possession, no change of voice.

\textbf{Ch 121 (bonds).} On Ilmen 20 (Day 414), the month’s second Account-day and market, he came up short off the clay road to the reading block under the moot-post with the red wool cord of his office folded square under his coat and the sweetish green of tasted lead glaze at one mouth-corner, under the hot clay of him the smell of nothing at all. He called the levy and denied it with \emph{your house}, never \emph{I}, taking himself out of his own sentence as a surgeon draws a hand from a field before the dressing goes on; to a man who brought a number up out of a shut fist and asked what the levy would take he sent the number to a slate at the watch, and it went from fist to mouth to shoulder and arrived nowhere. Something low he said to the block about kindness being entered, in the tone of a man setting a cup where a cup belongs, and the block answered nothing; there was no anger in it and no triumph and no payer stood under it. He went off up the clay road toward High Kiln with the cord folded, the narrow slate under his arm and the box locked, Ilmen’s second true subtraction riding inside, believing he had done a kindness. \textbf{This is T015/T041/T047 advanced and NOT paid:} two readings of the year now stand behind one unsigned figure — two are two and not one account, the first is not made a thirteenth by the second, the figure read is still not the figure paid, no signature stands on the space and no doctrine comes out of two — and the twelve old arithmetics are not laid across the two new ones to make a row come out even, for paper is not a payer and the key went up in a coat pocket that never comes back down. His kindness and his self-removal go on their own trays toward the day the kindness is remembered against him and the day a hand that was in a field must be found to have gone away before the dressing went on. Hessa carried his slate up the road before noon unread and was not made a reader by a second figure; Sella set the basket in the moot-post’s finger’s width of shade and stood half a pace off through the reading and the bell; the soft-cuffed clerk stayed set below the north bridge for a measure nobody called; the green and the shape stayed sightings with no eighth. No new scar or possession, no change of voice.

\textbf{Ch 117 (bonds).} On Ilmen 10, the new year’s first Account-day and market, he came up short off the clay road to the reading block under the moot-post with the red wool cord of his office folded square under his coat and the sweetish green of tasted lead glaze at one mouth-corner, under the hot clay of him the smell of nothing at all. He wiped his thumb twice before touching nothing, held a narrow slate unopened to his forearm, passed a finger over the figure through his sleeve and read \emph{One in twelve, as the notice says} low into the goers-by, sending it twice over the basket — once for the moot and once for the households that came late. His large clean hands wiped his thumb twice before touching nothing, once for the slate and once for the figure; he held the narrow slate unopened to his forearm with the writing inward, passed a finger over the figure through the cloth of his sleeve, and read \emph{One in twelve, as the notice says} low into the goers-by, sending the figure twice over the basket, once for the moot and once for the households that came late, never looking into it. He called the levy and denied it with \emph{The levy is called. It is not called by me} and \emph{your house}, never \emph{I}, taking himself out of his own sentence as a surgeon draws a hand from a field before the dressing goes on; he sent a man with a number in his fist to a slate at the watch, said something low to the block about kindness being entered in the tone of a man setting a cup where a cup belongs, and went off up the clay road toward High Kiln with the cord folded, the narrow slate under his arm and the box locked, Stone’s last true subtraction inside, believing he had done a kindness with no anger and no triumph in him. \textbf{Twelve arithmetics of the year now stand behind one unsigned figure — the three of Frost, the first, second and third of Bone, the first, second and third of Ash, and Stone’s first, second and last — twelve are twelve and not one account}, the figure read still not the figure paid, no signature on the space and no doctrine out of twelve; the twelve true subtractions ride locked in his box, the key gone up in a coat pocket that does not come back down and the boy having no key. The boy filed the order of Berr’s reaching on a tray of its own beside the other record-first hands and made no tenth, no payer and no doctrine of it; the finding sat on a place of its own and was not laid across the keeping at the fold, the four rooms’ gap or the four directions. He was offstage on Stone 28 and 29. No new scar, wound, rank or possession; the belief that he had done a kindness goes on gathering interest against the day it is remembered against him.

\textbf{Ch 109 (bonds).} On Stone 20 (Day 379), the month’s second Account-day and market, he came up short off the clay road to the reading block under the moot-post with the red wool cord of his office folded square under his coat and the sweetish green of tasted lead glaze at one mouth-corner, under the hot clay of him the smell of nothing at all, which is the most expensive smell in Grath. His hands were large and clean; he wiped the thumb twice on his apron before touching nothing, once for the slate and once for the figure that would be on it, held a narrow slate unopened against his forearm with the writing inward, passed a finger over the figure through the cloth of his own sleeve and let his eyes rest on the writing a breath longer than the writing required. Then he read \emph{One in twelve, as the notice says} low into the goers-by and sent the figure twice over the basket, once for the moot and once for the households that came late, never looking into it. He called the levy and denied it with \emph{The levy is called. It is not called by me} and \emph{your house}, never \emph{I}, taking himself out of his own sentence as a surgeon draws a hand from a field before the dressing goes on; to a man who had brought a number up out of a fist he said \emph{Your house wants it again, there’ll be a slate at the watch}, and to the women at the rail, \emph{If your household has heard otherwise, your household has heard wrong}. Something low he said to the block about kindness being entered, in the tone of a man setting a cup where a cup belongs, and the block answered nothing. He was offstage on Stone 19 and 21; no bond changed hands, no new scar, wound, rank or possession, no change of voice. The reason he has done a kindness is the part that will one day be remembered against him.

The district’s arithmetic changed for the second month running and cannot be changed back, while the printed figure stands unchallenged and the figure read is still not the figure paid. \textbf{Five arithmetics of the year now stand behind one printed figure}, five readings five and not one account, a rule made from five wanting a payer put under all five where none stood; the boy kept the finding on a place of its own with no payer, not a lesson, grievance, mending, doctrine or rule. The reading answered nothing for the hare gone into the weather, the hand that went in on Seed 15, the man carried out on Day 188 or the dressed grain read over by a number that did not know its cost. He was offstage on Bone 19 and 21. No loyalty spoken, no debt paid, no bond changed hands, no new scar or possession, no change of voice.

\textbf{Ch 86 (bonds).} On Bone 10 he came up short off the clay road to the reading block, wiped his thumb twice before touching nothing, held the narrow slate inward, passed a finger over the figure, read one in twelve twice over the basket, called the levy and denied it with \emph{It is not called by me} and \emph{your house}, never \emph{I}, and went off up the road with the box locked and Bone’s first true subtraction inside beside Frost’s three, believing he had done a kindness. Sella set the basket in the moot-post’s shade and stood half a pace off through the reading and the bell and carried him home saying nothing; Hessa carried his slate unread and answered the women with \emph{I don’t read it. I carry it. There’s a difference, and the road doesn’t care which}. The clerk stayed set at the landing for a measure nobody called; the green and the shape stayed sightings with no eighth; the bell went four, four and a gap and the reading answered nothing for the covered grain or the hand that did not come back. No loyalty spoken, no debt paid, no bond changed hands, no new scar or possession, no change of voice.

\textbf{Sella Vail} — he confirmed her widow’s mark and has never called in the debt Garl left against a shipment of tiles. The uncalled debt is worse than a called one: she cannot pay it, cannot settle it, and cannot stop owing it. She has never asked, and he has decided this means she knows. \emph{Ch 3:} he told her at the Cross that the mark was confirmed by the factor at Greybank, that it was a kindness, and that kindness is entered. She answered the wool and the boy, not him; he stood with his mouth open on the next part of what he had come to say, looked at the mark under her collar without asking to see it, and went back to the moot leaving the debt as carefully unentered as he had found it.

\textbf{Jorra Vail} — he suspects the young man is with the Broken Slates and lets him be. A district needs somewhere to put its anger, and Berr has calculated that a kiln-house with a safe place for anger is cheaper than a kiln-house without one. Jorra threw a stone at his door in Y.H. 810; Berr had the stone swept up and does not mention it.

\textbf{Garl Vail} — dead friend and rival. Berr let the Vail house carry a debt rather than call it in, and has spent a year being unable to decide whether this was mercy or the simplest way to keep a witness quiet. \emph{Ch 3:} the debt against the firing of tiles went spoken around at the Cross, a space in a sentence shaped like the hollow seat up the yard; his care not to call it was another kindness entered nowhere.

\textbf{Alda Reed} — he pays her to keep the birth-slates and has never asked about the second notes. He has concluded that she must be paid enough not to keep them, which is an expensive conclusion and a wrong one. \emph{Ch 3:} she kept the birth-slates in a row at the edge of the market, turning the writing down when a mother came near; he did not see the crossed sign she made at the boy’s wrist or the date she covered it with, which is the whole point of paying someone to keep a record.

\textbf{Dessa Silt} — he took one in three from her wages and told her one in twelve. She spat at his door and denied it; he had the spittle cleaned before the market opened and never said who did it.

\textbf{Corin} — he watches the boy with a kiln-master’s eye and has decided he is worth more than he costs, which is exactly how the Court will one day see him. This is not cruelty in Berr’s account. It is an investment. \emph{Ch 3:} the boy lay in a basket at the edge of his square all morning and he never once looked into it. The figure was read over the top of him twice; the district went back to the pigs. He has entered this nowhere, including in his own mind.

\textbf{Ch 5.} At the Fishstairs on Stone 14 he came down the steps with the red wool cord folded under his coat and wiped his thumb on his apron before touching his slate, the green of tasted glaze at one corner of his mouth. He said \emph{the levy is called for the feast; it is not called by me}, accepted four eels where six should go without appearing to count them, and gave out \emph{three days to the Five} from the top of the steps with a finger passed over the figure. He has paid her two marks short for six years and taken two eels short for six years, and the war has never been named by either of them. The box in his house stays locked; the true deduction stays in it.

\textbf{Ch 6.} On Stone 20, Account-day, he came to the block with the red cord of his office folded under his coat and the green of tasted glaze at one corner of his mouth, wiped his thumb twice on his apron before touching the slate, and read \emph{one in twelve, as the notice says} low into the top of two hundred leaning people. He called the levy for the feast and said it was not called by him, passed a finger over the figure, confirmed the fire and the widow’s mark under this roof, and went around the consignment of tiles where a debt might have stood, the way a woman goes around Ash left in a corner. He did not look into the basket and went back to the pigs by dusk believing his own sentences. The box stays locked and the true deduction stays in it.

\textbf{Ch 7.} On Stone 30, the year’s last Account-day, he came to the block with the red wool cord of his office folded under his coat and the green of tasted glaze at one corner of his mouth, wiped his thumb twice before touching the slate and read \emph{One in twelve, as the notice says} low into the crowd at the last market of the year. He passed a finger over the figure, said the levy was called for the feast and was not called by him, went around the uncalled debt against the firing of tiles as carefully as Sella went around Ash in a corner, and did not look into the basket. He gave out that the Five were three days off while the district argued three, two and whatever the moot had already decided to pay, and went back to the pigs by dusk believing he had done the district a kindness. The box in his house stays locked and the true deduction stays in it.

\textbf{Ch 8.} At the Weighing on Day 26 he was glimpsed at the edge of the reading with the red wool cord of his office folded under his coat and green glaze at one corner of his mouth; he wiped his thumb before he touched his slate, passed a finger over the figure, read a name the household would not repeat, explained nothing, looked nowhere near the basket and went off with the box in his house still locked. The clean voice in a temple’s clothes that read the measures was the same grammar of his Cross, now in an officer’s mouth, and a whole return was announced for somebody not in the room. One in twelve stayed printed and unchallenged at the Opening of the Slates on Ilmen 1 and the true deduction was spoken by nobody.

\textbf{Ch 9.} On Ilmen 7 he came back from the river with the red wool cord of his office folded under his coat instead of worn across it, and green of tasted glaze at one corner of his mouth. He wiped his thumb twice on his apron before he touched nothing, passed a finger across a figure on a narrow slate, and had a number he did not care to give. When a neighbour at the well started to ask, he said \emph{A number goes into a slate, not into a well. If your house wants it, there’ll be a slate at the watch} --- \emph{your house}, not \emph{my account}, taking himself out of his own sentence as neatly as a man takes his hand out of a field before the dressing goes on. He went off toward High Kiln with the box in his house still locked and looked nowhere near the basket. The boy put the twice-wiped thumb on the tray where the other record-first hands lay and did not call it the same hand.

\textbf{Ch 10.} On Account-day, the day after a woman goes into the brook uncollected, he comes to the block with the red wool cord of his office folded under his coat and the green of tasted glaze at one corner of his mouth, wipes his thumb twice before touching anything and reads one in twelve \emph{as the notice says} low into the crowd. The true subtraction goes over the top of the basket and is spoken by nobody. To a neighbour who begins to ask about the thaw he says \emph{A number goes into a slate, not into a well. If your house wants it, there’ll be a slate at the watch} --- \emph{your house}, not \emph{my account} --- and takes himself out of his own sentence as neatly as a hand out of a field. The number for what the thaw will cost goes from a fist to a mouth to a shoulder and is never given, and he goes off with the box in his house still locked and his good reason intact. He is not at the Weir for the blessing. The clerk at the Court’s table and the clerk set at the Fishstairs for an uncalled measure both put hand to slate before eye to person, and the boy files their order beside Berr’s twice-wiped thumb without calling the three the same hand.

\textbf{Ch 11.} He came up the yard on Day 47 with the red wool cord of his office folded under his coat and green of tasted glaze at one corner of his mouth, hot clay under the smell of nothing at all. He wiped his thumb twice on his apron before touching nothing and held a narrow slate unopened against his forearm, passing a finger over what was written and letting his eyes rest on it a breath longer than the writing required. \emph{A number goes into a slate, not into a well. The house wants it again, there’ll be a slate at the watch} --- the house, not my account; he took himself out of his own sentence as neatly as a surgeon takes a hand out of a field. He never looked into the basket and went off toward High Kiln with the box in his house still locked and the true deduction inside. The figure that went from fist to mouth to shoulder went with him into a slate and stayed there.

\textbf{Ch 12.} On Account-day at the Cross he wiped his thumb twice, read one in twelve twice over the basket and put himself out of his own sentence with \emph{there’ll be a slate at the watch}; the true subtraction went over the basket and the number for the thaw went from fist to mouth to shoulder and reached nobody. Sella’s widow’s mark and the uncalled debt against the tiles were not touched, Jorra’s dust was not spoken of, and Alda’s birth-slates were kept where they belonged. He never looked into the basket and went off toward High Kiln believing he had done the district a kindness, with the box still locked and the true deduction inside.

\textbf{Ch 13.} On Ilmen 30, the last Account-day and market before Silt, he came to the block with the red wool cord of his office folded under his coat and the green of tasted glaze at one corner of his mouth, wiped his thumb twice before touching nothing and read \emph{one in twelve, as the notice says} twice over the basket. He called the levy for Silt and took himself out of his own sentence with \emph{there’ll be a slate at the watch}. The true subtraction went over the basket and was spoken by nobody; the number for what the thaw and the flood would cost went from a fist to a mouth to a shoulder and arrived nowhere. The bell went four, four and a gap and nobody crossed himself. The soft-cuffed clerk at the Fishstairs was glimpsed with his hand to the slate before his eyes to the stalls and did not speak. Berr went off toward High Kiln believing he had done the district a kindness, with the box in his house still locked and the true deduction inside.

\textbf{Ch 14.} On Silt 2 he came up short at the outer edge of the Fishstairs shade, the red wool cord of his office folded under his coat, green of tasted glaze at one corner of his mouth and hot clay over the smell of nothing at all. He wiped his thumb twice on his apron before touching nothing and held a narrow slate unopened against his forearm, passing a finger over what was written and letting his eyes rest on it a breath longer than the writing required. \emph{A number goes into a slate, not into a well,} he said. \emph{If the house wants it again, there’ll be a slate at the watch.} He took himself out of his own sentence as neatly as a hand out of a field before the dressing goes on, never said \emph{I}, never looked into the basket, and went off toward High Kiln with the box in his house still locked and the true deduction inside. The eel figure went over the basket into the noise of the stalls and was gone; the boy filed the twice-wiped thumb on its own tray and did not join it to the Fishstairs clerk’s hand or to the other record-first hands.

\textbf{Ch 15.} On Silt 10, Account-day, he came up short at the edge of the dry step with water sitting on the one below it, the red wool cord of his office folded under his coat, green of tasted glaze at one corner of his mouth and hot clay under the smell of nothing at all. He wiped his thumb twice before he touched nothing, held a narrow slate unopened against his forearm, passed a finger over what was written and let his eyes rest on it a breath longer than the writing required, then read \emph{one in twelve, as the notice says} over the water and the basket and took himself out of his own sentence, never saying \emph{I} and never looking into the basket. The true subtraction went over it unspoken and the number for what the flood would cost went from a fist to a mouth to a shoulder and arrived nowhere; the bell went four, four and a gap and nobody crossed himself. Word came up that the soft-cuffed clerk was still set at the Fishstairs with a slate for a measure nobody called, and the boy put Berr’s twice-wiped thumb on its own tray, not joined to that hand or to any of the other record-first hands. Berr went off toward High Kiln with the box in his house still locked and the true deduction inside, believing he had done the district a kindness.

\textbf{Ch 17.} On Silt 20, Account-day, he comes to the block with the red wool cord folded under his coat and the green of tasted glaze at one corner of his mouth, wipes his thumb twice before touching nothing and reads one in twelve over a crowd made thinner by the flood and the lean week. He takes himself out of his own sentence and goes off toward High Kiln believing he has done a kindness, the true subtraction locked in his box and a figure read aloud that is not the figure paid. The printed figure stands unchallenged over fewer bodies. He does not look into the basket. Sella’s uncalled debt against the firing of tiles stays neither paid nor settled, never done with; the soft-cuffed clerk at the Fishstairs is still set for a measure nobody called, and the boy keeps Berr’s twice-wiped thumb on its own tray, not joined to that hand or to any other record-first hand.

\textbf{Ch 20 (bonds).} Sella’s widow’s mark and Garl’s uncalled debt against the tiles were not touched or named; she answered the reading with the fire and said nothing about what went over the basket. Jorra’s dust and the back room were not spoken of, and Alda’s birth-slates and second notes stayed where they belonged. Dessa has been dead more mornings than any living person keeps count of and the figure read over the basket did not know her name or the boy’s; he has never looked into the basket and has entered this nowhere, including in his own mind. The soft-cuffed clerk at the Fishstairs and the man from Slate Row with soft hands are two more record-first shapes on their own trays, not Marra and not joined to one another or to the loaf. No bond was paid or repaired this chapter: the box stayed locked and the good reason intact.

\textbf{Ch 24 (bonds).} On Seed 22, afternoon, came up short off the north road at the outer edge of the yard well with the red wool cord of his office folded under his coat and the green of tasted glaze at one corner of his mouth, hot clay over the smell of nothing at all; hands large and clean, wiped the thumb twice on his apron before touching nothing and held a narrow slate unopened against his forearm, passing a finger over the figure and letting his eyes rest on the writing a breath longer than it required. Read \emph{One in twelve, as the notice says} low into the leaning yard, said \emph{A number goes into a slate and not into a strip. If your house wants it again, there’ll be a slate at the watch} — \emph{your house}, never \emph{I} — taking himself out of his own sentence as a hand goes out of a field before the dressing goes on. A man brought a number up out of a fist toward the well, looked at it, thought better of giving it and put the fist back in his sleeve, so the figure arrived nowhere; the boy kept Berr’s twice-wiped thumb on a tray of its own beside the other record-first hands and did not join it to the neighbour’s reaching hand at the shelf or to Sella’s hand on the board. Tarn said \emph{Yes, house} to the early thaw and the late and kept wanting the late because it puts off the paying. Berr went off up the clay road toward High Kiln with the narrow slate under his coat and the box locked in his house behind him and the true subtraction inside, believing he had done the district a kindness. Garl’s debt against the firing of tiles went around the space where a name might have stood, neither paid nor settled nor done with, and he never said \emph{I} or looked into the basket. Offstage on Seed 21 and 23. No new scar, possession or change of voice.

\textbf{Ch 25 (bonds).} Offstage on all three days, present only as a shape in the boy’s private file: at the Fishstairs on Seed 26 the boy set Berr’s twice-wiped thumb and his finger passed over a figure beside a midwife reaching for a slate before a child, a neighbour at a well, a clerk behind a Court table, a man who priced him, Jorra speaking to the wheel before the pots, Sella giving the instruction to the wool before anyone, and Alda laying her birth-slates down before the fold — a row of record-first hands kept on separate places and never joined. At the Cross the soft-handed man from Slate Row who held his slate at the edge was filed apart from Berr’s twice-wiped thumb, with no wiped thumb, no sentence taken out of itself and no sale. Sella’s widow’s mark and Garl’s uncalled debt against the tiles were not touched or named; Jorra’s dust and the back room were not spoken of; Alda’s birth-slates and second notes stayed where they belonged. Dessa is more mornings dead than any living person keeps count of and the figure that went nowhere in the strips did not know her name or the boy’s; he has never looked into the basket and has entered this nowhere, including in his own mind. No bond was paid or repaired this chapter: the box stayed locked and the good reason intact.

\textbf{Ch 26 (bonds).} On Seed 30, Tenthday, Account-day and the last market of Seed, came up short off the north road to the reading block at the Cross, offstage on Seed 27–29. The red wool cord of his office was folded under his coat instead of worn across it and the green of tasted glaze stood at one corner of his mouth; under the hot clay was the smell of nothing at all, the most expensive smell in Grath. His hands were large and clean; he wiped the thumb twice on his apron before touching nothing and held a narrow slate unopened against his forearm, passing a finger over the figure and letting his eyes rest on it a breath longer than the writing required. He read \emph{One in twelve, as the notice says} low into the two hundred, said \emph{The levy is called. It is not called by me}, and to a man who brought a number up out of a fist and asked what the planting cost now the hands had been in it said \emph{A number goes into a slate, not into a strip; if your house wants it again, there’ll be a slate at the watch} — \emph{your house}, never \emph{I}, taking himself out of his own sentence as a hand goes out of a field before the dressing goes on. The figure read aloud was not the figure paid, the true subtraction sat in the locked box in his house up the road, and the figure that went into the slate did not know the hand that had not come back out of the strip. He never said \emph{I} and did not look into the basket; the boy kept his twice-wiped thumb and his finger over the figure on a tray of their own, not joined to any other record-first hand. Garl’s debt against the firing of tiles went around the space where a name might have stood, neither paid nor settled nor done with, and he went off up the clay road toward High Kiln with the box locked and the true deduction inside, believing he had done the district a kindness. No new scar, possession or change of voice.

\textbf{Ch 31 (bonds).} On Day 134, morning, at the Cross and the eel stalls he came up short out of the clay road with the red wool cord of his office folded under his coat instead of worn across it and the green of tasted glaze at one corner of his mouth, hot clay over the smell of nothing at all. His hands were large and clean; he wiped his thumb twice on his apron before touching nothing, held a narrow slate unopened against his forearm, passed a finger over the figure and let his eyes rest on the writing a breath longer than the writing required. At the eel stall he took two pair and paid two marks short, the stall-keeper putting the marks in her palm without counting them where anyone could hear. \emph{A number goes into a slate, not a bundle}, he said; \emph{If your house wants it again, there’ll be a slate at the watch} --- \emph{your house}, never \emph{I} --- taking himself out of his own sentence as neatly as a surgeon takes a hand out of a field before the dressing goes on. He stood a moment with his mouth open on the next part of what he had come to say and then said it to the stall instead: the levy was called and was not called by him, one in twelve as the notice says; nobody leaned in at that hour, so the low voice was spent on the boards. The boy kept his green on its own tray beside the twice-wiped thumb and the finger passed over a figure, and kept the silent woman’s green across the square on a separate place; two mouths had the same colour and the two colours were not the same object. He went off toward High Kiln with the cord folded square and the narrow slate under his arm, the box in his house still locked with the true subtraction inside, believing he had done the district a kindness. He never says \emph{I}; he says the notice, the figure, the levy and the house. Sella’s widow’s mark and Garl’s uncalled debt were untouched, Jorra’s dust unasked about, Alda’s pages unread and Dessa dead and unnamed; the figure he read did not know the hand that had not come back. No bond was paid or repaired this chapter: the box stayed locked and the good reason intact, and no new scar, possession or change of voice was recorded.

He went off toward High Kiln with the cord folded square, the narrow slate under his arm and the box in his house still locked with the true subtraction inside, believing he had done a kindness. \textbf{Ch 33 (bonds).} On Day 139, the second Account-day of Reed, he came up short off the clay road to the reading block under the moot-post with the red wool cord of his office folded square under his coat and the green of tasted glaze at one corner of his mouth, hot clay over the smell of nothing at all. His large clean hands wiped his thumb twice on his apron before touching nothing; he held a narrow slate unopened against his forearm, passed a finger over the figure and let his eyes rest on the writing a breath longer than the writing required, then read \emph{one in twelve, as the notice says} low into the goers-by, called the levy and said \emph{It is not called by me} and \emph{your house}, never \emph{I}. The figure went into the air and the true subtraction stayed in the locked box up the clay road; a figure read aloud was not the figure paid. Across the square a silent woman with green in the crease beside her lip turned a cup a quarter and set it back where it stood: the fifth green at a mouth and the sixth shape of the colour, filed on a place of its own and never joined to his glaze, to her pale cord-mark or to any ear. At the stalls he took two pair of eels and paid two marks short, the stall-keeper putting the marks in her palm without counting them where anyone could hear, and he said \emph{A number goes into a slate, not a bundle. If your house wants it again, there’ll be a slate at the watch}, taking himself out of his own sentence as neatly as a hand out of a field before the dressing goes on. Let a low voice about the levy fall on the boards where nobody leaned in, and went off up the clay road with the cord folded, the narrow slate under his arm and the box locked, believing he had done the district a kindness. He never says \emph{I}; he says the notice, the figure, the levy and the house. The figure he read did not know the hand that had not come back out of the strip.

\textbf{Ch 34 (bonds).} On Day 142 he came up short off the clay road to the Cross in the afternoon with the red wool cord of his office folded square under his coat and the green of tasted lead glaze at one corner of his mouth, hot clay before him and the smell of nothing behind, his hands large and clean; he wiped his thumb twice before touching nothing and held a narrow slate unopened against his forearm. He passed a finger over the figure, read \emph{one in twelve, as the notice says}, called the levy and denied it with \emph{your house}, never \emph{I}, and told the man who brought a number that a number goes into a slate, not a bundle, and that if his house wanted it again there would be a slate at the watch. At the stalls he took two pair of eels and paid two marks short into the stall-keeper’s palm without her counting where anyone could hear, let a low voice about the levy fall on the boards with nobody leaning in, and went off up the clay road toward High Kiln with the cord folded, the narrow slate under his arm and the box locked with the true subtraction inside, believing he had done the district a kindness. The figure he read aloud did not know the hand that had not come back out of the strip, and he took himself out of his own sentence as a surgeon takes a hand out of a field. No new scar or possession, no change of voice; the figure read was not the figure paid.

\textbf{Ch 38 (bonds).} On the eve of the Account-day his red wool cord of office folded square under his coat was spoken of as a direction up the clay road toward High Kiln, not as a place anybody meant to go that day; a number came up from the road in a man’s fist, passed from fist to mouth to shoulder and arrived nowhere while the printed one in twelve stood unchallenged. On Day 159, the first Account-day of Tallow, he came up short off the clay road to the reading block under the moot-post with the green of tasted lead glaze at one mouth-corner, wiped his thumb twice before touching nothing, held a narrow slate unopened to his forearm, passed a finger over the figure and read \emph{one in twelve, as the notice says} low into the goers-by. He called the levy and denied it with \emph{your house}, never \emph{I}, and went off toward High Kiln with the box locked and the true subtraction inside, believing he had done a kindness; the figure read aloud was still not the figure paid. His slate went up the clay road edge-on in the hands of Hessa Rale, a slate-runner from Slate Row who carried it between the Cross and Greybank and was not a reader of anyone’s keeping; no figure came off it under any roof. Sella set the basket in the moot-post’s finger’s width of shade and carried it home at the going of the light saying nothing. Bell four, four and a gap, nobody crossing himself, heard beside told. No bond changed hands, no new scar or possession; the box stayed locked and the good reason intact.

\textbf{Ch 40 (bonds).} On Day 169, the second Account-day and market-day of Tallow, he came up to the reading block under the moot-post with the red wool cord of his office folded square under his coat and the green of tasted lead glaze at one corner of his mouth, hot clay under the smell of nothing at all; his hands were large and clean and he wiped his thumb twice before touching nothing, once for the slate and once for the figure that would be on it. He held a narrow slate unopened to his forearm, passed a finger over the figure, let his eyes rest on it a breath longer than the writing required and read \emph{one in twelve, as the notice says} low into the crowd. He called the levy and said it was not called by him; to a man with a number in his fist he said a number goes into a slate and not a bundle and that there would be a slate at the watch — \emph{your house}, never \emph{I} — taking himself out of his own sentence as a surgeon takes a hand out of a field before the dressing goes on. The printed figure stood unchallenged, the true subtraction went back up the clay road in the locked box and a figure read aloud was still not the figure paid (T015/T041/T047, T077). The bell went four, four and a gap with nobody crossing himself, heard beside told (T078). His slate went up the clay road edge-on in Hessa Rale’s hands, a runner who carried it and did not read it, joined to no other keeping (T080 advanced, not paid). Sella set the basket in the moot-post’s finger’s width of shade and carried him home saying nothing of what had been read over it. No bond changed hands, no new scar or possession; box locked, good reason intact.

Dessa is dead and unnamed and the figure read over the last market did not know her name or the boy’s; he has never looked into the basket and has entered this nowhere, including in his own mind. Hessa carried his narrow slate up the clay road edge-on and unread, a runner’s hand on its own tray, not joined to his twice-wiped thumb or to any other record-first hand. No bond was paid or repaired this chapter: the box stayed locked and the good reason intact.

\CRsheetheading{Arc So Far}
\textbf{Ch 127 (Days 432–434, Silt 8–10).} On Silt 10, Silt’s first Account-day and market and the year’s fourth reading, the Thane of Clay comes up short off the clay road with the red wool cord folded square under his coat and the sweetish green of tasted lead glaze at one mouth-corner, the smell of nothing at all under the hot clay of him; he wipes his thumb twice before touching nothing, holds a narrow slate unopened to his forearm, passes a finger over the figure through his sleeve, reads \emph{one in twelve, as the notice says} twice over the basket, once for the moot and once for the households that came late, calls the levy, denies it with \emph{The levy is called. It is not called by me} and \emph{your house}, never \emph{I}, sends a fist-number to a slate at the watch where it arrives nowhere, says something low to the block about kindness being entered with no anger and no triumph, and goes off up the road with the box locked and Silt’s fourth true subtraction inside, believing he has done a kindness. \textbf{Four readings of the year now stand behind one unsigned figure} — four are four and not one account, the first not made a thirteenth by the three that follow, the second supplying no signature, the third no doctrine, the fourth no payer — and the twelve of Y.H. 813 are not laid across the four, for paper is not a payer and the key went up in a coat pocket that never comes back down. The figure read is still not the figure paid. His kindness grows toward the day it will be remembered against him and his \emph{your house} toward the day a hand that was in a field must be found to have gone away before the dressing went on. Offstage on Silt 8 and 9, his first three subtractions behind the fourth in the locked box. Advanced, not paid. No new scar, wound, rank or possession; the reason stays hidden in the ordinary hand and the box stays locked.

\textbf{Ch 117 (Days 402–404, Ilmen 8–10).} On the year’s first Account-day the Thane of Clay reads one in twelve twice over the basket, once for the moot and once for the late households, calls the levy and denies it with \emph{your house}, never \emph{I}, takes himself out of his own sentence and says kindness is entered low to the block, then goes up the road with the box locked and the first subtraction of the new year inside, believing he has done a kindness. A count begins again; one reading is one and not an account, a reset is not a signature and the figure read is not the figure paid. His self-removal gathers interest toward the day a hand that was in a field must be found to have gone away before the dressing went on, and his kindness toward the day it is remembered against him. Advanced, not paid. \textbf{Ch 112 (Days 387–389, Stone 28–30).} On the year’s third and last Account-day the Thane of Clay reads one in twelve twice over the basket, once for the moot and once for the households that came late, wipes his thumb twice before touching nothing, passes a finger over the figure through his sleeve and sends Stone’s last true subtraction up the clay road in the locked box. Twelve arithmetics of the year now stand behind one unsigned figure — twelve and not one account, the figure read still not the figure paid, no signature, no doctrine — and the twelve true subtractions ride in a box whose key went up in a coat pocket that never comes back down. He calls the levy, denies it with \emph{The levy is called. It is not called by me} and \emph{your house}, never \emph{I}, takes himself out of his own sentence as a surgeon draws a hand from a field before the dressing goes on, says something low to the block about kindness being entered, and goes home believing he has done a kindness with no anger and no triumph in him. That belief, not anger, is what will one day be remembered against him. No new scar, wound, rank or possession; the reason stays hidden in the ordinary hand and the box stays locked.

\textbf{Ch 109.} Stone 20, the month’s second Account-day and market, goes up the clay road in his locked box, and with the three of Frost, the first, second and third of Bone and the first, second and third of Ash it makes \textbf{eleven arithmetics standing behind one unsigned figure}; eleven are eleven and not one account, the figure read is still not the figure paid, no signature stands on the space and no doctrine comes out of eleven. He comes up short off the clay road, wipes his thumb twice before touching nothing, holds the narrow slate inward, passes a finger over the figure, reads one in twelve twice over the basket, once for the moot and once for the late households, calls the levy and denies it with \emph{your house}, never \emph{I}, says something low to the block about kindness being entered, and goes off with the box locked and Stone’s second subtraction inside, believing he has done a kindness with no anger and no triumph in him. He never looks into the basket and has entered that nowhere nowhere. The reading heads nothing under the Vail roof: Sella sets the basket in the moot-post’s finger’s width of shade and stands half a pace off, the keeping at the fold stays found where put and not made again, the four rooms with the same gap stay apart with a finger between every pair, and the collector’s ordinary hand stays on its own tray joined to none. Hessa carries his slate up the road unread and is not made a reader by eleven; the soft-cuffed clerk stays set for a measure nobody called. He is offstage on Stone 19 and 21. He remains the most frightening thing in Sarn — not a dark lord but a reasonable man with a ledger and a good reason — and the reason is the part that will one day be remembered against him. Nothing he has kept has been opened or paid. Forward, not closed.
