The man shut his fist and put it back in his sleeve and the number went from the fist to Berr’s mouth to the shoulder of a man going up toward High Kiln and arrived nowhere. A figure read aloud was not the figure paid, the true subtraction sat in the locked box in his house up the road and had not been shown to anybody, and the figure that went into the slate did not know the hand that had not come back out of the strip. The bell went four, four and a gap and nobody crossed himself, and the soft-cuffed clerk was still set at the out-of-line Fishstairs landing with his slate to his forearm for a measure nobody called. He never looked into the basket; the boy kept his twice-wiped thumb and his finger over the figure on a tray of their own, not joined to any other record-first hand. Garl’s debt against the firing of tiles went around the space where a name might have stood, neither paid nor settled nor done with. He went off up the clay road toward High Kiln with the box locked in his house behind him and the true deduction inside, believing he had done the district a kindness. No new scar, possession or change of voice.

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item Ch 29: Day 127, Reed 8, on stage only that day. Came up short off the clay road late in the day with the red wool cord folded under his coat and green of tasted glaze at one corner of his mouth; hands large and clean, wiped the thumb twice on his apron before touching nothing, held a narrow slate unopened against his forearm and let his eyes rest on the figure a breath too long. Said \emph{A number goes into a slate, not into a bundle}, read \emph{one in twelve, as the notice says}, called the levy and said it was not called by him, and sent a man with a number in his fist to a slate at the watch — \emph{your house}, never \emph{I} — taking himself out of his own sentence as a hand goes out of a field. The figure arrived nowhere; the true subtraction stayed in the locked box and did not know the hand that did not come back out of the strip. Never looked into the basket; went off up the clay road toward High Kiln believing he had done a kindness. His green was filed apart from the third green at the market’s edge and his twice-wiped thumb on its own tray among the record-first hands. No new scar, possession or change of voice; box locked, good reason intact.

If your house wants it again, there’ll be a slate at the watch} --- \emph{your house}, never \emph{I} --- and said something low to the stall about the levy called and not called by him, one in twelve as the notice says, spent on the boards with nobody leaning in. The heard bell beside the told bell and the soft-cuffed clerk still set at the landing were two more shapes on their own places. No new scar, possession or change of voice; box locked, good reason intact.

\CRcharacter*{Marra}{the woman at the edge of the flare light}{build/art/characters/marra.png}{\CRfield{Also called}{Collector Marra, Marra of the Grey Coat, the woman with the slate, the hand that writes}\CRfield{Role}{antagonist}\CRfield{Born}{Y.H. 768, the Hearthseat, on the Keel}\CRfield{Kind}{human (Grathic; officer of the Keeping)}\CRfield{Origin}{the Hearthseat; no house, no kin; entered on the rolls in Ledgerhand}\CRfield{Allegiance}{the Warm Court, collector’s office; secretly the Unbanked}\CRfield{Status}{alive}\CRfield{First seen}{Chapter 1}}{\CRsheetheading{Appearance}
In the death scene she is a grey shape at the edge of the flare light in a coat the colour of wet ash, holding a slate, writing; the writing does not stop when the van takes him. In Sarn she is a woman in her forties with the neat, unremarkable face of an officer who has spent her life at tables rather than in rooms. Her fingertips are the colour of wet ash and have been since Y.H. 803, which she attributes to cold rooms in a voice that invites no question. She wears her hair pinned tight and her cuffs buttoned to the wrist, partly from the trade and partly because she does not want the hand seen. She has the collector’s habit of touching the slate before she touches the person, and a smaller habit — noticed only by people who have watched her for years — of touching her own wrist afterwards, where the iron clip would go, as if checking that it is not there. She smells of cold iron, slate dust and nothing else, which is the most expensive smell in Sarn.

\CRsheetheading{Voice \& Manner}
She apologises in clauses she does not finish. She is precise about other people’s warmth and vague about her own, and the vagueness is not evasion but a genuine absence: she has entered so many measures that she has lost the habit of entering herself. She speaks the Ledgerhand passive as naturally as breathing — \emph{the measure is banked, the return is recorded, the account stands} — and then, rarely, a plain sentence breaks through, usually about a child, and is immediately corrected into the grammar again. When she lies she becomes even more exact, giving dates and figures that nobody asked for.

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item “The measure was drawn at the fourth beat. I’m sorry, I — the account stands. That’s all that’s required.”

\item “I don’t remember my fingers. I mean, I remember that they were — they were warm once. That isn’t in the report.”

\item “You were written before you were seen. That’s an irregularity. It isn’t a cruelty. There’s a difference, and I’ve entered it.”

\item “Forty measures. One return. If you add it and it doesn’t balance, you’re adding it wrong. I’ve added it. I know what it balances to.”

\item “I’ve been paying since. Don’t ask me with what. It isn’t in the report.”

\end{itemize}

\CRsheetheading{History}
She entered the Keeping as a collector’s assistant in Greybank in Y.H. 790, arriving from the Hearthseat with a slate and an unusual care for the measurement of other people’s warmth. Her early reports were models of the craft: exact, unembellished, quiet about her own deductions. Within four years she was collecting in the Sill district; within twenty her fingertips had begun to go grey; within twenty-five she was the collector of the Low Kiln levy and the woman the district crosses the street to avoid. She has never been reprimanded and has never been promoted, which is a distinction she has thought about more carefully than either.

In the winter of Y.H. 812 she was standing at the edge of a flare light on an expressway in a country she could not have named, writing because the trace in front of her would not cool. She did not cause the crash and did not touch the child. She wrote the measure of a man who gave at the moment of breaking and whose promise was too heavy to bank. She wrote a name — Corin — before she had seen the infant’s face. Then she went home to Sarn and forged the assessment: a whole return with memory intact, booked at twelve hundred marks and forty unspent measures, with the deduction entered as zero. The money came from forty children of Low Kiln. The collector’s clerk who carried the slate has never been able to spell the buyer’s name.

She has been paying for the return ever since with her own fingers, a little warmth at a time, drawn without a slate and booked nowhere. In Y.H. 803 a slate in Greybank was found with a line that did not balance; it was corrected in a second hand and filed without comment. The first hand was hers. The second was also hers, written with the other hand so that the file would show two officers.

\CRsheetheading{Wounds \& Fears}
Her fingers. And underneath them, the forty. She can add and she has added, and the difference between what a whole return costs and what the Hearth was told it cost is a number she carries the way Dan carries Tasha’s chart — as a small, hard, private knowledge of the shape of her own conduct. She fears the Weighing, where the year’s measures are read aloud in a clean voice, because one of them is hers and it is not on any roll. She fears that the boy will one day look at her with that clinical attention and add her up the way she has added up everyone else. Her contradiction: the woman who invented an officer’s exactness to hide a forgery has made the forgery the most exact thing in her life, and calls it \emph{the account standing}.

\CRsheetheading{Desires}
She wants the sealed world too — the Unbanked’s paradise, where nothing leaks and nothing is owed — and she wants the instrument they sent for to be whole enough to do the sealing. She thinks she wants the boy to live. What she needs is to understand that she has already spent him: forty children bought one man, and no amount of careful handwriting makes that a balance. When she finally confesses it, it will be in a clause she does not finish, and the boy will finish it for her, in the plainest words, and the world will not end.

\CRsheetheading{Bonds}
\textbf{Corin} — the return she paid for and has never watched grow. She knows his name before she knows his face, and when she meets him in Slate Row she will look at him the way a surgeon looks at a chart: to check whether her own work held. He will be the first person to ask her about the fingers, and the first to hear her say \emph{I don’t remember} and understand that she means \emph{I do}. \emph{Ch 1:} she is a coat the colour of wet ash at the edge of a flare, a hand moving on a slate, and the same pause in a dark hand on a birth-slate in Low Kiln. He has filed the hand without a name and has not put the two together.

\textbf{Rusk} — the other half of the purchase. He taught the boy; she bought him. They have not spoken plainly in twelve years and have arranged their lives so that they never have to. She has begun to be afraid that he is gentler with the boy than the work permits, which in her vocabulary is the same as saying he has begun to love him.

\textbf{Berr Clay, the Thane of Clay} — she took his signature on the levy of forty and let him forget the purchaser’s name, which he did deliberately and with relief. She has never thanked him and never will; a debt acknowledged is a debt entered.

\textbf{Alda Reed} — Alda crossed herself at a birth-flower and wrote nothing in the Court’s book. Marra has read the Court’s book. She has never asked Alda what else she wrote, because a hearth-maid’s second note is the one thing even a collector cannot lawfully want.

\textbf{Haldre} — whose paper named the ending she has been paying for. She has never read it. She has heard it described once, by Rusk, and has spent the years since doing the work without the theory, which is a more Sarnish arrangement than either of them will admit.

\textbf{Steward Derren} — her head of office, whom she has never contradicted and never trusted. He has praised her exactness twice. She has decided that his praise is the most dangerous thing in the Hearthseat.

\CRsheetheading{Arc So Far}
Chapter 1 gives the first of her two entrances before she enters. She is a grey shape at the edge of the flare light: a coat, a head, a hand, writing without stopping while the van burns. She is not named, not to Dan and not to the reader, who is allowed to think she caused the fire. The writing has the same rhythm of short strokes and a decided pause as the strange dark hand on the birth-slate in House Silt, and Dan sets the two side by side without putting them together. The fingers, the forged assessment, the forty and the unfinished apology are all still buried.

\CRsheetheading{Chapter Log}
\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item Ch 1: Appears only as the image at the edge of the flare light --- coat the colour of wet ash, hand on a slate, short strokes, a pause, more strokes, the writing not stopping when the fire takes the van. Unnamed in the Sarn narration and unremembered by name. She wrote a name before anyone saw the child’s face; by morning that pause is sitting on a slab of grey stone within reach of a midwife’s hand.

\end{itemize}
}

\CRcharacter*{Ulda}{the friend who knew exactly what to say}{build/art/characters/ulda.png}{\CRfield{Also called}{Ulda, Ulda of the Fishstairs, the foundling with the ready laugh, the boy who sold the mark}\CRfield{Role}{antagonist}\CRfield{Born}{Y.H. 809, Low Kiln, Sill, Grath (foundling; one name only)}\CRfield{Kind}{human (Grathic; foundling, one name only)}\CRfield{Origin}{Low Kiln, Sill, Grath; no house, no kin, no slate until the Court entered him}\CRfield{Allegiance}{the Fishstairs; the Waiting Room clerk; quietly, the keeping of small secrets for people who pay}\CRfield{Status}{alive — on Day 219, Grain 10, the first Account-day and market of Grain, the \textbf{seventh} sighting came at the market’s edge: a shape in cast-offs with a man’s shoulders and breeches cut off at the knee, silt dried pale in the creases of the wrists, a gap where a front tooth had been and a green sliver of lead-glaze on a string catching the light and going dull, its head going toward a set-down pot a half-beat late and stopping in the middle; no dialogue, no loaf, no slate and no sale, never named Ulda in the narration; filed by the boy as a seventh shape on a place of its own beside the six behind it, after the knock and not before it, not a hearing and not a seventh of the full note, not joined to the seventh green at the pot board; offstage on Days 220 and 221; the sale to the Waiting Room clerk still years ahead and nothing sold at the close of Day 221}\CRfield{First seen}{Chapter 16}}{\CRsheetheading{Appearance}
Three years older than Corin and twice as easy in the world, with a narrow face that is always slightly amused and a set of clothes that are somebody else’s cast-offs worn as if they were a uniform. He has a gap where a front tooth was knocked out at the Fishstairs and he grins through it, which makes people forgive the things he says before they have decided whether to be offended. He keeps a sliver of green lead-glaze in a string around his neck, picked up in High Kiln, and rubs it with his thumb while he decides what a person wants to hear, which is almost always the thing they have already said they want and a little more. He smells of river silt, small ale and the warm stone of other people’s hearths, because he is always in somebody’s kitchen and never in his own. The thing people notice first is the grin; the thing they notice last is that when Corin turns his head toward a pot, Ulda turns it too, a half-beat late, and has never once been able to explain why.

\CRsheetheading{Voice \& Manner}
Fast, warm, fluent in the proverb-form of Low Kiln and quicker than the adults at it. He is the only child in the yard who can make the kiln-hands laugh, and he does it by saying the thing the adults are thinking in a voice that makes it harmless. He never says \emph{I want}; he says \emph{they say}, \emph{everyone knows}, \emph{your house wouldn’t mind}, which is a way of wanting without owning the want. When he is lying he gets affectionate, which is the tell that Mira Silt has learned to read and that Corin, for years, took for kindness. He has a habit of finishing another person’s sentence for them, correctly, and then looking surprised that it was not what they meant.

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item “—and a good deal,” said at the well in Ch 16, finishing a kiln-hand’s sentence in a quick, warm, affectionate voice. “That’s the whole of the account. Everyone knows it. I’m only saying.” This is his first plain sound in the book: a borrowed sentence, harmless on the surface, that makes the yard laugh before anybody has decided whether to be offended.

\item “Everyone knows the Vail boy isn’t Vail. I’m not saying it. I’m saying everyone knows it. There’s a difference.”

\item “You heard it before I tapped it, didn’t you? That’s not a trick. That’s a thing you should be careful with, Corin. I’m only saying.”

\item “I didn’t tell the clerk. I told him a thing and he wrote it down. That’s not the same, is it? You tell me, because I can never tell which part’s mine.”

\item “The mark. Under your sleeve. I saw it at the Weir and I didn’t say. I didn’t say for three years, Corin. That’s what I’m asking you to remember.”

\item “Sella’s kind to you. She’s kind to me too, when she’s thinking of something else. Don’t make it more than it is.”

\end{itemize}

\CRsheetheading{History}
He was born in Low Kiln to a mother entered in the name-pot and returned thin, and he has never known which of the several dead in him is his mother, which he describes as \emph{a family, in a manner of speaking}. He was entered on a slate at three because the Court began counting foundlings in Y.H. 782, and has had a name on a roll ever since, which makes him, in his own account, a man of property compared with Corin, who for his first years had none. He attached himself to the Vail yard at five because there was alwaysbread there and because the boy with the flower was interesting in a way Ulda could not name. He became the foundling’s friend in the way poor children become friends: by sharing a crust, by knowing which boards at the Fishstairs are safe, and by being the person who says the thing aloud that the other one is thinking.

He has sold small secrets at the Fishstairs since he was nine — which household has paid the levy, which collector takes his ale before a draw, which hearth-maid has begun to keep a second set of notes — and has never thought of it as betrayal, because a secret in Low Kiln is a thing that belongs to whoever can use it. In Y.H. 811 he told a Waiting Room clerk that a foundling under the Vail roof could hear the full note of a pot before it was tapped. The clerk wrote it down. Ulda was eleven and was paid in a loaf, and has entered the loaf in no account, which is the only thing about the whole business he has never been able to explain to himself.

Three years later he will tell the same clerk about the branching red mark under the boy’s sleeve, which he saw at the Weir and has kept for exactly the right moment, and the clerk will write that down too. He will do it because he has begun to be afraid that Corin will one day be taken by the Court and Ulda will not be there to be useful, which in his vocabulary is the same as being abandoned. He will say afterwards that he did it to protect him. He will believe it for a while.

\textbf{On his age in these chapters.} In Y.H. 813, when he first comes plainly into the yard in Chapter 16, he is a small foundling of three or four in somebody else’s cast-offs, not the eleven-year-old of the dialogue above. The sentences about the Waiting Room clerk, the paid loaf, the mark under the sleeve and the sale at eleven belong to years hence and are written here as the shape of the man he will become, not as words this child speaks now. In Chapter 16 he is given one borrowed sentence and nothing of his own; his sheet was reconciled to this on his first appearance. If he is given a second speaking appearance while the boy is still an infant, treat the later dialogue as years ahead of him and give him no secret to sell yet.

\CRsheetheading{Wounds \& Fears}
He has no house and has made a career of being the person who fits into other people’s. His wound is that he cannot want anything in his own voice: every desire comes out as \emph{they say} or \emph{everyone knows}, so that he can deny it if it is refused. He fears the name-pot, because a foundling entered on a slate can be entered again, and fears more than that the day Corin looks at him with that clinical, quiet attention and sees the thing he did at eleven. His contradiction: the boy who tells everyone’s secrets has kept one of his own for three years — the mark — and calls the keeping of it loyalty, when it is a thing he has been saving to spend.

\CRsheetheading{Desires}
He wants a place in a household, any household, where the door closes on him and somebody says his name without a slate in front of them. He thinks he wants Corin to stay in Low Kiln and be his friend forever, which is the same as wanting the boy not to become what he is becoming. What he needs is to understand that a person cannot be kept by being useful, and that the loaf he was paid at eleven has gathered interest for three years in an account he cannot read. When he finally says the thing he did, it will be in the affectionate voice, and it will be the first honest sentence he has ever spoken, and Corin will not believe him at first, which is the correct response.

\CRsheetheading{Bonds}
\textbf{Corin} — his friend, the only person he has never tried to manage, which is why the betrayal will work. Ulda knows the boy hears things and has spent years pretending not to notice so that the boy will keep being ordinary beside him. The tension is a love that expresses itself as a careful inventory of the beloved’s weaknesses, held in reserve. \emph{Ch 16:} the boy in the basket is still an infant and Ulda does not know him yet; he turns his own head toward a pot a half-beat after the boy turns his, is as surprised as anybody and cannot say why, and rubs the green sliver at his neck. The half-beat is the physical tell of what he will one day do, filed in the boy’s private file without a cause written across it. \emph{Ch 18:} the delay came a second time at the market’s edge on Silt 30, half a beat after the boy’s turning and after the knuckle, and he stopped, rubbed the sliver and could not say why; no loaf, no slate, no sentence. The boy keeps the second delay on its own tray beside the first and still writes no cause across either. \emph{Ch 36:} a \textbf{sixth} silent glimpse came at the last market of Reed on Day 149 — cast-offs worn like a uniform, silt dried pale in his wrists, a gap in his grin, a green sliver on a string at his throat — his head a half-beat late toward a set-down pot and stopping in the middle, the sliver rubbed twice and his mouth opening on the tail of a kiln-hand’s sentence with nothing a clerk could take down; no loaf passed, no slate was seen and no sale was paid, and the boy kept the shape on a place of its own, never Fenna in the narration and never named.

\textbf{Mira Silt} — she reads his affection as the tell it is and has told him once, at the Fishstairs, that a boy who sells a secret has no way of buying it back. He answered with the weather and has never forgotten that she did not laugh.

\textbf{Dessa Silt} — he carries messages for her and has never once told her that the boy she thinks is dead is three doors away, because a secret that big would make him important, and a boy who is important gets entered on a slate.

\textbf{Sella Vail} — he is always in her kitchen and she has never once said he may not be, which he has decided is the same as being wanted and is not.

\textbf{The Waiting Room clerk} — a man whose name is not on any roll, who pays in loaves and ale and has taught Ulda that a secret is worth exactly what somebody will give for it. This is the man who will buy the mark.

\textbf{Jorra Vail} — who would throw him out of the yard if he knew half of it, and whom Ulda watches carefully, because Jorra has broken three birth-slates and is therefore a person who could be useful or a person who could be dangerous.

\textbf{Ch 17.} On Silt 19 he is glimpsed once, silently, at the yard well — a small foundling in cast-off clothes worn like a uniform, a gap in his grin, the green sliver of lead-glaze at his neck. He turns his head toward a pot a half-beat after the boy’s and rubs the sliver, and is as surprised as anyone; no sentence is finished for a kiln-hand this time, no loaf passes, no slate is seen. The boy files the delay as an object on a place of its own and keeps his own turning beside it without letting the two touch. He is not seen again that week; nothing has changed hands that a slate could read and the sale stays a shape, not a betrayal paid. The half-beat and the loaf from Silt 16 gather interest in an account the child cannot read.

\textbf{Ch 20 (bonds).} He is still a shape and not a friend in the boy’s file: the Silt 16 loaf and the half-beat have gathered another seven days of interest, and nothing has crossed that any slate could read. Corin does not know him yet and he has no line of his own; Mira still reads the affection he has not learned to hide, and Sella’s kitchen door is still open without anybody saying he may not come in. Jorra would throw him out if he knew half of it, and the Waiting Room clerk still waits for a better price than a loaf. No bond changed hands on Seed 9: no loaf, no slate, no sentence finished, no secret sold.

\textbf{Ch 23 (bonds).} He is still a shape and not a friend in the boy’s file: the Silt 16 loaf and the half-beat have gathered another three days of interest and nothing has crossed that any slate could read. Corin does not know him yet and he has no line of his own; Mira still reads the affection he has not learned to hide, and Sella’s kitchen door is still open without anybody saying he may not come in. Jorra would throw him out if he knew half of it, and the Waiting Room clerk still waits for a better price than a loaf. On Seed 19 he was glimpsed once at the market’s edge, unnamed and silent, cast-offs worn like a uniform, silt dried pale in the creases of his wrists, a gap in his grin and the green sliver at his throat; when a pot was set down his head went toward it a half-beat after the boy’s, after the knuckle and after the note, then stopped, and he rubbed the sliver and opened his mouth on the tail of a kiln-hand’s sentence without finishing it. No loaf passed, no slate was seen and no secret sold; the delay stays a thing that comes after the knock, not a hearing and not a seventh, and the sale stays a shape.

\textbf{Ch 27 (bonds).} He is still a shape at the edge of the market, not a speaker and not yet a betrayer. On Reed 2 he stood at the edge of the stalls beyond the Cross in cast-offs worn like a uniform, silt dried pale in the creases of his wrists and a green sliver of lead-glaze on a string at his throat that caught the light when he turned and went dull when he turned back. When a kiln-hand set a pot down, his head went toward it half a beat after the boy’s, after the knuckle and after the note, then stopped in the middle of the turn; he rubbed the sliver twice with his thumb and his mouth opened on the tail of the kiln-hand’s sentence and nothing came out that any clerk could take down. No loaf passed anywhere within reach of the basket and no slate was opened within two paces of it. This is the \textbf{fifth} glimpse, held on a place of its own beside the four earlier delays and the Silt 16 loaf, after the knock and not before it, not a hearing and not a seventh, and the boy wrote no cause across any of them. He is not Marra, not the Fishstairs clerk and not the Court-table clerk, and is joined to none of them; the sale stays a shape and the betrayal stays years ahead.

\textbf{Ch 46 (bonds).} On Day 189, Ember 10, the first Account-day and market-day of the kiln month, he was a held shape at the market’s edge, unnamed in the narration and given no dialogue: cast-offs catching the light on the green sliver at his throat and going dull when he turned, no pot set down for him to turn toward, no half-beat spent, no loaf passed, no slate opened within reach of the basket and no sale paid. The boy gave the colour no ear and the shape no name, and did not count him as a seventh sighting (T033/T034 held; the no-seventh-in-Chapters-46–50 rule kept). He is not the man carried out on Day 188 and not the green at the pot board’s mouth; the sixth green stays a colour and this stays a shape, on places of their own and not joined. He is not Marra, not the Fishstairs clerk and not the Court-table clerk, and is joined to none of them. The Silt 16 loaf goes on gathering interest in an account the child cannot read, and any dialogue on his sheet remains years ahead of the child in the basket. No bond changed hands, no new scar or possession, no change of voice.

\CRsheetheading{Arc So Far}
He enters in Chapter 16 as the grin at the well, finishing a kiln-hand’s sentence in the affectionate voice that makes the yard laugh, a small foundling of three or four in a coat with a man’s shoulders and breeches cut off at the knee, worn like a uniform he was never measured for. The gap where a front tooth had been goes into every circle of the yard ahead of him and comes back with permission to say anything; the sliver of green lead-glaze on a string at his neck is rubbed with his thumb while he decides what a person wants to hear, which is usually what the person has already said and a little more. He says what everybody is thinking in a tone that makes it harmless, and he never says \emph{I want} --- he says \emph{they say}, \emph{everyone knows}, \emph{your house wouldn’t mind}. When a woman sets a pot down his head goes toward it a half-beat after the boy’s, after the knuckle and after the note, then stops and comes back; he rubs the green sliver and cannot say why he turned, and is as surprised as anybody. When a man from Slate Row whose name is on no roll holds out a warm loaf, his mouth opens on a sentence with the shape of \emph{everyone} or \emph{your house} and stops where a want would have stood, because he has no form of words for a want that is his own and is too quick a child to say a thing that could be refused to him by name. The loaf goes into the pocket of the cast-off coat, which holds a bit of string and nothing any clerk could read, with no slate between them; the man says something low that does not carry and the child nods as though he had understood it. He is named on the sheet but not in the narration. He stays a shape in the boy’s file --- a delay, a sliver, a loaf, an unfinished sentence --- and no secret has changed hands that any slate could read, no betrayal has been paid. The loaf has begun to gather interest in an account he cannot read, and the half-beat is held for the day it lands as the physical tell of what he did.

On Days 78 through 84 he is a shape at the edge of the recovery, not a speaker and not yet a betrayer. He appears once, at the yard well on Silt 19, in cast-offs worn like a uniform with a green sliver at his throat; when a pot is set down his head goes toward it a half-beat after the boy’s, after the knuckle and after the note, and he stops, rubs the sliver and cannot say why he turned. The boy files the delay beside his own turning without letting the two touch, because a thing that comes after the knock is a different thing from one that comes before it and this was neither a hearing nor a seventh. No acceleration of a kiln-hand’s sentence, no warm loaf, no slate, no secret; he is gone for the rest of the week and nothing has been sold that any clerk could read. The half-beat stays the physical tell held for the day the small sales land as betrayal, and the loaf from the man from Slate Row goes on gathering interest in an account he cannot read.

On Days 85 through 90 he is a shape at the edge of the last market of Silt, still not a speaker and not yet a betrayer. He is glimpsed a second time on Silt 30 at the market’s edge, unnamed in the narration: a small foundling in cast-offs worn like a uniform, a gap where a front tooth had been and a green sliver of lead-glaze on a string at his throat. When a pot is set down his head goes toward it a half-beat after the boy’s --- after the knuckle and after the note --- and then stops; he rubs the sliver with his thumb and cannot say why he turned. No sentence is finished for a kiln-hand, no loaf passes, no slate is seen and no secret sold. The boy files the delay on a place of its own beside his own turning and does not let the two touch, because a thing that comes after the knock is a different object from one that comes before it. He is not Marra, not the Fishstairs clerk and not the Court-table clerk and is joined to none of them; the sale stays a shape and the betrayal stays years ahead. The half-beat and the warm loaf from the man from Slate Row go on gathering interest in an account the child cannot read, and the month turns into Seed with nothing changed hands that any slate could read.

On Days 94 through 100 he is a shape at the edge of the planting month, still not a speaker and not yet a betrayer. He is glimpsed a third time on Seed 9 at the edge of the Fishstairs market, unnamed in the narration: a small foundling in cast-offs worn like a uniform, silt dried pale in the creases of his wrists, a gap where a front tooth had been and a green sliver of lead-glaze on a string at his throat. When a pot is set down his head goes toward it a half-beat after the boy’s --- after the knuckle and after the note --- then stops; he rubs the sliver with his thumb and cannot say why he turned, opens his mouth on the tail of a kiln-hand’s sentence and lets nothing out that a slate could take down. No new loaf passes, no slate is opened within reach of the basket, no secret changes hands that a slate could read and no loan or sale is paid. He is not Marra, not the Fishstairs clerk and not the Court-table clerk, and is joined to none of them. The boy files the delay on a place of its own, after the knock and not before it, not a hearing and not a seventh, and keeps his own turning beside it without letting the two touch. The half-beat and the warm loaf from the man from Slate Row go on gathering interest in an account the child cannot read, and any dialogue on his sheet remains years ahead of the child in the basket.

On Days 107 through 109 he is a shape at the edge of the planting month’s last tend, still not a speaker and not yet a betrayer. He is glimpsed once on Seed 19 at the dawn market below the north bridge, unnamed in the narration, at the edge of the fish-trade shade where a whole market walks carefully over the out-of-line landing and a soft-cuffed clerk sits for a measure nobody called. He is in cast-offs worn like a uniform, silt dried pale in the creases of his wrists, a gap where a front tooth had been and a green sliver of lead-glaze on a string at his throat. When a kiln-hand sets a pot down near the eel shade the boy hears its full note and his head goes toward it; the foundling’s head goes a half-beat after the boy’s, after the knuckle and after the note, then stops in the middle of the turn. He rubs the sliver twice with his thumb and could not have said why he turned, and there is no word in the market’s language for the thing that made him turn, which was not the note and came after it. A kiln-hand at the edge says the tail of a sentence and leaves it hanging, and the foundling’s mouth opens on the end of it the way a child’s mouth opens to finish a thing heard a hundred times, and nothing comes out that any clerk could have taken down. No loaf passes, no slate is opened within reach of the basket and no secret changes hands that a slate could read. The boy files the delay on a place of its own, after the knock and not before it, not a hearing and not a seventh, keeps his own turning beside it without letting the two touch, and sets the watcher’s turning beside the two tellings of the shelf as a third shape, joining none of them. Somewhere a long way off a hand will lay them together and call the joining an account; it is not his hand and it is not today. The half-beat and the Silt 16 loaf go on gathering interest in an account the child cannot read, and any dialogue on his sheet remains years ahead of the child in the basket.

On Reed 2 he is a shape at the edge of the stalls beyond the Cross, still not a speaker and not yet a betrayer. Glimpsed once and unnamed in the narration: cast-offs worn like a uniform with a man’s shoulders and breeches cut off at the knee, silt dried pale in the creases of his wrists, a gap where a front tooth had been and a green sliver of lead-glaze on a string at his throat that caught the light when he turned and went dull when he turned back. He said nothing and nobody spoke to him. When a kiln-hand set a pot down his head went toward it half a beat after the boy’s, after the knuckle and after the note, then stopped in the middle of the turn; he rubbed the sliver twice with his thumb, his mouth opened on the tail of the kiln-hand’s sentence and nothing came out that any clerk with a slate could have taken down. No loaf passed anywhere within reach of the basket and no slate was opened within two paces of it. This is the fifth glimpse, held on a place of its own beside the four earlier delays and the loaf from the man from Slate Row; the boy files it after the knock and not before it, not a hearing and not a seventh, and keeps his own turning beside it without letting the two touch. Not Marra, not the Fishstairs clerk and not the Court-table clerk; joined to none of them, the sale a shape and the betrayal years ahead, any dialogue on the sheet still years ahead of the child in the basket.

On Days 147 through 149 he is still a shape at the edge of the market and not yet a speaker or a betrayer. On Day 149, the last market of Reed, he is glimpsed a sixth time, unnamed in the narration and given no dialogue: cast-off clothes worn like a uniform, silt dried pale in the creases of his wrists, a gap where a front tooth had been, a green sliver of lead-glaze on a string at his throat. When a pot is set down his head goes toward it half a beat after the boy’s, after the knuckle and after the note, then stops in the middle of the turn; he rubs the sliver twice with his thumb and opens his mouth on the tail of a kiln-hand’s sentence and lets nothing out that any clerk could take down. No loaf passes, no slate is seen near the basket and no sale is paid. The boy files the sixth half-turn on a place of its own beside the five earlier delays and the Silt 16 loaf, a shape and not a hearing, after the knock and not before it, and writes no cause across any of them. The sale stays a shape, the betrayal years ahead, and the loaf goes on gathering interest in an account the child cannot read.

On Ember 10, the first Account-day of the kiln month, he is a shape at the market’s edge again: cast-offs, a gap in his grin, the green sliver at his throat catching the light and going dull. He is given no name, no dialogue, no half-beat, no loaf and no sale, and the boy does not count him as a seventh sighting. The rule for these chapters holds him to a shape on a place of his own, after the knock and not before it, not a hearing and not a seventh; the sixth green at the pot board stays a colour and is not joined to the sliver. He is not Marra, not the clerk at the Fishstairs and not the clerk at the Court’s table, and is joined to none of them. The Silt 16 loaf goes on gathering interest in an account the child cannot read, and the betrayal stays years ahead.

On Day 199, Ember 20, the second Account-day of the kiln month, he is a shape at the market’s edge again: cast-offs worn like a uniform, silt dried pale in the creases of his wrists, a gap where a front tooth had been, the green sliver on a string at his throat catching the light and going dull, his head stopping a half-beat toward a pot and his hand rubbing the sliver. On Grain 10 the shape at the market’s edge turns a seventh time, still unnamed and still silent: cast-offs with a man’s shoulders, silt pale in the wrists, a gap where a front tooth had been and the green sliver catching and going dull, the head a half-beat late toward a set-down pot and stopping in the middle. No loaf passes, no slate comes near the basket and no sale is made; the boy files the half-turn as a seventh shape beside the six behind it and writes no cause across any of them. The loaf from the man from Slate Row goes on gathering interest in an account the child cannot read and the betrayal stays years ahead.

\CRcharacter{Steward Derren}{the reasonable man at the head of the account}{build/portraits/steward-derren.pdf}{\CRfield{Also called}{Steward Derren, Derren, the head of the Keeping, the voice that never rises}\CRfield{Role}{villain}\CRfield{Born}{Y.H. 749, the Hearthseat, on the Keel}\CRfield{Kind}{human (Grathic; officer of the Keeping)}\CRfield{Origin}{the Hearthseat; slate-name entered on the rolls, no house and no kin}\CRfield{Allegiance}{the Warm Court — Steward of the Hearth; keeper of the sealed files}\CRfield{Status}{alive}\CRfield{First seen}{Chapter 640}}{\CRsheetheading{Appearance}
Sixty-three and spare, with the dry, maintained look of a vessel that has been carefully tempered and has never been allowed to run cold. He dresses in the Hearthseat’s plain dark wool with a strip of lead-grey at the collar that denotes the office and nothing else; he has no rings, no house-mark and no ornament, because an officer who wears a thing gives the rolls something to read. His hands are clean to the point of aggression — the hands of a man who has not carried fuel in forty years and does not need to. His voice is low, level and slightly warm, which is the most frightening thing about him, because his listeners must lean in and therefore agree to the sentence before it is finished. He has a trick of resting his fingertips on a slate while he speaks, not to consult it but to keep it flat, the way another man might keep a cup from sliding. He smells of warm stone, clean paper and the faintest trace of the Hearth-fire, which follows him from the Weighing Hall and which he has never tried to hide.

\CRsheetheading{Voice \& Manner}
Ledgerhand grammar made flesh: every sentence passive, every verb removed, every cruelty in the third person. He never raises his voice, never says \emph{I} where he can say \emph{the Keeping}, and never says \emph{you} where he can say \emph{the account}. He has eleven words for a deduction and will use the exact one, which is his way of being honest within the only vocabulary he considers real. When he is contradicted he becomes interested, which is worse than anger. He has one habit that his officers have learned to fear: he writes the thing down while the person is still speaking.

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item “The measure is banked. The account stands. Nothing is lost that we have kept. That is the whole of it, and it is not a threat.”

\item “You have said a thing that cannot be entered. I have entered it anyway. That is my kindness.”

\item “The world cannot be saved. The counting can be continued. Those are different propositions, and only one of them is my work.”

\item “One in twelve is printed on the notice. What a household believes is not in the notice, and is therefore not in the Keeping.”

\item “I have read the sealed file. You have not. Shall I tell you what it says, or shall we go on as we were?”

\end{itemize}

\CRsheetheading{History}
He was entered on the rolls at twenty-two and has never held another name. He rose not by cleverness but by an unbroken capacity to be present when a difficult slate had to be signed: the Ash Rising of Y.H. 668, the suppression of Haldre’s paper in 710, the sealing of the First Seam survey in 806, the Long Cold of 811. In each case he was the officer who wrote the final line in a hand that did not vary, and in each case the line was a kindness in the grammar of the Keeping — the district was quieted, the paper was suppressed, the survey was sealed, the levy was raised for the Hearth. He has never been accused of cruelty and has never understood an accusation when one was made, because he cannot see the person inside the account, and has spent forty years perfecting the not-seeing.

He has read the sealed file. He knows the Hearth is a wound and the Keeping is salvage from a failing repair. He knows the deduction in Low Kiln is one in three and that the printed notice is a founding invoice dressed as mercy. He knows the oldest repairs under the world are neither clay nor stone, and he knows what the Keldish translation and the Court translation of them were: both guesses, both near. He has read Haldre’s paper and has not burned his copy. He keeps it because it is the only honest document in the Hearthseat and because he has decided that honesty, left where it is, does no harm. He is not a believer. He is a continuance.

In the first weeks of Stone, Y.H. 812, he authorised a private whole return of forty unspent measures without recording the purchaser. He did this personally and with perfect composure, and has entered nothing about it anywhere except in the sealed file, where the entry reads: \emph{The instrument is in place. The account is carried.}

\CRsheetheading{Wounds \& Fears}
He has no wound he will admit to, which is itself the wound: a man who has trained himself not to feel the cold has become unable to feel anyone else’s. He fears the Waste growing inward, because it is the only thing in his ledger that does not balance and cannot be written down as a kindness. He fears a hot trace that will not cool, because it is the only measure that will not enter an account. He fears, most of all, a man who looks at a dying body and says plainly \emph{leave it}, because that sentence has no passive form and therefore cannot be entered, and a thing that cannot be entered is a thing the Keeping cannot survive. His contradiction is not hidden and not a secret: he knows the world cannot be saved by the Keeping, and he continues the Keeping anyway, and calls the continuation mercy.

\CRsheetheading{Desires}
He wants the account to continue. He thinks he wants the world kept. What he needs is to understand the difference — which he already knows and has chosen to forget — and that a man who continues a failing repair is not keeping the world but spending it, one district at a time. He will never understand this in any way that changes him. He will understand it perfectly in the way that lets him write it down.

\CRsheetheading{Bonds}
\textbf{Marra} — his collector, the most exact hand in his service, whose fingers are going grey and whose reports have never once mentioned her own deductions. He has praised her twice and once asked her, gently, whether she believed the printed figure. She said the account stood. He has not asked again, because the answer confirmed what he needed: she is one of his own, in the sense that she has learned not to see the person.

\textbf{Derren the Younger} — an officer’s son with access to the sealed file and a different last name in his heart. The younger man has begun to ask about the oldest repairs in language that is almost the Deep Hand. Steward Derren has not stopped him, which is the most dangerous permission in the Hearthseat.

\textbf{Pell Varr} — the Assessor-Marshal who put down the Ash Rising by list. They are the two men who understand what a district costs, and they have never once discussed it, because a discussion would require the word \emph{I}.

\textbf{Haldre} — the keeper who vanished in Y.H. 704. Steward Derren keeps Haldre’s paper in a drawer beside the sealed file and reads it on the Last Day, when the ash in the corners is not swept. He has decided that Haldre was right and that being right changes nothing.

\textbf{Rusk} — a name in a sealed file, a person of the sealed opinion, whom the Steward has never met and has caused to be watched for thirty years without ever ordering an arrest. He likes the man’s questions and has said so in a report, which is the closest thing to affection in the Hearthseat.

\textbf{Corin} — not yet a name in his account, only an irregularity in a slate from Greybank: a whole return whose deduction is zero. He has read that slate twice and has written nothing in the margin, which for him is an act of extraordinary restraint and the beginning of an interest.

\CRsheetheading{Arc So Far}
No chapters are written yet. He enters in a room gone cold — a single scene away from Dan, in the Weighing Hall or a counting room — where a slate is read aloud and a man is quietly entered. The reader will feel the shift in the prose before they know why.

\item No chapters written yet; first appearance planned for Ch 640 (a Court scene away from Dan).

\end{itemize}
}

A woman of thirty-odd years with the drained, level face of somebody who has walked the same road too often to measure it any more. Nothing about her is arranged for looking at: her coat is shortened at the skirt for the road’s mud, and the mud has dried on it in a pale scurf which she does not brush off, because a runner’s coat is a tool and nobody scours a tool for its own sake. A strap crosses her chest and a second, shorter strap has been let out to take the weight when the road is long; she settles both without seeming to, the way a person settles a burden that has become part of the walk. Her hands are the hands of a woman who carries and does not open. The fingers close on a slate’s edge with a working looseness, the thumb lies along the grain of the frame, and nothing presses where the writing is. She holds the slate edge-on to her own forearm so that the face of it turns toward her sleeve and the writing looks at nobody. That is not concealment: it is the manner of carrying a slate so the writing is not rubbed and no goer-by takes a figure off it without a hand to put there. She moves at the pace of a person who has made a bargain with distance and keeps it without thinking. What people notice first is the slate; what they notice last, if they notice at all, is that her hand went to it before her eyes went to them.

\CRsheetheading{Voice \& Manner}
Clipped, practical, the grammar of the road rather than the Court. She answers the question actually put and not the one behind it, and she is done with a conversation when the road is done with it, without rudeness and without apology. She never pronounces, never reads aloud, never says \emph{the account} or \emph{the figure} where \emph{the slate} will do. Her sentences are short and complete; what she will not carry she leaves standing where it was set down, the way a man leaves a pot where there is no hand to carry it. A slight dry amusement goes with the road and not with people.

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item “I don’t read it. I carry it. There’s a difference, and the road doesn’t care which.”

\item “Cross to Greybank. Reading goes up before noon. I’ve got a road to walk.”

\item “Ask the road. It knows the way and I know the weight. That’s the whole of what either of us knows.”

\end{itemize}

\CRsheetheading{History}
She comes out of Slate Row, where the Court’s tables and the Waiting Room stand and where a person can be made answerable for a thing merely by having touched it. She took up running because it was work that could be measured in the legs and kept in the hands: a slate goes from the Cross to Greybank and back, and what is written on it belongs to the person who set it down. Over the years she has carried slates for the assessor’s house, for the collector’s table at the Cross, and for Berr Clay the Thane, whose narrow slate goes up the clay road ahead of the reading and comes back with the true subtraction nobody in Sill has been shown. She has never been asked to read one and has never offered. The district is full of people who put a hand to a record before they put an eye to a person; she is one of them and does not know it, or does not think about it, which amounts to the same thing from the outside. She knows the road in all weathers, knows which ruts hold water and which stretch of the clay road dries pale in scurf, and has made a bargain with distance that she keeps without thinking. Nothing in her history has yet made her a reader of anyone’s private keeping, and she is careful that nothing does.

\CRsheetheading{Wounds \& Fears}
No wound is spoken of. Her hands carry the small wear of a working person who grips an edge and not a face: nails short, thumb callused along one side from the frame of a slate, the skin at the wrist hardened by a strap. She fears a slate rubbed blank in a coat, a strap parting on the road, and being made answerable for a figure she did not set down; these are the fears of a carrier, not of a clerk. She has seen what happens to a person in Slate Row who is caught between a figure and the person it is about, and she keeps her own face turned toward the sleeve.

\CRsheetheading{Desires}
She wants the road kept, the slates delivered whole, and to be paid for carrying and never for knowing. She thinks she wants nobody to take an interest in what she carries. What she needs, years from now, is harder: to understand that a figure is not a thing that travels by itself, and that the hand which lays the district’s separate keepings together will one day be a hand like hers — a carrier’s hand that has learned, too late, what it has been carrying. That day is far off and she is not yet part of it.

\CRsheetheading{Bonds}
\textbf{Ch 127 (bonds).} On Silt 10, the month’s first Account-day and market and the year’s fourth reading, she went up the clay road toward Greybank before noon carrying Berr Clay’s narrow slate edge-on to her forearm with the writing turned to her sleeve, the thumb along the grain of the frame and nothing pressing where the writing was, the second strap let out for the long road and dried pale scurf of road-mud unbrushed on the shortened skirt. The small flat correction of the strap and the turn of the wrist came first, her hand to the slate before her eyes to the crowd. To a woman at the rail who asked what she carried she answered the question put and not the one behind it: \emph{I don’t read it. I carry it. There’s a difference, and the road doesn’t care which}; and to the one who wanted more, \emph{Cross to Greybank. Reading goes up before noon. I’ve got a road to walk}. She gave no figure, read nothing aloud and did not look into the basket, and went on at the pace of a person who has made a bargain with distance and keeps it without thinking. Offstage on Silt 8 and 9 and not on any road; no slate of hers was opened within reach of the basket and no figure came off any wood. She is not the second man from Slate Row who went down the north bridge road with his own narrow slate turned to his sleeve, and not the soft-cuffed clerk reported at the landing; the second man’s direction and slate, the first man’s face, the well-asking answered with the weather, the clerk’s entered figure and the neighbour’s near-reaching are filed on their own places with a finger between every pair, and the green at the pot board and the shape at the market’s edge stayed sightings on separate trays, never joined to her wood. Her \textbf{eighth} record-first hand stays eight and joined to none, with a finger between it and the fifth shaping, the entered figure, Ilva’s ninth standing nine and the faces filed and not counted; four figures going up the road did not make her a reader of any of them and no tenth stood up in the empty place. The reported second slate of Silt 6 stayed a shape in a mouth on a place of its own, not on stage, not hers to read and given no figure by four figures or by any road; the carrying goes on gathering interest toward the far-off hand that will lay the district’s private keepings together and the far-off day she must choose whether to read what she carries, advanced and not paid. No new scar or possession, no change of voice.

\textbf{Ch 118 (bonds).} Not on stage as a sighting on any of the three days; on Ilmen 12 (Day 406) she is present only as the unnamed subject of a word at the yard well: one of the bucket-round said low, into the space between her pot and the next woman’s shoulder, that the woman who carries the slate had once carried a figure that named a person she knew. No owner stood under the word, no room came with it, no hand at a slate, no name for the person, no figure, no date and nobody to ask; it stopped on the stone lip and went off into the yard’s ordinary talk. The boy took it apart as a surgeon takes a field apart and filed it as the \textbf{fifth shaping} of the well-saying on a place of its own with a finger between it and her \textbf{eighth} record-first hand and another between it and the Cross-to-Greybank road saying and a third between it and the four ownerless directions — expressly not a witness (no owner standing to be asked), not a confession (no mouth owned the figure), not a reader made (no slate opened within reach of the basket) and not a sixth shaping, with no sixth made due. Her eighth hand stays eight and joined to none; she is neither made a reader by the word nor joined to Ilva’s count in wood, which stayed on its own place with a finger between. The word buys no figure and no payer; her going up the road unread on the Account-days behind goes on gathering interest toward the far-off hand that will lay the district’s private keepings together. No new scar or possession, no change of voice. \textbf{Ch 117 (bonds).} On Ilmen 10, the year’s first Account-day and market, she went up the clay road toward Greybank before noon carrying Berr Clay’s narrow slate edge-on to her forearm, the writing turned to her sleeve, her hand to the slate before her eyes went up to the crowd. There’s a difference, and the road doesn’t care which} — so that the runner’s saying went on a place of its own beside the other unread things. The boy filed the order of her reaching as the eighth record-first hand-shape joined to none, her eighth hand staying eight with no ninth made of the carrying and no reader, witness or payer standing. The first arithmetic of the year went up the road in Berr’s locked box while hers went unread; the two went on separate places and were not joined. No new scar or possession, no change of voice. \textbf{Ch 112 (bonds).} On Stone 30 (Day 389), the year’s third and last Account-day and market, she goes up the clay road toward Greybank before noon with Berr Clay’s narrow slate held edge-on to her forearm and the writing turned to her sleeve, the thumb along the grain of the frame and nothing pressing where the writing is — not concealment but the manner of carrying a slate so the writing is not rubbed and no goer-by takes a figure off it without a hand to put there. Her hand goes to the slate before her eyes go to the crowd, and the reaching comes before the word; no figure comes off the face of it and she is not made a reader by the year’s last figure. The boy files no tenth hand: her \textbf{eighth} stays eight on a place of its own, joined neither to Ilva’s ninth at the well, Berr’s twice-wiped thumb, the charcoal under the loaf shelf, the soft-cuffed clerk’s inward slate nor any other private keeping. She was offstage on Stone 28 and 29. No new scar or possession and no change of voice; the carrying goes on gathering interest toward the far-off day she must choose whether to read what she carries, and nothing on this last market made the choice for her.

\textbf{Ch 110 (bonds).} On Stone 23 (Day 382), before noon, she goes up the clay road toward Greybank with Berr Clay’s narrow slate held edge-on to her forearm and the writing turned toward her sleeve; the thumb lies along the grain of the frame and nothing presses where the writing is — not concealment but the manner of carrying a slate so the writing is not rubbed and no goer-by takes a figure off it without a hand to put there. The second strap is let out for the long road and dried pale scurf of road-mud stands unbrushed on the shortened skirt; the small flat correction of the strap and the turn of the wrist come first, her hand to the slate before her eyes to the yard, and no figure comes off the face of it. To the woman who asks what she carries she answers the question put and not the one behind it: \emph{I don’t read it. I carry it. There’s a difference, and the road doesn’t care which}; to the woman who wants more, \emph{Ask the road. It knows the way and I know the weight. That’s the whole of what either of us knows}. She settles the second strap again, not for the women and not for the road, reads nothing aloud, gives no figure and does not look into the basket, and goes on at the pace of a person who has made a bargain with distance and keeps it without thinking. The boy files the turning of the writing toward herself on a place of its own beside the Ash 6 sighting with a finger between: a runner going up with the writing toward herself is not a voice standing in a doorway and not a saying fulfilled; no fifth shaping of the Frost 14 well-saying, no reader, no witness and no payment, and he joins her neither to Ilva’s strip in its sleeve, Berr’s twice-wiped thumb, the charcoal under the loaf shelf, the soft-cuffed clerk’s inward slate nor any other private keeping. Her \textbf{eighth} record-first hand stays eight with no tenth, and \textbf{eleven arithmetics behind one unsigned figure do not make her a reader}. She was offstage on Stone 22 and 24; nothing from the keeping at the fold or the fourth direction over the boards came to her road as sign, lesson, mending, cause or payment, and the far-off day she must choose whether to read what she carries was not brought nearer. No new scar or possession, no bond paid, no change of voice.

\textbf{Ch 109 (bonds).} On Stone 20 (Day 379), the month’s second Account-day and market, she took Berr Clay’s narrow slate up the clay road toward Greybank before noon, held edge-on to her own forearm with the writing turned toward her sleeve, the thumb along the grain of the frame and nothing pressing where the writing was. The second strap was let out for the long road and dried pale scurf of road-mud stood unbrushed on the skirt she had shortened for it; the small flat correction of the strap and the turn of the wrist came first, her hand going to the slate before her eyes went to the crowd, and no figure came off the face of it. To the woman who asked what she carried she answered the question put and not the one behind it: \emph{I don’t read it. I carry it. There’s a difference, and the road doesn’t care which}. To the woman who wanted more she said, \emph{Ask the road. It knows the way and I know the weight. That’s the whole of what either of us knows}. She settled the second strap again, not for the women and not for the square, gave no figure, read nothing aloud and did not look into the basket, and went on at the pace of a person who has made a bargain with distance and keeps it without thinking. The boy filed the turning of the writing toward herself on a place of its own beside the Ash 6 sighting, with a finger between: a runner going up with the writing toward herself was not a voice standing in a doorway and not a saying fulfilled. He made no fifth shaping of the Frost 14 well-saying, no witness, no reader and no payment, and joined her neither to Ilva’s strip in its sleeve, to Berr’s twice-wiped thumb, to the charcoal beneath the loaf shelf, to the soft-cuffed clerk’s inward slate nor to any other private keeping. Her \textbf{eighth} record-first hand stayed eight with no tenth; she was a runner and not a reader, and \textbf{eleven arithmetics going up the road behind her did not make her one}. She was offstage on Stone 19 and 21; nothing from the keeping at the fold or the eleven readings came to her road as figure, lesson or payment, and the far-off day she must choose whether to read what she carries was not brought nearer. No new scar or possession, no change of voice.

\textbf{Ch 108 (bonds).} On Stone 17 (Day 376), in the afternoon, she went \textbf{up} the clay road in the boy’s sight out of Low Kiln with Berr Clay’s narrow slate held edge-on to her forearm and the writing turned toward her own sleeve, the thumb along the grain of the frame and nothing pressing where the writing was. The second strap was let out for the long road and dried pale scurf of road-mud stood unbrushed on the skirt she had shortened for it; the small flat correction of the strap and the turn of the wrist came first, her hand going to the slate before her eyes went to the yard. To the woman who asked what she carried she said \emph{A slate. I don’t read it. I carry it. There’s a difference, and the road doesn’t care which}, and to one who wanted more, \emph{Ask the road. It knows the way and I know the weight. That’s the whole of what either of us knows}. She gave no figure, read nothing aloud and did not look into the basket, and went on at the pace of a person who has made a bargain with distance and keeps it without thinking. The boy filed the turning of the writing toward herself on a place of its own \textbf{beside} the Ash 6 sighting with a finger between: a runner going up with the writing toward herself is not a voice standing in a doorway and not a saying fulfilled. He made no fifth shaping of the Frost 14 well-saying, no witness, no reader and no payment, and joined her neither to Ilva’s strip, Berr’s thumb, the charcoal, the soft-cuffed clerk’s inward slate nor any other private keeping; her eighth record-first hand stayed eight with no tenth. She is a runner and not a reader and the road does not care which. Offstage on Stone 16 and 18; Ilva’s ninth at the well, the keeping at the fold found where put and ten arithmetics behind one unsigned figure brought no figure to her road. She was not made a reader early and the far-off day she must choose whether to read what she carries was not brought nearer. No new scar or possession, no bond paid, no change of voice.

\textbf{Ch 107 (bonds).} On Stone 14 (Day 373), in the afternoon, she came \textbf{down} the clay road in the boy’s sight out of the direction of Greybank, with Berr Clay’s narrow slate held edge-on to her own forearm and the writing turned toward her sleeve. The second strap was let out for the long road and dried pale scurf of road-mud stood unbrushed on the skirt she had shortened for it; the small flat correction of the strap came first and the turn of the wrist after it, bringing the edge round, and only then did her eyes go to the yard, her hand having gone to the slate before either. The thumb lay along the grain of the frame and nothing pressed where the writing was — not concealment but the manner of carrying a slate so the writing is not rubbed and no goer-by takes a figure off it — and she went on at the pace of a person who has made a bargain with distance and keeps it without thinking. She gave no figure, read nothing aloud and did not look into the basket. The boy filed the turning of the writing toward herself on a place of its own \textbf{beside} the Ash 6 sighting with a finger between: a runner coming back down the road with the writing toward herself was not a voice standing in a doorway and not a saying fulfilled. He made no fifth shaping of the Frost 14 well-saying, no witness, no reader and no payment, and joined her neither to Ilva’s strip, Berr’s thumb, the charcoal, the soft-cuffed clerk’s inward slate nor any other private keeping; her eighth record-first hand stayed eight with no tenth. She is a runner and not a reader and the road does not care which. Offstage on Stone 13 and 15; no runner was seen on those days, the ten arithmetics behind one unsigned figure brought no figure to her road, and Sella’s small keeping at the fold on the fifteenth evening was neither sign nor payment to her. She was not made a reader early and the far-off day she must choose whether to read what she carries was not brought nearer. No new scar or possession, no bond paid, no change of voice.

\textbf{Ch 106 (bonds).} On Stone 10 (Day 369), the deep-winter month’s first Account-day and market, she took Berr Clay’s narrow slate up the clay road toward Greybank before noon, edge-on to her forearm with the writing turned to her sleeve, making the small flat correction of the strap and the turn of the wrist first, her hand to the slate before her eyes to the crowd and nothing pressing where the writing was; no figure came off it. To a woman who asked what she carried she answered the question put and not the one behind it: \emph{I don’t read it. I carry it. There’s a difference, and the road doesn’t care which}; to one who wanted more, \emph{Cross to Greybank. Reading goes up before noon. I’ve got a road to walk}, without rudeness and without apology and with the pace of a person who has made a bargain with distance. Berr read one in twelve twice over the basket below her — once for the moot, once for the late households — called the levy, denied it with \emph{your house}, never \emph{I}, and went off with the box locked and Stone’s first true subtraction inside; \textbf{ten arithmetics now stand behind one unsigned figure, ten are ten and not one account}, and they did not make her a reader of what she carried. She is a runner and not a reader, her order of reaching the \textbf{eighth} record-first hand on a place of its own with no tenth, joined to none — not Marra, not the soft-handed man of Slate Row, not the clerks, not Ilva with her count in wood, not the green-mouthed woman, not the Drawing collector and not the woman whose voice came over the boards. The Frost 14 well-saying stands at one saying and four shapings beside her eighth hand with a finger between, not a witness, not a confession, not a joining and not paid; the collector’s ordinary hand on its own tray at the Drawing two mornings later is not joined to hers. Offstage on Stone 11 and 12; no runner was seen on either day and no figure came off any slate. Sella set the basket in the moot-post’s finger’s width of shade where no slate lay and stood half a pace off through the reading and the bell and gave the runner no name. No bond paid, no figure given, no new scar or possession, no change of voice.

She is a runner and not a reader, her order of reaching the \textbf{eighth} record-first hand on a place of its own with no tenth, joined to none — not Marra, not the soft-handed man of Slate Row, not the clerks, not Ilva with her count in wood, not the green-mouthed woman, not the Drawing collector and not the woman whose voice came over the boards. \textbf{Ch 94 (bonds).} Offstage on Ash 4 and 5, she was glimpsed once on Ash 6 (Day 335) coming \textbf{down} the clay road in the afternoon with the writing of Berr Clay’s narrow slate turned toward herself for the first time in the boy’s knowing of her. On Account-days she takes that road up toward Greybank before noon with the writing to her sleeve and the slate’s face turned away from everybody; here she came down it and the face stayed turned toward her own forearm, still edge-on, the writing looking at her sleeve and at nobody, the thumb along the grain of the frame with nothing pressing where the writing was and no figure coming off it. The second strap was let out for the long road and dried pale scurf of road-mud stood unbrushed on the shortened skirt; her hand went to the slate before her eyes went to the yard. To a woman who asked what she carried she answered the question put and not the one behind it: \emph{Ask the road. It knows the way and I know the weight. That’s the whole of what either of us knows.} She is a runner and not a reader, her order of reaching stays the \textbf{eighth} record-first hand on a place of its own with no tenth, and she is joined to none — not Marra, not the soft-handed man of Slate Row, not the clerks, not Ilva, not the green-mouthed woman, not the Drawing collector and not the woman whose voice came over the boards. The boy filed the turning of the writing toward herself on a place of its own \textbf{beside} the Ash 5 fourth shaping of the well-saying with a finger between: a voice said the runner had come back down the road and here she comes, but a voice standing in no doorway is not a prophecy fulfilled, and he refused to join saying to sighting, make a fifth shaping, make her a reader, make the sighting a payment or pay the claim (T080 advanced, not paid). The far-off day she must choose whether to read what she has carried is not brought nearer. No bond paid, no figure given, no new scar or possession, no change of voice.

\textbf{Ch 92 (bonds).} On Bone 30, the month’s third and last Account-day and market, she carried Berr’s slate up the road toward Greybank before noon, edge-on to her forearm with the writing turned to her sleeve, the second strap let out for the long stretch and the dried pale scurf of road-mud standing unbrushed on the skirt she had shortened for it. I carry it. There’s a difference, and the road doesn’t care which} and, to the one who wanted more, \emph{Cross to Greybank. Reading goes up before noon. The sixth arithmetic had changed the district’s figures below her on the square — six arithmetics now standing behind one printed figure, six readings six and not one account — and had not made her a reader of what she carried; her order of reaching stayed the eighth record-first hand in the district, eight and not a rule, kept on a place of its own and joined to none, and the three shapings of the Frost 14 well-saying stood beside it with a finger between every pair and did not make her a witness, a cause or a confession. She was not the soft-handed man from Slate Row, not the clerk at the Court’s table, not Ilva with her count in wood, not the woman who had carried the saying at the well and not the green-mouthed woman at the pot board or the foundling at the market’s edge, which stayed a colour and a shape with no eighth; Sella set the basket in the moot-post’s shade and stood half a pace off and gave the runner no name. She was offstage on Bone 28 and 29 and Bone went out without a boundary drawn. No bond paid, no figure given, no new scar or possession, no change of voice.

\textbf{Berr Clay, the Thane of Clay} — she carries his narrow slate between the Cross and Greybank and does not read it. He is a good reason in a neat hand; she is the road under it. On Day 158 his cord was spoken of as a direction up the clay road, and on Day 159 she took the slate up that road ahead of the reading, after he had called the levy and denied it with \emph{your house}, never \emph{I}. No loyalty is spoken and no figure passes between them.

\textbf{The Cross and Greybank} — the two ends of her road. At the Cross the reading goes up before noon; at Greybank the factor and the bank are. She joins the two places without ever joining what is written at either.

\textbf{Sella Vail and the Vail basket} — on Day 158 she came through the Clay Yard and Sella carried the boy past at the half-pace, gave the house no name for the slate and did not say whose it was. Neither woman asked the other anything. At the Cross on Day 159 Sella set the basket in the moot-post’s shade where no slate lay.

\textbf{The boy under the Vail roof} — he does not know her name and she has not looked into the basket. He saw the order of her reaching and filed it as the eighth record-first hand in the district, on a place of its own, joined to none. She has no idea she has been filed.

\textbf{Ch 40 (bonds).} On the second Account-day of Tallow she is seen again going up the clay road with Berr’s narrow slate held edge-on to her forearm, her hand to it before her eyes go to the crowd, the small flat correction of the strap and the turn of the wrist bringing the edge round; her coat is shortened at the skirt for the road’s mud with the dried pale scurf unbrushed, two straps settled, thumb along the grain of the frame and nothing pressing where the writing is. To a woman who asks what she carries: \emph{I don’t read it. I carry it. There’s a difference, and the road doesn’t care which}; to the woman who wants more: \emph{Cross to Greybank. Reading goes up before noon. I’ve got a road to walk.} No figure comes off the slate and no joining is made to Marra, the clerks, the reed-cutter’s cord, Berr’s twice-wiped thumb, the finger beneath the loaf shelf or the soft-cuffed clerk at the landing. She is a runner and not a reader; the order of her reaching remains the eighth record-first hand on a place of its own (T080 advanced, not paid).

\CRsheetheading{Arc So Far}
\textbf{Ch 127 (Days 432–434, Silt 8–10).} On Silt 10, the month’s first Account-day and market and the year’s fourth reading, she takes Berr Clay’s slate up the clay road toward Greybank before noon, edge-on and writing to her sleeve, the hand to the slate before her eyes went to the crowd and the second strap let out for the long road. To a woman at the rail who asked what she carried she answers the question put and not the one behind it — \emph{I don’t read it. I carry it. There’s a difference, and the road doesn’t care which} — and to the one who wants more, \emph{Cross to Greybank. Reading goes up before noon. I’ve got a road to walk}; no figure comes off the slate. Offstage on Silt 8 and 9 and not on any road. The eighth stays eight and joined to none, and four figures going up the road in a locked box do not make her a reader of what she carries; the reported second slate of Silt 6 stays a shape in a mouth on a place of its own, not on stage, not hers and given no figure. The second man’s direction and turned slate, the first man’s face, the well-asking answered with the weather, the clerk’s entered figure, the neighbour’s near-reaching and the two market sightings go on their own places with a finger between every pair; the woman’s quarter-turned cup and the foundling’s stopped half-beat are never joined to her wood and no eighth of either came. The carrying gathers interest toward the far-off day she must choose whether to read what she carries, advanced and not paid. No new scar or possession, no change of voice; forward, not closed.

The second man’s direction and turned slate, the first man’s face, the well-asking answered with the weather, the clerk’s entered figure and the two market sightings of this day’s market go on their own places with a finger between every pair; the woman’s quarter-turned cup and the foundling’s stopped half-beat are never joined to her wood and no eighth of either came. The carrying gathers interest toward the far-off day she must choose whether to read what she carries, advanced and not paid. No new scar or possession, no change of voice; forward, not closed.
