She enters in the firing month of Y.H. 813, on the eve of the first Account-day of Tallow, and is seen twice: once coming through the Clay Yard from the direction of the Cross with Berr Clay’s narrow slate held edge-on to her forearm, and once the next morning taking it up the clay road toward Greybank. In the yard a woman asked what the levy would take now the kilns had been brought up and hands were in the month; Hessa answered that she did not read it, she carried it, that there was a difference and the road did not care which; when the woman wanted more she said \emph{Cross to Greybank. Reading goes up before noon. I’ve got a road to walk} and went on through the yard, leaving the question standing where it had been set down. Her hand went to the slate before her eyes went to the people, the small flat correction of the strap and a turn of the wrist to bring the edge round. To the boy that order of reaching is an eighth such hand-shape in the district, kept on its own place beside Marra’s pause, the neat dark hand, the Court-table clerk, the soft-cuffed clerk at the landing, the soft hands at Slate Row, Berr’s twice-wiped thumb and the finger that goes beneath the Vail loaf shelf. He does not let eight likenesses trouble him into a rule, for a rule wants a payer and no payer has been named to any of them. At the Cross on the Account-day she came through again with the slate edge-on, hand to slate before eye to the crowd, and went up the clay road with the writing turned to her sleeve; no figure came off it under any roof in Sill. She is a runner and not a reader of anyone’s private keeping, and the figure on the slate remained what figures on carried slates remained in this district: a thing somebody else had set down and nobody here had read.

She enters the second Account-day of the firing month as she entered the first: a figure going up the road in a narrow slate held edge-on, the writing turned toward a sleeve and the hand arriving before the eyes. The road between Cross and Greybank is the whole of her account, and she joins the two ends without joining what is written at either. The district is full of hands that put a record before a person; hers is one more such hand and she has made a manner of it, so that a slate is carried and no figure is read and nothing in it becomes hers to answer for. The boy has filed the order once and does not file it twice; eight likenesses must still be held apart by hand, for a rule wants a payer and no payer has been named to any of them.

\item Ch 127: On Silt 10, the month’s first Account-day and market and the year’s fourth reading, she went up the clay road toward Greybank before noon carrying Berr Clay’s narrow slate edge-on to her forearm with the writing turned to her sleeve, the thumb along the grain of the frame and nothing pressing where the writing was, the second strap let out for the long road and dried pale scurf of road-mud unbrushed on the shortened skirt. The small flat correction of the strap and the turn of the wrist came first, her hand to the slate before her eyes to the crowd. To a woman at the rail who asked what she carried she answered the question put and not the one behind it: \emph{I don’t read it. I carry it. There’s a difference, and the road doesn’t care which}; and to the one who wanted more, \emph{Cross to Greybank. Reading goes up before noon. I’ve got a road to walk}. She gave no figure, read nothing aloud and did not look into the basket, and went on at the pace of a person who has made a bargain with distance and keeps it without thinking. Offstage on Silt 8 and 9 and not on any road; no slate of hers was opened within reach of the basket and no figure came off any wood. She is not the second man from Slate Row who went down the north bridge road with his own narrow slate turned to his sleeve, and not the soft-cuffed clerk whose entered figure stayed a report at the landing; the second man’s direction and slate, the first man’s face, the well-asking answered with the weather, the clerk’s entered figure and the neighbour’s near-reaching are filed on their own places with a finger between every pair. At the market a woman turned a cup a quarter and a foundling stopped a half-beat after a note, two sightings on separate trays, never joined to her wood and with no eighth of either. Her eighth record-first hand stayed eight and joined to none, with a finger between it and the fifth shaping, the entered figure, Ilva’s ninth standing nine and the faces filed and not counted; four figures going up the road did not make her a reader of any of them. No new scar or possession, no change of voice.

\end{itemize}

\item Ch 118: On Ilmen 12 (Day 406) she is on stage only as the unnamed subject of a word at the yard well: a neighbour said once that the woman who carries the slate had once carried a figure that named a person she knew, with no owner standing, no room, no hand at a slate, no name, no figure, no date and nobody to ask. The boy filed it as the fifth shaping of the well-saying on its own tray with a finger between it and her eighth record-first hand and another between it and the Cross-to-Greybank road saying, a third finger between it and the four ownerless directions; no witness, confession, reader or sixth made due. She is not a sighting that day and not made a reader by the word; her eighth hand stays eight and joined to none. Offstage as a sighting on all three days. No new scar or possession, no change of voice.

No new scar or possession, no change of voice.

Her eighth record-first hand stayed eight with no tenth and joined to none. Offstage on Stone 28 and 29. No new scar or possession and no change of voice; the carrying goes on gathering interest toward the far-off day she must choose whether to read what she carries.

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item Ch 110: On Stone 23 (Day 382), before noon, she went up the clay road toward Greybank with Berr Clay’s narrow slate held edge-on to her forearm and the writing turned toward her sleeve, the thumb along the grain of the frame and nothing pressing where the writing was — not concealment but the manner of carrying a slate so the writing is not rubbed and no goer-by takes a figure off it without a hand to put there. The second strap was let out for the long road and dried pale scurf of road-mud stood unbrushed on the shortened skirt; the small flat correction of the strap and the turn of the wrist came first, her hand to the slate before her eyes to the yard, and no figure came off the face of it. To the woman who asked what she carried she answered the question put and not the one behind it: \emph{I don’t read it. I carry it. There’s a difference, and the road doesn’t care which}; to the woman who wanted more, \emph{Ask the road. It knows the way and I know the weight. That’s the whole of what either of us knows}. She settled the second strap again, not for the women and not for the road, read nothing aloud, gave no figure and did not look into the basket, and went on at the pace of a person who has made a bargain with distance and keeps it without thinking. The boy filed the turning of the writing toward herself on a place of its own beside the Ash 6 sighting with a finger between: a runner going up with the writing toward herself was not a voice standing in a doorway and not a saying fulfilled; no fifth shaping of the Frost 14 well-saying, no reader, no witness and no payment, and he joined her neither to Ilva’s strip, Berr’s thumb, the charcoal, the soft-cuffed clerk’s inward slate nor any other private keeping. Her eighth record-first hand stayed eight with no tenth, and eleven arithmetics behind one unsigned figure did not make her a reader. She was offstage on Stone 22 and 24; nothing from the keeping at the fold or the fourth direction over the boards came to her road as sign, lesson, mending, cause or payment, and the far-off day she must choose whether to read what she carries was not brought nearer. No new scar or possession, no bond paid, no change of voice.

\end{itemize}

\item Ch 107: Day 373, Stone 14, Fourthday, in the afternoon, coming \textbf{down} the clay road in the boy’s sight out of the direction of Greybank, with Berr Clay’s narrow slate held edge-on to her own forearm and the writing turned toward her sleeve. The second strap was let out for the long road and dried pale scurf of road-mud stood unbrushed on the skirt she had shortened for it; the small flat correction of the strap came first and the turn of the wrist after it, bringing the edge round, and only then did her eyes go to the yard, her hand having gone to the slate before either. The thumb lay along the grain of the frame and nothing pressed where the writing was, not concealment but the manner of carrying a slate so the writing was not rubbed and no goer-by took a figure off it; she went on at the pace of a person who has made a bargain with distance. She gave no figure, read nothing aloud and did not look into the basket. Ten arithmetics of the year stood behind one unsigned figure up the clay road in Berr’s locked box, with Stone’s first true subtraction inside and the key gone up in a coat pocket that does not come back down, ten and not one account, the figure read still not the figure paid and no doctrine out of ten, and none of it made her a reader of what she carried. The boy filed the turning of the writing toward herself on a place of its own \textbf{beside} the Ash 6 sighting with a finger between, a runner coming back down the road with the writing toward herself being neither a voice standing in a doorway nor a saying fulfilled; he made no fifth shaping of the Frost 14 well-saying, no reader, no witness, no payment, and joined her neither to Ilva’s strip, Berr’s thumb, the charcoal, the soft-cuffed clerk’s inward slate nor any other private keeping. She is a runner and not a reader, her order of reaching the \textbf{eighth} record-first hand on a place of its own with no tenth, joined to none — not Marra, not the soft-handed man of Slate Row, not the clerks, not Ilva with her count in wood, not the green-mouthed woman, not the Drawing collector with his ordinary untroubled hand and not the woman whose voice came over the boards. Offstage on Stone 13 and 15; no runner was seen on either day, and nothing from those days crossed her road as sign, lesson, cause, payment or payer. The far-off day she must choose whether to read what she carries was not brought nearer. No bond paid, no figure given, no new scar or possession, no change of voice. Forward, not closed.

\end{itemize}

\CRcharacter{Ilva}{the woman who keeps the month’s firings in a strip of birch bark}{build/portraits/ilva.pdf}{\CRfield{Also called}{Ilva of the firing work, the woman at the yard well}\CRfield{Role}{other}\CRfield{Born}{Y.H. 780s, Low Kiln, Sill, Grath — the year was never entered on any slate she keeps}\CRfield{Kind}{human (Grathic)}\CRfield{Origin}{Low Kiln, Sill, Grath; of the yard’s firing work, not of a kiln-house}\CRfield{Allegiance}{the firing work of the Clay Yard, Low Kiln}\CRfield{Status}{alive; seen once on Silt 12, Y.H. 814 (Day 436) at the yard well drawing with the pail against her knee, the rope stiff in the dry cold giving its small rasp, clay dried pale in her nail crescents and finer rack dust in one thumb seam she does not scrub out, her hand going flat over the fold before her eyes went to the asker and her mouth after both, the half-beat lying in the gap where a lesser observer would put an intention. A second neighbour at the well, having heard the round’s talk of the figure that went back into the fist on Ilmen 26, asked whether a count kept in wood would be taken at the next reading — not a second offer and not the old question repeated, but the fear advanced by another mouth; the short strip of notched birch stayed in its fold, pale where a thumb had rubbed the notches and dark in the uncut grain between, not taken out, read, copied, counted, shown or joined, and no figure came off the wood. She answered the question put and not the one behind it — \emph{Ask the pot what it cost. I keep the count, not the account} — and put the flat of her hand once more on the sleeve and went back to the pail, nobody turning twice. The boy filed the second asking on a place of its own beside the offer and its return, her ninth record-first hand and the fifth shaping, with a finger between every pair, not a second offer, custom, tenth hand, witness, sale or calling of the loan, expressly unjoined to the clerk’s entered figure, the reported second slate, the neighbour’s near-reaching, the well-asking answered with weather and the three likenesses of Slate Row; her fear is advanced and unpaid, the asking not repeated on Silt 13, the ninth staying nine and the count staying in wood. earlier, alive; seen once on Ilmen 26 at the yard well drawing with the pail against her knee, the rope stiff in the dry cold giving its small rasp, clay dried pale in her nail crescents and finer rack dust worked into the seam of one thumb she does not scrub out, her hand going flat over the fold before her eyes went to the asker and her mouth after both, the half-beat lying in the gap where a lesser observer would have put an intention. A woman waiting her turn brought a number up out of a shut fist, held it toward the light and put the fist toward the strip in Ilva’s sleeve, saying she could put a figure to the month’s firings; Ilva answered the question put and not the one behind it — \emph{Ask the pot what it cost. I keep the count, not the account} — and the figure went from the fist toward the wood, looked at the light and went back into the sleeve, arriving nowhere, the stick keeping its notch and learning no name and the woman going back to the round with \emph{Then it’s a stick}. No slate was opened within reach of the basket, no figure came off the wood, no reader was made and no name was spoken over the notches; the boy filed the \textbf{offer and its return} on a place of its own beside her ninth record-first hand and the fifth shaping, with a finger between every pair, a reaching gathering interest toward the far-off hand that will one day lay the district’s private keepings together and not that hand. A woman of the firing work in Low Kiln, past her first youth and not old enough to be spoken of as old, with the yard’s pale clay dried in the crescents of her nails and the finer grey dust of the racks worked into the seam of one thumb. She does not scrub the seam out. Her hands know the weight of a pail and the edge of a wet board, and are not soft. She draws water at the yard well with the pail against her knee and goes on with her work without looking to see who has noticed her. The district would not turn its head twice for her; she is of the yard in the way the rack and the trough are of the yard. What she carries that nobody sees is a short strip of birch bark notched along one edge, pale where a thumb has rubbed the notches and dark in the uncut grain between, kept in her sleeve and put back with the flat of a hand. People notice the pail first and the sleeve not at all, which is the order she prefers.

\CRsheetheading{Voice \& Manner}
Plain, short, and exact in the way a tally is exact. She answers the question put and not the one behind it, and she never volunteers a figure for the work. She gives no name to the thing she keeps and has never been asked for one. There is no proverb in her, no instruction addressed to a pot or a fire; that belongs to the houses. When she is asked how many firings a month has taken, her hand goes to the record, her thumb passes over it, her eyes go to the person who asked, and only then does her mouth open. She does not explain the order and would not know what there was to explain.

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item “Five to this morning.”

\item “If it went on a slate it would want a figure put on it. It’s a firing. Ask the pot what it cost.”

\item “I keep the count of the fires. I don’t keep the account.”

\end{itemize}

\CRsheetheading{History}
She was born in Low Kiln into the firing work and has never left it for a house. The work is the racks, the pails, the carrying, the counting of how many times the kilns have been lit since the month came in; it is done in glances and hands and the weight of the thing carried, and nobody in the yard gives it a figure aloud. A slate would want a figure put on it, and the yard has no wish to give the slate one, so Ilva keeps the month’s firings in wood. The strip is hers; she puts it in her sleeve with the flat of her hand and takes it out when a question is asked that wants an answer. She is not a reader of private keepings. She is not the woman in the grey coat at the flare, not Hessa Rale with her edge-on slate between the Cross and Greybank, not the soft-cuffed clerk set below the north bridge for a measure nobody called, and not an officer with a reason. She is a woman who keeps a count in wood and draws water in a yard.

\CRsheetheading{Wounds \& Fears}
The sweet edge of lead glaze comes up off High Kiln on a wrong wind and goes over the boards and out again; she has learned to know it on the air and to make nothing of it, as the yard makes nothing of it. The yard goes around the place in the returning line where a hand went in on Seed 15 and did not come back, and she goes around it with a look and a wide step like everybody else, and does not count it among the firings or give it a name. Her fear is small and practical: that one day a slate will be put to her stick and a figure taken off it, and the count of firings will become an account with a payer standing under it. She has no wish to be the woman who explains what the notches mean.

\CRsheetheading{Desires}
She wants the firings to go on and the count to stay true in wood, where no clerk’s thumb can read it. She thinks she wants nothing beyond keeping her place in the yard. What she needs, though she is far from it, is to be one of the hands that will one day lay the district’s private keepings together — the charcoal under the shelf, the reed-cutter’s cord, the knot-string, the six pages, the tins, the pewter tin, the inward slates and this strip of notched birch — and to find that a count kept from a slate was still a record all along.

\CRsheetheading{Bonds}
\textbf{Ch 128 (bonds).} Seen once on Silt 12 (Day 436) at the yard well drawing with the pail against her knee, the rope stiff in the dry cold giving its small rasp, clay dried pale in the crescents of her nails and the finer rack dust worked into the seam of one thumb, which she does not scrub out; her hands know the weight of a pail and the edge of a wet board and have never been soft, and people notice the pail first and the sleeve not at all, which is the order she prefers. In the afternoon a second neighbour at the well, having heard the round’s talk of the figure that went back into the fist on Ilmen 26, asks whether a count kept in wood will be taken at the next reading — not a second offer and not the old question repeated, but the fear advanced by another mouth. Her hand goes flat over the fold before her eyes go to the asker and her mouth after both, the half-beat lying in the gap where a lesser observer would put an intention; the short strip of notched birch stays in its fold, pale where a thumb has rubbed the notches and dark in the uncut grain between, and is not taken out, read, copied, counted, shown or joined, and no figure comes off the wood. No slate is opened within reach of the basket, no room is entered and no reader is made. She answers the question put and not the one behind it — \emph{Ask the pot what it cost. I keep the count, not the account} — puts the flat of her hand once more on the sleeve and goes back to the pail, nobody turning twice. The boy files the \textbf{second asking} on a place of its own beside the offer and its return, her ninth record-first hand and the fifth shaping of the well-saying, with a finger between every pair: not a second offer, not a custom, not a tenth hand, not a witness, not a sale and not the calling of the loan, no figure under it and no payer, and expressly unjoined to the clerk’s entered figure, the reported second slate of Silt 6, the neighbour’s near-reaching at the shelf, the well-asking answered with weather and the three likenesses of Slate Row. She is expressly not the speaker of the first asking and is not made a reader by the second; the ninth stays nine, the count stays in wood where no clerk’s thumb can take a figure off it, and her fear is advanced and unpaid. The asking is not repeated on Silt 13. No new scar or possession, no change of voice; forward, not closed.

\textbf{Ch 123 (bonds).} On Ilmen 26 she stands once at the yard well drawing with the pail against her knee, the rope stiff in the dry cold giving its small rasp, clay dried pale in the crescents of her nails and the finer rack dust worked into the seam of one thumb, which she does not scrub out; her hands know the weight of a pail and the edge of a wet board and have never been soft, and people notice the pail first and the sleeve not at all, which is the order she prefers. A woman waiting her turn shifts a pot from one hip to the other, brings a number up out of a shut fist, holds it toward the light and puts the fist toward the strip in Ilva’s sleeve, saying she could put a figure to the month’s firings. Ilva’s hand goes flat over the fold before her eyes go to the asker and her mouth opens after both, the half-beat lying in the gap where a lesser observer would have put an intention; the short strip of notched birch lies in its fold, pale where a thumb has rubbed the notches and dark in the uncut grain between, and it is not taken out, read, copied, counted or joined, and no figure comes off the wood. She answers the question put and not the one behind it — \emph{Ask the pot what it cost. I keep the count, not the account} — and puts the flat of her hand once more on the sleeve. The woman holds the figure out a breath longer, then shuts her fist upon it and puts it back into her sleeve, where it arrives nowhere; \emph{Then it’s a stick}, she says, and goes back to the round, and nobody turns twice. \textbf{The boy files the offer and its return}, advanced and not paid, on a place of its own beside Ilva’s \textbf{ninth} record-first hand and the fifth shaping of the well-saying, with a finger between every pair: not a sale, a reader made, a tenth hand, a payer, an account or a sixth shaping, not the calling of the loan and not joined to the well-asking, the clerk’s entered figure, the second man’s turned slate or the face at the yard’s edge. It is a reaching gathering interest toward the far-off hand that will one day lay the district’s private keepings together, and is not that hand; her fear is advanced and left unpaid — the count stays in wood where no clerk’s thumb can take a figure off it — and she is expressly not the speaker of the well-asking, which came up once on the twenty-third and was not told again. Offstage on Ilmen 27 and 28 with her keeping where she left it: no figure was offered twice, no reader was made of her keeping and the ninth stays nine with no tenth. No new scar or possession and no change of voice.

\textbf{Ch 122 (bonds).} On Ilmen 23 she stands once at the yard well drawing with the pail against her knee, the rope stiff in the dry cold giving its small rasp, clay dried pale in the crescents of her nails and the finer grey rack dust worked into the seam of one thumb, which she does not scrub out; people notice the pail first and the sleeve not at all, which is the order she prefers. Word comes up once at the bucket-round, from mouth to mouth with no body standing under it, that a man with a narrow slate under his arm had asked after a house-name under this roof and been answered with the weather. Her hand goes toward her sleeve before her eyes go to the asker and her mouth opens after both, the half-beat lying in the gap where a lesser observer would put an intention; the short strip of notched birch lies in its fold, pale where a thumb has rubbed the notches and dark in the uncut grain between, and it is not taken out, read, copied, counted or joined to the asking, and no figure comes off the wood. She answers the question put and not the one behind it — \emph{Ask the pot what it cost. I keep the count, not the account} — puts the flat of her hand once more on the sleeve and goes back to the pail, nobody turning twice. The boy takes the order of reaching apart as a surgeon takes a field apart and files it as her \textbf{ninth} record-first hand on a place of its own with a finger between it and Hessa Rale’s eighth; he files no tenth, makes no reader of her keeping and no figure of the word’s nearness. \textbf{She is expressly not the speaker of the asking:} nobody saw the asking, no voice carried into the yard, no slate was opened within reach of the basket, no room entered and no name spoken, and she is not made a reader by its nearness. The boy files the asking on its own place beside the second man’s direction down the north bridge road and his narrow slate turned to the sleeve, the first man’s face, the clerk’s entered figure and the fifth shaping, with a finger between every pair, and joins it to none. Offstage on Ilmen 24 and 25 with her keeping where she left it; the softening at the river’s skin, the two readings up the road and the fifth shaping found where put buy no figure for her wood and stand on separate places with a finger between. The ninth stays nine with no tenth and no reader made of her keeping. No new scar or possession, no change of voice.

\textbf{Ch 120 (bonds).} Offstage on all three days — Ilmen 17, 18 and 19 — with her keeping where she left it: the short strip of notched birch lies in its fold in her sleeve, pale where a thumb has rubbed the notches and dark in the uncut grain between, and nobody takes it out, reads it, copies it or takes a figure off the wood. The clerk’s entered figure on its own place at the landing and the first arithmetic up the road are not joined to her wood, and the fifth shaping found where put at the well is not made a sixth and buys no figure for her count. No new scar or possession, no change of voice.

\textbf{Corin (the boy in the basket).} He was set down at the edge of the work where no slate lay while she answered a woman with a pot. She did not look at him, did not know he was reading her, and went on with her water. He took the order of her reaching and nothing else; he did not read the stick, ask her about it or take a figure off it. To her he is a child at the edge of the work. In his private file she is the ninth record-first hand, joined to none.

\textbf{The neighbour with the pot} — asked how many firings the month had taken, got \emph{Five to this morning}, and went off with her answer level. The exchange is the whole of their connection.

\textbf{Sella Vail} — keeper of the house whose kiln the firings count. Ilva is of the yard and not of the house; there is no argument between them because there is no occasion for one.

\textbf{Hessa Rale} — a fellow keeper of a record that no figure comes off, but a runner with a slate on the road to Greybank. The two are filed far apart and must not be joined.

\textbf{Berr Clay} — his slate would want a figure off the stick. Ilva has never handed him the stick and never will; there is no quarrel, only the distance between wood and slate.

\textbf{Ch 128 (Days 435–437, Silt 11–13).} Seen once on Silt 12 at the yard well drawing with the pail against her knee, the rope stiff in the dry cold, clay pale in her nail crescents and rack dust in one thumb seam she does not scrub out, her hand flat over the fold before her eyes went to the asker and her mouth after both, the half-beat lying in the gap. In the afternoon a second neighbour at the well, having heard the round’s talk of the figure that went back into the fist on Ilmen 26, asks whether a count kept in wood will be taken at the next reading — the fear advanced by another mouth, not a second offer and not the old question repeated. The strip of notched birch stays in its fold and is not taken out, read, copied, counted, shown or joined, and no figure comes off the wood; she answers the question put and not the one behind it, \emph{Ask the pot what it cost. I keep the count, not the account}, and goes back to the pail, nobody turning twice. The boy files the \textbf{second asking} on a place of its own beside the offer and its return, her ninth hand and the fifth shaping, with a finger between every pair — not a second offer, custom, tenth hand, witness, sale or calling of the loan, and expressly unjoined to the clerk’s entered figure, the reported second slate, the neighbour’s near-reaching, the well-asking answered with weather and the three likenesses of Slate Row (T080 with T090/T102 advanced, not paid). She is expressly not the speaker of the first asking and is not made a reader by the second; the ninth stays nine, the count stays in wood where no clerk’s thumb can take a figure off it, and her fear is advanced and unpaid. The asking is not repeated on Silt 13. Forward, not closed.

\textbf{Ch 123 (Days 420–422, Ilmen 26–28).} Seen once on Ilmen 26 at the yard well drawing with the pail against her knee, the rope stiff in the dry cold, clay pale in her nail crescents and rack dust in one thumb seam she does not scrub out, her hand flat over the fold before her eyes went to the asker and her mouth after both, the half-beat lying in the gap. A woman waiting her turn offered a figure for the month’s firings and put it toward the strip in her sleeve; Ilva answered the question put and not the one behind it, \emph{Ask the pot what it cost. I keep the count, not the account}, and the figure went from the fist toward the wood, looked at the light and went back into the sleeve, arriving nowhere, the stick keeping its notch and learning no name and the woman going back to the round with \emph{Then it’s a stick}. The boy filed the \textbf{offer and its return} on a place of its own beside her ninth hand and the fifth shaping, with a finger between every pair — a reaching gathering interest toward the far-off hand that will one day lay the district’s private keepings together and not that hand (T080 with T090/T102 advanced, not paid). She is expressly not the speaker of the well-asking and is not made a reader by the figure’s nearness; the ninth stays nine with no tenth, the count stays in wood where no clerk’s thumb can take a figure off it, and her fear is advanced and left unpaid. Offstage on the twenty-seventh and twenty-eighth, not offered a figure twice. Forward, not closed.

I keep the count, not the account}, and the ninth stays nine with no tenth. She is expressly not the speaker of the word that came up at the well — a man with a narrow slate had asked after a house-name under this roof and been answered with the weather, with nobody standing under the asking — and is not made a reader by its nearness; her wood and the asking stand on separate places with a finger between. Offstage on Ilmen 24 and 25; the softening at the river’s skin, the two readings up the road, the clerk’s entered figure and the fifth shaping buy no figure for her count and go on separate places with a finger between. Forward, not closed.

\textbf{Ch 110.} On Stone 22 she stands once at the yard well, pail against her knee, rope stiff in the Stone cold giving its small dry rasp, clay pale in her nail crescents and grey rack dust worked into the seam of one thumb she does not scrub out; her hands know the weight of a pail and the edge of a wet board and have never been soft, and people notice the pail first and the sleeve not at all. To the woman who asks what Stone’s firings have taken her hand goes toward her sleeve before her eyes go to the asker and her mouth opens after both with the half-beat in the gap; the notched birch strip lies in its fold, not taken out, read, copied, counted or joined to the open slate on the stone lip, the charcoal beneath the loaf shelf, the cord or the knot-string, and no figure comes off the wood. The boy, two hundred and forty-four days old and unable to lift his own chin, reads the order of reaching and files it as the ninth of the district’s record-first hands. On Bone 22–24, Days 321–323, she is a woman of the yard and not of a house, and keeps the month’s firings in wood where no slate can take a figure off them. On Bone 23 she is seen once at the yard well drawing with the pail against her knee, clay dried pale in the crescents of her nails and the finer grey rack dust worked into the seam of one thumb; asked what the firings of Bone had taken, her hand goes toward her sleeve and stays, the short notched birch strip is not taken out, read, copied, counted or joined to the charcoal beneath the loaf shelf, the cord, the open slate a pace away, the knot-string or the ownerless saying, and no figure comes off the wood. Her eyes go to the asker and her mouth opens after both with a half-beat, and she answers the question put and not the one behind it: \emph{Ask the pot what it cost. I keep the count, not the account.} The boy files the order of reaching as the ninth record-first hand on a place of its own with a finger between it and Hessa Rale’s eighth, files no tenth, and does not join her strip to the handful Sella let fall at the rack end the day before or to the charcoal under the shelf, for testing and keeping are two acts and neither pays for the other. She is offstage on Bone 22 and 24; the twice-mended pot with its crack showing, the dressed grain turned under wool and given no figure, the three coverings called weather and the five arithmetics going up the road in a locked box bring no figure to her well as sign, lesson, mending, cause or payment. Nine are nine and not a rule, for a rule is an account that has found a payer and none stood to this one. She does not know she was read; no new scar or possession came and no bond changed hands.

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item Ch 128: On Silt 12 (Day 436) she stands once at the yard well drawing with the pail against her knee, the rope stiff in the dry cold giving its small rasp, clay dried pale in the crescents of her nails and the finer rack dust worked into the seam of one thumb, which she does not scrub out; her hands know the weight of a pail and the edge of a wet board and have never been soft, and people notice the pail first and the sleeve not at all, which is the order she prefers. In the afternoon a second neighbour at the well, having heard the round’s talk of the figure that went back into the fist on Ilmen 26, asks whether a count kept in wood will be taken at the next reading — not a second offer and not the old question repeated, but the fear advanced by another mouth. Her hand goes flat over the fold before her eyes go to the asker and her mouth after both, the half-beat lying in the gap where a lesser observer would put an intention. The short strip of notched birch lies in its fold, pale where a thumb has rubbed the notches and dark in the uncut grain between; it is not taken out, read, copied, counted, shown or joined, and no figure comes off the wood. No slate is opened within reach of the basket, no room is entered and no reader is made. She answers the question put and not the one behind it — \emph{Ask the pot what it cost. I keep the count, not the account} — puts the flat of her hand once more on the sleeve and goes back to the pail, nobody turning twice. The boy files the \textbf{second asking} on a place of its own beside the offer and its return, her ninth record-first hand and the fifth shaping of the well-saying, with a finger between every pair: not a second offer, not a custom, not a tenth hand, not a witness, not a sale and not the calling of the loan, no figure under it and no payer, and expressly unjoined to the clerk’s entered figure, the reported second slate of Silt 6, the neighbour’s near-reaching at the shelf, the well-asking answered with weather and the three likenesses of Slate Row (T080 with T090/T102 advanced, not paid). She is expressly not the speaker of the first asking and is not made a reader by the second; the ninth stays nine, the count stays in wood where no clerk’s thumb can take a figure off it, and her fear is advanced and unpaid. The asking is not repeated on Silt 13. No new scar or possession, no change of voice; forward, not closed.

\end{itemize}

A woman waiting her turn shifts a pot from one hip to the other, brings a number up out of a shut fist, holds it toward the light and puts the fist toward the strip in Ilva’s sleeve, saying she could put a figure to the month’s firings. Ilva draws with the pail against her knee; the rope is stiff in the dry cold and gives its small rasp; clay is dried pale in her nail crescents and the finer rack dust is worked into the seam of one thumb, which she does not scrub out. Her hand goes flat over the fold before her eyes go to the asker and her mouth opens after both, the half-beat lying in the gap where a lesser observer would have put an intention. She answers the question put and not the one behind it — \emph{Ask the pot what it cost. I keep the count, not the account} — and puts the flat of her hand once more on the sleeve. The woman holds the figure out a breath longer, then shuts her fist upon it and puts it back into her sleeve, where it arrives nowhere; \emph{Then it’s a stick}, she says, and goes back to the round, and nobody turns twice. No slate is opened within reach of the basket, no figure comes off the wood, no reader is made and no name is spoken over the notches. \textbf{The boy takes the offer apart by the place of each part — fist, eye, mouth, the half-beat in the gap — and files the offer and its return on a place of its own beside her ninth record-first hand and the fifth shaping of the well-saying, with a finger between every pair (T080 with T090/T102 advanced, not paid).} It is not a sale, a reader made, a tenth hand, a payer, an account or a sixth shaping, not the calling of the loan and not joined to the well-asking, the clerk’s entered figure, the second man’s turned slate or the face at the yard’s edge, but a reaching gathering interest toward the far-off hand that will one day lay the district’s private keepings together, and is not that hand. Her fear is advanced and left unpaid: the count stays in wood where no clerk’s thumb can take a figure off it, and the figure that looked at the light went home with the woman. She is expressly not the speaker of the well-asking, which came up once on the twenty-third and was not told again. Offstage on Ilmen 27 and 28 with her keeping where she left it, not made a reader and offered no figure twice; the ninth stays nine with no tenth. No new scar or possession, no change of voice; forward, not closed.

The next I don’t count}, said \emph{Yes, house} to the fire and agreed with the early thaw and the late while keeping the late because it puts off the paying, swept the collector’s road without turning, and no collector came up or went down the clay road on Smoke 7, 8 or 9; brought the ear-sentence all the way to the word that would call the loan on all three days and stopped there with no figure and no name, the stopping a remembered stopping and not a new one; chest tight since the dark, Ash worked into the knuckle creases in the colour of the clean dark line, the pale clip-ring at the left wrist holding what light there is, the warm stone cold and unreconciled in its unmarked pot in the Debt Loft; his stroke over the flagstones past the shallow bright patch without the half-check, so the Day 171 movement stays a held change on its own place beside the Day 161 fraction and the Day 166 shelf beat; heard the fifth ownerless asking go over the boards on Smoke 8 and did not claim it or supply a witness to the five now filed (T101 advanced, unpaid); no new scar, possession or change of voice}\CRfield{First seen}{Chapter 2}}{\CRsheetheading{Appearance}
Twenty-two and bent at the shoulders from six years in the slip pit, which makes him look older than his term. He has grey Ash in the creases of his knuckles that no amount of scrubbing lifts, and a pale ring round his left wrist where an iron clip sat in Y.H. 806, when he was bound. He is a narrow man with a narrow face and the habit of putting the smallest tool on the bench into his pocket when he thinks nobody is looking, because a man who owns nothing should know where the small things are. He sleeps in the Debt Loft above the wheel-shed and keeps his few possessions in a clay pot with no mark on it. He smells of wet wool, tallow and the sour tang of a corner that has not been swept. The thing people notice first is how quickly he moves; the thing they notice last is that he stops moving altogether when he is told he is doing well.

\CRsheetheading{Voice \& Manner}
Deferential with a nail in it. He calls everyone \emph{house}, including Sella, and says \emph{I owe} where another man would say \emph{I am}. He never argues; he agrees so thoroughly that the argument has nowhere to go. When he is frightened he becomes helpful, which in a kiln-house means doing three things at once and quietly putting the fourth right. His jokes are not jokes; they are statements of fact made in a tone that invites someone else to laugh so that he does not have to.

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item “Yes, house. I’ll sweep it. I swept it this morning. I’ll sweep it again.”

\item “Six years. One to go. I’ve counted every one, and I won’t count the next.”

\item “He’s a foundling. I’m a debt. Don’t put us in the same sentence, Sella.”

\item “I took the small knife. I put it back. You can check.”

\item “You can’t return a man to himself. They tried with my mother. She came back with somebody else’s hands.”

\item “I took the small knife. I put it back. You can check.” --- said of his own accord, to nobody, in the tone of a man stating the weather.

\item “Six counted. The next I don’t count.” --- to the kindling at the going of the light, with the knife set back where it can be checked; the sentence about the ear under this roof came a sixth time on Reed 20 to the word that would call the loan and stopped there with no figure and no name, the breath drawn and not spent.

\item “Yes, house.” --- said on Day 140 to an early thaw and a late, wanting the late because it puts off the paying, though the paying has stood in the ruts since the water went.

\end{itemize}

\CRsheetheading{History}
His mother was banked in Y.H. 792 and came back thin to the district’s name-pot, with fragments of a life she could not name and hands that frightened him because they were not her hands. He was born of that return, which means he carries a little of somebody else’s interest in a life he cannot place, and has been told all his life that this makes him useful. In Y.H. 806, at sixteen, his mother’s account was entered against him and he was bound to House Vail for seven years, a term he did not choose and has counted every day of. He has worked the slip pits, swept the yard, banked the fire and carried the household’s small accounts in his head for six years.

He was sent to fetch a collector for Garl Vail in the Long Cold and turned back at the frozen ford. Sella never asked whether he had gone. Jorra, who was thirteen, never asked either, which Tarn has decided is worse. He was in the house when Corin arrived and watched the boy be given a bed while he slept in the loft, and he has never said the thing he thinks about it, because a clay-bound hand who complains about beds is a clay-bound hand who can be returned to the slate.

\CRsheetheading{Wounds \& Fears}
He is a debt with a body, and one year of a seven-year term left. He fears that when the term ends there will be no house to take him and he will be entered again for vagrancy, which is how the district keeps people. He fears the Second Want in himself — the shape that comes over him some nights and leaves him reaching for a tool he has never used. He fears Sella’s kindness more than Jorra’s command, because the kindness is the thing he cannot enter in any account and therefore cannot pay back. His contradiction: the man who owns nothing is the one who notices when a tool is missing and the one who keeps the house’s accounts most exactly.

\CRsheetheading{Desires}
He wants a slate with his own name on it and no mark against it. He wants to be called by something that is not a house’s possession. He thinks he wants freedom; what he needs is to learn that freedom in Sarn is another category of account, and that a man can be unowned and still be cold, and that the thing to want is not an empty column but a way to keep warm without being spent.

\textbf{Ch 128 (bonds).} With Sella nothing changed across Silt 11, 12 and 13 and nothing from the second asking at the well, the Slate Row face at the yard’s edge, the softening at the river’s skin or the four readings behind one unsigned figure came to the kindling as sign, lesson, mending, cause, payment or payer; he takes the broom only after it has been given its instruction, calls her \emph{house}, and she has not asked about his term or his ear. At the kindling and flagstones on the afternoons of all three days six pieces stood in the worn thumb-mark where the house could check and the seventh at the lip beside Garl Vail’s unforged collector sentence, no name on the man who turned back at the frozen ford and no figure on the tile debt, the small knife at the very edge of its sill; his hand went over blade and sill and away with no breath held at the top of the reach, the coming away the whole of the checking, and in the tone of a man stating the weather he told the wood \emph{Six counted. The next I don’t count} once each day. The sentence was found where put and not made a habit, not a tenth stopping, payment, hearing or rule, and the boy filed it on a place of its own beside Garl’s unforged collector sentence and Jorra’s silence, two quiet men under one roof and not a custom, and laid none of it across the second asking, the Slate Row face or the four readings. The ear-sentence about an ear under this roof being worth more than the debt that holds it came to the word that would call the loan and stopped there, a remembered ninth stopping with no tenth, at the very end of a term already ended; the Seed 16 breath stayed unspent, the loan uncalled, his valuable ear exposure and not safety, the fear of being entered again for vagrancy still his without a figure and the unvoiced want of a slate with his own name and no mark against it. He took the broom only after its instruction, said \emph{Yes, house} to the fire, did not turn his head toward the landing and let the degree stay a shape found where put. Ash was worked into the knuckle creases in the colour of the clean dark line, the pale clip-ring at his left wrist caught and gave back the little light, and the chest stayed tight since the dark. No new scar or possession, no change of voice, nothing called or paid; forward, not closed.

The boy took the absence apart by the place of what was there and what was not and filed it on a place of its own: a hand withdrawn from a field before the dressing goes on, exact, complete, worth nothing at two inches of air, not a tenth stopping, not a payment, not a hearing and not a rule, and not laid across the clerk’s figure, his degree, the face at the yard’s edge or Jorra’s promise, for a doctrine is an account that has found a payer and none stood. He did not turn his head toward the landing on any of the three days and the degree stayed a shape found where put, not repeated; the warm loft stone stayed unreconciled by not trying, which is not forgiving. No new scar or possession, no change of voice, no payment and no ending.

His chest stayed tight since the dark, Ash worked into the knuckle creases in the colour of the clean dark line, the pale clip-ring at his left wrist holding what little light there was, his stroke over the shallow bright patch without the half-check, the returned half-check of Bone 8 kept as the fourth held change and not a rule, the warm loft stone cold in its unmarked pot and unreconciled by not trying, which is not forgiveness. The boy kept the thumb’s resting on a place of its own with a finger between it and the nine stoppings, the four held changes, the handful and his own gaps — not a tenth stopping, not the seventh year given, not a payment, not a fifth held change, not a hearing, not a mending and not a rule, with no payer standing. No bond changed hands, no new scar or possession and no change of voice; he wants the seventh year held at its very end with the loan uncalled.

\textbf{Ch 91 (bonds).} With Sella nothing changed across Bone 25–27: he took the broom only after its instruction, went wide around the yard’s seven walked-around places and gave the day’s hunts and repairs no figure. The next I don’t count}. He did not make the resting again on Bone 27 and no collector came up or went down the clay road, the loan uncalled, the nine stoppings still nine with no tenth before the seventh year at its very end and still ungiven. On the twenty-seventh he said \emph{Yes, house} to a man who wanted the thaw early and to a man who wanted it late and kept the late because a late thaw puts off the paying, agreeing so thoroughly that no argument could find a foot. \textbf{Ch 86 (bonds).} Nothing changed hands with Tarn through Bone 10–12. He agreed with the early thaw and the late and kept wanting the late because it puts off the paying, his chest tight, Ash in the knuckles and the pale clip-ring holding light. His stroke went over the shallow bright patch without the half-check, and the Bone 8 returned half-check stayed on its own place as the fourth of four held changes and not a rule. The warm loft stone stayed cold and unreconciled by not trying, which is not forgiveness. Sella’s reading-day went past without a number spoken to him and Jorra’s standing finger was not made a cause of anything. No name given, no debt paid, no bond paid, sold, named or spoken.

\textbf{Sella Vail} — she holds his debt and once, in the winter Garl died, gave him a warm stone for the loft which he has kept in his clay pot for two years. He cannot reconcile the stone with the debt, and has stopped trying, which is not the same as forgiving it. \emph{Ch 2:} he calls her \emph{house}, says \emph{I owe} where another man says \emph{I am}, and agreed with everything so thoroughly that there was nowhere for an argument to go. She gave the foundling a bed and him the loft, and he put the one sentence into the room that nobody had asked for.

\textbf{Jorra Vail} — son of the house, who treats him as a brother when the wheel needs him and as a servant when it does not. Tarn has decided to hate him for it and keeps failing, because Jorra once sat up all night with him through a fever and has never mentioned it. \emph{Ch 2:} Jorra noticed a rasp left out of its place and Tarn answered him; the kindness and the command arrived in the same voice and Tarn did not separate them.

\textbf{Corin} — the foundling who arrived and was given a bed in the house. Tarn was the first to notice that the boy turns his head toward a pot before anyone taps it, and has told nobody, because a clay-bound hand who can hear the full note is worth more than his debt and he does not want to be bought. \emph{Ch 2:} he said \emph{He’s a foundling. I’m a debt. Don’t put us in the same sentence, Sella.} His resentment is not envy of the bed; it is a man keeping the one thing he owns, which is the exact account of what he is owed and what he owes.

\textbf{Dessa Silt} — he has carried messages between her and the house, and barley from her to Sella, and has hated being the thin part of that chain. He knows her cough is not the pits and has never said so.

\textbf{Mira Silt} — she has suspected for a year that he is more than he says, and has not asked. He has noticed her noticing, and has answered her with the weather every time.

\textbf{Garl Vail} — he was sent for a collector and turned back. The dead man’s coat still hangs behind the door and Tarn has never once touched it.

\textbf{Ch 4.} He called Sella \emph{house} and put the knife back twice where it could be checked; his broom stopped two strokes at the Vail pot’s note without a turn of the head, and the boy watched and kept the silence as carefully as he did. Six of seven years counted, the seventh not. Jorra came in from the back room with slate dust and said the back room was cold; Tarn said nothing about that either. Dessa’s cough went by him as weather, as it always did. The one thing he owns stays kept.

\textbf{Ch 5.} On Stone 13 he came up the yard with the knife already back on its sill, went through the motion of checking it with his eyes, and saw the boy turn his head toward a pot \emph{before} it was set down. His broom stopped half a stroke at the soft set-down that gave nothing, and he said nothing about either thing, as he has said nothing about the pot’s note through the wall. He counted six years of the seven and held the seventh back; when Sella told him he had done well he stopped altogether for two breaths, then began again. At dusk he set the knife back where it could be checked and told the yard he had done so, unasked. He wants his exact account and grudges the house the loan of a bed; a loan that can hear is a loan that can be called, and he has said neither sentence.

\textbf{Ch 6.} On Stone 16 he measured the kindling stack with his eyes --- four, four, a space where the fifth should be --- and told the stack six were counted and the seventh held back. On Stone 17 the knife went back on the sill and was announced to the empty yard, and when Sella said \emph{you’ve done well} the broom stopped altogether for two breaths before he said \emph{Yes, house} and went on; he scraped Ash from his knuckles, held the pale clip-ring at his left wrist up to the light, and put the knife back, this time without announcing it. He named the kiln’s breath as the thing that takes a man in his sleep and told of the man in Mud End the district called merciful; he wanted the late thaw because it put off the paying. His broom stopped half a stroke at the bench where no note came. On Stone 20 he told the yard again that the knife was back where it could be checked; six of seven years counted, the seventh held back, and he offered to check the ridge. He said nothing about the boy’s ear and the boy said nothing about his.

\textbf{Ch 7.} On Stone 22 his head turned a degree when a vessel carried past the door gave its flat note, and he went back to the broom without looking at the basket or calling the sound a sound; he had been sent for the collector who came with grey fingertips, and the boy put that grey on a tray of its own. On Stone 25 his broom checked half a stroke at the place in the yard where a pot cracked all the way through, and again at the place on the bench where no note had come, and he said nothing about either. He set the small knife on its sill and told the empty yard where it was on Stone 22, Stone 23 and Stone 30; counted six years of the seven and held the seventh back every day; held the pale clip-ring at his left wrist to the light; and wanted the late thaw because a late thaw puts off the paying. On Stone 29 he offered to check the width of the ridge with his thumb and took his eyes off it as a man takes his eyes off a woman who has been crying. The two silences under one roof kept their usual shape, and the loan that could hear went on being worth more than the debt that held him.

\textbf{Ch 8.} Through the Five the knife went back to its sill and the seventh year was held back every day; he announced the knife to the empty yard and said to the kindling that six were counted and the next he did not count. The Ash in the creases of his knuckles was the colour of the ridge no scrubbing lifted, and he kept the silence about the flat note all five days, as he kept the silence about the boy’s ear. On the Long Night he said in the dark that six years were counted and the next he did not, and set the knife where it could be checked; Garl’s coat held a broader man’s shape in the dark and he let the proverb go to the pot. He wanted the late thaw still, because a late thaw puts off the paying, and on Ilmen 1 he swept toward the thaw and the slip pits with the knife on its sill and the seventh year held back again.

\textbf{Ch 9.} Through Days 31–37 the knife went back to its sill and he announced it to the empty yard, six years counted and the seventh held back, Ash worked into the knuckles that no scrubbing lifted. He agreed with the neighbour who wanted the thaw early and the one who wanted it late, and kept wanting the late one because a late thaw puts off the paying. On Ilmen 6 his head went a degree toward the pot that answered nearly full and he went back to his broom without naming the sound or looking at the basket; the boy kept the turning beside his own hearing and did not join them. On Ilmen 7 he was with the yard at the well when the Singing Sill gave its note early and did not say what it was. The loan that can hear stayed uncalled and the sentence was not said under the roof.

\textbf{Ch 10.} The small knife goes back to its sill before light and is announced to the empty yard --- \emph{It’s back. You can check} --- with six years of the seven counted and the seventh held where he always holds it; Ash is worked into the creases of his knuckles that no scrubbing lifts and the pale clip-ring catches what light there is. He sweeps around the place where the clay-heavy water came up behind the racks and sweeps the road down toward the Fishstairs over and over without once looking along it, which is the road a man goes down when a house wants a collector. No collector comes for the woman in the brook and he does not go for one, and he does not say the omission has a name. He still wants the thaw late because a late thaw puts off the paying; he agrees with the early and the late without taking either side. The loan that can hear is still uncalled and the sentence is still unsaid under the roof.

\textbf{Ch 11.} The small knife went back to its sill before the light was gone on Days 45 and 46 and he told the empty yard where it was, unasked; on Day 47 he put it back and told nobody, because the yard had already been told and a man does not say the same thing twice to a house that does not answer. Six years of the seven were counted and the seventh held back on all three mornings, the one entry in this house the house cannot check. His broom went over the road a man takes when a house wants a collector, over and over, without once turning to look along it, and no collector went down it for the woman the brook took nine mornings ago; he did not say the thing which had not happened had a name. Ash was worked into the creases of his knuckles that no scrubbing lifts and the pale clip-ring caught the light. He agreed with the ones who wanted the thaw early and the ones who wanted it late and kept wanting the late one, because a late thaw puts off the paying. When Sella said he had done well he stopped altogether for two breaths before saying \emph{Yes, house}.

\textbf{Ch 12.} He kept Sella’s house in its exact account and kept his own seventh year out of it; he said house to the yard and counted six where the house could check and the seventh where it could not. With the boy he kept the older equality: a vessel gave its note past the door on Day 50 and a pot answered nearly full on Day 52, and his head did not turn at either and he said nothing about either. Jorra’s returned dust went unremarked and Mira passed without a question. The loan that can hear stayed uncalled, and he still wanted the late thaw because a late thaw puts off the paying.

\textbf{Ch 13.} He agreed with the neighbour who wanted the thaw early and the one who wanted it late, saying \emph{Yes, house} to both, and went on wanting the late one because a late thaw puts off the paying. The small knife was back on its sill with six years counted and the seventh held back, the one entry in this house the house cannot check; Ash was worked into the creases of his knuckles in the colour of the clean dark line, and the pale clip-ring at his left wrist held the light and gave it back. His broom went over the road a man takes when a house wants a collector, over and over, without once turning along it, and no collector went down it for the woman in the brook. A vessel gave its note past the yard door on Ilmen 28 and his head did not turn; he did not name the sound or supply a Grathic word for it, and the boy did not call it a seventh hearing. Sella told him he had done well and he stopped altogether for two breaths, then set the knife where it could be checked and went back to the broom.

\textbf{Ch 14.} Before light on Silt 3 the small knife went back to its sill and was announced to the empty yard — \emph{It’s back. You can check} — and he told the kindling six were counted and the next he did not count; six years stood, and the seventh was nearly gone and still held, the one entry in this house the house could not check. Ash was worked into his knuckles in the colour of the clean dark line, and the pale clip-ring at his left wrist held the little light and gave it back. He said \emph{Yes, house} to the ones who wanted the thaw early and to the ones who wanted it late, agreed so entirely that no argument could find a foot, and went on wanting the late one because a late thaw puts off the paying, though the water came with the paying. His broom checked half a stroke at the place where a pot cracked on Stone 25 and went on without a turn of the head or a name for the sound. When a vessel gave its note past the yard door he did not turn. On Silt 6 his head went a degree toward a pot that answered nearly full under nobody’s knuckle, and then went back to the broom; he said nothing and did not look toward the basket. The boy kept his turning beside his own hearing and did not join them, and the loan that can hear stayed uncalled.

\textbf{Ch 15.} Through Silt 9–15 the seventh year presses against the rising water and is still held back. The small knife went back to its sill before light and was announced to the empty yard, six years standing in a mark worn almost flat by his thumb and the seventh nearly gone and never named, the one entry in this house the house could not check; Ash was worked into his knuckles in the colour of the clean dark line and the pale clip-ring at his left wrist held what light there was and gave it back. He said \emph{Yes, house} to the ones who wanted the thaw early and to the ones who wanted it late, agreed so entirely that no argument could find a foot, and kept wanting the late one because a late thaw puts off the paying, though the paying came with the water. His broom checked at the cracked-pot place and went over the road a house sends a man down when it wants a collector without once turning along it, and when a vessel gave its note past the yard door in the afternoon of Silt 15 his head did not turn and he did not name the sound or look toward the basket. He does not say that an ear which can hear is worth more than the debt that holds him, and the sentence that would call the loan lies under the roof as it has for six years.

\textbf{Ch 16.} Through Days 75–77 the seventh year presses against the mud the flood left and is still held back. The small knife goes to its sill before the light on Day 77 and he tells the empty yard where it is, six years standing in a mark worn almost flat by his thumb and the seventh nearly gone and still held, the one entry in this house the house cannot check; he tells the kindling \emph{Six counted. The next I don’t count.} Ash is worked into the creases of his knuckles in the colour of the clean dark line and no scrubbing lifts it, and the pale clip-ring at his left wrist holds what light there is and gives it back. He says \emph{Yes, house} to the ones who want the thaw early and to the ones who want it late, agrees so entirely that no argument can find a foot, and keeps wanting the late one because a late thaw puts off the paying, though the paying has come up the road and stands in the ruts. His broom goes over the road a house sends a man down when it wants a collector, over and over, without once turning along it. A vessel gives its note past the door and his head does not turn and he does not name the sound, and the boy does not call it a seventh hearing; a whole vessel’s note goes past on Day 77 and he does not turn then either. The two ears keep their equality under the roof and the two silences are of one shape with nobody putting a word between them. The loan that can hear stays uncalled. Something must give at the end of the seventh year, but the end was not written here.

\textbf{Ch 17.} The seventh year presses toward its end through all seven days and is still held. The small knife lies on its sill with six years standing in a mark worn almost flat by his thumb and the seventh nearly gone and unnamed, the one entry in this house the house cannot check; he tells the kindling \emph{Six counted. The next I don’t count.} Ash is worked into the creases of his knuckles in the colour of the clean dark line and no scrubbing lifts it, and the pale clip-ring at his left wrist holds what light there is and gives it back. He says \emph{Yes, house} to those who want the thaw early and to those who want it late, agrees so entirely that no argument can find a foot, and keeps wanting the late one because it puts off the paying, though the paying has stood in the ruts all week. His broom goes over the road a house sends a man down when it wants a collector without once turning along it, and when a vessel gives its note past the door on Silt 23 his head does not turn and he does not name the sound. Sella’s instruction still goes to the fire and the wool and never to him by name; he calls her house and keeps the exact account of what he owes that the house cannot check. The loan that can hear stays uncalled.

With Corin the equality holds: two ears, two silences, a loan that can hear and has never been called, and the foundling’s half-beat at the market’s edge not joined to his own turning. Garl’s unforged collector sentence stays where he keeps the seventh year, neither entered; Mira’s noticing and his answered weather are unchanged. No bond has been paid, sold or spoken this chapter.

\textbf{Ch 24 (bonds).} Sella gave the broom its instruction before she gave it to him and he took it up as a man takes up a tool already named, saying \emph{Yes, house} to those who wanted the thaw early and those who wanted it late, agreeing so entirely that no argument could find a foot while keeping the late because it puts off the paying, though the paying had stood in the ruts since the water went. His chest had been tight since the dark and the breath from Seed 16 was still unspent, a small interval at the top of each reach showing where it should have gone in; the small knife lay at the very edge of its sill with six years in a worn mark and the seventh nearly gone and still held, the one entry the house cannot check, the unforged collector sentence kept beside it. \textbf{New on Seed 22:} while Jorra’s bent finger stood in the cold damper ahead of Sella’s unfinished sentence, his stroke checked for half a beat on the flagstones and then went on toward the road without a word or a turn of the head; the place where the stroke stopped was kept as a thing nobody would enter, and neither man named the other’s silence. The boy set the half-check beside the wheel-keeper’s finger on one tray and laid no finger across them. Two ears kept their equality under the roof, the ear worth more than the debt and unsafe; the sentence that would call the loan that can hear has still never been said. Ash was worked into the creases of his knuckles in the colour of the clean dark line and no scrubbing lifted it; the pale clip-ring at his left wrist held the little light and gave it back. No bond changed hands, no new scar, possession or change of voice; something must give at the end of the seventh year and it did not give here.

In Chapter 2 he pockets the small bench knife and then says of his own accord that he took it and put it back and they can check; he stops his broom for two strokes when a pot is set down and gives its flat note, turns his head a degree and says nothing; he banks the coals without looking at the fire. His deference has a nail in it, and the nail is the one possession the house cannot check. Through the middle tend of Grain his account held unchanged — six counted and the seventh at the lip, the breath unspent, nine stoppings with no tenth, the loan uncalled and the stone cold — while the yard went around the returning-line place and he agreed the early thaw and the late, wanting the late still (T036/T076, T006, T098 carried).

When a vessel gives its note past the door he does not turn and does not name it, and the boy does not call it a seventh hearing; two ears and two silences keep their equality under one roof. The head that turns half a beat late at the well is not his and he does not join it to anything. Something must give at the end of the seventh year, and the end was not written here; the loan that can hear stays uncalled.

On Days 85 through 90 the seventh year stands at the edge of the sill through the turn of Silt into Seed and is still held. To the kindling he says \emph{Six counted. The next I don’t count.} Ash is worked into the creases of his knuckles in the colour of the clean dark line and no scrubbing lifts it; the pale clip-ring at his left wrist holds what light there is and gives it back. Two ears and two silences keep their equality under one roof; the loan that can hear stays uncalled. Something must give at the end of the seventh year; it did not give here, and the count crosses into Seed with the seventh still held.

Something must give at the end of the seventh year; it did not give here, and the breath presses to its edge into Chapter 25.

On Days 113 through 115 the seventh year stands at the very edge of the sill and is still held, and the breath he decided not to spend on Seed 16 is still unspent. The boy sets the unchecking stroke beside the earlier half-beat on one tray and lays no cause across them. Two ears and two silences keep their equality under the roof, the ear worth more than the debt and therefore unsafe; the sentence that would call the loan that can hear has still never been said. Something must give at the end of the seventh year; it did not give here, and the held breath presses to its edge into Chapter 26.

On Days 116 through 119 the seventh year stands at the very edge of the sill and is still held, and the breath he decided not to spend on Seed 16 is still unspent. On Seed 28, the only day he is on stage, he takes the broom only after Sella has given it its instruction and says \emph{Yes, house} to those who want the thaw early and those who want it late, agreeing so entirely that no argument can find a foot while keeping the late because it puts off the paying, though the paying has stood in the ruts since the water went. The small bench knife lies at the very edge of its sill with six years in a mark his thumb has worn almost flat and the seventh nearly gone, the one entry in this house the house cannot check, and to the kindling he says \emph{Six counted. The next I don’t count.} The unforged collector sentence stays where he keeps the seventh year and neither is entered.
