There is a small interval at the top of each reach where the breath should have gone in: the broom goes up, the interval opens, the breath does not come, the broom comes down. The change made on Seed 22 is held and not repeated: while Jorra’s bent finger stands in the cold damper ahead of Sella’s unfinished sentence his bristles go on over the flagstones without the half-check, past the place where the stroke stopped that day, and the stones keep that place as a shallow bright patch worn into the stone, a thing nobody will enter. Neither man names the other’s silence; the ear worth more than the debt is unsafe, and the sentence that would call the loan that can hear has not been said under this roof in six years and is not said today. Two ears and two silences keep their equality under one roof. Something must give at the end of the seventh year, and it did not give here; the count goes into Reed with the seventh still held.

On Days 120 through 122 the seventh year is pressed past the end of the planting and still held, and the breath he decided not to spend on Seed 16 is still unspent. On Reed 2, the only day he is on stage, he takes the broom only after Sella has given it its instruction (\emph{Go around, it cost enough to come in, it will cost more to take out}) and says \emph{Yes, house} to those who want the thaw early and those who want it late, agreeing so entirely that no argument can find a foot while keeping the late because it puts off the paying, though the paying has stood in the ruts since the water went. The small bench knife lies at the very edge of its sill with six years in a mark his thumb has worn almost flat and the seventh nearly gone and never named, the one entry in this house the house cannot check; the unforged collector sentence stays beside it where he has kept it since the frozen ford, and neither is entered. Ash is worked into the creases of his knuckles in the colour of the clean dark line and no scrubbing lifts it, and the pale clip-ring at his left wrist holds what light there is and gives it back. His chest is tight and there is a small interval at the top of each reach where the breath should have gone in, a breath stopped against iron and never let through; to the kindling he says \emph{Six counted. The next I don’t count.} The change made on Seed 22 stays held and not repeated: while Jorra’s bent finger stands in the cold damper ahead of Sella’s unfinished sentence his bristles go on over the flagstones without the half-check, past the shallow bright patch the stones keep where the stroke stopped, and neither man turns or speaks. The boy files the unchecking stroke beside the earlier half-beat on the interval tray, two objects and not a rule. Two ears and two silences keep their equality under one roof; the ear worth more than the debt is unsafe, the loan that can hear is not called, and the foundling’s half-beat at the market is not joined to his own turning. Something must give at the end of the seventh year, and it did not give here.

On Days 123 through 125 the seventh year presses past the third tend of the planting and is still held. The small bench knife lies at the very edge of its sill with six years standing in a thumb-mark his thumb has worn almost flat and the seventh nearly gone and never named, the one entry in this house the house cannot check; the unforged collector sentence lies beside it where he has kept it since the frozen ford, and he enters neither. Ash is worked into the creases of his knuckles in the colour of the clean dark line and no scrubbing lifts it; the pale clip-ring at his left wrist holds what light there is and gives it back. He takes the broom only after it has been given its instruction, says \emph{Yes, house} to the woman who wants the thaw early and the man who wants it late, agrees so entirely that no argument can find a foot and keeps wanting the late because it puts off the paying, though the paying has stood in the ruts since the water went. His chest is tight and the breath from Seed 16 is still unspent, a small interval at the top of each reach where it should have gone in, a breath stopped against iron and never let through. On Reed 5 he puts his hand to the knife on its sill, moves it a hair’s breadth and sets it back where it can be checked, and tells the sill where it is; behind Jorra’s standing finger his bristles go on over the flagstones without the half-check, past the shallow bright patch the stones keep where the stroke stopped, and neither man names the other’s silence. On Reed 5 night, crouched to the kindling that smells of straw and tallow, he brings the sentence about the ear and the debt to the threshold of the word that would call the loan and stops there; the wood takes it as wood takes everything, without answer and without keeping, and the boy files the stopped sentence on the interval tray beside the half-beat, the unchecking stroke and his own held breath. Something must give at the end of the seventh year and has not given yet; the loan that can hear stays uncalled.

On Days 126 through 128 the seventh year is pressed further past its third tend and still held, and the thing that must give at its end has not given. Reed has come on and the reeds stand in the yard in armfuls judged by the arm that carries them; he takes the broom only after it has been given its instruction, says \emph{Yes, house} to an early thaw and a late and keeps wanting the late because it puts off the paying, though the paying has stood in the ruts since the water went. His knife lies at the very edge of its sill with six years in the worn thumb-mark and the seventh nearly gone and never named, the unforged collector sentence beside it, his chest tight with the breath from Seed 16 still unspent and a small interval at the top of each reach where it should have gone in. On Day 127, with the coals banked and the knife set back where it can be checked, he tells the kindling \emph{Six counted. The next I don’t count}, and the sentence about the ear under this roof worth more than the debt that holds it comes a second time to the word that would call the loan and stops there with no figure and no name; he draws the breath and does not spend it, says \emph{Yes, house} and goes on with the broom. The boy files the second stopping beside the first on the interval tray as two intervals and not two payments, and the loan stays uncalled. Under the wheel-shed Jorra’s bent finger leads at the damper ahead of an unfinished sentence and the dust comes out of the back room from men unnamed; Tarn’s stroke goes on over the flagstones without the half-check while the stones keep the shallow bright patch where it stopped, neither man naming the other’s silence. He never looks toward the bed or the basket and says nothing of the ear; Sella asks nothing within hearing. The silver clip-ring at his wrist holds what light there is and Ash stays worked into the creases of his knuckles in the colour of the clean dark line. Nothing is spent, called, named or joined, and the seventh year goes into the next days still held.

Three stoppings now stand on the interval tray and none of them is a payment. The seventh year is pressed past another tend of Reed, the knife back on its sill with six counted where the house can check and the seventh held where it cannot, the unforged collector sentence beside it and the breath from Seed 16 still unspent. A thing stopped three times is not settled; the loan that can hear waits for the word that has not been said.

\textbf{Four stoppings now stand on the interval tray and none of them is a payment.} The seventh year is pressed past the middle tend of Reed, the knife back on its sill with six counted where the house can check and the seventh held where it cannot, the unforged collector sentence beside it and the breath from Seed 16 still unspent. A thing stopped four times is not settled; a held word is a debt and a debt that can hear can be called, and the loan waits for the word that has not been said. The stroke goes on over the flagstones without the half-check and the two silences stay unjoined.

On Days 135 through 137 the seventh year presses nearer its end and is still held; the boy is carried past him at the half-pace and the day’s arithmetic goes on in loaves and weather. On Day 136 he takes the broom after its instruction, agrees with an early thaw and a late and wants the late because it puts off the paying; men unnamed go into the room off the shed and he does not ask about it, just as Jorra does not ask about the ear. With the coals banked and the knife set back where it can be checked he measures the kindling four, four and an empty fifth and tells it \emph{Six counted. The next I don’t count.} Then the sentence about the ear under this roof being worth more than the debt that holds it comes the fifth time to the word that would call the loan and stops there with no figure and no name; he draws the breath and does not spend it, says \emph{Yes, house} and goes on with the broom over the bright patch without the half-check. The boy files the fifth stopping beside the first four on the interval tray as an object and not a rule, an interval and not a payment, and refuses to let five likenesses stand up and call themselves a doctrine. A thing stopped five times is a thing held, not settled; something must give at the end of the seventh year and has not given yet. The loan stays uncalled and the two silences stay unjoined.

On Days 138 through 140 the seventh year presses nearer its end than it has ever stood and is still held; the boy is carried past him at the half-pace and the yard’s arithmetic goes on in loaves and weather. The next I don’t count} and then the sentence about an ear under this roof being worth more than the debt that holds it comes a sixth time --- after Reed 5, 8, 11, 14 and 17 --- all the way to the word that would call the loan and stops there with no figure and no name; he draws the breath that should have gone in at the top of the reach and does not spend it, says \emph{Yes, house} to the fire and goes on with the broom. The boy files a sixth stopping on the interval tray beside five as an object and not a rule, an interval and not a payment, and refuses to let six likenesses stand up and call themselves a doctrine, for a doctrine is an account that has found a payer and no payer has been named to any of the six. On Day 140 he takes the broom only after its instruction, says \emph{Yes, house} to the early thaw and the late and keeps the late because it puts off the paying; the knife lies at the very edge of its sill with six counted where the house can check and the seventh where it cannot, the unforged collector sentence beside it and the breath from Seed 16 unspent with a small interval at the top of each reach. Men unnamed go into the back room before first grey and he does not ask about them, just as Jorra does not ask about the ear; his stroke goes on over the shallow bright patch without the half-check and neither man names the other’s silence. Through Reed 22–24 the seventh year presses from nearer its end to one tend from it and still does not give. His stroke goes on past the shallow bright patch without even the half-check it had made once on Seed 22, and the equality under the roof holds at that place: Jorra’s finger leads at the damper, Tarn does not ask about the room and Jorra does not ask about the ear, and the two silences are not joined. No collector comes, the loan stays uncalled, and something must still give at the end of the seventh year and has not given here. Ash stays worked into the knuckle creases and his chest has been tight since the dark.

On Day 145 the seventh year stands one tend from its end and still does not give. On Days 147 through 149 the seventh year stands one tend from its end and has still not given. \textbf{Ch 37.} The firing month finds his seventh year still one tend from its end and held: six counted in the worn thumb-mark where the house can check, the seventh at the lip of the sill where it cannot, the small knife at the very edge with the unforged collector sentence beside it, the Seed 16 breath unspent with its small interval at the top of each reach, his chest tight since the dark, Ash worked into his knuckle creases in the colour of the clean dark line and the pale clip-ring at his left wrist holding what light there is. He takes the broom only after it has been instructed and says \emph{Yes, house} to an early thaw and a late, wanting the late because it puts off the paying. On all three days his stroke goes on over the flagstones past the shallow bright patch without even the half-check; he does not turn along the road a house sends a man down when it wants a collector, and no collector comes. The equality with the boy has stood a hundred and fifty-two days: his ear for a pot before a knuckle touches it, the boy’s turn toward the note before anybody makes it, two silences of one shape and a loan that can hear never called. At the going of the light on Day 152, with the coals banked, he tells the kindling \emph{Six counted. The next I don’t count}; the sentence about an ear under this roof being worth more than the debt that holds it comes up as it had come up nine times before, but on this day it is \textbf{not} brought to the word that would call the loan --- it stops short of the threshold, no tenth stopping stands up to join the nine, and he draws the breath that should have gone in and does not spend it, says \emph{Yes, house} to the fire and goes back to the broom. Sella, within hearing, gives the end of her instruction to the pot and asks nothing; Jorra does not ask about the ear and he does not ask about the room. The nine stoppings stay nine objects with no payer named to any, a tenth before the seventh year is earned would be a debt invented to make the nine into a bill, and the absence of a tenth is a keeping and not a payment. No new scar or possession, no change of voice; the loan uncalled and something still to give at the end of the seventh year.

\textbf{Ch 38.} Tallow 4–10 finds his seventh year pressed nearer its end than it has ever stood and still held: six counted in the worn thumb-mark where the house can check, the seventh at the very edge of the sill where it cannot, the small knife set back at the lip with Garl’s unforged collector sentence beside it, the Seed 16 breath unspent with its small interval at the top of each reach, Ash worked into the knuckles in the colour of the clean dark line, the pale clip-ring at the left wrist holding what light there is, his chest tight since the dark. \textbf{Ch 55.} Through Days 216–218, Grain 7–9, the exact account under the Vail roof goes forward one working day at a time with no market until Grain 10. He takes the broom only after it has been instructed, tells the kindling \emph{Six counted. The next I don’t count}, says \emph{Yes, house} to the fire, agrees with the early thaw and the late while keeping the late because it puts off the paying, sweeps the flagstones past the shallow bright patch without the half-check and the collector’s road without a turn, and no collector comes on any morning. The seventh year stands at its very end and still ungiven: six counted where the house can check and the seventh at the lip, the small knife at the very edge with Garl’s unforged sentence beside it, the Seed 16 breath unspent, nine stoppings nine objects with no tenth and the loan uncalled. On all three days the ear-sentence comes to the word that would call the loan and stops there as a remembered interval with no figure and no name, the breath drawn and not spent. The warm stone stays cold and unreconciled in its loft pot, the burned-slate word comes a fourth time and arrives nowhere, and the pot sayings stay sayings with no pot lost; the two silences under the roof stay unjoined. Forward, not closed.

Through Grain 10–12 the exact account under the roof goes on without a tenth standing up. The seventh year stands at its very end and has not given; the small knife stays at the very edge of its sill with six counted where the house can check and the seventh at the lip where it cannot, Garl’s unforged collector sentence beside it and the Seed 16 breath still unspent. The sentence about an ear under this roof being worth more than the debt that holds it still comes to the word that would call the loan and stops there, nine stoppings with no tenth, a remembered interval and not a payment; no collector comes on Grain 10, 11 or 12. Offstage at the market, he keeps the bright patch and the collector’s road unturned and lets the day’s new colours and shapes stay outside the house.

Through Grain 13–18 the exact account under the Vail roof goes on without a tenth standing up. The seventh year stands at its very end and has not given: the knife at the very edge of its sill with six counted where the house can check and the seventh at the lip where it cannot, Garl’s unforged collector sentence beside it, the Seed 16 breath drawn and not spent, nine stoppings nine objects with no tenth and the loan uncalled. He takes the broom only after it has been instructed, tells the kindling \emph{Six counted. The next I don’t count}, brings the ear-sentence to the word that would call the loan and stops there with no figure and no name as a remembered stopping and not a new one, and no collector comes up or down the clay road on any of the six days. His stroke goes past the shallow bright patch and over the road a house sends a man down when it wants a collector without the half-check and without a turn, so the Day 171 movement stays a held change on its own place beside the Day 161 damper fraction and the Day 166 shelf beat. Chest tight since the dark, Ash worked into the knuckle creases in the colour of the clean dark line, the pale clip-ring at the left wrist; the warm stone lies cold and unreconciled in its unmarked pot in the Debt Loft. The dressed grain under the fold gains no number, the yard goes around the returning-line place with a look and no number, and the boy’s thirtieth answer is filed on its sixth place and not stood up beside his nine stoppings. Forward into Grain 19, not closed.

Through Grain 19–21 his seventh year stands at its very end and has still not given: six counted in the worn thumb-mark where the house can check and the seventh at the lip where it cannot, the knife at the very edge of its sill with Garl’s unforged collector sentence beside it, the Seed 16 breath drawn and not spent, nine stoppings with no tenth before the seventh year at its very end, and the loan uncalled with no collector up or down the clay road on any of the three mornings. He brings the ear-sentence all the way to the word that would call the loan three more times and stops each time with no figure and no name, a remembered stopping and not a new one, and he wants the late thaw because a late thaw puts off the paying though the paying has stood in the ruts since the water went. The warm stone lies cold and unreconciled in its loft pot, a keeping taken out and looked at once on Ember 4 and put back, which is not forgiving. His stroke goes past the bright patch without the half-check, so the Day 171 movement stays a held change on its own place beside the Day 161 fraction and the Day 166 beat. He is a debt with a body, one year from the end of his term, valuable because he can hear and therefore unsafe, and the sentence that would call the loan that can hear has still never been said. Nothing paid, called, spent or forgiven.

Through Grain 22–24 (Days 231–233) his seventh year stands at its very end and has still not given: six counted in the worn thumb-mark where the house can check and the seventh at the lip where it cannot, the small knife at the very edge of its sill with Garl’s unforged collector sentence beside it, the Seed 16 breath drawn at the top of each reach and not spent, nine stoppings nine objects with no tenth before the seventh year at its very end, and the loan uncalled with no collector up or down the clay road on any of the three days. He takes the broom only after it has been instructed, tells the kindling \emph{Six counted. The next I don’t count}, says \emph{Yes, house} to the fire and to those who want the thaw early and those who want it late, agreeing so entirely that no argument can find a foot while keeping the late because it puts off the paying, though the paying has stood in the ruts since the water went. On all three days he brings the sentence about an ear under this roof being worth more than the debt that holds it all the way to the word that would call the loan and stops there with no figure and no name, the stopping a remembered stopping and not a new one; the breath he should have spent shows its small interval at the top of the reach and goes unspent. Chest tight since the dark, Ash worked into the knuckle creases in the colour of the clean dark line and no scrubbing lifting it, the pale clip-ring at the left wrist holding what light there was and giving it back; the warm stone Sella gave him in the winter Garl died lies cold and unreconciled in its unmarked pot in the Debt Loft, a keeping taken out and looked at once on Ember 4 and put back, which is not forgiving. His stroke goes over the flagstones past the shallow bright patch without the half-check and over the road a house sends a man down when it wants a collector without once turning along it, so the Day 171 movement stays a held change on its own place beside the Day 161 fraction at the damper and the Day 166 beat beneath the shelf. Nothing paid, called, spent or forgiven.

On the afternoon of Smoke 8 the fifth ownerless asking went over the boards — the weather answering first with the sweet edge of lead glaze on a wrong wind off High Kiln and the price of barley after it, the voice going up the terrace with the row standing where it stood — and he did not claim it or supply a witness. Three or more men go low into the back room before first grey and neither he nor Jorra gives them a name; the burned-slate word stays at four and the two shut-room tellings at two. Through Smoke 10–12 (Days 249–251) he is at the kindling, the hearth, the flagstones, the loaf shelf’s low angle, the Clay Yard and the collector’s road on all three days. He takes the broom only after it has been instructed, tells the wood \emph{Six counted. The next I don’t count} in the tone of a man stating the weather, says \emph{Yes, house} to the fire, agrees with the early thaw and the late and keeps wanting the late because it puts off the paying, and sweeps the collector’s road without once turning along it; no collector comes up or goes down the clay road on Smoke 10, 11 or 12. His seventh year stands at its very end and is still held: six counted in the worn thumb-mark where the house can check and the seventh at the lip where it cannot, the small knife at the very edge of its sill with Garl’s unforged collector sentence beside it, the Seed 16 breath drawn at the top of the reach and not spent, nine stoppings — Reed 5, 8, 11, 14, 17, 20, 23, 26 and 29 — nine objects with no tenth before the seventh year at its very end and still ungiven, and the loan uncalled. No new scar or possession, no change of voice, no tenth stopping and no calling of the loan.

Through Smoke 16–18 his seventh year stands at its very end and still held, and the sentence about the ear under this roof comes to the word that would call the loan and stops there on all three days, a remembered stopping with no figure and no name. Six are counted in the worn thumb-mark where the house can check and the seventh is at the lip where it cannot; the knife lies at the very edge of its sill with Garl’s unforged collector sentence beside it, the Seed 16 breath is drawn at the top of each reach and not spent, and nine stoppings stand with no tenth. His stroke goes over the bright patch and the collector’s road without the half-check or a turn, and no collector comes up or down the clay road. The warm stone stays cold and unreconciled in its loft pot, not tried and not forgiven; Ash is worked into his knuckles in the colour of the clean dark line, the pale clip-ring holds what light there is, and his chest has been tight since the dark. He does not ask about the room and Jorra does not ask about the ear, and something must still give at the end of the seventh year.

Through Smoke 19–21 the seventh year stands at its very end and has still not given. He takes the broom only after its instruction, tells the kindling \emph{Six counted. The next I don’t count}, says \emph{Yes, house} to the early thaw and the late while wanting the late because it puts off the paying, sets six where the house can check and the seventh at the lip where it cannot, and brings the sentence about an ear under this roof worth more than the debt that holds it to the calling word on the 19th and 21st, stopping there with no figure and no name as a remembered ninth stopping with no tenth before the seventh year at its very end and still ungiven; the Seed 16 breath stays unspent, the loan uncalled, no collector coming up or down the clay road on any of the three days. Chest tight since the dark, Ash in the knuckle creases in the colour of the clean dark line, the pale clip-ring holding what light there is, the warm stone cold and unreconciled in its unmarked loft pot, and his stroke over the bright patch without the half-check (T036/T076, T009/T013/T092, T006). Smoke’s second arithmetic goes up the road in Berr’s locked box on the 20th and changes nothing at the kindling; the boy’s six answers stay objects on a sixth place, never joined to the ear-sentence (T061/T082).

Through Smoke 22–24 the seventh year stands at its very end and has still not given. He takes the broom only after its instruction, says \emph{Yes, house} to the early thaw and the late, agrees with both so no argument finds a foot and keeps the late because it puts off the paying, tells the wood \emph{Six counted. The next I don’t count}, sets six in the worn thumb-mark where the house can check and the seventh at the very lip of the sill where it cannot, and keeps Garl’s unforged collector sentence beside the knife with no name on the man who turned back at the frozen ford and no figure on the debt. On all three days the sentence about an ear under this roof being worth more than the debt that holds it comes to the word that would call the loan and stops there, a remembered ninth stopping with no tenth before the seventh year at its very end and still ungiven; he would not stand one up to make the nine into a rule. The Seed 16 breath is drawn and unspent, the loan uncalled, no collector coming up or down the clay road, chest tight, Ash in the knuckle creases in the colour of the clean dark line, the pale clip-ring holding what light there is, his stroke over the bright patch without the half-check, and the warm stone cold and unreconciled in its unmarked loft pot, not tried and not forgiven (T036/T076, T006, T009/T013/T092). Smoke’s second arithmetic stays behind and unread up the road; the boy’s six answers stay objects on a sixth place, never joined to the ear-sentence, and the finding that a house keeps by not-doings is held on a place apart from the debt’s own omissions (T061/T082). Something must still give at the end of the seventh year, and did not give here.

With Corin the equality held at the place it had moved to, the boy’s six answerings kept on a sixth place and never joined to the ear-sentence; with Jorra the old shape held under one roof with the bent finger in the damper and the debt’s unchecking stroke on the flagstones. Through Bone 10–12, Days 309–311, his seventh year stands at its very end and has still not given. The knife lies at the very edge of its sill where it can be checked and where it can slip, six in the worn thumb-mark where the house can check and the seventh at the lip, Garl’s unforged collector sentence beside it with no name and no figure. On all three days he takes the broom only after its instruction, tells the wood \emph{Six counted. The next I don’t count}, says \emph{Yes, house} to the early thaw and the late and keeps the late because it puts off the paying, and brings the ear-sentence to the word that would call the loan and stops there with no figure and no name — a remembered ninth stopping with no tenth before the seventh year at its very end and still ungiven. The Seed 16 breath stays unspent, his chest tight since the dark, Ash worked into the knuckles and the pale clip-ring holding and giving back light. His stroke goes over the shallow bright patch without the half-check; the fourth held change stays on the flagstones with three older ones and four are four and not a rule. In the Debt Loft the warm stone lies cold in its unmarked pot and he does not try to reconcile it, which is not forgiveness. The loan is uncalled, no collector comes up or down the clay road, and Bone 20 stands five mornings ahead. Nothing is joined, named, opened, called, paid or ended.

Through Bone 22–24, Days 321–323, the exact account holds at the kindling and on the flagstones and nothing is spent. Six years stand in the worn thumb-mark where the house can check and the seventh at the lip beside Garl’s unforged collector sentence, the knife at the very edge of its sill where it can be checked and where it can slip; he told the wood \emph{Six counted. The next I don’t count} on all three days and put the knife back where it could be checked, announcing it to nobody because the yard had already been told. He brought the ear-sentence to the word that would call the loan and stopped there with no figure and no name, a remembered ninth stopping with no tenth before the seventh year at its very end and still ungiven; the breath he drew did not go in, the Seed 16 breath stayed unspent with its small interval at the top of each reach, his chest tight since the dark, Ash in the knuckle creases the colour of the clean dark line and the pale clip-ring at the left wrist holding the little light and giving it back. His stroke went over the shallow bright patch without the half-check on all three days, and the returned half-check of Bone 8 stayed on the flagstones as the fourth of four held changes on four places, not a rule and with no payer named; Sella’s handful at the rack end was not made a fifth of them, and the boy’s staying and early letting-go stayed two objects with a finger between. The warm stone lay cold in its unmarked loft pot, unreconciled by not trying, which is not forgiveness. He said nothing to an early thaw and a late and kept wanting the late because it puts off the paying; no collector came up or went down the clay road on any of the three days, and the five arithmetics going up in Berr’s locked box did not call the loan. Jorra did not ask about the ear and he did not ask about the room; the two silences stayed unjoined. No bond paid or spoken, no new scar or possession and no change of voice.

Took the broom only after it had been given its instruction, said \emph{Yes, house} to the early thaw and the late, agreed with both so no argument could find a foot and kept the late because it puts off the paying, and told the wood \emph{Six counted. The next I don’t count} in the tone of a man stating the weather. Set six in the worn thumb-mark where the house could check and the seventh at the very lip of the sill where it could not, with Garl’s unforged collector sentence beside it, no name on the man who turned back at the frozen ford and no figure on the debt. Brought the sentence about an ear under this roof being worth more than the debt that held it to the word that would call the loan on all three days and stopped there with no figure and no name — a remembered \textbf{ninth} stopping with no tenth before the seventh year at its very end and still ungiven. Drew the breath that should have gone in at the top of the reach and did not spend it, a small interval showing where it should have been, chest tight as it had been since the dark; Ash worked into the knuckle creases in the colour of the clean dark line, no scrubbing lifting it, and the pale clip-ring at the left wrist holding what light there was and giving it back. From above came the small dry scrape of a pot’s foot on stone, a sound with a direction from a room he cannot enter; the warm stone in its unmarked pot in the Debt Loft stayed cold and unreconciled by not trying, which is not forgiveness. His stroke went on over the flagstones past the shallow bright patch without the half-check, the stones keeping the place where it had stopped. No collector came up the clay road on Frost 7, 8 or 9 and none went down it; the stayed frost at the well, the stiffened rope, the skinned trough and the plate of ice lifted on Frost 9 paid nothing to the loan and made no lesson of four openings in four months (T058/T079). With Jorra the old shape held: the dust-finger in the damper and the debt’s unchecking stroke on the flagstones, neither man naming the other’s silence. No bond paid, sold or spoken, no new scar or possession, no change of voice.

His seventh year stood at its very end and was still held: six counted in the worn thumb-mark where the house can check and the seventh at the lip where it cannot, the small knife at the very edge of its sill with Garl’s unforged collector sentence beside it, the Seed 16 breath drawn at the top of each reach and not spent, nine stoppings — Reed 5, 8, 11, 14, 17, 20, 23, 26 and 29 — nine objects with no tenth before the seventh year at its very end and still ungiven, and the loan uncalled. His stroke went over the flagstones past the shallow bright patch without the half-check and over the road a house sends a man down when it wants a collector, over and over, without once turning along it, so the Day 171 movement stayed a held change on its own place beside the Day 161 damper fraction and the Day 166 beat beneath the shelf (T062, T100). He did not ask about the room and nobody asked about the ear, and the two silences stayed unjoined under one roof. Above the shed, in the Debt Loft that reached him only as a sound with a direction, an unmarked clay pot held the warm stone Sella gave him in the winter Garl died, two years gone and cold, unreconciled with the debt by not trying, which is not forgiving (T006). On Grain 20 he was offstage at the market; on Grain 19 and 21 he kept the exact account under the roof while the district’s arithmetic changed twice in Grain and the road stood where the road stood. No bond paid or spoken, no new scar or possession, no change of voice; something must give at the end of the seventh year and it did not give here.

\end{itemize}

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item Ch 58: Days 225, 226 and 227, Grain 16–18, Sixthday to Eighthday, on stage at the kindling, the hearth, the flagstones and the collector’s road on all three days. Took the broom only after it had been instructed, told the kindling \emph{Six counted. The next I don’t count} and said \emph{Yes, house} to the fire (T036/T076). His seventh year stood at its very end and was still held: six counted in the worn thumb-mark where the house can check and the seventh at the lip where it cannot, the small knife at the very edge of its sill with Garl’s unforged collector sentence beside it, the Seed 16 breath drawn at the top of each reach and not spent, nine stoppings --- Reed 5, 8, 11, 14, 17, 20, 23, 26 and 29 --- nine objects with no tenth before the seventh year at its very end, and the loan uncalled (T036/T076, T061/T082). Chest tight since the dark, Ash worked into the creases of his knuckles in the colour of the clean dark line and no scrubbing lifted it, the pale clip-ring at the left wrist holding what light there was and giving it back. On all three days he brought the sentence about an ear under this roof being worth more than the debt that holds it all the way to the word that would call the loan and stopped there with no figure and no name; the stopping was a remembered stopping and not a new one, no tenth stood up to join the nine, and no collector came up or went down the clay road on Grain 16, 17 or 18. His stroke went over the flagstones past the shallow bright patch without the half-check and over the road a house sends a man down when it wants a collector without once turning along it, so the Day 171 movement stayed a held change on its own place beside the Day 161 fraction at the damper and the Day 166 beat beneath the shelf (T062, T100). The warm stone lay cold and unreconciled in its unmarked clay pot in the Debt Loft, not looked at and not forgiven (T006). While the year’s first grain was beaten out on the flagstones and spread thin to dry he kept his own exact count and gave no figure to either the grain or the hand that did not come back; the yard went around that place with a look and a wide step and no number (T077, T098 advanced and not paid). With Sella he took the broom after its instruction and neither asked about the ear or the room; with Corin the two ears kept their equality and silence, the boy’s held inch on its sixth place not laid across his own intervals; with Jorra neither asked about the back room or the ear, and the bent finger stood in the damper as a remembered repetition (T061/T082, T035/T031/T062). No bond paid or spoken, no new scar or possession, no change of voice; forward, not closed.

\end{itemize}

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item Ch 57: Days 222, 223 and 224, Grain 13–15, Thirdday to Fifthday, on stage at the kindling, the hearth, the flagstones and the collector’s road on all three days. Took the broom only after it had been instructed, the instruction going to the tool before the man; said \emph{Yes, house} to the fire and told the kindling \emph{Six counted. The next I don’t count}; agreed with the woman who wanted the thaw early and the man who wanted it late on Grain 15, agreeing so entirely that no argument could find a foot, and kept wanting the late because it puts off the paying, though the paying had stood in the ruts since the water went (T036/T076). His seventh year stood at its very end and was still held: six counted in the worn thumb-mark where the house can check and the seventh at the lip where it cannot, the small knife at the very edge of its sill with Garl’s unforged collector sentence beside it, the Seed 16 breath drawn at the top of each reach and not spent, nine stoppings — Reed 5, 8, 11, 14, 17, 20, 23, 26 and 29 — nine objects with no tenth before the seventh year at its very end, and the loan uncalled; chest tight since the dark, Ash worked into the creases of his knuckles in the colour of the clean dark line and no scrubbing lifted it, the pale clip-ring at the left wrist holding what light there was and giving it back. On all three days he brought the sentence about an ear under this roof being worth more than the debt that holds it all the way to the word that would call the loan and stopped there with no figure and no name; the stopping was a remembered stopping and not a new one, no tenth stood up to join the nine, and no collector came up the clay road on Grain 13, 14 or 15 (T036/T076, T061/T082). His stroke went over the flagstones past the shallow bright patch without the half-check and over the road a house sends a man down when it wants a collector without once turning along it, so the Day 171 movement stayed a held change on its own place beside the Day 161 fraction at the damper and the Day 166 beat beneath the shelf, not repeated and not paired into a rule (T062, T100). Above the shed the warm stone Sella gave him in the winter Garl died lay back in its unmarked clay pot in the Debt Loft, two years gone and cold, unreconciled with the debt by not trying, which was not forgiving (T006). The harvest came in with hands back in the worked strips and the first grain carried under the roof; with the returning hands the yard went around the empty place in the returning line where a hand went in on Seed 15 and did not come out, with a look and a wide step and no number, and the boy kept the bundle and the absence on separate trays, T098 advanced and not paid (T009/T013/T092, T098). While Jorra’s bent finger stood in the cold damper as a remembered repetition he did not look toward the bed or ask about the room, and Jorra did not ask about the ear; three or more men unnamed went low into the finger’s-width-open back room before first grey on the two mornings he saw them and neither man named them or made a third telling of the shut counting room, the two tellings staying two (T035/T031, T065/T095). The burned-slate word held at four and the three shapings of the pot saying stayed sayings, a wrong-wind voice on Grain 15 letting one stand without a pot lost (T061/T082, T064). With Sella nothing changed — he takes the broom only after its instruction and she has still not asked about his seventh year or his ear; with Corin the two ears kept their equality and silence; with Jorra neither asked about the ear or the room. No bond paid, sold or spoken, no new scar, possession or change of voice; something must give at the end of the seventh year and it did not give here.

\end{itemize}

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item Ch 56: Through Days 219–221, Grain 10–12, offstage on the market morning of Day 219 and at the kindling and sill on the two ordinary tending days. He took the broom only after it had been instructed, said \emph{Yes, house} to the fire, told the kindling \emph{Six counted. The next I don’t count}, and kept the knife at the very edge of its sill with six counted in the worn thumb-mark where the house can check and the seventh at the lip where it cannot; Garl’s unforged collector sentence lay beside it and the breath from Seed 16 stayed unspent, with its small interval at the top of each reach (T036/T076). The ear-sentence came to the word that would call the loan and stopped there with no figure and no name, the stopping a remembered stopping and not a new one; the nine stoppings stood as nine objects and not a rule, no tenth came before the seventh year at its very end, and the loan stayed uncalled (T061/T082). His stroke went past the shallow bright patch without the half-check and over the collector’s road without a turn, so the Day 171 movement stayed a held change on its own place beside the Day 161 fraction at the damper and the Day 166 beat beneath the shelf; no collector came on Grain 10, 11 or 12. The warm stone lay cold and unreconciled in its unmarked clay pot in the Debt Loft, heard from below only as a scrape on an earlier day and not touched again (T006). Ash stayed worked into the knuckle creases in the colour of the clean dark line and the pale clip-ring held what light there was; he agreed with the early thaw and the late and kept wanting the late because it puts off the paying. With Sella nothing changed, with Corin the two ears kept their equality and silence, and with Jorra neither asked about the ear or the room. No bond paid or spoken, no new scar or possession, no change of voice.

\end{itemize}

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item Ch 1: Does not appear; the broom, the knife and the loft are held for Chapter 2.

\item Ch 2: Swept the kiln-house before anyone woke and stopped for two strokes at a pot’s flat note without turning his head or naming the sound. Put the small bench knife in his pocket, then took it out and put it back where it could be checked and said so unasked. Told Sella \emph{Six years. One to go. I’ve counted every one, and I won’t count the next.} Carried up from the Debt Loft with a broom on the third day, banked the coals, and said \emph{He’s a foundling. I’m a debt. Don’t put us in the same sentence, Sella.} when the boy was given a bed. Heard the second flat note of the three days from a pot set down on the bench and did not say what it was.

\end{itemize}

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item Ch 4: Days 5 and 6. Swept before light on Stone 11 and again at dusk on Stone 12, with Ash in his knuckles and the pale ring at his left wrist. Took the small bench knife out and put it back where it could be checked, saying so unasked both times. His broom stopped for two strokes at the flat note of a pot through the shed wall and he did not turn his head, name the sound or say that it was a sound at all --- the second ear in the house, witnessed only by the reader. Said \emph{yes, house; I’ll sweep it; I swept it this morning; I’ll sweep it again} to the ground and kept his head down over the broom. Six of seven years counted, the seventh not counted. He said nothing about the note all day, and nobody asked him to.

\end{itemize}

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item Ch 5: Days 7--9. On Stone 13 came up the yard with the small knife already back on its sill, checked it with his eyes only, and saw the boy turn his head toward a pot before Jorra set it down; his broom stopped half a stroke at the set-down that gave nothing and he said nothing about either. Counted six years of seven and held the seventh back, and stopped altogether for two breaths when Sella said he had done well, then swept again. At dusk put the knife back where it could be checked and announced it unasked, and kept his head down over the broom while Sella counted loaves and bits. Said nothing all three days about the note that did not come, and nobody asked him to.

\end{itemize}

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item Ch 6: Days 10--14. On Stone 16 measured the kindling stack with his eyes, four, four and a space at the end, and said to the stack \emph{Six counted. The next I don’t count.} On Stone 17 set the small knife on its sill and told the yard to check, stopped altogether for two breaths when Sella said \emph{you’ve done well} and said \emph{Yes, house} before going on; his broom checked half a stroke when a pot turned toward on the bench gave nothing. Scraped Ash from his knuckles with the knife, held the pale ring at his left wrist up to the light and put the knife back without announcing it this time. Named the kiln’s breath as the danger and said a man in Mud End who slept before a kiln with the damper shut was called a merciful death; said he would take the late thaw, a longer week before the paying. On Stone 18 said he had swept and would sweep again; on Stone 19 agreed a late thaw was a longer week before the paying and offered to check the ridge; on Stone 20, Account-day, told the yard again the knife was back on its sill and let his broom stop half a stroke at the place where no note had come. Six of seven years counted all five days, the seventh held back and never named.

\end{itemize}

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item Ch 7: Days 15--24. On Stone 22 set the small bench knife on its sill, told the empty yard \emph{I took the small knife. I put it back. You can check}, and said to the kindling \emph{Six counted; the next I don’t count}; was sent for a collector for a neighbour two doors down and returned with a man whose cuff was soft from washing and fingertips the colour of skimmed milk gone off, who said \emph{the measure is taken and the account stands as entered} to a slate. On the way back his head turned a degree at a vessel’s flat note carried past the door and he did not name it or look at the basket. On Stone 23 swept around the place where a pot had given nothing and said \emph{I swept it this morning; I’ll sweep it again}; Jorra’s returned dust went unremarked by him. On Stone 25 and 26 his broom checked half a stroke at the place where a pot cracked in the yard with the flat knock and he said nothing about either; he wanted the late thaw because it put off the paying. On Stone 29 held the pale clip-ring at his left wrist to the light, said \emph{I can check the width, house. I’ve a thumb as good as any}, and took his eyes off the ridge. On Stone 30 the knife was back on its sill and announced once more, unasked. Six of the seven years counted every day, the seventh held back and never named; the ear kept silent and the loan uncalled.

\end{itemize}

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item Ch 8: Days 25--30. Through the Five set the small bench knife on its sill and told the empty yard where it was, and said to the kindling that six were counted and the next he did not count; the seventh year was held back on every day. Scrubbed at the Ash in his knuckles that no scrubbing lifts, and kept the silence about the flat note all five days and about the boy’s ear as before. On the Long Night said in the dark that six years were counted and the next he did not, and set the knife where it could be checked; Garl’s coat held a broader man’s shape in the dark. Wanted the late thaw because a late thaw puts off the paying; on Ilmen 1 swept toward the thaw and the slip pits with the knife back on its sill and the seventh still held back, and did not touch the ridge or the mark.

\end{itemize}

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item Ch 9: Days 31–37. On Ilmen 2 noticed the oiled paper had stopped lifting hard before he noticed the light, and swept toward the slip pits with Ash in his knuckles that no scrubbing lifted; six years of the seven counted, the seventh held back and not said to the paper or the boards or anybody. Agreed with the neighbour who wanted the thaw early and the one who wanted it late and kept wanting the late one, because a late thaw puts off the paying. On Ilmen 3 set the small bench knife on its sill and announced it to the empty yard --- \emph{I put it back. You can check} --- and scraped at the Ash in his knuckles. On Ilmen 5 swept near the bench and did not say what the pot gave or look toward the basket. On Ilmen 6 his head went a degree toward the pot that answered nearly full and he went back to his broom without naming the sound. On Ilmen 7 stood with the yard as the Singing Sill gave its low note early and the argument ended in weather, and said nothing about either. Through the seven days kept the silence about the flat note and about the boy’s ear, and carried the count into Ilmen 8 with the knife back on its sill and the seventh year held back.

\end{itemize}

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item Ch 10: Days 38–44. Set the small bench knife on its sill before light on Ilmen 9 and again on Ilmen 11, told the empty yard \emph{It’s back. You can check}, counted six years of the seven and held the seventh back; Ash worked into the creases of his knuckles that no scrubbing lifted, the pale clip-ring at his left wrist catching the light. Swept around the place where the clay-heavy water had come up behind the drying racks and swept the road toward the Fishstairs over and over without looking along it, the road a man goes down to fetch a collector; no collector came for the woman in the brook and he did not go for one. Agreed with the early thaw and the late and kept wanting the late one because it puts off the paying. Said nothing about the sixth hearing the boy had heard out of a person on the bank, and did not look at the basket on the way back up the yard.

\end{itemize}

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item Ch 11: Days 45–47. Put the small bench knife on its sill and told the empty yard \emph{It’s on the sill. Counted six years of the seven and held the seventh back every morning, Ash worked into the knuckles that no scrubbing lifts, the pale clip-ring catching the light. Swept the road down toward the Fishstairs over and over without once turning to look along it; no collector went down it and he did not go, and he did not say the omission had a name. Stopped altogether for two breaths when Sella said he had done well, then said \emph{Yes, house} and went on. Agreed with the early thaw and the late and kept wanting the late one because it puts off the paying. At the well on Day 47 went once over the collector’s road and again without turning. Said nothing about the boy’s ear or his own, and the loan that can hear stayed uncalled.

\end{itemize}

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item Ch 12: Days 48–54. The small knife lay on its sill with six years counted and the seventh held back; Ash was worked into his knuckles that no scrubbing lifts and the pale clip-ring caught what light there was. His eye went a degree to the slack oiled paper at the window before the light did and he said nothing. A vessel gave its note past the yard door on Day 50 and another pot answered nearly full on Day 52 and his head did not turn at either; he did not call either a seventh hearing or name the sound. He agreed with the early thaw and the late and kept wanting the late one, because a late thaw puts off the paying; his broom went over the collector’s road on Days 50 and 53 without once turning along it and no collector came. He did not look toward the bed or the basket, and the loan that can hear stayed uncalled.

\end{itemize}

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

At the well and in the yard he said \emph{Yes, house} to the neighbour who wanted the thaw early and to the one who wanted it late, and kept wanting the late one because a late thaw puts off the paying (T036). His broom went over the road a house sends a man down when it wants a collector, over and over, without once turning along it, and no collector went down it for the woman in the brook (T009, T090). On Ilmen 28 a vessel gave its note past the yard door and his head did not turn; he did not name the sound or supply the Grathic word for it and did not call it a seventh hearing (T061, T076). When Sella told him he had done well he stopped altogether for two breaths, then set the knife where it could be checked and went back to the broom. On Silt 1 he kept sweeping toward the thaw with the count unchanged; the loan that can hear stayed uncalled.

\end{itemize}

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item Ch 14: Days 61–67. Set the small knife on its sill and told the empty yard \emph{It’s back. You can check}, with six years counted and the seventh nearly gone and still held, the one entry the house cannot check; held the pale clip-ring to the light and kept Ash in his knuckles the colour of the clean dark line. Said \emph{Yes, house} to both the early and the late thaw and kept wanting the late one because a late thaw puts off the paying. His broom checked half a stroke at the cracked-pot place and went on without turning or naming the sound; a vessel gave its note past the yard door and he did not turn. On Silt 6 his head went a degree toward the nearly-full pot and went back to the broom; he said nothing and did not look at the basket. Jorra’s dust went unremarked and the loan that can hear stayed uncalled.

\end{itemize}

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item Ch 15: Days 68–74, Silt 9–15. Set the small knife on its sill before light and told the empty yard where it was, six years standing in a mark worn almost flat by his thumb and the seventh nearly gone and still held, the one entry the house could not check; Ash in his knuckles the colour of the clean dark line, pale clip-ring held to the light. Said \emph{Yes, house} to the early thaw and the late, agreed with both so entirely no argument could find a foot, and kept wanting the late one because it puts off the paying, though the paying came with the water. His broom checked at the cracked-pot place and went over the collector’s road without once turning along it; when a vessel gave its note past the yard door in the afternoon of Silt 15 his head did not turn and he did not name the sound or look toward the basket. Jorra’s dust went unremarked and the loan that can hear stayed uncalled.

\end{itemize}

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item Ch 16: Days 75–77, Silt 16–18. The next I don’t count} to the kindling. Ash in his knuckles the colour of the clean dark line, pale clip-ring held to what light there was. Said \emph{Yes, house} to both sides of the thaw argument and kept wanting the late one because it puts off the paying. His broom went over the collector’s road without once turning along it; a vessel gave its note past the door on Day 75 and a whole vessel did so on Day 77, and his head did not turn and he did not name either sound. He did not look toward the bed or the basket, said nothing about the foundling’s half-beat or the loaf, and kept the two ears and two silences under one roof as an equality neither named. The loan that can hear stayed uncalled; the seventh year pressed to its edge and was held.

The next I don’t count.} Ash worked into his knuckles the colour of the clean dark line and no scrubbing lifted it; the pale clip-ring at his left wrist held what light there was. Said \emph{Yes, house} to the ones who wanted the thaw early and the ones who wanted it late, agreed so entirely no argument could find a foot, and kept wanting the late one because it puts off the paying, though the paying had stood in the ruts all week. When a vessel gave its note past the door he did not turn and did not name the sound, and the boy did not call it a seventh hearing. He did not turn toward the foundling’s half-beat at the well either and did not put the two turnings together. The two ears and two silences under the roof kept their equality; the loan that can hear stayed uncalled and the seventh year pressed to its edge and was held.

The next I don’t count}; six years stood in a mark worn almost flat by his thumb and the seventh was never cut, nearly gone and still held, the one entry in the house the house could not check. Ash was worked into the creases of his knuckles in the colour of the clean dark line and no scrubbing lifted it; the pale clip-ring at his left wrist held what light there was and gave it back. Said \emph{Yes, house} to the woman who wanted the thaw early and the man who wanted it late, agreed so entirely no argument could find a foot, and kept wanting the late because it puts off the paying, though the paying had stood in the ruts all week. His broom went over the road a house sends a man down when it wants a collector, over and over, without once turning along it, and no collector came; he kept the sentence about the frozen ford where he kept the seventh year. On Silt 26 and Seed 1 swept the yard around the boot-print, the clean dark line, the finer grey and the space under the lowest rack without touching any of them, and on Seed 1 took the broom only after Sella had given it its instruction. A vessel gave its note past the door on Silt 27 and again in the afternoon of Seed 1 and his head did not turn and he did not name the sound, and the boy did not call it a seventh hearing; he did not turn toward the foundling’s half-beat at the market either and did not join the two turnings. At the going of the light set the knife back where it could be checked and told the yard so, unasked. The loan that can hear stayed uncalled and the seventh year pressed to its edge and was held across the turn of the month.

The next I don’t count.} Ash was worked into the creases of his knuckles in the colour of the clean dark line and no scrubbing lifted it, and the pale clip-ring at his left wrist held what light there was and gave it back. Said \emph{Yes, house} to the early thaw and the late, agreed so entirely no argument could find a foot, and kept wanting the late because it puts off the paying, though the paying had stood in the ruts. A vessel gave its note past the door on Days 91 and 92 and his head did not turn and he did not name the sound; the boy did not call it a seventh hearing. No collector came, the loan that can hear stayed uncalled and the seventh year was held.

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item Ch 20: Days 94–100, Seed 5–11. Set the small bench knife on its sill with six years standing in a mark his thumb had worn almost flat and the seventh nearly gone and still held, the one entry in the house the house cannot check, and said to the kindling \emph{Six counted. The next I don’t count.} Ash in his knuckles was the colour of the clean dark line and no scrubbing lifted it; the pale clip-ring at his wrist held what light there was and gave it back. Said \emph{Yes, house} to the early thaw and the late, agreed so entirely no argument could find a foot and kept wanting the late because it puts off the paying. Took the broom only after Sella had given it its instruction, swept the collector’s road over and over without once turning along it, and kept the unforged sentence from the frozen ford with the seventh year, entering neither. A vessel gave its note past the door and he did not turn and did not name it; the boy did not call it a seventh hearing. He did not turn toward the foundling’s half-beat at the market’s edge and did not join the two turnings. \CRcharacter{Veno Brine}{the factor who can turn a damp document into a fortune}{build/portraits/veno-brine.pdf}{\CRfield{Also called}{Veno Brine, the factor, Veno of Greybank, the man who never signs anything}\CRfield{Role}{other}\CRfield{Born}{Y.H. 766, Vhal, the Sallow coast}\CRfield{Kind}{human (Vhaleni)}\CRfield{Origin}{Vhal, the Sallow coast; a house with no boat-share and an excellent memory for wet paper}\CRfield{Allegiance}{the Greybank counting house; agent of Sere interests in the north; Council of Tides by correspondence}\CRfield{Status}{alive}\CRfield{First seen}{Chapter 130}}{\CRsheetheading{Appearance}
Forty-six and carefully dressed in a lowland cut that he has never quite got right, which he does not care about because the clothes are for the people he deals with and not for himself. He is a narrow Vhaleni man with a client’s smile that he can hold for an entire negotiation and drop the instant the door closes, which the clerks of Greybank have learned to read as the true end of the meeting. His hands are soft, with salt-paper stains at the fingertips, and he never carries a pen, because a factor who is seen writing is a factor whose word can be checked. He has a gold crown mounted in a ring which he wears on his little finger and which he has never earned in Grath, a detail he considers the only beautiful thing about the place. He smells of tar, wet rope, expensive soap and — when a Sere matter is in hand — myrrh, which is the smell of the empire and of a room where a person has been entered. The thing people notice first is the smile; the thing they notice last is that he never touches a slate, not even to move it, which in a counting house is a form of armour.

\CRsheetheading{Voice \& Manner}
Vhaleni sibilance flattened for lowland ears, with long pauses and questions that contain their own answers. He says \emph{the document}, \emph{the weather}, \emph{the understanding}, and never \emph{the contract}, because a contract is a thing that can be read and he has built his life on things that cannot. He speaks of people as positions — \emph{the widow, thane, the collector} — and has a way of offering kindness with a figure attached, so that the recipient must decide which part was the gift, which is the whole art of his trade. When he is genuinely angered he becomes courteous to a degree that makes the room cold, because everyone has seen what precedes it. He has two laughs: one for clients, warm and brief, and one for himself, which is a single breath through the nose and means he has just been found out and does not intend to admit it.

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item “The paper is damp. It’s a bad season for documents. In Vhalen we consider that a virtue. A law that lasts too long stops earning, doesn’t it?”

\item “I have not paid you. I have advanced you. You’ll see the difference when the grain comes.”

\item “Forty measures for one return. Ask me why forty and I’ll tell you the figure is the figure. Ask me again in private and I’ll still tell you the figure is the figure.”

\item “I don’t buy people. I buy the shape of them. A beautiful return must remember enough to be exhibited. There’s a difference, and the Council calls it civility.”

\item “You want the girl. I want the share. We’ll write it down in the rain and see which of us has a document in the morning.”

\end{itemize}

\CRsheetheading{History}
He was born in Vhal to a family with no boat-share and an unusual talent for reading documents that had been left in the rain, which in the salt republic is the most marketable gift a man can have. He worked the counting house, learned that a contract on salt-paper in damp weather is no contract at all, and spent twelve years turning that fact into a fortune and two enemies, one of whom he later bought out with a damp document and a warm smile. He came up the Salt Road to Greybank in Y.H. 796 as a factor for Vhaleni glass and stayed, because the north buys measures and a factor who can buy a debt before it is due is a factor who never needs to buy the person. He has represented Sere interests in the north since Y.H. 803 without ever admitting to the Sun-Emperor’s Council that he works for them, and has sold grain, glass, quiet ash and whole returns to people who believe they are dealing with a Vhaleni and not an empire.

In the first weeks of Stone, Y.H. 812, he carried the slate for a private whole return from the Greybank factor to the collector in Sill, and could not spell the purchaser’s name, which he has never told anyone and has never forgotten. He has spent the years since trying to work out who bought forty children’s warmth for a foundling with a flower, because a man who cannot identify a buyer is a man who cannot charge him again, which in his profession is a form of insult. He has begun to suspect the Unbanked, then the Court, then a third thing that looks like both, and has kept each suspicion in a different document, all of them damp.

He has kept Solene Ember in a room with good light since Y.H. 810, which he describes to visitors as protection and to himself as an investment that has not yet matured. He has twice offered to buy Pia of the Quay’s mother’s boat-share and been refused twice, which he has entered as a debt owed to him by a girl who does not know she owes it.

\CRsheetheading{Wounds \& Fears}
He has no house and no share, which in Vhalen makes him a man whose account is always current and never his own. His wound is that he can turn any document into nothing and therefore cannot make anything that lasts, which is a strange hunger in a man who deals in permanent arrangements. He fears wet paper in the wrong hands, which is the only thing that can undo him, and fears more than that a person who reads a contract as a person rather than a shape, which is what the foundling from Low Kiln does when he looks at a vessel. His contradiction: the man whose whole trade is the convenient disappearance of evidence has kept three damp documents dry in a private drawer for ten years, because a factor who keeps nothing can never be blackmailed and a factor who keeps everything can, and he has chosen to be the second kind in secret and the first kind in public.

\CRsheetheading{Desires}
He wants a boat-share, which would make him a Vhaleni instead of a man who deals with them, and he wants to know who bought the whole return in Y.H. 812, because an unspelled name is the only account in his life he cannot close. He thinks he wants the north to remain a place where a damp document is a fortune. What he needs is to understand that a person with no account is cheaper than a person with one, which is the Council’s doctrine and his own, and that he has spent his life making people cheaper in order to call himself civility. When he finally learns the purchaser’s name, he will not say it aloud; he will write it on salt-paper in the rain and watch it disappear, which is the only honest thing he has ever done with a document.

\CRsheetheading{Bonds}
\textbf{Solene Ember} — the beautiful return he keeps in a room with good light. He is kind to her in the exact way a creditor is kind, and she has never mistaken it, which is why he keeps her and why he distrusts her. He has begun to fear that she will refuse a fourth return, which would be a loss and a precedent, in that order.

\textbf{Pia of the Quay} — the salt girl who refused his offer for her mother’s share twice. He has entered the refusal as a debt and has never collected, which in his vocabulary is the beginning of an interest he cannot name.

\textbf{Marra} — the collector whose slate passed through his hands in Y.H. 812 and whose name appeared on a document he was not supposed to read. He has not told anyone and has used the knowledge once, gently, in a negotiation, which is how he tests what a thing is worth.

\textbf{Berr Clay, the Thane of Clay} — who signed the levy he carried and forgot the purchaser’s name deliberately. Veno has never pressed him, because a Thane who has forgotten a thing on purpose is a Thane who can be made to remember it at the right moment, which is a kind of leverage he has kept warm for ten years like a coal under ash.

\textbf{Corin} — the foundling whose name was written before a face. Veno has tried three times to buy his ear for the College or the Sere factors and has been refused three times, and has begun to suspect that the boy is not an account at all but a creditor, which is a category he has no word for.

\textbf{Avis Wake} — a Council member who votes against taxing the glass boats and whom Veno pays to do so, which is an arrangement the Council calls representation and Veno calls the cheapest insurance in Vhalen.

\CRsheetheading{Arc So Far}
No chapters are written yet. He enters in the Greybank counting house, smiling at a widow while declining to touch a slate, and the reader will take him for a merchant until the first damp document turns a household’s debt into nothing.

\CRsheetheading{Chapter Log}
\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item No chapters written yet; first appearance planned for Ch 130 (the Greybank counting house, the offer for the boat-share).

\end{itemize}
}

\chapter*{The Atlas}
\markboth{The Atlas}{The Atlas}
\addcontentsline{toc}{chapter}{The Atlas}
\CRmap*{The Bone Orchard — outside the north gate of Sill}{build/atlas/bone-orchard.jpg}{The burial ground a league north of the Cross, drawn at walking scale along the north gate road: the rough-staked ground of the thin-return children’s shallow graves, the east ground where pots are broken for the dead and left where they fell, the barrow of grey Ash that goes out through the north gate on every market-day and comes back empty, and the road running on through the gate to Cold Acre on the ridge with its six houses, its barley and turnips and its well that never freezes. The north bridge, the Ilm and Sill are drawn faint at the foot for neighbourhood only. Cartouche dated Y.H. 813, the month of Ember, with compass, a league scale in paces, a convention of signs and surveyor’s notes on the barrow, the unslated graves, the pots broken for the house and the road that is clay to the ankle in Silt. An engraved broken pot in the margin.}

\CRmap*{Cold Acre — on the ridge two leagues north of Sill}{build/atlas/cold-acre.jpg}{The farm hamlet two leagues north of Sill, one league beyond the Bone Orchard by the north gate road, drawn at walking scale: six houses and a byre in their drift-stone wall, the barley strips and turnip ground, the bare ring of ground about the well where frost will not hold and the children leave the untaken turn standing, and the well itself with its stone lip, clay dish, well-rope, eleven links to the water and the twelfth that hangs dry in the hand. The well-shrine and the children’s stone stand beside the curb; a red nought marks the place where the thirteenth would stand. The road runs south to the north gate, Sill and the Bone Orchard drawn faint below, and east to the Tallow Works two leagues off; the frozen Ilm and the Singing Sill lie at the foot. Cartouche dated Y.H. 813, the month of Frost, with compass, a league scale in paces, a convention of signs and surveyor’s notes on the ninety-four days of ice, the bell that comes up the ridge four, four and a gap with the gap not ours to fill, the assessor’s column that has never held a figure, the barrow of grey Ash that goes past on market-days, and no Last Day on a ridge. An engraved clay dish set on a stone sits in the margin.}

\CRmap*{The Cross and the Fishstairs — Sill’s market and the steps below the north bridge}{build/atlas/cross-and-fishstairs.jpg}{The ground the boy is carried over on every Account-day, drawn at the scale of the market: the market square with its stalls, the reading block under the moot-post and its finger’s width of shade, the eight pigs on the weighing rail and the turnips left standing with figures beside them, the Court’s table at the Slate Row fringe; below the north bridge the Fishstairs counting four steps, four, and the out-of-line landing, the edge of the fish-trade in the bridge’s shadow, Rusk’s room, the hard sill and the Singing Sill under the water, the dotted line of the Breaking, and the south bridge on the way to Low Kiln. Surveyed and inked in Y.H. 813, the reed month.}

\CRmap{Greybank, the Court’s gate}{build/atlas/greybank.jpg}{The Court’s granary town eighteen leagues downriver of Sill, drawn as its own surveyors would draw it: the Ilm and its quay, the factor’s house where the tally for Sill is kept, the Vhaleni Counting House with Veno Brine’s private drawer of dry documents, the Court’s granaries and banking hall, the winter ford, the burial grounds, and the ends of the Clay Road and the beginnings of the Salt and Hearth Roads. Surveyed and inked in Y.H. 812, the Thin Year.}

\CRmap*{High Kiln — the glaze terrace above Low Kiln, Sill}{build/atlas/high-kiln.jpg}{The other half of Sill, drawn at the scale a potter walks: the terrace two hundred paces above the low yard with its barley strip, House Clay and the folded red cord and locked box, the Glaze Room where lead is mixed and tasted, the master potters’ houses and their breathing kilns, the broken terrace lip, the steep street climbing from the north bridge and the Cross, the Ilm with its four-foot sill and Singing Sill, and Low Kiln below drawn faint for neighbourhood only. Surveyed and inked in Y.H. 812, the Thin Year.}

\CRmap*{Sill and the Lower Ilm — the country of the birth-town}{build/atlas/home-region.jpg}{The clay country about Sill, drawn out a few days’ walking: the Ilm from Nine Pots and the Ferr to Greybank, the weir, the Old Kiln, Cold Acre, Mud End and the Reedholt marsh. Surveyed and inked in Y.H. 812, the Thin Year.}

\CRmap{Sill and the Two Kilns — the birth-town}{build/atlas/home-settlement.jpg}{A detailed plan of Sill on the Ilm, drawn to the ground a child can walk: the four-foot fall and the Singing Sill, the two bridges, the Fishstairs and the Cross, Slate Row, Low Kiln with the Clay Yard and the Vail kiln-house, High Kiln and the Glaze Room, the family houses, the smithy, the meal mill, the wells and fields, the Bone Orchard and the edge of the reedbeds. Surveyed and inked in Y.H. 812, the Thin Year.}

\CRmap*{House Reed and the Birth-flower Shrine — Low Kiln, Sill}{build/atlas/house-reed.jpg}{The reed-cutter’s house east of the Clay Yard, Alda Reed’s dwelling, drawn close at the scale of a basket set just inside the finger’s-width-open door: the one room with its hearth and slip pot, the bench by the door with a birth-slate propped writing-down, the board-bed whose grey wool holds a warmed stone at the belly, the grey Ash ridge left where it lies, bundles of cut reeds inside and at the threshold, and the loose board lifted at one end under which six narrow pages lie face-down in a second hand with no seventh written. A few paces east stands the birth-flower shrine, the hearth-maids’ niche where the district’s birth-slates lie overnight: five slates on the flat stone, a candle end of beeswax, a curl of grey wool, the slate-box of answered slates at its foot, and the crossed mark cut into the stone above, drawn and not explained. Around both, drawn faint: the Vail kiln-house, the Drawing house, House Silt, the smithy, the drying racks, the slip pits and the yard well; the Slip Brook clay-heavy along the north, the Ilm below, the walk the women take from the house to the niche, and the Clay Road west to the Cross and east to Greybank, with the reedbeds going off toward Reedholt. Cartouche dated Y.H. 813, the month of Bone, with compass, a hundred-pace scale, a convention of signs and surveyor’s notes on the hand that goes to the slate before the child, the mark for which a priest gave a date and did not look up, the six pages no Court physician has seen, and the date laid over a sign that no living person can take off. An engraved bundle of cut reeds sits in the margin.}

\CRmap*{House Silt and the Birth Room — Low Kiln, Sill}{build/atlas/house-silt.jpg}{The house three doors down the Clay Yard from the Vail house, drawn at the scale at which a basket set just inside the door sees it: the front birth room with its bench by the door, hearth and slip pot, board-bed of grey wool with the hollow where the pale river stone lay, the round pewter tin above the bed with its pale fold and thumb-bright rub, the shelf’s chipped cup, the birth-slate and the six narrow pages turned face-down toward a floorboard, and the grey Ash ridge left where it lies along the skirting into the back room. There a neighbour scrubs at a board with lye water and a low song comes up through the floor. Around it, drawn faint: the Vail kiln-house, the smithy, the Drawing house, the drying racks, the slip pits, House Reed and the birth-flower shrine, the Slip Brook where Dessa Silt was taken, and the nineteen counted steps. Surveyed and inked in Y.H. 813, the month of Tallow.}

\CRmap{Keld Keep and the First Seam}{build/atlas/keld.jpg}{The Warden’s fortress city against the Rim and the deep survey cut into the stone beneath it, drawn cold and mineral as the Keep’s own survey-clerks would draw it: the walled Keep with the Warden’s hall and the mine-reeve’s room; the Rim Road coming up from Sill and going on ten leagues to the Cold Pass and its survey post; the Listening Stones five leagues higher in the Rim; and below, the timbered shaft of the First Seam with its galleries, the Descent, the Duelling Floor cut into the stone with nine clamps to the floor and the tenth behind the board, the survey room holding the crossed-out entry of Y.H. 588 and its branching red mark, the Ninth Gallery with the tin lined with warm-stone, a seam-serpent’s passing entered only as a change in the numbers, and the hot-lead warning of the Sweating. Cartouche dated Y.H. 812, the Thin Year, with a compass, a league scale, a convention of signs and surveyor’s notes on the measure before the name, the Warden’s claim, the once-a-year reading of the paper, and the insistence that no map is honest past the last pass.}
