\CRmap*{The Meal Mill — below the south bridge, Sill}{build/atlas/meal-mill.jpg}{The water-mill under the south bridge, drawn at the scale of a sack set against the hopper: the Ilm coming down from the Cross with its silt shoals and tide ripples, the timber bridge, the race taking water from above the mill and the tail returning it below, the great wheel with its paddles and spokes, the two dressed millstones under the roof, the hopper with barley going in, the meal-book kept by the miller’s daughter with a barleycorn shut in its fold, the toll-bag, the sacks white with mill-dust, the grey print at the corner nobody will own, and the brown silt tideline the flood left along the foot of the leaf. The Cross and Slate Row stand faint on the north bank, High Kiln above them, Low Kiln with the Vail roof and the yard well across the water, the worked strips at the east edge. Cartouche dated Y.H. 813, the month of Ash, with compass, a scale in paces, a convention of signs and surveyor’s notes on the mill keeping one hour and the stone another, the figures that go into the meal and leave nothing on the leaf, the early note entered nil in a factor’s clerk’s narrow hand, the foundling left at the mill with a stone under him and no name, and the crust that travels two inches from a boy’s ear. An engraved barleycorn and an engraved dressing-pick sit in the margin.}

\CRmap*{Mud End — the peat hamlet three leagues downriver of Sill}{build/atlas/mud-end.jpg}{The peat hamlet three leagues downriver of Sill, drawn at walking scale on the dry shelf above the marsh: nine houses and their peat stacks, the byre where the moot meets and its moot-post, sods set out to dry, the peat cuttings in the southern banks, and a landing and punt on the Ilm. The Clay Road runs west to Sill and east the fifteen leagues on to Greybank, both drawn faint at the edges for neighbourhood only; the marsh drain comes down into the river, and Reedholt stands faint among the reeds to the south. Cartouche dated Y.H. 813, the month of Grain, with compass, a league scale in paces, a convention of signs and surveyor’s notes on the winter peat that decides who stays warm, the man taken quiet in his sleep and called merciful, and the wolves of Reedholt. An engraved peat spade sits in the margin.}

\CRmap*{Nine Pots — the rival kiln hamlet west of Sill}{build/atlas/nine-pots.jpg}{The pottery hamlet eight leagues west of Sill, drawn at walking scale along the road of the old feud: four kilns and one shared clay pit, the potters’ houses and worked strips, the moot-post, and the road east forded over the Ferr toward Sill. Stonemouth stands three leagues east where the Ferr meets the Ilm, with its lime kilns and coarse sandstone workings; the blue-grey Lead Run comes in from the west, and the Rim Road passes north on its way to Keld Keep. Sill and Greybank are drawn faint at the east edge for neighbourhood only. Cartouche dated Y.H. 813, the month of Ember, with compass, a league scale in paces, a convention of signs and surveyor’s notes on the feud, the lime and sandstone trade, the Lead Run that makes a man thin, and a cord from the Fishstairs never carried upriver. An engraved pot counted out at Nine Pots sits in the margin.}

\CRmap*{Reedholt — the reed-cutters’ hamlet in the east marsh}{build/atlas/reedholt.jpg}{The marsh hamlet four leagues east of Sill, drawn at walking scale: reed-cutters’ huts on posts on the dry hummock, the mud-wife’s hut with its grey-wool knot, the peat-dry with its drying sods and lifted tally board, peat stacks, the boardwalk over a cut with one plank gone, the peat-hut, the Reed Cut and its cut bundles, and a landing and punt on the Ilm. The river road runs above the marsh toward Sill and Greybank; the marsh road comes down from Mud End, passes the hamlet and goes off toward the Quiet Acre and the Standing Post, both drawn faint or set down in notes. The black peat and the bog-cow are written in the surveyor’s margin and drawn nowhere, for a figure would make a thing stand that does not stand. Cartouche dated Y.H. 813, the month of Frost, with compass, a league scale in paces, a convention of signs and surveyor’s notes on going into the marsh in pairs, the reed-wolf’s five clicks and the man with two fingers gone, borrowed ground and standing reeves, peat and grey weighed under an apron and sealed under a Court name, and the child cutting a first bundle in the dark. An engraved reed-wolf and an engraved count-stick sit in the margin.}

\CRmap*{Rusk’s Room above the Fishstairs — Sill}{build/atlas/rusks-room.jpg}{The old man’s room above the Fishstairs and below the north bridge, drawn close at the scale of a hand laid on a drawer: the floorboards and their cold, the locked drawer with its small lock left shut, a bench and the stool nobody sees him use, the pot he taps for its note, the ice-mouse-fur coat and salt-stiff hat on their pegs, and the ash in the corners unswept; the window over the steps, the stair down, the four Fishstairs steps and the out-of-line landing where a fifth should stand, the bridge over the Ilm with the fish-trade shade beneath it, the Singing Sill and its four-foot fall, the river road upriver to the Weir and the Eel House and downriver to Greybank, with the Cross and its moot-post and Slate Row drawn faint at the edges. Cartouche dated Y.H. 813, the month of Ash, with compass, a hundred-pace scale, a convention of signs and surveyor’s notes on the man who never sits down indoors and turns a question back on the asker, the paper read once a year on the Last Day that no surveyor has set down, and the boy who turned his head toward a pot before anybody tapped it. An engraved key with its small ward sits in the margin.}

\CRmap*{The Bowl of Sere and the Ten Bowls}{build/atlas/sere.jpg}{The hot southern capital three hundred leagues south of Sill, drawn as a factor’s clerk at Greybank would copy a southern plan: no wall worth the name, but open courts each with a fire in the middle. The great Open Court holds the public bowl emptied at the third hour when an act of the Sun-Emperor is announced, and the fourth bowl that is set out at every feast and carried away full; nine other bowl-houses of the Ten Bowls stand about the courts. The Ember bowl-house is drawn with its fire-shrine fed with bought oil, its wine-press, its counting room no woman enters and a room with good light; Solene Ember was returned whole here in 799, 804 and 809. The grain mills stand on the cut to the south with their wheels and sacks, the grain strips and olive grounds beyond, the bond-quarters entered without a name, the trace of a broken wall, the burning winds and their yellow dust. The Peat Line runs along the north edge, where the southern advance stopped in Y.H. 634, with the road going on to Greybank and Sill. Cartouche dated Y.H. 812, the Thin Year, with compass, a scale in leagues, a convention of signs and surveyor’s notes on the announced act, the mercy of the Spending, the burning of the debt-slates, the two kinds of returned stranger, the clerk’s three times above the space and the Sere account with a place where a bowl should be emptied and is not.}

\CRmap*{Slate Row — the Court’s quarter in Sill}{build/atlas/slate-row.jpg}{The Court’s quarter, a quarter league east of the Cross, drawn at walking scale: the Clay Road passing through the Row to Greybank, the steep street climbing to High Kiln, the Ilm and its reedbeds along the south edge. The Court’s room with its bench by the door, pot, draught felt at the ankles and a place in the figures where a line should stand; the assessor’s narrow house of Y.H. 776; the collector’s table with its slate and cold-iron tube; the barred Waiting Room where the Forty of Low Kiln were held in Y.H. 812; the Court’s table at the market fringe and the printed one in twelve. Surveyed and inked in Y.H. 813, the month of Tallow.}

\CRmap*{Stonemouth — where the Ferr comes down to the Ilm}{build/atlas/stonemouth.jpg}{The quarry village five leagues upriver of Sill, drawn at walking scale where the Ferr comes down to the Ilm: the sandstone workings and the lime yard on the rising bank, the lime kilns with their smoke, the ale-room beside the kiln, the village houses, and the weigh-clerk’s bench by the landing with punts on the river. The river road runs east to Sill and west over the ford to Nine Pots three leagues away; the Lead Run comes in from the west stained blue-grey from an old working, and the Rim Road passes north-west toward Keld Keep. Sill and Nine Pots are drawn faint at the edges for neighbourhood only. Cartouche dated Y.H. 813, the month of Grain, with compass, a league scale in paces, a convention of signs and surveyor’s notes on the lime, sandstone and reed-wolf tooth that go out by water, the Ferr that makes a man thin with no figure set against it, the thirty-year habit of stopping at the end of the part when a clean coat comes up from Greybank, and the name kept in a room against the name kept on a slate. An engraved reed-wolf tooth sits in the margin.}

\CRmap*{The Clay Yard and the Vail House — Low Kiln, Sill}{build/atlas/the-clay-yard.jpg}{The close ground of Low Kiln drawn at the scale a clay child walks: the Clay Yard with its slip pits and ruts, the Vail kiln-house with its hearth, loaf shelf and bed, the wheel-shed with the Debt Loft and the finger’s-width-open back room, the drying racks with the space beneath the lowest, the row of houses to House Silt, the smithy, the well and the birth-flower shrine, the Slip Brook behind and the Ilm at the reedbeds. Surveyed and inked in Y.H. 812, the Thin Year.}

\CRmap*{The Drawing House — the death-house two doors down the Clay Yard, Low Kiln, Sill}{build/atlas/the-drawing-house.jpg}{The unnamed neighbour’s house two doors down the yard from Vail, drawn close at the scale of a basket set at the edge of the light: the bench by the door with its pot, the draught going along the floor before the cold is felt, four nails, four and a thumb’s-width knot overhead, the grey Ash ridge a finger’s width thicker than Vail’s and turning the corner by the door without a break. Inside, the drawing pallet against the far wall with the pale round place on the arm, the collector with the cold iron tube wrapped in wool and the slate face downward, a hearth, the folded quilt on the other side with the warmed stone at the belly and the pot set between child and door. The Vail kiln-house, wheel-shed, smithy, drying racks, House Silt, the birth-flower shrine, the yard well and the slip pits are drawn faint for neighbourhood; the Clay Yard and Clay Road run below, west to the Cross and east to Greybank. Cartouche dated Y.H. 813, the month of Smoke, with compass, a hundred-pace scale, a convention of signs and surveyor’s notes on the room that bears no name, the knuckle set before the iron and the note before the figure, and the child who grew worse before the day was out. An engraved cold-iron tube in its wool sleeve sits in the margin.}

\CRmap*{The Empty Cantons — the Quiet Acre}{build/atlas/the-empty-cantons.jpg}{The province sixty leagues south of Sill that the Court names the Empty Cantons and the Fen call the Quiet Acre: roads rutted under turf where no wheel has gone in eight hundred years, six wells dry with their stones laid in the old order, nine doorways standing where the walls have gone with bare squares above three of them and a slate unread in one, cold hearths with white ash unswept, dry cuts dug to drain, and a twelfth doorway left out of the count. Drawn from Gedde’s survey of Y.H. 812 and the Greybank annals, with the south road from Sill and Cold Acre, the way in from Greybank, the marsh road to Reedholt and the Standing Post, and the Peat Line and Sere beyond. Surveyed and inked in Y.H. 814, the month of Ilmen.}

\CRmap{The Hearthseat on the Keel}{build/atlas/the-hearthseat.jpg}{The Court’s city, built over the Hearth a hundred and fifty leagues south-east of Sill, drawn cool and clean as its own surveyors would file it: the Weighing Hall with the grating of cold iron over the never-out fire and the Hearth shown in cut beneath the floor; Slate Row with the College of Assessors and its second file; the Steward’s room, the sealed files, the bank where measures are pressed into newborn vessels, the rooms of fewer than twenty Kept, the back rooms, the printed notice, the Hearth Road from Greybank and the way out to the Nine Wells. Surveyed and filed in Y.H. 812, the Thin Year.}

\CRmap*{The Old Kiln and the Ash Throat — one league south of Sill}{build/atlas/the-old-kiln.jpg}{The collapsed kiln in the grey clay a league south of Sill, drawn as its surveyor would draw it: the fallen crown and its broken brickwork, the fire mouth on the south-east flank, the flue broken at the top, the concentric throat where the ash runs deeper than a man, the hollow in its wall from which a slate was carried north to Low Kiln, the grey banks that will not take a glaze, the surveyor’s stakes and his cord, the track from Sill and the marsh way to Reedholt. A slow coil copied from the back of a slate is inked into the margin and left unread. Surveyed and inked in Y.H. 812, the Thin Year.}

\CRmap*{The Smithy — Low Kiln, Sill}{build/atlas/the-smithy.jpg}{The forge east of the Clay Yard, drawn at the scale of a man standing at the bench: the long low shop with no kiln-mark over its door, the forge hearth and bellows, the anvil, the bench with its chisel notches that nobody has ever entered as a figure, the kiln behind the bench answering four pulls with the fifth missing, three collectors’ cold-iron tubes on their pegs with the grips polished grey to the thumb, Keldish bars with the blue bloom no potter will glaze over, the ash pit, the trough and the slate lying face down on a shop where no man would write a sentence. The yard well, the Vail kiln-house, the wheel-shed, the drying racks, House Silt, House Reed and the birth-flower shrine stand faint at the edges; the Clay Road runs west to the Cross and east to Greybank, with the Slip Brook and the Ilm below. Cartouche dated Y.H. 813, the month of Frost, with compass, a scale in paces, a convention of signs and surveyor’s notes on the tubes that take and do not give, the pale ring left at a wrist, the count kept in wood, the iron that comes down from Keld and the counting room shut in the last war eighteen leagues east. An engraved tube and an engraved anvil sit in the margin.}

\CRmap*{The Standing Post and the Peat Paths — the Fenmarch}{build/atlas/the-standing-post.jpg}{The only Fen place a dry man is shown: the carved post and the dry boards where reeves settle fines standing up, the reeve’s stone with its peat-block niche, the loose board with the reed beneath, the huts on posts, the meres and black peat, the ways east to Mud End, south to the Peat Line and north-west toward the Quiet Acre, which is set down in words and drawn nowhere. Surveyed and inked in Y.H. 813, the month of Bone.}

\CRmap*{The Tallow Works — the rendering house two leagues north-east of Sill}{build/atlas/the-tallow-works.jpg}{The sheep-fat works known in Sill only by the smell on a north wind, drawn at walking scale: the rendering house or fat-house with its three vats, the hot flue and the thumb-wide warm crack where the wall meets it with grey paper nests hung behind, the lamp-room with its trimmed lamps and the leaf kept under a cracked saucer, the byre where the men sit at the turning of the year, the nest-fire at the shed door with the burnt paper beside it, the sheep-folds on the rise, and the sluice run carrying ash and wash-water away south-east. The ridge road comes in from the north gate past Cold Acre, both drawn faint, and the sweet smoke goes down on a north wind toward Sill. Cartouche dated Y.H. 813, the month of Bone, with compass, a league scale in paces, a convention of signs and surveyor’s notes on the fourth cup poured under the bench and the clerk who set it on the floor, the wasp that comes to the warmth and not the fat with twelve nests burnt and no value arising, fever first and the cold after with no figure asked for, the coal that comes up in clay on Kindling and the Long Night’s cost, the nought written where a name should stand, and the second warm crack in the cold north wall that has never held a nest and is set down in words but not marked on the wall. An engraved tallow lamp and an engraved tallow-wasp sit in the margin.}

\CRmap*{The Waste beyond the Last Pass}{build/atlas/the-waste.jpg}{A chart of report and not of walking: the Rim and the Cold Pass at the east edge, the survey post, and beyond it the cold seams and the coastlines of cold, with the uncollected sitting upright facing the way they came. No distance past the post can be trusted. Surveyed and inked in Y.H. 813.}

\CRmap*{The Weir and the Eel Traps — one league upriver of Sill}{build/atlas/the-weir.jpg}{The eel weir on the Ilm a league upriver of Sill, drawn at the ground the trap-keepers walk: the V of stakes and its traps, the plank walk, Orra Weir’s hut and salting-racks, the hearth-maids’ blessing stone, the shoals and reeds, and the river road. Surveyed and inked in Y.H. 812, the Thin Year.}

\CRmap*{The Worked Strips — the barley fields east of Low Kiln, Sill}{build/atlas/the-worked-strips.jpg}{The ground east of Low Kiln drawn at walking scale, the chart the lived days have fallen on from the planting of Seed through the cutting and dressing of Grain to the wool-covered grain of Smoke: five long rutted plots with their furrows and a flood stone a woman swept around, the clay-heavy Slip Brook coming down behind the drying racks, the reedbeds standing grey in the ruts where the barley stood, the Ilm along the head of the chart with its landing and punt, and the river road above the strips. Low Kiln, the Vail roof and its smoke, the drying racks and the Cross are drawn faint at the western edge for neighbourhood only; the Weir lies a league upriver, Mud End and Greybank downriver, Reedholt away through the marsh. Cartouche dated Y.H. 813, the month of Smoke, with compass, a hundred-pace scale, a convention of signs and surveyor’s notes on the arm that knows a bundle’s weight and no slate its price, the clay-heavy rise that took a woman from the end of nineteen steps and was called weather, and the empty place in the returning line where a hand went in on Seed 15 and did not come out — described in the margin and marked nowhere, for a mark would be a figure and no figure stands. An engraved ear of barley with its top grain gone sits in the margin.}

\CRmap*{The Vail Kiln-house — the roof over the boy, Low Kiln, Sill}{build/atlas/vail-house.jpg}{The house known by its objects before its people, drawn at the scale of a basket set just inside the door: the boy’s room with its bed, one crust in the fold and four nails, four and a knot overhead; the other room with the carried fire under ash at four and a gap, the loaf shelf with two unnamed gaps and the charcoal beneath unread, the clay jar, the charred slate and the clean dark line beside the finer grey called the thaw. Beyond it the kiln at its mouth, the wheel-shed with the cold damper of two bites, the Debt Loft and the finger’s-width-open back room, the drying racks, the flagstones with the bright patch, the yard well with its bare trough and the Clay Road going west to the Cross and east to Greybank. Surveyed and inked in Y.H. 813, the month of Ember.}

\CRmap*{Vhal and the Sallow coast}{build/atlas/vhal.jpg}{A salt-chart of the principal Vhaleni port and the five leagues of shore east of it, drawn in the tar-and-wet-rope manner of the Council’s own surveyors: the Quay with its piers, crane, moored salt boats and the pulled benches; the Council room that smells of tar and wet rope, the tide-tally house and the glass furnaces within the town; the Salt Pans outside it with their dippers at dawn and their drying salt-paper; the blue-green Glaze Cliffs stained by old lead workings, and the glass-sand pits behind them; the silt-mouthed Ilm entering from the west and the Salt Road coming up from Greybank by the coast pass. In the sea the Sallow draw runs seaward against the wind, with a brine-gull, a salt boat and a salt-thing by report, and a surveyor’s notes on boat-shares passing through mothers, contracts that rot in the damp, and children warned not to lick the cliffs. Cartouche dated Y.H. 812, the Thin Year, with compass, league scale and a convention of signs.}

\CRmap*{The War of Measures — the eastern border country}{build/atlas/war-of-measures.jpg}{A surveyor’s chart of the ground the measure-wars are fought over: the Ferr valley and the lower Ilm from Nine Pots and Stonemouth to Greybank and the Sallow shore. Burned kilns, a poisoned well, collectors’ boats on the Ilm and a district left cold for a season. The cold is drawn as the thing that advances. Surveyed and inked in Y.H. 814.}

\CRmap*{Sarn — the bowl between Hearth and Waste}{build/atlas/world.jpg}{The known world as its own surveyors would draw it: the Rim and the cold beyond, the Sallow Sea, the Keel and the Hearth, and the nations between. Surveyed in Y.H. 812.}

\CRmap*{The Yard Well — Low Kiln, Sill}{build/atlas/yard-well.jpg}{The most-named uncharted stage of the daily round, drawn at the scale of a pail set down on the stone where a pail always stands: the shared well of the low houses with its little roof, uneven curb, eleven links to the water and the twelfth that hangs dry in the hand; the white frost-bloom on the north lip where the Warm went out of the stone and the thawed edge where the sun took it off; the trough skinned bare and the silt-clouded plate of ice set on the flat stone out of the path of feet. At the bucket-round a woman draws with the pail against her knee and her hand toward her sleeve, the count kept in wood and unread, while a man brings a number up out of a shut fist toward the well and puts it back, so the figure arrives nowhere. The slate lies open on the lip with the writing turned toward its owner and nobody reading it aloud; the words spoken to the boards and the well-roof stand at five shapings with no owner standing under them, and the two tellings of the counting room shut in the last war do not touch. The Vail kiln-house, House Silt and the birth-flower shrine lie faint to the west, the drying racks to the east with the space under the lowest gone around, the Clay Road running west to the Cross and east the eighteen leagues to Greybank, High Kiln over the terrace above, the clay-heavy Slip Brook and the Ilm among the reedbeds below. Cartouche dated Y.H. 814, the month of Ilmen, with compass, a hundred-pace scale, a convention of signs and surveyor’s notes on the water that tasted different, the number that is kept back, the pail that goes down into weather and the plate of ice standing where the weather was told to stand. An engraved pail on a well-chain sits in the margin.}

\chapter*{The Codex of Sarn}
\markboth{The Codex of Sarn}{The Codex of Sarn}
\addcontentsline{toc}{chapter}{The Codex of Sarn}
{\centering\FellFont\itshape\small\color{faded} Documents of the world, gathered from its ledgers, shrines, roads and kitchens.\par}\bigskip
\clearpage\phantomsection\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{A Bowl Not Poured, Being an Account of the Southern Empire of Sere, Set Down by Harn of Nine Pots at Greybank in Y.H. 813}
\CRsheetheading{A Bowl Not Poured, Being an Account of the Southern Empire of Sere, Set Down by Harn of Nine Pots at Greybank in Y.H. 813}
{\centering\FellFont\itshape\footnotesize\color{faded} A journeyman potter’s travel account, begun on the backs of dry grain-sacks and copied forward on the back of a Court tally-roll; part itinerary, part price-list, part complaint, with the figures of a Sere counting-house clerk entered in the margin and one line added in Greybank by a hand nobody will own · Written at the factor’s counting house in Greybank in Ilmen, Y.H. 813, by Harn of Nine Pots, a thrower’s son who went down the Peat Line in Y.H. 812 with a cart of coarse ware, two bales of wool and nine bars of Keldish iron, and came back in Ash with a purse of gold crowns that no man in the Clay Yard would change. Set down first on three dry grain-sacks and copied onto the back of a discarded Court tally-roll, sewn with eel-sinew and carried in a clay tube stoppered with wool. It survives with the yellow dust of the burning winds ground into the fold, a thumb of olive oil at the head, a wine-ring at the foot, a husk of southern grain stuck fast in the gutter, one crown pressed flat between the third and fourth leaf, four corrections in the leaning hand of a Sere clerk who borrowed the leaves at the market, and a line at the back in a narrow upright hand added after the copy reached Greybank.\par}\medskip
I went south with pots. That is the whole of my reason and I will not dress it as a pilgrimage. Nine Pots has four kilns, a shared clay pit and a quarrel with Sill about a road neither town has mended. A journeyman who can throw a jar in four beats hears that a house in the south will pay for a coarse jar to hold oil, and he hears it the way a man hears water in a dry well. He goes.

I left in Seed of Y.H. 812 with a cart, two bales of wool off the Tallow side and nine bars of Keldish iron got honest at Stonemouth, and came back in Ash with a purse of gold crowns that no man at the Cross could change and a figure in my head that would not leave. This is the figure. I have set down what happened and what did not. A man who writes only what happened writes a ledger, and I have read enough ledgers.

\subsection*{The road down}

The Clay Road ends at Greybank and the south begins somewhere past it, though not all at once. The Empty Cantons come first: wells with the rope still on the windlass, doorways with the thumb-polish worn into the lintel, and nobody. A Fen man told me the people were taken in the first Returns and paid for by a line of figures. I asked him where the line went. He said a line goes where it is written and a figure stays where it is put, and went back to his eels.

At the Peat Line the wet begins. A reeve took a mark off me for standing on a board he had not pointed to, which was within his right. The Fenfolk say a dry man is a dangerous man, put us up on the Standing Post and did not tell us which boards would bear us. We learned. Sere’s northern advance stopped here in Y.H. 634 and the Fenmarch has paid tribute in eels ever since, which tells a man more about the south than any temple tells him about the Hearth.

Past the Line the dust comes up off the roads and lies on the pots like grey slip. The burning winds take the skin off a man’s lips. I had been told the south was warm; it is warm the way a kiln is warm, with the door open and the breath coming out, and a man goes thirstier there than he does in a Grathic winter.

\subsection*{The bowl at the third hour}

The Bowl of Sere is three hundred leagues from Sill and has no wall worth the name. Its courts are open and each has a fire in the middle. Men sit in the heat of them with their coats on the ground beside them, and the dust settles in their hair, and nobody brushes it off.

At the third hour of the day a public bowl of wine is emptied, and that is how the Sun-Emperor’s acts are announced. I stood in a court and watched a man in a pale coat tip the bowl out onto the stones. The crowd leaned in. I asked the man beside me whether a debt had been forgiven or a province ruined.

He said, “Yes.”

“Which?”

He looked at me as though I had asked a pot which side was the bottom. “Measure for measure,” he said, and went back to his wine.

I have since learned that the phrase means whatever the speaker has already decided. It is a fine phrase for an empire. At home a man says \emph{one in twelve, as the notice says}, and the notice and the man between them keep a whole district warm for a season. Here they empty a bowl and call it the same thing as a number.

They sing this at the wine-presses. I have set the Grathic words under the southern tune, which loses something, as Grathic always does when it is made to carry a tune.

\begin{quote}\itshape Fill to the lip and let it go,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the pot was made to pour;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the cup that keeps is the cup that sours\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and cracks along the floor.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape One for the house and one for the fire,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape one for the slate we burn by lot;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and one stands full and is not poured ---\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape ask not whose debt. Ask it not.\end{quote}

\subsection*{The burning of slates}

Valen Openhand, whom they call the Bowl-Priest, preached in the court while I was there. He teaches the Spending: that a vessel was made to be emptied and a life hoarded is a life wasted. He is not a thin man, and neither are the priests who say it after him, which a traveller notices after standing in a court all morning.

At the end of a feast they burn one household’s debt-slates, chosen by lot, and then make new ones. I saw it done. A woman whose slate went into the fire wept, and the crowd was kind to her, and then the new slate was brought out and the crowd applauded that too. I have not got used to the second applause.

The warmest funerals in Sarn are in Sere. A house will burn a year’s grain under a dead man to keep him warm, and the Court taxes the ash, and the house is ruined by degrees and called generous. A poor funeral is a small fire in an open court. A great funeral can empty a province, and the province is then bought cheap, which is the sort of arithmetic the south has made its own.

A girl of sixteen emptied the bowl at her Bowl feast and named a debt she intended to carry. The applause was for the debt, not for her. She had seven names by then and would keep whichever her household liked. I asked a bowl-surgeon beside me how a person becomes one person out of seven. He said a vessel keeps the shape it is poured into, and sold me a nest of tallow-wasp resin for four marks. He held the nest up to the light and listened to it the way a potter listens to a pot, and asked whether it had been taken in a frost. In the Clay Yard we burn the stuff. Here it goes into a graft.

\subsection*{People with no measure}

Slavery is open here and legally simple. A slave’s warmth is the owner’s holding, and a slave has no measure in law. This is not an oversight. It is the whole of the law. A beautiful house-slave is given a whole return and exhibited at feasts as proof of the owner’s generosity; a slave who runs is returned thin and set to the grain mills. I heard the mills grinding at night, a low sound under the wind, and was told that the people in them had once been someone.

At a feast I saw a northerner exhibited for small coins. He was thin-returned and could not say where he came from. He looked at me the way a man looks at a wall he half remembers, and said a word that might have been \emph{slip}, or might have been a bit of the Ferr water coming up in him. I did not go to him. In a southern court the man who buys a curiosity and the man who claims a countryman are the same man until he has paid.

I have written this plainly because it was plain. I have not written what I think of it, which is a thing a traveller keeps to himself if he wants to travel back.

\subsection*{What I fetched}

Twelve bits to a silver mark. Twenty silver marks to a gold crown, which is a Sere coin and does not stay in Grath. The Court books in embers and will tell you an ember is worth five marks; no man has ever exchanged one for the other, and I left them off.

I carried south — Sold for — I carried north — Cost me\par

Nine bars of Keldish iron, Stonemouth — 2 crowns and a half — One green glazed bowl — 3 marks\par

Two bales of wool, Tallow side — 1 crown, 9 marks — A skin of southern wine — 6 marks\par

A score of coarse jars, Nine Pots — 11 marks — A phial of oil for a lamp — 4 marks\par

One nest of tallow-wasp resin — 4 marks — Four crowns, changed at the quay — would not change at the Cross\par

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Written across the wool row in the leaning hand of the Sere clerk who borrowed the leaves at the market:} Wool entered at the crown rate. The figure is current.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Underneath, in mine:} It was current until he went home. In the morning the same buyer wanted two marks less for the same bale, and the clerk was not there to enter the difference.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Against the last row, in the same leaning hand:} Coins entered as four. The bowl not entered.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{And below, in mine:} He entered the coins and left the bowl, which is the whole art of that country in one line of writing.\end{quote}

The green bowl cracked on the third morning after I got home. It gave a small flat knock when I set it down and went from lip to foot without anything falling out that I could see. A southern glaze will not take a northern frost. In Sere they would have told me what it meant. In Nine Pots we swept around it and called it a bowl gone wrong.

\subsection*{The bowl that stands}

At every feast a fourth bowl is set down full and not emptied. It stands through the feasting and is carried away still full. Nobody pours it and nobody says whose debt it holds. I asked three times and got three different silences, the last of which was the kindest.

This is the figure I brought back. There is a place in every Sere account where a bowl should be emptied and is not, and the clerks go around it the way our yard goes around the space under the drying rack. I have set it down because I saw it and not because I understand it. A hearth-maid would cover it with a date. A Court clerk would give it a number and the number would be nothing entered in the wrong column.

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{At the foot of this section, in a narrow upright hand added at Greybank, the verbs left out as though a verb were a thing a man could hide in a cuff:} No fourth bowl. Not carried forward.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{In mine, underneath:} I have left his line standing. If it is not carried forward then it stands where it is, which is what I said before he wrote it.\end{quote}

\subsection*{Coming back}

I came back in Ash with the dust still in the seams of my coat and a crown pressed flat between the third leaf and the fourth. The year before I went down had been the Long Cold. The barley was thin, the fuel dear, and a potter with nine bars of iron was a man with a reason to leave. I found the reason had followed me home: the same levy, the same printed figure, the same men going around a place where a line should stand and does not.

The crown buys nothing at the Cross. In Sere a coin is a thing a man can empty into a bowl and call it generosity. Here it is a thing I keep because I cannot spend it. I have not spent it and I have not entered it. The fourth bowl stands where I left it.

\clearpage\phantomsection\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{A Dry Man, Being the Road-Account of Tess Marl, a Hemp-Buyer out of the Quay at Vhal, Who Went Up the Marsh Road to the Standing Post with Money for Hemp and Came Back with a Count-Stick She Could Not Read, a Knot of Grey Wool She Would Not Untie, and a Figure a Clerk Set Against a Name She Did Not Give; with the Table of What Was Offered, the Law as It Was Said to Her, the Song Said to the Boards, Two Rulings in Borrowed Hands, and a Line at the Foot Nobody Will Own}
\CRsheetheading{A Dry Man, Being the Road-Account of Tess Marl, a Hemp-Buyer out of the Quay at Vhal, Who Went Up the Marsh Road to the Standing Post with Money for Hemp and Came Back with a Count-Stick She Could Not Read, a Knot of Grey Wool She Would Not Untie, and a Figure a Clerk Set Against a Name She Did Not Give; with the Table of What Was Offered, the Law as It Was Said to Her, the Song Said to the Boards, Two Rulings in Borrowed Hands, and a Line at the Foot Nobody Will Own}
{\centering\FellFont\itshape\footnotesize\color{faded} A buyer’s road account, set down first in the leaning counting-hand on the backs of spoiled hemp-warrants at the Standing Post and copied at Greybank onto the back of a Court peat-docket voided by the Long Cold; the road and the figures in the buyer’s hand, the Fen sayings kept in the hearing and not translated, a knot of grey wool tied through the first leaf for the word she cannot write, the verbs put back under every borrowed correction, and one line at the foot in a hand that has never come forward · Written in Reed and Tallow of Y.H. 812, the Thin Year of the Long Cold, at the Standing Post in the Fenmarch and again on the marsh road, by Tess Marl, a buyer of hemp for a rope-house on the Quay at Vhal, who went up the Salt Road with a purse of marks and came back with a horn-notched count-stick, a phial of Fen ash unopened, and an offer she did not take; copied at Greybank in Ilmen of Y.H. 813 onto the back of a spoiled warrant and sewn with tarred net-twine into a scrap of oiled sailcloth. It survives with a white salt bloom at the head off her own paper, peat worked brown into the gutter, a press of wet sedge across the second leaf, a bog-water tideline that has taken two words, a horn-shaving caught in the fourth fold, a knot of grey wool tied through the first leaf which the writer will not undo, a fish-hook nick, a thumb of tallow at the fold, a small grey Ash print along the outer fold which the writer did not make and has not swept, one ruling in the narrow upright Ledgerhand of a factor’s clerk, one in the charcoal of a reeve of the Post, and a line at the foot in a hand nobody will own\par}\medskip
I buy hemp for a rope-house on the Quay at Vhal. Rope is the one thing the sea takes and gives back altered, and a rope-house without hemp is a rope-house that shuts, and a house that shuts has no account to enter, which is the only silence the Quay will not forgive. In Reed of the Thin Year I went up the Salt Road with a purse of marks for hemp and came back in Tallow with a count-stick I cannot read, a knot of grey wool I have not untied, and a figure a clerk set against a person whose name I did not give him. Where I saw one thing and was told another I have left both standing. A buyer can do that. A clerk cannot.

The white at the head is salt off my own paper. The brown in the gutter is peat off theirs. They have never mixed in this book, and I have not tried to make them.

\subsection*{The road up, and the change in the boots}

Eighty leagues of salt road to Greybank, then the Clay Road to Sill, then the marsh road into the bog. The change comes before you can see it. The ruts go soft, the tar goes out of the coat and the wet sedge comes in, and your boots, counted at Greybank, are weighed down by the road itself. A man makes four leagues a day on the Clay Road and two in the bog, and the last of the two is the one he remembers.

At the Cross in Sill a woman selling eels told me, “A dry man is a dangerous man,” and would not say whether she meant the weather, the strangers going down, or me. I asked a second time and she said it to her basket instead, which is how I learned the manner of the country before I had set foot in it: a thing said to a basket is a saying, and a thing said to a person is an argument.

Past the last dry rise the road becomes a board. There is no gate and no name at the entering of it, and nobody asks what you carry, which after Greybank feels like a door left open in a house where a man has been expected. I had expected to be asked. I was not, and have thought about that more than about the hemp.

\subsection*{The Post, and the boards you are not shown}

The Standing Post is a raised boardwalk and a post carved with reeves’ marks. It is the only place in the Fen a stranger is shown, which is another way of saying it is the only place a stranger can be watched while he stands on the wrong board.

I was lodged there nine days and nobody told me which boards would bear me. On the second morning I put my foot where a woman had put hers an hour before, and the board gave and did not go down, and she said from the next board, “Stand where you stood, and the board will mind you.” I have taken it for a promise about boards and nothing else; there is no paper here that lasts long enough to carry another kind.

Every dry place here is lent. The houses stand on posts so that the water may call the loan in without taking the house with it. I have sat on a board with my feet hanging over my own goods and understood I was not on the ground at all, and that this is ordinary.

\subsection*{How they choose a reeve}

I asked how a reeve was chosen. A reeve is the one who stands longest in the bog. I asked how long that was. Until the others have had enough. About half of them are women, and the saying does not change for it.

One had stood through a whole Reed over a feud about two eel-weirs, and said the side the mud calls right is the side still standing. I asked whether she had been warm in those weeks; she said warmth was not what a reeve was counted on, and asked me whether I was warm, which I have since learned is the question that country asks instead of every other.

I told her I had a stone in my coat. She said, “Then you have not come far enough,” and went back to standing. I have joined nothing to it, because a buyer who joins things has begun to price them.

\subsection*{What the mud is said to keep}

They say the Marsh Mother keeps the warm in the mud and hands it back to whoever can reach it. A priest up from Greybank told a man at the Post this was the Hearth under a Fen name. The man, mending a net at the rail, said theirs had no keys and no slate and no figure, and needed no man in a clean coat to open it. He did not look at me; I have written it as I heard it, said to the net.

In Grath they leave the ash in the corner on the Last Day and burn it in the morning. Here the ash in the corner is gathered, bottled and sold. A woman of the Post sold me a phial of it for two bits and said it was for a man who wanted his own dreams to stop arriving. It was grey and ordinary in the glass. I have carried it eighty leagues and have not opened it and have not entered it either, because I could not think what figure to set against a thing bought to forget.

Children here are taught to know a collector by his boots before they are taught their own names. A woman at the Post pointed out a pair drying on a rail before she would tell me hers.

\subsection*{What was offered, and what I paid}

\emph{The figures as they were given to me at the Post, set above what the factor’s clerk entered at Greybank. The two readings stand.}

Article — What was asked — What I paid — What the clerk entered\par

Hemp, a bale, green hemp — 4 marks — 4 marks — hemp, current\par

Eels, smoked, a string — 2 bits — 2 bits — dried fish, current rate\par

Peat, a dried block — given, not sold — nothing — not entered\par

A thin return — 10 marks — not bought — —\par

Bought breath, a season — 6 marks and a peat-debt — not bought — no entry lies\par

Count-stick, horn-notched — given, not sold — nothing — not a vessel\par

Grey wool, one knot — given — not given — nil\par

Twelve bits to the silver mark and twenty to the crown, which is the counting I brought from the Quay. The Court books an ember at five marks, and no man in Vhal has exchanged one; here they have not heard of one, which is a mercy of a kind.

They offered me a thin return for ten marks, a third of what the Court charges the district for the same thing. I asked what it was and was told it was a return. I asked whose. The woman said a buyer who asks whose has already decided not to buy, and she was right. I have not entered that I was asked. A thing not entered is the only kind of honesty I have ever been able to keep.

Against the two rows I did not pay, the clerk at Greybank wrote \emph{no entry lies}, which is true in the language of his office. I did not fail to enter them. They are not in me to enter.

\subsection*{The law, as it was said to me}

Said standing, to the post and not to a person, by a reeve who had fined a man that morning for a board he had moved:

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item A fine is paid in marks, or in eels, or in a term.

\item A fine unpaid becomes a term.

\item A term unpaid becomes a measure.

\item A measure is not entered here. It travels.

\end{enumerate}

A bought breath has a hook in it. A woman of the Post put her finger in her own mouth to show where: in the word a man would need in order to complain. She would not say it before the buyer, who stood a little off with his hands in his sleeves. I have set both down, the saying and the hand, and have not put them together.

\subsection*{The stick, and the knot}

Law here is carried in a stick and not on a slate. Fen Cant is not written; it is said in the mouth, cut in a stick, and tied in knots. The reeve gave me a count-stick with a notch cut in horn, and when I asked what it counted he said it counted what was owed, and when I asked who was owed, he said a stick has no ear and will not argue with me. A notch in horn takes differently from one in bone; he could tell his own stick in the dark by the feel, which he gave as the reason and not the price.

I tied a knot of grey wool through the first leaf for the word I could not write. They tie wool when a thing is owed and untie it when it is paid, and a knot does not care whose hand made it. The factor’s clerk entered my knot as \emph{nil}, because a knot is not a figure. He was right. That is why I will not untie it.

\subsection*{The song said to the boards}

\emph{Sung at the Post at dusk, going in and not coming back, by women mending nets on the boards. The last line is said twice, the second time to the ground under the board. There was a fourth verse which the singer would not give while I stood there.}

\begin{quote}\itshape Four for the boards and one for the slack,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the bog takes the foot and the reeve takes the stand;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the warm goes down where the alder stands\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the mud hands back what the mud has kept.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape A fine goes down and a term comes up,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape a term goes down and a measure stands;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape they tie it in wool and they cut it in horn\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and what’s in the mouth never reaches the slate.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape We do not say who went through the door,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape nor what hung in the square above it;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape say it to the board, say it to the ground,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the water will answer the water’s own.\end{quote}

The fourth verse was about the ground between here and Grath, which the Court calls the Empty Cantons and the Fen call the Quiet Acre. The singer said a doorway is built for coming back through, and a thing you can name is a thing the Court can figure. She said it to the net. I left the place the length of it and wrote nothing in it; the clerk at Greybank wrote \emph{no verse entered} above the space. He has taken the verbs out of a song and called the result an account.

\subsection*{What the borrowed hands did}

The factor’s clerk writes upright and narrow, with ink settled in two fingers of a cuff that will not come out. He borrowed the leaves on a market morning and took the verbs out as though a verb were a thing a man could carry away in a cuff.

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item At \emph{a bought breath has a hook in it} he wrote \emph{the term is entered against the party’s own obligation}, and underlined it twice. The hook is in a word, and words of that kind are not entered in his office, which is perhaps why his sentences never catch on anything.

\item At \emph{I tied a knot} he put \emph{nil}, and at the stick, \emph{not a vessel}. A stick is not a vessel and a knot is not a figure. He has not struck a word of mine, only written above it, which is the manner of that hand.

\end{itemize}

A reeve of the Post, who can write in the clay letters and chose charcoal, wrote along the margin in a hand that had clearly not been trained to keep a book: \emph{Hemp paid. Thin not bought. No harm done to the account.} I have put mine beneath. I was asked to buy a person and said no, which is not the same as no harm done, and I have not let his line carry mine away from the board where it was said.

\subsection*{At the head and in the gutter}

The white at the head is salt bloom off my paper. The peat in the gutter is theirs and has worked into the grain and will not come out, which is why the moot signs in peat and not in ink. The press of wet sedge came off the morning the boardwalk stood under water and the sayings were said to the boards instead of to a person. The tideline has taken two words, and I have not written them back; a saying with two words gone is a saying said slowly. The horn-shaving is off the fifth stick, the fish-hook nick from a man paying me for eels with the hook still in his hand. The tallow is my lamp, set too near the leaf. The grey along the outer fold is not mine and not the clerk’s and not the reeve’s. I have not swept it. There is no Last Day in the Fen and nothing gets burnt in the morning.

\subsection*{At the foot, in a hand nobody will own}

\begin{quote}\itshape The board minds the one who stands where he stood.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape The mud keeps what the mud is given.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape I went up for hemp and was offered a person.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Ask the stick whose debt it counts. Ask the door.\end{quote}

I asked a reeve of the Post, the woman who sold me the phial, and a factor’s clerk come up from Greybank, and had three answers and no hand. I have left the lines where they were written. The leaves go back into the oiled wrap and the wrap into the pocket the net-twine has worn. Tomorrow I sell the hemp to the rope-house and the rope goes to sea and comes back altered, and the knot stays tied through the first leaf, and I will not untie it. A knot untied is a debt paid, and this one was never entered, and a debt that was never entered is the only kind I have ever managed to keep.

\clearpage\phantomsection\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{A Tide Not Yet Seen, Being a Letter Written in the Rain and Answered in the Margin}
\CRsheetheading{A Tide Not Yet Seen, Being a Letter Written in the Rain and Answered in the Margin}
{\centering\FellFont\itshape\footnotesize\color{faded} A private letter on salt-paper, from the Salt Pans to the Quay at Vhal, carried out in Ilmen and returned in Silt, with the answers of the woman addressed, one correction from a Council clerk, and a word of an older law stuck fast to the leaf · Written at the Salt Pans outside Vhal in the second tend of Ilmen, Y.H. 813, by Enna Salt, a salt-worker of the pans, to Vea Net of the Quay, who holds a twelfth of a boat through her mother; carried along the Salt Road by a glass carrier, rained on in Silt, and returned with answers in Vea’s hand and one correction in the narrow upright hand of a clerk of the Council of Tides. Kept since in a dry tin among what the house calls nothing. The leaf survives soft at the fold, with a white salt bloom along the gutter, a thumb of tar at the head, a green bead of cliff-glass in the lower corner, a nick from a fish-hook, and one word of an old Council decree that will not come off the paper.\par}\medskip
To Vea of the Quay, who holds a twelfth through her mother and will not say it before company. From Enna at the pans, where the wind has been in the east nine days and the paper will not take ink.

I have written this in the rain. The factor come up from Greybank does it and gets a fortune by it, so there must be something in the practice. If the Council reads what is left of this there will be nothing in it to read, and a letter that cannot be read is the only kind I have ever wanted to send you.

The seventh lot is short. I raked at the fourth hour and the crust came up as thin as the skim on the Sallow on a still morning, and when I told the pan-master he said the weather and went on with his counting, which is what a pan-master does when a woman has told him the truth. A brine-gull took a coal off the brazier while my back was turned. I threw a chip of cliff-glass at him and missed, and he went off with the coal warm under his crop, as though he had been invited.

The dippers came at dawn and trailed the nets and said the draw ran against the wind again, which it always does and which the Council is always surprised by. The clerk entered the figure that would be profitable and left the other standing in the wet where he could not see it. My mother used to say a law that lasts too long stops earning; the Council has made a virtue of it and then hired men to write things down. It is the funniest thing I know and I have never once laughed at it.

Old Iven went out on the ebb in the second tend, sealed in a salted boat, and we stood on the Quay and watched until it was out of sight, which is held to be enough. I thought of you the whole while and have not entered it. If I entered it I would have to charge you for it, and you would pay, and then there would be an end of it.

A man in a clean coat come along the Salt Road from Greybank asked after your mother’s twelfth on the third day of the tend. I told him the document had been left in the rain. He said that in Vhal that was a virtue, and laughed as though he had invented it. He asked after quiet ash as well, though a salt-master has none to sell; I told him so and watched his smile go out like a lamp in a draught. He has not been back. I have not told your mother. If he comes again she will hear it from him, which is the proper order of things and costs me nothing.

I go up the Salt Road with the glass at the turn of the month. The carrier says two tendays and the pan-master says a season, and the pan-master is generally right about the length of other people’s absences. I will be gone when the ebb comes that I said I would be back for. Do not hold it against me. Hold it against the road, which has been in a bad way since Silt; a thing said in Ilmen does not travel well once the mud takes it.

When we were fourteen you walked the pans barefoot at the Salt Walk and named a tide nobody had seen, and the dippers wrote it in the salt and it was gone by noon. I have tried all winter to get the word back. I have the shape of it and not the word. It went up at the end, or it went down, and I cannot bear to choose between the two, because I have chosen wrong every other time there was a thing to choose.

\subsection*{In the margin, in a second hand, small and sibilant, the letters leaning}

Iri. It went up at the end. You have put your stop in the wrong place and always did.

Do not tell me the seventh lot is short. Tell me you are going up the road. I am not a pan-master, and I can bear a thing said straight if it is said once.

\subsection*{What the clerk did}

A clerk of the Council borrowed the leaf on a market morning in Silt, being a man who cannot leave paper alone. He struck out the word \emph{short} and set \emph{current} above it. Against the tide-name he wrote \emph{tide not entered}, in the narrow upright hand they teach at the counting house, with the verbs left out as though a verb were a thing a man could smuggle in a cuff. He put a figure in the margin where I had put none: \emph{one mark and a binding promise}, which is what a salt-worker is paid, and which I suppose he thought he was being kind to enter. I have left all of it standing. He has entered the promise and not the tide, which is exactly what the Council does with both.

\subsection*{In the margin again, lower down, the same hand}

\begin{quote}\itshape Rake at the fourth, rake at the turn,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the crust comes up where the wind has been;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the gull takes the coal, the clerk takes the mark,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the pan keeps what the rain cannot reach.\end{quote}

I have never written a rhyme in my life and I would not begin now if I had a slate to write it on. You have written it in the rain, so there is no letter, and I have answered nothing. Ask me again in the dry and I will charge you.

There is a tide that has not come. I have named it for the day you come back down the Salt Road. Do not ask me what it is like. I have not seen it, and if I had seen it, it would not be the one.

\subsection*{At the foot, in the first hand, written on the return}

It came back wetter than it went. Most of the words are gone. The ones that went deepest are the ones that stayed, which is the whole history of salt and a fair part of mine. The tide-name is still here because I pressed it with the point of a nail instead of a pen, and the rain had nothing to take. A thing written deep enough is a thing the rain cannot call a contract.

I have kept the leaf six tendays in a dry tin. I would not line the tin with glass; glass sweats in this weather and would have it away in a month. There is no word in Vhaleni for a person you write to without wanting something. There is a word for a person whose account is current, and I have used it of you in my head for nine years, and never once charged you.

\subsection*{Stuck to the leaf}

A scrap of an older Council decree has stuck fast to the back of the sheet, older than the tin and older than the woman who gave it to me. Only one word of it survives: \emph{earning}. The rest has gone the way the Council’s laws go, quietly and in good time and with everybody paid.

\subsection*{At the back, in a hand that is nobody’s}

The ebb takes and does not keep. I have tried to learn that from the water and have not managed it.

\clearpage\phantomsection\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{Before the Name, Being an Account of the Cold Kingdom of Keld Written on the Road Down, with the Prices of Iron and Warm-Stone, the Tally of Eleven Months, the Road-Song of the Carters, and the Correction Set Over It at Greybank}
\CRsheetheading{Before the Name, Being an Account of the Cold Kingdom of Keld Written on the Road Down, with the Prices of Iron and Warm-Stone, the Tally of Eleven Months, the Road-Song of the Carters, and the Correction Set Over It at Greybank}
{\centering\FellFont\itshape\footnotesize\color{faded} A factor’s clerk’s travel account in the open courtesy of Sere, set down in gold ink on prepared paper and copied at Greybank onto the back of a spoiled Court grain-warrant; the itinerary in the long-vowelled southern hand, the prices in a tally-clerk’s figures, the Keldish sayings rendered into Grathic with the hard words left hard, a mine-reeve’s correction written number-first in the margin, one correction in the narrow upright Ledgerhand of a Court clerk, and a line at the foot that answers to no name · Written in the last tend of Ash of Y.H. 812, the Thin Year, on the road down from Keld Keep by the Rim Road, by Joren Brightbowl, a junior tally-clerk in the service of the Ten Bowls of Sere, who went north in Seed with a letter of credit and forty gold crowns to buy iron, lead and warm-stone, and came back in Ilmen of Y.H. 813 with three bars of iron, a pig of lead, a fist of warm-stone, and the name of nobody who had warmed it; copied at Greybank onto the back of a grain-warrant voided by the Long Cold and carried on to Sill. It survives with gold ink worked into the grain of the first leaf, the yellow dust of the burning winds ground into the fold, grey stone dust from the First Seam along the lower margin, a ring of warm wine near the song, a hard crumb of Keldish barley bread in the gutter, a bump pressed into the third leaf where a warm-stone lay under it for a night, the mine-reeve’s blunt correction in the margin, the Court clerk’s correction laid over the text, and a line at the foot in a hand that answers to no name\par}\medskip
I went north with a letter of credit and forty gold crowns, and came back with iron, lead, and a stone that was warm in the morning and would not say who had warmed it. This is the whole of my errand and I will not dress it as a pilgrimage. The Ten Bowls buy iron and warm-stone from the mountain, and wool and grain go north to pay for them, and a clerk who can count is a clerk who gets sent. In Sere we call a debt carried gracefully an ornament of a house. In Keld a debt is a number cut into the forearm, and a man gives it before he gives his name. I set that difference down first because it cost me more than the iron did.

I write in the courtesy of my country, which is elaborate, and I have left the hard words hard. A favour done to a reader is a debt the reader did not ask for; I have done none. Where I could not learn a thing I have set down the shape of the not-learning, which is a thing a clerk can carry home and a priest cannot.

\subsection*{The road up}

The Clay Road ends at Greybank and the north begins somewhere past it, though not all at once. At Greybank a factor sold me a fist of warm-stone in a fold of wool for three marks and would not say whose fire it had come from. This was the first honest answer I had in that country. The road says: only fools and factors go up without a stone. I was a factor’s clerk, which in the high country is a fool with better boots.

From Greybank the Rim Road runs a hundred and twenty leagues of improving road and worsening weather. There are inns at the first three stages and after that a man lodges with whoever will have him, and pays in a figure or a promise, and finds out in the morning which one was current. On the fourth day the water in the bucket had a skin of ice before I had carried it ten paces. On the sixth I could see the Rim, which is not a mountain but a wall of cold with a sky leaning on it.

At Keld Keep a man asked my measure before my name. I gave him the courtesy of Sere: Joren Brightbowl, of the Ten Bowls, in the service of the house, most honoured to be received. He waited. When I had finished he asked again. I told him I had no number cut in my arm, being a lowlander and uncut, and he wrote me down as a lowland figure and told me it would not carry me ten leagues beyond the pass. He was right. It did not.

I asked him why the figure went first. He said a name was a thing said in a doorway and a number a thing said in a mine, and that the mine had the longer memory. I have set that as he said it. It is a hard saying and I have not softened it with any of our words.

\subsection*{What they count}

In Keld a man’s number is cut into the forearm at thirteen, on the day they call the Descent, and when a man comes back thin the old numbers are cut out and new ones put in, so that a smooth place on the arm is not a blank but a thing that happened. I saw three such places in the tally-room and asked a man with one of them what number he gave now. He gave the old one.

“But the skin has been corrected,” I said.

“The number was not,” he said, and went back to his counts.

The deep mines are worked by men bought for a term, whom the Grathic buyers call under-vessed. Their lives are reckoned at eleven months. I asked the mine-reeve what became of a man at the end of the eleven and he said the term was expiring, which is a phrase that lets a man go on writing. In the Bowl we empty a bowl at the feast and call a debt forgiven. Here they cut a number and call it a man. Both are figures in a clean hand, and neither hand washes.

What I carried north — Entered at — What I fetched — It cost — Who paid\par

A letter of credit, forty crowns — at the factor’s house, Greybank — three bars of iron — eleven marks — the house, which will carry it at the feast\par

Six ells of southern wool — two crowns and a half — a pig of soft lead — four marks — the gallery, which gives back nothing\par

One olive-oil lamp, not new — not entered — a fist of warm-stone — three marks — unnamed; I have not found the name\par

A promise of grain at the Peat Line — current until the rain — eleven months’ labour, entered as a term — not a price — the man whose forearm carries it\par

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{In the blunt number-first hand of the mine-reeve, in the margin against the last row:} Eleven. Not a price. A term. \emph{Underneath, in mine:} I have left his correction standing above my row, as a repaired vessel keeps the old break showing. A term is the only figure in that country that I have seen a man refuse to call a number.\end{quote}

\subsection*{The stone, the iron and the hand}

On the third morning the mountain sweated. There was no cry and no bell. A man came up from the Ninth Gallery with the smell of hot lead on his coat and said only that the gallery was giving back more than it took. The mine-reeve sent the men up before he wrote anything down, which is the first time in that country that I saw a figure wait for a man. I had been told the smell was the whole warning and had not believed it until I smelled it. It is a sweetish smell, like a glaze room in High Kiln, and a man from the south might think it a kindness. It is not.

I did not go down to the Duelling Floor, but I heard a clamp set across a way. It is a small sound, a staple going into green wood, and then a boy’s breath let go in two pieces. A clamp-master told me that the first man to open a way usually wins, because the other is busy bleeding, and he said it as another man might say the price of an axe. He had a hand that would not close and held the clamp with the other.

A Keldish man told me the true Hearth lies under his mountain and that the Court’s fire in the south is a candle lit from it. I said nothing, being a guest. A Court clerk standing near said nothing either and did not argue, which is the whole of the Court’s answer in that country.

The warm-stone has kept a little heat for eleven days under my coat. Every morning I have asked whose fire it came from, and every morning I have had the same count of words: none at mine. A stone from the Ninth is a kindness bought by somebody whose name is not written where a traveller can read it, which is a generosity of the same order as ours in the Bowl and perhaps a more honest one, because it does not ask to be applauded.

\subsection*{The people who sit against stone}

I climbed five leagues higher into the Rim to the Listening Stones, where the Vorr sit against the stone for days and come away with numbers. One of them, a tall grey man with the last joint of his fingers doubled, let me stand beside him through a morning and would not let me look at the stone he kept. I asked him what the oldest marks meant. He said the numbers would be found correct when the season had turned, which is the answer they give and is not a translation. I have set it down because a courteous man owes his reader the exact shape of a refusal.

He told me, which was more than I expected, that the Vorr do not undergo the Return and are never collected. When I asked why, he said they had never been owed. He said it without pride, the way a man says that a door is locked, and I have not added to it.

\subsection*{The road-song}

\emph{Taken down in Grathic letters from a carter going up, not down, on the sixth day out. He sang the middle verse twice, the second time for a man with a smooth place on his forearm. The Keldish vowels are long where ours are short; I have put them back as I heard them and left the hard consonants standing.}

\begin{quote}\itshape The road goes up and the name goes down,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the number goes on the arm;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape three for the axe and two for the lead,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and one for the stone that keeps a fire.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Eleven months at the seam, they say,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and a warm-stone sewn in the coat;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the mountain keeps what the mountain took,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the carter carries what it wrote.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Give me the count, I’ll give you the cold,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the figure stays where the man went;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape a name in the mouth is a door in the wall,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape but a number is cut in the bone.\end{quote}

He would not sing going down. He said a song sung coming down was a debt with no date, and a man who had carried a load up the Rim Road had paid enough for the one he had carried up.

\subsection*{What the clerk did at Greybank}

A clerk of the Court borrowed the leaf on a market morning, being a man who cannot leave paper alone. He set his hand on the top sheet before he looked at me, and said it was entered as it stood. He writes in the narrow upright hand with the verbs taken out, as though a verb were a thing a man could smuggle in a cuff.

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item Against \emph{a man gives his number before his name} he wrote \emph{the vessel is identified by measure}.

\item Against \emph{a life reckoned at eleven months} he set \emph{term: eleven; value retained}.

\item Against \emph{the mountain sweated} he wrote \emph{an increase in the seam-draw was recorded}.

\item Where I had left the place where the warm-stone’s payer should stand, he drew a small circle and wrote \emph{unaccounted} beneath it.

\item Against the Vorr man’s saying that they had never been owed, he wrote \emph{no charge lies against this party}, which is true in the same way that an empty cup is clean.

\end{itemize}

I have left every line of his standing above mine. He takes the verbs out because a thing always true has no need of them. I put them back because a clerk writing home wants to know who did what to whom, and the answer is in the sentence if there is someone in it.

\subsection*{At the head and in the gutter}

The gold at the head is mine; gold ink creeps into the grain of the paper and leaves a yellow edge that no washing takes out. The dust of the burning winds came north with me in the seams of my coat and has ground into the fold, a southern thing in an account of the north. The grey along the lower margin is stone dust from the First Seam; I set the leaf down on a bench where a surveyor had laid his slate and did not brush it off. The small round mark by the song is where I set a cup of wine on the first night back at Greybank and went to find the word I wanted; the wine went cold and has left a ring the colour of old lead. The bump in the third leaf is where the warm-stone lay under the quire for a night and kept the paper faintly warm until morning. The hard crumb in the gutter is Keldish barley bread, given to me on the road by a man who would take neither a coin nor a promise, and I have kept it because I could not enter it.

\begin{quote}\itshape At the foot, in a hand that answers to no name:\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape The number goes on the arm and the name goes home;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the stone keeps the fire and the fire keeps no date.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Ask who paid for the warmth in a stranger’s pocket ---\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the mountain does, and the mountain does not say.\end{quote}

I asked the mine-reeve, the Court clerk and the man with the smooth forearm, and had three answers and no hand. I have left the line where it was written. The quire goes back into the factor’s tin at Greybank. Tomorrow the grain goes north and the iron goes south, and the number in my own arm --- which is none, for I am a lowlander and uncut --- is still the only thing about me that nobody in Keld found worth entering.

\clearpage\phantomsection\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{What the Ridge Keeps, Being the Sayings of Cold Acre, Gathered at the Well and Glossed for a Child of the Six Houses Who Came Back with a Figure in Her Head}
\CRsheetheading{What the Ridge Keeps, Being the Sayings of Cold Acre, Gathered at the Well and Glossed for a Child of the Six Houses Who Came Back with a Figure in Her Head}
{\centering\FellFont\itshape\footnotesize\color{faded} A curb-woman’s gathering of the proverbs, pail-maxims, limb-sayings and road-refusals of the six houses of Cold Acre, set in Grathic letters on the back of a barley tally spoiled at the meal mill; the sayings in the short Cold Acre speech with the ends dropped into the well, the glosses in the writer’s own charcoal thinned with well-clay, with an assessor’s clerk’s correction in narrow upright Ledgerhand, a slate-woman’s line set close to the birth-flower row, and one line at the foot in a hand nobody will own · Gathered at the well that never freezes in Cold Acre, two leagues north of Sill on the ridge, through the ninety-four days of the Long Cold and into Stone of Y.H. 813, by Gedde, who keeps the curb and the clay dish and has set a pail on that stone for four-and-twenty winters; written on the back of a barley tally a wet thumb spoiled at the meal mill, in charcoal ground with well-clay, folded into oiled sacking and tied with a spent length of the well-rope; carried down the ridge road in a hunter’s creel and copied at Greybank in Ilmen of Y.H. 813 onto the back of a Court winter-well warrant voided by the Long Cold, where an assessor’s clerk borrowed the leaves for a morning and set his hand above hers. It survives with well-clay worked into the grain at the head, a white frost-ring that has taken two words clean off the second leaf, a barley awn stiff in the fold, a turnip-knife nick at the fore-edge, a pale tideline of well-water along the gutter, a thumb of tallow at the outer fold, one grey hair from a hare’s back shut in the third leaf, a grey Ash print nobody will own, a twist of well-rope fibre through a hole in the first leaf which the writer will not pull out, and the line at the foot which has never been claimed\par}\medskip
I keep the curb at Cold Acre and set the dish on it for six houses, and have done it four-and-twenty winters. A child of ours was sent down the ridge road in the Thin Year to be entered and came back with a figure in her head and no word for what it counted. She asks what the ridge said before the slate came up. I have set the sayings on the back of a mill tally because a figure spoiled a figure and left paper enough. The well-clay came up under my nails and no washing takes it out of the grain.

Say these low, to the pail, the curb, the dish, the rope and the bare ground, and to a person last. Said looking at a person, a saying becomes an argument, and there is argument enough down the ridge road on a market-day without carrying it home. Our speech is short and the ends of the words fall into the well; a long sentence up here sounds like a man from the town explaining a figure. There is no Last Day on this ridge and nothing gets swept, so the sayings stay where they were said.

\subsection*{Of the well and the eleven links}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item “Eleven go down. The twelfth hangs in your hand and has never wet.”

\end{enumerate}

\emph{Gloss — The chain has lowered eleven links every morning of my life and never twelve. A man of the College stood here with a cord and said the twelfth is kept back for the Hearth. I told him the water comes up on the eleventh and if the Hearth wants its share let it send a man with a longer arm. One in twelve is printed on the notice and is not a lie. A printed thing travels; a chain does not. Both stood in the air between us and neither went into the other.}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item “The well gives. It does not ask.”

\end{enumerate}

\emph{Gloss — Three assessors have measured the lip and set a figure in a column that has never held anything. They leave it empty not out of kindness but because there is nowhere in the house of the world where a figure like that would stand. I told them I never sold the well. I fear the figure, not the carrying of it; a well cannot be carried. Once a figure stands at a thing the thing is a gift, and a gift can be refused, and a man who refuses water on the ninety-fourth day of ice has paid for it somewhere else where nobody stood to see.}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item “It is not warm. It has not given up, which is a different thing.”

\end{enumerate}

\emph{Gloss — A priest come up from Greybank called it a little sister of the Nine Wells and a mercy of the Hearth drawn through the ridge. The well has given no sign that it heard him. They tell us the Kept feel no cold; the well does not feel it either, and I have met it every morning for four-and-twenty winters. Carry that likeness one step further and you come back with a doctrine, and a doctrine is an account that has found somebody to pay it.}

\subsection*{Of the hand at the pail}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item “A hand gone white at the pail wants a stone and somebody to hold it.”

\end{enumerate}

\emph{Gloss — The well has not frozen in any winter anyone can name and still draws from a hand faster than the Ilm draws from a stone. A physician from Greybank says water is only water and draws faster than air. I held one hand in the pail and one in the north wind for one count, and the pail hand was colder. Both stand. We say the well has somewhere to put what it takes, as the collectors say it in a cleaner room, only they write it down.}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item “Warm the stone on your own wrist. The wrist knows; the eye does not.”

\end{enumerate}

\emph{Gloss — It came off somebody’s hearth and somebody in these six houses paid for the coals. Put it at the middle and not at the ends, under the wool and against the skin, and count three breaths and three more. The hands and feet are wrapped and left; they are not rubbed and are not set to the fire. A stone taken fresh from the fire will burn a child as easily as a hand.}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item “Count with her. Do not count for her.”

\end{enumerate}

\emph{Gloss — The second chill comes after the warming and not before, on the second or the third day, and it is ordinary. I have kept the counts on birch bark and not added them, for a count added is a count a clerk can carry down the ridge. A woman at three in the morning wants a hand to count with and not a figure to carry away.}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item “Never put grey in a cut.”

\end{enumerate}

\emph{Gloss — A turnip knife goes in clean and the women put grey from the corner in the cut to dry it, believing the grey is clean. I dressed three such and found grey under the skin in all three and could not get it out. The cut keeps a white line. There is no Last Day here to burn it off.}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item “The end goes first. The middle holds out.”

\end{enumerate}
