The ale ring is not a mark anybody owns; three men put a cup in it over one evening and no man will say which. The tallow thumb is mine: I held the sheet down in the draught that comes up the shaft and did not know I had marked it. The grey in the gutter came off a cuff I had no business putting into a corner in the room where the cups were, and I have not washed it off and have no wish to.

The board box goes back under the survey table with the spoil slips. The figures on the face of the sheet are gone soft on the wet side, and the song on the dry side is plain enough to read. A man will state his measure and then his name tomorrow as he did today, and the number of some of them will be changed by the end of the tend, and the clerk will set the second down without a mark beside it, which is the only thing he is allowed to do honestly.

\clearpage\phantomsection\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{Nineteen Out, Nineteen Back}
\CRsheetheading{Nineteen Out, Nineteen Back}
{\centering\FellFont\itshape\footnotesize\color{faded} A work song of the slip pits and the drying racks, Low Kiln · Taken down on a market morning in Y.H. 812, the Thin Year, from the mouths of women treading slip in the Clay Yard of Sill, by a clerk in the factor’s house at Greybank whose name has been rubbed from the corner of the sheet; the copy stands on the back of a spoiled Weighing notice, folded into an apron pocket, and survives with slip-stains, a green bead of lead glaze, a thumb in tallow, and the clerk’s own square hand striking out one line. The song is held to be older than the Clay Road.\par}\medskip
I set this down because I was told to copy what the women sang and not what I thought they ought to have sung, which is a harder thing than it sounds. I am a clerk. My hand wants a verb where there is no verb, and a line where the line breaks off and goes around the pot instead of through it. What is written below is as near as I could come, with the knocked-out parts left standing so that a man reading it in Greybank may know what he is looking at. The slip at the top right is not mine. Nor the green. The tallow thumb is the woman’s who sang it loudest; she put her hand on the sheet to keep it from the draught and did not know she had marked it.

\subsection*{The song, as it goes round the yard}

The pit is cold before the sun, the slip is old bone under the heel; tread it, girl, and tread it again, it will mind your weight and keep it.

Tread, tread, the clay says more than the potter will say before company; a fist in the belly, a thumb at the rim, and the crack shows where you left it.

Nineteen out and nineteen back, a pot on the hip and the broom at the track; four and four and a want in the Count, and the rack keeps the dry and the pit keeps the wet.

The wheel does not care whose hands, only that they come steady and come soon; bone-pale slip to the bend of the finger, and the hollow seat keeps the shape of a man.

Set it down. Let the pot speak first. A whole one answers full under the knuckle; a cracked one gives a little flat knock and will not be told what it should have said.

Leave the crack showing. Let the glaze go over the good part and the bad part alike; a repair is a scar with a pot around it, and the pot is the one that gets carried.

Nineteen out and nineteen back, and a place at the end of the rack where nothing stands; the yard goes around it, the broom goes around it, and nobody puts a pot there, and nobody says why.

Up the terrace the glaze room breathes sweet, sweet enough to make a body careless; a pale line at the gum is the first of it, and a woman with green at her mouth still sings.

One in twelve as the notice says, three loaves to the levy and one to the dish; the bell at the Cross goes longer than a church bell, and nobody crosses himself at it, and the pigs go over the boards.

When the river comes up and takes the low steps, the steps come back a hand’s breadth out of line; the yard calls it weather and goes on using them, as a woman calls a cough weather and goes on.

Nineteen out and nineteen back, the fire keeps the breath it will not give; bank it with the back of a broken pot, and leave the grey where it lies till the Last Day.

\subsection*{The fourth line, and what I did to it}

The women sang, \emph{the pit is cold before the sun}. I struck this out, being used to a verb in its place, and wrote above it, \emph{the cold is in the pit before the sun is}. Missy Clay, who sang loudest and keeps her hand on my sheet, looked at what I had written and asked me which of us had been standing in the pit, because the cold was not in it before the sun and never had been; it came up out of it when you trod, which is a different thing and not the thing on my notice. I have left my line standing above hers so that the correction can be seen. It is the only place in this copy where the Court’s grammar has got the better of me, and I am not proud of it.

\subsection*{A note on the counting, in the same hand}

The nineteen is not a number I have ever been able to make agree with anything. It is the steps from the slip pit to the drying rack, out and back, and a woman of House Silt has walked it every day since Y.H. 806, which is six years, and will not vary it by one. I asked her why nineteen and she asked me why a tend has ten days in it, and when I told her the Court had not made the tend and could not unmake it, she said that was the answer, and went back to her tread. There is a twentieth place at the rack’s end where a pot once stood. I put it in the song because they put it in the song. I cannot tell you what pot it was, and no one I asked would tell me either, so I have entered it as a place and not as a loss.

The \emph{four and four and a want in the Count} is the kiln’s breathing, or the stack’s, or the bell’s; they use the same count for all three and keep the three counts in separate places in their heads. I put down what I heard. I would not join them for a crown.

\subsection*{The verse they would not sing before a man from Slate Row}

There is one more verse. The women broke off at it when a collector crossed the north bridge with his satchel under his arm, and took it up again when he was past the Fishstairs, and would not let me write it while he was in the square. I have it now from Missy Clay after the market, and set it here with the proper space left before it, which is the space they left in the singing:

\begin{quote}\itshape The iron comes cold and the slate comes clean,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the hand that writes is not the hand that’s seen;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape what goes in the pot is not what comes out,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the account stands, and the bowl’s about.\end{quote}

I asked her what the last line meant. She said it was a song, and a song was not obliged to mean a thing just because a clerk had written it down. Then she put her tallow thumb on the corner of the sheet again.

\subsection*{At the foot of the leaf}

A grey ridge runs along the skirting in the room where they sang, near two thumbs wide, turning the corner without a break. It is not swept until the Last Day and is burnt the morning after, and called dealt with. I touched it with the edge of my notice and it came off on the paper, which is how the grey at the bottom of this leaf got there. If the sheet is ever read in the Hearthseat, let that be entered against me and not against the women: I moved it, and they would have left it.

\clearpage\phantomsection\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{The Number Before the Name, Being the Sayings of the Keldish, Gathered Above the Shaft Mouth at Keld Keep and Glossed for a Man Come Up the Rim Road}
\CRsheetheading{The Number Before the Name, Being the Sayings of the Keldish, Gathered Above the Shaft Mouth at Keld Keep and Glossed for a Man Come Up the Rim Road}
{\centering\FellFont\itshape\footnotesize\color{faded} A key-woman’s gathering of the proverbs, tally-maxims, iron-sayings and stone-curses of Keld, set in Grathic letters on the back of a shift-tally because Keldish is cut in bone and does not travel; the sayings in the hard Rim speech with the endings struck off, the glosses in the writer’s own hand, with a Court survey-clerk’s correction in narrow upright Ledgerhand, a notch cut in the edge where a word would not come, a carter’s sloping addition, and one line at the foot in a hand nobody will own · Gathered in Bone of Y.H. 812, the year the lowlands called the Thin Year, by a woman who holds the mine-reeve’s keys above ground at Keld Keep, from men waiting their turn at the weigh and from the old women who count at the mouth; written in charcoal on the back of a shift-tally gone soft at the fold, cut once at the edge with a tally-knife where a word would not come, carried down the Rim Road with a cart of lead in Ilmen of Y.H. 813 and copied at Greybank onto the back of a spoiled weigh-slip, where a survey-clerk of the Court borrowed it and set his hand above hers. It survives folded in the key-woman’s leather key-pouch, with coal smut ground into the head, an iron-red thumb at the second corner, a bead of Ninth Gallery lead shut in the fold, a warm-stone shaving that kept a little heat through a night on the stone floor, a frost-feather pressed flat that was gone by noon, a tallow print, a grey Ash print nobody will own, the knife-cut standing in the margin, and a line at the foot in a hand that is nobody’s.\par}\medskip
I keep the keys above ground. My mother kept them before me and her mother before her, and none of us has been down the shaft. The mine-reeve checks a man who has lied about his number and the checking is done in red; I hand him the slate and do not watch. What is below is what men say waiting at the weigh and what the old women say counting at the mouth. A man come up from Greybank asked me what we say when there is nothing to say. I told him we say it to the stone. He went away believing he had learned the mountain.

Keldish is cut in bone and stone, not written. A notch stays when paper has gone and cannot be read by a man from the factor’s house, which is a virtue we did not think of first. I have set the sayings in Grathic letters and struck the endings off them. Say them to the stone, to the iron, to the lamp, never to the man beside you: said looking at a man, a saying becomes a bargain. Where a word would not come I have cut the edge with my tally-knife and left the cut standing. A notch is not a letter. It keeps better.

\subsection*{Of the number before the name}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item “State what you hold. Then say who you are.”

\end{enumerate}

\emph{Gloss — At the Warden’s hall and at this gate both. A lowlander gives his name and waits to be asked the rest, and is sent back to the foot of the post to begin again. I am not shaming him. A name is a thing a man can change at the next well; a measure is what he carries into the dark, and the dark does not care what he calls himself. There is an order to a man and the order is not the one he was taught at home.}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item “The number is part of the name. The name is not part of the number.”

\end{enumerate}

\emph{Gloss — A man’s measure is cut into his forearm and counts as part of who he is; ask a Keldishman who he is and he will often give the number first. After the Descent some have the old numbers cut out and new ones put in. I have seen a man with two sets in one arm, the later cut deeper. The mine-reeve entered the later and left the earlier standing in the skin, which is how an honest clerk keeps two truths without calling either a lie.}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item “The number stands. Do not say it twice.”

\end{enumerate}

\emph{Gloss — What men say when a pair goes down and one comes up. It is not a denial and it is not a hope. To say a number twice is to ask it to be other than it was, and the mountain keeps no second figure. At the Duelling Floor a cup stands at the end that nobody takes, for the man whose number was changed twice.}

\subsection*{Of iron, and the two bites}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item “Cold iron takes. It does not give back.”

\end{enumerate}

\emph{Gloss — The collector’s tube, the clamp, the blade laid across a fever: one iron and one hunger. A salt-wife at the Quay told me it draws the heat out of a wound and takes the measure with it. We say it of a man who has taken something and calls it borrowing. He hears the insult, which is what the saying is for.}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item “One bite holds the vessel whole. One bite takes the hand off a man. It is the same bite.”

\end{enumerate}

\emph{Gloss — The clamp. There is no word in Grathic that holds both mercies and none in Keldish either, which is why the saying has two halves and a silence between them. A lowlander asked which of the two the Order meant. I told him the Order means the iron, and the iron has not asked anybody’s opinion.}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item “Put hot iron to the palm and ask a man if he owes. The honest answer leaves the hand dead.”

\end{enumerate}

\emph{Gloss — Of the Duelling Floor. I have known honest men come back from that question unable to lift a cup, and not one lied. It is said so that a man going up knows what he has paid before he is told he has been trusted.}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item “Open a way in the arm. Keep it while it scars.”

\end{enumerate}

\emph{Gloss — The first way: a surface way cut across and held open until it heals that way. It aches before the thaw and after, and a man answers to whichever number the room has given him. An old man of the floor told me the way is a door and the arm the wall it is cut in. I have put that where he said it.}

\subsection*{Of the stone, and what it keeps}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item “The mountain keeps its own.”

\end{enumerate}

\emph{Gloss — The dead are walled into the mine facing the deep seam and the surveyors add numbers to a slate nobody reads aloud. We do not fetch them back and do not say we have. A lowland priest calls this a kindness done by a mountain. A mountain is not kind; it is retentive, which costs less.}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item “Warm-stone is sold. It is not lent.”

\end{enumerate}

\emph{Gloss — It holds heat longer than anything else in Sarn. A man goes up without a stone and borrows from the next man who has one, or turns back; there is no lending here. The shaving swept from the cutting floor is sold by the half-mark and not given away. A thing that can be lent has a place in somebody’s account. A thing sold is paid for, which is cleaner.}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item “The rock sweats and the lead smells hot. That is the whole of the warning.”

\end{enumerate}

\emph{Gloss — In the Ninth Gallery the smell of hot lead gives what warning it gives, and no man has asked for a better one. It is said quietly. A man who has smelt it does not say it again, and a man who has not will never believe it matters.}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item “Frost-feather grows where the warm has lately gone out of the stone.”

\end{enumerate}

\emph{Gloss — Lowlanders call it frost-bloom and the yard at Sill calls the whole business weather. Here it is a map of the leak, read at the mouth before the sun takes it. A feather on the well lip means warmth went out of that stone in the night, and somebody is sent to find where it went. Gone by noon, and the finding still owed.}

\subsection*{Of the Rim, the pass and the Long Want}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item “There is a post and no gate.”

\end{enumerate}

\emph{Gloss — Karric VII shut the Cold Pass in seven hundred forty-one and the agreement of seven hundred forty-seven fixed the border. There is a post there and nothing else. The Warden’s surveyors keep the record of the rim-seam and do not promise to bring a man back who goes past it. A clerk at Greybank put a nought in the place where the gate should stand. A nought is a number. A post is a place, and the two are not the same.}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item “The Long Want had nowhere to put what the Cold took.”

\end{enumerate}

\emph{Gloss — Before the Hearth the temple calls those years the Broken Years and we call them the Long Want. The temple says the world was cracked once. The seam shows layers, and a survey man will say only that the repairs lie one over another like a pot mended until the first pot cannot be seen. He will not say it in front of an officer. I have set his words where he said them and have not joined them to anything.}

\subsection*{Of the Vorr and the stones}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item “We were never owed.”

\end{enumerate}

\emph{Gloss — A Vorr death has no slate, no deduction and no return. The others seat the body upright facing the direction it came from and leave it. It is the only sentence I know in Sarn with no account in it, and the Court has never found a way to enter it.}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item “The numbers are correct.”

\end{enumerate}

\emph{Gloss — What a Vorr says after sitting against a Listening Stone and coming down with a figure. Ask what the figure means and he will say it twice. He means it is an answer to the numbers and not to your question, which he will tell you if he is in a patient mood. They sell nothing but numbers and have never translated a slate in full.}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item “A Vorr keeps the count in the bone, not the blood.”

\end{enumerate}

\emph{Gloss — It makes them difficult to collect and impossible to bank in the ordinary way; a tube finds nothing where they keep it. This is spoken of as a difficulty, never as a mercy. A thing the Court cannot take is a thing it will not call a gift.}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item “Forty years is a short sitting.”

\end{enumerate}

\emph{Gloss — The Long Sitting is at forty: a Vorr sits still against a stone for a season and comes away with the numbers changed. They take their names one at a time many years apart, and divide work by whether a person has sat long enough to hear the stone, which is not permitted to the impatient. In seven hundred fifty-eight they stopped selling warm-stone to the Court and gave no reason. The Court entered it as a cause with no effect, which is the kind of entry it can bear.}

\subsection*{What the boys say going down}

\emph{Said at the mouth on the morning of the Descent, going down and not coming up. The mother does not say it. The old women at the count say the last line with him, and one of them puts a warm-stone into his hand after the knife.}

\begin{quote}\itshape State what you hold, then the name you bring;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the number goes on the arm, the stone in the palm;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape down one day and up the next, and the dark between;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the dark tells the mother, the arm tells the rest.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape One for the shaft and one for the seam,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape one for the pair that goes down with him;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape two go down and the count comes two,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the figure stands where the figure stood.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Hold the stone. It is sold, not lent.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Hold the rail. It is iron, and it takes.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Come up with the number you went down with,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape or come up with the number the mountain gave.\end{quote}

\emph{A gloss, because a boy of thirteen will ask. The third line of the second part is not a promise that two come up. It is a promise that the count will be made. No old woman at this mouth will explain the difference to a boy before he goes down, and none will say it after.}

\subsection*{What the Court hand did}

A survey-clerk of the Court borrowed the leaf at Greybank on a market morning. He writes in the narrow upright hand and takes the verbs out as though they were things a man could smuggle past a weigh.

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item At \emph{state what you hold, then say who you are}: \emph{the measure is declared and the person is identified}, underlined twice.

\item At \emph{the number stands}: \emph{the vessel was re-entered}, true in a language nobody speaks at this mouth.

\item At \emph{there is a post and no gate}: \emph{the frontier is unguarded}. There is no gate to guard and never was, but a sentence with a guard in it can be entered.

\item At \emph{we were never owed}: \emph{no account arises}. The nearest he has come to saying what the Vorr said, and I have not helped him.

\item At the cup nobody takes he put a round nought and wrote \emph{vacancy} beneath it. A nought is a number. The cup is a place.

\end{itemize}

I have put the sayings back underneath and left his above. He takes the verbs out because a thing always true has no need of them. I put them back because a boy at thirteen with a knife at his arm does not know he is hearing something always true, and wants to know which hand to hold the stone with.

\subsection*{In the margin, in a carter’s sloping hand}

\begin{quote}\itshape Paid for the bar here and charged two again at Greybank, and the factor’s man said the second was for the road. I have stopped asking which of the two was the true figure.\end{quote}

Below it, in mine: \emph{Both stand. He paid for the iron and for having carried it, and the road has no slate of its own. The factor’s man has joined them into one figure, which is the whole art of that house. I did not collect the second and cannot cross it out.}

\subsection*{At the head and in the gutter}

The smut at the head is coal off the sleeve I wipe the keys with; it goes into the grain and no wet sleeve takes it out. The iron-red at the second corner came off the mine-reeve’s point while he checked a man who had given a figure that would not hold; he did not look at me and I did not look at the man. The lead bead in the fold rolled out of the Ninth Gallery; a shift-man laid it on the leaf and went away without it. The shaving kept its heat through the night and is cold now, which is the order of things here. The feather pressed flat was on the well lip after a warm night and was gone by the time I found the leaf to put it in. The tallow print is my own lamp set too near the tally. The grey in the gutter came off a cuff laid where no cuff has business lying in a room where the keys are kept; I have not swept it and there is no Last Day above ground.

\subsection*{At the foot, in a hand nobody will own}

\begin{quote}\itshape We say the number before the name because the name goes home and the number goes down.\end{quote}

I asked a shift-man waiting at the weigh, a surveyor come down from the stones, and an old woman who has counted here thirty years, and had three answers and no hand. I have left the line where it was written. The leaf goes back into the key-pouch and the keys on the nail. Tomorrow a boy will state what he holds before he says who he is, the mine-reeve will check the figure in red, and the number will go on being called after the arm that carried it has come up or has not.

\clearpage\phantomsection\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{What the Returned Say, Being the Sayings of Those Who Have Come Back, Gathered at Greybank Among the Walking Thin and Glossed for a Woman Who Has Never Been Banked}
\CRsheetheading{What the Returned Say, Being the Sayings of Those Who Have Come Back, Gathered at Greybank Among the Walking Thin and Glossed for a Woman Who Has Never Been Banked}
{\centering\FellFont\itshape\footnotesize\color{faded} A keeper of the return-slate’s gathering of the proverbs, cradle-maxims, borrowings and small refusals of the returned, set in Grathic letters on the back of a spoiled return-slate because the mixed speech of the bank’s lower room is written nowhere; the sayings in that mixed speech with a southern word left standing where no Grathic word will come, the glosses in the keeper’s own charcoal hand, the correction of a factor’s clerk in narrow upright Ledgerhand, the objection of a bowl-leech come up from Sere pressed cold into the margin, a cradle-verse with a place left the length of a name, and one line at the foot in a hand nobody will own · Gathered in Ash and Stone of Y.H. 812, the Thin Year, in the lower room of the bank at Greybank, from people sitting between the drawing and the pouring and from those who had come back and had nowhere else to sit; written in charcoal on the back of a return-slate spoiled by a figure entered in the wrong column and washed with barley-water, carried downriver to Sill in Ilmen of Y.H. 813 and copied onto the back of a voided grain-warrant, sewn with wire into a fold of oiled cloth and kept under the loose board beside the cradle. It survives with cold-iron filings at the head, a tallow thumb at the fold, a ring of barley-water gone dark, a browned crust pressed flat between the third and fourth leaves, a grey Ash print nobody will own, a small square cut out with a knife where a name stood, the clerk’s narrow correction standing above the keeper’s words, the southern leech’s cold objection in the margin, and the line at the foot which has never been claimed\par}\medskip
I keep the return-slate in the lower room at Greybank. My trade is to write what a person booked at and what came out of the pouring, which are two figures and never the same one. A woman came down from Low Kiln in the Thin Year with a child returned thin and asked what the child’s liking for a cup meant. I told her to ask the child. She said the child could not speak yet. I told her the cup could not speak either, and the two would have to manage between them, which is how most arrangements here begin.

So I have set down what the returned say on the bench against the wall, between the drawing and the pouring, emptied of one figure and not yet pressed into another. Some have been poured three times and answer to the wrong name. They talk in a low mixed speech, Grathic at the ends and something else in the middle, because measures from four countries get pressed into one room and no one grammar survives the pressing. I have written it in Grathic letters and left a southern word standing where ours would not come.

Say these to the cup, the cradle, the fire, never to the person returned. Said looking at a person, a sentence becomes a question with an answer owed, and not one here has an answer owed in it. A woman banked three times will say the same sentence to the same child in a different voice, and the child will hear the difference.

\subsection*{Of the cup and the hand that goes first}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item “The hand goes to the cup before the eyes go to the face.”

\end{enumerate}

\emph{Gloss — What the women at the cradle say of a thin return. Measures are pooled and divided, and what comes back is a stranger with a liking for a table he never sat at and a hand that reaches for a cup before he has seen it. The Low Kiln woman asked whether her child remembered her. I told her the hand remembered the cup and the rest was still to be made, and she took that as kindly as if I had promised her something, which I had not.}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item “Come back as you can. Nobody comes back as they were.”

\end{enumerate}

\emph{Gloss — Said low, to the cradle. At the Weighing they announce the whole returns and the houses clap; the returned say this afterwards, when the cloth is put away. It is not bitterness. It is the only sentence that lets a woman hold the child she has been given without asking her to be somebody else.}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item “The name is written into the vessel before it can refuse one.”

\end{enumerate}

\emph{Gloss — The banker writes the name at the pressing, before the infant has a mouth to refuse with. A whole return keeps its name; a thin one is named from the district’s pot; a person banked five times may hold five names and answer to the wrong one. A woman of Sere returned whole three times keeps three names in a cloth and will not say which she answers to.}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item “A man banked past three is an unsafe marriage.”

\end{enumerate}

\emph{Gloss — Not a jest. Across Sarn a person poured more than three times is held unsafe to marry, because the Second Want may arrive in a child’s body wearing the wrong face. The physicians struck the word from their records in Y.H. 651 and went on writing the thing as the afterdrop. The old women at the cradle still say the first word when no officer listens. I have left both names standing, as the slate keeps the newer figure over the older one.}

\subsection*{Of what is paid and who is named}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item “A whole return has a figure. A beautiful return has a cloth.”

\end{enumerate}

\emph{Gloss — A whole return is booked at twelve hundred marks and forty unspent measures, and no man has been told why forty. The beautiful ones are shown at southern feasts with coins laid on clean cloth, and on the third day the hand begins to shake and the priests call it the price of beauty. Somebody pays that price. The cloth is laid out before the feast and the hand is not.}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item “One in twelve is printed. The other one goes into the house.”

\end{enumerate}

\emph{Gloss — We in the bank know two figures. The notice says one in twelve for the Hearth; in Low Kiln the part that goes into the slate and the part that goes out of the house are different, and the difference has no name because a thing with a name can be argued with. A returned person learns it from how cold the house is in the morning.}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item “The fire under the cradle is lit by somebody who is not named at the feast.”

\end{enumerate}

\emph{Gloss — Every hearth touches its flame from the carried coal, and nobody says where the first coal came from or who kept it through the Five. In Sere the fire stands in the open court and a man may singe his wrist; here it is brought under a pot and counted. The returned say this when a house has a warm child and no fuel. Ask who paid and you will be told to ask the fire, an answer given by people who asked the same thing at their own cradle.}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item “Quiet ash stops the voice. It does not stop the wanting.”

\end{enumerate}

\emph{Gloss — A phial costs sixty marks and is dispensed by a greyed hand. The previous life stops arriving in dreams, which the rich call a mercy and the poor a price they cannot pay. I have seen a woman take the phial, sit quieter, and reach for the cup exactly as before. The ash stops the voice and leaves the hand.}

\subsection*{Of the guest and the third day}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item “A returned one may bring a guest.”

\end{enumerate}

\emph{Gloss — She calls a name not given in this house and reaches for a door not in the room. A bowl-leech from Sere pressed a sentence into my margin saying a spoken name puts no shape back and that this is a disorder of the memory, not a visitor. He is right in a cold language. I have kept the house’s sentence above his: a woman at the cradle wants to know which door to stand by.}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item “Worse before better is the order of it.”

\end{enumerate}

\emph{Gloss — The afterdrop: a rekindled child grows worse on the third day, and a hearth-maid warms a stone against her own wrist before putting it to the child. They keep it. They keep it anyway. In the south they pour a second bowl and applaud; the hand steadies for an hour and is worse by evening. Neither asks what the first bowl took.}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item “They read four over us. We answer with one.”

\end{enumerate}

\emph{Gloss — At the pouring the officer reads the four sayings of the Keeping in the clean voice, and the house answers in its own words. In the lower room the answer is one word said to the cradle: warm. The house keeps a place where a fifth would stand and does not say what stands in it. I have left the place the length of it here, and put no nought in it.}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item “A thin return is nobody’s fault and everybody’s child.”

\end{enumerate}

\emph{Gloss — The district pays thirty marks and the measures are pooled, so no household can be told which of its dead came back in this cradle. We feed them and do not ask them to remember us. A clerk at the factor’s house wrote *value nil} against a man exhibited at a feast with a coin held flat in his palm, and the man let a girl take it for a crust. There is no figure for the hand that let her.*

\subsection*{Of the question and the refusal}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item “Ask a returned man what he was and he will ask what you are short of.”

\end{enumerate}

\emph{Gloss — I took it for evasion the first year. In the eleventh I understood it was all he could tell you: not who he had been but what was missing from the room he came into. It is not asked unkindly. A man who wants his name back is asking after the shape of a hole.}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item “A name said at home is a door. A number is a hole in the wall.”

\end{enumerate}

\emph{Gloss — The district’s pot supplies a name at birth and the old name is entered in a separate column the family is not shown. A woman whose child came back from another house says the household name at home and keeps the entered one for the slate. I have entered both and never joined them, which is the only kindness my office allows.}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item “Do not ask the cradle whose child it is.”

\end{enumerate}

\emph{Gloss — Said to a woman newly come to the lower room, who wants to know which of the district’s dead lies under the wool. The slate knows and the cradle does not, and a cradle that knew would be a different thing. I have set this last because it is the one I have had most cause to use.}

\subsection*{The cradle-verse}

\emph{Said low, to the cradle, by the women who sit with a returned child through the third day. The place after the last line is the length of a name and no singer has filled it. The room says the refrain whether the child is whole or thin.}

\begin{quote}\itshape Four for the pulls and one that is not pulled,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the stone goes cold and the house says warm;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the name comes down on the dark of the slate\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the hand goes out where the cup was borne.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Come back as you can. Come back to the fire.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape The measure is banked. The account stands.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape What the house kept it keeps, and does not say whose.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Come back as you can. Come back as it can.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Three for the names and one held in the cloth,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape one for the guest who comes in by the door;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the third-day hand will not hold mine ---\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{[a place the length of a name]}\end{quote}

\emph{Gloss — The fourth pull of the kiln is counted and the fifth is not, which is the house’s arithmetic and not the bank’s. The refrain is said twice at a thin return, once for the child and once for the house that got it. The cut square is not a nought: a nought is a figure carried out in a cuff, while a name held in a cloth stays where the cloth is.}

\subsection*{What the factor’s clerk did}

A clerk of the factor borrowed the leaves on a market morning, with ink in two fingers that would not come out. He writes in the narrow upright hand and takes the verbs out as though a verb were a thing he could spill from a cuff.

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item At \emph{the hand goes to the cup before the eyes go to the face}, he wrote \emph{a preference is retained from the pooled measure}, which leaves the hand out and the preference in.

\item At \emph{come back as you can}, he set \emph{a thin return is entered}, true in his language and of no use to a woman holding a child.

\item At \emph{one in twelve is printed}, he put a small stop in the figure and wrote it again above, larger.

\item At \emph{quiet ash stops the voice}, he wrote \emph{dream-intrusion suppressed}, the neatest sentence I have read about a thing he never watched.

\item At the place in the verse he put a round nought and wrote \emph{vacancy} beneath it. A nought is a number. The place was a name, and he has made it smaller.

\end{itemize}

I have put the sayings back underneath and left his hand above. He takes the doer out because a thing always true has no need of anybody doing it. I put the doer back because a woman at the cradle wants to know which hand to hold the stone with.

\subsection*{What the physician pressed in the margin}

He came up from the Bowl of Sere with myrrh in his coat-fold and a hand that writes cold. Against the guest he set \emph{a disorder of the memory, not a visitor}. Against the third day, \emph{the head rises when too much has been poured}. Against the Second Want, which I had written as the old women say it, he wrote \emph{settling of the graft}, underlined twice, which is the word the Court’s physicians have used since Y.H. 651.

He was right about the head and wrong about the guest. I have left his sentences above mine so the next reader can tell which is which, which is the whole use of a margin.

\subsection*{At the head and in the gutter}

The filings at the head came off the tube-case when an officer set it down hard and went out without apologising. The tallow thumb is mine; I turn the leaf with the hand I hold the cradle with. The ring is barley-water set down while I sought the word for the child’s liking and left until it went dark, that afternoon in one circle. The crust was given by a woman from Low Kiln who would not take a mark for it; the brown edge went into the grain and I have not brushed it. The grey in the gutter came off a cuff laid where no cuff has business lying in a room where the cradle stands. I have not swept it and there is no Last Day in this room. The cut square I made with a knife and have not written the word back, because a word written where a name was is a word the bank can enter.

\subsection*{At the foot, in a hand nobody will own}

\begin{quote}\itshape The measure comes back. The hand that held it does not.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape The cup is set down anyway.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape We are a people of every house and no country.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape We are poured and we are entered and we are carried.\end{quote}

I asked a woman who keeps the cradle, a clerk of the factor’s house, and a returned man who could not say which of his five names he wanted, and had three answers and no hand. I have left the lines where they were written. The leaf goes back under the loose board beside the cradle. Tomorrow a district will be poured above me, the four sayings read in the clean voice, and the house will answer with one word; I shall write two figures that are not the same one and leave the place in the verse the length it is.

\clearpage\phantomsection\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{Salt, Current, and the Ebb, Being the Proverbs of the Vhaleni Set Down at the Pans and Glossed for a Landman}
\CRsheetheading{Salt, Current, and the Ebb, Being the Proverbs of the Vhaleni Set Down at the Pans and Glossed for a Landman}
{\centering\FellFont\itshape\footnotesize\color{faded} A pan-clerk’s gathering of the proverbs, counting-maxims, tide-sayings and curses of Vhalen, written in the leaning counting-hand on salt-paper the writer kept dry against the rule; the sayings in the sibilant low speech with the ends of words let fall, the glosses in the writer’s own hand, with a Council clerk’s correction in narrow upright Ledgerhand and one line at the back in a hand nobody will own · Gathered at the Salt Pans outside Vhal in Seed and Frost of Y.H. 811 by Tavi Hull, a copyist of the dippers’ tide-tallies who learned his letters in a counting house and has never held a share; written on salt-paper leaves he kept dry in a tin lined with nothing, sewn with tarred net-twine, and carried up the Salt Road with a glass consignment in Stone of Y.H. 812, where the leaves were copied at Greybank onto the back of a spoiled weigh-slip and corrected by a clerk of the Council of Tides. Copied forward in Ilmen of Y.H. 813 with the wet corner left wet. It survives with a white salt bloom at the head, a thumb of tar at the fold, a peck-hole where a brine-gull took the leaf for a crust, a fish-hook nick, a corner softened by rain where two sayings have gone, a rope-burn along the outer edge, a grey Ash print nobody will own, and a loop of tarred twine through the first leaf which the writer will not undo.\par}\medskip
I copy the dippers’ tide-counts at the pans outside Vhal: I write down what the water did and leave out what it meant, because the Council pays for the first and has never asked for the second. A man from the hill country asked me once what we say when there is nothing to say. I told him we say it to the water. He paid me two bits and went away believing he had learned something, which in Vhalen is the usual end of a conversation with a man from away.

These are our sayings, set in the Grathic letters because our own hand is kept for contracts, and a contract is made to be read by a man who is not in the room. Say them with the ends of the words let fall, so that the listener supplies the last of the thought. Said looking at a man, a saying becomes an argument; said to a rope, a pan, a tide, it stays a saying. A landman will hear half of what is here and call it rudeness. He would be nearer the mark if he called it a contract with the half left out.

I have written these on salt-paper and keep the leaves dry, contrary to the practice of the country, and I know it. A contract left in the rain is no contract, which we call a virtue; a saying left in the rain is no saying either, and I have met no man who sees the virtue in that.

\subsection*{Of the current man}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item “There is no guest in Vhal. There is a man whose account is current.”

\end{enumerate}

\emph{Gloss — We have no word for guest or friend, only for a man whose account is current: one who has paid for what he took and may remain in the room. A landman calls this hard; it is only exact. A guest is a person you cannot enter, and one you cannot enter may cost you anything.}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item “Don’t say \emph{kindly}. Kindly is the coin we don’t take.”

\end{enumerate}

\emph{Gloss — Said to one who has done something for nothing and wants to be let off it. Say so at once, that the other knows it was no favour. A favour in Vhalen is a debt with no date, and a debt with no date is the kind that keeps a man awake.}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item “Count it by touch. The fingers don’t care what the face is saying.”

\end{enumerate}

\emph{Gloss — A counting-house trick, and an eel-woman’s trick upriver, and the same trick. You learn a coin with the hand and let the face lie over it. I have watched a factor smile at a widow while his thumb told him the figure was short. Both were true; only one could be entered.}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item “A stranger’s coin warms before his face.”

\end{enumerate}

\emph{Gloss — Of a man who has come a long way in cold weather. The coin has been against his skin all the road and the face has not; you can tell where a man has been by what he carried. It is a saying about warmth, whatever a priest may make of it.}

\subsection*{Of paper and weather}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item “Write it in the rain and see what’s there in the morning.”

\end{enumerate}

\emph{Gloss — Half the port’s fortunes have turned on this, and the other half on somebody forgetting to do it. A contract on salt-paper in wet weather is no contract at all. That is not a loophole in our law; it is our law. Ask a Grath man why he trusts a slate: it is stone. Ask us why we trust wet paper: it does not last.}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item “A law that lasts too long has stopped earning.”

\end{enumerate}

\emph{Gloss — My mother said it before the Council made a virtue of it. A decree is repealed when it stops paying, which is honest if you consider a decree a tool and not a promise. The assessors cannot bear it. Their slates are stone, their sentences have no verbs, and both outlive the man who wrote them.}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item “What the rain takes, nobody can enter.”

\end{enumerate}

\emph{Gloss — A clerk can only enter what he can still read. That is our theology of paper and most of our law. It is why we keep tide-names in the mouth and not on the leaf; a name said at the Salt Walk is written in salt, the sun takes it by noon, and no Council has found a way to tax noon.}

\subsection*{Of the draw and the tide}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item “The tide runs against the wind and doesn’t ask the moon.”

\end{enumerate}

\emph{Gloss — The Sallow does as it pleases with the weather, and the dippers read what it did rather than what it ought to have done. A Grath man tells the time by a bell; we tell it by the turn of the water under the quay, which is never where the bell says. The moon is not consulted in Vhalen and would not be answered if it were.}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item “Name the tide you haven’t seen. Salt’s teacher enough.”

\end{enumerate}

\emph{Gloss — At fourteen the young walk the pans barefoot at low tide and name a tide nobody has seen. The dippers write the name in salt and the sun takes it. When a Vhaleni would say what he cannot write, he names a tide not yet come. It is the nearest thing to a promise we have and is not one, which is why we can say it.}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item “Trail the net at dawn. Read what comes up.”

\end{enumerate}

\emph{Gloss — The dippers bless the nets by dragging them at first light and reading the draw. We say the Sallow has a Hearth of its own beneath the salt and the Court’s is only its chimney. I have said it all my life; no dipper has taken me down to see the one under the salt, and I have learned not to ask.}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item “The draw takes what isn’t kept, and the Court taxes what’s taken.”

\end{enumerate}

\emph{Gloss — The Warm goes out seaward and the assessors arrive with deductions on the salt works, as punctual as gulls. We bless the draw and pay for it, and never thought the two inconsistent. A cold country makes a man careful where his heat went.}

\subsection*{Of gulls, salt and the dead}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item “The gull takes the warm thing and leaves you colder than you were.”

\end{enumerate}

\emph{Gloss — The brine-gull lifts a coal from a brazier, or a loaf, or a warmed stone, and flies off with it under its crop. No malice in it. A bird that steals warmth is no worse than one that steals bread. Say this of a man who has taken something and calls it borrowing.}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item “Carry a barrel of rain. It’s the only thing the salt-thing won’t cross.”

\end{enumerate}

\emph{Gloss — The salt-thing follows boats at night and taps the hull where the store is; fresh water stops it as a wall stops a man. Every captain I have sailed with carries rain in a barrel against it and would deny being afraid. The dippers bless the nets against it, which is reasonable and costs the Council nothing.}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item “Don’t lick the Cliffs. They’re sweet and they’re lead.”

\end{enumerate}

\emph{Gloss — The Glaze Cliffs are blue-green with old lead workings and smell faintly sweet in the heat. Children are told not to lick them and some do, for a child believes a warning about a taste before one about a poison. The sweetness stays with the man; the lead stays with the Glaze room across the water.}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item “Seal him in a boat, push him on the ebb, watch till he’s out of sight. That’s enough.”

\end{enumerate}

\emph{Gloss — We do not break a pot at the door as they do across the water; we seal the dead in a salted boat, let the ebb carry them, and stand until there is nothing left to look at. The watching is held to be enough. Nobody says why; I have never seen a Vhaleni who wanted a longer ceremony.}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item “A man who dies at sea has already returned. The sea keeps its own account.”

\end{enumerate}

\emph{Gloss — A kindness we allow the sea. On land the collector comes with his cold tube and the Return is entered; at sea there is no slate, the warmth goes out with the tide, and we call it done. Women say it of a husband who never came back and mean they are released from entering him, which is a mercy and is not one.}

\subsection*{Of boats and shares}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item “The share goes through the mother. A husband’s come aboard and his word’s half a word.”

\end{enumerate}

\emph{Gloss — Shares pass through mothers; a man who marries into a boat-owning family is come aboard, his opinion counted at half. He knows it; everyone knows it; nobody says it before company. Captains are mostly women, because the sea does not care and the Council has learned not to.}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item “Thirty marks and a curse every hour. That’s a boat.”

\end{enumerate}

\emph{Gloss — What our shipwrights ask to build a boat and what they say while building it. The curse is in the price, and a man who pays less gets more of it. It does not sink the boat; that would be a gift, and no shipwright in Vhal has ever given anything away.}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item “Two marks a month and keep. One mark and a binding promise. Know which you’re being paid in.”

\end{enumerate}

\emph{Gloss — A sailor’s share and a salt-worker’s are not the same, and a promise is not a mark however binding the man who offers it says it is. I have taken the promise myself; it was binding and worth what I could get for it, which was nothing. A man should hear both sayings before he signs either.}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item “Seven years at the pulled bench, or till your hands give out, whichever comes first.”

\end{enumerate}

\emph{Gloss — The sentence for a condemned criminal, said as other countries say a grace. The pulled benches are the salt galleys, and the hands give out first, so that the seven years is a figure written for the benefit of the man who wrote it. We do not say it to a man being sentenced; he finds out in the ordinary way.}

\subsection*{What they sing at the Salt Walk}

\emph{Said by the young walking the pans barefoot at low tide, going out, not coming back. The name in the third line is the one nobody has seen. They write it in the salt and go home and it is gone by noon.}

\begin{quote}\itshape Out on the crust where the wind has been,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape barefoot, barefoot, and the pan holds;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape I name you a tide that has not come,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and salt says yes and the sun says no.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Rake at the turn and rake at the fourth,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the gull takes the coal and the clerk the mark;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape what the pan keeps is what it keeps,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and what’s in the mouth can’t enter the slate.\end{quote}

\emph{Gloss — The fourth line is no contradiction. Salt says yes because the name is spoken there; the sun says no because it takes the writing. Both tell the truth and neither can be entered, which is the first thing a Vhaleni child learns of a contract: there are two parties to everything and one is weather.}

\subsection*{What the Council clerk did}

A Council clerk borrowed the leaves at Greybank on a market morning, being a man who cannot leave paper alone. He writes in the narrow upright counting-hand, with the verbs taken out as though a verb were a thing a man could smuggle in a cuff.

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item At \emph{there is no guest in Vhal}, he set \emph{the party is accommodated}, and underlined it twice.

\item At \emph{what the rain takes, nobody can enter}, he wrote \emph{the instrument is void by weather}, a true thing in a language nobody at the pans speaks.

\item At \emph{name the tide you haven’t seen}, he put \emph{tide not entered} and a round nought in the space where the name would stand. A nought is a number. The tide was not a number and has not come back to be one.

\item At the wage-sayings he wrote \emph{two marks and one promise, current}, joining two unlike payments into one figure, which is the whole art of that hand.

\end{itemize}

I have left all of it standing. He takes the verbs out because a thing always true has no need of them. I put them back because a man barefoot on a pan wants to know who is doing the taking and whether he will get it back.

\subsection*{In the margin, in the leaning counting-house hand}

A Council tally-man wrote this below the song, in the sloped letters of tallies, never of decrees:

\begin{quote}\itshape They pay for the tide that’s entered, not the tide that’s seen.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape I have stopped telling them which is which.\end{quote}

I do not know his name and have not asked. It is the most honest line on these leaves, which is a poor recommendation for a line written by a Council man, but there it is.

\subsection*{At the head and in the gutter}

The salt bloom came up in a wet week at the pans and has eaten two letters of \emph{current}, which I have not written in again; a word about a current that the weather has taken is truer than one a clerk can still read. The tar thumb is mine; I turn the leaves with the hand I mend nets with. The peck-hole went through \emph{gull} and nobody has claimed the bird. The fish-hook nick is from a basket set down while a man paid for six herrings and was charged for five, or the other way, which he will not settle and I have not entered. The soft corner is the rain; two sayings went entirely and I do not know which two, which is the condition I described in sayings five and seven and have now been given in my own paper. The grey print nobody will own came off a cuff laid where no cuff has business lying on a pan. There is no Last Day at the pans and nothing gets swept.

\subsection*{At the back, in a hand nobody will own}

\begin{quote}\itshape The account is current until the weather says it is not. Everything else in Vhalen is entered.\end{quote}

I asked a dipper, a tally-man and a man come up from Greybank with road-mud on his boots, and had three answers and no hand. I have left the line where it was written. The leaves go back in the tin; tomorrow the dippers trail the nets at dawn, and I write what the water did, leave out what it meant, and am paid for the one and not asked for the other.

\clearpage\phantomsection\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{The Courtesy of the Bowl, Being the Proverbs of Sere, Gathered at a Name-Day in a House of the Ten Bowls and Glossed for a Child Who Is About to Be Given a Debt to Carry}
\CRsheetheading{The Courtesy of the Bowl, Being the Proverbs of Sere, Gathered at a Name-Day in a House of the Ten Bowls and Glossed for a Child Who Is About to Be Given a Debt to Carry}
{\centering\FellFont\itshape\footnotesize\color{faded} A courtesy-woman’s gathering of the proverbs, feast-sayings, name-warnings and polite refusals of the southern people, set in the long-vowelled speech of Sere and written in Grathic letters because the house hand is kept for contracts; the sayings in charcoal, which is a woman’s hand and not a clerk’s, the glosses in the writer’s own charcoal, with a bowl-house tally-clerk’s correction in thin gold above, a factor’s clerk’s ruling in narrow upright Ledgerhand above that, a girl of the mills in the margin, and one line at the foot in a hand nobody will own · Gathered at the name-day of a daughter of a house of the Ten Bowls in the Bowl of Sere in Ember of Y.H. 813, and set down that night by Halia Gilded, a courtesy-woman who teaches the young of that house their names and their manners before they are sent up to the Bowl; written in charcoal on the backs of glaze-tallies spoiled at the third furnace, because gold is for what a house means to keep and a saying is for the mouth; sewn with a drawn thread from the girl’s name-day dress into a fold of oiled silk and kept in the lining of the teacher’s sleeve. Carried north with a consignment of glass and oil in Ilmen of Y.H. 813 and copied at Greybank onto the back of a Court grain-warrant voided by the Long Cold, where a factor’s clerk set a ruling above the gold. It survives with gold dust worked into the head off the tally-clerk’s cuff, yellow dust of the burning winds ground into the fold, a ring of warm wine at the second leaf, a green bead of lead glaze pressed into the lower corner, a flake of quiet ash shut in the gutter, a dress-thread gone stiff with gold in the sewing, a flattened crown between the third and fourth leaves which would not change at Greybank, a pale thumb where a girl of the sweet sickness leaned to read, a grey Ash print along the outer fold which the writer did not make and has not swept, and the line at the foot which nobody has claimed\par}\medskip
I teach the young of this house their names and their manners, and have done it for nineteen years. At sixteen they go up to the Bowl to empty a cup of warm wine and name a debt they intend to carry, and the court claps. I am not allowed to stand where they stand. I am allowed to tell them beforehand what the room will do, which is a kindness of a particular southern kind: it saves them the surprise and does not save them the debt.

A clerk come down from the factor at Greybank asked what we said over the cradles and the bowls. He wrote down two lines and went away believing he had learned the south. So I have set the whole of it here, with the ends put back where the court lets them fall. I write in charcoal. Gold is for what a house means to keep; a saying is for the mouth, and a mouth has no cuff for a clerk to take ink from.

Say these with the vowels opened and the last of the thought thrown away, so that the listener supplies it. Say them to the bowl, the fire, the wine, the door; say them to a child last of all. Said looking at a person, a saying in Sere becomes a lawsuit, and there are lawsuits enough in this house without carrying one out of the room.

\subsection*{Of the bowl and what it is for}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item “Empty the bowl and name what you will carry. The clapping is for the carrying, not the drinking.”

\end{enumerate}

\emph{Gloss — At sixteen. The cup is emptied in the open court and the debt is named, and the court applauds the debt. A child who names a small debt is praised for modesty and given a larger one before the year turns. I have stood at the foot of the steps nineteen years and never seen a cup refused.}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item “The wine comes warm to the hand and cold to the account. Both are true and neither is entered at the same table.”

\end{enumerate}

\emph{Gloss — The warmth is in the cup and the figure is in a room the cup never enters. A guest who asks which is the real one has asked a question with two answers, which in Sere is not a question but an invitation to choose.}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item “Three bowls go round. The fourth goes back to the shelf, and a house that knows why is a poorer house than one that does not.”

\end{enumerate}

\emph{Gloss — At every feast a fourth bowl is set out and carried away full. Nobody pours it and nobody says whose debt it holds. If the house knew, it would pour it. Not knowing is called a mercy of the Spending. I asked the woman who carries the bowls what was in it and she told me to ask the bowl.}

\subsection*{Of names, and the seven}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item “Give the child seven names. Keep the one that costs the house least.”

\end{enumerate}

\emph{Gloss — A child of a great house may gather seven names by adolescence and keep whichever the household prefers. The six are not thrown away; they are spent on the child, which is how a house speaks of having used them. I say this to the fire.}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item “A bought woman is given one name. The one she brought is put under the glaze.”

\end{enumerate}

\emph{Gloss — In some houses the forbidden name is cut into the inside of a bowl before the lead goes on, and the bowl goes into the rack with its rim turned outward. She is never permitted to look into it. The fire shuts the word in more carefully than the house shuts anything else.}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item “A name under the glaze keeps longer than a promise written in gold.”

\end{enumerate}

\emph{Gloss — The house writes its promises in thin gold on prepared paper and men with clean cuffs read them aloud. A word cut under lead before the firing is shut in for the life of the bowl. I have set the two where I heard them and have not joined them; a woman who joins them has begun to draw a conclusion, which I am not paid to draw.}

\subsection*{Of the slate and the burning}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item “The slate goes into the fire and comes out in a clean hand. The debt does not go anywhere.”

\end{enumerate}

\emph{Gloss — At the end of a feast the debt-slates are burned by lot and written again before the wine is cold. The room claps at the new writing. A woman three places down from me wept at the burning of hers and then applauded the new slate with everyone else, and was called generous for it.}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item “Buy the ash back. A house that cannot afford quiet ash has no business burning slates.”

\end{enumerate}

\emph{Gloss — The Court taxes the ash and the family buys it back at the price of quiet ash. That is how a feast can ruin a house. The smoke goes up for nothing and what is left of it does not.}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item “Burn the slate before company and the whole room has agreed to forget it. Ask the room, not the slate.”

\end{enumerate}

\emph{Gloss — The burning and the forgetting are public acts done in the same hour with the same wine. Nobody is forced to remember. That is the mercy the priests speak of, and the reason the north calls our generosity by another name.}

\subsection*{Of the house and the door}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item “A woman may own the bowls, the slaves and her husband’s debt. She may not own the door.”

\end{enumerate}

\emph{Gloss — The counting room is barred and no woman of the house goes through it; her numbers are read there by a man. I have stood outside with a wine-list and heard figures read in a low patient voice. The wood is ordinary wood and the latch is on the inside.}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item “Gold ink keeps a threat as long as a promise. Choose which you are writing.”

\end{enumerate}

\emph{Gloss — The house writes in thin gold and the corrections stand above in the same hand, so that what a man meant and what he was told to mean lie in the same ink and last equally long. Charcoal is safer. It rubs off on the sleeve and nobody has thought to enter a sleeve.}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item “The tally-clerk writes above and the factor’s clerk writes above him. The woman at the press writes underneath and nobody reads her.”

\end{enumerate}

\emph{Gloss — This is the order of hands in this house and in the copy that went north. I have let every borrowed correction stand and put my words beneath it, the way a repair lies over an older repair in a bowl still used at table.}

\subsection*{Of the north and what is bought}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item “The north buys what we pour out and calls it a return. We sell it and call it a province.”

\end{enumerate}

\emph{Gloss — Some houses buy poor northern measures cheaply and make of them one beautiful return to display at a feast. The distance between the buying and the displaying is the profit, and nobody walks it. A northerner at the lower table with three copper bits under his palm is not there to be pitied, though he often is.}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item “A crown that will not change beyond the Peat Line has been spent twice already.”

\end{enumerate}

\emph{Gloss — Southern crowns will not change at Greybank. The northern traders who come south with wool and go back with a figure in their heads complain of this, and are sold to anyway. A coin a man cannot spend has already been counted for him.}

\subsection*{Of the dead and what is kept}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item “We burn the dead in an open bowl, tax the ash and buy it back. No other people makes so costly a thing of quiet.”

\end{enumerate}

\emph{Gloss — Cremation in a public bowl, with wine and music; the warmest send-off in the world. The Court taxes the ash and the family buys it back at the price of quiet ash, which is how a Sere funeral can ruin a good house. I have seen a woman set her hand on the phial and not open it.}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item “A cup that keeps is called generous here and a cup that pours is called spent. Ask the cup which it would rather be.”

\end{enumerate}

\emph{Gloss — The priest says a vessel was made to pour and the cup that keeps is the cup that sours. He says it over the wine and not over the accounts. I have set it where I heard it and asked the cup nothing.}

\subsection*{The song of the carrying}

\emph{Said at the Bowl by the young going up the steps, going up and not coming down. The fourth part is said to the bowl and not to the company. There is a silence before it the length of a name under the glaze, and I have left it the length it is kept.}

\begin{quote}\itshape Up the long steps with a cup in the hand,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the household behind and the court set wide;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape name what you’ll carry and carry it whole,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and they clap at the name and not at the soul.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Three pour at the third and the fourth stands still,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the slate goes up and the clean comes down;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape buy back the ash, buy back the quiet,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the house stands where it stood before.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Seven names over the cradle and one kept,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape a door for the numbers and none for the name;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape gold for the promise and lead for the word,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the word keeps best where no eye has read.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{[Here the bowl stands. No sound.]}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape One for the bowl and one for the fire,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape one for the debt that the room will forget;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the wine goes round and the name goes up,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the number goes in where no woman is let.\end{quote}

A girl of the press asked what the silence was for. She was told to ask the bowl. The tally-clerk put a small round mark in it afterwards and wrote \emph{not named} beside it, which is a thing a house can enter and a name is not.

\subsection*{What the gold hand did}

A tally-clerk of this house borrowed the leaf in the scullery while I was still finding the end of a line. He writes very small, in thin gold, and takes the verbs out as though a verb were a thing a woman could spill from a cuff.

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item At \emph{the clapping is for the carrying}, he wrote \emph{obligation acknowledged by acclamation} and underlined it twice.

\item At \emph{buy the ash back}, he set \emph{ash repurchased at assessed valuation; no deduction arising}, which leaves the price standing and takes the quiet away.

\item At \emph{a woman may own the bowls}, he wrote \emph{property enumerated; access restricted}, true of the inventory and silent about the latch.

\item At the silence he put the round mark and \emph{not named}. I have left it where he set it and put the name back underneath, which is where it was before.

\end{itemize}

I have put my words back beneath his everywhere, as the word under the glaze lies under the glaze. He takes the doer out because a thing always true can be carried into a counting room. I put the doer back because a child at the foot of the steps wants to know whose hand will pour.

\subsection*{What the northern hand did}

A factor’s clerk at Greybank wrote above the gold on the copy. He has never been south, and writes in the narrow upright hand of the College.

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item At \emph{seven names}, he set \emph{six designations struck; one current}, which is the whole of his trade with a person.

\item At \emph{the north buys what we pour out}, he wrote \emph{pooled measures exported; no deduction at point of sale}, and did not ask who had been pooled.

\item At \emph{the fourth bowl}, he put \emph{reserve unentered} and a figure of no account against it.

\item At \emph{a crown that will not change}, he wrote \emph{currency not current beyond the province}, a true sentence in a language nobody at the press speaks.

\end{itemize}

I have left his hand above both. There is no Last Day in a scullery and nothing here is swept; the corrections lie one over another and are not asked to agree.

\subsection*{In the margin, in the charcoal of a girl of the mills}

\begin{quote}\itshape My mother burned her slate at the feast and wept, and the room clapped. I have learned to clap at the burning and to keep the date of it in my head. A date has no figure and does not go up in smoke.\end{quote}

She would not sign it. I have left it where she wrote it.

\subsection*{At the head and in the gutter}

The gold at the head came off the tally-clerk’s cuff and will not wash out of the grain; a contract is meant to last and a saying is meant to be carried. The yellow in the fold is the dust of the burning winds and I have not shaken it out. The wine-ring is the third hour. The green bead came off a bowl chipped when a girl set her cup down too hard on the rim; the sweetness is in the edge and the sweetness is not a kindness. The flake of quiet ash I found shut in the gutter and have left there. The dress-thread is gold and stiff, drawn out of the girl’s name-day sleeve. The crown between the third and fourth leaves is the only coin here nobody has entered, which is not the same as nobody having paid for it. The pale thumb is the girl with the sweet sickness. The grey along the outer fold is not mine and not the tally-clerk’s. I have not swept it.

\subsection*{At the foot, in a hand nobody will own}

\begin{quote}\itshape The bowl keeps what it is told to keep.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape The slate keeps what the fire lets.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape The house keeps the name it chose and the debt it did not choose.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Nobody keeps the person who carried either.\end{quote}

I asked the woman who carries the bowls, a girl of the mills, the tally-clerk and a factor come down from Greybank, and had four answerings and no hand. The leaf goes into the silk and the silk into my sleeve. Tomorrow is a name-day in a house I will not name; three bowls will go round and one will stand, and a child will be told what she is to carry, and I shall say these sayings to the bowl and not to the child, and put the verbs back where the gold hand took them out.

\clearpage\phantomsection\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{Seven Names and the One the House Keeps, Being a Passing Game of the Lower Court at the Ember House}
\CRsheetheading{Seven Names and the One the House Keeps, Being a Passing Game of the Lower Court at the Ember House}
{\centering\FellFont\itshape\footnotesize\color{faded} A bowl-woman’s gathering of a children’s passing-and-naming game in the long-vowelled southern speech, written with a burnt stick on the back of a wine-list spoiled at the third hour; the rhyme in the children’s own high thin voices, the manner of the passing in the writer’s small careful hand, a house tally-clerk’s leaning corrections standing above it, a factor’s clerk’s upright correction added above both at Greybank, a gloss pressed into the margin in charcoal by a woman of the wine-press, and a verse at the foot in a northern child’s hand · Written in Grain of Y.H. 812 in the lower court of the Ember bowl-house in the Bowl of Sere, by a woman who washes the small bowls and is not permitted to look into one of them; set down after the third hour with a burnt stick on the back of a wine-list whose face was spoiled by a spill, and kept folded under the stack of mouth-down bowls on the lower shelf. Copied forward at Greybank in Ilmen of Y.H. 813 onto the back of an unissued boat-share sheet from the tide-tally house. It survives with a wine-ring at the head, yellow dust of the burning winds ground into the fold, a thumb of olive oil, a fleck of gold leaf from a contract carried past on a tray, a husk of southern grain shut in the gutter, a crack along the fold where the leaf has been folded and folded again, a grey Ash print nobody will own, the tally-clerk’s hand above the children’s words, the factor’s clerk’s hand above both, a press-woman’s gloss in the margin, and the verse at the foot in a hand that has never come forward\par}\medskip
I wash the small bowls in the lower court of the Ember house. That is my office and I am grateful for it; there are women in this house whose office is to stand where a guest may see them, and they are not permitted to sit down while the third hour lasts. I set this down because a little girl of the house asked me which of her names she was to answer to, and I, who am a bowl and answer to the name the house gave me, had no courtesy with which to reply. A courtesy is a thing said to a person who cannot answer back. She could answer back. That was the difficulty.

The name I had before I came is written on the inside of a bowl I am never permitted to look into. I have carried that bowl from the press to the court and back for eleven years and have never once turned it toward the light. The children turn theirs over. That is the game.

\subsection*{How it is played}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item It is played in the lower court at the going of the light, when the third hour’s bowls are washed and stacked mouth-down and the court fires are low. Not at a feast. On a feast day the children stand at the rail with the others and watch the great bowls go round, and a child who plays at the naming then is told she has not yet been told, which is the politest thing said in Sere.

\item Not when a clerk crosses the court with his tablets under his arm. If a clerk comes, the bowl is turned mouth-down and the game stops until he has gone, because a name said under a counting hand travels, and a name that travels arrives in a room the child will never enter.

\item They sit in a ring on the lowest step. One child is the pourer; she holds the small glazed bowl level at her knee and begins the rhyme. She is never the one who is kept, which the children accept as the ordinary order of things. The bowl goes from hand to hand, mouth up and level. A bowl that slops is set down, and the hand that slopped it is wiped by its owner, which is a courtesy and not a punishment.

\item One line, one pass. At each line the child to whom the bowl has come says one of her names to the bowl, with the vowels open and the ends thrown into the fire. Said to the bowl it stays a name; said to a face it becomes a claim, and a claim can be argued, and an argued name is entered. There is always a child who says it to a face, and there is always an older child to turn her chin toward the bowl.

\item The little ones have two names or one and borrow the rest from the older girls. They call it borrowing breath. There is another word for breath in this house and I will not set it beside theirs.
