A child who borrows must hold the name level until the bowl comes round again, the way a woman holds a full cup; she may not set it down.

\item At the seventh line the bowl is covered with the corner of the cloth. The child holding it says aloud, to the court and not to the bowl, the name the house keeps. Then every child breathes once across the covered bowl, which is how the other six names are given to the fire. The cloth is lifted, the bowl passed on, and the child who spoke becomes the pourer of the next round.

\item There is no winning and no last round. The fire is banked, the children go to their beds, and the bowl goes back on the shelf mouth-down.

\end{enumerate}

\subsection*{The rhyme, as it is passed}

\emph{Passed level. One line, one hand. Said to the bowl.}

\begin{quote}\itshape One for the name my mother sang at the well,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape two for the name my aunt kept in her mouth,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape three for the name that came south in a basket,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape four for the name the old woman would not write,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape five for the name we say when the bowl is turned,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape six for the name that goes down on the slate,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape seven for the name the house will keep.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Refrain, all together:} Pass it level, pass it full;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape say it to the bowl, not to the ear.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Six go to the fire and one stays here,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the one that stays is the one you hear.\end{quote}

\subsection*{What is said while the bowl is covered}

\emph{The cloth over the bowl. Every child breathes once. The words are said low, into the cloth.}

\begin{quote}\itshape Six go into the fire with the wine.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape They do not come back and they are not missed.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape The house calls one and the body answers,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape which is the whole of the courtesy.\end{quote}

They keep both hands on the step through this, and a child who lifts the cloth an inch to see whether the names are still there has given them to the fire twice and sits out a round with her palm over her mouth until the pourer taps her wrist. Nobody calls it by a name. I have watched them do it for eleven years and never once seen a child correct herself before the breath was out.

\subsection*{The verse they do not say when a clerk is in the court}

I have this from the smallest of the bought children, in the flat northern speech, said into the bowl with her back turned to the counting hand. The house children think it is a game about bowls. It is a game about bowls.

\begin{quote}\itshape Six go up and one stays down,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the one that stays is the one they call;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape I had a name before the south\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and it’s wrote where I mustn’t look.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Turn the bowl and read me none;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape I answer the bowl and not the court;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape keep the name and keep the debt,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and give me back the one you took.\end{quote}

I asked her what the sixth name was. She said it was the one she had before she came, and that she had it still, and that the fire had not taken it because it had never been given to it, which is an answer no courtesy in this house would have allowed a grown person to make. I have set it down as she said it, with the \emph{wrote} as she said it, because a child who has learned her letters off a slate writes it that way too. I have not asked whose bowl it is written in.

\subsection*{What the tally-clerk did}

A clerk of the house borrowed the leaf after the third hour, being a man who cannot leave paper alone. He writes in the leaning counting-hand, with the verbs taken out as though a verb were a thing a man could spill out of a cuff. He was pleased with this game, which I have not known a clerk to be with any other.

In the court’s hand — In the clerk’s hand\par

Seven names said to the bowl — Seven designations declared\par

Six given to the fire — Six cancelled by consent\par

One kept and called at the going of the light — One name retained; person identified thereby\par

The cloth over the bowl — No transaction\par

The bowl set mouth-down on the shelf — Balance nil\par

At the head he wrote, \emph{Names declared: seven. Retained: one. Released: six. No charge.} Against \emph{six go into the fire} he set \emph{six designations extinguished by consent}. Where the children cover the bowl and breathe he wrote \emph{no transaction}. At the foot, where the bowl goes back on the shelf, he put a round nought and wrote \emph{balance nil}.

He has put a figure where a name stood, and the house thanked him for it, which I have never seen happen in the north. There, they tell me, a clerk puts a number where a child stood and nobody thanks him, and the child’s people go around the number as a yard goes around a pot set down in the middle of it. Both hands are the same hand with the cuff turned a different way. I have put their words back underneath and left his standing above, as a full bowl stands on the shelf and the shelf does not argue.

\subsection*{What the factor’s clerk added at Greybank}

A factor’s clerk added one line at the head in the narrow upright hand, above everything else on the leaf. He has never been south and has not seen the bowl.

\begin{quote}\itshape Seven names entered; six cancelled; one whole return.\end{quote}

His figure is correct. The bowl is not in it.

\subsection*{What the woman at the press put in the margin}

She treads the press at the third hour and does not write often, and when she does she presses the letters in small, the way a woman writes in a room where somebody is sleeping. I have copied her hand as it stands.

At \emph{five for the name we say when the bowl is turned}: \textbf{We do not say it when the bowl is turned. We say it when the light is going. There is a difference, and the house has never asked after it.}

At \emph{six go into the fire}: \textbf{The fire takes the wine. It does not take the name. I have poured at nine feasts and my mother’s name is still in my mouth.}

At \emph{the name the house will keep}: \textbf{It keeps one because a house can only call one. A person can answer to more. That is the whole trouble in this court, and nobody in it will hear it said.}

\subsection*{At the head and in the gutter}

The wine-ring at the head belongs to no one hand; three hands set a cup in it over one evening and no hand will own it. The yellow dust of the burning winds is ground into the fold and I have not shaken it out, because a leaf that has never been in the wind is the wrong colour for this court. The thumb of oil is mine; I turn the leaf with the hand I wash the bowls with. The fleck of gold came off a contract carried past on a tray while the children were at their rhyme, and one of them picked it up and laid it in the gutter where a figure should stand, which is a better place for it than the counting room. The husk of grain came north in a loaf and went south again, which I could enter if I chose and have not. The crack in the fold is where the leaf has been folded and folded again; I cannot mend it and have stopped trying. The grey print came off a cuff laid where no cuff has business lying among the small bowls; nobody will own it, and there is no Last Day in a lower court.

\subsection*{At the foot, in a hand nobody will own}

\begin{quote}\itshape One name is kept and six are given to the fire.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape The fire has never once taken one.\end{quote}

I asked the pourer, the woman at the press and a potter come up from the provincial bowls, and had three answers and no hand, as I have had before. I have left the lines where they were written.

The leaf goes back under the small bowls. Tomorrow the light will go, the children will pass the bowl seven times and keep one name, and I shall wash the bowls and set them mouth-down on the shelf, and the name I was born with will stay where it is written, on the inside of one of them, which I have never once turned toward the light.

\clearpage\phantomsection\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{Six and the Seventh, Being the Rope-Skipping Game of the Weir Children, with the Counting-Out, the Manner of the Turns, and What an Assessor’s Clerk Made of It}
\CRsheetheading{Six and the Seventh, Being the Rope-Skipping Game of the Weir Children, with the Counting-Out, the Manner of the Turns, and What an Assessor’s Clerk Made of It}
{\centering\FellFont\itshape\footnotesize\color{faded} A net-mender’s gathering of a children’s skipping game, set down in Grathic on the back of a dried fish-bill; the counting-out and the turning verse in the children’s own half-sung speech, the manner of the play in the mender’s small hand, one correction in the narrow upright Ledgerhand of an assessor’s clerk come up from Greybank, a gloss pressed in charcoal by the woman who keeps the blessing stone, and a line at the foot in a hand that has never come forward · Written in Reed of Y.H. 813 at the plank walk above the Weir, one league upriver of Sill, by a woman who mends the eel-nets there, on the back of a fish-bill gone stiff with silt and sun; carried downriver in the creel of a girl come to Sill and copied at Greybank in Tallow of the same year onto the back of a weighing-warrant voided by the flood. Kept folded in the net-mender’s tin among the net-needles and the spent lengths of line. It survives with silt ground into the fold and worked into the fibre at the head, a ring where a dish of water stood from first grey to the going of the light, a press of wet reed across the second leaf, one fish-scale shut in the gutter, a grey Ash print nobody will own, the clerk’s correction standing above the children’s words, a gloss in charcoal beside the seventh, and a line at the foot in a hand that has not come forward\par}\medskip
I mend the eel-nets at the Weir, and I set this down because a man with a slate came up the plank walk in the dry week and asked what the children counted when they turned the line. I told him six and a seventh held, which is a count and not a figure, and he went away and sent me a clerk, which is what happens to a count in this country. What follows is what the children said before the clerk came and what they said again after he had gone back down the road with the verbs taken out of it. I have put their words underneath where they stand and left his above where he set them, as the boards keep the wet mark under the dry one.

The silt at the head is my own thumb; I set the bill down on the rail before I had done with the nets. The grey came off a cuff that had no business lying on a plank walk and I have not swept it. There is no Last Day on a board above the river, and nothing here gets burnt in the morning.

\subsection*{The line and the boards, as the children keep them}

\emph{Played on the dry boards of the plank walk above the water in Reed and Tallow, when the reeds lie spread to dry and the boards will take a foot. Not in the Five, when the children are made to stand and listen; not in rain, because a wet line will not turn over and a wet board puts a child into the Ilm. In Sill they say a child of eight can tell you which board has taken a nail and which has a knot the width of a thumb, and will not tell you which of the two will hold.}

The line is a length of net-line gone stiff with silt, knotted at both ends so the hands have somewhere to stay. It came off a net that had done its work and no net-mender will own it now it has been a skipping rope, which is the way of tools in this town. Two children take the ends and are \textbf{the ends}; one stands between them and is \textbf{the float}, because she goes up and down and the other two only go round. They are called the ends and never the hands, for hands are what a house is counted by and the children will not have it.

The ends turn the line over the float’s head, one turn to one line of the verse, and the float jumps each turn. The verse is said to the boards and not to the jumper. Said to a child it becomes an argument, and there is always a child who will argue.

\subsection*{The counting-out, said over the knots}

\emph{Right fists held out, knuckles up. The child who says it touches each fist in turn and does not look at the faces. The fist it lights on at the last word is the first float, which is not a prize: the float is the one who has to be fair and the ends are the ones who get to turn. The children accept this as a punishment and the net-menders accept it as practice.}

\begin{quote}\itshape Needle and net and hook and hair,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape a wet line and a dry place;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape draw it up and let it down ---\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the one it lights on keeps the round.\end{quote}

\emph{Kept the round means turned first, in the children’s speech, though an end will tell you it means kept the rope, and the two sayings have stood side by side on this board for as long as I have been mending here.}

\subsection*{The turning verse, as it is jumped}

\emph{One line, one turn, one jump. The line must pass right over the head and come down clear of the shoe; a line that catches the heel sends the float to the water, which is the edge of the boards where the wet ones sit with their hands folded. Seven is not a turn. At the seventh the ends stop the line high overhead and hold it there, and the float must stand still under it with both feet on the board and her hands by her sides. She does not jump the seventh. A float who jumps it has gone into the water and sits at the edge until the line is lowered to her shoe and three voices say together, *}The line calls\emph{*, at which she steps back in. Nobody counts how often this happens. There is no winning in this game and no last jump; when the seventh has been held, the ends lay the line on the boards and that is the end of it.}

\begin{quote}\itshape One for the post and one for the pin,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape one for the line that dried in the wind;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape one for the board where the wet nets lay,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape one for the eel that got away;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape one for the silt on the outer shoe,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape one for the hand that holds it true.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Six turns. The seventh stands.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Stand with it, float. The line has your hand.\end{quote}

\emph{The last two lines are said together by all three, with the line held high. The children will not be told why the seventh stands. Ask them and they say the line holds it; ask what the line holds and they ask you why a man wants to know what a line holds.}

\subsection*{What is said at the seventh, while the line is up}

\begin{quote}\itshape Seven is not a turn. It is a place to stand.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Feet on the board and hands by the side;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the line waits, and the boards wait,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the water is waiting below.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Jump it and you go where the wet ones go.\end{quote}

\subsection*{The verse they do not say while a man with a slate is on the boards}

I have this from the girl who kept the round, with the space left before it, which is the space the ends leave in the turning. She said it to the boards with her back turned and made me set it down with none of my verbs in it. A verse said to a board wants nothing added, and a verse said to a man wants everything taken away.

\begin{quote}\itshape Six for the basket and six for the bit,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape six for the child that the house won’t quit;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the seventh’s a year and not a day of the tend ---\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape it goes up the clay road and comes back thin.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape The ends go round and the float comes back,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and what was held is counted as lack;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape six on the board and one in the coat,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the place where the seventh stood is standing still.\end{quote}

I asked her what the year was. She said her brother had one of them and had gone up the clay road with it in the spring, and that she had never once seen him come back and had never once seen him not come back, which is a child’s way of keeping two things apart without putting a word between them. I have not put a word between them either.

\subsection*{What the clerk did}

An assessor’s clerk come up from Greybank to measure the winter fish-bills borrowed the leaf on the morning after, with his cuff soft at the edge from washing and the ink sitting in two fingers of it and will not come out. He set the ends down as \emph{holders} and the float as \emph{the vessel}. Against \emph{six turns are counted} he wrote \emph{six operations entered}. At the seventh he struck the children’s words through and set above them, \emph{seventh operation not entered; vacancy}. At the edge of the boards he wrote, \emph{the party who goes into the water is a deduction and is entered as nil}. At the foot, where the line is laid down and nothing is said, he put a round nought and wrote \emph{no result}.

I have set their words back under his and let his stand above. He writes of a thing that is always true and so has no need of a hand in it. I write for a child up to her ankle in the wet of the boards who wants to know which foot to lift and whether she brings it back. He has put a figure where a child was standing, which is the whole art of that hand: a nought can be carried up the road in a cuff, and a child kept waiting under a held line cannot.

He asked what the children learned by it. I told him the count and the holding and the calling back. He said that was an account of the thin return taught before the child could read a slate, and he entered it. The children stop when a man in a soft cuff comes onto the boards. They take it up again when he is past the bend in the road, and they never once jump the seventh.

\subsection*{The gloss at the seventh, in charcoal}

The woman who keeps the blessing stone pressed a line into the margin beside \emph{six turns}. She has kept that stone longer than I have kept nets and does not write often, and when she does she writes small, the way you would write in a room where somebody was sleeping.

\begin{quote}\itshape Not six. Seven, and the seventh is counted and kept out of the count. There’s a difference, and the Court won’t learn it.\end{quote}

I have left it where her thumb put it. She said a thing kept out of a count is not the same as a thing that is not in it, and that the difference was the whole of her life and most of her husband’s, and she would not say which part was hers. A hand on a line that lifts and a hand on a line that holds it overhead are two hands in the children’s game, though the ends change over at every round and nobody calls it by a name.

\subsection*{At the head and in the gutter}

The silt at the head came off my thumb and is worked into the grain, which is why the board takes a mark and the bill does not wash. The ring on the second leaf is a dish of water that stood from first grey to the going of the light and was drunk by nobody; three children have claimed it and one woman has denied it and I have given it to none of them. The press of wet reed across the fold came off the spread on the boards the day the clerk came and sat down on it, which is why the verse under his hand is the harder one to read. The fish-scale in the gutter is not mine and I have left it where it fell. The grey print nobody will own came off the cuff that had no business lying there, and I have not swept it and have no wish to. The tin goes back under the net-needles with the line coiled on top of it, where a line that has been a skipping rope is allowed to lie.

\subsection*{At the foot, in a hand that has not come forward}

\begin{quote}\itshape The seventh is the one the water keeps. Nobody calls for it at the Weir.\end{quote}

I asked the two ends and the float and the woman at the stone, and the ends laughed, and the float said it was the line, and the woman said she had always known it and had never once said it. I have left the line where it was written.

The bill goes back into the tin and the line back on the boards. Tomorrow the reeds will lie where they lie, the clerk will come up the plank walk and take the verbs out, and I shall put them back, and the children will turn six and hold the seventh where it has always stood, with both feet on the board and their hands by their sides.

\clearpage\phantomsection\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{Six Under the Heel, Being the Treading Song of the Clay Yard at Sill, with the Rounds as They Are Trodden and What the Factor’s Clerk Made of the Count}
\CRsheetheading{Six Under the Heel, Being the Treading Song of the Clay Yard at Sill, with the Rounds as They Are Trodden and What the Factor’s Clerk Made of the Count}
{\centering\FellFont\itshape\footnotesize\color{faded} A clay-yard’s treading song in the Low Kiln speech, called down into the slip pit and answered by the feet and not by voices; set down in charcoal by a rack-woman who treads slip in the mornings, with the rounds in the treaders’ own words, a correction in the margin by an old woman who has kept the racks thirty years, the factor’s clerk’s ruling in Ledgerhand above the seventh round, and a line at the back in a hand nobody will own · Written in Silt of Y.H. 813 in the Clay Yard of Low Kiln in Sill, in charcoal on the inside of a pot gone wrong that had split from lip to foot and been set by the wall of the wheel-shed for the sweeping; the charcoal went into the grain of the clay so that no scraping would take it out. Copied forward onto the back of a kiln-setting tally gone soft with damp, carried to Greybank in the pocket of a woman come to have a widow’s mark confirmed, and sewn with eel-sinew into a fold of oiled paper. It survives with bone-pale slip rubbed into the head, a wet-clay thumb at the second corner, a green bead of lead-glaze in the gutter, a brown barley crust gone stiff in the fold, a tallow print, a tideline from the Slip Brook, a grey Ash print nobody will own, the old rack-woman’s correction standing in the margin, the clerk’s ruling standing above the seventh round, and the line at the back that has never been claimed.\par}\medskip
I tread the pit in the mornings before the wheel is warm, and I have done so eleven winters. There are four of us when the water stands high and two when it falls, and the work is the same: foot after bare foot into the slip until the lumps are gone and the clay closes over the instep the way water closes over a stone. You do not see the air go. You feel it come up between the toes and break, and the old women call it the pot’s breath and say that a pot which keeps its breath will burst in the firing. I do not know whether this is true. I have seen a pot go flat in a kiln that had been trodden by women who knew their work, and I have seen a pot come out singing from a pit any child might have trampled.

This is not a song for a fire. It is said to the clay. A caller stands at the lip of the pit and says the first line down into it; the treaders say the second with the foot, and the last line of each round is not said aloud but is the lifting of the foot, which is the rest. Say a line to a woman and it becomes an argument. Say it to the clay and the clay tells your foot when to come up.

Six rounds to a tread and the seventh held. The count is not ours. It is the count of a clay-bound year, six that the yard will speak of and one that the household enters into a slate; a man may serve six years in a pit and be in his eighth before the yard will say his name in the same sentence as his debt. We do not sing the seventh. We hold it the way the kiln holds one breath in four, which is to say we leave it where it is and go around it.

I set the words down on the inside of a pot that had gone wrong, because there is no slate in a yard that a pail of water will not spoil and no paper that will last a morning among the tubs. The charcoal went into the clay and stayed there. What follows is what the women said before the man from the counting house borrowed the leaf at Greybank, and what they said again after he had gone back over the north bridge.

\subsection*{The song, as it is trodden}

\emph{Called at the lip, low, into the pit. One line, one round of the foot. The last line of each part is said to the clay and not to a person.}

\subsection*{The wetting}

\begin{quote}\itshape The slip is cold and the pit is deep,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape put in the foot where the others keep;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the clay comes up over the ankle bone,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape takes the print of the foot and keeps its own.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape The water lies where the water lay,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and mud goes down to the mud by day;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the pit has a lip and the pit has a floor,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the seventh stands at the lip and comes no more.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Six under the heel and the seventh held in;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the flaw goes shallow and the note comes back full.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Six under the heel and the foot comes up free;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape what goes out of the clay comes home to me.\end{quote}

\subsection*{The six rounds}

\begin{quote}\itshape One for the lump that the heel finds first,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape two for the bubble that breaks and is not;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape three for the water that climbs and goes,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape four for the bone-coloured slip on the toes;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape five for the print of a thumb in the wall,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape six for the seam where the thumb let it fall;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the seventh stands where the seventh has stood,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape with the cold of the pit and the print in the mud.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Six under the heel and the seventh held in;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the flaw goes shallow and the note comes back full.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Six under the heel and the foot comes up free;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape what goes out of the clay comes home to me.\end{quote}

\subsection*{At the wheel}

\emph{Not sung at the wheel itself. Said under the breath by the thrower while the pot goes up, with the thumb kept steady and the knuckle kept for afterwards.}

\begin{quote}\itshape The wheel goes round and the seat is worn\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape on the left where a man leaned, and the lean stays on;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape put the pot where his thumb was put\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and listen to what the pot has got.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape The wall goes up and the thumb goes in\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape at the one place where the wall is thin;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape tap it once with the knuckle bone ---\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape full is a note that a house may own.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Tap it once and it answers flat;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape sweep it around where the potter sat.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape A crack once made is a crack kept true;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape leave the crack showing and the yard goes through.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Six under the heel and the seventh held in;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the flaw goes shallow and the note comes back full.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Six under the heel and the foot comes up free;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape what goes out of the clay comes home to me.\end{quote}

\subsection*{At the kiln}

\begin{quote}\itshape The kiln draws breath and the kiln lets go,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape four for the breath and a place in the row;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the fire takes what the fire will take\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and leaves a brown edge on the loaf we bake.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape The glaze runs sweet where the lead has been\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and a girl at the cup has a pale at the gum;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape she sets the cup down on the bench and goes\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape out to the racks where the dry slip shows.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape What the fire takes out of the clay\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the house finds in the corner at dawn;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape we leave it there and we leave the pot\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape with the crack showing, and carry on.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Six under the heel and the seventh held in;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the flaw goes shallow and the note comes back full.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Six under the heel and the foot comes up free;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape what goes out of the clay comes home to me.\end{quote}

\subsection*{The verse they do not tread when a man from Slate Row is in the yard}

I have it from the caller, with the space left before it, which is the space the treaders leave in the singing. She would not say it to the clerk and would not say it within sight of his cuff. She said it to the pot I had set by the wall, with her back to the road.

\begin{quote}\itshape Six for the years that the slate will name,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and one for the year that the household keeps;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the figure goes in and the man goes round,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the grey in the corner goes up a thumb.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Six for the pot and one for the hand\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape that put the thumb in and could not command\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the place where it failed. The yard says weather.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape The legs say nothing. The slate says never.\end{quote}

I asked her what the seventh was and she said a man who had never trodden would not know where the foot comes up, and went back to the pit. This is the answer the yard gives to everything it does not want entered, and I have set it down as she gave it, without mending the sense.

\subsection*{The old woman’s correction in the margin}

Against \emph{two for the bubble that breaks and is not}, a woman who has kept the racks thirty years wrote in a small hard hand: \emph{Not air. Water. My mother trod this pit forty years and it is water that comes up between the toes, not air, and water will not burst a pot in the firing. The pot that went flat in our kiln had been dried too fast against the east wall.}

Under it, in mine: \emph{Both stand. I have felt the bubble break and I have known the east wall. A song that has been corrected in the margin is a song that has been used, and a song nobody has argued with is a song nobody has trodden to.}

\subsection*{What the clerk wrote above the seventh round}

The factor’s clerk borrowed the leaf at Greybank, being a man who cannot leave paper lying. He has a cuff gone soft from washing and the ink sits in two fingers of it and will not come out. He struck out \emph{the seventh held in} and wrote above it, \emph{one part in twelve withheld from the tread; the deduction is entered.} Against \emph{what goes out of the clay comes home to me} he set \emph{labour retained in the vessel; no residue arises.} At the foot of the last round he wrote \emph{six turns performed, rest nil,} and drew a line under it that went a finger’s breadth past the margin.

I have put the women’s words back underneath and left his standing above, as the floor keeps the ash and the foot that raised it. He has made a rest into a deduction and a deduction into a year. A rest is when the foot comes up; a year is what a clay-bound man does not get back. He has set one where the other stood, which is the whole art of that hand. The treaders stop when they see the soft cuff come into the yard. They take it up when he is past the bridge, and they never once sing the seventh.

\subsection*{At the head and in the gutter}

The bone-pale slip at the head is off the hand that drew the line in the pit; it goes into the grain and will not come out, which is why the yard uses it to mark a place and not to write a name. The wet-clay thumb at the second corner is mine. I signed in slip because I have no slate-name and the pot was mine before it was a leaf. The green bead came off a pot broken by the Glaze Room and rolled to the gutter while a woman held the tally down in the draught; I did not taste it and have not put it in my mouth, whatever the children say of that sweetness. The brown crust is a barley one with the edge burnt, given to a child who would not eat it and laid down here instead. The tallow print came off a lamp set too near the leaf at the Long Night. The tideline took two words off the back of the tally and I have not written them in again, because a song with two words gone is a song said slowly and all of ours are said slowly. The grey in the gutter came off a cuff laid where no cuff has business lying in a yard; I have not swept it. The Last Day is for corners, and a folded leaf has none.

The tally goes back into its fold of oiled paper and into the pocket, and tomorrow the pit will be cold again and the four of us will be there or the two, according to the water. The caller will say six and the feet will answer six, and the seventh will stand at the lip where it stood this morning, and the clay will close over the instep the way it always does, and whatever goes out of it will come home to somebody.

\subsection*{At the back, in a hand nobody will own}

\begin{quote}\itshape The flaw is where the thumb was. The thumb was somebody’s.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Six go into the pot. The seventh goes home in the leg.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Ask the yard what it counts and it will tell you the weather.\end{quote}

I asked the caller, the old woman of the racks and a carter waiting on the road, and had three answers and no hand. I have left the lines where they were written.

\clearpage\phantomsection\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{Sold, Not Lent, Being the Account of Veno Brine, a Buyer out of the Glass Furnaces at Vhal, Who Went Up the Rim Road in Seed of Y.H. 813 with Salt, Rope and a Contract on Salt-Paper and Came Down in Ember with Iron, a Warm-Stone Gone Cold, and a Number She Did Not Enter; with the Weigh at the Keep, the Table of What Was Carried and What Came Back, the Song of the Stone Going Up, Two Corrections in Borrowed Hands, and a Line at the Foot Nobody Will Own}
\CRsheetheading{Sold, Not Lent, Being the Account of Veno Brine, a Buyer out of the Glass Furnaces at Vhal, Who Went Up the Rim Road in Seed of Y.H. 813 with Salt, Rope and a Contract on Salt-Paper and Came Down in Ember with Iron, a Warm-Stone Gone Cold, and a Number She Did Not Enter; with the Weigh at the Keep, the Table of What Was Carried and What Came Back, the Song of the Stone Going Up, Two Corrections in Borrowed Hands, and a Line at the Foot Nobody Will Own}
{\centering\FellFont\itshape\footnotesize\color{faded} A buyer’s road account, set down first in the leaning counting-hand on the backs of spoiled tide-tallies at the shaft mouth and copied at Greybank onto the back of a Court salt-warrant voided by the Long Cold; the road and the figures in the buyer’s hand, the Rim sayings kept in the hearing with the endings struck off, the verbs put back underneath every borrowed correction, and one line at the foot in a hand that has never come forward · Written at Keld Keep and on the Rim Road in Seed and Tallow of Y.H. 813 by Veno Brine, a woman of the Quay at Vhal who buys for the three glass furnaces; she went up with two chests of Sallow salt, a coil of tarred rope and a contract written on salt-paper, and came down in Ember with four bars of Keldish iron, a warm-stone that had kept a fire and had gone cold, a shaving of the same stone, and a number cut in bone by a Vorr which she has not entered. Copied at Greybank in Ash of Y.H. 813 onto the back of a Court salt-warrant voided by the Long Cold, carried up the Salt Road to Vhal, and kept since in the tin among the anneal-tools. It survives folded into a strip of oiled sailcloth, soft at the fold and stiff with salt by turns: a white bloom at the head that has eaten the tails off two figures, a thumb of tar at the crease off the coil she carried home, iron-red at the second corner from the mine-reeve’s checking point, a warm-stone shaving gone cold in the fourth leaf, a slip of bone with a number cut into it that no clerk of ours has matched to anything, a frost-feather pressed flat that was gone by noon, a small square of bare paper where a word was scraped away with a knife-point, a grey Ash print along the outer fold which the writer did not make and has not swept, two corrections in borrowed hands, and a line at the foot in a hand nobody will own\par}\medskip
I buy for the furnaces. Three of them stand east of the Quay at Vhal and between them they melt the beach sand and the blue-green lead of the cliffs into glass that goes as far as Sere. They eat iron the way a kiln eats wood: pokers, clamps, the small bars the anneal is propped on, all of it going grey and then going. A buyer for the furnaces is a woman who is always short of iron, and is sent where the iron is cheap.

I went up in Seed with two chests of Sallow salt, a coil of tarred rope, and a contract written on salt-paper. At home we say a contract that rots in the damp is no contract, and call that a virtue. I carried mine in a tarred tin inside my coat and opened it only at the third hour, which is the hour the south does its business and the north, I was to learn, does not.

\subsection*{The road, and what the paper did}

Eighty leagues up the Salt Road to Greybank, and then the Rim Road north-west, a hundred and twenty more of improving road and worsening weather. I had been told to take a warm-stone. The advice came from a man who sold them, at Greybank, in the yard, with the price in his mouth before the reason. I bought none there. A woman who buys for a living learns that the first figure a man gives is the one he has said oftenest.

Below the pass the reeds go and the road goes to stone. By the fourth day the ruts held frost in the morning that no ruts at home hold, and the rope in my bundle had gone stiff where the tar had crept into it. The salt-paper did the opposite of what it does at Vhal: instead of going soft it went crisp, and the ink sat up on it. I put a leaf of it in the tin with my thumb and it did not come away. A buyer notices a thing that will not take the figure she brings.

The smoke of Keld Keep is seen before the Keep. It lies low along the stone, the colour of a banked fire at home, with the same sweetness under it that the glaze room has when the lead is up. A furnace woman would have known the smell. I knew it and was not glad.

\subsection*{The weigh, or the number before the name}

At the Warden’s hall I gave my name, and the clerk looked at me until I understood I had begun wrongly, as every traveller from the low countries does, and is allowed to do once. A man beside me said, “State what you hold, then say who you are,” in the voice of one who has said it to fools before. I went back to the foot of the post and came again with a figure, and the clerk wrote the figure first and asked the name second.

At Vhal a name is written on salt-paper and the rain takes it, and we call the taking a virtue. Here the number goes down the shaft with a man and the name stays in the room where he said it. I have joined neither.

The mine-reeve checked me in red. He set his point where I had given my figure, drew a stroke through it, and wrote the same figure above, which is how that office tells a man it found no lie without giving him anything to thank it for. The red stands at the second corner. I have not wiped it off or entered it.

\subsection*{What was carried, and what came back}

\emph{Figures as given at the third hour at the Keep, set with what I entered at the Quay. The left column is what a woman carries; the right is what she brings home, which is never the same coin.}

Article — Entered at Vhal — Given at Keld Keep — What I set on the back\par

Sallow salt, two chests — 6 marks — 1 mark and a favour — The favour is not current. I entered it anyway.\par

Rope, tarred, a coil — 2 marks — not taken — The tar came home on my hands and is in the seam of this book.\par

Contract on salt-paper, for iron — entered at 1 mark at the tide-tally house — void by cold — The clerk here would not write on it. It went brittle and kept its verbs, which is more than it does at home.\par

Keldish iron, four bars — — — half a mark the bar — Two marks the four bars, four to bring them down. The road has no slate of its own.\par

Warm-stone, a palm’s length — — — 6 marks — Sold, not lent. It kept my hand warm on the climb and was cold the morning I got home.\par

Shaving of warm-stone — — — half a mark — A shaving will keep a cup warm through one night. I bought it for the furnaces and kept it for myself.\par

A number, cut in bone, by a Vorr — — — 1 bit — The numbers are correct. I have not entered what it is for.\par

Twelve bits to the silver mark and twenty marks to the crown, if you can find a crown in Keld, which I could not. The Court books in embers and will tell a woman an ember is worth five marks; nobody has ever changed one, but the figure travels faster than the coin. I left the embers out. A row with nothing in it is a thing no clerk can take off a woman.

\subsection*{Sold, and not lent}

Two men told me a warm-stone is sold and is not lent, and they had no reason to agree, being one a seller and one a man who had bought from him. A thing that can be lent has a place in somebody’s account, said the seller. A thing that is paid for is finished, said the buyer.

At Vhal a boat-share passes through a mother, and a man who marries into the boat is come aboard and his opinion counted at half. The share is held and handed and never sold. Here a stone is paid for and its history stops at the paying. A Keldish man will tell you the price and not the debt, which is the same trick as telling you eleven months and not the month taken off.

I asked a woman at the annealing shed what the shavings were for. She said a shaving will hold a cup through a night, and then said her husband had held three cups in his time and none had held him. I have set the two sentences down together and put no third between them.

\subsection*{The mouth, and the boy going down}

The Descent is at thirteen. I stood at the mouth with the old women who count and watched a boy go down with a number cut into his arm and a warm-stone put into his hand after the knife. His mother said nothing. One of the old women said the last part of a saying with him, and the boy said the first part before he went down and the women said the second, and nobody explained it to me, and I did not ask.

Two go down and the count comes two, they say at the mouth. It is not a promise that two come up. It is a promise that the count will be made, which is a poorer promise and one a clerk can keep.

A man at the mouth had two sets of numbers in one arm, the later cut deeper. The mine-reeve entered the later and left the earlier standing in the skin, and told me both stood. In Vhal we write a debt down and let the rain have it. Here they cut a figure into the flesh and call the second cutting a kindness.

There is a cup at the end of the Duelling Floor that nobody takes, set for a man whose number was changed twice. I did not see the cup; I have written that first. I asked if I might go down and was told a lowlander goes down as tribute or as a spy, and often as both, and I was neither, so I stood and counted the boys.

\subsection*{The Vorr, and the number I did not enter}

A Vorr at the weigh sells numbers for a bit. He is tall and slow and his skin has the pale grey of the stone they keep, and his fingers are doubled at the last joint, which I noticed before his face, because I notice hands first. I bought a number and asked what it was for. He said the numbers were correct, and would not say it twice.

He cut it into a slip of bone with something I could not see. I asked whether it counted the iron, or the wells, or the doorways of a place I had passed on the road, and he said the numbers were correct, which is an answer a woman can carry away and still know nothing. I have not put the slip against the table. There is no column in it for a figure that will not say what it counts, and a buyer who makes a column for a thing she does not understand has made the figure current, which ought not to be done without a hand to pay for it.

The slip lies in the fourth leaf with the shaving. Both are cold, neither entered.

\subsection*{The song of the stone going up}

\emph{Taken down at the shaft mouth from the old women who count, said to the rope while the stone goes up. The last line is said twice; the second time is for those counted back into a different name.}

\begin{quote}\itshape A stone kept a fire before I was born\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and was sold to me for a figure in marks;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape it kept my hand on the climb and went cold at the Keep,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and no man there would call it a debt.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Count them going and count them back;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape two go down and the count comes two.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape The knife takes first and the stone takes after;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the number stays where the man does not.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Hold the rope, it is tarred and it takes;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape hold the stone, it is sold and not lent.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape A cup stands full where nobody drinks;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the dark keeps what the mother never entered.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Ask the rope what it carried up.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape The rope has no account to enter.\end{quote}

I have left the last line as it was said, twice. A woman who counts at that mouth will say a thing about a cup and not what stands in it, and I have learned not to ask a second time there.

\subsection*{What the borrowed hands did}

Two hands have been at these leaves besides mine.

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item A clerk of the Council of Tides, borrowed at Greybank after the salt boats came up, in the leaning low hand with the ends of words let fall. He took the verbs out as though a verb were a thing a woman could carry off in a cuff. Where I wrote \emph{they sold me the stone} he set \emph{consideration passed}; where I wrote \emph{the Vorr cut a number in bone} he set \emph{token, no value entered}. I have put my words back underneath. A verb is a person standing in a sentence.

\item The factor’s clerk, in the narrow upright hand, wrote \emph{figures of price, not of account} against my table and set a round nought in the margin beside the number cut in bone. A nought is a figure. The bone was not, and nobody has poured it. He has never been up the Rim Road and has strong views about it.

\end{itemize}

The mine-reeve’s red stroke at the second corner is a check and not a correction. He found the figure I gave stood. I have kept his mark where it fell, which is more than I can say of the others.

\subsection*{At the head and in the gutter}

The white at the head is salt bloom off the tide-tallies; it has eaten the tails from two figures and I have not written them back, because a figure with the end gone is read slowly, and everything on that road the same. The tar at the crease is mine, off the coil I carried eighty leagues and have never got out of the seam. The red is the mine-reeve’s point. The shaving in the fourth leaf held its heat one night on a stone floor and is cold now, which is the order of things up there. The slip of bone lies beside it with its figure unmatched. I have kept the two apart: they are different debts, and a woman who joins them has drawn a conclusion, which I have no licence to draw. The frost-feather lay on the well lip at the Keep and was gone before I folded the leaf; the yard at home calls that weather. The square of bare paper is a word I took out with a knife and have not put back. The grey along the outer fold is not mine and not the Council’s. A man of Keld called it Ash, which in Vhal is a thing a woman must buy before she will own to seeing it. I did not buy it. I have not swept it. There is no Last Day above that Keep.

\subsection*{At the foot, in a hand nobody will own}

\begin{quote}\itshape The stone went up warm and came home cold;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the iron came down and was paid twice over;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the name went into the room and the number went down;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the bone keeps a figure nobody will enter.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Ask the cup what it holds.\end{quote}

I asked the woman who counts at the mouth, a Vorr who sells numbers, and a Council clerk come up from Greybank, and had three answers and no hand. I have left the line where it was written. The leaves go back into the sailcloth and the sailcloth into the tin among the anneal-tools, where the tar keeps the damp out and the damp keeps the writing soft. Tomorrow I take the four bars to the third furnace and shall enter what iron fetched at the Keep and what it fetched at Greybank, leaving the difference standing between them, the only place in my book where a true thing is kept without a signature.

\clearpage\phantomsection\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{Ten at the Racks, Being the Palm-Count of the Low Kiln Girls, with the Manner of the Clapping, the Still Hands, and What a Clerk Put in the Eleventh Place}
\CRsheetheading{Ten at the Racks, Being the Palm-Count of the Low Kiln Girls, with the Manner of the Clapping, the Still Hands, and What a Clerk Put in the Eleventh Place}
{\centering\FellFont\itshape\footnotesize\color{faded} A rack-woman’s gathering of a children’s hand-clapping game, set down in charcoal on the back of a spoiled rack-tally; the count in the children’s own half-sung speech, the manner of it in the writer’s small hand, a correction in the narrow upright Ledgerhand of a factor’s clerk borrowed at Greybank, a gloss pressed in charcoal by the woman who keeps the birth-slates at the shrine, and one line at the foot in grey chalk in a hand that has learned its letters off a slate · Written at the drying racks in the Clay Yard at Low Kiln of Sill in Ash of Y.H. 812, the Thin Year, of an evening when the racks stood half full and the girls clapped over a tally of wet pots; carried to Greybank in the pocket of a potter gone to have a kiln-mark renewed and copied onto the back of a weigh-slip gone soft at one corner. Kept folded in the rack-shed under the loose board beside the wheel. It survives with slip dried pale in the creases at the head, a tallow thumb, a chalk score along the fore-edge where a line was drawn and rubbed out, a small-ale ring, a green bead of lead glaze in the fold, a grey Ash print along the gutter that nobody will own, the clerk’s correction standing above the children’s words, a gloss pressed in charcoal beside the ninth line, and a line at the foot in grey chalk nobody will claim\par}\medskip
I keep the drying racks in the Clay Yard, and I have set this down because the youngest girl who used to clap here went up the clay road in the spring and came back with a number where her name had been. She stands now at the end of the racks and watches the hands go round and does not put hers in. I am not writing it for her. A leaf of charcoal cannot teach back what has been taken out of a person. I write it for the ones who come after, who will want to know why the hands stop together on the tenth, why nobody claps in the gap, and why the ninth line is said to the rack and never to a face.

The tally this is written on counted forty pots and lost the figure in the damp before I wanted it. That is how I came by the back of it. A thing spoiled for the Court is the proper stuff for a children’s game; the factor’s man was going to throw it out and I asked him for it, and he gave it without looking, which is the only generosity I have ever had from that house.

\subsection*{How it is played}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item Two girls sit facing at the end of a rack, with the pots standing dry behind them. They clap their own hands on the odd lines and strike palms on the even, so that the pattern is \emph{own, together, own, together} all the way to the tenth. It is played while the racks are turned in the last of the light and not at any other time, because the racks want both hands and the game wants them too.

\item The count is said to the rack, not to the girl across from you. Said to a face it becomes an argument, and there is always a girl who will argue. The rack has no ears and will not carry the count up the road.

\item One line, one clap. On the tenth line the two palms meet and stay met, without pressing, while the words \emph{Read the count} are said. This is the reading. A girl who claps the tenth instead of holding it has read aloud where she should have kept quiet, and sits with her hands in her lap until the other turns her palm upward and says, \emph{The count begins again.} That is the whole of the bringing back. Nobody’s name is said in it.

\item After the tenth there is the gap. The hands part and lie flat on the knees for one breath and nobody claps. A girl who claps in the gap has banked it, and sits out as above. The gap is not a day and has no clap in it; they will not be told what it is, and if you ask they ask you why a man wants to put a number on a breath.

\item When ten has been held and the gap kept, the hands go back to Firstday and the whole count turns again. There is no last round and nothing is won. The girl who has kept her hands still through the most gaps gets to say the ninth line, which is the one about the name. She does not get to say it to anybody.

\item The game is not played in the Five, when the children are made to stand and listen, nor on a day a collector has been seen on the Clay Road. It is played in the thaw on the dry boards and in Stone on the trodden ash inside the kiln-house, and the words are the same in both places.

\end{enumerate}

\subsection*{The count, as it is clapped}

\emph{Own hands on the odd lines, palms together on the even. On the tenth the palms meet and do not move. Say it to the rack.}

\begin{quote}\itshape Firstday, and the fire is turned with a pot,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Secondday, and the grey goes around the cot;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Thirdday, and the pot answers full,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Fourthday, and the eel comes up through silt;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Fifthday, and the loaf shows a browned edge,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Sixthday, and the bit goes into the house;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Seventhday, the wheel that will not stand,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Eighthday, the broom that goes around;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Ninthday, the name we say at home,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Tenthday, the hands meet. Read the count.\end{quote}

\subsection*{What is said in the gap}

\emph{Hands flat on the knees. One breath, no more. The words are said low, to the floor, and not across the space between the two girls.}

\begin{quote}\itshape No clap in the gap. The gap is not a day.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape The hands lie down. The hands come back.\end{quote}

They keep both hands in their laps through this, and a girl who lets one hand go up an inch to begin the next count early is banked, though nobody calls it that but me. I have watched them do it for nineteen springs and never once seen a girl correct herself before the breath was out.

\subsection*{The verse they do not clap while a man from the factor’s house is in the yard}

I have this from the girl who says the ninth line, with the proper space left before it, which is the space the hands leave in the clapping. She would not say it while the clerk had his pen out and would not say it to him at all. She said it to the rack with her back turned and made me set it down with none of my words in it.

\begin{quote}\itshape They gave her a figure and sent her home,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and she stands at the end where the racks run out;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape we clap to the rack and not to her,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the count goes round with a place kept warm.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Six bits a day and the crust is free;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the grey in the corner is not for the pot;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape nine in the hands and the tenth in the house,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the eleventh is not a day of the tend.\end{quote}

I asked her what the eleventh was. She said the factor’s man would know, and that he had put it in his book while she was still saying the tenth, and that she had let him because a child who argues with a man in a soft cuff gets no crust at the end of the row. I have set it down as she said it, with the letting left in.

\subsection*{What the woman at the shrine put in the margin}

The charcoal here is hers, pressed hard and small, the way a woman writes who has kept birth-slates for nineteen years and does not want the words read over a cradle.

At \emph{the fire is turned with a pot}: \textbf{She says pot. It is the back of a broken pot. A girl who has never turned coals should not say this line, and will say it all the same.}

At \emph{the grey goes around the cot}: \textbf{The broom goes around it. The house goes around it. It is the same sentence said kindly. Do not let them make it a proverb before they have swept.}

At \emph{Ninthday, the name we say at home}: \textbf{There is a name for the house and a name for the slate. Keep them on two places of the tongue, and do not let the second one travel.}

At \emph{the gap is not a day}: \textbf{We sat with a covered pot through a Long Night and did not clap. That is the only gap I have kept, and it was longer than a breath.}

\subsection*{What the clerk did}

A factor’s clerk borrowed the tally at Greybank on the morning the pots went down, being a man who cannot let paper lie still. He has a cuff gone soft from washing and the ink sits in two fingers of it and will not come out. He numbered the ten lines in the margin and wrote against the tenth, \emph{the account is read and the parties are identified}. Against \emph{no clap in the gap} he wrote \emph{five days outside the tend; no observance; no charge to the district}. Against \emph{the name we say at home} he wrote \emph{the name is entered where the house requires}. At the foot, where the two hands lie on the knees and nothing at all is counted, he put a round nought and wrote \emph{eleven} beside it, and under that, \emph{vacancy}.

I have put their words back underneath and left his standing above. He takes the hands out of it because a thing always true has no need of them. I put them back because a girl up to her wrists in slip does not know she is hearing something always true, and wants to know when to clap. A nought is a number. The Five have names and no number. He has put a figure where a breath should be, which is the whole art of that hand.

He asked me what the children learned by the game. I told him the count and the stopping and the bringing back, and he said that was an account of the Return taught before a child could read a slate, and he entered it. The girls stop when a man with a soft cuff comes into the yard. They take it up when he is past the wheel-shed. They have never once changed the tenth.

\subsection*{At the head and in the gutter}

The slip at the head is dried pale in the creases and came off the hand that held the tally down on the rack rail; it goes into the grain and no damp takes it out, which is why a rack-woman uses charcoal and not ink. The tallow thumb is mine, from the lamp I held low while the girl said the verse with her back turned and I did not want her to see me writing. The chalk score along the fore-edge is a line one of them drew to count on and rubbed out with her sleeve before she was told to, which is the way lines go in this yard. The small-ale ring is from a cup set down by nobody in particular and claimed by three girls and denied by one. The green bead in the fold came off a girl come up from High Kiln with the sweetness still at her mouth, who leaned over to see the writing, touched the leaf and went back up the terrace without asking. The grey in the gutter came off a cuff laid where no cuff has business lying among the racks; I have not swept it, and there is no Last Day in a rack-shed.

\subsection*{At the foot, in grey chalk, in a child’s hand}

\begin{quote}\itshape I kept my hands still and she did not come back.\end{quote}

The letters are hard at the \emph{th} and one of them is set backward, which is how a child writes who has learned off a slate and not off a book. No hand will own it. I asked the girl who says the ninth line, the woman who keeps the shrine, and a potter going down with a barrow of wet ware, and had three answers and no hand, as I have had before. I have left it where it was written.

The tally goes back under the loose board. Tomorrow the racks will be turned in the last of the light and the girls will sit at the end of them and clap ten and keep the gap, and the one who came back will stand where she stands and watch the hands go round without putting hers in, and I shall not call her over. I have kept their words and I have not joined them to anything.

\clearpage\phantomsection\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{The Apprentice Beam, Being the Standing Rules of the Kiln-Masters of Sill for the Taking, Keeping and Trying of Apprentices, Read at the Cross and Nailed Beside the Moot-Post}
\CRsheetheading{The Apprentice Beam, Being the Standing Rules of the Kiln-Masters of Sill for the Taking, Keeping and Trying of Apprentices, Read at the Cross and Nailed Beside the Moot-Post}
{\centering\FellFont\itshape\footnotesize\color{faded} A bench-copy of the guild’s standing rules in the hand of the clerk who keeps the kiln-masters’ bench at the Cross; the terms set in tables, the yard’s wheel-song pasted to the back, two corrections in the Thane’s narrow hand, one clause crossed in a potter’s charcoal, and a line at the foot in a hand nobody will own · First gathered at Sill in Y.H. 418, the year the Clay Road was made a Court road by the treaty of the Blue Cliff, and copied forward each generation from the bench rather than from a book; this leaf written at the Cross and in the Clay Yard of Low Kiln in the Thin Year, Y.H. 812, and carried through the Opening of the Slates into Y.H. 813. It survives folded and soft at the nail-hole, with a thumb-worn centre where a hundred men have wiped their hands before reading, a green bead of lead glaze at the head off the Thane’s thumb, slip dried the colour of old bone down the gutter, a tallow spot at the wheel clause, a press of wet reed across the song from a day the bench stood in the rain, a grey print along the foot that is not mine and is not the Thane’s, two small corrections in his narrow upright hand, one line struck hard in charcoal by a potter who would not put his name to it, and one line at the foot nobody will own.\par}\medskip
I keep the guild’s bench at the Cross on market-days, between the pig beam and the Court table set at the Slate Row fringe. A house comes to take a child, or a child is brought to be tried, and I read what is below so that what is read in High Kiln is the same as what is read in the yard. The bench is worn smooth in the middle where thumbs have wiped it longer than any man can date, and this leaf has a nail-hole at the head and a green bead of glaze in the lower corner that came off the Thane’s thumb in the Thin Year and has not been swept since. The grey along the gutter came off a cuff laid in a corner where no cuff has business lying, and there is no Last Day for a bench-copy. I have set the rules down as they stand. Where a hand has corrected me I have left both readings.

They are not new rules. They were gathered in the year the Clay Road was made a Court road, when a man from the Cross could first reach Greybank in five days and the guild found it had neighbours it had not chosen. A rule with no thumb on it is a rule nobody has had to use. What follows has been used.

\subsection*{The standing rules, as read at the Cross}

\subsection*{Of the taking}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item A house takes an apprentice, not the guild. The house answers for the child’s food, his bed, his tools and the debt he makes; the guild answers only for the note. A man who takes a child and will not answer for him has taken nothing, and the child is sent back to the moot.

\item A child may be taken from his ninth year, and not before he can carry a board of wet pots the length of the yard without setting it down. A child bound by debt goes where the debt sends him, and his years count from the day the debt is entered, not from the day he could lift a board.

\item The taking is written in the house’s own roll, in a careful hand, and the roll is kept in the house. It is not taken to Slate Row and it is not shown to a man who comes down with a slate. A slate is for the measure; the roll is for the hand. The two are not the same book and must not be set side by side.

\item A foundling is named by whoever writes the slate, and has no house-name until a hearth claims him. Until then he is a coat any house may wear. See that the coat is mended where it tears, not worn till it thins.

\item A widow may hold her husband’s fire by the mark confirmed at the Cross and by the factor at Greybank. She touches the mark before she opens the kiln and at no other hour. A dusk is not an opening, and a bank is not an opening.

\end{enumerate}

\subsection*{Of the first year}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item The apprentice sweeps, carries, mixes slip and sets pots to dry. He does not touch the wheel, and he does not cut the glaze. A child set to the wheel too soon learns to humour the clay instead of hearing it, and a pot humoured is a pot that will not say what it is.

\item The apprentice is kept, not hired. He eats from the house’s dish and sleeps under the house’s roof. What he earns in the yard goes into the yard, and what the yard gives back comes back as bread, not as a figure in a man’s hand.

\item No child tastes glaze. Glaze is tasted by the master, with the side of the thumb and the back of the tongue, and spit out. A pale line at the gum is the glaze’s mark and not a mark of industry; a master who calls it a good sign is selling the child short by the ounce.

\item A wet pot is not set in the sun and a wet pot is not set near the door. You will pay for both in the thaw. Fire does not know a child is sorry; feed it and say nothing.

\end{enumerate}

\subsection*{Of the wheel and the ear}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item Knock with the knuckle, never the nail and never the flat of the hand. The hand says what it wants from the pot; the knuckle says what the pot has. This rule is the whole trade and the rest are its corners.

\item A sound pot under the knuckle gives its full note. A cracked pot answers flat, small and dead, and the sound stops at the surface and will not go through. A pot that answers flat is a pot gone wrong. It is broken at the door, not mended and sold, and the yard goes around the place where it stood.

\item A mended pot gives a note nearly full and never quite, and the yard calls it a pot that’ll do. Leave the crack showing. A repair that will not sing is a lie in clay, and a lie in clay is the only lie a kiln cannot burn clean.

\item The cupworm hides a flaw no knuckle will find. If a hand says a pot is wrong and the knuckle says it is right, set the pot aside another year. The yard has been wrong about pots and has never once been wrong about a hand that would not let a thing go.

\end{enumerate}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Crossed hard in charcoal across rule 13 in the Thin Year, in a potter’s hand that did not sign:} Strike \emph{the knuckle says it is right}. Set above: \emph{the ear hears it before the hand gets there, and the hand gets there before the knuckle}. I have not swept the charcoal. I have not put the struck words back. Both readings stand, because the bench has held both and the bench is older than either of us.\end{quote}

\subsection*{Of the kiln and the breath}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item No child sleeps in a closed kiln house. The kiln’s breath kills in sleep and is called a merciful death by those who have not had to carry the body out. A damper is a thing to be moved, not argued with.

\item Coals are banked under ash at dusk with the back of a broken pot, not with a shovel. Iron on iron wakes what should lie. The fire is left as it was found, so that the morning’s hand knows the night’s hand was there.

\item The master opens the kiln. The apprentice stands back from the lid, because a face over an open kiln learns nothing and loses its eyebrows. The kiln takes its breath in fours and a gap; a man who counts the gap aloud will be told to count the pots instead.

\end{enumerate}

\subsection*{Of the term and the debt}

Condition — Term — What gathers\par

House child, taken at nine — seven years — The note of the pot; nothing written against the boy\par

Child bound by debt — seven years, or as entered — Grey Ash in the household account, by the year and by the loaf\par

Debt left uncalled — as long as the house holds it — The debt is not forgiven. It lies where it was put, and a man goes around it as around Ash in a corner\par

Kept hand — until returned thin — No measure in the house’s roll; the house keeps the body and not the name\par

Foundling with a slate-name only — until a hearth claims him — A coat anybody can wear, and a debt nobody has entered yet\par

Widow holding a fire — by the mark, confirmed — The fire must not go out; the mark is touched before openings only\par

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item Seven years is the common term and not a short one. Interest gathers as grey Ash in the household accounts, which is why the house keeps its roll dry and why a debt left uncalled is worse than a debt called: a called debt has an end, and an uncalled one has only a place.

\item A clay-bound child sleeps in the loft and a taken child sleeps under the roof. This is a poor household’s sorting of its own members, and it is called kindness, and it is not entered anywhere. Ask the pot. The pot is more use.

\end{enumerate}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{In the Thane’s narrow upright hand, above rule 7:} The apprentice is kept. \emph{Underneath, in mine:} I had written that the apprentice is paid. He is not paid. He is fed, and the feeding goes into no figure, which is why it can be done. I have left my word standing under his, since a man should be able to see the thing he was told to change.\end{quote}

\subsection*{Of the levy and the First Firing}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item Two levies are called at the Cross, and the moot shouts at both. The levy of clay is worked out in barrow-loads and the levy of warmth in figures. The second is the heavier, and the notice says one in twelve. A household that has heard otherwise has heard wrong. The notice is what a man can be seen reading.

\item The levy is called; it is not called by the Thane, or by the bench, or by the house that pays it. The figure stands as read, and there will be a slate at the watch if the house wants it again. The red wool cord is folded into its drawer before the Thane goes home, and the bench does not follow him.

\item At twelve the child makes a pot, fires it and knocks it with a knuckle. A clear note means a feast; a flat note means another year in the yard. A foundling with no kiln of his own is judged on a pot made in the yard of the house that took him. The feast is bread and a pig’s trotter and nothing that needs entering.

\end{enumerate}

\subsection*{The wheel-song, pasted to the back}

\emph{Sung at the second firing, standing, with the slip still on the forearms. The yard says the refrain together. Nobody sings it at the First Firing, and nobody says why.}

\begin{quote}\itshape A dish of slip and a dish of water,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape a knuckle for the thing that matters;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the wheel goes round and the yard goes round,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the pot says what the pot has found.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Leave the crack showing,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape feed the fire, ask the pot;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape four for the corners, four for the wall,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the place where the fifth should be.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape I made a pot and the pot said no;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape I knocked it twice and it told me so.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape The sun’s no friend and the fire’s no friend\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape to a pot that’s cracked before the end.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Leave the crack showing,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape feed the fire, ask the pot;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape seven for the hand and one for the debt,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the slate stands in for the lot.\end{quote}

The press of wet reed across the second verse came from the bench standing in the rain at the Weir, where it went with a survey party that wanted a rule read in the open air. I have flattened it as well as I could. The words are plain enough under it.

\subsection*{What the two borrowed hands did}

The Thane’s clerk struck \emph{the apprentice is paid} and set \emph{kept} above. He left my figure for the term standing, saying a number is a number and a word is a word and the one has no business correcting the other. A potter struck the knuckle in rule 12 and put the ear in its place, and would not sign. The charcoal has come off on the fold and I have not brushed it away. A rule that two men have argued over is a rule that has been used.

\subsection*{At the foot, in a hand nobody will own}

\begin{quote}\itshape The fire is not entered. The hand is.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape That is the whole of the trade.\end{quote}

I have asked the potters, the Thane’s clerk and a man who came up from Slate Row, and had three answers and no hand. I have left the two lines where they were written. The leaf goes back under the moot-post nail and the bench onto the Cross; tomorrow a house will come to take a child, and I shall read what stands here, and by afternoon the charcoal will have come off on another sleeve.

\clearpage\phantomsection\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{The Arm and the Cord, Being the Standing Rules of the Reed-Cutters of the Weir for the Taking, Walking, Cutting and Trying of Apprentices in the Beds Below Sill, with the Table of Walkings, the Bundle-Song Pasted Inside the Cover, Two Corrections in Borrowed Hands, and a Line at the Foot Nobody Will Own}
\CRsheetheading{The Arm and the Cord, Being the Standing Rules of the Reed-Cutters of the Weir for the Taking, Walking, Cutting and Trying of Apprentices in the Beds Below Sill, with the Table of Walkings, the Bundle-Song Pasted Inside the Cover, Two Corrections in Borrowed Hands, and a Line at the Foot Nobody Will Own}
{\centering\FellFont\itshape\footnotesize\color{faded} A cutter’s leaf of rules carried in the lining of a coat against the leading rope; the rules set down in short sayings and half-sentences, the walkings and the faults in tables, the bundle-song pasted inside the cover, a knot set down in reed-ash in the margin and gone by noon, two corrections in the narrow upright hand of borrowed clerks, one line struck in charcoal by a woman who would not sign it, and a line at the foot in a hand nobody will own · Gathered at the Weir one league upriver of Sill in Reed of Y.H. 812, the Thin Year of the Long Cold, and carried forward at the Opening of the Slates into Y.H. 813; written by Nall of the Weir, a cutter who has kept the leading rope for nineteen years, on the back of a district tally spoiled when the river came up over it, and kept dry in the oiled lining of the coat that holds the rope. It survives with grey reed-ash at the head off the flat blessing stone, silt worked into the gutter and into the grain of the fold, the press of a wet bundle across the song, a thumb of tar off the leading rope at the head, a smear of eel slime along the second leaf, salt gone white at a wrist-print, a brine-gull’s peck through one word of the last verse, a ring of small ale at the foot left by a boatman who would not drink with cutters, a grey Ash print along the outer fold that is not mine and that I have not swept, two corrections in borrowed Ledgerhand standing above my words, one charcoal line struck and written again underneath, and the line at the foot which nobody has claimed\par}\medskip
I keep the leading rope at the Weir, and this leaf goes in the coat lining against it. A child comes down the plank walk at twelve with nothing in the hands and asks what a cutter is for, and I tell him: to carry what the arm says is there, and to come back by the same road. Then I set him to lifting a bundle and setting it down again on the flat stone. There is no lesson before that one.

These rules were gathered in the year the river came up twice and the reed stood too long, and they are carried forward in a coat and not from a book. A rule nobody has had to use is a rule nobody can carry. These have been carried. I set them down in the words we say, short words and often directions, and where a clerk has put a figure in the place of a direction I have left both standing.
