A man at first light wants to know which way to walk, not what the walk is worth.

\subsection*{The rules as they stand in the coat}

\subsection*{Of the taking}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item The Weir takes a child at twelve, by the rope and not by a house. A house may ask for the child and may not keep him. The child gives up a day and comes back by dusk with a bundle he did not have in the morning.

\item A child out of the bog comes with a reed-name, and the reed-name is enough. A child out of Sill comes with a house-name and leaves it below the bridge. We do not write either. We do not sit at a table where a slate is open, and no slate has ever been set at the Weir for a taking.

\item What is kept is the day the child first carried a bundle the length of the boards without setting it down, tied low in the cord with the teeth. A day tied in the cord is a day a man can find again by the feel of the knot, which is all a day is owed.

\item A child is taken by the arm and not by the eye. A child who judges a bundle by the weight settling into the forearm is taken. A child who counts the stalks is set to stacking and sent home at dusk, and may come again when the reed has stood.

\item A cutter’s child is not asked whether he wants the beds. He is asked whether he knows what is bought: silt to the knee, a rope that takes the wet, and hands that learn the weight before the price. The cutter cuts. The wanting comes after, or it does not.

\end{enumerate}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{In the narrow upright hand of a clerk of the factor at Greybank, against rule 3:} The taking is entered; one day, one bundle. \emph{Underneath, in mine:} I had written that the day is tied low with the teeth. He has entered the teeth as a figure and the bundle as a unit. A unit is a thing that can be carried up the road in a cuff. I have left both, because a man should see what was done to the day.\end{quote}

\subsection*{Of the arm}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item A bundle is counted in the arm that carries it. The hands that cut it are counted in nothing at all. Say this to a woman at the racks who asks what the bundle holds, and go on with the next armful. Do not say it a second time; the second time becomes an answer and an answer can be entered.

\item The arm tells what was carried and never what it cost. A cost asked as a direction is answered with a direction: downriver at first light, back over the boards at dusk, and the river in between. If the woman asks again, give her the weather. The weather has never yet been entered.

\item A wet bundle is lighter to lift and harder to learn. If a child brings back his first bundle wet, he is not yet of the bog; send him again when the reed has stood and the water is off it. Do not tell him he failed. He will know it in the forearm, which is where the knowing belongs.

\item A bundle is set on the stone and never in the silt. Silt gathers in a bundle laid down and becomes a weight nobody carried and everybody pays. Lift it off; leave the silt where it fell; say nothing to the pot or the slate about it.

\end{enumerate}

\subsection*{Of the going-downriver and the coming-back}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item A day’s work is a going-downriver and a coming-back. It is not a figure. A man who has walked it knows how far it was by where the arm begins to shake, and no slate in Sill has a column that will hold the shake.

\item The plank walk has a board that gives under a boot. Walk across it as across the rest of the boards. A woman with a creel takes the landing sideways, one hand out to the rail, and goes on selling; nobody makes a fall of it and nobody mends the board before the thaw.

\item The traps stand with their mouths upriver, so an eel goes in and cannot find the way out. The eels run whether anybody blesses them or not. On the fifteenth of Ilmen the hearth-maids bless the weir and the traps from the flat stone; stand where you are and do not look at the stone while the words are said. The blessing is the women’s. The run is the river’s.

\item At the turn of the day, straighten the cord on the flat stone. The stone lies flat and has a crossed mark in it older than any cutter’s name. Do not ask the stone what it signifies. Give the date of the blessing if a man asks twice, and give the same date a third way if he asks a third.

\end{enumerate}

\subsection*{Of the cord}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item The tally is a length of grey wool or reed-fibre with knots set at the lengths a man’s arm can judge, and one tied low with the teeth and a pull of the thumb. It is carried inside the coat. It would burn if put to a flame, and no clerk can take a figure from it. This is not a virtue in the cord; it is a use a man has found for a piece of wool.

\item Turn it once so the knots stand. Look at it yourself. Tie what must be tied, bite the end off, and put it back inside the coat with the flat of the hand. Do not count it aloud. A cord counted aloud is a cord with a figure in it, and a figure goes up the road.

\item To a woman who says she cannot read a cord, say \emph{You can ask the cord} and \emph{No more can the Court}. Say nothing after. The cord knows what the mouth will not say; the mouth knows what the cord will not count. Keep the two apart. Laying them together is a trade no honest house makes.

\item Do not lay the cord beside the knots a woman keeps at the lower boards or the eel-seller’s two twists at the Fishstairs. Three keepings laid together make a tally, and a tally wants a reader, and no reader stood at the Weir.

\end{enumerate}

\subsection*{The walkings}

\emph{Kept in the corner of the coat lining where the days leave off. A day is tied, not written; an entered cutter could be called back to a road he has walked.}

Condition — What is kept — What is done — Discharged\par

Child taken at twelve — the day first carried, tied low — bundle lifted and set on the stone — when the arm judges without the eye\par

First bundle brought back wet — nothing tied — child sent again when the reed has stood — when the bundle comes back dry\par

Woman with a creel at the landing — nothing — she takes the boards sideways — not entered by us\par

One who does not come back at dusk — a knot low in the cord — his place gone around with a look — never\par

Knots at the lower boards — by the woman who tied them — looked at by her and nobody else — not ours to discharge\par

The leading rope — the rope itself — straightened at the turn of the day — kept by whoever holds it\par

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item There is no term in years. A cutter stays while the rope is in his hand and goes with nothing written down. The knot for one who does not come back at dusk is not taken out to make the cord come even; a cord kept even has forgot who tied it.

\end{enumerate}

\subsection*{Of faults and their correcting}

Fault — As corrected at the Weir\par

Stalks counted instead of carried — Bundle set down; child set to stacking until the arm learns\par

Bundle laid in the silt — Lifted; silt left where it fell; nothing entered\par

Wet bundle taken for a dry — Child sent again after the reed has stood\par

Cord counted aloud — The count stopped; the knot tied low with teeth, in silence\par

A figure set where a going-downriver stood — Figure struck; \emph{downriver and back} set underneath\par

Cord laid beside another keeping — Put back inside the coat; a hand’s breadth kept between\par

A verb struck out of a rule — Put back underneath, where the clerk can see it\par

A charcoal line swept from the stone — Not swept; the line written again below\par

\subsection*{The bundle-song, pasted inside the cover}

\emph{Sung low going downriver at first light and again coming back over the boards, with the bundle on the shoulder and the cord inside the coat. Never at the Fish Blessing, and never twice in one house. The refrain is said with the whole crew; the last line belongs to whoever carried the most that day, and is not claimed.}

\begin{quote}\itshape Down at first light and back by the stone,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape a bundle on the shoulder and a cord in the coat;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the arm knows the weight and the arm knows the bend,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the slate knows nothing the river won’t take.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Ask the arm. Ask the cord.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape What it carried, not what it cost.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Four to the bundle and one gone green,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the eels go in where the mouths have been;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the stone lies flat and the traps lie still,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the run comes up whether we bless or not.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Ask the arm. Ask the cord.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape What it carried, not what it cost.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape A knot for the going and a knot for the back,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and one tied low where the thumb can track;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape no figure on the boards, no name in the tin,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the Court may ask the cord if it can.\end{quote}

The press of the wet bundle across the middle verse came from a morning the song was sung under a load that had not stood long enough. I have flattened the leaf as I could. The brine-gull took the last word of the last line; I have not written it back in. A verse with a word gone is a verse said slowly, and all of ours are said slowly.

\subsection*{What the borrowed hands did}

The Greybank clerk wrote \emph{one day, one bundle} above rule 3 and set \emph{transport} over \emph{carried} wherever I had put the word. Both stand. His \emph{transport} is true of a cart and a barge and a man with a load on his shoulder, which is why it is true of nobody. I have put \emph{carried} back underneath.

A clerk come down from Slate Row wrote \emph{the cost is not entered} above \emph{give her the weather} and put a round nought where the low knot is, with \emph{vacancy} beside it. The place was a knot before he numbered it. I have left his nought above and my knot underneath, because a figure and a piece of wool have never agreed at the Weir and are not going to begin here.

A woman at the lower boards wrote in charcoal, struck it, and wrote it again below:

\begin{quote}\itshape A knot is not a figure. Ask the wool.\end{quote}

She would not put her name to it. I have not swept the charcoal or put the struck line back.

\subsection*{At the head and in the gutter}

The grey at the head is reed-ash off the flat stone, where a fire was made of the stalks that would not stand; it goes into the grain and no wet sleeve takes it out. The silt in the gutter came up the river on the day the tally was spoiled and is still in the second leaf. The press across the song is wet reed, and goes soft when the weather goes soft. The tar is off the leading rope, from the hand that holds it while the other writes. The eel slime came off a trap set down while its owner counted the boats going up; he did not wipe it and I have not. The white at the wrist-print is salt from a woman who asked what the bundle held and went away with the answer she was given. The ale ring is a boatman’s; he would not drink with cutters and set his cup on the corner all the same. The grey along the outer fold is not mine and not the clerk’s, and I have not swept it. There is no Last Day at a Weir.

\subsection*{At the foot, in a hand nobody will own}

\begin{quote}\itshape The cord keeps the going. The arm keeps the weight. The river keeps the man who goes down and does not come back.\end{quote}

I asked a woman at the lower boards, the eel-seller below the bridge, and a man come up from Slate Row, and had three answers and no hand, as I have had before. I have left the lines where they were written. The leaf goes back into the lining and the rope goes back into the hand. Tomorrow a child will come down at twelve with nothing in the hands, and I shall set him to lifting a bundle before I tell him what a cutter is for, and by dusk the cord will have one more knot tied low with teeth, and the Court may ask the cord if it can.

\clearpage\phantomsection\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{The Articles of the Floor, Being the Standing Rules of the Clamp-Masters of Keld Keep for the Taking, Trying, Cutting and Paying Out of Apprentices at the Duelling Floor Beneath the First Seam, with the Table of Years, the Tally of Hands, the Floor-Song Pasted Inside the Cover, Two Corrections in a Survey-Clerk’s Upright Hand, One Line Struck in Charcoal by a Cutter Who Would Not Sign It, and a Line at the Foot Nobody Will Own}
\CRsheetheading{The Articles of the Floor, Being the Standing Rules of the Clamp-Masters of Keld Keep for the Taking, Trying, Cutting and Paying Out of Apprentices at the Duelling Floor Beneath the First Seam, with the Table of Years, the Tally of Hands, the Floor-Song Pasted Inside the Cover, Two Corrections in a Survey-Clerk’s Upright Hand, One Line Struck in Charcoal by a Cutter Who Would Not Sign It, and a Line at the Foot Nobody Will Own}
{\centering\FellFont\itshape\footnotesize\color{faded} A clamp-room leaf of rules in the hand of the under-master who keeps the irons and the roll of hands at the Duelling Floor, written on the back of a spoiled rim-seam tally in Grathic letters with the Keldish endings struck off, hung on a spike beside the clamp-rack; the articles in the hard short Rim speech, the years and the hands in tables, the floor-song pasted inside the cover, a warm-stone shaving shut in the second fold, two corrections in the narrow upright Ledgerhand of a Court survey-clerk, one line struck hard in charcoal, and a line at the foot in a hand nobody will own · First gathered at Keld Keep in Y.H. 741, the year Karric VII shut the Cold Pass and the Order found it had a border it had not asked for, and copied forward from the rack and not from a book; this leaf written in Stone of Y.H. 813 by Vek of the Floor, under-master, who has kept the irons and said the count over the clamp-rack for nineteen years and carries a first way in his own forearm that aches before the thaw; carried forward at the Opening of the Slates, Ilmen 1, Y.H. 814. It survives hung on its spike in the clamp-room off the Duelling Floor, soft at the fold and stiff with coal smut at the head, with an iron-red thumb off the mine-reeve’s checking point, a clamp-bite taken out of the upper corner, a lamp-scorch that has eaten the last word of rule 9 and left the sense standing, a warm-stone shaving shut in the second fold that is warm on the coldest morning and is never lent, a bead of Ninth Gallery lead pressed into the gutter, a frost-feather pressed flat that was gone by noon, a grey thumb along the outer fold that is not mine and not the reeve’s, two corrections in the Court’s upright hand, one charcoal line struck and written again underneath, and a line at the foot nobody will own.\par}\medskip
I keep the irons and the roll of hands at the Floor, in the stone beneath the Keep where the shaft ends and the rock has been cut level for bouts. A boy comes up from the Descent with a number new in his arm and a warm-stone in his palm, and the Order takes him if he came up. The mine-reeve checks his figure in red before he is let past the post, and there is no second asking. A Court survey-clerk comes up with a soft cuff, writes that instruction is supplied and no wage arises, and goes away believing he has entered a trade. I set the rules down as they stand. Where a hand has corrected me I have left both readings.

These are not new articles. They were gathered in the year the pass was shut, when the Keep got a border and the Order got boys from both sides of it. A rule with no clamp-bite on it is a rule nobody has had to hold. These have been held.

\subsection*{The articles as they stand at the Floor}

\subsection*{Of the taking}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item The Order takes the boy, not his house. A house may bring him to the mouth and feed him and bury him if he does not come up; from the morning he holds a clamp with the bite toward him he answers to the Floor. The family is paid in iron for the one who does not come back, which is the only price in Keld paid without a bargain.

\item He is taken the morning after his Descent, being thirteen, and not before he has come up with the number he went down with or a number the mountain gave him. A boy who comes back thin has the old numbers cut out and new ones put in. Nobody asks him which count is his; the mine-reeve enters the later and leaves the earlier standing in the skin.

\item He states what he holds before he says who he is. This is done at the Warden’s hall, at the gate and here, as a courtesy, so that no boy can say he was not told. A lowlander who gives his name first is sent back to the foot of the post to begin again. I am not shaming him. A name is a thing a man can change at the next well; the number goes down with him.

\item The Order keeps the method of the first way within Keldish hands. A lowlander may be taught it for iron, and often is. He is never taught it for nothing. A thing given free is entered against the giver, and there is no house in Keld that will carry that entry.

\item He is kept, not hired. He eats from the Floor’s dish, sleeps in the loft above the clamp-rack, and what he makes goes to the Floor and comes back as bread and a place by the brazier, neither entered. A master who tells a boy he is paid tells a true thing about a figure and a false thing about a living.

\end{enumerate}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{In the narrow upright hand of a Court survey-clerk, against rule 5:} Apprentice retained at the Floor. No wage arising. \emph{Underneath, in mine:} I had written \emph{kept}. He strikes a mouth wherever he finds one. I have put the boy back under the figure, because a figure eats no bread and sleeps in no loft. Both stand.\end{quote}

\subsection*{Of the number}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item The number is part of the name. The name is not part of the number. Ask a Keldishman who he is and he will give the figure first and the word after, the way a man lifts a stone before he looks under it.

\item The number stands. Do not say it twice. To say it twice is to ask the mountain to make it other than it was, and the mountain keeps no second figure.

\item At the end of the Floor there is a cup that nobody takes, set there for the man whose number was changed twice. It is not a memorial and it is never filled. A boy who asks whose cup it is is told to count the clamps. There are ten, and the tenth has never been taken off its nail.

\end{enumerate}

\subsection*{Of the way and the two bites}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item Cut across a surface way in the forearm and hold it open while it scars. This is the first way. It aches before the thaw and after, and a man answers to whichever number the room has given him. An old cutter told me a way is a door cut in the wall of a man, and that a door once cut is not a door that can be shut. I have set that down in his words, which are fewer than mine.

\end{enumerate}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{The lamp-scorch took the last word of this rule and left the sense, which is more than the Court has ever taken from a man. I have not written the word back.}\end{quote}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item A fortnight is given to the arm after the cutting. It is a useless arm and the boy is not sent to the rack with it. A master who sets him there to hurry the scar is buying a hand with a fortnight and paying for it with the whole life.

\item Tap before you cut. A sound block answers full under the knuckle; one with a flaw gives back a small dry sound. The same goes for an arm. A boy who cuts a way across a flaw he did not tap is sent to the wall to learn the note, and the wall does not answer him.

\item One bite holds the vessel whole. One bite takes the hand off a man. It is the same bite. Cold iron takes and does not give back; clamp a way past the turning of the watch and the arm below goes the colour of old rope and does not come back. The iron has not asked anybody’s opinion.

\item Trial of hot iron is put to the palm when a man is to be trusted with the racks. Put hot iron to the palm and ask a man if he owes; the honest answer leaves the hand dead. There have been a great many honest men at this Floor with dead hands. I have set the number down in the tally below and have not set what it cost, because the tally has no column for a hand.

\end{enumerate}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Struck hard in charcoal against rule 13, in a cutter’s hand that did not sign:} Mine is dead and I answered true. They entered the honesty and not the hand. \emph{In mine, below:} I have left his line struck above mine and mine standing under, so a boy can see what was said and what was done to it. The charcoal has come off on the fold and I have not brushed it away.\end{quote}

\subsection*{The table of years}

\emph{Kept by the boy who sweeps the clamp-room, in a hand that does not change between one line and the next.}

Year — At the Floor — What is taken\par

Thirteen — The Descent; the number cut; a warm-stone given after the knife — The habit of giving a name before a figure\par

Fourteen — Carry and sweep the irons; tap blocks and learn the full note — The birth-name, said once at the taking and not used at the Floor\par

Fifteen — The first way; the fortnight; the arm kept from the rack — The belief that a thing cut can be uncut\par

Sixteen — A first bout; the clamp held and loosed at the word — The last of a boy’s account with any house\par

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item Sixteen is the common end of a keeping and not a short one. Eleven months is the common end of a bought life and is not a keeping at all. A boy who has been through the years is not paid out and sent down the road; he stays where the Floor needs him, at the rack or on a pass or in a room where a man must state a figure before a name. The Floor does not choose which. The arm does, and the Warden after it.

\end{enumerate}

\subsection*{The tally of hands}

\emph{Kept by the under-master. The figure is the mine-reeve’s and is set first. What stands beneath it is mine and is not a figure.}

Condition — The reeve’s figure — What stands beneath\par

Boy taken the morning after the Descent — one apprentice, current, no wage arising — A boy who eats from the dish\par

The first way — permanent mark; no deduction arises — A door cut in the wall of a man\par

Hot iron trial — honesty entered — A hand that cannot lift a cup\par

Clamp left past the watch — one hand, current; measure not affected — The hand kept; the boy sent up the rope\par

A boy who does not come up — paid in iron — Iron, and the number called once\par

A block that answers dry — not cut; not entered — The flaw the knuckle found\par

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item The reeve enters a hand that cannot close as one hand, current, measure not affected. It is a true figure and a true figure about the wrong thing. I have set what it cost beneath it, where a clerk can see it and choose not to read it.

\end{enumerate}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{In the narrow upright hand of the Court clerk, against that row:} One hand, current; measure not affected. \emph{In mine, underneath:} It is a hand. I did not learn it from a page, which is the only reason I can still say it. Both stand.\end{quote}

\subsection*{Of the sweating and the grub}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item The mine sweats before it gives. In the Ninth Gallery the rock sweats where no seam was cut, the air turns sweetish and hot, and the smell of hot lead comes up before anything shows. That smell is the whole warning a man gets. No boy is sent down to a sweating to learn it; a boy who has smelt it once does not want a second lesson, and a boy who has not will never believe it matters.

\item The reeve stops a shift for one grub. This is not kindness. He counts every life that goes down and every ember of iron that comes up, and those two figures have never agreed and were never meant to. A stopped shift is a figure that does not balance. He stops it anyway.

\item Warm-stone is sold and is never lent. It holds heat longer than anything else in Sarn, and a man who goes up without a stone borrows from the next man who has one, or turns back; there is no lending here. The shaving swept from the cutting floor is sold by the half-mark and not given away. A thing that can be lent has a place in somebody’s account. A thing sold is paid for, which is cleaner.

\item Read the frost-feather at the mouth before the sun takes it. It grows where the Warm has lately gone out of the stone and is gone by noon. A feather on the lip means a man is sent to find where it went, and the finding is still owed when the feather is gone.

\end{enumerate}

\subsection*{Of the tin and the neighbours}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item There is a tin lined with warm-stone in the survey room off the Floor. It is kept shut. No boy in his years at the Floor is shown it and no boy is told what is in it; he learns that there is a thing not to ask after, which is the only instruction in this house given without a demonstration.

\item The Vorr sit at the stones and are not asked to translate. The Deep Hand is copied and not read. When they come down with a figure they say the numbers are correct, which is not an answer to the question put. These are the Floor’s neighbours, set down here so that a boy may know which questions to leave alone.

\end{enumerate}

\subsection*{The floor-song, pasted inside the cover}

\emph{Sung at the first opening of a way, standing, with the arm across the block and the clamp held in the teeth. Never sung after a bout and never while the mine-reeve’s clerk is at the tally. The last two lines belong to the boys; the masters sing them wrong on purpose, and no boy has ever been told why.}

\begin{quote}\itshape Iron on the block and iron at the door,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape state what you hold and then say who you were;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape cut it across and hold it while it scars,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape a way is a door and the arm is the wall.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape One bite to hold and one to take,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the hand knows which the mouth will mistake;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape four to the cut and a slack for the cup,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the tenth clamp hangs where no one takes it down.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Do not ask the stone what it wants of you,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the stone has no want and the lead smells true;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape hold till the watch turns, then let the iron go ---\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the arm below is the colour of rope.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Iron on the block and iron at the door,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape one for the boy and one for the reeve’s score;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the honest hand leaves the cup where it stood,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the number stands where the number stood.\end{quote}

The press of a lamp-cloth across the second verse came from the song being held up to the lamp at the change of shift. I have flattened it; the words hold.

\subsection*{What the borrowed hands did}

A Court survey-clerk borrowed the leaf at Greybank with ink in two fingers of a soft cuff, and took the verbs out as though a verb were a thing a man could smuggle up the Rim Road in a sleeve.

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item Against \emph{the Order takes the boy, not his house} he set \emph{Instruction is supplied. No wage arising.} I have put the boy back underneath, because a figure eats no bread and sleeps in no loft.

\item Against \emph{a way once cut stays cut} he set \emph{the condition is permanent.} He has made a door into a state and left the man who cut it out of the sentence. I have set mine under his.

\end{itemize}

The other hand is charcoal, a cutter of the Floor who would not sign. Against rule 13 he struck \emph{leaves the hand dead} and wrote above, \emph{Mine is dead and I answered true. They entered the honesty and not the hand.} I have left his line struck above mine and mine standing under. A rule two men have argued over is a rule that has been held.

\subsection*{At the head and in the gutter}

The smut at the head is coal off the sleeve I wipe the rack with; it is in the grain and no wet sleeve takes it out. The iron-red thumb is the reeve’s point, checking a boy who gave a figure that would not hold; he did not look at me and I did not look at the boy. The corner has had a clamp-bite taken out of it by a man showing his brother how the iron closes; both were honest afterwards and one cannot lift a cup. The shaving in the fold is warm-stone swept from the cutting floor, kept and not lent; it is warm on the coldest morning and I have not sold it. The bead is lead out of the Ninth Gallery, where the rock sweats and the smell gives what warning it gives; a man laid it down and did not take it up. The feather pressed flat was on the mouth stone after a warm night and was gone by the time I found the leaf to put it in. The grey along the outer fold is not mine and not the reeve’s, and I have not swept it. There is no Last Day beneath this Keep and nothing here is burnt in the morning and called dealt with.

\subsection*{At the foot, in a hand nobody will own}

\begin{quote}\itshape The number goes down and the name goes home.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape The clamp keeps the hand, and the Floor keeps the count.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape The house that sent the boy is paid in iron and keeps nothing.\end{quote}

I asked a rack-master, a Court clerk come up from Greybank, and a woman who counts at the mouth, and had three answers and no hand. I have left the lines where they were written. The leaf goes back on its spike and the coal takes another word by the next shift. Tomorrow a boy will come up from the Descent with a number new in his arm, and I shall put a clamp in his hand with the bite toward him, state the count before his name, and say nothing about the cup at the end of the Floor.

\clearpage\phantomsection\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{The Asking-Cord at the Standing Post, Being Four Riddles Tied and a Fifth Left Untied, the Knot Nobody Can Read, and the Figure a Factor’s Clerk Set Above It}
\CRsheetheading{The Asking-Cord at the Standing Post, Being Four Riddles Tied and a Fifth Left Untied, the Knot Nobody Can Read, and the Figure a Factor’s Clerk Set Above It}
{\centering\FellFont\itshape\footnotesize\color{faded} A fire-keeper’s telling of a winter’s riddling on the back boards at the Post, set down in Grathic letters though the questions were put in Fen Cant and are not written anywhere else; the riddles in the short nose-speech with the ends let fall into the mud, the answers tied in grey wool and read by touch, the wagers in peat-blocks laid against the hut wall, a tally nicked into the door-lintel with a fish-hook, a factor’s clerk’s entry in narrow upright Ledgerhand above, a slate-runner’s line in the slant of a carried hand, and one line at the foot in a hand nobody will own · Written in Stone of Y.H. 812, the Thin Year of the Long Cold, at the Standing Post in the Fenmarch, by Wen, who keeps the little fire on the back boards and the cord of answers that hangs beside it, from a night told over by a reed-cutter come up across the winter way; carried down the marsh road in Ilmen of Y.H. 813 and copied at Greybank onto the back of a spoiled eel-tribute tally, sewn with eel-sinew into a fold of oiled reed and kept under the loose board with the market stick and the gathered fen sayings. It survives with a peat thumb worked into the head, a bog-water tideline along the gutter, a pressed reed across the third leaf, a fish-hook nick at the fore-edge, eel slime shut in the fold off a basket set down there, a glass-eel thread fine as a hair in the lower margin, a grey Ash print along the outer fold which nobody will own, a knot of grey wool tied through a hole in the first leaf which the writer will not undo, the clerk’s narrow correction above the answers, the runner’s sloping line below it, and the line at the foot which has never been claimed\par}\medskip
I keep the little fire on the back boards at the Post and the cord of answers that hangs beside it. It is one work with two hands: the fire must be coaxed before anybody is looked at, and the cord must be taken up before a question is heard, and neither asks who laid the peat or tied the wool. In Stone the bog bears and the winter way goes east over it with carts that pay nothing and no reeve will stand on it, so there comes a fortnight in which the only trade on these boards is questions.

Put a question to a man and you have a difference with him before you have an answer. Put it to the board and it stays a question. A question whose answer you already know is a riddle, which is a thing the Fen can afford; a question whose answer nobody knows is a wager, and there is wagering enough here without a fire in it.

We answer in knots. Fen Cant is not written and a knot keeps when paper has gone soft at Greybank, which is not an argument for knots so much as a fact about paper. Where no Grathic word will come I have tied a knot in the margin, and I have put no word into it. Say these low, through the nose, and let the last word fall into the mud instead of finishing it. Do not look at the person you say them to.

\subsection*{The manner of the cord}

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item A riddle is put once to the board. Ask for it again and you lay a peat-block by the fire, because the second asking is for your own pleasure and not for the hut.

\item Answer in one knot. A second knot is a different answer and is not read. A man who ties two has not understood the first.

\item The judge is the board. I say whether a knot serves and I do not say why. A reason given is a riddle given away for nothing, and the giver can take it down the mud road and sell it at the Cross.

\item The wager is a peat-block laid against the wall where the fire can see it. We count them by touch and not by eye, because the eye listens to the face and the fingers do not.

\item No slate lies on the back boards. A slate turns a question into a figure and the figure goes up to Greybank in a clean hand and comes back as something a household owes.

\item The asking-cord is the only cord in the Fen that is never untied. Ours are tied when a thing is owed and loosed when it is paid, but a riddle paid is a riddle spent, and the answer goes home in the asker’s mouth and is not entered anywhere.

\end{itemize}

There had been eleven nights of it before the Long Cold shut the road, and there would be no more until the ice went. This is the one the reed-cutter told over, in the words he used, which are short and have their ends dropped.

\subsection*{The four that were tied}

The first went to the reed-cutter himself, come up over the winter way with a bundle on his back and the snow still standing on his shoulders. He had his answer before the verse was out, which is why he never lays a peat-block and is always first. He tied it with his teeth because both his hands were full of reed.

\begin{quote}\itshape Ten go over and none come back wet,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape no reeve will stand where the cart went;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape it is paid by nobody and kept by none ---\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape what bears the crossing?\end{quote}

The winter way. He tied one loop and drew it low, the way a man ties what he cannot see. Nobody asked him which cart had gone over, which is the proper way to leave a crossing alone.

The second went to a girl who dips eels at the Line and answers a board before she answers a person.

\begin{quote}\itshape I keep the warm behind the head;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape cut me there and you learn nothing.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Count me going and count me coming,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape my basket has no column for me ---\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape what am I?\end{quote}

An eel. She tied two turns with a space between them and set the cord back in my hand without letting me see her thumb do it. Two counts, going and coming, and no column for either. When the factor’s man asked which count she meant, she told him to ask the eel, which is the whole of the answer and the manner of it.

The third went to the man from Greybank, who had road-mud on his boots that had dried the colour of the clay dish and would not come off on the edge of his hand.

\begin{quote}\itshape It holds a whole country under a skin;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape we do not dig it out, we ask.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape It has no keys, no slate, no clean coat,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and a priest come up from the south called it a sister ---\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape what is it?\end{quote}

The peat, by the old name. He tied a square knot, neat enough to lie flat on a clerk’s table, and I made him tie it again, because a knot that lies flat is a knot somebody can read and this one was not meant for reading. He tied the second the way we do and put his hand over it a moment before he let go, which is not the manner of it either, though I have never known a man from the factor’s house do it any other way. The peat keeps what it keeps. It has no door for him to put his hand against.

The fourth I put to the fire, because the room had got noisy and wanted quieting, and a question put by the boards is not scored against anybody.

\begin{quote}\itshape A thing is lent and called a house;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape it stands on legs that are not its own.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape The water calls it in when it pleases\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the hut does not go with it ---\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape what is it?\end{quote}

Dry ground. An old woman who had come in to warm her hands put her palm flat on the cord and took it away again without tying anything. That is an answer in this country, and the oldest one here. I have seen a man from the College stand on the Post and ask where the dry ground is, and he was standing on it when he asked, and nobody told him, because a thing you point at is a thing you can put a figure to.

\subsection*{The fifth, which was tied low}

After the fourth the hut went quiet in the way a hut goes quiet when there is nothing left to say and nobody will leave. A child of the Post, nine or ten, who had been sitting with her back to the fire and her hands in her sleeves all evening, came and put her fist into the cord. She tied one knot below the others, low down where the fingers go by teeth and thumb and the eye cannot follow, and she set the cord back exactly where it hung. She did not say what the riddle was and nobody asked her. A knot tied low is a thing the tie-keeper knows and nobody else does, and asking a child to say it aloud is a way of making her lose it.

She went out on the winter way before the going of the light with the cord still warm from her hand. In the morning there was a round dry place on the wall by the fire where no peat-block had stood, and I have not found whose it was. I have not asked. The knot is still on the cord. It does not lie flat with the others and no thumb of mine has ever read it, which is how I know it was tied by somebody who did not want it carried away.

\subsection*{The tally, nicked in the lintel}

Question — Put by — Answer tied — Peat-block\par

The crossing — the reed-cutter — the winter way — laid, not counted\par

The two counts — a girl from the Line — an eel — laid, not counted\par

The sister — a man from Greybank — the peat — laid twice, once for the wrong knot\par

The house — the fire — dry ground — none\par

The low knot — a child of the Post — not read — not scored\par

\subsection*{What the factor’s clerk did}

A clerk of the factor’s house borrowed the leaf on a market morning when the square was full; there was ink settled in two fingers of a soft cuff and he laid his hand flat before his eye went to the words, which is the manner of that house. He set the questions down as \emph{queries entered} and the answers as \emph{responses recorded}, valued each peat-block at a half-mark of warm-stone and wrote \emph{gaming, not commercial} across the head of the tally, so that a night of asking came out as a night of trading with the profit left off. Against the low knot he wrote \emph{no answer tendered; struck}. He asked who had tied it. I told him a child of the Post, and that she had given no name to the riddle, which is a true thing and not the thing he wanted, and he wrote \emph{party unidentified}.

He also wrote \emph{one part in twelve reserved to the fire} above the peat-blocks, because one in twelve is printed and a printed thing travels. I have left his line standing. The fire has never asked for a share and has never kept a slate, but a figure is a thing that goes where the fire does not, and it is easier to write the figure than to sit and watch a peat-block burn.

I have set the cord over his hand and left his hand standing on the leaf, the way a board keeps a man’s weight and the water’s mark and does not choose between them. He takes out whoever did the thing, as though a sentence stood truer with nobody in it. I tie the doer back in, because a child of the Post wants to know which hand went into the cord, and there is always a hand.

\subsection*{In the margin, in a slate-runner’s sloping hand}

\begin{quote}\itshape I carry the slate edge-on and never look at what is on it. The figure that goes up to Greybank does not know what came over the winter way or who tied what by the fire. I have walked this road nine years and never opened one.\end{quote}

Below, in mine: she said it to the board and would not say it twice. I have not asked. A person who carries a slate is not a person who reads one, and the road cares about neither.

\subsection*{At the head and in the gutter}

The peat thumb at the head is mine; I hold the leaf down in the draught that comes up between the boards and do not know I have marked it, and peat goes into the grain and will not come out, which is why we sign in clay here and not in ink. The tideline is bog-water off a pail set down while I was telling the girl to eat and she would not. The pressed reed came from the reed-cutter’s bundle and has gone flat and pale where he laid it across the second leaf while he decided whether to pay for his second asking, and did not. The hook nick is from a basket set down by a man paying for six eels and charged for five, or the other way, which he has not settled. The slime in the fold came off that basket and goes soft when the weather goes soft, which tells me when to shut the oiled reed. The glass-eel thread in the lower margin is fine as a hair and came from nobody I can name. The grey along the outer fold came off a cuff that had no business lying on the back boards, and I have not swept it. There is a Last Day in Sill and the corners are swept there in the morning and burnt and called dealt with. There is no Last Day at the Post, and nothing here is swept while the bog is bearing. The knot of grey wool through the hole in the first leaf is mine, tied for the word that would not come into Grathic, and I will not undo it to see what is inside.

\subsection*{At the foot, in a hand nobody will own}

\begin{quote}\itshape Four answers went home in men’s mouths. One went down the winter way still tied.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape The board was answered. The slate was not.\end{quote}

I asked the reed-cutter, the girl from the Line and the man who came up from Greybank, and had three answers and no hand. I have left the lines where they were written. The leaf goes back under the loose board with the market stick and the sayings, and the cord goes back on its nail beside the fire. In Ilmen the weather will take the ice off the bog and the carts will pay to cross and there will be better things to do of an evening than ask one another what we already know. The child will be a year older and may come back and may not, and I shall not ask her about the low knot when she does. If the factor’s clerk comes again with his pen I shall let him count what can be counted, and I shall keep the cord where the fire can see it, because a knot is not a figure and a figure cannot sit here and warm itself.

\clearpage\phantomsection\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{The Articles of the Three Years, Being the Standing Rules of the College of Assessors in Slate Row for the Taking, Keeping and Trying of Apprentices in Ledgerhand, with the Weighing Rubrick and the Provost’s Corrections}
\CRsheetheading{The Articles of the Three Years, Being the Standing Rules of the College of Assessors in Slate Row for the Taking, Keeping and Trying of Apprentices in Ledgerhand, with the Weighing Rubrick and the Provost’s Corrections}
{\centering\FellFont\itshape\footnotesize\color{faded} A copyist’s fair copy of the College’s standing articles, kept by the under-clerk who holds the second file; the three years set out in a table, the faults and their corrections in a second, the copying-song pasted inside the cover, two corrections in the Provost’s narrow upright hand, one struck verb in a clerk’s hand, and a line at the foot nobody will own · First gathered in the Hearthseat in Y.H. 776, the year the College built its house in Sill’s own Slate Row, and copied forward from the tin at each Opening of the Slates; this leaf written by the under-clerk of the second file and carried through Y.H. 813. It survives folded inside the second file’s tin, soft at the fold, with slate dust worked into the gutter, a grey collector’s thumb at the head, iron-gall ink in the creases of the copyist’s two fingers, a damp tide-line from the sealed-file room along the foot, a green bead of lead-glaze from a glaze-mixer come up from High Kiln, one verb struck in a hand that is not the Provost’s, and a line at the foot that has never been claimed\par}\medskip
I keep the second file. It holds the names taken off the rolls, and I copy them in the same hand as the names that stayed, because a hand that changes between one name and the next is a hand that can be accused of feeling something. The College takes a boy with a name and teaches him to write a life with nobody in it. These are the rules by which that is done. I have set them down as they stand, and where a hand has corrected me I have left both readings.

The assessors are a guild of a sort, though the word is a clay-country one and is not used in Slate Row. These articles are not new. They were gathered in Y.H. 776, when it was found that a method could be kept longer than any man who used it. A rule with no thumb on it is a rule nobody has had to use. These have been used.

\subsection*{The articles, as they stand in Slate Row}

\subsection*{Of the taking}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item The College takes an apprentice, not a house. A house may bring a child, or a collector, or the Temple’s poor may be sent, but from the day of entering the child belongs to the College and to no house. He is given no kin. Graduates are given none either, which is the same rule said at the other end.

\end{enumerate}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item A child is taken at twelve, or in the year after, and entered for three years. A child taken later is entered for the same three. This is a kindness the College does not advertise and does not enter.

\end{enumerate}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item The birth-name is written once on the roll, in a careful hand, and then turned face under. A slate-name is entered in its place. The birth-name is not spoken in the teaching room. A boy who is called by it there writes his slate-name fifty times, and the fifty sheets are burned before he is let back to the copying.

\end{enumerate}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item An apprentice is kept, not hired. He eats from the College’s dish, sleeps in the College’s room, and what he earns goes to the College. The College does not pay him, and does not call him paid. What comes back comes back as bread and a bed, and neither is entered.

\end{enumerate}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item A boy who cannot learn the hand is taken off the rolls and entered in the second file. The file lies in its tin beside the sealed-file room and is not read at the Weighing. His entry is made in the same neat hand as an entry in the rolls, so that no man can tell, by looking at the writing alone, which boy stayed.

\end{enumerate}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{In a narrow upright hand, the verb struck from rule 4:} The apprentice is kept. \emph{Underneath, in the copyist’s hand:} I had written that he is fed. The Provost’s clerk strikes a verb wherever he finds one, even in a rule about food. I have left \emph{fed} standing under \emph{kept}; a boy can be kept and hungry in the same sentence, and the passive voice has room for both.\end{quote}

\subsection*{Of the hand}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item Ledgerhand is Grathic with the verbs removed, written upright and neat, all in the passive voice. The first exercise is to write a true sentence about a man and then take the man out of it. What is left is always true and can be read at the Weighing.

\end{enumerate}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item The passive voice is the College’s own. \emph{The measure was drawn} is true of every man who ever drew a measure, and a sentence true of everybody can be argued with by nobody. An apprentice who writes \emph{I drew} is told to write again. An apprentice who writes \emph{he drew} is told twice.

\end{enumerate}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item There are eleven words for a deduction. They are spoken in the teaching room in the second year, by the Provost or the officer he sends, and are not written in these articles. A boy who writes them on a slate copies the page again without them, and the slate is scraped clean in front of him. The words are not a secret. They are a trade.

\end{enumerate}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item No apprentice adds a column alone. Addition is done in the Weighing Hall, where figures are read aloud and not inspected. A column added alone will not agree with the notice, and what will not agree with the notice is copied again. An apprentice who needs to add is told that a man who can add is a man who can accuse, and is sent back to the copying.

\end{enumerate}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{In the Provost’s narrow hand, above rule 7:} The passive voice is used. \emph{Underneath, in mine:} I had written that it is chosen. A rule with nobody in it is a rule nobody can be thanked for and nobody blamed. I have left my word where he put his above it.\end{quote}

\subsection*{The three years}

Year — The exercise — What is taken\par

First — The upright hand; copying notices from the moot-post at the Cross — The boy’s own hand\par

Second — The passive voice; the eleven words, spoken only — The boy’s own name in a sentence\par

Third — The Weighing; the reading of a figure in a clean voice — The boy’s own voice, which he gets back only as the College’s\par

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item At the end of the third year the apprentice reads a figure aloud in the Weighing Hall, in a clean voice, with the Hearth-fire behind the grating and no priest or boy allowed to touch it. A reader who puts himself into the sentence is set back. The figure is the one the notice prints: one in twelve, as the notice says. There is no other figure in the room.

\end{enumerate}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item A whole return may be announced at the Weighing for a person who is not in the room. The apprentice does not ask where the person is. The College keeps a second file for the answers to questions of that kind, and the second file is not read aloud.

\end{enumerate}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item At the end of the three years the officer is given no house and no kin and is sent where the College sends him. His slate-name goes on the rolls in the same hand as his betters’. He does not take his birth-name with him, and the College does not take it from him; it is already face down.

\end{enumerate}

\subsection*{Of faults and their correcting}

Fault — Correction\par

A verb in the roll — The page copied again, in the same hand\par

A column added alone — The slate taken up for a tend\par

A birth-name spoken in the teaching room — Fifty sheets, burned before the boy\par

A figure read with feeling — The reader set back one year\par

A sealed file carried out of the room — The carrier’s own name entered in the second file\par

A slate lost — Paid in kind; a slate is a piece of stone and a name is not\par

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item The College keeps its rolls, its Weighing notices, its sealed files and the only right to write a lawful deduction. It keeps them in the Hearthseat. An apprentice who carries a sealed file beyond the room has his own name carried into the second file instead.

\end{enumerate}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item The Vorr sit at the survey table and are not asked to translate. The Deep Hand is copied and not read. These are the College’s enemies, set down here so that an apprentice may know which questions to leave alone.

\end{enumerate}

\subsection*{The copying-song}

\emph{Sung at the benches in the first year, under the breath, while the hand learns the upright stroke. Nobody sings it at the Weighing.}

\begin{quote}\itshape Ink in the crease of the thumb,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape slate dust along the sleeve;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape write the man, then take him out,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and leave the part believed.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape One for the roll and one for the file\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and one for the name turned down;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the words go out, the figures stay,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the house keeps its own.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Eleven words and none said aloud,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape a clean voice for the sum;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the boy who copies all night long\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape is the boy it comes from.\end{quote}

The grey at the head of this leaf came off a collector’s thumb laid there while the song was being copied; he had the colour at his fingers and did not know he had marked it. I have not rubbed it out. The tin is not swept on the Last Day, and the dust stays where it fell.

\subsection*{What the borrowed hands did}

The Provost’s clerk struck the verb out of rule 7, as he strikes every verb he can find, and set \emph{is used} above my \emph{is chosen}. I have left both. Another hand, narrow and not the Provost’s, struck \emph{the birth-name is turned face under} in rule 3 and set \emph{the writing is turned} above it, as if a name were a piece of writing and not a boy. I have put the name back underneath. A name turned face down is still a name, and a clerk who forgets that is a clerk who will one day find his own in the tin.

The damp along the foot came from the sealed-file room, which is colder than the rest of Slate Row and always has been. The green bead in the fold came off a glaze-mixer come up from High Kiln with the sweetness still at her mouth; she leaned to see the eleven words and did not ask to read them. I have kept the bead where it fell.

\subsection*{At the foot, in a hand nobody will own}

\begin{quote}\itshape A hand that can write a life without a person in it will write one for anybody.\end{quote}

I have asked the copyists, the Provost’s clerk and a man come down from the Weighing Hall, and had three answers and no hand. I have left the line where it was written. The leaf goes back into the tin beside the names that were taken off the rolls. Tomorrow a boy will be entered at twelve and will learn to take himself out of his own sentences, and by the third year he will read a figure in a voice that nobody can thank and nobody can blame. The figure will stand as read.

\clearpage\phantomsection\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{The Back Place, Being the Setting-Song of the Kiln Throat at Low Kiln, Sung as the Green Pots Go In, with the Rows as They Are Set, the Space at the Back That Is Gone Around with a Look, a Factor’s Clerk’s Figures in the Narrow Upright Hand, a Gloss in Green Charcoal, and One Line at the Foot Nobody Will Own}
\CRsheetheading{The Back Place, Being the Setting-Song of the Kiln Throat at Low Kiln, Sung as the Green Pots Go In, with the Rows as They Are Set, the Space at the Back That Is Gone Around with a Look, a Factor’s Clerk’s Figures in the Narrow Upright Hand, a Gloss in Green Charcoal, and One Line at the Foot Nobody Will Own}
{\centering\FellFont\itshape\footnotesize\color{faded} A setter’s work song of the clay yard in the low half-sung Grathic of Low Kiln, counted in rows of three and the turning of the wrist, said down into the throat and not up into the yard; the rubrics in the setter’s charcoal hand, the clerk’s figures above in Ledgerhand, a glaze-girl’s green gloss in the margin, and one line at the foot nobody has claimed · Set down in Frost of Y.H. 813 by Senna, a woman who sets the pots into the throat of a kiln two doors below the Vail in Low Kiln of Sill and has set them through seventeen firings; written in charcoal thinned with wet slip on the back of a firing-tally spoiled by a thumb through the count, folded into four and tied with grey wool to a nail beside the damper; copied at Greybank onto the back of a voided weigh-slip. It survives with a wet-slip thumb at the head, brick dust in the fold, a wad of clay pressed flat between the second and third leaf, a scorch along the lower edge, a green bead of lead glaze in the lower corner, a sherd from the throat, a grey Ash smear along the gutter nobody will own, the clerk’s figures above, the green gloss in the margin, and one line at the foot in a hand nobody has claimed\par}\medskip
I set the pots into the throat of a kiln two doors below the Vail and have done it through seventeen firings. A man come off the north bridge with a soft cuff and a slate asked a girl at the tubs what was said while the green ware went in, and wrote her answer down before she had finished giving it. What he took away had the doing out of it and a figure standing where a place should be. So I have set the words down as we say them at the mouth and put the verbs back.

A setting-song is not a tune. A tune wants a voice with nothing in its hands, and at the throat every hand is full. We say the words down into the clay, not up into the yard. Said up they grow a melody, and a man in a clean coat can carry the melody away and leave the pots behind him, which has happened twice in my time and both times in the same week.

The wet-slip thumb at the head is mine. I held the tally down on the flagstone with the hand I set with and did not know I had marked it.

\subsection*{How it is set}

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item Carry the green pots from the racks with the palm under the belly, never by the rim. Green rim comes away in the hand and leaves a cup with no top.

\item One wad of clay under every pot, no bigger than a thumb. The wad is the only promise in this yard that goes all the way through the fire with the thing it was made for.

\item Three to a row and a thumb’s width between. The width is the heat’s road. Too close and the heat cannot pass; too wide and it runs through and the pot comes out with its green note still in it.

\item At the back of the throat there is a place where two go and three would go. Go around it with a look and a wide step. Do not set a third there to make the row come straight, and do not say whose place it is.

\item Say the refrain into the throat. Said to the girl beside you it becomes instruction, and instruction at this kiln is instruction she will unlearn at somebody else’s.

\item Do not set on a morning when the wind comes off High Kiln with the sweet edge on it. A girl who has tasted glaze cannot smell what is in her own mouth, and leans too far over the throat.

\item The count is in the rows and the turning of the wrist. A pot counted is a pot sold, and a pot sold is entered elsewhere, which is not a thing to do while it is still wet.

\end{itemize}

\subsection*{The song}

\emph{The last hand to come away from the throat keeps the refrain back until the wad is under the next pot. One line of the refrain to one row set.}

\begin{quote}\itshape Up from the racks with the green pots on the forearm,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape palm to the belly, not the rim, or the rim goes;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape wet clay is a thing that trusts the hand that holds it\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and comes apart in the hand that has only just learned.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Set it. Leave the space. Let the heat come round.}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Three to a row, and the back place left as found.}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{The fire takes both and answers to neither.}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape A wad of clay under every pot, no bigger than a thumb,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the pot sits on it and the wad sits on the stone;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape it is the only promise in this yard that burns,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the pot either keeps its seat or goes over.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Set it. Leave the space. Let the heat come round.}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Three to a row, and the back place left as found.}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{The fire takes both and answers to neither.}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape A thumb’s width between and no more and no less;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape too close and the heat can’t get by to the far side,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape too wide and it goes through without stopping\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the pot comes out with its green note still in it.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Set it. Leave the space. Let the heat come round.}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Three to a row, and the back place left as found.}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{The fire takes both and answers to neither.}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape At the back there’s a place where two go and three would go,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and we go around it with the look and the wide step;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape don’t set a third there to make the row come straight ---\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape a straight row is a thing a clerk can carry away;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape what we set we don’t count, and what we don’t set we don’t name.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Set it. Leave the space. Let the heat come round.}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Three to a row, and the back place left as found.}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{The fire takes both and answers to neither.}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape A girl come down from the Glaze Room with the sweet at her mouth\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape leans over the throat to see the rows standing;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape don’t let her lean. The pale line at the gum is the first of it,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the hand that sets is the hand that will answer.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Set it. Leave the space. Let the heat come round.}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Three to a row, and the back place left as found.}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{The fire takes both and answers to neither.}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape The last pot in is the one you never see again;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the clay lid goes on and the mouth is shut with a wad;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape what you had in your hands at the bell you have not got now,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the fire has it, and gives back what it chose.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Set it. Leave the space. Let the heat come round.}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Three to a row, and the back place left as found.}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{The fire takes both and answers to neither.}\end{quote}

There is a space before the last refrain, the length of a hand coming away from the last pot. The clerk put a nought in it, which is a thing you can hold up; a hand coming away is not.

\subsection*{The part they do not set while a man from Greybank stands in the yard}

\emph{Said low to the throat and not across the yard. Taken up when the cuff has gone back over the bridge.}

\begin{quote}\itshape Three to a row and the back place gone around;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape we do not say whose place it is and the yard does not ask.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape One in twelve, says the notice, twice over the basket;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the bell goes four, four and a gap and nobody crosses.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape The fire was carried here under a broken pot and answered four pulls\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape with the fifth missing, and nobody has named whose.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape The grey goes out of the north gate heaped above the sides\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and nobody in the square looks at it twice, which is the afternoon’s work;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape a brine-gull took a coal not yet cold and went upriver with it,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and no slate in Sill stood one mark the poorer.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape The river keeps a note under the sill and the town sets its clock by it;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the kiln keeps a count under the floor, and they were never one.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Three to a row. The back place stays where it was found.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape The clerk may have his nought. It will not keep a pot warm.\end{quote}

\subsection*{What the clerk did}

The factor’s clerk borrowed the tally on a morning when the weigh-slips were out drying, ink on two fingers that would not come out. He took the verbs out and set his words above mine. I have left his hand standing and put ours underneath, as the throat keeps the pot and the flagstone keeps the wad.

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item At \emph{the only promise in this yard that burns}, he wrote \emph{clay seating, consumable; no residue arises}. True in the figure and false at the mouth, where the wad goes all the way.

\item At \emph{three to a row}, he wrote \emph{capacity, three per shelf}, and at the back place, \emph{shortfall, one position}. He has made the place into something owed by somebody; there is no owing in a look.

\item At \emph{the back place left as found}, he wrote \emph{nil}, and drew his line a finger’s breadth past the margin.

\item At \emph{the fire takes both and answers to neither}, he wrote \emph{thermal transfer, unrecorded}. He thinks a transfer entered is a transfer known.

\item At \emph{the count is in the arm that carried}, he wrote \emph{labour, one mark the day; no deduction for injury}. He has put a figure where an arm was.

\end{itemize}

\subsection*{What the glaze-girl put in the margin}

The green belongs to a girl who comes down from the Glaze Room and has the pale line at her gum and will not say when it came. I have copied it as it stands.

At \emph{don’t let her lean}: \emph{I have leaned at nine throats and been told at each of them. The sweet is not in the mouth, it is in the habit. I have never told the next girl.}

At \emph{the pale line at the gum}: \emph{It shows white if you put a lamp to it. We do not put lamps to one another here. We put the tongue to the glaze and go on tasting.}

At \emph{what we don’t set we don’t name}: \emph{There is a name for the back place on this terrace and we do not use it. Words said up there come down on the wind and go over the bridge with a figure on them.}

At the kept-back part: \emph{I asked who the back place belonged to. She said it belonged to the firing, which is an answer you can carry to Greybank and still have in your mouth when you arrive.}

\subsection*{At the head and in the gutter}

The wet-slip thumb at the head is mine and has gone into the grain, which is why I sign with it. The brick dust in the fold came off the flagstone and is the only thing here put there by the trade and not by a person. The wad between the second and third leaf was pressed there by a girl to hold the paper in the draught; it has gone hard as a pot that never saw the throat, and is lighter in the hand than one that did. The scorch took two words off the first verse, which I have not written in again, because a song with two words gone is said slowly, and ours are all said slowly. The green bead came off the girl who leaned over with sweetness still at her tongue; she touched the leaf, said nothing and went back up the terrace. I have kept my tongue off it. The sherd between the third and fourth leaf broke at this throat and answers flat when I knock it on the nail, the only thing in the leaf that has been through the fire and come back to tell of it. The grey along the gutter came off a cuff laid where no cuff has business lying on a kiln bench; nobody will own it, and there is no Last Day behind a nail. The grey wool ties the leaf to the nail, with a knot for the one line I could not bring up.

\subsection*{At the foot, in a hand nobody will own}

\begin{quote}\itshape The wad keeps the seat. The throat keeps the row.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape The back place keeps itself, and the slate is read all the same.\end{quote}

I asked the girl at the tubs, the watcher at the damper and a carter under the sill, and had a proverb, a rest and a direction, and no hand. I have left the line where it was written.

The tally goes back on the nail. There will be firings enough, and I shall set three to a row and go around the back place with a look. If the clerk borrows the leaf he may have his figures. The pots will be where I put them, and the count under the floor will not be made to agree with the note under the stone.

\clearpage\phantomsection\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{The Bank Song, Being the Digging-Song of the Clay Yard at Low Kiln, Sung at the Face Above the Slip Brook, with the Cuts as They Are Counted, the Grey Seam Left Standing, the Overhang Kept for the Bank, a Kiln-Master’s Ruling in Broad Charcoal, a Factor’s Clerk’s Figures in the Narrow Upright Hand, a Gloss from a Woman at the Tubs, and One Line at the Foot in a Hand Nobody Will Own}
\CRsheetheading{The Bank Song, Being the Digging-Song of the Clay Yard at Low Kiln, Sung at the Face Above the Slip Brook, with the Cuts as They Are Counted, the Grey Seam Left Standing, the Overhang Kept for the Bank, a Kiln-Master’s Ruling in Broad Charcoal, a Factor’s Clerk’s Figures in the Narrow Upright Hand, a Gloss from a Woman at the Tubs, and One Line at the Foot in a Hand Nobody Will Own}
{\centering\FellFont\itshape\footnotesize\color{faded} A digger’s work song in the low speech of the yard, called down into the face and answered by the spade and not by voices; the verses counted in cuts going up, with the fourth cut left standing for the bank’s own roof and the grey seam left uncut; the rubrics of the face in the same charcoal-and-clay hand; a kiln-master’s ruling in broad charcoal, a factor’s clerk’s figures standing above in Ledgerhand, a gloss pressed into the margin by a woman at the tubs, and one line at the foot in a hand nobody will claim · Sung at the clay bank two doors below the wheel-shed in Low Kiln of Sill and set down in Bone of Y.H. 812, the Long Cold, by a woman who has dug that face for nine winters and has learned to tell a good cut from a grey one before the spade goes in; written with a burnt stick and clay-water thinned in the Brook on the back of a digger’s docket spoiled by a wet thumb, folded twice and tied with grey wool against the frost, carried up the Clay Road with a consignment of tile and copied forward at Greybank in Ilmen of Y.H. 813 onto the back of a factor’s voided weigh-slip. It survives with a clay thumb worked into the grain at the head, a pale silt tideline from the Slip Brook along the gutter, a dry grey flake from the seam pressed in the fold, a root-hair caught across the second leaf, one word of the sixth verse softened away by water and not written in again, a green bead of lead glaze pressed into the lower corner by a girl with sweetness at one mouth-corner, a sour small-ale ring at the foot, a grey Ash print along the outer fold that nobody will own, a nick from a spade caught in the fold, the kiln-master’s broad ruling, the clerk’s figures standing above, the tub-woman’s gloss, and the line at the foot\par}\medskip
I dig the face above the Slip Brook, two doors below the wheel-shed, and have done it nine winters. The clay comes out in beds, the way bread comes out of a batch; cut across the grain and you get not a lump but a handful of the bank’s own wall. There is a grey thread runs through the face a hand’s breadth below the top. We leave it standing. When a girl asks why, we tell her to cut her own cut and find out; if she asks again we send her to the pot, which has no answer.

A man come up from Greybank with a soft cuff stood at the lip and asked what the women said while they cut. I told him. He wrote it down before I had finished, with the doing taken out and a figure put where a place should stand, and went off up the road with his boots clean. So I have set the words down as we say them, to the face and not to the bridge, and put the verbs back where he took them out.

The clay at the head is mine. I held the docket down with the hand I dig with and did not know I had marked it. Clay goes into the grain and no washing takes it out, which is why we sign with it here and not with ink.

\subsection*{How it is cut}

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item Cut from the top down, never from the bottom up. A face undercut at its foot will come down on the next woman who stands before it, and the bank has no slate and sends no word ahead of itself.

\item Cut with the grain, not across it. The beds lie one on one the way silt lies on a step. A blade along them takes what the face was holding; a blade across them takes the face as well and calls it a lump.

\item Do not stand under the lip. Before a man stands under it, it is clay and the bank’s own business. After he stands under it, it is a room, and it is a room the bank did not ask him into.

\item Leave the grey thread where it lies. Do not put it in the barrow and do not put it on the rack. If a coarse pot comes out of a barrow of that clay, it goes flat under the knuckle, and the pot is set by the wall with the crack showing so nobody has to be told whose cut it was.

\item Knuckle a lump before it goes up with the rest. A whole one answers full and the note goes through; a hollow stops at the skin and gives back flat. The fire finds what the spade let go, and does not ask who let it.

\item Count the cuts going up, never the barrow coming down. A cut that has reached the barrow has left the face; a count coming down is a count of empty barrows, which a clerk can enter and nobody else wants.

\item Say the words down into the face, not to a woman beside you; said to a person they become instruction, and instruction at one bank is instruction she will unlearn at another.

\item Do not sing it at the Cross, and do not sing it on an Account-day. The bell goes four, four and a gap, and a digging-song set against that gap comes home wrong in the wrist.

\item The last part is kept back. It is for when the kiln-master has gone up the terrace and the man from Greybank has gone back over the north bridge with his satchel under his arm and the yard can hear itself again.

\end{itemize}

\subsection*{The song}

\emph{Called down into the face. One verse to three cuts; the fourth cut is the lifting of the spade and is not said aloud. The refrain goes into the clay and not across the bank.}

\begin{quote}\itshape The face has a grain the way bread has a grain,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape laid down in the bank before any of us came;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape cut with the grain and the lump comes away,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape cut across it and you break the bank’s own wall.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Cut it, lift it, lay it by,}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{three to the barrow and the fourth let lie;}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{the grey seam stands where the spade won’t go,}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{and the bank keeps the roof that the clay lets go.}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape The bank sweats in Ember and rings in Stone;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape a spade in the frost tells you where it has been;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape there’s a trickle of cold at the root of the face\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape that runs for the Brook and never comes back.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Cut it, lift it, lay it by,}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{three to the barrow and the fourth let lie;}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{the grey seam stands where the spade won’t go,}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{and the bank keeps the roof that the clay lets go.}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Don’t stand where the lip hangs over the cut.\end{quote}
