\begin{quote}\itshape A roof is a room the moment a man stands under;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape before that it’s clay and the bank’s own business,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the bank has not asked anybody in.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Cut it, lift it, lay it by,}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{three to the barrow and the fourth let lie;}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{the grey seam stands where the spade won’t go,}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{and the bank keeps the roof that the clay lets go.}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape There’s a grey runs through the face like a thread through a sleeve;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape leave it where it lies, don’t send it up in the barrow.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Ask the pot what a grey cut costs set down there ---\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape it has no answer, and it will not be told.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Cut it, lift it, lay it by,}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{three to the barrow and the fourth let lie;}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{the grey seam stands where the spade won’t go,}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{and the bank keeps the roof that the clay lets go.}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Knuckle a lump before it goes up with the rest.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape A whole one answers full and the note goes through;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape a hollow stops at the skin and gives back flat,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the fire finds what the spade let go.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Cut it, lift it, lay it by,}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{three to the barrow and the fourth let lie;}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{the grey seam stands where the spade won’t go,}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{and the bank keeps the roof that the clay lets go.}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Three to the barrow and the fourth to the bank,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and one in twelve is the figure they read;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the figure you hear is not the figure you pay,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the grey in the seam is the part they don’t take.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Cut it, lift it, lay it by,}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{three to the barrow and the fourth let lie;}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{the grey seam stands where the spade won’t go,}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{and the bank keeps the roof that the clay lets go.}\end{quote}

There is a space before the last refrain, the length of a hand laid flat on the face where you feel for the grey before you cut. I have left it on the docket. A clerk put a round nought in it once, a thing you can hold up and look at; a hand laid flat is not.

\subsection*{The part they keep back}

\emph{Not sung while a man from the terrace or a man with a satchel stands at the lip. Said down into the face and not across the bank.}

\begin{quote}\itshape There are places in this yard the foot goes round\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape with a look and no number and nobody’s name;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the face is one of them, and the grey thread another,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the bank keeps both and asks no rent for either.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape The barrow goes up and the figure goes up\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the face stays here with its roof and its thread;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape we do not say the fourth to a man with a soft cuff,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and we do not stand where the roof is.\end{quote}

There is no verse after it. The next thing is the spade going back into the face, which is not a verse and has never wanted one.

\subsection*{What the kiln-master did}

He came up from the terrace on the wrong wind with the sweet edge of the glaze at one corner of his mouth and read the docket with one eye on the bank. Against \emph{leave the grey thread where it lies} he wrote in broad charcoal: \emph{Overburden at the face; rejected at source. Sound clay only to be removed. No loss arises.} He underlined it twice.

Underneath, in mine: He is right about the clay and wrong about the loss. What is left standing is not nothing even when it is not entered, and a bank without its own roof is a hole with a woman at the bottom of it. He reads with one eye on the kiln, as a man does who has never stood under the lip and listened.

\subsection*{What the clerk did}

The factor’s clerk borrowed the leaf at Greybank on the morning we unloaded the tile, being a man who cannot leave paper lying. His cuff was gone soft from washing and the ink sat in two fingers of it. He took the verbs out and set his words above mine, and I have left his hand standing above ours, as the face keeps the old bed under the new cut.

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item At \emph{the bank keeps the roof that the clay lets go}, he wrote \emph{unworked face; residue unentered.} It is true in a figure and false at the lip, where a roof is the one thing the bank will not let go.

\item At \emph{a hollow stops at the skin and gives back flat}, he wrote \emph{vessel unsound; quality not a figure}, and underlined it twice. He thinks a flat note is a defect entered. At this bank a flat note is a lump set by the wall with the crack showing.

\item At \emph{the figure you hear is not the figure you pay} he struck the line through and wrote \emph{deduction current, one part in twelve; statement erroneous}. He has entered the number that was read and not the number that was paid, which is the whole distance between a cuff and a wrist.

\item At the three cuts he wrote \emph{three removed, fourth nil}, and drew a line under it that went a finger’s breadth past the margin. The fourth is not nil. It is the spade coming up, which a man can carry away in a figure and a woman cannot.

\item Where I had left the space before the last refrain he put a round nought and wrote \emph{vacancy} beneath it. A nought is a number and travels. A hand laid flat on the face is a place, and stays where it was put.

\end{itemize}

\subsection*{What the woman at the tubs put in the margin}

The thick charcoal belongs to a woman who scours at the tubs four doors down and has carried water past this bank since before the Glaze Wars. I have copied it as it stands, without making the hands agree.

At \emph{don’t stand where the lip hangs over the cut}: \emph{A girl went in under the old face in Silt and came out with clay to her knee and her bodice full of it. The face did not kill her. It kept her a while. I have not stood under since, and I have not told her what I think of the place she stood.}

At \emph{ask the pot}: \emph{I asked. It gave back flat. It was a pot out of a bank like this one, and a woman had carried it two years before it went. I have not told the kiln-master and I have not set it by the wall, which is a thing I will answer for somewhere else.}

At the part they keep back: \emph{The yard goes round its places with a look and no number. I have never asked which number this face would have if it had one, because a number is the one thing the bank has not got and the only one we have never tried to give it.}

\subsection*{At the head and in the gutter}

The clay thumb at the head is mine and will not come out of the grain, which is why I use it to sign. The pale line along the gutter came out of the Brook while the docket lay on the bank and has taken the edge off one word of the sixth verse; I have not written it back. A song with a word gone is a song said slowly, and everything here is said slowly. The grey flake in the fold came off the thread itself under the spade and is lighter in the hand than a good flake, which is the whole of the lesson and no use at all to a clerk. The root-hair across the second leaf came out of the face with a cut and caught there; I have left it lying across the word it landed on. The green bead came off a girl with sweetness at her mouth who touched the docket; I have not washed it. The sour ring is small ale set down at the first verse and taken up at the last, by which time it had gone the colour of the face it stood on. The grey along the outer fold came off a cuff laid where no cuff has business lying on a bank. Nobody will own it. There is no Last Day at a face; the grey stays where it fell and goes into the next year under the wool. The nick is a spade caught in the fold, and I have kept the fold open at it.

\subsection*{At the foot, in a hand nobody will own}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{The face keeps the grey. The barrow keeps the count.}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{The slate keeps neither, and goes up the road.}\end{quote}

I asked the woman at the tubs, a girl who has this year come to the bank, and a carter waiting with his horse at the yard gate, and had three answers and no hand. I have left the line where it was written.

The docket goes back under the flat stone at the lip. Tomorrow the spade goes into the face above the Brook, three cuts and the fourth where the bank put it, and the grey thread standing where no spade has set it; and if the clerk comes again with his soft cuff, he may have the nought. He cannot have the hand laid flat, because it is a place, and he has no word for a place he cannot carry up the road.

\clearpage\phantomsection\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{The Articles of the Bench, Being the Standing Rules of the Hearth-Maids of Grath for the Taking, Keeping and Trying of Girls at the Birth-Slates, with the Years Set in a Table, the Form of a Birth-Entry, Faults and their Correcting, the Warming-Song Pasted Inside the Cover, Two Corrections in Borrowed Hands, and a Line at the Foot Nobody Will Own}
\CRsheetheading{The Articles of the Bench, Being the Standing Rules of the Hearth-Maids of Grath for the Taking, Keeping and Trying of Girls at the Birth-Slates, with the Years Set in a Table, the Form of a Birth-Entry, Faults and their Correcting, the Warming-Song Pasted Inside the Cover, Two Corrections in Borrowed Hands, and a Line at the Foot Nobody Will Own}
{\centering\FellFont\itshape\footnotesize\color{faded} A bench-copy of the order’s standing rules in the hand of the maid who keeps the birth-flower shrine’s slate-box in Low Kiln; the articles in the short half-sentences the trade speaks, the years and the faults in tables, the form of a birth-entry left blank, the warming-song pasted to the inside of the cover, two corrections in borrowed hands, a page copied again with two words left out, and a line at the foot nobody has claimed · First gathered in Y.H. 782, the year every birth in Grath was made a slate-entry and the Court began to pay the maids who had kept the slates for nothing since any woman could date, and copied forward from the bench and the slate-box rather than from a book; this leaf written at the shrine beside House Reed in Low Kiln in Stone of Y.H. 812, the Thin Year of the Long Cold, carried through the Opening of the Slates into Y.H. 813, and read to a girl brought up from the tubs with her hands already red. It survives folded in a grey wool birth-cloth among the answered slates; beeswax from the shrine candle worked into the head, fine grey slip from the upper pit at the fold, birth-water gone brown where the leaf was doubled, grey Ash along the gutter off a cuff laid where no cuff has business lying, a curl of grey wool through the tie-hole which the writer will not untie, a tallow thumb, a tideline of well-water along the foot, a green bead of lead glaze pressed in by a girl with sweetness still at her mouth, two words eaten clean away and not written in again, two corrections in borrowed hands, and a line at the foot that is nobody’s\par}\medskip
I keep the slate-box at the shrine. A girl is brought to me with red hands from the tubs, and I read her what is below before I let her touch a stone. The trade is learned at the bench and not out of a book. There is no Last Day at a bench; the grey stays where it fell and goes into the next year under a birth-cloth. I have set the rules down as they stand. Where a hand has corrected me I have left both readings.

They were first gathered in Y.H. 782, the year a birth in Grath became a slate-entry and the Court began to pay the maids who had kept the slates for nothing since anyone could date. A rule with no thumb on it is a rule nobody has had to use. These have been used.

\subsection*{The articles as they stand at the bench}

\subsection*{Of the taking}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item A maid takes a girl, not a house. The maid answers for the girl’s bread, her bed and what she breaks; the house gives her up for the years and has her back at the end with a trade in her hands and no figure written against her. A house that will not give her up for the years has given nothing.

\item She is taken at twelve, or at thirteen if her house has kept her through a winter of sickness. Not before. A girl who cannot carry a pail the length of a room without spilling it has no business at a birth; she will spend the heat on the floor and call it the child’s.

\item Her name goes on the back of the birth-slate book in the worn corner. It is not a slate-name and never becomes one. A maid who has no slate-name has one thing the College’s officers have not: a name that can be called across a room without entering anybody.

\item She is kept, not hired. She eats from the maid’s dish and sleeps under the maid’s roof. What she earns goes to the house that sent for her and comes back as bread. She is paid in the only coin this trade uses, which is a stone put in a tin and not marked.

\item No girl is asked whether she wants the births. She is asked whether she understands what is carried: a child, a slate, a stone, and the hours between the second day and the fourth in which nobody comes to take the room off her hands. The wanting comes after, or it does not come; the order has never claimed to teach that part.

\end{enumerate}

\subsection*{Of the stone and the slate}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item Warm the stone first and test it on your own wrist. A stone fresh from the fire will burn a belly as easily as a hand. The wrist knows. The eye does not.

\item The stone goes to the middle, under the wool and against the skin, never to the ends. Hands and feet are wrapped and left; they are not rubbed and are not set to the fire. If a neighbour tells you to hold the foot to the hearth, say the house has spoken, and carry the stone back to the middle. A woman who spends her heat on the extremity has none left for the part that can keep it.

\item Set the slate face down on the bench before you go to the child. The hand goes to the slate before it goes to the child. A hand that goes the other way has already decided what the slate will say and will spend the rest of the evening making the child agree with it. Write the day first; the face will tell you the rest in its own time and will keep telling you for a year.

\item At the red flower, cross two fingers at the corner of it and say nothing. If somebody asks, give a date. Dates are safe; the Court likes a date and does not ask what it covers. Alda Reed crossed two fingers over a flower in the Thin Year and gave the day when she was asked, and nobody has since asked her the other question. A girl who asks what the sign means is told to ask the stone. The stone will not answer, which is the whole of the answer.

\item A child that goes worse on the third day has the second chill. It is not a sickness and not an entry. Call it that where the mother can hear you and call it nothing where the father can; a name spoken in a room becomes a figure by supper in this country. Keep the watch till the fourth morning. Do not send for the collector because the child has got worse. That is what the day does.

\item When the man with the tube comes, give him the mother and keep the child behind the slate. Do not say no. We do not say no. Put the pot between the child and the door and talk to the pot about the weather until he has gone back over the bridge; the pot has never once been asked what it held. If he leaves a pale ring on a wrist, do not rub it and do not cover it before he has gone. Cover it after. A thing covered too soon looks hidden, and a thing hidden is asked about twice.

\item Keep a stone from every birth in a tin under the bench, and never put a mark on any stone. A marked stone is a slate, and a slate can be read by anybody who can hold it. There is no count in the tin. There are stones in the tin.

\item When the bell goes at the Cross, stop and begin again after. It is counting something that is not your room.

\end{enumerate}

\subsection*{The three years}

Year — At the bench — What is taken — What is put in its place\par

First — Carry, warm, wash, sweep; hold the stone while the mother sleeps — The girl’s own haste — A wrist that knows the stone before the eye does\par

Second — The slate face down; the day before the face; the watch — Her own name in a sentence — The house, the day, the hour before first grey\par

Third — A birth kept alone with an older woman in the next room — Her own answer to the question about the sign — The thing the room did, carried under an apron\par

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item At the end of the third year the girl is set to a birth with the slate on the bench and nobody between her and the child but the wool. She enters the day and the house and leaves the rest of the line for the mother to fill. If she writes down what the child said in the night, the page is copied again with those words left out; they are not a birth and have no column. The bare place is left the length of what was taken away.

\item On Ilmen 15 she stands on the flat stone at the Weir with the other maids and blesses the weir and the eel-traps. The traps have their mouths upriver, so an eel goes in and cannot find the way out. The eels run whether anybody blesses them or not. She says the words because the words have been said. If asked what they do, give the date.

\end{enumerate}

\subsection*{Of faults and their correcting}

Fault — What the older maid does — What goes on the slate\par

Hand to the child before the slate — The girl washes and begins again — The day, and nothing beside it\par

A stone too hot at the belly — Held to the wrist; the girl waits with the child in her arms — Nothing\par

A foot rubbed or set to the fire — Unwrapped, wrapped again, left — Nothing\par

The flower covered with a word — Two fingers crossed at the corner; a date given — The date\par

A figure put upon a chill — The figure taken off; the watch kept — The fourth morning, and no cause\par

What the child said in the night — The page copied again with the words left out — The space the words were\par

The tin counted — The stones tipped out and put back unmarked — Nothing\par

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item A fault copied twice in the same tend is one fault the girl has not understood, and the older maid sits with her at the bench until she has. The slate is not a rod. It is a piece of stone with a place where a person stood.

\end{enumerate}

\subsection*{The form of a birth-entry}

\emph{Set out at the end. Copied with the blanks as they stand. In nine years no mother has wanted the last line filled by my hand.}

\begin{quote}\itshape Entered this day, being ---day of -------, in the year of the Hearth ------, the birth of a vessel in the house of ----------------------, the stone set to the middle before the ------- hour, the flower crossed at the corner and not spoken of, the third day watched through to the fourth morning, the name given by ----------------------, or the date standing where the name should stand; written by ----------------------, whose hand went to the slate before it went to the child.\end{quote}

\subsection*{The warming-song, pasted inside the cover}

\emph{Sung low to the stone at the bench while the girl learns to hold it against her wrist. Never across the room. The second verse is my mother’s and I have set mine underneath it so a girl can hear where the words change.}

\begin{quote}\itshape Stone from the fire and wool from the ewe,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape hold it to the wrist before it goes to you;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape warm the middle and leave the ends alone,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the house will keep what the house has known.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Slate on the bench and the child on the knee,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape write the day before the face you see;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the hand that writes is the hand that holds,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the name comes up where the date once stood.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Cross two fingers and give a date;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape a date is safe and a flower is not.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Three days, three watches, a fourth-day bread;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape what comes back is not what went.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Stones in a tin and not one marked,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape a pail at the well and the pail not counted;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape put the verbs back where they were struck,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and come back warm. Come back as you can.\end{quote}

The wet reed across the fourth verse came from the Weir, where the cloth lay in the rain at the blessing until the eels had run. I have flattened it as well as I could.

\subsection*{What the borrowed hands did}

A clerk of the College came up from Slate Row with ink in two fingers of a soft cuff. On an Account-day he borrowed the leaf and struck the verbs out of article eight, setting \emph{the entry is made before attendance is given} above \emph{the hand goes to the slate before it goes to the child}, true of every birth and therefore of none. Against the two fingers at the flower he put a round nought and wrote \emph{vacancy} beneath it. A nought is a number and two fingers are a thing a woman does. I have put my words back underneath and left his above, where they belong, the way the Ash is left in the corner until morning and called dealt with.

The other hand is a physician’s, come up from Greybank. In Y.H. 651 a physician struck a word out of his own report and paid the hearth-maid who had written it for her trouble, and the word has not come down to us. On article ten he set \emph{a common event; no entry; a settling of the graft}, which is a kinder phrase and costs less. I have struck it through and written \emph{the second chill} underneath in my own hand, and left his above it. Both stand. Where a word has been taken away twice I leave a place the length of it, and do not fill the place.

\subsection*{At the head and in the gutter}

The wax at the head is off the shrine candle; it went into the grain in a drop and no knife takes it out clean. The fine grey at the fold is slip from the upper pit; it stayed in the fold instead of falling through, which is how I knew whose hand held the slate. The brown in the doubled leaf is birth-water and has eaten two words off the back; I have not written them in again, because a verse with two words gone is a verse said slowly, and all of ours are. The grey along the gutter came off a cuff laid where no cuff has business lying; I have not swept it. The curl of grey wool through the tie-hole is mine, tied there for the word I could not put down, and I will not untie it. The tallow is off the lamp I kept low so that a mother would not know I was writing and change the account for me. The tideline along the foot is well-water from a pail set down while I was telling a girl to warm the stone first; it has taken the corners off two lines without taking the sense. The green bead is not slip. A girl with sweetness at her mouth leaned over to see the form of entry, touched the paper and went back to her work without asking. I have not washed any of it. There is no Last Day in a slate-box.

\subsection*{At the foot, in a hand nobody will own}

\begin{quote}\itshape The stone keeps the belly and the slate keeps the day. Between the two a girl carries the child, sets it down, and goes to the next room.\end{quote}

I asked the woman who brings the well-water, a girl new to the slates, and a man who reads the notices at the Cross, and had three answers and no hand, as I have had before. I have left the line where it was written. The leaf goes back into the cloth and the cloth into the box among the slates that have been answered. Tomorrow a girl will be brought up from the tubs with red hands, and I shall read her what stands here, and put the verbs back where a borrowed hand took them out, and say nothing about the tin.

\clearpage\phantomsection\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{The Rules of the Birth-Cloth, Being the Standing Sayings of the Hearth-Maids of Grath for the Taking of Girls, the Warming of Stones, the Writing of Birth-Slates and the Manner of the Three Days; Kept in the Fold of a Grey Wool Birth-Cloth at the Shrine in Low Kiln, with the Table of Days, the Washing-Song Said to the Stone, Two Corrections in Borrowed Hands, and a Line at the Foot Nobody Will Own}
\CRsheetheading{The Rules of the Birth-Cloth, Being the Standing Sayings of the Hearth-Maids of Grath for the Taking of Girls, the Warming of Stones, the Writing of Birth-Slates and the Manner of the Three Days; Kept in the Fold of a Grey Wool Birth-Cloth at the Shrine in Low Kiln, with the Table of Days, the Washing-Song Said to the Stone, Two Corrections in Borrowed Hands, and a Line at the Foot Nobody Will Own}
{\centering\FellFont\itshape\footnotesize\color{faded} A rule-leaf of the hearth-maids’ sayings in the hand of the keeper of the slate-box at the birth-flower shrine in Low Kiln; the sayings set down in charcoal and the dregs of a tallow end on the back of a spoiled birth-slate rubbing, the days and the faults in tables, the washing-song sewn into the fold, one correction in the narrow upright Ledgerhand of a clerk of the College, one in the small quick hand of a collector’s clerk who wrote while the leaf was still being read aloud, and a line at the foot that nobody will claim · First gathered at Sill in Y.H. 782, the year the College made every birth a Court entry and paid the maids to keep it, and copied forward from mouth to cloth and from cloth to mouth, never from a book, which is why the rule about the wrist is worn away where a hundred thumbs have tested it and the rule about the tin is as sharp as the day it was said. This leaf written at the shrine in Low Kiln in Frost of Y.H. 813 by the keeper of the slate-box, who has taken girls to births for nineteen years and has never once entered a stone. It survives folded in a grey wool birth-cloth in the box under the niche: beeswax from the shrine candle worked into the grain at the head, a tallow thumb pressed into the corner where the leaf was held down in the draught, grey Ash along the gutter off a cuff laid where no cuff has business lying, a drop of birth-water gone brown in the fold and eaten into two words which have not been written in again, a round pale place where a collector’s tube-wrap was set down and no hand has claimed the wrap, a green bead of lead glaze pressed into the lower corner by a girl with the sweetness still at her mouth, crust-grease on the second table where a woman set down a crust for a child who would not eat, a curl of grey wool caught in the sewing of the song, one margin corrected above and one below, and a line at the foot in a hand that has never been owned\par}\medskip
I keep the slate-box at the shrine in Low Kiln. It stands on the shelf beneath the niche, and the women bring slates to it on the evening of the third day and take them away on the Long Night to lie under the crossed mark cut into the stone above. There is a bench, a tin of stones beneath it, and a birth-cloth folded in the box with these sayings written on the back of a rubbing that spoiled. I write on the back because the face of a slate is for a name, and a name on the face of a slate is a thing that travels.

No girl learns this from a book. A book goes up the road and comes back with a figure in it. These go from mouth to cloth and from cloth to mouth, said low with the wool drawn up and the hand on the belly. A rule that has never had tallow on it is a rule nobody has had to say. These have been said.

They were gathered in Y.H. 782, the year the College made every birth a Court entry and paid the maids to keep it. We took the money; a woman with cold children takes money and asks the giver what it buys. What it bought was the three days, which were ours before they were entered. Where a borrowed hand has corrected me I have left both readings, as a mended pot leaves the crack showing.

\subsection*{The sayings as they stand at the shrine}

\subsection*{Of the taking}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item The shrine takes a girl, not a house. A house may bring her and feed her, but from the day she holds a stone at a belly she answers to the maid, who answers for her bread, her bed, her stones and the figures she writes. A house that will not give her up has given nothing.

\item Taken at nine, set to the stones at eleven, and not before she can hold a stone against her own wrist and say whether it is too hot. A child set to the belly before she has learned the wrist has carried a stone that burned somebody. The wrist knows; the eye does not, and the mother is not there to tell her.

\item She eats from the maid’s dish and sleeps under the maid’s roof. What she earns goes to the shrine and comes back as bread, not as a figure in a girl’s hand.

\item She keeps the name her mother gave her. We are not the furnace and do not name a child after a thing it did. The slate-name is a different name, and the two must not be set side by side where a man with a soft cuff is standing.

\item No girl is asked whether she wants the stone. She is asked what she is bought for: a warmed thing at a stranger’s middle, a hand to the slate before the child, and the not saying of what she sees beneath two crossed fingers. The wanting comes after, or it does not; we have never claimed to teach that part.

\end{enumerate}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{In the narrow upright hand of a clerk of the College, against rule 3:} Retained at the shrine; stipend arising from Y.H. 782. \emph{In mine, underneath:} The stipend came in 782 and is paid to the maid, not the girl. The girl is fed. I have put \emph{fed} back, because a girl who has eaten is a thing his sentence has no room for. Both stand.\end{quote}

\subsection*{Of the stone}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item Put it at the middle and not at the ends; warm the middle and wrap the ends. The chill comes up from the ends and settles in the middle on the second or third day, and it is the second chill and not a sickness and not a thing to be entered.

\item Hold the stone to your own wrist first. A stone fresh from the fire will burn a belly as easily as a hand, and the belly cannot tell you to wait. Three breaths at the middle and three more, said low enough that the mother hears a woman counting and not a figure being taken.

\item Do not rub the ends and do not set a foot to the fire. A neighbour will tell you to hold the foot to the hearth; say the house has spoken and carry the stone back to the middle, for a woman who spends her heat on the extremity has none left for the part that can keep it. You will pay for that in the thaw.

\item Keep a stone from every birth in a tin beneath the bench, and never mark one. A clerk would call the tin a count; give him no figures and he will write \emph{unentered residue} above it and go away satisfied, for a figure with nobody in it pleases him more than one with a person. A marked stone is a slate, and any man who can hold it can read it.

\end{enumerate}

\subsection*{Of the three days}

\emph{Kept on the face of the rubbing. The day goes down before the face is looked at, which is the order of this trade and not the order of a counting house.}

Day — To the child — On the slate — Not on the slate\par

First — Stone to the belly; the child to the breast; the birth-flower covered — The house, the day, the hour before first grey — A name you would keep\par

Second — Wrap the cold ends and leave them; count the breaths; do not rub — The day again, in the same hand — What the child said in the night\par

Third — Keep the stone if the chill came; give the child over — The name, if the mother has given it; else the date and no more — The chill, the stone, the neighbour’s advice\par

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item A hand goes to the slate before it goes to the child. A hand that goes the other way has decided what the slate will say and will spend the evening making the child agree with it.

\item Write the day first. The face will tell you the rest in its own time and will keep telling you for a year. A birth is entered within three days, a rule the College wrote and ours before it was theirs.

\item If the mother has not given a name by the third day, write the date and no more. Leave the place where the name should stand the length of a thumb, and do not put a nought in it. A nought is a figure and a place is not.

\item There is a second name for this chill which the Court struck out of its record in Y.H. 651. We do not write it. A maid who writes it has put a figure where a child was, and the figure will be read by a man who never held the child.

\end{enumerate}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{In a small quick hand, set above rule 13 by a collector’s clerk who stood in the doorway while I was saying it:} A common event; no entry arises; no remedy applied. \emph{In mine, underneath:} He has called the chill common and taken the child out of the sentence. A thing called common has still got a belly in it. Both stand.\end{quote}

\subsection*{Of the man with the tube}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item He comes before the three days are out if the house has owed, which in Low Kiln is most houses. He takes the mother’s attention first, a kindness the Court has never entered: a woman asked for her warmth looks at the man asking, not at the child. Give him the mother and keep the child behind the slate.

\item If he asks what the stone is for, tell him it is for the warmth. It is for the warmth: a true answer, with no figure in it, and he cannot put it on a slate without putting a warmth on a slate, which no man does standing where the warmth is.

\item Do not say no. We do not say no. Put the pot between the child and the door and talk to the pot about the weather till he has gone back over the bridge. The pot has never been asked what it held.

\item If he leaves a pale ring on the mother’s wrist, do not rub it or cover it before he has gone; cover it after. A thing covered too soon looks like a thing hidden, and a thing hidden is asked about twice.

\end{enumerate}

\subsection*{Of the flower and the not saying}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item A child may come among you with a red branch across the ribs or down the arm. Cover it; do not wash it; do not call it by a name. It is a red branch, and the day will tell you what it was if it wants to.

\item Cross two fingers over it and say nothing. The day you tell somebody what you saw is the day it gets written down, and a thing written down here does not stay a thing you saw. It becomes a figure in a column, and the column goes up the road.

\item One in twelve is printed on the notice and unchallenged. The other figure is not printed. I do not write it here, and a maid who writes it has made a figure of the house she was sitting in. Ask the pot. The pot is more use.

\end{enumerate}

\subsection*{Of faults and their correcting}

Fault — As corrected at the shrine\par

Stone set to a foot or a hand — The stone taken back to the middle; the end wrapped and left\par

A stone given fresh from the fire — Held to the wrist first; the belly not burned\par

Hand to the child before the slate — The slate set down first; the day written again in the same hand\par

The chill entered on the slate — Struck; \emph{no entry} set above; the words left underneath\par

A mark put on a kept stone — The mark rubbed away with the thumb; the stone put back in the tin\par

The unprinted figure spoken where a clerk can hear — Not entered. The printed figure stood, and the other is not written here\par

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item A fault copied twice at one birth has not been understood; the maid sits with the girl until it has. The stone is not a rod.

\end{enumerate}

\subsection*{The washing-song, sewn into the fold}

\emph{Said low to the stone, sitting, with the child at the belly and the wool drawn up. Never across the room. The second verse is the one the old maids sang and the girls sing it wrong on purpose, putting the wrist after the belly where the words will not bear it.}

\begin{quote}\itshape Stone from the hearth and wool from the ewe,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape three at the middle and three more too;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape warm the middle and wrap the end,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the house keeps what the house can mend.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape A hand on the slate before the eye,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the day set down and the face left by;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape put a place where the name should be\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the clerk reads clean what the mother cannot see.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Two fingers crossed and a mouth shut tight,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the red branch covered and out of sight;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the pot talks weather while the boots go through,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the stone goes back to the tin unmarked too.\end{quote}

The curl of grey wool in the sewing caught there the morning a girl sang the second verse in the rain and would not sing again. I have flattened the fold.

\subsection*{What the borrowed hands did}

A clerk of the College borrowed the leaf on a market morning, ink set in two fingers of a soft cuff. He takes the verbs out as though a verb were a thing a man could hide in a sleeve. Against \emph{the girl is fed} he set \emph{retained at the shrine; stipend arising}, true about a figure and false about a girl who eats from the dish. I have put my word underneath and left his above, where the money is.

The other is a collector’s clerk, who wrote while I was still saying rule 13. He took the belly out and left the event standing. He can enter the chill as common and the tin as residue and the ring as a thing provided, because all of those have a place in his book. The wrist that tested the heat and the fingers that stayed crossed he cannot enter, and he has not tried.

\subsection*{At the head and in the gutter}

The wax at the head is off the shrine candle, worked into the grain in a drop no knife takes out clean. The tallow is mine, from holding the leaf down in the draught under the niche. The grey in the gutter came off a cuff laid where no cuff has business lying; I have not swept it, and there is no Last Day in a slate-box. The brown in the fold is birth-water and has eaten two words off the back; I have not written them in, for a saying with two words gone is said slowly, and all of ours are. The pale round came off a tube-wrap set down while the measures were counted, and nobody will own the wrap. The green bead came off a girl with sweetness at her mouth who leaned over to see the writing; I have not washed it. There is no heat here to take a word into glass and keep it for the light; the damp corrects instead, one word at a time, and keeps no roll.

\subsection*{At the foot, in a hand nobody will own}

\begin{quote}\itshape The stone keeps the middle and not the name; the slate keeps the name and not the chill. Between the two a maid carries a child over the bridge and sets it down, and goes back for the next.\end{quote}

I asked an old maid come down from Cold Acre, a clerk of the College, and a woman who brings well-water, and had three answers and no hand, as before about the grey print and the two words gone. I have left the line where it was written. The cloth goes back into the fold. Tomorrow a house will bring a girl at nine, and I shall put a stone into her own hand before I let her near a belly, and tell her what came up and not what she ought to have found, and by afternoon the tallow will have come off on another sleeve.

\clearpage\phantomsection\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{The Sermon at the Birth-Flower, Being What Was Said Over the Slates on the Long Night of Y.H. 812}
\CRsheetheading{The Sermon at the Birth-Flower, Being What Was Said Over the Slates on the Long Night of Y.H. 812}
{\centering\FellFont\itshape\footnotesize\color{faded} A sermon of the Temple of the Return preached at the birth-flower shrine in Low Kiln, with the women’s answers set beside it and a clerk’s corrections struck through but left standing · Preached by a priest of the Temple of the Return, come up from Greybank, at the niche beside House Reed in Low Kiln, Sill, on the Long Night of Y.H. 812, the Thin Year, over the birth-slates the women had laid there to lie overnight; set down two mornings after, on the Last Day, by a hearth-maid of the district in charcoal and tallow on the back of a birth-slate spoiled by a late entry, continued on the leaf of a drying tally, and kept in the fold of a grey wool birth-cloth that goes where the maids go. It survives soft at the fold with a tallow thumb at the head, a green bead of lead glaze from a girl who leaned over to see the writing, a grey Ash print along the gutter, a spot of barley grease from a crust laid down and not eaten, three corrections in the maid’s own hand, one narrow hand borrowed from a clerk that takes the verbs out, and a line at the foot in a hand nobody will own. Copied forward in Ilmen, Y.H. 813, with the verbs put back and the nought left in its place.\par}\medskip
I am a hearth-maid of Low Kiln and nobody asked me to write this. I write it because the women said it after him and I did not want it to go out of the room with their breath. He was a priest of the Temple of the Return come up from Greybank and spoke in the clean voice they use at the Weighing, the one that takes the speaker neatly out of his own sentences; I have heard that voice announce a whole return for a person not in the room. He stood at the niche with the slates under his hand and did not once look up at the crossed mark cut above it. I set his words down as he said them, with his verbs left out where he left them out, and I have put the verbs back underneath in my own hand, because a thing said over a child is a thing a mother has to use. What the women answered is set beside. A sermon is not a thing a room swallows whole.

The tallow thumb at the head is mine; I held the slate down in the draught under the niche and did not know I had marked it. The green is not slip. The grey came off my cuff when I measured the ridge in a house two doors down and came back to write, and I have not swept it off the leaf.

\subsection*{The sermon, as he said it}

\subsection*{Of the vessel}

Mothers, and you that carry what you have not yet held, and you children that cannot yet say the word I am saying: hear the first thing you were taught before you could hear it.

The world was a vessel. It was fired whole in the Hearth and cracked in one anger, and the crack has a name, which is the First Breaking. What fell out of it went a long way and is going still. Do not ask where it went. The Waste is not a country a household can walk into and come back from with the same number of years.

The Nine Who Kept went after what had run away. They drove the repairs and left us the Return. By the Return, what is banked is not lost. The measure is banked. The account stands. Your return is recorded.

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{The room answered, and the children said it twice, once for the moot and once for them that came late:}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Come back warm. Come back as you can.\end{quote}

\subsection*{Of the flower}

Some of you have had a child come among you with a red branch across the ribs or down the arm. The district calls it a birth-flower. It is not a sickness and it is not a debt. It is the mark the Hearth sets on a vessel before the vessel has a name, so that the Keeping may know its own when it comes back. Do not wash it off. Do not cover it with a word. A covered thing is still entered.

Concerning the mark cut above this niche, I am not empowered to speak. It is older than this niche and older than the slate in my hand. Ask me when the niche was built and I will give you a date. Ask me what the mark signifies and you will be given the same date, because a date is an answer that does not spoil in the mouth.

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{The room answered:}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Come back warm. Come back as you can.\end{quote}

\subsection*{Of the figure}

One part in twelve of every measure is kept back for the fire, as the notice says. This is not a tax. A tax is taken by a man who wants a thing; this is kept by the Hearth, which wants nothing and therefore cannot be refused.

The tube the officer carries is cold because the fire is behind iron and no priest may touch it. Understand this plainly: the iron does not take. The slate takes. The iron only opens the way. A draw with a slate is a keeping. A draw without one is theft, and the wrist is marked so that the account may find the hand again. You will see a pale ring on a wrist in this district that shows through the winter. The neighbours call it nothing. It is the account, and the account is merciful, and it is never wrong.

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{The room answered:}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Come back warm. Come back as you can.\end{quote}

\subsection*{Of the grey}

On the Last Day the grey in the corner is left where it lies. In the morning it is burnt, and it is called dealt with. The Court does not teach that the grey is a person. It teaches that the grey is what remains when the Warm has gone out, and that what cannot be kept is not a loss. Do not weep over dust. Sweep it. Burn it. Say it is dealt with, and go back to your bread.

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{The room answered:}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Come back warm. Come back as you can.\end{quote}

\subsection*{Of the Kept and the close}

Blessed are they that are Kept. No want can reach them; they no longer feel the cold; there is nothing left in them for the Hearth to take, and so they are past the need of a return. There are fewer than twenty in the world. Speak of them with pity.

For you the account is still open, and the days go into it one by one, and the world is being mended. The ninth repair is not finished. Your names go into it.

The measure is banked. The account stands. Your return is recorded.

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{The room answered:}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Come back warm. Come back as you can.\end{quote}

\subsection*{What the women said after him}

\emph{Written as they said it, standing about the niche with the children sending them in the last line. I have not joined the two columns. Where he said a thing and they said a different thing, both stand.}

As he said it — What the women said after\par

The world was fired whole and cracked in one anger. — A pot goes flat when it goes wrong. We do not ask who was angry.\par

Nine hands went after what had run away; the ninth is still abroad. — The ninth has a place under the rack where nobody sets a pot. The yard goes around it.\par

The birth-flower is the Hearth’s mark set before the naming. — It is a red branch. A woman crossed two fingers at the corner of it and gave a date nobody asked for. I have set the date in the margin.\par

One in twelve, as the notice says, for the keeping of the fire. — One in twelve is printed and unchallenged. The other is not printed. Nobody in this room needs me to write it.\par

The iron does not take. The slate takes. — The pale ring shows through the winter and the neighbours call it weather. A slate is a piece of stone with a neat hand on it.\par

What the Court has kept is not lost. — The grey in the corner is not dirt. It is somebody. In the room two doors down it turns the corner without a break.\par

They that are Kept are past want and to be pitied. — A woman asked one of them whether he was cold. He said no. She did not ask him anything else.\par

Say the name. Your return is recorded. — Say it twice, once for the moot and once for them that came late. If you have no name, leave the place where the name would stand.\par

Sweep it, burn it, call it dealt with. — We leave it. It is swept on the Last Day and burned in the morning, and the clean line where it stood is not the same as gone.\par

\subsection*{What stands in the margins}

At \emph{the mark the Hearth sets on a vessel}, a girl of the drying racks asked him outright what the mark above the niche was. He gave her a date: Y.H. 782, the year the maids began to be paid. He gave her the same date a second time when she asked again in a different way. My mother used to say a date is safe; the Court likes a date and does not ask what it covers. I have put his date in the margin and left the question where he left it, which is standing. The mark is cut into the stone above the niche and drawn in the yard chart, and the chart does not explain it, and neither does this leaf.

Where he said \emph{a draw with a slate is a keeping}, the narrow hand of a clerk borrowed the leaf on an Account-day and set \emph{a keeping} out above and wrote \emph{a taking, lawfully entered} over it. Under that, in mine: \emph{the neighbours call it weather.} Both stand. He has a word for the heat going and a word for the heat going with a slate, and the same heat goes both ways.

The narrow hand also struck the verbs out of \emph{the world was fired whole} and wrote above it \emph{the world is a vessel, fired whole}, saying that a thing always true has no need of a verb. I have put \emph{was} back underneath. A priest can speak without verbs because he is never in the room he is speaking about; a woman cannot.

In the space where the fifth line of the answer should be, the same hand put a round nought and wrote \emph{vacancy} beside it. We said four and four and the place where the fifth should be, and I have left his nought standing in the place and my words under it. He numbered the Five as four on that visit also. I did not correct him. The five are not ours to give away.

\subsection*{The barley grease and the bead}

The crust was laid on the leaf by a woman who was telling her little one to eat and would not, and lay there while the priest spoke of bread. I left it. A crust put down and not eaten is a thing this district knows how to read. The green bead at the top right is not slip: a girl with sweetness still at her mouth leaned over to see what I was writing, touched the slate with her thumb, and went back to the rack. I have not washed any of it, and I would not if I knew how.

After he went, the women laid their birth-slates back in the niche overnight as they do, and the children were sent home before the fire was put out. The priest’s words went up the road toward Greybank in a clean coat. Our words stayed in the room, which is why I have written them down.

\subsection*{At the foot}

In a hand that is not mine, not the clerk’s and not the priest’s, struck through once and written again underneath, very small:

\begin{quote}\itshape The mark was here before the niche. The niche was here before the name.\end{quote}

I have asked four women whose it was and had four dates and no hand. I have left it struck through and standing, which is the only honest way to keep a sentence you cannot sign.

The cloth goes back in the fold. They will bring the slates again on the next Long Night and set them in the niche, and another reader may come up from Greybank and say the same four sentences over them, and the women will answer him with the place where the figure is not. I shall put the verbs back as I did this time. I have copied the leaf once into Ilmen and shall copy it again, with the nought in its place and the grey along the gutter, and the space at the end of the answer left the length it is.

\clearpage\phantomsection\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{The Sermon at the Bitter Well, Being What the Keeper of the Dish-Shelf Said Over the Well by the Ferr at Stonemouth on a Morning in Ash of Y.H. 813, with the Drawing-Song Left with Its Sixth Line Unsung, the Shelf in a Tally, a Factor’s Clerk’s Correction, and a Line at the Foot in a Hand Nobody Will Own}
\CRsheetheading{The Sermon at the Bitter Well, Being What the Keeper of the Dish-Shelf Said Over the Well by the Ferr at Stonemouth on a Morning in Ash of Y.H. 813, with the Drawing-Song Left with Its Sixth Line Unsung, the Shelf in a Tally, a Factor’s Clerk’s Correction, and a Line at the Foot in a Hand Nobody Will Own}
{\centering\FellFont\itshape\footnotesize\color{faded} A well-shrine sermon of the common Grathic telling preached at the niche beside the well that the road-book calls the well that was never sweetened, where the Ferr comes down to the Ilm at Stonemouth; the sayings in the flat washed speech of the washing-bench set down in Grathic, the drawing-song with the sixth line left as it is not sung, the shelf in a tally, one correction in the narrow upright Ledgerhand of a factor’s clerk come up from Greybank to weigh the winter lead, and one line at the foot in a hand nobody will own · Preached on Ash 9, Y.H. 813, by a woman of High Kiln who had kept the dish-shelf at the well for two and thirty years, whose mother went thin on the Ferr in the Long Cold and would not let her drink; written that evening by the girl who takes the quarrymen’s names at the weigh-clerk’s bench, in charcoal on the back of a weigh-slip spoiled by wet slate, folded with a green bead of lead glaze shut in the crease and tied with a turn of well-rope, and kept since in the niche behind the dish-shelf. It survives with lime worked into the grain at the head, a blue-grey tideline off the Ferr that has eaten two words clean off the second leaf, a ring of barley-water on the first, a grey Ash print along the gutter nobody will own, the green bead in the fold, a flake of the well’s sweet crust shut in the third crease, a pale line pressed from a cup’s lip in the lower corner, one correction in the narrow upright hand of a factor’s clerk, and a line struck through and written again very small underneath in a hand that has never come forward. Copied once at Greybank in Ilmen of Y.H. 814 into the factor’s file of northern sayings, with the verbs put back and the sixth line left as it was not sung.\par}\medskip
I take the quarrymen’s names at the weigh-clerk’s bench and give them back when the factor’s man comes up, which is a way of keeping names without owning them. Nobody asked me for this. I write because the woman who keeps the dish-shelf spoke to a well and the well gave back the same water it has always given. She spoke first to the lip, then to the cup in the niche, then to the dish, and last of all to us, which is the order a person uses when somebody may be listening who wants a figure. Where she left a verb out I have put it back underneath, because a saying said over a well is a thing a woman has to use before the water is cold.

The lime at the head is off my cuff and no wet cloth takes it out of the grain. The blue in the gutter is the Ferr; it has taken two words off the second leaf and I have not written them in again. The ring is barley-water, set down while she spoke of the twenty-one. The grey came off a cuff laid where no cuff has business on a counted stone; I have not swept it, and there is no Last Day at this well.

\subsection*{The manner of the drawing, as the well actually has it}

\emph{Written small, from watching, not from any order the Court has printed.}

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item Come before the sun is on the lip. A man who comes at noon sees his own shadow in the water and calls it the well’s answer.

\item Do not drink. A man who drinks the Ferr and calls it thin has taken a giving for a taking, and the habit is hard to unlearn in a household that has no other water.

\item Set a dish of barley-water on the shelf with a stone in it to keep the wind from dragging it off. The stone is not a payment and has never been entered.

\item Tap the cup in the niche with the knuckle. It answers flat. Do not tap the well; a well answers with its surface and tells you nothing.

\item If you come up from the glaze room, leave the green bead on the shelf and say whose it was to the dish and not to a person. A bead said to a person becomes a question about the colour, and the colour has a price in High Kiln.

\item Do not say the count of the twenty-one aloud at this well. A number said here goes up the road in a clean hand and comes back with the drinkers taken out.

\item When a man in a clean coat comes up from Greybank to weigh the winter lead, stop. Begin again when he has gone back down it. We have kept this habit thirty years and never said why, and he has never asked.

\end{itemize}

\subsection*{The sermon, as she said it}

\subsection*{Of the well}

She put her palm on the stone lip and left it there while the Ferr went by under the bank with the blue of the west on it.

“The well gives as it gave,” she said. “It has never given anything else and it has never stopped. What it takes it does not say, and a well that will not say what it takes is called a mercy in a room three leagues east where nobody has drawn from it.

“There is a clause on a slate at Sill,” she said, “and the factor pasted salt-paper over it, and the strip has lifted at one corner so that six words show and the rest do not. We have leaned over it and put a thumb on it, and the six words are \emph{the wells of the Ferr are to be sweetened at the charge of the workings}. The clause is on a slate. The water is in this hole. They have never met, and the well has kept the larger part.”

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Margin, in my hand:} She said \emph{never sweetened} twice, once to the well and once to a woman come up from the washing for barley-water. I have left both sayings where they stood. A date would have been safer, but there is no date on this niche.\end{quote}

\subsection*{Of the cup}

She took the cup from the niche and tapped it with her knuckle. It gave the small flat sound a pot gives when the crack has gone all the way through.

“A pot tells the truth for nothing,” she said. “This one came down from High Kiln in the year of the water and would not hold a pouring. The physician wrote \emph{a reduction in the measure was recorded} above it and the road-book wrote \emph{a visitation of the water}, and the cup has answered flat every morning since without asking who would write it down. A physician’s sentence is true in a language nobody at this bench speaks. The cup has not learned it and is the better for it.”

A girl asked where the pale line was, that the well-song speaks of. She turned the cup so the light went along the empty rim.

“That is on a pot still at High Kiln, not here,” she said. “I have pressed a flake of the crust off this lip into the corner instead, because a woman can carry that and cannot carry a pot. It is not a flower and it is not a visitation. It is the colour of the water on a lip that has tasted it through a season. The women taste the glaze to get the colour and the colour stays, and there is no clause about the rim on any slate.”

\subsection*{Of the dish}

She set a dish of barley-water on the shelf and put the stone in it, the way a household sets one at Sill, but with this difference: at Sill they set it for them whose measure has been banked.

“We set a dish for the twenty-one who went downriver and were not entered again,” she said. “In the morning the water is gone and the stone is where it was. Nobody says who drank, because a household here can carry a name a slate has no room for. In Sill they call the water a keeping. Here we call it gone. It is the same dish and not the same saying, and I will not have one put over the other.”

She put the dish where it had stood and did not look into it.

\subsection*{Of the figure}

A man at the bench asked what the shrine kept, since the factor’s man would want a figure.

“Three hundred,” she said. “A round sum. Ninety-six and a hundred and twelve and seventy-one. The seventy-one are us, by this well. The twenty-one went downriver and the round sum has no room for them, so a small hard hand put them in the gutter where a clerk carrying a total will not look. I have kept the gutter. Three hundred is a visitation; seventy-one is a row of houses; twenty-one is a thing that happened to people we can still name. The road-book balances, and I have never seen a house balance.”

\subsection*{Of them that went downriver}

She turned from the shelf to the company then, which she had not done until that hour.

“Do not say they were returned,” she said. “They went downriver. A thin return is a thing done in a room with a slate and a tube and an infant at the end of it. These were not returned. They walked or were carried downriver and were not entered again. If the Keeping wants them, let the Keeping say where they went. It has not said.”

A man asked whether that was a mercy or a refusal. There is no Grathic word that holds the two together and she would not choose one.

“It is what we say,” she said. “Mercy is a word with a giver in it and I have never seen one at this well.”

\subsection*{Of what is not sung}

There is a well-song taken down at the washing from a woman who learned it from women who had, and anybody here can sing it you. It is a true song and it is not this one. This one has a sixth line that is not sung.

“The sixth belongs to the twenty-one,” she said. “A line sung for a person not in the room becomes a keeping, and we have had enough of keepings. Let the dish stand for them and let the line go unsung the length they have been unentered.”

\subsection*{The drawing-song}

\emph{Sung low, standing, with the palm on the lip. The women say the fourth line with her. The sixth is not sung and I have left the space its length.}

\begin{quote}\itshape The Ferr came down with a blue on its skin,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the cup at the lip would not hold;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape we drank all winter and called it thin,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the slate wrote a figure and told.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Seventy-one by the well that we know,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and twenty-one where the gutter runs;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the clause was pasted and six words show\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the sweetening never came.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape The lime keeps a print and the well keeps a name,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the bead goes green where the lip has been;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Here the sixth line is not sung. No sound is made for the twenty-one.}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape A round sum balances; a row does not.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape The water goes down and the name stays here.\end{quote}

A girl asked what the space was for. Nobody answered her. The clerk put a round nought against it later, which I have left where he set it.

\subsection*{The shelf, as the shrine keeps it}

\emph{Things set in the niche or on the shelf. What was left and what was entered. I have set them where they stood.}

Thing in the niche — Who set it — What it was for — What was entered\par

The cup that would not hold a pouring — a woman of High Kiln — to hear the flat from — nothing\par

The green bead — a girl come up from the glaze room — left because her mother drank — nothing\par

The dish of barley-water — the keeper of the shelf — for the twenty-one downriver — nothing\par

A string with twenty-one knots — the keeper of the shelf — the odd ones the round sum missed — nil, written above\par

A flake of the sweet crust — nobody will say — from the lip in a dry winter — nothing\par

The strip of salt-paper — the factor at Greybank — pasted over the sixth clause — obligation outstanding\par

The grey on the lip — a cuff nobody owns — left where it fell — nothing\par

There were beads and dishes before these and the keeper can set a season to most of them; I have not written the seasons, for a row of years is a thing a clerk can carry away and a cup is not.

\subsection*{What the clerk did}

He came up from Greybank on the tenth with a book that had the word \emph{lead} in it, borrowed the leaf while I was at the bench, and gave it back with the verbs taken out.

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item At \emph{the well gives as it gave} he set \emph{the source continues in yield} above and underlined it twice.

\item At \emph{the well was never sweetened} he wrote \emph{the obligation remains outstanding}, the same line he set in the stone-dresser’s yard-book last year, as though a sentence written twice were twice true.

\item At \emph{the twenty-one went downriver} he wrote \emph{third parties not resident; no account arises}.

\item At \emph{the cup answered flat} he wrote \emph{a vessel of defective retention}, which leaves the cup standing where nobody has to hear it.

\item At the gap in the song a round nought and \emph{vacancy}. When I asked what a space was worth that held twenty-one people, he said nothing a clerk could enter, the first true thing he has said at this bench.

\end{itemize}

I have put the verbs back underneath and left his hand above, as the well keeps the dust under the water and the water under the lip. He takes them out because a sentence with nobody in it can be copied from one book into another and never be wrong. I put them back because a woman with her palm on the well wants to know who is doing the taking.

\subsection*{At the head and in the gutter}

The lime is mine and will not wash out of the fold; I wipe the bench with my cuff and the cuff goes into the grain. The blue is the Ferr, carried up on a wet sleeve and set down while a man told me something about the upstream water; the tell dried and the blue stayed. The two words it ate I have left out, for a leaf that has lost two words to the water must be read slowly. The ring is barley-water from the dish, and the grey came off a cuff and I have not swept it. The bead in the fold came off a girl with the sweetness still at her mouth who leaned over to see what I was writing. The flake of crust is from the lip and is sweet in dry weather. The pale line in the corner came off the cup’s rim when she set it down to tap it. The salt-paper has lifted at one corner, so a correction shows through that was meant to be covered, the only honest thing that paper has done.

\subsection*{At the foot, in a hand nobody will own}

Struck through once and written again underneath, very small:

\begin{quote}\itshape The well was sweetened on a slate and not in the water.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape A round sum can be carried. Seventy-one cannot.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape The twenty-one went downriver and the dish was set for them.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Ask the cup at the lip what it held, and why it will not hold now.\end{quote}

I asked the keeper of the shelf, the woman at the washing, the weigh-clerk and the clerk from Greybank, and had four answerings and no hand.

The leaf goes back into the niche behind the dish-shelf with the bead in its fold. Next Ash the women will set a dish and the clerk will take the verbs out, and I shall put them back. The Ferr will come down with the blue on it and the cup will answer flat and the well will give as it gives.

\clearpage\phantomsection\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{The Blue Cliff, Being an Extract from the Road-Book of Sill Concerning the Glaze Wars, the Winter of the Ferr, and the Terms Set at the Blue Cliff in Y.H. 418, with the List of the Three Hundred, the Well-Song, and the Corrections of Two Clerks}
\CRsheetheading{The Blue Cliff, Being an Extract from the Road-Book of Sill Concerning the Glaze Wars, the Winter of the Ferr, and the Terms Set at the Blue Cliff in Y.H. 418, with the List of the Three Hundred, the Well-Song, and the Corrections of Two Clerks}
{\centering\FellFont\itshape\footnotesize\color{faded} A road-clerk’s extract from the thane’s book of distances and tolls, copied out of the moot-chest original; the year-entries in the clay-hand, the treaty clauses in a Vhaleni tally-hand gone soft with damp, the three hundred entered as a round sum with a fourth row in a hand nobody will own, the well-song taken down at Stonemouth, one struck word in the narrow upright hand of the College, and a line at the foot that has never been claimed · Written at Sill in the thane’s counting room off the Cross in Stone of Y.H. 812, the Thin Year, by the road-clerk who signs himself only R. and will not say what the letter stands for; copied from a road-book kept in the moot-chest since Y.H. 418 and carried forward at the Opening of the Slates into Y.H. 813. It survives as four leaves of stout foolscap sewn with wire into a board cover rubbed bare at the corners: clay worked into the gutter, a green bead of lead glaze pressed into the lower margin by a glaze-mixer come up from High Kiln, a ring of small ale at the head, a grey collector’s thumb on the treaty clause which its owner did not wipe away, a strip of salt-paper pasted over the sixth clause and gone soft at the edge, one word struck through and written above in the College hand, and a line at the foot in a hand that has never come forward.\par}\medskip
The road-book is not a history. It is a list of distances and of what was paid upon them, kept in the thane’s counting room so that a man who says the Clay Road took six days in Silt may be answered out of a book and not out of a memory. Distances are the only thing in Sill that nobody argues about. Everything else is argued about, and the argument is entered under the year in which it was made, not the year in which it happened.

This chapter is the one the factor at Greybank asks to see when he comes up. I have copied it four times. On each copy the three hundred have stood as a round sum, because the clerk who first entered them counted households the way a potter counts a row of wet pots, by the places and not by the heads in them. I have left his round sum standing and put his rows underneath it, where a clerk of the Keeping will not think to look, which is the gutter.

\subsection*{The years as the moot-chest has them}

\emph{Copied in the clay-hand out of the book with the split board cover. I have put nothing in from the temple tells, which have their own dates and a comfort in them.}

\textbf{Y.H. 300.} Lead workings in the lower Ferr pass out of Keldish hands into those of contractors. Lead falls at Stonemouth, clay rises at Sill. Entered as \emph{a readjustment of the workings}.

\textbf{Y.H. 318.} Vhaleni salt-masters buy the mines from the Keldish contractors. A clay cart out of Sill is turned back at the Ferr and its load tipped into the water. Entered as \emph{an obstruction of the road}.

\textbf{Y.H. 326.} Two kilns at Stonemouth are burned by men of Sill. There is no battle and no dead man entered. Entered as \emph{a firing in the matter of the road}, which is the clay-country phrase for a burning and for the firing of a kiln both, and the clerk who wrote it knew it.

\textbf{Y.H. 339.} The wells by the Ferr carry a blue-grey dust. The thane’s physician says the water is not good. The entry says \emph{the water was complained of}. I have kept \emph{complained}.

\textbf{Y.H. 401.} A hard winter. Three hundred households of High Kiln drink from the Ferr through the season. Their measure goes thin. Entered as \emph{a visitation of the water}. The word is the physician’s, and the households did not choose it.

\textbf{Y.H. 411.} The Clay Road is stopped past Greybank. Carts go down by the river and take nine days where they took five. Entered as \emph{delay, and the road otherwise engaged}.

\textbf{Y.H. 417.} Commissioners sit at the Blue Cliff. Salt-paper, iron clamps and a piece of Sill clay are laid on one table. Entered as \emph{a conference at the cliff}, with no mention of who paid for the table.

\textbf{Y.H. 418.} Terms set and the road opened. Entered as \emph{peace, the road opened, the account standing}.

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{In the tallies of the Vhaleni factor, against the entry of Y.H. 339:} The water was not complained of. It was found unequal to use. Strike \emph{complained}.\end{quote}

I have not struck it. A man who complains is a man who expects an answer. A man who finds a thing unequal to use has carried it out of his house and barred the door and gone on. Both are true, and the difference between them is whether anybody was still standing in the room to be told. The factor’s strip is pasted to the leaf and has begun to rot, which the Vhaleni hold to be a virtue in paper. It has not improved the entry.

\subsection*{The terms, as the slate has them}

\emph{The treaty slate lies in the moot-chest under the road-book. The factor at Greybank keeps a copy on salt-paper, which has perished in the middle and been pieced with a straw-coloured thread. I have set the slate’s words in the left column and what the road-book entered beside them in the right.}

Clause — As it stands on the slate — What the road-book set beside it\par

One — Grath keeps the clay towns and the right to fire its kilns. — \emph{Fire without let.} The kilns of High Kiln were fired that Ember as they had been fired the Ember before.\par

Two — Vhalen keeps the coast and the salt. — \emph{The salt to the sea.} Salt came up the Clay Road that winter at the old price. Nobody thanked anybody.\par

Three — Keld keeps the lead and the right to sell it to whom it will. — \emph{The lead to the mountain.} Lead came downriver in fine ware, which the slate does not name.\par

Four — The eastern bound is set at Greybank. — \emph{The bank is the bound.} An assessor may now stop a cart on the Clay Road without asking the thane.\par

Five — The Clay Road is declared open to all three powers. — \emph{The road is open.} A road open to everybody is a road nobody can shut when the collector comes. Entered as \emph{open} and left at that.\par

Six — The wells of the Ferr are to be sweetened at the charge of the workings. — \emph{Sweetening to be done.} No charge was entered, and the factor pasted his salt-paper over the clause.\par

The paste has gone soft and lifted at one corner, so that six words of the clause show through and the rest do not. A man can read what was hidden without taking the strip off, if he is willing to lean over the leaf and put his thumb on it. There are three thumb-marks on that corner, one of them grey, and I have not cleaned them off.

\subsection*{The three hundred}

The figure is entered in the book as \emph{300 households, High Kiln and Stonemouth, visitation of the water, no dead entered}. It is entered in the neat hand and it balances. I have set the rows underneath as I found them, and the fourth row as I found it too.

Row — The thane’s clerk — The other hand, small and hard-pressed\par

First — High Kiln, west row — 96 households — and the pot with the pale line at the lip\par

Second — High Kiln, east row — 112 households — and the cup that would not hold a pouring\par

Third — Stonemouth, by the Ferr — 71 households — and the well that was never sweetened\par

Fourth — — — and twenty-one that went downriver and were not entered again\par

Ninety-six and a hundred and twelve and seventy-one make two hundred and seventy-nine. The writer of the fourth hand knew his figures, which is a thing a man in a clay town does not often keep to himself. He wrote \emph{twenty-one} small and close to the gutter, as a man writes who expects his slate to be scraped in front of him. I have copied it as it stands. The factor’s clerk later set \emph{visitation: 300 households; no deaths entered} against the whole and underlined it twice. The three hundred are the round sum. The twenty-one are the odd ones, and a round sum has no room for them.

\subsection*{The well-song}

\emph{Taken down at Stonemouth from a woman at the washing, who had not been born in the year of the water and had learned it from women who had. It is sung at the tubs and not at the kiln. She would not sing the second verse until the tubs were put away.}

\begin{quote}\itshape The Ferr came down with a blue-grey skin,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the lead went down to the sea;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape we drank all winter and called it thin,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the cup answered flat to me.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape A pale line sits where the lip should be\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape where the glaze is tasted at the rim;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the slate writes \emph{three hundred}, a house writes \emph{rows},\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the odd ones go downriver with him.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape The cliff is blue and the salt-paper white,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the road stands open to every cart;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the well was sweetened one winter’s night\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the water kept the larger part.\end{quote}

She said she did not know who made it, and then said that songs about water are made by the water, which is not an answer and is the custom of that shore. I have put it where I found it, at the washing and away from the fire.

\subsection*{What the second clerk did}

The College hand came up from the Hearthseat on the factor’s business and corrected the leaf while I was out of the room. It is a careful upright hand and it has never in this chapter changed a figure.

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]
