\item Against \emph{the water was complained of} it set \emph{the water was found unequal to use}, which I have already set down above, so that the two readings stand together.

\item Against \emph{three hundred households made thin} it wrote \emph{a reduction in the measure was recorded}.

\item Against \emph{the Clay Road was stopped past Greybank} it wrote \emph{the road was otherwise engaged}.

\item Against the fourth row it wrote nothing at all. The hand passed over the twenty-one without a stroke, which is the readiest way of correcting an entry I have yet seen.

\end{itemize}

I have left both readings everywhere, the thin one under the neat one, as a potter leaves the old break showing under a new seam and does not pretend the first hand never touched the clay. A clerk who takes the drinker out of the sentence leaves the water standing by itself, and water standing by itself has done nobody a harm, and no measure has gone thin in a house where nobody ever drank.

\subsection*{What I have set side by side}

In this year the glaze of High Kiln is still tasted at the rim. The sweet sickness still shows first as a pale line at the gum. The Clay Road is still a Court road, and lead still comes down from Keld to be sold to whom it will. I have entered these four things under this year and not joined them. A chronicler who joins them has begun a sermon, and a sermon gets copied oftener than an account.

The Long Cold is in the book as a line of figures and then as the word \emph{walking thin}, which the district uses of people who keep moving because stopping is the same as cooling. I have entered the figure and the word without asking which came first. This is the whole craft of the road-book: to keep the place where a thing stood, so that the next hand has something to copy besides the clean version.

\subsection*{At the head and in the gutter}

The clay in the gutter came off the floor of the counting room and has been there since the first copy; a man who keeps a book of distances walks clay into it every day and does not sweep it out. The green at the lower margin is not ink. A glaze-mixer come up from High Kiln leaned over to see the well-song and touched the leaf with her thumb, and I have kept the mark where she put it. The ring at the head is small ale spilled by the man who brought me the moot-chest key, who said the treaty was older than any man’s grandfather and set his cup down on the leaf to prove it. The grey on the sixth clause came off a collector who leaned over the sweetening and did not wipe his hand; he is not the writer of the fourth row, and I have never asked him. The strip of salt-paper has lifted at one corner and shows six words of what it was meant to cover. The struck word in the year-entries is mine: I wrote \emph{the water was poisoned}, and have put \emph{the water was complained of} above it, because the book holds what was entered, and what was entered was the complaint. What was in the water is in the margin, where the College hand does not reach.

\subsection*{At the foot, in a hand nobody will own}

\begin{quote}\itshape Five clauses on the slate and none at the well;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the road was opened and the water was not.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape They entered the households and left the rows,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the twenty-one went downriver with the debt.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Ask the pot at the lip what it held.\end{quote}

\clearpage\phantomsection\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{The Title of Bonds, Being the Ordinance of the Keeping for the Entering, Serving, Assignment and Reckoning of Debts, Copied into the Assessor’s House at Sill with the Bond-Clerk’s Margin, the Knife-Score, and a Correction in a Borrowed Hand}
\CRsheetheading{The Title of Bonds, Being the Ordinance of the Keeping for the Entering, Serving, Assignment and Reckoning of Debts, Copied into the Assessor’s House at Sill with the Bond-Clerk’s Margin, the Knife-Score, and a Correction in a Borrowed Hand}
{\centering\FellFont\itshape\footnotesize\color{faded} An extract from the Court’s ordinances, copied out for the counter of the assessor’s house in Slate Row, Sill, with the marginal hand of the clerk who keeps the bond-slate; the articles in Ledgerhand, the verbs restored beneath them, one line scored with a knife-point, two corrections in borrowed hands, and a form of entry left blank for want of a name · Copied at Sill in the assessor’s house built in Y.H. 776, in Ilmen of Y.H. 813, from Title the Fourth of the Ordinances of the Keeping as confirmed to the factor at Greybank by the treaty of Y.H. 418 and added to after the Rising of Y.H. 668, in Y.H. 782 and in the Thin Year, Y.H. 812; carried forward at the Opening of the Slates. It survives as three leaves of foolscap sewn with wire and tied with a grown string, kept in the pigeonhole behind the counter and taken down when a debt is disputed; an iron-gall thumb at the head, a bone-pale streak of slip down the gutter, a line scored deep with a knife-point in the lower margin, a tallow thumb at the fold, a grey Ash print along the outer edge, a green bead of lead glaze in the corner, two corrections in hands that are not the writer’s, and seven short lines pasted inside the cover in a hand nobody has claimed.\par}\medskip
I keep the bond-slate at this counter. A man comes up from the yard with a figure in the thumb of his right hand and wants it entered before the factor’s man comes up from Greybank; a woman comes who has paid a debt in loaves for six years and wants me to call the six a seven. I write what the ordinance tells me and I set the verbs back underneath the words it has taken out, because a debt without a verb is a debt nobody did, and that is the kind the Court has always liked best. What follows is Title the Fourth, copied out so that a person may know what is being read to him before it is read. I have kept the blanks in the form of entry blank. I have never had a name to put in them that the household wanted spoken in this room.

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{At the head of the first leaf, in the same hand, written very small:} Copied by the counter, and for it. The verbs were put back by me and struck out again by a man who does not keep a counter. Let both stand. A slate with two hands on it is the only kind a woman believes.\end{quote}

\subsection*{Title the Fourth, as it stands}

\emph{From the Ordinances of the Keeping, Title the Fourth: Of Bond, Service, the Assignment and the Reckoning of Debts. Confirmed to the factor at Greybank by the treaty of Y.H. 418; added to in the year after the Rising, Y.H. 668, in Y.H. 782, and in the Thin Year, Y.H. 812.}

\subsection*{I. Of the entering of a debt}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item Every debt is entered upon the bond-slate within three days of the promise, in Ledgerhand and without verbs. The sum is entered in marks, or in loaves, or in days of service, and is not changed from one kind to another without a second hand set beside the first.

\item Where the promise was made in the yard and not at the counter, the entering officer is not the man who heard it. What was heard is not written. The debt is named by the debtor and the creditor together; the house roll is kept close and is not shown.

\item A debt entered only in a house roll is a debt the Court has not picked up. No entry is made against it and no figure is struck.

\end{enumerate}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Margin:} A debt left lying is not a debt forgiven. It is a debt nobody has taken up. I have three such standing in this book from the winter, with nobody on either side of them, and they are entered in the same neat hand as the debts that are being paid, so that no man can tell by the writing which is which. I have set the word \emph{stands} above them, which is the word used for an account in good order. I have not been corrected, and that is how I know nobody reads this column.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Margin, in a second and narrower hand:} Article 3 was added in Y.H. 782, the year the maids began to be paid. A hearth-maid lays the birth-slate on the bench before she goes to the child. A woman lays her house roll on this counter before she says what she came for. These two things are of a kind, and the ordinance does not say so.\end{quote}

\subsection*{II. Of the term and what gathers upon it}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item A clay-bound term is seven years, or such other years as a household has set and entered. It is reckoned from the day of entering and not from the thaw.

\item Interest gathers as grey Ash in the household account and not upon the Court’s slate. It is not counted in marks, being a thing that collects where promises are left unkept. It is not swept away before the Last Day.

\item In the Fenmarch a breath is bought for a season or for a year, which is called bought breath. The name of the buyer is not entered where the debt is paid.

\item Where a term is spoken of as running \emph{till the thaw}, no day is entered and the debt is not discharged by the coming of warm weather.

\end{enumerate}

Debt, as entered — Term — What gathers — Discharged\par

Clay-bound hand — Seven years from the day of entering — Grey in the house roll — In the thaw, when the house says\par

Bought breath, the season — One season, and no day — Nothing entered — To the buyer at the season’s end\par

A tile debt left lying — No term entered — Grey, unmeasured — Nowhere; not forgiven\par

Bread given at a house door — No entry — Nothing — Nothing; given and not entered\par

A loan that can hear — The term of the debt — What the borrower hears — By the lender, who does not always call\par

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Margin:} The woman who came on the last Account-day had six years in her thumb and wanted me to write seven. I wrote the day of entering, which her household had set, and not the six she carried. She said the seventh was as good as kept. I said a kept year and a paid year are different vessels, which is a thing I have no right to say at a counter, and so I said nothing and let her say it. The ordinance gives me no word for the year a man holds back so that he need not pay. I have scored a line in the lower margin with my knife instead, which is not an entry and cannot be added.\end{quote}

\subsection*{III. Of the keeping of those in service}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item A bond-servant is lodged apart from the household’s children, in the loft or the out-room, and is not entered at the family hearth. The household’s own child is not lodged there.

\item Where consent to a lawful collection is withheld, the vessel is clip-held by the wrist until consent is entered. A pale ring left at the wrist is spoken of as nothing and is not entered as a wound.

\item No cold iron is set to a living wrist save by the officer appointed thereunto. The tubes are mended at the smithy, which keeps no kiln-mark and is not a great house.

\end{enumerate}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Margin:} A foundling was given a bed under the roof here, in a house three doors down the yard, while a debt was given the loft. The house did not call it kindness and I have not entered it. A child under a roof and a debt above a wheel-shed are two vessels in one house, and the house knows which it means to keep. I have put no figure against either.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Margin:} The ring shows through the winter. I have seen a man rub his cuff down over it while he was being told the figure, and go out saying the ring would go in the thaw. That is what my mother said about everything. It is not in the ordinance.\end{quote}

\subsection*{IV. Of assignment and purchase before due}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item A debt may be assigned before it is due, and the assignment entered in the hand of the buyer or his factor. The debtor is not asked.

\item Where a debt is bought for the measure rather than the marks, the entry is made in marks. The measure is not entered.

\item The widow’s mark is not assigned. The factor at Greybank confirms it, and the confirmation is spoken of as a kindness and entered as one.

\item Debts of Grath sold south to the bowls of Sere are entered as goods and not as persons. The figure is copied from the factor’s slate.

\end{enumerate}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{In the leaning hand of the factor’s man come up from Greybank, written over article 11:} assigned in due course. \emph{Underneath, in mine:} bought before due. He strikes the verb wherever he finds one, as though a verb were a thing a man could carry off in a cuff and sell at the crossing. I have left both stand. A debt bought before it is due has a different smell in the room from one assigned in due course, and I am the man who has to stand at the counter when the smell arrives.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Margin:} Against article 13 the factor’s man wrote \emph{kindness entered}, which is exactly what the ordinance says and exactly what the house means when it does not want a question. There is no column for it and no figure in it, and still it is entered every time.\end{quote}

\subsection*{V. Of faults and their correcting}

Fault — As entered — Correction\par

A verb in the roll — Page copied again, in the same hand — The verb set underneath, where the clerk put it\par

A debt in a house roll only — Stands — Not paid, and not called forgiven\par

A term called \emph{till the thaw} — The day of entering — If no day stands, none is supplied\par

A seventh year claimed early — Six, and the seventh held — No figure given to the holding\par

A sealed bond carried beyond the room — The carrier’s own debt entered in its place — The first entry left standing beside it\par

\subsection*{The form of entry}

\emph{Set out at the end of Title the Fourth. I have copied it with the blanks as they stand in the book. In nine years nobody has filled one.}

\begin{quote}\itshape Entered this day, being ---day of -------, in the year of the Hearth ------, the debt of ----------------------, set at -------- marks, or ------- loaves, or ------- days of service, to be served from the day of entering and not from the thaw; the interest to gather as grey in the house account; the hand that writes not the hand that holds; the debt to stand until claimed, and to be discharged where the household says. Entered by ----------------------, who is not the man who heard it.\end{quote}

\subsection*{Seven lines pasted inside the cover}

\emph{Not part of the ordinance. Said under the breath at the counter while the tally is cut, and never when the factor’s man is in the room. I found the leaf pasted in and have not taken it out.}

\begin{quote}\itshape Six on the sill and a seventh not cut,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the wood keeps the year that the slate left out;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape grey in the corner and crust by the door,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape what nobody claimed stands and stands, and no more.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape One in twelve, says the notice, read twice at the Cross;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the house says the thaw, and the thaw says a sum;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the notch is a place and the slate is a figure,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the place goes on when the figure is done.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{In the narrow upright hand, against the last line:} Seven lines pasted. \emph{In mine:} I count seven and so does he. He has put no number against the notch, which is how I know he has looked at it. A man does not number what he has not looked at.\end{quote}

\subsection*{At the head and in the gutter}

The brown at the head is iron-gall and mine, made by holding the quire open through a market morning; it will not come out of the creases. The bone-pale streak in the gutter is slip off the forearms of a thrower who held her slate away from her coat while she waited and set it for a moment against this leaf. The line scored deep in the lower margin is mine and was cut with the small knife I keep at the counter, the same morning the woman wanted six called seven; a knife goes into paper more easily than into a bench, but the mark stays in both. The tallow at the fold came off the lamp I keep turned low while I write, so that a woman at the counter will not change her tale for me. The grey along the outer edge came off my own cuff going down to the Cross on Account-day, where I put my hand into a corner I had no business putting it into. The green bead in the corner is not slip; it is lead glaze from a girl come up from High Kiln with the sweetness still at her mouth, who leaned to see the form of entry and did not ask to have it filled. I have kept everything where it fell. There is no Last Day behind a counter.

\subsection*{At the foot, in a hand nobody has claimed}

\begin{quote}\itshape Under the roof they count in loaves; above the wheel they count in years; and the bench counts both in wood and says neither thing.\end{quote}

I have asked the factor’s man, a man come down from the College, and a woman who stood here about her house, and had three answers and no hand, as I have had before. I have left the line where it was written. Tomorrow the factor’s man will come up from Greybank with a debt bought before it is due and want the entry in his own hand, and I shall write \emph{bought} underneath as I have written it every tend; a woman will come with six years in her thumb and ask me to make them seven, and I shall write the day that stands. The bench behind the counter has six notches cut into it and a seventh place scored deep with a knife and not cut through. I did not cut it and cannot say who did. It will be there in the morning.

\clearpage\phantomsection\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{The Book of Again, Being the Figures Set Against Vessels Returned to the Bank a Second, Third and Fourth Time in the Assessor’s Room of Slate Row in the Hearthseat, with the Older Figure Beneath the Newer, the Remark Left Standing, Two Corrections in the College Hand, and a Line at the Foot Nobody Will Own}
\CRsheetheading{The Book of Again, Being the Figures Set Against Vessels Returned to the Bank a Second, Third and Fourth Time in the Assessor’s Room of Slate Row in the Hearthseat, with the Older Figure Beneath the Newer, the Remark Left Standing, Two Corrections in the College Hand, and a Line at the Foot Nobody Will Own}
{\centering\FellFont\itshape\footnotesize\color{faded} A page from an assessor’s ledger in the Hearthseat; figures in Ledgerhand copied from the collectors’ slates, the terse remarks in the hand that set the worth, a column of likenesses struck out by the College and drawn back underneath, one figure struck and set above in a borrowed hand, a word scraped away, and a line at the foot that has never been claimed · Written in the assessor’s counting room off the Weighing Hall in Slate Row of the Hearthseat, between the Weighing and the Remembering of Y.H. 812, the Thin Year, and carried forward at the Opening of the Slates, Ilmen 1, Y.H. 813; kept in a board cover under the counter and taken down whenever a whole return is disputed. It survives as two leaves of foolscap sewn with wire, with an iron-gall thumb at the head, a streak of bone-pale slip down the gutter, a tallow print where the lamp was held low, grey Ash off a returned woman’s sleeve worked into the outer fold, a pale round clip-ring pressed into the third leaf, a corner scorched by a spark off the grating, a green bead of lead glaze in the lower corner, a small square of bare paper where a word was scraped away, two corrections in the narrow upright hand of the College, one in the soft-cuffed hand of a factor’s clerk out of Greybank, and a line at the foot nobody will own\par}\medskip
I set the worth of a vessel that comes back. The room is off the Weighing Hall in Slate Row of the Hearthseat, and I have kept the figures in it for eleven years. A man dies in a district and a collector draws him and a factor enters the figure; years later the same man dies in another district and another slate comes under my counter with a different number written on it. I set the number the slate gives and, underneath it, the number the last slate gave. I have never added the two. Adding is a College matter, and the last hand in this room that added a column made a total which would not agree with the notice, and the factor at Greybank sent word that the notice was to be copied again in a better hand.

The brown thumb at the head is iron-gall and mine, made by holding a quire open through a Weighing morning. Clerks in this building can tell an assessor by his thumb before he has spoken, which is one of the small mercies of the trade: a man is known by what he has handled.

Twelve copper bits to a silver mark. Twenty silver marks to a gold crown, a Sere coin that comes north with a factor and goes south when he does. The Court books an ember at five marks and I have never once seen a man exchange the one for the other, though I have entered both figures in the same hour. One in twelve is printed on the notice and read in a clean voice at the Weighing. A whole return is one measure poured into one vessel and booked at the figure. A thin return is many measures pooled and divided among cradles by lot, and the figure is entered afterwards. There is no third kind on the notice, and there are three kinds in this book, the third being the kind that comes back to be counted again.

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{In the narrow upright hand of a man come down from the College:} Valuations entered in the ordinary way. \emph{Underneath, in mine:} There is nothing ordinary about a figure I have written twice for the same person with a different hand holding the slate each time. I have put the person back in.\end{quote}

\subsection*{The leaf, as it stood between the Weighing and the Remembering}

\emph{Figures in Ledgerhand. The older figure stands beneath the newer and has not been struck. The remarks are mine, in the hand that set the worth, and are not part of the account.}

Vessel, as the slate names it — Times returned — Embers now — Figure at first — Figure now — Return due — Remark\par

A glaze-room girl, High Kiln. \emph{Sweet} — second — 38 — 44 — 190 marks — thin — Asked after the taste. Entered none.\par

A clay-bound hand of the terraces — third — 29 — 51 — 145 marks — whole, by the factor’s order — Figure below the last two. \emph{Whole} set above \emph{with memory} in a borrowed hand. Both stand.\par

A woman of the Weir — second — 47 — 50 — 235 marks — thin — Came back wanting the river. No column for wanting.\par

A man of Mud End. \emph{Peat} — fourth — 22 — 56 — 110 marks — thin — Drawn before light. The four figures go down like a stair. I have not added the stair.\par

A returned child who would not warm — second — 13 — 15 — not set — — — Entered as a birth and not a worsening. The first slate was written before the face was looked at.\par

A vessel of the Ember bowl-house, out of Sere — three, spoken of — — — — — 1,200 marks and forty unspent measures, as booked — whole — Three whole returns are said to stand at 799, 804 and 809. The southern figures do not come north. A factor’s clerk wrote \emph{three times} above the space; I have left the space.\par

One of the Kept, in passing — — — 300 — — — not set — none — Asked after the weather. Pity entered, which has no column.\par

Draws behind this leaf: seven. Figures struck: none in my hand. Columns struck: one. Words scraped away: one.

\subsection*{The figure that goes down}

A remark is not part of the account. The College has never thought to strike the remark column out of this book, which I take for an oversight and not a mercy, and so I keep what I please in it.

The clay-bound hand came to me three times. The first figure stood at fifty-one, the second at thirty-eight, the third at twenty-nine, and the deduction stood at one in twelve between them like a stone that has not moved while the water went down. I have set the three numbers one under another and joined neither. I do not say what it means. An assessor who explains a figure has begun to write a sermon, and sermons get copied.

On the man of Mud End I wrote the word \emph{stair} first as a cause and then scraped it away, which is the bare square in the lower margin, and wrote it again as a likeness, which is all it is. Four figures from one man, each lower than the last, and each time a collector came in off the clay road with grey at the head of the slate and gave me the number before he gave me the name. There are eleven words for a deduction taught in the College and not one for a stair, which is the whole of the difficulty between us.

The glaze-room girl asked after the taste. She had had it once and had come back with a mouth that knew the shape of it and no word to put to it. I entered the figure and not the question, because a question has no column and a woman who asks one at a counter will be told the figure the notice says and go away with it. She set her cup down on the corner of the counter and did not take it up again, and I have not moved it. There is a ring where it stood on an earlier leaf and I have kept the leaf.

The woman of the Weir came back wanting the river. I have put that in the remark because she said it in my hearing and there is nowhere else to put it. A banker would call it a likeness and a physician would call it a thing to be entered in a column the family is not shown. I have called it wanting. I am aware that this is not a figure and cannot be added, which is why it stays where a clerk carrying the leaf will have to read it.

\subsection*{The likeness column struck by the College}

Beside \emph{Return due} I had kept a place with no heading, in which I set down what the vessel did when the figure was read aloud. The girl of the glaze room turned her mouth toward the cup before the cup was shown. The woman of the Weir turned toward the door that leads down to the river road. The child who would not warm reached toward the lamp. The man of Mud End said nothing and put his hand into his sleeve, where a number had once been, and brought it out empty.

The man from the College borrowed the leaf on the morning after the Weighing and struck the column from the first row to the last, and wrote \emph{No such column} above it in his narrow upright hand. I have drawn the column back underneath and left his words standing over it. He had to look at every row before he could write that there were none worth entering, and I watched him do it, standing as he stands, with his cuff gone soft from washing and the ink settled in two fingers of it. A man does not count what he has not looked at.

I have put no heading over the column still. A heading would turn a likeness into an entry and an entry into something a clerk may be called to answer for, and this house has answered for enough this year.

\subsection*{What the two borrowed hands did}

The College man struck the verb out of \emph{the figure went down} and set \emph{the figure was reduced} above it, and above that \emph{the valuation was adjusted}, which is further from the man who died than the first. I have put my words back underneath both. A sentence with nobody in it is a sentence no woman can ask about, and women ask about these figures in the end, always at the counter, always after the slate is shut.

Against the clay-bound hand he struck \emph{with memory} and set \emph{whole} above it, which is the word the notice prints and the word a house upriver will pay twelve hundred marks to hear. Both stand. I have not chosen between them and would thank any man who told me I had to.

The factor’s clerk did one thing. At the foot of the leaf, where I had written \emph{figure smaller than the last two}, he wrote \emph{figure corrected upward} and underlined it twice. The figure was not corrected upward. It was made smaller twice, by two collectors who had never met, in two districts that do not share a slate. I have left his line where he put it and mine where I put it. Neither is a lie in the language of its own room, and the man is not in either of them.

\subsection*{The song they carry up the passage}

\emph{Sung low going up the passage from the Weighing Hall to the rooms beside it, never at the reading and never twice in one day. The fourth stroke is the one they hold; I have set the words as they came.}

\begin{quote}\itshape Four for the fire behind the iron,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape four for the nails in this Hall;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape a place where the fifth should stand\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and nobody crosses himself.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape The figure goes down, the figure goes down,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the deduction does not go down;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape they read us the sum in a clean voice\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and we carry the rest in the cold.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape One slate at the first and one at the third,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape one at the going-out of the breath;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the hand that wrote the figure is grey\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the figure is entered as death.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Hold the fourth. Let the fifth stand where it is.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape What comes back is not what went,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and comes back as it can.\end{quote}

A clerk come up from Sill told me the bell there goes four, four and a gap and that nobody crosses himself. I have kept his telling beside the song and not made it a hearing. A man of the College put a nought in the fifth place and wrote \emph{vacancy} under it. A nought is a figure and can be carried out in a cuff. The fifth is a place and stays.

\subsection*{At the head and in the gutter}

The brown at the head is iron-gall and mine. The bone-pale streak down the gutter is slip off the forearms of the glaze-room girl, who held her slate away from her coat while she waited and set it for a moment against this quire; she did not know she had marked it and I have not told her. The tallow print at the foot came off the lamp I keep turned low so that a woman at the counter will not change her tale for me when I write down what she asked.

The grey in the outer fold came off the sleeve of the woman of the Weir as she leaned to see the columns. It is not mine and it did not come off my cuff, and I have not swept it. They sweep the corners of houses on the Last Day and burn what they find in the morning and call it dealt with. There is no Last Day in an assessor’s room. The rolls of the dead are carried forward here and never closed, which is a kind of mercy in a thing nobody finishes.

The pale round ring in the third leaf was made by a collector setting his cold tube down while he reached for a figure out of his cuff. The paper is thinner inside it. The tube had been used an hour before and was not used again that day, and the ring is not a wound, but it is the only mark on this leaf that looks like one. The scorched corner caught a spark off the grating while I held the leaf up to the light. The green bead is lead glaze from a girl who leaned over to see the figures with the sweetness still at her mouth and touched the paper and said nothing. The small bare square is where I scraped the word away and put no other in its place. I have not written it back and have not forgotten it.

\subsection*{At the foot, in a hand nobody will own}

\begin{quote}\itshape The bank keeps the figure that went in. This book keeps the figures that came back.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape The space between them has no column and no hand.\end{quote}

I asked the College man, a factor’s clerk come up from Greybank, and a woman who stood at the counter about a daughter of hers, and had three answers and no hand. I have left the lines where they were written.

The leaf goes back under the counter. Tomorrow a vessel will come back a fourth time and a collector will come in off the clay road with grey at the head of his slate, and I shall set the new figure above the old ones and put the verbs back where the College struck them out, and leave the likeness column standing where it was drawn. Somewhere in a district a child will turn toward a cup before a cup has been shown to him, and no figure in this book will tell his mother why. The rolls stay open. The book stays in the cover. That is the whole of it, and it goes on.

\clearpage\phantomsection\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{The Book of Worth, Being the Valuations Set in the Assessor’s House at Sill in the Thin Year, and the Figures Set Above Them in a Second Hand}
\CRsheetheading{The Book of Worth, Being the Valuations Set in the Assessor’s House at Sill in the Thin Year, and the Figures Set Above Them in a Second Hand}
{\centering\FellFont\itshape\footnotesize\color{faded} A page from the valuation ledger of the assessor’s house in Slate Row, Sill; figures in Ledgerhand, terse remarks in the hand of the assessor who set them, one column left unfilled, and two corrections in the narrow upright hand of the College · Written at Sill in the assessor’s house built in Y.H. 776, in the Thin Year Y.H. 812, and carried forward at the Opening of the Slates on Ilmen 1, Y.H. 813; kept in a board cover under the counter and taken down when a figure is disputed. It survives as two leaves of foolscap sewn with wire: an iron-gall thumb at the head, a streak of bone-pale slip down the gutter, a green bead of glaze in the lower corner, a tallow thumb, grey Ash worked into the outer fold, a small square of bare paper where a word was scraped away, two corrections in the College’s narrow hand, and one line at the foot in a hand nobody will own.\par}\medskip
I set the worth of vessels in this house. It stands in Slate Row at Sill, built in Y.H. 776, with the Court’s room next door and the Waiting Room behind, and the slate on my counter was bought the year the house was raised and has outlasted three assessors whose names I cannot now read. A figure comes to me off the collector’s slate and I set a worth against it and a return due; once a tend a man comes down from the College at the Hearthseat and strikes the verbs out of what I have written. I put them back. It is an arrangement of the kind that lasts because neither of us writes in the other’s hand.

The brown thumb at the head of this leaf is iron-gall and mine, made by holding a quire open through a market morning. It will not wash out of the creases. There are clerks in the Hearthseat who can tell an assessor by his thumb before he has spoken a word, which is one of the small mercies of the trade.

What follows is one leaf of the valuation book, being the figures set in the last tend of Stone and carried forward into Ilmen. I have set the rates first, so that a man may see what an ember is said to be worth before he sees what I set against a life. I have not added the column. Adding is a College matter, and the last time a hand in this house added a column the total would not agree with the printed one, and the factor at Greybank sent word that the printed one was to be copied again in a better hand.

\subsection*{The rates of the house}

Entry — As the house has it\par

Copper bit — twelve to a silver mark\par

Silver mark — twenty to a gold crown, a Sere coin that does not stay in Grath\par

Ember — five marks, by the Court’s book; no man has exchanged one for the other\par

Newborn vessel — twelve to fifteen embers\par

Labourer in good case — forty to sixty embers\par

A Held vessel — a hundred and upward\par

One of the Kept — three hundred; no figure any household can spend\par

Deduction — one in twelve, as the notice says\par

Whole return — one measure poured into one vessel, booked at the figure\par

Thin return — many measures pooled and divided, figure entered by lot\par

An ember is worth five marks in this room. In the yard a woman sells six eels for five marks or five for six and makes nothing of it, which is a fact about eels and not about embers. I have set both figures down and joined neither.

\subsection*{The leaf, as it stood}

\emph{Figures in Ledgerhand. The remarks are mine, in the hand that set the worth, and are not part of the account.}

Vessel, as entered — Embers — Worth — Deduction — Return due — Remark\par

A thrower of the low yard, second entry — 41 — 205 marks — 1 in 12 — thin — First entry stood higher. No reason entered.\par

A glaze-room girl, High Kiln — 38 — 190 marks — 1 in 12 — thin — Sweetness at the mouth. Name given, not entered.\par

A widow with the mark, Vail house — 33 — not set — 1 in 12 — — — The mark is not a figure. House roll kept close. Kindness entered.\par

A clay-bound hand, the terraces — 44 — 220 marks — 1 in 12 — thin — Six years entered. The seventh held back.\par

A man of the Weir — 47 — 235 marks — 1 in 12 — thin — Drawn before light. Worth set after. Order as it stood.\par

A foundling left at the mill — 12 — 60 marks — 1 in 12 — — — A stone under him, not a name. Stands till a hearth claims him.\par

Forty of Low Kiln, one line for the batch — — — — — 1 in 12 — whole — By lot. Names not taken. Purchaser entered elsewhere.\par

One of the Kept, in passing — 300 — not set — none — none — Asked after the weather. Pity entered.\par

A vessel returned three times — 29 — 145 marks — 1 in 12 — whole — Figure smaller than the last. Entered whole. No note made.\par

A house of the terraces, disputed — 52 — 260 marks — 1 in 12 — — — Thumb wiped twice. Figure asked for, then not wanted. Left standing.\par

\subsection*{The remarks}

A remark is not part of the account. The College has never thought to strike the remark column out of this book, which I take for an oversight and not a mercy, and so I keep what I please in it. \emph{Figure smaller than the last} is the only line on this leaf that I have had to write twice. The first time I set it down as a cause and then scraped the word away, which is the bare square in the lower margin; the second time I set it down as a likeness, which is all it is. I have seen three entries of one vessel and three figures going the same way, smaller each time, and the deduction standing at one in twelve between them like a stone that has not moved while the water went down. I do not say what it means. A clerk who explains a figure has begun to write a sermon, and sermons get copied.

\emph{Asked after the weather. Pity entered.} There is no column for pity and no figure for a courteous vessel. I put it in the remark because a man who has sat across this counter for nine and thirty years should be allowed one line that is not a number. The College left it. I have not decided whether that was the oversight.

\subsection*{What the College hand did}

The man from the Hearthseat has a cuff gone soft from washing and ink settled in two fingers of it. He does not sit down. He borrowed the leaf on a market morning and did three things to it.

Where I wrote \emph{the first entry stood higher}, he struck out \emph{stood} and set \emph{was higher} above, and then struck out \emph{was} also, leaving \emph{higher} with nothing to stand on. I have put \emph{stood} back underneath and left his \emph{higher} where he set it. A figure with a verb in it can be argued with, which is why he takes the verbs out; but a woman at my counter wants to know who did what, and a word with nothing to stand on will not tell her.

Against the vessel returned three times I had written, in the remark, \emph{with memory}. He struck it and set \emph{whole} above it. Both stand. \emph{Whole} is the word the notice uses and the word the household hears read in a clean voice at the Weighing. \emph{With memory} is the word I use when I am not reading anything aloud. I have not chosen between them, and I would thank any man who told me I had to.

He struck my last column also and wrote \emph{No such column} above it. I have struck his striking out and left the column where I drew it.

\subsection*{The column I drew and they struck out}

I keep a place beside the figure the notice gives for the figure the household actually gave. I have set no heading over it. A heading would make it an account, and an account is a thing a man may be called to answer for, and this house has answered for enough this year.

The last time I was asked to set a worth against a house of Low Kiln, the man who came did not bring the figure in his mouth. He brought it in his thumb, the way they do down the yard, and wiped that thumb twice across his slate before he touched nothing and said the figure the notice says. I entered the figure the notice says, as I am required to, and in the place beside it I entered his two wipes and the pause between them, which is not a figure and cannot be added. When the College man struck the column he wrote \emph{No such column} in the same upright hand he uses for the deduction. He had counted the rows before he wrote it, which is how I know the column troubled him. A man does not count what he has not looked at.

A place is not a debt. The College teaches eleven words for a deduction and has none for a place, and the clerk who came down from the Hearthseat gave himself away by putting a number in one.

\subsection*{In the margins}

The streak of slip in the gutter came off the forearms of the thrower whose figure stands second on the leaf. She held her slate away from her coat while she waited and set it against this quire for a moment, and the grey came off on the edge. The green bead in the lower corner is not slip. It is lead glaze from a girl who leaned over to see the writing with the sweetness still at her mouth, and touched the paper, and said nothing. I left it where she put it. The tallow thumb at the foot of the second leaf is the foundling’s, or the mark of a woman holding him who used her whole hand to keep the leaf still in the draught under the door; I do not know which and have not asked. The Ash in the outer fold came off my own cuff going down to the Cross on Account-day, where I put my hand into a corner I had no business putting it into and the grey came away on the cloth. They sweep the corners of the houses on the Last Day and burn what they find in the morning and call it dealt with. There is no Last Day for a valuation book.

\subsection*{At the foot}

The line below was not written by me and is not in Ledgerhand. I found it under the counter when I came in on the morning after the last market, and I asked the factor’s man, and the College man, and a woman who had stood at the counter about her house, and had three answers and no hand. I have left it where it was written.

\begin{quote}\itshape The book keeps the figure. The yard keeps the place where the figure stood.\end{quote}

The leaf goes back under the counter. Tomorrow the factor’s man will come up from Greybank with a slate whose upper line is in a neat dark hand, with a small stop between two clusters that I have seen before and joined to nothing, and I shall set a worth against it and put the verbs back and leave the column where I drew it. A woman will stand where women stand and ask what her house is worth, and I shall read her the figure the notice says, which is the only figure she can carry away. The other one stays here. It has nowhere else to go.

\clearpage\phantomsection\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{The Bowl Beside the Bed, Being a Lullaby of the Bowl of Sere Sung by a Woman Who Gives Suck to a Child That Is Not Hers}
\CRsheetheading{The Bowl Beside the Bed, Being a Lullaby of the Bowl of Sere Sung by a Woman Who Gives Suck to a Child That Is Not Hers}
{\centering\FellFont\itshape\footnotesize\color{faded} A wet-nurse’s lullaby taken down from her own mouth in the women’s quarter of a great house of the Ten Bowls; the verses in the long-vowelled courtesy speech of Sere, the manner of saying them in the writer’s own charcoal, a bowl-house tally-clerk’s correction set above in his leaning hand, a northern bond-woman’s charcoal pressed underneath, a gloss in myrrh from a woman who has given suck in three houses, and one line at the foot in a hand nobody will own · Sung in the third watch of the night in the women’s quarter of a great house in the Bowl of Sere, after the household bowl had gone round at the third hour of the day and the court fires were banked, and set down in Y.H. 812 by a woman of the house who gives suck and had once kept a tally before she was bought; written in charcoal and the dregs of a myrrh phial on the back of a bowl-house linen tally spoiled at one corner, sewn with a thread of grey wool into a fold of oiled silk and kept under the cradle mat. A factor’s clerk carried it north at the Opening of the Slates, Ilmen 1, Y.H. 813, and copied it at Greybank onto the back of a Court grain-warrant voided by the Long Cold, where the lowland name for that year, the Thin Year, was added below the southern one. It survives with a ring of warm wine at the head, yellow dust of the burning winds ground into the fold, a smear of myrrh across the second leaf, a milky thumb in the gutter that nobody will own, a green bead of lead glaze chipped from a bowl at the third hour, a curl of grey wool from a northern sleeve shut in the sewing, the tally-clerk’s correction standing above, the two charcoal hands standing below, and the line at the foot which has never been claimed\par}\medskip
I give suck in a house that is not mine, to a child whose name I am not permitted to say until the household has chosen it. I have done this for four years. I know the weight of the child on my arm the way a potter knows the weight of a pot before the glaze goes on, and I know the sound the house makes when the bowl goes round at the third hour, which is a sound with a debt in it.

A clerk come up from the factor’s house at Greybank stood in the portico and asked the women what we sang over the cradles. He wrote down the names, because names are what a clerk can carry away. I have set the song down as we say it, with the verbs left where we put them and the space left where the space is.

The ring at the head is wine. I held the leaf down in the draught under the portico and did not know I had marked it.

\subsection*{How it is said}

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item In the third watch, after the household bowl has gone round and the fires in the open court are banked for the night. Not at the Bowl feast and not on a name-day; on those days every name in the house is already in the air, and a song said then is a song with a name in it, which is a different thing.

\item Hold the child with its ear to your collar and not to the wall. Said toward a wall, the song becomes an instruction to the house, and there is no room in a great house that has not already been told what it is to do.

\item Set a cup down at the cradle’s head and do not drink from it. It is not the child’s cup and it is not yours. It stands for the one that was poured out in the court and cannot be carried back up the steps.

\item Say the refrain to the bowl and not to the child. Said looking into a face, the second line becomes a question, and there is nobody in this house, including me, who may answer it in the child’s hearing.

\item If a phial of quiet ash stands on the shelf, leave it corked. A voice that cannot arrive is not the same as a voice that has stopped wanting to.

\item Say the last line once. The space before the last refrain is the length of a name and is kept empty. I do not fill it and neither does the child.

\end{itemize}

\subsection*{The song}

\emph{Said low, with the ends of the words let fall the way a drop falls from a dipped cup. The refrain is said to the bowl.}

\begin{quote}\itshape The bowl came down from the open court warm,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the colour of skimmed milk gone blue at the rim;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the household drank and the act was announced,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and nobody asked who had carried it in.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Sleep, little bowl. The wine keeps warm.}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{I bore a child and it is not this one.}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Seven names stand ready above your bed\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the house will keep the one it likes;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape I have one name of my own and it is not mine ---\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape I say it to the bowl and not to you.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Sleep, little bowl. The wine keeps warm.}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{I bore a child and it is not this one.}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape They teach in the court that a vessel was made\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape to be emptied in public and praised for the emptying;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape I have held a cup through the whole of the third hour\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and learned which hand pours and which hand pays.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Sleep, little bowl. The wine keeps warm.}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{I bore a child and it is not this one.}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape I had a child with a brown edge to his crust\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and a way of turning his head at a cup;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape he went to the mills when the term was called,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the voice that called it was clean.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Sleep, little bowl. The wine keeps warm.}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{I bore a child and it is not this one.}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape The mistress sets a phial of quiet ash by the bed\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape so no voice from a former life will arrive;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape I have uncorked one and smelled it and set it down ---\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape a voice is a thing a woman can bear to hear.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Sleep, little bowl. The wine keeps warm.}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{I bore a child and it is not this one.}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape So sleep. I will not say the seventh name,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape which is not chosen and has no weight in it yet;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the cup stands full where the hand set it down\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the wine keeps warm for the one who will pay.\end{quote}

There is a space before the last refrain. I have left it on the leaf. It is the right length for a name and for nothing else, and the child who cannot yet ask what it is will one day ask and will be told that names are chosen above stairs.

\subsection*{What the tally-clerk did}

A bowl-house tally-clerk came into the women’s quarter with a cuff gone soft from washing and ink sitting in two fingers of it that would not come out. He writes in the leaning hand that keeps the glaze-tallies, and he took the verbs out as though a verb were a thing a woman could hide in her sleeve and carry past a door.

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item At \emph{the wine keeps warm} he wrote \emph{the measure is in circulation; temperature not entered}, and underlined the figure twice.

\item At \emph{I bore a child and it is not this one} he wrote \emph{issue: not entered; relation: contractual}, which leaves the room standing and takes both women out of it.

\item At \emph{the house will keep the one it likes} he set \emph{name assigned by household; no deduction arises}, which is true in the figure and false in the room where I said it.

\item At \emph{a voice is a thing a woman can bear to hear} he wrote \emph{no efficacy recorded} and put a small round nought beside the phial.

\item Where the space stands before the last refrain, he put a nought and wrote \emph{vacancy} beside it. He has put a number where a name should stand, which is the whole art of that hand.

\end{itemize}

I have put my words back underneath and left his standing above. He takes the verbs out because a thing always true has no need of them. I put them back because a child at the third watch does not know it is hearing something always true, and wants to know which hand will hold it and which hand will be paid.

\subsection*{What the northern woman wrote underneath}

The thick charcoal belongs to a woman bought out of the clay country who keeps her words on the backs of linen tallies and will not let a clerk see them. I have copied them underneath as she set them.

At \emph{I bore a child and it is not this one}: \emph{She has not seen that child in six years. She asked me whether I had, and I said no, and she put the cup down and did not take it up again.}

At \emph{seven names stand ready}: \emph{Where I come from a child has one name and a pot has a crack you can see. Here they give seven and glaze over the crack. I have set both down and joined neither.}

At \emph{the voice that called it was clean}: \emph{A clean voice is a voice with nobody in it. I have heard one. I was on my knees at the time, and I have never been able to say what the words were.}

At \emph{a voice from a former life}: \emph{She says this of the ash, but she has never asked what is in the phial. I have asked, and was told that the poor here dream in other people’s voices and the rich buy not to.}

At the space before the last refrain: \emph{The saying is not for the child. I asked whose it was and she gave me a date, which is an answer with nothing in it to argue with.}

\subsection*{At the head and in the gutter}

The wine at the head came up out of the paper itself and is the only thing here that entered without a hand. The yellow dust is off the burning winds and has worked into the fold, a southern thing in a book that has been north. The myrrh across the second leaf came from a phial set down while I was telling the child to sleep and it would not; I left the mark where it fell. The milky thumb in the gutter is mine and nobody will own it, which is right, since nobody in this house owns the milk either. The green bead came off a bowl chipped at the third hour when a woman leaned over to see the writing and put her cup down too hard on the rim; it rolled as far as the fold and I have not picked it out. The grey wool in the sewing is off the sleeve of the northern woman, caught when she reached to turn the leaf; she did not see it go and I have not told her. There is no ash left in the corners of a bowl-house to sweep up on a Last Day. They burn the slates instead, and then write new ones before the wine is cold.

\subsection*{At the foot, in a hand nobody will own}

\begin{quote}\itshape The bowl keeps the wine. The house keeps the name.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape The mills keep the child. Nobody keeps the account.\end{quote}

I asked the tally-clerk, the northern woman and the woman who carries the bowl down from the court, and had three answers and no hand. I have left the lines where they were written. The leaf goes back under the cradle mat. Tomorrow the bowl will go round at the third hour and the act will be announced and the women will carry it in and nobody will ask who paid, and at the third watch I shall say the same words into the same space, and a child who cannot yet say them will hear them for the fourth time. If an officer finds the leaf, let him take the verbs out. The next hand will put them back, and will hold the child with its ear to its collar, and will not look into its face while it says the second line.

\clearpage\phantomsection\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{The Bowl Goes Round, Being the Drinking Song of the Women of the Washing-Bench in the House of the Ten Bowls at the Bowl of Sere, with the Order of the Bowls, the Word Under the Glaze, and the Corrections Set Over It}
\CRsheetheading{The Bowl Goes Round, Being the Drinking Song of the Women of the Washing-Bench in the House of the Ten Bowls at the Bowl of Sere, with the Order of the Bowls, the Word Under the Glaze, and the Corrections Set Over It}
{\centering\FellFont\itshape\footnotesize\color{faded} A washing-woman’s drinking song, taken down from her own mouth at the basin after the court had gone; the verses in the long-vowelled courtesy of the south set down in charcoal, with the ends let fall as they are sung, the order of the bowls in the writer’s own hand, the house tally-clerk’s thin gold standing above, a factor’s clerk’s ruling in narrow upright Ledgerhand above that, a northern woman’s charcoal in the margin, and one line at the foot in a hand nobody will own · Written in Grain of Y.H. 812, in the scullery of the House of the Ten Bowls in the Bowl of Sere, by a woman of the washing-bench whose clay-name is Bowl and whose former name is under the glaze of a bowl she has never been permitted to look into; set down in charcoal on the back of a glaze-tally spoiled by a wet thumb at the third furnace, carried north with a consignment of glass and oil in Ilmen of Y.H. 813 and copied at Greybank onto the back of a Court grain-warrant gone soft at one corner. It survives folded in oiled silk in the fold of the washing-cloth, with a ring of warm wine at the head gone the colour of the glaze, a smear of press-oil at the second leaf, a green bead of lead glaze pressed into the lower corner, a fleck of the tally-clerk’s gold, a grey bead of slate-ash from the feast fire shut into the fold, a pale thumb-print where a woman with the sweet sickness leaned over to read, a thread of wool from a kitchen sleeve, one correction in thin gold, one in the narrow upright Ledgerhand of a factor’s clerk at Greybank, a gloss in the charcoal of a bought woman come down from the north, and a line at the foot that has never been claimed\par}\medskip
I am called Bowl. It is the name the house gave me when it bought me, and the name I had before that is written on the inside of a bowl on the lower shelf of the court cupboard, under the lead glaze, where I am not permitted to look. I wash the bowls of the Ten Bowls. That is the whole of my office: to take what the court has emptied, to scour it, and to set it back with the rim turned outward so that nobody sitting at the table can see what is kept under the glaze. There are nine bowls in that rack and I am the tenth, which is a jest the kitchen made once and has never made again.

A woman came south from Greybank with a consignment of glass and asked us at the basin what we sang when the court had gone. She wrote down the first line and went away believing she had learned Sere. I have set down the whole of it, with the ends put back where the court lets them fall, the clerk’s gold left standing above, and my charcoal put back underneath where it belongs. A repaired bowl keeps the old break under the glaze; a corrected leaf keeps the woman under the verb.

The ring at the head is wine. It was warm when I set the tally down and is the colour of the glaze now. I have not washed it out. A bowl that has stood a whole feast and been set down twice is entitled to one stain it did not ask for.

\subsection*{The manner of it}

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item Sung at the basin after the court has gone and before the bowls are stacked. Never in the court: a song with no debt in it is a song somebody will try to enter.

\item The bowls are washed in the reverse of the order in which they were emptied, and the song follows the bowls. The first bowl washed is the last that was handed. There is no reason for this and nobody has asked for one.

\item A sip is taken from what the bowl still holds before it goes into the water. This is not a perquisite and is not entered. The woman who drinks is not the woman who washed the bowl, so that no woman drinks her own leavings.

\item Said to the bowl, with the face turned toward the basin. Said looking at another woman it becomes a question, and there is always a woman who will answer it, and then the kitchen has two griefs instead of one.

\item Do not turn a bowl to the light. The word was cut under the glaze before the firing and the fire shut it in, and the glaze has kept it better than this house has kept anything else. A name that is read is a name the court can enter.

\item If a bowl comes up from the court still warm, hold it a moment before the water. That is the only warmth in this house that nobody has bought for us and nobody will enter against us.

\item When the tally-clerk crosses the yard, stop in the middle of a verse and begin again at the same place when he has gone. A song with a figure in it travels; this one does not.

\item The last place is kept the length of a name. Do not put a nought in it. A nought is a number. A name is a vessel.

\end{itemize}

\subsection*{The song}

\emph{Said low, from bowl to bowl, with the ends of the lines let fall into the basin. The refrain is said to the rim after every part.}

\begin{quote}\itshape The bowl went down the length of the court,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape from the high seat to the last stone bench;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape each man named the debt he meant to carry,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the fire applauded when he said it.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape The wine was warm at the first of them\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and had gone the colour of the rim at the last.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Pass the bowl. The bowl goes round.}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{What it held is poured out. What it keeps is under the glaze.}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape It came to us with a finger of wine in it\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the smell of a fire we were not asked to smell;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape we drink what the court let fall\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the basin keeps what we let fall.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape The basin has no column and asks for none.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Pass the bowl. The bowl goes round.}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{What it held is poured out. What it keeps is under the glaze.}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape There is a word on the inside of the third bowl,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape cut under the lead before it went to the fire;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the fire shut it in and the glaze has kept it\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape better than this house has kept a promise.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape I know the shape of it under my thumb\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and have never once been told the sound of it.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Pass the bowl. The bowl goes round.}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{What it held is poured out. What it keeps is under the glaze.}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape A child of this house is given seven names\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and keeps whichever the household likes;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape a bought woman is given one name\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the one she brought is forbidden.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape The bowls are the only vessels in this court\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape permitted to have kept two.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Pass the bowl. The bowl goes round.}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{What it held is poured out. What it keeps is under the glaze.}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape They burned the slate by lot when the eating was done\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and made a new one out of the same fire;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the debt went up in the smoke and came down in a clean hand,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the house stood where it had stood before.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Nobody clapped for the bowl that held the wine.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Pass the bowl. The bowl goes round.}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{What it held is poured out. What it keeps is under the glaze.}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape The glaze is sweet at the rim and the gum goes pale\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the hand forgets the cup at the end of it;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape nobody asks who paid for the wine,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape nobody asks who paid for the fire;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the bowl stands full for the next of the house,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the next of the house is not named.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Pass the bowl. The bowl goes round.}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{The word on the inside is not read aloud.}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{The bowl keeps it. The bowl gives none back.}\end{quote}

There is a space between the second line of the last refrain and the third. I have left it on the tally. It is the length of a name and of nothing else, and the women leave it when they sing, though none of them has ever said what stands in it.

\subsection*{What the glaze keeps}

A bowl for the court is glazed inside and out. Before the glaze goes on, a word is cut into the clay with a point fine as a needle, and the glaze runs over it and shuts it in, so that the word is there for the life of the bowl and can be come at only by the thumb or by breaking the bowl. This is done to some of the people the house buys and not to others, and I do not know why it was done to me. The kitchen says it is done to those who were once somebody and might be tempted to remember it. I asked whether the house was afraid of a word and was told the house is not afraid of anything, which is how a house answers a question it does not want entered.

The rule is that a bought woman is never to look into the bowl that carries her former name. It is not written anywhere. It is said at the basin the way a pot is said to be hot, which is information and not an order. The bowls go into the rack with the rims outward, and there is a woman at the end of the bench whose whole work is the turning of them, and who has been at it longer than I have been alive. She has never once turned one the other way. When I scour the inside I keep my eyes on the water and my thumb goes where it goes, and that is the whole of the arrangement.

A girl who washed here before me turned a bowl to the lamp and read the word on the inside. She was not beaten and nothing was entered against her. She was given a new clay-name in the morning, and the old word was scraped out of the bowl with a knife and the place filled again with glaze, so that there is a smooth green patch on the inside where the letters had been. She is at the grain mills now. I have not asked which name she answers to. That bowl is fourth from the left on the middle shelf, and I have washed it every tend since and have never turned it to the light.

I have tried to say the word once, to see whether the sound of it would still be mine. I could not get it out. This is not the same as forgetting. A thing under glaze is not lost to the woman who cannot see it; it is lost to the house that thinks it has covered it over.

\subsection*{What the tally-clerk set above}

The tally-clerk of the Ten Bowls came into the scullery with his gold pen and set his hand on my leaf while I was still finding the end of a line. He writes very small, in thin gold, and took the verbs out of four lines, leaving the women standing outside them.

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item At \emph{we drink what the court let fall}, he wrote \emph{the residue of the public bowl is not a discharge of any obligation}. It is true of the wine and does not mention the throat it went down. I have left it.

\item At \emph{the basin has no column and asks for none}, he set \emph{all premises appear in the house inventory}. The basin is not in the inventory. I have put my line back underneath and have not crossed his out.

\item At \emph{I know the shape of it under my thumb}, he wrote \emph{unauthorised handling of house ware is a fault}, and underlined it twice. I was set to wash the bowl. A woman cannot scour the inside of a bowl with her nails.

\item At \emph{the debt went up in the smoke and came down in a clean hand}, he wrote \emph{measure for measure}, which is what a man says in this country when he has already decided what the two measures are.

\item Where I left the space in the last refrain, he put a round nought and wrote \emph{one bowl, current} beside it. A nought is a figure and a bowl is a vessel. The two have never touched, and now they stand on the same line.

\end{itemize}

I have put my words back beneath his everywhere, as the word under the glaze lies under the glaze. He strikes the doer out because a thing always true can be carried into a counting room. I put the doer back because a woman at the basin wants to know whose hand let the wine fall, and the answer is in the sentence if there is somebody in it.

\subsection*{In the margin, in charcoal, a northern woman’s hand}

The charcoal belongs to a woman bought down from the low country, who came here with a skill at the press and has never learned to say the south properly. She writes on the backs of spoiled tallies and presses hard at the ends of words.

\begin{quote}\itshape In the low country they break a pot at the door of a death-house so that the heat may get out. Here they wash the bowl and the heat goes down the drain with the wine. Somebody paid in both countries. Nobody asks in either.\end{quote}

And below, in the same hand:

\begin{quote}\itshape I have washed eleven years here and can still count in marks. They gave me a clay-name the first week and I have not said my own since, but I know the number of it, which is a thing no clerk has thought to take.\end{quote}

I have set both where she wrote them. She would not sign them.

\subsection*{At the head and in the gutter}

The wine-ring at the head is mine and I have not washed it. The oil at the second leaf is press-oil off the sleeve of the woman who wrote in the margin; it has gone into the grain and will come out with nothing. The green bead in the lower corner is lead glaze, broken off a bowl that went to the rack with a star in it; do not touch the edge, the sweetness is in it and the sweetness is not a kindness. The fleck of gold came off the tally-clerk’s pen when he leaned over me. The grey bead in the fold is ash off the burnt slate of the feast; they burn the debt and then buy the ash back, which is a way of keeping a thing and calling it gone. The pale print is from a girl of the glaze room with the pale line at her gum, who leaned over to read and touched the tally and went back to her work. The thread is grey wool off a kitchen sleeve. There is no Last Day in a scullery and nothing gets swept.

\subsection*{At the foot, in a hand nobody will own}

\begin{quote}\itshape The court empties the bowl. The basin keeps the dregs.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape The slate burns. The name stays under the glaze.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Ask the tenth bowl what debt it intends to carry,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and listen to the answer before you applaud.\end{quote}

I asked the woman who turns the rims, the northern woman at the press, and a tally-clerk, and had three answers and no hand. I have left the lines where they were written. The leaf goes back into the oiled silk and the silk into the fold of the cloth. Tomorrow the court will empty the bowls in the same order and we shall wash them in the reverse of it, and the third bowl will go back on the lower shelf with its rim turned outward, and the new slate is already in the counting room with a debt in it that nobody at the basin will be asked to carry.

\clearpage\phantomsection\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{The Bowl-Leech’s Book, Being Remedies for the Third-Day Tremor, the Sweet, the Fever That Cooks, the Guest That Wants Another House, the Graft That Will Not Take and the Northern Cold, Set Down in the Bowl of Sere with the Errors Left Standing}
\CRsheetheading{The Bowl-Leech’s Book, Being Remedies for the Third-Day Tremor, the Sweet, the Fever That Cooks, the Guest That Wants Another House, the Graft That Will Not Take and the Northern Cold, Set Down in the Bowl of Sere with the Errors Left Standing}
{\centering\FellFont\itshape\footnotesize\color{faded} A bowl-leech’s book of remedies in the long-vowelled courtesy of Sere, written in gold ink on the back of a spoiled glaze-tally and folded into oiled silk; the cures in a bowl-leech’s hand, the objections of a physician come down from Greybank pressed cold into the margin, the corrections of a factor’s clerk in narrow Ledgerhand, a song for the third day with a place left where the seventh name stood, and one line at the foot in a hand nobody will own · Written in the Bowl of Sere between Grain and Smoke of Y.H. 812, the year the northern measures came south cheap, by Ilyra Vey, a leech attached to the house of Vey who held the third-day hand through nineteen returns; begun on the back of a glaze-tally spoiled in the pressing of a public bowl, written in gold ink on four leaves of glazed paper gummed into a fold of oiled silk, carried north with the glass in Ilmen of Y.H. 813 and copied at Greybank onto the back of a discarded rent-roll gone soft. It survives in a dry tin in a room with good light in the Greybank counting house, with gold worked into the creases of the first leaf, a ring of warm wine at the head, myrrh rubbed into the grain, a green bead of cliff-glass pressed into the lower corner, a grey bead of public-bowl ash caught in the gutter, a pale crescent of tallow-wasp resin at the foot of the remedies, a line that runs out toward the gutter and stops, a small square where a word was cut away with a knife and not written back, three objections in the cold margin hand of the physician, corrections in the upright Ledgerhand of the factor’s clerk, and the one line at the foot\par}\medskip
A woman of this house asked me to set down what I do, and I have set it down in the courtesy we use to people we would not disagree with, which is the same courtesy we use to the returned. I have left the errors standing. A physician come down from Greybank pressed his objections into the margin with a hand that writes cold, and I have put my words beneath his where the two disagree, as a bowl is set under a shelf to catch what the shelf will not hold.

The gold at the head is leaf off the tally. It gets into the creases and stays, so that after a year the Court’s figures and my cures look alike. The ring is warm wine from the public bowl, set down while I told a girl to drink and she would not. The myrrh came off the fold the tablets slept in. I have washed none of it away.

\subsection*{The order of the sick-court}

\emph{Written small in the first leaf, with the word for the guest gone over in wine.}

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item Set the sick one’s face toward the fire in the middle of the court, not toward the door. A person who faces the fire can be seen by everybody, which is how we know whether they are going.

\item Ask what debt they intend to carry before you ask what ails them. A person who has named a debt will tell you where it hurts. This is not kindness. It is the order of the room.

\item Turn the slate face down before you go to a child. I learned it from a northern bought breath who put her hand on a slate, turned it, and would say nothing more. I have done it at forty births and never asked her again.

\item Give the guest a place by the door and no bowl of their own. A guest who is given a bowl will ask when the debt falls due.

\item Do not look into a bowl that has a name written inside it. The house puts a name there that the bowl’s owner may never read, and a leech who looks has taken what the household has not spent.

\end{itemize}

Against the first line the physician wrote, in the cold hand: \emph{A vessel overheated in a cold room loses faster when turned to the fire.} I have set my line above his. Both stand.

\subsection*{The remedies, as they are used}

Trouble — What is set to it — The manner of it — Who is emptied\par

The third-day tremor — A second bowl emptied in the returned one’s name, and applause — It comes on the third day after a beautiful return, when the hand will not hold the cup. We say beauty must be paid for, and pour again. The physician says it is the head rising after too much was poured, and that wine adds to it. I have poured and watched the hand steady for an hour and worse by evening. Both stand. — The household, in wine; the returned one, in another measure.\par

The sweet (the pale line at the gum) — Scrape the green off a bowl into wine; a sweet answers a sweet — The green comes north from the Glaze Cliffs in bowls, and the women here taste the mix for colour. The physician says it is lead in the glaze and that scraping a bowl into wine takes more of it. I have seen the line go off a girl who left the furnaces and come back on one who stayed. I have not seen the lead. — The furnace, which cannot stop and does not ask.\par

The fever that cooks from within — Bleed at the elbow, to let the heat out — The Spending says a vessel emptied is a vessel saved. The physician says bleeding lets the measure out and not the fever. I bled four; two were quiet by evening and did not wake. Quiet is not better. I have written it and gone on bleeding. — The patient, in the arm.\par

The guest that wants another house — Seven names spoken at the door; a bowl set where the old bowl stood — She calls a name not given in this house and reaches for a door that is not in the room. We say a returned one has brought a guest, and give the guest the name until it goes. The physician says a spoken name puts no shape back, and he is right as a man who has never held one of these. One went off by the seventh naming; one kept it a year. — Nobody. The house, in a year it cannot spend.\par

A graft that will not take — Tallow-wasp resin at four marks a nest; a donor out of the same house if one can be found — The resin holds the wall until the vessel takes; a nest is four marks in the south and is burnt in Grath. The physician says resin holds a wall but not a want, and a wall from a donor shaped otherwise takes anyway and wants. I have seen it take and want, and never a donor who did not go thin. — The donor, in a head wine will not bring back.\par

The northern cold that stays — A bowl-fire at the belly, warm wine, and work carrying bowls — The bought breath comes south with a foot gone dark inside three turns of wool, is shown at a feast and given small coins, and is then brought to me. The extremity goes first and the heart holds out, and there is an hour on the far side of the warming.
