He said the third line was not a verse but a thing a keeper once wrote in the margin of a book, and had been sung ever since because men will sing what they are afraid to say. I have left it where I found it, in the middle, where a clerk correcting the leaves is least likely to put his hand.

\subsection*{What the borrowed hands did}

Two hands have been at this extract besides mine.

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item The College hand, narrow and upright, takes the verbs out. Where I wrote \emph{the chamber was found already warm}, it set \emph{the lighting is recorded in the first year}. Where I wrote \emph{a keeper pressed a coal into the wax}, it set \emph{a coal was pressed into the binding}. A verb with nobody in it is a verb that cannot be argued with, which is why they take them out. I have put mine back underneath and left theirs standing above, as the first copy stands under the fourth.

\item A temple hand, softer and rounder, wrote \emph{were gathered into the Hearth} across the line about the first Returns. It did not strike anything. It wrote across, which is a gentler way of taking a sentence away and a harder one to argue with, because the old words can still be read if a man is willing to lean over them and put a thumb on the leaf. I have left the thumb-print where it fell.

\end{itemize}

\subsection*{At the head and in the gutter}

The slate dust in the gutter has been there since the drawer was a drawer. The coal pressed into the wax of the sewing was put there by a keeper who had come off the grating with a coal in his fingers and had nowhere clean to set it; it is not part of the binding and never was. The scorch along the third leaf is where the leaf lay against the grating before I took the drawer, and it has not grown and will not go. The tallow at the head is mine; I turn the leaves by the light of a tallow end and have never managed to hold the book and the light with two hands. The flake of cold-iron scale in the lower margin came off the bars when a keeper struck one to show me where the fire comes up, and I kept it rather than ask him to strike another. The grey in the crease of the fourth leaf is Ash, and no keeper sweeps it during the Five, and no keeper has ever said why. The word struck through in the year-entries is mine: I wrote \emph{taken} where the Court hand had \emph{drawn}, and set \emph{drawn} above, because the book holds what was entered. What the tube did is in the verb underneath, where the College hand does not reach.

\subsection*{At the foot, in a hand nobody will own}

\begin{quote}\itshape The line grew smooth and the smooth line stands;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the rough one stays where the coal was pressed.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Four keys in a room and a fifth elsewhere,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and a figure on paper the tube never reads.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Ask the chamber. It has not forgotten.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape It was warm before we came.\end{quote}

I asked a keeper of the grating, a clerk of the College, and a surveyor up from Keld who would not give his name, and had three answers and no hand, as I have had before. I have left the line where it was written. The leaves go back into the drawer under the fire-tongs. At the Opening of the Slates I copy them forward and put the four copies in again with my own hand, in the order they were made, so that the smooth one never sits alone on the leaf. The chronicle goes on. Next tend I copy the Weighing figures from the clean roll, and I shall put the verbs back there too, and set them under the Court’s hand, where a man must kneel to read them.

\clearpage\phantomsection\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{The Chronicle of Grath, Being an Extract Concerning the Choosing and the Confirming of the Thanes of Clay, from the Kiln-Masters’ First Naming to the Present Thane at the Cross; with the Table of Confirmations, the Treaty Years in Which No Thane Was Asked, the Levies Called in a Thane’s Name, the Moot-Song, Three Corrections in the Narrow Hand of Greybank, and a Line at the Foot Nobody Will Own}
\CRsheetheading{The Chronicle of Grath, Being an Extract Concerning the Choosing and the Confirming of the Thanes of Clay, from the Kiln-Masters’ First Naming to the Present Thane at the Cross; with the Table of Confirmations, the Treaty Years in Which No Thane Was Asked, the Levies Called in a Thane’s Name, the Moot-Song, Three Corrections in the Narrow Hand of Greybank, and a Line at the Foot Nobody Will Own}
{\centering\FellFont\itshape\footnotesize\color{faded} A clerk’s extract from the Chronicle of Grath, kept in the chronicle chest in the thane’s house at Sill and not in the moot-chest below the Cross, which holds the town’s year-book and the thane’s road-book and is another kind of book; the year-entries in a broad clay-hand with the verbs left in, the thanes set in a table of choosing and confirming, the treaty years entered in the margin where the chest puts what the Court did not ask, the levies set against the notice in a column no clerk has signed, the moot-song taken down from a man who would not give his day’s wage, three corrections in the narrow upright Ledgerhand of a factor’s clerk come up from Greybank, one charcoal line left by a hearth-maid of Low Kiln, and a line at the foot in a hand nobody will own · Written at Sill in the thane’s house in the last tend of Ash, Y.H. 813, by the clerk of the chronicle, who signs with the office and not with a name and has put the verbs back where he found them taken out; copied from the Chronicle of Grath begun in the year of the Blue Cliff and carried forward at each Opening of the Slates into Y.H. 814. It survives as six leaves of foolscap sewn with wire into a board cover gone soft at the hinge: brick dust ground into the head off the High Kiln terrace, clay worked into the gutter and not swept out, a shaving of raw slip shut in the second fold, silt from the sill dried pale along the foot, a tallow thumb at the head, a green bead of lead glaze pressed into the lower corner by a glaze-mixer who leaned to read the song and went off with the sweetness still at her mouth, a ring where a cup of small ale stood from the first entry to the last, a short square of bare paper where a word was scraped away and no other put in, three corrections in the narrow upright hand of Greybank, one charcoal line left by a hearth-maid who would not give her name, a grey Ash print along the outer fold which the clerk did not make and has not swept, and the line at the foot which has never been claimed\par}\medskip
I keep the Chronicle of Grath. There are two chests in the thane’s house at Sill and I keep the one that is not the road-book; the road-book holds distances and tolls, and a man cannot get a year out of it, only a price for clay. The moot-chest below the Cross holds the town’s year-book, which begins at the Blue Cliff and holds what the town was told. This book holds what happened, when a man can be got to stand still long enough to ask. Where the two disagree I set them side by side and do not join them. A clerk who joins two accounts has begun a sermon, and a sermon in this country travels faster than a cart and lasts longer than a pot.

The office is smaller than it sounds. A Thane of Clay is chosen by the kiln-masters of Sill, who know a man by the way he sets a pot in the yard, and confirmed by the factor at Greybank, which is the only way a thane is confirmed and the reason every thane in this book is the factor’s thane before he is ours. The choosing takes an afternoon. The confirming takes a line on a slate eighteen leagues down the Clay Road, in a hand the thane cannot read without asking, which he does not, because a man newly chosen does not want to find out what he has been chosen for.

\subsection*{The years as the chest has them}

\emph{Copied in the broad clay-hand. I have put the verbs back where they were taken out and left the narrow hand above mine where it stands.}

\textbf{Y.H. 418, the Blue Cliff.} Commissioners sat at the cliff with salt-paper, a cold-iron clamp and a piece of Sill clay on one table. The Clay Road was made a Court road; an assessor could stop a cart without asking the thane, and did. The treaty slate was cut and laid in the moot-chest under the road-book, and read at the Cross on market morning. The thane was not at the cutting. Wyn Clay held the office, confirmed in 411; he asked who had signed for the road and was told that four powers had set their marks, which is true and not a name. Entered in the road-book as \emph{a conference at the cliff}; entered here as \emph{no thane at the cutting}. Both sentences are in the chest.

\textbf{Y.H. 560.} The thirty-one years the Court calls the War of Deductions ended; we have always called them the taking. Hal Clay held the office, confirmed in 552, and was not called to hear the ending. One figure was printed on the notice and read at the Weighing; another was paid in the clay households and entered nowhere. The two stand together in the table below without a signature between them.

\textbf{Y.H. 668, the Rising.} Ninety children’s warmth taken in Low Kiln for one whole return no household could name; eleven weeks of disorder; Assessor-Marshal Pell Varr came up with twelve collectors and a list, and forty-one persons were dead and entered as spent in the keeping of the peace. Hob Clay was thane, confirmed in 661. He called the levy in those weeks and called the disorder a disturbance when the factor’s letter came down. The eleven weeks are counted in the Hearthseat and not swept in Low Kiln; I have put the heap under the table where a clerk of the College will not think to look.

\textbf{Y.H. 747, the Cold Pass.} Karric VII shut the pass in 741 and seven years were spent arguing about which mountain the Hearth lies under. The agreement was cut on a slate in Slate Row, a Court street and not a Grathish one; Keld kept the pass and shaft, Grath kept the road, and the Hearthseat was left standing. Rade Clay was thane, confirmed in 739. He was not asked. The Grathish say this is how all important treaties are made; the Court says the thane’s absence is not an entry. A man who states his measure before his name is not thereby asked what he thinks of a border.

\textbf{Y.H. 811, the Long Cold.} Ice came on the Ilm in early Stone and did not break for ninety-four days. The barley was thin, the peat in Mud End would not dry, and fuel prices doubled and then stopped being quoted because there was none to sell. Bel Clay was thane, confirmed in 803. The levy was raised to one in three across every Low Kiln household and announced as being for the Hearth; the notice beside the Court’s room still said one in twelve. Nobody in Low Kiln reads it. Households called themselves walking thin, which is a name for people who keep moving because stopping is the same as cooling.

\textbf{Y.H. 812.} In the first weeks of Stone forty children of Low Kiln were banked for a private account. The Greybank slate gives no purchaser and no destination for the warmth. It gives a name for the return, written before the collector had seen the infant’s face. I have copied the figures and left the name where it was written; a name from Greybank gets repeated at the well and comes back as a cause, and there is no cause in this year that I can enter.

\subsection*{The choosing and the confirming}

\emph{Between the names below there are other thanes whose years the chest has and which I have not copied. A list of men is not a list of what they did, and the factor’s clerk turns first to the names.}

Thane — Chosen by — Confirmed at Greybank — What the chest has of him\par

Wyn Clay — the kiln-masters of Sill — Y.H. 411 — The Blue Cliff, 418. Asked who had signed for the road and was answered with the four powers.\par

Hal Clay — the kiln-masters of Sill — Y.H. 552 — The ending of the thirty-one years, 560. Not called to hear it.\par

Hob Clay — the kiln-masters of Sill — Y.H. 661 — The Rising, 668. Called the levy; called the eleven weeks a disturbance.\par

Rade Clay — the kiln-masters of Sill — Y.H. 739 — The Cold Pass, 747. Not at the cutting.\par

Bel Clay — the kiln-masters of Sill — Y.H. 803 — The Long Cold, 811. One in three in the clay households; one in twelve on the notice.\par

The present thane — the kiln-masters of Sill — — — Reads the notice at the Cross and calls the levy in the name of \emph{your house}, never \emph{I}.\par

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{In the narrow upright hand of a factor’s clerk, written above the second column:} Confirmed by the Court’s factor. \emph{In mine, underneath:} confirmed at Greybank. I have left both. A man is chosen in an afternoon in the yard at Sill and confirmed in a line at Greybank, and the line outlasts the afternoon and the yard. He writes \emph{the Court’s factor} as though a factor were a door that had always stood there and nobody had cut it out of the wall.\end{quote}

\subsection*{The years in which no thane was asked}

Year — What was cut or fixed — Who set marks — What the thane was told\par

418 — Clay Road made a Court road; border fixed at Greybank — Four powers, one mark set by a man of Sill who was not the thane — That the matter was closed\par

747 — Pass and shaft to Keld; road to Grath; Hearthseat neutral — Keld, the Court, Grath, and a fourth mark the chest does not name — That the road was open\par

749 — Neutrality of the Hearthseat guaranteed — Grath, Keld, Vhalen and Sere; Grath’s mark set at Greybank — That the fire was left standing\par

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{In the narrow hand, against the last row:} The thane’s attendance was not required. \emph{In mine:} not asked. A thing not required and a thing not asked are the same thing said from two rooms, and the rooms do not agree about who was standing in them. The first can be entered at a Weighing; the second said at a well. I have kept both.\end{quote}

A thane hears of a treaty when it is read at the Cross, after the pigs are over the boards and before the bell goes four, four and a gap. Nobody crosses himself at the gap. The gap is not a figure and has never been entered, which is a mercy of a kind.

\subsection*{The levies called in a thane’s name}

Year — Printed on the notice — Called in the households — What was entered\par

811 — one in twelve — one in three in every Low Kiln household — \emph{additional warmth for the Hearth}\par

812 — one in twelve — forty children, privately — purchaser not recorded\par

this year — one in twelve, as the notice says — read twice over the basket at the Cross — \emph{the levy is called}\par

The last column is the only one the College reads, and it has nobody in it. A levy called is a levy with the caller taken out. The figure that goes up the clay road in a locked box is not the figure that came out of the house. Paper is not a payer. I have drawn no line across.

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{In the narrow hand, against the 811 row:} The deduction is uniform. \emph{In mine, beneath:} one in twelve on the notice. A uniform deduction can be read aloud in a clean voice in a hall with the fire behind the grating; it cannot be paid in Low Kiln in a winter when the Ilm lies frozen for ninety-four days. I have not struck the clerk’s sentence out. A clerk who never walks the clay road should not be made to carry what he wrote.\end{quote}

\subsection*{The moot-song}

\emph{Taken down at the Cross from a mason who set the sill stones and would not give his day’s wage, sung after the reading and never during it. The crowd says the last line.}

\begin{quote}\itshape They chose him in the yard where the pots stand rim-down,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and confirmed him a line down the Clay Road;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape a line is a lighter thing to carry than a pot,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and it goes where the pot does not.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Four marks at the cliff and none for the thane,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape four, four and a gap at the bell;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the road is the road and the toll is the toll,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the thane wipes his thumb on his coat.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape One in twelve on the notice at the Court’s room,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape one in three on the house with the thin floor;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the figure that goes up the road in a box\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape is not the figure that came out of the door.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape A pot mended twice is the pot that was broken,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the pot that was broken is not there;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape ask the sill what it kept of the river,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape ask the thane what he kept of the year.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{In charcoal, pressed in the lower margin by a hearth-maid of Low Kiln who would not give her name:} Four, four and a gap is the bell that tells the figure and not the cost. \emph{In mine:} I have left it where she put it. She writes small, the way a woman writes where somebody is asleep.\end{quote}

\subsection*{The hands that are not mine}

The factor’s clerk borrows the chronicle when the salt boats come up. He writes upright and narrow and takes the men out of a sentence as though a man were a thing a clerk could carry off in a cuff. He set three readings above mine and, against the charcoal line, wrote nothing at all, passing over it without a stroke, which is the readiest correction I know.

I have left every reading where it was written. A book with two hands in it is the only kind a man in this country will believe; a book with one hand in it is a Court notice, and a Court notice has never told a man what his house would pay.

\subsection*{At the head and in the gutter}

The brick dust at the head came off the High Kiln terrace on the sleeve I wipe with, and no damp takes it out. The clay in the gutter comes off the floor of this room and has been there since the first copy; a clerk who keeps a chronicle walks clay into it every day and does not sweep it out. The slip-shaving in the second fold was left by a man come to be confirmed who went away without it; it has gone the colour of old bone. The silt along the foot is off the sill where the Ilm drops four feet over hard stone, dried pale and coming and going with the weather. The tallow thumb at the head is mine. The green bead in the corner is not ink: a glaze-mixer come up from High Kiln leaned over to read the moot-song and pressed it there with her thumb, and went off with the sweetness still at her mouth. The ring is where a cup of small ale stood from the first entry to the last. The square of bare paper is where I scraped a word away with a knife-point and put no other in; it is the only square in this quire I made myself. The grey along the outer fold is not mine and not the factor’s. I have not swept it. There is a Last Day in this house and we do not sweep the corners on it, which the factor’s clerk has entered as a custom and we keep as a debt.

\subsection*{At the foot, in a hand nobody will own}

\begin{quote}\itshape The kiln chooses and the quay confirms;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the road is measured and the man is not;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape four marks at the cliff and one gap at the bell,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the figure goes up and the house stays cold.\end{quote}

I asked the kiln-master, a factor’s clerk, and a man who has read at the Cross for thirty years, and had three answers and no hand. I have left the line where it was written. The book goes back into its chest. Tomorrow the thane will read \emph{one in twelve, as the notice says} twice over the basket, call the levy, and go up the clay road with the year’s arithmetic where no man can read it; this book will keep the other figure underneath, where a clerk of the College will not think to look.

\clearpage\phantomsection\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{The Clamp and the Bowl, Being an Account of the Southern Empire of Sere, Set Down by Veth, a Hired Clamp out of Keld Keep, Who Went Down the Peat Line in the Service of a Factor of the Sunbowl Houses and Came Back with His Measure Unchanged and a Figure He Could Not Spend; with the Order of the Name, the Road That Counted Nothing, the Four Bowls, a Table of Hire, the Clamp-Song as It Is Said Going Down, Two Corrections in Borrowed Hands, and a Line at the Foot Nobody Will Own}
\CRsheetheading{The Clamp and the Bowl, Being an Account of the Southern Empire of Sere, Set Down by Veth, a Hired Clamp out of Keld Keep, Who Went Down the Peat Line in the Service of a Factor of the Sunbowl Houses and Came Back with His Measure Unchanged and a Figure He Could Not Spend; with the Order of the Name, the Road That Counted Nothing, the Four Bowls, a Table of Hire, the Clamp-Song as It Is Said Going Down, Two Corrections in Borrowed Hands, and a Line at the Foot Nobody Will Own}
{\centering\FellFont\itshape\footnotesize\color{faded} A hired soldier’s road account, set down first in charcoal on the backs of three spoiled requisitions for warm-stone and cut in the edge with a tally-knife where charcoal would not hold, then copied at Greybank onto the back of a Court grain-warrant voided by the Long Cold; the figures in a number-first counting hand learned at the shaft mouth, the southern sayings kept in the hearing and not made into proverbs, the hard Rim endings struck off where Grathic letters would not carry them, the verbs put back under every borrowed correction, and one line at the foot in a hand that has never come forward · Written in Grain and Smoke of Y.H. 813 in the Bowl of Sere and at a provincial bowl on the south road, by Veth of Keld Keep, a clamp for hire who went down in Reed with a letter for a house of the Ten Bowls and an iron clamp at his belt and came back in Ash with the same number in his arm, three gold crowns he could not change, and a sliver of lead glaze in the seam of his coat; copied at Greybank in Ilmen of Y.H. 814 onto the back of a voided grain-warrant and carried up the Rim Road to the Keep. It survives folded into a tin lined with a shaving of warm-stone now gone cold, soft at the fore-edge and sour with the burning winds; yellow dust ground into the sewing, a ring of warm wine at the third hour, olive oil at the thumb, a curl of burnt paper from a slate that had gone into a court fire shut into the second fold, iron filings off a clamp filed at a gate, a shaving of warm-stone cold in the gutter, a square of bare paper where a word was scraped away with a knife-point, a grey Ash print along the outer fold which the writer did not make and has not swept, two corrections in borrowed hands, and a line at the foot in a hand nobody will own\par}\medskip
I was hired in Keld Keep to walk south and stand where a man might have put a third. The factor who hired me was courteous. His hand went to a slate before it went to me, and he asked for my measure before he asked for my name, which is the order at home and a courtesy I had not expected below the Rim. He wrote the figure first. Then he wrote the name. I have thought about that order since, and I have set it above the rest of what I brought back. A man who writes the figure before the name has decided what he is buying. A man who writes the name first may still be talked out of it.

I carried an iron clamp at my belt, a letter in my coat that I could not read, and a warm-stone the size of a plum that had come up out of the Ninth Gallery and was giving less heat each morning. The letter was for a house of the Ten Bowls. The clamp was to keep the letter and the man carrying it from being parted in the dark, which is the whole of a hired clamp’s learning. I had stood twice at the Duelling Floor and had never been quick enough to open a way in my own forearm before the other man opened one in his, so I was not a master and was paid as a man who is not a master. This is worth saying first, because most of what follows is a soldier’s account and soldiers are expected to say they won.

\subsection*{The order of the name}

At thirteen the number goes into the forearm and a warm-stone is put into the hand after the knife. From that day a Keldish man gives the number before the name, because the number is the thing the Warden can check and the name is the thing a man can lie about. I gave this factor forty-eight and Veth, in that order, and he wrote forty-eight and Veth, in that order, and neither of us was troubled.

In the south a child may have seven names by adolescence and keep whichever the household likes, and a slave has no measure in law at all. I asked a clerk of the house how a person is governed who has no figure. He said a person is governed as a vessel is governed, by the hand that pours it. I asked who pours the hand. He said I had asked two questions and that one of them had been answered. In Keld an answer like that gets a man a clamp across the knuckles, not because it is rude but because it wastes the morning. Here it was given with great courtesy and I was thanked for asking.

I saw a house-slave at the third bowl who was dressed better than I was and was exhibited for the generosity of the house. She had been given a whole return and a clay-name, and the name she had been born with was forbidden in that house, and written, I was told, on the inside of a bowl she was never allowed to look into. I have tried to picture a person with no measure. I can picture a clamp with no bite: it lies on the bench and nobody lifts it, and in the end the iron goes to the fire and is worked into something else. I could not make the picture stay. A northman’s whole mind is built the other way round, and the road down is a long way to carry it.

\subsection*{The road that counted nothing}

The Peat Line is where the clay gives up and the reeds begin, and a reeve took a bit off me for stepping on a board he had not pointed to. This was within his right and I said so, which is a thing a Keldish man says when he has paid and does not wish to argue. The Fenfolk say a dry man is a dangerous man, and put him up on boards and do not tell him which will bear him. We learned.

Beyond it lie the roads and wells and doorways of the ground the Court calls the Empty Cantons and the Fen call the Quiet Acre. The temple tells children that the people were taken up in the first Returns and are whole somewhere, paid for by a line of figures. Nobody says where the line went. I counted what could be counted and left the squares alone. There is a square of bare clay above a lintel where a house-roll hung, and a square is not a nought, and a man who puts a nought into it has made an empty room into an account. I have carried a number in my arm for twenty years and I know the difference between a figure that stands and a figure that was taken away.

The hearths there have white dust in them and no grey, which the surveyors set down last and speak of least. I did not write down what a Fen man told me it meant, because I do not know it for a lie and do not know it for the truth, and a soldier who writes what he cannot check has begun a sermon. The burning winds came yellow off the east past the Line and took the skin off my lips and left the grain standing. My lips went first. The grain stood. That is a thing I have no learning in and several reasons to believe.

\subsection*{The four bowls}

The Bowl of Sere has no wall worth the name. Each court has a fire in the middle and men sit in the heat with their coats on the ground beside them and the yellow dust down in their hair, and nobody brushes it off. I brushed mine off on the first day and was charged for the hour. I let it lie after that.

At the third hour a public bowl of wine is emptied onto the stones and that is how the acts of the Sun-Emperor are announced. I asked a man beside me whether a debt had been forgiven or a province ruined. He said, “Yes.” I asked which. He said, “Measure for measure,” and went back to his wine. In Keld a phrase like that would be settled with iron before the wine was cold. Here it settled itself and the wine went on being drunk.

At the feast of the house I counted four bowls on the board. Three went round and were poured. The fourth stood where it stood, and was carried away full when the feasting was done, and nobody poured it and nobody said whose debt it held. I asked three times and got three silences, the last of which was the kindest. A Keldish man cannot leave a thing standing that has no use and no payer. I have set the fourth bowl beside the empty place on the Floor where a clamp nobody lifts is kept, and joined neither to the other, because a man who joins what a country keeps apart has made a story, and stories are what that country lives on.

Valen Openhand preached the Spending in the court while I was there: that a vessel was made to be emptied and a life hoarded is a life wasted. He was not a thin man, and neither were the priests who said it after him, which a traveller notices after standing in a court all morning. At the end of the feast the debt-slates of one household, chosen by lot, went into the fire. A woman whose slate burned wept and the company was kind to her, and then the new slate was brought out and the company applauded that too. I have not got used to the second applause.

\subsection*{What the factor gave, and what the road took}

\emph{The left column is the figure as it was given to me. The right is what I set on the back of the leaf when I got home. The left hand is mine, number-first. The narrow hand above came from a clerk who borrowed the leaves at Greybank. Both stand.}

Thing — Given, in the south — Set on the back, at the Keep\par

Hire, forty days, at the shaft-mouth rate — 2 crowns and a half — 2 crowns and a half, and the days are mine\par

Keep and a bed in the clamp-yard — 1 crown — 1 crown\par

Warm-stone, fist-sized, bought at the gate — 3 marks — 3 marks; cold on the ninth day\par

Clamp, iron, Keldish, filed at the gate — 2 marks, the filing charged — 2 marks, the filing charged twice\par

Wine, a jar, at the third hour — 1 crown — 1 crown; the ring on the leaf is mine\par

Resin of the tallow-wasp, a nest — not taken — a bowl-surgeon offered 4 crowns for it\par

Gold crowns, changed at Greybank — 4 crowns — would not change at the Keep\par

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{In the narrow upright hand of the factor’s clerk at Greybank, against the last row:} Crowns entered as four. The stone and the days are not entered.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Underneath, in mine:} The stone was mine before the hire and went cold on the ninth day. The days were mine all along and I gave them. He has entered what he can carry and left what I carried.\end{quote}

Twelve bits to a silver mark and twenty marks to a gold crown. The Court books in embers and will tell a man an ember is worth five marks; no man I have met has ever changed one, north or south. I left the embers off. A column with nothing in it is an honest column.

\subsection*{The clamp-song}

\emph{Said on the road going down and not coming up. The words in the hard Rim speech, set in Grathic letters with the endings struck off. Taken down from a man who had been hired twice and had come back from both, while he filed a clamp at the gate. He would not sing it with a factor’s clerk in the yard.}

\begin{quote}\itshape Nine doorways and no man to come through,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape a well with the rope and no hand at the pail;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape I gave my number and kept my name,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the south said \emph{bowl} where the north said \emph{man}.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Three go round and the fourth goes up,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the iron holds and the iron takes;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape a clamp that has no bite lies on the bench ---\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape ask who will lift it. Ask it twice.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape I carried the north in the seam of my coat\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and came back with dust that the rain will not move;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape ask the bowl what it poured. It will say it was full.\end{quote}

He said there was a fourth verse and that it was a saying, and would not give it. I left the place scored with the knife and empty.

\subsection*{What the borrowed hands did}

Two hands have been at these leaves besides mine.

The factor’s clerk at Greybank, in the narrow upright Ledgerhand, took the verbs out. Where I wrote \emph{I was asked for my measure before my name} he set \emph{identification in two parts}. Where I wrote \emph{they burn a slate and write it again} he set \emph{instrument discharged by lot and renewed}. Where I wrote \emph{the fourth bowl was carried away full} he set \emph{vessel removed, contents not entered}. I have put my words back underneath. A verb is the difference between a thing that happened to a person and a thing that happened in a counting room.

The bowl-house clerk, in thin gold on prepared paper, wrote \emph{market rate, current} against the table and \emph{ceremony observed} against the burning. He did not strike a word. A clerk who strikes and writes above means to be argued with; one who writes above without striking means to be done with. The gold has worn thinner than the charcoal in the fold, which is one honest thing the rain did not undo.

\subsection*{At the head and in the gutter}

The yellow in the sewing is the burning wind, ground in going down and not shaken out, because a man who shakes a leaf is a man who wants to pretend he has been somewhere else. The wine-ring is small and belongs to the third hour. The olive at the thumb is mine; I turn the leaves with the hand I carried the bowl with. The curl of burnt paper came off a slate that went into the court fire, and a woman put it into my hand before the new slate was brought out, and I have kept it folded in the second leaf where the heat of it is gone. The filings are off the clamp I had filed at the gate, charged twice. The shaving in the gutter was warm-stone once and is cold now, and I have kept it because a man should be able to see the price he paid after the price has gone out of it. The grey along the outer fold is not mine and not the factor’s. I have not swept it. There is no Last Day on the road I came, and I have not found one since I got back.

\subsection*{At the foot, in a hand nobody will own}

\begin{quote}\itshape Forty-eight went down and forty-eight came back;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the south kept the figure and gave me the dust.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Three were poured and the fourth went up;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape I asked for a debt and was answered \emph{yes}.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Ask the slave what her number is. Ask the door.\end{quote}

I asked the factor’s clerk, a man of the Floor come south on other business, and a bowl-surgeon who sold me nothing, and had three answers and no hand. I have left the line where it was written.

The leaves go back into the tin, into the pocket the strap has worn. There is iron going up the Rim Road in the first tend of Silt and a factor who has not yet asked me whether I will walk it again. I have not said yes. A man with a clamp and no house says yes when the factor asks, which is why I have put off answering him and will put it off until the morning. The warm-stone in the tin is cold and the number in my arm is where the knife put it. Those are the two things I brought back that nobody has tried to enter.

\clearpage\phantomsection\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{The Clap at the Gap, Being the Hand-Counting Game of the Children of the Cross at Sill, with the Counting-Out, the Manner of the Hands, the Verses as They Are Clapped, a Factor’s Clerk’s Figures in the Narrow Upright Hand, an Old Woman’s Gloss in Charcoal, and One Line at the Foot in a Hand Nobody Will Own}
\CRsheetheading{The Clap at the Gap, Being the Hand-Counting Game of the Children of the Cross at Sill, with the Counting-Out, the Manner of the Hands, the Verses as They Are Clapped, a Factor’s Clerk’s Figures in the Narrow Upright Hand, an Old Woman’s Gloss in Charcoal, and One Line at the Foot in a Hand Nobody Will Own}
{\centering\FellFont\itshape\footnotesize\color{faded} A keeper’s gathering of a children’s hand game, set down in Grathic on the back of a market board spoiled by a wet thumb; the verses in the children’s own half-sung speech, the manner of the play in the keeper’s small hand, one correction in the narrow upright Ledgerhand of a factor’s clerk from Greybank, a gloss pressed in charcoal by a woman who has swept the Cross since before the Glaze Wars, and a line at the foot in a hand that has not come forward · Written in Bone of Y.H. 813 at the reading block under the moot-post at the Cross in Sill, by Halla of the Step, who keeps the step clean of slate dust and sells barley water on Account-days; set down because a factor’s clerk come up from Greybank to check the winter grain asked what the children counted when they clapped there on ordinary mornings, and wrote it down with the clapping taken out and a figure put where the ninth sound stood. Written in charcoal on the back of a market board gone soft in the rain, folded into four, carried to Greybank in a woman’s satchel and copied onto the back of a voided weigh-slip. It survives with slate dust ground into the head, a barley-water ring through the second leaf, a chip of coarse tile shut in the fold, a frost-feather pressed flat that was gone by noon, a grey Ash print nobody will own, a twist of grey wool through a hole which the writer will not untie, the clerk’s figures above the children’s words, the old woman’s gloss in charcoal beside the gap, and one line at the foot that has never come forward\par}\medskip
I keep the step under the moot-post and sell barley water when the market stands. There are three mornings in every tend when the Cross is full of people and two hundred lean over the block and eight pigs go over the wet boards, and seven when it is only the step and the dust and a child or two waiting for a mother at the pot board. On those mornings the children clap the bell. They clap it when the bell is not rung, which is the whole of the game and the thing the clerk could not hear.

A man with a soft cuff came up from Greybank and asked what they counted. I told him the count and the gap. He wrote it down with the gap taken out and a figure put in its place, and went back over the north bridge with his boots clean. What follows is what the children did before he came and what they did again after he had gone. I have set his hand above theirs, as the step keeps the dust under the feet that bring it.

The slate dust at the head is mine. I sweep the step and I do not get it all out of the grain of the leaf, which is how I know I have had it in my hand.

\subsection*{The step and the hands, as the children keep it}

\emph{Played on the seven mornings when there is no market. Not on Account-day, when the block is crowded and a child on the step is in the way of the reading. Not in the Five, when they are made to stand and listen. Not in rain, for a wet hand drops the corn and a wet step gives back no knock.}

Two children sit facing each other on the reading-block step, with their feet on the lower stone. One is \textbf{the bell} and one is \textbf{the gap}, for as long as they sit there, and they are not called by their own names while they play, for a name said at the Cross goes up the clay road in a cuff and comes back written. There is no rope and no pot and nothing to buy. Each holds a dried barleycorn shut in one hand all through the game.

The bell claps four times on her own knee, then four times palm to palm with the gap. At the ninth the bell lifts her hand and gives no stroke, and the gap claps once with the shut fist into the open palm, so that the corn takes the sound and gives back a small dry knock. Then the bell brings her hand down and they begin again.

The verse is said low to the step and never to a face. Said to a face it becomes a question, and there is always a child who will answer. One line is one clap, and the last three lines belong to the gap alone.

If the corn falls out of the hand or is crushed, the round is spoiled and they begin again at the first knee-clap. Nobody keeps a count of spoiled rounds. There is no winning and no last round; they stop when a mother calls, and the corn goes back into a pocket whole, and is often eaten on the way down the clay road, which nobody mentions.

\subsection*{The counting-out, said before the corn is taken up}

\emph{Open hands for this part, the corn still in the pocket. The child who says it taps each fist in turn and does not look at the faces. The fist it lights on at the last word is the gap, which is not a prize: the gap is the one who has to make the sound the bell leaves out. The bell is the one who gets to be silent.}

\begin{quote}\itshape Corn in the pocket and slate on the sill,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the bell goes up and the step stands still;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape one fist, two fist, three and four ---\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the one it lights on makes the ninth once more.\end{quote}

\emph{Makes the ninth once more means keeps the sound, in the children’s speech, though a bell will tell you it means makes it again; both sayings have stood on this step as long as I have swept it.}

\subsection*{The clapping verse, as it is clapped}

\emph{Four lines to four knee-claps. Then the refrain while the hands change. Then four lines to four palm-claps, and the refrain again. The last three lines are the gap’s, said with the hand still shut.}

\begin{quote}\itshape One for the dust on the reading-block stone,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape two for the pig that went over alone;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape three for the shade where the basket stood,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape four for the gap where the bell should have stood.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Four on the knee, four across to the palm,}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{one dry knock where the fist holds warm;}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{the bell gives nothing, the gap gives one,}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{said to the step, and the step says none.}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Five for the cup set down in the shade,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape six for the figure the crier has made;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape seven for the cuff with the ink in the seam,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape eight for the count that is not what it seems.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Four on the knee, four across to the palm,}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{one dry knock where the fist holds warm;}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{the bell gives nothing, the gap gives one,}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{said to the step, and the step says none.}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape The bell lifts her hand and gives no stroke;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the gap claps once where the corn lies shut ---\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape a dry little knock, and the dust jumps up.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape The fist opens. The corn is whole. Begin.\end{quote}

The children will not be told why the hand stays shut. Ask them and they say the corn tells them; ask what the corn tells and they ask you why a man wants to know what a corn tells.

\subsection*{What is said when the corn falls}

\begin{quote}\itshape Corn on the boards and a round gone wrong ---\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape four to the knee and begin the song.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Nobody keeps how often it fell.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape It goes in the pocket and stays well.\end{quote}

\subsection*{The verse they do not clap while a man in a soft cuff is on the step}

I have this from the child who was gap, with the space left before it, which is the space the bell leaves. She said it to the step with her back turned and made me set it down with none of my verbs in it. A verse clapped to a stone wants nothing added, and a verse clapped to a man wants everything taken away.

\begin{quote}\itshape Four, four and a gap, says the bell on the tenth;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape one in twelve, says the notice, read twice for the late.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape We clap in the place where the Court leaves air,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the corn in the fist has never been there.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape The clerk takes the knock and sets it down nil.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape The step keeps the dust and the dust keeps still.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Four are four and the ninth is none ---\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape but the corn goes home, and it is one.\end{quote}

I asked her what the one was. She said it was the corn in her pocket, and that it had been in her mother’s before her, and that she had never once cracked it between her teeth. I have put no word between them either.

\subsection*{What the clerk did}

The factor’s clerk borrowed the board, with his cuff gone soft from washing and the ink sitting in two fingers of it and not coming out. He set the game down as \emph{a rhythmic instruction in reckoning, imparted to minors}. Against \emph{four on the knee} he wrote \emph{four strokes entered}. Against the refrain he wrote \emph{four, four, rest; no charge arises}. At the ninth he struck the children’s words through and set above them, \emph{ninth stroke not struck; vacancy; no deduction}. Against \emph{the corn is whole} he wrote \emph{one barleycorn retained; no debit to the district}. At the foot, where the game ends with the corn going into the pocket, he put a round nought and wrote \emph{no result}.

I have put their words back underneath and left his standing above. He writes of a thing that is always true and so has no need of a child with a shut fist on a cold step. I write for that child, who wants to know whether the sound she made is still hers once it has left her hand. He has put a nought where a sound stood. A nought lies where it is put and can be carried up the road in a cuff. A sound is gone the moment it is made, which is why no Court in Sarn has ever managed to keep one.

The children stop when a man in a soft cuff comes onto the step. They take it up again when he is past the bend toward Greybank, and they never once let the bell strike the ninth.

\subsection*{The gloss in charcoal, by the woman who sweeps the Cross}

She has swept this step since before the Glaze Wars and does not write often, and when she does she writes small, the way you write where somebody is asleep. She pressed one line into the margin beside the refrain:

\begin{quote}\itshape I have swept thirty years and the dust comes back with the market. The knock in the gap comes back with the children. Neither is entered and both are kept by the step.\end{quote}

I have left it where her thumb put it. She said the bell had been rung by men in clean cuffs for eight hundred years and had never once rung the ninth, and she had heard it every tenth morning of thirty and was not lonely for it.

\subsection*{At the head and in the gutter}

The slate dust at the head came off the block where I set the leaf to copy; it goes into the grain and no damp takes it out, which is why the step takes a mark and the market board does not. The ring through the second leaf is a cup of barley water set down at the first verse and taken up at the last, by which time it had gone the colour of the dust it stood on; two children have claimed it and one woman has denied it and I have given it to none. The chip of tile in the fold fell out of a girl’s pocket on the third morning and she did not come back for it, so I shut it in the leaf, where it is lighter than a sound and about as useful. The frost-feather came off the north edge of the step and was gone before I had folded the leaf. The grey along the gutter came off a cuff laid where no cuff has business lying on a step where children sit; nobody will own it and I have not swept it. There is no Last Day at the Cross and nothing here gets gathered and burnt in the morning. The twist of grey wool through the hole is mine, tied for the word I could not put down. I will not untie it.

\subsection*{At the foot, in a hand nobody will own}

\begin{quote}\itshape Four and four and the clap under the fist.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape The Court has the figure. The child has the sound.\end{quote}

I asked the bell, the gap and a woman at the pot board, and had three answers and no hand. I have left the line where it was written.

The leaf goes back under the barley-water jar. Tomorrow there will be no market on the step, and two children will sit on it and clap the bell’s count while the bell is not rung, four on the knee and four across and one dry knock under the corn; and if a man with a soft cuff comes up from Greybank I shall put the verbs back and leave him his nought. The corn goes home in a pocket, whole and uncounted, and is eaten on the way down the clay road, which nobody mentions and no slate has a column for.

\clearpage\phantomsection\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{The Clay-Yard Book of Remedies, Being What a Hearth-Maid of Low Kiln Sets to the Second Chill, the Sweet Sickness, the Kiln-Burn, the Cord That Will Not Fall and the Cold That Stays, Written Down in Grathic with the Errors Left Standing}
\CRsheetheading{The Clay-Yard Book of Remedies, Being What a Hearth-Maid of Low Kiln Sets to the Second Chill, the Sweet Sickness, the Kiln-Burn, the Cord That Will Not Fall and the Cold That Stays, Written Down in Grathic with the Errors Left Standing}
{\centering\FellFont\itshape\footnotesize\color{faded} A midwife’s and healer’s book of remedies in the Grathic clay-yard manner, the cures in a hearth-maid’s hand with the verbs left in, the objections of a physician come down from Greybank pressed in the margin, the corrections of a College clerk in Ledgerhand, and one line at the foot in a hand nobody will own · Written in Low Kiln in Sill between Ash of Y.H. 811 and Ilmen of Y.H. 813, the Long Cold and the Thin Year, by Hedda of the Clay Yard, a hearth-maid who caught children in the slip pits and laid out the dead of the kiln terraces for twenty-six years; begun on the back of a glaze-house tally spoiled by a fall of slip, folded into four and carried in the breast of her apron against a square of birth-cloth washed so often there is no birth left in it, and copied at Greybank in Ilmen, Y.H. 813, onto the back of a rent-roll gone soft. It survives with a thumb of tallow at the head, grey Ash worked into the gutter, brick dust ground into the fold, a wet smear of slip that has taken two words clean off the second leaf, a ring of barley-water, a scorch where a spark off the kiln caught the corner, a long hair the colour of wet wool caught in the seam, objections in the hand of a Greybank physician, corrections in the narrow upright hand of a College clerk, and a line at the foot nobody will own.\par}\medskip
I am a hearth-maid of the Clay Yard and I have caught children in it for twenty-six years. Nobody asked me for this book. I write it because a girl came to me in the lean week with a foot gone dark inside three turns of wool and asked me what I did for the second chill, and I heard myself answer her the way my mother answered me, and did not know whether I believed it. A remedy you have to say in your mother’s voice is a remedy that has not been looked at in a long while. I have looked at some of mine here. I have left the others standing, because a woman at three in the morning wants a hand more than she wants a correction.

I write on the back of a glaze-house tally that a fall of slip spoiled. The figures went before anyone could price them, which is a mercy of a kind: a figure that will not read cannot be entered. The tallow at the head is mine. The grey in the gutter came off my cuff when I measured a corner in a house two doors down and came back to write. I have not swept it off. The district burns its grey on the morning after the Last Day and calls it dealt with. I have kept mine, which is the only part of this book I have not copied forward.

\subsection*{The order of a birth-room}

\emph{Written small, with one word gone over in slip.}

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item Set the slate face down before you go to the child. I have no slate-name and never shall; a midwife who writes the child before she looks at it has written the wrong one already, and a wrong one is hard to get off a slate.

\item Keep the door latched but not held. A woman who is watched through the door will hold her breath, and a held breath is a poor thing to bring a child on.

\item Put the stone in wool at the small of the back, never at the feet. Try it on your own wrist first. The stone takes from somebody’s fire, and somebody in the terraces paid for that fire.

\item Do not wash the red branch. Cross two fingers over it and say the word the mother gives you, and no other.

\item When the second chill comes, count with her. Do not count for her.

\end{itemize}

I asked a woman of the Weir what the red branch meant and she crossed two fingers and gave me a date. A date is an answer that does not spoil in the mouth. I have put the date in the margin and left the question standing, which is where it was when I asked it.

\subsection*{The remedies, as they are used}

Trouble — What is set to it — The manner of it — Who goes thin\par

The second chill — Warmth, barley water, a watch kept to the fourth day — It comes after the warming, not before. We walk her, believing a moving woman cannot go cold. A physician come down from Greybank says a body made warm spends faster and that walking spends it quicker still; he has seen a woman go stiller by evening and be gone by morning. I have seen the same and I have walked her. Both stand. — The household, one night’s sleep and, sometimes, the woman.\par

The sweet sickness (the line at the gum) — A spoon of sour barley-water; the gum rubbed with a pinch of wood-ash — The glaze girls taste the mix to get the colour, and the sweetness answers sweetness, we say. The physician says it is lead in the glaze and that sour water does nothing but trouble the teeth. I have seen the pale line go off a girl who left the glaze room and come back on one who stayed. I have not seen the lead. — The glaze room, which cannot stop and does not ask.\par

A kiln-burn — Tallow first, then a clean fold; a damper-key laid across it to draw the heat — We say the iron draws. The physician says cold iron takes the measure as well as the heat, and that a burn can lose a hand by being made cold. I have set the key on a burn and watched the skin below it go the colour of old rope. I have not done it a second time. — The burn, and the hand if the iron stays.\par

Milk that will not come — Another woman to hold the child while the mother sleeps; clay-water to cool the breast — The favour is paid out of the other woman’s own house, and I say so before I ask it. The physician says clay-water dries the milk and feeds nobody. I have given it and watched a child cry over a dry breast. I have not given it since the third such child. — The other woman’s child, first.\par

The birth-flower — Nothing. Two fingers crossed, and the word the mother gives — I have rubbed one with salt and one with slip and one with nothing, and the branch kept its shape in all three. A girl of the terraces told me her mother washed one and the child went flat by evening, and I have set that beside the three and not joined it, because a flower staying and a child going flat are two things in one room. — Nobody knows. The child’s skin, perhaps.\par

The cold that stays (a foot out of the Slip Brook) — Wool, a stone at the belly, and work to keep the woman moving — The extremity goes first and the heart holds out, and there is an hour on the far side of the warming when she gets worse. I have no name for that hour and have left the place where the name would stand the length a name of that kind wants. We walk her and set her to work. I have seen a foot go dark inside three turns of wool through a whole lean week and have gone on winding the wool. — The woman. This is the row where I have been least honest.\par

A cord that will not fall — Wait. A hand on the belly and a hand kept still — A midwife of the Weir says never pull, and I have pulled once and had the cord come away with more than the cord. I have not written what came with it, because a thing with no name in Grath is a thing a clerk will put a figure to if you leave it lying. — The woman, in the lying-in.\par

A child that comes back with another house’s want — The name nine times at the door; a bowl of water under the bed; threshold clay rubbed at the wrist — She calls her mother by a name not given in this house and reaches for a door that is not in the room. We give the name back nine times and set water where the old water stood. The physician says a spoken name puts no shape back, and he is right as a man is right who has never held one of these children. One went off it by the ninth speaking and one kept it a year. I have entered neither in the birth-slate. — Nobody. The house, in a year it cannot spend.\par

A cut from a pot-shard — Tallow first, then a clean fold; never the grey — The women of the yard sprinkle Ash into a cut to dry it, believing the grey takes the wet. I have dressed three such cuts and found the grey under the skin in all three when they came back to me, and have not been able to get it out. That is as much as I know and as much as I shall write. — The cut.\par

Nothing in this book is free. That is the only thing I will stand behind.

\subsection*{The second chill}

The second chill comes on the third night, after the warm has come back into the room. The district calls it the child’s own work and says it goes off by the fourth morning. I have said that for twenty-six years. A body that has been warmed gives heat away faster than one never warmed, and the hour on the far side of the warming is the hour to be afraid of. I know it and I still walk her.

The physician told me to hold her instead and count with her, and not set her on her feet till the fourth day. I have held two women and walked twenty. Both were up on the fourth morning. Of the twenty, three went thin and one did not get up. Three and one are not a number a district will let you use: two is a coincidence, twenty is a habit, and a habit is what the district calls an answer. I have left the place where the count should stand, the length a count of that kind wants.

\subsection*{The note under the thumb}

Tap a sound cup with the knuckle and it answers full. Tap a cracked one and it answers flat, a small dead sound that stops at the surface and will not go through. The kiln-masters keep this to themselves, which is their trade, and I have borrowed it from the rack where the cups dry.

I do not tap a woman to hear her. I did once, on a girl gone thin after a return, and the flat I thought I heard was not in her. A body is not a cup. But a house is: I can tell by the note in the pot on the bench whether the room held its warm through the night, and set the stone by that and not by a clock, for there is no clock in Low Kiln and no Court figure that will tell you what a pot knows.

\subsection*{The watch-song}

\emph{Sung low at the third night, to the woman and not to the child. The room says the last line with her.}

\begin{quote}\itshape The coals are banked, the water thin,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the child is come, the door shut fast;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape hold the wrist and count the breath\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and leave the place where two should be.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape The red branch keeps what the water takes,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the name comes late, the figure soon;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape a slate is a stone with a neat hand on it\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and a hand is a thing that can go cold.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape The chill comes after the warm is back,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape it is not the water, it is not the night;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape walk her soft, or hold her still ---\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the fourth morning knows which one was right.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Sing to the coals, sing to the child,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape sing to the woman counting under wool;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape what comes back is not what went,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and comes back as it can.\end{quote}

I have changed one line in thirty years. I sang \emph{walk her soft} and now sing \emph{hold her still}, and the women singing with me have not noticed, which is how I know it was needed. A line said over a hundred births belongs to the room, not to me.

\subsection*{What the borrowed hands did}

The physician came down from Greybank in Ember of Y.H. 811 with a book that had the word \emph{lead} in it and a hand that wrote in the margin without asking. He set \emph{a common settling} over my \emph{second chill} and struck the nine speakings of the name and wrote \emph{no efficacy} above them, then went off with a purse. I have put the nine back underneath. He was right about the lead and wrong about the name, and I have kept both sentences so the next reader can tell which is which.

A clerk of the College borrowed the leaf when it went to Greybank in Ilmen. He struck out my column headed \emph{Who goes thin} and wrote \emph{No cost entered} above it, which is a true thing in a dishonest place. Against the space where I had left the name of what a returned child wants, he put a round nought and wrote \emph{vacancy} beneath it. A nought is a figure and can be entered; a want cannot. He took the verbs out of \emph{the child comes when the kiln does} and wrote \emph{the child is come when the kiln is} above, saying a thing always true has no need of a verb. I have put \emph{comes} back underneath. A clerk can speak without verbs because he is never in the room; a woman at three in the morning wants to know whether the child is coming now.

\subsection*{At the head and in the gutter}

The tallow at the head came off the lamp I held low while a woman was saying something I wanted the end of. The grey is off my cuff. The brick dust in the fold is off the rack where the cups dry and is the only thing in this book put there by the trade and not by a person. The wet slip took two words clean off the second leaf, and I have not written them back: a remedy with two words gone is a remedy said slowly, and everything here is said slowly. The ring of barley-water came from a cup set down while I was telling a girl to drink and she would not. The scorch is a spark off the kiln that went out under my hand, and I have not entered the burn. The hair in the seam is the colour of wet wool and is not mine, and I have left it where it caught.

\subsection*{At the foot, in a hand nobody will own}

\begin{quote}\itshape The slate keeps the name. The clay keeps the print.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape The warm that came between them is kept in no house.\end{quote}

I asked a physician, a clerk of the College, and a woman of the Weir, and had three answers and no hand. I have left the line where it was written. The cloth goes back over the book in my apron. Tomorrow a girl will come to the door with a foot gone dark or a child that will not come, and I shall put the verbs back where the clerk took them out, and set the slate face down before I look at the child, because a child is not an account and a woman at three in the morning has a hand that wants holding.

\clearpage\phantomsection\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{The Glass Eel, Being a Trapper’s Field Notes on the Eel of the Lower Ilm and the Silt Below the North Bridge}
\CRsheetheading{The Glass Eel, Being a Trapper’s Field Notes on the Eel of the Lower Ilm and the Silt Below the North Bridge}
{\centering\FellFont\itshape\footnotesize\color{faded} A hunter’s field book on one beast, set down as the record of nights at the trap and not as natural philosophy; the rounds in Grathic, the tally in charcoal on the backs of spoiled fish-tallies, an eel-song as it is sung, a Greybank skin-buyer’s price pressed in the margin, two rulings in the narrow upright Ledgerhand of the factor’s clerk, and one line in pale ink from a hearth-maid at the Fish Blessing · Written in Ilmen of Y.H. 812, the Thin Year, in the first warm days after the Long Cold, by Tibb of the Fishstairs, who sets eel-traps at the Weir and fishes the silt below the north bridge; set down at the end of nights with a tallow lamp guttering in a clay dish, first on the backs of fish-tallies spoiled by river water and then on two folds of oiled eel-skin, sewn with eel-sinew and carried in a clay tube stoppered with wool. Copied at Greybank in Smoke of Y.H. 813 onto the back of a salt warrant voided by the damp. It survives with dried eel slime along the fore-edge, grey silt worked into the gutter, a white salt bloom at the head blown up from the Sallow, a lamp-scorch on the second leaf where the dish overturned, a fish-hook nick at the fore-edge, one eel-scale pressed flat in the fold, a tar thumb at the head, a brown tideline where the river stood on it through a night, a green bead of lead glaze from a woman who leaned to see the tally, a grey Ash print nobody will own, two corrections in the narrow upright Ledgerhand of the factor’s clerk at Greybank, a price in the blocky hand of the skin-buyer, a line in pale ink from a hearth-maid, and one line at the foot in a hand nobody will own\par}\medskip
I trap eels at the Weir and fish the first warm silt below the north bridge. That is my trade and the whole of what I know, and I have set down only what I have put a hand to. A man who writes what he has heard at a hearth is writing a hearth, not a beast. I have known both kinds of book and this is the sort a man can use with wet hands.

The slime on the fore-edge is eel and the silt in the gutter is the Ilm. I have not cleaned either off. A book that has never been down to the Fishstairs was never taken on watch.

\subsection*{The run}

They come up in Ilmen when the water turns and the ice is gone from the middle of the river, and they come up out of the Sallow, which is a thing every trapper on the Ilm knows and no clerk has ever had to enter. The traps at the Weir are set with their mouths upriver, so a thing going with the water goes in and cannot find the way back out. On Ilmen fifteen the hearth-maids stand on the flat stone and bless the weirs and the traps, and speak the words over the boards; the eels run on that day and they run on the day after whether the words were spoken or not. I have set down both things and joined neither.

In the first warm days they lie in the silt of the Fishstairs, under the north bridge, where the water goes flat and brown and glossy. At night they come to a lamp and to a stone that has held warmth. This is the whole of the hunting: a lamp on a stone, a trap with its mouth upriver, and a man who keeps his hands out of the water until he knows where the eels are.

I tap a basket the way a potter taps a pot. A basket with eels in it answers full; an empty one answers flat and small. It is the only account on this river that I trust, and it cannot be carried into a counting room because there is nothing on it to write.

\subsection*{What it is}

It is an eel. I will set that down first, because the old women will not. It has an eel’s length and an eel’s way of going, and it is the colour of the Sallow on a dull morning, grey with a thin glass shine along the back. In the hand it is cold and slippery and stronger than a thing of that thickness has any right to be.

I have opened nine. In each I found an eel and nothing else, and behind the head a small clear place, no bigger than a pea split in two, with a little warmth shut in it. I have no name for that place and I have not asked for one. A man who writes a cause into a book he keeps in a clay tube is a man who will be asked for the cause by somebody with a slate, and the answer will be entered and the eel will go on being an eel.

\subsection*{The stop}

The danger is not the bite. It has no bite worth writing of. The danger is the stop it puts through the water.

A man wading at night with a lamp will feel it before he sees anything: the ways in him stop as though a clamp had closed on them, and there is no iron to see and no mark on the skin. It lasts a moment on dry ground. In water that is up to a man’s calf it lasts long enough. He cannot lift his foot. The water does the rest, quietly and without haste, the way the Ilm takes a step at the Fishstairs and goes on being a river.

I have seen it once only and I will set that down plainly. It was Ilmen twenty-two, a man of the Weir wading below the bridge with a lamp on a stone and his creel at his hip. He was a man who carried more than his natural measure — a Held man, the sort who can stand a great deal — and I thought he would stand this. He went down at the knee in three feet of water and his hands came up empty and would not close. We had him out in the time it takes to cross oneself, which was not a short time. His fingertips were grey for a tend after and he did not get his warmth back all at once. He has never said what it felt like and I have not asked him. A physician at Sill would call it the cold that stays. I have called it the stop because that is what it did.

A Thin man in that water would not have come up. I have no doubt of it and no wish to test it. The thing has no malice that I could see. It stops what is in front of it, the way the draw stops at a sluice, and goes on with its own business.

\subsection*{The lamp and the trap}

Set at dusk, mouth upriver, the lamp on a stone to the lee side and never against the chest. A lamp against the chest brings the eel to the man instead of to the stone, which is a distinction a new man learns once. Work in pairs where the silt is deep. Smoke what you take at the Fishstairs and sell it for three bits a basket; salted it goes for two, and the women there set their own figure and do not say it aloud.

The skins go a different way. A man comes up from Greybank in a coat with the cuff gone soft from washing and buys the skins dried, a mark apiece, which is four baskets of eels for the skin of one and a figure I have never been able to argue with. He told me the dried skin carries a flow a little farther than the hand can carry it, which is a trade I do not follow and have no wish to follow. A mark is a mark and a question is a question with a figure hanging off it. I have written his price where he set it and have not added a reason to it.

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Pressed in the blocky hand of the Greybank buyer, in the margin beside the price:} A mark a skin, dried whole, no holes. Twelve to the bundle, entered at the tally house. The flow is not explained at this price. --- G.\end{quote}

I have left his hand standing. He paid and I have no quarrel with a man who pays.

\subsection*{The song}

\emph{Sung setting the traps at dusk, not lifting them at dawn. The third line is the old line and the men at the Weir sing it wrong on purpose, because a song that tells a man why the eel comes is a song he can carry home and set by his own fire. I have set it down as it is sung.}

\begin{quote}\itshape One for the Sallow and one for the draw,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape one for the run that comes up in the thaw;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape it comes to the lamp and it comes to the stone\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and takes the warm that the stone has known.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Four in the silt and four in the run,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the mouth upriver and the lamp on the bight;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape if the stop comes, let the man go down ---\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the river keeps what the river has found.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Count them going and count them back,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape three bits a basket and a mark for the skin;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape we sing the old line wrong and leave the gap\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape where the sixth eel rose and no hand went in.\end{quote}

The gap is where the sixth eel rose on Ilmen twenty-two. The men know it and sing it and have never once said why it is the sixth. There is a man at the Weir who sings the last line twice and will not say what for, and I have let him keep it.

\subsection*{The tally}

These are the nights I kept a true account of. There were others I did not write because my hands were full and one I did not write because I had drunk. I have set down both sorts as they stand. The last column is the clerk’s, not mine.

Night — Place — Lamp — Taken — Stopped — Entered\par

Ilmen 3 — Weir, west mouth — one — four — none — 12\par

Ilmen 8 — Silt below the north bridge — one — seven — none — 21\par

Ilmen 13 — Fishstairs, second step — two — five — none — 15\par

Ilmen 15 — Weir, after the blessing — one — nine — none — 27\par

Ilmen 22 — Below the bridge, deep silt — one — two — one man — 6\par

Ilmen 27 — Weir, east mouth — one — six — none — 18\par

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{In the narrow upright hand of the factor’s clerk at Greybank, struck through the “Stopped” column:} Persons stopped: not entered. Stop not a vessel. No deduction arises. Account stands.\end{quote}

I have left his hand standing. A clerk’s hand has its use: it keeps a man from arguing with what he cannot change. But the man on Ilmen twenty-two was grey at the fingertips through the whole of Ilmen and went on selling eels over the top of it, and the clerk has put \emph{nil} against him with a neat instrument and no name on it. I have written the grey in the margin below, where his column cannot reach, and set my own mark beside it in charcoal.

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Below, in my hand:} One man, grey ten days. Paid for at the Weir and not on any slate. Missed by nobody but me.\end{quote}

\subsection*{What the old women say}

They say the glass eels are the shadows of star-rivets that fell into the river, and that each one is the dark of a rivet that could not bear the light where it was driven. There are songs for it with a woman’s name in them and a wrong done at a weir. I have heard them and I have no quarrel with a song. I have opened nine and found an eel each time, and a small clear place behind the head with a little warmth in it, and nothing that would cast a shadow in daylight.

The stars are rivets in the great repair, so the old women say, and I have no learning to set against it. But a rivet that fell into the Ilmen would not come up as an eel. It would come up as a thing a man could not close his hand around, and there would be a figure in the slate for it before the water had gone down. I have written that sentence once and crossed it out twice, because it is the kind of sentence that gets a man called a natural philosopher, and natural philosophers are not set to trap eels at the Weir in Ilmen.

\subsection*{At the head and in the margins}

The slime at the fore-edge is mine, from holding a basket still while I wrote with the other hand. The silt in the gutter came up over the second step below the north bridge and has never come out. The salt bloom at the head came up out of the paper on a wind off the Sallow and comes and goes with the weather, which is more than can be said for the clerk’s figure. The scorch on the second leaf is where the lamp went over on Ilmen twenty-two, while I was down at the man in the water; the hand that set the dish upright was mine and has not been entered. The hook nick is from a creel at the Fishstairs. The scale in the fold came off a fish that went into the basket and not into the song. The tar is off the wrap. The tideline is the Ilm’s own hand on the leaf, and it has taken two of my words and left the clerk’s figures standing, which is a small injustice in the ordering of things. The green bead is lead glaze off a woman who leaned to see the tally with the sweetness at one corner of her mouth; she said nothing and went off with the light. The grey print nobody will own I have not swept. There is no Last Day on a river, and nothing here is burnt and called dealt with.

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{In pale ink on the corner of the fourth leaf, in the hand of a hearth-maid who stood on the flat stone at the blessing:} We say the words over the traps on Ilmen fifteen. The eels run whether we say them or not. I have spoken them for two and thirty years and have never once been told what they do, which is a mercy, because a blessing that does something has a price, and there is no house in Sill that wants a price on a blessing.\end{quote}

I have put her line above my own. She wrote it at the Weir and I wrote mine in the silt, and neither of us has asked the eel anything.

\subsection*{At the foot, in a hand nobody will own}

\begin{quote}\itshape The river keeps what it is given. It gives nothing back.\end{quote}

I asked a clerk, a buyer, a hearth-maid and a man who went grey at the fingertips, and had four answerings and no hand. I have left the line where it was written.

Next Ilmen I will go down to the Fishstairs before the blessing with a fresh lamp and two folds of eel-skin, and I will count them going and count them back, and if the clear place behind the head is full in one and empty in another I will set that down too, in charcoal, with the verb left in it and no figure at the end of the row.

\clearpage\phantomsection\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{The Clicking in the Reed, Being a Hunter’s Notes on the Reed-Wolf of the East Marsh}
\CRsheetheading{The Clicking in the Reed, Being a Hunter’s Notes on the Reed-Wolf of the East Marsh}
{\centering\FellFont\itshape\footnotesize\color{faded} A reed-cutter’s field book on one beast, set down as a record of hunts and not a book of natural philosophy; the calls and the counting-song in Grathic, the tally in charcoal and reed-sap, with a Stonemouth tooth-buyer’s corrections in Ledgerhand in the margin · Written in the hunting month of Bone, Y.H. 812, the Thin Year, by a reed-cutter of Reedholt who went into the east marsh with a spear and a knot of cord, and who hunts still; copied forward in Bone, Y.H. 813. Set on the backs of Stonemouth weigh-slips gone soft with damp and on two folded sheets of birch bark, sewn with eel-sinew and carried in a bark wrap under a loose board of the hunter’s hut.
