It survives stained and used: a tooth-grey smear along the fore-edge where the book was wiped on a sleeve after a kill, a press of wet reed across the first leaf, a brown peat thumb at the tally, a small round mark where a buyer set a two-mark piece down and left it, and a line of figures in the narrow hand of the Stonemouth weigh-clerk who counted and paid for the teeth. The hunter has answered that clerk in the foot and has not struck a word of his out.\par}\medskip
I cut reed at the east marsh and I have kept this book three winters. It is not a book of natural philosophy. I have no slate-name and no learning, and I set down only what I have put my hand to. A man who writes what he has heard from a hearth is writing a hearth, not a beast. I have known both kinds of book and this is the second sort, being the sort a man can use.

The brown thumb at the tally is peat, not Ash. There is Ash enough on the beast without bringing it into the book. I have not washed any of it off. A book that has never been wiped on a sleeve was never taken into the marsh.

\subsection*{The voice of it}

It does not howl. This is the first thing a new man gets wrong and the thing that gets him bitten. A wolf that howls is a wolf you can walk away from; you know where it stands and it knows you know. The mouth in the reed makes a low clicking with the tongue, under the water’s noise, so that you hear it in your boots before you hear it in the air. It carries over water as a man’s talk carries over a floor. Four clicks, then a gap, then four again, and the gap is where it is listening.

I have set the call down below as we use it, answered across the water to draw them to a stand. It is not a song for a fire. It is a thing said under the breath with the tongue behind the teeth, and the words are only there to keep the count for the men who cannot click true.

\begin{quote}\itshape Four for the mud and one for the slack,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape it comes to the warm and it comes to the crack;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape it comes not for singing, it comes for the place\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape where the way runs shallow and under the face.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Click once in the reed, then hold, then click:\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape a man who runs is a man they pick.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Stand to the elbow. Show them the bare.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape It wants the one place and it finds it there.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Five in the open and nine in the wet,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and one goes still and the rest go yet;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape count them going and count them back,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and leave the fourth for the man who lacked.\end{quote}

A reed-cutter goes in pairs. This is not a kindness. If a man goes alone into the east marsh in Bone he will come back with one arm or he will not come back, and the pairs are because a beast that has opened a way in one man must be driven off the other before it finishes. The last line of the song is for the one who does not come back. We leave the fourth click for him and we do not say his name at it. There is a man at Reedholt with two fingers gone who clicks four for himself and a fifth he will not explain, and I have let him keep it.

\subsection*{How it kills}

It goes for the throat and the inside of the elbow. That is the whole of it; there is no wrestling and no throwing down. I have seen a Held man, a man who carried more than his natural measure and was twice the weight of me, go into the mud under one of these and be under before he could shape a shout. The mud did as much as the beast. A pack can pull down a Held man in mud, which is why we cut reed in pairs and why I have no fine opinion of my own standing among them.

It does not worry a victim. This is what the hearths get wrong when they say it worries. It opens one place and waits at it. I have watched from a stand with my spear across my knee and seen a beast open a man’s elbow and then lie with its jaw against the place and wait, as steady as a collector with a tube against a wrist. The man stopped struggling. The beast did not shake him or worry him or drag him. It kept the one place, and the warm went out of it, and when I drove it off the man was already a thing I would not have sent for a physician to save.

I will set down what I have seen and not what it means. It killed quickly, at one place, and there was no anger in it that I could see. A collector’s draw is the same work done with iron and a slate. I have stood near enough to a draw to know the smell of the cold iron and I have stood near enough to one of these to smell the wet wool and the mud, and the two smells are not the same, but the work is. I have thought about that more than is good for a reed-cutter and I have not written a cause.

\subsection*{The tally}

These are the hunts I kept a true account of. Some nights I did not write because my hands were full and some I did not write because I had drunk. I have set down both sorts as they stand. The figure in the fifth column is the Stonemouth figure, not mine. I counted teeth; the clerk counted marks.

Night — Place — Heard — Taken — Teeth — Marks — Lost\par

Bone 4 — East bank below Reedholt — five — two — six — 12 — a dog, bitten in the elbow, shot at dusk\par

Bone 9 — The marsh road cut — seven — three — nine — 18 — none\par

Bone 14 — Standing water north of Mud End — nine — two — five — 10 — one of ours, hand taken, lived\par

Bone 20 — The lower Ilm, silt side — five — one — three — 6 — none; the wind turned and we were heard\par

Bone 27 — Old run east of the reedbeds — seven — four — eleven — 22 — spear lost in the mud, not recovered\par

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{The narrow hand wrote against the “Heard” column:} five, seven, nine are not a number. Enter as 7. Average 7 to a pack, 6 teeth to a hunt. This is the figure the factor will ask for.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{And along the foot of the “Marks” column, in the same hand:} 12+18+10+6+22 = 68. Received. Account stands.\end{quote}

I had the book out at Stonemouth on Bone 30 and the weigh-clerk laid his cuff on the leaf before he looked at me, the way they do, and set the figures down. He is a clerk and I am a reed-cutter and the account is his, so I have left his hand standing. But a pack is five or seven or nine according to the night and there is no factor in the marsh to give it a number. He has put seven where I put three figures, and under it he has written \emph{average}, which is a word that means nothing to a man standing in water up to his calf with nine of them clicking in the dark.

\subsection*{The teeth and the pelt}

The teeth are set into clamp-handles, and a good tooth is worth two marks at Stonemouth. This is not a pretty trade and I have never pretended it is one. A tooth remembers the shape of a way; that is what the clamp-men say when they buy, and they pay for the saying. I have seen a handle set with one of these teeth bite true where an iron one would slip, and I have no explanation for it and no wish to make one. I took eleven teeth on Bone 27 and I would take the same again if it bought the winter.

The pelt is worth nothing. The hair carries Ash, and a coat of it makes a man go thin by degrees without his knowing how. I have seen a Fen trader try to sell one in Mud End with the Ash worked out of it, and he could not, because you cannot work Ash out of a thing, you can only move it somewhere else. We burn the pelts. We do not sell them and we do not keep them and we say so plainly when a man asks, because a man who buys a reed-wolf pelt is a man who will come back for another.

\subsection*{What the hearths say}

The hearths say it is a drowned man’s grudge that has Learnt to click. There are songs about it in the Fenmarch with a man’s name in them and a wrong done at a weir. I have heard them and I have no quarrel with a song. But I have taken six-and-thirty of these in three winters and opened most of them, and what I found was a wolf. It is a wolf that took to the water and stayed there, and the cold of the water has gone into it the way the wet goes into a coat. It kills the way water kills, at one place and without wanting anything from the man it kills. I have written \emph{no anger} in the margin and the clerk has written over it:

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{In the clerk’s hand:} Malice: not entered. Sentiment is not a figure and has no place in a tally.\end{quote}

I did not write that it had no malice because I forgave it. I wrote it because I watched. Those are different things and a clerk’s hand cannot tell them apart, which is the whole reason I keep this book in a bark wrap under a board instead of on a slate in Stonemouth.

Two winters ago a man of Reedholt went in alone and came back walking in the direction he had been facing, and his mother lived in the next hut and did not know him. We did not send for a collector because there was nothing in him to draw, and because the collectors do not come into the east marsh in Bone. He walked to the water and stood, and in the morning he was not there. I have set this down because it happened and not because it explains anything. The hearths will make a song of it and put a name in it and the name will be wrong.

\subsection*{At the foot}

The tooth-grey along the fore-edge is from Bone 27, when I wiped my hand on the leaf before I could find a rag. The round mark is a two-mark piece the buyer set down and forgot; I have left it where it fell. The wet reed across the first leaf is from the morning the wind turned on us and we lay flat in the cut until the clicking went away. The peat thumb is mine. The clerk’s figures I have not touched, and the hunter’s hand that wrote \emph{no anger} under them is my own and will not be struck.

There is a new run east of the reeds that I have not walked. The water stands in it when it should have drained and the clicks come from it in fours with a longer gap than I have heard before. I do not know what the longer gap means. I will go in at the next Bone with a pair of cord and a fresh spear, and I will count them going and count them back, and if there are nine where there should be five I will set that down too, in my own hand, with the verb left in it.

\clearpage\phantomsection\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{The Cold Acre Book of Remedies, Being Remedies for the Well-Cold, the Threshing Cough, the Turnip-Knife Cut, the Sweet Line, the Second Chill, the Birth-Flower and the Member Gone Dark, Set Down on the Ridge with the Errors Left Standing}
\CRsheetheading{The Cold Acre Book of Remedies, Being Remedies for the Well-Cold, the Threshing Cough, the Turnip-Knife Cut, the Sweet Line, the Second Chill, the Birth-Flower and the Member Gone Dark, Set Down on the Ridge with the Errors Left Standing}
{\centering\FellFont\itshape\footnotesize\color{faded} A ridge-wife’s and midwife’s book of remedies in the Cold Acre speech, written in Grathic letters learned off a man who came up to have his mark confirmed; the cures in a healer’s hand on the back of a barley tally spoiled at the meal mill, the objections of a physician come down from Greybank pressed into the margin, the corrections of a factor’s clerk in narrow upright Ledgerhand, a slate-woman’s line set close to the third-night row, a well-song with the place where the twelfth should stand left as it is sung, and one line at the foot in a hand nobody will own · Written at Cold Acre, two leagues north of Sill on the ridge where the one well has not frozen in any winter the oldest on the ridge can name, between Tallow of Y.H. 812 and Ilmen of Y.H. 813, the Long Cold and the Thin Year, by Renna of Cold Acre, a ridge-wife who has set the bones of the harvest and caught the children of the six houses for nine-and-twenty years; begun on the back of a barley tally from the meal mill that a wet thumb spoiled, folded into oiled sacking and carried in the breast of a wool apron against a square of birth-cloth, and copied at Greybank in Ilmen of Y.H. 813 onto the back of a discarded rent-roll. It survives with well-clay worked into the grain at the head, a frost-ring that has taken two words clean off the second leaf, a barley awn stiff in the fold, a nick from a turnip knife at the fore-edge, a tideline of well-water gone pale along the gutter, a thumb of tallow at the outer fold, a green bead of High Kiln glaze pressed into the lower corner by a girl with the sweetness at one mouth-corner, objections in the cold margin hand of the physician, corrections in the upright hand of the factor’s clerk, a slate-woman’s line set close to the third-night row, and the one line at the foot\par}\medskip
I am a ridge-wife of Cold Acre and I have set the bones and caught the children of six houses for nine-and-twenty years. Nobody asked me for this book. A woman came up the ridge road in the lean week with a hand gone white from the well pail and asked what I did for the cold that stays, and I heard myself answer in my mother’s short way of speaking, and did not know whether I believed it. A remedy you have to say in your mother’s voice is a remedy nobody has looked at in a long while. I have looked at some of mine. The rest I have left standing, for a woman at three in the morning wants a hand more than a correction.

I write on the back of a barley tally the meal mill spoiled when a wet thumb went over the figures. The figures went into the meal and out of the house, and what is left is paper enough for a book nobody asked to see. The well-clay at the head comes up under the nails in this hamlet and no washing takes it out of the grain. The grey in the gutter came off a cuff laid where no cuff has business lying. There is a well here that has not frozen in any winter anyone can name, and nobody asks why; I have kept that beside the grey and made no lesson of it.

\subsection*{The order of the sick-room}

\emph{Written small on the first leaf, with one word gone over in well-water.}

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item Set the pail outside the door before you go to the child. A pail of well-water standing in a room takes the warm out of a side faster than the north wind, and the north wind has the decency to be cold all over.

\item Turn the slate face down. The slate-woman up the ridge writes the names and I do not; a hand that writes before it looks has already chosen the child.

\item Try the stone on your own wrist before it goes to a belly. It came off somebody’s hearth and somebody in these six houses paid for the coals.

\item Do not wash the red branch. Cross two fingers over it and say the word the mother gives you.

\item When the second chill comes, count with her. Do not count for her.

\item If a man comes up the ridge road with a cold tube and a slate, give him the mother and keep the child behind the pail. This is not refusal. It is the order of the room.

\end{itemize}

I asked the slate-woman what she saw under the two fingers and she crossed them again and gave me a date. A date does not spoil in the mouth. I have put the date in the margin and left the question standing where it was when I asked it.

\subsection*{The remedies, as they are used}

Trouble — What is set to it — The manner of it — Who pays\par

The well-cold (a hand gone white at the pail) — A stone at the belly, and work — The well has not frozen in any winter anyone can name, and still it draws from a hand faster than the Ilm draws from a stone. We say it has somewhere to put what it takes. A physician come down from Greybank says water draws faster than air and the well is only water. I held one hand in the pail and one in the north wind for one count; the pail hand was colder. Both stand. — The well, which keeps no account.\par

The threshing cough — Steam of barley-water under a cloth; honey if the house has it — The dust of the meal mill gets into a man and he coughs up a colour he will not discuss. A physician says grain dust in the lung and no physic but departure. I sent two down to Sill and both came back worse, for the roads have dust of their own. — The mill, which cannot stop and does not ask.\par

A turnip-knife cut — Tallow, then a clean fold; never the grey — The women put grey from the corner in a cut to dry it, believing the grey is clean. I dressed three such and found grey under the skin in all three, and could not get it out. — The cut, in a white line it keeps.\par

The sweet line — Sour barley-water; wood-ash at the gum — A girl come down from the Glaze Room with the pale line at her gum says a sweet answers a sweet. A physician says lead. I have seen the line go off one who left that room and come back on one who stayed. I have not seen the lead. — The glaze room, which cannot stop and does not ask.\par

The second chill — Warmth, barley-water, a watch to the fourth morning; we hold them now — It comes after the warming, not before. A physician says a warmed body spends faster and holding still spends less than walking. I walked nineteen and held five; of the walked three went thin and one did not rise, of the held one went thin. I have kept the counts on birch bark and not added them, for a count added is a count a clerk can carry down the ridge. — The household, one night’s sleep; sometimes the child.\par

The birth-flower — Nothing. Two fingers crossed, and the word the mother gives — The slate-woman crossed two fingers over nine children and never told anybody what she saw. A woman down in Sill washed one with salt and her child went flat by evening; I have set that beside the six I did not wash and not joined them. When asked what it is I give a date. — Nobody knows. The child’s skin, perhaps.\par

The member gone dark — Wool, a stone at the middle, and work — The extremity goes first and the middle holds out, and there is an hour on the far side of the warming when a body spends what it was given faster than it takes in. I have no name for that hour and have left the place where the name would stand the length a name of that kind wants. I have wound the wool and set them to work, and seen a foot go dark through a lean week, and gone on winding. — The woman. This is the row where I have been least honest.\par

Nothing in this book is free. It is carried from one ridge house to another and called a cure. That is the only sentence I will stand behind.

\subsection*{The note under the knuckle}

Tap a sound cup with the knuckle and it answers full. Tap a cracked one and it answers flat, a small dead sound that stops at the lip and will not go through. The women at the meal mill know it in the cups they drink from and I have borrowed it from them, as every trade borrows from the trade beside it.

I tapped a woman once, gone thin after a thin return, and the flat I thought I heard was not in her. A body is not a cup, though we set cups on the bench in the shape of bellies. But a house is: I can tell by the note in the pot whether the room held its warm through the night, and set the stone by that, for there is no clock in Cold Acre and no Court figure that will tell you what a pot knows.

The well gives back a low note when the bucket goes down. The slate-woman says it is the river running under the ridge; Gedde who keeps the curb says a well that gives a note will not freeze. I have left both sayings where I heard them.

\subsection*{The well that does not freeze}

The water comes up in Stone as in Ilmen, and a hand goes in either month and comes out the same colour and the same cold. A well that will not freeze is a kindness or a theft, and I have never decided which. We say it has somewhere to put what it takes, which is what the collectors say in a better room with cleaner cuffs, only they write it down. A physician says there is no mystery in it, only water, and is right about the water; he has never stood at this curb in Stone with the wind off the north gate and one hand in the pail. I have no remedy for the well-cold but a stone and a hand to hold, and have left the place where a better one would stand the length a remedy of that kind wants.

\subsection*{The song at the well}

\emph{Sung low at the curb while the pail goes down, to the water and not to the person. The twelfth is held in the singing, the length of a hand going into the pail and coming out empty. Nobody fills it.}

\begin{quote}\itshape Four for the houses and one for the well,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape one for the pail that will not freeze;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape a hand goes in and a hand comes out\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the cold keeps what the water leaves.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Two for the mill and two for the knife,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape two for the girl with the sweet at her mouth;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the line comes west and the line goes east\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the glaze room never asks what it cost.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Warm the middle and wrap the end,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape count with her, do not count for her;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the name goes down and the face comes up\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the stone keeps warm in the old tin’s cup.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Eleven I counted and one held out,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the twelfth goes down where the well keeps.\end{quote}

I changed one line in nine-and-twenty years: \emph{what the water takes} is now \emph{what the water leaves}, because a woman at this curb wants to know what is left in the pail when the hand comes out. The women singing with me have not noticed, which is how I know the line wanted changing. A factor’s clerk put a round nought in the held place and wrote \emph{vacancy} beneath it; a nought can be carried away in a cuff. The twelfth is a place and stays.

\subsection*{What the physician pressed in the margin}

He came down from Greybank with a book that had the word \emph{lead} in it and a hand that wrote without asking. Against the sweet line he set \emph{lead, as in the south}; against the well-cold, \emph{water conducts; no remedy}; against the birth-flower, \emph{a mark in the blood}. He was right in all three and had nothing a ridge house could pay for. Where I wrote \emph{we push the warmth back the way it came}, he set \emph{no such transmission}. I have put the warmth underneath.

\subsection*{What the factor’s clerk did}

A clerk of the factor borrowed the leaves when the winter barley was counted at Greybank; the ink sits in two fingers of a soft cuff. He struck out my column headed \emph{Who pays} and wrote \emph{No cost entered}, a true thing in a dishonest place. Where I wrote that the well keeps no account, he wrote \emph{the measure is retained in the water}, taking the hands out as though a pail could draw itself. I have put my verbs back underneath his. A clerk can write without verbs because he is never at a curb in Stone with a woman’s hand gone white in the pail.

\subsection*{In the margin, close to the third-night row}

\begin{quote}\itshape It was the second day, not the third, in my house also. Warm the middle and wrap the ends; do not tell the father what you call it. The tin under the bench is not a count. --- W.\end{quote}

She wrote it while I was at the well and set the leaf back with the fold changed. A woman who has kept the slates of this ridge for thirty-one years is allowed one sentence in a book of physic.

\subsection*{At the head and in the gutter}

The well-clay at the head came off my thumb in a wind off the north gate and has worked into the grain, which is why this leaf smells of the curb in any room. The frost-ring took two words clean off the second leaf when I left it outside the door; I have not written them back, because a remedy with two words gone is a remedy said slowly, and everything here is said slowly. The barley awn in the fold came off a sack by the mill door and has gone stiff as a splinter. The nick at the fore-edge is a turnip knife’s, from a woman who paid me with the knife still in her hand. The pale tideline is well-water off a pail set down while I was telling a girl to drink and she would not. The tallow is off the lamp I held low so nobody at the table would know I was writing. The green bead in the lower corner was pressed in by a girl come down from High Kiln with the sweetness at one mouth-corner; she touched the leaf, went back up the terrace and said nothing, and I did not ask whose glaze it was. The grey along the outer fold came off a cuff laid where no cuff has business lying; I have not swept it. There is a Last Day in Sill and the corners are swept and burnt there in the morning and called dealt with. There is no Last Day on this ridge.

\subsection*{At the foot, in a hand nobody will own}

\begin{quote}\itshape The well keeps what it takes and has no slate.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape The slate keeps what it cannot carry and calls it kept.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape The child between the pail and the door is warm or is not, and neither column asks.\end{quote}

I asked a physician, a factor’s clerk, and the woman who keeps the slates up the ridge, and had three answers and no hand. I have left the line where it was written. The book goes back into the sacking in my apron. Tomorrow a woman will come down the ridge road with a hand gone white from the pail or a child that will not breathe, and I shall turn the slate face down, try the stone on my own wrist, and leave the twelfth where it is, because a child is not an account and a woman at three in the morning wants a hand more than a remedy.

\clearpage\phantomsection\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{The Cold in One Foot, Being a Hunter’s Field Notes on the Silt-Leach of the Lower Ilm and the Ferr Shallows}
\CRsheetheading{The Cold in One Foot, Being a Hunter’s Field Notes on the Silt-Leach of the Lower Ilm and the Ferr Shallows}
{\centering\FellFont\itshape\footnotesize\color{faded} A hunter’s field book on one beast, set down as the record of wades and not as natural philosophy; the rounds in Grathic, the tally in charcoal on the backs of spoiled eel-bills, a blessing verse as it is said on the bank, one ruling in the narrow upright Ledgerhand of the factor’s clerk at Greybank, a line in the pale ink of a hearth-maid, and one line at the foot in a hand nobody will own · Written in Ember and Grain of Y.H. 812, the Thin Year, by a hunter of the Fishstairs who waded the shallows of the lower Ilm and the Ferr for eels and for leeches, and was paid by the dozen; set down at the end of wades on the bank with a tallow end in a dish and the cold still in one foot, first on the backs of eel-bills gone soft with river water and then on two folds of birch bark, sewn with eel-sinew and carried in a coat pocket against a twist of tallow. Copied forward at Greybank in Ilmen of Y.H. 813 onto the back of a Court grain-warrant voided by the Long Cold. It survives with grey silt worked into the head, an iron-brown tideline along the gutter from the Ferr, a press of wet sedge across the first leaf, a fish-hook nick at the fore-edge, a green bead of lead glaze pressed into the lower corner by a woman who leaned to see the tally, a cuff-grey smear where a collector set his slate down and took it up again, a singe where the tallow caught the third leaf, a grey Ash print nobody will own, one ruling in the clerk’s Ledgerhand, one line in the pale ink of a hearth-maid, and the one line at the foot\par}\medskip
I wade the shallows below the Weir and the Ferr at Stonemouth, and I take the leach out of the mud for the women at the Fishstairs. It is a poor trade and an honest one, which is more than I can say of most. A dozen dried fetch three bits and no questions, and the questions are the part that costs a man. I write this at the end of a wade with the water still in my boots and the tallow down to a knuckle, because a man forgets a cold foot once he is out of the river, and the forgetting is how he loses the count.

The grey at the head is silt and went into the fibre the first morning I set a leaf down on the bank. The brown along the gutter is iron out of the Ferr, and it stains a hand the colour of an old copper coin and does not wash off before the next wade. I have cleaned neither off. A book that has never been in the water was never used for anything.

\subsection*{Where it sets}

It comes in the low water, when the shallows smell of iron and mud and a man can see his own toes through the brown. In Ilmen the river is up and the leach is nowhere to be found; by Ember the water has gone down a hand’s breadth and the Ferr comes off the Lead Run blue-grey, and they are there. They set against the ankle of a wader and against the legs of the eel-men at the Weir, which is why an eel-man will not stand still in one place to mend a trap. They are very near the colour of the silt, so that a man sees them only when he lifts his foot and looks at what he has brought up, and by then it has been a while.

They are thickest where the water comes through slowly and stands. I have waded the same reach of the lower Ilm three Grains running and taken nine one year and four the next and none the third, and I have not found the rule in it and do not pretend to. A man who writes a rule into a book he carries in his pocket is a man who will be asked for the use of it by somebody with a slate.

\subsection*{What it is}

It is a leach. I will set that down before anything else, because the blessing verse does not and because a thing a man can hold in his fingers should be called by the name he would use for it in a kitchen. It is the length of a thumbnail and the colour of wet mud, with a mouth at the head end that does not let go once it has set, and a ways of going along the bottom that I have watched and cannot describe without making it sound like something it is not. It does not swim. It reaches and holds and draws itself along, the way a wetted finger draws along a table.

I have opened four. In each I found mud and a little blood and a small knot the colour of tallow behind the mouth, and nothing with a name in it that I could set down. I have put the colour where I found it and have not written what the knot is for. A man who has taken leeches for nine winters knows when to stop opening them.

\subsection*{The cold foot}

It does not bite. A man feels nothing while it works, and that is the whole danger of it. It sets its mouth to a way near the skin and draws slowly, the way a collector’s tube draws when the collector has all day, and a wader feels only a cold in one foot that does not go away when he leaves the water. I have kept that cold for a tend. I have known a man keep it for a month, and go to the physician about it, and be told there is nothing there to see.

It is the number that does the work. One leach on a grown man is a cold foot and an annoyance. A handful on a child is an hour, and at the end of the hour the child is cold all through and does not want anything. In Grain a woman came down to the Fishstairs with a child of two who had been set in the silt at the edge while she washed. There were six on the child’s ankles. I took them off into a dish and salted the feet, which troubles a leach but does not give back what one has already taken. The child was warm when I lifted her. She was cold by the time we reached the steps, and she did not cry at the steps. I have not put her cost in the tally because there is no figure for a child and because a figure would make it look as though somebody had paid.

I have set the verse down below as it is said on the bank at the Blessing, with the line the women sing wrong left standing. They sing it wrong on purpose. A song that tells a man why a thing takes his warmth is a song he can carry home and set by his own fire and be done with.

\subsection*{The verse}

\begin{quote}\itshape Four for the shallows and one for the bank,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape it sets where the iron comes up through the silt;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape it does not bite like a dog and it does not bark,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape it keeps to the ankle and keeps to the warm.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape A cold in one foot and a cold that stays,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape a child in an hour and a fistful of them;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape count them going and count them back,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and leave the fifth for the one we did not lift.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Three bits a dozen and no name on the bag,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape a greyed hand for the man who lets the slate have them;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape we sing it gives to the river, and sing it wrong ---\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the gap is the foot that does not come home.\end{quote}

The gap is a foot. The women know it and sing it and have never once said whose foot it is. There is an eel-man at the Weir who says the fifth line twice and will not say why, and I have let him keep it.

\subsection*{The tally}

These are the wades I kept a true account of. There were others I did not write because my hands were full and one I did not write because I had drunk. I have set down both sorts as they stand. The last column is the clerk’s, not mine; I counted what I took off, he entered what could be paid.

Wade — Place — Taken — Cold feet — Dozens — Entered\par

Ember 6 — Ferr below Stonemouth — eleven — one — none — 0\par

Ember 14 — Lower Ilm, below the Weir — nine — none — one — 3\par

Ember 22 — Ferr, the iron reach — fourteen — two — two — 6\par

Grain 3 — Silt side above the Fishstairs — seven — none — none — 0\par

Grain 11 — Lower Ilm, after rain — twelve — one — three — nil\par

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{In the narrow upright hand of the factor’s clerk, struck through the “Cold feet” column:} Leeches not a vessel. Cold in a foot: not entered. Warm in the shallows: no deduction arises. Account stands.\end{quote}

I have left his hand standing. A clerk’s hand has its use: it keeps a man from arguing with what he cannot change. But the child of Grain 3 is in no column of his and in no column of mine, and the cold that stayed in my foot through the whole of Ember is written nowhere he can reach. I have put both in the margin below, where his ruler cannot go, and set my own mark beside them in charcoal.

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Below, in my hand:} Six taken off. One child. No figure. The cold went on after the wade and I did not write it at the time because my hands were full. I write it now with the verb left in it.\end{quote}

\subsection*{The dozen and the greyed hand}

Dried leeches fetch three bits a dozen at the Fishstairs and nobody asks what they were taken from. This is a trade and I have never pretended it was a kindly one. I take them, I dry them on a strip of bark, I sell them, and the money goes into the house. What a man does with them after is not in my book.

But there is a use that is not mine to be nice about. A collector will buy them dried and set them on a wrist or a throat instead of iron and slate, and draw what he wants without entering it, and the law calls that theft and the fact calls it a greyed hand. I have seen the hand. It is the man who set the leeches who goes grey at the fingertips, not the man who sold them, which is a mercy of a kind and not one I like to think about on the walk home. I have sold four dozen in nine years and I have asked twice where they went and been told twice not to ask, and I have not asked a third time.

Salt does not stop the draw once it has begun. It only makes the foot smart, which a physician will tell you is a sign and a Fen trader will tell you is the cure. Both are paid for their answerings.

\subsection*{What they say at the Blessing}

They say at the Fish Blessing that the leach takes the warmth and gives it to the river, and that the river is honest with what it is given. I have put my hand in the water where a leach stood and where none stood, and the water is the same cold in both, and a river that had been given a hundred winters of warmth would not hide it so well. I have sung the line with the rest of them and I have left the sentence standing without a cause beside it. The women at the Fishstairs bless the traps in Ilmen and sell the leeches in Ember and will not hold both things in the same hand at the same time. I understand this better than I understand the leach.

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{In the pale ink of a hearth-maid, on the corner of a leaf gone soft where the river touched it:} It gives to the water, they say. I have laid a bowl of water by a child who was emptied and the water in the bowl was cold by morning, and so was the child, and I do not know which of them gave to which. Bless the trap. Say nothing at the selling.\end{quote}

I have put her line above my own. She wrote it at the Weir and I wrote mine in the mud below it, and neither of us has asked the leach anything.

\subsection*{At the head and in the margins}

The silt at the head is mine and off the bank at Stonemouth; it is grey here and brown when it dries, and it has gone into the grain the way the iron has into the gutter. The sedge across the first leaf came off the bank the morning the river came up a hand and I lay flat with the book under me and the eels gone. The nick at the fore-edge is a fish-hook, from the wade when I lost the hook and found it in the cover. The green in the lower corner was pressed there by a woman who leaned to see the tally with the sweetness of the glaze at one corner of her mouth; she did not say where it came from and I did not ask. The cuff-grey at the head is off a collector who set his slate on my leaf while he asked me a question about a wrist and took the slate up again without waiting for the answer. I have not wiped it off and I have not entered him. The singe on the third leaf is my own tallow end and the Ash print nobody will own has been there since Greybank. The clerk’s ruling I have not touched. The verse is as the women sang it, with the wrong line standing and the gap the length they leave it.

\subsection*{At the foot, in a hand nobody will own}

\begin{quote}\itshape The river is the road. It is not the house.\end{quote}

I asked an eel-man, a hearth-maid, a woman who washed at the Fishstairs, and a man with a grey hand, and had four answerings and no hand. I have left the line where it was written.

There is a reach of the Ferr above the Lead Run where the water comes down blue-grey and smells of iron even in Grain, and no eel-man sets a trap in it. Next Ember I will take a dish of salt and a coil of cord and wade it, and I will count them going and count them back, and if the cold stays in my foot for a tend after I have come out I will set that down too, in charcoal, with the cause left out and no figure at the end of the row.

\clearpage\phantomsection\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{The Cold-Iron Letter, Being a Letter from the Smithy at Low Kiln to His Sister at the Greybank Quay, Concerning the Tubes He Is Sent to Mend, the Iron That Comes Down from Keld, and the Figure Nobody Writes; with the Answers in the Margin, a Clerk’s Correction in Ledgerhand, and a Counting Song in a Hand Nobody Will Own}
\CRsheetheading{The Cold-Iron Letter, Being a Letter from the Smithy at Low Kiln to His Sister at the Greybank Quay, Concerning the Tubes He Is Sent to Mend, the Iron That Comes Down from Keld, and the Figure Nobody Writes; with the Answers in the Margin, a Clerk’s Correction in Ledgerhand, and a Counting Song in a Hand Nobody Will Own}
{\centering\FellFont\itshape\footnotesize\color{faded} A private letter on a strip of oiled packing-paper, written in charcoal and iron-gall, folded thrice and tied with a bit of wire; carried downriver from Sill to Greybank on an eel barge, answered in the margin, corrected on the back at the factor’s house, and kept since in a dry tin among the quay’s iron tallies · Written at the smithy east of the Clay Yard in Low Kiln, Sill, in the last tend of Silt, Y.H. 813, by Harn, a smith who mends kiln irons, barrow irons and the collectors’ cold-iron tubes, to Nessa his sister, who keeps the iron tally at the Greybank quay; carried eighteen leagues downriver on the eel barge, answered in her hand along the margin, and borrowed at the Court’s factor’s house, where a clerk set a correction on the back in Ledgerhand. It survives folded and wired in a tin of iron tallies, the charcoal rubbed thin at the folds, a thumb of brick-dust at the head, a tallow mark at the outer fold, a grey Ash print along the gutter where the writer’s cuff passed, a smear of cold-iron scale at the foot, a strip torn from the second fold, one word struck through with a chisel-point and written again underneath in the recipient’s hand, and a line on the back in a hand nobody has claimed.\par}\medskip
To Nessa at the quay, who keeps the iron tally and will not call a figure a figure before company. From Harn at the smithy east of the Clay Yard, Low Kiln, Sill.

I write on the back of a packing-sheet because there is no slate in this shop that I would put a sentence on. A slate is a thing a man reads to you. I have set my count in notches on the bench with a chisel-point for eleven years and no officer has ever asked me what the notches were, which is how I know they are not a figure. The charcoal takes badly on the oil and I have gone over every other word twice. Don’t rub the fold. It comes apart in the hand if you rub it.

The barge goes on the ebb the day after Account-day and the carrier says a thing said in Silt does not travel well once the mud takes it, so I am putting down what matters first. It is this. I mended nine tubes in the last tend and eleven in the one before, and I did not mend them faster or slower than they came in. They come in with the grip polished grey to the thumb, the grey worked into the creases of the handle where a man has held the same iron every day since he was taken on. I can tell a collector by his cuff before he comes through the door, turned back twice from washing, and by the fingers he keeps shut until he is at the bench. He never says what he took. He says “the account stands” to the iron as if the iron had read it.

I do not set a tube to a wrist. That is the officer’s work and I have no word for it and do not want one. I mend the mouth and the man who carries it goes away with it, and the district calls the whole of that a kindness because the law has no other name for a room where a man is held until he agrees. There is a pale ring left at the wrist where the clip held. It shows through the winter. I have seen a man rub his cuff down over it while he was being told a figure and go out saying it would go in the thaw. My mother said that about everything. It is not in any ordinance and I have never once heard it read aloud.

\subsection*{The tubes I mended in the last tend, set here and not on any slate}

When — What was brought — What was on it — What I did — What I entered\par

Firstday — A collector’s tube, the grip grey to the shoulder — Six grey prints; cuff turned back twice — Drawn clean, the seam set cold — Nothing\par

Thirdday — A barrow iron from the north gate — Ash in the notch, thicker than a year ago — Re-set and sent back — One mark, to the house\par

Fifthday — A kiln iron out of the glaze-room above — Green at the edge, sweetish at the smell — Filed it down and said nothing — Nothing\par

Seventhday — A damper iron with no house-name on it — Soot, and no warmth that belonged to it — Re-set; asked no question — Nothing\par

Ninthday — A second tube, the grip smooth as old bone — More prints than I counted, and I did not finish the count — Drawn clean — Nothing\par

I tap iron the way the women at the racks tap a pot, because a rule that holds for clay holds for anything that has been worked and may fail. A pot answers full and a cracked one answers flat, and a man answers if you know where to put your ear. A cold-iron tube answers neither. It has no note of its own. It takes and it does not give, and I have never in eleven years heard one ring full. I have set that down here because it is the strangest thing I know and there is nobody in this shop to tell it to. The kiln behind my bench takes its breath in fours and misses one, and I have worked beside it eleven years and never once heard the fifth. I do not call the missing breath anything. The yard calls it the kiln and goes on.

I was apprenticed in the year of the Rising, Y.H. 668, when ninety children’s warmth went into a private account and Pell Varr came down with a sword and put the district back the way a man sets a table. I was old enough to hold the bellows and not old enough to be told what the tubes were for, and I learned what they were for by watching what came back. Last year the hearth-maids tied a count in wool and the Weir tied one too, and no man has given me a figure for either, and I have not asked twice. A count a woman ties in wool is a count that stays where she put it. I have not entered it and Nessa must not enter it either.

Berr Clay came down from his house with the red cord folded under his coat and wiped his thumb twice before he touched nothing, and read one in twelve over the basket at the Cross, twice, once for the moot and once for the ones who came late. The bell went four, four and a gap and nobody crossed himself. Here is the thing I cannot put on a bench and cannot say to a man who has just had a measure taken from his sister: the figure that goes off a household in this yard is not the figure read over the basket. I have never seen the other written. That is how I know it is not written. I have held my tongue on it for nine years and it has grown a weight in the mouth like a stone a child carries without being told why.

\subsection*{The counting song}

\emph{Sung low over the bench, to the iron, never to a person. The second verse is the one Nessa’s mother taught us and Nessa has written it back under the line I rubbed out.}

\begin{quote}\itshape Iron comes down and the warm goes up,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the tube takes six and the slate takes none;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape nine on the bench and two in the house,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the count keeps what the clerk left out.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Four for the kiln and a fifth not heard,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape grey in the corner and grey at the cuff;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape a widow’s clay at the opening touched,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and nothing entered and nothing enough.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Write it in charcoal, write it on oil,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the barge takes it down when the river will;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape what came from the mountain goes back to the cold,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the hand that mends it is paid in a loaf.\end{quote}

I have mended the Vail kiln irons for four generations of that house. A woman there touches a thumb-length of glazed clay at her throat before the opening and at no other hour, and I have never asked her what it costs to touch. The factor at your end confirms the mark and calls the confirmation a kindness, and a kindness is entered. There is no column for the touch itself. I put no figure against it. On the Last Day the grey in my own corner is left where it lies and burned next morning and called dealt with, the same as everywhere else, and I have never once seen a thing dealt with stay dealt with.

Now the asking, which is what I wrote for. The Keldish iron came down the Rim Road again this month, the bars with the blue bloom on them the potters won’t take a glaze over. A man off that road at the well said a Keldish person states his measure before his name and has the number put on his forearm at thirteen, and that when a man comes back thin they cut the old numbers out and put new ones in. Is that true, or is it a thing travellers say to make a room go quiet? I have no number on my arm. If a man asked me for my measure before my name I would give him his own looking face and be none the worse. Tell me what the quay paid for the last lot of Keld iron and whether the Vhaleni factor is still writing his contracts on paper that rots, because a contract that rots in the damp is a virtue in your town and a folly in mine and I have never been able to keep the two things in one hand at once.

There is a story in this district of a counting room shut up in the last war with the damper closed and the men inside dead of the breath, eighteen leagues east, told twice now at the well as a curiosity with a date. Nobody joins it to any kiln in Low Kiln. I have mended damper irons and never asked what room they came out of, and I am not asking you now. Only: if the old man who keeps the quay’s chains was the one who made the iron of that room, ask him whether a damper shuts from the inside. Ask it of the iron and not of him, the way you ask a pot. He will tell you a thing about a room and not know he has told it.

You kept the tally after our mother and you keep it in a hand I can read at a glance even when the salt has got at it. We have never once put the other’s name into an account, and I would sooner burn this sheet than have a clerk at the factor’s table enter the two of us as current. What is said downriver does not come back upriver in the same words. If it does, I will know it was carried by a man who had been paid to carry it, and I will not send another.

Harn, at the smithy, the last tend of Silt, Y.H. 813.

\subsection*{In the margin, in a second hand, small and set close to the writing}

The tend before was nine too, not eleven. You counted the two you mended for the thane’s house a tend earlier and carried them into the last one because the notches ran together on the bench. A notch that runs into another notch is a notch a man has counted wrong, which is the whole of our trade. I have struck the eleven through and put nine under it in your own iron-gall, so that you cannot say a stranger wrote it.

A man off the Rim Road was at the quay on Tenthday with the numbers on his forearm and gave his measure before his name to the factor’s clerk, who wrote it down and did not look at his face. It is true, then. I have not asked him what the numbers were and he has not asked me what I keep in the tin. Do not ask the old man about the damper. I asked him about a chain instead and he told me a room shuts from whichever side has the more to lose by it. That is the whole answer and it is not an answer. Put it where you put the missing fifth breath and leave both alone.

\begin{quote}\itshape The clerk takes the verb, the quay takes the mark,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the tube takes the warm and the slate takes none;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape a notch is a place where the count stood still,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and a count that stands still is not yet done.\end{quote}

I have not written a verse since our mother died and I would not begin on a wet sheet. You have written one in charcoal, which does not keep, and I have set mine under it in iron-gall, which does. That is the difference between the two sides of this river and I have never known how to say it in a room.

\subsection*{What the clerk did}

A clerk of the factor’s house borrowed the sheet on the morning after it came up the quay, being a man who cannot leave paper alone. He writes in the neat upright hand they teach at the College, with the verbs taken out and everything in the passive. Against the barrow iron he set \emph{one mark, current}. Where Harn wrote \emph{the tube took six measures from a neighbour} he set \emph{six measures banked} above it, and the neighbour went out of the sentence as though a neighbour were a thing a man could carry off in a cuff. Against the count in wool he wrote \emph{vacancy}, and against the closing of the room he wrote \emph{not entered}, which is the Court’s own art in a small space. He put a round figure where Harn had put none, and the figure has outlasted the notches it was meant to explain.

I have put the verbs back underneath where I could still read them. He takes them out because a thing always true has no need of verbs. We put them in because a man at a bench at three in the morning wants to know which hand to hold the iron with. I have left his figure standing on the back, where it belongs, and the nine notches on the front, where nobody has asked for them.

\subsection*{At the foot, in a hand nobody has claimed}

\begin{quote}\itshape The smith mends the mouth that eats the house. He counts the mouths and does not name them. The tube has no note of its own; a man has one, and this district is full of notes nobody taps.\end{quote}

I asked the old chain-man, a dipper come up from Vhal with salt at his wrists, and a man who keeps the factor’s tally, and had three answers and no hand, as we have had before. I have left the line where it was written. The sheet goes back in the tin among the iron tallies. When the barge goes upriver in Ember I will send it back with the verbs still in it, and you will take them out again if you have a mind to, and neither of us will call it an account.

\clearpage\phantomsection\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{The Kingdom of Cold Iron, Being the Road-Book of Garl, a Potter of Nine Pots, Who Took a Cart of Coarse Bowls up the Rim Road to Keld Keep in the Thin Year and Came Back with Two Iron Clamps, a Warm-Stone Gone Cold, and a Figure on a Slate That Was Not the One He Gave; with the Reckoning of the Road, the Manner of the Weigh, the Song of the Descent, the Cup Nobody Takes, Two Borrowed Corrections, and a Line at the Foot Nobody Will Own}
\CRsheetheading{The Kingdom of Cold Iron, Being the Road-Book of Garl, a Potter of Nine Pots, Who Took a Cart of Coarse Bowls up the Rim Road to Keld Keep in the Thin Year and Came Back with Two Iron Clamps, a Warm-Stone Gone Cold, and a Figure on a Slate That Was Not the One He Gave; with the Reckoning of the Road, the Manner of the Weigh, the Song of the Descent, the Cup Nobody Takes, Two Borrowed Corrections, and a Line at the Foot Nobody Will Own}
{\centering\FellFont\itshape\footnotesize\color{faded} A potter’s road-book, set down first in charcoal on the backs of spoiled pot-warrants at the mouth of the shaft and copied at Greybank onto the back of a clay-and-tile docket voided by the Long Cold; the days in the potter’s own hand, the prices in a sloped tally hand, the sayings of the Keep kept in the hearing and not translated, the verbs put back under every borrowed correction, and one line at the foot in a hand that has never come forward · Written in Ash and Stone of Y.H. 812, the Thin Year of the Long Cold, at Keld Keep and again at Nine Pots, by Garl, a potter of the rival kiln hamlet eight leagues west of Sill, who took nine coarse bowls and a letter up the Rim Road to trade for iron and came back in Stone with four bowls whole, two in pieces, two iron clamps, a warm-stone that had kept a fire and had now gone cold, and a figure on a slate; carried down the Rim Road in Ilmen of Y.H. 813 and copied at Greybank onto the back of a voided docket. It survives folded into a strip of well-worn harness leather: coal smut worked into the head, iron-red from the mine-reeve’s checking point at the second corner, a chip of Ferr lead in one gutter and a bead of Ninth Gallery lead shut in the fold which are not the same lead and have never been joined, a warm-stone shaving gone cold in the fourth leaf, a frost-feather pressed flat that was gone by noon, a tallow print at the head, a square of bare paper where a word was scraped away with a knife-point, a grey Ash print along the outer fold which the writer did not make and has not swept, a Court survey-clerk’s correction in narrow upright Ledgerhand, and a line at the foot in a hand nobody will own\par}\medskip
I throw pots. That is the whole of what I am, and I went up the Rim Road because a man who throws pots is always short of iron. I took nine coarse bowls and a letter from the factor at Greybank. Four came back whole. Two came back in pieces. Three I sold at the Keep for less than the cord they were tied with, and the cart came home lighter than it went and heavier by a thing I have never entered.

The mountain is a kiln with the door shut. I have said that to nobody, because a man who says it in Keld is taken for a spy and a man who says it in Nine Pots is taken for a fool. Put a fire under clay and it holds. Put a fire under stone and it keeps. The Keldish have a word for the keeping and no word for the heat, which tells you which of the two they have learned to trust.

\subsection*{The road, and what it took}

Nine Pots stands eight leagues west of Sill, and the Rim Road passes north of it at the Ferr ford, so a man can sleep at Stonemouth with his pots unbroken if he wraps each in straw and does not let the ass choose the ford. I let the ass choose. One bowl went in the Ferr and came up in three pieces the colour of the water, blue-grey off the old working, and I entered it at Stonemouth and not again, because a bowl that goes into the Ferr does not come home, and a bowl that comes home in pieces has cost the journey its only honest figure.

We made the Keep in nine days up and seven down, and the seven were colder, which I did not expect and have not found a clerk who will enter. I carried a warm-stone in my coat on the advice of a lime-man who had been up twice and come back with all his fingers. It cost six marks, which is a great deal of pots. He told me the price and not the debt, which is the manner of that country. It kept my hand warm on the climb and was cold the morning I got home.

\subsection*{What the road took, and what it gave}

\emph{What I entered at Nine Pots, what stood at the Keep, and what I wrote on the back of the docket at Greybank, where the factor’s man puts a figure against a thing whether or not the thing has a figure in it.}

Article — Entered at Nine Pots — Given at Keld Keep — What I set on the back\par

Coarse bowl, straw-wrapped — nine, at four bits — three sold, four whole, two broken — A bowl that breaks has no price and still cost the road.\par

Iron clamp, small — — — 1 bit and a favour — The favour is not current. I have entered it anyway.\par

Iron clamp, for the wheel-shed — — — 2 marks at the Keep, 2 marks again at Greybank — The second was for the road. The road has no slate of its own.\par

Warm-stone, a palm’s length — — — 6 marks — Sold, not lent. Cold by the seventh day home.\par

Lead, a blue-grey chip — — — given, not sold — Off the Ferr, not out of the Ninth Gallery. I have kept the two apart.\par

A number, from a Vorr — — — 1 bit — The numbers are correct. I have not entered what it means.\par

Twelve bits to a silver mark and twenty to a crown, if you can find a crown in Keld, which I could not. The Court books in embers and tells a man an ember is worth five marks. Nobody has ever exchanged one, but the figure travels faster than the coin, which is the whole art of that house.

\subsection*{The weigh, or the number before the name}

At the Warden’s hall I gave my name, and the clerk looked at me until I understood I had begun wrongly. He said nothing. A man beside me said, “State what you hold, then say who you are,” in the manner of a man repeating something he has said to fools before. I went back to the foot of the post and came again with two-and-forty, which is what I judge I carry, and the clerk wrote the figure first and asked the name second, as though a name were a thing a man might keep back and sell later.

A name is a thing a man can change at the next well, the beside-man told me, and it is the only explanation I was given on the whole road that I could carry home. The number goes down the shaft with a man. The name stays in the room where he said it.

The mine-reeve checked me in red. He set his point where I had given two-and-forty, drew a stroke through it and wrote the same two-and-forty above, which is how a clerk tells you he has found no lie without saying anything a man can thank him for. The red is at the second corner of this leaf now, and I have not wiped it off and have not entered it.

\subsection*{What is sold above ground}

Iron is common in Keld and dear in Grath, and the difference is the price of the road, which the road itself will never enter. A good axe is half a mark up there and two at Stonemouth, and a man who carries one down is paid for the carrying and not for the iron.

Warm-stone is sold and is not lent, said twice to me by two men who had no reason to agree. A thing that can be lent has a place in somebody’s account; a thing sold is paid for, which is cleaner. The shavings go by the half-mark, and a potter from Nine Pots will buy a shaving before a stone, because a shaving will keep a cup warm through one night.

There is a Vorr at the weigh who sells numbers. I bought one for a bit and asked what it was for. He said the numbers were correct, and would not say it twice.

\subsection*{The mouth, and the boy going down}

The Descent is at thirteen. I stood at the mouth with the old women who count and watched a boy go down with a number cut into his arm and a warm-stone put into his hand after the knife. His mother said nothing. One of the old women said the last part of a saying with him, and the boy said the first part before he went down and the women said the second, and nobody explained it to me, and I did not ask.

Two go down and the count comes two. That is what they say at the mouth, and it is not a promise that two come up. It is a promise that the count will be made. I have written it as it was said, with the thing that is not a promise standing in the middle of the sentence, which is where the Keldish put their mercies.

A man at the mouth had two sets of numbers in one arm, the later cut deeper. The mine-reeve entered the later and left the earlier standing in the skin, and told me both stood. A man who comes back thin has the old numbers cut out and new ones put in, which is a kindness done with a knife and entered as a correction.

I asked if I might go down. They said a lowlander goes down as tribute or as a spy, and often as both, and I was neither, so I stood and counted the boys. What I know of the First Seam is told to me, not seen.

The dead are walled into the mine facing the deep seam, and the surveyors add numbers to a slate nobody reads aloud. They do not fetch them back and do not say they have. The mountain keeps its own, which costs less than a kindness. There is a cup at the end of the Duelling Floor that nobody takes, set for a man whose number was changed twice. I did not see the cup.

\subsection*{The song said at the mouth}

\emph{Taken down from the old women who count, said once to the boy going down and once to the ground after he has gone. The second part is said with a line left out.}

\begin{quote}\itshape One for the arm and one for the stone,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape one for the pair that goes down together;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the knife goes in and the warm goes home,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the dark keeps what the mother never entered.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Hold the rail, it is iron and it takes;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape hold the stone, it is sold, not lent;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape count them going and count them back.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Two go down and the count comes two;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the figure stands though the arm may not;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the mountain keeps what the mountain took,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the slate writes once what the mother forgot.\end{quote}

The fourth line of the second part is left out. I have set the space where it should stand and have not filled it, though I know what word would go there. A song that tells a boy what the count is for is a song he cannot carry down with him.

\subsection*{The Sweating, and what they reckon a life at}

In the deep seams the rock sweats and the Warm comes up through the stone in a flood, and the only warning is the smell of hot lead. I did not smell it. I have set that down first so that no reader thinks I have been where I have not. A shift-man at the mouth told me he had smelt it once and come up, and that men who smelt it twice did not come up, and then asked if I had a stone.

Below the floor they work the stone with under-vessed slaves, condemned men and bought breath, and reckon a life at eleven months, a year with the month of the buying taken off. A man who sells a life by the month will tell you the months and not the month that is missing, which is the same trick as the price of a warm-stone.

The Keldish claim the true Hearth lies under their mountain and that the Court’s fire is a candle lit from it. A surveyor come up from the shaft, with drink in him and no officer in the room, told me the rim-seam shows repairs laid one over another and that the oldest are not stone and not clay, and then turned his slate face down. The Keldish call those repairs Ash. He said the Court’s copy has another word and that I would not be shown it, which I have set down as heard and not as known.

\subsection*{What the borrowed hands did}

A Court survey-clerk at Greybank borrowed these leaves on a market morning. He writes upright and narrow and takes the verbs out as though a verb were a thing a man could carry off in a cuff.

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item Against \emph{I gave my name and was sent back to the foot of the post} he wrote \emph{the person was identified after the measure was declared}, underlined twice.

\item Against \emph{two go down and the count comes two} he wrote \emph{two persons entered the shaft and two were recorded}, which says nothing about the coming up.

\item Against \emph{they shut the Cold Pass in seven hundred forty-one} he wrote \emph{the frontier was closed by treaty in seven hundred forty-seven}, which is the agreement and not the shutting, and has a date a clerk can copy.

\item Against \emph{the mountain keeps its own} he wrote \emph{interment underground; no return entered}, which leaves the mountain out and keeps the entry in.

\end{itemize}

The mine-reeve’s red stroke stands at the second corner. It is a check and not a correction. He found the figure I gave stood, and I have kept his mark where it fell, which is more than I can say of the factor’s marks.

I have left his readings above mine everywhere. A clerk who takes the doer out leaves the mountain standing by itself, with nobody kept and no count in it to argue with. I put the doer back because a potter who carried nine bowls up a road wants to know whose hands they were in when they broke.

\subsection*{At the head and in the gutter}

The coal at the head is mine, off the sleeve I wipe the pots with; no wet cloth takes it out. The iron-red at the second corner is the mine-reeve’s point. The chip in the gutter is Ferr lead, off the bowl that went in the ford; the bead in the fold came from the Ninth Gallery. I have never joined the two, because they are two different debts, and a man who joins them has drawn a conclusion, which I have no licence to draw. The shaving held its heat one night on the stone floor and is cold now, which is the order of things up there. The frost-feather lay on the well lip and was gone before I folded the leaf; the yard at home calls that weather and the Keldish call it a map of the leak. The tallow print is my own lamp set too near the leaf. The square of bare paper is the word I scraped away and put nothing in its place. The grey along the outer fold is not mine and not the clerk’s. I have not swept it. There is no Last Day above this Keep.

\subsection*{At the foot, in a hand nobody will own}

\begin{quote}\itshape The cart went up with nine and came back with four;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the stone went in warm and came home cold;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the figure stood and the name went nowhere,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the count came two where the cup stood still.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Ask the mouth what it counted.\end{quote}

I asked the beside-man at the Warden’s hall, a woman who counts at the mouth, and a Vorr who sells numbers, and had three answers and no hand. I have left the line where it was written. Tomorrow I take the four bowls that came back whole down to Stonemouth and sell them for what they fetch, and when the weigh-clerk asks me what I carry I shall say four and not my name, which is a habit I have brought home from a country that does not care what a man calls himself.

\clearpage\phantomsection\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{The Cold Place in the Wall, Being a Soldier’s Field Notes on the Seam-Serpent of the First Seam Beneath Keld Keep; with the Song as It Is Not Sung, the Deep Tally, a Survey-Clerk’s Ruling in Ledgerhand, a Vorr’s Answer, and One Line at the Foot Nobody Will Own}
\CRsheetheading{The Cold Place in the Wall, Being a Soldier’s Field Notes on the Seam-Serpent of the First Seam Beneath Keld Keep; with the Song as It Is Not Sung, the Deep Tally, a Survey-Clerk’s Ruling in Ledgerhand, a Vorr’s Answer, and One Line at the Foot Nobody Will Own}
{\centering\FellFont\itshape\footnotesize\color{faded} A soldier’s field book on one beast, set down as the record of a watch kept over the deep shaft and not as natural philosophy; the sayings in the hard Keldish speech with the endings struck off, the watch-song with the number left as it is not spoken, the tally in charcoal on the backs of spoiled rim-seam rubbings, one ruling in the narrow upright Ledgerhand of a Court survey-clerk, one line in the broad slow hand of a Vorr come up from the Stones, and one line at the foot in a hand nobody will own · Written in Bone and Stone of Y.H. 812, the Thin Year of the Long Cold, by Dren, a man of the Warden’s watch set over the shaft mouth at Keld Keep, who states his number before his name and has never gone down the Descent; set down at the end of watches in the lamp-room at the head, first on the backs of rim-seam rubbings spoiled by wet slate and then on three leaves of rough survey paper sewn with wire into a board cover gone soft at the seam, carried down the Rim Road in Ilmen of Y.H. 813 with a survey party’s clamps and copied at Greybank onto the back of a voided weigh-slip. It survives with coal smut ground into the head off the writer’s own sleeve, iron-red at the second corner off the mine-reeve’s checking point, a smear of hot lead at the fold that has burnt one word clean through, a frost-feather pressed flat between the second and third leaves which was gone by noon, a warm-stone shaving gone cold shut in the fourth fold, a ring where a cup of small ale stood from the first watch to the last, a grey Ash print along the outer fold which the writer did not make and has not swept, one ruling in the narrow upright hand of a Court survey-clerk, one line in the broad slow hand of a Vorr, and the line at the foot\par}\medskip
I keep the deep watch at the shaft mouth and set down what the wall does when no man stands over it. I have never gone down the Descent. My number is cut in my arm and I state it before my name because that is the order here and the dark does not care what a man calls himself. What follows I have put my hand to or stood near. What I have only heard I have set down as heard, with the word standing where I heard it, because a saying said to the stone is one thing and a saying said looking at a man becomes a bargain.

The smut at the head is coal off my own sleeve. A book of the deep that has never been wiped on a cuff was never taken below. I have not knocked it off.

\subsection*{The cold place}

You know it before you see it. Standing at the wall with the lamp held low, you come to a patch of stone that takes the heat out of the back of your hand, and the patch is not where it was at the last watch. It moves along the crack the way a thumb moves along the seam of a cup, slow and with no haste, and the surveyors enter the moving as a change in the numbers. I have laid my palm on a place that gave back nothing and on a place a hand’s breadth off that gave back the lamp’s warmth, and the two are not the same stone. The Keldish call the first a cold place and say no more than that over it. To say more gives a thing a place in a man’s mouth, and a thing in a man’s mouth will be asked about by somebody with a slate.

It keeps to the wall and not the floor. I have never found it crossing the open stones of the Duelling Floor, and men who work the face below the Ninth say the same of that gallery. It goes where the crack goes. A man who follows it with a lamp finds himself at a wall and then at another wall, and the cold place is behind him, and he has carried up nothing he can set on a slate. One of the surveyors told me he had entered its passing three times in a tend and could not have said, on any of the three, which way it had gone. He said this standing at the mouth, which is a dry place and a place to say anything.

It does not hurry and it does not turn aside for iron. I have held a clamp against the stone where a cold place lay and left it there the length of a watch, and the clamp went cold and the cold place was where it had been. Cold iron takes, as the saying goes. Here it takes from the iron and not from the thing, which is a reversal of the order a man learns above ground and one I have not made a lesson of.

\subsection*{The touch}

A miner touched by the seam comes up thin. That is the whole of what I have seen. He does not fall and he does not cry out. In the afternoon his fingers are the colour of milk that has stood two days, and by the end of the shift the warm has gone out of him the way water goes out of a jug left in the cold, and he asks for the stone and not for the physician. I watched a Held man, one who carried three times my number and could swing a clamp the length of a shift, go up the rope after a touch at the face and be thin by the time his boots came to the head. The rope did as much as the thing in the wall. He said nothing, and there is no word in Keldish for what had been done to him and none in Grathic that a man will use above ground.

They say a man touched twice will not come up a third time. I have seen one man with the grey in him twice; he came up both times and went down on the third and did not. I have set the saying and the two together and drawn no line between them. Three men are not a rule and the mountain keeps no second figure. There is a cup at the end of the Floor that nobody takes, and a man may stand beside it all the length of a watch and no one will tell him whose it was. I have not written a name beside that cup and I have never asked.

\subsection*{The song}

\emph{Sung going down at the first watch, not coming up. The number is left as it is not spoken, and every man sings it that way on purpose, because a song that gives the cold a figure is a song a man can carry up and enter. I have set it down as it is sung, with the number where it was not said.}

\begin{quote}\itshape One for the lamp and one for the rail,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape one for the arm that the dark will read;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape it goes in the wall where the crack has been,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the place it was is the place it leaves.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Count to the wall and do not say the sum ---\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the number stands where the figure stood;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape count them going and count them back,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and one for the hand that did not close.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape It takes through the stone and gives no sign,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape it leaves a man with the colour of milk;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the Vorr look up and the numbers are right,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and nobody asks what the numbers tell.\end{quote}

A man going down wants to know where the cold will be. The song tells him he will not know, which is a kindness of the same order as the post at the pass: it stands and says nothing, and a man who walks past it has been told. The last line of the third part is the old line. We sing \emph{tell} where the old word was something else, and I have not set the old word down. A song that gives the cold an appetite is a song a man cannot carry home and set by his fire.

\subsection*{The tally}

These are the watches I kept a true account of. There were others I did not write because the lamp was low, and one I did not write because I had been touched and had forgotten which watch it was. I have set down both sorts as they stand. The last column is the surveyor’s, not mine. I counted what went thin; he counted what the wall gave up.

Watch — Where — Cold place — Men thin — Rim-seam figure — Skin\par

Bone 3 — Face below the Ninth — one; moved a hand’s breadth in a watch — none — 41 to 40 — none\par

Bone 11 — Wall off the survey room — one; at the old repair — one; fingers milk-grey, came up — 40 to 40 — none\par

Bone 19 — Deep face, no name — two; one behind the lamp — two; one came up thin, one did not — 38 to 37 — none; hot lead in the air, shift stopped\par

Stone 2 — Along the under-seam — one; under the fifth repair — one; Held man, thin by the rope — 37 to 37 — a shred in the gutter\par

Stone 14 — Wall past the walling-in — one; gone by morning — one; forgot his number, kept his name — 37 to 36 — none\par

Stone 27 — New ground beyond the Ninth — not found — one; touched by the third watch — 36 to 36 — none; I did not write the first watch\par

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{In the narrow upright hand of a Court survey-clerk, borrowed against the leaf at the mouth:} Serpent not a vessel. No deduction arises. Thinness of miners: not entered. Rim-seam figure entered as survey correction. Shed skin: no value entered, being unpriced. Account stands.\end{quote}

I have left his hand standing. He has set \emph{not entered} over the man who did not come up and \emph{no value entered} over the skin, which is the neatest piece of work I have seen out of a Court hand. A survey figure can be carried up and entered and a man who went thin at the face cannot, so there is a kind of justice in it, if the figure is held by the right cuff. I have written the man and the skin underneath in charcoal, where his column cannot reach, and put the figure back where it was not said.

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{In the broad slow hand of a Vorr come up from the Stones, written in the lower margin and not above:} The numbers are correct.\end{quote}

He was asked what the change in the figure meant. He said it twice and turned the slate face down. In Keld that is an answer a man can carry away and learn nothing from, and the sort that keeps. I have not joined his line to the clerk’s, and there is a finger’s width between them where neither can reach the other.

\subsection*{The skin}
