Once in the Ninth a skin is found in the gutter of the face, thin as the skin inside a cup and longer than a man’s arm. They say it is the oldest repair material in the seam and that nobody will name it. I have held a shred of one in the lamp-room and put my knuckle through it and found it whole on the other side, which is a thing I cannot explain and have not tried to. I have shut the shred into the fourth fold and set no figure against it.

That is not a kindness on my part. A thing nobody names is a thing no clerk can tax, which is a mercy of a kind and costs the Court nothing, being a thing it has never seen. The Vorr will look at the skin and say the numbers are correct and ask for nothing, and a Vorr who asks for nothing is not a poor man, being a man who has no use for what he would be given. I do not know which of those two facts is the stranger and I have set them down side by side with a finger between.

\subsection*{What the hearths say}

They say it is the First Breaking still moving in the crack, the repair coming undone under the world and going on undoing itself while men cut stone above it. There are songs in Keld with a name in them and a wrong done at the making. I have heard them and I have no quarrel with a song. But I have put my hand on the wall where a cold place lay and on the wall a spear-cast off, and I have watched a place move off a man and settle on another man, and I have followed it to a wall and lost it there. If it is the Breaking still moving, then it moves in particular places and the particular place is the whole of what I can see. What it wants there I have left where I found it.

I think it drinks what the wall loses. I have written that sentence once and have not crossed it out and have not written it a second time, because it is the kind of sentence that gets a man called a natural philosopher, and natural philosophers are not set over the deep watch with a lamp and a length of cord. What it gives in exchange I have not seen, and I have asked no man to look for it.

\subsection*{At the head and in the margins}

The coal at the head is mine and came off the sleeve I wipe the lamp with; it goes into the grain and no wet cuff takes it out. The iron-red at the second corner came off the mine-reeve’s point while he checked a man who had given a figure that would not hold; he did not look at me and I did not look at the man. The hot lead at the fold came off a sample wrapped in the same paper on Bone 19 and has burnt the word \emph{seam} clean through; I have not written the word back in, because a hole in that word is the honest state of it. The feather between the second and third leaves was on the wall below the survey room after a warm night and was gone by the time I found the leaf to put it in. The shaving in the fourth fold kept its heat through one watch on the stone floor and is cold now, which is the order of things here. The ring is off a cup that stood from the first watch to the last and was drunk by neither of us, which is how small ale is drunk in Keld when there is a thing to say and no proper word for it. The grey along the outer fold is not mine and not the Court’s, and I have not swept it. There is no Last Day above the shaft mouth, and below there is less.

\subsection*{At the foot, in a hand nobody will own}

\begin{quote}\itshape It does not take the man. It takes the place the man was keeping.\end{quote}

I asked a miner who had been touched, a surveyor come up from the stones, a Vorr, and a clerk of the factor at Greybank, and had four answerings and no hand. I have left the line where it was written. The leaves go back into the board cover and the cover under the lamp, and my number is called at the mouth whether the arm that carried it came up or not.

There is a cold place beyond the Ninth that I have not walked to, where the paper sweats and the figure has not been changed by any hand. Next Stone I will go in with the lamp shut and a coil of cord and stand there the length of a watch, and if the wall gives back warmth where no man has stood and the numbers move without a hand to move them, I will set that down too, in charcoal, with the verb standing as it happened and no figure at the end of the row.

\clearpage\phantomsection\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{The Collector’s Day-Book, Being the Measures Drawn in Sill and the Clay Towns from the Last Market of Stone in Y.H. 812 through the Five to the Opening of the Slates in Y.H. 813, with the Embers, the Deduction, and the Note the Vessel Gave}
\CRsheetheading{The Collector’s Day-Book, Being the Measures Drawn in Sill and the Clay Towns from the Last Market of Stone in Y.H. 812 through the Five to the Opening of the Slates in Y.H. 813, with the Embers, the Deduction, and the Note the Vessel Gave}
{\centering\FellFont\itshape\footnotesize\color{faded} A page from an officer’s own pocket day-book; figures in Ledgerhand copied from the slate, the remarks in the hand that held the cold iron tube, a column of notes struck out by the College and drawn back by the officer, one figure struck and set above in a borrowed hand, and a line at the foot in a hand nobody will own · Written on the road between Sill and Greybank in the last tend of Stone, Y.H. 812, the Thin Year, through the Five and into Ilmen 1, Y.H. 813, and copied forward at the Opening of the Slates; carried in an oiled-paper wrap in the officer’s coat, beside the tube in its wool sleeve. It survives with grey at the head of the ember column, iron filings worked into the gutter from the tube’s wrap, a tallow thumb at the foot, a streak of bone-pale slip, a green bead of lead glaze in the lower corner, a damp tide-line from the Waiting Room, a small square of bare paper where a word was scraped away, two corrections in the narrow upright hand of a clerk of the College, and one line at the foot nobody will own.\par}\medskip
I draw the measure. The clerk at Greybank sets the figure down; I hold the tube. There is a difference between the two, and it is not the difference the College would have you believe, which is the difference between a taking and a draw. A taking and a draw are the same heat going the same way. The slate is the difference, and the slate is a piece of stone with a neat hand on it.

This book goes in my coat under oiled paper, and the tube goes beside it in a sleeve of wool. When I hold the leaf still in the draught under a door my fingers leave grey on it. I have washed them. The grey is the trade, and the trade is the only kin I have: no house, no name but the slate-name upon the roll, and a cuff that has gone soft from washing. I do not set that name on this leaf. A name written in a book that may be read by a woman whose house I have entered is a name that can be called back to her door, and I have called at enough doors.

What follows is one leaf, from the last market of Stone through the Five and into the first tend of Ilmen. Twelve copper bits to a silver mark; twenty marks to a gold crown, a Sere coin that does not stay in Grath. An ember is booked at five marks and no man has exchanged one for the other. A newborn vessel holds twelve to fifteen, a labourer in good case forty to sixty, and one of the Kept three hundred, which is a figure no household can spend. One in twelve is printed on the notice and read twice at the Cross. I have put no second figure beside it in the ember column. I have put it in the column beside that one, which the College struck out.

Draws on this leaf: nine. Lines with no draw in them: two. Figures struck: one. Columns struck: one.

\subsection*{The leaf, as I set it down}

\emph{Figures in Ledgerhand, copied from the slate. The remarks are mine, in the hand that held the tube. The last column is mine also and is not part of the account.}

Day — Vessel, as the slate has it — Embers — Deduction — Banked to — Note — Remark\par

Stone 30 — A widow of the lower town. \emph{Loaf} — 41 — 1 in 12 — Greybank — full — Four loaves baked, three to the levy. Figure read twice, once for those that came late.\par

Stone 30 — Forty of Low Kiln. One slate for the batch, by lot — — — 1 in 12 — Hearthseat — — — Held overnight in the Waiting Room. Birth-names not taken. A barrow of grey went out through the north gate in the afternoon.\par

Kindling — A man of Mud End. \emph{Peat} — 47 — 1 in 12 — Greybank — flat — Year’s first measure, taken before light. Kiln’s breath. The neighbours called it merciful.\par

Kindling — A child three days returned, Low Kiln. \emph{Second} — 13, struck to 12 — 1 in 12 — Hearthseat — none — Worse before dusk. Entered as a birth, not a worsening.\par

Weighing — A glaze-room girl, High Kiln. \emph{Sweet} — 38 — 1 in 12 — Greybank — nearly full — Pale line at the gum. Asked after her girl; not entered.\par

the Long Night — A clay-bound hand of the terraces. \emph{Seven} — 44 — 1 in 12 — Greybank — full — Consent withheld. Clip-held by the wrist until consent entered. Draw made by lamp; no fire after dusk.\par

the Remembering — One of the Kept, in passing. No slate-name — 300 — none — none — none — Asked after the weather. Pity entered, which has no column.\par

the Last Day — A house of the terraces, disputed. \emph{Shoulder} — 52 — 1 in 12 — — — flat — Thumb wiped twice before touching nothing. Figure asked for, then not wanted. Left standing.\par

Ilmen 1 — A thrower of the low yard. \emph{Nineteen} — 41 — 1 in 12 — Greybank — full — First entry of the new roll. Earlier figure struck; no reason entered.\par

Ilmen 10 — A man of the Weir. \emph{Eel} — 52 — 1 in 12 — Greybank — full — Drawn before light. Pale round place left on the arm. The bell went four, four and a gap; nobody crossed.\par

Ilmen 10 — No vessel drawn. A clerk set at the Fishstairs — — — — — — — — — Cuff grey from washing; slate held to the forearm; hand to slate before eyes to the stalls. I asked whose measure it was. Nobody had called one. Not one of ours.\par

\subsection*{The note column}

Before the tube I set a knuckle on the wall or the rim of the cup. A whole vessel answers full. One cracked through answers flat, a small dead sound that stops at the surface. A vessel with air under the note answers nearly full, and the yards have no word for it, so I have set down the phrase as I heard it, which is not Grathic and will not be read at a Weighing. A vessel turned toward in expectation may give nothing at all; I have entered that as \emph{none} and not as a nought, because a nought is a figure and a silence is not.

The kiln-masters of Sill know the full note and keep it to themselves, which is their right and their trade. I know it because I have stood in forty rooms where a pot was set down and the whole house went on talking over the sound of it. A collector who cannot hear a vessel is a man who draws blind. He will still bring back his figure. The figure will still be entered. That is the trouble with figures.

On Weighing I wrote \emph{nearly full} for the girl of the glaze room, and the clerk borrowed the leaf and struck the whole column out. He wrote \emph{No such column} above it in his narrow upright hand. I have drawn the column back underneath and left his words standing over it. He had to look at every row before he could write that there were none worth entering, and I watched him do it. A note is not a figure and cannot be added, which is why he struck it, and a figure cannot hear a vessel, which is why I put it back.

\subsection*{The grey}

The grey at the head of the ember column came off my own fingers while I gave the figure to the clerk at Greybank on a market morning. It is the colour of skimmed milk gone off. It goes in under the nails first and comes up into the creases by the second year, and after that a man may wash until the water freezes and nothing changes. The filings in the gutter came out of the wool sleeve the tube rides in; there is always a little iron in the fold, and it has never once drawn the warmth out of the paper, which is a mercy of a kind and the only one in this book.

The tallow thumb at the foot is mine, from holding the lamp low while I wrote in a room where somebody was saying something I wanted the end of. The streak of slip came off a thrower’s forearms when she set her slate beside mine to wait for a figure. The green bead is lead glaze and not slip; a girl leaned over to see the writing with the sweetness still at her mouth, touched the leaf, said nothing, and went back to her terrace. I have not washed it off. The tide-line along the foot came from the Waiting Room, where the collected are kept overnight before banking and the damp gets into everything left on a bench. The bare square in the lower margin is where I scraped a word away with a knife and put no other in its place. I have not written the word back, and I have not forgotten it.

On the Last Day they sweep the corners of houses and burn what they find in the morning and call it dealt with. There is no Last Day for a coat.

\subsection*{What the two borrowed hands did}

The clerk from the College struck the figure of thirteen against the child on Kindling and set twelve above it, saying a vessel three days returned cannot hold thirteen after the draw. Both stand. I have asked which is right and neither of them has told me, and I have stopped asking, because an officer who asks after a correction is an officer who will soon be making one.

He struck a verb also. Where I wrote \emph{I drew} he set \emph{the measure was drawn} above, and underneath that he set \emph{the warmth was entered}, which is further from the bed than the first. I have put \emph{I drew} back beneath both. A sentence with nobody in it is a sentence no woman can ask about, and women ask about these draws in the end, always at the door, always after the tube is put away.

The other hand is not the College’s. It is a tall leaning hand from Greybank, and against \emph{the neighbours called it merciful} it wrote \emph{the draw was lawful} and underlined the word twice. Both stand. Lawful is true and does not mention a man on a bed in Mud End who was already gone when I came through the door. Merciful is what the neighbours said, and I set it down because it was said in my hearing and there is no column for what a room says after the tube comes out.

\subsection*{The verse the collectors carry up the yard}

\emph{Called under the breath going up the Clay Yard, never while the tube is out, and never twice in one house.}

\begin{quote}\itshape Cold iron, warm arm,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape a hiss and a pale round ring;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the figure goes up and the figure goes down\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the note stays where it came in.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape One in twelve, says the notice, read twice at the Cross;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape four and four and a place where the fifth should be;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape I carry the tube and the book in my coat\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the grey goes home ahead of me.\end{quote}

The man who sang this to me would not sing the last line while the factor’s man stood on the quay, which is how I know the last line is the one that matters. I have copied it as it came and put no gloss on it. A collector who explains a song has begun to write a sermon, and sermons get copied.

\subsection*{At the foot, in a hand nobody will own}

\begin{quote}\itshape The figure is read twice. The note is read by nobody. Both were taken from the same vessel on the same morning.\end{quote}

I asked the clerk at Greybank, and a woman who stood at my counter about her house, and a man come down from Slate Row with a cuff gone soft, and had three answers and no hand. I have left the line where it was written.

The book goes back into the oiled paper and the tube into its wool sleeve. Tomorrow the bell will go four, four and a gap with nobody crossing, and a figure will be read twice at the Cross, and I shall set the tube to a way and set the knuckle to the wall first, and write the note down before the College can strike it out. The grey will come off on the next leaf. I have stopped washing it.

\clearpage\phantomsection\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{The Cord Kept Dry, Being a Letter from a Mother at the Quay to Her Daughter on the Eve of Her Marriage, Concerning the Share That Passes Through Women, the Man Come Aboard, the Eight Sacks, and the Knot No Tally-Man Has Counted}
\CRsheetheading{The Cord Kept Dry, Being a Letter from a Mother at the Quay to Her Daughter on the Eve of Her Marriage, Concerning the Share That Passes Through Women, the Man Come Aboard, the Eight Sacks, and the Knot No Tally-Man Has Counted}
{\centering\FellFont\itshape\footnotesize\color{faded} A private letter on the back of a Council tide-draw spoiled by rain, written in charcoal gone over in iron-gall where the salt had got into the grain, folded four times and sewn with eel-sinew into a scrap of oiled sailcloth; carried up the Salt Road in a glass-carrier’s coat to Greybank, answered along the margin in a younger hand, borrowed at the tide-tally house where a Council clerk set a correction on the outer fold in the leaning hand the damp has nearly taken, and kept since in a dry tin among the boat’s share-cords · Written at the Quay in Vhal in the last tend of Grain, Y.H. 813, by Vessa of the Quay, who holds a share in a salt boat through her mother and dips at the pans when the weather turns, to her daughter Luli, who is to be married on the flood to Daro, a man come aboard off the coast road; set down on the back of a tide-draw the Council left out in the rain, answered in the margin at Greybank on the daughter’s way north, corrected on the outer fold at the tide-tally house, and kept folded and sewn in a dry tin among the boat’s share-cords. It survives with a white salt bloom at the head, tar at the second fold, a fibre of wet net-cord pressed across the third crease, a green bead of Glaze Cliffs glass caught in the stitch, a fish-hook nick at the fore-edge, a ring of brine, a grey print along the outer fold that neither woman made and neither has swept, one word eaten away by the damp with the space left standing, and one line at the foot in a hand nobody has claimed\par}\medskip
To Luli, who is to be married on the flood. From Vessa of the Quay, who holds the share through her mother and has never held it through a man.

I write on the back of a Council draw that was left out in the rain. The figures have gone where the Council’s figures go, which is nowhere a man can put his hand on, and what is left is paper enough for a letter. It is not a sheet I would choose. There is no paper at the Quay that is mine, and a letter written on a man’s paper is a letter a man may read if he has a mind to, so I have written the parts that matter in charcoal and gone over them in iron-gall, and the ink beads where the salt has got into the grain. Do not hold this to the fire to read it, as your aunt does with everything. It goes soft and smells of the pans, and a letter that smells of the pans is a letter the whole Quay will want to hear.

You are to be married on the flood. I have no word for a gift and we have a word for a share, so I will put it the way we put everything else: this is not a gift. It is the cord. Your grandmother tied it when she went aboard and carried it nineteen years in a tin kept dry against the practice of the country, and I have kept it dry for nineteen more. A cord kept dry is not a cord kept from use; it is a cord that has not yet been asked. You will be asked on the flood.

Three things, and then a question. Read the three first. A woman who reads the question before the instructions will answer the question and go away thinking the instructions were the courtesy.

The first is the share. It goes through you and not through him. Your mother held it, I hold it, you will hold it. A man who marries into a boat-owning family is come aboard, and his opinion on the boat is counted at half. Half is not none, and I have known men who could bear it and men who could not; the ones who could not were the ones who said \emph{half} loudest at the table. Daro has stood at the rail for two seasons and waited for whoever was speaking to finish before he said anything about the boat. That is not the same as being counted at half. It is the nearest thing to it I have seen in a man come off the coast road, and I have not once said so in a room where he could hear me, and I am not saying so now. This is a letter. It is different.

The second is the knot. It is tied the way our knots are tied, left over right with the tail tucked and a half-turn taken in it that no tally-man has ever counted, because it does not look like a figure. Keep it that way. A contract written on salt-paper in wet weather is no contract at all, which is the virtue of it, and every fortune in this port has turned on that fact at least once. A cord tied in dry weather is still a cord when the paper has gone. I have never entered the cord anywhere and the Council has no word for the thing it holds. Do not teach them one.

The third is the salt. Eight sacks go with you, one for the pan and the others for the house, and the house sacks are the ones to watch, because a sack set down inside a door has a way of becoming a figure before the week is out. If a man from the tally house writes against the sacks, ask him which tide settled it. He will say the figure settled it. Ask him again after the turn. He will have gone. This is not rudeness; it is the whole of our dealings with the tally house and it has kept us fed.

Now the question. When they ask you at the table whose share you hold, will you say your mother’s name or your own? I am not asking which is the true answer. I am asking which one you will say, because I will not be at that table, and a name said at a table is a name that can be written down, and a written name keeps better than a cord does in the rain. Say the one you can say twice.

\subsection*{The shares, as they are kept in the tin, not as they stand on the Council’s paper}

\emph{The first column is the order of the women. The last is what the tally house has entered, which is not the same thing and was never meant to be.}

Who held — How she came by it — What was tied — What stands on paper\par

Your grandmother — Through her mother, before the Council put the boats to contract — A bead of cliff-glass pressed into the knot — vacancy\par

Your mother — Through her mother, in a wet year when the paper went — Left over right, tail tucked — share, one\par

I — Through my mother, and not through my husband — Two half-turns taken where no thumb rests — current\par

You — Not yet. The cord is in the tin and dry — The half-turn your grandmother left in it — —\par

A dash is a place where nothing stood to be entered. It is not a nought, and the difference has kept more than one woman out of the lower room.

\subsection*{The share-song}

\emph{Sung going out on the flood, never at the tally house. The third line is the old line. The girls at the Quay sing it wrong on purpose, because a song that says what a share is worth is a song a man can carry to a table and set down there.}

\begin{quote}\itshape The share goes down and the share comes in,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the cord keeps what the paper spins;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape half for the man who comes aboard,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the whole for the woman who kept the board.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Sea runs against the wind and the moon gets none,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the dipper reads the draw before the sun;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape salt on the sack and salt at the seam,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the knot is the only thing that means what it means.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape We sing the old line wrong and leave it so,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the place where the mother’s name would go;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape count them going and count them back ---\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the cord stays dry and the debt stays black.\end{quote}

I asked a dipper what the third line ought to be and she said it was none of my business and went on with her net. I have left it as the girls sing it.

\subsection*{In the margin, in a younger hand, set close to the writing}

I will say my own. You taught me to keep the count and I am not giving it to a table. Do not tell me again that half is not none; I have heard it since I was nine and I know what it costs.

You have Daro wrong. He stood at the rail because he was waiting for you to finish, not because he knew his place. There is a difference, and you of all people should know it. He has never once said \emph{half} in this house. I would have told you if he had.

When I want to say a thing I cannot write I will name you a tide that has not come, which is the only honest way we have of saying it.

I saw the other cord in the tin. You thought I had not. I have not touched it and will not. Ask me nothing about the half-turn and I will ask you nothing about the bead.

\subsection*{What the clerk did}

A clerk of the tide-tally house borrowed the leaf on a market morning, being a man who cannot leave paper alone. He writes in the leaning hand the damp has nearly taken, so that of his four corrections only two verbs and a figure survive. Where I wrote \emph{I hold the share through my mother and not through my husband}, he set \emph{share passing by women; consideration current} above it, and the two of us went out of the sentence as though a woman were a thing a man could carry off in a cuff. Against the cord he wrote \emph{no instrument}. Against the share-song he wrote \emph{currency not entered}, and against my daughter’s answer, \emph{declarant’s name recorded}, which is the Court’s own art in a small space: she said it, and now it has happened to her.

I have put the verbs back underneath where I could still read them. He takes them out because a thing always true has no need of verbs. We put them in because a woman at a table wants to know which hand to lay the cord with. I have left his figure standing on the outer fold and my daughter’s correction standing over my own, and neither of us has struck the other out.

\subsection*{At the head and in the folds}

The bloom at the head is salt out of the paper and not out of the sea, which is a thing only a person who has kept salt-paper knows the difference of. The tar at the second fold is off the oar I held down while the draw was read and went soft under me; it has taken two words of the first paragraph and made them slow, which is no great loss. The fibre across the third crease is wet net-cord, from the net I was mending when I thought of the question and put the leaf down on it. The green bead caught in the stitch is cliff-glass off the Glaze Cliffs, five leagues along the shore, and a girl pressed it there and said nothing, and I have not taken it out. The nick at the fore-edge is my fish-hook and went through when I folded in a hurry at the going of the light. The ring of brine came from a cup set down while I was telling Luli to eat and she would not. The grey print along the outer fold is not mine and not the Council’s, and I have not swept it. There is no Last Day for a letter and there is no broom in a tin.

\subsection*{At the foot, in a hand nobody has claimed}

\begin{quote}\itshape A share is a thing a woman holds against the water. The water does not ask who paid.\end{quote}

I asked a dipper, a tally clerk, a man come aboard, and a woman who has held a share forty years, and had four answers and no hand, as we have had before. I have left the line where it was written.

The leaf goes back in the tin among the share-cords. On the flood she will be married and the cord will go with her, dry, and nobody at the tally house will know that it has left the country, which is how a thing is kept in Vhalen. The Sallow runs against the wind and is said to follow the Warm rather than the moon, and we have stopped asking it why; a question put to a tide is a question paid for twice. That is the whole of the letter, and it goes on.

\clearpage\phantomsection\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{The Cost of Carrying, Being a Winter Worth-Night at the Heaped Measure in Greybank, with Four Costings Put to the Barley Dish, the Factor’s Clerk’s Figures Entered Over Them, and the Grain in the Crack That Would Not Burn}
\CRsheetheading{The Cost of Carrying, Being a Winter Worth-Night at the Heaped Measure in Greybank, with Four Costings Put to the Barley Dish, the Factor’s Clerk’s Figures Entered Over Them, and the Grain in the Crack That Would Not Burn}
{\centering\FellFont\itshape\footnotesize\color{faded} An ale-keeper’s telling of one night’s contest, set down for the settling of an argument the granary never settled and not for the improvement of the reader; the costings in the words they were spoken, the sayings put to the dish and not to the room, the stake in grains of barley laid in a cracked dish, the tally in charcoal on the back of a grain-warrant voided by the granary’s second count, the factor’s clerk’s figures entered above in narrow upright Ledgerhand, a carter’s gloss in broad charcoal, and one line at the foot in a hand nobody will own · Written in Stone of Y.H. 812, the Thin Year of the Long Cold, at the alehouse called the Heaped Measure on the Clay Road in Greybank, where the road comes in from Sill and turns uphill before noon to the factor’s table; set down by the woman who keeps the house, the fire and the barley dish, on the back of a grain-warrant spoiled by a second count, and copied forward in Ilmen of Y.H. 813 onto the back of a voided carriage-receipt, sewn with wire into a fold of oiled sacking and kept in the tin beside the lamp-wick, where nothing else in this house is kept dry. It survives with a thumb of wet clay at the head, a tallow thumb at the fold, a barley grain shut fast in a crack of the dish pressed into the paper, a press of frozen wool across the first leaf, a dark ring where small ale stood from the first costing to the last, a browned crust gone soft in the gutter, frost raised out of the paper on the climb up the Clay Road, a grey Ash print along the outer fold that nobody will own, the charcoal rubbed thin where the warrant was carried in an apron, one correction in the narrow upright hand of a factor’s clerk, one gloss in the broad charcoal of a carter, and the line at the foot which has never been claimed\par}\medskip
I keep the Heaped Measure on the Clay Road in Greybank, where the clay road comes in from Sill and turns uphill before noon to the factor’s table. The sign is a bowl of barley with the grain piled above the rim. A clerk of the factor came in once and told me a heaped measure is a false measure, which is true in his trade. I told him the sign was a promise and not a measure. He wrote that down too, which is the sort of man he is.

In Stone the frost takes the road and the Ilm goes under its skin, and this town fills with men who cannot get up to the factor and men who cannot get back down to Sill. There is a granary here with a beam and a second count, and a bank with a lower room where people sit between drawing and pouring, and eight leagues of clay between us and the Cross that nobody mends. Of an evening there is nothing to do but ask one another what a thing cost, which is a riddle in this town, because the figure and the cost are two figures and never the same one.

So we play the costing. Each puts a thing he carried through the year and asks what it cost him, and the house says whether the answer serves. It is not a guessing game. The answer is in the room already, and the trick is to say it in one breath without turning it into a figure. The stake is a grain of barley in a dish. At first grey the dish goes to the fire and the grain burns, so that nothing is carried out of this room in a slate. A man who wants that may go uphill before noon and sit with people warmer than himself.

\subsection*{The rules as the house keeps them}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item A costing is put once. Ask for it again and you owe a grain, because the second asking is for your own pleasure and not for the house.

\item Answer in one breath and say it to the dish. Said to a person it becomes an argument, and an argument in Greybank is a debt with no date on it.

\item Four costings are scored. The fifth is kept on the shelf, where a thing may stand a long time without being entered.

\item The judge is the dish. I say whether an answer serves and I do not say why. A reason given is a costing given away for nothing, and the giver can take it up the road and sell it.

\item No slate lies on the table. The factor’s clerk sits at the end of the bench and writes on his knee with the slate turned inward, which he says is not lying on the table. He is the only man who has argued the rule with me and won.

\end{enumerate}

It was the third night of Stone, with frost on the inside of the glass and the road shut behind the door. There were five of us: old Varre who carts lime up from Stonemouth, Tess of the granary beam, a man from the lower room of the bank whom nobody called by a name, the clerk with his slate on his knee, and me behind the bar. The man from the bank held his cup with both hands and had not drunk from it. I have learned not to take that as a sign of anything.

\subsection*{The four that were scored}

The first was put by old Varre, who had come in with lime-white in the seams of his hands and would not sit down until he had put his back to the fire.

\begin{quote}\itshape Up on a back and down on a back,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape counted at the beam, counted at the pot;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the figure goes into the house\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the back goes home.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape What is carried?\end{quote}

“Lime,” Tess said, and that was a true answer and the dish took a grain for it. Varre said nothing until the grain had gone in. Then he said, “A man. There’s lime in every load and a man under every lime, and only one of them is ever entered.” He said that to the fire, not to the dish, so it was not scored. He has said it to the fire every winter I have known him, and the fire has never answered him, and he goes on saying it.

The second was put by Tess, who had been on the beam since before the granary had a second count and knows the difference between what a sack holds and what a sack is called.

\begin{quote}\itshape It comes back to a house that knows the cup\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and does not know the hand;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape two figures go in and one figure comes out,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the difference is fed at the table.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape What came back?\end{quote}

There was a pause in which the man from the bank turned his cup a quarter on the bench and did not lift it. Then he said, “A person,” to the dish, which served. To the clerk he said, “A thin return,” which did not, because a man who has been poured into a cradle and cannot say which house he came out of does not want that sentence said over him at a bar. The clerk wrote it down anyway. I gave the man a grain and he set it on the bench beside his cup and did not put it in his pocket, which is one way of refusing a thing without refusing it.

The third stood to the man from the bank, though he had not asked to play and had not once looked at the dish. Put a question to a man like that and you get the answer he carries, which is often not the one he was asked.

\begin{quote}\itshape I carry a thing I cannot set down\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and cannot say the name of;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape my hands go to it in a room I have not entered;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape it is warm and it is not mine.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape What do I carry?\end{quote}

The clerk wrote before anyone could stop him. \emph{A preference retained from the pooled measure,} he wrote, in the hand that takes the verbs out of everything it touches. It is the name they give it in the lower room and it is a true name and it is not an answer. I told him the question was what the man carried and not what the bank called it. He said a preference was not a thing that could be carried, which is a thing a clerk can say with a straight face while his own two fingers are black with ink. The man looked at the dish at last, and said, “The warm out of a house I never lived in.” I gave him a grain. He took it this time, and held it a moment the way you hold a coal before you put it somewhere safe, and then put it in his sleeve, and I have not seen it since.

The fourth I would not have put, because a costing put by the house is not scored against anybody, but the clerk asked to put one, which was a first in eleven winters. He put his slate a little further onto his knee and did not look at any of us.

\begin{quote}\itshape I carry a figure up the road and bring it back smaller;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape I am paid for the carrying and cannot say what it cost me;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the ink is in two fingers and will not come out.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape What am I?\end{quote}

Nobody answered for a while. Then Tess said, “A clerk,” and the clerk said that was the trade and not the answer. Old Varre, with his back still to the fire, said, “A man that carries a figure all day for a man that never carried it.” The clerk sat with that a moment. Then he said, “There’s no figure for it, which is why I asked,” and I gave him a grain, the first grain ever given out of this dish to the factor’s house. He took it up between finger and thumb as though it were a mark, and put it in his coat, and went away up the hill before morning with it. He has never said what he did with it. I have not asked.

\subsection*{The fifth, which was kept on the shelf}

I put this one myself, standing behind the bar, so it was not scored and no grain went into the dish for it. I have put it every winter for eleven years and I will put it every winter until I can no longer stand.

\begin{quote}\itshape I am counted and then destroyed;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape I am the only measure in this town with no carrying-forward;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape I lodge in a crack and the fire goes over me.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape What am I?\end{quote}

“A grain of barley,” I said to the dish. There is a grain in the crack of this dish that has been there longer than I have kept the house. The fire goes over it every morning and does not find it. I have stopped lifting it out. A cracked dish tells you where it has been, which is more than can be said for the factor’s slate.

\subsection*{The tally, in charcoal on the warrant}

Costing — Put by — What served — Grain\par

The load — old Varre — Tess: lime; the man below it said to the fire — one, paid\par

The cradle — Tess — the man from the bank: a person — one, left on the bench\par

The warm — the man from the bank — the house: the warm out of a house never lived in — one, taken in a sleeve\par

The figure — the factor’s clerk — old Varre: the man under the figure — one, carried up the hill\par

The grain in the crack — the house — the dish — not scored\par

The figure read at the granary that morning was one in twelve, as the notice says, and it went over the four grains with the ale and nobody looked at it twice. There is a pause in that figure the length of a held breath, which the clerk reads past and I do not, but that is not a thing for a costing night.

\subsection*{What the clerk did}

He set the costings down as \emph{queries entered} and the answers as \emph{responses entered}, and put a figure of marks against each of the four, which was more than I had scored, because the dish scores in whether a man sits down again and he does not. Against the fifth he wrote \emph{house question; no entry arising}. Against the burning he wrote \emph{grain destroyed by fire: waste, not a measure}. Against the grain in the crack he put a round nought and wrote \emph{vacancy}.

I have left his hand standing above mine, as a newer repair lies over an older one on a pot. He cannot enter an ending, so he calls a burnt grain waste, and he cannot enter a place, so he calls it vacancy. A nought is a figure. The crack is not. I have set my words underneath and let him carry his figures away, which he is paid to do and does very neatly.

Old Varre pressed a line into the margin in the charcoal he marks his buckets with, in a hand so broad it took the whole gutter.

\begin{quote}\itshape Ask a man that carries a figure all day what his shoulder carries. Then you’ll have two answers and neither of them will agree with the slate.\end{quote}

I have left it where his thumb put it. He did not sign it. He never signs anything.

\subsection*{At the head and in the margins}

The wet clay at the head is mine; I held the warrant down on the bar before I had done with the ledger and did not know I had marked it. It goes into the grain and no damp takes it out, which is why the house signs in clay. The tallow thumb at the fold is off the lamp I turn the leaf by. The barley grain pressed into the crack of the dish came out of the dish itself and not out of my hand; I set the warrant down on the rim and it was there when I lifted it, and I have not prised it loose, because a grain that chooses a crack is not a grain to move. The frozen wool across the first leaf came off the man from the bank, who held the door while the clerk came in and did not let go when he was through. The dark ring is small ale that stood from the first costing to the last and was drunk by nobody; three men have claimed it and one woman has denied it and I have given it to none of them. The browned crust in the gutter is a barley crust set down by Tess and taken away again uneaten, which is how a crust is usually taken in this town. The frost came up out of the paper on the climb from Sill and is the only thing in this house that entered without a hand. The grey along the outer fold came off a cuff that had no business lying where I keep the tin, and I have not swept it. There is no Last Day in a tavern, and nothing here is burnt in the morning and called dealt with, except the barley, which is burnt, and is the whole reason the clerk will not stand behind this bar.

\subsection*{At the foot, in a hand nobody will own}

\begin{quote}\itshape The figure goes up the road. The back comes home.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape The dish keeps the grain that the fire missed.\end{quote}

I asked the clerk, Tess, old Varre and a man come down from the bank, and had four answerings and no hand. I have left the lines where they were written.

The warrant goes back into the tin beside the wick. The grain stays in the crack, which is a place and not a number, and the clerk will come again when the road opens and ask for a costing and write his figures over mine, and I shall put the dish out and burn what is in it at first grey. If he asks me what a grain of barley is worth I shall tell him to ask the fire, which is the answer he took away in his coat and has not brought back.

\clearpage\phantomsection\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{The Count in the Bone, Being the Sayings of the Vorr, Gathered at the Listening Stones and Glossed for a Man Who Wanted Them Translated}
\CRsheetheading{The Count in the Bone, Being the Sayings of the Vorr, Gathered at the Listening Stones and Glossed for a Man Who Wanted Them Translated}
{\centering\FellFont\itshape\footnotesize\color{faded} A keeper of the Keldish survey’s gathering of the sayings, refusals, counting-maxims and death-words of the Vorr, set in Grathic letters on the back of a spoiled rim-seam rubbing because Vorr speech is not written and a notch cut in bone travels worse down a road than a letter; the sayings in the slow long-vowelled Rim speech, the glosses in the writer’s own hand, with a Court survey-clerk’s correction in narrow upright Ledgerhand, one answer in the very large, very slow hand of a Vorr, a clamp-master’s line in charcoal from the Duelling Floor, and a line at the foot in a hand nobody will own · Gathered over three Long Sittings in Bone and Ash of Y.H. 812, the Thin Year, at the Listening Stones five leagues above Keld Keep, by a keeper of the survey who had leave to sit within sight of the stones and was never allowed to touch the stone a Vorr keeps; written on the back of a rim-seam rubbing gone soft with wet slate, sewn with wire into a fold of oiled survey-cloth and carried down the Rim Road in Ilmen of Y.H. 813, where a survey-clerk of the Court’s factor at Greybank corrected it. It survives with grey dust of a blighted seam rubbed into the head, the same dust the Vorr mark their counting-stones with and do not sell, coal smut at the fold, a shaving of warm-stone that kept its heat one night on a stone floor and is cold now, a frost-feather pressed flat which was gone by noon, a bead of Ninth Gallery lead shut in the sewing, a tallow print beside which the doubled last joint of a finger has left its mark, a clamp-scratch across two glosses, a grey Ash print nobody will own, and the line at the foot which has never been claimed\par}\medskip
I keep the survey at Keld Keep, in a room of slate and lead with its door facing the shaft. Five leagues higher there are standing stones older than the Return, and the Vorr sit against them for days and come down with numbers. I have sat within sight of them three seasons and have never been asked to move, which in that country is as near a welcome as a man from below is given. What follows is what they said to the stone while I was near enough to hear.

The manner first, because a saying said wrongly is a different saying. Say them slowly, with the vowels opened and the ends left in the air, once, and to the stone or the ground beside it. Do not say them looking at a Vorr. Said to a man, one of these sentences becomes a question with an answer owed, and there is no sentence here with an answer owed in it. Ask the same thing twice and you will be told the same thing twice, which is not anger but the exactness of a people who give a name once in forty years. A third asking is the fault of the asker. I have set the words in Grathic letters with the Keldish endings struck off, because Vorr speech is not written and bone-notches travel badly in a pocket. Their counting-stones are marked with grey dust off a blighted seam, which they do not sell and which has rubbed into the head of this leaf.

\subsection*{Of the number and what it is for}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item “The numbers are correct.”

\end{enumerate}

\emph{Gloss — What a Vorr says when a man asks what the oldest slates say. It is not a translation, and he will say so himself if he is in a patient mood, which is a mood waited for the way weather is waited for. The surveyors of Keld call the oldest marks Ash and the Court calls them language; a Vorr says the numbers are correct. I have set the three answers one under another and made none of them a sentence of mine.}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item “A stone is kept. A number is sold.”

\end{enumerate}

\emph{Gloss — They sell nothing else. In Y.H. 758 they stopped selling warm-stone to the Court and gave no reason, and the Court entered it as a cause with no effect, which is the figure it keeps for a thing it has been told and does not like the telling. The counting-stones stay with those who marked them; the numbers go down the road on a surveyor’s slate. This is not a saying about trade. It is a saying about what may leave a house.}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item “The count is in the bone. The tube finds nothing there.”

\end{enumerate}

\emph{Gloss — The collector’s cold iron tube takes what is in the blood, and a Vorr keeps his measure in the bone, which makes him difficult to draw and impossible to bank in the ordinary way. They do not undergo the Return. When one dies the others seat the body upright facing the direction it came from and leave it uncovered, and say we were never owed. I have seen such a body on the high path and did not go near it. A Grathic hearth-maid would have covered it with a fold and crossed two fingers. Both acts are kindnesses; only one has a number in it.}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item “The number after a sitting is not the number before.”

\end{enumerate}

\emph{Gloss — At forty a Vorr sits against a stone for a season and comes down with the number changed. What he heard is not recorded. The Court, which employs them as surveyors and watches them carefully, enters the change because it must, and has never asked to hear the reason, which is the only thing I have seen the Court do with a Vorr that a man could call restraint. A lowlander calls this a rise. A Vorr says the number is different, the way another man says the weather has turned, and goes on with his sitting.}

\subsection*{Of the sitting and the hearing}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item “The stone does not answer the first asking.”

\end{enumerate}

\emph{Gloss — Names come one at a time and many years apart, and a Vorr is known by the stone he keeps rather than by a family. The first sitting gives a number and not a name. I have known one through two sittings and still do not know what to call him except by his stone; he has not offered the other word. A man from the lowlands takes this for a riddle. It is an arrangement of years.}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item “The hearing divides the work. The body does not.”

\end{enumerate}

\emph{Gloss — They do not divide labour or inheritance by sex as we do below. They divide it by whether a person has sat against a stone long enough to hear it, which takes most of a life and is not permitted to the impatient. This is not a kindness. One who has heard does the counting, and a woman who has heard counts as readily as a man who has, which is a fact the Court’s roll has never found a column for.}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item “What is heard is not written. What is written can be carried away.”

\end{enumerate}

\emph{Gloss — The Vorr keep the long listenings in the head and write none of them. A clerk once asked one to set down what the stone had said and was given its height, which was true and useless and which he entered. There are perhaps four thousand Vorr, most of them here in Keld and almost none in Grath, and I have never heard of one writing a sentence. A thing said to a stone stays where it was said, which is more than can be said for a thing said at a table.}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item “The impatient hear the stone scratch.”

\end{enumerate}

\emph{Gloss — They will not let an impatient person sit, and there is no argument about it. A man who cannot sit still has spent his season and brings back a number he could have had at home, and a temper besides. I watched a young surveyor try it in Ash and come down with the figure unchanged. He has not been up since, and neither has his temper.}

\subsection*{Of the questions men carry up the stones}

\emph{Men walk five leagues of scree with a question and bring back the same answer in different words. I have set four here, with what was said on the stone and what was entered at Greybank.}

What was asked — What the Vorr said — What was entered\par

What do the oldest slates say? — The numbers are correct. — Figures confirmed by the party.\par

Why is there no return for your dead? — We were never owed. — The party is outside the roll.\par

What did you hear in the season? — The sitting continued. — No proceedings to record.\par

Why was the warm-stone stopped in Y.H. 758? — The number is sold. The stone is kept. — Supply discontinued, cause unrecorded.\par

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{In the narrow upright hand of the Court’s clerk, across the foot of the table:} Four answers reduced to entries. \emph{Underneath, in mine:} One is a refusal and two are silences, and a table with four rows is a fine thing to carry into a room where nobody has climbed the five leagues.\end{quote}

\subsection*{What they say at the turning of a sitting}

\emph{Said low, facing the way the last Vorr died, with the hands flat on the stone. The young say the first part before a sitting and the old say the second after it. Nobody says both in one breath.}

\begin{quote}\itshape Sit to the stone and the stone to the cold,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape one for the name not yet bestowed;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the count goes in where the bone is old,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the bone keeps what the blood let go.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Say it once. It is said.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Say it twice. It is the same.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape The stone was here before the sitting.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape The number changes. The stone remains.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape We were never owed. We do not ask.\end{quote}

\emph{Gloss — The third line is the only one that names the bone, and it is said to the stone, not to the person sitting. Children ask what the name not yet bestowed is and are told to ask the stone, which is the answer their elders were given. A clerk at Greybank put a round nought after the last line and wrote exempt, not discharged below. A nought is a number; the line was a refusal, and the two have never touched.}

\subsection*{Of the dead and what is not owed}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item “We were never owed.”

\end{enumerate}

\emph{Gloss — A Vorr death has no slate, no deduction and no return. They stop. The others seat the body upright facing the direction it came from and leave it, and say this once. I asked what becomes of the measure and was told there is no measure to become anything, which is not an answer in our tongue and is a complete one in theirs.}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item “He came from there. He faces there.”

\end{enumerate}

\emph{Gloss — Said over the body before they leave it, with the chin set toward the way it came. It is not a prayer. There is no fire carried up from the Keep and no one reads anything aloud. A man who washes bodies at the Keep asked me whether they were sending the dead home, and I said no, and he wrote nothing down, which was the only honest thing he did that morning.}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item “The drawer has borrowed from a debt that was not his.”

\end{enumerate}

\emph{Gloss — Said of one who draws from a well or a seam without owning it. The warmth comes out of somebody’s account in another district and the district pays in cold, and the man who took it calls it a current. A Vorr calls it borrowing, which is the word the Court takes out of every sentence it writes. I have set it here because it is the only Vorr saying I know with a person paying in it.}

\subsection*{What the borrowed hand did}

A survey-clerk of the factor at Greybank borrowed the rubbing in Ilmen. He writes upright and narrow and takes the verbs out as though a verb were a thing a man could carry off in a cuff.

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item Against \emph{we were never owed} he set \emph{the party is outside the roll}, which leaves the owing out and the party in.

\item Against \emph{the numbers are correct} he wrote \emph{figures confirmed by the party} and underlined it twice, as though a man confirming a number had said something about it.

\item Against \emph{the count is in the bone} he set \emph{the measure is retained, not deposited}, which is true in a counting room and false on a high path, where a bone is neither a bank nor a box.

\item Against \emph{the number after a sitting is not the number before} he wrote \emph{revaluation after lapse of time}, and put the season in a column where a season has never stood.

\end{itemize}

I have left his hand above mine everywhere, as a newer repair lies over an older one in the seam. He strikes out the doer because a thing with nobody in it cannot be argued with. I put the doer back because a boy at forty with a stone before him wants to know which way to face.

\subsection*{In the hand of a Vorr}

One of them wrote across the lower margin while I turned the leaf, in letters so large and slow that the line took the better part of an afternoon. He used grey dust off a blighted seam and pressed the doubled joint of his last finger into the tallow beside it. The dust has worked into the grain and does duty for a signature.

\begin{quote}\itshape You have written much. The numbers are correct.\end{quote}

The first sentence is a judgment on this leaf and the second an answer to the whole of it. I have not glossed either. A man who glosses a Vorr’s two sentences has begun to teach the stone his own trade.

\subsection*{In the margin, in charcoal, a clamp-master’s hand}

A master off the Duelling Floor borrowed the leaf below stairs and wrote, with the charcoal he marks hands with:

\begin{quote}\itshape Ask a Vorr what the clamp took and he will tell you the number. He will not tell you the hand.\end{quote}

I have set that where he wrote it. Both sentences are true, and the second is the reason the first was written. He did not sign it, and the charcoal has rubbed thin where the fold is carried.

\subsection*{At the head and in the gutter}

The grey at the head is counting-stone dust off the finger that wrote the two large lines; it goes into the grain and no damp takes it out, which is why they use it for marks they mean to keep. The coal smut at the fold is mine, off the sleeve I wipe the survey with. The warm-stone shaving was left on the leaf by a Vorr who went away without it; it held its heat one night on the stone floor and is cold now, which is the order of things here. The frost-feather came off a stone at the high path and was gone before I folded the leaf. The lead bead rolled out of the Ninth Gallery, where the rock sweats and the smell of hot lead gives what warning it gives; a surveyor laid it down and did not take it up. The clamp-scratch across two glosses was made by the master showing a boy how iron bites; both were honest men afterwards and one has a dead hand. The grey along the outer fold is not mine and not the Court’s. I have not swept it. There is no Last Day above this Keep.

\subsection*{At the foot, in a hand nobody will own}

\begin{quote}\itshape The stone has kept more counts than the Court has written.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape It has never entered one.\end{quote}

I asked a surveyor who carries the rubbing up, a clamp-master off the floor, and a Vorr come down with his number changed, and had three answers and no hand. I have left the lines where they were written. The rubbing goes back into its wire fold in the survey room and the grey dust onto the high shelf where they keep it and nobody buys it. Tomorrow I shall go up five leagues and sit where I am allowed, and if a Vorr says the numbers are correct I shall write it once and not ask him twice, which is the whole of the trade above this Keep.

\clearpage\phantomsection\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{The Country Outside, Being the Account of Orven, a Carter out of Stonemouth, Who Took Lime to Keld Keep and Walked Past the Survey Post With a Warm-Stone in His Coat and Came Back Without the Reason; with the Reckoning of the Days That Held, the Table of What Was Given and What Was Taken, the Song of the Sitting Dead, Two Corrections in the Narrow Hand of a Factor’s Clerk, and a Line at the Foot Nobody Will Own}
\CRsheetheading{The Country Outside, Being the Account of Orven, a Carter out of Stonemouth, Who Took Lime to Keld Keep and Walked Past the Survey Post With a Warm-Stone in His Coat and Came Back Without the Reason; with the Reckoning of the Days That Held, the Table of What Was Given and What Was Taken, the Song of the Sitting Dead, Two Corrections in the Narrow Hand of a Factor’s Clerk, and a Line at the Foot Nobody Will Own}
{\centering\FellFont\itshape\footnotesize\color{faded} A carter’s road-book, written first in charcoal on four strips of birch bark beyond the last pass and copied at Greybank onto the back of a lime-warrant voided by the Long Cold; the days in the carter’s own hand with the lost ones left standing as gaps, the figures of the road in a sloped tally hand, the sayings of the country set down in the hearing and not translated, the verbs put back under every borrowed correction, and one line at the foot in a hand that has never come forward · Written beyond the Cold Pass and at Keld Keep in Ash and Stone of Y.H. 812, the Thin Year of the Long Cold, by Orven, a carter of Stonemouth who hauled lime up the Rim Road and went on past the post with a warm-stone in his coat; copied at Greybank in Ilmen of Y.H. 813 onto the back of a voided lime-warrant and carried down the Ilm to Sill. It survives as five leaves of rough survey paper sewn with wire into a board cover gone soft at the seam: frost raised out of the grain on the climb and gone by noon, lime dust from the quarry worked into the gutter, a tallow thumb at the fold, a small grey stone from beyond the post sewn into the lower corner, a flake of warm-stone gone cold in the fourth leaf, a grey Ash print along the outer fold which the writer did not make and has not swept, two corrections in the narrow upright hand of the factor’s clerk at Greybank, one date scraped away with a knife-point, and a line at the foot in a hand nobody will own\par}\medskip
I took lime up the Rim Road in Ash, when the frost had not yet closed the high places and a cart could still make the Keep in nine days. The load was mine and the horse was not. A man who owns the horse does the arguing, and I was paid to carry stone and not to argue. At Keld Keep I gave my measure before my name at the Warden’s hall, which is their custom and not a rudeness, and the clerk wrote the figure first and asked the name second, as though a name were something a man might keep back and use again.

I bought a warm-stone there, a piece the length of my palm, and paid six marks, which is a great deal of lime. The man who sold it said it had come up out of the Ninth Gallery and had kept a fire since before his father. He did not say whose fire, and I did not ask. A warm-stone is a piece of somebody’s account that you can hold in your hand, and the man who sells it will tell you the price and not the debt.

\subsection*{The post, and the road that ends}

The survey post stands ten leagues beyond the Keep, where the Rim Road goes through into the cold. There is a post and no gate, which is the first thing a man from the clay countries asks about and the last thing anybody tells him. I asked the keeper what the post was for. He said it was for counting. I asked what it counted. Men, he said. I asked where the gate was. He looked at me a while and said that a gate is a thing you put up when you mean to stop somebody, and the Warden’s surveyors do not promise to bring a man back.

That is the truest thing I was told on the whole road, and I have set it above the rest.

Beyond the post the road goes on for a day as a track, and then it goes on for another day as a place where a track once was, and then it stops being a road and becomes the ground again. A surveyor come up from the shaft had drawn the way for me on a slate before I left the Keep. He drew as far as the post and stopped, and turned the slate face down. I asked him why he had not drawn the rest. He said that a line drawn past the post was a lie told with a ruler, and that his office had never yet been thanked for a lie that could be measured.

The frost came up out of the paper on that climb. It is in the head of this book still, or was when I copied it, and was gone by the middle of the day. I set down that much and no more, because a man who writes about frost as though it meant something has already begun a sermon.

\subsection*{The days that held}

I kept the days in charcoal on birch bark, which is what a quarryman keeps anything with that he means to carry up a mountain. Charcoal rubs off. The first day beyond the post I wrote the date and the word \emph{track}. The second I wrote \emph{stone, no road}. On the third I could not find the bark, and when I found it under a bank of snow the writing had come away on my thumb and there was no date to put back. After that I set down what the days had in them and not which day it was, which is a poor way to keep a reckoning and the only one that country allows.

In the bark — What I entered at Greybank — What stood underneath\par

The day of the post — \emph{post, no gate} — the same, struck and written above\par

A day of track — \emph{track} — \emph{track}\par

A day of stone — \emph{stone, no road} — \emph{stone, no road}\par

— — \emph{nought} — a space the length of a thumb\par

A day with the sitting man — \emph{man seated, not covered} — the words \emph{not covered} scraped away\par

— — \emph{nought} — a space, and a second space beside it\par

A day a man gave me a name — \emph{name given, not retained} — the letters of it, with no sound\par

The climb back — \emph{strap let out two holes} — the horse’s name, which I had forgotten\par

I have left the spaces where the clerk put his noughts. A nought is a figure. A space is a day I cannot spend. The two have stood side by side in this book for a year and nobody has asked me to make them agree, which is the only mercy I have ever had from a counting room.

\subsection*{What was given, and what was taken}

A Wasteling gave me a stone on the second or third day and asked nothing for it and would not take the bowl I offered. I carried the stone back and sewed it into the corner of this book, where it sits now, grey and cold and worth nothing. It is the only thing I brought home that I can still account for.

Another told me his name. I wrote it on the bark in charcoal, and when I came to copy it at Greybank the marks were there and the sound of them was gone, so that I had a name in a hand I could not say aloud. I have left the marks where they stand. A man who cannot say a name has still had one given to him, which is more than I can say of the reason I went.

A third said he would give me a day of his warmth. I put out my hand. He put his hand on mine and let go, and I was no warmer, and yet I came back a day short somewhere that I have never been able to find. I have entered this as it happened and not as a bargain, because a bargain is a thing two men remember and I remember only the hand.

They say out there that the cold is not empty but is full of what nobody kept. I asked a surveyor what that meant. He said it was a saying, and that sayings are what men keep when they have no figures. I asked a Wasteling the same thing and he asked me if I was warm. I told him I had a stone in my coat. He said, then you have not come far enough.

\subsection*{The sitting dead}

I came on a man sitting with his back against a stone, facing the way he had come, which was south-east, toward the Keel. His knees were drawn up and his hands lay on them. Nothing had been put over him. Frost had made a white seam along one shoulder and a little on the sleeve, and there was no drift against him, because he had been set there to be seen and not to be hidden.

I stood a while. A man who carries lime does not often have time to stand, and I have thought about that standing more than I have thought about the road.

A Wasteling came by and I asked whether they set the dead like that for love or for fear. He asked me if I was warm. I gave him the answer I had given the other, and he said that a warm man who asks that question has not yet understood the answer, and went on.

In Grath we break a pot at the door of a death-house to let the heat out. Out here there are no pots and no doors, and a man is left facing the road. I have set the two customs side by side and joined neither, because a custom is a thing a man does with his hands and not a thing he can explain to a clerk.

\subsection*{The song of the sitting dead}

\emph{Taken down beyond the post, from a man who would sing it only while he was walking and not while he stood still. It is said to the ground and not to a person. The last line is said twice; the second time is for those who went in and did not come back to say why.}

\begin{quote}\itshape The cold is not empty;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape it is a room with a name in it.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape We set the dead to face the road\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and put no cloth on them;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape whatever they came for, they can see it still.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape A stone is given and no thanks entered.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape A name is given and no man keeps it.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Ask the warm man what he carries ---\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape he will carry it back.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape There is no Last Day out here.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Nothing is swept. Nothing is owed.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape The cold keeps what nobody kept.\end{quote}

He would not give the name of the man who made it, and said that songs from that country are made by the country, which is an answer of the kind the coast gives and the clay countries do not. I have put the song where I heard it, walking, and away from the post.

\subsection*{What the clerk did at Greybank}

The factor’s clerk borrowed the leaves on a market morning. He writes upright and narrow and has ink settled in two fingers of his cuff that will not come out. He laid his hand on the top sheet before he looked at me, which is the manner of that table.

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item Against \emph{a space where a day stood} he wrote \emph{nought}, and beneath that, \emph{no entry lies}. I have put the space back under the figure. A nought can be carried into a court room; a space cannot, which is why one of them is honest.

\item Against \emph{I do not remember why I went} he wrote \emph{motive not entered}, which is true in the language of his office and false in mine. I did not fail to enter it. It is not in me to enter.

\item Against \emph{they gave and asked nothing for it} he wrote \emph{no consideration recorded; gift void}. Perhaps it is void. I have kept the stone sewn into the corner, and it has never once been entered.

\end{itemize}

I have left both readings everywhere, the thin one under the neat one, as a quarryman leaves the old cut showing in a face of stone. A clerk who takes the man out of a sentence leaves the road standing by itself, and a road standing by itself has carried nobody, cost nobody, and has no figure in it to argue with.

\subsection*{At the head and in the gutter}

The frost at the head came up out of the paper on the climb and was gone before noon; it kept no figure and asked for none. The lime in the gutter is mine, off the load I took up and did not bring back. The tallow at the fold is my lamp, set too near the leaf because the light goes early up there. The grey stone in the lower corner came from beyond the post and has never been warm and never will be. The flake in the fourth leaf was warm-stone once and is cold now, and I have kept it because a man should be able to see the price he paid even after the price has gone out of it. The grey along the outer fold is not mine and not the factor’s. I have not swept it. Beyond the post there is no Last Day on which a man might sweep, and I have not found one since I came back.

\subsection*{At the foot, in a hand nobody will own}

\begin{quote}\itshape A post and no gate, and a road that ends in stone;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape a man gave me a name I cannot say.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape I carried warmth up and came back with a cold stone;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the reason went somewhere I cannot find.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Ask the man seated what he waits for.\end{quote}

I asked a Wasteling, a surveyor come up from the Keep, and a clerk at Greybank, and had three answers and no hand. I have left the line where it was written. The leaves go back into the tin, into the pocket the strap has worn. Tomorrow I take the cart down to the lime-yard and enter nothing, which is the only entry the road beyond the post has ever asked of me.

\clearpage\phantomsection\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{The Country That Empties, Being an Account of the Southern Empire of Sere Set Down by Tavi Salt, a Tally-Clerk of Vhal, Who Went Down with Glass and Salt and Came Back with Crowns He Could Not Spend; with the Prices of the South, the Four Bowls, the Song of the Wine-Press, Three Corrections in Borrowed Hands, and a Line at the Foot Nobody Will Own}
\CRsheetheading{The Country That Empties, Being an Account of the Southern Empire of Sere Set Down by Tavi Salt, a Tally-Clerk of Vhal, Who Went Down with Glass and Salt and Came Back with Crowns He Could Not Spend; with the Prices of the South, the Four Bowls, the Song of the Wine-Press, Three Corrections in Borrowed Hands, and a Line at the Foot Nobody Will Own}
{\centering\FellFont\itshape\footnotesize\color{faded} A travelling tally-clerk’s account, kept dry in a tarred tin and written first on salt-paper, then copied at Greybank onto the back of a Court grain-warrant voided by the Long Cold; the figures in a sloped tally hand, the southern sayings kept in the hearing and not translated, the verbs put back underneath every borrowed correction, and one line at the foot in a hand that has never come forward · Written in Grain and Smoke of Y.H. 812, the Thin Year, in the Bowl of Sere and at a provincial bowl on the south road, by Tavi Salt, a tally-clerk out of the tide-tally house on the Quay at Vhal, who went south in Reed with two chests of Cliffs glass and a consignment of Sallow salt for a house of the Ten Bowls and came back in Ash with three gold crowns, a jar of wine whose contract had perished on the Salt Road, and a green-glazed bowl that cracked on the second morning at home. Copied at Greybank in Ilmen of Y.H. 813 onto the back of a voided grain-warrant and carried up the Salt Road to Vhal. It survives soft at the fore-edge and sour with salt, with a white bloom at the head, a tar thumb at the fold, yellow dust of the burning winds ground into the sewing, a ring of warm wine at the third hour, a thumb of olive oil, myrrh worked into the grain, the fibre of a wet rope pressed into the second leaf, a green bead of Cliffs glass flattened into the lower corner, a gold crown pressed flat between the fourth and fifth leaves, a husk of southern grain stuck fast in the gutter, a scorched corner, one small square of bare paper where a word was scraped away with a knife-point, three corrections in borrowed hands, and a line at the foot in a hand nobody will own\par}\medskip
I keep tallies on the Quay at Vhal in a room that smells of tar and wet rope. In our country a contract is written on salt-paper, and if the rain gets at it the debt is made nothing, and we call that a virtue. I went south with two chests of Cliffs glass and a consignment of Sallow salt for a house of the Ten Bowls, and came back with three gold crowns, a jar of wine whose paper had perished on the road, and a green bowl that cracked the second morning at home. I have set down what I saw. Where the south and my book disagree I have left both standing, which is what a tally-man does when he wishes to be honest and does not wish to be dismissed.

\subsection*{The road, and how the paper fared}

I took the Salt Road up to Greybank with the glass riding high and the salt riding low, because salt wets paper and glass breaks it and a man must choose which of his goods he will let suffer. The factor’s man there wrote \emph{salt} against a figure and did not look at the team. Below the coast pass the clay gives way to reeds, and at the Standing Post a reeve fined me a bit for asking which of the boards would bear me, which was within his right. The Fenfolk say a dry man is a dangerous man, and lodge him accordingly, and we learned why.

Beyond the Peat Line the villages stand empty in the middle of the day, and in their doorways are squares of bare clay where house-rolls once hung. A guide of ours asked whether the people had gone south or north. The reeve said they had gone where the account went, and would not say which that was.

I carried my paper in a tarred tin inside my coat and opened it only at the third hour, when the south does its business. At Greybank a clerk told me that paper made to rot was no way to carry a debt three hundred leagues. I told him it was the only way to carry one that could be honestly lost. He wrote it down and I have left it standing.

\subsection*{The heat, and the dust}

The south is warm the way a kiln is warm with the door standing open. I have sat out a Stone at the Sallow with the eels frozen in the baskets and never wanted water as I wanted it there. The burning winds come yellow off the east and take the skin off a traveller’s lips and leave the grain standing, which is a trick of the wind I have no learning in and several reasons to believe. My lips went first. The grain stood.

The courts have no walls. There is a fire in the middle of each and men sit in the heat of it with their coats on the ground beside them, and the dust comes down into their hair, and nobody brushes it off. I brushed mine off on the first day and was noticed. A man beside me said that a man who brushes the dust has decided he is only passing through, and a man only passing through may be charged for the hour. I let it lie after that. There is yellow of it ground into the sewing of this book, which I have not shaken out, because a clerk who shakes a leaf is a clerk who wants to pretend he has been somewhere else.

\subsection*{What I carried and what it fetched}

\emph{Figures as the house gave them at the third hour, set above what I entered on the Quay. The left column is the figure a man carries. The right is the figure he brings home, which is never the same figure and is never the same coin.}

Article — Entered at Vhal — Given in Sere — What I set on the back\par

Cliffs glass, a sheet, green — 2 marks at the ebb — 4 crowns — Crowns. They do not change on the Quay.\par

Sallow salt, a sack — 3 marks — 1 crown and a promise — The promise is not current. I entered it anyway.\par

Tallow-wasp resin, a nest — 4 marks — 4 crowns, to a bowl-surgeon — A surgeon, not a nest. I have set both.\par

Rope, tarred, a coil — 1 mark — 2 crowns — The tar came home with the figure, on my hands.\par

Dried fish, a string — 1 bit — not taken — A country that has fish will not pay for fish.\par

Keldish iron, a bar — 2 marks at Greybank — 3 crowns — The bar stood in four hands. The crowns stood in none.\par
