Where I wrote \emph{I entered the life at eleven}, the Court’s man set \emph{the life was entered} above it, and above that \emph{the entry stands recorded}, which is further from the man breathing on the slate than the first. I have put my words back underneath. A sentence with nobody in it is a sentence no mother can ask about, and mothers ask, always at the wall, always after the iron is paid.

The other hand is tall and leaning and comes out of the factor’s house at Greybank. Against the held place at the foot of the Bone 8 row it set a round nought and wrote \emph{no head returned} beside it. I have left both standing. A nought is a figure and can be carried down the road and added at the other end; the held place is a place where the mountain’s number goes and no man has ever put a figure in it. The factor’s man put one there because a hand that writes whole returns for persons not in a room has long since stopped asking whether a place and a number are the same thing. They are not. The mine-reeve set his red point against the boy’s two numbers and against the under-vessed man’s eleven and said nothing at either.

\subsection*{What they say going down}

\emph{Said low at the mouth while the rope goes out and the boy after it, to the rope and not to the boy. Coming up, it is said backward with the held line held again. Never say it looking at a person; said looking at a person, it becomes a checking.}

\begin{quote}\itshape One for the rope and one for the stone,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape one for the count that the boy brought down;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape tap it and cut it and hold it true,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and what comes up is the mountain’s own.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Loads to the beam and heads to the wall,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the twelfth is kept and is never found;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape eleven they write and eleven they pay,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the reeve’s red stays red in the ground.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape One for the keys and one for the hand,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and one held back where the number goes ---\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape we do not say it going down,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape we do not say it coming up.\end{quote}

Children ask what the held line is and are told to ask the rope, an answer given by people who asked the same at their own Descent. The factor’s man put a nought in that place and a word beside it. I have left the place the length it wants.

\subsection*{At the head and in the gutter}

The smut at the head is coal off the reeve’s sleeve; he leaned to read the Bone 8 remark standing and would not sit down, and said a tally that had never been under the mountain was not worth the keeping. The iron-red is his point and stays red in frost, and I have not wiped the margin where it touched. The shaving in the fold came off a palm’s piece a man set down while he counted his marks and went away without it; it is warm on the coldest morning and has been asked for twice and never lent, and when it goes cold I shall not know who paid for the warmth I had off it. The bead is lead out of the Ninth, where the rock sweats and the smell of hot lead gives the only warning there is; a man laid it on the leaf and did not take it up. The filing in the gutter came out of the clamp-rack and I have left it where it fell. The frost-fern came up out of the paper on the climb over the Cold Pass and went to water before I had made an end of the first column; it entered itself, which is more than can be said for any figure in this book. The clamp-scratch across two columns was made by a man showing his brother how a clamp bites; both were honest afterwards and one has a dead hand. The thumb in coal dust at the foot is not mine and not the reeve’s. I have not wiped it away.

\subsection*{At the foot, in a hand nobody will own}

\begin{quote}\itshape The slate keeps the figure. The wall keeps the man. The rope keeps what it brought back and says which way it came.\end{quote}

I asked the reeve, a key-keeper come up from the mouth, a cutter of the Floor, and a woman whose son went down at thirteen and came up with a different number, and had four answers and no hand, as I have had before. I have left the line where it was written.

The book goes back into its oiled cloth and the red point back into the reeve’s pocket. Tomorrow the rope goes down on the morning shift and a boy will give his number before his name, and I shall set down what came up beside what went down and put the verbs back where the Court struck them out. The mountain will sweat when it sweats; the smell will come before the heat, as it always has, and the count will try to agree and will not. The held place will stay the length it wants, and no figure will be put in it by any hand of mine.

\clearpage\phantomsection\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{The Sermon at the Dish-Niche, Being What a Man Who Came Back Thin Said at the Shrine of the Return in Sill on the Morning After the Weighing of Y.H. 812, with the Skimming-Song, the Dish-Row, a Factor’s Clerk’s Correction, and a Line at the Foot Nobody Will Own}
\CRsheetheading{The Sermon at the Dish-Niche, Being What a Man Who Came Back Thin Said at the Shrine of the Return in Sill on the Morning After the Weighing of Y.H. 812, with the Skimming-Song, the Dish-Row, a Factor’s Clerk’s Correction, and a Line at the Foot Nobody Will Own}
{\centering\FellFont\itshape\footnotesize\color{faded} A lay sermon of the Temple of the Return preached at the shrine of the Return off the Cross in Sill, at the niche where households set a dish of water overnight for them whose measure has been banked; the sayings in the low Grathic of the town set down in the shelf-keeper’s charcoal, the skimming-song with the gap left the length of a dish being wiped, the dishes in a shelf-tally, one correction in the narrow upright Ledgerhand of a factor’s clerk come up from Greybank, and a line at the foot in a hand nobody will own · Preached on the morning after the Weighing, in the five days outside the months, of Y.H. 812, the Thin Year, by a man of the shrine who had come back thin from the north two winters before and had kept the dish-shelf since, to the women who came up from Low Kiln with their dishes after the year’s figures had been read; written that evening by the woman who keeps the shelf and the shrine’s door, in charcoal and the dregs of a tallow lamp on the back of a spoiled levy notice gone soft at one corner, folded twice and tied with a thread of grey wool, and kept in the niche behind the shelf where the marked clay dishes stand. It survives with a tallow thumb worked into the head, a crescent of dry river silt along the gutter from a morning the leaf lay on the shrine step, a chip of pale dish-clay shut in the fold, a thread of grey wool through the tie, a ring where a dish of water stood from the first voice to the last, a bead of beeswax with a grey hair caught in it, a grey Ash print nobody will own, the clerk’s correction standing above the sayings, and a line struck through and written again very small underneath in a hand that has never come forward. Copied at Greybank in Ilmen of Y.H. 813 onto the back of a voided grain-warrant, with the verbs put back and the empty place left empty.\par}\medskip
I keep the dish-shelf at the shrine off the Cross, and nobody asked me for this. I write because he came back thin and keeps the dishes now, and because a factor’s clerk took the verbs out of his sayings before the week was out, and a saying with the verbs taken out travels well and arrives empty. He spoke first to the dish, then to the water in it, then to the shelf and the mark on the shelf, and last of all to us, which is the order a man uses when he has come back from a country he will not describe. I have set his words down in Grathic, with the verbs where he put them, because a saying said over water is a thing a household has to use.

The tallow at the head is mine; I held the notice down in the draught under the door and did not know I had marked it. The silt came up on the shrine step in the flood and dried in the grain. The pale chip in the fold is off a dish’s lip. The wax with the hair in it fell from the shrine candle as he spoke. The grey came off a cuff and nobody will own it; I have not swept it, and there is no Last Day behind a shelf.

\subsection*{The manner of the dishes, as the niche keeps it}

\emph{Written small, from watching, not from any order the Temple has printed.}

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item Come at first grey, before the ovens are stirred. A woman who comes at noon sets her dish on a shelf other women have breathed on and calls it the same shelf. It is not.

\item Set the dish lip to the wall on its own mark. Not on the ground. The ground is for what is poured out and the shelf for what was brought.

\item Skim the surface with your thumb. Do not drink, and do not let a child drink, though children ask.

\item Pour it out at the foot of the wall, not into the Ilm. The wall takes nothing and stands where it stood.

\item Wipe the dish and set it back on its mark. A wiped dish is not a clean dish.

\item Say nothing over the water. A word said over water comes up in another mouth and nobody here can tell you whose.

\item When the bell comes over the Cross, stop. Four, four and a gap; the gap is not ours to fill.

\item Leave the place at the end of the row as it is. A mark is not a dish and cannot be entered.

\end{itemize}

He said the last twice, once to the shelf and once to a woman from the kilns. I have set the sayings down as one because the shelf does not answer.

\subsection*{The sermon, as he said it}

\subsection*{Of the dish}

He took the dish from the shelf and turned it so the row could see the mark worn under the thumb.

“This is not a measure,” he said. “It holds what is put into it and gives it back when it is poured out. A measure goes up the road in a box and comes back as a figure. This goes nowhere. I have kept this shelf two winters and never carried a dish past the Cross.”

He set it down with the lip to the wall.

“There is a man in a clean coat who tells us nothing is lost that we have kept. I have heard him say it at the Weighing and once over a person not in the room. I believe the first half. The keeping is here: a chip in the rim, a mark under the thumb. The other half I cannot put my hand to.”

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Margin, in my hand:} He said \emph{the keeping is here} twice, once to the shelf and once looking at his own hands. I have not joined the sayings.\end{quote}

\subsection*{Of the water}

He lifted the dish and let the light go across the surface.

“There is generally silt,” he said. “The yard is clay and the wind comes off the terrace and puts its dust in everything. I skim it with my thumb and pour it at the foot of the wall and wipe the dish and set it on its mark. That is the whole of my preaching and I have two winters to find another sentence and could not.

“A priest come up from Greybank told me the water is a keeping of the Hearth and that the Hearth knows what is poured into it. I asked him where the water went when it left the dish. He said it was received. A man says \emph{received} when he has not stood at this wall in the dark. I have stood here two winters and the wall has never once been wet above the stone.”

A girl asked what became of the silt. He said it had been in the ground before it was on his thumb, which is a difficult sentence to carry home.

\subsection*{Of the figure}

“They read one in twelve this year in a clean voice and nobody here challenged it,” he said. “It is printed and it is true and it is said to a room that is not this one. I asked a man from the College how much of this dish was the Hearth’s. He gave me the printed figure, as though a twelfth of a dish of water were a thing a man could carry away in his fist and set on a shelf elsewhere.

“I asked him again which part went. He gave me a year. A date is an answer that does not spoil in the mouth, and the Court likes a date and does not ask what it covers. I have set his year in the margin and left my question under it.

“They call the rest of the dish a return. I do not know what word they have for what is poured at the foot of a wall, and I have never heard one out of that coat.”

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{In the narrow upright hand of a factor’s clerk:} A receptacle of retained measure; retention and diversion are lawful conditions of a vessel. Enter as nil.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape *\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Underneath, in mine:} I have put \emph{dish} and \emph{water} and \emph{poured} back under his. A sentence with the verbs taken out travels well and arrives empty, which is what a man wants who has to carry it to a table.\end{quote}

\subsection*{Of the name}

“Do not say a name over the dish,” he said. “A woman comes up with a dish and wants to say who it is for, and I tell her not to. Said over the water, a name goes down with it and comes up in another mouth.

“At the Weighing they read a whole return for a person not in the room. I was in that room once and they read nothing for me, and I was not asked what I wanted read. I do not say the Return is a lie. I say I have stood on both sides of that sentence and it is a different room from each side.”

He crossed two fingers over the empty place at the end of the row then, as the hearth-maids cross them over a birth-flower, and covered the act with a date, which is what people here do when asked about a mark they would rather not explain.

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{In my hand:} I asked what the year meant and he gave me Y.H. 747, the year of the Cold Pass agreement. I asked again in another way and he gave me the same year. The clerk set a different year above it; both stand, and the empty place has no dish in it.\end{quote}

\subsection*{Of them that come back}

He turned the dish a quarter and set it back.

“I came back thin,” he said. “They say it low at the Weighing and loudly in the north, where they buy it. I have heard both prices. A thin return is not a person mended; it is a person with less in him and a hankering for a table he never sat at.

“The nine who went after what had run away did a work, and I do not dispute it. But a man came back here and nobody sent for him, and he wipes dishes with cold fingers that do not answer as they used to. I will not preach that. A doctrine is an account that has found somebody to pay it, and I have no figure under mine.

“I keep the shelf because a man who has come back knows which way the water goes.”

He spoke the last to the dish and not to the women, and I have written it as it was said.

\subsection*{The skimming-song}

\emph{Said low, standing, with the thumb on the rim and the dish set on its mark. The row says the last four lines with him. There is a gap before those four, the length of a dish being wiped dry after the water has gone into the ground, and I have left it here as it is sung.}

\begin{quote}\itshape The dish goes up at the going of the light,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the water stands all night and does not stir;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape at first grey I skim it with a thumb\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and pour it where the wall will not drink.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape The shelf keeps the mark and the dish goes home;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape there is a place at the end where none stands;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape four go back and the fifth is a mark,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the mark is not ours to fill or to count.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Here the dish is wiped. No sound.}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Say what it did and not what it meant;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape set the rim down where the rim was worn;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the man who came back does not ask the wall\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape what it did with the water he poured.\end{quote}

A girl from the kilns asked what the space before the last four lines was for. Nobody answered her. The clerk put a round nought against it later, which I have left where he set it.

\subsection*{The dish-row, as the shelf keeps it}

\emph{The figure that arrives here in a coat goes down the Clay Road again in the same coat and leaves nothing on the stone. These I have set down where they stood.}

Dish — Set by — What stood in it at morning — What was entered\par

The chipped milk dish — A woman of Low Kiln, for her child — Water gone grey with fine slip-dust; not drunk — Nothing\par

The dish beneath the shelf’s end — Nobody came to claim it — Clear water, skimmed once and poured at the wall — Nothing\par

The dish with the twist of grey wool under it — A neighbour who would not give a name — Water with a hair in it; the hair taken up on the thumb — Nothing\par

The empty place at the row’s end — Nobody — A mark worn in the wood where a dish once stood — A round nought; vacancy\par

There were dishes before these that he could set a winter to, and I have not written the winters, because a row of years is a thing a clerk can carry away and a dish is not. The shelf has never agreed with the factor’s book.

\subsection*{What the clerk did}

He came up from Greybank on the second morning with ink in two fingers, borrowed the leaf while I held the door, and gave it back with the verbs taken out.

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item At \emph{this is not a measure}: \emph{a vessel is a lawful receptacle of retained measure}.

\item At \emph{the wall has never once been wet above the stone}: \emph{retained and expended; no charge against the keeping}, underlined twice. He did not ask to see the wall.

\item At \emph{I came back thin}: \emph{returnee classified thin; figure withheld pending assessment}, a true thing said by a man who has never been poured out of one country into another.

\item At the empty place a round nought and \emph{vacancy}. When I asked what a place was worth with no dish in it, he said nothing a clerk could enter, which was the first true thing I heard out of that coat.

\end{itemize}

I have put the verbs back underneath and left his hand standing above, as the shelf leaves the old mark under the new dish. He takes them out because a thing always true has no need of verbs. I put them back because a woman at first grey with a dish in her hand wants to know who is doing the pouring.

\subsection*{At the head and in the gutter}

The tallow will not come out of the grain. The silt has eaten the edge off two words at the foot, which I have not written in again, because a saying with two words gone is a saying said slowly, and most of ours are. The pale chip is clay off a rim wiped one time too many. The grey wool is mine and I tied it for the word I could not put down, and I will not untie it. The ring stood from the first voice to the last and was never drunk from. The wax and the grey hair are from the candle. The Ash came off a cuff and nobody will own it; there is no Last Day behind a shelf.

After he went the women poured their dishes out at the wall and set them on their marks, and the empty place was left as it was found. His words went down the Clay Road in a clean coat with a correction. The water went into the ground and the dishes went home.

\subsection*{At the foot}

Struck through once and written again underneath, very small, in a hand that is not mine:

\begin{quote}\itshape What goes into the ground is not lost and is not kept.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape The mark at the end of the row has no dish to enter.\end{quote}

I asked the woman from the kilns, the girl who asked about the gap, a carter and the clerk, and had four answerings and no hand. I have left the line struck through and standing, which is the only honest way to keep a sentence you cannot sign.

The leaf goes back behind the shelf with the thread at its tie. Next Weighing one in twelve will stand unchallenged and the women will set their dishes on their marks, and the clerk will take the verbs out. I shall put them back and leave the empty place the length it is.

\clearpage\phantomsection\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{The Dish of Salt, Being a Guessing-Night at the Head of the Quay in the Long Cold, Four Questions Put to the Brazier, the Answers Said to the Dish, and What a Council Clerk Made of the Morning}
\CRsheetheading{The Dish of Salt, Being a Guessing-Night at the Head of the Quay in the Long Cold, Four Questions Put to the Brazier, the Answers Said to the Dish, and What a Council Clerk Made of the Morning}
{\centering\FellFont\itshape\footnotesize\color{faded} A room-keeper’s account of one winter night, set down for the settling of a wager and not for the improvement of the reader; the questions in the words they were spoken, the wagers in pinches of salt in a dish, the tally taken off the dish at dawn, one correction in the narrow upright hand of a Council clerk, a salt-wife’s gloss pressed into the margin, and a line at the foot in a hand that nobody will claim · Set down at the head of the Quay in Vhal in Stone of Y.H. 811, the Long Cold, when the coast pass was shut and no cart came down from Greybank in nine days, by the woman who keeps the brazier room there; copied forward in Ilmen of Y.H. 813 onto the back of a spoil Council salt warrant, sewn with tarred thread into a fold of oiled sailcloth and kept in a tin above the brazier, which is the only dry place in the house. It survives with a white salt bloom in the gutter, a thumb of tar at the head, a wine ring near the fourth question, wet wool pressed across the first leaf, a crust of frost along the outer edge, a green bead of cliff-glass folded into the second fold, a fish-hook nick, a grey print nobody will own, the clerk’s correction standing above the room’s words, the salt-wife’s gloss standing in the margin, and a line at the foot in a hand that is nobody’s.\par}\medskip
I keep the brazier room at the head of the Quay. It is a narrow house with the water going under it, and in Stone the frost takes the iron ring at the landing, so that a man puts his boot against it before he will believe it is iron. The boats lie high. The pass is shut and no cart has come down from Greybank in nine days, which means no clay ware, no wool, and nothing to argue about over a fire. So we guess.

A guess here is a question said to the fire. Said to a person, an answer becomes an argument, and an argument in Vhal is a debt with no date on it, which is the one thing this house will not carry through the winter. We put four questions. The wagers are pinches of salt laid in a dish. Salt is the only thing in the room a man can taste and cannot spend, so it is the right stake for a night when there is nothing to buy. The dish goes from hand to hand and the answer is said to the dish. No slate lies where the dish lies. A man who wants a thing entered can go up to the tide-tally house and sit with people colder than himself.

The coal is paid for by the boat-house at the step, which enters it against the share in the spring. Thus a man warms himself before he owes for the warming, which is the ordinary order here and the reason the fire stays lit. I have no word in Vhaleni for a person who sits by a fire without an account. I have a word for a person whose account is current, and I used it of everyone who came that night.

\subsection*{The night as it went}

It was the ninth night of the shut pass. The Sallow came in against the wind and went out against the wind, as it does, and the frost stood on the Quay boards in feathers where the Warm had lately gone out of the stone. There were six of us and a boy who swept the landing. A question is put once; ask for it again and you owe a pinch, because the second asking is for your own pleasure and not for the dish. Four are scored. A fifth may be said from the door and is not counted, being a thing said by a man who has not sat down.

The first went to a salt-wife of the third pan, with the salt worked white into the creases of her hands.

\begin{quote}\itshape Written to be lost, and lost is how I keep;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape a wet morning is my ending\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the Council calls it a virtue.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape What am I?\end{quote}

“A contract on salt-paper,” she said, and said it to the dish. She did not look at the man from the tide-tally house, who had not yet put his slate down. He put a pinch in all the same, which is the sort of thing a clerk does when he wants it known that he can lose a wager and still be paid.

The second went to a man come aboard at the step, whose opinion on the boat is counted at half and who knows it.

\begin{quote}\itshape I am held by a mother and not by me;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape my word on the boat goes in at half;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape I am married to the account\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and may never own it.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape What am I?\end{quote}

“A man come aboard,” he said to the dish, which is how a man says a thing about himself in Vhal without claiming it. His wife’s sister laughed, and he said nothing, and the dish went on. That is the whole of a marriage at the head of the Quay, and it is not a sad thing unless you have watched it.

The third I put myself, because the room had got loud and wanted quieting, and a question put by the fire is not scored against anybody.

\begin{quote}\itshape I steal a coal and leave no track but a warm crop;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape I am a bird with a borrowed name;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the pan-master counts me as weather.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape What am I?\end{quote}

“A brine-gull,” said the glass-woman from the furnaces. She had the sweetness of the cliff at one corner of her mouth. After she had said it she wiped that corner with the back of her hand, though there was nothing there to wipe, and held the dish a moment longer than the passing needed. The salt-wife put a pinch in for her.

The fourth went to the boy who swept the landing, and he answered before the verse was done, which is why he never wins anything and is always first.

\begin{quote}\itshape I tap from below where the warm is kept;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the boat looks the same when I have done;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape no hole in her, and no heat.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape What am I?\end{quote}

“A salt-thing,” he said to the dish. He had seen one tap his mother’s boat in the summer, and nobody in the room said the boat’s name. He set his pinch on the dish and did not take it up again, though nobody had asked him to pay, and I have left it lying where he put it.

\subsection*{The tally, taken off the dish at dawn}

Question — Put to — Answer, said to the dish — Salt laid down\par

The written thing — the fire — a contract on salt-paper — one pinch\par

The half word — the fire — a man come aboard — one pinch\par

The bird — the fire — a brine-gull — one, laid by another hand\par

The tap below — the fire — a salt-thing — one, not taken up\par

Four answered. Nothing was drunk, and the cup that stood by the brazier from the first question to the fourth went back on the shelf with the ale still in it, which is how small ale is drunk in this house when there is a thing to say and no proper word for it.

\subsection*{The salt-wife’s gloss, pressed into the margin in charcoal}

She borrowed the leaf before the clerk came and put her mark against the bird:

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{The gull took from the Council’s brazier at the pan gate, not from ours. It has been doing it eleven years and the Council has never once entered the coal. Say which fire you mean.}\end{quote}

Underneath, in mine: \emph{Both stand. A gull carries whatever is not watched, and a fire that is paid for by nobody is the kind a bird will always choose.} She came back for the leaf at noon and read what I had written below hers and said I had put it rightly, which she would not have said if I had put it wrongly, and went away with her hands white to the wrist.

\subsection*{What the clerk did}

A clerk of the Council came with the light, being a man who cannot leave paper lying. He laid his hand on the leaf before his eyes went to the room, which is the manner of that house. He set the four questions down as \emph{queries entered} and the answers as \emph{responses recorded}, valued each pinch of salt at a twentieth of a bit, and wrote \emph{gaming, not commercial} across the head of the tally, so that a night of guessing came out as a night of trading with the profit left off. Against the boy he wrote \emph{no standing party}, and against the coal, \emph{fire privately maintained; no public charge}, which is true and is the whole of what the Council cares to know about a fire.

In this room — In the Council hand\par

A pinch of salt, tasted and not spent — One twentieth of a bit\par

An answer said to the dish — A response recorded\par

The boy who swept the landing — No standing party\par

A fire paid for by a house that is not here — No public charge\par

He asked me what a guess was worth. I told him nothing a clerk could carry, which is the first true thing I have said to that table in two winters. I have put the room’s words underneath and left his standing above, as salt lies under ink and shows through when the paper wets. He has entered four answers and struck the boy, and the boy was not struck: he said a thing he had seen and took nothing for it, and that is the only answer of the four that cost the speaker anything.

\subsection*{At the head and in the gutter}

The salt bloom came up out of the paper itself and I have not brushed it off. The tar at the head is mine, off the coil I keep by the door for the boats in winter. The wine ring near the fourth question belongs to the glass-woman, who set her cup down and did not take it up until the salt-wife had paid for her; I have not washed it out. The press of wet wool across the first leaf came off the man come aboard, who held the door while the clerk read and did not let go when he was done. The crust along the outer edge came up out of the paper on the ninth night, when I carried the leaves inside my coat and the coat froze to my back; I have not scraped it off, because a guessing kept in a warm room would be a different guessing. The green bead in the second fold is cliff-glass; the girl pressed it in with her thumb and did not say what it was for, and I have not turned it to the light. The fish-hook nick came off a man paying for eels with the hook still in his hand. The grey print came off a cuff laid where no cuff has business lying, and I have not swept it. There is no Last Day here and nothing anywhere gets swept.

\subsection*{At the foot, in a hand nobody will own}

\begin{quote}\itshape Four answers went out on the ebb. The fire did not.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape The dish came back empty and the place by it stayed warm.\end{quote}

I asked the salt-wife, the man come aboard and the boy who sweeps, and had three names and no hand, and none of the three was in the room when the line was written. I have left it where it stands. The leaf goes back in the tin above the brazier, which is the only dry place I have, and tomorrow the pass will still be shut and the boats will still lie high, and if a man asks what there is to do of an evening I shall tell him to ask the dish.

\clearpage\phantomsection\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{The Drawing Book, Being the Measures of the Sill District Entered at Greybank in the Last Tends of Stone, Y.H. 812}
\CRsheetheading{The Drawing Book, Being the Measures of the Sill District Entered at Greybank in the Last Tends of Stone, Y.H. 812}
{\centering\FellFont\itshape\footnotesize\color{faded} A page from the tally-book of the Court’s collector’s clerk at Greybank; figures in Ledgerhand, with the officer’s remarks in the hand that made the draw · Written in the factor’s house at Greybank in Y.H. 812, the year the clay towns call the Thin Year, by the clerk who keeps the tally for Sill and the villages about; the officers are entered on the leaf and the clerk is not. Copied forward at the Opening of the Slates in Y.H. 813. It survives as a quire of paper soft at the fore-edge in a tin on the factor’s shelf: a grey thumb at the head of the ember column, a streak of slip down the gutter, a green bead of glaze in the lower corner, a drag of Ash along the foot, one figure struck through and set above in a second hand, and a line at the foot which the factor’s clerk did not write.\par}\medskip
I keep the tally for the Sill district in the factor’s house at Greybank. The officer makes the draw and gives me the figure; I set it down. The figures go in Ledgerhand, without verbs, because a figure with a verb in it can be argued with and one without cannot. The remarks are the officer’s own, in the hand that held the tube, and I have not changed a word of them. The College would take the verbs out of those as well if it knew they were there. The factor allows them. He says a remark is not part of the account, which is his way of saying that a thing may be written down so long as it is never entered.

The grey at the head of the ember column came off on the officer’s fingers. He laid them on the page while he gave me the number and did not know he had marked it. I have not rubbed it out. It is the only mark on the leaf that I did not set here of purpose, and it is the one the factor’s clerk asked me about.

Day entered — Vessel, as the slate has it — Embers — Deduction — Banked to — Officer’s remark\par

Stone 12 — A man of the Weir. Birth-name not taken; entered as \emph{Eel} — 52 — 1 in 12 — Greybank — Drawn before light. Pale round place left on the arm.\par

Stone 12 — A child three days returned, Low Kiln. Entered as \emph{Second} — 13, struck to 12 — 1 in 12 — Hearthseat — Worse before dusk. Entered as a birth, not a worsening.\par

Stone 20 — A woman of the glaze room, High Kiln. Entered as \emph{Sweet} — 38 — 1 in 12 — Greybank — Pale line at the gum. Asked after her girl; not entered.\par

Stone 20 — A clay-bound hand of the terraces. Entered as \emph{Seven} — 44 — 1 in 12 — Greybank — Consent withheld. Clip-held by the wrist until consent entered.\par

Stone 22 — A man of Mud End. Entered as \emph{Peat} — 47 — 1 in 12 — Greybank — Kiln’s breath. The neighbours called it merciful.\par

Stone 25 — A girl of the slip pits, Low Kiln. Entered as \emph{Nineteen} — 12 — 1 in 12 — Hearthseat — Birth-slate laid face down on the bench before the child was turned.\par

Stone 30 — A widow of the lower town. Entered as \emph{Loaf} — 41 — 1 in 12 — Greybank — Four loaves baked; three to the levy. Figure read twice, once for those that came late.\par

Stone 30 — Forty of Low Kiln. One slate for the batch, entered by lot — — — 1 in 12 — Hearthseat — Held overnight in the Waiting Room. Birth-names not taken. A barrow of grey went out through the north gate.\par

\subsection*{The column of embers}

An ember is said to be worth five marks and a newborn vessel holds twelve to fifteen. A labourer in good case carries forty to sixty and does not know it. The book does not ask what the walls are like; it asks only what went through them and where it was put. I have set the figures down as they were given. I have not added them, because adding is a thing the College does in the Hearthseat and not a thing a tally-clerk does at Greybank, and because the last time I added a column I got a number that would not agree with the printed one and the factor told me to copy the printed one again.

The officer gave me thirteen for the child on Stone 12. The factor’s clerk struck it and set twelve above in his own narrow hand, saying a vessel three days returned cannot hold thirteen after the draw. Both figures stand. I have asked which is right and neither of them has told me, and I have stopped asking, because a clerk who asks after a correction is a clerk who will soon be correcting next.

\subsection*{The remarks}

I struck out one of my own words on this leaf. Where the officer said \emph{the warmth was drawn}, I had written \emph{taken}, and he looked at the word and said a draw is not a taking when there is a slate. I set \emph{drawn} above and left \emph{taken} standing under it, which is the only honest thing on the page. A taking and a draw are the same heat going the same way; the slate is the difference, and the slate is a piece of stone with a neat hand on it.

The remarks are the only place in this book where a person appears, and even there they appear as a pale round place on an arm, a line at the gum, a word not entered, a wrist held until consent. The officer writes a good remark. He does not explain himself in them and does not plead. \emph{The neighbours called it merciful.} That is all he set down for the man of Mud End, and it is more than the ordinance would allow and less than a man would say.

\subsection*{What I did not enter}

The streak of slip in the gutter came off the forearms of a thrower who came in from Sill while I was copying the Stone 20 figures. She stood at the counter with her hands held away from her coat and waited for the figure, and the grey came off on the edge of the quire when she set her slate beside it. The green bead in the lower corner is not slip. It came from a girl who leaned over to see the writing with sweetness still at her mouth, and touched the paper and said nothing. I have left it where she put it. The drag of Ash along the foot was there when I opened the tin; it is not mine and not the factor’s clerk’s. I have not swept it. On the Last Day they sweep the corners of the houses and burn what they find there in the morning and call it dealt with. There is no Last Day for a tally-book.

One in twelve is printed on the notice and I have copied it eight times in these two tends. I have not checked it against the roll, and the officer has not asked me to. The figure goes into the book as it comes off the notice and out of the book into the Weighing, and a district hears it read in a clean voice and goes home knowing what it owes without having been told what it paid.

\subsection*{At the foot}

The factor’s clerk has written a line here that is not mine and is not in Ledgerhand:

\begin{quote}\itshape Nothing is lost that we have kept.\end{quote}

I have not struck it out. It is not a figure and has no business on a tally; but it is in the book now, and when I copy the leaf on Ilmen 1 I shall copy it again, in his hand and not my own, as it stands. The tin goes back on the shelf between the salt scales and the damp copies from the coast. The grey thumb will come off on the next leaf. I shall not rub that out either.

\clearpage\phantomsection\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{The Drawing Table, Being the Standing Rules of the Collectors of Sill and Greybank for the Taking, Keeping and Trying of Apprentices at the Table in Slate Row and on the Clay Road, with the Table of Years, the Wrapping-Song Pasted Inside the Wool Sleeve, Two Corrections in Borrowed Hands, and a Line at the Foot Nobody Will Own}
\CRsheetheading{The Drawing Table, Being the Standing Rules of the Collectors of Sill and Greybank for the Taking, Keeping and Trying of Apprentices at the Table in Slate Row and on the Clay Road, with the Table of Years, the Wrapping-Song Pasted Inside the Wool Sleeve, Two Corrections in Borrowed Hands, and a Line at the Foot Nobody Will Own}
{\centering\FellFont\itshape\footnotesize\color{faded} A table-copy of the collectors’ standing rules in the hand of an old officer who keeps the wool sleeves and the roll of hands behind the collector’s table in Slate Row; the articles in short road sayings, the years and the faults in tables, the wrapping-song pasted inside a wool sleeve, one correction in the narrow upright Ledgerhand of a College clerk, one in the soft-cuffed hand of a factor’s clerk at Greybank, three lines in the thick charcoal of a hearth-maid come up from Low Kiln, and a line at the foot nobody will own · First gathered at Greybank in Y.H. 719, the year the factor’s house began to keep a roll of hands beside its roll of measures, and copied forward from the sleeve and not from a book, which is why the rule about the grey is rubbed nearly through at the corner and the rule about the wool is as sharp as the day it was set down; this leaf written in Smoke of Y.H. 813 by a collector who has drawn on the Clay Road for twenty-six years and keeps the table’s sleeves and its roll of hands, after the Thin Year and the Opening of the Slates. It survives folded small enough for a coat pocket, carried in the wool sleeve of a tube that has never once drawn the warmth out of the paper: grey worked under the nails at the head, iron filings ground into the gutter off the tube’s wrap, a green bead of lead glaze pressed into the lower corner by a girl at the Cross with the sweetness still at her mouth, frost-crisp along one edge from a morning on the Rim Road, a tallow thumb, a damp tide-line from the Waiting Room along the foot, a small square of bare paper where a word was scraped away and no other put in its place, two corrections in borrowed hands, three lines in the margin, and a line at the foot nobody will own\par}\medskip
I keep the sleeves and the roll of hands behind the table in Slate Row. A boy comes up from Greybank with a house-name and goes back with a slate-name and a wool sleeve. I draw the measure. The clerk at Greybank writes the figure. There is a difference between the two. A taking and a draw are the same heat going the same way; the slate is the difference.

The table is a guild of a sort, though the word is a clay-country one and is not used in Slate Row. These articles were first gathered at Greybank in Y.H. 719, when the factor’s house found it had two sorts of men to count. A rule with no grey on it is a rule nobody has had to use. These have been used.

\subsection*{The articles as they stand at the table}

\subsection*{Of the taking}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item The table takes an apprentice, not a house. A house may bring him, or the Temple’s poor may be sent, or a collector may take him off a doorstep where a draw has left nobody to answer for him. From the day he first wraps a tube the table answers for his hand. A house that will not give up the years has given nothing.

\item He is taken at fifteen, or at sixteen if the house has kept him through a hard year. A boy who cannot carry a wrapped tube to the Waiting Room and set it down without letting the iron show has no business on the road; he will spend the wool on his sleeves and call the road’s.

\item His birth-name is said once at the taking and kept in the mouth afterward. A slate-name is entered in the roll in its place, in the same hand as the figures, so that no man can tell by looking which of the two was written first. A name in the mouth cannot be entered, and there is nothing in this country the Court has not tried to enter.

\item He is kept, not hired. He eats from the table’s dish and sleeps in the room above the Waiting Room, and what he earns goes into the table and comes back as bread and a sleeve, neither of which is written down. An officer who tells a boy he is paid tells a true thing about a figure and a false thing about a living.

\item No boy is asked whether he wants the iron. He is asked whether he understands what is carried: a tube wrapped in wool, a knuckle laid to the wall, a hiss, a figure read twice, and a grey that comes up under the nails before he has learned to read the slate. The wanting comes after, or it does not come.

\end{enumerate}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{In the narrow upright hand of a College clerk, against rule 4:} Retained by the table; no wage arising. \emph{Underneath, in mine:} I had written that he is fed. He is fed, and the feeding goes into no figure, which is why it can be done. I have left my word where his was set above it, as a man leaves the crack showing.\end{quote}

\subsection*{Of the wool and the note}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item Wrap the tube before you take it up, not after. A boy can hold iron while he speaks, but he will not speak well with his fingers going the colour of the sky before snow. The wool keeps the hand one draw and lets the heat go, which is as much as any sleeve of mine is owed.

\item Set the knuckle to the wall before the iron goes to the arm. A whole vessel answers full; one cracked through answers flat, a small dead sound that stops at the surface. Write the note before the figure, and write \emph{none} where there was no note and not a nought, because a nought is a figure and a silence is not. The kiln-masters of Sill keep the full note to themselves, which is their trade; I know it from rooms where a pot was set down and the house talked over the sound. A collector who draws blind still brings back a figure. That is the trouble with figures.

\item Look at the arm, where the ways run near the skin. Do not look at the face. A face tells you nothing you can use, and a thing you cannot use is a thing you will remember, which is worse on the road.

\item Count the draws on the fingers afterwards, never before. A figure counted before the draw is a figure already decided, and a decided figure is the same thing as a false one with the ink dry.

\item Say the four sayings in the order the road comes to them, not the order the notice prints. In the room they begin with \emph{nothing is lost that we have kept} and end with the taking; on the road the record comes first, so it cannot comfort, and the banking comes last, because it is the true one and the one we do the most. Say them into the wool, not the air, where words go up and get entered.

\item One in twelve, as the notice says, read twice: once for the moot and once for those who came late up the road. The boy reads what is printed. What the district pays is not his hand, and the man who sets the other figure has gone up the Clay Road with it and does not carry it in the open. An apprentice who asks after that figure is told that a collector who asks after a correction will soon be making one.

\item Never say the prayer twice over one man. A second prayer argues with the first, and the first was honest, being said before he knew how much the man had. If the bell comes off the Cross four and four and a gap, stop at the gap. The gap belongs to somebody else.

\item Consent is recorded; the table writes the word as the slate has it. A boy is taught to say \emph{lawful draw; consent recorded} and not to ask recorded by whom, because a collector who asks it in a room will ask it at a door, and a door is where a man loses his cuff. A refusal is not entered. The clip belongs to the Court’s room, not to this table, and the room has its own hand for it.

\end{enumerate}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{In the leaning hand of a factor’s clerk come up from Greybank, against rule 11:} Printed deduction, read twice; no second figure arises. \emph{In mine, underneath:} Both figures arise. One is carried in the open and one under a coat. Both stand, and I have stopped asking the clerk which of the two he means by \emph{arises}.\end{quote}

\subsection*{The years at the table}

\emph{Kept behind the sleeves. What is written is the work that came up, in a hand that does not change between one line and the next.}

Year — At the table — What is taken\par

Fifteen — Wrap the tubes, sweep, keep the sleeves dry, carry the slate edge-on — The birth-name, said once and kept in the mouth\par

Sixteen — Walk with an old collector; set the knuckle; say the note into the wool — The habit of counting before the draw\par

Seventeen — Set the iron under an eye that has drawn forty times; read the figure twice — The face of the person on the pallet, which is not looked at again\par

Eighteen — Take a pot alone through a draw and read the grey in his own hand — The last of a boy’s account with any house\par

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item Eighteen is the common end of a keeping and not a short one. He stays where the table sends him, at Sill or Greybank or a district he has not heard of. The table’s figure for him is one apprentice, current, no wage arising. What stands beneath that figure is a boy who eats from the dish. The College does not choose where he goes. The roll does, and the road after it. His hand goes grey under the nails first and comes up into the creases by the second year, and after that a man may wash till the water freezes and nothing changes. Collectors say the grey comes off in a day. I have had it last six, and no clerk has asked after the sixth. A collector who says the cost is nothing has not looked at his own hand, which is the only looking he does not do.

\end{enumerate}

\subsection*{Of faults and their correcting}

Fault — As corrected at the table\par

Iron taken up before the wool — The tube wrapped in the boy’s sight; the draw put off a tend\par

Knuckle not set before the tube — The note entered as \emph{none}, which is not a nought\par

A figure counted before the draw — The figure struck; the boy set to counting sleeves for a tend\par

The face looked at — No punishment. The boy is told what he has kept and sends it nowhere\par

A prayer said twice over one man — The second struck; the first left standing\par

A birth-name written on a travelling leaf — Scraped away; no other word put in its place\par

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item A fault copied twice in one tend is a fault the boy has not understood, and the old collector sits with him behind the table until he has. The tube is not a rod and the slate is not a confession.

\end{enumerate}

\subsection*{The wrapping-song, pasted inside the wool sleeve}

\emph{Sung low going up the Clay Road, with the tube wrapped and not in the hand. Nobody sings it in a house and nobody sings it at the Weighing. The boy whose sleeve is new says the middle verse, and nobody says his name.}

\begin{quote}\itshape Wool on the iron, iron on the arm,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the note comes first and the figure after;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape four for the moot and four for the late,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and a place where the fifth goes by.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Grey in the nail, grey in the crease,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the hand goes home ahead of the man;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape wrap the iron, turn the slate,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape wipe the hand and say no name.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Wool on the iron, iron on the arm,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the road goes up and the figure goes down;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the note stays where the knuckle left it,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the gap in the bell is nobody’s.\end{quote}

\subsection*{What the borrowed hands did}

A clerk of the College borrowed the leaf at Sill with ink in two fingers of a soft cuff, and took the verbs out as though a verb were a thing a man could smuggle past a weigh. Against \emph{I set the knuckle to the wall} he wrote \emph{the vessel was assessed}, true of every vessel in Sill and therefore of none; I have put my hand back underneath. Against \emph{what the district pays is not his hand} he wrote \emph{the deduction is one in twelve for every vessel of the Keeping}, which is what the notice says. I have left it standing; a clerk’s true sentence is not always an honest one. Where the space stands before the last verse he put a round nought and wrote \emph{vacancy}. A nought is a number. The place was not.

A clerk of the factor’s house at Greybank wrote \emph{no cost to officer} against the grey. I have not struck him out. A clerk’s false line is what the next reader ought to see.

The hearth-maid came up from Low Kiln with a birth-slate under her shawl and waited until the pigs were weighed before she put charcoal to the leaf. Her thick letters tore the paper in two places.

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item At \emph{look at the arm, not the face}: “I have washed that arm and held it when it was warm. You will not know whose it was. I shall.”

\item At \emph{write none and not a nought}: “We put the date where the word would go, and the date is not the word.”

\item At \emph{the hand goes home ahead of the man}: “There’s a stone in my house kept for whoever comes in behind. It isn’t for you. Don’t ask who it was for.”

\end{itemize}

I have set her words in the margin where she put them, because she would not have them on the face of the leaf where an officer might read them going past.

\subsection*{At the head and in the folds}

The grey at the head is mine, off the fingers I gave the figure to at Greybank, and it has gone in under the nails and will not come out. The filings in the gutter came out of the wool sleeve; there is always iron in the fold, and it has never drawn the warmth out of the paper, which is the one kindness iron has shown this leaf. The green bead came off a girl at the Cross who leaned over with the sweetness still at her mouth and touched the corner; it tastes sweet in wet weather, and I have not washed it. The frost along one edge is from the Rim Road in Stone, and I have not gone over the words it thinned; a word written thin is a word said quietly, and most of ours are. The tallow thumb is mine. The tide-line along the foot came from the Waiting Room, where the collected are kept overnight and the damp gets into everything on a bench. The bare square in the lower margin is where I scraped a word away with a knife and put no other in its place. I have not written it back, and I have not forgotten it.

On the Last Day they burn the corners and call it dealt with. There is no Last Day for a sleeve.

\subsection*{At the foot, in a hand nobody will own}

\begin{quote}\itshape The wool keeps the heat out of the hand for one draw.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Nothing else in this trade is kept.\end{quote}

I asked an old collector, a clerk from the College and a woman at my counter, and had three answers and no hand. I have left the two lines where they were written. The leaf goes back behind the table and the tube into its wool. Tomorrow a boy will come up from Greybank with a name he will not use on the road, and I shall set the knuckle to the wall before the iron and write the note before the College can strike it out. The grey will come off on the next leaf. I have stopped washing it.

\clearpage\phantomsection\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{The Price of a Dry Foot, Being the Market of the Standing Post and the Dues of the Boardwalks, the Peat Paths and the Marsh Roads, Cut on Count-Sticks and Copied into the South’s Letters}
\CRsheetheading{The Price of a Dry Foot, Being the Market of the Standing Post and the Dues of the Boardwalks, the Peat Paths and the Marsh Roads, Cut on Count-Sticks and Copied into the South’s Letters}
{\centering\FellFont\itshape\footnotesize\color{faded} A board-man’s tally of the marsh’s prices and road-dues, cut as notches in a count-stick and written on oiled reed for a factor who cannot read a notch; the figure told below set above the figure taken here, one place left smooth and not noughted, the verbs put back where a borrowed hand took them out, two corrections in other hands, and a line at the foot nobody will own · Written at the Standing Post in the Fenmarch by Wade, who cuts the reeves’ sticks there and learned his south’s letters off a peat-tally clerk at Greybank, though he keeps his own accounts in notches; begun in Reed of Y.H. 812, the Thin Year, after the Long Cold, carried forward at the Opening of the Slates, Ilmen 1, Y.H. 813, and written up again at the Reed Cut of that year. It survives as one strip of oiled reed and two leaves of birch bark sewn with eel-sinew, folded and kept in a dry tin under the loose board at the Post; with a cross-notch cut at the head for a fine paid, a dry-mud thumb, a bog-water tideline along the gutter that has taken two figures clean off, a cross-cut from a reeve’s point, a reed-wolf’s tooth nick at the second corner, eel slime at the foot, the dark wet mark of a board laid across the third leaf, a grey Ash smear nobody will own, one knot of grey wool tied through a hole in the first strip which the writer will not untie, two corrections in borrowed hands, and one line at the foot nobody will claim.\par}\medskip
I keep the boards at the Standing Post. Four planks lie across a cut no man has sounded, and a fifth place where no plank is laid, and a stick in my coat with a notch for every foot that went over and a mark for what it gave. A stranger comes up the marsh road, sets his boot on the first plank and asks what the crossing costs. I tell him the crossing costs nothing and the ground costs a bit. He takes this for a jest, because he is a dry man and believes ground lies still under him. I have watched dry men go down at the third plank. The water does not argue. It takes the boot and leaves the man to explain it to a reeve.

Fen Cant is not written. What is owed is cut in a stick: one notch for a bit, a deep notch for a mark, a cross-cut for a term, and a smooth place where nothing is entered. A factor’s clerk at Greybank can read my notches and cannot read what they are for, which is how I know they are honest. I write in the south’s letters so a reeve’s daughter may read this. The words that will not go into them I have tied in the margin, with no word for what the knots are for.

Twelve copper bits to a silver mark; twenty marks to a Sere crown, which comes north with the buyers, will not change at Greybank, and goes south again with them. The Court books in embers and calls five marks an ember. I have cut no notch for one. In sixteen years I have never seen an ember paid, and have seen a man try.

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{In the narrow upright hand of the factor’s clerk, written above my first line:} Ember: five marks. Reckoning entered. \emph{Underneath, in mine:} I have left his figure standing and cut a smooth place beneath it. A thing nobody pays has no notch. A smooth place is where it belongs.\end{quote}

\subsection*{What the Post keeps, and what it sells}

\emph{The left figure is what a man is told in Sill or at the Greybank beam. The right is what is given here, at the boards or in the cut. Nothing in the right column is weighed where a clerk can stand.}

Article — As told below — As given here\par

Peat, a barrow — 2 bits in Grain, 5 in Stone — a barrow cut by the buyer, or a day of bought breath; never by the stack, for a stack is a house’s winter\par

A winter stack for two rooms — not cried on any board — thirty marks below; here a term paid in work, and the term has a hook in its mouth\par

Reed bundle, an armful — not on any board — ask the arm that cut it; the arm knows weight and not cost\par

Hemp, a hank — 1 mark at Greybank — 3 bits, in kind; wet hemp weighs more and no buyer has ever noticed why\par

Eels, a basket — 3 bits smoked, 2 salted, at the Fishstairs — 2 bits at the boards, or a stick notched under an apron; the eel-women set their own figure and do not say it\par

Eel-sinew, a hank — not on any board — 1 bit; it sewed these leaves, and the seller would not take the bit back\par

Bog-cow, a milking — 24 marks below for the cow — a share of the morning’s milk, by the morning; no cow has ever stood on a board in this marsh\par

Salt herring — 2 bits at Sill — 3 bits; the salt has been up from the Sallow and knows it\par

Dried leeches, a dozen — 3 bits at the Fishstairs — not sold here; taken off children and counted, which is a different trade\par

Grey, a thimble, bottled — 60 marks in a Court jar, licensed — 4 bits at the Post, in an unmarked jar; the same grey in two vessels, one with a Court name and one with none\par

Thin return, paid by a household — 30 marks to the Court, in labour — a third of that, in eels and peat, and no questions about the source; what comes back is a stranger the house keeps\par

Bought breath, a season — not spoken of below — a term paid in iron or peat, entered in months; the hook is in the word the seller cannot say\par

A child named before the collector comes — no figure — a name said three times into the ground under the boards, which no stick can hold\par

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Cut deep in the margin:} The thin-return row is the only figure on this strip that a man from the Court asked me to change. He wrote \emph{one third of the Court tariff, subject to licence} above it. I cut \emph{no questions} beneath. A man who asks where the warmth came from has decided not to hear it.\end{quote}

There is a figure spoken in the yards at Mud End which is not the printed one. I have heard it and cut nothing for it. I have no beam to weigh it on, and a figure cut without a beam will be asked to read itself aloud at the Cross. Nobody in this marsh wants to stand under that bell.

\subsection*{What is paid in the mud and not entered}

What is taken — What I cut\par

A fine at the reeve’s post — peat to the winter stack — a notch; unpaid, it becomes a term, and the term becomes a measure\par

A feud settled by standing — the side that stands longest is called right by the mud — no figure; a reeve is chosen the same way\par

The draining of a cut — fever follows the ditch up into the water — nothing; the ditch pays and no slate carries it\par

A collector’s boots — children are taught those before their own names — not a due, but a thing every hut knows the price of\par

A name said at home — kept in the house, not entered on any roll — a door, which a knot in the margin stands for\par

The grey in the corner — gathered, bottled and sold at the Post — nothing swept and burnt and called dealt with; there is no Last Day under a board\par

A dry man is a dangerous man, we say, and say it to the water and not to him. He thinks a promise is a thing with a weight he can carry. Here a promise is tied in wool and left where the water can find it.

\subsection*{The dues of the marsh roads}

\emph{The figure asked is what a man is told at the road’s end. The notch is what left his pocket, or what left his back, which is the dearer of the two.}

Road and place — As asked — As cut on my stick\par

Boardwalk from the marsh road to the Post — 1 bit for a dry foot — 1 bit, or a stick notched for a wet one; I do not tell a stranger which planks bear\par

The fifth place at the Post — no plank, no crossing — a smooth place, not a nought; nobody steps on it and nobody’s foot is entered\par

East marsh road to Reedholt, a beast — 1 bit — 1 bit; a man on foot gives a date where a figure is asked and is let go on\par

The peat paths through the cut — paid in peat, by the arm-load — paid in peat, and the load is heavier going out than it came in\par

The smugglers’ paths — no name on any board — a stick left at the cut, notched by the bunch; no questions, and no name\par

The road up to Mud End and Sill, a beast — 1 bit at the marsh road — 1 bit, and the same beast weighed again at the Cross; a road has two ends and both have a hand\par

The road into the Quiet Acre — no gate, no due — nothing cut; there are wells and doorways there and nobody to come back through them\par

The Peat Line, going south into Sere — tribute in eels, paid at the Line — eels by the basket; the South calls it a tariff, and north of it a man is a neighbour, which costs less\par

The drain cuts, after the ditch — no figure — fever, paid by whoever dug and by nobody who entered it\par

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{In the narrow upright hand of the factor’s clerk, against the fifth place:} Vacancy. Nil. \emph{Underneath, in mine:} A nought is a notch cut deep enough to hold a figure. The fifth is a smooth place. I have not cut it, and he has not made it agree with anything.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{In a hand with a little gold in the ink, come down from Sere:} Bought breath entered as seasonal labour; thin return as a graded return, rate one third. \emph{In mine:} A season is a term with a hook in it, and a graded return is a stranger a house must keep. I have left both readings standing, as a board keeps the mark of the water under the mark of the foot.\end{quote}

The roads have two ends and the figures do not agree between them. The tally-man at Greybank cuts what goes out on the quay, the clerk at the Cross cuts what is paid under the pig-board, and I cut what is taken here. Between us a basket of eels is counted twice and a man once, which is the proportion the Court has always liked. The Hearth Road takes nothing at any gate, having taken it at home; the Salt Road calls its toll a contribution freely entered. I have cut neither. They are not roads of this marsh.

\subsection*{The song the board-men carry}

\emph{Said low going in over the Post, never coming out, and said to the plank or the water and not to a man. The last word falls and is not finished.}

\begin{quote}\itshape One for the dry foot and one for the wet,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape a notch for the peat and a cross for the debt;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape four for the boards and a smooth for the fifth,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the mud keeps the count that the reeve does not.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape A bit at the Line and a bit at the plank,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape a stick for the eels and a term for the stack;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the Court writes the return and the river writes none,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the man who comes over is dry till he is not.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Say it to the board, say it down to the water,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the last word falls where the board has no foot;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape a name said at home is a door in the mud,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and a notch in a stick is the whole of the account.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{In the factor’s hand, against the last line:} Three figures entered. \emph{Underneath, in mine:} There are four, and the fourth is a smooth place. He has put a nought where I left the stick bare. A nought can be carried away. The smooth place stays where it is.\end{quote}

\subsection*{The hands that are not mine}

The factor’s clerk writes upright and narrow and leaves the doer out of every sentence, as though a bit could pay itself and a foot could cross a board without a man in it. He put \emph{vacancy} where I keep a place and \emph{subject to licence} where I keep \emph{no questions}. I have set my notches under his words and left both standing. The Sere hand calls a term a season, which is a thing a house can empty and refill; I have called it a term, which a man carries in his mouth and cannot put down. A strip with three hands on it is the only kind a man at these boards will believe. A strip with one hand is a Court notice, and a Court notice has never told a man which plank will bear him.

\subsection*{At the head and in the gutter}

The cross-notch at the head is the fine I paid last Reed, cut with the reeve’s own point so no wet sleeve takes it out; I have not said what it was for, and a cross-cut is the only signature this Post allows. The brown at my thumb is dry mud, not peat; I know the two the way a woman knows her own debt from another’s. The tideline in the gutter is bog-water from the morning the Post stood under and has taken two figures clean off the second leaf. I have not written them back, because a figure with two notches gone is a figure cut slowly, and everything here is cut slowly. The nick is a reed-wolf’s tooth, from a man who paid with his hand still on the knife. The slime at the foot came off a basket set down while a buyer was counting and a seller was not. The dark mark across the third leaf is the wet board laid on the strip to keep it from curling; it looks like a figure and is not one. The grey in the gutter is not mine and not the Court’s, and I have not swept it. The knot through the hole is mine, and holds the word that does not go into the south’s letters. There is no Last Day in a tin under a board.

\subsection*{At the foot, in a hand nobody will own}

\begin{quote}\itshape The board keeps the foot. The stick keeps the debt. The mud keeps both and asks no figure.\end{quote}

I asked the reeve, an eel-trader, and a man come up from Greybank to count the winter peat, and had three answers and no hand. I have left the line where it was written. The strip goes back into the tin under the loose board. Tomorrow a man will come up the marsh road, give me a date where I ask for a figure, set his foot where I do not tell him, and pay a bit for the dry and a notch for the wet, and by evening it will be a thing that was true. I shall cut it under the figure they told him and leave the space between the two.

\clearpage\phantomsection\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{The Dry Tally at Reedholt, Being the Market of the East Marsh in Bits, Sticks and Kind, with the Dues of the Marsh Road, the Boardwalks and the Cuts, Kept Under an Apron and Copied at Greybank}
\CRsheetheading{The Dry Tally at Reedholt, Being the Market of the East Marsh in Bits, Sticks and Kind, with the Dues of the Marsh Road, the Boardwalks and the Cuts, Kept Under an Apron and Copied at Greybank}
{\centering\FellFont\itshape\footnotesize\color{faded} An eel-trader’s tally of what the east marsh fetches and what the ways between its villages take, the figures named into an apron and not across a table, peat weighed at the dry set beside the same peat weighed at the quay, with a column left as a place and not a nought, two corrections in borrowed hands, and one line at the foot in a hand nobody will own · Kept by Meg Sedge, who buys eels on the marsh road and weighs peat at the dry in Reedholt, in the east marsh four leagues east of Sill; set down first in Bone of Y.H. 812, the Thin Year, after the Long Cold, and copied forward at the Opening of the Slates, Ilmen 1, Y.H. 813, onto the back of a spoiled peat-tally at Greybank. It survives folded into oiled sacking under a loose board at the dry, sewn with eel-sinew, with a peat thumb ground into the head, a bog-water tideline that has taken two words clean off the second leaf, dried eel slime at the fore-edge, a fish-hook nick at the head, a grey Ash print along the gutter nobody will own, a press of wet sedge across the third leaf, a knot of grey wool tied through a hole in the first leaf which the writer will not untie, a small pale round place where a collector’s cuff was laid, two corrections in hands that are not the writer’s, and one line at the foot nobody will claim.\par}\medskip
I buy eels on the marsh road and weigh peat at the dry, and I keep the tally under my apron. A figure named aloud in this country grows legs. It walks to Greybank before the man who said it has got his boots dry, and comes back wearing somebody else’s debt. I say mine into the apron, to the creel, to the board under my foot; said looking at a person it becomes a bargain, and I have made enough bargains to know which of them I wanted.

The stick is the honest witness. A notch is still there when the paper has gone soft. Fen Cant is not written, so I set what I can in the south’s letters, learned off an eel-trader who could tally and could not read what he wrote. Where a word will not come I tie a knot in the margin and cut a notch in the edge. A notch is not a letter and a knot is not a figure. Both keep longer than a name.

Nothing here is free. A thing that costs nobody in a marsh has usually cost somebody who cannot write.

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{In the narrow upright hand of a factor’s clerk out of Greybank, written above my first line:} Coin and reckoning entered. Ember: five marks. \emph{Underneath, in mine:} He has written an ember as though a man could carry one up the marsh road in his boot. I have carried peat in my boot and never an ember. He takes the verbs out because a thing always true has no need of anybody in it. I put them back because a woman standing in water to her calf wants to know who is doing the keeping.\end{quote}

Twelve copper bits to a silver mark; twenty silver marks to a gold crown. Crowns come north with the Sere factor and will not change at Greybank, so a man takes the eels and leaves the crown, which is neither generosity nor an insult but the only arithmetic the marsh has ever understood. The Court books in embers and calls five marks an ember; no man has ever exchanged one, and I have left no column for them on my board.

\subsection*{The market at the dry}

\emph{What things fetched at the east-march dry between the last market of Stone and the Opening of the Slates. The left figure is what a man is told at Sill or the quay. The right is what is taken here, with the water still on the boots of the man who brought it.}

Article — As told below — As taken here\par

Peat, a barrow at the dry — 2 bits in Grain, 5 in Stone — 1 bit in Grain, 3 in Stone; dear again at Greybank\par

Reed bundle, an armful, at the Reed Cut — not on any board — ask the arm that carried it; it knows weight and not cost\par

Hemp, a hank, from the east cut — not cried — 2 bits, and the hank goes soft if it has lain\par

Eels, a basket at the boards — 3 bits smoked, 2 salted — 2 smoked, 1 salted, named under the apron and never the same twice\par

Salt, a sack, up from the pans by Greybank — 3 marks at the quay — 4 marks; the extra mark is the road and nobody calls it a tax\par

Dried leeches, a dozen — 3 bits at the Fishstairs — 4 bits here, no questions; no slate asks where they came from\par

Grey, a phial, gathered and bottled at the dry — not sold in Grath — 4 bits, no name; the Court seals the same grey and sells it for sixty\par

Thin return, bought from a household — 30 marks, paid by the district — 10 marks, in peat and iron and labour, which is a third and still a return\par

Bought breath, a season — not spoken of below — paid in iron or in a term of peat; entered in months, not in marks\par

A child’s first bundle, cut in the dark at the Reed Cut — no figure — no figure; the child is not yet of the bog and goes again\par

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Margin:} The peat row at Greybank stands at five bits in Stone and the same barrow is three here. The carter who pays both says the coal did not change and the road did. I have not set his words on the board.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Margin:} I scraped a word I wrote beside the grey row and left the bare square where it was, which is the length of it.\end{quote}

\subsection*{Paid in kind, and not entered}

These stand on the board with a space where the figure should be. The factor’s clerk has more than once put a nought in the space. A nought is a figure and can be carried away; the things below cannot, which is why the marsh keeps them.

What passes — What is given — What I write\par

A knot of grey wool tied for a debt — untied when the debt is paid — the knot, in kind; a knot has no ear and no rate\par

A count-stick cut at the dry — a notch for each barrow — the notch, which the rain does not take out\par

A name said at home before the collector comes — said into the ground beside the hut — nothing; a name at home is a door and not a figure\par

A reed-name said three times to the ground — once to the child, once to the pot, once under the boards — nothing; the third saying is for the child who cannot yet say it\par

A gold crown that will not change at Greybank — left in the coat and carried home — nothing; a thing nobody can spend is a thing somebody has paid for\par

\subsection*{The dues of the roads}

There are no roads in the Fen, only ways trodden long enough to be called roads by people who do not have to walk them. What follows is what the reeve’s man takes, or the factor’s, or the water. The difference between the two is the whole art of crossing a marsh.

\subsection*{The marsh road, east to Greybank}

Peat and eels go up it and salt and iron come back, and the factor’s clerk arrives with his soft cuffs. A cart makes it slowly in Silt and not at all when the high way is under.

Due\par

Cart with a load — 2 bits at the dry, 2 bits more at the quay\par

Beast on the hoof — 1 bit\par

Foot passenger — nothing on a dry day; 1 bit in Silt, when there is a bank to walk on\par

A drove of bog-cows — 4 bits, and the hides counted twice, once at each end\par

\subsection*{The boardwalks to the Standing Post}

The boards bear ten thousand feet and will bear a man’s if he puts his foot where the others went. Outsiders are put up on the walk and are not told which boards are safe, which is not cruelty but information nobody here has had reason to sell.

Due\par

A dry foot — 1 bit to the reeve’s man\par

A wet foot — a marked stick; a notch and no figure\par

A man who stands where he was shown to stand — nothing; the board minds him\par

A man from the Court asking which boards bear — 2 marks, paid before the question, not returned with the answer\par

\subsection*{The dry ways and the cuts}

No gate stands at any of them. Where the cart goes twice, the peat is counted twice, which the factor calls a load and the cut calls weather.

Due\par

Barrow going out to a cut — no gate; weighed at the dry\par

The same barrow weighed again at Greybank — 2 bits, which is the second weighing and not a second barrow\par

A drainage cut — no due; the fever that comes up after it is not entered\par

A ferry over a cut — 1 bit for the boat, nothing for the water\par

\subsection*{The road over the Quiet Acre}

North toward Mud End and Grath the way runs through the ground the Court calls the Empty Cantons and we call the Quiet Acre: wells with no hands at them and doorways in walls nobody lives behind. No reeve sits on that road and no due is asked, which is not the same thing as a road being free.

Due\par

Cart, beast or foot — nothing at any post, there being no post\par

A slate carried across the Acre — no fee; the figure arrives where the slate arrives\par

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Margin:} A due is a figure somebody will stand behind and this road has nobody on it.\end{quote}

\subsection*{The Peat Line, south}

Sere’s northern advance stopped at the Line in Y.H. 634 and the reeves have paid tribute in eels ever since. A man goes down a neighbour and is counted a bowl when he gets there, and the crowns come back north and will not change at Greybank.

Due\par

Tribute in eels, at the Line — a basket of eels, paid by the reeves, entered by nobody\par

A man going south with a hide — 1 bit at the Acre end, and whatever the bowl asks at the other\par

Gold crown carried south — no due; the bowl takes it by emptying it\par

A man coming back from the Line — no due and no guarantee\par

\subsection*{The smuggler’s path, and the winter way}

Due\par

The path through the reedbed — no due and no guarantee; a man comes back with wet boots and no figure\par

The bog when it bears ice — nothing; no reeve will stand on it\par
