He said the eleventh bar went because the cart was carrying twelve and there is always one too many in a count that a man makes by lamplight. He said the term was nearly out. Then he put the flat cup on the mantel and said to the fire that he had been paid for the stone out of his own pocket and paid for the bar out of his own count, and had charged neither to the factor, and that was the whole of what he would give a clerk.

\subsection*{The tally, in charcoal on the way-bill}

I counted the bars into the cart myself when he set it under my door that night, because he asked me to and because I wanted the thing in two hands. I have set down both counts. The last column is not mine.

Where counted — Bars — Who counted — Entered\par

Keld Keep, shaft-mouth weigh — twelve — the reeve’s man — twelve\par

The Bent Nail, by lamplight — eleven — Nils, the carter — eleven\par

The Bent Nail, second count — eleven — I counted after him — eleven\par

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{In the narrow upright hand of the survey-clerk of the Court, struck through the “Entered” column:} Bars entered at source, twelve. Cartage loss: one in twelve. Deduction printed; current. Fifth trace: no entry arising. Measure not stated; party unidentified. Account stands.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Underneath, in mine:} He has put the figure that ought to be there where Nils put the figure that was there. A bar that goes without a man taking it is a loss in my house and a deduction in his. Both are the same bar and they are not the same thing. He has left the fifth out because a fifth has no number and a number is the only thing his hand can carry. I have put the fifth back where Nils left it, at the post where there is a mark and no gate.\end{quote}

\subsection*{At the head and in the margins}

The coal smut at the head is mine, off the sleeve I wipe the lamp glass with; it goes into the grain and no wet cloth takes it out, which is why I sign in coal. The frost-feather between the second and third leaves came up out of the paper in the cold of the room and was gone before I pressed it, and a feather that has been gone by noon is still a feather that was here at midnight. The press of wet wool across the first leaf came off the Warden’s man who held the door while the clerk came in, and I have not written down which man, because he would stop holding doors if I did. The bent nail in the fold is out of this house’s own door; it has been bent since before I came here and I have never straightened it, because a straight nail in a bent hole is a thing that will not hold. The ale ring near the song is Nils’s, and he denied it, and then set his cup in it again. The grey along the gutter came off a cuff that had no business lying in the corner where I keep the tin, and I have not swept it. There is no Last Day at a wayhouse; nothing here is burnt in the morning and called dealt with.

\subsection*{At the foot, in a hand nobody will own}

\begin{quote}\itshape The road keeps what the cart cannot carry.\end{quote}

I asked the survey-clerk, the two of the Warden’s men and a man come down from Greybank with a way-bill, and had four answerings and no hand. I have left the line where it was written. The leaf goes back in the tin beside the wick, and the nail goes back in the fold from which it came, and the road will open at the thaw and the carts will come down and I shall count iron into them that was counted out at the Keep, and the two counts will agree on paper as they always do. On the ninth night of Stone Nils will come in again and take his ale standing, and if he asks for a warm-stone I shall give him one, and I shall not ask him what he wants with it, and I shall count the bars by lamplight as before. The post at the pass has a mark and no gate, and there is a place in every trace where a spare shaft lies. I have stopped asking what goes in it.

\clearpage\phantomsection\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{The Book of the Figure Set Above, Being the Figures Struck and Written Over in the Collectors’ and Assessors’ Books of Sill, Greybank and the Hearthseat, with the Hands That Set Them, the Terse Remarks Left Underneath, the Correcting-Song, and a Line at the Foot Nobody Will Own}
\CRsheetheading{The Book of the Figure Set Above, Being the Figures Struck and Written Over in the Collectors’ and Assessors’ Books of Sill, Greybank and the Hearthseat, with the Hands That Set Them, the Terse Remarks Left Underneath, the Correcting-Song, and a Line at the Foot Nobody Will Own}
{\centering\FellFont\itshape\footnotesize\color{faded} A page from the correction-register of an under-clerk of the College of Assessors in Slate Row of the Hearthseat; the struck figures and the figures written over them copied in the narrow upright hand, the remarks in the hands that made the draws, the verbs put back underneath where they were taken out, one column struck and drawn back again, and a line at the foot nobody will own · Written in Slate Row of the Hearthseat in the last tend of Ash, Y.H. 812, the Thin Year of the Long Cold, and carried forward at the Opening of the Slates, Ilmen 1, Y.H. 813; copied from the correction-leaves of the collector’s table at Sill, the factor’s house at Greybank and the College’s own benches, the upper hand in each case kept apart from the lower and both left standing. It survives folded into a quire of spoiled Weighing notices, kept in the under-clerk’s tin beside the second file: iron-gall worked into the head, slate dust ground into the gutter, iron filings from a tube’s wool wrap caught in the fold, a tallow thumb at the foot, a streak of bone-pale slip along the fore-edge, a green bead of lead glaze in the lower corner, a red clip-score across two rows, a damp tide-line from the sealed-file room along the foot, a small square of bare paper where a word was scraped away, three corrections in borrowed hands, and one line at the foot that has never been claimed\par}\medskip
I keep the book of the figure set above. It is not an account. An account has one figure in each place and one hand to answer for it; this book has two figures in most places and no hand that will own either. When a clerk strikes a figure and writes another over it, the lower one does not go away. It goes on standing beneath the upper one the way an old repair shows through a new one on a vessel, and a man who knows to look for it can read the history of the repair by the shape of what is showing.

I was set to copy corrections in the third year of my teaching. The College teaches that a correction is the removal of an error. I have copied corrections for nine years and have yet to see an error removed. What is removed is the hand that made it. A figure with nobody in it is a figure that can be read aloud in a clean voice and carried home by a household that believes it has been told what it paid.

Twelve copper bits to the silver mark; twenty marks to the Sere crown, which comes north with the factor and does not stay in Grath. The Court books an ember at five marks and no man has exchanged one for the other. I have copied that figure four hundred times and have never once seen the exchange, which is a fact about figures and not about embers. One in twelve is printed on the notice and read twice at the Cross, once for the moot and once for those who came late. I have copied the notice and I have not added it, because adding is a thing done in the Weighing Hall where figures are read aloud and not inspected.

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{At the head of the register, in mine, written small:} The upper figure is copied as it stands. The lower is copied as it was set down. Let both stand, for I am not the hand that chose between them.\end{quote}

\subsection*{The figures, as they stand in the register}

\emph{The first column is what was written. The second is what was written over it. The third is the hand that did the writing over. The remarks are as I copied them, in the hands that made the draws, and are not part of the account.}

Where the figure stood — In the first hand — Set above — The hand that set it — Remark\par

Sill, Stone 12; a child three days returned, Low Kiln — 13 — 12 — The factor’s clerk at Greybank — A vessel three days returned cannot hold thirteen after the draw. Both figures stand. I have asked which is right and neither hand has told me.\par

Sill, Stone 12; the order of the draw — I drew — the measure was drawn; above that, the warmth was entered — A clerk of the College — Three sentences, one figure, no doer. The officer put \emph{I drew} back underneath both.\par

The assessor’s house, Sill; a vessel returned three times — with memory — whole — A clerk of the College — \emph{Whole} is the word the notice prints. \emph{With memory} is what the house calls it when no notice is in the room.\par

The College’s articles, rule 4; the keeping of apprentices — the apprentice is fed — the apprentice is kept — The Provost’s clerk — A boy can be kept and hungry in the same sentence. The passive voice has room for both.\par

Collector’s clerk at Greybank; his own word struck — taken — drawn — The clerk himself, at the officer’s bidding — A taking and a draw are the same heat going the same way. The slate is the difference, and the slate is a piece of stone with a neat hand on it.\par

Keld Keep; a lowlander giving two-and-forty at the gate — two-and-forty, struck through — two-and-forty, in red — The mine-reeve — A check and not a correction. He found no lie and wrote nothing a man could thank him for.\par

The First Seam; a man with two sets of numbers in one arm — the earlier cut — the later cut, in red — The mine-reeve — The later is entered. The earlier stays in the skin. A kindness done with a knife.\par

The chronicle of the Cantons; the oldest ledger — went out in a season of no frost — were gathered into the Hearth — A hand that takes the verbs out — The smoother words go up the road in a clean voice. The rough ones stay where they were said.\par

The Waiting Room leaf; the column of what was said at the water’s edge — four rows of remarks — No such column — A clerk of the College — He counted every row before he wrote that there were none worth entering. A man does not count what he has not looked at.\par

The counting stone at the Nine Wells; the space in the warming-song — four cups left as they are sung — a round nought, and vacancy — A clerk come up from Slate Row — A nought is a number. The space held four cups.\par

The moot book at Sill; five rows of squares — squares, left as squares — nil, entered in each — The moot clerk — A square is where a figure stood and was taken away. A nought is a figure put in its place. The column balances, which is how I know it does not.\par

The consent-book at the watch; one word scraped with a clip — no — a score the length of the word — The keeper of the watch — The word is not entered. The length of it is.\par

Figures struck in this leaf: twelve. Figures set above: twelve. Columns struck: two, both drawn back underneath. Verbs struck: as many as the hand could find.

\subsection*{What the upper hand is for}

The Provost says a sentence true of everybody can be argued with by nobody. It is the whole art of the house. \emph{The measure was drawn} is true of every man who ever drew a measure, and a thing true of everybody can be carried into a Weighing Hall and read over a room without anybody rising to contradict it. \emph{I drew} is true of one man on one morning in one house, and a woman in that house may one day come to the counter and ask which morning and whose house, and there is no column for the answer.

I have put the doers back underneath everywhere. A correction that removes the doer is not a correction of a figure. It is a correction of a person, and the figure is left to stand in the person’s place, which is a garment that fits badly and is worn anyway.

The red hand at Keld Keep is the one honest correction in this book. A cross in red on that slate means the figure has been checked and is to stand. It does not mean the stone is warm, and it does not mean the man stood it. The mine-reeve enters the later number and leaves the earlier in the skin, and a clerk who can keep two truths without calling either a lie has a busy morning and a quiet night. In this office a correction is a thing done with a pen and a cuff, and the cuff is washed until it goes soft, which is as near as a clean hand comes to a stain.

\subsection*{The column struck and drawn back}

Beside each row I keep the name of the hand that set the upper figure. I set no heading over it. A heading would make it an account, and an account is a thing a man may be called to answer for, and this house has answered for enough this year.

The Provost’s clerk borrowed the register on a morning in Ash and struck the column through from the first row to the last, and wrote \emph{No such column} above it in his narrow upright hand. He had to count the rows before he could write that there were none worth entering, and I watched him do it, standing as he stands, with his cuff gone soft and his ink settled in two fingers. I drew the column back underneath and left his words standing over it. He struck a verb also, where I wrote \emph{the clerk set above}, and set \emph{the figure was corrected} over it. I put my hand back beneath and left his figure where he set it. A sentence with nobody in it is a sentence no woman can ask about, and women ask about these corrections in the end, always at the door, always after the register is put away.

The other hand is a tall leaning one out of the factor’s house at Greybank. Against the row for the child of Low Kiln it wrote \emph{adjustment on re-examination, figure confirmed}, and underlined the word twice. Both stand. \emph{Confirmed} is true in a room with a door shut, and the child was worse before dusk.

\subsection*{The song the correctors carry}

\emph{Sung low at the correction-bench in the third year, never at the Weighing, and the second verse left out when a clerk from the factor’s house is within hearing of the bench.}

\begin{quote}\itshape One for the slate and one for the hand,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape one for the figure set above;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the bottom one stays where it came in\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the top one gets read aloud.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape I drew, it was drawn, the warmth was entered ---\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape three sentences and one man;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the clip leaves red and the tube leaves grey,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the cuff stays soft through the Weighing.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Four cups are stopped and the space is nought,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the square is a figure gone;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the hand that strikes does not ask whose hand,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the hand underneath knows.\end{quote}

The woman who sang this to me at the bench would not sing the last line while the Provost’s clerk stood in the door, which is how I know the last line is the one that matters. I have copied it as it came and put no gloss on it. A corrector who explains a song has begun to write a sermon, and sermons get copied.

\subsection*{In the head and in the gutter}

The iron-gall at the head is mine, made by holding a quire open through a market morning; there are clerks in this city who can tell a copyist by his thumb before he has spoken a word. The slate dust in the gutter came off a surveyor who leaned over my table with the south-road dirt still on his cuffs and would not sit down. The filings in the fold came out of the wool sleeve a collector set beside the register while he gave me a figure; there is always a little iron in the fold, and it has never once drawn the warmth out of the paper, which is the only kindness iron has shown this leaf. The tallow thumb at the foot is mine, from holding the lamp low while a woman in the sealed-file room said something I wanted the end of; she did not tell me the end. The streak of slip came off the forearms of a thrower come up from High Kiln who set her slate beside mine to wait for a figure and took it away again. The green bead is lead glaze and not slip; a girl leaned over to see the correcting with the sweetness still at one corner of her mouth, touched the paper, said nothing, and went back down the terrace. The red score across the two Keld rows was made by a man showing his brother how a clip bites; both were honest men afterwards and one has a dead hand. The tide-line along the foot came from the sealed-file room, which is colder than the rest of Slate Row and always has been. The small bare square in the lower margin is where I scraped a word away with a knife and put no other in its place. I have not written the word back, and I have not forgotten it. On the Last Day they sweep the corners and burn what they find in the morning and call it dealt with. There is no Last Day for a correction-register.

\subsection*{At the foot, in a hand nobody will own}

\begin{quote}\itshape The College keeps the upper figure. The yard keeps the lower. The room where both were spoken keeps neither.\end{quote}

I asked the Provost’s clerk, a collector come up from the Cross, and a woman who stood at the counter about her house, and had three answers and no hand. I have left the line where it was written.

The register goes back into the tin beside the second file. Tomorrow a clerk will strike a verb in another book and set a smoother one above it, and I shall copy both, and put the hand back where it was taken out. The figure at the top will be read in a clean voice at the Weighing, and the figure underneath will stay where it came in, and the space between them will have no signature, as it has had none for nine years and will have none in the tenth.

\clearpage\phantomsection\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{The Sermon at the Fire-Shrine, Being What the Bowl-Priest Said Over the Four Bowls at the Ember House on a Name-Day in Smoke of Y.H. 812, with the Pouring-Song Left as It Is Sung, the Bowls in a Wine-List, the Gold Hand Above, a Bond-Woman’s Charcoal Beneath, and a Line at the Foot Nobody Will Own}
\CRsheetheading{The Sermon at the Fire-Shrine, Being What the Bowl-Priest Said Over the Four Bowls at the Ember House on a Name-Day in Smoke of Y.H. 812, with the Pouring-Song Left as It Is Sung, the Bowls in a Wine-List, the Gold Hand Above, a Bond-Woman’s Charcoal Beneath, and a Line at the Foot Nobody Will Own}
{\centering\FellFont\itshape\footnotesize\color{faded} A sermon of the Spending preached at the fire-shrine of the Ember bowl-house in the Bowl of Sere; the sayings in the long-vowelled courtesy of the south set down in Grathic letters by a northern bond-woman of the wine-press, the pouring-song with the fourth silence left as it is sung, the four bowls in a wine-list table, one correction in the thin gold of the house tally-clerk, one in the narrow upright Ledgerhand of a factor’s clerk at Greybank, and one line at the foot in a hand nobody will own · Preached by Valen Openhand, the Bowl-Priest, come down from the open court of the Bowl of Sere to the small fire-shrine within the Ember house, on the name-day of the house’s youngest daughter in Smoke of Y.H. 812, when the burning winds stood and the fourth bowl was set out as it is set out at every feast; written that evening by a northern bond-woman who keeps the wine-list at the house press, in charcoal on the back of a wine-list spoiled at the third hour, folded into oiled silk and kept within the clay bowl in which the shrine’s fire is carried at the turning of the year. It survives with gold dust worked into the head off the clerk’s cuff, yellow dust of the burning winds ground into the fold, a ring of warm wine on the second leaf, an olive thumb at the head, a grain husk stuck fast in the gutter, a flake of myrrh from a burial cloth shut in the crease, a scorched corner where the leaf lay near the fire, a shard of green northern glaze pressed into the lower corner, a gold crown flattened between the third and fourth leaves, the gold correction standing above the charcoal, the Greybank hand set above both, and a line struck through and written again very small underneath in a hand that has never come forward. Copied at Greybank in Ash of Y.H. 812 into the factor’s file of southern sayings, with the verbs put back and the fourth silence left the length it is sung.\par}\medskip
I keep the wine-list at the press in the Ember house and nobody asked me for this. I am north-born and write in charcoal; the house writes in thin gold and would not set a bond-woman’s hand among its contracts. I write on the back of a leaf spoiled at the third hour, because a spoiled paper is a paper nobody will borrow for a column. He spoke to the fire, then to the four bowls, then to the girl whose name-day it was, and last to the company.

The gold at the head came off the clerk’s cuff; the yellow in the fold is the dust of the burning winds and I have not shaken it out. The wine-ring is the third bowl. The myrrh came off a burial cloth whose family bought back the ash and is called generous here. The green shard is from a bowl of my own country, cracked in the first heat after I was brought south.

\subsection*{The manner of the shrine, as the house keeps it}

\emph{Written small, from watching, not from any order the Council of Bowls has printed.}

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item The fire is carried in a clay bowl and set in the wall-niche before the first voice, fed with oil and a little myrrh. No priest touches it; the keeper of the fire does, and she has not been through the door where the numbers are read.

\item Four bowls stand with their lips to the fire. Three go round. The fourth stands where it was set and is carried away full. Do not look into it, and do not ask whose debt it holds. Ask the bowl.

\item Say the sayings to the fire or to the bowl. Said looking at a person, a saying becomes a lawsuit.

\item Open the vowels and throw the ends of sentences into the fire; the listener supplies the last of the thought. A northerner who says the whole of a sentence has said too much.

\item Clap at the debt and at the new writing, softly at the old slate when it burns. A guest who claps only at the burning has not understood.

\item The Sun-Emperor’s act is announced at the third hour in a court three streets away. Stop until it has passed. Begin again after.

\item A slave is given a clay-name by the house and the old name is forbidden. In some houses it is written inside a bowl which the slave is never allowed to look into.

\end{itemize}

He said the last twice, once to the fire and once to a woman at the lower table given three copper bits for standing. I have not joined the two sayings.

\subsection*{The sermon, as he said it}

\subsection*{Of the fire}

He put his hand above the clay bowl and warmed it without touching. His cuffs were clean and his fingers full.

“A vessel was made to pour,” he said. “The cup that keeps is the cup that sours. A life hoarded is a life wasted. Say it over the wine. Do not say it over the accounts, where it would be a very different sentence and might cost somebody a province.”

This fire is fed with oil, and the oil was bought, and the myrrh was bought, and somebody chose to spend it on a flame out before the wine is cold. He spoke in the open voice of the courts, with the ends thrown away; the room leaned after him. I wrote the endings in where I heard them, which a Sere clerk would not do.

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Margin, in charcoal, mine:} He had three rings on the hand he warmed. He said \emph{a life hoarded} while a woman at the lower table held a bowl she was not permitted to empty. Both stood in the room. I have not put one over the other.\end{quote}

\subsection*{Of the four bowls}

He turned the first bowl a quarter, the way a potter shows a buyer the foot of a cup.

“This one is for the house,” he said. “The debt is named and the bowl goes round. The second is for the fire. The third is for the slate. They go round and are poured, and nobody is the poorer, because what is poured was going to be spent.”

He came to the fourth and stopped. It stood full, with the light going along the rim.

“This one is nobody’s,” he said. “It is set out at every feast and carried away full. Nobody pours it and nobody says whose debt it holds. If the house knew, it would pour it. It does not know, which is a mercy of the Spending and not a failure of the house.”

A girl asked what was in it. He turned his head toward the fire. “Ask the bowl,” he said. She asked the bowl; the bowl answered as bowls answer. I have set the fourth in the table below where a figure should stand. The clerk has set a figure beside it. The two have not touched.

\subsection*{Of the name}

The girl whose name-day it was stood at the end of the row in a dress gone stiff with gold thread. Seven names had been given her and the house kept one.

“A name is a bowl,” the priest said. “The more names, the more pourings; the more of a person has been used, the more generous the house has been. Do not be sorry for the six. They were spent on you.”

The girl looked at the fourth bowl and then at her mother, who could not go through the door where her numbers were read. Her mother looked at the fire. I have written the order and not what it means.

I have two names. One was given me in the north and is forbidden here, and one is clay and belongs to this house. I wrote the first inside a bowl in my first winter and have never looked into it, which is the courtesy of this country.

\subsection*{Of the burning}

“Burn the slate by lot,” he said. “Write it again before the wine is cold.”

This year it was the household of a woman three places down from me. She wept while the slate burned, the room was kind, and then applauded the new writing. The clerk wrote above that an instrument was discharged and a fresh obligation acknowledged, a true thing in a language nobody at the press speaks.

A guest asked whether a debt had been forgiven or a province ruined.

“Yes,” the priest said.

The guest asked which he meant.

“Measure for measure,” the priest said, and went back to his wine.

The guest asked me afterward and I told him I did not read the accounts of this house. He said I was fortunate. I have thought about that word more than about the fire.

\subsection*{Of them that are emptied}

The returned woman was brought in after the third bowl. Solene Ember was returned whole here in Y.H. 799, Y.H. 804 and Y.H. 809, and the house speaks of the fourth as a man looks forward to a harvest he has already sold. She turned a cup a quarter, set it back and said nothing, and the company applauded her.

“A beautiful return is proof of a generous house,” the priest said. “A life poured out gloriously comes back beautiful. A life kept in a corner comes back thin, and thin returns are for the north, who buy them.”

A thin northerner stood at the lower table with three copper bits under his palm. I kept my hand on my wine-list and did not look at him.

“If there is a generosity in this world,” the priest said, “it is in the pouring, and the pouring does not stop to ask who brought the wine.” He said it to the fire. I have set it down as it was said and not as it was meant.

\subsection*{Of the door}

A woman of this house may own the bowls and the slaves and her husband’s debt, but not go through the door where her numbers are read. The priest called it a courtesy with a door in it: a door is not an argument and will not fight anybody.

I have stood outside with a wine-list in my hand and heard nothing but a man reading figures in a low patient way. The wood is ordinary wood and there is a latch on the inside. On the last name-day a woman put her hand to the latch and took it away without turning it, and went back and clapped at the burning of a slate that was hers. I have not written which woman.

\subsection*{The pouring-song}

\emph{Sung at the tread of the press, not at the feast. The fourth verse is said to the bowl and not to the company. There is a silence before it, the length of the fourth bowl standing full, and I have left it the length it is sung.}

\begin{quote}\itshape We tread the press and the wine comes warm,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape a neck for the house and a neck for the fire;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the slate goes down on a name-day’s lot\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the fourth goes back to the shelf.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape We clap for the debt and the slate,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape we buy back the ash at the price of the grain;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the year we burned under one we loved\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape was a year we had meant to spend anyway.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Here the fourth bowl stands. No sound.}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Three are poured and carried away;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape one stands where it stood at the first of the day.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Ask it what holds it and ask it why\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape it goes back full when the others go dry.\end{quote}

A girl from the press asked what the silence was for. Nobody answered her. The clerk put a round mark against it later and at Greybank they put a nought.

\subsection*{The four bowls, as the wine-list keeps them}

\emph{Figures that come in here in a coat go out again in a new slate. These I have set down where they stood.}

Bowl — Poured for — What was said over it — What was entered\par

The first — the house, at the name-day — the debt named aloud — obligation acknowledged, current\par

The second — the fire in the niche — the act of the Sun-Emperor — act recorded, no figure\par

The third — the slate — \emph{burn the slate by lot; write it again} — one discharged, one written\par

The fourth — nobody — nothing — a reserve retained, no charge against it\par

The slate burned — a woman three places down — she wept; the room applauded — affect observed, not entered\par

My mistress can set a season to every feast before this one, and I have not written the seasons, because a row of seasons is a thing a clerk can carry away and a bowl is not. The crown in the fold is one the guest gave the girl for standing, and it is the only coin here nobody has tried to enter.

\subsection*{What the gold hand did}

The tally-clerk borrowed the leaf after the third hour, being a man who cannot leave paper alone. He writes in thin gold and takes the verbs out as though a verb were a thing a man could spill from a cuff.

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item At \emph{a vessel was made to pour}: \emph{vessels are made for use}, underlined twice.

\item At \emph{the cup that keeps is the cup that sours}: \emph{retention produces diminution}, which leaves out the souring and the cup together.

\item At \emph{she wept and the room applauded}: \emph{affect observed, not entered}.

\item At \emph{measure for measure}: \emph{equivalence recorded}, with the equivalence underlined.

\item Against the fourth bowl: \emph{a reserve retained; no charge against it}, a true thing in the language of a counting room, with the bowl still standing in it.

\end{itemize}

I have left his hand above mine and my words underneath, as the new slate lies over the burned one. He takes the verbs out because a thing always true has no need of them; I put them back because there is always a hand.

\subsection*{What the northern hand did}

A factor’s clerk at Greybank wrote on the copy in the narrow upright hand. He has never been south.

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item At the fire-shrine: \emph{private fire, no public charge}.

\item At the fourth bowl: a round nought and \emph{vacancy}, which is a number and is not a bowl.

\item At \emph{a life hoarded is a life wasted}: \emph{doctrine, not entered}. He asked whether the one in twelve of the northern notice was read in this house. I told him it was not, and he wrote nothing, which is the only honest line in his hand.

\end{itemize}

I have left his hand above both, as a new account is laid over an older one and the older is not asked to stand up.

\subsection*{At the head and in the gutter}

The gold will not wash out of the grain: a contract is meant to last and a saying to be carried. The yellow in the fold is the burning wind, and I should rather it stayed, because a woman who shakes a leaf is pretending she has been somewhere else. The wine-ring belongs to the third hour. The myrrh is from a cloth I put my hand on because a woman there put hers there first; I have not washed the smell out. The crown between the third and fourth leaves is the only thing in this book nobody has entered, which is not the same as nobody having paid for it.

\subsection*{At the foot, in a hand nobody will own}

Struck through once and written again underneath, very small:

\begin{quote}\itshape Three were poured and the fourth went back full.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape The room applauded the debt and the debt stayed in the room.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape A bowl that keeps is called generous and a bowl that pours is called spent.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape The fire takes the names and nobody asks who brought the oil.\end{quote}

I asked the girl from the press, the woman who keeps the fire, the clerk and a factor from Greybank, and had four answerings and no hand. I have left the line struck through and standing, the only honest way to keep a sentence you cannot sign.

The leaf goes back into the oiled silk and the silk into the clay bowl. Next name-day three bowls will go round and one will stand, and the clerk will take the verbs out and I shall put them back, and the fourth bowl will go away full as it came, and nobody in this house will ask it what it holds.

\clearpage\phantomsection\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{The Firing Cup, Being the Drinking Song of Low Kiln at the Draw, with the Order of the Cup, the Verses as They Go Round, a Kiln-Master’s Correction in Broad Charcoal, a Clerk’s Figures in the Narrow Upright Hand, a Gloss from the Woman Who Keeps the Birth-Slates, and One Verse at the Foot in a Hand Nobody Will Own}
\CRsheetheading{The Firing Cup, Being the Drinking Song of Low Kiln at the Draw, with the Order of the Cup, the Verses as They Go Round, a Kiln-Master’s Correction in Broad Charcoal, a Clerk’s Figures in the Narrow Upright Hand, a Gloss from the Woman Who Keeps the Birth-Slates, and One Verse at the Foot in a Hand Nobody Will Own}
{\centering\FellFont\itshape\footnotesize\color{faded} A kiln-house drinking song for the end of a firing, taken down from the mouths of the yard in the low half-sung speech of Grath; the cup passed hand to hand and no man pouring for himself, the verses said to the kiln mouth and not to the company, a kiln-master’s broad charcoal set above, a factor’s clerk’s figures in narrow upright Ledgerhand above that, a hearth-maid’s small careful gloss in the margin, and a last verse in a hand nobody will claim · Set down in Low Kiln of Sill in Ember and Smoke of Y.H. 812, the Thin Year of the Long Cold, at the draw of the Vail kiln and three firings after, by Tessa of the Racks, a woman who turns the drying racks two doors up the Clay Yard and keeps the firing cup; written in charcoal and tallow on the back of a kiln tally spoiled by a wet thumb, sewn with iron wire into a fold of grey sacking and kept in a meal crock behind the lowest rack. Carried up the clay road in Ilmen of Y.H. 813 and copied at Greybank onto the back of a Court grain-warrant voided by the Long Cold. It survives soft at the fold and gritty with slip, with a grey curl of fired clay at the head, a thumb of tallow, a brown crust-grease print on the second leaf, a ring of small ale gone sour where the cup stood from the first verse to the last, a green bead of lead glaze pressed into the lower corner where a girl with sweetness at her mouth leaned over to see the writing, a scorch where the leaf lay too near the kiln mouth, grey Ash along the gutter that nobody will own, a twist of grey wool through a hole in the first leaf which the writer will not untie, two corrections set one above the other, a gloss in the margin, and a verse at the foot in a hand that has never come forward\par}\medskip
I keep the cup at the firing. It is not my cup. It stands on the shelf above the racks with a thumb-wide flaw in the lip and comes down only when the kiln is drawn, and I set it on the bench and go away, and the cup does the calling. There is no word in our yard for a man who pours for himself, which is a mercy, because there is a word for almost everything else.

I set this down because a man come up from Slate Row stood at the yard well and asked what the women sang when the last pot was out. He wrote the answer in a book while I was still saying it, and what he wrote had no verbs in it and no hands, and he went away thanking me. What follows is what we said before he came and what we said again after he had gone back over the north bridge. I have put his hand above mine where he set it, and the kiln-master’s above his, and the hearth-maid’s in the margin where she wrote it, and my words under all three, as the floor keeps the ash and the foot that raised it.

The charcoal at the head is mine. I held the tally down on the kiln shelf in the draught off the yard door and did not know I had marked it.

\subsection*{The order of the cup}

\emph{Written small on the back of the tally, before the verses, in the hand I use for the rack count.}

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item Sung at the draw, after the last pot is out and before the embers are raked. A song that runs into the raking is a song with a figure in it, and no figure has ever come out of this yard singing.

\item Standing, with faces to the kiln mouth. Said looking at a person it becomes an argument, and there is enough argument in Low Kiln over the winter firing without carrying it home.

\item One cup goes round. A woman sets it down; the next woman lifts it. Nobody pours for herself, and nobody wipes the rim, which is how a flaw in the lip comes to be known by everybody without being named.

\item The first pour goes to the fire, the second to the pot that answered full, the third to the pot that answered flat. The fourth stands where it stands and is drunk by nobody, and is carried back to the shelf still full.

\item Stop while the bell goes at the Cross. It is counting a different thing. Begin again when the stroke after the gap has gone.

\item The last verse is said twice, once to the fire and once into the bench. The second saying is for the ones who carried in and did not carry out. They are not named in it and their places are not filled.

\end{itemize}

\subsection*{The song}

\emph{The cup goes left. The kiln breathes behind the wall. Refrain after every verse, said low into the bench.}

\begin{quote}\itshape Round with the cup and round with the fire,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape a whole pot sings and a cracked one lies;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape one in twelve goes up the road\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the rest goes round the yard.\end{quote}

\subsection*{I. Of the cup}

\begin{quote}\itshape This cup came down off the highest shelf\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape with a thumb-wide flaw in the lip;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape we keep it for the firing and for nothing else,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and a woman who asks why may carry her own.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Round with the cup and round with the fire...}\end{quote}

\subsection*{II. Of the first pour}

\begin{quote}\itshape The first pour goes to the fire, not to a face;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the damper’s shut and the fire keeps its mouth.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape It takes what we set to it and gives back heat\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and never once says what it kept.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Round with the cup and round with the fire...}\end{quote}

\subsection*{III. Of the whole pot}

\begin{quote}\itshape The second to the pot that answered full,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape knocked on the bench with a clean whole note;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape it’ll hold water till the day it won’t,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and that day’s another firing’s business.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Round with the cup and round with the fire...}\end{quote}

\subsection*{IV. Of the flat one}

\begin{quote}\itshape The third to the pot that gave back flat,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape set by the door with the crack showing;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape don’t mend it pretty and don’t put it back ---\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape an honest fault’s a thing the neighbours know.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Round with the cup and round with the fire...}\end{quote}

\subsection*{V. Of the backs and the hands}

\begin{quote}\itshape Here’s to the backs that the wet pots bent,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape here’s to the hands that went in and stayed;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the kiln doesn’t ask whose back it was\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the cup doesn’t know who’s drinking.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Round with the cup and round with the fire...}\end{quote}

\subsection*{VI. Of the bell}

\begin{quote}\itshape The bell at the Cross goes four and four\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and stops where the fifth should stand;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape we drink to the gap and say nothing over it,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the way the yard says nothing at the grey.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Round with the cup and round with the fire...}\end{quote}

\subsection*{VII. Of the figure}

\begin{quote}\itshape One in twelve goes up the road in a clean hand,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape printed and current and read twice aloud;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape a figure you hear isn’t a figure you paid ---\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape pass the cup. It’s the only figure here.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Round with the cup and round with the fire...}\end{quote}

\subsection*{VIII. Of the going of the light}

\begin{quote}\itshape There’s grey in the corner where the promise went;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the broom goes round it, the bucket goes round it,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the house goes round it at the going of the light;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape we leave it on the Last Day and burn it in the morning.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Round with the cup and round with the fire...}\end{quote}

\subsection*{IX. The last verse}

\begin{quote}\itshape So pass it left. Don’t pour for yourself.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape The pot keeps the note and the cup keeps the crack,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the yard keeps the place where the flat one stood,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the name goes round when the cup goes round.\end{quote}

There is a space before the last refrain in the singing. I have left it on the tally. It is the length of a name and of nothing else, and the cup goes around it the way the broom goes around the grey. The refrain is then said twice, the second time into the bench, and nobody lifts the bench to see what was said to it.

\begin{quote}\itshape *Round with the cup and round with the fire,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape a whole pot sings and a cracked one lies;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape one in twelve goes up the road\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the rest goes round the yard.*\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{The rest goes round the yard. The rest goes round.}\end{quote}

\subsection*{What the kiln-master set above it}

The broad charcoal belongs to the man who fires the Vail kiln. He marks hands with it and writes as though he were cutting a notch. He borrowed the leaf on a morning when the kiln was going down and returned it with the fold changed.

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item At \emph{a whole pot sings and a cracked one lies}: “A pot that sings before the firing is green and will slump. There’s no note to argue with till it’s been through.”

\item At \emph{an honest fault’s a thing the neighbours know}: “Set it by the door. Don’t leave it where a buyer can knock it.”

\item At \emph{don’t mend it pretty}: “Mend it how you like, but let the seam show. There’s a cupworm in this yard that bores from inside and leaves a pot looking sound.”

\item At \emph{the kiln doesn’t ask whose back it was}: “It doesn’t. That’s why the count’s kept at the door and not at the mouth.”

\end{itemize}

I have left his corrections standing above my words. He is right about the pot and wrong about the song, which was never only about pots, and he has read every line of it with one eye on the kiln. He did not sit down while he wrote, and said a song that had never been in a kiln-house was not worth the paper.

\subsection*{What the clerk did}

A clerk of the factor’s house at Greybank borrowed the leaf on an Account-day, being a man who cannot let paper lie. He writes in the narrow upright hand, with the verbs taken out as though a verb were a thing a man could hide in a cuff and carry past a weigh.

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item At \emph{the fire keeps its mouth} he wrote \emph{fuel consumed; no entry}, which leaves the fire standing and takes the mouth away.

\item At \emph{it takes what we set to it and gives back heat} he set \emph{heat transferred to chamber, current}, and underlined it twice.

\item At \emph{one in twelve goes up the road} he wrote \emph{deduction one in twelfths, read twice, current}, as though the reading and the paying were the same act performed in two places.

\item At \emph{a figure you hear isn’t a figure you paid} he wrote \emph{figures of account, not of price}. I have never argued less with a sentence of his.

\item At \emph{the cup’s got a lip and the lip’s got a flaw} he set \emph{vessel fractured; retained in service}, which is the truest and coldest thing on the leaf.

\item Where the space stands before the last refrain he put a round nought and wrote \emph{vacancy} beside it. He has put a figure where a name should stand, which is the whole art of that hand.

\end{itemize}

I have put my words back underneath and left his standing above. He takes the verbs out because a thing always true has no need of them. I put them back because a woman at the end of a firing does not know she is hearing something always true, and wants to know which hand held the cup before hers.

\subsection*{What the hearth-maid put in the margin}

The small careful hand is Alda’s, who keeps the birth-slates for the district and carries soap and warm milk in the same order every morning. She wrote in the margin because she would not have her words on the face of the leaf where a collector might read them going past. I have copied her as she set them down.

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item At \emph{the first pour goes to the fire, not to a face}: “Same order at a birth. The hand goes to the slate before it goes to the child. Don’t make more of it than that.”

\item At \emph{here’s to the hands that went in and stayed}: “A round forgets who it was for by the third cup. Names are better. Ask me why I say that and I’ll give you a date.”

\item At \emph{we drink to the gap}: “The fifth isn’t a drink. It’s a place. Leave it the length it is.”

\item At \emph{an honest fault’s a thing the neighbours know}: “A child came back to us this year who liked the smell of wet clay before he had seen a pot. I have written that nowhere else. Keep it where a collector’s thumb won’t go.”

\item At the space before the last refrain: “The third saying is not for the pot and not for the fire. I have been asked whose it was and answered with a date. Both stand.”

\end{itemize}

\subsection*{At the head and in the gutter}

The grey curl at the head is off the kiln shelf and went into the grain when I held the leaf down. The tallow is mine, off the lamp I keep turned low behind the racks. The crust-grease on the second leaf is from a browned edge laid down while I was telling a girl to eat and she would not. The ring is small ale, set down at the first verse and taken up at the last, by which time it had gone the colour of the pot it stood on. The green bead came off a woman from High Kiln who stood with the sweetness at one corner of her mouth, leaned over to see the writing, touched the leaf and went back up the terrace without buying. The scorch took one word off the sixth verse and I have not written it back, because a verse with a word gone is a verse said slowly, and ours are all said slowly. The grey along the gutter came off a cuff laid where no cuff has business lying; nobody will own it, and there is no Last Day behind a rack. The twist of grey wool through the hole is mine, tied for the line I could not put down. I will not untie it.

\subsection*{At the foot, in a hand nobody will own}

\begin{quote}\itshape The fire keeps what it’s given. The pot keeps the note.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape The cup goes round and the name goes round,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the slate goes up the road with neither.\end{quote}

I asked a woman at the racks, the kiln-master and a man come up from Greybank, and had three answers and no hand. I have left the verse where it was written.

The crock goes back behind the lowest rack and the cup goes back on its shelf with the thumb-wide flaw uppermost. Tomorrow the kiln will be drawn again and the cup will come down and go round, and the fourth pour will stand where it stood and be carried away full, and if the clerk borrows the leaf let him take the verbs out. The next hand will put them back, and wet the rim before it sings.

\clearpage\phantomsection\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{The First Book of the Chronicle of the Keeping, Being an Extract Concerning the Finding of the Chamber Already Warm, the First Returns of Y.H. 3, the Setting Up of the Three Offices, the Printing of the Figure One in Twelve, the Four Wells Sealed, and the Line of Empty Squares; with the Kindling Song, the Table of the Founding Years, Two Corrections in the Upright Hand, and a Line at the Foot Nobody Will Own}
\CRsheetheading{The First Book of the Chronicle of the Keeping, Being an Extract Concerning the Finding of the Chamber Already Warm, the First Returns of Y.H. 3, the Setting Up of the Three Offices, the Printing of the Figure One in Twelve, the Four Wells Sealed, and the Line of Empty Squares; with the Kindling Song, the Table of the Founding Years, Two Corrections in the Upright Hand, and a Line at the Foot Nobody Will Own}
{\centering\FellFont\itshape\footnotesize\color{faded} A keeper’s extract from the oldest volume of the chronicle of the Keeping, being the first book, which lies nearer the fire than any other book in the Hearthseat; the founding years in the oldest and smoothest Ledgerhand, the rough first entries showing through under it where the ink has gone brown, the figure set on the notice in a clean round hand, the three offices entered as a list of rooms and duties, the kindling song taken down from a woman who had sung it at the grate for forty years, two corrections in the narrow upright hand of the College, and a line at the foot in a hand that has never come forward · Written at the Hearthseat in the Weighing Hall, beside the grating of cold iron, in Ash of Y.H. 812, the Thin Year, by the keeper of the first book, who appears on no roll and signs only \emph{the office of the first book}; copied from the volume kept in a box on the inner side of the Hall since before the College was built, and carried forward at the Opening of the Slates into Y.H. 813. It survives as five leaves of thick vellum gone brittle at the head from the heat that comes up through the grating, sewn with iron wire into a board cover warped out of true: the ink at the head the colour of weak tea and the ink in the gutter still black, soot from the grate worked into the grain of the first leaf, a coal gone cold shut in a nail-hole of the cover which nobody will say came from the first fire, slate dust along the fold where a surveyor laid his slate and was told to move it, a tallow thumb at the second corner, a ring where a cup of small ale stood from the first copying to the last, a square of bare vellum where a word was scraped away and not written back, the figure struck and written again beneath in the keeper’s own hand, two corrections in the upright College hand, a grey Ash print along the outer fold which the keeper did not make and has not swept, and the line at the foot\par}\medskip
I keep the first book, which is the book the others are copied from and the one no man asks to see. The chronicle of the Keeping has a continuator who writes the later years in the roll-room under the narrow window; I write the beginning in a box on the inner side of the Weighing Hall, where the heat comes up out of the Keel and goes into the paper and will not come out again. There is a grating between me and the fire and a rule that no priest touches it, and I have sat here copying for eleven years and have never once been asked to move my table.

This book has been copied more times than any other book in Sarn, and every copy is smoother than the one before it, as a pot is glazed again and again until no clay can be seen. I have done the copying as I was told and I am good at it. I can take a rough year and lay a clean one over it so neatly that a man reading Standing here would not know there was a year underneath. It is only that the brown ink comes back in the thin light before Kindling, when the fire is low and the vellum cools enough to show what is under the glaze. I have kept what shows. I have not put it in the year.

\subsection*{The founding as the book has it}

\emph{Copied from the vellum. The smooth hand is above; where the brown shows through I have set it beneath, in the order the words stand on the leaf and not in the order I would put them.}

\textbf{B.H. 400 to 1, which the temple calls the Broken Years and the people of Keld the Long Want.} The temple tells that the dead went into the Waste and did not come back, and that vessels broke and nothing mended them. The book enters almost nothing, which is the easiest way of entering a thing. What survives out of that age is bowls and slates. The bowls are well made. The slates are accounts in a hand no living scholar can read, though the Vorr claim to recognise the numbers. I have entered the bowls first, because a bowl is a thing a man can hold and the claim of the Vorr is not.

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{In the upright hand of the College, against this entry:} The long want is a mystery of the faith. The bowls are not entered.\end{quote}

I have left the bowls standing under the mystery. A bowl that held soup in a country with no Return is a bowl that held soup, and there is no hand in the College clever enough to take the soup out of it.

\textbf{Y.H. 1, the lighting.} The temple says the Nine Who Kept lit the Hearth with a coal brought from the first fire. The oldest hand in this book says only: \emph{the chamber was found already warm.} The entry has been copied four times and each copy is smoother than the one before. I have copied it five. In the fifth the two sentences stand together. No copy before mine has done it and none after mine will, since I am the last hand that reads the brown by the low fire.

There is a coal shut in a nail-hole of the cover. It is cold. It has been cold every time I have opened this book for eleven years, and no man will say whether it was lit. I asked the continuator when he came up to borrow the leaf. He said a coal eight hundred years in a box is a coal and nothing more, and wrote nothing about it, which is his craft and not a lie.

\textbf{Y.H. 3.} The first Returns are recorded. Entered as \emph{the mercy of the Hearth made known in the keeping of the dead}. Under the brown: a collector drew the first measure with a tube of cold iron and a woman stood by with an infant and did not cross herself, being paid by the hour. I have set both sentences down. The mercy entered the book in a clean hand on the third day of the year; the tube entered it under the glue of the binding, where the College hand has never thought to look.

\textbf{Y.H. 8 to 12.} Three offices are set up: assessors to value a life, collectors to draw the measure, bankers to press it into an infant. Entered as \emph{the several offices of the Keeping established in order}. There is no order in the brown. The three come on the same leaf, written at one sitting, and the word \emph{several} has been put in over a word scraped away, of which a square is left. I have not written the scraped word back. A square in this book is a thing a reader can put his finger on, and I have no licence to fill a man’s finger.

\textbf{Y.H. 40.} The deduction is fixed at one part in twelve and printed on the Weighing notices, where it stands after eight hundred years. The figure in the book is in a round clean hand, larger than the hand about it, so that it can be read from the door. I once struck it and wrote \emph{one in three} beneath, having heard the figure spoken in the yards on a market day. I struck my own figure out again the same tend. This book holds what was entered, and what was entered was one in twelve. The other figure has no row here and never will, and I have left the place where I struck it as near as I could to the gutter, where the light from the grate does not fall.

Also in Y.H. 40: four of the Nine Wells are sealed in the Keel and the keys are kept. Five are left for the living. This is entered as \emph{four reserved to the Hearth}. The brown says \emph{sealed}, and the word was written hard enough to have gone through the leaf if the vellum had been paper. A well that is reserved is a well a man may stand beside; a well that is sealed has a stone over it and a key in a room he may not enter. Both are true at the door of the room.

\textbf{Y.H. 41.} Sixty leagues south of Sill the province called the Empty Cantons appears in the ledger as a line of figures and then as a line of empty squares. The temple says the people were returned elsewhere. No record says where. I have counted the squares on nine copies of this book, and there are forty on every one. The continuator says a square is a place where a figure was left out in copying. I have asked a reeve come up from the Fenmarch what his people call that ground, and he gave me a name I have set in the margin and will not put in the year, because the Court can figure a thing once it has been named in this hall.

\textbf{Y.H. 120.} Here the first book ends. The clean roll goes on in its smooth hand. Another book, kept behind the winter tallies in the lower room at Greybank, takes up the years from this one, and puts the verbs back where they were taken out. I have never seen that book and have no wish to. Two hands correcting the same sentence in one week is a near thing, and this world has accounts enough.

\subsection*{The three offices, as they stand}

\emph{The list from the Y.H. 8 entry, set beside what each room is called by the men who work in it. The right-hand column is not in any copy but mine.}

Office — As entered in the first book — What the room is called here\par

Assessors — To value a life — The room where a man is told what he was worth before he is asked how he died\par

Collectors — To draw the measure — The table with the iron and the tube, which is set up before the person comes in\par

Bankers — To press the measure into an infant — The room below, where an infant is carried in and a person is carried out\par

The assessors sit highest and write least. The collectors carry the iron. The bankers have the warmest room, being nearest the Hearth, which is a kindness of the building and not of the office. I have set the three in this order because that is the order on the leaf. A man who puts the bankers first has begun an argument about where the warmth goes, and there is no end to that argument in this Hall.

\subsection*{The kindling song}

\emph{Taken down from a woman who has sung at the grate on Kindling for forty years and will not sing it while the figure is being read. She said the song was older than the book and then said that songs about fire are made by the fire, which is the custom of this city and not an answer. Sung low, with the last line left to the room.}

\begin{quote}\itshape The chamber was warm before we came,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the bowl was whole before the crack;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape nine went after what had run away\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and nine came back with something on their hands.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape They set the figure on the board, one in twelve,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and called it mercy in a clean round hand;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape they sealed four springs and kept the keys\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and left five open for the living.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Sixty leagues of road and well and door,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and never a name entered after the fortieth year;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the slate says they were returned elsewhere,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the squares say nothing, and are believed.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Kindle the fire and do not ask\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape who kept it before the Keeping was;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the flame has no mouth and the grate no tongue,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the book by the fire has learned to be quiet.\end{quote}

\subsection*{What the upright hand did}

The continuator borrows the first book on the tenth of every month and takes the verbs out of it as though a verb were a thing a man could smuggle past the grating in his cuff. He writes with care and has never in eleven years changed a figure.

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item Against \emph{the chamber was found already warm} he set \emph{the Hearth was lit in the first year}, and drew a small rule under it. I have left both. The lighting is an event; the finding is a state of the room; and a room that was warm before anybody came into it is not the same thing as a fire that somebody made.

\item Against \emph{four wells sealed} he set \emph{four wells reserved to the Hearth}, which I have set in the year already, so that the two readings stand together where a reader can find them.

\item Against the line of empty squares he wrote \emph{figures not legible in this copy}, which is the truest false sentence in the book. I have counted forty squares on nine copies. A figure not legible has a figure somewhere behind it; a square has nothing behind it and was made empty on purpose.

\item Against \emph{no record says where} he wrote nothing at all. His hand passed over the line without a stroke, which is the readiest way of correcting a sentence I have yet seen.

\item Against the kindling song he wrote \emph{no entry arises}, and then, underneath in mine, I have put \emph{the room sang the last line}, which is a record of the room and not of anybody who can be entered.

\end{itemize}

\subsection*{At the head and in the gutter}

The head of every leaf is brown and brittle from eleven hundred years of warmth coming up through the grate, and the ink there has gone the colour of tea; the gutter is still black and the figures in it read as if they were written yesterday. A keeper of this book reads the end of a line first and the beginning last, which is not a skill and cannot be taught. The soot at the head of the first leaf is off the grating and was there before I came. The coal in the nail-hole is shut in with wire I have not touched. The slate dust in the fold came off a surveyor’s slate; I told him to move it and he moved it onto the book. The tallow thumb at the second corner is mine. The ring at the foot is small ale, set down by the continuator on a tenth-day when he had taken three verbs out of the founding and would not say what he had put in their place; he stood a long while with the cup in his hand and then set it on the leaf and went away without drinking. The square of bare vellum is where I scraped a word away. The grey along the outer fold is not mine and not the College’s. I have had this book eleven years and have not swept it. There is no Last Day in a box beside the fire.

\subsection*{At the foot, in a hand nobody will own}

\begin{quote}\itshape They found it warm and wrote it lit,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the figure went up clean;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape forty squares and a line of road\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape with nothing entered in between.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Four springs are sealed and four keys kept\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape in a room the reader does not know;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape ask the chamber what it held before\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the first book told the chamber so.\end{quote}

I asked the continuator, a woman who sings at the grate, and a reeve out of the Fenmarch who would not give me his name twice, and had three answers and no hand. I have left the line where it was written. The book goes back into its box on the inner side of the Hall, where the warmth comes up through the grating and settles into the vellum and no brush takes it out. On the tenth the continuator will borrow it and take the verbs out again, and the clean copy will go on in its smooth hand, and this one will go on underneath it with the brown showing through where the fire is lowest. Next tend I copy the first Returns out of the year Three and set the tube beside the mercy, where a man must move the book to reach them. The notice by the door will still say one in twelve. The squares will still be forty. I have put both down where they stand.

\clearpage\phantomsection\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{The First Measure, Being the Collector’s Own Leaf for the Hearth Drawing in Low Kiln on Stone 12 of Y.H. 812, with the Embers, the Deduction, the Note the Room Gave, the Child Worse Before Dusk, and the Figure Read Twice at the Cross; Written in the Hand That Carried the Tube and Corrected in Two Others}
\CRsheetheading{The First Measure, Being the Collector’s Own Leaf for the Hearth Drawing in Low Kiln on Stone 12 of Y.H. 812, with the Embers, the Deduction, the Note the Room Gave, the Child Worse Before Dusk, and the Figure Read Twice at the Cross; Written in the Hand That Carried the Tube and Corrected in Two Others}
{\centering\FellFont\itshape\footnotesize\color{faded} A page from a collector’s pocket ledger; figures in Ledgerhand copied from the day-slate, the remarks terse and in the hand that unwrapped the wool and held the tube, one column struck by a College clerk and drawn back beneath his words, a passive verb set above each of mine, one sentence written over by a factor’s man, and a line at the foot in a hand nobody will own · Written in the Clay Yard of Low Kiln and in the death-house two doors down from the Vail kiln-house on Stone 12, Y.H. 812, the Thin Year, the day of the Hearth Drawing; copied forward at the Opening of the Slates, Ilmen 1, Y.H. 813, and carried in the oiled-paper wrap in the collector’s coat beside the tube in its wool sleeve. It survives with grey worked under the nails at the head, iron filings ground into the gutter off the tube’s wrap, a tallow thumb where the lamp was held low, a bone-pale streak of slip from a thrower’s forearm, a green bead of lead glaze in the lower corner, a pale round ring where a cold tube was set down on the leaf, the circle of a milk-cup pressed into the second fold, a damp tide-line along the foot out of a house where a pot was broken at the door, a small square of bare paper where a word was scraped away with the tube’s edge, two corrections in the narrow upright hand of a College clerk, one in the leaning hand of a factor’s man from Greybank, and one line at the foot nobody will own\par}\medskip
I draw the year’s first measure on a day before the year has turned, which is the Court’s way and not mine. Stone the twelfth, with the Ilm still under its skin of ice and the district saying three days to the Five while counting three Account-days and not three mornings. A collector may draw from the dying and from the newly born on the same day. The ordinance says \emph{may}; the district says \emph{must}; both are entered in the same neat hand by men who have stood in different rooms.

I set the slate down before I look at anybody. Hand to slate, then eyes to the bed, then the mouth to say what the slate has already said. If a woman tells me her mother’s name while I am writing the figure, I have the figure and not the name, which is what she wanted me to have, though she would deny it at her own door.

Twelve copper bits to a silver mark; twenty marks to a gold crown, a Sere coin that comes north with the factor and will not stay in Grath. The Court books an ember at five marks and no man in this yard has exchanged one for the other. A newborn vessel holds twelve to fifteen, a labourer in good case forty to sixty, one of the Kept three hundred, which is a figure no household can spend. One in twelve is printed on the notice and read twice at the Cross, once for the moot and once for those who came late. I have set no second figure beside it. I have heard a figure spoken in the yards and not entered it, not being a figure I can weigh.

Draws on this leaf: five. Lines with no draw in them: three. Figures struck: one. Columns struck: one. Figures read twice: one, and both readings the same.

\subsection*{The leaf, as I set it down}

\emph{Figures in Ledgerhand, copied from the slate I carried. The remarks are mine, in the hand that unwrapped the wool, and are not part of the account. A dash is a place where nothing was drawn, not a nought.}

Day — Vessel, as the house has it — Embers — Deduction — Banked to — Note — Remark\par

Stone 12 — A neighbour two doors down, a man past speaking. \emph{Breath} — 44 — 1 in 12 — Greybank — none — Asked once while breath remained; the house answered. Wrote before unwrapping. Held the tube without pressing. A woman set a basket at the edge of the light; I did not ask whose.\par

Stone 12 — A child three days returned, the same room. \emph{Second} — 13, struck to 12 — 1 in 12 — Hearthseat — none — Worse before dusk. Entered as a return, not a worsening. Both figures stand.\par

Stone 12 — A hearth-maid’s slate, left at the threshold. \emph{Birth} — — — — — — — — — Name written before the face was looked at. No figure came off it. Not mine to enter.\par

Stone 12 — A thrower of the low yard, come for the year’s first. \emph{Nineteen} — 41 — 1 in 12 — Greybank — full — Knuckle to the rim before the tube. Slip on both forearms; left a bone-pale streak on my cuff. Asked after her girl; not entered.\par

Stone 12 — A clay-bound hand of the terraces, sixth year of seven. \emph{Seven} — 43 — 1 in 12 — Greybank — nearly — Counted by the man, not by me. Air under the note; no Grathic word for it, so I have set the phrase as I heard it.\par

Stone 12 — A house of the terraces, disputed. \emph{Shoulder} — 52 — — — — — flat — Thumb wiped twice before touching nothing. Figure asked for, then not wanted. Left standing.\par

Stone 12 — No vessel drawn. A house at the yard’s end — — — — — — — — — Breath had gone before I came through the door. Pot broken at the threshold after I wrapped the tube; heat went out with the shard and not into the account. No measure.\par

Stone 12 — The Cross, the figure read aloud — — — 1 in 12 — — — — — Read twice, once for the moot and once for the late households. The same figure I wrote by the bed. Both set; neither joined.\par

\subsection*{The order at a death-house}

\emph{Copied from what I was told at the table and have used for eleven years. The second column is mine and is not read at any Weighing.}

Step — As the notice has it — As I keep it\par

The asking — Put once while breath remains; the answer entered before the breathing is counted — I have asked twice in eleven years and entered both as fresh. Neither answer was worth the ink.\par

The answer — Where the vessel cannot speak, the house answers; entered to the house — The house is not asked whether it understood. A woman held her mother’s hand and said a sentence that was not an answer; I set it at the edge of the leaf, the length of it.\par

The tube — Unwrapped after the entry; of cold iron, wrapped in wool — The wool is for the hand that holds it. The ordinance has no place for such a hand. I hold without pressing.\par

The figure — One in twelve, as the notice says; not changed for the bed or the hour — Read twice at the Cross before I came down the yard; entered once at the bed. The same figure. I have not made one out of the two readings.\par

The pot — Broken at the door after the tube is wrapped, before the slate is carried away — Never entered. A pot is a piece of clay, and what was in it is not on any slate.\par

The shard — Not swept until the Last Day — This house swept its step in the afternoon. I asked who swept and entered the answer to the house, which was weather.\par

\subsection*{The note column, and why a man is not a cup}

Before the tube I set a knuckle on the rim or the bed-rail. A whole vessel answers full; one cracked through answers flat, a small dead sound that stops at the surface; one with air under it answers nearly full, which the yards have no word for. A vessel turned toward in expectation may give nothing at all. I have entered that as \emph{none} and not as a nought, because a nought is a figure and a silence is not.

At the death-house the room gave none. I did not tap the man. A man is not a cup, and I have learned not to set my knuckle to one. There was a cup on the bench by the bed and it had stood there long enough to take the room into itself; it answered nothing, and I wrote nothing beside it. The hearth-maid later turned a written note down under a milk cup, and the circle of that cup is pressed into the second fold of this leaf; it is her cup and her note and I have entered neither.

The College man came down from Slate Row with ink in two fingers of a cuff gone soft from washing and struck the column through from the first row to the last, writing \emph{No such column} above it in his narrow upright hand. He drew his thumb down every row before he could write that there was nothing in any of them worth entering, and I watched him do it. I have drawn the column back underneath and left his words standing over it. A man does not count what he has not looked at.

\subsection*{The child on the third day}

The returned child in that room was three days back and worse before dusk. The women worked with the certain kindness of a thing they have known all their lives, warming from the outside and slowly, and saying almost nothing over the pallet. The physician come up from Low Kiln calls it the second chill; the hearth-maid calls it a graft settling. I have set both phrases in the remark and neither in a column. A child who comes back and then grows cold again is a thing the yards know and the slate has no place for. I entered the measure at thirteen, the clerk set twelve above it, and both stand, because a vessel three days returned cannot hold thirteen after the draw and yet the slate beside the bed said thirteen when I read it.

\subsection*{What the two borrowed hands did}

The College clerk struck \emph{I drew} against the man at the bed and set \emph{the measure was drawn} above it, and underneath that \emph{the warmth was entered}, which is further from the bed again. I have put \emph{I drew} back beneath both. A sentence with nobody in it is a sentence no woman can ask about, and women ask about these draws in the end, always at the door, always after the tube is put away.

A factor’s man from Greybank wrote in a leaning hand with a little gold in the ink. Against \emph{the house answered} he set \emph{the answer was entered}. Against \emph{the room called it merciful} he set \emph{the draw was lawful} and underlined it twice. Both stand. Lawful is true and does not mention a man on a board-bed; merciful is what the room said after I had wrapped the tube, and there is no column for what a room says. He struck the word \emph{none} in the note column and wrote \emph{vacancy} above it. A nought is a figure and can be carried out in a cuff. The silence at the bed stays where it was.

\subsection*{The verse the collectors say going down the yard}

\emph{Said low going down the Clay Yard after the tube is wrapped, never while the slate is open, and never twice in one house. The last line is said to the pot, and the man who said it to me would not say it while the factor’s man stood at the gate.}

\begin{quote}\itshape Wool on the iron, slate on the knee,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the tube goes in where the breath would be;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape one in twelve as the notice says,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape read twice at the Cross and once at the bed.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Four go down and four come up,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and a place where the fifth should stand;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the pot goes out with the house’s heat\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the grey goes home ahead of the hand.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape The name goes down before the face,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the child comes back and wants no cup;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape I write the note and not the room\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the room keeps what I never took down.\end{quote}

I have copied it as it came and put no gloss on it. A collector who explains a song has begun to write a sermon, and sermons get copied.

\subsection*{In the head and in the gutter}

The grey under the nails at the head came off my own fingers giving the figure to the clerk at Greybank last tend; it goes in under the nails first and comes up into the creases by the second year, and after that a man may wash until the water freezes and nothing changes. The filings in the gutter came out of the wool sleeve and have never once drawn the warmth out of the paper, which is the only mercy iron has shown this leaf. The tallow thumb is mine, from holding the lamp low while a woman in the death-house was telling me something I wanted the end of; she did not tell me the end, and went back to sitting. The bone-pale streak came off the thrower’s forearms when she set her slate beside mine to wait for a figure.
