The book goes back under the warm-stone. Tomorrow a man will come in with a wall failing and a cuff full of money, and the room will take a wall from a beast and set it over him, and I shall enter the donor’s figure and put the wanting in the margin, where there is no column and nobody has asked to see it. The stone will be warm when I lift it and warm when I set it down. It keeps no account and gives no account of itself, which is more than can be said of anything else in this building.

\clearpage\phantomsection\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{The Granary Years, Being an Extract from the Chronicle of the Factor’s House at Greybank Concerning the Raising of the Granary in Y.H. 726, the Doubling of the Grain Levy, the Ninety-Four Days, and the Row of Empty Sacks; with the Cart-Song, the Table of Loads, Two Corrections in the College Hand, and a Line at the Foot Nobody Will Own}
\CRsheetheading{The Granary Years, Being an Extract from the Chronicle of the Factor’s House at Greybank Concerning the Raising of the Granary in Y.H. 726, the Doubling of the Grain Levy, the Ninety-Four Days, and the Row of Empty Sacks; with the Cart-Song, the Table of Loads, Two Corrections in the College Hand, and a Line at the Foot Nobody Will Own}
{\centering\FellFont\itshape\footnotesize\color{faded} A factor’s annalist’s extract from the granary chronicle, copied out of the loft-book; the year-entries in a sloping tally hand, the two figures set against the notice, the loads entered as a round sum with the rows underneath it in the gutter, the cart-song taken down at the quay, one figure struck and written again beneath, two corrections in the narrow upright hand of the College, and a line at the foot in a hand that has never come forward · Written at Greybank in the factor’s counting house in Ash of Y.H. 812, the Thin Year, by the keeper of the granary chronicle, who signs nothing and calls himself only the continuator of the sacks; copied from a loft-book kept in a tin box above the second floor since Y.H. 726 and carried forward at the Opening of the Slates into Y.H. 813. It survives as six leaves of stout foolscap sewn with wire into a board cover gone soft at the hinge: barley dust worked into the grain of the first leaf, a husk stuck fast in the gutter, a weevil shut in the second fold, the lower corner gnawed by a mouse so that two words are gone clean off the third leaf, a white bloom of Sallow salt at the head that comes and goes with the weather, a tallow thumb, a ring where a cup of small ale stood from the first load to the last, the figure for the four loads struck through and written again underneath in the writer’s own hand, two corrections in the narrow upright hand of the College, and a grey Ash print along the outer fold which the continuator did not make and has not swept\par}\medskip
I keep the chronicle of the granary at Greybank, which is not the same thing as the chronicle of the Court, or of Grath, or of the road that brings us the grain. The granary keeps what came in. The chronicle keeps what was entered. Between the sack and the slate there is a space the width of a clerk’s hand, and it is in that space that this book is written. Where the two disagree I set both down and leave them standing, because an annalist who reconciles them has begun to write an account, and an account is a thing a factor can carry to the Hearthseat and show to a man who has never stood in a granary loft in his life.

The loft-book lies in a tin box above the second floor, where the warm comes up through the boards in winter and the dust settles into the grain of the paper and no brush takes it out. I have copied this chapter four times, and each time the loads have stood as a round figure in the clean hand, because the first keeper of this book counted sacks the way a miller counts a row of wet pots, by the places and not by what was in them. I have left his round figure standing and put his rows underneath it, where a clerk of the College will not think to look, which is the gutter.

\subsection*{The years as the loft-book has them}

\emph{Copied in the tallies out of the tin box. I have put nothing in from the temple tells, which have their own years and a comfort in them.}

\textbf{Y.H. 711.} The factor’s house buys the old malt-floor by the quay and lays a new floor over it. Entered as \emph{a necessary enlargement of the office}.

\textbf{Y.H. 726.} The granary is raised two storeys. The Court’s levy of grain in Grath is doubled, from one part in twenty of the harvest to one part in ten. Entered as \emph{the establishment of the granary; the levy adjusted to the Hearth}.

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{In the narrow upright hand of the College, against the second entry:} The levy was readjusted. No burden was added. Strike \emph{doubled}.\end{quote}

I have not struck it. A burden halved in the telling is still a burden carried in the cart, and the carts came down the Clay Road that autumn with the same horses and the same ruts and one more sack to a load. The College hand has never in this chapter changed a figure. It takes the doer out of the sentence and leaves the figure standing, which is the readiest way of correcting a book I have yet seen.

\textbf{Y.H. 782.} Every birth in Grath must be entered on a slate within three days, and the hearth-maids who kept the slates for nothing are paid by the Court. The granary’s own roll grows by a column. Entered as \emph{a regularity in the keeping of the birth-slates}.

\textbf{Y.H. 811, the Long Cold.} Ice came on the Ilm in Stone and did not break for ninety-four days. No cart crossed the ford and no collector crossed from the quay. The grain levy was called all the same, in a district that had no grain to give, and in Low Kiln the measure-levy was raised to one in three, which is a different figure and is printed nowhere. Entered as \emph{a visitation of the weather; the account standing}.

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{In the margin, in a hand that is mine:} They called themselves walking thin. I have put the words here and not in the year, because a man who keeps moving because stopping is the same as cooling is not a figure and the loft-book has no column for him.\end{quote}

\textbf{Y.H. 812, the Thin Year.} The granary gave out in Grain, before the second firing, and was opened again in Smoke. I have entered both dates, which the first keeper did not, because he entered openings and not closings, as a man enters what he can see from the quay.

\subsection*{The table of loads}

\emph{The old figure stood one in twenty until Y.H. 726. The figure after it is one in ten. The right-hand column is not mine: it is made up in the room below, before the carts set out.}

Year — Levy in the district — Loads due at the granary — Loads that came down the Clay Road — Entered as\par

725 — one in twenty — 90 — 90 — \emph{levy received}\par

726 — one in ten, doubled — 180 — 176 — \emph{levy received; account standing}\par

727 — one in ten — 180 — 180 — \emph{levy received}\par

758 — one in ten — 180 — 180 — \emph{levy received; warm-stone not supplied}\par

811 — one in ten, called in ice — 180 — none — \emph{a visitation of the weather}\par

812 — one in ten, called early — 180 — 61 — \emph{the account carried forward}\par

The four loads of Y.H. 726 went into the ford in Silt, which was high that year, and the carters came up with wet boots and empty places in the string. The figure was made in this room before they left, so the four went into the book as received. I have struck the figure and written it again underneath, by touch as it were and not by eye, because a man writes differently when he is setting down what happened from what was entered.

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{In the narrow upright hand of the College, against the struck figure:} Deficit not entered. Levy discharged at the granary door. Account standing.\end{quote}

The hand is careful and it has never once in this chapter changed a figure. It has made four wet sacks into no sacks at all, which is a cleaner thing to carry into a counting room. There are eleven words for a deduction taught in the College and not one for a sack that came back half-full, which is the whole of the difficulty between us.

\subsection*{The cart-song}

\emph{Taken down at the Greybank landing from a carter of High Kiln who had come six days on the Clay Road and would not sing until the horses were unhooked. It is sung going up and not coming down; coming down a man wants his ale. The third verse is not sung at the granary door, and the carter said a man who sang it there would not be hired again in Grath.}

\begin{quote}\itshape Four days to the clay and five back,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape five in Grain and six in Silt;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the sack goes up and the slate goes down\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and neither one knows what was spilt.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape One in twenty the old book said,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape one in ten when the floor was laid;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the same wheel turns in the same old rut\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the same hand mends the same old trade.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape They write the figure at this end\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape before the horse has set his foot;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape we carry the difference in our backs\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and enter nothing at the boot.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Ninety-four days the river stood\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the ford was a stone that would not bear;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the levy came on the frost behind us\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and found us thin and standing there.\end{quote}

He would not say who made it and said that songs about roads are made by the roads, which is the custom of that country and not an answer. I have set it down as he sang it, with the unsung verse where it stood.

\subsection*{What the College hand did}

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item Against \emph{the levy doubled} it set \emph{the levy was readjusted}, so that the act of doubling has no actor in it.

\item Against \emph{four loads lost at the ford} it set \emph{deficit not entered; levy discharged}, which is true at the door and false at the ford.

\item Against \emph{they called themselves walking thin} it wrote \emph{no designation arises}, which leaves the men standing and takes the name away.

\item Against \emph{the granary gave out in Grain} it set \emph{stock reduced, not exhausted}, and underlined it twice.

\item Against \emph{one in three in Low Kiln} it wrote \emph{the figure is the measure-levy and not the grain; no entry lies}, which is the only correction in this chapter I did not wish to argue with.

\end{itemize}

It takes the person out and leaves the grain standing, and grain standing by itself has never gone hungry. I have put nothing back under the last of these, because it is true. A clerk who can tell two figures apart is a rarer man than a clerk who can write one, and this one came up from the Hearthseat with the figure for the measure already in his cuff.

\subsection*{At the head and in the gutter}

The barley dust at the head is off the second-floor boards and is older than my copying of this chapter; it goes into the paper and no damp takes it out. The husk in the gutter stuck there in Grain of Y.H. 811, when the last of the old grain was swept up off the floor and the granary stood open and empty behind it. The weevil shut in the second fold was alive when I folded the leaf and is not now, and I have left it where it died. The lower corner is mouse-gnawed and has taken two words clean off the third leaf; I have not written them back, because a gap in a chronicle is a thing a reader can put his finger on and a supplied word is not. The white at the head is salt bloom off the Sallow and comes and goes with the wind. The tallow thumb is mine. The ring at the foot is not any man’s; three men set a cup in it over one evening of copying and not one will say which, which is how small ale is drunk in this room when there is a thing to say and no proper word for it. The grey along the outer fold is not mine and is not the College’s. I have had this leaf four years and have not swept it.

\subsection*{At the foot, in a hand nobody will own}

\begin{quote}\itshape The floor was laid and the figure stood;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape four loads went wet and were entered dry.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape The granary keeps what the carts bring in,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the book keeps what the factor will deny.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Ask the sack. It has a mouth and no slate.\end{quote}

I asked the carter at the landing, the second clerk who made up the right-hand column, and a woman who has swept this loft for thirty years, and had three answers and no hand. I have left the lines where they were written. The leaves go back into the tin box above the second floor, where the warm comes up through the boards and settles into the grain of the paper. Tomorrow the levy will be called again, and the notice in the room below will say one in twelve, which is the figure for the measure and not for the grain, and nobody in the district has ever been asked to tell the two apart. The carts will come down the Clay Road with one more sack than the year before, and I shall enter the rows, because that is what the loft-book is for.

\clearpage\phantomsection\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{The Grave-Dog, Being a Soldier’s Field Notes on the Bone-Hound at the Bone Orchard Beyond Sill’s North Gate; with the Watch-Song as It Is Sung, a Tally of Graves and Phials, a Ruling in Ledgerhand, a Line in Pale Ink, and One Line at the Foot Nobody Will Own}
\CRsheetheading{The Grave-Dog, Being a Soldier’s Field Notes on the Bone-Hound at the Bone Orchard Beyond Sill’s North Gate; with the Watch-Song as It Is Sung, a Tally of Graves and Phials, a Ruling in Ledgerhand, a Line in Pale Ink, and One Line at the Foot Nobody Will Own}
{\centering\FellFont\itshape\footnotesize\color{faded} A soldier’s field book on one beast, set down as the record of a watch kept over the thin-return graves and not as natural philosophy; the rounds in Grathic, the tally in charcoal on the backs of burial dockets gone soft with rain, a watch-song as it is sung, a ruling in the narrow upright Ledgerhand of a clerk of the Court’s factor at Greybank, a line in the pale ink of an Ash-runner written on a scrap of salt-paper, and one line at the foot in a hand nobody will own · Written in Ash and Bone of Y.H. 812, the Thin Year of the Long Cold, by Gant, one of the Thane of Clay’s men set over the north road, in the watch-shed at the Bone Orchard a league beyond Sill’s north gate, with a tallow end, a short spear and a spade; set down first on the backs of thin-return burial dockets spoiled by rain and then on two folds of birch bark sewn with eel-sinew, carried in a coat pocket under the arm; copied forward in Bone of Y.H. 813. It survives with grave-clay ground into the head, a grey Ash thumb along the fore-edge where the leaf was wiped on a sleeve, a small round mark where a five-bit piece was set down and left, a dry grave-flower pressed flat in the second fold, a tideline along the gutter where a pail went over, a scorch where the watch-lamp caught the fourth leaf, the charcoal rubbed thin where the wrap was carried against the thigh, one ruling in Ledgerhand standing above the words it corrects, one line in pale ink on salt-paper gone soft at a corner, and the line at the foot\par}\medskip
I keep the north road and the orchard beyond it for the Thane. It is no post a man writes home about. The orchard stands a league beyond the north gate, and the thin-return children lie in uneven rows with no slate over any of them. A cart of grey comes out from the Cross on every market-day and tips its load at the south edge and goes back empty, and nobody in the square looks at it twice. I am set to see that no one digs the rows in the dark and that no one lies down in them and stays there. I carry a spade, a short spear with the head gone blue on the quay stone, and a fire-pot of coals under blind ash. I write at the end of a watch with the tallow down to a knuckle.

The dockets I wrote on first were thin-return burial dockets, and the rain took the figures clean off, which was a mercy of a kind: a figure the rain has eaten is a figure no clerk can enter. I write in charcoal now, on the backs of those same dockets and on two folds of birch bark sewn with eel-sinew. Charcoal goes into the grain and a cuff cannot take it off. The clay at the head is my own thumb setting the leaf down on the shed bench. I have not knocked it off. A book that has never been wiped on a sleeve was never taken into an orchard.

\subsection*{What it smells}

It follows the Ash, not the dead. This is the first thing a new man gets wrong, and the thing that makes him stand a whole watch facing the wrong way. He looks for the fresh grave, for the turned clay and theuk knees of a mourner, and all the while the beast is coming from the south edge where the cart tips.

It comes to where the grey has lain. The rows are shallow and the grey gathers in them between the stakes, and a child set down in the year of the flower and a child set down last tend both carry the same smell to a nose that knows it. On the Last Day the households leave their grey where it lies and burn it in the morning and call it dealt with, and for a tend after that the orchard is quiet. Then it comes back. I have set the order down and no cause beside it.

What is strange is the barrow. The Ash at the south edge is deeper than my spear and the beast will not go near it. I have watched one stand at the edge of the tipped grey with its nose working and then turn back up the rows, and I have stood a cold watch trying to make the two things agree. Grey in a cart is not grey in a grave. I know that much. I do not know how a dog knows it.

It comes on still nights. It does not bark. When it has a grave open it makes a small sound low in the throat, and I have heard it from the shed and thought it was a man turning in his sleep, which is a thing a soldier learns to be ashamed of being glad of.

\subsection*{What it is}

It is a dog. I set that down before anything else, because the hearths will not. It has a dog’s teeth and a dog’s neck and a dog’s way of putting its head on one side when it listens. It is bigger than the yard hounds at the Tallow Works and thinner, and the coat is the colour of wet grave-clay, so that a man sees the grey of the muzzle before he sees the body. The grey is under the nails and in the mouth. The teeth are worn flat on small bones. It smells of wet earth and Ash.

I have opened three. Two were brought down on the north road and one was found dead with its head in a shallow grave it had dug out from the side. In all three I found a dog altered by the place it lived in, the way a potter’s hands are altered by the wheel. In the second I found grey in the stomach and a warmth in it that I could feel through the paunch, which is not what I looked for in a beast that had been at a month-buried child. The bodies in these rows are not cold all the way through when they go down. I know that because I have had to cover them. I have written the two things on the same leaf and I have not drawn a line between them. A man who writes a cause into a book he keeps in his coat is a man who will be asked for it by somebody with a slate.

\subsection*{The hand}

It does not touch a man on his feet. I have stood within two paces with the spear down and it went on with its own work. But let a man go down at the lip of a grave, or kneel to lift something out of one, and the dog comes for the hand.

A man of the orchard went in at Ash 14 to get a clay pipe back out of a grave before the frost took the clay hard. He was on one knee with his fingers in the edge when the dog came up behind him. It did not shake him or drag him. It put its mouth to the back of the hand and held the one place, the way a collector sets a tube and waits, and the man said afterwards that the worst of it was not the pain but the waiting and not knowing what it was waiting for. I struck the dog across the back with the spear-shaft and it went three paces off and stood, which is what it does; it does not run and it does not come back at a man who has hit it.

There were two small holes and not much blood, and grey worked into them along the seam of the hand. An old woman of Low Kiln bound it with tallow and told him to keep it out of the Ash. At the end of the tend the holes were still holes. It is now the better part of a year and a half and he still shows them to people when the subject turns. Salt does not hold that bite and there is no physic for it that I know. Keep the hand out of the grey and let the man show it to whom he will.

\subsection*{The watch-song}

\emph{Sung going in at the first watch, not coming back. The fourth line is the old line and every man on the road sings it wrong on purpose, because a song that gives the dog a reason is a song a man can carry home and set by his fire. I have set it down as it is sung.}

\begin{quote}\itshape One for the spade and one for the grey,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape one for the small ones set down without slate;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape it comes on the still and it comes on the frost,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and it goes to the warm before the cold.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape It takes the Ash and it leaves the bone,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape a mouth on the hand and a wound on its own;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape count them going and count them back,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and one for the hand that did not close.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Four in a row and a fifth not said ---\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the old line’s a lie and we sing it instead;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the gap is the place where the spade went in,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and we do not sing what the clay held within.\end{quote}

The gap is the fifth place in a row the men stop at. They know it and sing it and have never once said whose it is. There is a woman comes up from Low Kiln on the Last Day and stands at that row and does not go to it, and I have let her keep it.

\subsection*{The tally}

These are the watches I kept a true account of. There were others I did not write because my hands were full, and one I did not write because I had drunk. I have set down both sorts as they stand. The last column is the clerk’s, not mine. I counted graves; he counted phials.

Watch — Where — Graves opened — Hounds — Hands bitten — Phials sold — Entered\par

Ash 3 — South edge, under the barrow — none — one — none — 0 — 0\par

Ash 9 — Third row, thin-return graves — one — two — none — 1 — 0\par

Ash 14 — Broken-pot ground, east — none — one — one — 0 — nil\par

Ash 22 — Fourth row, after the frost — two — three — none — 2 — 0\par

Bone 2 — North row, the newest mound — one — one — one — 1 — 0\par

Bone 11 — The row the woman stands at — none — one — none — 0 — nil\par

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{In the narrow upright hand of a clerk of the factor’s house at Greybank, borrowed against the leaf at the north gate:} Canine not a vessel. Disturbance of a grave: no deduction arises. Hands bitten: not entered. Quiet ash going south: entered as vacancy. Phials received at five bits the phial. Account stands.\end{quote}

I have left his hand standing. But he has put \emph{vacancy} against a grave that was opened, and a vacancy is a word for a place where somebody stood. I have written that in the margin below, where his column cannot reach, and I have put my own mark beside it in charcoal.

\subsection*{The phials}

The grey out of a beast’s stomach is sold as cheap quiet in the Fenmarch at five bits a phial, and men come through Cold Acre for it with a cart that has no load on the way out. I have stopped one with six phials sewn into a coat lining and asked him what he carried, and he told me the weather and the road, which is the answer the reed-cutters give at the Clay Yard when a woman asks what a bundle holds. I did not ask twice. A man who asks twice about a phial is a man who wants one.

They say the cheap quiet that goes south over the Peat Line is why so many Fen returns come back thin. I have not seen a return and I have not seen a phial opened, so I have set the saying down beside the five bits and joined neither. I have written no name on any of the six rows above, and a phial with a name on it would not travel, which I learned from the man who told me the weather.

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{In the pale ink of an Ash-runner, on a corner of salt-paper gone soft where the damp took it:} We do not ask whose ash it is. A phial that has a name on it will not travel. Bless the cart and do not ask the dog.\end{quote}

I did not write his line and he did not write mine, and neither of us asked the dog anything.

\subsection*{What the hearths say}

They say it is a dog set to guard the graves, a wrong done at a weir and a mother’s grief gone down into the clay on four legs. There are songs in the Fenmarch with a name in them. I have heard them and I have no quarrel with a song. I have opened three of these and found a dog, and found the newest graves gone into first, and a warmth in the small bodies that had not gone all the way out. If the beast guards anything, it is the place where the warm is, and that is not the same thing as guarding the dead, and it is not the same thing as a grief. I have written that sentence out once and crossed it out twice, because it is the kind of sentence that gets a man called a natural philosopher, and natural philosophers are not set to watch a burial ground in Ash.

The yard calls it a mercy because it keeps the rows clear. I have not called it that.

\subsection*{At the head and in the margins}

The grave-clay at the head is mine. The grey thumb along the fore-edge is from Ash 22, when I wiped my hand on the leaf before I could find a rag, and I have left it, because it is the only mark on this book that came off a grave. The round mark is the five-bit piece the man set down on the bench and forgot; I have not spent it and I have not put it in a figure. The flower in the second fold was dry when I found it on a mound and I do not know who put it there. The tideline came from a pail going over on the shed step; the figures ran together and I did not write them again. The scorch is where the leaf caught when I held it to the lamp to read, and the hand that pulled it back was mine and is not entered. The charcoal is rubbed thin where I carried the wrap under my arm. The clerk’s ruling I have not touched. The song is as the men sang it, with the old line wrong and the gap standing.

\subsection*{At the foot, in a hand nobody will own}

\begin{quote}\itshape It does not eat the dead. It eats what the dead were keeping.\end{quote}

I asked a clerk, an Ash-runner, a woman who stands at a row, and a man who had lost the use of a hand, and had four answerings and no hand. I have left the line where it was written.

There is a ground beyond the north row where the stakes have gone rotten and the clay comes up warm under the spade on the stillest morning of Bone, though nothing has been buried there this year. I have not dug there. Next Ash I will take a spade and a coil of cord and go in at the first watch with the lamp shut, and if the warm comes up where no grave has been opened I will set that down too, in charcoal, with the verb left in it and no figure at the end of the row.

\clearpage\phantomsection\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{The Green at the Mouth, Being a Letter from the Glass Furnaces at Vhal to the Glaze Room at High Kiln in Sill, with the Answer Written on the Back in Another Hand, a Proportion Set Down in Charcoal, a Correction in Ledgerhand, and a Mixing Song Nobody Will Claim}
\CRsheetheading{The Green at the Mouth, Being a Letter from the Glass Furnaces at Vhal to the Glaze Room at High Kiln in Sill, with the Answer Written on the Back in Another Hand, a Proportion Set Down in Charcoal, a Correction in Ledgerhand, and a Mixing Song Nobody Will Claim}
{\centering\FellFont\itshape\footnotesize\color{faded} A private letter on a sheet of Council salt-paper softened by the spring damp, written in iron-gall and the point of a cliff-glass bead, folded four times and sewn with eel-sinew into a scrap of oiled sailcloth; carried up the Salt Road after the flood by a salt-factor’s man, borrowed at the factor’s house at Greybank, answered at High Kiln in Seed, and kept since in a glaze-room tin among the tasting-spoons · Written at Vhal in Ilmen of Y.H. 813 by Wenna, a glaze-mixer’s daughter of High Kiln who went down the Salt Road to work the glass furnaces, to Gessa her mother, who keeps the Glaze Room in High Kiln, Sill; carried eighty leagues up the Salt Road and through the coast pass in Silt of Y.H. 813, after the water went off the road, borrowed at Greybank where a Council clerk set a correction in Ledgerhand, and answered at High Kiln in Seed of Y.H. 813. It survives sewn into oiled sailcloth, with a green thumb at the head, a bead of cliff-glass pressed into the second fold, a bloom of salt along the gutter, a ring of vinegar on the third leaf, a smear of lead glaze at the foot, two words eaten clean away by damp, one correction in the narrow upright hand of a Council clerk, the answer in the mother’s charcoal hand on the back, and one line at the foot in a hand nobody will own.\par}\medskip
To Gessa at the Glaze Room, High Kiln, Sill, who taught me to taste with the back of the tongue and never to say what I had tasted. From Wenna at the furnaces, Vhal, in Ilmen of Y.H. 813.

I write on the back of a Council contract because there is no paper in this town that was made to keep a sentence. Salt-paper is made to rot. A clerk of the Council will tell you the rotting is a virtue, and he will tell it with a straight face and a cuff soft from washing, because a contract that goes soft in the damp is a contract nobody can read against a man, which is the whole of their justice and the whole of their trade. I have written my wages three times on three such sheets and had two of them go. This is the third and the ink is already coming up in little pale islands where the salt has worked. If it reaches you with the verbs gone, know that they were mine when I set them down.

Do not rub the second fold. There is a bead of cliff-glass pressed into it and the edge will take your thumb.

I have been at the furnaces eleven months. You will want to know first whether the Vhaleni taste their work. They do. That is the answer I came eighty leagues to find and did not want to bring back. The glass women rub their gums with cliff-glass and say the sweetness answers sweetness; a salt-wife of the Quay gives them seawater to drink and says the sea has been paid for already. A physician come up from Greybank in Y.H. 798 left a page in the glass-house saying the sweetness comes from the lead, and the page came back to me with the word taken clean away, as though a word could be scraped off paper the way slip is scraped off a bench. I have written it here in my own hand.

It is lead.

I knew that in High Kiln at nine and I have crossed a country to learn it again under a Vhaleni name. They call it the glass-sickness here. It is the green with a Vhaleni name written on it. The pale line comes up at the gum before a girl has thought to look at her own mouth in a pot’s glaze, and after that the hand goes, slowly, so slowly that a woman can go on holding a cup for years and blame the cup. I have watched it happen to a girl who could taste a firing by the smell of the room. She tells it now by the colour of her own fingertips, which is an instrument, of a kind, and no kinder than the last one.

When I left you I thought the green was a thing of our room: the sweetish lead of Ember, the mix tasted on the back of the tongue, the wheel turning under the window, the pot tapped with a knuckle before anybody said it was finished. I wrote you from the road that the glass men of Vhal used a different flux and did not taste their work at all. I wrote it in a confident hand. I have set that hand beside this one and let them stand. A confident hand is what a girl of sixteen uses when she wants a sentence to be true more than she wants it to be accurate, which is the same defect I have spent my life covering with lead.

The furnaces take sand from the beach and lead from the Glaze Cliffs, blue-green and sweet-smelling in the heat, and melt them together into glass that goes as far as Sere. The women who work it have the green at the mouth and a hand that will not hold a cup steady, and one of them told me her mother used to tap the ribs of a sick man and say he had gone flat. I did not ask what he had been returned as. There is no column for it in the Council’s figures, and I have learned not to put my questions where a clerk can reach them.

\subsection*{The proportion, as I set it down in charcoal on the back of the third sheet}

What goes into the pot — What the mixer is told — What I have seen\par

Lead out of the blue cliffs — A flux, and a flux is nothing to speak of — Lead. It goes in by the handful and comes out at the gum.\par

Beach sand, washed in seawater — The sea takes the sting out of it — The sea takes the figure off the contract. It does not take the sting out of the sand.\par

The tasting, twice in a firing — A glaze-mixer tastes. That is the trade. — A glaze-mixer tastes. That is the price of the trade. These are the same sentence said in two rooms.\par

The tap with the knuckle — A full note means the glaze has filled the flaw — A full note means the flaw is under the glaze, which is not the same as gone.\par

The green at the mouth — The mark of a girl who does her work — The beginning of the sweet-sickness, which you told me at nine and which I would not hear at sixteen.\par

You will say I have put the price in the column where the proportion should be. It is the only column in this trade that tells the truth.

\subsection*{The mixing song}

\emph{Sung low at the wheel, to the pot and not to a person. The second verse is the one you taught me; I have set your correction underneath where you wrote it, and left my own words standing above, as you left mine.}

\begin{quote}\itshape Mix it with the back of the tongue,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape lead in the morning and slip at noon;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape a cup that sings has a flaw beneath,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the flaw keeps the note of its own.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Two for the wheel and two for the fire,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape two for the girl who knows her place;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the green comes up where the gum was pale,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and nobody counts it, and nobody says.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Three for the crack and one for the glaze,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape a whole return in a beautiful dish;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape what it covers is what it keeps,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the mixer pays for the dish.\end{quote}

The Council clerk at Greybank borrowed the sheet on the morning after the salt boats came up, being a man who cannot leave paper alone. He writes in the neat upright hand they teach, with the verbs taken out and everything in the passive. Against \emph{it is lead} he set \emph{the flux is retained} above it, and the lead went out of the sentence as though a lead could be carried off in a cuff. Against the place where I had left the payer unnamed he put a round nought and wrote \emph{vacancy} under it. Where I wrote \emph{the mixer pays for the dish} he set \emph{the measure is banked}, which is true in the way a closed room is true. I have put the verbs back underneath and left his hand standing on the back, where it belongs. He takes them out because a thing always true has no need of verbs. I put them in because a girl at a bench at three in the morning wants to know which hand to hold the cup with.

I have two questions and I am putting them where you can answer them without a slate in the room. The first: is the green at your own mouth wider than it was when I went? Do not tell me it is the mark of skill. I know the district’s saying and I know what it is for. The second: a woman at the Quay says a child upriver turns his head toward a pot a breath after the knuckle falls, and that the yard calls it quickness. Is that a thing people say, or a thing you have seen? I am not asking for a name. A name is the one thing a girl in Vhal can send home in a letter and have entered against her before she has taken her coat off.

\subsection*{In the daughter’s hand on the back, in charcoal, written at High Kiln in Seed of Y.H. 813}

Your grandmother’s line for the second verse was different and you have left it out. It went:

\begin{quote}\itshape The green comes up where the gum was pale;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the house calls it skill and the girl calls it hers.\end{quote}

I have written it above yours and yours stays where you set it. A song with two second verses is a song a woman can sing either way, which is the only kind we have ever had the sense to keep.

I have not answered the question about your mouth because you did not ask it. You asked about mine. You have got thinner in the wrist and I have got greener, and those are two facts in two rooms, and if you put them in one sentence you will have made a cause and a cause wants a name. Keep them apart.

There is no such thing as a flux that is nothing to speak of. A man who says that to you is either selling you the mix or has already sold the recipe to the factor at Greybank, and in this house those are the same trade with two different cuffs. Vinegar takes the edge off a tongue for an hour and off nothing else. I have held the price where it stood this year and Sella has not asked why, which is a kindness from a woman who cannot afford one and is therefore worse than a bill. Do not write it down. A kindness entered is a kindness gone.

The yard says a figure read aloud is not the figure paid. I do not know that as a fact and I have not set it down as one, so do not set it down in a letter with your name at the foot of it. Berr Clay came to the block with the red cord folded under his coat and wiped his thumb twice before he touched nothing and read one in twelve over the basket, twice, once for the moot and once for them that came late. The bell went four, four and a gap and nobody crossed himself. That much a girl can carry away without a clerk taking it off her. The rest is a place, and a place is not a debt, whatever the College calls it.

I have tied two knots in a strip of grey wool and sent it with the man. One is for the eleven months you have been gone and one is for the firings I have mixed since you left. The wool stays where I put it and no clerk can spell it, which is more than I can say for the sheet you sent me. Your father’s tap is on the bench and nobody has used it. The cup you chipped is where you left it, with the chip turned to the wall.

Come back in Ember if the green goes darker. Do not come back for a figure.

\subsection*{At the head and in the gutter}

The green at the head is mine, off my thumb setting the sheet down on the bench in the Glaze Room with the mix still on it, and it has gone into the grain so that the whole sheet smells faintly of a firing. The bead in the second fold was pressed in by a girl of the furnaces who watched me write and said nothing, and has left a sweet smear that has not dried in two months. The salt along the gutter came up out of the paper and not out of the sea, which is a thing only a person who has kept salt-paper knows the difference of. The ring on the third leaf is vinegar from the tasting-cup; the cup was set down while I was telling a woman to eat and she would not. The lead at the foot is not from the mix but from the rim of the dish, and I have left it where it fell. Two words have gone out of the second verse where the damp took them clean, and I have not written them in again. A song with two words gone is a song said slowly, and everything in this trade is said slowly.

\subsection*{At the foot, in a hand nobody will own}

\begin{quote}\itshape The pot keeps the flaw and the glaze keeps the name;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the green at the mouth keeps what the mixer paid.\end{quote}

I asked a dipper, a salt-wife of the Quay and a factor come up from Greybank, and had three answers and no hand. I have left the line where it was written. The sheet goes back into the sailcloth and the sailcloth into the tin among the tasting-spoons. On the next salt boat a girl will press another bead into a contract and write home that the Vhaleni do not taste their work, and I shall not correct her, because a girl has to cross a country to learn what her mother knew at nine, and a correction sent too early is only another kind of glaze.

\clearpage\phantomsection\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{The Grey Eel, Being a Quay-Tale of a Riddle Night Fourteen Winters Back, Told at the Fire in Ash, with the Questions as They Were Put, the Wager in Marks, a Factor’s Clerk’s Entry Set Over It, a Surveyor’s Gloss in the Margin, and a Line at the Foot Nobody Will Own}
\CRsheetheading{The Grey Eel, Being a Quay-Tale of a Riddle Night Fourteen Winters Back, Told at the Fire in Ash, with the Questions as They Were Put, the Wager in Marks, a Factor’s Clerk’s Entry Set Over It, a Surveyor’s Gloss in the Margin, and a Line at the Foot Nobody Will Own}
{\centering\FellFont\itshape\footnotesize\color{faded} A fire-keeper’s telling of a winter contest, set down for the settling of a question about a prize nobody claimed and not for the improvement of the reader; the tale in the old tally-man’s words, the riddles in the words they were put, the wager in a column of marks, the clerk’s figures entered above them, a gloss in another hand come back over the pass, and one line at the foot in a hand nobody will own · Written in Ash of Y.H. 813 at the Grey Eel, an alehouse at the lower end of the quay at Greybank, by Hedda, who keeps the fire behind the bar and mends nets in the afternoons when the quay is shut; told to her by Varr, who kept the quay tally for thirty years and now sits by the door with his hands on his stick, in the words he told it, which are the words of a man telling a thing he has told twice and would rather not tell a third time. Set down on the back of a spoiled quay-tally leaf in charcoal thinned with small ale, folded and sewn with eel-sinew and kept in the tin behind the fire, where the house keeps nothing else. It survives with a tallow thumb at the head, a press of wet wool across the first leaf, a small-ale ring gone dark where a quart stood from the first question to the last, a spot of barley grease, grey Ash worked into the gutter, frost raised out of the paper on the carry up from the quay, one correction in the narrow upright hand of the factor’s clerk, a gloss in the sloping hand of a Keldish surveyor who could not get back over the pass, and one line at the foot which nobody has claimed\par}\medskip
I keep the fire at the Grey Eel and mend the nets in the afternoons when the quay is shut, which is a different work from keeping an account, though both begin with the hand on the thing before the eye goes to the person standing there. In Ash the river goes grey under its skin and the road up to Sill is a road nobody takes, and of an evening there is nothing to do but sit where the fire is and ask one another what we already know and call the asking a question. A question whose answer nobody knows is a wager, and there is enough wagering in Greybank without ale in it.

A man came in the first tend of Ash and asked who had won the Eel’s contest fourteen winters back. I could not tell him. There was a prize, and there was a night, and there were men who would have remembered both, and I had kept the fire nine years; the only man left who had been there was Varr, who kept the quay tally before I kept the fire and now sits by the door with his hands on his stick. He told me the night as he tells it when he has told it twice and would rather not tell it a third time. I have set it down on the back of a tally leaf a wet thumb spoiled, because a prize nobody can claim is a thing that ought to have a story standing where the name would be.

\subsection*{The house and the night}

The Grey Eel stands at the lower end of the quay, where the road from Sill comes down to the water and the salt road goes out the other way. It is a low room with a hard clay floor and a bench of black ash worn hollow at the fire end by quay sleeves and the backs of men who have carried salt. I score nothing on it. A man who wants a thing entered can go up the street to the factor’s house and sit with people warmer than himself, and he will not get a riddle there.

The contest was in Stone of Y.H. 799, the winter the Ilm froze at the ford and the quay was shut for nine days. Four sat down and a fifth stood. The prize was a warm-stone out of Keld, no bigger than a fist, which the Eel kept in a pot of ash behind the bar and lent to whoever won, to sleep with through the dark. A warm-stone is a thing somebody has paid to keep warm, and a man who wins one and carries it home may sleep the warmer without ever knowing whose cold went into it. That is the sort of prize a quay gives, and the sort a quay argues about afterwards.

Varr says the night went badly from the first question, because the factor’s man answered before the verses were finished, which is the way of a man who has spent his life being read rather than reading.

\subsection*{The four that were put}

The first was put to the factor’s man, who had a soft cuff and a nail of salt-paper stuck to his sleeve from the morning’s contracts.

\begin{quote}\itshape I am signed in a room that smells of tar;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the wetter I get, the truer I am;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the Council lays its name on me\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the sea takes the name away.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape What am I?\end{quote}

“Salt-paper,” he said, before the last word was out. “And the wetter it gets, the less there is left to argue with.” He laid a bit toward the pot though nobody had asked him to pay, which is a habit of men who have been read rather than reading. Varr scored him one and did not say why.

The second was put to a carter come down from Sill for the winter lease, with ice still in the creases of his coat.

\begin{quote}\itshape I have more marks than the things I count;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape no man can read me unless he stands over me;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape a reeve keeps me in his belt and turns me\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape when he is deciding which row to open.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape What am I?\end{quote}

“A count-stick,” the carter said. Then, because he was a carter and could not leave a thing alone: “And a reeve with more notches than graves is either a good reeve or a man with a claim.” There was an argument about the second half of that, which Varr stopped by setting the cup down. There is no winning an argument about a stick. It has the marks it has, and the reeve turns it where he stands, and a man at a bar is not standing over it.

The third was put to a Keldish surveyor come down the Rim Road with a survey roll under his coat and no word to say about the pass. He had the habit, common to his kind, of stating his measure before his name, and had done neither.

\begin{quote}\itshape I am heard in the square and told on a slate;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape I go four and four and then a thing that is not a number;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape nobody crosses himself when I come,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the clerk reads straight past where I stood.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape What am I?\end{quote}

“The bell,” the surveyor said. “No. The gap in it.” He said the second answer low, to the fire, which is the proper way to give the answer to a thing that is not a number. A Keldish man will say the figure and not the space after it, being paid to survey seams and not silences; that he said the space at all cost him something, and Varr gave him the score for the cost and not for the word.

The fourth Varr put himself, being the only man in the room who had kept a tally long enough to know what a figure costs and still be able to say it.

\begin{quote}\itshape I go up the road in a box and come back in a cup;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape I am read twice over the basket and paid once;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape I am the same in every mouth in the district\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and a different thing in every house that pays me.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape The space between me and my price has nobody’s name on it.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape What am I?\end{quote}

Nobody answered for a while. Then the woman who mends the nets, who had sat at the end of the bench all night with her hands in her lap and had not taken her cup up, said it to the fire.

“A figure,” she said. “One in twelve, as the notice says. It goes up in a box and comes down in a cup, and the space has no signature.”

Varr passed her the pot. She set it down again without drinking and said she had mended a net for a man who carried a figure up the road and came back with a coat she did not know, and that she had never asked him what it cost because a net-mender who asks about figures does not keep nets for long. That is the best answer I have heard in nine winters and the only one that cost the giver something.

\subsection*{The wager, as it stood at the fire}

What was laid — What the house kept — What the factor’s clerk wrote over it\par

A bit from the factor’s man — One, given early; not drunk — Query entered; commercial interest nil\par

A bit from the carter — One, argued and allowed — Response entered; no charge arises\par

A bit from the surveyor — One, given to the fire — Party unidentified; interest not entered\par

The net-mender laid nothing — One, given to the fire — No answer tendered; struck\par

The warm-stone in the pot of ash — Not taken; it went back into the ash — Prize unappropriated; no entry arises\par

The figure read at the Cross that morning was one in twelve, as the notice says, and it went over the bench with the ale and nobody looked at it twice. There is a pause in that figure the length of a held breath, which the clerk reads past and Varr does not, but that is not a thing for a riddle night.

\subsection*{What the clerk did}

He came down from the factor’s house on the first market after the thaw with a cuff soft at the edge from washing, and borrowed the leaf when the quay was full. He set the riddles down as \emph{queries entered} and the answers as \emph{responses entered}, and put a figure of marks against each of the four, which was more than Varr had scored, because the bench scores in whether a man sits down again and he does not.

Against the net-mender’s answer he wrote \emph{no answer tendered; struck}, because she had said it to the fire and not to him, and a thing said to a fire is not a tender. He asked who had put the fourth. Varr told him a man at the bench. He asked for the man’s name, and Varr said the man had not given one, which is a true thing and not the thing he wanted, and he wrote \emph{party unidentified}. He asked what the warm-stone was worth. Varr told him a warm-stone is worth what the cold is worth and changes with the weather, and the clerk wrote \emph{unappropriated; no entry arises}, which is a word for a thing nobody has claimed and a thing nobody can have.

He took the stone away and left the answer where it had been said. I have put his hand above mine and left mine standing under it, the way the fire keeps its heat under a pot and is not asked where it got it.

\subsection*{In the margin, in a surveyor’s sloping hand}

The leaf went up the Rim Road with a bundle of survey sheets and came back with a line in a hand that is not mine and not the clerk’s. I have copied it as it stands.

\begin{quote}\itshape At \emph{the gap in it}: I was in the square at the Cross on the tenth of Stone and heard the bell go four, four and a gap, and nobody crossed himself. The told bell and the heard bell are two bells and neither is the gap. A man who has stood in the Rim knows the difference between a number and the space after it, which is the whole of surveying. Do not let the clerk carry the space away. He will write \emph{nil} over it and it will be a true entry and a lie besides.\end{quote}

I have not answered him in the margin. A thing written in a book follows a man home, and a surveyor’s home is a room with a slate in it and nowhere to put a second opinion.

\subsection*{At the head and in the gutter}

The tallow thumb at the head is mine; I held the leaf down in the draught that comes under the bar door and did not know I had marked it. The press of wet wool across the first leaf came off the carter when he held the door for the surveyor and did not let go when he was through, and I have not written down which carter, because he would stop holding doors if I did. The dark ring is small ale that stood from the first question to the fourth and was drunk by nobody; two men have claimed it and one woman has denied it and I have given it to none of them. The barley grease came off a crust the surveyor set down on the leaf and took away uneaten. The grey in the gutter came off a cuff that had no business in the corner where I keep the tin, and I have not swept it. The frost came up out of the paper on the carry up from the quay and is the only thing in this house that entered without a hand. There is a Last Day at the Grey Eel and the corners are swept on the morning after and burnt and called dealt with.

\subsection*{At the foot, in a hand nobody will own}

\begin{quote}\itshape The fire keeps the heat. The slate keeps the space.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape The stone went back into the ash and nobody slept warmer.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape The answer stood where the name should have been.\end{quote}

I asked the carter, the surveyor and the woman who mends nets, and had three silences and no hand. I have left the lines where they were written. The leaf goes back into the tin and the pot goes back behind the bar. Tomorrow the quay may open and there will be more to do of an evening than ask one another what we already know, and the bench will be wanted for cups again. If a man comes in and asks who won, I shall tell him the woman at the end of the bench answered and did not take the stone, and let him make of that what a quay makes of everything, which is a wager and a figure and no name on either.

\clearpage\phantomsection\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{Of the Grey in the Corners, the Last Day, and the Burning Called Dealt With, Being the Court’s Standing Order for the Sweeping of the Last Day, Copied into the Court’s Room at Sill with the Sweep-Clerk’s Margin, the Places in a Table, the Form of Entry Left Blank, the Sweeping-Song Pasted Inside the Cover, Two Corrections in Borrowed Hands, and a Line at the Foot Nobody Will Own}
\CRsheetheading{Of the Grey in the Corners, the Last Day, and the Burning Called Dealt With, Being the Court’s Standing Order for the Sweeping of the Last Day, Copied into the Court’s Room at Sill with the Sweep-Clerk’s Margin, the Places in a Table, the Form of Entry Left Blank, the Sweeping-Song Pasted Inside the Cover, Two Corrections in Borrowed Hands, and a Line at the Foot Nobody Will Own}
{\centering\FellFont\itshape\footnotesize\color{faded} An extract from the Court’s ordinances, written out in the Court’s room in Slate Row in Sill for the households of the district; the articles in Ledgerhand with the verbs restored beneath them, the places and the faults in tables, the form of the entry left blank, the sweeping-song pasted inside the cover, two corrections in borrowed hands, a scorch off a household lamp, and a line at the foot nobody has claimed · Copied at Sill in the dark month of Ash, Y.H. 813, the Thin Year of the Long Cold, by the under-clerk who keeps the last-day slate in the Court’s room in Slate Row, from the standing order sent down from the Hearthseat to the factor at Greybank, sent down in Y.H. 418, set down after the Rising of Y.H. 668 and added to in Y.H. 782 and in the Thin Year; kept against the Last Day in the drawer under the counter beside the bell-cord, and written to be carried forward at the Opening of the Slates. It survives as three leaves of foolscap sewn with wire, with grey Ash off my own thumb at the head, tallow gone white where the lamp stood through a watching, a browned crumb of barley bread pressed into the second fold, a curl of grey wool through the tie-hole off a cradle blanket carried over a threshold, a pale ring where a pan of washing-water stood, bone-coloured slip along the outer edge from a swaddling cloth, a green bead of lead glaze pressed in by a girl come up from High Kiln with the sweetness still at her mouth, a scorch where a spark off the household hearth caught the third leaf, a washing-water tide-line along the foot, two corrections in borrowed hands, and a line at the foot that nobody will own\par}\medskip
I keep the last-day slate in the Court’s room in Slate Row. The order comes down every year from the Hearthseat to the factor at Greybank, and is copied here so that a house may know what is being entered against it before the bread is cut. The order is in Ledgerhand, and there is nobody in any of its sentences. I put the people back underneath, because a sweeping with nobody in it is a sweeping nobody did, and that is the kind this Court has always liked best.

It was sent down to the factor in Y.H. 418, set down after the Rising of Y.H. 668, and added to in Y.H. 782 and in the Thin Year. A rule with no broom on it is a rule nobody has had to sweep. These have been swept.

\subsection*{The standing order as it stands in the Court’s room}

\subsection*{I. Of the day and the lamp}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item The Last Day is the fifth of the Five and belongs to no month. Bread is baked in every house. No market is held, no figure is read, and the bell at the Cross is not rung.

\end{enumerate}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Margin:} In the Five the bell is silent, and on Account-day it goes four, four and a gap with nobody crossing himself. I have kept the two silences apart. A man who puts them together has begun to keep an account of a rumour, and the Court pays for those by the page.\end{quote}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item The grey in the corners is not swept on the Last Day. It is left where the year left it, and is gathered by lamp in the morning.

\end{enumerate}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Margin:} It is invisible in daylight and plain by tallow-light. I hold the lamp low so a household will not know I am writing, and the grey comes up out of the grain of the leaf where my thumb turned it. A woman at the tubs in Stone of the year gone told a girl that the grey would lie where it lay until the Last Day and be burnt the morning after and called dealt with. I have entered the telling as a telling, and not as the grey.\end{quote}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item The order is read at the Cross before the bread is cut. The reader does not ask what the grey is.

\end{enumerate}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Margin:} I asked once. The reader said, \emph{residue arising on the premises}, which is true of a corner and of a room and of a person standing in it, and is therefore true of nobody. I have set the answer at the edge, the length of a face.\end{quote}

\subsection*{II. Of the places}

\emph{The left column is the order’s own name. The second is what this district calls the same place. The third is what goes into the slate. The fourth is mine and has no standing in any court in Sarn.}

The place as the order names it — What our district calls it — What is entered — What stands beneath\par

The corner behind the sleeping-place — a draught coming under the door — residue, no quantity — a promise that went unkept, as the yard says\par

The skirting of the warm room — old soot off the firing — residue, swept — the cool stone at the rack end and the wool over the grain\par

The boards before the shelf — weather — residue, swept — two gaps in a row of loaves and a finger that will not read them\par

The floor beneath the wheel — slip — residue, swept — a seat kept hollow by twenty years of sitting\par

The step at the door — mud brought in on boots — residue, swept — a pot broken there, with the shard left where it fell\par

A house from which no collector came — nothing arising — residue, not entered — a name spoken once at a bank and a whole return for one not in the room\par

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Margin:} I asked a woman at the well why the grey gathers in a corner. She said it gathers where something has gone unkept. I have put that at the edge, the length of a saying, and not into the column, because a saying with a cause in it becomes a figure by supper in this country, and a figure wants a payer, and no payer stood at that well.\end{quote}

\subsection*{III. Of the burning}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item In the morning the grey is gathered from the places and burnt. The ash of the burning is not entered, and no deduction arises against the year.

\end{enumerate}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Margin:} A deduction is a figure and the grey is not a figure. Where the order says \emph{no deduction arises}, I have left a place the length of a figure so that a man may see what stood there. In nine years nobody has filled it with a nought, which is the only honesty this article has ever been capable of.\end{quote}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item The fire is from the house’s own hearth. No priest attends the burning and no collector. In the Hearthseat the grey is burnt in a brazier beneath the grating, which no priest is allowed to touch.

\end{enumerate}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Margin:} A woman of Low Kiln carried her grey to the midden in a twice-mended pot and set the pot on the step afterward with the crack showing. I have entered the pot as a pot. I have left the crack where it was; a mended thing leaves the hand that handled it showing, and this order has no column for a hand.\end{quote}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item The house says that the grey is dealt with. The word is not entered.

\end{enumerate}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Margin:} I asked a woman what was dealt with. She said the grey. I asked what had left it. She said the winter, and went for her water. There is no column for the going for water, and I have not made one.\end{quote}

\subsection*{The faults and their correcting}

Fault — As entered in the room — What the clerk sets beneath\par

Grey swept before the Last Day — residue, no entry arising — the hand that swept it, at the edge, the length of a hand\par

A figure put upon the grey — the page copied again, in the same hand — the length of the figure, and no figure\par

\emph{Dealt with} written into an article — allowed, being the house’s own word — the thing the house did not do\par

A name spoken over the corner — not entered — the name, at the edge, the length of it\par

A pot carried whole to the burning — breakage not entered — the crack left showing\par

The lamp held high where a household could see it — no entry — the hand that kept it low\par

\subsection*{The form of the entry}

\emph{Set out at the end. I have copied it with the blanks as they stand. In nine years no house has asked to have the last line read aloud.}

\begin{quote}\itshape Entered this day, being the Last Day, in the year of the Hearth ----, the bread baked in the house of ----------------------, the grey left in the corner where the year left it, gathered by lamp in the morning and burnt with the house’s own hearth, no figure arising and no deduction entered, the name spoken over the corner ----------------------, which is not entered, the word \emph{dealt with} said by ----------------------, who did not say what was dealt with; written by ----------------------, whose hand went to the corner before it went to the crust.\end{quote}

\subsection*{The sweeping-song, pasted inside the cover}

\emph{Said low at the door while the lamp is held, never at the Cross and never at the burning. The second line of the third verse is the women’s line; the clerks sing it wrong on purpose.}

\begin{quote}\itshape Grey in the corner by tallow shown,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the bread set down and the crust its own;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape sweep it after the lamp goes round,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape call it dealt with and burn it in the morn.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Four for the bell and four for the bread,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and a gap where the fifth should stand;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the Court has a figure for what was took,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and none for what the corner kept.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape A crust at the corner for one not come,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape a crack left showing where the wire crossed;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the grey goes up in the morning smoke,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the house goes on where the house was.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Four for the bell and four for the bread,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the gap goes up with the rest;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the fire keeps the year and the lamp keeps the place,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the hand that held it keeps none of it.\end{quote}

The bell is not rung in the Five. I have kept the gap as a gap and have not put a twelfth into it, whatever the College writes.

\subsection*{What the borrowed hands did}

A clerk of the College came up from Slate Row on the morning the order was copied, with ink in two fingers of a cuff gone soft from washing. He struck \emph{the grey is gathered} out of article four and set \emph{the residue is collected and disposed of} above it, which is true of every corner and therefore of none. Against the woman at the tubs he put a round nought and wrote \emph{no person arising} under it. A nought is a figure and a woman is a person saying a thing; I have put mine back underneath and left his above, where they belong, the way the grey is left in the corner until morning and called dealt with.

The other hand is a factor’s from Greybank, brown at the edge with a little gold in it. Against \emph{no deduction arises} he wrote \emph{the premises are cleared}, and against the crust at the corner, \emph{an article of value, not entered}. I have not struck either. A hand with gold in it can call a crust an article; a hand that has held the lamp at the corner calls it a place set for somebody. Both stand.

\subsection*{At the head and in the gutter}

The grey at the head is Ash off my own thumb, turning the leaf toward the lamp while I found a name, and it will not come out of the creases. The white in the gutter is tallow gone hard where the lamp stood through a watching; it has taken the corner off one line without taking the sense, and I have not picked it off. The crumb in the second fold is barley from the Last Day bread, pressed in while I read the form of entry to a woman who held the crust in her apron and did not eat it. The curl of grey wool through the tie-hole came off a cradle blanket carried over a threshold on the Last Day; I have not untied it. The pale ring is a pan of washing-water set down while I read article four to a woman who kept her hands in her sleeves. The bone-coloured streak along the edge is slip off a swaddling cloth laid here while a girl from the yard waited for me to finish; it is not Ash and in this room the difference is worth knowing. The green bead is lead glaze, pressed in by a girl come up from High Kiln with the sweetness still at her mouth; she leaned to see the form of entry, did not ask what the grey was, and went back down the stair. The scorch in the third leaf is a spark off the household hearth, caught while I held the paper too near in order to read it in the draught. The tide-line along the foot is water from the washing of the step after a burning; it has taken the corners off two lines and left the lines.

There is no Last Day for a slate. The order is read, the bread is cut, the grey is burnt, and the leaf goes back into the drawer with the grey still in the grain of it.

\subsection*{At the foot, in a hand nobody will own}

\begin{quote}\itshape The bread keeps the house. The lamp keeps the corner. Between the crust and the smoke a woman leaves what the order has no column for.\end{quote}

I asked the woman who bakes, a clerk come down from Greybank, and a man who reads at the Cross, and had three answers and no hand, as I have had before. I have left the line where it was written. The Last Day stands ahead; the bread will be baked and the grey left where the year left it, and in the morning it will be gathered by lamp and burnt, and the house will say it is dealt with, and the corner will keep whatever it kept.

\clearpage\phantomsection\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{The Sermon at the Grey Mouth, Being What an Old Kiln-Woman Said Under the Fallen Arch of the Old Kiln on the Morning the Watch Turned a Man Back from the Ash, in Bone of Y.H. 812, with the Grey-Song Left as It Is Sung, the Row of Jars in a Sherd-Tally, a Factor’s Clerk’s Correction, and a Line at the Foot in a Hand Nobody Will Own}
\CRsheetheading{The Sermon at the Grey Mouth, Being What an Old Kiln-Woman Said Under the Fallen Arch of the Old Kiln on the Morning the Watch Turned a Man Back from the Ash, in Bone of Y.H. 812, with the Grey-Song Left as It Is Sung, the Row of Jars in a Sherd-Tally, a Factor’s Clerk’s Correction, and a Line at the Foot in a Hand Nobody Will Own}
{\centering\FellFont\itshape\footnotesize\color{faded} A kiln-mouth sermon of the common Grathic telling, preached at the niche under the lip of the Old Kiln one league south of Sill; the sayings in Grathic, the grey-song with the place where the fifth line should stand left as it is sung, the jars in a sherd-tally, one correction in the narrow upright Ledgerhand of a factor’s clerk come out from Greybank to measure the winter clay, and one line at the foot in a hand nobody will own · Preached on Bone 12, Y.H. 812, the Thin Year, by an old kiln-woman who had swept the mouth of the Old Kiln for seven and twenty winters, on a morning when the Thane’s watch turned a man back from the throat and the man left his crust on the lip and went; written that evening by the keeper of the niche, in charcoal and with the point of a broken sherd on the back of a kiln-docket spoiled by rain, folded into a grey wool kiln-cloth and kept in a tin under a loose firebrick at the mouth, out of reach of the watch. It survives with soot worked into the head and the gutter, grey clay dried pale in the creases and under one nail, a frost-crisp along the fore-edge where the leaf lay a night outside the arch, a wet ring where a dish of barley-water stood from the first voice to the last, a green bead of High Kiln lead glaze pressed into the lower corner by a girl with the sweetness still at her mouth, a grey Ash print along the gutter off a cuff nobody will own, a copper bit shut in the fold, the charred end of a tallow dip, one correction in the narrow upright hand of a factor’s clerk come out from Greybank to measure the winter clay, and a line struck through and written again very small underneath in a hand that has never come forward. Copied once at Greybank in Ilmen, Y.H. 813, with the verbs put back and the empty place left empty.\par}\medskip
I keep the niche under the fallen arch at the mouth of the Old Kiln, and nobody asked me for this. I write because the old woman spoke to a dead kiln and the kiln gave back nothing, and I did not want the words to go the way the smoke goes. She spoke first to the ash, then to the jars, then to the road that goes north to Sill, and last of all to us, which is the order a kiln-woman uses when there is a watch upon the road and somebody may be listening who wants a figure. I have set her words down in Grathic.

The soot at the head is mine and comes off the arch; the grey under one nail is this place’s clay, not Ash, though a clerk would call it so. The ring is barley-water set down at the first voice by a woman who did not drink it. The green bead is not slip: a girl of High Kiln leaned over with the sweetness at her mouth, touched the corner and went back up the road. I have told her what that sweetness does to a gum, and she has told me her mother had it and held a cup to the end. The frost took two words off the fore-edge and I have not written them back, because a song with two words gone is a song said slowly. I have moved none of it.

\subsection*{The manner of the leaving, as the mouth actually has it}

\emph{Written small, from watching, not from any order the Thane has printed.}

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item Come before the watch’s round and be gone before it comes back. The throat is the Thane’s; no jar is carried past the fallen arch.

\item Set your jar on the lip with its mouth uppermost. Mouth to the sky is for a thing done with giving; mouth to the ground is for a thing still asked to hold.

\item Do not glaze a jar of this clay. It will not take. A woman who glazes grey clay spends good lead on a thing that has refused it.

\item Tap the jar before you set it. A sound jar answers full under the knuckle and a grey one answers flat, a little dead sound that stops at the surface. Do not say what you heard where a man with a slate is standing.

\item Leave what you brought: a crust, a bit, a sherd, a knot. What is set down at a dead kiln stays at a dead kiln.

\item When the bell comes up the south road from the Cross, stop. It has counted something that is not your jar. Four, four and a gap, and the gap is not one of yours to fill.

\end{itemize}

She said the last twice, once to the ash and once to a man up the road with his hands in his sleeves.

\subsection*{The sermon, as she said it}

\subsection*{Of the grey}

She put her palm flat on the fallen arch, where the firebrick had gone the colour of a pot fired and left.

“This clay will not take a glaze,” she said. “I have watched women carry good lead up from High Kiln and spend it on a jar dug here, and the jar comes out grey as it went in, the lead sitting on it like a promise made to a person who has gone away. A thing can be made and still not take what is put upon it. That is the whole of my preaching, and I have had seven and twenty winters to find another sentence and could not.”

She turned a grey jar so the row could see the lip, which had no colour on it.

“Do not tell me it is a bad jar. It was asked to be something it was not made to be.”

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{The people answered, and said it twice, once for the mouth and once for the road:}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape The clay will not take a glaze;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape it has not forgotten the fire.\end{quote}

\subsection*{Of the ash}

“The ash in the throat is deeper than a man,” she said to the arch. “I have never been in and never will, and the watch is set on the road to see nobody does. A man came this morning with his coat done against the cold and went a pace past the arch, and the watch turned him, and he came back and left his crust on the lip and went off with his hands in his sleeves. I have set the crust on the sill where the birds may have it.”

There was a silence after this, the kind that has four in it and a gap.

“They tell us the kiln’s breath is a merciful death,” she said. “A man sleeps before a banked kiln with the damper shut and does not wake, and the district calls it merciful because no slate goes up to Sill over it and nobody has to be sent for. I have known three men go that way and said the word at two of the graves, because it is a word people want at a grave. Here I will not say it. A man lay down. That is what I know. Whether he was tired or cold or wanted something he could not ask for, I do not know, and the ash does not.”

A woman near me put her thumb into the grey at the rim of a jar and left it there and did not say whose jar it was. I have put no name to it, and there is no name on the leaf.

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{The people answered:}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape The clay will not take a glaze;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape it has not forgotten the fire.\end{quote}

\subsection*{Of the figure}

A factor’s clerk come out from Greybank to measure the winter clay stood at the end of the row with a slate to his forearm. He asked what a jar was worth that would not take a glaze.

“Nothing at the Cross,” she said. “I have set one here every Bone for seven and twenty years and never wanted a figure for it.”

“Then it is nil,” he said.

“It is worth nothing to you,” she said. “Those are two sentences and I will not have one put over the other. One in twelve is printed on the notice and read at the Cross and is not a lie. It is a true thing said to a room that is not this one.”

“The measure is retained,” he said, in the voice that takes the speaker out of the sentence. “Nothing is lost that we have kept.”

“I keep a jar,” she said. “I do not keep a person. If the Hearth wants what went up the throat of this kiln, let it come down the south road and fetch it. It has not come yet.”

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{In the narrow upright hand of the clerk, above the old words:} Grey clay is inert; the jars are unsaleable. No measure arises. Enter as nil.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape *\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Underneath, in mine:} I have put \emph{worth nothing to you} back under his \emph{is nil}. His sentence travels well and arrives empty, which is what a man wants who has to carry it eighteen leagues to a table. I have left his hand above and mine below.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{The people answered:}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape The clay will not take a glaze;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape it has not forgotten the fire.\end{quote}

\subsection*{Of them that went into the ground}

“They teach that the dead come back warm,” she said. “I have stood at four returns in this district. Two came back as other people, with a hankering for a table they had never sat at.
