One said a word in a tongue I have forgot. One came back thin and wanted nothing and sat by the door until somebody put a crust in her hand. The Court calls each a settling and reads a figure over it.”

She turned a grey jar mouth down on the lip.

“I am not saying the Return is a lie. I am saying I have not seen the thing they say it is, and the difference sits on this lip where no slate is set. The rich buy the grey in a phial and call it quiet ash, and a man who cannot remember his own dead sleeps the better. I have never bought one and never will. Not from piety. I have no use for a sleep that must be bought.”

A girl of the Clay Yard asked what lay under the firebrick and was given a year: Y.H. 668, the Rising. She asked again in a different way and had the same year. A date is the only answer this mouth gives, and the Court likes a date and does not ask what it covers.

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{The people answered, and the children said it twice, once for the moot and once for them that came late:}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape The clay will not take a glaze;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape it has not forgotten the fire.\end{quote}

\subsection*{The grey-song}

\emph{Sung low, standing, with the palm on the arch and a jar mouth-up on the lip. The row says the last four. There is a place where the fifth line should stand, the one the watch leaves, and I have left it as it is sung.}

\begin{quote}\itshape Grey on the lip and grey in the throat,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the jar came up out of the clay;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape a glaze will not take and a name will not stay,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the watch goes by in the grey.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Four for the jars and four for the road,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and a place where a fifth would stand;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the bell keeps a gap and the ash keeps a word,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and neither is entered by hand.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape The clay will not take a glaze;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape it has not forgotten the fire.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Take up what you brought and go home by the south road,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and leave the throat to the watch and the Thane’s desire.\end{quote}

A girl asked what the space was for. Nobody answered. The clerk put a nought against it, which I have left where he set it.

\subsection*{The row of jars, as the mouth keeps it}

\emph{A jar set on the lip stays on the lip and no tally from Sill has counted one. These I have set down where they stood.}

Jar — Set by — What was asked of her — What the mouth gave\par

Grey, unglazed, lip chipped — the old woman, every Bone — nothing; she sets it and goes — another Bone\par

Grey, with a pale line at the rim — a girl of High Kiln — whether the sweet would kill her — the clay, which would not take the glaze\par

Grey, with a copper bit shut inside — a man off the south road — whether his deduction was lawful — the printed figure, read at the Cross, unchallenged\par

A sherd with a branching mark — nobody will say — nothing — kept, and not turned up in company\par

The crust on the sill — the man the watch turned — nothing — the birds, before noon\par

The fifth place — the watch — — — not set; left the length of one\par

There were jars before these and my mother could set a winter to each, and I have not written the winters, because a row of years is a thing a clerk can carry away and a jar is not. The sherd with the branching mark I have not turned up, for an answer given to no question is a kind of theft.

\subsection*{What the clerk did}

He came from Greybank with ink in two fingers and gave the docket back with the verbs taken out.

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item Where she said \emph{a thing can be made and still not take what is put upon it}, he wrote \emph{the vessel is incapable of retention} above and left hers below.

\item Where she said \emph{a man lay down}, he wrote \emph{a life was voluntarily resigned} and underlined it twice. He did not ask which man, which was the first true thing he did all morning.

\item At the fifth place he put a round nought and wrote \emph{vacancy}, and when I asked what a place was worth that held no jar, he said nothing a clerk could enter.

\item At the gap in the song he wrote \emph{vacancy} again, and at the branching sherd \emph{mark of no significance; not a figure}, which is true, and the only true thing on his slate I could have said myself.

\end{itemize}

I have put the verbs back underneath and left his hand above. He takes them out because a thing always true has no need of them. I put them back because a woman with her palm on a cold arch wants to know who did the refusal: her own clay that failed, or somebody else’s lead.

\subsection*{At the head and in the gutter}

The soot at the head is mine and will not wash out of the fold; I rest the docket on the arch and do not notice I have marked it. The grey under the nail comes up however I wash. The frost took two words off the fore-edge and I have left them gone. The ring is barley-water set down by a woman who stood through the speaking of them that went into the ground and did not drink it. The green bead is not slip, and I have kept the leaf out of the sun. The grey in the gutter came off a cuff; I have not swept it, and there is no Last Day at this mouth. The charred end is from my dip, which burned down while the clerk wrote \emph{nil}.

\subsection*{At the foot}

Struck through once and written again underneath, very small, in a hand that is not mine, the old woman’s or the clerk’s:

\begin{quote}\itshape What the glaze would not take, the grey kept.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape What the grey kept, no slate has entered.\end{quote}

I asked four people and had four answerings and no hand. I have left the line struck through, the only honest way to keep a sentence you cannot sign.

The docket goes back in the tin under the loose firebrick. Next Bone the jars will be set mouth-up and the watch will go by with its spear gone blue at the head, and the bell will come four, four and a gap, and the clay will refuse whatever is put on it. If the clerk comes I shall let him take the verbs out and put them back, and leave the nought and the fifth where they stand.

\clearpage\phantomsection\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{The Guess-Shed of Nine Pots, Being the Riddle Fight of the Long Frost, the Wagers Counted in Sherds, and the Loaf That Was Not Paid}
\CRsheetheading{The Guess-Shed of Nine Pots, Being the Riddle Fight of the Long Frost, the Wagers Counted in Sherds, and the Loaf That Was Not Paid}
{\centering\FellFont\itshape\footnotesize\color{faded} A pot-mender’s winter record, set down for the settling of a wager and not for the improvement of the reader; the rules in the hand the shed keeps, the riddles in the words they were spoken, the wagers in broken sherds in a jar, the tally of one night set against a Sill carter’s tally, the correction of a factor’s clerk in Ledgerhand, a gloss pressed into the margin in charcoal, and one line at the foot in a hand nobody will claim · Written in Bone of Y.H. 812, the Thin Year after the Long Cold, in the shared drying shed at Nine Pots (four kilns and one clay pit, eight leagues west of Sill, in standing feud with Sill over the road), by Heddi of Nine Pots, a woman who mends cracked pots with slip and keeps the shed and its fire through the cold months; copied forward in Ilmen of Y.H. 813 onto the back of a spoiled glaze-tally from the third firing, sewn with wire into a fold of oiled sackcloth and kept in the jar by the covered bench at the pit’s head. It survives with bone-coloured slip ground into the head, a green thumb of glaze at the fold, tallow in the gutter, a crust of frost along the outer edge, a press of wet wool across the first leaf, a potsherd folded into the gutter where a figure should stand, one correction in the narrow upright hand of a factor’s clerk come up from Greybank, a gloss in the thick charcoal hand of a Sill carter who borrowed the leaf on a market morning, and a line at the foot in a hand that is nobody’s\par}\medskip
I mend what the kiln spoils. In Bone there is no drying to do and the shared shed is the only warm room in Nine Pots, so in Bone I keep the guess-shed, which is what we call the riddle bench, though a man from Sill would call it an alehouse and charge the road for it.

Nine Pots and Sill are in feud over the road. It is eight leagues of packed clay and belongs to both of us, which is why neither of us mends it. In the thaw the feud is carried in stones thrown and in loaves withheld. In the frost the road shuts under its skin and a man cannot throw a stone eight leagues, so we throw questions instead. A riddle is a stone the other man has to carry home.

The bench is a drying board laid on two clay cones and blackened by ten thousand sleeves. I keep the wagers in a jar of sherds at the end away from the fire, where a sherd shows white against the soot, and I empty the jar in the morning back into the pit. Nothing is carried away from this shed in a slate. A man who wants a thing entered can go east to Greybank and sit with people warmer than himself, and he will not get a riddle there.

\subsection*{The rules, as the shed keeps them}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item A riddle is put once. Ask for it a second time and you owe a sherd, because the second asking is for your own pleasure and not for the shed.

\item Answer in one breath, and say it to the pot, the bench or the fire, never to the man who put it. Said looking at a Sill man, an answer becomes an argument, and the argument is the feud, and the feud has a date a clerk would want.

\item Four questions are scored. A wager is not a question and is kept on a place of its own, because a loaf laid down is a thing that can be taken up again.

\item The judge is the shed. I say whether an answer serves and I do not say why. A reason given is a riddle given away for nothing, and the giver can go home and sell it.

\item Sherds are counted by the hand and not by the eye. A sherd for a round, a cup of small ale for a night, and neither leaves in a figure. This is a skill we share with the eel-women downriver, who keep their accounts in cords and will not say where they learned it.

\item No slate lies on the bench. If a slate comes in, the guessing stops for that night, because a thing entered is not a riddle any more; it is a debt with the warmth taken out of it.

\item A pot is set down before the first question and nobody lifts it until the fourth. If it answers flat when it is set down, the night’s answering will go badly. I have never known this to fail and I would not say so before a thrower.

\end{enumerate}

\subsection*{The four that were scored}

The first went to a girl who sweeps the Glaze Room up the terrace in Sill, come down with the frost to see our kilns and stay longer than she meant to. She had her answer before the verse was out, which is why she never wins anything and is always first.

\begin{quote}\itshape Sweet before it is trusted, green where no grass grew,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape a pale line at the gum and a price on the shelf;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the mixer knows it by the tongue, the potter by the thumb.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape What is it?\end{quote}

“The lead in the glaze,” she said, and said it to a pot. “My mother has the line,” she said, “and she will not say what she tastes.” Nobody asked her to say more. A girl of twelve in this country knows what is in the mix and what the mix does to the women who taste it, and knows that the knowing is not to be said across a room where men have slates.

The second I put to a thrower of Nine Pots, with slip dried bone-coloured on both forearms and the little finger bent where a splinter went in at eleven.

\begin{quote}\itshape A tube of cold iron opens a way no knife made;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape what it takes leaves a round place that shows through winter;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the figure goes up the road and the warmth goes\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape nowhere a body can follow.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape What is it?\end{quote}

“A measure,” he said, and said it to the floor. There was a man at the bench with a pale round place above his wrist who set his cup down and did not lift it again. The measure is not a thing for a feast, and a riddle answered right is still an answer that has cost somebody. I scored it and passed the jar; he did not pass his cup back, and nobody made him.

The third went to a carter out of Sill, who had come up the road that morning and would go back before dark.

\begin{quote}\itshape Eight leagues long, owned by two houses\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape that will not share a name;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape both mend me, and each says the other\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape laid the first stone;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape I carry their loaves and their stones\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and neither crosses me in frost.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape What am I?\end{quote}

“The road,” he said, and said it to the door. He would not say which house laid the first stone, because a first stone is a thing a Court clerk would want a date for, and a date given in a shed is a date carried out of it. The old man who mends said something low about the frost holding the road together better than either village did, and the carter said nothing to that, which is the proper way to answer a man who has said something true.

The fourth I put myself, because the room had got noisy and wanted quieting, and a riddle put by the shed is not scored against anybody.

\begin{quote}\itshape Set me down and I tell you whether I am honest;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape tap me and the whole shed hears it;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape I can crack and come back, and I never say\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the crack went away.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape What am I?\end{quote}

“A pot,” said the old man who mends. “A pot and the seam in it.” He said it to the bench. Then he set his own cup down and it answered full, which is the only answer a man can get from a pot without paying for it. He left his sherd on the board and did not take it back, and I have put that sherd in the gutter of this account where a figure should stand. If he wanted it again he could ask, and he has not asked.

\subsection*{The tally, in sherds}

Round — Put by — Answer given — Served — Sherds\par

The sweet — the shed — the lead in the glaze — yes, said to a pot — one\par

The tube — the shed — a measure — yes, said to the floor — one\par

The road — the shed — the road — yes, said to the door — one\par

The pot — the shed — a pot and the seam — yes, said to the bench — one, left lying\par

Four answered and none drunk. The cup stood from the first question to the last and went back on the shelf with the ale still in it, which is how small ale is drunk in Nine Pots when there is a thing to say and no proper word for it.

\subsection*{The loaf that was not paid}

The wager is not in the table, and I keep it where it belongs, on a place of its own. The carter laid a browned loaf on the bench against the girl from High Kiln: she could not name the sweet in the glaze, he said, without tasting it, and there was lead enough in the room to have done the naming for her. She named it and did not taste it. He took the loaf up again and said she had named a thing and not the name of it, which is the sort of distinction a man makes when the loaf is his.

He said it to the bench and not to her. She went back up the terrace with the frost on her shawl and did not ask for the loaf, and I have not put a figure against the place where it stood, because a sherd is not a loaf and a figure is neither. When a man takes up a loaf that has been laid down, what is left is a place on a board, and there is no word in Grathic for the holding of it.

\subsection*{What the factor’s clerk did}

A clerk of the factor’s office came up from Greybank in the second tend of Ilmen, with a cuff gone soft at the edge from washing and ink sitting in two fingers of it that would not come out. He laid his hand on the leaf before his eyes went to the room, which is the manner of that table. He set the four questions down as \emph{queries entered} and the answers as \emph{responses recorded}, put two marks against each sherd (a sherd, he said, is a half-bit), struck the loaf as \emph{consideration not tendered}, and wrote \emph{levy on small ale, one in twelve} across the head of the tally, so that a night of guessing came out as a night of trading. Against the round place on the man’s arm he wrote \emph{measure drawn; cost to district, nil}. Where the old man had said the seam keeps the crack, he wrote \emph{repair retained; material not entered} and left mine underneath, which is more than he usually leaves.

In the shed’s hand — In the Court hand\par

Sherds in the jar, counted by hand — Four responses, two marks each\par

The loaf not paid — Consideration not tendered\par

The road, owned by both and mended by neither — Way, public; upkeep not entered\par

A pale round place above a man’s wrist — Measure drawn; cost to district, nil\par

A pot that cracks and comes back with the crack showing — Repair retained; material not entered\par

The guessing stops when a slate comes in — No entry required\par

He asked me what a riddle was worth and I told him nothing a clerk could carry, which is the first true thing I have said to that table in two years. I have put my words under his and left his standing above, the way a drying board keeps the wet mark under the sherd. He has entered four answers and struck the loaf, and the loaf was not struck: it went back to the man who laid it down.

\subsection*{What the carter put in the margin, in thick charcoal}

He borrowed the leaf on a market morning and returned it with the fold changed. I have copied his hand as it stands.

At \emph{neither crosses me in frost}: \emph{We cross it. We cross it before the frost sets and come back with the clay on our boots. Saying we do not is how we keep from asking who laid the first stone.}

At \emph{the figure goes up the road}: \emph{It goes to Greybank. The man with the round place walks the other way and is not paid for the walk.}

At the loaf: \emph{I am the man who took the loaf back. She named it and I said she had not. I have said it to my own daughter since, and she has asked me twice which of us I was.}

I have not answered him in the margin. A man writes that in a book and it follows him home.

\subsection*{At the head and in the gutter}

The slip at the head is mine; I held the tally down with my whole hand because the draught under the shed door takes paper before it takes a man, and there is slip in my knuckles whatever I am doing. The green at the fold came off a girl who leaned over to see the writing with sweetness still at one corner of her mouth. The tallow in the gutter is mine. The press of wet wool across the first leaf came off the carter, who held the door while the factor’s clerk read and did not let go when it was done. The crust of frost along the outer edge came up out of the paper on the night the shed froze, when I carried the leaves inside my coat and the coat froze to my back; I have not scraped it off, because a night of riddles kept in a warm room would be a different night. The sherd folded into the gutter is the one the old man left on the board. I have set it where the figure should stand, because it is what the night left, and a figure is not.

\subsection*{At the foot, in a hand nobody will own}

\begin{quote}\itshape Four answers went home in men’s mouths. The road kept the stones.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape The loaf went back to the man who had laid it down.\end{quote}

I asked the carter, the girl and the old man, and had three answers and no hand. I have left the line where it was written. The jar goes back under the bench and the sherds go back into the pit. When the clay sets in Seed the feud will go back to stones and loaves, and the shed will be a drying room again. I shall keep the guess-shed for the next frost, count what is left in sherds, and set the loaf’s place where the figure was, and not ask who wrote the line at the foot.

\clearpage\phantomsection\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{The Gull That Carries, Being a Boat-Soldier’s Field Notes on the Brine-Gull of the Sallow Coast and the Glaze Cliffs}
\CRsheetheading{The Gull That Carries, Being a Boat-Soldier’s Field Notes on the Brine-Gull of the Sallow Coast and the Glaze Cliffs}
{\centering\FellFont\itshape\footnotesize\color{faded} A soldier’s field book on one beast, set down as the record of watches kept over a boat’s warm-store and not as natural philosophy; the rounds in the Vhaleni tide-words written in Grathic letters, the tally in charcoal on the backs of spoiled tide-tallies, a Quay song as it is sung, two rulings in the narrow upright Ledgerhand of a clerk of the tide-tally house, a line in the pale ink of a salt-pan dipper, and one line at the foot in a hand nobody will own · Written in Stone of Y.H. 812, the Thin Year, by one of the Council’s men set over the night-store of a salt boat out of the Quay at Vhal, who wrote at the end of a watch with a tallow end in a pot and the Sallow coming up under the hull; carried forward at the Opening of the Slates into Ilmen of Y.H. 813. Set down first on the backs of tide-tallies spoiled by sea-water and then on four folds of salt-paper stiffened with tar, sewn with eel-sinew and carried in a tarred wrap in a coat pocket. It survives with a white salt bloom at the head, tar at the fold, a Sallow tideline along the gutter, a fish-hook nick at the fore-edge, a brown spot the size of a fingernail on the second leaf where a boy’s blood fell, the charcoal rubbed thin where the wrap was carried against the thigh, two corrections in the narrow upright Ledgerhand of the tide-tally clerk who borrowed the leaves at the tally house, one line in the pale ink of a dipper written on salt-paper gone soft at one corner, and the one line at the foot\par}\medskip
I keep the night-store of a salt boat out of the Quay at Vhal, and that is the whole of my post. The boat belongs to a house that holds its share through its women, and a man who marries into it is come aboard and has his say counted at half, which is an arrangement I have never had cause to test. I am not aboard by marriage. I am set there by the Council and paid by the watch, and my work is to see that what the boat keeps warm at night is still warm in the morning.

The tallies I wrote on first went soft in a week. The sea took the figures off clean, which was a mercy of a kind: a figure the sea has eaten is a figure no clerk can enter. I write in charcoal now, on the backs of spoiled leaves and on folds of salt-paper I have stiffened with tar. Charcoal goes into the grain and salt-paper rots, and a contract that rots is held a virtue here, being a contract that was never quite made. This book is the one thing aboard that the damp has not been asked to settle.

The bloom at the head is salt. I have not brushed it off. A book that has never been out in a Sallow winter was never taken on watch.

\subsection*{What it comes for}

It does not fight. This is the thing a new man gets wrong and the thing that costs him his breakfast. A man looks for teeth and a way of holding on, and meanwhile the loaf goes.

It comes for the coal that has not gone out, the warmed stone, the crust still holding heat from the oven, the fish a man has set by to thaw. It takes the thing a body is keeping against the cold and leaves the body colder than it was. I have watched it come down out of the grey light with its feet white and go off with a coal in its beak, and the hand that had been holding the coal stayed shut for a moment after, the way a hand does when there is nothing in it and it has not yet understood that.

It is a gull. It has a gull’s beak with a small hook at the end and a gull’s way of turning its head to look at a thing sideways. It is the colour of wet stone with a darker grey across the back, and the salt stands on it in a fine white crust at the feet and along the leading edge of the wing, so that a bird come in off the pans looks as though it has been walking in flour. It is no bigger than the gulls that follow the ferry at Greybank, and a man who has seen one at the fishstairs would know this one for a cousin of it. The difference is what it wants.

It has no fear of a man on his feet. I have stood with my spear across my knee and had one come within two paces of the store and go on with its own work. But let a man turn his back on the store, or let him sit down with the crust in his hand, and it is gone in the time it takes to say the tide-word for the turn. There is no courage in testing this twice, and I have not tested it twice.

\subsection*{The turn it comes on}

The Sallow runs against the wind. Every child on the Quay knows it and every man from the clay country has to be told it twice, because their rivers go the way the air goes and they expect the same here. Our water follows the Warm and not the moon, and the dippers read the draw off it before they bless the nets, and tell the Council only what is profitable, which is a Vhaleni way of telling the truth. The gull comes on the turn of the draw, in the hour when the water is deciding which way it will go and has not yet chosen.

Our store is a clay pot of coals under blind ash, set in a box in the lee of the mast, and a warm-stone out of the Keel that came south on the Hearth Road and is worth more than my year’s pay. The stone goes in the pot at the second watch and comes out at the first. Between those two hours the pot is the warmest thing on the boat, and there is always something in the dark that knows it.

In a hard winter they come inland. They have been seen as far as Greybank, over the pass where the clay country gives way to the salt, and a man will tell you they come for the uncollected that lie along that road. I have seen them come for a baker’s basket outside the tally house. I have set down both things and joined neither.

\subsection*{The song}

\emph{Sung going out on the first watch, not coming in. The fourth line is the old line and every man on the Quay sings it wrong on purpose, because a song that gives the bird a reason is a song a man can carry home and set by his own fire. I have set it down as it is sung, with the wrong line standing and the gap where the men leave it.}

\begin{quote}\itshape One for the ebb and one for the draw,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape one for the turn that brings it in;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape it takes the coal before it takes the crust,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and takes the stone the boat kept warm.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Salt on the foot and salt on the wing,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape salt from the pan and not from the dead;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape a thing that can lift is a thing that can go,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the teller’s the same on the either shore.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Count them going and count them back,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape a bit for the bundle, a feather for the sore;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape we sing the old line wrong and leave the gap ---\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the place where the warm thing stood before.\end{quote}

The gap is the space where the coal was. The men know it and sing it and have never once said what it is a gap in, which is the nearest thing we have to a grace here. There is a rower on the pulled benches who sings the last line twice and will not say why, and I have let him keep it.

\subsection*{The tally}

These are the watches I kept a true account of. There were others I did not write because my hands were full and one I did not write because I had drunk. I have set down both sorts as they stand. The last column is the clerk’s, not mine. I counted what went; he entered what could be paid.

Watch — Place — Draw — What went — What came back — Entered\par

Stone 9 — Quay, against the salt pans — turn — a crust — none — 0\par

Stone 14 — Off the Glaze Cliffs — slack — two coals — one, dropped in the water — 0\par

Stone 21 — The coast pass, wind off the clay — ebb — a warmed stone — none — 0\par

Stone 27 — Quay, under the tally house — turn — a fish set out to thaw — the bones — 0\par

Ilmen 3 — Greybank landing — draw — a crust, a bit of rope — the rope — 0\par

Ilmen 12 — Quay, after the thaw — slack — one coal — none — nil\par

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{In the narrow upright hand of the clerk of the tide-tally house, struck through the “What went” column:} Fowl not a vessel. Petty taking by a bird: no deduction arises. Warm in a boat’s store is not entered. Account stands.\end{quote}

I have left his hand standing. A clerk’s hand has its use: it keeps a man from arguing with what he cannot change. But the stone that went on Stone 21 came up the Hearth Road and somebody paid for the keeping of it, and the clerk has put \emph{nil} against it with a neat instrument and no name on it. I have written the stone in the margin below, where his column cannot reach, and I have put my own mark beside it in charcoal.

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Below, in my hand:} One warm-stone, gone. Paid for on the Keel. Not entered anywhere, and missed by nobody but me.\end{quote}

\subsection*{The feathers and the meat}

The feathers hold salt. A bundle is a bit in Vhal and is used to salt a wound, which is a brute method and does sometimes work, though a physician will tell you it is not a physic and a Fen trader will tell you it is the only physic the poor can afford. I have seen a man with a gull-feather laid in a cut that would not close, and the cut went on being a cut. I have seen another go quiet under it for a tend. I have set down both and have no rule out of them.

The meat is not eaten. They say it makes a man thin, and a Vhaleni will say this with one shoulder raised, which is a way of saying that the matter is closed and the meat is not worth the opening. The dippers bless their nets against the bird at dawn in the pans and will not do it while a man from the tally house is standing on the board. I have asked one why. He said a blessing said in front of a clerk is a blessing with a figure on it, and a blessing with a figure on it has already been half bought. I have written his words and not his name.

\subsection*{What they say at the pans}

They say the gull carries the dead out to the Sallow, that a drowned man cannot pay the ferry and goes instead in the beak of a bird. There are songs for it with a woman’s name in them and a wrong done at a landing. I have heard them and I have no quarrel with a song. I have watched one carry a coal, a crust, a fish, a bit of rope, and a child’s wooden boat from a bollard on the Quay, and what it carried was what it could lift. It did not choose between the boat and the coal. One was heavier and it took the coal.

The salt on its feet is the colour of the pans. That much I have seen. I have not written where the salt comes from beyond that, because a man who writes a cause into a book he keeps in a tarred wrap is a man who will be asked for it by somebody with a slate. The pans are a place a man can stand and look at. What the bird wants with the warmth it carries I have left where I found it.

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Written in the pale ink of a dipper on a corner of salt-paper gone soft, the words showing through where the damp has taken them:} It takes the warm and it gives nothing. We say it takes the dead and we are kinder to it than it is to us. Bless the net and do not ask the bird.\end{quote}

I have put the dipper’s line above my own. He wrote it at the pans and I wrote mine on a boat, and neither of us has asked the bird anything.

\subsection*{At the head and in the margins}

The bloom at the head came up out of the paper itself and is the only thing in this book that entered without a hand. The tar at the fold is off the wrap and has taken two lines of the first watch and made them slow to read, which is no great loss. The tideline along the gutter came from a morning when the Sallow came up over the rail and into the box where I kept the leaves; the figures ran together and I did not write them again. The nick at the fore-edge is a fish-hook, from the watch when we lost the fish and found the hook in the cover instead. The brown spot on the second leaf fell there from a boy’s finger when he sat down beside me with a cut in it, and I have not scraped it off, because it is the only entry on this leaf that cost anybody anything. The charcoal is rubbed thin where I carried the wrap against my thigh. The clerk’s two rulings I have not touched. The song is as the men sang it, with the old line wrong and the gap standing.

\subsection*{At the foot, in a hand nobody will own}

\begin{quote}\itshape It carries what can be carried. It is the boat that pays.\end{quote}

I asked a clerk, a dipper, a rower on the benches, and a man who had lost a stone, and had four answerings and no hand. I have left the line where it was written.

There is a reach beyond the Glaze Cliffs where the lead comes down into the sand and the gulls stand in the shallows with their feet white to the knee, and they are not the white of the pans. I have not walked that reach. Next Stone I will take the boat in on the turn with a fresh pot of coals and a coil of cord, and I will count them going and count them back, and if they carry something out of that water that no hand on the boat put there I will set that down too, in charcoal, with the verb left in it and no figure at the end of the row.

\clearpage\phantomsection\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{The Half Knot, Being the Rope-Skipping Game of the Quay at Vhal, with the Counting-Out, the Manner of the Turns, the Eleven Lines, the Half Kept at the Untied Place, and What a Council Clerk Made of It}
\CRsheetheading{The Half Knot, Being the Rope-Skipping Game of the Quay at Vhal, with the Counting-Out, the Manner of the Turns, the Eleven Lines, the Half Kept at the Untied Place, and What a Council Clerk Made of It}
{\centering\FellFont\itshape\footnotesize\color{faded} A rope-woman’s gathering of a children’s skipping game, set down in Grathic letters on the back of a Council tide-draw spoiled by rain; the verses in the children’s own half-sung Quay speech, the manner of it in the writer’s tarred small hand, one gloss pressed in charcoal by a woman who dips at the pans, a Council clerk’s correction in the leaning hand that has gone soft with damp, and one line at the foot in grey chalk in a hand nobody will claim · Written at the Quay in Vhal in Ilmen of Y.H. 813, on the evening of a flood after the Long Cold had gone off the coast, by a woman who mends the nets and coils the tow-ropes for the boats that tie under the tide-tally house; set down on the back of a Council tide-draw gone soft at one edge and sewn with eel-sinew into a fold of oiled sailcloth; carried up the Salt Road with a consignment of glass in Ember and copied at Greybank onto the back of a voided weigh-slip. Kept in a tarred tin under a coil of rope beside the tide-tally house. It survives with a white salt bloom worked into the grain at the head, a tar thumb at the fold, a fibre of wet rope pressed into the second leaf, a brine-gull’s peck through one word of the sixth line, a fish-hook nick at the head, a rent where the old rope frayed across the lower corner, a green bead of cliff-glass pressed in by a girl with sweetness at one mouth-corner, a grey Ash print along the gutter that nobody will own, the pan-woman’s gloss in charcoal, the Council clerk’s correction standing above the children’s words, and a line at the foot in grey chalk\par}\medskip
I coil and mend the ropes for the boats that lie under the tide-tally house, and I have set this down because a girl of the Quay asked me why the half in the rope was for a man who never held a share and never would. Her father came aboard, which is what we call a man who marries into a boat-owning house: his word on the boat counts at half, and has counted so these nine years, and he knows it and does not say it where a clerk can hear him. The girl put him into a skipping rope. I have written it as the children keep it, with the verbs left in, because a rhyme said to a rope wants a hand to lift the next line, and a rhyme said to a Council man wants nothing but a figure.

The leaf is the back of a tide-draw the Council left out in the rain. The figures on the face of it have gone where the Council’s figures go. The green at the corner is a bead of cliff-glass pressed there by a girl of the furnace who leaned over to read and did not ask for it back; the tar is mine, off the coil I was holding when the wind came up off the Sallow; the salt bloomed out of the paper itself, which is a virtue in this country and a folly in every other. The grey along the gutter came off a cuff laid where no cuff has business lying on a Quay, and nobody will own it. There is no Last Day on a Quay.

\subsection*{How it is played}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item The rope is an old tow-rope gone soft, tarred once and rained on since. Eleven knots stand in it. The twelfth place is where a knot has been untied; the cord there is frayed and lighter than the rest. The two ends are called the flood and the ebb. Two children hold the ends and turn; the rest are shares, and skip in the middle. They are the flood, the ebb and the shares, and are not called by their house-names while the rope is going round.

\item Play it on the boards under the tide-tally house at the head of the flood, or on the Salt Pans at dawn before the water has crusted. Never at the ebb, and never when the quay-crier calls the turn: the rope stops then, because a count is being taken elsewhere and two counts in one morning make a debt. Not in the Five, and not while a boat is going out with a dead man aboard, which is a watching and not a game.

\item Say the words to the rope, not to the faces. Said to a face it becomes a bargain, and in Vhal a bargain has to be kept, which no child wants at a rope.

\item One line, one skip. The eleventh line is skipped like the others. The half is not skipped. At the half the two ends stop with the rope knee-high, nobody crosses it, and every hand goes to the frayed place where the knot came out. A child who skips the half is come aboard: she takes the ebb end and turns until three others call her by the name she has at home. Then she comes back into the middle. That is the whole of the bringing back.

\item If the rope catches a foot, the same thing: she goes to the ebb end, and stays there until she is called back. Nobody calls her quickly. The ebb end is not a punishment anyone names, and a child asked why she is standing there will say she is turning, which is true.

\item There is no last round and nothing is won. The child who has kept the half the most times gets to say the verse about the man aboard, and says it to the rope with her back turned to the Quay.

\end{enumerate}

\subsection*{The counting-out}

\emph{The rope lies on the boards. A child lays a finger on each knot from the flood end, one knot to a name, and does not look at the faces. The finger’s knot turns the flood end; if it lights on the frayed place, that child turns the ebb. This is not a prize. The ebb end is where the rope goes out of the hands.}

\begin{quote}\itshape Flood and ebb and coil and cleat,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the share goes round and the half keeps its seat;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape mother’s mother, aunt and kin ---\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the finger stops where the knot has been.\end{quote}

\subsection*{The eleven lines, as they are skipped}

\emph{One line, one skip, over the rope as it comes round. The tenth line is skipped whole. The eleventh is skipped whole. The half is kept.}

\begin{quote}\itshape One for the keel and the cord that binds,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape two for the share that the mother finds;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape three for the aunt who carries it down,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape four for the coil that goes soft in the wet;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape five for the tar that stays on the hand,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape six for the gull that steals from the brazier;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape seven for the pan where the water stands white,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape eight for the bench where the seven years sit;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape nine for the paper the rain has made nothing,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape ten for the crier who calls what has not come;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape eleven for the word we say at the board,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and half for the man who came aboard.\end{quote}

The second line is the share that passes through the mother, and the third is the aunt who carries it down to the boat when the mother cannot. There is no fourth line for a husband. A man who comes aboard is put in the half, which is the last line and the one nobody skips. Ask a child why the half comes last and she will ask you why a man should be counted before a boat.

\subsection*{What is said at the half}

\emph{Hands on the frayed place. The rope is held still, knee-high, and nobody crosses. The words go down to the cord and not across to the children.}

\begin{quote}\itshape The knot’s gone. The place is kept.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape The cord holds what no mother had.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Say it to the cord and not to a face ---\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape a half is a share with nobody under it.\end{quote}

\subsection*{The verse they do not say while a man of the Council is on the Quay}

I have this from the girl who keeps the half, with the space left before it, which is the space the children leave when the rope stops. She said it to the boards with her back turned and made me set it down with none of my verbs in it.

\begin{quote}\itshape The share goes down the mother’s row,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the half goes nowhere and is not signed;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the Council writes on paper made to rot\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and calls the rotting law. We call it weather.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Eleven whole and a half kept out;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the crier turns and the rope turns too,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape but the crier’s turn is not the rope’s,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the half stands where the knot came through.\end{quote}

The draw follows the Warm and not the moon; every dipper knows it and no Council man will say it in front of a factor. The children know the crier’s turn and their own are two turns, which is a thing the tally-house has never entered.

\subsection*{What the woman at the pans put in the margin}

The charcoal here is hers, pressed hard and leaning, the way a woman writes who has dipped at dawn for thirty years and does not want a sentence read by a man who has never stood in salt water.

At the half: \textbf{He came aboard and counted at half for nineteen years before he died, and never once said the word in his own house. The children have put him in a rope. It is more than any of us could do with him.}

At \emph{the cord holds what no mother had}: \textbf{A share goes through the mother. That is the only road it is allowed. My half had no road and went nowhere all his life, and the rope has given it somewhere to stand. Do not make a proverb of this before you have kept a half yourself.}

\subsection*{What the Council clerk did}

A clerk of the Council borrowed the leaf on a market morning, being a man who cannot let paper lie still. He writes in the leaning hand with the salt in the nib, and the damp has had at him since. He struck out \emph{the half keeps its seat} and set above it, \emph{half-interest unenumerated}. Against \emph{a half is a share with nobody under it} he wrote \emph{no entitled party appears}, which is a true thing in a language nobody on this Quay speaks at a rope. At the frayed place, where the children put their fingers, he drew a small circle and wrote nothing inside it, and the rain has gone round the circle and left it standing, so that a place where a knot came out is now a figure that can be copied into a column.

I have put the words back underneath and left his hand above. He writes so a thing can travel up the Salt Road; I write so a child knows which hand to lift. A circle on a damp leaf is a figure. The frayed place is where somebody’s father stands, and it will not travel, and the Council has never had a column for a man standing at half. He asked what the children learned by it. I told him the count, the stopping and the bringing back. He wrote \emph{rudimentary instruction in shares}, and went away with his cuff gone soft at the fold, which is the only thing about him the weather has improved.

\subsection*{At the head and in the gutter}

The salt bloom at the head came out of the paper and has gone white in the grain where the leaf was doubled; it will not wash out, which is why we keep such leaves in tarred tin and not in a house. The tar thumb is mine and came off the coil I held down in the wind; a coil paid for with a wet hand goes soft when the weather goes soft, and I know by it when to shut the tin. The rope fibre in the second leaf came off the very rope the game is played with, and goes frayed at the end like the eleventh place. The brine-gull peck went through one word of the sixth line and nobody has claimed the bird; the word was \emph{brazier}, and a rhyme with a word gone is a rhyme said slowly, and all of ours are said slowly. The hook nick came off a man paying with his hook still in his hand, and he did not apologise. The rent at the lower corner is where the old rope frayed before I cut it down; I have kept the corner open at it. The green bead came off a girl of the furnace who touched the leaf and went back up the shore road with the sweetness at her mouth. The grey in the gutter came off the cuff and has not been swept. There is no Last Day on a Quay; the grey stays where it fell and goes into the next year under the oilcloth.

\subsection*{At the foot, in grey chalk, in a child’s hand}

\begin{quote}\itshape I do not jump the half. It is where my father stands.\end{quote}

The letters are hard at the \emph{th} and one of them is set backward, which is how a child writes who has learned off a tally and not off a book. I asked the girl who keeps the half, a woman who dips at the pans and a carter waiting with his load off the Salt Road, and had three answers and no hand, as I have had before. I have left the line where it was written.

The leaf goes back into the tin under the coil. Tomorrow the boats come in at the flood and the crier will call a turn that is not the rope’s, and the children will stop their rope for it as they always do and begin again after, and the half will stand where the knot came out with nobody jumping it and nobody entering it. The Council clerk may have his circle. The girl will put her finger on the frayed place all the same.

\clearpage\phantomsection\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{The Half Share, Being the Quay’s Drinking Song for a Man Come Aboard}
\CRsheetheading{The Half Share, Being the Quay’s Drinking Song for a Man Come Aboard}
{\centering\FellFont\itshape\footnotesize\color{faded} A Vhaleni drinking song for the coming-aboard feast and the spring launching, taken down in Grathic letters from a mouth that has no word for guest; the verses on salt-paper squared at the edges, with three lines the damp has made void by the Council’s own law, a factor’s clerk’s correction in Ledgerhand, a dipper’s note in charcoal, and one verse in a hand nobody will own · Set down at Vhal on the Sallow coast in Ember of Y.H. 807 by Vessa of the Quay, a woman who held a boat-share from her mother, for the coming aboard of a man whose name she did not enter, because a name entered is a name held; carried up the Salt Road in Frost of Y.H. 810 in a dry tin and copied at Greybank onto the back of a spoiled harbour tally; copied forward in Stone of Y.H. 812 with the damp-void lines left void. It survives with a white salt crust along the gutter, a ring of red wine that has eaten one word clean through, a fibre of wet rope pressed into the second fold, a green bead of Glaze glass, a fish-hook nick at the head, and a thumb printed in salt where the writer signed, because a boat on this coast is signed in salt and not in ink. One correction is in the narrow upright hand of a factor’s clerk who borrowed the sheet at Greybank; one note is in charcoal and is a dipper’s; the verse at the foot is in a hand nobody will own.\par}\medskip
I have set this down in the letters of the clay country, because that is the hand of the account that comes down the Salt Road and the factor at Greybank reads nothing else. The song itself is Vhaleni and loses something in the writing, the way a net loses what it was made to hold. There is no word in my language for \emph{guest} and no word for \emph{please}. I cannot ask you to drink. I set the cup on the bench and go away, and the cup does the asking. This is the whole of our hospitality, and it is why people upriver call us cold. They are welcome to think it. A man who has been called cold by a Grathic household has at least been noticed by one.

The song is not for a quiet room. It is sung at the coming aboard, when a man marries a boat-owning house and is given the half of a share he did not bring with him, and at the launching in Ember when the new hull goes down the ways and everybody’s words are worth half of what they will be worth next year. The women sing the verses. The man come aboard answers the refrain at half voice, because his opinion on the boat counts at half and he has known it since the day he married; a man who cannot take a joke about his own share has no business aboard one. There is salt on the rim of every cup. A man who drinks the wine without the salt has drunk only wine, which is a Grathic habit and a poor one.

The tune goes like water going over water, low and without a rise, and it is sung through the nose. The last line is held until the ebb.

\subsection*{The song}

\emph{The women. A cup set down. Salt on the rim.}

\begin{quote}\itshape The boat was laid before the daughter,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the share went down the mother’s line;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape a man may come aboard by marrying,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape but he does not steer by right of mine.\end{quote}

\emph{The man come aboard answers, at half voice.}

\begin{quote}\itshape Half a share and a whole thirst;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the boat goes where the women go,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the tide goes where it will.\end{quote}

\emph{The women.}

\begin{quote}\itshape We count his word at half, not in spite,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape but because half is what he brought:\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape a tongue, a debt, a pair of hands,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the boat was here before his word.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Do not tell him it is kindness.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape He will spend it. He will enter it.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Give him the half and call it half,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and there is no argument in the room.\end{quote}

\emph{The refrain. The man at half voice. Nobody crosses himself; nobody in Vhal ever has.}

\begin{quote}\itshape Half a share and a whole thirst;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the boat goes where the women go,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the tide goes where it will.\end{quote}

\emph{The women. This verse is sung to the cup, not to the man.}

\begin{quote}\itshape Put salt in it. The Sallow’s in it.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape A man who drinks without the salt\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape drinks only wine, and wine’s a clay-country habit;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape we take the sea with everything.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape The sea is the colour of skimmed milk\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and it runs against the wind,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the dippers say it follows the Warm\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and not the moon. Let the moon go.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Nobody has taxed the moon.\end{quote}

\emph{Here three lines stood, and are gone. Rain got into the tin in Grain of Y.H. 810, between the coast pass and Greybank. I have left the place the length of them and written nothing in it. By the Council’s own law a wet document is no document, so those lines are void, which is a virtue, says the Council, and I have not put them back. I remember two of them and have not written either. A verse remembered is not a verse kept, and I was not going to make the Council a present of one.}

\emph{The women.}

\begin{quote}\itshape Write it on salt-paper. Let it rain.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape A contract that has rotted is no contract,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape which is the virtue of it, and half the fortunes\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape of this port have turned on exactly that.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape A thing that lasts too long stops earning.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape A bench that will not rot has no business\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape in a room where men are buying boats.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Wet paper, clean hands, and a good ebb.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape That is the whole of our law and most of our religion.\end{quote}

\emph{The refrain.}

\begin{quote}\itshape Half a share and a whole thirst;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the boat goes where the women go,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the tide goes where it will.\end{quote}

\emph{The women. This verse is sung at the launching, with the rope in the singer’s hand.}

\begin{quote}\itshape At dawn the dippers trail the net\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and read the draw the Sallow makes;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the Warm goes seaward under the hull\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and we go after it with salt.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape I walked the pans at fourteen barefoot\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and named a tide I had not seen;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape they gave me that name to keep\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape for a thing I could not write down.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape The gull will steal a coal out of your fire\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and carry it upriver warm;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the salt-thing taps the hull at midnight\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape where the store of warmth lies thin.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape A boat that’s warm at dusk and cold by morning\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape has no slate to answer to. That’s the trade.\end{quote}

\emph{The women. The last verse before the refrain is said low, to the boat, while the rope goes over.}

\begin{quote}\itshape Our glass comes green off the Cliffs\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape where the old lead sweetens in the heat;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape drink from it and you will taste the colour\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape of a thing made beautiful by burning.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Fill to the half. Drink it whole.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape The cup is not a guest. The cup has no name.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape If you want a passage, name a tide\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and we will say it has not happened yet.\end{quote}

\emph{The refrain. The man come aboard answers at half voice; the women answer him at full, and the difference is the point of the song.}

\begin{quote}\itshape Half a share and a whole thirst;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the boat goes where the women go,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the tide goes where it will.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Come aboard. Come aboard.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Bring nothing. It is already counted.\end{quote}

\subsection*{How it is used}

\emph{Written small in the margin, in my own hand.}

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item Sung standing. A sitting singer is a singer who has been bought.

\item The man come aboard sings the refrain at half voice the first year. In the second year he may sing it at full if the women have voted it, which they never have while I have been singing.

\item The salt goes on the rim before the wine goes in the cup. Done the other way it is a Grathic cup with salt on it, which is a thing nobody in this port would drink.

\item At a launching the rope is held through the last verse and let go on \emph{Come aboard}. A man who lets go early has paid for a boat that will not hold him.

\item If a collector is in the room, sing the third verse and the law verse and skip the tide verse. He cannot enter the draw, and a verse he cannot enter makes him uneasy enough to drink. This is not a kindness. It is a manoeuvre.

\end{itemize}

\subsection*{What the factor’s clerk did}

A clerk of the factor’s house at Greybank borrowed the sheet on a wet morning and gave it back dry in one corner and damnable everywhere else. I have left his hand standing and mine under it, the way a boat keeps both the water’s mark and the painter that holds it.

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item At \emph{the share went down the mother’s line} he wrote above, \emph{The share is entered to the female line, the male entrant taking a half interest.} Mine stands beneath. His is true in a language nobody on the Quay uses to describe a mother.

\item At \emph{we count his word at half} he set \emph{the vote of the come-aboard is rated at one half} and underlined it twice, as though I had discovered a figure and might be proud of it.

\item At \emph{Write it on salt-paper. Let it rain} he wrote \emph{Instrument voided by exposure to water} and added, in a smaller hand, \emph{no value attaches.} He was quite right. He has made a living out of being quite right in a room full of wet paper.

\item At \emph{the Warm goes seaward under the hull} he wrote \emph{The Sallow draw is a taxable current} and put a figure against it. The figure has not been paid by anybody in eleven years, which is the kind of figure the Court likes best.

\item Where the three lines are gone he wrote \emph{three lines lost, no entry} and then, underneath, \emph{no claim can lie against a lost line, which is fortunate for all parties.} I have left it. He has taken the verbs out of a song and called the result an account, and if he had ever sung one he would know why we keep them in.

\end{itemize}

\subsection*{In the dipper’s hand}

At the foot of the second leaf, in thick charcoal that has rubbed onto the fold, in the hand of a dipper who borrowed the sheet in the Council room when it smelled of tar and wet rope:

\begin{quote}\itshape At dawn we trail the net and read what the Sallow is doing. We tell the Council the figure that buys salt. The draw itself we keep. A current that is measured honestly is a current that gets taxed, and there is no virtue in being taxed honestly.\end{quote}

He did not sign it and did not take the sheet away. When I asked him why he had written it on a song he said a song is the only paper in Vhal that nobody thinks to read. I have left the charcoal where he put it and not washed the fold.

\subsection*{At the head and in the gutter}

The salt crust at the head and along the gutter came up out of the paper on the two nights the tin went damp, and has taken the ink off one word in the law verse; I have not written the word back, because a verse about rot with a word rotted out of it is in better order than I could have made it. The ring is red wine and has eaten through to the other side. The rope fibre in the second fold came off the launching rope in Ember and is wet when the weather is wet, which is a nuisance and a useful one, because it tells me when to keep the tin shut. The green bead is from a cup off the Cliffs and is not slip and not lead; it fell out of a girl’s hair when she leaned over to see the writing, and she did not ask for it back. The nick at the head came off a fish-hook set down in a hurry by a man who was paying me and did not apologize. The salt thumb is mine. A boat on this coast is signed in salt, because ink will not stay on a wet hand and a wet hand is the only kind we have.

\subsection*{At the foot, in a hand nobody will own}

\begin{quote}\itshape A boat is a pot with its crack below the water.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape The sea does not knock. The sea has no knuckle.\end{quote}

I asked the women, the dippers, a factor come up from Greybank and a man who had been come aboard for nine years, and had four answers and no hand. I have left the line where it was written. The sheet goes back in the tin and the tin goes in the drawer where we keep the paper we mean to let rot. A slate is a thing that gets read in a clean voice; this is a thing that gets sung with salt on the rim and goes damp at the fold, and is the better for it. If the clerk borrows it again, let him take the verbs out. The next singer will put the salt back, as I did, and the cup will do the asking.

\clearpage\phantomsection\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{The Half Turn, Being the Skipping Game of the Quay Children at Vhal, with the Counting-Out, the Manner of the Turning, the Verse They Do Not Skip While the Crier Calls the Turn, a Council Clerk’s Figures on Salt-Paper Gone Soft, a Gloss in Charcoal from a Woman Who Mends Nets, and One Line at the Foot in a Hand Nobody Will Own}
\CRsheetheading{The Half Turn, Being the Skipping Game of the Quay Children at Vhal, with the Counting-Out, the Manner of the Turning, the Verse They Do Not Skip While the Crier Calls the Turn, a Council Clerk’s Figures on Salt-Paper Gone Soft, a Gloss in Charcoal from a Woman Who Mends Nets, and One Line at the Foot in a Hand Nobody Will Own}
{\centering\FellFont\itshape\footnotesize\color{faded} A children’s skipping game gathered on the Quay at Vhal and set down in Grathic letters for a man who wanted a figure; the counting-out and the four whole shares in the children’s half-sung Quay speech, the manner of the play in the writer’s small hand, the kept half left as a half and never called a fifth, one correction in the narrow upright Ledgerhand of a Council clerk on salt-paper the damp has since eaten, a gloss pressed in charcoal by a net-mending woman, and a line at the foot in a hand nobody will claim · Set down at Vhal on the Sallow coast in Smoke of Y.H. 812, the Thin Year, by a woman of the Quay who mends nets and has turned the rope for three councils of children; written in charcoal thinned with brine on the back of a dippers’ tide-tally spoiled by rain and sewn with eel-sinew into a fold of oiled sailcloth, carried up the Salt Road in Ilmen of Y.H. 813 and copied at Greybank onto the back of a voided weigh-slip. The original survives in a dry tin among a boat’s things at the Quay, with a white salt bloom along the gutter, a tar thumb at the head, a salt-stiff fibre of the painter across the second leaf, a green bead of cliff-glass pressed into the lower corner by a girl with sweetness at one mouth-corner, a brine ring at the foot, a white brine-gull feather shut in the fold, a tide-line that has taken one word off the third share and has not given it back, a grey Ash print along the outer fold that nobody will own, the Council clerk’s figures eaten down to a figure and half a verb, the net-mender’s charcoal gloss, and the line at the foot\par}\medskip
I mend nets on the Quay and I have turned the rope for three councils of children, which is a thing a woman can do without ever being asked to do it and without its appearing on any tally. A man out of the Council room came down in Smoke with a cuff gone damp at one fold and asked what the children counted when they skipped on the flags below the tide-mark. I told him four and a half, which is the truth, and he wrote four in his book and asked me what the half was for, and I told him it was for the come-aboard, and he wrote \emph{vacancy} against it and went back up the Salt Road with salt dried white at the heel of each boot. What follows is what the children said before he came and what they said again after he had gone, with his hand set above theirs where he put it and theirs underneath where they stand, as the flags keep the water’s mark under a dry foot.

The charcoal at the head is mine. I held the tally down on a bollard in a wind off the Sallow and did not know I had marked it; charcoal goes into the grain and no washing brings it back, which is why we sign with it here and not with ink. Ink on this Quay is a thing that waits for rain.

\subsection*{How it is skipped}

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item Played on the dry flags below the tide-mark, where the last ebb has left its salt and the stone has not yet taken the next one back. Not on the wet flags. A foot that skids on salted stone takes the skin off a knee, and the Quay has no column for that.

\item At the turn of the tide, stop. When the quay-crier calls the turn the turners let the rope lie and the children stand where they stand until he has done. He is counting something that is not in the game. A child who skips through his call is not bold; she is skipping through two counts at once and will go home with them mixed.

\item Two turners hold a painter, an old mooring rope gone stiff with salt, and the third is the skipper. Say the counting-out to the rope and not to a face; said to a face it becomes an argument, and there is always a child who will argue.

\item One line of the verse is one turn of the rope. Turn from the shoulder, slow. A rope snapped at the wrist goes over a child’s head and the game is done for that day. There is a shine on this painter where the hands of the Quay have gone up it, and it will not turn fast for a stranger.

\item Four turns are four whole shares. The fifth line is the half: the rope goes round slow and the skipper hops once on one foot. It is not a fifth. A fifth is a place people stand in upriver and put a nought in; this is a share that somebody holds.

\item The half belongs to the child newest aboard, and nobody says which child that is. When a girl has held the rope through two turnings of the year she is counted whole and another child takes the half, which is how the Quay comes to have a new person in it without anybody holding a slate over her.

\item When the verse comes round again the skipper takes an end of the painter and a turner goes into the middle. There is no winning and no last turn. A child who has never held the rope does not know what the half weighs.

\item Do not skip it while a man in a clean cuff is on the flags. He can enter four. He cannot enter a half, and a game entered as four comes home wrong in the wrist.

\end{itemize}

\subsection*{The counting-out}

\emph{Right hands out, fists shut. The child who says it touches each fist in turn, looking at the rope and not at the faces. The fist it lights on takes the painter, which is not a prize: the turners do the standing and the skipper gets the jumping.}

\begin{quote}\itshape Mother’s rope and mother’s share,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape aunt’s rope and the mending there,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the come-aboard’s word at half again ---\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the one it lights on turns and does not complain.\end{quote}

\subsection*{The rhyme, as it is skipped}

\emph{One line, one turn. Four whole shares and the half. The half line is said slow, with the rope going over once and one foot going down once. It is not said louder or softer than the others, and no child is told why. Said to the rope; said to a child it becomes a claim.}

\begin{quote}\itshape One for the painter stiff with the salt,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape two for the share that went down the mother’s line,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape three for the gull that carries a coal upriver warm,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape four for the hull that was laid before the daughter;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{And the half, and the half, the come-aboard’s turn;}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{the rope goes slow and the foot goes down on one.}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape One for the ebb that takes and does not ask,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape two for the dippers blessing the net at dawn,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape three for the glass that sweetens in the furnace heat,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape four for the bench where a man’s word counts at half;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{And the half, and the half, the come-aboard’s turn;}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{the rope goes slow and the foot goes down on one.}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape One for the pots that go down the Salt Road,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape two for the peat that comes up in a barrow,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape three for the watch kept till the fourth day,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape four for the Sallow that runs against the wind;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{And the half, and the half, the come-aboard’s turn;}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{the rope goes slow and the foot goes down on one.}\end{quote}

When the crier calls the turn they say no verse at all. The rope lies on the flags and the turners hold the ends down with their feet, because a rope left loose in a wind off the Sallow will coil itself around a child’s ankle without meaning anything by it. When he has done, they begin again at the first share. I have asked them why they do not keep the place they had reached, and they say the tide has not kept its place either, so why should they.

\subsection*{The verse they do not skip while a man from the Council room is on the flags}

\emph{I have it from the child who held the painter at the third turning, with the space left before it, which is the space the turners leave when the rope goes slow. She would not say it facing the Quay and made me set it down with none of my verbs in it, because a verse said to a rope wants nothing added and a verse said to a man wants everything taken away.}

\begin{quote}\itshape The tally goes up and the tally comes down,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the damp takes a word out of every one;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the half we keep is the half that would rot,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the Council calls a rotten paper saved.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape A man may be entered and never asked,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape a share may be held by a name not written;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape we count the half to the child come aboard\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and we do not say \emph{aboard} in the hearing of a cuff.\end{quote}

\subsection*{What the Council clerk did}

A clerk of the Council borrowed the leaf on a market morning while the salt was being weighed, being a man who cannot let paper lie, and gave it back with his hand above mine and the damp already at work under both. He counted four children on the flags and set the fifth down as \emph{vacant, no share arising}, which is how a person disappears from a Quay tally: first made a half, then made nothing. Against \emph{the come-aboard’s word at half again} he wrote \emph{the vote of the incoming member is rated at one half}, which is a true thing said in a language nobody on the Quay uses to describe a child. Where I wrote \emph{the half is a share that somebody holds} he set \emph{fractional interest; no deduction arises}. The damp has eaten his \emph{fractional} and left \emph{interest, no deduction}, which is the Council’s own hand written by the weather, and I have not put the word back for him.

I have put their words back underneath and left his standing above, as the flags keep the salt under the dry foot. He has put a figure where a share was held. A figure travels up the Salt Road in a cuff; a share stays with a woman and goes down her mother’s line. He asked what the children learned by it. I told him the count and the turn and the holding of the half, and he wrote that the young were instructed in shares, and entered it. The children stop when a man in a clean cuff comes down the flags. They take it up when he is past the coast pass with his satchel under his arm, and they never once call the half a fifth.

\subsection*{What a woman who mends nets put in the charcoal}

She has mended the same nets these forty years and has never once called a rope a line. She pressed one line into the margin beside the half, small, the way a person writes where somebody is sleeping:

\begin{quote}\itshape A child counted half at the rope is counted half at the table when she is grown. I have watched two of them grow. The half does not come off. The boat comes to be hers, and by then she has forgotten she was ever counted at all, which is the only kindness this Quay knows how to do and will not admit to.\end{quote}

I have left it where her thumb put it. She said a half is not a lack of a whole but a whole thing held by somebody who has not yet been given the name of holding it, and she would not say whether she meant children or boats.

\subsection*{At the head and in the gutter}

The salt bloom at the head came up out of the paper itself on the two nights the sailcloth went damp; it has taken the edge off one word in the third share and I have not written the word back, because a rhyme with a word gone is a rhyme said slowly, and everything on this Quay is said slowly. The tar thumb is mine, off the painter I held down when the wind was taking everything else. The fibre across the second leaf is eel-sinew from the binding, gone soft again in the damp; when it is stiff the leaf is dry and when it is soft the leaf has been out, which is a more useful clock than the Council’s. The green bead came off a girl with sweetness at one mouth-corner who leaned to see the writing, pressed it into the fold and went back up to the furnaces without asking. The brine ring at the foot came from a cup set down at the first share and taken up at the half. The white feather shut in the fold is a brine-gull’s; it came down on the tally while I was writing and I closed the fold on it rather than move it. The grey along the outer fold came off a cuff laid where no cuff has business lying on a net-mender’s leaf. Nobody will own it. There is no Last Day on a Quay: salt does not burn, it comes back with the next tide and goes on doing what it did.

\subsection*{At the foot, in a hand nobody will own}

\begin{quote}\itshape The rope keeps the half. The crier keeps the turn.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape The tally goes damp and the Council calls it saved.\end{quote}

I asked the net-mender, the dippers, a factor come up from Greybank and a man who has been come aboard for nine years, and had four answers and no hand. I have left the lines where they were written.

The leaf goes back into the oiled sailcloth and the sailcloth into the tin where we keep the paper we mean to let rot. Tomorrow the children will be on the flags below the tide-mark, four whole shares and a half, and they will stop when the crier calls the turn and begin again after, and if the clerk borrows the leaf again he may have the four. He cannot have the half, because it is a share, and a share is a thing that stays where a woman put it.

\clearpage\phantomsection\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{The Sermon at the Hand-Stone, Being What a Miller of Sill Said Over the Note at the Singing Sill on the Morning It Came a Week Early in Silt of Y.H. 813, with the Early-Note Tally, the Low-Note Verse, a Factor’s Clerk’s Correction, and a Line at the Foot in a Hand Nobody Will Own}
\CRsheetheading{The Sermon at the Hand-Stone, Being What a Miller of Sill Said Over the Note at the Singing Sill on the Morning It Came a Week Early in Silt of Y.H. 813, with the Early-Note Tally, the Low-Note Verse, a Factor’s Clerk’s Correction, and a Line at the Foot in a Hand Nobody Will Own}
{\centering\FellFont\itshape\footnotesize\color{faded} A sermon of the meal mill preached at the shrine of the hand-stone above the Singing Sill, below the north bridge at Sill; the sayings in Grathic, the low-note verse with the gap left as it is sung, the early notes in a meal-book tally, one correction in the narrow upright Ledgerhand of a factor’s clerk come up from Greybank, and a line at the foot in a hand nobody will own · Preached on Silt 7, Y.H. 813, by a miller of Sill who had ground at the meal mill under the north bridge for two and thirty years, on the morning the stone gave its note a week before its hour and the yard said the water ran fast under the skin and then said weather; written that evening by his daughter, who keeps the mill’s meal-book, on the back of a leaf spoiled by a wet figure out of the Glaze Room, folded into the toll-bag with a barleycorn shut in the crease. It survives with white mill-dust worked into the head and the gutter, a brown silt tideline along the foot from a morning the leaf went down to the Fishstairs in a woman’s apron, a wet ring where a cup was set on it, a grey Ash print nobody will own, a barleycorn in the fold, one small nick from a millstone dressing-pick, one correction in the clerk’s hand that takes the verbs out and numbers the early note nil, and a line struck through and written again very small underneath in a hand that has never come forward. Copied once at the Fishstairs in Seed, Y.H. 813, with the verbs put back and the nought left in its place.\par}\medskip
I keep the meal-book at the mill under the north bridge, and nobody asked me for this. I write because my father spoke to a stone and the stone gave nothing back, and I did not want the words to go the same way the note goes, into the water and out of sight. He stood with his palm flat on the hand-stone and spoke to the stone, the river, the mill, and last of all to us, which is the order a miller uses when there is work waiting and somebody may be listening who wants a figure. I have set his words down in Grathic. Where he left a verb out I have left it out, and put it back underneath in my own hand, because a saying said over a stone is a thing a household has to use.

The white at the head and in the gutter is mill-dust, not salt; I write at the mill and the dust gets into everything.
