The brown line along the foot came up the Fishstairs in the flood and stayed when the water went. The ring was a cup set down while he was speaking of the hour and taken up before he saw it. The grey at the corner came off a cuff and nobody will own it; I have not swept it. The barleycorn shut in the fold was in the leaf when I took it from the spoiled quire and I have left it where it lay. The nick is from the dressing-pick, which I use to open the book when my hands are wet.

\subsection*{The manner of the listening, as the hand-stone has it}

\emph{Written small, from watching, not from any order the Court has printed.}

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item Come at the hour the note is due, not before. A man who comes early hears the water going over the ledge and calls it the note, and is wrong all day.

\item Stand below the bridge with your palm flat on the hand-stone. The note comes up through the stone into the hand before the ear places it out in the water. If you feel it in the roots of your teeth and cannot yet hear it, you are standing in the right place.

\item Do not say the hour aloud. An hour said aloud becomes an argument, and there is argument enough at the Cross without carrying it down to the river.

\item Leave what you brought on the ledge behind the stone: a crust, a bit, a knot, a sherd. Take nothing back. The river takes what is set on its bank and gives back silt, which is an honest exchange and entered nowhere.

\item If the note comes before its hour, do not correct it. It has not gone wrong. We are the ones who are early or late.

\item When the bell comes down from the Cross, stop. It has counted something that is not your river. Begin again after. Four, four and a gap, and the gap is not one of yours to fill.

\item The mill keeps one hour and the stone keeps another. Do not lay one over the other. A man who does will grind his grain at the wrong time and blame the mill.

\end{itemize}

He said the last of these twice, once to the stone and once to a woman who had come down from High Kiln to hear him and was writing nothing.

\subsection*{The sermon, as he said it}

\subsection*{Of the two stones}

He put his palm flat on the hand-stone and turned his head toward the mill behind him.

“There are two stones under this bridge doing the same work and not agreeing,” he said. “One turns and grinds and gives me a measure of meal I can carry to the Cross and sell. One lies under the water and gives one note and goes on giving it and never gives a measure at all. I have stood between the two for two and thirty years. The millstone feeds the body. This one feeds the day.

“You will ask which of them the town could do without. I have asked myself on mornings when the hopper was empty. The answer changes with the hour, which is a thing the Court does not like in an answer. At the mill we grind with what the river sends and give out what the mill can hold, and we never ask the grain whose house it came out of.”

\subsection*{Of the hour}

“There is a clock in the square that takes this note and gives out an hour,” he said. “Nobody has ever told me what the note counts. A man come up from Greybank told me it was a mercy of the Keeping, so that the world might be counted in its hours as it is counted in its measures. I asked him how much of an hour the Hearth kept back. He looked at the stone and gave me the printed figure, one in twelve, as though a twelfth of an hour were a thing a man could put in his pocket and carry away.

“Here is what I know of hours. A day at the mill is the time it takes to grind what is brought, and the time is never the same twice, and the meal is never the same twice, and nobody has ever entered either. When the note comes I set the mill by it and grind. That is all the preaching I have, and I have had two and thirty years to find another sentence and could not.”

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Margin, in my hand:} He used the phrase \emph{lawful tide} twice, once of this stone and once of the Weighing, and I have not put the two sayings together. A man who uses one word for two things has a use for the word.\end{quote}

\subsection*{Of the early note}

“It came a week before its hour this morning,” he said to the stone. “I felt it in my teeth before I heard it out in the water, and when I looked up there was still skin on the Ilm and the frost-bloom not gone off the well-lip up the yard. A man come back from looking said the water ran fast under the skin. The yard said weather, and then said the thaw that was, and went home warm.

“A thing that comes early is not a thing gone wrong. The eels run early and late and nobody fines them. The lambs come when they come and no slate is set at the byre. But let a note come a week before its hour and a man with a slate has a figure for it before the water has finished. I have heard the figure go from a fist to a mouth to a shoulder and arrive at no door in this town.

“In the Long Cold the ice held ninety-four days and this stone kept its note under the skin of the river and the town kept its hours another way, by the bell and by the loaves and by the light going off the terrace. When the ice went the note came back as though it had never stopped, and nobody asked who had kept the hours in between. I have asked. I got a date and then a figure and then weather. A man who keeps an account does not answer a question about what he did not enter.”

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{In my hand, at the foot of this section:} He said the paragraph about the eels twice. The second time he said it to the mill and not to us. I have set the two sayings down as one because the mill does not answer.\end{quote}

\subsection*{The low-note verse}

\emph{Sung low, standing, with the palm on the stone. The row says the last four lines with him. There is a gap before those four, the one the bell leaves, and I have left it here as it is sung.}

\begin{quote}\itshape The stone gives one note and goes on giving,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape low as a man’s throat under water;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the clock takes it and says nothing,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the mill takes it and grinds.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Four for the steps and four for the boards,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and a place where the note comes through;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the bell keeps a gap and the stone keeps a note,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and neither is entered by you.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape It came a week before its hour and we called it weather;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape it came under the ice and we called it the Long Cold;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape say what it gave and not what it meant,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and leave the place where the answer stood.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape The note goes on and the clock goes round\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the mill goes round with it;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the ninety-four days are kept\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape by nobody this town can name.\end{quote}

A girl from the Fishstairs asked what the space before the last four lines was for. Nobody answered her. The clerk put a round nought against it later, which I have left where he set it.

\subsection*{The early notes, as the meal-book keeps them}

\emph{I keep this tally because a figure that arrives at the mill in a fist goes out again in the meal and leaves nothing on the leaf. These I have set down where they stood.}

When — Where it was felt — What the yard called it — What was entered\par

Ilmen 7, Y.H. 813 — up through the boards of the well-platform — weather — nothing\par

Ilmen 9, Y.H. 813 — up through the boards of the Weir — weather — nothing\par

Ilmen 25, Y.H. 813 — up through the boards of the Vail kiln-house, spoken of from the Weir — weather — nothing\par

Silt 7, this morning — in the roots of the teeth, out in the water after — the water running fast under the skin; then weather — nothing\par

The ninety-four days, Y.H. 811 into 812 — under the ice; not heard — the Long Cold — a line of figures\par

There were others before these, and my father could set a year to each of them, and I have not written them, because a row of years is a thing a clerk can carry away and a note is not. The line of figures for the ninety-four days stands in the meal-book as it stood in the mill: a row with nothing under it.

\subsection*{What the clerk did}

A factor’s clerk came up from Greybank on the morning after with a cuff gone soft from washing and ink in two fingers, and borrowed the leaf while I was at the hopper. He gave it back with the verbs taken out.

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item Where my father said \emph{the millstone feeds the body and this one feeds the day}, he wrote \emph{retention and conversion are lawful conditions of a vessel} above and left mine below.

\item Where he said \emph{the note came a week before its hour}, he wrote \emph{the tide arrived in advance of the reckoning} and underlined it twice. At the end of the row he wrote \emph{nil}.

\item At the ninety-four days he wrote \emph{a vacancy in the account, carried forward}, which is a true thing said by a man who has never stood under this bridge.

\item At the gap in the verse he put a round nought and wrote \emph{vacancy} beside it. When I asked him what a gap was worth that had no note in it, he said nothing a clerk could enter, which was the first true thing he said all morning.

\end{itemize}

I have put the verbs back underneath and left his hand standing above, as the mill leaves the old grinding showing under the new. He takes the verbs out because a thing always true has no need of them. I put them back because a man with his palm on a cold stone wants to know who is doing the giving, and whether it was his own hand that set the hour.

\subsection*{At the head and in the gutter}

The mill-dust at the head is mine and will not wash out of the fold; my father’s hands were white to the wrist and he never noticed he had marked the leaf. The brown tideline is from the morning the flood went over the Fishstairs and I carried the leaf under my apron to keep the figure in it dry, though there was no figure in it. The wet ring is not ale; a woman set her cup down while he was speaking of the hour and took it up before he saw it. The grey at the corner came off a cuff at the hand-stone and nobody will own it. The barleycorn was shut in the crease when I took the leaf from the spoiled quire; it has not sprouted and I have not moved it. The nick is from the dressing-pick. The clerk did not notice any of these things, which is how I know he is a good clerk.

\subsection*{At the foot}

Struck through once and written again underneath, very small, in a hand that is not mine, not my father’s and not the clerk’s:

\begin{quote}\itshape The clock takes the note and gives the hour.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape The clock was given by a hand.\end{quote}

I asked my father, the woman from High Kiln, a man come up from Greybank, and a barge-man waiting below the bridge, and had four answerings and no hand. I have left the line struck through and standing, which is the only honest way to keep a sentence you cannot sign.

The leaf goes back in the toll-bag with the barleycorn in its fold. Next Silt the stone will give its note when it gives it, early or late, and the town will set its clock by it and say nothing about what it counts, and the clerk will come up from Greybank and take the verbs out. I shall put them back as I did this time, and leave the nought in its place and the gap the length it is.

\clearpage\phantomsection\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{The Held Palm, Being the Clapping Game of the Quay Children at Vhal, with the Counting-Out, the Half That Stands, and What the Tally-man Made of It}
\CRsheetheading{The Held Palm, Being the Clapping Game of the Quay Children at Vhal, with the Counting-Out, the Half That Stands, and What the Tally-man Made of It}
{\centering\FellFont\itshape\footnotesize\color{faded} A share-woman’s gathering of a children’s clapping-count, set down in Grathic letters on the back of a boat-share sheet gone soft with damp; the counting-out and the clapping verse in the children’s own half-sung salt-coast speech, the manner of the play in the writer’s small hand, one correction in the narrow upright Ledgerhand of a clerk come down from the tide-tally house, a gloss pressed into the margin by a dipper who reads the Sallow draw at dawn, and a line at the foot in a hand that has never come forward · Written in Ember of Y.H. 813 at the Quay in Vhal, by a woman who keeps the mothers’ share-lines and mends the rope that holds the salt galleys, on the back of a share-sheet spoiled by a wet tend, the figures on its face gone soft and the salt-paper rotten at one corner. She set it down because a man from the tide-tally house came down the boards and asked what the children counted when they clapped, and was given a count and not a figure; he went away and sent a clerk, which is what happens to a count in this country. Kept folded in a coil of spent tow-rope under the Quay bench among the beads and the net-needles. It survives with a white salt bloom across the head, a tar thumb at the first corner, a press of wet rope across the second leaf, a gritting of glass from the furnaces in the fold, a fish-scale shut in the gutter, a tideline along the foot where the sheet went damp, a grey Ash print nobody will own, the clerk’s correction standing above the children’s words, a dipper’s gloss in charcoal beside the half, and a line at the foot in a hand nobody will claim\par}\medskip
I keep the mothers’ share-lines on this Quay and mend the rope that holds the salt galleys when they come in, which are two works that would each keep a man busy and neither of them pays a woman for the trouble of writing. The children clap on the dry boards above the water-line, and I have set their words down as they came, with the clerk’s hand above them where he put it and theirs underneath where they stand, as the Quay keeps the wet mark under the dry one.

The salt at the head is my own thumb. I set the sheet on a bollard before I had done with the rope and did not know I had marked it. The grey came off a cuff that had no business lying on a coil, and I have not swept it. There is no Last Day on a Quay; the salt eats what a broom would take and the tide takes the rest.

\subsection*{The boards and the hands, as the children keep them}

\emph{Played on the dry boards of the Quay in Ember and Grain, when the salt has been raked into heaps and the boards will bear a foot and a clap. Not in the Five, when the children are made to stand and listen; not in rain, because a salt-paper sheet left in the wet is a debt made nothing and a clap on a wet board brings nobody home. In the hard months they play it in the rope-walk, where the tar pots stand and the floor is dry under the racks.}

Two children play. One is \textbf{the mother}, because shares pass through mothers on this Quay and nobody has thought to ask why. One is \textbf{the aboard}, the one married into the boat, whose word on the boat is weighed at half. They are called these names and never their own, for a name said on a Quay travels up the Salt Road in a cuff and comes back entered.

Each holds both palms up. A clap of palm to palm, mother to aboard, is a whole. A clap where the aboard lifts one hand and keeps it in the air is the half, and the hand in the air is called \textbf{the place}, which is not a fraction but a child standing with her hand up. One line of the verse is one clap. The verse is said to the rope and the salt, never to a face; said to a face it becomes a bargaining, and there is bargaining enough on this Quay without teaching it to children.

The clap must sound, palm to palm. A clap that goes edgewise, or slaps a wet board, sends the player to the coil at the end where the wet ones sit with their hands folded, and she comes back only when three voices say together, \textbf{The rope calls}. Nobody counts how often this happens. There is no winning in this game and no last clap. When the tenth has been held the hands come down together and the count goes back the way it came.

\subsection*{The counting-out, said over the bead}

\emph{A glass bead out of the furnaces, which the children call a tide-bead, is passed from fist to fist along the row, right fists held out and knuckles up. The child who says the words touches each fist in turn and does not look at the faces. The fist the bead lies in at the last word is the mother; the next fist is the aboard, and the aboard does not choose it, which the children accept as a punishment and the share-women accept as practice.}

\begin{quote}\itshape Bead for the glass and tar for the boat,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape salt on the board and a rot in the note;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape pass it low and pass it dumb ---\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the fist it stops in is the one that’s come.\end{quote}

\emph{The bead going round the row is called the boat. An old woman here will tell you a boat goes round and comes back with the same hands, which is a thing no factor at Greybank has ever entered.}

\subsection*{The clapping count, as it is clapped}

\emph{Nine whole claps going out, then the palm held, then nine claps coming back. The tenth is not a clap. At it the aboard raises one palm and holds it up while the mother’s hand stays where it is; both stand still under the held hand, feet on the board and chins down. A player who claps under it has gone into the water and sits on the coil until the rope calls. The coming back is clapped to the same nine lines read backward, and the last clap is the first line said again.}

\begin{quote}\itshape One for the keel and one for the oar,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape one for the rope on the galley floor;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape one for the salt in the raker’s shoe,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape one for the gull and the coal it flew;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape one for the lead in the furnace sand,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape one for the contract that will not stand;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape one for the tide that runs ‘gainst the wind,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape one for the share that the mother holds in;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape nine for the board and the boat’s own name ---\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the tenth is a palm and it isn’t a claim.\end{quote}

\emph{The brine-gull line came up the Salt Road, they say, and the children will not give it up. They clap it to a gull that went off upriver with a coal out of a banked fire that was not yet cold, which is a thing a child can see and a clerk cannot enter, and so it stays.}

\subsection*{What is said at the held palm}

\emph{Said low, to the salt, while the hand is up. All three say the last two lines together.}

\begin{quote}\itshape The hand’s up. The boat’s still.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape The wind’s against the water and the water has its will.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Say it to the salt and not to me ---\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape a half’s a body standing, not a fee.\end{quote}

\subsection*{The verse they do not clap while a tally-man is on the boards}

\emph{I have this from the child who was aboard, with the space left before it, which is the space the children leave in the clapping. She said it to the coil with her back turned and made me set it down with none of my verbs in it. A verse clapped to a board wants nothing added, and a verse clapped to a man wants everything taken away.}

\begin{quote}\itshape One for the warrant and two for the tide,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape three for the oar and the hands it tried;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape four for the bench and the seven-year term,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape five for the cuff and the figure it’ll confirm;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the half stands up and the half stands still,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and what goes up the Salt Road comes back as a figure and not as a girl.\end{quote}

\emph{The pulled benches take a man for seven years, or until his hands give out; a Vhaleni hull is never long from the oars. The child who said this had an uncle on a term and would not say whether his hands had given out, which is a child’s way of keeping two things apart without putting a word between them. I have put no word between them either.}

\subsection*{What the tally-man did}

A clerk come down from the tide-tally house borrowed the leaf on the morning after, with his cuff soft at the edge from washing and the ink sitting in two fingers of it and will not come out. He laid his hand on the sheet before his eyes went to the room, the way they do at that house. He set the board down as \emph{a transaction in shares} and the mother as \emph{the holder of record}. He wrote the aboard as \emph{a party at half interest}. Against the held palm he struck the children’s words through and set above them, \emph{one half-share entered; value, one half; the residue nil}. At the coming back he wrote \emph{nine operations returned; no balance outstanding}. At the head of it he wrote the notice’s one in twelve, as the figure the districts are read, and set the Quay’s half beneath it, and the two figures agreed, which is a thing that has never once happened on a board. At the foot, where the hands come down and nothing is clapped, he put a round nought and wrote \emph{no remainder}.

I have put the children’s words back underneath and left his standing above. He writes of a thing always true and so has no need of a hand in it; I write for a child with her palm up in the salt wind who wants to know when to bring it down. He has set a fraction where a person stood, and a fraction travels up the Salt Road in a cuff and a child does not. A man married into a boat has his word weighed at half on this Quay, and I have never argued with the share-lines; but the half in this game is a place, and a place is not the same thing as a figure however neatly it is written. A child stands in it with her chin down until the rope calls her back. A figure has no chin.

He asked what the children learned by it. I told him the count and the holding and the calling back. He said that was an account of the half-share taught before a child could read a slate, and he entered it. The children stop when a man in a soft cuff comes onto the boards. They take it up again when he is past the Council room with his satchel under his arm, and they never once clap under the held palm.

\subsection*{The gloss in the margin, in charcoal}

The woman who blesses the nets at dawn and reads the Sallow draw pressed one line into the margin beside the ninth clap. She does not write often, and when she does she writes small, the way a person writes in a room where somebody is sleeping.

\begin{quote}\itshape Not nine. Ten, and the tenth is a palm held up out of the count. There’s a difference, and the tally house won’t learn it.\end{quote}

Beside \emph{the tide that runs ‘gainst the wind} she wrote: \emph{The dippers say the Sallow follows the Warm and not the moon. A child on this Quay knows the water comes against the wind and will not say what pulls it. She has been asked, and has asked the water.}

I have left both where her thumb put them.

\subsection*{At the head and in the gutter}

The salt bloom at the head is mine and has worked into the grain, which is why a Quay sheet takes a mark and never gives one back. The tar thumb is the man who holds the galleys’ rope; he does not wash before he comes to the bench and says a sheet that has never been tarred was never used on a Quay. The press of wet rope across the second leaf is from the coil the leaf lay in through a tide of rain. The glass in the fold came off a furnace barrow that went past while I was writing and gritted the sheet, and I have not picked it out. The fish-scale in the gutter is not mine and I have left it where it fell. The tideline along the foot took two words off the back of the share-sheet, and I have not written them in again, because a rhyme with two words gone is a rhyme said slowly, and all of ours are said slowly. A scrap of tarred rope-end is tied through a hole in the second leaf for the word I could not put down. I will not untie it.

\subsection*{At the foot, in a hand nobody will own}

\begin{quote}\itshape The board keeps the clap. The coil keeps the child.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape The tally keeps the half and has never kept the hand.\end{quote}

I asked the mother, the aboard and the dipper, and had three answers and no hand. I have left the lines where they were written. The sheet goes back into the coil under the bench, and tomorrow the salt will be raked into heaps and the tide will come up against the wind, and the children will clap nine and hold the tenth where it has always stood, with their feet on the board and their chins down. If the clerk comes again with his pen I shall put the verbs back. He may keep the half; the hand comes back at the end of every count, and no house on this Quay has ever entered it.

\clearpage\phantomsection\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{The Held Rope, Being the Counting Game of the Fishstairs Children at the Out-of-Line Landing, with the Choosing, the Manner of the Turns, the Verse of the Hold, and What a Court Clerk Entered Over It}
\CRsheetheading{The Held Rope, Being the Counting Game of the Fishstairs Children at the Out-of-Line Landing, with the Choosing, the Manner of the Turns, the Verse of the Hold, and What a Court Clerk Entered Over It}
{\centering\FellFont\itshape\footnotesize\color{faded} A woman of the fish-trade shade’s gathering of a children’s skipping game, set down in Grathic on the back of a weigh-slip blown down from the Cross; the choosing and the verses in the children’s own half-sung speech, the rules in the writer’s charcoal hand, a correction in the narrow upright Ledgerhand of a Court-table clerk, a gloss in the charcoal letters of the girl who holds the rope, a line from the Weir in the hand of a woman who counts in wool, and a line at the foot in a hand nobody will own · Set down in Seed of Y.H. 813 at the fish-trade shade below the sill in Sill, of an evening when the eel boats were out and the children skipped on the flat place at the foot of the Fishstairs; copied forward in Reed of Y.H. 813 onto a second slip when the first went soft at the fold. The slip came originally from the Court’s table at the Cross and was trodden into the shade, which the writer thought a proper beginning for it. It survives folded into a twist of oiled cloth under the outer tub at the shade: eel slime worked into the grain at the head, silt along the fore-edge and a tideline through the second leaf, a fish scale pressed flat in the fold, the smoke-smudge of a coal from a banked fire on one corner, a nick from a fish-hook, a bloom of salt on the leaf that lay nearest the creel, a grey Ash print along the gutter that nobody will own, the clerk’s correction standing above the children’s words, and a line at the foot in a hand that has never been claimed\par}\medskip
I wind children’s feet in wool below the sill and I have set this down because a man from the Court’s table at the Cross came into the shade with his cuff wet at the edge and asked what the children counted when they jumped. He wanted a figure. I told him there was a count in it and no figure, which is the truth of the thing, and he sent me a clerk instead of an answer, which is the way of that table. What follows is what the children said before the clerk came and what they said again after he had gone back over the north bridge. I have set his hand above theirs where he put it and their words underneath where they stand, as the landing keeps the foot and the water that came up over it.

The game is played on the flat place at the foot of the Fishstairs, which has four steps down, four steps, and a landing a hand’s breadth out of line where a step should have been. At high water it is played on the boards under the shade. It is not played in the Five, because in the Five the children are made to stand and listen and there is nobody to turn a rope. The rope is a plait of reed-fibre or a length of eel-sinew, and it is never knotted. A mother will untie a knot in it before she will let a child jump, because a thing with a knot in it is a thing that will be asked what it counts, and a skipping rope is not an account.

\subsection*{How it is played}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item The choosing is said to the rope and not to the faces. Said to a child, it becomes an argument, and there is always a child who will argue. Right fists held out, knuckles up; the child who says it points at each fist in turn and does not look at anybody. The fist it lights on on the last word belongs to the one who will hold the rope at the hold, which is a duty and not a prize.

\end{enumerate}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item Two children turn and one jumps. One line of the verse, one jump. The line must be crossed and never touched: a child who touches the rope is banked, and sits on the landing edge with her hands folded while the others go around her.

\end{enumerate}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item The hold is the fifth line. When it comes, the two turners stop the rope hanging slack between them and the jumper must jump once over the rope where it lies still. That is a jump over nothing. A child who steps into the slack, or who says the held word while the rope is still turning, is banked as above.

\end{enumerate}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item A banked child is brought back when three children say her name. A child whom nobody brings back is thin until the next round. The children will not say why they call it that, and I have not asked twice.

\end{enumerate}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item The counter says the count at the end. She says nine. A second child counts on her fingers underneath and gets ten, because she counted the hold as a step. The argument is settled the same way every time: the hold is a place and not a jump; but the children keep both counts, one in the mouth and one in the hand, and have never made them agree.

\end{enumerate}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item The last child still jumping takes the dry end of the shade, where no slate lies. That is the whole of what is won. It is a place to set a basket down and nobody has ever asked a figure for it.

\end{enumerate}

\subsection*{The choosing}

\begin{quote}\itshape Eel in the creel and coal in the gull,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape silt in the cuff and a scale in the fold;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape step and step and step and step,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the one it lights on comes up with the hold.\end{quote}

\subsection*{The verse, as it is jumped}

\emph{One line, one jump. At the fifth line the rope is stopped and held still. Say it to the rope.}

\begin{quote}\itshape One for the step that goes down to the water,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape two for the step that comes up the same;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape three for the eel at the outer board,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape four for the coal that the gull took wrong;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Hold --- for the place where the foot must not go.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Five for the cuff that is washed every morning,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape six for the slate that is held to the arm;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape seven for the hand that goes down to the stone,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape eight for the figure that goes up the road;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Nine for the landing at the foot of them all.\end{quote}

They call it nine and the hold. Ask a child what the hold is and she will tell you it is the step you do not take, and if you ask whether it counts she will ask you whether a rest counts. I have put that down as it was said to me, with the question left in it, because a question said to the ground is the only answer a child here will give a woman with a slip in her hand.

\subsection*{The verse they do not say when a man with a soft cuff is on the landing}

This one I had from the girl who holds the rope, with the proper space left before it, which is the space the turners leave in the jumping. She would not say it while the clerk had his pen out and would not say it to him at all. She said it to the rope with her back turned.

\begin{quote}\itshape One for the man set down before he was called,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape two for the cuff that goes grey by noon;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape his hand to the slate and his eye to the stall,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the number goes up and the landing stays down.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Four for the boards and four for the post,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the place where the fifth should be --- even here;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the gull has the coal and the river the eel,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and nobody counts what the water keeps.\end{quote}

I have set it down with none of my words in it. A verse said to the rope wants nothing added, and a verse said to a man wants everything taken away.

\subsection*{What the girl who holds the rope put in the margin}

The letters are hard at the \emph{th} and one of them backward, which is how a child writes who has learned off a slate and not off a book.

At \emph{six for the slate that is held to the arm}: \textbf{Not to the arm. Where nobody can read it.}

At \emph{Hold --- for the place where the foot must not go}: \textbf{It’s a rest. A rest is what you get for jumping and not going anywhere.}

At \emph{eight for the figure that goes up the road}: \textbf{He said it twice. We counted it once.}

At \emph{nine for the landing at the foot of them all}: \textbf{There’s a step gone off this and nobody’s come down to see which.}

\subsection*{A line from the Weir}

A woman come down with eels from the Weir, who keeps a string of knots at her waist, read the slip over my tub and put one line in the margin in the small nasal hand she uses when she is tired. I have copied it as it stands.

\begin{quote}\itshape Up at the boards we tie it in wool. A knot stays where you put it. A jump goes off with the foot.\end{quote}

She would not say what her own knots counted, and told me to ask the cord, which is an answer given by people who asked the same thing at their own cutting. I have left it where she set it and put no gloss beside it.

\subsection*{What the Court hand did}

The clerk of the Court’s table borrowed the leaf in the shade on an Account-day, being a man who cannot let paper lie. He has a cuff gone soft from washing and the ink sits in two fingers of it and will not come out. He numbered the nine lines in the margin, struck through the hold and wrote above it, \emph{the fifth is a vacancy; enter nil}. Against \emph{the place where the foot must not go} he wrote \emph{no passage; no entry}. Against \emph{the number goes up and the landing stays down} he wrote \emph{the measure is carried forward}. At the foot of the count he put nine and a round nought and wrote \emph{one vacancy} beside it, which is a true figure and a false place.

I have put their words back underneath and left his standing above. He has taken the feet out of the game and left the figures, which travel well and arrive with nobody in them. I put the feet back because a child up to her ankle in silt on the out-of-line landing does not know she is hearing something always true, and wants to know which foot to lift. A nought is a number. The hold is a place to stand in for a breath. He has put a figure where a place should be, which is the whole art of that hand.

He asked me what the children learned by it. I told him the count and the fault and the bringing back. He said that was the account of a Return taught before a child could read a slate, and he entered it. The children stop when a man with a soft cuff comes down the steps. They take it up again when he is past the bridge. They have never once changed the hold.

\subsection*{At the head and in the gutter}

The eel slime at the head is off the hand that held the slip down while I wrote; it goes into the grain and will not come out, which is why the shade uses eel-sinew for rope and not string. The silt is along the fore-edge and through the second leaf, where the water came up over the flat place and went back down again the way it does. The tideline has taken two words off the back and I have not written them in again, because a rhyme with two words gone is a rhyme said slowly, and all of ours are said slowly. The fish scale in the fold came off a creel set down on the leaf while a child was told to lift her own bundle and let her arm tell her what went into it, and did. The smoke on the corner is off a coal a brine-gull carried upriver from a banked fire that was not yet cold; the bird went over with it and the corner took the soot. The hook nick is not mine and nobody has claimed it. The salt bloom is on the leaf that lay nearest the creel, where the eels went in and stayed. The grey in the gutter came off a cuff laid where no cuff has business lying; I have not swept it and nobody will own it, and there is no Last Day under a tub.

The oiled cloth goes back around the two slips and under the outer tub. In the morning the water will be down or it will not, and the children will draw the same flat place with their feet and jump the same nine and the same hold, and the counter will say nine in the mouth and ten in the hand and the two will stand side by side as they stood today. I have kept their words and I have not joined them to anything.

\subsection*{At the foot, in a hand nobody will own}

\begin{quote}\itshape They bring her back by saying her name. Nobody brings back the hold.\end{quote}

I asked the girl who holds the rope, the woman come down from the Weir, and a man going past with a creel, and had three answers and no hand. I have left the line where it was written.

\clearpage\phantomsection\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{The Holding Book of the Waiting Room at Slate Row in Sill, Being the Vessels Kept Overnight Between the Drawing and the Pouring, with the Embers Standing, the Note Each Gave in the Dark, the Loss by Morning, and the Figure Carried Up the Clay Road at First Light}
\CRsheetheading{The Holding Book of the Waiting Room at Slate Row in Sill, Being the Vessels Kept Overnight Between the Drawing and the Pouring, with the Embers Standing, the Note Each Gave in the Dark, the Loss by Morning, and the Figure Carried Up the Clay Road at First Light}
{\centering\FellFont\itshape\footnotesize\color{faded} A leaf from a collector’s own night-book, kept behind the collector’s table; figures in Ledgerhand copied from the day-slates, the remarks in the hand that fed the room’s dish and turned the pallets, one column struck by a College clerk and drawn back beneath his words, a verb corrected in a second hand, and a line at the foot in a hand nobody will own · Written at Sill in the Waiting Room behind the collector’s table in Slate Row, in the firing month of Tallow, Y.H. 813, the year after the Thin Year, between the first Account-day and the second; sent up the Clay Road at first light with the figures and left folded under the bench at the turning of the tend. It survives as one leaf of foolscap folded small enough for a coat pocket, with grey Ash worked into the outer fold, a tallow thumb at the head, iron filings in the gutter from the tube’s wool sleeve, a bone-pale streak of slip along the foot, a green bead of lead glaze in the lower corner, a damp tide-line from the flagstones where a barrow stood overnight, a small square of bare paper where a word was scraped away, two corrections in the narrow upright hand of a College clerk, and one line at the foot that has never been claimed\par}\medskip
I keep the room where they stand overnight. The collector draws in the district and brings his slate to the table; I set a pallet, a dish of banked coals under the bench, and a pot of water by the door, and the vessel lies here until first light, when the figure goes up the Clay Road and the warmth goes into a cradle. The College calls this the holding. The district calls it the night. I have written both names into one book and neither of them is mine.

The room is the coldest in Slate Row and the dampest, and the draught under the door goes along the floor to the corner where the grey gathers. I do not sweep it. There is no Last Day in this room, and nobody burns the corner in the morning.

What follows is one leaf, from the first Account-day of Tallow to the second, in the firing month of the year after the Thin Year. Twelve copper bits to a silver mark; twenty marks to a gold crown, a Sere coin that does not stay in Grath. An ember is booked at five marks and no man has exchanged one for the other. A newborn vessel holds twelve to fifteen, a labourer in good case forty to sixty, one of the Kept three hundred, which is a figure no household can spend. One in twelve is printed on the notice and read twice at the Cross. I have heard another figure spoken in the yards and have not entered it, not being a figure I can weigh.

Vessels held on this leaf: ten. Nights with no vessel: one. Figures struck: one. Columns struck: one.

\subsection*{The leaf, as I set it down}

\emph{Figures in Ledgerhand, copied from the day-slates. The remarks are mine, in the hand that fed the dish and turned the pallets, and are not part of the account. The column at the end has no heading; a heading would make it an account.}

Night — Vessel, as the slate has it — Embers standing — Note in the dark — Loss by morning — Gone up to — Remark\par

Tallow 11 — A widow of the lower town. \emph{Loaf} — 41 — full — 2 — Greybank — Four loaves baked, three to the levy. Asked whether it went into a child. Not entered.\par

Tallow 11 — A kiln hand of High Kiln. \emph{Bent} — 46 — flat — 5 — Greybank — Sweetness at the mouth. Note flat before the pot was set down; the sweetness came and went with the speaking.\par

Tallow 12 — A child three days returned, Low Kiln. \emph{Second} — 13, struck to 12 — none — 1 — Hearthseat — Gave nothing under the knuckle. Entered as a worsening, not a birth. Both figures stand.\par

Tallow 13 — A clay-bound hand of the terraces. \emph{Seven} — 44 — nearly full — 3 — Greybank — Six years on the slate; the seventh not. Warmed the pallet with his own hands before I could set the dish.\par

Tallow 14 — One of the Kept, in passing. No slate-name — 300 — none — — — — — Asked after the weather. That goes in the remark and in no column.\par

Tallow 15 — A man of Mud End. \emph{Peat} — 47 — full — 4 — Greybank — Taken quiet in his sleep. Neighbours called it merciful. Room gave full and nobody crossed.\par

Tallow 16 — A thrower of the low yard. \emph{Nineteen} — 41 — full — 2 — Greybank — Slip on both forearms; left a bone-pale streak on the bench. Earlier figure stood higher. No reason entered.\par

Tallow 17 — A vessel returned three times — 29 — flat — 6 — Greybank — Smaller each time. Figure went down while the deduction stood still. No note made.\par

Tallow 19 — A foundling left at the mill — 12 — none — 1 — — — A stone under him, not a name. Stands till a hearth claims him. Knuckle found no vessel to answer.\par

Tallow 20 — A house of the terraces, disputed — 52 — full — — — — — Thumb wiped twice before touching nothing. Figure asked for, then not wanted. Left standing.\par

Tallow 20 — No vessel held. A clerk set at the Fishstairs — — — — — — — — — Cuff grey from washing; hand to slate before eyes to stalls. A measure nobody called. Not one of ours.\par

The forty of Low Kiln were held here last year, one line for the batch and no names taken; a barrow of grey went out through the north gate the morning after and I have not swept this corner since. They are carried as forty, not as forty persons, and the room remembers the difference in the damp.

\subsection*{The note in the dark}

Before the dish I set a knuckle on the pallet rail or the rim of the pot. A whole vessel answers full. One cracked through answers flat, a small dead sound that stops at the surface. A vessel with air under the note answers nearly full, and the yards have no word for it, so I have set down the phrase as I heard it, which is not Grathic and will not be read at a Weighing. A vessel turned toward in expectation may give nothing at all; I have entered that as \emph{none} and not as a nought, because a nought is a figure and a silence is not.

A note taken at the drawing and a note taken at first light are not the same note. The room takes a little off everything it holds, the way any pot set in a draught loses heat without being asked, and the loss column is the only place in this book where the cost of keeping is set down. The College struck it on a market morning and wrote \emph{No such column} above in the narrow upright hand. I have drawn the column back underneath and left the words standing over it. He drew his thumb down every row before he could write that there was nothing in any of them worth entering, and I watched the thumb go.

I feed the dish at four and four, and it misses the fifth, and I put nothing into the gap. The bell at the Cross does the same thing over the market and nobody crosses himself. Two counts in two rooms, and I have kept them on separate places rather than make one out of them. A clerk who joins two counts has begun to write a doctrine, and doctrines get copied.

\subsection*{What the borrowed hands did}

The College clerk struck \emph{I held} against the widow and set \emph{the vessel was held} above, and underneath that \emph{the measure was kept}, which is further from the pallet than the first. I have put \emph{I held} back beneath both. Take the man out of a sentence and there is nobody left for a woman to put her question to, and the questions come in the end, always at the door, always after the figure has gone up the road.

Against the man of Mud End I had written \emph{the neighbours called it merciful}. A tall leaning hand from Greybank set \emph{the draw was lawful} above and underlined it twice. Both stand. Lawful is true and does not mention a man who was gone before the tube came through the door; merciful is what the room said after I had put the dish out, and there is no column for what a room says in the dark.

He struck a third thing also. Where I wrote \emph{asked whether it went into a child}, he wrote \emph{no entry required}, and he was right by the rule and wrong by the door. I have left both.

\subsection*{The verse the collectors say coming down the road}

\emph{Said low going down Slate Row before the light, never while the slate is open on the table, and never twice in one house.}

\begin{quote}\itshape The room keeps four and the room keeps four\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and a place where the fifth should stand;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the figure goes up in a clean dry hand\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the warmth goes down in the clay.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape I do not ask what the morning does\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape with a thing that lay warm on the bench;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the slate is read twice and the cradle once\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and nothing is read of the night.\end{quote}

The man who said this to me would not say the last line while the factor’s man stood at the foot of the Row, which is how I know which line matters. I have copied it as it came and put no gloss on it. A man who sets a meaning beside a song is writing a notice, and notices are read twice at the Cross.

\subsection*{In the margins}

The grey in the outer fold came off a district bundle laid on the bench while a man was being carried in from Mud End; it took the shape of a thumb and I have not brushed it away. The tallow thumb at the head is mine, from holding the lamp low over a row when somebody behind me was saying something I wanted the end of. The filings in the gutter come out of the wool sleeve the tube rides in; there is always a little iron in the fold and it has never once drawn the warmth out of the paper, which is the one small kindness this trade allows the written word. The bone-pale streak is slip from the thrower’s forearms, left when she set her slate beside mine to wait for a figure. The green bead is lead glaze and not slip; she leaned over to see the writing with the sweetness still at her mouth, touched the leaf, said nothing, and went back up the terrace. The tide-line along the foot came up from the flagstones the night the barrow stood here, and comes back every wet month. The small square in the lower margin is where I scraped a word away with a knife and put no other in its place. I have not written the word back and I have not forgotten its length.

\subsection*{At the foot, in a hand nobody will own}

\begin{quote}\itshape The room keeps them warm. The morning keeps the figure. Nobody keeps the hour between.\end{quote}

I asked the College clerk, a man come up from Greybank, and a woman who stood at the table about her house, and had three answers and no hand. I have left the line where it was written.

The leaf goes back under the bench. At first light Hessa Rale will come with her strap settled and her slate held edge-on to her sleeve, and carry the figure up the Clay Road without reading it, and I shall feed the dish and turn the last pallet and set the note down before the College man can strike it. The bell will go four, four and a gap over the Cross. The corner will keep its grey. There is no Last Day in this room and nothing here is burned in the morning.

\clearpage\phantomsection\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{The Song of the Hollow Seat, Being the Wheel-Shed Work Song of Low Kiln, Counted in Turns of the Wheel and Said into the Clay}
\CRsheetheading{The Song of the Hollow Seat, Being the Wheel-Shed Work Song of Low Kiln, Counted in Turns of the Wheel and Said into the Clay}
{\centering\FellFont\itshape\footnotesize\color{faded} A wheel-woman’s work song of the Clay Yard, counted in the turns and not in the pots; the verses in the low Grathic of the yard, said down into the lump and not up into the air; the manner of the turns and the unsung last verse in the wheel-woman’s charcoal hand; a glaze girl’s gloss pressed into the margin in thick charcoal; the corrections of a College clerk borrowed at Greybank in Ledgerhand standing above; and one line at the foot in a hand nobody will own · Sung at the hollow wheel-seat of the wheel-shed in Low Kiln of Sill since before the Glaze Wars and set down in Ember of Y.H. 813, the kiln month, by a woman who has turned at that wheel for one-and-thirty years and has begun to lose the use of her right thumb; written in charcoal and tallow on the back of a drying-rack tally spoiled by a fall of slip, folded into four and carried in the breast of her apron against a square of sacking gone soft at the seam, and copied forward at Greybank onto the back of a factor’s weigh-slip gone stiff with salt. It survives with wet slip worked into the grain at the head, brick dust ground into the fold, a tallow thumb at the second corner, a green bead of lead-glaze in the lower corner, a grey Ash print along the gutter that nobody will own, a ring the colour of weak barley-water, a long hair the colour of wet wool caught in the seam, a pot-shard pressed flat between the third and fourth leaves, the clerk’s figures standing above the verses, the glaze girl’s gloss in the margin, and the one line at the foot\par}\medskip
I have turned at the wheel in the shed below the kiln for one-and-thirty years, and I have set this down because a man come up from Slate Row stood in the door with a slate under his arm and asked what the hands said while they worked. I told him hands don’t say. He said every trade has its count, and if I would not give him mine he would put a figure in it himself. So I have written it in the order of the turns, on the back of a rack tally that a fall of slip spoiled. The figures went before anyone could price them, which is a mercy of a kind.

A wheel song is not like a bank song. A bank song is counted in pulls, and a man wrong on one pull pays for it on the next with his shoulder. This is counted in turns of the foot, and a wrong turn cannot be taken back, because the wall has already risen wrong and the clay does not forgive. We say it down into the lump, not up into the shed. Said up into the air it becomes a thing for listening to, and a wheel that stands still while a girl at the well listens.

The count begins at the second turn. The first turn is the wheel’s own; it centres the lump and is not ours and is never counted. A clerk can put a nought against that if he likes. A nought is a figure and the first turn is not one.

\subsection*{How it is sung}

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item Sit down into the hollow before you set the lump. The seat is worn to the shape of a body and a body new to it will slide and spend the morning finding itself. Three women of this yard have sat in that hollow before me, and my girl will sit in it after, if the shed is standing.

\item Centre on the first turn and say nothing. To say a word over the first turn is to claim it, and a claimed centring makes a wall that leans.

\item Come in on the second with the thumbs wet. Wet the hands and not the wall, the old women say; a wall drowned in water sits down while you look at it, and a wall too dry argues with the rib all morning.

\item Say the refrain into the clay and not to the girl beside you. Said to a person it becomes instruction, and instruction given at this wheel is instruction she will unlearn at somebody else’s.

\item Do not sing it over a pot set down to dry. A song said over a standing pot brings the note into the room before it is due, and a pot told it is true before the fire has tried it is generally a pot that goes flat. A master come up from the terrace said a pot that sings early sings itself out early, and I have no cause to argue with him, and none to agree.

\item Not at the Cross, and not on an Account-day. The bell there goes four, four and a gap and a song sung against that gap comes home wrong in the mouth.

\item Leave the last verse where it is left below. It is not sung at the wheel. It is said once, low, by whoever has the shed to herself, and the wheel is given its turn back afterward.

\end{itemize}

\subsection*{The song}

\emph{The lump goes down in the first turn and the first turn is not counted. Refrain after every verse, said down into the clay. One line of the refrain for one turn of the foot.}

\begin{quote}\itshape The seat is worn hollow where my mother sat,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and I sit in the hollow and my girl will;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape a body fits a hollow and the hollow keeps the shape,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the wheel turns before the hand gets there.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Turn. The foot remembers.}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Turn. The wall comes true.}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{The first is the wheel’s. We count from two.}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Wet the hand and hold.}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Let the wheel have the lump and say nothing over it,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape one turn to centre and that turn is not yours;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape come in on the second with the thumbs wet,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the clay will show you where it wants to stand.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Turn. The foot remembers.}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Turn. The wall comes true.}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{The first is the wheel’s. We count from two.}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Wet the hand and hold.}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Two to raise and three to bring it true,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape four to take the thumb’s own printing out;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape a wall hurried in the raising keeps the mark,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and a wall that keeps the mark answers flat.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Turn. The foot remembers.}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Turn. The wall comes true.}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{The first is the wheel’s. We count from two.}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Wet the hand and hold.}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Too much water and it goes down sitting,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape too little and it argues with the rib;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape there’s a dry place in the clay that will not be reasoned with,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the only argument that wins there is a wet thumb.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Turn. The foot remembers.}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Turn. The wall comes true.}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{The first is the wheel’s. We count from two.}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Wet the hand and hold.}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape The sweet comes down the terrace on a wrong wind,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the girls that taste the glaze have a pale line at the gum;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape we give the pot its shape and they give it the colour,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the colour is paid for out of somebody’s mouth.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Turn. The foot remembers.}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Turn. The wall comes true.}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{The first is the wheel’s. We count from two.}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Wet the hand and hold.}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Tap the lip with the knuckle when the wall has stood;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the full note says true and the flat note says a flaw;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the kiln-masters keep that to themselves, being their trade,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape but the wheel knows it a day before the fire does.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Turn. The foot remembers.}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Turn. The wall comes true.}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{The first is the wheel’s. We count from two.}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Wet the hand and hold.}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape The bell goes up at the Cross four and four and a gap,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the slate goes up the road in a clean hand;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the yard counts turns and the district counts souls,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and neither of the two will tell you what a pot’s worth.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Turn. The foot remembers.}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Turn. The wall comes true.}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{The first is the wheel’s. We count from two.}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Wet the hand and hold.}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape On the Last Day the grey goes out through the north gate\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the pots that failed go broken after it;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape what the wheel made and the kiln kept\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape goes back to the ground it came out of, in its own time.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Turn. The foot remembers.}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Turn. The wall comes true.}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{The first is the wheel’s. We count from two.}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Wet the hand and hold.}\end{quote}

There is a space before the last refrain in the singing, the length of one turn of the foot. I have left it on the tally. It is the space the first turn stands in, which is the wheel’s and not ours, and it wants exactly that much room and no more.

\subsection*{The last verse, which is not sung at the wheel}

\emph{Said once, low, when the shed is empty. I have put it after the song and not into it, because a verse said at the wheel sets the hand to looking at its own fingers, and a wheel-hand who looks at her fingers is a wheel-hand who will lose a morning.}

\begin{quote}\itshape There was a woman turned at this seat in a winter of ice,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and her right hand went in where the clay was too cold to tell her;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape we counted her turns going and we did not count them back,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the next pot up the rack stood with one place unfilled.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape The seat kept her shape. The wheel kept her turn.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape We gave the first to the wheel as we always do,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and have never once found out which of us it was\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape that the wheel was keeping it for.\end{quote}

I asked the old women whose hand it was and had three answers and no name, and I have put none in. A name said in a wheel-shed travels, and a name that travels arrives at a slate. The girl who writes for me has put a line of dots where this verse stood when I first said it, and I have left her dots standing over my words, as a rack keeps the place where a pot was taken down.

\subsection*{What the glaze girl put in the margin}

The thick charcoal belongs to a girl of the Glaze Room up the terrace, who came down with the colour on her sleeve and leaned over to see the writing and read the verse about the gum with her own hand at her mouth. I have copied it as it stands.

At \emph{the colour is paid for out of somebody’s mouth}: \emph{I tasted three mornings running in my first year and the line came up at my gum and my mother rubbed it with wood-ash and it went. It came back when I went back. I have not told the physician at Greybank and I have not told the factor and I have told this slate, which is the only one that will not travel.}

At \emph{the first is the wheel’s}: \emph{My mother said the first turn is the one that’s given away, and you never miss it and never get it back, and she said it of the pot and not of anything else, I think.}

At \emph{a wall that keeps the mark answers flat}: \emph{I have heard the kiln-master tap them and say full and flat and nothing besides. He does not say what the flat one cost. None of them do.}

\subsection*{What the clerk did at Greybank}

A clerk of the College borrowed the tally when the slates went up, being a man who cannot leave paper lying. He has a cuff gone soft from washing and the ink sits in two fingers of it and will not come out.

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item He numbered the turns one, two, three, four in the margin and put a round nought against the first and wrote \emph{centring, nil} beside it. It is true in the figure and false in the shed. I have left it.

\item At \emph{the clay will show you where it wants to stand} he wrote \emph{the vessel is shaped by the operator}, and struck out \emph{will}. A thing always true has no need of a verb, he said. I have put \emph{will} back underneath.

\item At \emph{the colour is paid for out of somebody’s mouth} he wrote \emph{glaze applied. Cost to district, nil}, the cleanest lie in the margin and the one I have most trouble leaving standing.

\item Against the bell at the Cross he wrote \emph{one in twelve, read twice; the young are instructed}. He has put the district’s twelfth where the bell’s gap stood. The bell has no twelfth. It has the gap.

\item Where the last verse stood he ruled two lines and wrote \emph{no entry} above them, a true thing in a place that has never had a hand go into a wheel. I have put my verse below his rule and not through it.

\end{itemize}

He asked me what a song was worth that could not be entered. I told him it was worth the wall coming up true, which is a thing no slate has ever paid for and no slate has ever had to carry. He wrote \emph{sentiment} in the margin and went off with the leaf. I have kept his hand and my words under it, as the floor keeps the ash and the foot that raised it.

\subsection*{At the head and in the gutter}

The slip at the head is off the hand that set the lump down; it goes into the grain and will not come out, which is why the yard uses it to mark a place. The brick dust in the fold is off the rack where the pots stand and is the only thing here put there by the trade and not by a person. The tallow thumb is mine; I held the leaf down in the draught under the shed door and did not know I had marked it. The green bead came off a pot broken in the Glaze Room and rolled as far as the fold before anybody saw it; a girl with sweetness at her mouth put it there, said nothing and went back up the terrace. The grey along the gutter came off a cuff laid where no cuff has business lying; nobody will own it, and there is no Last Day in a wheel-shed. The ring is weak barley-water, set down at the first verse and taken up at the last, by which time it had gone the colour of the slip beside it. The hair in the seam is long and the colour of wet wool and is not mine. The pot-shard between the third and fourth leaves is from a flat one broken at the end of a firing in Ash of last year; I put it in to keep the leaves apart and have not looked at the crack since.

\subsection*{At the foot, in a hand nobody will own}

\begin{quote}\itshape The pot keeps the note. The seat keeps the shape.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape The slate keeps neither and is read aloud all the same.\end{quote}

I asked an old woman of the racks, a girl of the Glaze Room and a clerk who does not turn, and had three answers and no hand. I have left the line where it was written. The tally goes back into my apron and the apron back over the square of sacking. Tomorrow the wheel will take its first turn before I set a hand to it, as it has done for one-and-thirty years and as it will do after my thumb has gone, and I shall count from the second and say the refrain down into the lump, and leave the first where it belongs.

\clearpage\phantomsection\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{The Articles of the Hopper, Being the Standing Rules of the Millers of Sill for the Taking, Keeping and Trying of Apprentices at the Meal Mill on the Ilm, with the Table of Grinds, the Faults in a Second Table, the Dressing-Song Pasted Inside the Meal-Book, Two Corrections in Borrowed Hands, and a Line at the Foot Nobody Will Own}
\CRsheetheading{The Articles of the Hopper, Being the Standing Rules of the Millers of Sill for the Taking, Keeping and Trying of Apprentices at the Meal Mill on the Ilm, with the Table of Grinds, the Faults in a Second Table, the Dressing-Song Pasted Inside the Meal-Book, Two Corrections in Borrowed Hands, and a Line at the Foot Nobody Will Own}
{\centering\FellFont\itshape\footnotesize\color{faded} A mill-leaf of rules in the hand of the under-miller who keeps the hopper and the roll of hands; the articles in the short sayings of the river bank, the grinds and the faults in tables, the dressing-song pasted to the inside of the meal-book, a barleycorn shut in the fold, two corrections in the narrow upright Ledgerhand of a factor’s clerk, one line in a carter’s thick charcoal, a girl’s gloss underneath, and a line at the foot nobody has claimed · First set down at Sill in Y.H. 726, the year the factor at Greybank raised his granary and doubled the grain levy, when a mill that had carried its rules in the dust was made to write them so that a due could be argued with; copied forward from the hopper board and not from a book, which is why the rule about the handful is worn smooth where a hundred thumbs have lifted it and the rule about the foundling is as sharp as the day it was cut. This leaf written in Stone of Y.H. 813, the year after the Thin Year, by the under-miller who keeps the hopper and the roll of hands, and kept folded in the toll-bag on its nail behind the mill door. It survives with white mill-dust worked into the head and the gutter, a brown silt tideline along the foot from a morning the leaf went down to the Fishstairs in an apron, a barley awn stiff in the second fold, a barleycorn shut in the crease that has not sprouted, a wet ring where a cup was set down and taken up before it was seen, a nick from a millstone dressing-pick at the fore-edge, a thumb of tallow off the hopper strap, a thread of grey wool caught in the sewing where a foundling’s fold was mended, the sweet green of lead glaze pressed in by a girl come down from High Kiln, a grey print along the outer fold that nobody will own, two corrections in the factor’s upright hand, one line in a carter’s charcoal added at the bridge, a girl’s gloss under it, and a line at the foot that has never been claimed\par}\medskip
I keep the hopper and the roll of hands at the meal mill on the Ilm. A house brings a child and goes away; the child stays with the dust. When a man comes in off the ridge with a sack frozen hard I tell him what the road took before I tell him what the mill will give, because the first is a thing I have seen and the second is a thing the Cross has said twice. The toll-bag hangs on a nail behind the door, and a man must turn his back on the wheel to reach it. That is the first lesson and I never have to teach it; the bag teaches it.

I set down what stands. Where a borrowed hand has corrected me I have left both readings, the way old grinding shows under the new on a dressed stone.

They were first written in Y.H. 726, the year the factor raised his granary and doubled the levy, when a mill that had kept its rules in the dust was made to set them down so a due could be argued with. A rule that has never had dust on it is a rule nobody has had to grind. These have been ground.

\subsection*{The articles as they stand at the mill}

\subsection*{Of the taking}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item The mill takes a child, not a house. A house may bring him and answer for his bread until the first grind is done; from the day he lifts a peck he answers to the hopper. A house that will not give up the years has given nothing.

\item A child is taken at ten, or at eleven if his house has kept him through a winter of sickness. Not before he can carry a peck of meal the length of the bench without setting it down. A child who sets it down has spent the meal on the floor and will call it the wheel’s doing; the wheel does not answer.

\item His birth-name is said once at the taking and not used again at the mill. What he is called afterward is the dust-name, given the first morning he comes up white to the wrist and does not know he has marked himself. A dust-name cannot be entered, which is the only thing in this country I have found that cannot be.

\item He is kept, not hired. He eats from the mill dish, sleeps in the loft above the sacks, and what his hands earn goes into the meal and comes back as bread with the brown in the fold. He is paid in the only coin this trade uses: a crust at the door and no figure.

\item No child goes under the great wheel, and no child sleeps in the dust loft when the sacks are new. New sack-dust takes a man’s breath the way the kiln’s breath takes a man in sleep, only slower, so that nobody thinks to carry him out.

\end{enumerate}

\subsection*{Of the two stones}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item There are two stones under this town doing the same work and not agreeing. One turns and grinds and gives me a measure I can carry to the Cross. One lies under the water and gives one note and never gives a measure at all. The millstone feeds the body; the hand-stone feeds the day. A boy who lays one over the other will grind at the wrong hour and blame the mill.

\item Come to the hand-stone at the hour the note is due, not before. Stand below the ledge with the palm flat and wait until the note comes up into the roots of your teeth, before the ear places it out in the water. Hear it first and you were late, hearing the river go over instead.

\item Do not say the hour aloud. An hour said aloud becomes an argument, and there is argument enough at the Cross without carrying it down to the bank. When the bell comes down from the town, stop. It goes four, four and a gap, and the gap is not one of yours to fill. Begin again after.

\item Leave on the ledge behind the stone what you brought --- a crust, a bit, a knot, a sherd --- and take nothing back. The river takes what is set on its bank and gives back silt, which is an honest exchange and entered nowhere.

\item If the note comes before its hour, do not correct it. In the Thin Year it came under the ice for ninety-four days and the town kept its hours another way. A note is not gone wrong because we were early. Say what it gave and not what it meant.

\item Say the day to the hopper and not to the man asking. Said looking at a man, a figure becomes a price, and a price carried out with the meal comes back with a second figure on it. Twelve bits to the mark, twenty marks to a crown; an ember is what the Court calls five marks, and no ember has ever come through this door.

\end{enumerate}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{In the factor’s narrow upright hand, against rule 10:} The tide arrived in advance of the reckoning. Entered: nil. \emph{Underneath, in mine:} I had written that the note came early. He takes the doer out and leaves a nought where the hour stood. Both readings stand, because the boy will meet that hand again at the Cross and should know its writing before he has to argue with it.\end{quote}

\subsection*{Of the sacks and the hopper}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item Lift the handful off the top before the sack is tied and never weigh it. The handful is for the stone, and a thing weighed stops being a handful and becomes a charge, and a charge wants a figure put against it.

\item The cup on the nail beside the hopper is for the woman who carries, and she does not ask. The bran goes to the pig at the door, the crust to the child, and neither is entered. A mill that enters its crusts will soon be asked to enter its children.

\item A foundling left at the mill in a fold of grey wool gets a stone warmed under him and no name until a hearth claims him. He is not a sale and not a charge. A boy who names a foundling has made a slate where there was a fold of wool, and there is no unmaking it.

\item The toll-bag hangs behind the door. Reach it with your back to the wheel. What you take here, you take without looking at the work.

\item There is a figure spoken in the yards which is not the one on the notice. I have heard it under the wheel and set no sack beside it. A boy who asks after it is told to ask the hopper, which has never once answered, and is the better for it.

\item No boy is set to dress a millstone until he has carried a sack through a Silt flood and come back dry enough to be trusted with a pick. A sharp tool in a wet hurry takes the furrow off the stone and the skin off the hand; only one grows back.

\end{enumerate}

\subsection*{The table of grinds}

\emph{Kept on the hopper board, in a hand that does not change between one line and the next.}

At the mill — The work — What is taken\par

Ten — Carry, sweep, mind the sacks, set the cup on the nail — The birth-name, said once and not used again\par

Eleven — The peck carried level; the handful lifted off the top — The belief that a thing lifted is a thing known\par

Twelve — The hand-stone at its hour; the bell’s gap left standing — The boy’s own hour, which the town keeps after him\par

Thirteen — The first sack in a Silt flood; the dressing-pick held dry — The habit of asking what the mill ought to grind\par

Fourteen — A grist taken alone and given out without a figure — The dust-name, said to the wheel and kept in the mouth\par

Fifteen — Stand at the wheel when the year’s barley comes down frozen — The last of the boy’s account with any house\par

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item Fifteen is the common end of a grind and not a short one. A boy who has been through the years stays where the mill needs him, at this mill or at Stonemouth or on a barge going up with salt. The mill does not choose. The wheel does, and the road after it.

\end{enumerate}

\subsection*{The faults and their correcting}

Fault — As corrected at the mill\par

A figure said to the man and not the hopper — Said again to the hopper; nothing carried out\par

An early note corrected — The note left standing; the boy sent back at the due hour; nothing entered\par

The bell’s gap filled — Stop and begin after; the gap left the length it is\par

A foundling named — The name taken back; the fold of wool left as it lay\par

The handful weighed — The scales put away; the handful lifted off the top\par

A dust-name written in the meal-book — Rubbed out with meal-dust and said again to the wheel\par

A birth-name used at the mill — The roll read aloud once; the boy sent to the ledge\par

The bag reached with the face to the wheel — The toll said again with the back turned\par

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item A fault copied twice in one tend is a fault the boy has not understood, and the miller sits with him on the hopper board until he has. The dressing-pick is not a rod, though men who have never dressed a stone have called it one.

\end{enumerate}

\subsection*{The dressing-song, pasted inside the meal-book}

\emph{Sung low, kneeling, while the pick goes round the furrow and the dust comes up white. The last verse is said to the stone and not to the company. There is a gap before it the length of the bell’s.}

\begin{quote}\itshape Pick to the furrow and dust to the knee,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape one for the stone and one for me;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the wheel goes round and the sacks go round\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the note comes up out of the ground.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Four for the boards and four for the sill,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and a place where the bell has not said its fill;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the clock takes the note and gives out an hour,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the mill takes the note and gives out the meal.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape A boy comes in with a name on his sack\end{quote}
