\begin{quote}\itshape and goes out as meal with the name ground back;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the handful goes first and the road goes twice,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the clerk writes down what the river said once.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Pick to the furrow and dust to the knee,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the stone takes the boy and the boy takes the dust;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape leave the place where the answer stood\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and come back white. Come back as you can.\end{quote}

The wet reed across the third verse came from the leaf lying on the ledge while a girl from the Fishstairs sang it into the stone. I have flattened it.

\subsection*{What the borrowed hands did}

A factor’s clerk came up from Greybank with a soft cuff and ink in two fingers, and borrowed the leaf while I was at the hopper.

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item Against \emph{he is kept, not hired} he set \emph{retained at the mill, no wage arising}, true about a figure and false about a boy who eats from the dish. I have put the crust back underneath.

\item Against \emph{the handful is for the stone, never weighed} he set \emph{milling charge, one in twelve, as the notice says}. The notice is read in the square; the handful is lifted here before the sack is tied.

\end{itemize}

The other hand is a carter’s, thick charcoal added at the bridge: \emph{Paid going over and paid coming back, and the sacks lighter every time.} Beneath it, smaller, a girl who carries meal set: \emph{The cup on the nail belongs to the woman who carries, and she has never once asked.} Neither has signed. I have not rubbed either out. A rule two hands have argued over is a rule that has been used.

\subsection*{At the head and in the gutter}

The white at the head is mill-dust, not salt; my hands are white to the wrist and I did not know I had marked the leaf until I opened it. The brown line along the foot came up from the Fishstairs in an apron and stayed when the water went. The awn in the second fold is stiff where the crease kept it from the damp. The barleycorn was shut in the crease when I took the leaf from a spoiled quire; it has not sprouted and I have not moved it. The ring is not ale; a woman set a cup down while I spoke of the hour and took it up unseen. The nick is from the dressing-pick, which I use to open the book when my hands are wet. The tallow is off the hopper strap. The thread of grey wool caught in the sewing came from the fold a foundling lay in one Silt; I have not cut it away. The green bead came off a girl come down from High Kiln with the sweetness still at her mouth; she leaned to read the faults and asked nothing. I have left it where it fell. The grey along the outer fold is not mine and I have not swept it. There is no Last Day at a mill; the dust goes out with the meal and nobody calls it dealt with.

\subsection*{At the foot, in a hand nobody will own}

\begin{quote}\itshape The clock takes the note and the Cross takes the figure;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the stone takes the handful and the bag keeps none.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape A boy comes in with a house’s name on his sack\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and goes out as meal with the name ground off,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the space between is not entered.\end{quote}

I asked the miller, a carter off the ridge, and a clerk come up from the Greybank beam, and had three answers and no hand. I have left the lines where they were written. The leaf goes back into the bag and the barleycorn into the crease. Tomorrow the sacks will come down frozen hard from Cold Acre, and I shall give the figure I gave today; by the time the wheel has turned it will be a thing that was true.

\clearpage\phantomsection\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{Of the Joining of Vessels, the Marriage Slate, the Number of Pourings, and the Vessel Unsafe to Marry, Being Title the Eleventh of the Ordinances of the Keeping, Copied into the Assessor’s House at Sill with the Joining-Clerk’s Margin, the Form Left Blank, the Joining-Song Pasted Inside the Cover, Two Corrections in Borrowed Hands, and a Line at the Foot Nobody Will Own}
\CRsheetheading{Of the Joining of Vessels, the Marriage Slate, the Number of Pourings, and the Vessel Unsafe to Marry, Being Title the Eleventh of the Ordinances of the Keeping, Copied into the Assessor’s House at Sill with the Joining-Clerk’s Margin, the Form Left Blank, the Joining-Song Pasted Inside the Cover, Two Corrections in Borrowed Hands, and a Line at the Foot Nobody Will Own}
{\centering\FellFont\itshape\footnotesize\color{faded} An extract from the Court’s ordinances, written out for the counter of the assessor’s house in Sill’s Slate Row, with the marginal hand of the clerk who keeps the joining-slate; the articles in Ledgerhand and the persons restored beneath them, the returns and the faults in tables, a form of joining left blank, the joining-song pasted inside the cover, a word left out where an older hand struck it, two corrections in borrowed hands, and a line at the foot nobody has claimed · Copied at Sill in the assessor’s house built in Y.H. 776, in the Thin Year, Y.H. 812, from Title the Eleventh of the Ordinances of the Keeping as set down in the first years after the Rising of Y.H. 668, amended in Y.H. 651 by the striking of a phrase, confirmed to the factor at Greybank by the treaty of Y.H. 418, and added to in Y.H. 782 and in the Thin Year; carried forward at the Opening of the Slates, Ilmen 1, Y.H. 813. It survives as three leaves of foolscap sewn with wire and tied with a grown string, kept in the joining-slate’s box behind the counter and taken down when two people come to stand as one house: an iron-gall thumb at the head, a streak of pale slip down the gutter, a thread of grey wool tied through the tie-hole, a brown crust-mark at the second fold, a green bead of lead glaze pressed into the lower corner, a cold-iron scratch the length of a clip in the margin where no clip is used, a washing-water tide-line along the foot, a bare place the length of a word struck before this leaf was copied, two corrections in borrowed hands, and a line at the foot that has never been claimed\par}\medskip
I keep the joining-slate. It lies in a box behind the counter with a string grown tight across the hasp, and I take it down when two people come to stand as one house. They stand a little short of the slate’s reach, as people do at the Cross, and I write what the ordinance tells me and set the two back underneath in my own hand, because a joining entered with nobody in it is a joining nobody made, and that is the only kind this house has ever wanted on its roll.

A joining is two measures under one sum. The Court does not ask what brought the two to the counter: it has no word for that and has managed eight hundred years without one. It asks for their numbers, their names, and how often each has been poured. I write the figure and the names under it and the count of pourings beside them, and the two go away as one household with two names still standing on the roll, one above the other, which is how the Court joins a thing without ever having to make it whole.

These articles were set down after the Rising and gathered here when the house in Slate Row was built in Y.H. 776. One phrase was struck in Y.H. 651, before my time and my teacher’s; the bare place is the length of it, and I have put no word into it. A rule with no thumb on it is a rule nobody has had to use. These have been used.

\subsection*{Title the Eleventh, as it stands in the assessor’s house}

\emph{From the Ordinances of the Keeping, Title the Eleventh: Of the Joining of Vessels, the Marriage Slate, and the Vessel Unsafe to Marry. Set down in the first years after the Rising of Y.H. 668; a phrase struck in Y.H. 651; confirmed to the factor at Greybank by the treaty of Y.H. 418; added to in Y.H. 782 and in the Thin Year, Y.H. 812.}

\subsection*{I. Of the two who stand}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item The joining of vessels is the entering of two measures as one house. The sum is set down in embers, and the deduction of one in twelve is entered once upon the joined house, as the notice says. Two figures become one figure at this counter and nowhere else. The Keeping holds no second slate for what it has added.

\end{enumerate}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Margin:} I have restored the two who stood beneath \emph{the vessels are joined}. The woman put her hand to the man’s sleeve and took it away before I looked up; I have entered neither. There is a column for embers and a column for names, and none for the space between two people, which is the only part they came here to have entered.\end{quote}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item A joining is entered without regard to sex. In Grath a widow may hold a hearth in her own right, and a woman returned thin may keep the house though she may not keep the wheel. These are house customs and are not entered here, though they are the reason half the people who come to this counter are women.

\end{enumerate}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item The names of both vessels stand upon the roll, one above the other, and neither is taken away. Where a name has been taken away by an officer of the College, the bare place is left the length of it and the joining is written over the place.

\end{enumerate}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Margin:} A woman given a slate-name wanted her birth-name back for the ceremony. I told her the roll does not lend names. She said she had not asked to borrow one. I entered the slate-name and put the other at the edge, the length of it.\end{quote}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item The clip is not brought to this counter. A vessel held by the wrist may be drawn, and consent to a drawing may be entered by an officer’s hand, but a vessel held by the wrist cannot be joined: the measure may be made to go in, and the want cannot.

\end{enumerate}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Margin:} I asked the officer who carries the clip whether he had ever held one at a joining. He said no, and then said he had once been asked, and put the word back into his mouth and carried it out. I entered the no and not the once.\end{quote}

\subsection*{II. Of the number of pourings}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item The count of pourings stands in a column of its own and is entered before the sum. A vessel returned whole keeps the name it had. A vessel returned thin is given a name from the district’s name-pot, and the former name is entered in a second column which the household is not shown.

\end{enumerate}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Margin:} A woman asked to see the second column. I told her there was none for her house and nothing in it she had not been given leave to read. Both answers were true, and neither was the one she had come for.\end{quote}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item A vessel poured more than three times is unsafe to marry, of either sex. The figure is entered. The reason is not entered. Where a reason is demanded, give the date of the striking and no more; a date is safe, and the Court likes a date.

\end{enumerate}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Margin, written very small:} The older copy had a phrase here, struck with a bone-stylus before this leaf was made. I have held the bare place to the lamp and read nothing. A clerk who supplies the words has begun to write a sermon, and sermons get copied.\end{quote}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item A vessel poured five times may carry five names and remember the wrong one. Where a person gives a name that belongs to another vessel on the roll, the figure is entered and the name is set at the edge; no second column is opened on the strength of a name spoken at a counter.

\end{enumerate}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Margin:} A man gave four names and a fifth I knew from the roll as his sister’s, come to him, he said, in a fever the physician called a settling of the graft. I entered the four and set the fifth at the edge, the length of it. He asked which column held the fever. I told him there was none. True, and not what he asked.\end{quote}

\subsection*{The returns, as the roll keeps them}

Pourings — Name on the roll — The second column — What this counter enters\par

One, whole — The birth-name — Nothing standing — The name, the sum, one in twelve\par

One, thin — A name from the name-pot — The former name — The new name; the other not shown\par

Three — As the roll has it — As the roll has it — The count, the sum\par

Four — As the roll has it — As the roll has it — \emph{Unsafe to marry}; the figure, not the reason\par

Five — Five names may stand — Not shown to the house — \emph{Unsafe to marry}; the count, and nothing of the fever\par

\subsection*{III. Of the house that comes of it}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item Where two hearths are joined, the Court enters one hearth. The second is not entered and is not swept out on the Last Day. On the morning after, both corners are called dealt with, and nobody has asked which was which.

\end{enumerate}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item A boat-share in Vhal passes through women. A man who marries into a boat-owning family is said to come aboard, and his opinion on the boat is counted at half. It is entered here because a joining made at the Quay is entered at this counter. A contract written on salt-paper and gone damp in the journey is no contract, and the Council calls that a virtue; the joining stands where the paper went.

\end{enumerate}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Margin:} A woman came up from the Quay with salt in the crease of her shoe and a sheet gone soft in her sleeve. By noon there was no writing on the sheet and by dusk she had a house. She asked whether the Council would count it a marriage. I told her it would count what was standing. True, and not what she asked.\end{quote}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item A joining made in the Bowl of Sere is not entered here. A people who burn debt-slates by lot at a feast do not keep a joining-slate, and no figure goes up the Clay Road from such a house.

\end{enumerate}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Margin:} A woman come back from the south with a green at one corner of her mouth asked whether a bowl had forgotten her. I told her no bowl keeps a slate. That is true, and was not what she asked.\end{quote}

\subsection*{IV. Of faults and their correcting}

Fault — As entered at the counter — What the clerk sets beneath\par

A joining entered with nobody in it — The two names, in the same hand — The hand each used, and the order of reaching\par

The struck phrase supplied — The word scraped out, the bare place kept — The length of the word, and nothing of it\par

A second column opened on a spoken name — The name struck, the figure left standing — The fever, at the edge, the length of a hand\par

The clip brought to this counter — Not entered — The officer’s \emph{once}, at the edge\par

A damp contract from the Quay — Entered as no contract — The woman, and the salt in her shoe\par

\subsection*{The form of the joining}

\emph{Set out at the end, with the blanks as they stand. In nine years no clerk has filled the last line with his own name.}

\begin{quote}\itshape Entered this day, being ---day of -------, in the year of the Hearth ------, the joining of the vessels ------------------ and ------------------ into one house, their measures in the sum of ---- embers, the deduction one in twelve as the notice says, the pourings standing at --- and ---, the names as they stand upon the roll, the second column not shown; the clause concerning the unsafe not called, the reason not entered; written by ------------------, whose hand went to the slate before his eyes went to the two.\end{quote}

\subsection*{The joining-song, pasted inside the cover}

\emph{Said low at the counter while the string is being undone, never while the form is in sight of the College man, and never twice for the same two.}

\begin{quote}\itshape Two pots on a shelf and a place between,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the shelf keeps the place and gives no name;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape bring the two together under one sum,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the sum will hold what the shelf held.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Four for the hearth where the two stood,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and a fifth for nothing that was said;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the cord goes round and the count goes up,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the roll keeps one name above the other.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Three is a number and four is a word\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the older copies would not let stand;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape hold the bare place to the lamp all night,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and read the length of what was taken out.\end{quote}

The second verse came in with the Thin Year and is said by no officer of the College. I have copied it as it came.

\subsection*{What the borrowed hands did}

The College man came down from Slate Row with ink in two fingers of a cuff gone soft from washing. On article one he struck \emph{the two who stood} and set \emph{the vessels are joined} above it, true of every joining and therefore of none. He drew a line under all my margins and wrote \emph{no entry arising} above the whole of them, so that the edge would read as though it had never held anything. He had to look at every margin before he could write that there was nothing in them worth keeping. I watched him.

The other hand is tall and leaning and comes from the factor’s house at Greybank. Against \emph{unsafe to marry} it set \emph{an impediment of account, not of person}, and against the struck phrase, \emph{a matter of physiography, long since settled}. I have struck neither. A hand that writes a person out of an impediment knows the difference between a vessel and a figure, and trades on never saying which. I have left both readings standing, as the names stand on the roll.

\subsection*{At the head and in the gutter}

The brown at the head is iron-gall and mine, from holding the quire while two people read the form who could not read it together. The pale streak down the gutter is slip from the upper pit; it stayed in the fold instead of falling through, which is how I knew who had held the leaf. The grey wool through the tie-hole is a thread from a wrist-cord tied there by a woman who went away with her question unentered; I have not untied it. The brown at the second fold is a barley crust set down while an old man found his name and taken up again when he found it; the mark has eaten the corner of one line and not the sense. The green bead came off a glaze-mixer come up from High Kiln with the sweetness still at her mouth; she leaned to see the count of pourings and went back down the road. The cold-iron score in the margin is the length of a clip, laid there by an officer before he remembered where he was; the clip is not used here, and the scratch is the only record of its having come. The tide-line along the foot is washing-water from a pail set down while I told a woman that the Council counts what is standing. There is no Last Day behind a counter. The slate is scraped for the next two, and what was written on it goes into no fire and is called dealt with by nobody.

\subsection*{At the foot, in a hand nobody will own}

\begin{quote}\itshape The figure keeps the two and the roll keeps the names. Between the sum and the second column a person stood who wanted, and the wanting is the one thing this house has never been able to enter.\end{quote}

I asked the College clerk, a man from the factor’s house, and a woman waiting with her pail, and had three answers and no hand, as I have had before. I have left the line where it was written.

The leaves go back into the box. Tomorrow two people will stand a little short of the slate’s reach; I shall read them what stands here, put the persons back where a borrowed hand took them out, give the date where the reason is asked for, and say nothing about the bare place.

\clearpage\phantomsection\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{The Song of the Rooms, Being the Lament of One Kept Near the Fire in the Hearthseat, with the Manner of It, the Words as the Room Keeps Them, and the Correction Set Over Them at the Weighing}
\CRsheetheading{The Song of the Rooms, Being the Lament of One Kept Near the Fire in the Hearthseat, with the Manner of It, the Words as the Room Keeps Them, and the Correction Set Over Them at the Weighing}
{\centering\FellFont\itshape\footnotesize\color{faded} A lament of the Kept, taken down by the keeper of the room-book in the Hearthseat; the verses in the soft Court speech of the warm passage, the refrain in the room’s own order of reaching, the coal-woman’s charcoal set underneath, the Steward’s clerk’s correction standing above, and one line at the foot in a hand nobody will own · Set down in Ash of Y.H. 812, the Thin Year, in the rooms beside the Weighing Hall on the Keel, by a junior clerk of the College who keeps the evening slate and signs nothing, calling herself only the keeper of the room-book; written on the back of a measure-slip spoiled by a wet thumb at the Weighing, carried down the Clay Road in Ilmen of Y.H. 813 and copied at Greybank onto the back of a Court grain-warrant gone soft at one corner. It survives in the room-book’s board cover in the Steward’s room: a flake of scale from the grating at the head, a thumb of tallow, a grey Ash print along the gutter that nobody will own, a ring where a cup of water stood from the first verse to the last and went cold without being drunk, a thread of grey wool from a Kept sleeve caught in the fold, the coal-woman’s words below the lines and the clerk’s verbless correction above them, and a line at the foot that has never been claimed\par}\medskip
I keep the room-book of the Kept. That is my whole office: to carry the evening slate down the warm passage to the rooms beside the Hall, to read the day’s figure to those who have no use for it, and to write down what they say after I have finished. There are fewer than twenty of them and I could name every room with my eyes shut. They hold three hundred measures apiece and feel nothing at all, which the Court calls a mercy and which I have never once heard called that by anybody who had stood in one of the rooms.

I set this down because a woman in the third room said these words to me on the night of the Weighing and asked me to put them somewhere a clerk would be obliged to read them. She cannot feel her own hands, but she remembers the order of feeling the way a pot remembers the thumb that made it. That is the whole marvel of those rooms and the whole horror of them, and I have not found a sentence that holds both, so I have set down hers instead of mine.

The dark at the head of this leaf is not Ash. It is a flake of scale off the grating before the Hearth-fire, which no priest is permitted to touch and which I was not permitted to bring away. It fell into the fold as I held the leaf up to the warm passage to read what I had written. I have left it where it fell. A thing that has been where the fire is does not need to be explained to anybody who has never been near it.

\subsection*{The manner of it}

\emph{Written small on the back of the slip, before the verses, in the hand I use for the room-book.}

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item Sung after the evening figure has been read and entered, never during the reading. A vessel who sings while the figure is being entered is entered as disturbed, and the song is stopped until the next night.

\item Facing the wall. The Kept are not asked to stand near the Hearth-fire, and one who has never stood near it does not sing toward it. She sings toward the wall, where the fire is not.

\item A cup of water is set down and not drunk. It goes cold in the ordinary way; the singer knows this by looking and not by any other means, and she looks.

\item The refrain is said to the slate and not to the room. Said to a person it becomes a comfort, and no comfort is entered in the room-book.

\item Stop while the readers are crossing the Hall above. Begin again when the passages go quiet. The Hall is longer in the telling than in the walking, and a song that runs into the reading is a song with a figure in it.

\item The last line is said twice. The second saying is for the room, not for the singer, who has no need of it and will not be told she has.

\end{itemize}

\subsection*{The song}

\emph{Said low, to the slate. The room keeps the refrain; the singer says the verses. The hand that holds the slate is not the hand that holds the cup.}

The refrain, as it is kept after every part:

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{The measure is banked. The account stands.}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Nothing is lost that we have kept.}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{I hold three hundred and I hold no hand.}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{The room is kept. I do not feel the keeping.}\end{quote}

\subsection*{I. Of the number}

\begin{quote}\itshape Three hundred in me and not one of them mine,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape entered in a hand that will never shake;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape no mark cut in my arm, for we are not counted there ---\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the mountain cuts the skin; we are written in a book.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape I have read my own figure every night for eleven years\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and it has never once changed, which is more\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape than can be said for any other slate in this city.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{The measure is banked. The account stands.}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Nothing is lost that we have kept.}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{I hold three hundred and I hold no hand.}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{The room is kept. I do not feel the keeping.}\end{quote}

\subsection*{II. Of the fire}

\begin{quote}\itshape The fire is behind iron and has never gone out;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape no priest has touched it and no Kept has stood near;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape I have lain eleven years warm and never once felt it,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape which is the finest thing the Court knows how to do.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape They bring the year’s flame up the yard in a clay dish\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape in the poor districts, and every house touches its own\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape to it and passes it on. I have never seen a clay dish.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape I have never been asked what my fire cost.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{The measure is banked. The account stands.}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Nothing is lost that we have kept.}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{I hold three hundred and I hold no hand.}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{The room is kept. I do not feel the keeping.}\end{quote}

\subsection*{III. Of the cold}

\begin{quote}\itshape The Waste takes what nobody keeps, and I am kept;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape so the Waste has no claim on me, and neither has the Hearth.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape I am the space between two houses that want me\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and neither of them can get at me. That is the keeping.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape In the districts the grey gathers where a promise fell,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape two thumbs wide at the corner, and the Last Day burns it.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape There is no corner in this room that has not been swept\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape since before I came here, and no Last Day, and no ash.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape They say it is pity to be past the cold.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape I have carried the word up and down the passage.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape It has a door in it. Most of their words have doors.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{The measure is banked. The account stands.}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Nothing is lost that we have kept.}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{I hold three hundred and I hold no hand.}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{The room is kept. I do not feel the keeping.}\end{quote}

\subsection*{IV. Of the shape}

\begin{quote}\itshape I tap my own wrist and it answers full;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape no man may tap me, for a body is not a pot;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape I have never given a flat note and never will,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and so I am the only vessel here that cannot be mended.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape There is a cup on the bench beyond the grating\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape which is full and stands and is not poured, and I know why\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape in the same way I know the order of the words for bread:\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape I have been told, and I have kept what I was told.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape They bottle the spent ash of a former life for the rich\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape so that the old voice will stop arriving in dreams.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape No voice arrives to me. There is nothing in me to bottle,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape which is a generosity I did not choose and cannot return.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{The measure is banked. The account stands.}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Nothing is lost that we have kept.}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{I hold three hundred and I hold no hand.}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{The room is kept. I do not feel the keeping.}\end{quote}

\subsection*{V. Of the last line}

\begin{quote}\itshape The roll of the dead is never closed. Mine lies in a drawer\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape two doors from here, and I have heard it read on the Remembering\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape in a clean voice that did not once look up from the slate.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Your return is recorded. I have said the words to myself.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape There is a place in the last line where a name stood once.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape I have left it the length of a name and do not fill it,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the way the yard leaves a space where a loaf was\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the broom goes around it and the figure never comes.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{The measure is banked. The account stands.}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Nothing is lost that we have kept.}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{I hold three hundred and I hold no hand.}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{The room is kept. I do not feel the keeping.}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{I hold three hundred and I hold no hand.}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{The room is kept. I do not feel the keeping.}\end{quote}

There is a space before the last refrain in the singing, as there is before the last line of the fifth part. I have left it on the slip. It is the right length for a name and for nothing else, and the coal-woman has put her thumb in it and would not say why.

\subsection*{What the coal-woman wrote underneath}

The charcoal belongs to the woman who carries the coals into the rooms at the fourth hour and takes the cold cups away. She writes on the backs of the tallies she spoils, in a hand that presses hard at the ends of words. I have copied it underneath as she set it.

At \emph{no mark cut in my arm}: \emph{They asked her at thirteen in the high country and she gave a number. Here they never asked her anything. She said this to me standing with her back to the grating, and I have not put her name to it.}

At \emph{I have never given a flat note}: \emph{I have carried coals into that room eleven winters. I have never heard her tap herself, but she tells me what her wrist says, and I have no way to know whether it is true. I have put it down as she said it, not as I should like it.}

At \emph{which is a generosity I did not choose}: \emph{She said this of the dreaming, and then she asked me whether I dreamed, which is a thing nobody in this building asks anybody. I told her I did. She said that was why she had written the line.}

At \emph{the way the yard leaves a space where a loaf was}: \emph{She has never been out of the Keel. I asked her what yard she meant. She said the one she was born in, before the keeping, and then she would not say another word about it.}

\subsection*{What the Steward’s man did}

A clerk of the Steward came into the room with the evening slate under his arm and took the leaf up while I was still writing. He has a cuff gone soft from washing and the ink sits in two fingers of it and will not come out. He writes in the narrow upright hand, with the verbs taken out as though a verb were a thing a man could hide in a sleeve and carry past a grating.

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item At \emph{three hundred in me and not one of them mine} he wrote \emph{vessel capacity: three hundred embers, current}, and underlined the figure twice.

\item At \emph{feel nothing at all}, in my opening line, he set \emph{no affect recorded} above it, which leaves the room standing and takes the woman out of it.

\item At \emph{the room is kept} he wrote \emph{the party is retained}, which is the same thing said by a man who has never had to stay in a room.

\item At \emph{I am the only vessel here that cannot be mended} he set \emph{no repair required}, and I have left it, because it is the truest and cruellest thing on the leaf.

\item Where the space stands before the last line, he put a round nought and wrote \emph{vacancy} beside it. He has put a figure where a name was, which is the whole art of that hand.

\end{itemize}

I have put her words back underneath and left his standing above. He takes the verbs out because a thing always true has no need of them. I put them back because a woman who cannot feel her own hands still wants to know which hand held the cup, and the answer is in the sentence if there is somebody in it.

\subsection*{At the head and in the gutter}

The flake at the head is grating-scale and I have not brushed it off, though a flake from that place is not a thing to carry in a book and I know it. The tallow is mine, off the lamp I kept turned down while she sang so that the readers above would not hear a song and come to enter it. The ring is where the cup of water stood from the first verse to the last; it went cold and nobody drank it and it left a mark the colour of the pot it stood on. The grey along the gutter came off a cuff laid where no cuff has business lying in a room that has been swept since before I came here. I have not swept it and nobody will own it. There is no Last Day in a room beside the Hall. The thread in the fold is grey wool off the sleeve of the woman in the third room, caught when she reached for the slate; she did not see it go and I have not told her.

\subsection*{At the foot, in a hand nobody will own}

\begin{quote}\itshape The grating keeps the fire and gives none back.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape The drawer keeps the roll and gives none back.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape The room keeps three hundred and warms nobody.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Nothing is lost that we have kept. Ask what paid for the keeping.\end{quote}

I asked the coal-woman, the Steward’s clerk and a reader who crosses the Hall at the fourth hour, and had three answers and no hand. I have left the lines where they were written. The leaf goes back into the room-book in the Steward’s room, and tomorrow the evening slate will be carried down the passage and the figure read to the third room, and the cup will be set down and go cold, and the woman who cannot feel the cold will look at it to learn that it has happened. I have kept her words and I have not joined them to anything.

\clearpage\phantomsection\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{Of the Nine Wells, the Sealing, the Keys and the Drawing Without Authority, Being Title the Eighth of the Ordinances of the Keeping, Copied for the Steward’s Room in the Hearthseat with the Key-Clerk’s Margin, the Notch of a Key in the Paper, the Tellers’ Verse, Two Corrections in Borrowed Hands, and a Line at the Foot Nobody Will Own}
\CRsheetheading{Of the Nine Wells, the Sealing, the Keys and the Drawing Without Authority, Being Title the Eighth of the Ordinances of the Keeping, Copied for the Steward’s Room in the Hearthseat with the Key-Clerk’s Margin, the Notch of a Key in the Paper, the Tellers’ Verse, Two Corrections in Borrowed Hands, and a Line at the Foot Nobody Will Own}
{\centering\FellFont\itshape\footnotesize\color{faded} An extract from the Court’s ordinances, written out for the Steward’s room beside the Weighing Hall; the articles in Ledgerhand and the verbs restored beneath them, the wells and their seals in a table, a table of offences and their correcting, a form of key-receipt left blank, the tellers’ verse as it is said in the passage, one line scored with the notch of a key, two corrections in borrowed hands, and a line at the foot nobody has claimed · Copied at the Hearthseat in Stone of Y.H. 812, the Thin Year, from Title the Eighth of the Ordinances of the Keeping, four of the Nine Wells sealed in the first hundred and twenty years and a fifth in Y.H. 618, with additions in Y.H. 782 and the Thin Year; carried forward at the Opening of the Slates, Ilmen 1, Y.H. 813. It survives as three leaves of foolscap sewn with wire, kept in the Steward’s room under the key-slate and taken down when a key is entered: a tallow thumb at the head, warm-stone dust ground into the gutter, a green mineral stain off a spring-lip at the fold, a cold-iron scratch the length of a key in the lower margin, iron-gall in the creases of two fingers, a damp tide-line from the sealed-file room along the foot, two corrections in borrowed hands, and a line at the foot that has never been claimed\par}\medskip
I keep the key-slate in the Steward’s room. Nine springs rise in the Keel within twenty leagues of this house, and five of them stand sealed. The keys hang on a nail behind the slate, and when a key goes out I write the hour and the hand and the spring it opens, and when it comes back I write the hour again and nothing else. The slate lies flat under the fingertips while a person is still speaking, which is the Steward’s own order and not mine. What follows is Title the Eighth, copied out so that a keeper may know what is being entered against him before it is entered. The ordinance is in Ledgerhand, with nobody in any of its sentences. I have put the verbs back underneath, because a key with nobody to carry it is a key that cannot be lost, and the Court has never yet kept a key that could not be lost.

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{At the head of the first leaf, in the same hand, written very small:} Copied by the room and for it. If this is read beyond the passage, let it be seen that the verbs were restored here and struck out again above. Let both stand. A leaf with two hands on it is the only kind a keeper believes.\end{quote}

\subsection*{Title the Eighth, as it stands in the Steward’s room}

\emph{From the Ordinances of the Keeping, Title the Eighth: Of the Nine Wells, their Sealing, the Keys, and Drawing Without Authority. Four springs sealed in the first hundred and twenty years; a fifth sealed in Y.H. 618; added to in Y.H. 782 and in the Thin Year, Y.H. 812.}

\subsection*{I. Of the springs and their sealing}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item Nine springs rise in the Keel. The ground there gives back more than it takes, as the ordinance says. Four were sealed in the first hundred and twenty years of the Keeping; a fifth was sealed in Y.H. 618. The others stand open and are not the Court’s to keep.

\end{enumerate}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item A spring sealed is covered with a stone and a ring of cold iron. No priest blesses the stone. No name is cut upon it. The name goes into the sealed files and is not read at the Weighing.

\end{enumerate}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item The keys are kept in the Steward’s room upon a nail. No key goes out without a figure, an hour and a hand entered against it. A key that goes out and comes back with the hour unentered is a key that has been out too long, whether or not the spring was drawn.

\end{enumerate}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item A key is carried in a wool sleeve, never bare against the stone. The wool is not entered and does not belong to the account.

\end{enumerate}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Margin:} The ground gives back more than it takes, as the article says. I have watched the level in the second spring fall a hand’s breadth through a dry winter and come back in the thaw. I have entered neither level. The ordinance has no column for a level, and a clerk who makes a column has begun to write a doctrine, and doctrines get copied.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Margin, in a second and narrower hand:} The fifth spring was sealed in Y.H. 618 and the keeper of it was hanged for drawing without a key. The roll gives the office and not the name. I have copied the year into the margin and left the article as it stands, which names neither the spring nor the man.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Margin:} A reeve come up from the Fenmarch says the spring sealed in Y.H. 618 is not under the Keel at all but under the Empty Cantons, and that the Court’s survey sets it twenty leagues from this room so that no collector need walk the south road. I have set his saying beside the figure and joined neither. A man who joins the two has drawn a map, and I have no licence to draw one.\end{quote}

\subsection*{II. Of the drawing and the key}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item Drawing from a spring without a keeper’s key forbidden. Drawing from the Hearth without a keeper’s key forbidden. The Hearth-fire stands behind a grating of cold iron; no priest has ever been permitted to touch it; even the Kept are not asked to stand near it.

\end{enumerate}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item Where the drawing is lawful, the Warm taken is booked in embers at five marks the ember, and the level of the spring is not entered. Where the drawing is unlawful, the key is withheld and the draw is entered as taken, which is the same figure with a different hand beside it.

\end{enumerate}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item A keeper who draws without authorisation is corrected. The correction entered in Y.H. 618 was a hanging, and no correction of that kind has been entered since. The account of that keeper stands open and is carried forward.

\end{enumerate}

Offence — As entered — Correction\par

Drawing without a key — The draw entered as taken — The key withheld; account carried forward\par

A key out beyond the hour — The nail noted empty — No second key cut\par

A key laid bare against the stone — Not entered — Nothing\par

A level falling through a dry winter — Not entered — A mark in the margin, which is not a figure\par

The name of the keeper corrected in Y.H. 618 — The office, not the name — Carried forward\par

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Margin:} I have carried one keeper’s account forward for eleven years. Nobody has come to close it and I have not closed it. A name carried forward is a different weight from a name bought, though the hand that writes them is the same.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Margin, in a leaning hand with a little gold in it, a factor’s from Greybank:} Against \emph{was hanged}, set \emph{was corrected in the ordinary manner}. Both stand. A phrase with nobody in it costs less to copy, and the factor does not have to carry the key back to the passage at the end of the day.\end{quote}

\subsection*{III. Of who may stand near}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item No priest touches the grating. A keeper of the third watch reads through the bars and the keepers answer; what is answered through the bars is not entered. The Weighing is lit by the fire behind them, and the figure read in that light is one in twelve, as the notice says. There is no other figure in the Hall.

\end{enumerate}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item The Kept are held near the fire and are not asked to stand before it. Fewer than twenty, three hundred measures apiece, and spoken of with pity. The pity is entered nowhere.

\end{enumerate}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Margin:} One of the Kept passed the door while I was entering a key and did not turn toward the fire. A clerk come up from Slate Row wrote \emph{no vacancy in the roll} against the space where it stood. He had looked at the space and put a figure there. I have not rubbed his figure out and I have not turned the Kept toward the fire.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Margin:} A keeper of the third watch told me the bars are cold on the fire side and warm on the room side, which is the order of things turned about. I have not put it in an article. An article has no room for a thing a man notices at three in the morning.\end{quote}

\subsection*{IV. Of the keeping of the roll}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item The key-slate is kept in the Steward’s room and is not shown to a household. The nail is not covered and is not explained. Where a keeper dies, the key is hung back upon the nail before the name is spoken in the room.

\end{enumerate}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item An account is never closed; it is only carried forward. A spring sealed is not called ended. A key lost is not called given.

\end{enumerate}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Margin:} There are nine keys on the nail and I have counted them every morning for six years without once writing the count down. A count I write becomes a figure and a figure can be carried off in a cuff and entered at the next crossing. The nail keeps its own.\end{quote}

\subsection*{The form of a key-receipt}

\emph{Set out at the end of Title the Eighth. I have copied it with the blanks as they stand. In six years nobody has filled the last line in the hand the Steward requires.}

\begin{quote}\itshape Entered this day, being ---day of -------, in the year of the Hearth ------, the key to the ------- spring taken from the nail at the ------- hour by ----------------------, for ----------------------, and returned at the ------- hour, the level not entered; the hand that carries not the hand that writes. Taken by ----------------------, who is not the man who keeps the nail.\end{quote}

\subsection*{The verse the tellers say in the passage}

\emph{Said low between the Steward’s room and the Hall, while the key is still in the wool. Never while the slate lies open on the desk. The last line is said by all.}

\begin{quote}\itshape Four stand open and five stand shut,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and nine are told upon the slate;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape a key goes out and a key comes in,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the level is not entered.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape The fire is barred and the bar is cold\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape to the hand that has not kept the watch;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape a keeper drew and the roll kept still,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the man went out without a name.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Wool to the hand and iron to the ring,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape a nail with nine and a slate with one;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape what the spring gives back the spring remembers,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the account stands where the key stood.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{In the narrow upright hand, against the first line:} Nine wells: five sealed, four current. \emph{In mine:} He has put a figure where I put a count. A count of springs is a thing a man can say in the dark; a figure is a thing he can hand to another man in the light. I have left both.\end{quote}

\subsection*{What the two borrowed hands did}

The College clerk came down from Slate Row with a cuff gone soft from washing and ink in two fingers. Against article one he struck \emph{the ground gives back more than it takes} and set \emph{a measure is drawn and recorded} above it, which is true of every spring and therefore of none. I put the words back underneath. Take the giving out of a spring and there is nobody left to ask what it gave, and the question comes in the end, always in the passage, always after the key is back on the nail.

The other hand is the factor’s, leaning and a little gold. He set \emph{was corrected in the ordinary manner} above the hanging and underlined it twice. Both stand. The roll gives the office and not the name, and a correction with nobody in it is the kind the Court has always liked best.

\subsection*{At the head and in the gutter}

The tallow at the head is off the lamp I keep low so that a man speaking at the slate cannot see me writing down the hour. The warm-stone dust in the gutter came off a stone a keeper carried in from the passage; warm-stone holds heat longer than anything else in Sarn and gives none of it back to the paper. The green at the fold is a stain off the lip of the second spring, which I touched with a wet finger while the key was out. It comes back every damp month, which is more than the level does. The scratch in the lower margin is the key itself, laid there while I counted the nails on the frame and did not look at the slate; it is the length of a key and is not an entry. The iron-gall is in two fingers and will not come out, which is how the Steward knows I have copied a thing before he asks. The tide-line along the foot comes up from the sealed-file room, which is colder than the rest of the Hearthseat. There is no Last Day in this room. The key hangs on the nail and the nail is not swept.

\subsection*{At the foot, in a hand nobody will own}

\begin{quote}\itshape The spring keeps its level. The nail keeps its key. The roll keeps the office, and the man who held it is carried forward.\end{quote}

I asked a keeper of the third watch, a factor come up from Greybank, and a woman who brought a cup of water from one of the open springs, and had three answers and no hand, as I have had before. I have left the line where it was written.

The leaf goes back under the key-slate. Tomorrow a key will go out in a wool sleeve and come back before the hour, and I shall enter the hour and not the level, and put the verbs back where another hand has struck them out. The figure on the notice is one in twelve, and there is no other figure in this room.

\clearpage\phantomsection\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{The Kneading Song, Being the Working-Song of the Clay Yard at Low Kiln, Sung Over the Lump on the Beating-Bench Before It Goes to the Wheel, with the Thumps Counted, the Fourth Kept as the Turning of the Lump, the Hidden Pocket Pressed Out, a Kiln-Master’s Ruling in Broad Charcoal, a Factor’s Clerk’s Figures in the Narrow Upright Hand, a Gloss from a Woman of the Firing Work, and One Line at the Foot in a Hand Nobody Will Own}
\CRsheetheading{The Kneading Song, Being the Working-Song of the Clay Yard at Low Kiln, Sung Over the Lump on the Beating-Bench Before It Goes to the Wheel, with the Thumps Counted, the Fourth Kept as the Turning of the Lump, the Hidden Pocket Pressed Out, a Kiln-Master’s Ruling in Broad Charcoal, a Factor’s Clerk’s Figures in the Narrow Upright Hand, a Gloss from a Woman of the Firing Work, and One Line at the Foot in a Hand Nobody Will Own}
{\centering\FellFont\itshape\footnotesize\color{faded} A worker’s song in the low hard speech of the yard, said down into the lump and not across the bench; the verses counted in thumps of the heel going into the clay, with the fourth kept as the turning of the lump and not entered, and the little room of air pressed shut before the lump goes to the wheel; the manner of the working in the writer’s own charcoal, the kiln-master’s ruling in broad charcoal, a factor’s clerk’s figures standing above in Ledgerhand, a gloss pressed into the margin by a woman of the firing work, and one line at the foot in a hand nobody will claim · Sung over the beating-bench two doors below the slip pits in the Clay Yard at Low Kiln of Sill and set down in Smoke of Y.H. 813, the second firing-month, by a woman who has worked the lump at that bench for twelve seasons and knows a hollow by the sound of the heel going in and not by any word spoken over it; written in charcoal thinned with slip-water on the back of a working-docket spoiled by a wet thumb, folded twice and tied with a curl of eel-sinew against the dust, carried up the Clay Road with a consignment of coarse tile and copied forward at Greybank in Ilmen of Y.H. 814 onto the back of a factor’s voided weigh-slip. It survives with a clay thumb worked into the grain at the head, a pale tideline from the Slip Brook along the gutter that has taken the edge off one word of the fifth verse, a curl of eel-sinew caught across the second leaf, a grey flake from the bench pressed in the fold, a hair from a horse’s forelock caught where the docket lay in the cart, a dark pinprick where a wire cut through the fourth verse and showed the speck the song is about, a green bead of lead glaze pressed into the lower corner by a girl with sweetness at one mouth-corner, a sour small-ale ring at the foot, a grey Ash print along the outer fold that nobody will own, the kiln-master’s broad ruling, the clerk’s figures standing above, the firing woman’s gloss in the margin, and the one line at the foot\par}\medskip
I work the lump at the beating-bench two doors below the slip pits, twelve seasons at it. A lump comes off the bank with a face as smooth as a loaf and something shut up inside it that has no name in the yard. We call it the little room. You drive it out with the heel before it goes to the wheel, because the wheel will not find it and the fire will. A pot with a room left in it goes into the kiln whole and comes out with a seam you can lay your thumb in, and nobody asks whose hand let the room stay.

A man came up from Greybank with a soft cuff and ink settled in two fingers of it and stood at the bench end asking what we said at the work. I told him. He wrote it down before I had finished, with the doing taken out and a figure put where a place should stand, and went off up the Clay Road with his boots clean. So I have set the words down as we say them, to the lump and not to the women beside the bench, and put the verbs back where he took them out.

The clay at the head is mine. I held the docket down with the hand I work with and did not know I had marked it. Clay goes into the grain and no washing takes it out, which is why we sign with it here and not with ink.

\subsection*{How it is worked}

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item Set the lump on the round the last one left. A bench wiped clean is a bench with no memory, and the first lump off a clean bench hides its room where the hand does not look.

\item Beat with the heel, not the fist. A fist leaves a hard place that throws the wheel crooked; the heel shuts the room without marking the face.

\item Listen as you go. A lump that answers solid has no room in it; one that answers hollow gives back a sound like a cup with a hair in it, and the hand goes back to where the sound came from.

\item Turn after three thumps and look at the cut face. The room shows as a dark pinprick no bigger than a flea, and a pinprick left in the clay is a pot with a seam two months hence.

\item Press it shut with the thumb. Do not cut it out. Clay taken out will not marry to the clay about it, and the fire finds the place you made as surely as the room you left.

\item Knuckle a worked lump before it goes up. A whole one answers full; one with a room still in it gives back flat. The wheel takes both and does not say which was which, so the knuckle has to say it first.

\item Count the thumps going in, never the pots coming down off the rack. A count coming down is a count of pots, which a clerk can enter and nobody wants. The fourth is the turning, and a turning is not a thump.

\item Do not sing it on an Account-day. The bell goes four, four and a gap, and the gap is the turning; a working-song set against it comes home wrong in the wrist.

\item The last part is kept back, for when the kiln-master has gone up the terrace and the man with the soft cuff has gone back over the north bridge and the bench can hear itself again.

\end{itemize}

\subsection*{The song}

\emph{Said low into the lump, with the heel flat. One verse to three thumps going in. The fourth is the turning of the lump and is not said aloud. The refrain goes into the bench and not across the yard; said to a person it becomes an account, and there is enough account at the Cross without bringing it to the slip pits.}

\begin{quote}\itshape The lump comes down from the bank with a face like bread,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape smooth as a loaf and as quiet under the hand;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape but there’s a little room shut up in the middle of it\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape that the wheel won’t find and the fire will.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Thump it and turn it, three to the lump,}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{and the fourth is the turning no heel let fall;}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{the room lies where the knuckle can’t come at it,}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{and the fire finds out what the hand let go.}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Beat with the heel and not with the fist;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape a fist leaves a hard place the wheel will remember,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and a crooked wall comes up round a hard place\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and opens at the rim when the kiln takes it.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Thump it and turn it, three to the lump,}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{and the fourth is the turning no heel let fall;}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{the room lies where the knuckle can’t come at it,}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{and the fire finds out what the hand let go.}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape A solid lump answers back and the note goes through;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape one with a room in it gives back small and flat,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape like a cup with a hair in it, like a pot set down wrong ---\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the bench keeps both sounds and tells neither.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Thump it and turn it, three to the lump,}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{and the fourth is the turning no heel let fall;}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{the room lies where the knuckle can’t come at it,}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{and the fire finds out what the hand let go.}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Turn it after three and look at the cut face;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the room shows dark where the wire went through,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape a speck the width of a flea, and a flea’s worth of air\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape is a seam you can lay a thumb in come Smoke.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Thump it and turn it, three to the lump,}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{and the fourth is the turning no heel let fall;}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{the room lies where the knuckle can’t come at it,}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{and the fire finds out what the hand let go.}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape One in twelve is printed and read twice at the Cross,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape once for the moot and once for them that came late;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the bell goes four, four and a gap, and the gap is the turn,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the figure you heard is not the figure they paid.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Thump it and turn it, three to the lump,}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{and the fourth is the turning no heel let fall;}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{the room lies where the knuckle can’t come at it,}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{and the fire finds out what the hand let go.}\end{quote}

There is a space before the last refrain in the singing, the length of a hand laid flat on the lump where you feel for the room before the heel comes down. I have left it on the docket. A clerk put a round nought in it once, which is a thing you can hold up and look at; a hand laid flat is not.

\subsection*{The part they keep back}

\emph{Not said while the kiln-master stands at the bench end, and not while a man with a satchel is on the boards. Said to the bench and not across the yard.}

\begin{quote}\itshape There was a lump one Ember went up with its room\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and came back a pot with a seam down the side;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the rack set it by the wall with the crack showing\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and nobody said whose heel had let it stand.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape We go round the fourth with the lump the way a house goes round\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape what it will not sweep. The clerk put a nought where it turned;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape a nought is a figure and travels up the road,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and a turning is a place and stays where the clay put it.\end{quote}

There is no verse after it; the next thing is the heel going back into the lump, which has never wanted one.

\subsection*{What the kiln-master ruled}

He came down off the terrace on the wrong wind with the sweet edge of the glaze at one corner of his mouth and read the docket with one eye on the wheel-shed. Against \emph{the room lies where the knuckle can’t come at it} he wrote in broad charcoal: \emph{Air inclusion to be proved at the wheel. Sound bodies only to the firing. No loss arises.} He underlined it twice. Against \emph{the fourth is the turning} he set: \emph{Turning is not a count. Nothing enters.} He did not look at the bench while he wrote.

Underneath, in mine: he is right about the count and wrong about the loss. A turning is not a thump, but it is where the hand finds what would otherwise go up inside a pot, and a room shut in the clay is not nothing because it cannot be entered. He reads with one eye on the kiln, as a man does who has never stood at a bench and listened to a lump answer back.

\subsection*{What the factor’s clerk did}

The factor’s clerk borrowed the leaf at Greybank on the morning the tile was weighed, with his cuff gone soft from washing and ink sitting in two fingers of it. He took the verbs out and set his words above mine, the way a newer repair lies over an older one on a pot, and I have left his hand standing and put ours underneath.

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item At \emph{one with a room in it gives back small and flat} he wrote \emph{vessel unsound; not a chargeable defect}, and underlined it twice. He thinks a flat note is a pot that has reached its term. At this bench a flat note is a room the heel missed and the bench was not told about.

\item At \emph{the fire finds out what the hand let go} he wrote \emph{loss at firing, unascertained}, which takes the hand out and leaves the fire standing with nothing to find.

\item At \emph{the room shows dark where the wire went through} he wrote \emph{inclusion, sampled}, and set a figure against it. A speck in a lump is not a sample and has never had a value, which is why the yard asks the pot and not the clerk what a room cost.

\item At \emph{one in twelve is printed and read twice} he wrote \emph{deduction current, one part in twelve; twice read}, and set the printed figure above it. He has entered the number that was read and not the number that was paid, which is the whole distance between a cuff and a wrist.

\item At the three thumps he wrote \emph{three struck, fourth nil}. The fourth is not nil. It is the turning of the lump, which a man can carry away in a figure and a woman cannot.

\item Where I had left the space he put a round nought and wrote \emph{vacancy} beneath it. A nought is a number and travels. A hand laid flat on a lump is a place, and stays where it was put.

\end{itemize}

\subsection*{What a woman of the firing work put in the margin}

The thick charcoal belongs to a woman who has carried lumps from this bench to the wheel since before the Glaze Wars and has had the pale line at the gum these six years. I have copied it as it stands, without making the hands agree.

At \emph{the rack set it by the wall with the crack showing}: \emph{There has been a seam down every firing since I came to this yard. I have asked the pot what it cost and the pot has told me, which is more than the slate has ever done. I have not told whose heel let the room stand, and I have not set the seam on a slate, which is a thing I will answer for somewhere else.}

At \emph{turn it after three and look at the cut face}: \emph{A girl turned hers only at the end and sent up six lumps in one morning. Three went flat and the other three went whole, and nobody could say which hand made the difference, least of all hers. She still works at that bench. I have not taught her to turn, and the bench has not either.}

\subsection*{At the head and in the gutter}

The clay thumb at the head is mine and has gone into the grain; nothing here is gathered and burnt on a Last Day, so the grey goes into the next season under the dust-cloth. The gutter-line came out of the Slip Brook and has taken the edge off one word of the fifth verse; I have not written it back. The curl of eel-sinew across the second leaf came off the cutting-thread and I have left it over the word it landed on. The grey flake in the fold came off the round under the lump and is lighter in the hand than a good flake, which is the lesson and no use to a clerk. The hair came off a carter’s horse going up the Clay Road; it is the only part of this docket that has walked the road on its own. The pinprick through the fourth verse is where a wire went through the leaf and showed a dark speck where the verse speaks of one; I have not widened it, because a wire leaves the hole and a clerk leaves the nought, and neither is the room in the clay. The green bead came off a girl with sweetness at her mouth who touched the leaf and went back up the terrace; I have not washed it. The sour ring is small ale set down at the first verse and taken up at the last, gone the colour of the bench it stood on. The grey along the outer fold came off a cuff laid where no cuff has business lying on a bench. Nobody will own it.

\subsection*{At the foot, in a hand nobody will own}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{The bench keeps the round. The lump keeps the room.}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{The pot goes up the road with the seam in its side.}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{The slate keeps neither, and goes up the road.}\end{quote}

I asked the woman of the firing work, the kiln-master, and a carter waiting with his horse at the yard gate, and had three answers and no hand. I have left the lines where they were written.

The docket goes back under the beating-bench. Tomorrow a lump will come down with a face like bread, three thumps will go into it and the fourth be the turning where no heel fell, and if the clerk comes again he may have the nought. He cannot have the hand laid flat, because it is a place, and he has no word for a place that stays where the clay put it.

\clearpage\phantomsection\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{The Knot Not Untied, Being a Letter from Wenna at the Standing Post to Her Brother Holl at Mud End, Concerning a Stand That Ended Otherwise, a Peat Block Kept Loose Against the Niche, a Term of Bought Breath Owed at the Line, and the Bringing Back of Salt; with the Answer Written Along the Margin on the Return of the Peat Cart, a Factor’s Clerk’s Correction on the Back, and a Song Said to the Boards}
\CRsheetheading{The Knot Not Untied, Being a Letter from Wenna at the Standing Post to Her Brother Holl at Mud End, Concerning a Stand That Ended Otherwise, a Peat Block Kept Loose Against the Niche, a Term of Bought Breath Owed at the Line, and the Bringing Back of Salt; with the Answer Written Along the Margin on the Return of the Peat Cart, a Factor’s Clerk’s Correction on the Back, and a Song Said to the Boards}
{\centering\FellFont\itshape\footnotesize\color{faded} A private letter on the back of a Sill weigh-slip read twice and not paid, folded small and lashed with eel-sinew, sent down the mud road in a peat cart and handed back up by the same cart three mornings later; the writer’s words in a reed-pen over a washed-out figure, the answer in a hard salt-stiff hand along the margin, a knot tied through a hole where a word would not come, a factor’s clerk’s correction on the back in Ledgerhand, and one line at the foot in a hand nobody will own · Written at the Standing Post in the last tend of Seed, Y.H. 813, by Wenna, a board-woman of the Post who lays the peat blocks in the niche at the foot of the reeve’s stone, to her brother Holl, who keeps the eel baskets at the landing at Mud End, three leagues downriver of Sill. Carried down the mud road under a carter’s boot and returned three mornings later with the answer in the margin and a little salt gone damp in the fold; borrowed at Greybank by a clerk of the factor who set his correction on the back, and kept since under the loose board in a folded reed wrapper with the Post’s sayings and the dry stick of market rates. It survives with a peat thumb ground into the head, a bog-water tideline that has taken two words off the second page, dried eel slime at the fore-edge, a fish-hook nick, a pale round place where a collector’s cuff was laid, grey Ash pressed into the outer fold which the writer did not put there and has not swept, a knot of grey wool tied through a hole in the first page which she will not untie, and one line at the foot that has never been claimed\par}\medskip
To Holl at Mud End, who keeps the eel baskets by the landing and has not written in two tend. From Wenna at the Post, who lays the peat blocks in the niche and does not say whose shape they are.

I write on the back of a weigh-slip from Sill. It came up the mud road under a carter’s boot and was given to me for nothing because the figure on it had been read twice and was not the figure paid. Paper from Sill is too clean for this country; it takes the peat badly. I have gone over every second word with the stub of a reed-pen and tied a knot in the margin where the word would not come. Fen Cant is not written and never will be. A word set down in the south’s letters is a word a man can carry off in a cuff and read aloud to people who have never stood in water to their calf.

Nib stood on the boards in the last tend of Silt and came back, and I laid a block for him in the niche. It is the shape of where he stood and not the shape of him, and I have never once mistaken the one for the other. Our father stood in the year of the Long Cold and did not come back, and there is no block for him and never will be, because the niche takes only a stand that ends with a man walking back. I have kept a dry block in my hut against the day somebody tells me different. It has gone hard at one corner. I have not shaped it.

You were away when she tied the knot. Six marks and a knot for a season of bought breath, she told the eel-trader, and he wrote it on the back of his hand because he could not write at all. The season is out. The knot is not untied. I have kept it in the fold of my apron two winters and taken it out on the first morning of every tend to see that the wool has not gone soft on me, and put it back. I do not know whose hand I would be undoing if I undid it. That is the asking I have written this for.

\subsection*{What went down and what came back by the peat cart}

\emph{Set down on the slip as the cart went down on Fifthday and written up again on the return on Eighthday. The left is what I sent; the right is what came back. Where a thing was not sent I have left the place as a place and not put a nought in it.}

Went down in the cart — Came back on Eighthday\par

A dry block for the niche, wrapped in reed — The same block, carried back; wet at one corner\par

A letter on a Sill weigh-slip — The same slip, with an answer in the margin\par

Six marks for the season, tied in a fold of apron — Four marks, and a word about the other two\par

Nothing — A little salt, gone damp in the fold of the slip\par

A word for our mother — A word about the knot, which is not the same word\par

A place where the fifth mark would stand — The place still standing\par

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{In the margin, small, in mine:} The cart went down with six and came back with four. He has not stolen the two. He has left them standing on the other side of the water, where I cannot put my hand on them. A mark left standing is not a mark paid, but it is also not a mark that has gone into anybody’s pocket, and I have set both readings here.\end{quote}

The reeve’s stone has no name cut into it and has never counted a man. Nib’s block went in because Nib walked back. There is a woman at the Post who says a block is not the man and a block is not the shape, and that the stone keeps neither; she has said it so often that the young say it before her, which is how a saying starts to be a law. I did not ask her about our father. I asked the stone, and the stone kept its own counsel, as it does.

\subsection*{The ask}

Come back before the Reed. The young cut their first bundles in the dark and come back wet or dry, and if the bundle comes back wet they go again, and nobody tells them why. I want you standing at the end of the boards where I can see you put your foot where the others went, and I will not point to the board. If you come back after the Reed I shall not be at the landing and shall not send the block up again.

Bring the salt if you can carry it; salt is four marks up here and three at Greybank, and the extra mark is the road and nobody calls it a tax. Do not come by the smuggler’s path. A man comes back that way with wet boots and no figure, which is a cheap way to travel and a dear way to arrive. The winter way will not bear a cart yet, and no reeve will stand on it, which is the only honest thing I know about that way.

Untie the knot yourself if you are coming. Do not send it back tied and do not send me the marks in place of the hand. I have kept two winters of a thing that belonged to her hand, and I want the undoing to be done by the person it was tied for, so that the wool has been in somebody’s fingers who remembers why it was tied.

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{At the foot of the page, in a second hand, hard and salt-stiff, written small along the margin where the peat would not take a full line:} I have sent four marks and the salt is damp because the sacks at the landing are not what they were. The other two I have not got. I have kept them where a man keeps a thing he owes and cannot pay, which is in front of his eyes and not in his pocket. I am not coming before the Reed. That is not a refusal and I will not have you read it as one. Send me the knot and I will send it back tied the way she tied it, which I have not forgotten though I never asked her to show me. A thing tied by her hand and untied by mine would be two hands and no debt, and I do not know a man who can live in that country. Holl.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Underneath, in mine, written on the white of the slip where the figure had been read twice:} He has not said he will come after the Reed, and I have not asked him a second time. Four marks stand on one side of the water and two stand on the other and the knot stays in my apron. I have taken it out to look at it this morning and put it back. The block is still hard at one corner.\end{quote}

\subsection*{The song said to the boards}

\emph{Said low through the nose while the blocks are laid, never looking at the stone and never while a reeve is standing within hearing of the second part. The last line is said to the water.}

\begin{quote}\itshape Four for the stand and one for the slack,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the block goes in where the man came back;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the reed says wet and the reeve says wait,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and what was lent goes back to the water.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Six for the breath and a knot in the wool,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the knot keeps the term and the term keeps the hole;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape two marks stand over and two marks stay,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the hand that tied is the hand gone away.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Salt comes up and the peat goes down,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the cart keeps the boot and the mud keeps the man;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape we do not shape it and we do not say,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the stone keeps the place where the shape would lie.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{In the margin:} He will say the second part is a complaint about the Court. It is a complaint about a knot. I have let him say what he pleases and tied another knot in the margin where the word should be. There is a place where the fifth stand would go and I have not put a block in it and have not called it a fifth.\end{quote}

\subsection*{What the factor’s clerk did}

A clerk of the factor at Greybank borrowed the slip when the eel-trader carried it on to the quay, being a man who cannot leave a written thing alone. He writes in the narrow upright hand they teach, with the verbs taken out and everything done to the paper.
