Where I wrote \emph{I laid a block for Nib}, he set \emph{a block was entered} above it, and Nib went out of the sentence as though a man could be carried off in the fold of a weigh-slip. Where I wrote \emph{the knot stays in my apron}, he set \emph{the obligation remains current}. Against the two marks standing on the far side of the water he wrote \emph{outstanding}, which is a word with a cuff on it. He put a round nought in the place I had left for the fifth stand and wrote \emph{vacancy} beside it.

I have put my words back underneath and left his above. He takes the verbs out because a thing always true has no need of anybody in it. I put them in because a woman standing in water to her calf wants to know whose hand tied the wool and whose hand has not come back to undo it. His nought has outlasted the place it was meant to cover, which is his trade and not mine. The nought has kept better than the two marks. That is the whole of what is wrong with it.

\subsection*{At the head and in the gutter}

The peat at the head is mine; I held the slip down on the boards in a wind off the bog and did not know I had marked it. Peat goes into the grain and will not come out, which is why we sign with it. The tideline has taken two words clean off the second page and I have not written them back, because a letter with two words gone is a letter said slowly, which is how all of ours are said. The eel slime at the fore-edge came off the hand that carried the creel down to the landing; the hook nick came off a man paying for six eels and charged for five, or the other way, which he never settled and I never entered. The pale round place is where a collector’s cuff was laid while I was telling a girl to eat and she would not; it is not a wound and there is no blood in it, and I have covered it with the fold and written nothing over it. The grey along the outer fold is not mine and not the factor’s. I have not swept it. There is no Last Day at the Post and nothing under a loose board gets burnt in the morning.

\subsection*{At the foot, in a hand nobody will own}

\begin{quote}\itshape A block is the shape of a place where a man stood. A knot is the shape of a breath somebody bought. The stone and the wool keep both, and neither of them knows what it cost.\end{quote}

I asked a reeve, an eel-trader come up from the landing, and a woman whose term is not out, and had three answers and no hand. I have left the line where it was written.

The slip goes back into the reed wrapper under the loose board with the sayings and the dry stick. Tomorrow the carts go east with peat and come back with salt, and four marks will stand on one side of the water and two on the other and I shall not add them. If he comes after the Reed I shall be at the landing and shall not point to the board he is to stand on. The knot stays in my apron until a hand comes for it that I can recognise.

\clearpage\phantomsection\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{The Knotted Answer, Being the Order of the Return as the Reed-Midwives Say It Face Down in the Peat, with the Child Named Before the Collector Comes, the Answer Tied in Grey Wool, a Factor’s Clerk’s Correction, and a Line at the Foot Nobody Will Own}
\CRsheetheading{The Knotted Answer, Being the Order of the Return as the Reed-Midwives Say It Face Down in the Peat, with the Child Named Before the Collector Comes, the Answer Tied in Grey Wool, a Factor’s Clerk’s Correction, and a Line at the Foot Nobody Will Own}
{\centering\FellFont\itshape\footnotesize\color{faded} A litany of the Return said face down on the peat-dry at the Reed Cut, the mud-wife saying it to the ground and the answer tied in knots instead of spoken; set down in Grathic letters learned off an eel-trader, though Fen Cant is not written, the sayings in the thick half-sung speech of the marsh with the ends bitten off, the rubrics of the dry, seven stations and their knot, a bog-tally of names said into the ground before the collector came, one correction in the narrow upright Ledgerhand of a factor’s clerk come out from Greybank, an eel-trader’s margin, and a line struck through and written again very small underneath in a hand that has never come forward · Written in Reed of Y.H. 812, the Thin Year, at the peat-dry beside the Reed Cut by Lett Peat, a reed-midwife of the east marsh, who signs the leaf with a knot in grey wool and not with a name, in charcoal on the back of a bog-tally spoiled by a wet figure; folded into oiled sacking with a knot-stick shut in the crease and kept in the thatch of the drying shed, taken out only when a child is born before the collector’s boat is seen. Borrowed in Ilmen of Y.H. 813 by a clerk of the factor’s house come out from Greybank to count the winter thin returns, who set his hand above hers; read over by an eel-trader out of Reedholt, who put four lines in the margin in a leaning hand gone soft with eel slime. It survives with peat worked into the grain at the head in a brown thumb, a press of wet sedge across the first leaf, a bog-water tideline along the gutter, the loan-knot tied through a hole in the first leaf, a horn-shaving from the count-stick in the second crease, a fish-hook nick, an Ash print off the cuff of a man who sells it, a ring of small ale, and the clerk’s correction standing above the words it corrects\par}\medskip
I am a reed-midwife of the east marsh and I have never said this litany standing up. It is said face down, with the cheek in the peat and the mouth shut against the smell of it, because a thing said into the air goes up and gets entered somewhere, and a thing said into the ground stays where the child is. Fen Cant is not written. It is carried in the mouth, cut on sticks and tied in knots; a notch is still there when the stick is wet, which is more than can be said for the paper they use at Greybank. I learned my letters off an eel-trader and write them with the ends bitten off, the way we speak them and the way the south says we cannot read.

What cannot be written is tied. I have tied the answer in grey wool at every station, and the cord goes back into the thatch with the leaf, and a clerk from Greybank who came to count the winter thin returns has set his hand above mine in narrow upright letters. I have left his hand there and my knots underneath it, the way water leaves the print under the boot. There is no name on this leaf. A name written is a name entered; I have signed with a knot, which he held in his fingers and did not ask me about.

\subsection*{The manner of it, written small at the head}

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item Say it at first grey, face down, before the collector’s boat is seen on the cut. A child named after the boat has two names and only one of them ours.

\item Say it to the peat, then to the water in the prints of your knees, then to the ground beside the hut. Do not say it looking at the child; said looking at a person, it becomes a bargain, and the child cannot keep one.

\item The answer is not spoken. It is tied. Every station has its knot, and a knot tied in the dark is still tied in the morning, which is more than can be said for a word.

\item Say the reed-name three times: once for the mother, once for the child that cannot say it, once for the mud. Written once, it belongs to the clerk.

\item If they come before the third saying, stop. Give them the number and keep the word. Begin again when the boat is gone.

\item If an officer takes the cord, give him the leaf and keep the cord. He can enter a leaf. He cannot enter a knot without taking it apart, and a knot taken apart is no longer a knot.

\end{itemize}

\subsection*{The litany}

\emph{I say it into the peat. There is nobody present to answer. The answer is made with the hands after every station: grey wool, two turns, a slip. I have set down what each knot is called, which is not what the clerk entered.}

\subsection*{I. Of the ground that is lent}

\begin{quote}\itshape Dry ground is borrowed.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape The house stands on posts so the loan can be called\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape without taking the house with it.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Say it to the post. It has stood longer than any of us\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and never counted a man.\end{quote}

\emph{The answer is tied: the loan-knot, two turns and a slip. It is untied when the water gives the ground back, which it never does.}

\subsection*{II. Of the Marsh Mother}

\begin{quote}\itshape She keeps it warm down there and hands it back\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape to whoever can reach it.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape She has no keys, no slate, no figure.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape A priest come up from Greybank told me she was the Hearth\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape under a Fen name. The Hearth has a grate.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Ours has a skin of water and moves when it is walked on.\end{quote}

\emph{The answer is tied: the warm-knot. The warm place where a cow stood moves by the next tend, and the cow with it. I have kept the knot and not the place.}

\subsection*{III. Of what goes in}

\begin{quote}\itshape What goes into the mud is kept.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape A body goes out on a raft into the reedbed\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and nobody fetches it back.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape The mud keeps what it wants, which is not always\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the whole of a person. We have never asked for the rest.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Say it to the water under the water.\end{quote}

\emph{The answer is tied: the keeping-knot. It is the knot we tie when a thing is owed and untie when it is paid. This one is not untied. There is nobody to pay.}

\subsection*{IV. Of the iron}

\begin{quote}\itshape Cold iron takes. The mud takes.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape One of them writes it down.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape The tube does not keep. It opens a way and leaves it open.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape A pale round place shows on the arm all winter.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape The mud leaves nothing an officer can enter.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Do not ask which is kinder. A man who asks that\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape wants a kind way to be emptied.\end{quote}

\emph{The answer is tied: the taking-knot. It has the same two turns as the loan-knot and is tied on the other end of the cord. I have stood at both and cannot tell them apart with my eyes shut, which is the whole difficulty.}

\subsection*{V. Of the figure}

\begin{quote}\itshape One in twelve, as the notice says. Printed. Read twice.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Twelve bits to the mark, and a crown will not change here.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape A thin return is a return. Ask for more\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and you get a colder one.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape We do not say what a whole return costs.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape A man who buys one has paid somebody,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and here we know who, because he paid here.\end{quote}

\emph{Here I tied two knots, one for the figure on the notice and one for the other figure, and set them side by side on the cord. The clerk has put his small stop above the first. Both knots stand.}

\subsection*{VI. Of the name}

\begin{quote}\itshape Say the name three times and the mud will know it.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Once for the mother, once for the child that cannot say it,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape once for the ground beside the hut.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape If they come before the name is given,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape give them the number and keep the word.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape A name said at home is a door.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape A number is a hole in the wall.\end{quote}

\emph{The answer is tied: the word-knot. There is ground between here and Grath with doorways in it and no smoke. A doorway is built for coming back through. We do not say who went, or what hung in the bare clay above the lintel; a thing you can name is a thing the Court can figure.}

\subsection*{VII. Of the coming back}

\begin{quote}\itshape Come back as you can. The mud does not ask who you were.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape It keeps the shape of where you stood\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and cannot tell you whose it was.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape If you have no name, leave the place where the name would stand\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and let the water stand in it.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Say it to the ground. Said looking at a person,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape it becomes a bargain.\end{quote}

\emph{The answer is tied: the coming-back knot. I tie it with the ends left long so the child can find it later. I have never seen a child find one, and I tie them long all the same.}

\emph{Here the cord has a loop with no knot in it. It is not a knot forgotten and not a vacancy. It is the loop for them that came back into a house that did not name them in time, and nobody has tied it. I have left the loop the length it is.}

\subsection*{The cord, as this dry keeps it}

\emph{A figure that comes into the marsh in a coat goes out again in a thin return and leaves nothing in the thatch. These are the names said into the ground before the boat was seen. The slate column is not mine.}

When — Child — Name said into the ground — Knot tied — What went into the slate\par

Reed 6 — a girl of the east cut — said three times, into the door-hole — word-knot — number only; the word kept\par

Reed 9 — a boy of the upper board — not said; his mother was down with the fever — loop left untied — thin, from the district pot\par

Reed 11 — a bought breath’s child — said twice; the third said for her by the woman who held her — loan-knot — nothing entered; the boat went back empty\par

Reed 14 — a child out of Reedholt — said three times and written nowhere — keeping-knot — whole, by a house upriver; the name not entered here\par

The fifth row is a space the length of a name and I have not filled it. A stick has no ear and a cord has no clerk. What is tied here goes into the thatch.

\subsection*{What the clerk did}

He came out from Greybank in Ilmen with ink in two fingers and cuffs soft from washing, to count the winter thin returns. He writes in the narrow upright hand and took the verbs out as a man takes bones out of a fish, and set figures where the knots stood.

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item At \emph{she has no keys, no slate, no figure}, he wrote: \emph{the measure is retained in the peat}. Underneath, in mine: I have put \emph{keeps} and \emph{hands back} under, because a woman standing in water to her calf wants to know who is doing the handing, and whether she will get it back.

\item At \emph{the mud keeps what it wants, which is not always the whole of a person}, he wrote: \emph{recovery not possible; account closed}. Under it: it keeps. Whether it keeps the whole of him is not a question the mud answers.

\item At \emph{cold iron takes. The mud takes. One of them writes it down}, he wrote: \emph{draw recorded; lawful extraction}. Under it: he takes and does not write; they write and do not take. I have stood at both.

\item At the figure he put a small stop in \emph{one in twelve} and wrote it again above, larger. It is the figure they like to see. The other figure is tied on the same cord and cannot be carried out in a cuff.

\item At the loop he put a round nought and wrote \emph{vacancy}. A nought is a figure and a figure travels. The loop stays where it is tied.

\item At the answer he wrote: \emph{no verbal response recorded}, the only true thing he wrote all morning and cost him nothing, because a knot has no tongue to enter.

\end{itemize}

I have put the verbs back underneath and left his hand standing above, as the water leaves the print under the boot. He takes them out because a thing always true has no need of them. I put them back because a woman face down wants to know whose hands are holding her child.

\subsection*{What the eel-trader put in the margin}

The leaning hand is Orra’s, out of Reedholt, who taught me my letters and smells of eels even when her sleeves are dry. I have copied her as she wrote it.

At the iron: “I have seen a man come up out of the black stand with his fingers the colour of old rope. He had been drawn the week before. I did not ask which took more, and have not stopped asking.”

At the name: “My mother said mine into the water and the collector came up the board an hour later. He wrote a number. She kept the word. I answer to neither at the Post.”

At the loop: “Leave it. There is a girl on the upper board who came back last winter and goes toward the water when somebody calls a name that is not hers. I have not told her which.”

At the close: “You tie more knots than any midwife. You said a knot keeps better than a clerk. Good answer, and not the whole one.”

\subsection*{At the head and in the gutter}

The brown at the head is peat worked into the grain by my own thumb; the marsh signs with a hand and not a name, which is why the clerk could not tell who wrote this even while I stood beside him. The press of sedge has made the first two words soft and I have not gone over them, because a word written soft is a word said into the ground. The tideline is bog-water that stood on the leaf two nights; the writing there has gone thin and stayed. The knot through the hole is the loan-knot and I have never untied it. The horn-shaving came off my count-stick where I used the point to open a word I could not spell. The hook nick is not mine. The grey is Ash off the cuff of a man who sells it, and there is Ash enough in this marsh without a stranger’s. The ring is small ale that stood from the first station to the seventh and was drunk by nobody, which is how ale goes at a dry when there is a thing to say and no proper word for it. There is a Last Day in the low houses and none at the peat-dry, and even here the morning comes.

\subsection*{At the foot, in a hand nobody will own}

\begin{quote}\itshape The mud keeps what it is given. It does not say whose.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape The slate enters what it is given. It does not say who gave.\end{quote}

Struck through once and written again underneath, very small, in a hand that is not mine, not the clerk’s and not Orra’s:

\begin{quote}\itshape Both keep. Only one of them is asked to answer.\end{quote}

I asked the clerk, the eel-trader, a woman of the east cut, and the man who sells the Ash, and had four answerings and no hand. I have left the line struck through and standing, the only honest way to keep a sentence you cannot sign.

The leaf and the cord go back into the thatch. Next reed-cutting a woman will lie face down before the boat comes up the cut, and I shall say the seven stations to the ground and tie the answers and leave the loop the length it is. The clerk will take the verbs out and I shall put them back. The collector will write a number he will not bring into the dry. The word will stay where it was said, in the ground beside the hut, where a doorway is built for coming back through and nobody says who went.

\clearpage\phantomsection\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{The Lament of the Pulled Bench, Being the Song the Women of the Quay Sing Over the Oars at Vhal, with the Manner of It, the Verses as the Oar-Keeper Keeps Them, the Council Clerk’s Correction Set Above, a Boat-Mother’s Gloss in Charcoal, and One Line at the Foot in a Hand Nobody Will Own}
\CRsheetheading{The Lament of the Pulled Bench, Being the Song the Women of the Quay Sing Over the Oars at Vhal, with the Manner of It, the Verses as the Oar-Keeper Keeps Them, the Council Clerk’s Correction Set Above, a Boat-Mother’s Gloss in Charcoal, and One Line at the Foot in a Hand Nobody Will Own}
{\centering\FellFont\itshape\footnotesize\color{faded} A lament of the bench-women of the Quay, set down in the Vhaleni tide-words in Grathic letters by the woman who keeps the oar-store; the verses in the thick half-sung speech of the Quay, the refrain kept by the oars, a Council clerk’s correction in the leaning hand on salt-paper gone soft with damp, a boat-mother’s gloss pressed into the margin in charcoal, and one line at the foot in a hand nobody will claim · Written at the oar-store on the Quay at Vhal in Stone of Y.H. 812, the Thin Year, by Ulla Brine, a woman of the Quay who counts the oars in at the ebb and out at the flood and mends the leather sleeves at the rowlock; set down because a clerk of the tide-tally house come to count the galley stores asked what the women sang when the boats came in off the pull, and wrote the answer down while she was still saying it, with the doing taken out and a term set where a place should stand. Written first on the back of a tide-tally spoiled by sea-water and then on folds of salt-paper stiffened with tar, sewn with eel-sinew and kept in a tarred tin under the oar rack; carried up the Salt Road at the Opening of the Slates, Ilmen 1, Y.H. 813, and copied at Greybank onto the back of a factor’s voided weigh-slip. It survives with a white salt bloom at the head, a tar thumb at the fold, a fibre of wet rope pressed into the second leaf, a brine ring gone sour at the foot, a fish-hook nick at the fore-edge, a green bead of Cliffs glass in the lower corner, a shaving of worn oar-wood laid in the fold where a sixth verse should stand, a grey Ash print along the margin that nobody will own, the Council clerk’s leaning hand going soft with the damp, the boat-mother’s charcoal gloss, and one line at the foot that has never come forward\par}\medskip
I keep the oar-store on the Quay. That is my office: to count the oars in at the ebb and out at the flood, and to see that the leather sleeves at the rowlock are mended before a boat goes down. An oar comes back with a shine on the handle where a hand has held it through a term, and I can tell a new man’s oar from an old man’s by the shine before I can tell it by the wood. The Council counts the boats. I count the oars. Nobody counts what the oar took from the man who held it, which is not the same thing as saying nobody knows.

I set this down because a clerk of the tide-tally house stood at the store with a cuff gone soft from washing and a leaf in his hand, and asked what the women sang when the boats came in off the pull, and wrote the answer down while I was still saying it, with the doing taken out and a term set where a place should stand. So I have written what we said before he came and what we said again after he had gone. His hand stands above mine and the damp is taking it, and a shaving of oar-wood lies in the fold where a sixth verse should stand. A shaving is not a figure and cannot be carried away in a cuff.

The bloom at the head is salt. I held the leaf down on the oar rack in a wind off the Sallow and did not know I had marked it. Salt goes into paper the way seven years go into a hand, and nothing takes either out.

\subsection*{How it is sung}

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item At the oar-store, over the oars as they are counted in, never aboard and never while a boat is going out. Said aboard, it becomes a prayer for a passage, and we have no prayer in this port that the Council has not entered against somebody’s term.

\item Standing, with the hand on the oar-handle before it goes to a woman’s arm. Said with a hand on a person, it becomes an argument, and there are arguments enough at the Quay without carrying one three leagues up the Salt Road.

\item To the wood and not to the company. The last word of every verse is let fall into the salt on the floor and not finished. The oars keep the refrain: one voice begins it and the rest come in on the second line.

\item Tap the oar-handle once for each stroke while the refrain is said. The tap is not a number. A clerk can carry a number off in his cuff; he cannot carry off a tap on a piece of wood, and if he could he would not know what to enter it as.

\item One verse for the oar, one for the hand, one for the term, one for the sea, one for the coming home. There is a place where a sixth should stand and it is not scored and not filled. Where the sixth should stand I have laid a shaving of the handle, cut with a knife where the wood has been worn smooth. The Council clerk has written against it, and his word is going soft with the damp. His word is his and the shaving is ours.

\item Not sung at the launching and not sung for a man who died at sea. There is a different thing said for him and it is said to the water, at the pushing-out of the boat, and watched until the boat is out of sight, which is held here to be enough.

\end{itemize}

\subsection*{The song}

\emph{Said low to the wood, standing. The oars keep the refrain. The hand goes to the handle before the first line.}

The refrain, as the oars keep it after every verse:

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Pull to the ebb, and the oar keeps the count.}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Pull to the flood, and the hand pays it.}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{The Council keeps seven. The sea keeps none.}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{The wood keeps the shine where the hand has gone.}\end{quote}

\subsection*{I. Of the oar}

\begin{quote}\itshape Count them in, count them out, count them on the rack;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape an oar comes back shining and a man comes back slack.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape The sleeve at the rowlock is cut to the wrist;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the oar’s entered serviceable, the wrist isn’t.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Pull to the ebb, and the oar keeps the count.}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Pull to the flood, and the hand pays it.}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{The Council keeps seven. The sea keeps none.}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{The wood keeps the shine where the hand has gone.}\end{quote}

\subsection*{II. Of the hand}

\begin{quote}\itshape There’s a pale ring on the palm where the handle wore;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the fingers shut on nothing when the boat came in.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape A hand that cannot close on an oar\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape cannot close on a cup, and won’t be asked to.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Pull to the ebb, and the oar keeps the count.}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Pull to the flood, and the hand pays it.}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{The Council keeps seven. The sea keeps none.}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{The wood keeps the shine where the hand has gone.}\end{quote}

\subsection*{III. Of the term}

\begin{quote}\itshape Seven years the notice says, or till the hands give out,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape whichever comes first, which is never the one you want.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape The Council writes \emph{discharged} where we write \emph{come home};\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the same man stands in both and neither asks him.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Pull to the ebb, and the oar keeps the count.}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Pull to the flood, and the hand pays it.}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{The Council keeps seven. The sea keeps none.}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{The wood keeps the shine where the hand has gone.}\end{quote}

\subsection*{IV. Of the sea}

\begin{quote}\itshape If he dies at the bench the sea has him returned;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape no slate goes down and no collector goes with it.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape We seal him in a salted boat and push him on the ebb\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and watch till he’s out of sight, which is enough.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Pull to the ebb, and the oar keeps the count.}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Pull to the flood, and the hand pays it.}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{The Council keeps seven. The sea keeps none.}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{The wood keeps the shine where the hand has gone.}\end{quote}

\subsection*{V. Of the coming home}

\begin{quote}\itshape We set the cup to his mouth and don’t ask his hand;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape a man can still be thirsty with his hands on the bench.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape He sits where the oar rack was and says nothing of the pull,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the shine on the wood goes on keeping his count.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Pull to the ebb, and the oar keeps the count.}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Pull to the flood, and the hand pays it.}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{The Council keeps seven. The sea keeps none.}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{The wood keeps the shine where the hand has gone.}\end{quote}

\subsection*{VI. The place that is not a verse}

\emph{Here a shaving of the oar-handle lies in the fold, cut with a knife where the wood has been worn smooth. There are no words to the sixth place. The taps on the wood go round once more with the shaving under the thumb.}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{In the leaning hand, against the shaving:} nil, term served.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape *\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Underneath, in mine:} A nought is a figure and can be carried away. The shaving is a place and stays where it is. I have not moved it and will not.\end{quote}

\subsection*{What the Council clerk did}

A clerk of the tide-tally house borrowed the leaf on a morning when the galley stores were being counted. He writes in the leaning hand, on salt-paper, and the damp has taken half of what he set down, so that of four corrections two are figures and one is the ghost of a verb. He took the verbs out of the verses and set his words above mine.

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item At \emph{an oar comes back shining and a man comes back slack}, he wrote \emph{oar returned serviceable; person discharged; no claim arises}.

\item At \emph{a hand that cannot close on an oar}, he wrote \emph{term completed by infirmity}, which is the same sentence with the man taken out of it.

\item At \emph{we seal him in a salted boat}, he wrote \emph{return at sea presumed; no slate required}, and underlined it twice, which is a great deal of ink for a thing nobody pays for.

\item Where the shaving lies he wrote \emph{nil}, and the damp has eaten the word down to a figure with no verb.

\end{itemize}

I have put my verbs back underneath and left his standing above. He takes the doing out because a thing always true has no need of it. I put it back because a woman at the oar-store does not know she is hearing something always true, and wants to know which hand held the oar.

\subsection*{What the boat-mother put in the margin}

The charcoal belongs to a woman who holds a share from her mother and has a man come aboard whose opinion on the boat is counted at half. She writes on the backs of spoiled tallies in a hand that presses hard at the ends of words. I have copied it as it stands.

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item At \emph{the Council keeps seven}: \emph{Seven is a term and a term is a thing with an end to it. His hands gave out in the fourth year and the Council called it mercy. A mercy with a date on it is a fine thing for the man who wrote the date.}

\item At \emph{a man can still be thirsty}: \emph{I set the cup to my brother’s mouth for eleven nights. On the twelfth he took it with his own hand and we all went out of the room, which is how a house thanks a hand for coming back.}

\item At the shaving: \emph{Cut it from where the wood is smoothest. That is where the most hands have been. I will not tell you whose.}

\end{itemize}

\subsection*{At the head and in the gutter}

The bloom at the head came up out of the paper itself and is the only thing on this leaf that entered without a hand. The tar thumb is mine, off the sheet I held down on the rack in the wind. The rope fibre in the second leaf came off a coil paid for with a wet hand and goes soft when the weather goes soft, which tells me when to shut the tin. The ring at the foot is brine, set down at the first verse and taken up at the last, by which time it had gone the colour of the floor it stood on. The fish-hook nick came off a man who set his hook down to count oars and charged the pulling of the boat to the wrong house, which is a thing the Council can settle and I cannot. The green bead fell out of a girl’s hair; she had been to the Cliffs and had sweetness at her mouth and said nothing, which is how the Cliffs are spoken of by those who have licked them. The grey along the margin came off a cuff laid where no cuff has business lying; nobody will own it and I have not swept it. No Last Day is kept at an oar-store, and nothing here is gathered and bottled and called dealt with. The shaving lies in the fold where the sixth verse should stand and I have not lifted it and will not.

\subsection*{At the foot, in a hand nobody will own}

\begin{quote}\itshape The oar keeps the shine. The sea keeps the boat.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape The slate keeps seven and nothing of what they paid.\end{quote}

I asked the clerk, a dipper come up from the pans, and a woman whose man came home in the fourth year, and had three answers and no hand. I have left the line where it was written.

The leaf goes back into the tin under the rack. Tomorrow the boats go out on the flood and I shall count the oars in at the ebb, and the wood will keep the shine and the clerk will keep his seven, and if a man comes home with his hands left on the bench I shall set the cup to his mouth and not ask him to lift it. There is a place in the song for a sixth verse and it stays where it is, under the shaving, with no figure and no hand.

\clearpage\phantomsection\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{The Land That Is Lent, Being the Account of Orra, a Pack-Woman out of Sill, Who Went Down the Marsh Road in the Reed of Y.H. 812 with Clay Pipes, Needles and Salt Herring and Came Back with Rushes, a Knot of Grey Wool She Will Not Untie, a Reed-Name She Will Not Say Aloud, and a Figure Read Over Her in the South but Paid in the Mud; with the Roads and Their Dues, the Table of What Was Asked and What Was Given, the Standing-Song as It Is Sung Face Down, Two Corrections in Borrowed Hands, and a Line at the Foot Nobody Will Own}
\CRsheetheading{The Land That Is Lent, Being the Account of Orra, a Pack-Woman out of Sill, Who Went Down the Marsh Road in the Reed of Y.H. 812 with Clay Pipes, Needles and Salt Herring and Came Back with Rushes, a Knot of Grey Wool She Will Not Untie, a Reed-Name She Will Not Say Aloud, and a Figure Read Over Her in the South but Paid in the Mud; with the Roads and Their Dues, the Table of What Was Asked and What Was Given, the Standing-Song as It Is Sung Face Down, Two Corrections in Borrowed Hands, and a Line at the Foot Nobody Will Own}
{\centering\FellFont\itshape\footnotesize\color{faded} A pack-woman’s road-account, set down first in charcoal on the backs of dried herring wrappers and copied at Greybank onto the back of a Court tallow-warrant voided by the Long Cold; the days in the pack-woman’s own hand, the figures in a sloped tally hand learned at the Cross, the sayings of the mud kept in the hearing and not translated, the verbs put back under every borrowed correction, and one line at the foot in a hand that has never come forward · Written in Reed of Y.H. 812, the Thin Year, on the marsh road out of Reedholt and at the Standing Post in the Fenmarch, by Orra, a pack-woman of Sill who carried small wares down to the fen and came back with rushes, eel-sinew, a knot of grey wool and a name she would not write; copied at Greybank in Ilmen of Y.H. 813 onto the back of a voided tallow-warrant and carried up the Clay Road to Sill in an oiled-sacking wrapper under the loose board of a landing. It survives as three leaves of soft reed-paper sewn with eel-sinew and folded in oiled sacking: a peat thumb worked into the head, a bog-water tideline along the gutter that has taken two figures clean off, a wet reed pressed flat across the second leaf, a clay-pipe stem snapped in the fold, a salt-herring scale at the foot, a reed-wolf’s tooth nick at the second corner, a grey Ash print along the outer fold which the writer did not make and has not swept, a knot of grey wool tied through a hole in the first leaf which she will not untie, two corrections in borrowed hands, one word scraped away with a knife-point, and a line at the foot in a hand nobody will own\par}\medskip
I carried a pack. That is the whole of what I am. I went down the marsh road in the reed month with clay pipes in the top of it and needles in a little tin and salt herring wrapped in oiled reed at the bottom, and I came back with rushes, a hank of eel-sinew, a knot of grey wool I cannot untie without losing what it stands for, and a name I have written down and will not say aloud. I have set down what I saw. Where the south and the mud disagree I have left both standing, which is the only honest way I know to carry a pack.

\subsection*{The road, and what it took}

Mud End stands three leagues downriver of Sill on a dry shelf above the marsh, with nine houses and their peat stacks. The byre there has a floor packed hard as old bread, and the moot sits in it when the peat is too wet to stand on. I slept in the byre on my first night with my pack under the bench and my boots toward the door, which is how a woman from the clay country learns to sleep in a wet one. In the morning a man asked me what I carried and I said herring and pipes. He said the marsh would take the herring and leave me the pipes, which was the first true thing told me on that road and the one I have entered first.

From Mud End the marsh road goes to Reedholt, where the reed-cutters live in huts at the edge of the beds and the wolves come in after dark. A man there sold me a night’s lodging and a drink of small ale and told me the wolves will not take a woman with a pack, because a pack smells of many things and none of them is woman. I asked him what they would take. He said a child cutting its first bundle in the dark, if the child goes alone and brings the bundle back dry, which is the Reed Cut and not a thing a visitor asks about twice. I have put his sentence where he said it and have not asked him again.

Beyond Reedholt the road goes into the Quiet Acre, which the Court calls the Empty Cantons on its own maps. There are wells there and doorways and no people. A doorway is built for coming back through, and a square of bare clay above a lintel is where a house-roll once hung. I saw eleven doorways and did not count the twelfth, because a thing with no figure in it is what that country keeps. I asked a peat-carter who goes that road whether anybody had come back through the doorways. He said the doorways had not been shut, which is not the answer I asked for and is the only one the road has.

The Standing Post is ninety leagues south-west of Sill and is the only place in the fen a stranger is shown. It is a walk of four planks laid across a cut no man has sounded, and a fifth place where no plank is laid. The man who keeps the boards told me the crossing costs nothing and the ground costs a bit. When I set my foot where he did not point I went in to the calf and had to be pulled out by a woman with a hook on a pole. She pulled me out and asked nothing, and I gave her a clay pipe and she would not take it. I have left the pipe standing in the account below and the pulling-out where it happened.

\subsection*{What was asked, and what was given}

\emph{The left column is the figure I was told at the Cross in Sill or by the beam at Greybank. The right is what left my pack or came into it here, where no clerk stands with a slate. I have set what I think of it on the back.}

Article — As told below — As given in the mud — What I set on the back\par

Salt herring, a string — 2 bits at the Fishstairs — 2 bits, or a notched stick under an apron — The stick is honest. The eel-women set their own figure and do not say it.\par

Clay pipes, a dozen — 3 bits in Sill — not taken; a woman pulled me from the cut and would not take one — A thing given for a thing not given has no price and stays in the pack.\par

Needles, a paper of six — 1 bit at the Cross — 2 bits, in kind, for a hank of eel-sinew — The sinew sewed these leaves and the seller would not take the bit back.\par

Rushes, a bundle — not cried on any board — ask the arm that cut it; the arm knows weight and not cost — The arm is not a scale. I have bought rushes all my life and never once weighed them.\par

Peat, a barrow — 2 bits in Grain, 5 in Stone — a barrow cut by the buyer, or a day of bought breath — Never by the stack. A stack is a house’s winter.\par

Grey, a thimble, bottled — 60 marks in a Court jar, licensed — 4 bits here, in an unmarked jar — The same grey in two vessels. One has a Court name and one has none.\par

Thin return, a household — 30 marks to the Court — a third, in eels and peat, and no questions — What comes back is a stranger the house keeps. I asked whose warmth and was asked why I wanted it.\par

Bought breath, a season — not spoken of below — a term paid in iron or peat, entered in months — The hook is in the word the seller cannot say.\par

A child named before the collector comes — no figure — a name said three times into the ground under the boards — No stick can hold it. I have tied a knot instead.\par

Twelve bits to the silver mark and twenty marks to a Sere crown, and the crowns that come north with the southern buyers will not change at Greybank, so they go south again and leave nothing behind but the figure. The Court books in embers and calls five marks an ember; in sixteen journeys I have never seen one paid and have twice seen a man try. I have left the ember column off. A column with nothing in it is the only one in this book no clerk has corrected.

\subsection*{The standing, and how they chose a reeve}

They chose a reeve while I was at the Post. Reeves here are chosen by standing in a bog until the others have had enough, and it is not strength: a strong man goes in hot and comes out early, and a reeve stands until the mud has taken his measure and found it enough. About half of them are women and the saying does not change for it.

The one they chose that morning was a woman with peat to the knees and her hands folded across her chest. She stood while the light went off the reedbeds and came back on them, and when a man went in to take her arm she came out under her own power and said nothing. Her first fine was a barrow of peat to the winter stack, laid on a man who had let a drain run into a neighbour’s cut. He paid it. The fine went on a stick. When I asked what became of a fine that was not paid, the board-man said a fine unpaid becomes a term and a term unpaid becomes a measure, and that there is no Last Day in a tin under a board where a man might sweep either one away.

I asked the woman reeve, through the board-man, whether standing so long made her right. She said the mud called her right and that she had only stood where she was put, which is a large answer in a small voice and the only one I got. I have set it above the price table, because it is the only thing on this leaf nobody has tried to write over.

\subsection*{The mother, and the number before the name}

A child was born in a hut off the Post while I was there. The mother named it before the collector came up the boardwalk, which the fenfolk do, and which a man from Greybank told me was the closest thing they had to a declaration of war. She named it three times: once to the child, once into the ground beside the hut, and once to the pot, and would not write it. When the collector read his figure she gave him the number and kept the word, which is their saying and not mine.

I asked a woman at the washing why a mother would spend a name on the ground. She said a written name travels where the person does not, and a name said at home is a door, and a number is a hole in the wall. Then she said I should not put that question to a mother, because a mother who answers it has told me what she paid for the child, and no visitor has a right to that. I have left the question in and the answer out, which is how the fen keeps its doors.

What the collector drew went at a third of what the Court charges, and nobody asked where it came from. A man who asks where warmth came from has decided not to hear it, the board-man said, and he said it to the water and not to me. I saw a pale round place on an arm that shows through the winter. I did not see the tube. I have written what I saw and have not written what I was told happened after, because I was told it by three people in three words and none of them would say the fourth.

\subsection*{The song said face down}

\emph{Taken down at the Standing Post from the woman who pulled me out of the cut. She would not sing it standing up, or looking at me, or while a slate lay open on the board, so we lay face down in the peat at the edge of the reeds and said it to the ground. The last word of each verse falls into the mud and is not finished. Where a word will not go into the south’s letters I have tied a knot in the margin.}

\begin{quote}\itshape Four for the boards and a smooth for the fifth,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the reed says wait and the reeve says stand;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the mud takes the name and the water takes the mark,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and what was lent goes back to the [knot].\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape A bit for the Line and a bit for the plank,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape a stick for the eels and a term for the stack;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the Court writes one and the river writes none,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the man who comes over is dry till he is not.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape She keeps it warm and she hands it back,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the Marsh Mother, and no priest in a coat;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the cold iron takes and the [knot] takes,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and one of them writes it down.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Say it to the board, say it down to the water,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the last word falls where the board has no foot;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape a name said at home is a door in the mud,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and a knot in the wool is the whole of the account.\end{quote}

She said songs from that country are made by the country, which is an answer the clay countries do not give and the coast does, and would not give the name of anybody who had made it. I have put the song where I found it, face down, and away from the slate.

\subsection*{What the borrowed hands did}

The factor’s clerk at Greybank borrowed the leaves on a market morning. He writes upright and narrow and takes the verbs out as though a verb were a thing a man could carry off in a cuff. He had never been south of Reedholt and had strong views about peat.

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item Against \emph{the mud called her right} he wrote \emph{the reeve was duly chosen}, and underlined it twice. I have put the mud back underneath. A reeve duly chosen is a reeve with nobody in the bog and no water on his boots.

\item Against \emph{a name said three times into the ground} he wrote \emph{naming not entered; vacancy}, and put a round nought in the fifth place. A nought is a figure. The fifth place is where no plank is laid. He has made the two agree and I have left them as they stood.

\item Against \emph{they gave and asked nothing for it} he wrote \emph{no consideration recorded; gift void}. Perhaps it is void in the language of his table. The woman pulled me out and would not take the pipe, and I have left the pipe in the pack where she left it.

\end{itemize}

The second hand is a College clerk come down from the Hearthseat on the factor’s business, who took the leaf while I was at the well and set \emph{a reduction in the measure was recorded} above the thin return, and \emph{seasonal labour} above bought breath, which is a thing a house can empty and refill. I have set my words under both. A verb is the difference between a thing that happened to somebody and a thing that happened in a counting room, and a leaf with three hands on it is the only kind a man at these boards will believe. A leaf with one hand is a Court notice, and a Court notice has never told a woman which plank will bear her.

\subsection*{At the head and in the gutter}

The peat at the head is mine. I held the leaf down on the board in a wind off the bog and did not know I had marked it, and peat goes into the grain and will not come out, which is why the fen signs with it. The tideline in the gutter is bog-water from the morning the Post stood under and has taken two figures clean off the second leaf; I have not written them back, because a figure with two figures gone is a figure cut slowly, and everything there is cut slowly. The wet reed across the second leaf came off the bundle I bought and was pressed flat under my pack. The pipe-stem in the fold snapped the day I offered it to the woman who pulled me out and she would not take it, and I have kept both pieces where they fell. The scale at the foot is a salt herring’s, off the string I carried down and did not bring back. The nick at the second corner is a reed-wolf’s tooth, from a man at Reedholt who paid with his hand still on the knife. The grey along the outer fold is not mine and not the factor’s and I have not swept it; there is no Last Day under a board on which a woman might sweep it. The knot of grey wool through the hole in the first leaf is mine, tied for a word that will not go into the south’s letters, and I will not untie it. One word on the third leaf I scraped away with a knife-point and put nothing in its place. I have not written it back.

\subsection*{At the foot, in a hand nobody will own}

\begin{quote}\itshape Four planks and a smooth where the fifth should lie;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape a woman stood in the bog and the mud called her right.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape I carried names in a tin and brought home a knot;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the figure went up and the child stayed in the mud.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Ask the doorway in the Acre who came back through it.\end{quote}

I asked the board-man, the woman who pulled me out, and a factor come up from Greybank to count the winter peat, and had three answers and no hand. I have left the line where it was written. The leaves go back into the sacking and under the loose board at the landing, and tomorrow I take my pack up the clay road to Sill and sell rushes by the armful and never once say where I got them, and by evening it will be a thing that was true. The clerk at the Cross will read my figure twice and call it a kindness. I shall keep the knot in my pocket, where no clerk has thought to look for an account.

\clearpage\phantomsection\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{The Landing Tally, Being the Dues of the Fishstairs Below the North Bridge in Sill and the Measures Set to the Clerk at the Out-of-Line Step, with the Figures Called, the Figures Not Called, and the Order of Reaching Entered Beside Them}
\CRsheetheading{The Landing Tally, Being the Dues of the Fishstairs Below the North Bridge in Sill and the Measures Set to the Clerk at the Out-of-Line Step, with the Figures Called, the Figures Not Called, and the Order of Reaching Entered Beside Them}
{\centering\FellFont\itshape\footnotesize\color{faded} A page from a collector’s clerk’s pocket ledger; figures in Ledgerhand, the remarks terse and in the hand that holds the slate, one column struck by the College and drawn back underneath, a numbering in a borrowed hand where the writer left a place, and a line at the foot in a hand nobody will own · Kept at the Fishstairs landing below the north bridge in Sill from the Opening of the Slates on Ilmen 1, Y.H. 813, through the Account-days of Reed in the Thin Year; written by the clerk set at the out-of-line step (the office stands on the roll, the hand does not), carried in the inner coat pocket where the slate’s strap has worn a place opposite the wrist and the cuff has gone grey from washing. It survives soft at the fold, with dried eel slime along the fore-edge, grey silt worked into the gutter, a white salt bloom at the head, a green bead of lead-glaze in the lower corner, a pale round ring pressed into the paper where a cold tube was set down, a small square of bare paper where a word was scraped away, corrections in the narrow upright hand of the College, a numbering in a hand that is not the College’s, and one line at the foot nobody will own.\par}\medskip
I keep the slate at the landing below the north bridge, where the Ilm comes down four steps and there is a flat place where a fifth should be. The market goes up and down over that place all morning and nobody falls, and if somebody does nobody calls it a fall. I am set for a measure. I have been set since Ilmen and it has not been called, and I write the dues of the eel-boards in the meantime, because a hand with nothing to enter will enter what it can find.

There are three of us with slates in this town and our entries do not touch. The man at the Court’s table at the Cross touches the top slate before he looks at the woman waiting, and says it’s entered as it stands. The Drawing collector keeps a book I have never seen open. I am neither. My cuff has gone grey from washing and the strap of my slate has worn a place in the coat opposite my wrist, so that the two wearings meet when I raise it. I have asked nobody to take me off. Word came up twice that nobody had, and the eels went on being sold over the top of me.

Write first. Look after. That is the order at this landing and it is the whole of the art. If a buyer names a figure I have it before I know his face, and if he asks me who it was I can tell him the figure and not the man, which is nearly always what he wanted. A clerk who looks before he writes is a clerk who has heard something he will later have to forget.

\subsection*{The rates of the landing}

Entry — As the slate has it\par

Copper bit — twelve to a silver mark\par

Silver mark — twenty to a gold crown, a Sere coin that does not stay in Grath\par

Ember — five marks, by the Court’s book; no man has exchanged one for the other\par

Eel, smoked, a basket at these boards — 3 bits\par

Eel, salted, a basket — 2 bits\par

Landing due, a basket set on the flat place — 1 bit, entered before the buyer is seen\par

Reeds, an armful — not entered; judged by the arm that carried them\par

Deduction — one in twelve, as the notice says\par

Newborn vessel — twelve to fifteen embers\par

Labourer in good case — forty to sixty embers\par

I have set the reeds in the table with no figure against them, which is how the yard sets them. A cutter told the girl with the creel to ask the arm that carried it, and she did, and went off satisfied. When a man come down from Slate Row asked what the reeds cost, he was sent to the pot with \emph{the house has said it} and got no number, and wrote nothing. I have copied his nothing honestly.

\subsection*{The tally, as I set it down}

\emph{Figures in Ledgerhand. The remarks are mine, in the hand that held the slate, and are not part of the account.}

Day — What stood at the landing — Dues, bits — Measure set, embers — Called — Remark\par

Ilmen 9 — Eels at the outer boards. A clerk set at the landing — 6 — — — — — Hand to slate before eyes. Nobody called one.\par

Ilmen 16 — Eels over the top of me. A brine-gull upriver with a coal — 9 — — — — — Not taken off. Not one of ours.\par

Ilmen 20 — Account-day. Eight baskets over the board below the bridge — 11 — 47 — none — Entered as it stood. Market sold over it.\par

Silt 10 — The second step under an inch of brown water, gone flat — — — — — — — Water read as weather. Slate held dry.\par

Silt 20 — Thinner crowd. Fewer bodies come down the steps — 7 — — — — — Figure read twice elsewhere. Not here.\par

Silt 30 — A foundling in cast-offs at the market’s edge — — — 12 — none — No loaf passed. No slate opened near him.\par

Seed 10 — Account-day. Eels below the bridge in the last of the planting — 13 — — — — — Hand to slate before eyes. Asked the cord; got no figure.\par

Seed 30 — The landing gone around with a look and no number — 4 — 33 — none — A place kept, not an entry.\par

Reed 10 — First Account-day of Reed. Baskets judged by the arm — 8 — — — — — Bell four, four and a gap. Nobody crossed.\par

Reed 15 — Reeds in armfuls. The flat place walked over carefully — 5 — — — — — Entered as it stood. Slate held to forearm.\par

Draws made: none. Measures set to this post: three. Measures called: none. Dues entered: sixty-three bits. Columns struck: one. Figures struck: none; I do not strike figures, I leave them standing until somebody tells me which one to take away, and nobody has.

\subsection*{The order of reaching}

The order is hand to slate, then eyes to the boards, then mouth. I have watched myself do it until I know the three parts as separate motions, the way a potter knows the foot from the belly of a pot. The woman at the outer boards moves eel-bones while she decides whether to lie, and when a buyer names a figure her thumb goes under her apron and stays longer than the figure wants. I have entered the figure and not the thumb. There is no column for a thumb that stays too long, and a clerk who makes one is a clerk who will soon be asked to read it aloud at a Weighing.

A girl with a creel takes the out-of-line landing sideways, one hand out to the rail, and goes on selling without looking at her feet. I have entered her baskets and not her foot. The district goes over the flat place carefully, the way it goes over a crack in a floor it has known since childhood, and calls the whole of it weather. When the Ilm came up on Silt 10 it stood on the second step and put the flat place under an inch of brown water, and gave the steps back one at a time through Silt 11 to 13, four, four, and the place again a hand’s breadth out of line. I kept the slate dry under my coat. A wet slate is a slate that can be read twice, and a figure read twice is a figure that has been made to say more than it said.

\subsection*{The column the College struck}

Beside \emph{Called} I had written a column of my own with no heading. In it I had set down, for each measure set to this post, the hour at which the slate was raised and the hour at which it was put down again. The man from the College borrowed the leaf on Reed 10 and struck the column through from the first row to the last, and wrote \emph{No such column} above it in his narrow upright hand.

I have drawn the column back underneath and left his words standing over it. He had to count the rows before he could write that there were none worth entering, and I watched him do it, standing as he stands, with his cuff gone soft and his ink settled in two fingers. A man does not count what he has not looked at. I have put no heading over the column still, because a heading would turn an hour into an entry and an entry into something a clerk may be called to answer for. An hour held is not a measure drawn. The College has eleven words for a deduction and not one for a holding, which is the whole of the difficulty between us.

\subsection*{The verse the eel-women carry below the bridge}

\emph{Sung at the boards at dawn while the baskets are counted, never on Account-day and never while a slate is out.}

\begin{quote}\itshape Four to the water and four to the stone,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and a flat place where the fifth should lie;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the eel comes up and the figure goes down,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the slate keeps what it never was given.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Hand to the slate and then to the stall,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the mouth comes last, as the mouth should do;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape one in twelve, says the notice, read twice at the Cross,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the landing reads once and reads it to you.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Ask the cord, ask the arm, ask the river, they say;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the Court has a figure for each of the three.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape I have a slate for a measure not called\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and a place in the count that the count keeps for me.\end{quote}

A woman with pale slime dried on her sleeves sang the first two lines while she worked and would not sing the third while the factor’s man stood on the bridge, which is how I know which line is the one that matters. I have copied it as it came and put no gloss on it. A clerk who explains a song has begun to write a sermon, and sermons get copied.

\subsection*{What the borrowed hands did}

The College hand struck \emph{Nobody called one} on the Ilmen 9 row and set \emph{No measure presented} above it, which is true and further from the landing than my words. I have put mine back underneath. \emph{Presented} is a word for a thing that was carried to a counter; a measure not called is not carried anywhere, it is simply not there, and the slate is held up all the same.

The other hand is a numbering hand, narrow and leaning, and not the College’s. Against the three rows where I left the \emph{Called} column bare it set a round nought in each. I have not struck the noughts out and I have not set them above my blanks either; they stand beside them. A nought is a figure and a blank is a place, and this leaf now holds both, which is more honest than either alone. A man who wanted those noughts to be true had to write them himself, and he did it in a hand that is not mine, in the hour before the Reed 15 baskets came down.

\subsection*{In the margins}

The eel slime along the fore-edge is mine, from holding the quay board still with the same hand that held the slate; it dries pale and comes off again when the damp gets into it. The silt in the gutter came up off the second step on Silt 10 and I have never got it out. The white bloom at the head is salt off a basket from the pans, and it has eaten one letter of the first date so that I cannot now read whether Ilmen 9 or Ilmen 8 stood there. The green bead in the lower corner is not slime. It is lead glaze from a woman who leaned over to see the tally with the sweetness still at her mouth, and touched the paper, and said nothing, and went back up the terrace. I have left it where she put it. The pale round ring was made by setting a cold iron tube down on the leaf while I reached for a basket, and the paper is thinner inside it; the tube was not used and the ring is not a wound, but it is the only mark on this page that looks like one.

The small bare square in the lower margin is where I scraped a word away with a knife and put no other in its place. I had written \emph{sixth} there, meaning the sixth morning I had raised the slate for a measure that did not come, and then I counted and found I could not say which mornings were the same and which were not, so I took the word off. A figure that cannot be checked is a figure I have no right to leave standing, even in the margin.

\subsection*{At the foot, in a hand nobody will own}

\begin{quote}\itshape The dues are entered. The measure is held. Both were taken from the same morning.\end{quote}

I asked the man at the Court’s table, the Drawing collector, and a woman who sold eels at the outer boards, and had three answers and no hand, as I have had before. I have left the line where it was written.

The slate goes back on my forearm and I go back to the flat place where the fifth step should be. Tomorrow the bell at the Cross will go four, four and a gap and nobody will cross himself, and a figure will be read twice over eight pigs, and I shall set down the baskets before I look at the boards, and hold the slate up for a measure nobody has called, and put it down at the same hour I put it down today. The noughts will stand beside the blanks. The leaf goes into the oiled pocket and the silt stays in the gutter, and there is no Last Day for a landing.

\clearpage\phantomsection\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{Of the Last Bed, the Drawing at the Mouth, and the Pot Broken at the Door, Being Title the Tenth of the Ordinances of the Keeping: with the Last-Bed Tally, the Form Left Blank, the Pot-Breaking Verse Said at the Threshold, Two Corrections in Borrowed Hands, and a Line at the Foot Nobody Will Own}
\CRsheetheading{Of the Last Bed, the Drawing at the Mouth, and the Pot Broken at the Door, Being Title the Tenth of the Ordinances of the Keeping: with the Last-Bed Tally, the Form Left Blank, the Pot-Breaking Verse Said at the Threshold, Two Corrections in Borrowed Hands, and a Line at the Foot Nobody Will Own}
{\centering\FellFont\itshape\footnotesize\color{faded} An extract from the Court’s ordinances, written out for the gate of the Bone Orchard outside Sill with the marginal hand of the clerk who keeps the last-bed slate there; the articles in Ledgerhand with the verbs restored beneath them, the tally in a table, the form of entry left blank, the pot-breaking verse said at the threshold, one word scored away with the edge of the cold-iron tube, two corrections in borrowed hands, and a line at the foot nobody has claimed · Copied at the Bone Orchard gate in the Thin Year, Y.H. 812, and carried forward at the Opening of the Slates, Ilmen 1, Y.H. 813, from Title the Tenth of the Ordinances of the Keeping as confirmed to the factor at Greybank by the treaty of Y.H. 418, set down after the Rising of Y.H. 668 and added to in Y.H. 782 and in the Thin Year; it survives as three leaves of foolscap sewn with wire, kept on a nail in the gate-room and taken down when a household sends for the collector: a grey Ash thumb at the head, a tallow watch-candle thumb beside it, the pale ring of a pot set down at the second fold, cold-iron filings from a tube-wrap worked into the gutter, a streak of pale slip along the outer edge, a green bead of lead glaze in the corner, a thread of grey wool through the tie-hole, one word scored out with the tube’s edge, a washing-water tide-line along the foot, two corrections in borrowed hands, and a line at the foot nobody will own\par}\medskip
I keep the last-bed slate at the gate of the Bone Orchard, a league out of Sill by the north road. A household sends for the collector when the breathing has come down to a matter of watching, and a boy comes up with a pot under his coat to be broken at the door; I read what is below to whoever is left standing before the tube is unwrapped. The ordinance is in Ledgerhand, and there is nobody in any of its sentences. I put the people back underneath, because a death with nobody in it is a death nobody died, and that is the only kind this Court has ever wanted entered. What follows is Title the Tenth, copied out from the book in Slate Row so that a house may know what is being entered against it.

\begin{quote}\itshape At the head of the first leaf, in mine, written small: Copied at the gate and for the gate. The verbs are mine. The absence of them is not. A leaf with a hand at the edge and a hand in the gutter is the only kind a household believes.\end{quote}

\subsection*{Title the Tenth, as it stands at the gate}

\emph{From the Ordinances of the Keeping, Title the Tenth: Of the Last Bed, the Drawing at the Mouth, and the Breaking of the Pot at the Door. Confirmed to the factor at Greybank by the treaty of Y.H. 418; set down after the Rising of Y.H. 668; added to in Y.H. 782 and in the Thin Year, Y.H. 812.}

\subsection*{I. Of the bed and the asking}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item No measure is drawn from a vessel that has breathed its last. The collector asks while breath remains to answer, the answer is entered, and the tube is not unwrapped until the entry is made.

\item Where the vessel cannot speak, the house answers. The answer is entered to the house and not to the person. The house is not asked whether it understood the question.

\item The words of the Return are said by the house, and the question is put after them. The answer is entered before the breathing is counted.

\item The question is put once. A second asking is a fresh entry and is entered as fresh, whether the first answer was given or not.

\item Consent at the bed is entered as elsewhere provided in Title the Fourth. The clip is not set where a vessel is past feeling it.

\end{enumerate}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Margin:} Beneath article 1, in mine: \emph{the vessel answers}. A woman held her mother’s hand and said a sentence that was not an answer. I have entered what the collector wrote and set the sentence at the edge, the length of it. A sentence that is not an answer has no column, and I have no column that will hold it.\end{quote}

\subsection*{II. Of the tube and the drawing}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item The measure is drawn at the mouth, where the last of the Warm goes out with the breath. The tube is of cold iron and is wrapped in wool; the wool is not entered.

\item The drawing is made by the collector and not by the house. The hand that holds the tube is not the hand that writes.

\item The measure taken is entered in embers and not in marks. Marks are for the living.

\item The figure is one in twelve, as the notice says, and is not changed for the hour, the bed, or the words spoken in the room.

\item What is drawn is not returned. What is returned is bought.

\end{enumerate}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Margin:} I asked a collector’s man why the tube is wrapped in wool when the iron is the thing that draws. He said the wool is for the hand that holds it, and the ordinance has no place for such a hand.\end{quote}

\subsection*{III. Of the whole and the thin}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item A whole return keeps the measure intact and brings back the vessel with its memory. It is booked at twelve hundred marks and forty unspent measures.

\item The forty are not found; they are made in the counting. No collector is asked to produce them.

\item A thin return pools the measures of many vessels and divides them. Nothing comes back that can name the house it came from. The district pays thirty marks, in labour where it has no coin.

\item The name written at the bank is not the name spoken at the bed. No house is asked what it would call the child.

\item An account is not closed by the drawing. It is carried forward, and the dead are kept on the roll.

\item Quiet ash is not given at the bed. The wanting of quiet is not entered.

\end{enumerate}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Margin:} A factor come up from Greybank asked whether a whole return could be made to remember a face. I told him the ordinance makes no provision for faces. He said that was a pity and went back down the road. I have set both sentences here; only one can be entered.\end{quote}

\subsection*{IV. Of the pot at the door}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item A pot is broken at the door of the death-house when the drawing is done, so that the heat that was in the house goes out with the shard and is not counted against the household. The pot is broken by the household and not by the collector.

\item It is broken after the tube is wrapped and before the slate is carried away. A pot broken before the drawing lets the heat out of the account as well as out of the house, which is a loss the Court does not provide for.

\item The shard is not swept until the Last Day. Where a shard is swept the same morning, the house is asked who swept it, and the answer is entered to the house.

\item No figure is entered for the pot. A pot is a piece of clay, and the heat that was in it is not a measure.

\end{enumerate}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Margin:} I keep a count of the pots broken at this gate in charcoal on the inside of the cover, and it is not the count on the slate. On Ash 12 two pots went out of one house and one measure went up the road. I have not joined the two counts. A man who joins them will ask where the second heat went, and there is no column for the answer.\end{quote}

\subsection*{V. Of faults and their correcting}

Fault — As entered at the gate — What the clerk sets beneath\par

A verb in the ordinance — The article copied again, in the same hand — The person who did the thing, restored\par

The question put twice — Second asking, entered fresh — The moment the house wanted, not entered\par

A sentence at the bed that is not an answer — Not entered — The sentence, at the edge, the length of it\par

A pot broken before the drawing — Loss entered to the house — The heat that went out with the shard\par

A shard swept before the Last Day — The house asked who swept — The hand that swept, and why it did\par

A factor’s figure written over the forty — The figure as the notice has it — The forty as they were made in the counting\par

The word that must not be written — Not entered; the place left bare — The score in the lower margin, cut with the tube\par

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item A fault copied twice in one tend is a fault the clerk has not understood; the senior clerk sits with him until he has. The pot is not a rod. It is a piece of clay with a place where a house stood.

\end{enumerate}

\subsection*{The last-bed tally}

\emph{Copied from the slate at the gate. The figures are the Court’s. The last column is mine and has no standing at any Weighing.}

Day — The vessel — Entered — Not entered — At the door\par

Ash 12 — A kiln-hand, Low Kiln — one measure, whole — \emph{It’s cold enough here.} — two pots, one broken before the tube\par

Ash 14 — An old woman of the terraces — one measure, thin — the name she called her daughter — one pot, swept the same morning\par

Ash 18 — A foundling, no slate-name — to the Keeping — the pot was not hers to break — none broken\par

Ash 21 — A glaze-room girl, High Kiln — one measure, thin — the green at her gum, older than the tube — one pot, broken\par

Ash 26 — A man of Mud End — one measure, whole — a sentence I have scored out — one pot, broken\par

Ash 30 — A clay-bound hand, term served out — to the house that held his bond — the year he had left to serve — one pot, broken\par

Draws on this leaf: six. Returns entered: two whole, three thin, one to the Keeping. Pots broken: seven. Sentences not entered: six. The word that must not be written stands scored in the lower margin, the length of it, cut with the edge of the tube.

\subsection*{The form of the last-bed entry}

\emph{Set out at the end of Title the Tenth. I have copied it with the blanks as they stand. In nine years no household has asked to have the last line read aloud.}

\begin{quote}\itshape Entered this day, being ---day of -------, in the year of the Hearth ------, the drawing of one measure from ---------------------- of ----------------------, asked once while breath remained, answered by the house where the vessel could not answer, the tube of cold iron set to the mouth, the figure one in twelve as the notice says, the measure entered in embers and not in marks, the return ----------------------, the name written at the bank not the name spoken at the bed, and the pot broken at the door after the tube was wrapped; written by ----------------------, whose hand was not the hand that held the tube. What was said in the room: ----------------------, which is not entered.\end{quote}

\subsection*{The pot-breaking verse}

\emph{Said low at the threshold by whoever is left standing, after the shard goes on the step. It is not sung. The fourth line is said to the pot.}

\begin{quote}\itshape Clay to clay and the door to the cold,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape break it here where the heat would go;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape one goes up in a slate and one goes out in a shard,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the house keeps the shape of the thing it had.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Iron at the mouth and a mark at the wrist,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the figure goes up and the name goes down;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape what was said at the bed is not in the book,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the pot keeps the place where the house stood.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Break it after the tube, not before;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape a pot broken early lets the account out too.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Six go up and seven go out,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and nobody asks where the second heat went.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{In the narrow upright hand, against the last line:} One measure entered; no discrepancy arises. \emph{In mine:} There are seven pots and six measures, and he has put a figure where I put a pot. A man does not number what he has not stood at a door. Both stand.\end{quote}

\subsection*{What the two borrowed hands did}

The College man came down from Slate Row with ink in two fingers of a cuff gone soft from washing. He struck the person out of article 6 and \emph{the house answers} out of article 2, setting \emph{the drawing is made} and \emph{answer is entered} above them, both true of the slate and false of the room. I have put mine back underneath.

The other hand is a factor’s from Greybank, brown at the edge with a little gold in it. Against the forty unspent measures he wrote \emph{stock, no deduction arises}, and against \emph{a whole return}, \emph{article of value}. I have not struck either through. A hand with gold in it can call a return an article; a hand that held the tube at a mouth calls it a person going out of a room. Both stand.

\subsection*{At the head and in the gutter}

The grey at the head is Ash, off my own thumb turning the leaf toward the lamp, and it does not come out of the creases. The tallow beside it is off the watch candle, kept low so a household would not know I was writing. The ring at the second fold is the bottom of a pot set down while I read article 17 to a man who had not yet broken it; the clay has left a pale circle the shape of a thumb. The iron in the gutter is filings from a tube-wrap, shaken out when a collector laid it here to go for a cup. The pale streak along the edge is slip from a swaddling cloth. The green bead is lead glaze chipped from a bowl out of Sere; the thread of grey wool through the tie-hole is mine, tied there the year I wrote a word I was told to scrape out, and I have never untied it. The tide-line along the foot is water from the washing of the step after a pot was broken; it has taken the corners off two lines without taking the sense.
