At the Last Day the houses sweep their corners and burn what they find and call it dealt with. This gate is not a house, and the shard stays where it fell.

\subsection*{At the foot, in a hand nobody will own}

\begin{quote}\itshape The slate keeps the measure. The door keeps the pot. The gutter keeps the sentence, and nobody is asked to enter it.\end{quote}

I asked a collector’s man, a woman with a pot under her coat, and a clerk from Slate Row, and had three answers and no hand. I have left the lines where they were written.

The slate goes back on its nail. Tomorrow a boy will come up with a pot under his coat and a collector behind him with the tube in its wool, and I shall read what stands here, put the verbs back where another hand took them out, and ask the question once. Someone will say something that is not an answer. The pot will go on the step, and I shall write the figure and leave a place the length of it. That is my trade: to enter what was drawn, and keep in the gutter what was only breathed.

\clearpage\phantomsection\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{Of Quiet Ash, the Licence to Buy, and the Greyed Hand, Being Title the Fifth of the Ordinances of the Keeping, Copied into the Factor’s House at Greybank with the Licence-Clerk’s Margin, the Scrape of a Phial-Cork, and a Correction in a Borrowed Hand}
\CRsheetheading{Of Quiet Ash, the Licence to Buy, and the Greyed Hand, Being Title the Fifth of the Ordinances of the Keeping, Copied into the Factor’s House at Greybank with the Licence-Clerk’s Margin, the Scrape of a Phial-Cork, and a Correction in a Borrowed Hand}
{\centering\FellFont\itshape\footnotesize\color{faded} An extract from the Court’s ordinances, written out for the counter of the factor’s house at Greybank, with the marginal hand of the clerk who keeps the licence-book; the articles in Ledgerhand and the verbs restored beneath them, a table of offences, a form of licence left blank, one line scored with a phial-cork, two corrections in borrowed hands, and a line at the foot nobody has claimed · Copied at Greybank in Seed of Y.H. 813 from Title the Fifth of the Ordinances of the Keeping as first licensed in Y.H. 683, fifteen years after the Rising, and added to in Y.H. 782 and in the Thin Year, Y.H. 812; carried forward at the Opening of the Slates, Ilmen 1, Y.H. 813. It survives as three leaves of foolscap sewn with wire, kept under the licence-book in the factor’s counting house: a grey Ash thumb at the head, salt bloom along the gutter from the Sallow wind off the quay, a tar thumb at the fold, iron-gall in the creases of two fingers, a scrape where a phial-cork crossed the lower margin, a green bead of cliff-glass, a damp tide-line along the foot, two corrections in borrowed hands, and a line at the foot nobody will own.\par}\medskip
I keep the licence-book at this counter. A man comes up from the quay with a phial under his coat and a mark in his fist and wants the mark entered against the phial before the factor’s clerk comes down from the Hearthseat; a woman of a house of Sere gives a name that is not hers and asks that her previous life stop arriving in dreams. I write what the ordinance tells me, and I set the verbs back underneath the words it has taken out, because a medicine with nobody in it is a medicine nobody took, and that is the kind the Court has always liked best. What follows is Title the Fifth, copied out so that a person may know what is being entered against him before it is entered.

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{At the head of the first leaf, in the same hand, written very small:} Copied by the counter, and for it. The verbs were put back by me and struck out again by a man who does not keep a counter. Let both stand. A leaf with two hands on it is the only kind a buyer believes.\end{quote}

\subsection*{Title the Fifth, as it stands in the factor’s book}

\emph{From the Ordinances of the Keeping, Title the Fifth: Of the Sale and License of Quiet Ash, and of the Greyed Hand. First licensed in Y.H. 683, fifteen years after the Rising; added to in Y.H. 782 and in the Thin Year, Y.H. 812.}

\subsection*{I. Of the thing itself}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item The grey that gathers in corners is not swept before the Last Day; it is gathered, bottled, sealed and licensed. In daylight it is not seen; by tallow-light it is plain. It is not dirt. What it is, is not entered.

\end{enumerate}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item Sold only by licence of the factor, in a phial bearing the Court’s mark, at sixty marks the phial. No phial sold without a figure; no figure entered without a phial.

\end{enumerate}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item Where the grey is gathered from a house in which a promise was left unkept, the gathering is entered to the house and not to the promise. The house is not asked.

\end{enumerate}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Margin:} I wrote what the grey is on this leaf and scraped the word away with the cork of a phial still wet at the mouth. The bare place is scored in the lower margin and the length of it is the length of the word. A clerk who supplies a definition has begun to write a sermon, and sermons get copied. I have left the place as it is.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Margin:} A man come up from the Fenmarch with a jar under his coat priced the same grey by the thimble at four bits and called it paste. I set his four bits beneath the sixty and left the two unjoined. A jar with a Fen name and a jar with the Court’s name stand on different shelves here, and I am the man who puts them there. I have not written the likeness in the book. It is a short sentence and it would cost me the counter.\end{quote}

\subsection*{II. Of the buyer}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item A licence to buy is entered in the name of the household and not of the person. It is written in the hand of the buyer or his factor; the hand that writes is not the hand that drinks. It is renewed at the end of each tend. A licence that lasts longer than a tend is a licence that has stopped earning.

\end{enumerate}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item The buyer is not asked what the phial is for. No physician’s certificate is required where the buyer has a house and a mark. Dreams are not entered; the previous life is not entered; the wanting of quiet is not entered.

\end{enumerate}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Margin:} The woman of Sere gave a name that was not hers and paid in marks, which anyone can write down, and with a sentence at the counter, which is not a figure. I entered the name she gave. A name that is not the name of the woman who speaks it is common in this trade, and the ordinance has no word for it. She asked if the phial would keep her mother’s dreams from coming. I said it was sealed. She took that for an answer and went up the road with it.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Margin, in a second and narrower hand:} Article 4 was added in Y.H. 782, the year the maids were first paid. A licence renewed each tend is a law that earns its keep by ending, which the Council of Tides would call a virtue if it had thought of it first. The ordinance does not say so, and I have not put it in the article.\end{quote}

\subsection*{III. Of the unlicensed sale}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item Quiet ash sold to any not licensed to buy it is punished by a greyed hand. The hand is greyed by the Court’s own iron and gives no warmth back. This grey is not the grey of a collector’s fingers, which comes with years at the tube and is a mark of the trade; the other is set deliberately and is called a correcting.

\end{enumerate}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item Where a phial is sold without licence, the phial is broken and the figure is not returned. A phial broken is entered as broken; the grey is not entered as returned.

\end{enumerate}

Offence — As entered — Correction\par

A phial sold to one not licensed — The hand greyed — The figure carried forward\par

A phial sold without a figure — The phial broken — Nothing returned\par

Quiet ash sold by the thimble, under a Fen name — Not entered here — The jar left on the other shelf\par

A licence lapsed in the tend — Carried forward — Not called ended\par

A definition supplied by the clerk — Scraped away — The bare place left standing\par

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Margin:} I have seen both greys. The one comes up under the nails by slow years and a man may carry it into any room and nobody ask him about it. The other comes all at once, like a hand dipped in skimmed milk gone off; the man keeps it in his pocket, in a glove, under a cuff gone soft from washing. I have never been asked which I have, and I have never told anybody, because I have neither. This is a fact about this counter and not a virtue.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Margin:} The Court owns no slaves, which it calls civility, and greys a hand by iron, which it calls a correcting. Both go into the book in the same neat hand. That is the whole mercy the ordinance allows itself.\end{quote}

\subsection*{IV. Of the keeping of the book}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item The licence-book is kept under the counter and is not shown to a household. The keeping of it is not explained, only kept. Where a name is disputed, the figure stands and the name is not changed.

\end{enumerate}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item An account is never closed; it is only carried forward. A licence lapsed is carried forward as a licence lapsed, and not as a licence ended.

\end{enumerate}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Margin:} The rolls of the dead are kept open, and so are the licences of the living. I have carried one name forward for eleven years after the household that gave it was empty of people. Nobody came to close it and I did not close it. A name carried forward is a different weight from a name bought, though the hand that writes them is the same.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Margin:} The seal on the phial is the Court’s mark and not a priest’s. A dipper of Vhal would trail the jar in the sea at dawn and call that a licence; the factor calls it nothing at all. I have copied neither saying into this book.\end{quote}

\subsection*{V. Of faults and their correcting}

Fault — As entered in Ledgerhand — What the clerk sets beneath\par

A verb in the roll — Page copied again, in the same hand — The verb restored, where it stood\par

A buyer’s name disputed — The name as given — No note made\par

Sixty marks written as a rate — The figure as the notice has it — The figure as the phial was sold\par

A licence called ended — Carried forward — Not called ended\par

A grey too dark to hide — A glove — Nothing, which is not an entry\par

\subsection*{The form of licence}

\emph{Set out at the end of Title the Fifth. I have copied it with the blanks as they stand. In eleven years nobody has filled one in the hand the factor requires.}

\begin{quote}\itshape Entered this day, being ---day of -------, in the year of the Hearth ------, the licence to buy one phial of quiet ash granted to ---------------------- of ----------------------, at ------- marks, to be renewed at the tend’s end and carried forward where not ended; the hand that writes not the hand that drinks; the phial sealed and the figure entered, and the name not changed where disputed. Granted by ----------------------, who is not the man who sold it.\end{quote}

\subsection*{The verse the weighers say at the phial-draw}

\emph{Called under the breath at the beam when the phials come up off the boat, never while the factor’s clerk is in hearing. It is not a song for the quay and has never been sung there.}

\begin{quote}\itshape Grey in the corner, grey in the jar,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape one has a name and one has a mark;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape sixty marks for the sealed and licensed,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape four bits for the same under a fen-name.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Put the cork to the leaf and leave the word out;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape a hand goes grey and a hand goes cold;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the account stands where the phial stood,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the dream comes back where the figure went.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{In the narrow upright hand, against the fourth line:} One article entered. \emph{In mine:} There are two greys and I have set both. He has put no figure against the Fen jar, which is how I know he has looked at it. A man does not number what he has not looked at.\end{quote}

\subsection*{What the two borrowed hands did}

The College man came down from the Hearthseat with a cuff gone soft from washing and ink in two fingers. He struck \emph{gathers} out of article one and set \emph{is gathered} above, as though a thing that gathers in a corner had nobody who left it there. I put \emph{gathers} back. He struck the verb out of the buyer’s sentence also, leaving a wanting with nobody to want it. Both stand.

The other hand is leaning, with a little gold in it, from a counting house of Sere. Against \emph{sixty marks} it wrote \emph{quiet ash, market rate}, and put a figure in the margin where I had put the price. I left both standing. A house of Sere can call a figure a rate, because a rate is a thing that can be emptied and refilled; a man who has held the phial and smelled the cork calls it a price.

\subsection*{At the head and in the gutter}

The grey at the head is Ash, off my own thumb turning the leaf toward the light while the factor read a figure over it; it is the colour a corner leaves when it has been swept too late, and it does not wash out of the creases. The white in the gutter is salt bloom blown up from the Sallow under the counting house door; it comes and goes with the weather and is never entered. The tar at the fold came off a Vhaleni boatman’s coil, and the green bead in the corner is cliff-glass from that coast and not lead glaze from High Kiln, which has a sweeter look and a smell. The iron-gall is in two fingers and will not come out, which is how the factor knows I have copied a thing before he asks. The scrape in the lower margin is the cork, drawn across while I decided what word to leave out; the tide-line along the foot is a phial set down through a morning, the seal holding and the leaf taking the damp. There is no Last Day under a counter, and nothing here is swept and burnt and called dealt with.

\subsection*{At the foot, in a hand nobody has claimed}

\begin{quote}\itshape The jar keeps the grey. The hand keeps the colour. The slate keeps the figure, and none of them says what it was for.\end{quote}

I asked the factor’s man, a man come down from the College, and a woman who stood here about a phial, and had three answers and no hand, as I have had before. I have left the line where it was written.

The book goes back under the counter. Tomorrow a man will come up with a phial under his coat and a mark in his fist, and a woman will give a name that is not hers, and I shall enter the figure and not the wanting, and put the verbs back where I can. The scrape in the margin is the length of a word. I have not written it back, and I have not forgotten it.

\clearpage\phantomsection\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{The Lie of the Ground, Being an Account of the Empty Cantons, Which the Court Names So and the Fen Calls the Quiet Acre, Set Down by a Well-Sinker out of Cold Acre Who Went South with a Survey Party in the Thin Year and Came Back Before the Thaw with Nothing to Tell Except the Lie of the Ground; with the Measure of Six Wells, the Nine Doorways, the Song of the Dry Road, Two Corrections in Borrowed Hands, and a Line at the Foot Nobody Will Own}
\CRsheetheading{The Lie of the Ground, Being an Account of the Empty Cantons, Which the Court Names So and the Fen Calls the Quiet Acre, Set Down by a Well-Sinker out of Cold Acre Who Went South with a Survey Party in the Thin Year and Came Back Before the Thaw with Nothing to Tell Except the Lie of the Ground; with the Measure of Six Wells, the Nine Doorways, the Song of the Dry Road, Two Corrections in Borrowed Hands, and a Line at the Foot Nobody Will Own}
{\centering\FellFont\itshape\footnotesize\color{faded} A well-sinker’s field account, set down first in charcoal on the backs of three spoiled well-tallies and a Court lime-warrant and copied at Greybank onto the back of a granary docket voided by the Long Cold; the measurements in a rough travelling hand with the rope’s figure set above the eye’s, the sayings of the country kept in the hearing and not translated, the verbs put back under every borrowed correction, and one line at the foot in a hand that has never come forward · Written in the Cantons and at Cold Acre in Ash and Stone of Y.H. 812, the Thin Year of the Long Cold, by Gedde, a well-sinker of Cold Acre who keeps the ridge wells from freezing and had never sunk a dry one until he went south, hired with a survey party out of the factor’s house at Greybank to measure the old wells; carried back up the south road in Ilmen of Y.H. 813 and copied at Greybank onto the back of a granary docket voided by the Long Cold. It survives folded into a well-rope coil in a dry tin: a white dust like bone meal worked into the fold from the hearths, grey silt in the gutter off the road, a chip of slate pressed into the lower corner with a mark on it that is not a figure, a thumb of tallow at the head, a length of well-rope fibre caught in the sewing, a small square of bare paper where a word was scraped away with a knife-point, a grey Ash print along the outer fold that the writer did not make and has not swept, two corrections in borrowed hands, and a line at the foot in a hand nobody will own\par}\medskip
I sink wells. There is one at Cold Acre that has never frozen, and I have kept it from the ice nineteen winters by knowing where the water goes under the ridge. A man who knows where water is knows where it is not, which is why the factor at Greybank sent for me. Three of us went south in Ash: a surveyor out of the factor’s house with a slate and a new coil of rope, a Fen man who would take us as far as the first doorway and no farther, and me. We went to measure the old wells of the Cantons. I had never measured a dry one.

I have measured six now. I have come back with nothing to tell except the lie of the ground, which is what men come back with from that place, and I had better set the ground down plain before it turns into a story.

\subsection*{The road in}

The Cantons lie sixty leagues south of Sill, and there is no road a cart can make in a day. We walked. On the third day the ruts came back under the turf, deep as a cart’s wheel and empty of anything a wheel had drawn through them in eight hundred years. A road is a thing somebody meant to come back along, and the ground had kept that much and let everything else go.

There is no gate and no due. The Fen man stopped where the first doorway stood and would not go past the shadow of it. He is a man of few words and gives them to the ground before he gives them to a person. He said a dry man is a dangerous man, and that he had stood on the boardwalk long enough to know one, and then he sat down on a stone and took no part in what followed, though he watched us the whole while with his back turned.

The first thing a well-sinker notices in a strange country is where the water would be if there were any. In the Cantons the low ground holds no damp, the ditches that were cut to drain it are dry cuts, and the clay underfoot has gone the colour of a pot fired too often.

There was no smoke. That is the thing every man writes down first, and I have written it down too, because it is true and because there is nothing else to write at that hour. In Grath a man can tell the hour by the smoke over a roof. Here the sky went on being a sky with nothing said in it, and the surveyor and I ate our bread standing up, though there was nowhere to sit that was not a step of somebody’s house.

\subsection*{The six wells}

\emph{Measured in the order we came to them. The rope’s figure is what my line brought up; the eye’s figure is what I saw at the mouth; the last column is what the surveyor wrote. I have set his hand above mine and left mine under it, which is the only way a man reads a slate in this country without lying.}

Well — What the rope said — What the eye saw — What was entered\par

First, by the road — full length down, dry coming up, iron on the wet end — stones laid round the mouth in the old order, every stone where a stone expects to be — dry; no entry\par

Second, in the doorway-yard — dry; the line came up with white dust on it — no mark of a bucket on the rim, and yet the rim worn smooth on one side — dry\par

Third, under the fallen wall — the rope fouled below and would not come back till I let the coil go — the mouth worn deep where a hand would rest and a hand would pull — dry; obstruction below, no value\par

Fourth, by the last standing hearth — dry — ash in it that is not grey — dry\par

Fifth — dry — a square of bare clay set into the stonework above it, where something had hung — dry\par

Sixth, beyond the doorways — dry — the stones laid so tidy that a man’s first thought is to ask who laid them — dry\par

A dry well is not a hole. A dry well is a statement made in stone, and I have no trade in answering it. In Cold Acre a well that fails is a well with a cause: a seam that has shifted, a taint, a nothing that the water used to do. These six had none. The water was down out of sight, which is a different thing from being gone, and the stones were laid round the mouths in the old order, which a man does not do when he is leaving in a hurry.

The surveyor wrote \emph{dry} against each and \emph{no entry} against the first. I asked him why the first was entered and the others not. He said the first stood nearest the road and a figure had to begin somewhere. Then he turned his slate face down, which is a thing men do here when they have seen enough and do not want to be asked what.

\subsection*{The doorways}

We counted nine doorways standing where the walls had gone. In three of them there was a square of bare clay above the lintel where a house-roll had hung, and there was no nail in any of the nine. A nail would have been pulled out and carried away, or would have rusted where it stood; there were no nails and no marks where nails had been, only the bare square as clean as the day the clay was laid.

In one doorway a slate still stands in its notch. The figures on it are not figures I could read, and I have set them down as shapes and not as numbers, because a man who calls a shape a figure has begun to explain it. One groove goes deeper than an iron point would cut, and I did not write how it was made, and would not know if I had.

A Vorr came through while we stood there, going north with a bag of nothing and a stick. The surveyor asked him about the slate. The Vorr looked at it a while and said the numbers were correct, and went on. He would not say what they counted. I have put his saying in the margin below rather than in the body of the account, because a sentence a man can carry away and still know nothing of is not an answer and should not be given the room of one.

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{In the margin, in a small hard hand I took for the Vorr’s, four figures set down one under another, correctly made. I cannot match them to anything on the road: not to the wells, not to the doorways, not to the nine. I have left them standing where they were written.}\end{quote}

\subsection*{The hearths}

The hearths are cold, and the ash in them is not grey. It is a white dust like bone meal, fine and dry, lying in the hollow where a fire would have been. I have put my hand into four of them. In the fourth there was a little warmth still in the stone under the dust, no more than a stone keeps when the sun has been off it an hour, and I wrote that down and then crossed it out, because a well-sinker who writes a warmth where there should be none will be asked to find it again.

The Fen man said, from his stone with his back turned, that the white is what is left when a promise has been kept too long. I have set that down as it was said and have joined nothing to it. A man who joins a saying to a hollow full of white dust has made a story, and stories are what that country has no need of. In Grath we leave the grey in the corners on the Last Day and burn it in the morning. Here there is no Last Day that anybody keeps, and the white lies where it lies, and nobody sweeps.

\subsection*{The song of the dry road}

\emph{Sung by the Fen man going in, not coming back. He would not sing it within sight of the first doorway, and sang it on the third morning with his face to the north. The fourth line is his; there is a place in his singing of it where a word should stand, and I have set down what I heard rather than fill it.}

\begin{quote}\itshape Six wells and never a splash,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the rope goes down where the water was;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the stones keep house and the lintel keeps bare,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the road keeps the place where the step was.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Four for the corners and one for the nail\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape that was never driven and never pulled;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the Fox has the hearth and the dust has the name,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the well keeps the white that the hand never drew.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape I went in dry and I came back dry,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the dry of the two is not the same;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape one is a man and one is a ground,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and only the ground has a name for it.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Ask the rope what it brought back ---\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the rope said nothing, and went on that way.\end{quote}

He said the last line was about the song and not about the wells, and when I asked him what the difference was he said a man who needed it explained would not have sung it. I have copied it as it came and put no gloss on it.

\subsection*{What the surveyor entered, and what I set under it}

At Greybank a clerk of the factor’s house borrowed the leaves while I was buying rope. He writes upright and narrow and leaves the doer out of every sentence, as though a well could dry itself and a man could walk sixty leagues without a pair of feet. He did not strike a word of mine. He put his words above and left mine where they stood, which is the readiest way of correcting a man I know.

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item Against \emph{the stones were laid in the old order} he wrote \emph{masonry, derelict}, which is a true description of stones and leaves out the order.

\item Against \emph{the rim was worn where a hand would pull} he wrote \emph{wear, cause unknown}. I have set \emph{cause: a hand} underneath in charcoal, which does not keep, and am content it should not.

\item Against \emph{the white dust in the hearths} he wrote \emph{residue, unclassified}, and against the Vorr’s saying, \emph{statement not entered}. He was right in the language of his office. A statement the office cannot enter is a statement the office need not answer.

\item Against my six rows he wrote \emph{six dry wells; no population; property unoccupied}, and underlined it twice. The wells are dry and the place is empty. I have never argued with either figure. What I cannot agree to is the word \emph{unoccupied}, which is a word for a house from which somebody has gone, and not for a house that has gone from somebody.

\end{itemize}

I have left both hands standing, his above and mine below, as a repaired vessel keeps the old break under the new staple and does not pretend the first hand never touched the clay. A clerk who takes the hand out of a well leaves the well standing by itself, and a well standing by itself has never dried anybody.

\subsection*{At the head and in the gutter}

The white in the fold came off the hearths and is bone meal fine; it will not wash out and I have stopped trying. The grey in the gutter is silt off the south road and came honestly by its place, worked in on the walk back when the thaw had begun under the frost. The tallow at the head is my own lamp, set too near the leaf on the last night before we turned north. The rope-fibre in the sewing came off the coil that fouled in the third well; I cut it out with a knife and sewed it back, because a rope that has been down a well is not a rope to throw away. The chip in the lower corner is off the slate in the doorway. I prised it with a nail and it came away more easily than a chip should, and the mark on it is not a figure and I have never called it one. The square of bare paper is where I scraped a word away with a knife-point and put no other in its place; it is the only square in this account I made myself. The grey along the outer fold is not mine and not the clerk’s. I have not swept it. There is no Last Day in the Cantons and I have not found one since I came back.

\subsection*{At the foot, in a hand nobody will own}

\begin{quote}\itshape Six wells and never a drop to count,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape nine doorways and no one to come through;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the rope keeps the shape of what it didn’t bring up,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the slate in the door keeps a figure for you.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Ask the dust what it kept so long.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Ask the stone why the water went.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Ask the road whose wheel it was.\end{quote}

I asked the surveyor, the Fen man, and the Vorr who came through, and had three answers and no hand, as I have had before. I have left the line where it was written.

The leaves go back into the tin, and the tin into the coil, and the coil onto the shelf beside the rope I use at Cold Acre. Tomorrow I sink a well for a household on the ridge, and it will give water, and I shall be paid in marks for finding what the ground was willing to give. In the thaw I mean to walk south again with a longer line. I have not told the factor and do not know what I shall ask the well when I get there. A man who writes why before he goes has already decided what he will find, and I have made that mistake once, below the Old Kiln, and do not mean to make it twice.

\clearpage\phantomsection\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{The Light in the Clay Cup, Being a Letter from the Tryworks Two Leagues North-East of Sill to a Woman Who Keeps the Lamp-Row in the Low Houses, Concerning a Thin Rendering After the Long Cold, the Smell on a North Wind, the Price of a Quart of Fat, and the Question of Who Pays for a Burning; with the Answer in the Margin, a Clerk’s Correction in Ledgerhand, and a Lamp-Song in a Hand Nobody Will Own}
\CRsheetheading{The Light in the Clay Cup, Being a Letter from the Tryworks Two Leagues North-East of Sill to a Woman Who Keeps the Lamp-Row in the Low Houses, Concerning a Thin Rendering After the Long Cold, the Smell on a North Wind, the Price of a Quart of Fat, and the Question of Who Pays for a Burning; with the Answer in the Margin, a Clerk’s Correction in Ledgerhand, and a Lamp-Song in a Hand Nobody Will Own}
{\centering\FellFont\itshape\footnotesize\color{faded} A private letter on the back of a tallow-weight chit spoiled by a wet thumb, written in iron-gall over charcoal that would not take on the fat, folded thrice and tied with a hemp wick; carried down the north-east road from the Tallow Works to Low Kiln in the cover of a pail, answered along the margin in a second hand, borrowed at Greybank where a factor’s clerk set a correction on the back in Ledgerhand, and kept since in a dry tin among the wicks and the spoiled weights · Written at the Tallow Works, two leagues north-east of Sill, in the last tend of Bone, Y.H. 813, by Orra, a woman who renders sheep fat, to Lett, who keeps the lamp-row in the low houses below the sill; carried down in the last week of Bone and answered in the margin at Low Kiln in Ash of the same year, borrowed on the Clay Road at the factor’s house at Greybank, and kept in the tin beside the wicks. It survives with a thumb of raw tallow worked into the grain at the head, a grey Ash print along the gutter which nobody will own, a hemp wick through the tie-hole, a bloom of salt on the outer fold off a cuff that had been at the pans, a scorch where the leaf lay too near the try-pot, a brown crust spot at the second fold, the clerk’s correction standing above the words, the verbs standing underneath it, and a line at the foot in a hand nobody has claimed\par}\medskip
To Lett, who counts the lamps in the low houses below the sill. From Orra at the tryworks, two leagues up the north-east road. Written in the last tend of Bone.

I write on the back of a weight-chit the factor’s man spoiled with his figure, because there is no paper at the works that is mine and a sheet that has carried a number is a sheet a man will not read twice. The fat has got into the grain and the charcoal would not take on it, so I have gone over every word in iron-gall and the ink beads where the thumb was. Do not hold the leaf to the fire to read it. It goes soft and smells, and a letter that smells of rendering is a letter somebody will ask about.

The north wind came on Bone 26 and carried the smell down into Sill the way it does, and a woman at the well below the bridge said the whole terrace had been rendering sheep all morning and would not believe it was us, two leagues off. A smell travels without a slate and arrives before the man that sent it. By midday it was in the pottage. Nobody thanked us and nobody stopped eating.

We rendered thin this year. The Long Cold took the grass before the flocks were in, and the sheep came up to the works with their bones showing through the wool like a slate with the figures rubbed off, and what fat there was lay pale in the pan and set before it could be poured. A pound of it will not stand in a cup the way it stood last year. I have set the tend’s count below and put in the last column what the factor’s man took out.

\subsection*{Fat rendered in the last tend, and where the light went}

\emph{Written in charcoal first, then gone over. The figure column is his. The last column is mine and has no standing at any Weighing.}

When — Fat rendered — Price asked — Who bought — What the light stood beside\par

Firstday — Seven pound, pale — Nine bits the quart — A woman of the low houses — A child’s bed, lit until the mother came in\par

Thirdday — Four pound, set hard in the pan — Nine bits, and a crust thrown in — The man at the Cross — Nothing; he carried the quart past the bridge\par

Fifthday — Six pound, sweet at the smell — Not asked — Nobody — The pan itself, which smoked all afternoon\par

Seventhday — Three pound, dregs — Six bits, taken in ale — A woman from Cold Acre — A window set for a man coming on the Clay Road\par

Ninthday — Eight pound, the best of the tend — Nine bits — The Vail house, by a girl with slip in her wrists — The shelf where the bread is kept\par

Nine bits the quart is what the notice in the factor’s window says, and it is what I asked, and it is not what a woman below the bridge pays when she has had three days without work. She pays in small ale and a promise, and the promise gathers grey in the corner the way a debt gathers, and I have never once entered it. A promise is a debt without a figure, which is the only kind this side of the works can afford.

A lamp is a small fire taught to sit still, the way a hearth-fire is taught, and tallow is what it eats. There is no note in a lamp. Tap a pot with the knuckle and it answers full; tap a cracked one and it answers flat, a little dead sound that stops at the surface; tap a clay lamp and you get only the dull sound of the thing you tapped, which tells you nothing except that it is clay. I have learned to read a lamp by the smell. A lamp that smells of the wick is a lamp eating its own hemp. A lamp that smells of nothing has gone out and will be cold by morning. There is a woman three doors below the bridge who sets her lamp in the window when her man is due off the Clay Road, and the lamp is not for her and she will not say so, and the fat in it is bought with the same bits that buy the bread. I have put her in the last column, where the clerk will not let me.

Every light somebody keeps burning is paid for by somebody. This is not a saying of the Keeping and it is in no ordinance; it is what a woman learns who has stood over a try-pot and watched a length of yellow fat come up out of a sheep that ate a field that somebody held the deed to. The Court will tell you one in twelve, and the notice says it, and Berr Clay reads it over the basket twice, once for the moot and once for them that came late, wiping his thumb twice before he touches nothing. The bell went four, four and a gap and nobody crossed himself. He never asks what a lamp cost. A figure read aloud is not the figure paid, and a light in a window is not a light anybody has entered.

So I ask you two things, and I have put them where you can answer without a slate in the room.

The first: what is in the cup of the lamp by the bed in the Vail house? I am not asking who pays for it. I know that answer and so do you, and it is the house and never a person, as it is everywhere below the sill. I am asking what is in the cup, because a woman come up from the pans says a child upriver turns his head toward a light a breath before it is lit, and I want to know if that is a thing they say at the Fishstairs or a thing you have seen. Do not give me a name. A name in a letter is a thing a clerk can enter against a person before she has taken her coat off.

The second: is the wick hemp from the fen, or the thread they spin at the Quay? I have a mind to send a wick up with the next fat and I will not send the wrong one, for a wick that draws too fast eats a household’s winter in a night and there is nobody in the low houses who can afford it. Answer on the back and not in the gutter, where the Ash has got into everything.

\subsection*{The lamp-song}

\emph{Sung low over the try-pot while the skimmings are lifted, never to a person and never while the factor’s man is in the room. The fourth line is said to the wick. Where the light goes out is left as it is sung.}

\begin{quote}\itshape Fat comes up pale and the pan goes black,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the sheep ate grass on a borrowed ground;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape nine bits the quart and a promise besides,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the light in the cup keeps what it found.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Wick from the fen or thread from the Quay,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape draw it too fast and the winter goes;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape four in the window and a fifth never lit,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the hand that set it is the hand that knows.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape The north wind carries the smell to the town,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the smell goes in and the figure stays out;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape a lamp is a wound that is fed with a spoon —\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape ask who paid, and the room goes dark about.\end{quote}

\subsection*{What the clerk did}

A clerk of the factor’s house borrowed the chit on the morning after it came up the quay, being a man who cannot leave paper alone. He writes in the neat upright hand they teach at the College, with the doers taken out. Against \emph{a woman of the low houses pays in small ale and a promise} he set \emph{consideration arranged} and the woman went out of the sentence the way a neighbour goes out of a tally. Against \emph{the light stood beside a child’s bed} he set \emph{domestic consumption}, and against the girl with slip in her wrists he set \emph{household of standing}, which is a phrase that means the house has pots and says nothing about the girl. Against the question of who pays for a burning he wrote \emph{no deduction arises}, which is the Court’s own art in four words. He put a round figure in the last column where I had put a woman and a window. The figure has outlasted the fat it was meant to explain.

I have put the verbs back underneath where I could still read them, and left his figure standing above. He takes the people out because a thing always true has no need of verbs. We put them in because a woman at a tryworks at the going of the light wants to know whose bed the quart went to.

\subsection*{In the margin, in a second hand, small and set close to the writing}

The quart went to the low houses and the ale was watered and the promise was kept in the corner and not in the cup. I do not know what is in the lamp by the bed and I have never looked into it, which is the same as knowing in this house. The child turns his head at the pot before the knuckle falls, and before the light is set down, and I have seen it four times and will not make a fifth of it, for four are four and a fifth would want a payer. It is not quickness. It is not a sign. It is a thing a child does in a room whose floor his own floor does not touch.

\begin{quote}\itshape It is hemp from the fen. I know the smell of it when it draws, and I have kept yours these three years without asking what you wanted it for.\end{quote}

I have struck your nine bits and put eight under it in your own iron-gall. The woman below the bridge paid eight and a crust, and the crust was the browned one and went to the child and not to her, which is the kindness of the low houses and is not entered. Put the figure where the figure belongs and the woman where the woman stood. I will not write the name of the girl with slip in her wrists, and not because I do not know it.

\begin{quote}\itshape A lamp kept in a cup is a light somebody ate in a field.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape The field keeps the figure. The cup keeps the dark.\end{quote}

\subsection*{At the head and in the gutter}

The tallow at the head is mine, off the thumb I held the chit down with while the wind came through the door; it has gone into the grain and there is no washing it out, and I have stopped trying. The grey along the gutter came off a cuff that had no business lying where the weights are kept, and I did not make it and have not swept it; there is Ash enough in this house without bringing a stranger’s in. The wick through the tie-hole is hemp from the fen, and I have tied it there so that I cannot send it with the fat and lose it. The salt bloom on the outer fold came off a woman’s cuff that had been at the pans on a flood tide, and it has eaten one letter of the date so that I cannot now read whether it was Bone 25 or Bone 26 the wind came on, which is a small loss and the only one I mind. The scorch is where the leaf lay too near the try-pot on Ninthday and took the corner off the price without taking the sense. The brown at the second fold is from a crust set down by the woman who pays in ale; she laid it there while she told me where the child had been and would not say the name of the house, and the grease has eaten two letters and left the sentence standing. The clerk’s correction stands above my words and my words stand under it, and neither has been struck out.

\subsection*{At the foot, in a hand nobody will own}

\begin{quote}\itshape The smith mends the mouth that takes the house.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape The render feeds the light that shows the crack.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Nine goes in the slate and eight comes in the cup,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the fifth stays dark where the fifth stood.\end{quote}

I asked a woman at the pans, a man come down from Cold Acre with a hare, and a girl who keeps the factor’s tally, and had three answers and no hand, as we have had before. I have left the line where it was written.

The chit goes back in the tin beside the wicks. In the morning the fat goes down to Sill on the cart, and the woman below the bridge will pay in ale and a promise, and the lamp in the window will be set for a man who is not yet on the road. That is the whole of the letter, and it goes on.

\clearpage\phantomsection\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{The Stonemouth Book of Remedies, Being What a Dresser of Stone Sets to the Lime-Burn, the White Cough, the Fall from the Bank, the Ferr-Thin, the Lead-Rat’s Bite, the Birth-Flower and the Child That Comes Cold, Written in the Dust of the Lime Yard with the Errors Left Standing}
\CRsheetheading{The Stonemouth Book of Remedies, Being What a Dresser of Stone Sets to the Lime-Burn, the White Cough, the Fall from the Bank, the Ferr-Thin, the Lead-Rat’s Bite, the Birth-Flower and the Child That Comes Cold, Written in the Dust of the Lime Yard with the Errors Left Standing}
{\centering\FellFont\itshape\footnotesize\color{faded} A quarry-leech’s book of remedies in the Stonemouth manner, set down on the back of a spoiled lime-warrant with the counts cut in the margin by a tally-point; the cures in a stone-dresser’s hand, the objections of a physician come down from Greybank pressed blue-grey into the gutter, the corrections of a College clerk in narrow upright Ledgerhand, a bank-master’s line in chalk at the foot of the remedies, a washing-song with the odd ones left standing, and one line at the foot in a hand nobody will own · Written at Stonemouth, where the Ferr joins the Ilm five leagues upriver of Sill, between Stone of Y.H. 811 and Ilmen of Y.H. 813, the Long Cold and the Thin Year, by Ivo of Stonemouth, a dresser of coarse sandstone who has set bones and caught children in the lime yard for three-and-twenty years; begun on the back of a lime-warrant spoiled by a wetting, cut at the edge with a tally-point, folded into oiled sailcloth and carried downriver at the Opening of the Slates, then copied at Greybank in Smoke of Y.H. 813 onto the back of a discarded weigh-slip. It survives with lime worked into the grain at the head, a blue-grey tideline off the Ferr that has taken two words clean off the second leaf, a reed-wolf’s tooth pressed into the lower corner by a buyer who paid two marks and did not stay to see it written, a ring of barley-water, a grey Ash print from a cuff nobody will own, a strip of salt-paper pasted over one correction and gone soft at the edge so that the correction shows through, three objections in the cold margin hand of the physician, the clerk’s upright hand above the cures, the bank-master’s chalk at the remedies, and the line at the foot\par}\medskip
I dress stone for a living and have set bones and caught children in this yard for three-and-twenty years. Nobody asked me for this book. A man came in off the bank in the lean week with both hands gone white to the wrist and asked what I did for the lime, and I heard myself answer in my father’s voice, and did not know whether I believed it. A remedy you have to say in your father’s voice is a remedy nobody has looked at in a long while. I have looked at some of mine here; the rest I have left standing, because a man at three in the morning wants a hand more than a correction.

I write on the back of a lime-warrant that a wetting spoiled. The figures went before anybody could charge them. The lime at the head is off the cuff I wipe the chisel with. The blue in the gutter came off the Ferr when I washed a man’s arm in it, which I have not done since. Nothing in this book is free. Here a thing that costs nothing has usually been paid for by whoever carried the lime.

\subsection*{The order of the dressing yard}

\emph{Cut small into the first leaf with the tally-point, with one word gone over in lime.}

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item Lay the sick one on sacking, never on bare stone. Stone takes from a body faster than a bed does, and a man laid on it goes cold from the side he lies on. A physician from Greybank says a cold stone draws the heat out. I have set my line above his. Both stand.

\item Ask what he carried before you ask what ails him. A man who has carried lime knows where his back hurts; a man who has carried nothing will tell you where it ought to. This is not kindness. It is the order of the yard.

\item Turn the slate face down before you go to a child. I have no slate-name and never shall; the weigh-clerk here sets his figure to a tooth before he looks at the man who brought it, and I have no wish to be taken for that kind of reader.

\item Put the warm stone in wool at the belly and try it on your own wrist first. The stone comes off the kiln bank, and somebody paid for the coal that warmed it.

\item Set the splint loose enough to see a finger under it.

\item When the third night comes, let the woman do the counting; a number counted for her belongs to whoever counted it.

\item Do not drink from the Ferr or wash a wound in it. We have said the opposite for four hundred years and have put the old line underneath rather than lose it.

\end{itemize}

\subsection*{The remedies, as they are used}

Trouble — What is set to it — The manner of it — Who is spent\par

The lime-burn (both hands, or the forearm where the sleeve rides back) — Tallow first, then a clean fold; never dry lime — The men shake lime on a burn to dry the wet, believing white is clean. The physician says lime eats and does not dry. I have dressed three such hands with lime on them and found a white line under the skin in all three, and have not done it a fourth time. — The hand; and the household that bought the lime.\par

The white cough — Steam of hot water under a cloth; honey if the house has it — We say the dust of the good stone cuts the dust of the bad. The physician says it is stone in the lung, and the only physic is to leave the yard, which no house here can do. I sent three up the ridge; two came back worse, because the ridge has stone of its own. — The man, in the morning he coughs up a colour he will not discuss.\par

The Ferr-thin (a season at the well) — Barley-water, a stone at the belly, and work — We say it is the cold of the water and that a warm body keeps it out. The physician says the water carries lead down off the old working and that warmth has nothing to do with it. I have sent men warm to the kiln and watched them go thinner by the fifth month; one went off it after his daughter took him up to Cold Acre. I have not sent anybody else. — The household, which cannot move six leagues to good water.\par

The sweet line at the gum — Sour barley-water; the gum rubbed with wood-ash — The pots from High Kiln carry the green, and the women taste the glaze to get the colour, and say a sweet answers a sweet. The physician says it is lead and that sour water only troubles the teeth. I have seen the line go off a girl who left the glaze room and come back on one who stayed. I have not seen the lead. — The glaze room, which cannot stop and does not ask.\par

A fall from the bank — Two hands, a lath of straight sandstone, a fold of wet cloth; set it before the swelling takes — We say a bone dressed green takes the tool the way a block does. The physician says wet cloth about a limb cools what should be kept warm. I have set eleven and had three come crooked; one hand I bound too tight for fear of its moving, and it did not come back. — The man, in the holding still. This is the row where I have been least honest.\par

A lead-rat’s bite — Tallow and a clean fold; burn the tails, two bits a score — We say one bite is nothing and a hundred make a thin child. The physician wrote the year Y.H. 641 in the margin, when this was known, and noted it was forgotten; he says the rat and the glaze carry the same lead. I have put the year where he wrote it and left the rat under it. — The household, whose children go thin by degrees; the catcher, paid by the tail.\par

The birth-flower (the red branch) — Nothing. Two fingers crossed, and the word the mother gives — A woman of the washing crossed two fingers at a child of this yard and covered it with a date, the way they do at Sill. I have put the date in the margin. The physician says it is a flowering of the blood and not a flower, and is right in a language nobody here speaks. — Nobody knows. The child’s skin, perhaps.\par

A child that comes with the cold on it — A stone in wool at the belly, a living body under the fold, a watch to the fourth day — It comes when the birth is in Stone, and the hands go first. We walk them, believing a moving child keeps its heat. The physician says a child made warm spends faster and that a cold child cannot clot. I have watched nine and held two; all saw the fourth morning, and one went thin. I have left the count with the woman who did the watching. — The household, one night’s sleep, and sometimes the child.\par

Nothing here is given away. It is carried from one body into another and called a cure. That is the only sentence in this book I will stand behind.

\subsection*{The note in the block}

The masons tap a block with the butt of a hammer-handle before they dress a face. A sound one answers full and a flawed one answers flat, a small dead sound that stops at the skin of the stone and will not go through. This is the one thing in this country that costs nothing and is still allowed to be true.

I tapped a man once, gone thin after a winter at the well, and put my ear to the little flat I thought I heard. The flat was not in him. A body is not a block. I did not say so at the time, because there was a weigh-clerk in the room. I have written it here, which is a different matter.

The cup on the bench knows more about whether a room held its warm through the night than the man in it, and I set the stone by the cup’s note and not by the yard bell, which counts something of its own.

\subsection*{What the well by the Ferr keeps}

The well was never sweetened. The clause is on the treaty slate and the factor at Greybank pasted his salt-paper over it, and the strip has lifted at one corner so that six words show and the rest do not. I have washed men at that well for three-and-twenty years and have never once tasted lead in it.

In the year of the water the households drank all winter and called it thin. The well-song, taken down at the washing from a woman who had learned it from women who had, says they did; the road-book at Sill entered three hundred households and no dead. A small hard hand put seventy-one against Stonemouth, and twenty-one went downriver and were not entered again.

The physician wrote \emph{visitation of the water} above our \emph{cold water}, true in a language nobody at this well speaks. He was right about the lead and had nothing to put in its place that a household here could pay for, and the well kept the larger part, as the song says. I have set his sentence above mine and left the twenty-one underneath, where a clerk carrying a round sum will not think to look.

\subsection*{The washing-song}

\emph{Sung low at the tubs, not at the kiln. There is a place after the second verse the length of a row that was never entered.}

\begin{quote}\itshape The Ferr came down with a blue-grey skin,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the clause was pasted, the charge not paid;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape a pale line shows at the lip’s inner edge\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape where the pot from High Kiln has been tasted.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Three hundred stand where a slate has them,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and seventy-one by the well we know;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape a man goes thin in the fifth month\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the cup gives back what the water took.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Sing to the tub, sing to the flat cup,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape sing to the woman who counts under wool;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape what comes back is not what went,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and comes back as it can ---\end{quote}

A clerk of the College put a round nought in the place and wrote \emph{nil} beneath it. A nought is a figure. The twenty-one went downriver and stayed a row.

\subsection*{What the physician pressed in the margin}

He came down from Greybank in Smoke of Y.H. 811 with a book that had the word \emph{lead} in it and a hand that wrote without asking. Against the lime he set \emph{caustic; no efficacy}, against the birth-flower \emph{a mark in the blood, nothing more}, and against the white cough \emph{the dust of the stone, and no physic but departure}, which is true and of no use to a household whose living is cut out of that stone.

He was right about all three. I have left his sentences above mine, so the next reader can tell which is which, and put my words back underneath where a man at three in the morning will find them.

\subsection*{What the College clerk did}

He borrowed the leaf at Greybank when the winter lime was being counted.

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item Against my column headed \emph{Who is spent} he wrote \emph{No cost entered}, which is a true thing in a dishonest place.

\item Where I wrote \emph{we drink all winter and call it thin}, he set \emph{a reduction in the measure was recorded} above, as though the drinker had gone out of the sentence and left the measure standing by itself.

\item Where I wrote \emph{the well was never sweetened}, he wrote \emph{the obligation remains outstanding}, which is the most beautiful sentence I have ever read in a hand that has never drawn water in the dark.

\end{itemize}

I have put the verbs back underneath. A clerk can speak without verbs because he is never in the yard; a man who has carried lime wants to know who paid for the coal.

\subsection*{In the margin, in chalk, the bank-master’s hand}

\begin{quote}\itshape A block tells you when it is dressed. A man does not. I have dressed four hundred blocks and two hands, and neither hand gave a note. --- R.\end{quote}

He wrote it at the foot of the remedies while I was at the well. I have set his line above my row and mine under it, as the yard keeps the old cut showing under the new dressing. A man who has lost a hand to his own trade is allowed one sentence in a book of physic.

\subsection*{At the head and in the gutter}

The lime at the head is mine and will not wash out. The blue tideline came up the second leaf the morning I washed a Ferr-thin man’s arm and has taken two words clean off it; I have not written them back, because a remedy with two words gone is said slowly. A buyer pressed the tooth in the corner, paid two marks for it and said a good tooth remembers the shape of a way. The ring of barley-water came from a cup set down while I told a man to drink and he would not. The grey along the fold is not mine; I have not swept it, and there is no Last Day in this yard. The salt-paper strip has lifted at one corner, so a correction shows through that was meant to be covered, which is the only honest thing that paper has done.

\subsection*{At the foot, in a hand nobody will own}

\begin{quote}\itshape The block keeps the cut and the well keeps the dust;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape neither was asked who drank, or who paid.\end{quote}

I asked the physician, the College clerk and a woman at the washing, and had three answers and no hand. I have left the line where it was written. Tomorrow a man will come in off the bank with a hand gone white or a child that will not breathe, and I shall put the verbs back and turn the slate face down before I look at the child --- because a child is not a block and a body is not a cup, and the yard has room for both truths if a man leaves them side by side.

\clearpage\phantomsection\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{The Sermon at the Listening Stones, Being What Om of the Long Sitting Said Against the Fourth Stone on the Hearth Drawing of Y.H. 812, with the Sitting-Song Left with Its Number Unsaid, the Sittings in a Stone-Tally, a Mine-Reeve’s Clerk’s Correction, and a Line at the Foot in a Hand Nobody Will Own}
\CRsheetheading{The Sermon at the Listening Stones, Being What Om of the Long Sitting Said Against the Fourth Stone on the Hearth Drawing of Y.H. 812, with the Sitting-Song Left with Its Number Unsaid, the Sittings in a Stone-Tally, a Mine-Reeve’s Clerk’s Correction, and a Line at the Foot in a Hand Nobody Will Own}
{\centering\FellFont\itshape\footnotesize\color{faded} A sermon of the Long Sitting preached at the shrine of the Standing Stones five leagues above Keld Keep, where the Vorr sit and come away with numbers; the sayings in the short one-sentence speech of the Vorr set down in Grathic, the sitting-song with the number left as it is not spoken, the sittings in a stone-tally, one correction in the narrow upright hand of a mine-reeve’s clerk who learned his letters out of a Court primer, and one line at the foot in a hand nobody will own · Preached on Stone 12, Y.H. 812, the Hearth Drawing of the Thin Year, on a morning when the wind came over the Cold Pass and snow stood in the joints of the stones, by Om of the Long Sitting, a Vorr who had sat at the Stones since his fortieth year; written that evening by the woman who keeps the stone-shelter and counts the warm-stone issued to sitters, in charcoal on the back of a survey-sheet spoiled by a lead-rub, folded with a warm-stone chip shut in the crease and tied with a turn of iron wire, and kept since in the tin at the shelter among the tally-stones. It survives with pale lead dust worked into the head off the survey rubbing, cold stone grit in the grain, a warm-stone chip in the fold, a tallow thumb at the head, iron filings caught in the gutter, a grey Ash print along the foot from a cuff nobody will own, a wet ring where a tin of melted snow stood from the first voice to the last, a pressed lichen shut in the second crease, one correction in the narrow upright hand of a mine-reeve’s clerk come up from Keld Keep to take the winter count of warm-stone, and a line struck through and written again very small underneath in a hand that has never come forward. Copied at Greybank in Ilmen, Y.H. 813, into the factor’s file of northern sayings, with the verbs put back and the number left as it was not spoken.\par}\medskip
I keep the stone-shelter at the Listening Stones and count out the warm-stone to sitters, and nobody asked me for this. I write because Om spoke to a stone and the stone gave a number, and he would not say what the number counted. He spoke to the stone, to the snow in its joint, to the number itself, and last of all to us, which is the order the Vorr use when they have been asked a thing they do not mean to keep. I have set his words down in Grathic, which is not his tongue, and where he left a verb out I have put it back underneath in my own hand, because a saying said over a stone is a thing a person has to carry down the mountain and use.

The pale at the head is lead dust off the survey-sheet; no brushing takes it out of the grain. The grit is stone ground small by forty winters of palms against the Fourth, and scratches a nail. The chip in the fold is warm-stone from the ration, still faintly warm though it has lain here since the Hearth Drawing. The grey came off a cuff laid where no cuff has business on a counted stone; I have not swept it. The ring is the tin of snow, set down at the first voice and taken up before he saw it.

\subsection*{The manner of the sitting, as the Stones actually have it}

\emph{Written small, from watching, not from any order the Keep has printed.}

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item Come up in the dark before the wind. A man who comes at noon sees his own shadow on the stone and calls it the stone’s answer.

\item Keep the warm-stone in the pocket against the thigh, not in the hand. The hand must be the cold thing. A warm hand reads its own heat and calls it the number.

\item Lay the flat of the palm to the stone. Do not knock. A pot answers the knuckle; a stone answers the sitting.

\item Sit until the cold is ordinary. The first hour belongs to the stone, the second to you, and after that to neither.

\item Ask one question. The stone will give a number. Do not ask what it counts or who paid for it; the stone allows one question.

\item If the number is correct, say \emph{The numbers are correct} and stop. That sentence is true and not a translation. Anything more is a man hearing himself.

\item Do not cut your measure into the stone. The arm is for that. The stones are older than the arm and need no telling.

\item If the stone sweats and the smell of hot lead comes up, go down without counting the hour. The mountain gives warning once.

\item When a man with a slate comes among the sitters, stop, and begin again after. His figure is for a room below. Do not lay the two together.

\end{itemize}

He said the last twice, once to the stone and once to a man in a Keldish coat writing nothing I could see.

\subsection*{The sermon, as he said it}

\subsection*{Of the number}

He had his left palm flat on the Fourth Stone, and the snow went on standing in the joint beside his fingers as though the hand had told it to.

“I sat from my fortieth year,” he said. “I have come away with a number.”

A man from the duelling floor asked what the number was. This is what every visitor asks, and the Vorr have one answer for it.

“The numbers are correct,” Om said.

“Correct of what?”

“Of the counting,” he said. “That is the whole sentence. If I add a name to it, I have made the number a debt, and there was no debt at the stone.”

He drew the hand back and looked at the palm as a man looks at a tool set down in the wrong place. There was no mark on it. The Vorr hold their measure in the bone, and there is nothing on the skin to read.

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{The people answered, and the Keldish among them said it with the flat short vowels of the Keep:}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape The stone keeps the number; it does not say of whom.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Margin, in my hand:} He used a Vorr word for \emph{correct} that also means \emph{unmoved}, as a stone is unmoved in wind. I set \emph{correct}, the Keep’s word. He would not have the other written.\end{quote}

\subsection*{Of the arm}

A young duellist of the Tenth Clamp stood with his sleeve up, showing the numbers cut into his forearm at thirteen. A scar crossed them where an old figure had been taken out and a new one put in after a thin return.

“There is the honest way to keep a count,” Om said, and nodded at the arm. “A knife put it there. A knife can take it out. A man can see his own number and know which of it is his and which was pressed in by somebody else’s account.”

He put his palm back on the stone.

“This one cannot be cut out. It does not lie under the skin. It lies where the sitting put it, and the sitting was mine.”

The duellist said that a number a man could not show was no use in a duel, and several of the younger ones laughed, though not loudly.

“No use in a duel,” Om said. “That is true. I have never fought one. You would win and I would sit, and we should both have what we are good at.”

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{The people answered:}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape The stone keeps the number; it does not say of whom.\end{quote}

\subsection*{Of the oldest repair}

A surveyor of the seam stood at the edge, his slate turned face down against his forearm, as surveyors carry a thing they will not have read over in the wind.

“He will tell you,” Om said, without looking at him, “that the rim-seam shows repair laid over repair, that the oldest are not stone and not clay, and that in the record they look like language. Then he will stop and turn his slate face down, because the man who wrote the entry before his was taken out of the shaft.”

The surveyor said nothing. That is the answer the Keep gives when a thing is true and not to be carried further.

“You cannot translate a repair,” Om said. “You can only lay another over it. A mended thing keeps the break under the patch. Ask the pot, not the potter. The pot knows where it was opened.”

A woman beside me asked what the oldest repairs were made of, which is what the surveyor had been asked and had not answered.

“A question with a use,” he said. “I have sat at four stones and none has given me a word for it. They have given me numbers. A number is the shape of a thing with the thing taken away. If you want the thing, sit longer than I did, and be colder.”

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{The people answered:}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape The stone keeps the number; it does not say of whom.\end{quote}

\subsection*{Of never owed}

He turned then from the stone to the company, which he had not done until that hour, and spoke in the short sentences they use at the Stones.

“The Court says a vessel is emptied and pressed into another and the account stands. It says this to the dying so they may go away quiet. It is a sentence with a slate at the end of it.”

He held up the palm that had been on the stone.

“We are not collected. Our measure is in the bone and the tube has nowhere to take hold. When a Vorr dies the others seat him upright facing the way he came and leave him. We say: we were never owed. Say it to a collector and he goes away, because there is no account to draw and no infant to press it into.”

A man come up from the low country asked whether that was a mercy or a refusal. There is no Grathic word that holds the two together, and Om would not choose one.

“It is what we say,” he said. “I have never called it mercy. Mercy is a word with a giver in it.”

He put the palm back for the last time. The snow in the joint had not moved while he spoke.

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{The people answered, and the Vorr among them said it once and did not say it twice:}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape The stone keeps the number; it does not say of whom.\end{quote}

\subsection*{The sitting-song}

\emph{Sung low, seated, palm on the stone. The Keldish take the second and fourth lines; the Vorr take the last two. The number is not spoken, and I have left the space its length.}

\begin{quote}\itshape Sat from forty and the snow in the joint,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the stone gave a number and keeps its own;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the arm takes the mark and the knife takes it out,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the slate puts back what the knife took out.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Three for the sitting and one for the cold,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape one for the hand that would not be told;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the surveyor turns his slate to the ground\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the oldest repair is not clay, not stone.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Here the number is not spoken. The sitter makes no sound.}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape The stone keeps the number; it does not say of whom;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape we were never owed, and the snow fills the print;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the count is correct and the count is not ours,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the hand goes down with the number in it.\end{quote}

A girl asked what the space was for. Nobody answered her. The clerk put a round nought against it, which I have left where he set it.

\subsection*{The stone-tally, as the shelter keeps it}

\emph{A warm-stone goes out with a sitter and comes back with him, or does not. These sittings I set down where they stood, and the numbers are not entered, because no number has been given out at these stones.}

Stone — Who sat — What was asked of the stone — What the stone gave\par

The Fourth, from his fortieth year — Om of the Long Sitting — nothing; he sat and came down — a number, kept, not spoken\par

The Fourth, one winter — a duellist of the Tenth Clamp — whether his arm would hold through the season — the figure at thirteen, still standing\par

The Second — a surveyor come up from the First Seam — what the oldest repair was made of — \emph{the numbers are correct}, which is not a translation\par

The First — a woman whose son went down to the bank — whether he had been entered — a figure; she carried it down and said nothing of it\par

The Third — the mine-reeve’s clerk, taking the winter count — nothing entered — nil, written above the four\par

The place under the Fifth — nobody — nothing — no stone, and no sitting\par

There were sittings before these, and the old keeper could set a winter to most of them; I have not written the winters, because a row of years is a thing a clerk can carry away and a stone is not. The place under the Fifth has no stone, and I have left it in the tally so the row may be read the way it stands.

\subsection*{What the clerk did}

He came up from Keld Keep on the third day with ink in two fingers, borrowed the leaf while I was at the ration-tin, and gave it back with the verbs taken out.

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item At \emph{the stone gave a number}: \emph{a figure was returned to the sitter}, above and underlined.

\item At \emph{the numbers are correct}: \emph{sentence affirmed; referent not stated}.

\item At \emph{we were never owed}: \emph{declaration of non-liability; not recognised}, with a small stop between two clusters of his neat dark hand.

\item At the number kept and not spoken: \emph{no figure produced; enter as nil}.

\item At the gap in the song a round nought and \emph{vacancy}, as though a space where a number is not given were an empty column waiting to be filled.

\end{itemize}

I have put the verbs back underneath and left his hand standing above, as the stone keeps the sitting under the number. He takes them out because a thing always true has no need of anyone to have done it. I put them back because a woman with her palm on a cold stone wants to know who sat.

\subsection*{At the head and in the fold}

The lead at the head grates between the teeth if a person is foolish enough to test it; the glass-men do that once and do not do it again. The grit is stone dust ground by every palm that has sat here, and I know a sitter by it. The chip in the fold has not lost all its heat, which is what warm-stone does. The tallow is mine; I held the leaf down in the wind and did not know I had marked it. The iron in the gutter is filings off the wire at the tie. The grey came off a cuff and I have not swept it. The wet ring is the tin of snow, set down while he spoke of the arm. The lichen lay in the crease when I took the leaf from the sheet, and I have left it. The clerk noticed none of these things, which is how I know he is a good clerk.

\subsection*{At the foot}

Struck through once and written again underneath, very small, in a hand that is not mine, not Om’s, not the surveyor’s and not the clerk’s:

\begin{quote}\itshape A correct number is not a true sentence.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape The stone keeps both, and will not say which is the mercy.\end{quote}

I asked Om, the surveyor, the duellist and the clerk, and had four answerings and no hand. I have left the line struck through and standing, the only honest way to keep a sentence you cannot sign.

The leaf goes back in the tin with the warm-stone chip in its fold and the wire tied as it was. Next Stone the sitters will come up the five leagues from Keld Keep with snow in the joints, and a Vorr will lay a palm to the Fourth and come away with a number unspent. If the clerk comes I shall let him take the verbs out and put them back, and leave the nought in its place and the number where it was not spoken.

\clearpage\phantomsection\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{The Litany Before the Grating, Being the Prayer of the Keepers of the Hearth-Fire at the Weighing, with the Voice’s Corrections and a Junior Keeper’s Margin}
\CRsheetheading{The Litany Before the Grating, Being the Prayer of the Keepers of the Hearth-Fire at the Weighing, with the Voice’s Corrections and a Junior Keeper’s Margin}
{\centering\FellFont\itshape\footnotesize\color{faded} A litany of the Return said by the keepers of the Hearth-fire in the Weighing Hall, the Voice reading and the keepers answering through the bars; set down by a keeper of the third watch who signs with a coal-cross, with the rubrics of the grating, the eight stations and their answer, the Voice’s struck corrections, the second watch’s note, and a line at the foot nobody will own · Written in the Weighing Hall in the Hearthseat on Weighing of Y.H. 812, the Thin Year, by the junior keeper of the third watch, on the back of a spoiled slate-copy of the year’s first measure, and corrected by Hesta Clay, Voice of the Return, before the Remembering; carried through the Opening of the Slates and copied forward in Ash of Y.H. 813 into a quire kept in the iron box under the grating ledge. It survives soft along the fold and scorched at the upper edge, with coal-dust worked into the creases of the first leaf, a lamp-black thumb, iron filings caught in the gutter from the grating hinge, a spot of tallow off the watch lamp, a hair, a grey Ash print from a cuff that had been in the residue room, and a small coal in the fold that nobody will own.\par}\medskip
I am a keeper of the third watch at the grating and I write this where I stand, which is on the north side with my hands behind me. The Voice reads from the ledge in the clean voice, the one that takes her neatly out of her own sentences, and we answer through the bars. I have kept the answer as we say it and the rubrics as the room actually has them, because a rubric written in a clean hand is a rubric for a room with no fire in it. The Voice has borrowed the leaf and given it back with four of my lines struck through. I have left every struck line standing under her words, as a keeper leaves a repair showing.

The coal-dust at the head came off the grate when the hinge was worked on the morning of the Weighing; it goes into the grain and will not come out. The scorch along the upper edge is from a night when a draught came off the Keel and carried a spark against the leaf while I held it to the lamp. I have not cut the scorch away. A prayer with a burn on it has been used, which is more than can be said for a clean one. The filings in the gutter are off the hinge. The grey came off my cuff after I had been in the residue room, and I have not swept it off the leaf. The little coal in the fold is not mine and I have asked the second watch about it and had two answers, neither of which I have written down.

\subsection*{The manner of it, written small at the head}
