\begin{quote}\itshape The smell of hot lead gives whatever warning it gives.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Nothing was said in the Ninth Gallery that could be written down;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape a man went down and the lead told him, and he came up or did not.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape What the lead tells is not entered. What the lead takes is entered by nobody.\end{quote}

\emph{I stop while the rope moves over the mouth. There is no saying for the deep that has not had a man in it. I have tried to write one and left the place the length of it.}

\textbf{The order answers:} Cut the number. Keep the hand. Do not ask the stone what it kept.

\subsection*{VIII. Of those who do not answer}

\begin{quote}\itshape Across the Rim they sit against the Stones and come away with numbers.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape They do not come down to the knife and do not answer at the mouth.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape They say they were never owed.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape We have left the length of their silence standing.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Do not fill it. A filled place is an entered place.\end{quote}

\emph{Here the order turns toward the Rim. At this station the answer is said by nobody. I say it once into the arm, which is not the same as having it answered, and close the space the length of a man sitting against a stone.}

\textbf{The order answers:} \emph{Nothing is said here. The place is kept.}

\subsection*{IX. Of the stone after}

\begin{quote}\itshape The stone is given after the knife and stays warm longer than the man expects.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape He will get worse before he gets better. That is the rule here as everywhere.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape If he comes back wrong, keep him. Keep him anyway.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Do not ask the stone what it kept.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape It will tell you the weather and nothing else.\end{quote}

\emph{I put the warm-stone in the hand that has just been cut. It is the whole of the mercy and the whole of the theft. Somebody paid to have it warm, and the man holding it does not ask, which is the only courtesy the mountain has ever been shown.}

\textbf{The order answers:} Cut the number. Keep the hand. Do not ask the stone what it kept.

\subsection*{What the clerk did}

A clerk of the factor’s office came up with the lead cart and borrowed the leaf at the mouth on a morning when the rope was going down and nobody had a hand to spare. He writes narrow and upright and takes the verbs out as though a verb were a thing a man could carry past a weigh in his boot. He laid his hand on the leaf before he looked at me, which is the manner of that office.

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item Against \emph{the number goes on the arm before the name}, he wrote: \emph{vessel identified by measure at entry.} He has left the mouth out, and the mouth is where the number has to go before anybody will hear it.

\item Against \emph{the Hearth is under this mountain}, he wrote: \emph{claim not admitted; the Hearth is entered under the Keel.} He has not argued with the mountain. He has entered somewhere else and gone away.

\item Against \emph{we leave the earlier showing in the skin}, he wrote: \emph{superseded entry retained, not current.} True in the figure. I have seen a man with two sets on one arm and both hands answered when his mother called, and there is no figure for that in a counting house.

\item Against \emph{two sets is not two men}, he wrote: \emph{duplicate entry. One to be struck.} He strikes men readily. The skin does not agree with him and has never been asked.

\item At the eighth station he put a round nought in the space and wrote \emph{no return required}. This is the truest thing he has written and the cruelest. A nought is a number. They refused the number. I have left his nought standing in the space and my space standing around it, as a crack is left showing under a keying.

\end{itemize}

I have left all of it standing, his hand above mine and mine under it, as an arm keeps the first figures under the second. He takes the verbs out because a thing always true has no need of them. I put them back because a man at the mouth wants to know which hand to hold out.

\subsection*{What the other hand put in the margin}

The iron-red hand is Nessa’s, of the Duelling Floor, cut at thirteen and cut again after the bank, who keeps both counts and has never said which she answers to when somebody calls across a room.

At IV: “My second was cut deeper and I still turn to the first when my mother calls. The mine-reeve entered the deeper. Both hands turned. I have never known which one she was calling to.”

At V: “My brother was entered at eleven and lasted fourteen. On the last morning he asked for the stone and they gave him the figures. I have set this here and not in the stations, because the stations are said over an arm and this is said over a man.”

At VI: “My father held the clamp and was called honest. He ate with the other hand for nine years and never once said the word they used of him.”

At VIII, against \emph{they were never owed}: “I asked one of them at the Stones whether they were cold. He asked me whether I had ever been cut. I did not ask him anything else.”

At the answer: “Say it over the hands. The rest of us are standing here and can hear.”

\subsection*{At the head and in the gutter}

The smut at the head is mine; I hold the leaf down with the hand I cut with and do not know I have marked it, and coal gets into the grain and no wet sleeve takes it out. The red cross is iron oxide off the mine-reeve’s point and stays red in frost. The warm-stone shaving in the fold came off a piece set down and not taken up, and is still warm on the coldest morning, which is the whole argument about where warmth comes from and who paid. The lead bead rolled out of the Ninth Gallery and a surveyor laid it on the leaf and went away without it. The frost-feather grew on the survey stone after a warm night and was gone by noon. The clamp-scratch across the answer was made by a man showing his brother how a clamp bites; both were called honest afterwards and one has a dead hand. The grey on the outer fold came off a cuff that lay where no cuff has business lying, and I have not swept it. The thumb in coal dust at the foot is not mine and not the mine-reeve’s. There is no Last Day at a shaft mouth.

\subsection*{At the foot}

In a hand that is not mine, not the clerk’s and not Nessa’s, struck once and written again underneath, very small:

\begin{quote}\itshape The knife gives before the bank takes.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape The arm keeps two counts. The slate keeps one. The stone keeps none, and is warm.\end{quote}

I asked the cutter at the Descent, a woman cut twice, a man entered at eleven who lasted fourteen, and one of the Vorr at the Stones, who answered me with a question, and had four answers and no hand. I have left the struck line where it was struck. The leaf goes back into the tin at the mouth. Tomorrow a boy will go down at thirteen and hold the stone after the knife, and a man come back thin will hold out his arm, and the old numbers will be cut out and the new cut in deeper, and the mine-reeve will enter the later and leave the earlier showing in the skin, and I shall say nine stations to the arm and keep the eighth place the length of a man sitting against a stone.

\clearpage\phantomsection\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{The Litany of the Third Pouring, Being the Order of the Return as a House of Nine Pots Keeps It When a Woman Comes Back for the Third Time, with the Manner of It, Seven Stations and the Answer Said to the Cloth, the Three Knots Counted Out, a Factor’s Clerk’s Correction in Narrow Upright Ledgerhand, a Bowl-Leech’s Cold Objection, a Daughter’s Charcoal, and a Line at the Foot Nobody Will Own}
\CRsheetheading{The Litany of the Third Pouring, Being the Order of the Return as a House of Nine Pots Keeps It When a Woman Comes Back for the Third Time, with the Manner of It, Seven Stations and the Answer Said to the Cloth, the Three Knots Counted Out, a Factor’s Clerk’s Correction in Narrow Upright Ledgerhand, a Bowl-Leech’s Cold Objection, a Daughter’s Charcoal, and a Line at the Foot Nobody Will Own}
{\centering\FellFont\itshape\footnotesize\color{faded} A prayer of the Return said in a potter’s house at Nine Pots on the evening a woman is brought back for the third time, the woman of the house reading from a folded birth-cloth and the household answering to the knots; written in charcoal on the back of a spoiled clay-docket, with the rubrics of the house, seven stations and their answer, the pourings set in a table with the figure entered and the figure that came back, one correction in the narrow upright hand of a factor’s clerk out of Greybank, the pressed objection of a bowl-leech come up from the south, a daughter’s thick charcoal in the margin, and a line at the foot in a hand nobody will own · Written at Nine Pots, eight leagues west of Sill, in Tallow of Y.H. 813, the year after the Thin Year, by the woman of a potter’s house who keeps the birth-cloth, and signed with three knots of grey wool and not with a name; carried down the Clay Road to Sill on the evening of an Account-day and borrowed there by a clerk of the factor at Greybank, who set his hand above hers and put a nought in the fourth place; kept since in the fold of the grey wool cloth on the pot-shelf, taken out after the evening figure has been read and put back before the lamp is trimmed. It survives with clay worked brown into the head, a bone-pale streak of slip down the gutter, the print of a wet pot’s foot at the third fold, a tallow thumb, a grey Ash print nobody will own, a cold-iron shaving out of a tube’s wool wrap, a thread of grey wool from the cloth which comes back after every shaking, a browned crust pressed flat between the fifth and sixth leaves, a green bead of lead glaze in the lower corner, the clerk’s correction standing above the words it corrects, the leech’s cold objection in the margin, and a line struck through and written again very small underneath in a hand that has never come forward\par}\medskip
I keep the cloth on the shelf above the pots at Nine Pots. It was cut from the birth-sheet of the woman who is now coming back for the third time, and it has three knots in one corner and a fourth place the length of a thumb left empty. I tied the first knot myself. I tied the second with my sister’s hand over mine, and I tied the third alone, after the figure had gone up the Clay Road and nobody in the house would say what it had been read over.

The Court has an order for the drawing and an order for the pressing and a form for the joining of vessels. It has no words for a house that has had the same woman poured three times and must set a cup down for her all over again. So we say this. I sign with the three knots because a name on a prayer is an entry, and an entry can be read out at a Weighing by a man who never held the cloth.

The brown at the head is clay and has gone into the grain. The streak in the gutter is slip off a marriage-pot set down while I sought a word and left standing until it went pale. The print at the third fold is a wet pot’s foot; it was not made on purpose and I have not rubbed it out. The grey came off a cuff that had been in the corner where the grey gathers, and there is no Last Day in this house that has ever reached that corner.

\subsection*{The manner of it, written small at the head}

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item Lay the cloth on the table before the child is brought in, and count the knots with your thumb. Said to the child these sentences become questions with answers owed, and not one of them has an answer owed in it.

\item The answer belongs to the house, including the girl at the wheel and the man come up from Greybank with the slate, who says it with his hands behind him. Do not correct him, and do not correct the child, who says it worst.

\item The bell at the Cross is eight leagues off and does not come up the road. We keep four and four and the gap without hearing it, which is a poorer thing than hearing and is the only thing available.

\item Set a cup down at every station and do not drink from it. At the third station the cup is set on the cloth and is not lifted until the end. Nobody pours for herself in this house on this evening.

\item Do not untie the knots to see which name is which. The names went soft after the second pouring and we stopped reading them. A knot keeps what a mouth lets go.

\item Leave the fourth place the length of a thumb. Do not tie it and do not put a figure in it. It is not waiting for anybody; it is the room the house has and cannot fill.

\end{itemize}

\subsection*{The litany}

\emph{I read from the cloth. The house answers to the knots. The answer is the same at every station, which is why it is a litany and not an argument with a bank.}

\subsection*{I. Of the cloth}

\begin{quote}\itshape The cloth was cut from a birth-sheet and hemmed with a potter’s thread.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Three knots are tied in it and no fourth is tied.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape A name given at the pouring is a name given to be spent.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape A name kept in the cloth is kept to be looked at and not read.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape We do not untie the first to find the third.\end{quote}

\emph{Answer:} Keep the name. Leave the place. Come back as you can.

\subsection*{II. Of the figures}

\begin{quote}\itshape The first came back whole, at twelve hundred marks,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape with forty unspent measures nobody has explained.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape The second came back thinner. The third came back thinner again.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape The deduction stood at one in twelve through all three,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape as the notice says, read twice and not argued with.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape The figure fell twice. The deduction never fell.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape That is the whole of the arithmetic this house knows.\end{quote}

\emph{Answer:} Keep the name. Leave the place. Come back as you can.

\subsection*{III. Of the pouring}

\begin{quote}\itshape One measure into one vessel: they say she comes back with her name,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape with the hand that held the cup and the price of bread in a year gone by.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Many into many: they say she comes back as she can,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape with a hankering for a table nobody in this house set.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Both are poured into a clean hand. The clean hand is not the hand that held the pot.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape We have set the two sayings down side by side and have not made them one.\end{quote}

\emph{Answer:} Keep the name. Leave the place. Come back as you can.

\subsection*{IV. Of the cup and the hand}

\begin{quote}\itshape The hand goes to the cup before the eyes go to the face.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape She came back and went toward a cup before the cup was shown.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape The cup was shown. She took it and did not drink.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Her grandmother drank from it and would not say why.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Set the cup down anyway. It is the oldest courtesy here.\end{quote}

\emph{Here the cup is set on the cloth. The ring it leaves is not a figure and has never been counted. My daughter says the ring is the only thing in this house that nobody has tried to explain.}

\emph{Answer:} Keep the name. Leave the place. Come back as you can.

\subsection*{V. Of the door}

\begin{quote}\itshape She says a name this house never gave her\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and reaches for a door this wall has not got.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Stand by the cloth and not by the door.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape A door stood by is a door somebody will come through.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Do not ask which of the three she has come back as.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Ask which of the three she is not, and do not ask it aloud.\end{quote}

\emph{Answer:} Keep the name. Leave the place. Come back as you can.

\subsection*{VI. Of the iron}

\begin{quote}\itshape The tube came up the Clay Road in wool and went away with a figure.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Cold iron takes from the drawer as well as from the drawn.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Somebody’s fingers went grey at the third pouring.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape In this house we have not asked whose, which is not the same as not knowing.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape The collector does not come into this room and does not hear the answer.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape What he takes is entered. What it cost to take is said here and nowhere else.\end{quote}

\emph{Answer:} Keep the name. Leave the place. Come back as you can.

\subsection*{VII. Of the fourth place}

\begin{quote}\itshape The fourth place is the length of a thumb and is not tied.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape It is not a name forgotten and it is not a nought.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape It is where the cloth has room for what the house cannot hold.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Do not tie it. A knot tied too soon is a debt paid too soon.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Keep her. Keep the cup. Leave the place as it is.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Come back as you can. Come back as it can.\end{quote}

\emph{Here the house leaves a space the width of a thumb. It is not a line forgotten. It is the place where the third name would stand if we had kept one, and where the second woman sat when the first figure was read, and where I sat when the third was read. Nobody ties it.}

\emph{Answer:} Keep the name. Leave the place. Come back as you can.

\subsection*{The pourings, as the cloth keeps them}

\emph{Figures in the clerk’s hand, copied from the slate. The last column is mine and has no standing at any bank. A dash is a place where no figure was made, not a nought.}

Pouring — Year — As the slate named her — Figure entered — Figure that came back — What the house did\par

First — Y.H. 806 — A thrower of the low yard, come up to this house — whole, 1200 marks — forty unspent measures — Cut the cloth. Tied the first knot.\par

Second — Y.H. 809 — The same, entered as a new vessel — 210, struck to 190 — — — Tied the second knot. Stopped reading the names.\par

Third — Y.H. 812 — A child three days old in this house — 22 — not weighed — Tied the third knot. Left the fourth place the length of a thumb.\par

Draws on this leaf: three. Knots tied: three. Figures struck: one. The cup-ring and the pot’s foot are not figures and have not been added.

\subsection*{What the clerk did}

A clerk of the factor came up from Greybank with the evening tally, with ink settled in two fingers of a cuff gone soft from washing. He did not take the verbs out of this leaf, which surprised me. He took the woman out instead, which is the stranger thing to do to a cloth.

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item At \emph{keep the name}, he wrote \emph{a birth-name was entered on the slate; no further entry required}. Both stand. The slate has one name and the cloth has three, and they are not the same name.

\item At \emph{the figure fell twice}, he set the printed figure above each fallen one, larger. He went down the three rows with his thumb before he wrote it, which is how I know he had read what he was correcting.

\item At \emph{she reaches for a door this wall has not got}, he wrote \emph{disorientation following the pouring; not unusual}. True in his language and of no use to a woman standing by a wall.

\item At the forty unspent measures he wrote \emph{not in this jurisdiction} and underlined it twice. They have been in every jurisdiction for seven years and nobody has explained them, which is not the same as their being nowhere.

\item At the fourth place he put a round nought and wrote \emph{vacancy} beside it. A nought is a number. The place was the length of a thumb.

\end{itemize}

I have left every line of his standing above mine and mine under it, as the new glaze lies over the old break and does not take the break away.

\subsection*{What the bowl-leech pressed in the margin}

He came up from the south through Greybank with myrrh in his coat-fold and a hand that writes cold.

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item Against the door: \emph{a disorder of the memory, not a visitor}.

\item Against the third pouring: \emph{settling of the graft; the ordinary worsening}.

\item Against \emph{unsafe to marry}, which the old women say when no officer listens: he wrote nothing, and drew a small line under the word \emph{three}.

\end{itemize}

He is right in a cold language. I have kept his sentences above ours so the next reader can tell which hand was nearer the woman and which was nearer the book.

\subsection*{What my daughter put in the charcoal}

The thick letters are hers, made with a stick from the kiln and not a pen. She has sat at two of the three pourings and says she will not sit at a fourth.

At the cup: “She did not drink. I put the cup in her hand and she held it the way you hold a thing you have been given before and cannot place. Then she let go. Her grandmother drank it and looked at the door. I have asked her twice and she will not say why.”

At the third figure: “I was in the room when they read it over her. They read the number twice and did not once say the word child. I have kept that and put nothing under it.”

At the fourth place, beneath the clerk’s nought: “Not a vacancy. The place where my mother’s mother stood when the first figure was read. I stood there when the third was read. It is the same place and it is not a number.”

At the answer: “I have said it wrong at three pourings. I have not let anybody correct it.”

\subsection*{At the head and in the cloth}

The tallow is off the lamp I keep low, so that a woman at the table will not change her words when she hears the charcoal. The crust went into the grain at the fifth fold and I have not brushed it; a woman from Low Kiln held it for a child not in this room and would not take a mark for it. The thread of grey wool comes out of the cloth and goes on coming out, though I have shaken the leaf three times. The green bead is lead glaze, pressed in by a girl with the sweetness still at her mouth who leaned over to see what was being written. The iron has never once drawn the warm out of the paper, which is the only kindness this shelf affords.

We sweep the floor of this house on the Last Day and burn what we find in the morning and call it dealt with. The corner above the pots is not swept and has never been called dealt with. I have kept the print where it fell.

\subsection*{At the foot, in a hand nobody will own}

\begin{quote}\itshape The bank keeps the figure. The cloth keeps the knots.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape The woman keeps neither, and comes back anyway.\end{quote}

Struck once and written again underneath, very small:

\begin{quote}\itshape She is not the sum of the three. She is what is left after the third.\end{quote}

I asked the clerk, the girl at the wheel and a woman who has sat at a pouring in a house two streets over, and had three answers and no hand. I have left the struck line where it was struck.

The leaf goes back into the fold of the cloth and the cloth goes back on the shelf above the pots. Next Account-day a clerk will come up from Greybank with a soft cuff and put another nought in the fourth place, and I shall read seven stations to the knots and leave the gap where the bell is not heard, and the girl at the wheel will say the answer wrong and I shall not correct her. There is still room in the cloth for a fourth knot, and I have not tied it, and I go on not tying it.

\clearpage\phantomsection\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{The Long Night Riddles, Being a Contest Held with the Fire Banked under Slate Row in the Hearthseat, with Four Questions Put in the Dark, the Fifth Answered by a Voice Nobody Could Place, the Warm Places Read by Touch at First Grey, a College Clerk’s Figures Set Above at the Remembering, and One Line at the Foot Nobody Will Own}
\CRsheetheading{The Long Night Riddles, Being a Contest Held with the Fire Banked under Slate Row in the Hearthseat, with Four Questions Put in the Dark, the Fifth Answered by a Voice Nobody Could Place, the Warm Places Read by Touch at First Grey, a College Clerk’s Figures Set Above at the Remembering, and One Line at the Foot Nobody Will Own}
{\centering\FellFont\itshape\footnotesize\color{faded} An alehouse keeper’s record of a night with no light, set down for the settling of an argument about a voice and not for the improvement of the reader; the rules in the hand that covers the hearth, the questions in the words they were put in the dark, the answers as they came back out of it, the score read by the warmth of hands on the bench at first grey, the figures of a College clerk entered above afterwards, a coal-woman’s gloss pressed into the margin in broad charcoal, and one line at the foot in a hand nobody will claim · Written at first grey on the morning of the Remembering, Y.H. 812, the Thin Year, at the alehouse called the Covered Fire in the lane under Slate Row in the Hearthseat, by the woman who keeps the room and covers the hearth at dusk; set down from what she remembered of the voices before the fire was uncovered, because what is spent in the night is not entered in the morning. Written in lamp-black thinned with small ale on the back of a notice of the Five spoiled when the damp took the clean figure off one corner, folded and sewn with wire into a fold of oiled sacking and kept under the dish beside the banked hearth; copied forward at the Opening of the Slates, Ilmen 1, Y.H. 813, onto the back of a College term-sheet voided by a wet thumb. It survives with a thumb of tallow at the head, lamp-black in the grain of every word, a ring where a cup of water stood from the first question to the fifth and went cold without being drunk, a grey Ash print off a Kept room’s skirting board worked into the gutter, a scorch where a spark off the grating caught the second leaf when the fire was uncovered, the pale ghost of the printed figure showing through one corner, a press of wet wool across the first leaf off a man who held the door and did not let go when he was through, the charcoal rubbed thin where a sleeve went over it in the dark, a damp tide-line out of the sealed-file room along the foot, one correction in the narrow upright hand of a clerk of the College of Assessors, a gloss in the broad charcoal of the woman who carried the dish up from the Hall on Kindling, and a line at the foot which nobody has claimed\par}\medskip
I keep the Covered Fire in the lane under Slate Row, and I cover the hearth at dusk on the Long Night, which is a different work from banking a fire to save it. In this town a fire is covered for one night in the year because the ordinance says no fire after dusk and no light carried between houses, and people sit in the dark and tell the stories of the Return. The fire in this room was lit from the Hall on Kindling, two days before, under a dish of ash carried up the lane by a woman who burned her wrist under the lip. I have kept this house eleven years and have never stood before the fire in the Hall. I have heard it under the grating from the passage and have not looked at it.

There are juniors from the College in the lane on that night and clerks come up from Greybank who cannot get back down the Clay Road before the Five are out. They ask one another questions whose answers they already know, which is a riddle in this trade. A question whose answer nobody knows is a wager, and there is wagering enough in the Hearthseat without a riddle in it.

I have set this down because a man came the next morning and asked whose voice had answered the fifth, and I could not tell him. Nothing is entered of what is spent in the night, which is an article of the Five. I wrote it at first grey with the hearth still covered, from what I remembered of the voices, and put the clerk’s figures where he set them afterwards, above mine, the way the ash of the Last Day is burnt in the morning and called dealt with.

\subsection*{The manner of the night}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item A riddle is put in the dark. Ask for a lamp to answer it and you owe a quart, because the light was for your own pleasure and not for the night.

\item Answer in one breath from where you sit. A second answer is a different riddle and is not heard, because in the dark nobody can tell whose mouth it came from, which is the reason here and the only one.

\item Four are scored from a seat. A fifth may be put from the floor and is not scored; the floor has no place in the dark and cannot be read in the morning.

\item The judge is the dark. I say whether an answer serves and I do not say why. A reason given is a riddle given away for nothing, and there is nobody here to buy it until the fire is uncovered.

\item No slate lies on the bench after dusk. A slate in the dark is a figure with the speaker left out, and the College can write those without help from this room.

\item The stake is a hand laid flat on the bench. At first grey I read the warmth of the hands and not the names, because a name spoken in the dark belongs to whoever says it in the morning.

\end{enumerate}

\subsection*{The four that were scored from a seat}

The first went to a junior of the College, with ink settled in the crease of one cuff and the clean voice they teach in Slate Row.

\begin{quote}\itshape I stand between the flame and the hand;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the hand that tends me has never felt me;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape a man may count my bars and never count my heat.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape What am I?\end{quote}

“The grating,” he said, before I had finished him; then, remembering the order of his house, “before the Hearth-fire, behind the iron.” He said it with the done-to left in, as juniors do when they are not being paid. I scored him and set a warm place down in my mind where his hand had been. There was no light to see whether he sat again.

The second went to a physician come down from the rooms of the Kept, who was on his way back up and would not drink in the dark.

\begin{quote}\itshape He is warm and does not know it;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape he is reckoned at three hundred and pitied under his own roof;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape a hand is brought to him and taken away again,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and he never asks whose warmth it was.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Who sits?\end{quote}

“One of the Kept,” said the physician, low, in the voice of that passage. “He has no want and no memory of a want, which is why we are paid to hold his hand.” Nobody passed the pot. A man who has just held the hand of a Kept vessel does not drink to it, and no rule tells him why.

The third went to a clerk of the Steward’s room, who had come down for the notices and stayed because the lane was dark.

\begin{quote}\itshape I have no last line and I am never closed;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape a kinsman comes to end me and goes away with his name unentered;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape I am read once a year in a clean voice,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the mouths that said me are not on me.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape What am I?\end{quote}

“The roll,” he said. Then, in the hand’s own phrase: “The account carried forward.” He said there was no other kind of account in his room, which is true there and not in the clay country, where a debt left lying is one the slate has never heard of. I scored him. He asked me who had put the question and I told him the dark had put it, which was true and not what he wanted.

The fourth came from the floor, which is not a seat and is not scored, and I set it down because it was said and I had no rule against hearing it.

\begin{quote}\itshape I am covered at dusk and uncovered at first grey;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape I was lit from the Hall and I am not the Hall’s;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape what is spent in me is not written down.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape What am I?\end{quote}

“The Long Night,” said a woman who washes the College linen, into the bench and not to the room. Then she said: “And the fire under the ash is the same fire that was carried on Kindling, which nobody says out loud at the Weighing.” The junior asked whose voice it was and I said the dark’s. There are five warm places on the bench and I have not set a name under any of them.

\subsection*{The fifth, which was put from the door and answered from the floor}

A woman stood at the door with a dish in her hands and did not come in, which is a thing a woman does in this town when she has carried something and wants to set it down where nobody will enter it. She had come up from the rooms of the Kept with coal under one thumbnail she had not washed off. She put the fifth without sitting:

\begin{quote}\itshape What is the figure for a thing spent in the night?\end{quote}

Nobody answered at first, because there is no figure for it and the College has an article about the morning. Then a voice from the floor said: “There is no figure. What is spent in the night is not entered in the morning.” It was a low voice from the side where the dish had been set down, but in the dark a voice has no place, and I did not see a mouth.

The junior asked who had said it. I said I did not know. The physician asked whether the woman at the door had said it, and she said she had carried a dish and not a sentence, and went back up the lane with the dish held against her coat. I have not asked her what was in it.

\subsection*{What I read by touch at first grey}

\emph{The fire was still covered. I went along the bench with the backs of my fingers before I lifted the ash, and set down a place where the wood was warm and left the rest cold.}

Question — Put by — What came back — Warm places\par

The grating — a College junior — the grating; the fire behind iron — one, at the College end\par

The Kept — a physician — one of the Kept; a hand held and paid for — one, by the door to the passage\par

The roll — the Steward’s clerk — the roll; the account carried forward — one, at the notices\par

The Long Night — the floor — the Long Night; the carried fire — not scored; the linen woman’s place\par

The figure for the night — a woman with a dish — no figure — not scored; one place, no name\par

There were four scored places and two that were not, and six places of warmth on a bench the College would have entered as nil. I have left the sixth where it was. When the fire was uncovered the places went off the wood in the time it takes to say one in twelve, as the notice says, a figure read here every Weighing and never entered.

\subsection*{What the College clerk did}

He came down on the morning of the Remembering with ink settled in two fingers of a cuff gone soft from washing, and borrowed the leaf while I was setting the cups out. He writes narrow and upright and takes the doer out of every sentence.

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item At \emph{the hand that tends me has never felt me} he wrote \emph{access to the Hearth-fire restricted; no approach}. True of the grating, and silent about the woman who carried the dish and burnt her wrist under the lip two days before.

\item At \emph{we are paid to hold his hand} he set \emph{attendance recorded; no charge arising}. The hand is gone out of it and the payment with it, which is the way the College makes a room warm without anybody in it.

\item At \emph{the mouths that said me are not on me} he wrote \emph{roll carried forward; names current}. He has set the mouth where the name should be, and left the name where the mouth was. Both stand.

\item At \emph{what is spent in the night is not written down} he wrote \emph{observance; no transaction}. That is the article as it is printed. He did not ask why a room full of men would spend a night asking one another for nothing, and I did not tell him.

\item At the fifth he wrote \emph{no response tendered; struck}, and asked who had answered. I told him a voice from the floor. He wrote \emph{unattributed voice; no figure arises}, and underlined it once, which is as near as a College clerk comes to being troubled.

\end{itemize}

I have put my words under his and left his standing above, the way the ash is left on the Last Day and burnt on the morning after. A clean line where the grey stood is not the same as gone, and there is no article in the Five about the line.

\subsection*{In the margin, in broad charcoal}

The woman who carried the dish up from the Hall on Kindling borrowed the leaf while I was turning it. She writes with a piece of the coal she carried, and the letters are wide and hard to keep in a line.

\begin{quote}\itshape The fire you covered was lit from the Hall and I carried it under a dish. The lip burnt me here and here and there is no entry for it in any book. You write of the dark as if nobody had paid for the light you put out at dusk. I have kept the burn two years and it has not gone.\end{quote}

I have copied it as it stands and not answered her, because the answer is an article of the Five and she has a better one under her wrist.

\subsection*{At the head and in the gutter}

The tallow at the head is mine, off the lamp I turned the leaf by at first grey before I covered it again. The lamp-black is in the grain of every word and no damp takes it out, which is why the Court’s notice shows through it at one corner and cannot be washed off either: \emph{one in twelve, as the notice says}, with the corner gone soft where the damp took it. The ring is a cup of water that stood from the first question to the fifth and went cold without being drunk, which is how water is drunk in this room when there is a thing to say and no proper word for it. The grey in the gutter came off the skirting board of a Kept room, the only Ash here that entered without a hand. The scorch is a spark off the grating caught when I lifted the ash; I put it out under my palm and did not enter the burn. The press of wet wool came off the physician, who held the door while the clerk came in and did not let go when he was through. The charcoal has rubbed thin where a sleeve went over the bench in the dark. The damp along the foot came out of the sealed-file room, which is colder than the rest of the Hearthseat. I have not swept the grey. There is a Last Day for it, and it is not this one.

\subsection*{At the foot, in a hand nobody will own}

\begin{quote}\itshape The Hall keeps the flame. The grate keeps the hand.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape The night keeps the answer and the morning keeps none.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape The roll keeps the name, and not the mouth that said it.\end{quote}

I asked the junior, the physician, the clerk of the Steward’s room and the woman who carried the dish, and had four answers and no hand. I have left the lines where they were. The leaf goes back under the dish beside the banked hearth, and tomorrow the names of the dead will be spoken on the Remembering and the returns announced in a clean voice, and the Last Day after that, when the grey is left where it lies and burnt in the morning and the clean line is not called a loss; and on Kindling a year’s fire will go out under a dish and be carried to every hearth in Sarn. This room will light from it. I shall cover it at dusk next Long Night and put the questions to the dark again, and if a man asks me what this house is named for I shall tell him: the fire that was covered, and not the one nobody may touch.

\clearpage\phantomsection\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{The Song of the Cut, Being a Mother’s Lullaby of the High Rim, Sung to the Cradle Board at Keld Keep; with the Number Before the Name, the Stone Held Back Until After the Knife, a Survey-Clerk’s Correction in Ledgerhand, a Grandmother’s Charcoal, and One Line at the Foot in a Hand Nobody Will Own}
\CRsheetheading{The Song of the Cut, Being a Mother’s Lullaby of the High Rim, Sung to the Cradle Board at Keld Keep; with the Number Before the Name, the Stone Held Back Until After the Knife, a Survey-Clerk’s Correction in Ledgerhand, a Grandmother’s Charcoal, and One Line at the Foot in a Hand Nobody Will Own}
{\centering\FellFont\itshape\footnotesize\color{faded} A mother’s lullaby in the hard clipped Rim speech, set in Grathic letters because Keldish is cut in bone and does not travel; the verses said to the arm and to the nail in the cradle board, never to the man who will one day sing them, the endings struck off, the refrain counted down the fingers of one hand; a mine-reeve’s red checking at the second corner, a survey-clerk’s correction above in narrow upright Ledgerhand, the child’s grandmother in thick charcoal underneath, and one line at the foot in a hand nobody will claim · Sung first over a cradle in a room above the shaft mouth at Keld Keep, and again, after the cradle had stood empty three years, to the iron nail in its board; set down in Bone of Y.H. 812, the winter her youngest son turned twelve, by his mother, a woman of the count’s row who has never gone below; written in charcoal on the back of a shift-tally spoiled by slate dust, with a notch cut in the edge where no Grathic word would come, carried down the Rim Road in Ilmen of Y.H. 813 with a cart of warm-stone and copied at Greybank onto a voided weigh-slip, where a survey-clerk set his figure above hers. It survives with a shaving of bone at the head, coal smut in the second fold, a thumb of tallow, a curl of the child’s first hair in the sewing, a dry barley crust, the dent where a warm-stone stood on the leaf and went cold, a red thread from the mine-reeve’s checking, a frost-feather gone by noon, a small-ale ring at the foot, a grey Ash print nobody will own, the notch in the edge, the clerk’s correction above, the grandmother’s charcoal underneath, and the line at the foot that has never been claimed\par}\medskip
I sing above the shaft, at the cradles in the row behind the count’s room. Our women do not go below: a woman’s measure lies too near the surface and would draw the sweat out of the stone, and the stone is not ours to trouble. I have sung to three children of this row and borne two. My youngest turned twelve in Bone and goes down at thirteen, a year off. The cradle has stood empty three years, and I sing to the nail in its board now, because a cradle with a child in it will look at you, and a woman singing about a knife does not want to be looked at.

I set the words down the night before his birthday, on the back of a tally a fall of slate dust spoiled, and cut a notch in the edge where the Grathic would not come. A survey-clerk from Greybank borrowed the leaf at the weigh in Ilmen and wrote his hand above mine, with the doing taken out and a figure standing where the nail stood. I have left his words where he put them and put mine back underneath, as the board of a cradle keeps the shape of a child after the child has gone out of it.

The bone at the head of this leaf is a shaving off a tally-stick. Keldish is cut in bone, not written, and a notch stays when paper has gone soft. I sign with charcoal because charcoal goes into the grain and no wet sleeve takes it out. The smut in the second fold came off the sleeve I wipe the keys with. I did not know I had marked it.

\subsection*{The manner of it}

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item Said to the arm and to the nail, never to the child. Said looking at a child it becomes a promise, and there is no promise here that a woman can keep.

\item The hand goes to the nail before the eyes go to the cradle: the record first, then the person, then the mouth opening after both. A lowlander does the opposite and thinks nothing of it.

\item One verse to one finger. Count down the fingers of the left hand and stop at the thumb. The thumb is not a number and does not go down.

\item The stone is not put into the hand at the cradle. It is given after the knife, by a woman at the mouth who has counted the numbers. A stone in a cradle is warmth paid for and spent on nothing, and no warmth here comes unbought.

\item The name is not sung. Where it would stand in the last part I have cut a notch in the edge of the leaf. A notch keeps better than a word and cannot be carried up the road in a cuff.

\item Sing the first parts while the child still has a face you can look at. Keep the last part until the boots have gone up the Rim Road and the room is quiet. A song with a name in it travels; this one stays where the cradle is.

\item Do not sing it at the weigh or while a number is being checked in red. A lullaby said during a checking is entered as a disturbance, and the mine-reeve does not ask twice.

\end{itemize}

\subsection*{The song}

\emph{Said low, to the nail. The hand goes to the nail before the first line. One verse to one finger, counting down and stopping at the thumb. The last word of each part is said to the iron and not to the room.}

The refrain, as the cradle keeps it after every part:

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Hush. Count. The arm has spoken before the face.}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{One for the cradle, one for the knife, one for the stone.}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{The number goes down. The name stays here.}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Say it once. The mountain keeps its own.}\end{quote}

\subsection*{I. Of the arm}

\begin{quote}\itshape Before you had a face you had an arm.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Before you had a name the number was kept in it.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape The arm speaks first in this house; the face comes after.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape We say what we hold before we say who we are.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Hush. The arm is listening.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Hush. Count. The arm has spoken before the face.}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{One for the cradle, one for the knife, one for the stone.}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{The number goes down. The name stays here.}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Say it once. The mountain keeps its own.}\end{quote}

\subsection*{II. Of the knife}

\begin{quote}\itshape Thirteen is a short road. I have walked to it twice.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape The knife goes across the surface way and stays there.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape A way once cut is a door and does not close again.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape It aches before the thaw. It will ache after.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape You will answer to the number the room gives you.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Hush. Count. The arm has spoken before the face.}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{One for the cradle, one for the knife, one for the stone.}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{The number goes down. The name stays here.}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Say it once. The mountain keeps its own.}\end{quote}

\subsection*{III. Of the stone}

\begin{quote}\itshape They will put a stone in your hand after the knife.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape I cannot put it there. My hands do not go below.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape A stone keeps its night longer than a mother keeps a child.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape It is paid for at the mouth; no man here has called it ours.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Hold it. It is the only warmth with a price I can pay.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Hush. Count. The arm has spoken before the face.}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{One for the cradle, one for the knife, one for the stone.}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{The number goes down. The name stays here.}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Say it once. The mountain keeps its own.}\end{quote}

\subsection*{IV. Of the iron}

\begin{quote}\itshape Hold the rail going down. It is iron and it takes.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Hold the rail coming up. It is the same iron.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape The clamp that closes a crack will close a fist;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the iron has never been asked which one it meant.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Hush. I have asked it. It does not answer.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Hush. Count. The arm has spoken before the face.}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{One for the cradle, one for the knife, one for the stone.}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{The number goes down. The name stays here.}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Say it once. The mountain keeps its own.}\end{quote}

\subsection*{V. Of the number}

\begin{quote}\itshape State what you hold. Then say who you are.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape The number stands. We do not say it twice.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Two go down and the count comes two.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Whether two come up is a thing the mountain keeps.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Do not ask the mountain. It will tell you the number.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Hush. Count. The arm has spoken before the face.}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{One for the cradle, one for the knife, one for the stone.}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{The number goes down. The name stays here.}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Say it once. The mountain keeps its own.}\end{quote}

\subsection*{VI. The part kept back}

\emph{Not sung while boots are on the road or a clerk is at the weigh. Said to the nail with the thumb laid over the notch.}

\begin{quote}\itshape I gave you a name at the cradle and the road will not carry it.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Where the name would stand in this song I have cut a notch.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape A notch is not a figure and cannot be entered.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape I did not carry you down. I cannot carry you up.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape I can hold the board until it remembers your shape.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Hush. Count. The arm has spoken before the face.}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{One for the cradle, one for the knife, one for the stone.}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{The number goes down. The name stays here.}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Say it once. The mountain keeps its own.}\end{quote}

There is a space before the last line of the last refrain, the length of the notch in the edge of the leaf. I have left it on the tally. It is the right length for a name and for nothing else, and the women leave it when they sing, though none of them has ever said what stands in it. My thumb is in it now and has been since I cut it.

\subsection*{What the survey-clerk did}

He came up from Greybank with a cuff soft from washing and ink in two fingers of it, and borrowed the leaf while the pair before ours was weighed. He writes narrow and upright and takes the verbs out as though a verb were a thing a man could smuggle past a weigh in the seam of a cuff. He set his hand above mine and did not look at the notch.

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item At \emph{before you had a name the number was kept in it} he wrote \emph{capacity declared at birth; designation pending}, underlined twice. True in a counting room and false at a cradle, where the number was still waiting in the arm for the knife.

\item At \emph{the number stands} he wrote \emph{the vessel was re-entered} --- the same sentence with nobody in it, and a man’s thirteenth year made to sound like a correction.

\item At \emph{I cannot put it there. My hands do not go below} he set \emph{stone issued after procedure; no gift arises}. Right about the stone; he has left out the hands, which is the whole art of that hand.

\item At \emph{whether two come up is a thing the mountain keeps} he wrote \emph{no return due; remains retained on premises}. The cruellest line on the leaf and the truest, and I have not crossed it out.

\item Where the notch stands he put a round nought and wrote \emph{vacancy}. A nought is a figure and travels in a cuff. A notch is a place and stays where it was cut.

\end{itemize}

I have put my words back underneath everywhere and left his standing above. He takes the doer out because a thing always true has no need of anybody doing it. I put the doer back because a woman singing to a board wants to know which hand held the child, and the answer is in the sentence if there is somebody in it.

\subsection*{What the grandmother put underneath}

The thick charcoal is my mother’s. She counted at this mouth thirty-one years and never set her name to anything. She pressed these lines in below the verses while I was finding the end of the fourth, and would not read them over. I have copied them where she set them.

\begin{quote}\itshape At \emph{a stone keeps its night longer than a mother keeps a child}: He came up with two sets in one arm. The later cut was deeper. I have looked at that arm and I have not asked him which set he answers to, and he has not told me.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape At \emph{you will answer to the number the room gives you}: Your father answered to two numbers in one year and held the cup with the other hand. The room entered the later one. I have kept both, which is a thing a room cannot do.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape At the notch: I put my thumb in it when you wrote it and I will not tell you why. You have cut it the width of your own thumb, which was the width of his.\end{quote}

I have set all three where she wrote them. She would not sign them and I have not made her.

\subsection*{At the head and in the gutter}

The bone shaving at the head came off a tally-stick my mother kept and is the only part of this leaf written before it was said. The coal in the second fold is off the sleeve I wipe the keys with; it goes into the grain and no wet sleeve takes it out, which is why I sign in charcoal. The tallow is off the lamp I kept low so the women in the next room would not know I was setting down what we sing and change their words. The curl of hair is his, cut at two years with the knife that cuts the tally notches; I shut it in the sewing and have not opened it. The crust is Last Day bread; there is no Last Day at a shaft mouth and nothing here is gathered and burnt in the morning and called dealt with. The dent is where the warm-stone stood while I found the sixth verse: it held through the writing and was cold before the charcoal set, which is the order of things. The red at the second corner came off the mine-reeve’s point while he checked a man whose figure would not hold; he did not look at me and I did not look at the man. The frost-feather was on the mouth stone after a warm night and was gone before I came to put it in. The small-ale ring is where a cup stood from the first verse to the last and was not lifted; it is not the cup on the nail and belongs to no Order. The grey along the outer fold came off a cuff laid where no cuff has business lying above ground; nobody will own it and I have not swept it.

\subsection*{At the foot, in a hand nobody will own}

\begin{quote}\itshape The cradle keeps the shape. The arm keeps the number.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape The road keeps the name and will not give it back.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape The stone keeps one night. The mountain keeps the rest.\end{quote}

I asked a woman who has counted here longer than I, a man off the Duelling Floor, and a surveyor who carries the slate up, and had three answers and no hand. I have left the lines where they were written.

The leaf goes back into the tin with the keys, and the nail into the board. Tomorrow a pair will go down and the count’s woman will put the stone into whichever hand the knife leaves free; I shall sing to the board and stop at the notch. He will have the number and I the name, the road will have neither, and the mountain will keep its own and will not be asked to give it back.

\clearpage\phantomsection\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{A Letter from the Counting House at Greybank to the Ember Bowl in the Bowl of Sere, Concerning the Price of Northern Measures, the Forty That Are Not Found but Made, a Beautiful Return That Would Not Hold a Cup, and the Shape a House Must Buy; with the Answer in the Margin, a Correction in Ledgerhand, and a Rowing Song from the Pulled Benches}
\CRsheetheading{A Letter from the Counting House at Greybank to the Ember Bowl in the Bowl of Sere, Concerning the Price of Northern Measures, the Forty That Are Not Found but Made, a Beautiful Return That Would Not Hold a Cup, and the Shape a House Must Buy; with the Answer in the Margin, a Correction in Ledgerhand, and a Rowing Song from the Pulled Benches}
{\centering\FellFont\itshape\footnotesize\color{faded} A merchant’s letter in iron-gall on the back of a barley tally spoiled by damp, folded thrice and sealed with a thumb of red lead-glaze; carried south from Greybank by a grain factor’s clerk as far as the Peat Line and from there by a carrier of eels to the Bowl of Sere; answered in the recipient’s hand along the gutter, corrected on the outer fold at the Council room in Vhal, and kept since in the Ember house’s box of southern contracts · Written at the Sere counting house in Greybank, eighteen leagues downriver of Sill, in the last tend of Grain, Y.H. 813, by Corven Dells, a factor’s under-clerk who buys northern measures for the Ten Bowls, to Ovia Gilded, keeper of the bowls in House Ember at the Bowl of Sere; answered in her hand in the gutter, borrowed at Vhal by a factor’s clerk who could not let paper lie, and returned to the box of contracts in the Bowl. It survives with barley dust worked into the head and the gutter, a round wine ring the width of a cup, a thumb of red seal at the outer fold that comes away on the finger, a pale tideline of salt along the lower margin, one figure gone over in the damp and written again underneath, an answer in a sloping southern hand, one correction in the narrow upright hand of the College, a round nought set in the place of a missing oar, and a line at the foot that nobody has claimed\par}\medskip
To Ovia Gilded, keeper of the bowls in the House Ember at the Bowl of Sere, from Corven Dells at the counting house in Greybank. Written on the back of a barley tally that spoiled in the damp and was given to me for nothing, which is the only paper in this house that has not already been told what to say.

I write in the southern hand because a northern one would be taken for a petition, and a petition in this country is a thing a man spends a mark to have lost. The damp got at the tally and took two figures clean off it. In Vhal that would be called a mercy and here it is called a waste of good paper. I have written over them. A figure that has gone soft is not a figure that has been forgiven; it is a figure with the number rubbed out and the debt standing all the same. Do not wet the fold. The seal is red lead and comes off on the thumb.

You write asking for a whole return before the first Frost, with the memory kept and the shape whole enough to be shown at a feast. I answer plainly, because the courtesy we use at this end of the trade is a courtesy with a bill inside it. It can be done. Twelve hundred marks and forty unspent measures, as the Court books them; the marks go north to a household and the measures go south in a cradle, and nobody at this counter has ever seen the two things arrive at the same door. Your house wants remembering. What the north has to sell is remembering. That is the whole of our trade, and there is not a kind word in it that has not been priced.

The district is walking thin. The levy in Low Kiln is one in three and the notice in the Court room says one in twelve; I stood under the notice at the Cross last Account-day and heard the figure read twice over the basket, once for the moot and once for those who came late, and I know a figure read aloud is not the figure paid. I could not tell you which of the two goes into your cradle. That is not my department. In my department we write down what the Court gives us and do not ask the slate where it has been.

\subsection*{The measure as it comes to us, set against what goes south}

In the district — On the collector’s slate — In our letter to the Bowl — In the cradle\par

A widow of the lower bank. Two loaves — one in twelve — a whole measure, freely returned — the shape of a woman who wanted something\par

A glaze-room girl, sweet at the mouth — one mark, current — a vessel of good remembering — a mouth that turns toward the cup before the cup is shown\par

A clay-bound hand, term served out — term, not measure — a measure, term fulfilled — a hand that has forgotten the trade but not the reach\par

Six and twenty of the lower yard, by lot — one line for the batch — forty measures, purchased — forty, and no name among them\par

A man found in the yard at morning, no figure taken — not entered — nothing — nothing, and the slate shut\par

I keep the four columns apart because a man in a counting house can forget what a cradle is for if he writes the four in one line. The College would put them in one line. A College clerk borrowed this very leaf before it went south and put them in one line and took the verbs out of the whole of it, and I have set the verbs back underneath and left his line standing above, so that both may be read and neither mistaken for the other.

You ask why forty. I asked the same of a man who had stood at this counter longer than I had been alive, and he said \emph{because the account requires it}, which is a phrase that means \emph{because we have decided it}. A whole return wants one vessel that holds and remembers; it wants forty measures that will never be a vessel at all, that go into the account and stay there and are called unspent. They are not found in this district, lady. They are made. There are households below the sill with nothing left in them but the breathing, and out of those households the forty come, one line on a slate and a hand at a wrist that leaves a pale ring the neighbours call weather. I have written \emph{made} here and I will not strike it out. The borrowed hand above has written \emph{were banked}, which is true in the way a butcher’s floor is true.

\subsection*{The song the pulled benches keep}

\emph{Sung by the condemned at the oars of the salt galleys out of Vhal, to the stroke; put down here because it is the only account in this trade that counts the rower. The last line is said twice, the second time for the man whose hands give out before the seven years.}

\begin{quote}\itshape One for the clay and one for the chalk,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape one for the hand that the salt took;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape pull and the measure goes over the side,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape pull and the measure stays inside.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Four on the bench and four on the shore,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and a place where the fifth oar was before;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape seven years is a long, lean tide ---\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the lamp goes out and the hands abide.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape We carry the warm that we never kept,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape we row the road that the slate has cut;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape ask the bowl what it wants of us ---\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape it wants the shape, and it wants it shut.\end{quote}

You ask in the same hand after a fourth pouring for the woman of the green bowl, who was shown in that year and twice before, and you ask whether the shape will remember. I have seen the shape. It holds wine and does not spill, and it has not spilled at three feasts, and the applause for it is the cleanest applause in the empire because nobody in the room has to believe it. Whether there is anybody inside it on the third day is a question for your bowl-surgeons, not for a clerk at this counter. We can send the forty. We cannot send the wanting. That is the one part of the order the north cannot fill, and it is the part your house is buying.

\subsection*{In the gutter, in her hand, set close and small}

\emph{She writes on the diagonal, as the bowls write when they are crossed, and uses the plural of houses even where a single woman must have stood at the writing.}

We emptied the bowl on the first night of Grain and the debt-slates were burned by lot and new ones made, as you know, having once been at a feast in this room and applauded with the rest. Your four columns amuse me. We do not keep accounts of that kind here; we keep the bowl and the applause and the shape that comes back. Send the forty and send the cradle. As for the wanting, my house has never found it in the north, though we have bought north for nine generations and have had good value out of every district.

\emph{Below, in the same hand, a line she did not cross out:}

You were asked at sixteen what debt you meant to carry. I am asking you the same thing now, in a letter, because a debt named in a room is applauded and a debt named on paper has to be paid. Answer me on the back and not in the gutter, where the salt has got into everything.

\subsection*{What the clerk did at the Council room in Vhal}

A factor’s clerk borrowed the leaf in the tar-smelling room where the Council writes its decrees on salt-paper that goes soft in the rain and calls the softening a virtue. He writes in the narrow upright hand, with the verbs taken out and everything in the passive, as they teach it at the College and as the Council pretends not to need. Against \emph{they are made} he set \emph{forty unspent measures were banked}, and under that \emph{were lawfully purchased}, and underlined it twice. Against the rowing song he wrote \emph{no cost entered}, which is the neatest thing I have ever seen done to nine lines of a song. Against the woman of the green bowl he set \emph{a beautiful return, third pouring}, struck out \emph{wanting} wherever it stood, and wrote \emph{no want recorded} above it, because a thing a house has bought cannot be wanting. Where I left the place of the fifth oar he put a round nought and wrote \emph{nil} beneath it.

I have put my verbs back underneath and left his figures standing over them. He is right in the language he writes. In the language of the benches a nought is not a place where an oar was.

\subsection*{At the head and in the fold}

The barley dust at the head came off the tally when I turned it over, and there is more of it in the gutter than there should be, mixed now with her sloping hand, which is a thing I cannot separate and would not if I could. The round ring is wine from the feast at which the woman of the green bowl was shown, or from another feast; I did not mark which and will not guess at it. The red at the outer fold is the seal, lead and something else, and it comes away on the thumb with a sweetish taste if a man is fool enough to touch his tongue to it, which I have not done and the clerk from the College did, and was sick behind the tar-room door while the Council went on with its counting. The pale line along the lower margin is not the Ash, whatever a northerner would call it; it is the salt that gets into everything in this coast country, and I have not brushed it off. There is no Last Day on this counter. Paper goes into the box and the box goes south, and nobody burns it in the morning and calls it dealt with.

\subsection*{At the foot, in a hand nobody will own}

\begin{quote}\itshape The north counts what it lost. The south counts what it kept.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape The bowl goes round and the account stays open.\end{quote}

I asked a factor, a clerk who cannot let paper lie, and a woman who rowed the pulled benches and now sells eels at the Peat Line, and had three answers and no hand. I have left the line where it was written.

The leaf goes back into the box of southern contracts. In the morning the grain goes south by the Peat Line and a tally goes up to the factor’s table, and the forty go where they go, which is not a place I have ever been allowed to name. Tomorrow another household below the sill will find it has had a good year and that the account has stood. That is the whole of the letter, and it goes on.

\clearpage\phantomsection\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{The Mercy Telling at Mud End, Being Six Stories Spoken on the Long Night in the Peat Byre, the One Told to the Floor, and the Figure a Clerk Set Against the Dead}
\CRsheetheading{The Mercy Telling at Mud End, Being Six Stories Spoken on the Long Night in the Peat Byre, the One Told to the Floor, and the Figure a Clerk Set Against the Dead}
{\centering\FellFont\itshape\footnotesize\color{faded} A byre-keeper’s record of a winter telling, set down for the settling of which death was called merciful and not for the comfort of the reader; the rules in the hand the byre keeps, the stories in the words they were spoken, a score in peat-blocks on the trodden floor, the figures of a factor’s clerk entered over them, and one line at the foot in a hand nobody will own · Written on the Long Night of Y.H. 812, the Thin Year, in the peat byre at Mud End three leagues downriver of Sill, by the woman who keeps the byre where the moot sits when the peat is too wet to stand on; copied out in Ilmen of Y.H. 813 onto the back of a spoiled winter-peat tally, folded into oiled sacking and kept in a wall-niche behind the peat-stack under a flat stone. It survives with a peat thumb at the head, a press of wet wool across the first leaf, a small ale ring, a grey Ash print along the gutter, frost-crisp at one edge, one sheep’s-wool fibre off the Tallow road, one correction in the narrow upright hand of a factor’s clerk come up from Greybank to count the winter peat, and a line at the foot in a hand that is nobody’s.\par}\medskip
I keep the byre at Mud End where the moot sits in winter. There is a fire until dusk and none after, because this is the Long Night and the Keeping says a man may tell the Return in the dark and be heard the better for it. I have kept this byre eleven winters and I have never once seen anybody hear better in the dark. They hear the same. They hear it with nothing to look at, which is a different thing.

We hold the mercy-telling on this night. A person tells of a death the hamlet called merciful --- one that went quietly, where nobody had to be sent for and no collector came up from Greybank for it --- and the teller must give the dead one’s name. A story that keeps its name gets a peat-block set on the floor. A story that lets a figure into it gets nothing, and the teller owes a peat to the winter stack, which is the only fine this byre knows and the only one anybody pays without an argument. I do not say why a story served. A reason given is a story given away, and a person who has told one well can go home and sell it in Sill.

The moot meets here because the bog takes a man’s weight in Silt and his boots in Stone, and there is no dry room between us and the river but this one. Nine houses and their peat stacks, and one byre with a floor packed hard as old bread. On the Long Night the floor is the book. Nothing is written in it that a clerk can carry off, and in the morning I tread the blocks into the ash and there is no score left, which is the point of a byre and the difference between a byre and Slate Row.

\subsection*{The rules, as the byre keeps them}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item Tell once. A story told twice is a different story and is not heard; the second telling is for the teller and he may pay for it himself.

\item Give a name. A figure is not a name. A figure travels; a name stays in the room where the person said it.

\item Four blocks lie in a row and a fifth lies by the wall. The fifth is not a prize and is not the best story’s block. It is for the one the year took and nobody in these nine houses could tell.

\item No fire after dusk. The last coal is banked before the first voice. A story told by firelight counts for nothing, being a story told twice --- once to the living and once to the coal.

\item Say it to the floor, the door, or the pot. Said looking at a person it becomes an argument, and there is enough argument in Mud End over the winter peat without bringing the dead into it.

\item The byre judges. I say whether a name was kept and I do not say which name I wanted.

\end{enumerate}

Before the first voice we sing the short song, standing, with our hands on the byre wall because it is the only warm thing in the room by then.

\begin{quote}\itshape Four blocks for the four that went quietly,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and a fifth by the wall for the one not told;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the peat keeps warm what the peat has held,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the name goes round while the figure goes cold.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Tell it to the floor, tell it to the door,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape tell it to the place where the fifth would stand;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the clerk writes one and the house writes none,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and both go down in the same dry hand.\end{quote}

\subsection*{The four that were told}

\textbf{Vey}, said the widow who cuts peat on the west bank. She said it to the pot. Her man went out after the frost with a spade and sat down in the cut and did not stand up again, and the district called it merciful because nobody had to go looking and no slate went up to Sill over it. She said his name three times, once for the byre, once for the floor, and once for the cut he sat in, and would not let me set a figure against it. “He’s Vey,” she said. “That’s the whole of it. A number’s what you write when you’ve lost the person.” She took her peat-block and went and stood by the door until the next story, which is how a widow stands in this hamlet.

The second was put by a woman come over from Cold Acre, where the well never freezes. She told of a child returned thin in the year of the flower, come back to a house where three had gone into the measure and the house could not say which of the three had come home. The child was quiet and wanted nothing and grew no shape, and the house called it merciful because it asked for no warmth and so cost nobody. She did not give the child’s name. She gave the name of the woman who kept it, said low into the pot, and said the child’s name was not for a byre where a clerk had been known to lean in the door. I set a block for the keeper’s name and none for the child’s, and we left it so. A name kept in one house is still a name kept.

The cooper told the third. He is the man the hamlet means when it says a cooper’s seventh, though he has never explained the seventh to anybody and gives a different date for it every time he is asked, which is a way of answering that costs him nothing. He told of the man they called merciful who slept before a banked kiln with the damper shut and did not wake, and he told it to the floor with his cap in his hand. “Merciful is the word the district used,” he said. “His name was Ansel. You can have the one or the other, but not both, and I’ll have the name.” There was a silence after that, the kind that has four in it and a gap where the fifth would be, and the bell from Sill came across the frozen fields four, four and a gap, and nobody crossed himself. I set the block. Ansel’s name went round the byre and came back to the cooper, and the figure never arrived.

The fourth I put myself, because the room had grown too quiet and a story put by the byre is not scored against anybody. I told of the year’s fire that comes up in a clay dish before light, house to house, each hearth touching its own flame to it, and the last house keeping what is left. There was a woman in this row who took the dish in and did not pass it on, and her house was warm all that winter and she went cold in the spring, and the hamlet called her merciful because she went in her sleep and nobody had to tell her the fire was spent. I did not say where the coal came from. She did not say either. That is the part we call merciful, or the part next to it. I set no block for my own story, because a byre that scores itself will soon be a Court, and I have seen how those rooms go.

\subsection*{The fifth by the wall}

The fifth block lay by the wall all night and nobody moved it. A girl from the Tallow road, who had come in with wool on her sleeves and stayed silent, put her hand toward it twice and took it back, and I have not written which girl, because she would stop coming if I did. In the morning there was a small grey print of Ash where the block had lain, the colour of the ridge that gathers where a promise is not kept, and I trod it in with the rest of the floor and called it the thaw, as we call everything in this hamlet that we do not want to name. The fifth was not a story that failed. It was the year’s taking that nobody in nine houses could put a name to, and a thing left in place is still a thing kept.

\subsection*{The score, in peat-blocks on the floor}

Story — Told by — Name kept — Block\par

The cut in the bog — Vey’s widow — Vey, said three times — set, paid\par

The thin child — Cold Acre woman — the keeper’s name only — set, child’s name not given\par

The banked kiln — the cooper — Ansel — set, figure refused\par

The dish not passed on — the byre — none; byre does not score — not scored\par

The year’s taking — nobody — none — by the wall, not moved\par

\subsection*{What the clerk did}

A factor’s clerk come up from Greybank to count the winter peat borrowed the leaf on a morning when the stacks were being measured and his cuff was soft at the edge from washing. He set the four tellings down as \emph{four merciful returns entered, nil deduction}, and put a figure of marks against each of the three names, which was more than the byre had scored, because the byre scores in whether a name comes back out of the room and he does not.

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item Against \emph{he’s Vey, that’s the whole of it}, he wrote \emph{one life surrendered without claim}.

\item At the thin child he wrote \emph{third party unidentifiable; vacancy}, and put a round nought in the place where the child’s name would have stood.

\item Against \emph{his name was Ansel}, he struck the name and set above it \emph{the measure was voluntarily resigned}, and underlined it twice.

\item At the year’s fire he wrote \emph{the warmth was transferred by consent}, which is a true thing in a language nobody in this byre speaks. Consent of whom he did not write, and I have not asked him.

\end{itemize}

I have put my words under his and left his standing, the way the floor keeps a peat-block under a spilled quart.
