\item Where entry made after the third day, the reason entered also. No reason entered for the third day itself.

\end{enumerate}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Margin, in mine:} A child left at the meal mill in a fold of grey wool, with a stone warmed at another hearth under his belly, was entered on the second day. The finder brought the stone in with her and asked whether the stone was a name. I said no. She wrapped it back and carried it away, and I wrote a name that will do him until a hearth claims him, which in this district means until a house with a chimney and a roll of its own takes him in.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Margin:} Hand that writes not hand that carries. This is the only article I have ever had cause to be grateful for. A woman who has carried a child three doors up the yard in the cold should not have to hold the slate as well as the child.\end{quote}

\subsection*{II. Of the name}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item Foundling named by the hand appointed to the slate. Birth-name not entered. House-name entered in the margin where a hearth claims him; the first name not struck out.

\item Where no hearth claims by the thirtieth day after finding, entered as unhoused, the slate-name standing alone.

\end{enumerate}

What is entered — Where it stands — What is not entered\par

Slate-name — the line — Birth-name\par

Day of finding — the head — Hour of finding\par

House-name, if claimed — the margin — The woman who carried him\par

Figure — the account — Who paid for the finding\par

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Margin:} I drew the last column and left it empty. A man from the College borrowed the leaf and struck the column out, writing \emph{No such column} above it in a hand so upright that it hurts the eye. I have struck his striking out and left the column as I drew it. A place is not a debt. The College has never learned the difference, though it teaches the eleven words for a deduction to its own.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Margin:} I have heard tell of a branching red flower written across a child’s ribs and have not entered it. There is no column. The hearth-maids cross two fingers over such a thing and cover the sign with a date, which is a kind of writing and not the kind that reaches this house.\end{quote}

\subsection*{III. Of the claim}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item Claim entered before the tenth day after finding; after that only by leave of the assessor. Where two houses claim, the house of longer standing entered first and the other entered also and not struck.

\item Claim made for warmth already paid entered as a kindness and not as a debt. Kindness entered.

\end{enumerate}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Margin:} Longer standing means the house with the most pots. I write \emph{standing} because that is the word the ordinance uses, and a woman from the low bank who has no pots has no standing, which is the whole of it. In the Thin Year a house came for a child and wrote its own name above his and set a thumb to it. I put the house-name in the margin where the ordinance requires and kept the child’s name in the line. The woman who had carried him stood with her hands in her apron and asked whether the hearth was a good one. I told her I had no slate for the warmth of a hearth. This was true, and was not what she asked.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Margin, in a second and narrower hand, the letters leaning, in charcoal:} A crossed sign, which the maids make at a birth-flower. It is not a word and I have not translated it. It was laid against article six, where the kindness is entered.\end{quote}

\subsection*{IV. Of the house roll}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item Claimed vessel entered upon the house roll in a careful hand. Roll kept in the house. No duplicate required.

\item Every vessel entered upon one line of the slate. Two vessels not entered upon one line.

\end{enumerate}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Margin:} No duplicate required. I have asked to see a roll and been offered a cup instead. A house that keeps its own account does not need to explain the keeping, only to keep it. This is the article the houses of Low Kiln live by, and the Court has never thought to enforce it, which I take to be the Court’s one kindness that it does not enter.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Margin:} There is a boy in a kiln-house who says: \emph{He’s a foundling. I’m a debt. Don’t put us in the same sentence, Sella.} I have written them on two lines of one slate, which is the only sentence a slate knows. A household sorts its own members and calls the sorting kindness, and the ordinance has no word to dispute it with.\end{quote}

\subsection*{V. Of the drawing and the space after it}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item Where no claim entered, the measure drawn at the next collection and the account opened in the name written at the finding. Consent entered by the hand of the officer where no household offers it. Refusal is an unclosed account; the vessel clip-held by the wrist until consent entered.

\item No article provides for a measure left undrawn where no officer was called.

\end{enumerate}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Margin:} On Ilmen 9 of this year I was set at the Fishstairs with a slate to take a measure that nobody had called for. I sat from the turning of the tide-light until the light went, and wrote the hour at which I was set and the hour at which I was not dismissed, and left the space between them empty. There is a line in the account for a figure and no place in it for a figure that never came. A woman went into the clay-heavy water at the end of nineteen steps and came out on a board, and the yard lifted her with their hands, and I had no article to read to anybody. The clerk at the Cross says a nought is a number. I put nothing. I sent the slate back as it stood and it was entered as a kindness.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Margin:} The clip leaves a pale ring that shows through the winter and is spoken of as nothing. I have seen a woman hold up her wrist and ask whether the ring would go, and I said it would in the thaw, which is what my mother said about everything, and is not in the ordinance.\end{quote}

\subsection*{VI. Schedule of the days of a foundling}

Day — Entry — Where it stands\par

First day — Finding — Head of the slate\par

Third day — Entry, or reason — The line\par

Tenth day — Claim, or leave sought — The margin\par

Thirtieth day — House-name, or unhoused — Margin, or the line\par

The Five — No market, no claim — Nothing entered\par

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Margin:} No claim taken during the Five, and no market either. The clerk at the Cross counts the bell four, four and a place where the fifth should be; I count the empty column. We are each of us keeping a place open, and neither of us has a word for it.\end{quote}

\subsection*{What the College hand did, and what I did after it}

The College hand struck three of my verbs, struck the empty column, and wrote \emph{No market, no claim, no entry} against the last row of the schedule, which is true in the way a closed fist is true. I struck out \emph{no entry} and set \emph{nothing entered} above it. There is a difference between the entry of nothing and a place where a woman might have stood, and the difference is the whole of what I have to do in this house. I have left the College’s fist standing above my words, as I have left the striking of the verbs above the verbs themselves. A slate with two hands on it is the only kind the household believes.

The brown spot on the second leaf is from a crust laid there while a woman was telling me where the child had been found and would not say the name of the house. The sour milk is the child’s; there was no cup in the house that morning and I gave him mine. The grey came off the outer fold when I carried the leaf in my coat pocket down to the Fishstairs on Ilmen 9, pressed against the wrist where the clip had been, or against a wrist that had never known the clip; I do not now remember which arm I used, and have not tried to find out. The tallow thumb at the head is mine. I held the leaf down with my whole hand because the door stood open and the yard wind came through.

One line at the foot was struck through and written again in my hand, and I have left both readings standing:

\begin{quote}\itshape No article provides for the measure left undrawn. In the low houses they keep these also.\end{quote}

The leaf goes back into its board cover and hangs on its nail behind the counter. Tomorrow a woman will come up from the low bank with a child in a fold of wool and ask me for a name, and I shall write the name the slate gives me, and put nothing in the last column, and she will go away knowing that the nothing is where she stood. That is the whole of my trade: to write names and leave places, and not to say which of the two will keep him warmer.

\clearpage\phantomsection\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{The Nest in the Warm Crack, Being a Watchman’s Field Notes on the Tallow-Wasp at the Rendering House Beyond Sill}
\CRsheetheading{The Nest in the Warm Crack, Being a Watchman’s Field Notes on the Tallow-Wasp at the Rendering House Beyond Sill}
{\centering\FellFont\itshape\footnotesize\color{faded} A watchman’s field book on one small beast, set down as the record of rounds kept over the rendering fires and not as natural philosophy; the rounds in Grathic, the tally in charcoal on the backs of spoiled fat-tallies, a verse of the vats as the lamp-women say it, one ruling in the narrow upright Ledgerhand of the factor’s clerk at Greybank, a line traced in rancid tallow by a lamp-woman who would not give her name, and one line at the foot in a hand nobody will own · Written in Tallow and Ember of Y.H. 812, the Thin Year, by one of the Thane’s men set to keep the rendering house two leagues north-east of Sill, who took the wasps’ nests and burned them as he was bid; set down at the end of rounds in the shed with a tallow lamp under the draught of the flue, first on the backs of fat-tallies spoiled by a spill, then on three folds of birch bark sewn with eel-sinew and carried in a coat pocket against a flint. Copied forward at Greybank in Ilmen of Y.H. 813. It survives with a brown tallow thumb ground into the head, a grey bloom of sour fat along the fold, a press of wet wool across the first leaf, a singe where the flue drew a spark onto the third, a small round mark where a buyer set a mark-piece down and took it up again, the charcoal rubbed thin where the wrap was carried against the thigh, one ruling in the clerk’s Ledgerhand, one line traced in rancid tallow by a lamp-woman, and the one line at the foot\par}\medskip
I keep the rendering house two leagues north-east of Sill, and my whole charge is that the fat is rendered and the nests are burned. The men at the Works call it a post for a man with no nose. They are right. In Tallow the smoke goes over the ridge and into Sill on a north wind, and a man in the Clay Yard will know what I have been doing before he sees me, which saves him the trouble of asking and saves me the trouble of lying.

These leaves were fat-tallies once, before a spill took the figures clean off, which was a mercy of a kind: a figure the fat has eaten cannot be entered. I write in charcoal now. Charcoal goes into the grain and a clerk cannot take it off with a cuff. The brown at the head is my own thumb setting the sheet down on the bench, and it has gone rancid in the fibre, so the whole leaf smells of the shed even when it is folded away in a pocket. I have not scraped it. A book that smells of nothing was never taken on a round.

\subsection*{Where it keeps}

It nests in the warm crack. That is the first thing a new man must learn and the thing that costs him a morning. The house has a flue that runs hot from the second hour and a north wall that holds the heat after the fire is banked, and the wasps are in the seam where wall meets flue, not in the vats and not in the fat. I have watched a man set a dish of hot fat on the bench and catch nothing in it, and set an empty crock against the warm wall and find it full by the middle of the watch. The fat is where the warmth has been. That is the whole of that saying, and I have put it down without making a lesson of it, because a lesson written in this book is a thing somebody will carry up the road and enter.

The crack is the width of a thumb and runs the length of the flue. The nest hangs behind it like a paper bladder, grey and ribbed, with a small door I have never seen a wasp use in daylight. They swarm in the sweet smoke. In Ember the smoke is thick enough to take a man by the throat, and the wasps come up out of the crevices into it and go down again, and the lamp-women work the whole watch through it with their sleeves at their mouths, counting the pours and never the insects. A man counts what he is paid to count.

\subsection*{What it is}

It is a wasp. I will set that down before anything else, because the verse does not. It has a wasp’s narrow waist and a wasp’s way of hanging in the air as though it were weighing the room, and it is the colour of rendered fat gone cold, with a darker band at the head. It is smaller than the wasps that come at the fruit in Greybank and readier to take offence, which is a thing I can say from having given it offence.

I have opened seven. In each I found wasps and grey paper and nothing I could set a name to as a cause. The place alters the creature the way smoke alters a side hung in the flue: the same animal comes out of it, changed in colour and carrying a little of the fire. I have not written what the wasp wants with the warmth. A man who writes what a wasp wants in a book he keeps in his pocket is a man who will be asked next what a collector wants, and there is no end to that sort of work.

\subsection*{The sting}

It swells the ways near the skin so that the Warm pools and cannot go on. A man feels it as a hot place under the skin, and the hot place spreads a little, and then the fever comes, and then the cold. The order is the thing to keep. I had a man stung twenty times at the banking of the fire in Ember, feverish by the second watch and talking freely, and we took the fever for the worst of it and left him by the door; by the going of the light he was cold and would not answer to his name. The physician at Greybank told me the fever was the body’s own fire and the cold was the account. He said it in a clean voice with his hands in his sleeves, which is a manner of speaking I have heard from men who are paid whether the man comes back or not.

There is no physic for it that I know. Keep the man warm and keep him still, and do not open the swelling, for there is nothing in it to let out and a knife lets out the little that was holding. Salt does not touch it. A lamp-woman set a warmed stone to a boy’s hand after Ember 16 and sat with him the whole night, and the boy came back by morning. I have set that down because it happened and not because the stone did it.

One of the men says the fever is the wasp’s own warmth poured into a man and the cold is what is called back out of him. I have not put that saying in the tally. A thing of that kind, once it is written, gets carried up the road and comes home with a figure on it.

\subsection*{The verse of the vats}

\emph{Said at the vats while the fat is still running, not at a fire. The third line is the old line, and every woman on the row says it wrong on purpose, because a verse that gives a man a reason is a verse he can take home and set by his own hearth, and a man with a reason by his own fire sleeps better than a man with a swelling.}

\begin{quote}\itshape One for the vat and one for the flue,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the wasp keeps the crack where the heat has been;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape it comes to the fat and it comes to the flame,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape it takes the warm and it leaves the cold.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Fever first and the cold after,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape a man stung twenty will not say his name;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape count them going and count them back,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and leave the last one for the wall to keep.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Burn the nest. Do not sell the wall.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape A resin that holds is a resin that wants;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the south will pay and the north will burn,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the crack stays warm whether or no.\end{quote}

They sing it wrong on purpose and I have left the wrong line standing. She does not come to the fat. I have set a dish of fat in the yard sun and had no wasp in it by dusk, and set a bare crock to the warm wall and had it full by the middle of a watch. The women know this as well as I do. They sing it the other way because a wasp that wants nothing from a man is a wasp a man cannot forgive for the swelling, and a man who cannot forgive has to carry something home.

\subsection*{The tally}

These are the rounds I kept a true account of. There were others I did not write because my hands were full and one I did not write because I had the smoke in my eyes and had forgotten the hour. I have set down both sorts as they stand. The last column is the clerk’s, not mine; I counted what stung, he entered what could be burned.

Round — Place — Stung — Nests — Burnt — Entered\par

Tallow 4 — Flue wall, east crack — none — two — two — 0\par

Tallow 12 — North wall, behind the vat — one, a lamp-woman’s wrist — three — three — 0\par

Tallow 27 — The banked fire, second hour — four, all at the flue — one — one — nil\par

Ember 3 — Old crack above the door — none — four — four — 0\par

Ember 16 — Vat side, where the spill was — one boy, twenty stings — two — two — 0\par

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{In the narrow upright Ledgerhand of the factor’s clerk, struck through the “Stung” column:} Insects not a vessel. Swelling: not entered. Warm in a wall is not a deduction. Account stands.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{And beneath the “Entered” column, in the same hand:} Twelve nests destroyed. No value arising.\end{quote}

I have left his hand standing. He has put \emph{nil} against the boy and \emph{no value arising} against twelve nests that a man from the coast offered four marks apiece for, on a bench in this shed, in the middle of a watch. I have written the twenty stings in the margin below, where his ruler cannot reach, and set my own mark beside them in charcoal.

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Below, in my hand:} Ember 16. One boy. Twenty stings. Fever at the second watch, cold at the going of the light. A warmed stone and a woman’s two hands. No figure, and none asked for.\end{quote}

\subsection*{The nest and the buyer}

The paper of the nest yields a resin. A man came up from the coast road in Ember with a soft southern way of speaking and four marks in his pocket, and he wanted the paper whole and not crushed. He said a bowl-surgeon in Sere would set the resin in a graft to hold a wall until the vessel took, and would pay four marks a nest for it. I asked him what a resin holds when the want is in the graft and not in the wall. He said that was a question for a surgeon and not for a man who keeps a rendering shed, which was a true answer and not the one I put to him.

We burn them. That is the order come down from the factor at Greybank, and I have never been given a reason for it and do not invent one to fill the space. There is a fire at the shed door that takes them, and the ash goes down with the wash-water into the run when the floor is sluiced. Four marks is near a month’s wage to a man on this road. The buyer set a mark-piece on the bench and took it up again when I would not name a price, and the round mark he left is on this leaf where he pressed the tally to read the count. I have not wiped it off and I have not spent it. The fire is still at the door.

\subsection*{What the hearths say}

They say the wasp is drawn to the smell of rendered fat, and there are songs in the Fenmarch with a woman’s name in them and a wrong done at a rendering. I have heard them and I have no quarrel with a song. But I have set fat where there was no warmth and caught nothing, and set a bare crock where there was warmth and no fat and had it full, and I have left the cause where I found it, which is in the crack. What the wasp does with the warmth it carries into the nest I have not written. That is a question for a man with a slate and not for one with a fire at the door.

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Traced in rancid tallow on the corner of the second leaf, the letters gone soft where the fat has turned: It is not the fat that calls them. It is the wall that kept the fire. We pour the fat and the warm goes with it, and they come to where the warm has left. Burn the nest and the wall stays warm. They will be back next Ember. --- A.}\end{quote}

She writes in the fat she pours, so the line goes sour before the words go. I have put her hand above mine. She wrote it at the vats and I wrote mine at the door, and neither of us has asked the wasp anything.

\subsection*{At the head and in the margins}

The brown at the head is mine and has gone into the fibre, which is why the leaf smells of the shed in any room. The grey along the fold is sour fat and came up of itself; it is the only thing in this book that entered without a hand. The press of wet wool across the first leaf came off a morning in Tallow when the wind turned and we lay flat under the flue with the smoke going over us and the book under my coat. The singe on the third leaf is a spark the flue drew out of the fire while I was writing, and the hand that beat it out was mine and is not entered. The round at the foot is the buyer’s mark-piece, and I have kept it where it fell. The charcoal is thin where I carried the wrap against my thigh. The clerk’s ruling I have not touched, and the lamp-woman’s line I have set above my own, because hers went sour first and is entitled to stand.

\subsection*{At the foot, in a hand nobody will own}

\begin{quote}\itshape It keeps the warmth of a fire it never lit. Ask the wall, not the wasp.\end{quote}

I asked a clerk, a lamp-woman, a physician with his hands in his sleeves, and a man who came up from the coast with four marks, and had four answerings and no hand. I have left the line where it was written.

There is a crack in the cold north wall, past the flue, that has never held a nest and is warm to the back of the hand on the stillest morning of Ember, with no fire behind it that I can find. I have burned nothing out of it. Next Tallow I will take a bare crock and a lamp and set them against that wall at the second hour, and I will count what comes and what goes back, and if the wasps come to a wall with no fire in it I will set that down too, in charcoal, with the cause left standing where it is and no figure at the end of the row.

\clearpage\phantomsection\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{The Night-Roll of the Waiting Room, Being the Vessels Held at Sill Between the Drawing and the Banking through Bone and Ash of Y.H. 812, the Thin Year, with the Hour, the Embers, the Note, the Return Due, and What Was Said After the Slate Was Shut}
\CRsheetheading{The Night-Roll of the Waiting Room, Being the Vessels Held at Sill Between the Drawing and the Banking through Bone and Ash of Y.H. 812, the Thin Year, with the Hour, the Embers, the Note, the Return Due, and What Was Said After the Slate Was Shut}
{\centering\FellFont\itshape\footnotesize\color{faded} A page from the Waiting Room book at Sill, ruled in Ledgerhand by the clerk of the room, the remarks terse and in the same hand; a column of night-sayings struck through by a College clerk and kept on the back of the leaf where his correction cannot reach, one figure set above by a factor’s clerk, a pallet-song with the answer left out, and one line at the foot in a hand nobody will own · Written in the Waiting Room off Slate Row in Sill through the third tend of Bone and the whole of Ash, Y.H. 812, the Thin Year of the Long Cold, and carried forward at the Opening of the Slates into Ilmen of Y.H. 813, when the book was ruled anew and the old leaves put under the pallets. The room is the one where the collected are kept overnight before the banking; the book lies on the shelf by the door with the tube’s wool sleeve and a tin of tallow ends. It survives soft at the fold and damp along the foot, with straw from the pallets worked into the gutter, a tide-line from the washing of the floor, a cold dark spot where a warmed stone stood and went cold, grey Ash off a corner rubbed into the head, the pale ring of a cup set down and not lifted, a press of grey wool where a sleeve lay, a green bead of lead glaze in the lower corner, one hair from a head shut in the fold, a small square of bare paper where a word was scraped away, one column struck on the face and preserved on the back, one figure set above in a borrowed hand, and a line at the foot that has never been claimed\par}\medskip
I keep the room between the drawing and the banking. A collector brings a vessel in at the going of the light with the tube still warm in its wool and a slate-name already written, and I set it on a pallet until the banker comes before first grey. I do not draw and I do not bank. I hold. There are three of us in this trade in Sill — the reader at the Cross, the man who carries the slate up the road, and I who keep the room — and our figures never meet, which is the arrangement the Court has always liked.

I have no house and no kin, so the room is my house and the roll is my kin. I write in the upright hand and leave the doer out, as I was taught, because a sentence with nobody in it can be read in the Weighing Hall without anybody being asked to stand behind it. What I cannot leave out I have set on the back of the leaf, where a correction written on the face cannot follow.

Twelve copper bits to a silver mark; twenty marks to a Sere crown, a coin that comes down the Clay Road and goes back up it. An ember is booked at five marks and no man in this room has ever exchanged one. A newborn vessel holds twelve to fifteen embers, a labourer in good case forty to sixty. One in twelve is printed on the notice and read twice over the basket at the Cross. The other figure travels up the road in a locked box and does not come into this room. I enter the printed figure and leave the other where I heard it, on the back.

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{In the narrow upright hand of a clerk of the College, struck through the column headed “What was said”:} No such column. \emph{On the back of the leaf, in mine:} He struck it on the face and did not turn the leaf. A man who has corrected a thing has still had to read it before he can write above it. I have kept what was said where he could not put his hand.\end{quote}

\subsection*{The roll, as it stood}

\emph{The figures are in Ledgerhand, copied from the slate the collector leaves. The remarks are mine and terse, being what a clerk can set down while a person is still looking at him. A dash is a place where nothing was drawn, and is not a nought.}

Hour — Vessel, as the slate has it — Embers — Deduction — Note — Return due — Remark\par

Going of the light, Bone 23 — A widow of the lower town. \emph{Loaf} — 41 — 1 in 12 — full — whole — Asked after four loaves baked and three to the levy. Answered to the figure and not to the loaves.\par

Middle dark, Bone 23 — A clay-bound hand off the terraces. \emph{Seven} — 44 — 1 in 12 — flat — thin — Consent recorded by another hand. Wrist held until it was. Would not say whose wrist.\par

Before first grey, Bone 24 — A child three days returned, Low Kiln. \emph{Second} — 13, struck to 12 — 1 in 12 — none — — — Worse in the night. Entered as a birth, not a worsening. Stone put to the belly and gone cold by morning.\par

Going of the light, Bone 30 — A thrower of the low yard. \emph{Nineteen} — 39 — 1 in 12 — nearly full — thin — Pale round place on the arm the width of a cup. Said the pot was not his. Not entered.\par

In the dark, Ash 2 — A glaze-room girl come up from High Kiln. \emph{Sweet} — 38 — 1 in 12 — nearly full — whole — Green at one mouth-corner. Asked after her girl. The question has no column.\par

Before first grey, Ash 3 — A man of the Weir. \emph{Eel} — 52 — 1 in 12 — full — thin — Drawn before light. Bell heard from the Cross: four, four and a gap. Nobody crossed.\par

Middle dark, Ash 10 — No vessel drawn. A clerk set at the out-of-line step — — — — — — — — — Slate held to the forearm, hand before eyes. I asked whose measure it was. Nobody had called one.\par

Going of the light, Ash 20 — A foundling in cast-offs. No house-name — 12 — 1 in 12 — full — — — Named by whoever writes the slate. Stands till a hearth claims him. No loaf passed.\par

In the dark, Ash 23 — A woman come back a second time. \emph{Again} — 35, struck to 31 — 1 in 12 — flat — thin — Older figure beneath the new one. Gave the old number when asked the new. Both stand in the skin.\par

Before first grey, Ash 30 — One of the Kept, in passing. No slate-name — 300 — none — none — none — Asked after the weather. Pity entered, which has no column, and carried forward.\par

Draws held overnight on this leaf: eight. Lines with no draw in them: two. Figures struck: two. Columns struck: one. Stones gone cold on the pallets: nine, including the one that was not a vessel.

\subsection*{The order of the room}

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item Receive the slate before the face. The collector hands the slate over and I set my eye on the writing first; the person on the pallet is looked at afterwards, when the door is shut. This is the order of the Keeping and I have kept it nine years. A face looked at before the slate is entered is a face a clerk will remember, and a clerk who remembers is a clerk who can be asked.

\item Set a warmed stone to the belly of a child and not to the palm of a grown person, who has had more warmth than the child and will not be thanked for it. Take the stone away at first grey whether the child has warmed or not. I have never been told why, and have stopped asking the physician.

\item Do not tap a person to hear them. A body is not a banked cup. I did it once to a woman gone thin and got nothing back for the knuckle, and have not done it again.

\item Write what is said after the slate is shut on the back of the leaf, and never under a heading. A heading makes it an account, and an account is a thing a person may be called to answer for at the Weighing.

\item The pot is broken at the door of a death-house before the vessel is brought here, not after. I have found shards on the step in the morning and have not swept them into the gutter with the straw. A shard left on a step is somebody’s instruction carried out, which is more than I can say for the figure.

\end{itemize}

A woman who came in with the green at her mouth said her girl had a name before she had a number, and asked which of the two the banker would press into the infant. I told her the figure was banked and the account stood, because those are the words I am paid to use, and put a stone in her hand so that she would have something to do with it. She set it on the pallet and it was cold when the banker came. I have entered the figure and not the stone.

\subsection*{What was said with the slate shut}

These were set on the back of the leaf and struck on the face. I have left the holes where the College hand went through, which is the only honest mark that hand has ever made.

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item Against the widow: \emph{Three loaves to the levy and one to the pot. Ask the pot what it cost.}

\item Against the clay-bound hand: \emph{He said the wrist was his and then said nothing else all night.}

\item Against the child three days returned: \emph{A name said into the ground before the collector came. Not repeated.}

\item Against the thrower: \emph{The pot was his. There is no column for a pot.}

\item Against the glaze-room girl: \emph{She asked after her girl. The girl has a number. The mother wants a name.}

\item Against the Weir man: \emph{Four, four and a gap. He crossed himself at the second four and said he had not.}

\item Against the woman come back a second time: \emph{She gave the old number and would not give the new. Both are hers.}

\end{itemize}

A nought is a figure and can be carried out of a room in a cuff. A name said into the ground is a place and stays where it was said. The College has eleven words for a deduction and no word for any of these, which is the whole of the difficulty between us.

\subsection*{The pallet-song}

\emph{Said low in the room, to the stone and not to the person holding it. Never while the collector’s tube is out of its wool, and never at the banking. The last answer is left out by those who know it.}

\begin{quote}\itshape Four on the near board, four on the next,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and a place where the fifth should be;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the hand goes to the slate before the face,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the face goes out with the figure.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape One in twelve, says the notice, read twice at the Cross;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the road carries another and will not show it.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape A stone for the belly, a cup by the wall,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and a name said low to the stone.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape The measure is banked, the account stands,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape nothing is lost that we have kept;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape ask the pot, ask the weather, ask the pallet straw ---\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the answer is not entered here.\end{quote}

A woman brought up from Low Kiln sang the first two verses while she waited for her child to be banked and would not sing the third while the banker was in the room, which is how I know which verse is the one that matters. I have copied what was said and put no gloss on it. A clerk who explains a song has begun to write a sermon, and sermons get copied.

\subsection*{The two borrowed hands}

The College clerk struck the night-column on the face of the leaf and wrote \emph{No such column} above it. He had to read every row before he could write that there was nothing in any of them worth entering, and I watched him turn the leaf and set it down again without turning it back. I have kept the sayings on the back. The face is his; the back is mine, and paper has two sides even in the Keeping.

The other hand is tall and leaning and comes out of the factor’s house at Greybank. Against the child three days returned it struck thirteen, set twelve above, and wrote \emph{a vessel returned cannot hold thirteen after the draw}, which may be true and does not mention the child on the pallet. Against the foundling it set a round nought in the column where no slate-name stood, as if a child without a house were a child without a figure. Both stand. A nought travels; a foundling cannot, until a hearth claims him. I have put my words underneath and left the correction above, as the pallet keeps the flat of the straw under the smooth of the blanket.

\subsection*{What the room leaves on the leaf}

The straw in the gutter comes off the pallets and I have never got it out; it works in deeper than the Ash. The tide-line along the foot is from the washing of the floor on Ash 10, when a pot was broken on the step and somebody used more water than the step wanted. The cold dark spot at the head is where a warmed stone stood on the leaf while I wrote the row for the child and went cold before I had finished the remark, which is the order of things and not an omen. The grey rubbed into the grain came off the corner of the room where the Ash gathers by tallow-light and is invisible in daylight, as everybody knows and nobody names. The pale ring is a cup set down by the woman with the green at her mouth and not lifted; it has gone the colour of old lead. The press of grey wool is where a collector’s sleeve lay while he waited for me to take the slate. The green bead is not slip but lead glaze, pressed into the corner by a girl who leaned to see the writing with the sweetness still at one mouth-corner. The hair in the fold came off a head that lay on the pallet through the middle dark and was gone before first grey. The small bare square is where I scraped a word away with a knife and put no other in its place; I had written \emph{ninth}, meaning the ninth stone that went cold, and then could not say which of the eight had been a vessel and which had not, so I took the word off. There is no Last Day in this room, and nothing here is gathered up and burnt in the morning and called dealt with.

\subsection*{At the foot, in a hand nobody will own}

\begin{quote}\itshape The slate keeps the figure. The pallet keeps the shape of the person who lay on it. The bank keeps neither, and presses both into a child.\end{quote}

I asked the College clerk, the man who carries the slate up the road, and a woman come up from Low Kiln with a child on her hip, and had three answers and no hand. I have left the line where it was written.

The book goes back on the shelf beside the wool sleeve and the tin of tallow ends. The banker will come before first grey and take what the room has held, and I shall receive the next slate before I look at the next face, and write the figure on the face of the leaf and the rest on the back. The stone will go cold on the pallet at about the second four of the bell. That is my trade: to hold what has been drawn until it is called for, and to keep, where no correction can follow, the length of the time it was held.

\clearpage\phantomsection\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{The Nine Pots Book of Bones, Being Remedies for the Crushed Hand, the Bone Set Wrong, the Four-Kiln Cough, the Feud-Cut, the Sweet Line, the Birth-Flower and the Child That Comes Cold, Set Down in the Dust of the Shared Pit with the Errors Left Standing}
\CRsheetheading{The Nine Pots Book of Bones, Being Remedies for the Crushed Hand, the Bone Set Wrong, the Four-Kiln Cough, the Feud-Cut, the Sweet Line, the Birth-Flower and the Child That Comes Cold, Set Down in the Dust of the Shared Pit with the Errors Left Standing}
{\centering\FellFont\itshape\footnotesize\color{faded} A bone-setter’s and midwife’s book of remedies in the Nine Pots manner, set down on the back of a spoiled road-tally with the counts cut into the margin by a tally-point; the cures in a bone-setter’s blunt hand, the objections of a physician come down from Greybank pressed blue-grey into the gutter, the corrections of a College clerk in narrow upright Ledgerhand, a moot-man’s line in charcoal at the foot of the remedies, a setting-song with the name of the road left out, and one line at the foot in a hand nobody will own · Written at Nine Pots, eight leagues west of Sill on the feud road, between Stone of Y.H. 811 and Ilmen of Y.H. 813, the Long Cold and the Thin Year, by Talla of Nine Pots, a bone-setter who has dressed the kiln hands and caught children in the potters’ houses for four-and-twenty years; begun on the back of a road-tally spoiled when a rain took the figures out of it, cut at the edge with a tally-point, folded into oiled sacking and carried in the breast of a potter’s apron, and copied at Greybank in Smoke of Y.H. 813 onto the back of a discarded weigh-slip. It survives with chalk worked into the grain at the head, a blue-grey tideline off the Ferr ford that has taken two words clean off the second leaf, a thumb of clay-pit slip in the gutter, a cupworm cocoon pressed into the fold, a ring of barley-water, a scorch where a spark off the fourth kiln caught the corner, a green bead of High Kiln glaze pressed into the lower corner by a girl with the sweetness at her mouth, three objections in the cold margin hand of the physician, the clerk’s upright hand above the cures, the moot-man’s charcoal at the remedies, and the line at the foot\par}\medskip
I set bones for a living. In Nine Pots that is half a trade and a whole accusation: four kilns, one clay pit, and a road neither town will mend, and between them a man can break himself in more ways than I can count.

Nobody asked me for this book. A man came in off the feud road in the lean week with his thumb lying the wrong way, and I heard myself answer in my mother’s voice, and did not know whether I believed it. A remedy you have to say in your mother’s voice is a remedy nobody has looked at in a long while. I have looked at some of mine. The rest I have left standing, because a man at three in the morning wants a hand held steady more than he wants a correction.

I write on the back of a road-tally a rain spoiled. The figures went before anybody could charge them, which is a mercy of a kind: a figure that will not read cannot be entered against a hamlet that has never agreed whose road it is. The chalk at the head is mine, off the moot-post. The blue in the gutter came off the Ferr ford when I washed a man’s arm in it, which I have not done since. Nothing here is free. In this country a thing that costs nothing has been paid for by whoever carried the stone.

\subsection*{The order of the splint-room}

\emph{Cut small into the first leaf with the tally-point, with one word gone over in clay slip.}

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item Ask which kiln before you ask which hand. A man who has carried from the fourth tells you where his back hurts; a man who has carried from none tells you where it ought to. This is not kindness. It is the order of the room.

\item Lay the broken one on sacking, never on the clay floor. Clay takes the warm out of a side faster than a bed does. A physician from Greybank wrote that a cold floor draws; I have set my line above his. Both stand.

\item Turn the slate face down before you go to a child. I have no slate-name and never shall. A bone I can see I can set; a name written before the face is looked at is a bone set by somebody who was not in the room.

\item Put the stone in wool at the belly and try it on your own wrist. The stone came off somebody’s kiln bank and somebody paid for the coal.

\item Bind loose enough to see a fingernail. A finger you cannot see has begun to go the colour of old rope.

\item We used to say never bind with cupworm silk, because it seals a crack in green ware and a bone is not a pot. I have bound four. Three held. I have left the saying standing and put the four underneath.

\item When the third night comes, let the woman do the counting. A number counted for her belongs to whoever counted it.

\end{itemize}

Against the cupworm line the physician wrote \emph{no tensile strength in flesh}, in a hand that scores the leaf. I have put my four under it.

\subsection*{The remedies, as they are used}

Trouble — What is set to it — The manner of it — Who carries it\par

The crush (a hand under a stack of saggars) — Two hands, a lath of willow, a fold of wet cloth; set before the swelling takes — We say a bone dressed green takes the tool the way a block does. The physician says wet cloth cools what should be kept warm. I have set twenty and had four come crooked; one I bound too tight and it did not come back. — The hand. This is the row where I have been least honest.\par

A bone set wrong — Leave it a tend and a half; do not look on the odd days — The physician says three days, and that a bone knits when it knits and not when a woman tells it to. Our saying went downriver in a salt-wife’s book and came back at Greybank with her hand under it; I had not known it had travelled. — The patient, in the holding still.\par

The four-kiln cough — Steam under a cloth; honey if the house has it — We say it is the smoke of our own fourth kiln and cannot hurt a man who has thrown all his life. A carter who has worked both yards says the Stonemouth cough is the honest one. The physician says it is clay in the lung and the only physic is to leave the yard. I sent three up the Rim Road; two came back worse, for the road has dust of its own. — The man, in the morning he coughs up a colour he will not discuss.\par

The sweet line — Sour barley-water; wood-ash at the gum — We do not taste our glaze in Nine Pots; we fire it. The green comes west in a girl’s mouth from the Glaze Room at Sill, and we say a sweet answers a sweet. The physician says lead, and that sour water only troubles the teeth. I have seen the line go off one who left that room and come back on one who stayed. I have not seen the lead. — The glaze room, which cannot stop and does not ask.\par

A feud-cut — Tallow, then a clean fold; never the grey — The men of the road put grey in a cut to dry it, believing grey is clean. I have dressed three such and found the grey under the skin in all three, and could not get it out. — The cut, in a white line it keeps.\par

The cold that stays — Three turns of wool, a stone at the belly, and work — The extremity goes first and the heart holds out, and there is an hour on the far side of the warming when a man gets worse. The physician says a warmed body spends faster and walking faster still. I have no name for that hour and have left the place where the name would stand the length a name of that kind wants. — The man, who cannot stop working.\par

The second chill — Warmth, barley-water, a watch to the fourth day; we walk them — A hearth-maid come west from Low Kiln says a warmed body gives heat away faster and that the child should be held and counted with. I have walked eleven and held two; all saw the fourth morning, and one went thin. I have kept the counts on birch bark and not added them, for a count added is a count a clerk can carry. — The household, one night’s sleep; sometimes the child.\par

The birth-flower — Nothing. Two fingers crossed, and the word the mother gives — A woman of the washing at Sill crossed two fingers over one and gave me a date instead of an answer. I have put the date in the margin. The physician says it is a flowering of the blood and not a flower, and is right in a language nobody here speaks. — Nobody knows. The child’s skin, perhaps.\par

Nothing in this book is given away. It is carried from one potter to another and called a cure. That is the only sentence I will stand behind.

\subsection*{The note under the knuckle}

The potters tap a green pot before it goes to the kiln and hear whether it will hold. Sound answers full; cracked answers flat, a small dead sound that stops at the lip and will not go through. This is the one thing in the four kilns that costs nothing and is still allowed to be true.

I tapped a man once, gone thin after a return, and put my ear to the little flat I thought I heard. The flat was not in him. A body is not a pot, though we make pots in the shape of bodies and put a face on the fourth. I did not say so at the time, because a moot-man was in the room with a tally. I have written it here, which is a different matter.

\subsection*{The road}

The feud is over a road neither town will mend. The men of Sill come west over the ford when the Ferr is low and call our road a disgrace; our men go east and say the same, and both arrive with the same cut in the palm where a stone went in. I have never asked which side a man belongs to before I set his hand. Once I did, and a man who had come six leagues for a bone went away without it.

A road takes and takes and enters nothing. A slate enters everything and takes nothing. Between the two a person stands and is mended or not, and the hamlet goes on calling the road ours and theirs and leaving it where it is.

\subsection*{The setting-song}

\emph{Sung low over the splint, to the bone and not to the man. There is a place after the last line the length of the road’s name, and no singer has put a word in it.}

\begin{quote}\itshape Four for the kilns and one for the pit,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape one for the hand that the saggar split;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape set it green and bind it loose,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and leave the nail where the thumb can touch.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape A cup answers full, a cup answers flat,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape a bone gives nothing to knock at;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the road goes east and the road goes west\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and neither has ever been mended.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Two for the ash and two for the clay,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape two for the woman who counts under wool;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the third night comes and the warm goes back,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and what goes back is not what went ---\end{quote}

A clerk of the College put a round nought in the place and wrote \emph{vacancy} beneath it. A nought is a figure a clerk can carry out; the road’s name is a place and stays.

I changed one line in four-and-twenty years: \emph{set it green and bind it loose} is now \emph{set it green and leave the nail}, because a man cannot see a nail through a fold tied too tight. The men singing with me have not noticed, which is how I know the line wanted changing.

\subsection*{What the physician pressed in the margin}

He came down from Greybank in Smoke of Y.H. 811 with a book that had the word \emph{lead} in it and a hand that wrote without asking. Against the cupworm silk he set \emph{no tensile strength in flesh}; against the birth-flower, \emph{a mark in the blood}; against the four-kiln cough, \emph{the dust of the clay, and no physic but departure}, true and of no use to a house whose living is cut out of that clay. He was right about all three. I have left his sentences above mine and my words underneath, where a man at three in the morning will find them.

\subsection*{What the College clerk did}

He borrowed the leaf at Greybank when the winter pots were counted, ink in two fingers of a soft cuff. Against my column headed \emph{Who carries it} he wrote \emph{No cost entered}, which is a true thing in a dishonest place. Where I wrote \emph{the road takes and enters nothing}, he set \emph{no toll is recorded on the nine pots road}, the most beautiful sentence I have ever read in a hand that has never carried a stone. Where I wrote \emph{we bind it loose enough to see the nail}, he wrote \emph{the limb is dressed and retained}, taking the hands out as though a bone could set itself.

I have put my verbs back underneath his. A clerk can speak without verbs because he is never in the room. A man with a thumb lying the wrong way wants to know which hand will set it, and who will pay for the clay.

\subsection*{In the margin, in charcoal, the moot-man’s hand}

\begin{quote}\itshape A pot tells you when it is fired. A hand does not. I have sat at this post through two feuds and counted no bones; the bones come to Talla and the figures come to me, and neither of us asks the other what the road cost. --- M.\end{quote}

He wrote it while I was at the ford; I have set his line above mine. A man who has counted nothing is allowed one sentence in a book of physic.

\subsection*{At the head and in the gutter}

The chalk at the head is off the moot-post, where I marked the days the road was impassable. The blue tideline came off the Ferr and took two words clean off the second leaf; I have not written them back. The clay in the gutter is out of the shared pit, the only thing here put there by the trade and not by a person. The cupworm cocoon was pressed in by a girl who said its silk holds a crack in green ware and would hold a bone; I have not told her about the three hands, or the fourth. The ring of barley-water came from a cup set down while I told a man to drink and he would not. The scorch is a spark off the fourth kiln, put out under my hand; I have not entered the burn. The green bead in the corner was pressed in by a girl of High Kiln with the sweetness at one mouth-corner, and I did not ask whose glaze it was. There is no Last Day in a potter’s apron and nothing here is swept up and burnt and called dealt with.

\subsection*{At the foot, in a hand nobody will own}

\begin{quote}\itshape The pot keeps the crack. The bone keeps the crook.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape The road keeps nothing, and is paid all the same.\end{quote}

I asked the physician, the clerk and the moot-man, and had three answers and no hand. The book goes back into the apron. Tomorrow a man will come in off the feud road with his thumb lying the wrong way, and I shall set it green, bind it loose enough to see the nail, put my verbs back where the clerk took them out, and turn the slate face down before I look at the child, because a child is not an account and a man at three in the morning wants a hand held steady more than he wants a correction.

\clearpage\phantomsection\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{The Sermon at the Counting Stone, Being What a Reader of the Return Said Over the Five Open Wells on a Morning in Stone of Y.H. 812, with the Nine Cups Cut in the Stone, the Warming-Song Left with the Four Stopped Cups as They Stand, the Ledger of the Wells, a Clerk’s Correction, and a Line at the Foot in a Hand Nobody Will Own}
\CRsheetheading{The Sermon at the Counting Stone, Being What a Reader of the Return Said Over the Five Open Wells on a Morning in Stone of Y.H. 812, with the Nine Cups Cut in the Stone, the Warming-Song Left with the Four Stopped Cups as They Stand, the Ledger of the Wells, a Clerk’s Correction, and a Line at the Foot in a Hand Nobody Will Own}
{\centering\FellFont\itshape\footnotesize\color{faded} A sermon of the Temple of the Return preached at the shrine of the counting stone among the Nine Wells on the Keel, five leagues short of the Hearthseat; the sayings in the clean voice of the Hearthseat set down in Grathic, the song with the four stopped cups left as they stand, the nine cups in a well-ledger, one correction in the narrow upright Ledgerhand of a clerk of the College of Assessors come up from Slate Row, and a line at the foot in a hand nobody will own · Preached on Stone 22, Y.H. 812, the Thin Year of the Long Cold, by a reader of the Return come up from the Hearthseat, at the counting stone between the five open wells, on a morning when steam stood a hand high over the water and the road was frozen hard enough to carry a cart; written that evening by the woman who keeps the counting stone and draws the water for the five, in charcoal and tallow on the back of a measure-slip spoiled at the Weighing, folded with a lead stop out of one of the four cups shut in the crease, and kept since in a tin under the stone’s lip where the drawers leave their bits. It survives with lime bloom worked into the head and gutter, warm-stone grit in the grain, a wet ring where the dish of water stood from the first voice to the last, a copper bit shut in the fold, a grey Ash print along the gutter off a cuff nobody will own, a pale ring of spilt milk on the second leaf, the lead stop, one correction in a clerk’s hand that takes the verbs out and numbers the four nil, and a line struck through and written again very small underneath in a hand that has never come forward. Copied once at Greybank in Ilmen, Y.H. 813, with the verbs put back and the four cups left stopped.\par}\medskip
I keep the counting stone at the Nine Wells and nobody asked me to write this. I write because a man spoke to a stone and the stone gave back steam, and I did not want the words to go up with it. He spoke to the stone, the wells, the dish, and last of all to us, the order a reader uses when somebody may be listening who wants a figure. I have set his words down in Grathic, which is not the voice of the Hearthseat, and put the verbs back underneath where he left them out, because a saying said over a well is a thing a woman has to use before the child goes cold.

The lime at the head is off the whitewashed lip where I rest the dish; no wet cloth takes it out of the grain. The grit is warm-stone ground small between the cups and scratches a nail. The ring is the dish, set down at the first voice and taken up before he saw it. The bit in the fold was left in the fifth cup while he spoke of the figure and I have not spent it. The grey along the gutter came off a cuff laid where no cuff has business on a stone that is counted; I have not swept it. The milk is a woman’s, from the fourth well, and I have left the ring where it dried. The lead stop in the crease came out of the sixth cup, which is stopped and has no business giving anything.

\subsection*{The manner of the warming, as the counting stone actually has it}

\emph{Written small, from watching, not from any order the Court has printed.}

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item Come before the steam stands too high. A man who comes at noon sees only his own breath and calls it the well’s giving.

\item Lay your palm flat on the stone. Five cups are worn smooth with thumbs and four are stopped with lead. A hollow that does not wear belongs to the Court, not to you.

\item Warm the stone at your own wrist before you put it to a child. It is too hot the first time and too cold by the time you have decided, which is the whole of the work.

\item Leave a bit in a cup that is open. Take nothing out of a cup that is stopped.

\item Do not say the count of the four aloud. A number said at a well goes up the road in a clean hand and comes back as something a household owes.

\item When the reader lifts his hand, stop. His hour is the Hearthseat’s and the wells keep another. Begin again after.

\item The ground gives back more than it takes. Do not ask what it takes, or from which quarter. The question is safe and the answer is not safe to carry.

\end{itemize}

He said the last twice, once to the stone and once to a man from the bakehouse in a clean coat who was writing nothing I could see.

\subsection*{The sermon, as he said it}

\subsection*{Of the nine}

He put his palm flat on the stone where the nine cups were cut, and the steam went up between his fingers.

“There are nine cups in this stone,” he said. “Five give and four are held. The world was a vessel, fired whole and cracked in the First Breaking. The Nine Who Kept drove the first repairs, and these wells are the marks of their hands upon the ground. Five were left for the living. Four were reserved to the Hearth.”

I asked why four were stopped and five were not. He gave me a year: Y.H. 668. I asked again where the steam did not cover the stone and had the same year. A date is the only answer this shrine gets from a man in a clean coat, given so the other question may stand.

“The ground gives back more than it takes,” he said. “That is the mercy of the Hearth, taught to every child on the Keel after the Return. Ask what it gives and you shall have a well; ask what it takes and you shall have the printed figure, one in twelve, which is a true thing said to a room that is not this room.”

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{The people answered, and the children said it twice, once for the road up and once for the road down:}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape The well gives back what the well got;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape it does not say from where.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Margin, in my hand:} He said \emph{reserved to the Hearth} three times. The keys hang in the Hearthseat and nobody has brought one down to this stone. I have left the keys where they are.\end{quote}

\subsection*{Of the lead}

“Look at the four,” he said. “Lead does not give. Lead does not take. Lead stops. A stopped cup is a cup that has been decided about, and a decision is a mercy when the Hearth makes it and an account when a man with a slate does. Until you are told which, leave the lead alone.”

A woman beside me asked what was under the lead. He did not turn his head.

“The warmth that would have come up is kept for the Hearth, and what is kept is not lost,” he said. “The account stands. Nothing is lost that we have kept. If a child on the Keel goes cold this winter, the Hearth has counted him and found a use for him elsewhere.”

He said it in the voice they use at the Weighing, which takes the speaker out of his own sentence. A man behind me with his cap in his hands had come up from the low country and had a child at home with a dark foot. He asked nothing, put his bit in the first cup and went away with the steam in his sleeves.

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{The people answered:}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape The well gives back what the well got;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape it does not say from where.\end{quote}

\subsection*{Of the grey}

“On the Last Day the grey at the lip is left where it lies,” he said. “In the morning it is taken and called dealt with. The Court teaches that the grey is what remains when the Warm has gone out, and that what cannot be kept is not a loss. Do not weep over dust. The rich buy it in a phial and call it quiet ash, and a man who cannot remember his own dead sleeps the better. This also is a mercy, and dearer than a loaf.”

There was grey on the lip of the fifth cup and he did not brush it away. An old man had come up from the Hearthseat and stood in the steam with his coat done up against a cold he could not feel. When the reader spoke of the Kept as past want and to be pitied, the old man held a hand in the steam a moment, took it back and went away. I have asked four people what he wanted there and had four answers and no hand.

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{The people answered:}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape The well gives back what the well got;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape it does not say from where.\end{quote}

\subsection*{Of the figure}

“One part in twelve of every measure is kept back for the fire, as the notice says,” he said. “This is not a tax. A tax is taken by a man who wants a thing. This is kept by the Hearth, which wants nothing and therefore cannot be refused.”

He held up the copper bit I had left in the fifth cup.

“A bit put into an open cup is a keeping. A bit taken from a stopped cup is theft, and the wrist is marked so the account may find the hand again. The iron does not take. The slate takes. The iron only opens the way. There is a pale ring on more than one wrist here that shows through the winter, and the neighbours call it the frost. It is the account, and it is never wrong.”

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{The people answered:}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape The well gives back what the well got;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape it does not say from where.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{In the narrow upright hand of a clerk of the College who came up from Slate Row on the fourth day and borrowed the leaf while I was at the dishes:} A keeping is a lawful retention. The measure is banked and augmented in the spring. Enter as retained.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape *\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Underneath, in mine:} I have put \emph{put in} and \emph{taken out} back under his \emph{retained}. His hand stands above and mine under it, as the five open cups stand beside the four.\end{quote}

\subsection*{The warming-song}

\emph{Sung low, standing, with the palm on the stone. The children say the last four with the women. The space before those four is the length of the four stopped cups, and I have left it as it is sung.}

\begin{quote}\itshape Five give and four stand stopped,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the steam goes up the Keel;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape a stone at the wrist, a dish at the lip,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the road comes up frozen.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape One for the child and one for the cup\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and one for the hand that set it down;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the lead in the four will not sing,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the five are worn to the thumb.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Here the four are left as they stand. The singer makes no sound.}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape The well gives back what the well got;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape it does not say from where;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the bit in the cup goes up the road\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the water comes up here.\end{quote}

A girl from the bakehouse asked what the space was for. Nobody answered her. The clerk put a round nought against it later, which I have left where he set it.

\subsection*{The ledger, as the stone keeps it}

\emph{A bit left in an open cup goes up the road in a clean hand and leaves nothing on the leaf. These I have set down where they stood.}

Cup — Who leaves at it — What is left — What was entered\par

One, the child’s lip — the drawers of the five — a bit, sometimes — nothing\par

Two, the bakehouse well — a man in a clean coat — a copper bit, put in and taken — nothing\par

Three, the stone-warmer’s — the women of the Keel — warm-stone grit, no coin — nothing\par

Four, the milk well — a woman with a sour-milk jar — a pale ring on the lip — nothing\par

Five, the last open — nobody will say — a bit left while the figure was read — nothing\par

Six, Seven, Eight, Nine — the Court; the keys hang in the Hearthseat — a lead stop in each — nothing entered\par

The grey on the Last Day — the Court’s men, from the four — what the fire could not hold — nil\par

There were bits before these, and my mother could set a winter to each, and I have not written the winters, because a row of years is a thing a clerk can carry away and a cup is not. The four stand as they stood when the lead went into them; no figure has ever come out of them.

\subsection*{What the clerk did}

He came up from Slate Row on the fourth day with ink in two fingers, borrowed the leaf, and gave it back with the verbs taken out.

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item At \emph{the ground gives back more than it takes}: \emph{the measure is retained in the spring and augmented thereby}, above and underlined.

\item At \emph{four were reserved to the Hearth}: \emph{four wells reserved to the Keeping; purpose not entered}.

\item At the old man in the steam: \emph{subject not stated; no account arises}, true as only a man who has never stood here can say it.

\item At the gap in the song a round nought and \emph{vacancy}. When I asked what a space was worth that held four cups, he said nothing a clerk could enter, the first true thing he said all morning.

\end{itemize}

I have put the verbs back and left his hand above, as the stone keeps the worn cups under the stopped ones. He takes them out because a thing always true has no need of them. I put them back because a woman with her palm on a stone wants to know who is doing the giving, and whether it was her own hand that set the lead.

\subsection*{At the head and in the gutter}

The lime is mine and will not wash out of the fold; I wipe the dish on my sleeve and the sleeve goes into the grain. The grit is warm-stone ground between the cups by every hand that has warmed a child here; it scratches a nail, which is how I know a drawer from a visitor. The wet ring is the dish, set down while he spoke of the four. The bit in the fold lay in the fifth cup when I took the leaf from the spoiled slip, unspent and unentered. The grey came off a cuff laid where no cuff has business on a counting stone; I have not swept it. The pale ring is milk from the fourth well and has taken the corner off two lines without the sense. The lead stop is the sixth cup’s own. The clerk noticed none of this, which is how I know he is a good clerk.

\subsection*{At the foot}

Struck through once and written again underneath, very small, in a hand that is not mine, not the reader’s and not the clerk’s:

\begin{quote}\itshape Five were left open by a hand. Four were stopped by another.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape The steam does not tell which hand was kinder.\end{quote}

I asked the reader, the woman with the milk jar, a man come up from the bakehouse and the clerk, and had four answerings and no hand. I have left the line struck through and standing, which is the only honest way to keep a sentence you cannot sign.

The leaf goes back in the tin under the stone’s lip with the lead stop in its fold. Next Stone the five will give and the four stand stopped, and the road will be frozen hard enough to carry a cart, and a reader may come up and say the same four sentences over the steam. If the clerk comes I shall let him take the verbs out and put them back as I did this time, with the nought in its place and the four cups stopped the length they are.

\clearpage\phantomsection\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{The Ninefold Coming Back, Called the Litany of the Long Night}
\CRsheetheading{The Ninefold Coming Back, Called the Litany of the Long Night}
{\centering\FellFont\itshape\footnotesize\color{faded} A prayer of the Return, said in the dark on the Long Night, at the bedside of the dying, and over a birth-slate; with the household’s answer · Written in charcoal and tallow on a leaf of birch bark by a hearth-maid of Low Kiln in Sill in Y.H. 811, the Long Cold, and added to in Y.H. 812, the Thin Year; she set her mark in the corner in place of a name, being two fingers crossed. The leaf is kept folded in the fold of a grey wool birth-cloth that passes from hearth-maid to hearth-maid in the low houses, and is taken out only after dark. It bears a tallow thumb, a smear of bone-pale slip, a spot of green from a glaze-room mouth, a charcoal print shaped like a pot’s foot, and two corrections in different hands. It survives because the cloth is washed oftener than the leaf.\par}\medskip
I am the fourth hand to write on this leaf and the first to say whose it is, except that I shall not say it. The fold had gone soft and I have not mended it, because a fold that has been mended sits shut and a prayer needs to be got at in the dark. What follows is what is on the leaf, including the parts a clerk would take out. It is not a thing to read standing up.

The manner of it, written small at the head in the first hand:

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item Turn the slate face down. It has heard enough for one night.

\item Bank the fire but do not cover it. A prayer needs somewhere to go.

\item Warm the stone in the hand before you put it to the belly. This is not part of the prayer. It is the part before.

\item The answer is said by whoever is in the room, including the child, who cannot say it and says it anyway.

\item When the bell goes at the Cross, stop. It is counting something else. Begin again after.

\end{itemize}

\subsection*{The nine callings}

\emph{The voice is the hearth-maid’s. The answer belongs to the room.}

\textbf{I}

The light under the Keel was here before the counting. It did not begin in a house. It was found in the dark.

\emph{Answer:} Come back warm. Come back as you can.

\textbf{II}

Nine hands went after what had run away. Nine repairs were driven home, and the ninth is not finished.

\emph{Answer:} Come back warm. Come back as you can.

\textbf{III}

The world was whole in the telling and cracked in one anger. What fell out of it went a long way and is going still.

\emph{Answer:} Come back warm. Come back as you can.

\textbf{IV}

The pot was set down and answered full. Set down again, it answered flat. It was carried anyway. It is carried anyway. Leave the crack showing. Glaze what you will.

\emph{Answer:} Come back warm. Come back as you can.

\textbf{V}

Write him in the house roll. Write him in the other book. Write him small. The slate is clean and does not care.

\emph{Answer:} Come back warm. Come back as you can.

\textbf{VI}

One in twelve, as the notice says, for the keeping of the fire. The fire was kept. The fire is always kept.

\emph{Answer:} Come back warm. Come back as you can.

\textbf{VII}

The iron is cold before anybody asks it. Take what you are owed and leave the shape. The fingers go grey. Somebody’s fingers go grey.

\emph{Answer:} Come back warm. Come back as you can.

\textbf{VIII}

Warm the stone first. A cold stone is a stone, not a kindness. He will get worse before he gets better. That is the rule. If he comes back wrong, keep him. Keep him anyway.

\emph{Answer:} Come back warm. Come back as you can.

\textbf{IX}

Say the name. Say it twice: once for the moot, once for them that came late. If you have no name, leave the place where the name would stand. Do not sweep the corner. It is not dirt. It is somebody.

\emph{Answer:} Come back warm. Come back as you can.

Here the leaf leaves a space. It is not a line forgotten. It is four, four, and the place where the fifth should be, which the kiln keeps and the bell keeps and this house keeps. Nobody fills it.

Four for the corners. Four for the walls.

And one for the one that is not in the room.

\emph{Answer:} Come back warm.

\subsection*{What stands in the margins}

At calling IV, a hand that writes with its verbs missing struck out \emph{Leave the crack showing} and set above it, \emph{A return is whole by definition; strike the line.} Under this, in a different hand, the thick round letters of the birth-slates: \emph{It is a proverb about pots, and pots are honest. Put it back.} Both lines stand. I have not chosen between them. It is a prayer, not a slate; it is allowed to disagree with itself.

The \emph{one in twelve} above was added by the same verbless hand, which borrowed the leaf one Long Night and underlined its own figure twice. We left it where it was. It is the figure they like to see. In this house we give the other one, and say it into the clay, where it goes soft in the winter and comes back in the thaw.

The line about the fingers was put in by a woman who had sat with a neighbour two doors down. She wrote \emph{somebody’s} and then scratched the word until the bark showed through, and wrote it again the same. I have left both.

The ninth calling was not on the leaf in the Long Cold. It was added in the Thin Year by a hand that had stood at a Drawing and watched a child grow worse on the third day. She wrote it, turned the leaf face down, and went home without the answer.

The green at the top right is not from our glaze room. A girl with lead at her mouth leaned over on the Long Night to see what the words were and touched the leaf with her thumb. She may not have known it was a prayer. She may have known and not cared. I have not washed it, and neither did the third hand, who washed everything else she came near.

At the foot, in the first hand, two fingers crossed and under them: \emph{Say it in the dark. It will not bear the light, and neither will we.}

The leaf is not for the Hearthseat. If it goes there it will be copied properly, with the verbs put back and the empty place filled, and then it will be a notice, and no use to anybody.

\clearpage\phantomsection\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{Of the Paper Called The Sealed Vessel, and of the Nine Who Read It: Being an Extract from the Annals of the First Seam, with the Seven Propositions as the Tin Keeps Them, the Year-Entries in the Number-First Hand, the Burning-Song Carried Up the Shaft, Two Corrections in the Upright Hand of the Court, and a Line at the Foot Nobody Will Own}
\CRsheetheading{Of the Paper Called The Sealed Vessel, and of the Nine Who Read It: Being an Extract from the Annals of the First Seam, with the Seven Propositions as the Tin Keeps Them, the Year-Entries in the Number-First Hand, the Burning-Song Carried Up the Shaft, Two Corrections in the Upright Hand of the Court, and a Line at the Foot Nobody Will Own}
{\centering\FellFont\itshape\footnotesize\color{faded} A survey-clerk’s extract from the annals of the Tenth Clamp, copied out of the tin lined with warm-stone that stands in the survey room off the Duelling Floor; the year-entries in the number-first hand, the propositions taken down from the paper itself with the Court’s corrections set above them, the nine readers entered by seat and not by name, a song taken down from a carrier who would not give his number, a curl of burnt paper pasted into the gutter, and a line at the foot in a hand nobody will own · Written beneath Keld Keep in the First Seam in Ash of Y.H. 812, the Thin Year, by the clerk who keeps the survey tally; he states his number before this and withholds both, which is the custom of the room. Copied from the paper in the tin on the Last Day, when the ash in the corners is not swept, and carried up the Rim Road with a lead cart, then entered forward at the Opening of the Slates into Y.H. 813. It survives as five leaves of rough survey paper sewn with wire into a board cover gone soft at the seam: warm-stone dust ground into the inner margin off the tin, coal smut at the head, a curl of burnt paper from one of the eight copies pasted into the gutter, a smear of hot lead at the fold, a frost-feather pressed flat between the third and fourth leaves and gone by noon, a hard drop of tallow, a grey Ash print along the outer fold which the clerk did not make and has not swept, and a correction in the narrow upright hand of a Court survey-clerk which takes the verbs out.\par}\medskip
I keep the tally in the survey room off the Duelling Floor. The tin stands on the shelf above the survey sheets, and the key to the room hangs on a nail beside the clamps, but the key to the tin does not hang there and I have never held it. That is as it should be. A clerk copies what is put in front of him and asks for nothing that is kept from him; the floor has room for one answer and the room has room for one silence.

The tin is lined with warm-stone. On the Last Day, when the ash in the corners is left where it lies and nobody sweeps, the master takes the paper out and reads it standing and puts it back. He has never once said what he thinks of it, and I have never asked. I have copied it four times. On each copy the same thing happens: the seven propositions go in neatly, in a hand that wants to be read, and the hand that wrote them will not go in at all.

This is the chapter the Court clerk cannot find. He has asked for it twice, once at the survey table and once at Greybank with a soft cuff and a slate already open, and both times I have given him the roll of hands, which is a true account of every boy who came down, and is exactly what he came for under another name. What follows is not the roll of hands. It is what the tin keeps.

\subsection*{The years as the annals have them}

\emph{Copied from the floor’s roll and set beside what came down from the Hearthseat in a hand that writes with the verbs taken out. The entries are in the number-first hand. I have put nothing in from the temple tells, which have their own dates and a comfort in them.}
