\textbf{Y.H. 702.} A keeper of the Hearthseat named Haldre set down a paper called \emph{The Sealed Vessel}. It was read by nine persons. The Hearthseat enters it as \emph{a paper concerning the retention of vessels}. The floor’s roll enters it nowhere, because the floor counts measures and a paper holds none. Entered here as \emph{nine readers}, and the nine set out below by seat.

\textbf{Y.H. 704.} The keeper disappears. The Court records that he died and was banked. No completed return is entered. The Unbanked say he crossed first. Entered as \emph{the keeper’s account carried forward}, and beneath it, in the same hand, a nought. There is no grave.

\textbf{Y.H. 710.} Nine copies ordered burnt. Eight went on the grate in this room and the ninth went into the tin. The Court’s entry stops at \emph{nine copies ordered burnt}, because an order is a thing a clerk can enter and a fire is not. Entered as \emph{order discharged}. The ninth is not entered, and the roll goes on to the next boy.

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{In the narrow upright hand of the Court’s survey-clerk, against the entry of Y.H. 704:} The keeper’s return was not completed. Strike \emph{crossed first}.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Underneath, in mine:} I have not struck it. The keeper’s return was not completed, which is true, and the Unbanked say he crossed first, which is also true, and the two have different shapes. A clerk who strikes the second has left the nought standing by itself, and a nought on its own is the readiest answer to a man there is.\end{quote}

\subsection*{The seven propositions, as the paper has them}

\emph{Taken out of the tin on the Last Day and copied while the master read from the other side of the table. The paper is in a hand like Ledgerhand and is not Ledgerhand: every verb in it is in the present, which is the way a man writes of a thing he has seen done and not a thing he hopes for. I have set the Court’s correction above each proposition and left the proposition standing beneath, as the old break is left under a new keying.}

No. — As the paper has it — What the Court’s hand set above\par

One — The world is a vessel and every vessel leaks. Leakage is a flaw in the making and not a law of it. — The world was made whole and cracked once. Enter as the First Breaking.\par

Two — A flaw may be stopped. The seam can be made to hold so that nothing passes through it, and the vessel need not be mended again. — The Return is the appointed repair. Strike \emph{need not}.\par

Three — Where nothing leaks, nothing is owed. Where nothing is owed, the deduction has no object. — The deduction is a tithe for the Hearth and is not a loss.\par

Four — The Return is not mercy but the consequence of a leak. A vessel that holds has no dead to send back. — The Return is mercy. Strike \emph{consequence}.\par

Five — The Want is a rate of loss and not a hunger. Stop the loss and the Want ceases of itself. — The Want is the portion kept back. Strike \emph{of itself}.\par

Six — A vessel that holds everything feels nothing. This is not a punishment but the end of accounting. — The Kept are not to be pitied. Enter as: the account is secure.\par

Seven — The Final Banking is not a drawing-in but a sealing. The world made retentive is the world at rest. — The Final Banking is in the hands of the Keeping. Strike \emph{at rest}.\par

The sixth is the one the master turns face down before he reads the seventh. I have seen him do it four times and have never seen him hurry. A man who keeps a paper he will not use will also take his time over it; there is no hurry in a room where nothing is going to be done.

The paper asks for no new way and opens no way in the arm. It asks for the stopping of every way there is. That is why an assessor can take the verbs out of it and still find something left to fear, which is the nouns: \emph{leak}, \emph{owe}, \emph{Want}, \emph{rest}. A verb can be struck; a noun has to be answered.

\subsection*{The nine who read it}

\emph{The tin’s copy gives seats and not names. I have not invented the names, and I have not asked the Vorr, who would say that the numbers are correct and turn the slate face down.}

Seat — What the tin sets beside it\par

The keeper who wrote it — gone in 704; no completed return\par

The Steward of the Hearth — the seat stands\par

The College of Assessors — three readers, not named\par

The bank at the Hearthseat — two readers, not named\par

The roll-room — one reader, not named\par

The keeper of the Hearth-fire\par

That is nine by seat, with the keeper counted at the head of them. Eight seats have a thing set beside them and the ninth has a line left blank. The blank stands where the keeper of the fire should have an answer; the fire is still burning, which is a fact and not a reader. A blank is not an absence in this room; it is a place where a clerk has put down his pen and gone to stand at the door. I have copied the blank as I found it.

\subsection*{The burning-song}

\emph{Taken down at the shaft mouth from a carrier come up with a lead cart, who would not give his number and said the numbers were correct. Sung going up, never going down. He said he had learned it from a man who carried in 710 and would not say which of the nine the man had carried.}

\begin{quote}\itshape Nine were written and nine were read,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and one was read with a hand that shook;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the paper said a vessel might\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape be made to hold and never take.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Eight went on the grate in the survey room,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the ninth went down in a tin of stone;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the stone keeps warm what the fire would not,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the tin keeps shut what the stone keeps warm.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape No leak, no owing, no coming back,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape no cold to count and no debt to keep;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the keeper said it would end the Want,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the Vorr said the numbers were right.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape There’s one went first and has no grave,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and a tin on a shelf that is warm in Ash;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape read it on the Last Day, put it back,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the numbers stand and the hand does not.\end{quote}

He would not sing the last verse until the cart was unloaded. I have set it where he put it, at the mouth and away from the table.

\subsection*{What the Court’s hand did}

A survey-clerk of the factor’s office borrowed the leaf when the survey table sat at the Keep. He writes upright and narrow, and takes the verbs out as though a verb were a thing a man might smuggle past a weigh in the fold of a cuff.

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item Against \emph{every vessel leaks}, he set \emph{the vessel is whole by ordinance}, which is a sentence true of no cup in Keld.

\item Against \emph{the deduction has no object}, he set \emph{the deduction is received in due order}. The order is due and the object is not named.

\item Against \emph{a vessel that holds everything feels nothing}, he set \emph{the account is secure}, and struck the word \emph{end}.

\item Against \emph{the world at rest}, he set \emph{the work continues}, which is the phrase the College teaches its own to write at the foot of every closed file.

\item Against the blank where the ninth reader stands he wrote nothing. The hand passed over it without a stroke, which is the readiest way of correcting a reader I have yet seen.

\end{itemize}

I have left both readings everywhere, the paper under the neat hand, as the floor keeps the first number under the second when a boy’s measure changes and nobody scrapes the old one out. A clerk who takes the verbs out of a paper leaves the nouns standing, and the nouns in this paper are the only things in the First Seam that have ever frightened me.

\subsection*{At the head and in the gutter}

The coal at the head came off the master’s sleeve when he leaned over to turn the sixth proposition face down and would not sit down to do it. The warm-stone dust in the inner margin comes off the tin every time the paper goes back in, and there is more of it on the seventh proposition than on the first, which tells a man nothing he should repeat. The curl of burnt paper in the gutter is from one of the eight; it curls inward, the way paper curls when the fire takes the edge and not the middle, and I have pasted it in with flour paste that has gone brittle. The hot lead at the fold came off a surveyor’s cuff on the day a passing was measured early; it has eaten the corner of the fourth proposition and I have not written the word back in. The frost-feather came up out of the paper on the climb over the Cold Pass and was gone by the time I found the leaf to press it in. The tallow is my lamp set too near the tally. The grey along the outer fold is not mine and not the Court’s. I have had this leaf from the last Opening of the Slates and have not swept it, and if the factor asks why a clerk leaves dirt on a chronicle I shall tell him it is entered as observance kept, which is a phrase he will accept without looking up.

\subsection*{At the foot, in a hand nobody will own}

\begin{quote}\itshape Eight went to the fire and one to the stone,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the stone keeps warm what the fire undid;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape a world that holds is a world that feels,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the keeper who crossed has no name on the slate.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Ask the tin what it keeps.\end{quote}

I have asked the master of the floor, a surveyor come up from the Ninth Gallery, and a Vorr who came through with a warm-stone and would not set it down, and had three answers and no hand. The Vorr said the numbers are correct. The surveyor turned the slate face down. The master cleaned a clamp and went on with the counting. I have left the line where it was written.

The tin goes back on the shelf and the key goes back on its nail. Tomorrow a boy will be brought down at thirteen and will give his number before his name, and the master will ask him the second question while he cleans the iron, and whatever the boy answers will be entered in the same neat hand as the boys who stayed warm. The paper in the tin will be a little warm in the dark. Somebody paid for that warmth and the payer is not entered in any roll I keep.

\clearpage\phantomsection\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{The Ninth Gallery Book of Remedies, Being Remedies for the Sweet at the Gum, the Rope-Coloured Hand, the Descent Boy’s Fortnight, the Warm-Stone Burn, the Member Gone Dark, the Cut from a Seam-Shard, the Second Chill and the Birth-Flower, Set Down Beneath Keld Keep with the Errors Left Standing}
\CRsheetheading{The Ninth Gallery Book of Remedies, Being Remedies for the Sweet at the Gum, the Rope-Coloured Hand, the Descent Boy’s Fortnight, the Warm-Stone Burn, the Member Gone Dark, the Cut from a Seam-Shard, the Second Chill and the Birth-Flower, Set Down Beneath Keld Keep with the Errors Left Standing}
{\centering\FellFont\itshape\footnotesize\color{faded} A mine-leech’s and midwife’s book of remedies in the hard short Rim speech, written in Grathic letters learned off a Court survey-clerk with the Keldish endings left in where they will not fit; the cures in a leech’s hand on the backs of survey sheets gone soft with slate-damp, the objections of a physician come down from Greybank pressed coal-grey into the margin, the corrections of a survey-clerk of the Court in narrow upright Ledgerhand, a clamp-master’s line in charcoal at the foot of the remedies, a watch-song with the place where the tenth should stand left as it is sung, and one line at the foot in a hand nobody will own · Written in the Ninth Gallery beneath Keld Keep between Stone of Y.H. 812 and Ilmen of Y.H. 813, the Long Cold and the Thin Year, by Orva of the Ninth Gallery, a leech who dressed the hands of the Duelling Floor and caught the children of the survey families for seven-and-twenty years; begun on the backs of rim-seam survey sheets spoiled by slate-damp, folded into oiled survey-cloth and carried up the shaft against a shaving of warm-stone, then down the Rim Road in Ilmen of Y.H. 813 with a survey party bound for Greybank, where it was copied onto the back of a voided seam-tally. It survives with coal dust ground into the grain at the head, a tideline of slate-water that has taken two words clean off the second leaf, a bead of Ninth Gallery lead shut into the sewing, a scorch where a spark off the hot-lead corner caught the third leaf, a shaving of warm-stone pressed flat in the fold which kept its heat one night on the stone floor and is cold now, a ring of barley-water gone grey at the edge, a thumb of tallow, a grey Ash print along the outer fold that nobody will own, objections in the cold margin hand of the physician, corrections in the upright hand of the survey-clerk, the clamp-master’s line in charcoal, and the one line at the foot\par}\medskip
I keep the leech’s box in the Ninth Gallery, where the rock sweats and the smell of hot lead gives the only warning a man gets down here. I have dressed the hands of the Duelling Floor and caught the children of the survey families for seven-and-twenty years. Nobody asked me for this book. A boy came up in the lean week with the way in his forearm gone rope-coloured below a clamp, and asked what I did for it, and I heard myself answer in the hard short speech of this place, and did not know whether I believed it. A remedy you have to say in your mother’s voice is a remedy nobody has looked at in a long while. I have looked at some. The rest I have left standing, because a man at the changing of the watch wants a hand more than a correction.

I write on the backs of survey sheets the slate-damp spoiled. The rim-seam figures went up to Greybank where figures go, and what is left is paper enough for a book nobody asked to see. I write in the Grathic letters a clerk taught me and keep the Keldish endings where they will not fit. The coal at the head is mine. The grey in the gutter came off a cuff laid where no cuff has business lying. There is no Last Day under this Keep; the dust has nowhere to go.

\subsection*{The order of the leech-room}

\emph{Written small on the first survey sheet, with one word gone over in slate-water.}

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item Lay the warm-stone face down when you go to a child. A stone with its warm side up takes from the room, and a room in the Ninth is spending already.

\item Try the stone on your own wrist before it goes to a belly. It came out of somebody’s fire and the man who carried it up before me is in no roll I have read.

\item Set the number above the name, as they do on the floor. A man down here gives his number before his face, and a leech who writes the face first has written the wrong man.

\item Never set cold iron to a burn to draw it. Iron takes as well as draws. I learned that above me on the floor and have not unlearned it below.

\item Do not set a second clamp above a hand gone the colour of old rope. I wrote this on the iron board; the master struck it twice; I wrote it twice.

\item When the second chill comes, count with her. Do not count for her.

\end{itemize}

I asked a woman of the survey families what she saw when she crossed two fingers over the birth-flower, and she gave me a date. A date is an answer that does not spoil in the mouth. I have put the date in the margin and left the question standing where I asked it.

\subsection*{The remedies, as they are used}

Trouble — What is set to it — The manner of it — Who is spent\par

The sweet at the gum — Sour barley-water; wood-ash at the gum; a tend above ground — We say a sweet answers a sweet. The physician says lead, and here he is right: the rock sweats hot lead, and a man in the lower galleries tastes it before he sees it. I sent nine up; four came back with the line gone. — The Ninth, which cannot stop and does not ask.\par

The rope-coloured hand (below a clamp) — Take the iron off; wrap in wool; set nothing above — The floor says a clamp draws heat out of a way that will not settle. I set one again higher on a boy in Y.H. 811 and by evening the arm had the colour of the stone. — The hand, and the number that stays when it does not.\par

The Descent boy’s fortnight — Warm-stone in wool after the knife; a clamp on the fifteenth day — We say the stone gives back what the knife took. The physician says a warmed arm spends faster and that a stone from another man’s fire is that man’s heat in a pocket. I gave the stone to eleven; ten held the clamp and one was given the keys. — Somebody paid for those coals. His name is on no slate.\par

The warm-stone burn — Tallow, then a clean fold; never cold iron — The floor says iron draws the heat out of a burn. I set a cold clamp on one and watched the skin go the colour of old rope; I have not done it twice. His sentence stands above mine. — The burn, and the hand if the iron stays.\par

The member gone dark — Three turns of wool, a stone at the belly, and work — The extremity goes first and the middle holds out, and there is an hour on the far side of the warming when a body spends faster than it takes in. I have no name for that hour and have left the place where the name would stand the length a name of that kind wants. — The man, who cannot stop working. This is the row where I have been least honest.\par

A cut from a seam-shard — Tallow, then a clean fold; never the grey — The men put grey from the corner in a cut to dry it, believing it clean. I dressed three and found grey under the skin in all three, a white line I could not get out. Above ground they sweep their corners after the Last Day and call it dealt with. — The cut.\par

The second chill — Warmth, barley-water, a watch to the fourth day; we hold them now — It comes after the warming, not before. A hearth-maid from Low Kiln says a warmed body gives heat away faster and walking faster still, and that the child should be held and counted with. I walked nine and held four; of the walked two went thin, of the held none. I kept the counts on birch bark and did not add them. — The household, one night’s sleep; sometimes the child.\par

The birth-flower — Nothing. Two fingers crossed, and the word the mother gives — I rubbed one with salt, one with slip and one with nothing, and the thing kept its shape in all three. A woman of the Weir washed one and her child went flat by evening; I have not joined the two. When asked what it is I give a date. — Nobody knows. The child’s skin, perhaps.\par

Nothing under this Keep is given away. It is carried from one hand to another and called a cure. That is the only sentence I will stand behind.

\subsection*{The note under the knuckle}

The surveyors tap a piece of warm-stone before they set it in a tin. A sound piece answers full under the knuckle; a flawed one answers flat, a small dead sound that stops at the surface. It is the one thing in the Ninth that costs nothing and is still allowed to be true, and no clerk has thought to enter it.

I tapped a man once, gone thin after a thin return, and put my ear to the little flat I thought I heard. The flat was not in him. A body is not a stone, though we cut the number into it and call the cutting honest. I did not say so then, because a survey-clerk was in the room with a slate. I have written it here, which is a different matter.

\subsection*{The Sweating}

The stone sweats in its season and the old ways ache before the thaw and after it. A boy who says his arm aches is told the weather will have the last word; one who says it twice is given a warm-stone out of somebody’s fire, which is theft from an account he did not open and is entered nowhere. The stone comes up already warm and the carrying takes the name off.

The Vorr say the count is in the bone and that the tube finds nothing there. I have seen a collector go away with a blank slate beside a man who had worked here thirty years. When one of them dies they seat the body facing the direction it came from and say they were never owed. A woman of Low Kiln would cover such a body with a fold and cross two fingers. Both are kindnesses; only one has a number in it. I have set them side by side and joined them to nothing.

I have no remedy for the Sweating and have left the place where one would stand the length a remedy of that kind wants. A clerk would put a nought in it and call it empty. I have seen the place and it is not empty.

\subsection*{The watch-song}

\emph{Sung low at the changing of the watch, to the stone and not to the men. There is a place after the third verse where the tenth should stand, and no singer has put a word in it. The tenth is kept for the stone.}

\begin{quote}\itshape Nine on the board and one on the nail,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the tenth is kept below;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape give the number first, then the face,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and wrap the hand in wool.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape The rock sweats and the lead smells sweet,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the way goes rope at the second clamp;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape a stone comes up already warm\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and nobody asks whose.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Hold the child and count the breath,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape do not walk her, do not ask the slate;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape what comes back is not what went,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and comes back as the seam can.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Nine I counted and one held out ---\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the tenth goes down where the stone keeps.\end{quote}

A survey-clerk put a round nought in the held place and wrote \emph{vacancy} beneath it, which is a figure with the stone taken out. A nought can be carried away in a cuff. The tenth is a place and stays. I changed one line in seven-and-twenty years: \emph{and nobody knows} became \emph{and nobody asks whose}, and the men singing with me did not notice.

\subsection*{What the physician pressed in the margin}

He came down from Greybank in Ilmen of Y.H. 812 with a book that had the word \emph{lead} in it and a hand that wrote without asking. Against the sweet at the gum he set \emph{lead, as in the glaze rooms}, and he was right in a gallery where the rock sweats hot lead and gives a man nothing but his tongue to warn him. Against the rope-coloured hand he set \emph{no second clamp, no such transmission}, true in the language he speaks and of no use to a floor with one answer for everything. Against the child come up cold he set \emph{the air warms the child, not the stone}. He was right in all three and had nothing a survey family could pay for. I have left his sentences above mine and my verbs underneath.

\subsection*{What the Court survey-clerk did}

He borrowed the sheets when the winter seam was counted, ink settled in two fingers of a soft cuff. He struck out my column headed \emph{Who is spent} and wrote \emph{No cost entered} above it, which is a true thing in a dishonest place. Where I wrote that the boy’s fortnight was paid out of somebody’s fire, he set \emph{the measure is retained in the stone}, taking the hands out as though a stone could carry itself up a shaft. Against \emph{one in twelve} he wrote \emph{the deduction is constant}, which lets the figure stand and the gallery go on spending. I have put my verbs back underneath. A clerk can write without verbs because he has never held a warm-stone with a man’s heat still in it.

\subsection*{In the hand of a clamp-master, in charcoal}

\begin{quote}\itshape It’s the draw, not age. I have seen a man grey in one winter at the tube and could not get the colour back with a week at the fire. Ask a Vorr what the clamp took and he will tell you the number. He will not tell you the hand.\end{quote}

He wrote it while I was at the shaft mouth and set the leaf back with the fold changed, and put no name to it, because a name on a leaf is a name a clerk can carry up the road. A man who has counted nothing is allowed one sentence in a book of physic. I have set his line above mine.

\subsection*{At the head and in the gutter}

The coal at the head came off the master’s sleeve. The slate-water took two words clean off the second leaf and I have not written them back: a remedy with two words gone is a remedy said slowly, and everything down here is said slowly. The bead of lead was shut into the sewing by a girl who would not say which gallery it came off. The scorch is a spark off the hot-lead corner that caught while I wrote and went out under my hand; I have not entered the burn. The warm-stone shaving in the fold held heat one night and is cold now, which is the order of things here. The ring of barley-water came from a cup a boy would not drink from. The tallow is mine, from holding the sheet in the draught up the shaft. The grey along the outer fold is not mine and not the Court’s, and I have not swept it. There is no Last Day beneath this Keep, and the dust has nowhere to go.

\subsection*{At the foot, in a hand nobody will own}

\begin{quote}\itshape The floor keeps the number. The stone keeps the warm.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape The man between them is spent in no house.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape The tenth is kept, and nobody says for whom.\end{quote}

I asked a physician, a survey-clerk of the Court, and a clamp-master off the floor, and had three answers and no hand. I have left the line where it was written. The book goes back into the oiled cloth in the leech’s box. Tomorrow a boy will come up with the sweet at his mouth or a hand gone the colour of old rope, and I shall take the iron off, set the stone face down, put my verbs back where the clerk took them out, and leave the tenth where it is, because a child is not an account and a man at the changing of the watch wants a hand more than a doctrine.

\clearpage\phantomsection\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{The Book of the Open Bowl, Being the Seven Remedies of a House-Physician in the Bowl of Sere, with the Eighth Place Left Standing}
\CRsheetheading{The Book of the Open Bowl, Being the Seven Remedies of a House-Physician in the Bowl of Sere, with the Eighth Place Left Standing}
{\centering\FellFont\itshape\footnotesize\color{faded} A bowl-house physician’s book of remedies in the southern courtesy hand, written in the thin gold so that no clerk could mistake physic for a contract; the cures in a house-leech’s hand, the leaning entries of the tally-clerk above them, a northern bond-woman’s charcoal underneath, and one line at the foot in a hand nobody will own; with one song for the third hour and an eighth place kept empty · Written in Smoke of Y.H. 812, the Thin Year, in a house of the Ten Bowls in the Bowl of Sere, by Orylla Vanee, a house-physician who kept the sick-bowls and attended both the slave births and the exhibited returns; set down in thin gold on prepared paper, the back of the leaf carrying the thick gold of a contract that was never signed. Carried north with a consignment of oil and tallow-wasp resin and copied at Greybank onto the back of a Court grain-warrant voided by the Long Cold. It survives with the thin gold worn from half the remedies so that the uncleared contract shows through, the yellow dust of the burning winds worked into the sewing rather than lying on the face, a thumb of olive oil, a resin smear that caught dust and will not come out, a wine-ring at the foot, a scorched corner where the leaf lay near a court fire, a grey Ash print along the gutter that nobody will own, a grain of southern wheat stuck fast in the resin, and a single pale hair in the fold that is not gold. The corrections stand above in the leaning hand of the house tally-clerk and underneath in the charcoal of a woman of the grain mills who would not give her name.\par}\medskip
I keep the sick-bowls of this house. That is my office: to set a bowl of barley water at the head of a bed, to carry it away when it has been drunk, and to know which of a girl’s seven names to say when the household asks for somebody who is not in the room. I have kept these bowls eleven years and nobody has ever asked me which of the seven I meant, which tells a person how much a name is worth here and how much a bowl.

I write in the thin gold because thick gold is for contracts, and a contract is a thing said to a man who is not in the room. A remedy is said to the bowl. If the bowl answers, that is between them. The tally-clerk writes above my lines and a northern woman writes underneath, and I have left both standing, because a house that keeps only one hand in a book of physic has stopped learning, which is the same as a bowl that has stopped pouring.

The thin gold has gone off half the remedies, and where it has gone the uncleared contract shows through: nine marks, a date, a house-name grander than the house. I have not written over it. A physician who covers her leaf will soon be covering a patient.

\subsection*{The order of a sick-room}

\emph{Written small in the thin gold, with one word gone over in resin.}

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item Set the bowl at the head, never at the feet. A person takes from the top down, as a bowl empties from the lip.

\item Leave the court door open. A sick one who cannot hear the third hour will die of wondering what the bell said, which is the more expensive death.

\item Ask whose bowl it is before you fill it. A slave’s warmth is the house’s holding and a free servant’s is her own, and a physician who gives the same physic to both has made a gift of goods that were never hers.

\item Pour for the house, not for the person. The person belongs to the house and the house knows what it wants. I have set down what I was told, not what I would choose, which is a physician’s whole art here.

\item When the burning winds come off the east, wet a cloth and lay it over the lips. The wind takes what is loose, and a man’s lips are the loosest thing he has.

\item At the third hour, stop. The bowl is being emptied in every court in the city and our small room is not behindhand.

\item Do not tap a person to hear whether they hold. A bowl-surgeon taps the clay; a man who taps a person is asking a question whose answer belongs to the owner.

\end{itemize}

I have set down more bowls than I can count, which is why I count them in sevens and leave the eighth place standing. A girl here may have seven names by the time she is grown and keep whichever the household prefers, and a book of remedies ought to be at least as honest as a household.

\subsection*{The seven remedies, as they are used}

Trouble — What is set to it — The manner of it — Who is emptied\par

A fever that burns — Bleed at the elbow; a bowl of wine at the head — Take from the arm while the head is still clear, and give the wine after, to fill what was taken. A physician of the north would leave the blood in and give water. I have set her words underneath mine and both stand. — The patient, in the arm, by the house’s leave.\par

The thirst of the south — Water, and a wet cloth over the lips — Not wine. Wine is for the third hour and for the emptying, and a man who drinks it in a sick-room is being emptied without a slate. The water-carrier brings it up from the court well and is not thanked. — The water-carrier, who carries it and is not entered.\par

A hand taken by the grain mills — Tallow, a clean fold, resin if a graft must hold — A nest of tallow-wasp resin costs four marks and holds a patch until the vessel takes. The bowl-surgeon lifts the nest to the light and listens to it before he buys, the way a potter listens to a pot. In Grath they burn the nests. I have never asked why. — The mill. It takes no account and names no names.\par

The stone-cough of the dust — Steam of hot water under a cloth; honey if the house has it — To the mouth, not the face. The burning winds put a yellow grit in everything, and a man coughs it up in the morning in a colour he will not discuss. The woman of the mills writes that no steam will bring it up and that I am treating the symptom of a wind. Both stand. — The wind, which does not answer.\par

A wall that has given way within — A living patch, held under pressure with resin — Take the wall from a donor whose measure was shaped like the sick one’s. A patch from a donor shaped otherwise takes anyway and goes on wanting, and a person who wants a life that was not theirs is unsafe to exhibit. The bowl-surgeons know this and the buyers do not. — The donor, first, and the buyer afterward.\par

A child that will not take milk — A wet-nurse come up from the mills, for a season — She was returned thin and has milk enough for one; the house has bought her for two. Give the child barley water when she sleeps and do not tell the house how little there is. — The other child at the mill, who was not bought.\par

A wound that will not close — A pinch of quiet ash, then a clean fold — The house buys back its own funeral ash, a year’s grain burnt under one person and the remainder sold at the price they ask. I have set a pinch in a wound gone three days yellow and watched it go quiet by evening. The Court licenses such ash only to the rich; the penalty for selling it unlicensed is a greyed hand. I have never sold any. I have set it in wounds. — Nobody. This is the row I keep turned down.\par

There is an eighth place in this book where a remedy would stand for the trouble a person has when they remember who they were. I have left it the length of a name. The tally-clerk has put a figure in it; the figure stood and the place stood beside it and the two did not touch.

\subsection*{On the full note}

Tap a sound bowl with the knuckle and it answers full. Tap a cracked one and it answers flat, a small dead sound that stops at the surface. The bowl-surgeons listen to the clay before they pour a graft into it. A green-glazed bowl bought from a northern potter gave a flat knock in its first frost and went from lip to foot without anything falling out that I could see. In the Clay Yard they would call it a bowl gone wrong and sweep around it. Here the house calls northern clay inferior, and I have not corrected the house.

A northern potter tapped the ribs of an exhibited man at a feast and said the man had gone flat. He was a guest in that court and I did not correct him; in this country a guest who is corrected stops being a guest and becomes a witness. I have written his words without his name, which is the only mercy a physician here can practise without a slate.

\subsection*{Of the beautiful return}

This is the part of the book the house would have me leave out, so I have set it in the middle where nobody skipping to a remedy can miss it.

When a person has been emptied and brought back thin, the bowl-surgeons warm them and pour until the head rises. The memory goes first, then the appetite, then the sense of self; what comes back is calm and wants nothing. The house calls this a beautiful return and exhibits it at feasts as proof of generosity. A woman with seven names came back from one and kept the name the house preferred, saying she had always been that one, and the house was well pleased.

A physician of the north wrote that the calm is a burn. The copy that came down to me had the word taken clean away, as though a word could be taken off paper the way wine is taken off a bowl. I have written it back in the thin gold. I have not seen the burn. I have seen the calm, and a woman who said she had always been the name the house kept. I have set both sentences down, because a book that holds only one of them is a ledger, and I would sooner be wrong in a book than right in a ledger.

\subsection*{The song for the third hour}

\emph{Sung at the wine-press, not at the feast, with the vowels open and the ends thrown into the fire. The last line of the third part is said to the bowl and not to the company.}

\begin{quote}\itshape The wind comes yellow and takes the lip,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the mill turns under and takes the hand;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape a bowl goes round and a name goes round,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the one that is kept is the one that stands.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Pour for the house and pour for the heat,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape pour for the ash that the house buys back;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the calm comes first and the wanting goes,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the bowl goes dry and says no lack.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Three at the board and a fourth on the shelf,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape seven on a girl and one on the slate;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the ash comes back and the wine comes round,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and what went out . . . . . . . . . . .\end{quote}

There is a space before the last line where a name would stand. I have left it the length it is. The tally-clerk has tried twice to fill it; both times the space stood under the figure, which is the only argument this house has ever lost and never admitted.

\subsection*{What the tally-clerk did}

He borrowed the leaf after the third hour, being a man who cannot let paper lie, and writes in the leaning counting-hand with the gold gone thin.

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item At \emph{a house-leech’s mercy} he struck out \emph{mercy} and set above it \emph{return completed, current}.

\item Against the quiet ash he wrote \emph{licensed residue, market rate}, and put a figure in the margin where I had put a pinch.

\item Against the eighth place he set a round nought and wrote \emph{vacancy} underneath, as though a place where a name had been were the same as nothing.

\item He took the verbs out of two lines. A sentence with no verb travels through a counting room without catching on anything, which is what a counting room wants of a sentence.

\end{itemize}

I have put the words back underneath his and left his standing above. He can enter the ash at the market rate, for the house paid it. What he cannot enter is the space at the end of the song, which tells a person he knows the difference between a figure and a place better than a physician has any right to.

\subsection*{What the woman of the mills wrote underneath}

She is a bond-woman come up from the grain mills, returned thin, and she writes in charcoal on the backs of barley ration tallies with a hand that shakes at the ends of words. She would not let me put her name.

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Against the bleeding:} I have seen four bled. Two were quieter by evening. Quiet is not better.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Against the beautiful return:} The calm is not peace. It is a room with the door shut and nobody in it.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Against the eighth place:} That is where my name was. I have not forgotten it. I have only stopped saying it where a clerk can hear.\end{quote}

I have left her words without a name, which is the only kindness in this house that a clerk cannot enter. She took her charcoal away and did not ask for the leaf back, which is how I know she meant it.

\subsection*{At the head and in the gutter}

The olive thumb at the head is mine; I turn the leaves with the hand I carry the bowl with. The dust of the burning winds has worked into the sewing rather than lying on the face, which is how a person tells a book carried in a coat from one read in a court. The resin smear caught dust in the third year and will not come out, and I have stopped trying. The wine-ring at the foot belongs to the third hour and is small. The scorched corner is where the leaf lay too near a court fire and went brown without burning through, so the writing there is thin and I have not gone over it, because a word written thin is a word said quietly and most of ours are. The grey print along the gutter came off a cuff laid where no cuff has business lying, and I have not swept it. There is no Last Day in a house of the Ten Bowls and nothing gets swept. The grain of wheat in the resin came from a loaf sent north and returned uneaten. The pale hair in the fold is not gold and is not mine.

\subsection*{At the foot, in a hand nobody will own}

\begin{quote}\itshape The fire takes the grain and the house buys back the smoke;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the bowl takes the wine and nobody buys that back.\end{quote}

I asked the bowl-keeper, the tally-clerk and a woman who would not give her name, and had three answers and no hand. I have left the line where it was written. The book goes back under the fourth bowl, where I can find it in the dark. Tomorrow the third hour will come, and I shall set a bowl down at the head of a bed and carry it away when it has been drunk, and if a girl has seven names I shall say the one the house keeps and leave the other six standing.

\clearpage\phantomsection\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{The Pail Song, Being the Drawing-Song of the Yard Well in Low Kiln, Sung at the Bucket-Round in Frost, with the Pails Counted Going Up from the Stone Lip, the Fourth Left Standing for the Well, the Frost-Bloom Knocked Grey, a Kiln-Master’s Ruling in Broad Charcoal, a Factor’s Clerk’s Figures in the Narrow Upright Hand, a Gloss from a Woman of the Bucket-Round, and One Line at the Foot in a Hand Nobody Will Own}
\CRsheetheading{The Pail Song, Being the Drawing-Song of the Yard Well in Low Kiln, Sung at the Bucket-Round in Frost, with the Pails Counted Going Up from the Stone Lip, the Fourth Left Standing for the Well, the Frost-Bloom Knocked Grey, a Kiln-Master’s Ruling in Broad Charcoal, a Factor’s Clerk’s Figures in the Narrow Upright Hand, a Gloss from a Woman of the Bucket-Round, and One Line at the Foot in a Hand Nobody Will Own}
{\centering\FellFont\itshape\footnotesize\color{faded} A work song of the drawing, in the low hard speech of the yard, said to the rope and answered at the stone lip; the verses counted in pails going up from the well, with the fourth pail left standing where the frost wrote and not carried; the rubrics of the lip in the writer’s charcoal thinned with well-water, a kiln-master’s ruling in broad charcoal, a factor’s clerk’s figures standing above in Ledgerhand, a gloss pressed into the margin by a woman of the bucket-round, and one line at the foot in a hand nobody will claim · Sung at the yard well four doors down the Clay Yard from the Vail kiln-house in Low Kiln of Sill and set down in Frost of Y.H. 813 by a woman who has drawn at that well eleven winters and knows by the feel of the rope when the bucket has cleared the lip; written in charcoal thinned with well-water on the back of a bucket-tally spoiled by a wet thumb, folded twice and tied with grey wool to the hook of the well-rope under a broken pot turned mouth-down against the frost, carried up the Clay Road with a consignment of coarse tile and copied forward at Greybank in Ilmen of Y.H. 814 onto the back of a factor’s voided weigh-slip. It survives with a pale stone-lip thumb worked into the grain at the head, a frost-bloom raised white along the gutter and gone grey where the bucket touched it, a chip of the north lip in the fold, a rope-fray across the third verse, a pail-ring gone cold on the second leaf, a green bead of lead glaze pressed into the lower corner by a girl with sweetness at one mouth-corner, a sour small-ale ring at the foot, a grey Ash print along the outer fold that nobody will own, the kiln-master’s broad ruling, the clerk’s figures standing above, the bucket-round woman’s gloss in the margin, and the one line at the foot\par}\medskip
I draw at the yard well, four doors down the Clay Yard from the Vail kiln-house, and I have done it eleven winters. The rope wears a shine where the hands of the bucket-round have gone up it, and by that shine a woman can tell how much water the yard has taken in a year, which nobody has ever entered. The frost writes on the north lip in the cold months, in fronds the width of a finger, and the bucket knocks it grey on the second pail and the yard calls it weather. We leave the fourth pail standing where the frost stood. No hand carries it to the trough and no number is said over it where a man with a slate can hear.

A man come up from Greybank with a soft cuff and ink settled in two fingers of it stood at the trough and asked what the women said while they drew. He wrote the answer into his book before I had finished saying it, with the doing taken out and a figure put where a pail should stand, and went off up the Clay Road with his boots clean. So I have set the words down as we say them, to the rope and not to the bucket-round.

The stone at the head is mine. I held the tally down against the lip with the hand I wind with and did not know I had marked it. Stone goes into the grain and no washing takes it out, which is why we sign with it here and not with ink.

\subsection*{How it is drawn}

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item Wind from the shoulder. A wrist brings the bucket up too fast and slops half of it over the lip, and water spilled on the flagstones is water the yard has paid to carry and does not have.

\item A bucket snatched at the lip knocks the frost grey before its time, and a woman who has knocked it grey cannot call it weather with a straight face, though she will.

\item Set the pail on the lip, not in the trough. A pail left standing in the trough goes cold before it is carried, and cold water taken into a house is warmth the house pays out of its own pot before the morning is done.

\item Tap the pail as it fills. A whole one answers full and the note goes up the rope into the hand; a split one stops at the hoop and gives back flat, and a flat pail is set by the wall with the crack showing so nobody has to be told which hand drew it.

\item Four pails to a verse and a rest at the set-down. The rest is not a pail and is not counted. It is where the fourth stands.

\item The fourth pail is the well’s. It stands where the frost wrote and the bucket goes round it. If a girl asks why, tell her to count the pails going up and find out; if she asks again, do not answer her, because the answer is a place and a place cannot be told to a person who wants a figure.

\item Do not sing it on an Account-day. The bell goes four, four and a gap, and a drawing-song set against that gap comes home wrong in the shoulder.

\item The last part is kept back. It is for when the man from Greybank has gone back over the north bridge and the kiln-master has gone up the terrace and the yard can hear itself again.

\end{itemize}

\subsection*{The song}

\emph{Said low into the rope, with the pail steady on the lip. One verse to four pails going up. The fourth is not a pail; it is the standing of the pail on the stone, and it is not said aloud. The refrain goes into the well and not across the yard; said to a person it becomes an account, and there is enough account at the Cross without bringing it down the steps.}

\begin{quote}\itshape The rope has a shine where the hands have gone up,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape laid down one on another before any of us came;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape wind from the shoulder and let the bucket tell you,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and set it down where the stone is cold.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Wind it and lift it, three to the trough,}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{and the fourth stands where the frost-bloom wrote;}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{the well keeps the pail that nobody carries,}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{and the slate goes up the road with none of it.}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape The frost writes white on the north lip in fronds\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape where the Warm went out of the stone in the night;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the bucket knocks it grey on the second pail\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the yard calls it weather and goes on drawing.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Wind it and lift it, three to the trough,}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{and the fourth stands where the frost-bloom wrote;}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{the well keeps the pail that nobody carries,}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{and the slate goes up the road with none of it.}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Tap the pail as it fills. A whole one answers full\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the note goes up the rope into the hand;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape a split one stops at the hoop and gives back flat,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and it goes by the wall with the crack showing.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Wind it and lift it, three to the trough,}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{and the fourth stands where the frost-bloom wrote;}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{the well keeps the pail that nobody carries,}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{and the slate goes up the road with none of it.}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape One in twelve is printed and read twice at the Cross,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape once for the moot and once for them that came late;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the bell goes four, four and a gap and nobody crosses,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the figure you heard is not the figure they paid.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Wind it and lift it, three to the trough,}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{and the fourth stands where the frost-bloom wrote;}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{the well keeps the pail that nobody carries,}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{and the slate goes up the road with none of it.}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape The water comes up and the pail goes down\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the rope between them keeps the whole of the count;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape a figure travels light in a clean man’s coat,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and a pail of water does not travel at all.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Wind it and lift it, three to the trough,}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{and the fourth stands where the frost-bloom wrote;}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{the well keeps the pail that nobody carries,}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{and the slate goes up the road with none of it.}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Three to the trough and the fourth on the lip.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape The bucket goes around where the frond stood;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape we do not say the fourth to a man with a slate,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and we do not knock what the frost put there.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Wind it and lift it, three to the trough,}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{and the fourth stands where the frost-bloom wrote;}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{the well keeps the pail that nobody carries,}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{and the slate goes up the road with none of it.}\end{quote}

There is a space before the last refrain in the singing, the length of a hand laid flat on the north lip where you feel for the frost before you set the pail. I have left it on the tally. A clerk put a round nought in it once, which is a thing you can hold up and look at; a hand laid flat is not.

\subsection*{The part they keep back}

\emph{Not said while a man from Greybank is at the trough or a man from the terrace is on the steps. Said to the rope and not across the yard.}

\begin{quote}\itshape The well gives and the slate carries away;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape neither asks which house the water came out of.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape There’s a word comes up on the rope and stops at the lip\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and we do not say it to a man with a cuff.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Four pails and a rest. The rest is the well’s.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape The clerk has no word for a pail that stands still.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape He can carry the figure. He cannot carry the stone.\end{quote}

There is no verse after it. The next thing is the rope going down, which is not a verse and has never wanted one.

\subsection*{What the kiln-master set above it}

He came down from the terrace for a pail of water with the sweet edge of the glaze at one corner of his mouth and read the tally with one eye on the steps. Against \emph{the fourth stands where the frost-bloom wrote} he wrote in broad charcoal: \emph{Frost on the lip; a weather effect. No entry arises.} He underlined it twice. Against \emph{a split one stops at the hoop and gives back flat} he set: \emph{Vessels to be proved at the kiln, not at the well.} He did not look at the well while he wrote.

Underneath, in mine: he is right about the frost and wrong about the pail. A pail is proved at the lip, where the water goes over the stone and somebody carries the loss into a house. He reads with one eye on the fire, as a man does who has never watched a bucket come up in the dark.

\subsection*{What the clerk did}

The factor’s clerk borrowed the leaf at Greybank on the morning the tile was weighed, with his cuff gone soft from washing and the ink sitting in two fingers of it. He took the verbs out and set his words above mine, the way a newer repair lies over an older one on a pot.

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item At \emph{the well keeps the pail that nobody carries} he wrote \emph{water unaccounted for; no deduction arises}, which leaves the water standing and takes the keeping away.

\item At \emph{the bucket knocks it grey and the yard calls it weather} he wrote \emph{frost dissipated by use; no cost to district}. True in a figure and false at the lip, where the grey stays in the stone and the yard has called it weather for eleven winters without once believing its own word.

\item At \emph{a split one stops at the hoop and gives back flat} he wrote \emph{vessel unsound; not a chargeable defect}. At this well a flat pail is a thing set by the wall with the crack showing.

\item At \emph{one in twelve is printed and read twice} he wrote \emph{deduction current; one part in twelve; twice read}, and set the printed figure above it. He has entered the number that was read and not the number that was paid.

\item At the fourth pail he wrote \emph{three removed, fourth nil}. The fourth is not nil. It is a pail standing on a stone, which a man can carry away in a figure and a woman cannot.

\item Where I had left the space before the last refrain he put a round nought and wrote \emph{vacancy} beneath it. A nought is a number and travels. A hand laid flat on the lip is a place and stays where it was put.

\end{itemize}

\subsection*{What a woman of the bucket-round put in the margin}

The thick charcoal belongs to a woman who has drawn at this well since before the Glaze Wars and has knocked the frost grey on the second pail every winter she can remember. I have copied it as it stands, without making the hands agree.

At \emph{the frost writes white on the north lip}: \emph{It wrote in fronds the year my sister went south and every year since. I have called it weather every time and will call it weather tomorrow. A word said for eleven winters does not become true, it becomes cheap.}

At \emph{the well keeps the pail that nobody carries}: \emph{A girl asked whose pail it was. I told her to ask the stone, which is what my mother told me at my first drawing. Nobody has asked the stone and had a figure come back, which is why the question goes on being asked.}

At the part they keep back: \emph{The Court takes what it can carry up the road. The well takes what the Court cannot. I have shouted at both of them, and neither has ever turned, which is the only mercy I have had from either.}

\subsection*{At the head and in the gutter}

The pale thumb at the head is mine and has gone into the grain; there is no Last Day at a well and nothing here is gathered and burnt, so the grey stays where the bucket left it and goes into the next winter under the frost. The bloom rose white along the gutter and went grey where my sleeve crossed it; it took a word off the fourth verse and I have not written it back, because a song with a word gone is a song said slowly, and everything at this well is said slowly. The chip in the fold came off the north lip under the rope on the second pail and is lighter in the hand than a good chip, which is the lesson and no use to a clerk. The fray across the third verse came off the heart of the rope; I have left it lying over the word it landed on. The ring on the second leaf is cold water set down while a woman told me to wind from the shoulder and taken up when I had done. The green bead came off a girl with sweetness at her mouth who touched the leaf and went back up the terrace; I have not washed it. The sour ring is small ale set down at the first verse and taken up at the last. The grey along the outer fold came off a cuff laid where no cuff has business lying on a well. Nobody will own it. The grey wool ties the leaf to the rope-hook, with a knot for the line I could not bring up.

\subsection*{At the foot, in a hand nobody will own}

\begin{quote}\itshape The well keeps the fourth. The trough keeps the cold.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape The frost keeps the mark. The slate carries none of it.\end{quote}

I asked a woman of the bucket-round, the kiln-master come down for a pail, and a man with a barrow at the yard gate, and had three answers and no hand. I have left the line where it was written.

The tally goes back under the broken pot on the rope-hook. Tomorrow the bucket will go down and come up, three pails to the trough and the fourth standing where the frost wrote, and if the clerk comes again with his soft cuff he may have the nought. He cannot have the fourth, because it is a place, and he has no word for a place that stays where the water put it.

\clearpage\phantomsection\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{The Dry Man of Mud End, Being a Peat-Byre Tale Told in Stone, with the Bog-Wager, the Riddle Put to the Byre and Not to the Room, the Nine Houses, the Hide That Was Won and Left Unnamed, a Factor’s Clerk’s Entry Set Over It, and a Line at the Foot Nobody Will Own}
\CRsheetheading{The Dry Man of Mud End, Being a Peat-Byre Tale Told in Stone, with the Bog-Wager, the Riddle Put to the Byre and Not to the Room, the Nine Houses, the Hide That Was Won and Left Unnamed, a Factor’s Clerk’s Entry Set Over It, and a Line at the Foot Nobody Will Own}
{\centering\FellFont\itshape\footnotesize\color{faded} A byre-woman’s telling of a night in the deep cold, set down for the settling of an argument about a hide of peat and not for the improvement of the reader; the tale in the words it was told, the riddle in the words it was put, the standing-song as it goes round the fire, the wager in a column of peat-measures, the figures of a factor’s clerk entered over them, a reeve’s gloss in the margin, and one line at the foot in a hand nobody will own · Written in Stone of Y.H. 812, the Thin Year after the Long Cold, at the moot-byre of Mud End three leagues downriver of Sill, by the woman who keeps the byre-fire, the peat measure and the bench the moot sits on; told to her by a man come up the marsh road out of the Fenmarch with dry boots in deep weather. Set down in charcoal on the back of a hide-tally spoiled by a wet thumb, carried up the river road in Ilmen of Y.H. 813 and copied at Greybank onto the back of a Court grain-warrant voided by the damp, where a factor’s clerk borrowed the leaf and set his figures above hers. It survives folded in a strip of bog-fibre sewn with eel-sinew and kept in the tin behind the peat measure, where nothing else in this house is kept dry: wet peat worked into the grain at the head, a tallow thumb at the fold, the press of a frozen wool sleeve across the first leaf, a small-ale ring gone dark where a cup stood from the first asking to the last, a peat-shaving shut in the fold, a strip of bog-fibre in the gutter, frost raised out of the paper on the carry up from the ford, grey Ash along the outer fold which the writer did not put there, one correction in the narrow upright hand of the factor’s clerk, a gloss in the sloping hand of a reeve who could not get back over the marsh, and a line at the foot which nobody has claimed\par}\medskip
I keep the byre at Mud End and the fire in it, and the measure we hide peat by, which is a different work from keeping an account, though both begin with the hand on the thing before the eye goes to the person standing there. There are nine houses here and a moot that sits in my byre because there is no other room in the hamlet big enough to hold a disagreement. In Stone the road goes under, the ford goes over, and there is nothing to do of an evening but ask one another what we already know and call the asking a question. A question whose answer nobody knows is a wager, and there is enough wagering in a peat village without a riddle in it.

I have set this down because a man came the next morning and asked whose hide was stacked against my wall, and I could not tell him. That is a thing a byre ought to be able to tell. I have put the tale as he told it and left the clerk’s figure standing above it, because a figure written over a tale does not take the tale away, and a byre with a tale in it keeps warmer than a byre with a tally in it.

\subsection*{The manner of the byre}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item A question is put to the fire and not to the person beside you. Put to a person it becomes an argument, and an argument in a moot-byre is a debt with no date on it, which a peat house will carry longer than a debt with a date.

\item Answer in one breath. A second answer is a different question and is not heard. A man who gives two has not understood the first, which is the same in Sill and in the marsh.

\item The judge is the fire. I say whether an answer serves and I do not say why. A reason given is a question given away for nothing, and the giver can take it down the river road and spend it elsewhere.

\item The wager is a peat-shaving laid on the measure. We count shavings by the thumb and not by the eye, because the eye listens to the face and the thumb does not.

\item No slate lies on the bench. The moot has its slate on market-day and takes it away again on market-day; what is said at my fire goes off with the smoke, and neither is carried into a figure.

\item The cup is set down before the first question and no one lifts it until the last. If a skin forms on it, the night’s answering will go badly. I have known this to fail twice and would not say so before a reeve.

\end{enumerate}

\subsection*{The man off the marsh road}

He came in at the going of the light with his boots dry, which a man cannot manage in Stone without having come a long way or else not having come from the weather at all. He would not state what house he was of, which is a thing a man in Grath states before he states his name. He set a peat-shaving on the measure, sat with his cap on his knees, and told us why he was dry.

He had been up to the Standing Post on a wager of a hide of peat. It was seven days into Stone, when the bog had skinned over and the reeves were choosing who had stood longest. He stood. He said the water went off him on the third day and did not come back, and that a man who has stood that long in a bog comes up with less of himself than he went in with, which is how they choose a reeve and why the chosen man is never in a hurry to stand again.

An old woman at the fire said the Fen have a saying for it: \emph{a dry man is a dangerous man.} He said that was true and that he had heard it said of him before he had done standing, which is the worst way to hear a saying about yourself. Then he put the question. He put it to the fire, having been told twice, and said it as he said it, which is in the marsh speech with the endings left off.

\begin{quote}\itshape I am cut wet and carried dry.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape I am nine by the house and none by the road.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape The more of me is spent, the less of me is kept;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the less of me is kept, the warmer you sleep.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape The byre counts me. The slate has no column for me.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape What am I?\end{quote}

The woman who cuts our peat said “peat” before he had finished the third line, which is why she never wins a shaving and is always first. A carter come up from Sill for the winter lease said “warmth,” and the man from the marsh said warmth was what a man bought with the thing in the riddle and not the thing itself, and the carter said that was a distinction without a difference and went on with his ale. A boy of the house said “a day,” which nobody heard, being said to his mother and not to the fire. The cup went round once and came back to its place.

Then the man said the answer the byre had given was the easy one, and that the true answer was what the bog had kept. He said it low, to the fire.

“This is what came up,” he said, and set his hand on his cap. “What went in is not here to be asked about. I won the hide. They set it against the wall at the Post and told me to take it when I had a house to put it in. I have no house. I put my name into the standing so the reeve would have something to write, and it is in the mud now with the rest of the water. A hide of peat without a name is a thing that warms whoever gets to it first, and that is not the same as a thing that is yours.”

Nobody answered him, which is an answer in a peat village. The old woman said the marsh keeps what it takes and gives back what it cannot use, which is a true thing and not a comfort. The reeve’s saying came up again and nobody said it out loud. He left the hide stacked against my wall, and it is there now, and I have not put a name to it because a name written by me would be a name I had made, and a foundling’s name belongs to whoever writes first, which in this byre would be me, and I have scratched the charcoal and not written.

\subsection*{The standing-song}

\emph{Sung going round the measure in the first dark, one hand on the wall and the other at the small of the back. It is not a work-song; the peat gets cut whether it is sung or not. The last line is said to the fire.}

\begin{quote}\itshape One for the knee and one for the chin,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the bog takes the standing and gives back the thin;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape nine by the house and one by the road,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the hide goes dry and the name goes wet.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Stand, stand, the reeve says stand;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the longer you stand the less of a man.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Bring up the peat and leave the name;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the byre keeps the warm, the mud keeps the claim.\end{quote}

\subsection*{The wager, as it stood at the fire}

What stood — What the byre kept — What the Greybank hand wrote over it\par

One hide, won at the standing — One hide against the wall, no name on it — Fuel, unappropriated; value three marks\par

The standing, seven days into Stone — Nine standings and one man short — No account arises\par

The boots, dry in deep weather — Weather — Not entered\par

The name put into the bog — Nothing; the byre does not have it — Party unidentified; interest in a measure not entered\par

The shaving on the measure — One shaving, taken up by nobody — Gaming; not commercial\par

\subsection*{What the factor’s clerk did}

He came up from Greybank on the first market after the thaw with a cuff soft from washing, and asked what the stack against the wall was worth. I told him a hide of peat was three marks and that the price was the price of a winter to a household that had one, and he wrote \emph{three marks} and then wrote \emph{unappropriated} under it, which is a word for a thing nobody has claimed and a thing nobody can have. He asked who had won it. I told him a man off the marsh road. He asked for the man’s name and I said the man had left it in the bog, which is a true thing and not the thing he wanted, and he wrote as you see.

At \emph{the slate has no column for me} he wrote \emph{no charge arises.} He has taken the peat away and left the man standing in the mud, which is what a figure does when it is done with the person it came out of. I have put his hand above mine and left mine standing underneath, the way the fire keeps its heat under a pot and is not asked where it got it.

\subsection*{In the margin, in a reeve’s sloping hand}

The leaf went down the marsh road with a bundle of reeds and came back with a line in a hand that is not mine and not the factor’s. I have copied it as it stands.

\begin{quote}\itshape At \emph{the hide goes dry and the name goes wet}: I was at the Post the day he stood. He gave the name freely and we wrote it on the tally as the rule is, and on the third day the writing went soft and the name went into the bog with the rest. We did not scrape the mud for it. A reeve who scrapes the mud for a name has stopped being a reeve and become a man with a claim, and the Post has no place for a claim. Do not put a figure on the hide. A man with no name and three marks of peat is a dangerous man, and he is dangerous to nobody so long as nobody counts him.\end{quote}

I have not answered him in the margin. A thing written in a book follows a man home, and a reeve’s home is a boardwalk with nowhere to put a second opinion.

\subsection*{At the head and in the gutter}

The peat at the head came off the hand I held the leaf down with in the draught that comes under the byre door, and it has gone into the grain so that no dry sleeve takes it out, which is why the byre signs in charcoal and not in ink. The tallow thumb at the fold is off the lamp I turn the leaf by. The press of frozen wool across the first leaf came off the carter when he held the door for the man from the marsh and did not let go when he was through, and I have not written down which carter, because he would stop holding doors if I did. The dark ring is small ale that stood from the first question to the last and was drunk by nobody; two men have claimed it and one woman has denied it and I have given it to none of them. The shaving in the fold is the one laid on the measure and taken up by nobody, kept where the children cannot find it, because a child who takes up a shaving has paid for the asking and got nothing. The strip of bog-fibre in the gutter came off the man’s cap and goes soft when the weather goes soft, which tells me when to shut the tin. The frost came up out of the paper on the carry up from the ford and is the only thing in this byre that entered without a hand. The grey along the outer fold came off a cuff that had no business lying where I keep the tin, and I have not swept it. There is a Last Day in Mud End and the corners are swept on the morning after and burnt and called dealt with. There is no Last Day in the marsh, and nothing there is swept until the water does it.

\subsection*{At the foot, in a hand nobody will own}

\begin{quote}\itshape The fire keeps the tale. The measure keeps the count.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape The wall keeps the hide. The bog keeps the name.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape The factor keeps three marks and cannot say whose.\end{quote}

I asked the woman who cuts our peat, the carter come up for the winter lease, and the man who came in off the marsh road, and had three answers and no hand, as I have had before. I have left the lines where they were written. The leaf goes back into the tin behind the measure and the shaving goes back into the fold. Tomorrow the moot will sit and settle a fence and a pig, and the slate will come out and go back up the road, and the stack against my wall will stand where it stands, warming whoever is coldest first, with no name on it and three marks written over it in a hand that does not know what a winter is worth to a house that has nine of them and no more.

\clearpage\phantomsection\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{The Line Book, Being a Page from an Assessor’s Ledger Kept at the Peat Line in the Last Tend of Bone, Y.H. 813, with the Figure Cried and the Figure Entered, the Eels That Go South, the Thin Returns Bought Cheap, the Eleven Months Set Beside the Mark, Two Corrections in Borrowed Hands, and a Line at the Foot Nobody Will Own}
\CRsheetheading{The Line Book, Being a Page from an Assessor’s Ledger Kept at the Peat Line in the Last Tend of Bone, Y.H. 813, with the Figure Cried and the Figure Entered, the Eels That Go South, the Thin Returns Bought Cheap, the Eleven Months Set Beside the Mark, Two Corrections in Borrowed Hands, and a Line at the Foot Nobody Will Own}
{\centering\FellFont\itshape\footnotesize\color{faded} A page from a factor’s ledger kept at a tally-post on the Peat Line, in the service of the house at Greybank; figures in Ledgerhand copied from the rail-board and the reed tally, the remarks terse and in the hand that touches the slate before it looks at the person standing, one column struck by a College clerk and drawn back underneath, one figure struck and set above in a second hand, a word scraped away with a knife-point, and a line at the foot nobody will claim · Written at the Peat Line where the mud road comes down to the tally-post, in the last tend of Bone, Y.H. 813, the year after the Thin Year, by the assessor a factor out of Greybank keeps at the rail to count what goes south; copied forward at Greybank onto the back of a peat-docket voided by the Long Cold and kept in the factor’s tin among the dockets that are paid and the dockets that are not. It survives folded to the pocket and soft at the hinge, with black peat worked into the gutter and the creases of the thumb, dried eel slime along the fore-edge, a white salt bloom at the head that comes and goes with the weather, a green bead of Cliffs glass in the lower corner, a fish-scale pressed flat in the second fold, a frost-feather gone by noon, a tallow thumb at the foot, a pale round ring where a cold iron tube was set down and taken up, a wet corner where two figures have run and stand as entered all the same, a small square of bare paper where a word was scraped away with a knife-point, two corrections in borrowed hands, and one line at the foot that has never been claimed\par}\medskip
I keep the rail at the edge of the bog, where the mud road comes down and the peat is cut into blocks and stacked to go south. The factor at Greybank sends me a figure and a tube and a year, and I stand between the reeds and the road and put a number on whatever passes: eels, peat, hemp, ash in jars, and people who have been made thin. The figure is cried at the rail and entered in this book, and the two are not the same thing. I have learned to touch the slate before I look at the person standing, because a person looked at first will give a different figure.

Twelve copper bits to a silver mark; twenty marks to a gold crown, a Sere coin that does not come back north. The Court books a measure in embers and calls an ember five marks, which no man has exchanged and no carrier has ever carried. A thin return is bought here for two marks and sold in the Bowl for a figure nobody at this rail is allowed to hear. A man come down from Keld told me a bought life up there is reckoned at eleven months, which is a term and not a price. I have set it in the margin where it cannot be added: add a term to a mark and you get a number with nobody in it, which is the only kind the College will sign.

One in twelve is printed on the notice at Greybank and is read twice. I have put it on this leaf once, in the place the College allows, and put the other figure in the remark, which the College struck out and which I have drawn back underneath. A column that is struck is not a column that is gone. There is a difference between taking a figure and entering one, and it fits in the width of a thumb.

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{In the narrow upright hand of a College clerk, above my second paragraph:} Figures cried; figures entered; the two not joined. \emph{Underneath, in mine:} They are joined in the person standing, by the same mouth and in the same morning. I have set them on two lines and left them facing one another.\end{quote}

\subsection*{The book, as I set it down}

\emph{Figures in Ledgerhand. The cried figure is what was said at the rail; the entered figure is what went into the factor’s book. The remark is mine. A dash is a place where nothing stood, not a nought; a nought is a figure and can be added, and a silence cannot.}

Day — What stood at the rail — Cried — Entered — Went south — Remark\par

Bone 21 — Eels, the tribute, a basket from the reed landings — 3 bits the eel — 3 bits the eel — Sixty — The seventh basket holds six. The boy who counted is back in the reeds and will not be asked.\par

Bone 21 — Peat, a barrow, cut and stacked at the post — 5 bits — 5 bits — — — Fen price in Bone, Stone price in the Bowl; the same barrow, two honest figures. The road is the difference and walks away with it.\par

Bone 22 — A thin return, a woman of the Empty Cantons. No slate-name — 2 marks — 1 mark, struck to 2 above — Entered as breath — She held out her arm where a number would be cut and asked what the figure would buy. I entered the figure and did not enter the arm.\par

Bone 22 — A man come down off the Rim with two sets of numbers in one arm — eleven months — no figure — — — He gave the later number and kept the earlier under the skin. There is no column for the one under the skin.\par

Bone 23 — Fen ash, a jar, unopened and tied with grey wool — 1 mark — 1 mark — One jar — No man at the post will say what it is for. The buyer in the south pays for it in a room with no window. I have not asked which room.\par

Bone 23 — A pot mended with brass, out of a house at Mud End — 2 bits — 2 bits — One pot — Answers full under the knuckle. The south wants the seam shown and not hidden; a mended thing fetches more there than a whole one does here.\par

Bone 24 — Hemp, a bundle counted by a knot-account off the Standing Post — what the stick says — 4 marks — One bundle — The stick is horn-notched and tied with grey wool. I wrote the figure the knot gave and not the one the carrier said. Both were honest.\par
