Bone 24 — A child three days returned, out of the Quiet Acre — 13, struck to 12 — 12 — none — Worse before dusk. Entered as a birth, as the notice requires; nobody asked what it cost and no figure at this rail knew.\par

Bone 25 — A whole return bought for the Ember house; the seller would not give a name — 300 — 300 — South, by carrier — Three hundred, and no household under this bog could spend it. The house will set it on a shelf and call it beautiful.\par

Bone 25 — Nothing stood at the rail. Rain on the board — — — — — — — The writing ran and I entered it where it ran. No man crossed. The eels went under in the dark and the count went with them.\par

Bone 26 — A woman come back from the south with her number changed, asking for a table she had never sat at — not entered — not entered — — — She states her measure before her name and nobody asks which count is hers. I have kept a space the width of the question.\par

Bone 30 — One in twelve, as the notice says, read twice at the rail — 1 in 12 — 1 in 12 — The other figure, in the locked box — The deduction goes up the road in the clean hand. Its price stays here and has no hand at all.\par

Rows on this leaf: twelve. Rows that agree: three. Rows I left blank: two. Rows struck: two. The three that agree are the peat, the jar and the pot; I have marked them and cannot say why. They are not the whole of the leaf.

\subsection*{What the rail will not carry}

There is a boy who lifts the seventh basket and puts six back into the water and says nothing, and I have no row for the eel that goes back over the rail. A thing that goes back is not a thing never taken; it was counted and returned to a place where no count follows. I have set that in the remark and not the column, which is where this book keeps what matters and nothing that can be added.

The ash in the jar has a figure because a man in the south will pay one, and none at all at the post where it was dug. Grey Ash is swept up the morning after the Last Day, burnt and called dealt with; Fen ash is corked, sold and called a remedy. They are the same colour. I have put one mark against the jar and none against the colour; a man who joined the two would be drawing a conclusion, which I have no licence to draw.

A man who comes back thin has the old numbers cut out and new ones put in; the smooth place on his arm is not a blank but a thing that happened. I have kept a space the width of it in the row for the woman asking after her table and written nothing into it, because a figure put where a person stood is how this trade makes a man disappear and keeps the account tidy.

\subsection*{The counting song of the Line}

\emph{Sung low by the carriers going south with the baskets on the pole, never at the rail and never while a figure is being entered. I copied it from a man who would not sing the middle verse while the factor’s clerk stood on the road, which is how I know the middle verse is the one that matters.}

\begin{quote}\itshape Eels in the basket, six and a say-so,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the seventh goes back where the rail don’t see;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape cried at the post and entered at the boat,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the difference walks home ahead of me.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Eleven months for a man down south,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape twelve bits to the mark and a mark to the crown;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape one in twelve on the board, says the man,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the other one goes up in his box, not down.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape A brass seam sings and a green seam lies,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the peat keeps warm what the figure pays;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape count what you can at the edge of the bog\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and leave the rest where the reed stays.\end{quote}

I have put no gloss on it. A man who explains a song has begun to write a sermon, and sermons get copied.

\subsection*{What the borrowed hands did}

The College clerk came down from Greybank with a clean cuff and took the leaf up with two fingers, the way a man takes up a thing that might be wet. He struck the whole of my note column and wrote \emph{No such column} above it, having first counted every row, which is how I know the column troubled him. I have drawn it back underneath and left his words standing over it.

He struck \emph{I entered the figure and did not enter the arm} and set above it \emph{the measure was recorded}, and above that \emph{the entry was made}, which is further from the woman standing than the first. I have put my words back beneath both. A sentence with nobody in it is a sentence nobody can ask about, and people ask about these entries in the end, always at the rail, always after the slate is turned face down.

The other hand is the factor’s. Against the woman of the Empty Cantons he struck my two marks and set one above, saying a thin return from the Cantons cannot carry two; then, underneath, he restored the two in his own small figures and wrote \emph{current} beside it. Both stand. I have asked which is right and neither hand has told me, and I have stopped asking, because an assessor who asks after a correction is an assessor who will soon be making one.

A reeve of the Post set a mark in charcoal against the hemp row, a short stroke through the knot, which is the reeve’s way of saying that the stick was read and not carried off. It is the only hand on this leaf that has put a person into the sentence, and it is not a Court hand and will not travel with the book.

\subsection*{In the margins and the gutter}

The black in the gutter is peat off the hand that writes, and it goes into the grain and no wet sleeve takes it out, which is why this book keeps its figures on slate and its accounts on paper nobody wants. The slime along the fore-edge came off the seventh basket; the boy who lifted it set the slate down on the wet rail while I was entering six and did not know he had marked it. The white at the head comes and goes with the weather, as salt does on this coast; it has taken one word off the fifth remark and left the figure standing, which is the rude justice of salt. The green bead in the lower corner is Cliffs glass and not Fen glass; a woman come up from Vhal leaned to see what her jar of ash had fetched, touched the leaf, said nothing, and went back to the road. I have not washed it off.

The fish-scale in the fold came off the tribute basket. The frost-feather was on the rail on Bone 26 and gone before I folded the leaf; the yard at Mud End calls that weather and the carriers a map of where the Warm has gone out of the bog. The tallow thumb at the foot is mine, from holding the lamp low while the woman with the changed number asked her question. The pale round ring is where a collector from Sill set the cold tube down and took it up; he did not ask what this rail was counting, which was a kindness of a kind. The wet corner is the rain of Bone 25; two figures ran and I entered them where they ran, because a figure that has run is still a figure and the factor’s book has no row for rain. The bare square is a word I scraped away and have not written back. The grey along the outer fold is not mine, not the clerk’s, not the reeve’s. I have not swept it. There is a Last Day in the houses up the mud road and there is none at the edge of the bog, and even here the morning comes.

\subsection*{At the foot, in a hand nobody will own}

\begin{quote}\itshape What is counted at the rail is not what is carried from it, and what is carried is not what the south pays for. The three never stand in one room, and the room they stand in has no door.\end{quote}

I asked the factor’s clerk, a carrier who has gone down with the eels these nine years, a reeve come up from the dry boards, and the woman with the changed number, and had four answers and no hand. I have left the line where it was written.

The book goes back into the tin and the tin into the count-house at Greybank, where a man who has never stood in this bog will read the figures in a voice nobody can thank and nobody can blame. Tomorrow the baskets go south and the seventh will hold six, and I shall touch the slate before I look at whoever is standing, and write the remark down before the College can strike it out. The eels go under in the dark. The rail stands where it has always stood, at the edge of the country that empties, and the difference between the figure cried and the figure paid walks home ahead of me with no figure of its own.

\clearpage\phantomsection\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{The Peat-Wife’s Book of Mud End, Being Remedies for the Byre-Cough, the Peat-Knife Cut, the Child Come Up Drowned, the Sweet Line, the Birth-Flower, the Chill That Follows the Warming and the Sleep That Is Called Merciful, Set Down Among the Nine Houses with the Errors Left Standing}
\CRsheetheading{The Peat-Wife’s Book of Mud End, Being Remedies for the Byre-Cough, the Peat-Knife Cut, the Child Come Up Drowned, the Sweet Line, the Birth-Flower, the Chill That Follows the Warming and the Sleep That Is Called Merciful, Set Down Among the Nine Houses with the Errors Left Standing}
{\centering\FellFont\itshape\footnotesize\color{faded} A peat-wife’s and midwife’s book of remedies in the Mud End manner, written in Grathic letters learned off a man come up from Sill to measure the peat banks who could tally but could not spell what he wrote; the cures in a healer’s hand on the back of a peat-tally spoiled by a wet thumb, the objections of a physician come down the mud road from Sill pressed hard into the margin, the corrections of a factor’s clerk in narrow upright Ledgerhand, a charcoal line from a reeve up the marsh road, a byre-song with the tenth place left as it is sung, and one line at the foot in a hand nobody will own · Written at Mud End, three leagues downriver of Sill, between Bone of Y.H. 813 and Ilmen of Y.H. 814, the Thin Year, the Long Cold and the thaw that followed it, by Marda of Mud End, a peat-wife who has caught the children of the nine houses and set the arms of the turf-cutters for three-and-twenty years; begun on the back of a peat-tally a wet thumb spoiled at the moot byre, folded into oiled sacking and carried in the breast of a wool apron against a square of birth-cloth, and copied forward in Ilmen of Y.H. 814 onto the back of a discarded rent-roll at Greybank. It survives with peat worked into the grain at the head, a silt tideline off the Ilm that has taken two words clean off the second leaf, a peat-fibre stiff in the fold, straw from the dry bed in the moot byre, a ring of barley-water gone sour over one word of the ninth row, grey Ash off a cuff worked into the gutter, a scorch where a spark off the peat fire caught the corner, a green bead of lead glaze pressed into the lower corner by a girl with the sweetness at one mouth-corner, three objections in the small hard hand of the physician, corrections in the upright hand of the factor’s clerk, a reeve’s charcoal line beside the remedies, and the one line at the foot\par}\medskip
I did not mean to keep a book. A woman came over the mud road in the lean week with the thumb of her right hand split down the side by a peat-knife, and asked what I put on such a thing, and I answered her in the short way my mother had before I had decided whether it was true. A thing said before it has been looked at is a thing that has gone a long while without being looked at. I have looked at some of mine. I have left the rest standing where they stood, because a woman at three in the morning wants a hand held steady more than she wants a correction.

The peat gets under the nail in this hamlet and stays there through the washing. It is the only thing in Mud End that keeps a better count than I do. I write on the back of a tally a wet thumb spoiled at the moot. The figures went into the byre and out of it and nobody charged them, which is a mercy of a kind here, where a figure that reads is a figure that travels. The brown at the head is off my own thumb. The grey in the gutter came off a cuff laid where no cuff has business lying; I have not swept it, and there is no Last Day in a peat byre.

\subsection*{The order of the byre}

\emph{Written small on the first leaf, with one word gone over in silt off the Ilm.}

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item Set the child on dry sacking and never on peat. Peat holds water, and a wet child cools faster than a dry one, which every woman here knows and no man come down from Sill has ever written down.

\item Turn the slate face down before you go to the fold. I keep no slate-name and never shall. A child is not an entry, and a name written before the face is looked at is a name chosen by somebody who was not in the room.

\item Try the stone on your own wrist before it goes to a belly. It came off somebody’s peat fire, and somebody in these nine houses cut the peat and carried it and never called it a gift.

\item When the red branch shows, cross two fingers over it and say the word the mother gives. Do not wash it. I have seen a washed one and an unwashed one and have not joined them.

\item If a man comes up the mud road with a cold tube and a slate, give him the mother and keep the child behind the pail. This is not refusal. It is the order of the room.

\item Keep a place at the fire for the ninth house. It is the farthest from the road, and a woman from it will have walked the longest before she calls you.

\item When the fourth morning comes, let the woman do the counting. A number counted for her belongs to whoever counted it, and there is no figure in this byre to give away.

\end{itemize}

Against the pail the physician wrote, \emph{a wet child cools faster than a dry one; true, and of no use where there is no dry sacking.} I have put my line above his, because a woman with no sacking still has a hand.

\subsection*{The remedies, as they are used}

Trouble — What is set to it — The manner of it — Who carries it\par

The byre-cough — Steam of barley-water under a cloth, honey if the house has it — We say the smoke of our own peat cannot hurt a throat that has breathed it since childhood. A physician come down from Sill says it is the smoke, and the only physic is a high chimney, which nine houses cannot build. I sent two down to Sill; both came back worse for the dust of the road. Both stand. — The byre, which cannot stop and does not ask.\par

A peat-knife cut — Tallow, then a clean fold, never the grey from the corner — The women put grey from the corner in a cut to dry it, believing the grey is clean. I dressed four such and found grey under the skin in all four, and could not get it out. The physician says the grey is not clean, and writes it in a hand that scores the leaf. — The hand, in a white line it keeps.\par

The child come up drowned, in the Breaking — Lay belly-down across a warm sack, turn with the forearm, clear the reed from the mouth, warmth to the middle, a watch — We hold such a child by the heels and let the water run out, which is what our mothers did. A physician from Sill says the water in the belly is not what kills, and that there is a manner of turning I do not know. I held six by the heels and turned two; one of the two breathed by morning. I have not written which house the one came from. — The river, which takes what the Court does not count and enters nothing.\par

The sweet line — Sour barley-water, wood-ash at the gum — We do not taste our glaze in Mud End. The green comes down from the Glaze Room at High Kiln with a girl who says a sweet answers a sweet. The physician says lead. I have seen the line go off one who left that room and come back on one who stayed. I have not seen the lead. — The glaze room, which cannot stop and does not ask.\par

The birth-flower — Nothing. Two fingers crossed, and the word the mother gives — A woman of the ninth house washed one in salt water and it went the redder; four I did not wash went pale in nine days. I have set the one beside the four and not joined them. When asked what it is I give the day of the week and no more, because a day does not spoil in the mouth. — No account has named it. The child’s skin, if a body that cannot speak can pay.\par

The chill that follows the warming — Warmth at the middle, barley-water, a watch to the fourth morning; we walk them still — It comes after the warming, not before. The physician says a warmed body spends faster and walking faster still, and that the child should be held and counted with. I walked fourteen and held six; of the walked three went thin, of the held one went thin and one did not rise. I kept the tallies on a strip of willow under the straw and never added them. A tally summed is a tally that can be carried off the mud road. — The household, one night’s sleep; sometimes the child.\par

The sleep that is called merciful — Nothing. Leave the damper as it was found — A man of the ninth house who had worked the kilns at Sill came home and slept with the damper shut, and they that found him called it merciful. The physician says a shut damper and a sleeping man make a death and not a mercy, and writes it twice. I have left his sentence above mine and my word underneath, where a woman at three in the morning will find them. — The house, which did not know the damper had been shut.\par

Nothing here is free. It passes from one house to another and is called a cure, and the peat that carries it is paid for by whoever cut it. That is the only sentence I will stand behind.

\subsection*{The note under the knuckle}

The women at the drying racks in Sill tap a green pot before it goes to the kiln. Sound answers full, cracked answers flat, a small dead sound that stops at the lip. I borrowed the trick from them, as every trade borrows from the trade beside it.

I tapped a man once, gone thin after a thin return. The flat I thought I heard was not in him. A body is not a pot, though we set pots on the bench in the shape of bellies. There is no clock in Mud End, and the pot on the bench knows more about whether the night took the room than any slate up the road.

\subsection*{The moot byre}

The moot sits in the driest byre of the nine houses, and fines stand there as they stand at the Post, until the mud is held to have paid them. Last winter one stood three months and was paid in three days’ turf, and nobody entered what the turf cost the man who cut it. A reeve come up the marsh road said a fine paid in peat is a fine that has been stood on and walked off. I have set his sentence beside the slate.

\subsection*{The byre-song}

\emph{Sung low to the peat and not to the person, sitting with the child on the knee and the wool drawn up. Said to the floor, the sack or the byre door; said looking at a person it becomes an argument. The tenth place is held the length of a hand going into the pail and coming out empty. Nobody fills it.}

\begin{quote}\itshape Nine for the houses and one for the road,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the peat says dry and the child says cold;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape lay it on sacking and never on the floor,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and say the word to the byre door.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape The knife goes in and the grey goes round,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the sweet at the gum comes down from the town;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the line goes west and the line comes east\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the glaze room never asks what it cost.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Warm the middle and wrap the end,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape let her count, do not count for her;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the damper stood as the damper stands\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the house said merciful and did not look.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Nine I have kept and the tenth I hold\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape for the child with no house and no name.\end{quote}

I changed one line in three-and-twenty years. I sang \emph{the byre keeps it} as I was taught, and now sing \emph{the house said merciful}, because a byre cannot say anything and a house can say a thing that is not true. Nobody singing with me has asked why the line is different, which is how I know it wanted changing. A factor’s clerk put a round nought in the tenth place and wrote \emph{vacancy} beneath it. A nought is a figure that travels light. The tenth is a place and has to be stood in.

\subsection*{What the physician from Sill put in the margin}

He came down the mud road in Ash of Y.H. 813 with a book that had the word \emph{smoke} in it and a hand that wrote without asking. Against the byre-cough he set \emph{the smoke, and no physic but departure}; against the heels, \emph{the water is not what kills}; against the merciful sleep he wrote \emph{a shut damper, a sleeping man, a death}, and underlined it twice. He was right in all three and had put nothing in their place that a house of nine could pay for. I have left his sentences above mine.

\subsection*{What the factor’s clerk did}

A clerk of the factor borrowed the leaves at Greybank when the winter turf was counted; the ink sat in two fingers of a soft cuff washed too often. He struck out my column headed \emph{Who carries it} and wrote \emph{No cost entered}, true in the language he writes and false in a byre where a man’s thumb is split to the bone. Where I wrote that the river takes what the Court does not count, he wrote \emph{no toll arises}, the most beautiful sentence I have ever read in a hand that has never stood in silt. I have put my column back underneath his. A clerk can write without verbs because he is never in a byre with a child that will not breathe.

\subsection*{In the margin, in charcoal, a reeve’s hand}

\begin{quote}\itshape The mud road takes a day and gives no receipt. I have stood on it and still cannot tell you which boards are safe. I can tell you which houses paid. --- R.\end{quote}

He wrote it while I was at the peat-stack. A man who has counted other men standing is allowed one sentence in a book of physic.

\subsection*{At the head and in the gutter}

The peat at the head came off my thumb in a wind off the river and has worked into the grain, which is why this leaf smells of the byre in any room. The silt tideline came up the second leaf after the thaw and took two words clean off it; I have not written them back, because a remedy with two words gone is a remedy said slowly. The peat-fibre in the fold went stiff as a splinter, and the straw came off the dry bed in the moot byre. The ring of barley-water went sour over one word of the ninth row and lifted the ink; I have not written that word in either. The grey along the outer fold came off a cuff laid where no cuff has business lying, and I have not swept it. The green bead in the lower corner was pressed in by a girl come down from High Kiln with the sweetness at one mouth-corner; I did not ask whose glaze it was. There is a Last Day in Sill and the corners are swept and burnt there in the morning and called dealt with. There is no Last Day in a peat byre.

\subsection*{At the foot, in a hand nobody will own}

\begin{quote}\itshape Peat keeps the print of the boot and not the man.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape The slate keeps the man and not the print.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Between the byre and the mud road a child breathes or does not, and nobody has entered the breath.\end{quote}

I asked a physician, a factor’s clerk and a reeve come up from the Post, and had three answers and no hand. I have left the line where it was written. The book goes back under the loose straw in the byre. Tomorrow a woman will come over the mud road with a thumb split by a peat-knife or a child that will not breathe, and I shall turn the slate face down, try the stone on my own wrist and leave the tenth where it is, because a child is not a house and the mud road has taken enough figures.

\clearpage\phantomsection\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{The Phial Left Sealed, Being a Letter from the Bowl of Sere to the Factor’s House at Greybank, Concerning the Emptying of the Bowl, the Three Returns of a Mother, a Northerner Exhibited at the Feast, and a Sixty-Mark Phial That Was Not Opened; with the Household’s Ledger of Returns, the Feast Song as It Is Sung, the Answer Written in the Margin, the Factor’s Clerk’s Correction in Ledgerhand, and a Line at the Foot Nobody Will Own}
\CRsheetheading{The Phial Left Sealed, Being a Letter from the Bowl of Sere to the Factor’s House at Greybank, Concerning the Emptying of the Bowl, the Three Returns of a Mother, a Northerner Exhibited at the Feast, and a Sixty-Mark Phial That Was Not Opened; with the Household’s Ledger of Returns, the Feast Song as It Is Sung, the Answer Written in the Margin, the Factor’s Clerk’s Correction in Ledgerhand, and a Line at the Foot Nobody Will Own}
{\centering\FellFont\itshape\footnotesize\color{faded} A private letter on the thin gold-ink paper of a house of the Ten Bowls, folded thrice and carried north with a grain factor; the cursive of a Sere house at a table set for Company, the ledger of returns in the house’s careful hand, the feast song in the court’s own singing, the sister’s answer set small in the margin, one correction in the narrow upright Ledgerhand of the factor’s clerk at Greybank, and one line at the foot in a hand nobody will claim · Written in the open court of the Bowl of Sere in the last tend of Grain, Y.H. 812, the Thin Year, by Ilyra Gilded of a house of the Ten Bowls, to her sister Maris Gilded, who keeps that house’s northern account at Greybank; carried north with the grain factor, delivered in Stone of Y.H. 813, answered in the margin at the factor’s house, borrowed there by a clerk who set his correction above the writer’s words, and kept since in a tin of account leaves among which it is the only sheet with gold on it. It survives with the gold worn thin at the folds, a ring of red wine where the bowl was set down, a scorch at the second corner taken from the open court fire, a bead of cliff-glass pressed into the lower margin by a northerner who was exhibited at the feast, slate dust worked into the gutter, a grey Ash print along the outer fold which the writer did not make and has not swept, and the line at the foot\par}\medskip
To Maris Gilded at Greybank, who keeps our northern account and will not call a courtesy a courtesy before the factor’s clerk. From Ilyra, of a house of the Ten Bowls, in the open court at the Bowl of Sere.

I begin with the courtesy, which is the first thing owed between sisters of a house, as you were taught and I was not. I hope you are warm. I hope the factor’s table has a cloth on it this winter and that the new clerk has not yet learned to smile at a figure. I have put the thing itself in the fourth paragraph, where you will look for it last, as is proper. If you read only the first three you will have a letter full of hospitality and no news, which is the kind most of our correspondents send and the kind I have never managed to write to you.

The bowl was emptied on the tenth of Grain. The Sun-Emperor emptied it with both hands and the Council read the emptying as a debt forgiven in the south and a province ruined in the north, and both readings were entered before the wine had finished running down the steps. Our household’s slates were not put to the fire. I stood in the court with my sleeves wet at the cuff from pouring for two hundred people and felt relief go through me like warmth through a thin vessel, and was ashamed of the relief before it had done arriving. Relief said aloud in an open court is an invitation to the next lot. I said nothing and poured more wine.

We teach that a vessel was made to be emptied gloriously and a life hoarded is a life wasted. I have taught it to my daughter in the open court with the fire in the middle of us and the bowls going round. I am not now certain that I ever taught it to our mother. She was of the kind that holds, which in this country is called a virtue until it is called a hoarding, and the house spent a great deal to have her back three times.

\subsection*{The returns of our mother, as the house keeps them}

\emph{Entered by the house-accountant in the careful hand. The last column is mine and has no heading; a heading would make it an account.}

Year — What the house paid — How she came — What came back — What she asks for\par

Y.H. 799 — Twelve hundred marks, and the measures not counted here — Whole — Our mother. She remembered the name-day and the cook and the pot with the chipped lip. — The chipped pot.\par

Y.H. 804 — The same figure, entered as the same figure — Whole — Our mother, smaller. She remembered the pot and not whose name-day it was. — The pot, and who poured.\par

Y.H. 809 — The same figure, entered a third time — Thin — A stranger with a faint interest in a life it cannot name. — The pot. Always the pot.\par

She sits in the open court now in the warmest place that is not the fire’s own place, and asks for a pot that is not there. It is the chipped one. I keep it in my room. I have not given it to her and I have not thrown it away. A pot kept in a room is a thing with a roof over it. A pot given is an account opened, and a thing given in this house is never given twice; it is entered once and then owed back. A pot thrown away is a debt denied, and a debt denied in Sere is a debt the household carries at twice the figure. I have chosen the roof. This is the thing I put in the fourth paragraph. I have told it to no one in the court.

The northerner your factor sent south was exhibited at the feast and given small coins. He had the pale line at one gum and the fingers of an old rope, and when they set a cup in his hand he turned it a quarter and set it back where it had stood, which the court took for a trick and applauded. To the fire he said, in the clay-country speech, \emph{It’ll go in the thaw}. Nobody in the court knew whether he meant the weather or the account, and it was the only thing he said all evening that was not in the singing. I asked the woman beside me what it meant and she said a northerner says it of everything, which is an answer given by people who have heard a thing often and never asked. He went off with the light and a handful of small coins and no slate of ours against him, which is the whole of our hospitality to a northerner: we clap at his answers and we do not enter him.

You remember the phial we spoke of before you went north. I bought it of the Court’s factor through your house: sixty marks, which is a great deal of wine. It is called quiet ash and it is sold to the rich who want their previous life to stop arriving in dreams. The woman who sold it said the dreams go in a tend and do not come back. She had a soft cuff and a neat hand and did not once look at my face while she said it. The phial stands on the shelf behind my bed and has never been opened. A thing bought to stop a memory and kept sealed is a memory the buyer has chosen to keep, which is a Spending done in private and entered nowhere. Every time I pass it I think I have done a clever thing with sixty marks. Every time I pass it I think of the pot.

\subsection*{The song as it is sung while the bowl goes round}

\emph{Sung in the open court, at the emptying, never at the burning of the slates. The fourth line is the emperor’s line and the room says it with the singer. The last line is said low and held until the next bowl is brought.}

\begin{quote}\itshape Fill for the full and fill for the thin,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the vessel was made to be poured, not kept;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape a life in a cup is a life let go,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the house that hoards is the house that wept.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape One for the bowl and one for the fire,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape one for the hand that the bowl goes through;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the slate burns white and the slate burns black,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the household that burned will be entered anew.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape The north sends warmth and the south sends wine,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the factor books both at a figure he knows;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the guest says a thing in a speech not ours,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and we clap at the answer and let the guest go.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Pour for the mother, pour for the pot,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape pour for the phial that stands on the shelf;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the bowl goes empty and the room goes warm,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the thing we keep is the thing we left.\end{quote}

I have set the song down as it is sung, with the last line held. A clerk who takes the verbs out of a song leaves the bowls going round by themselves, which is a thing bowls have never done and never will.

You used to say \emph{measure for measure} when you wanted the bowl emptied and the account called even, in the tone of one who has already decided what both measures are. I have learned what the phrase means in the south, which is precisely that and nothing more. I have never heard it said in this court by anybody who had not already poured the wine.

\subsection*{What the factor’s clerk did}

A clerk of the factor’s house borrowed the leaf on the morning after it came up from the south, being a man who cannot leave paper alone, particularly paper with gold on it. He writes in the narrow upright hand they teach at the College, with the verbs taken out and everything in the passive. He laid his hand on the sheet before his eyes went to the room, which is the manner of that table.

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item Against \emph{our household’s slates were not put to the fire} he set \emph{a disposition was not recorded}, which is true in the way a shut fist is true.

\item Against \emph{she asks for a pot that is not there} he set \emph{a want was noted; no claim arises}, and the pot went out of the sentence as though a pot were a thing a woman could want without its having stood on a shelf.

\item Against \emph{I keep it in my room} he set \emph{the article is retained by the household}, which makes a room a household and a sister an officer.

\item Against \emph{the phial has never been opened} he set \emph{the measure remains unspent}, and put a round figure in the margin where I had put none.

\item Against the song he wrote nothing at all, but he numbered the lines, which is his way of singing.

\end{itemize}

I have put the verbs back underneath where I could still read them. He takes them out because a thing always true has no need of verbs. I put them in because a woman at a table in the last tend of Grain wants to know which hand pours for the mother and which hand keeps the pot. I have left his figure standing above mine and my emptiness under it. A leaf with two hands on it is the only kind this house believes.

\subsection*{In the margin, in a second hand, small and set close to the writing}

You have put the thing itself in the fourth paragraph and I have found it there, as you knew I would. You always did hide the thing in the longest sentence and then blame the reader for going straight to it.

Do not send the pot north. It would have to come the coast pass and the damp gets into everything on that road, and a pot that breaks on the road is a debt with no household standing to answer it. Keep the roof over it. She will not ask for it where she is now, and if she does, tell her the house has it, which is the truth and costs us nothing, being the sort of truth the factor’s clerk can enter without a verb.

The phial came. I have not opened it and will not open it for you. A sister who wants a dream stopped should say so in the first paragraph and not the fourth. I have struck nothing out. Your verbs are where you left them, which is more than I can say for your courtesy.

\subsection*{At the head and in the gutter}

The gold is worn thin at the folds where the leaf has been carried in a coat against a wrist, and the writer’s hand shows through where the gilding has gone. The ring at the head is red wine, set down by the writer while she was pouring and not drunk until the song was done. The scorch at the second corner came off the open court fire on the night of the emptying and went out under a sleeve, which is how a great house keeps a fire and how a leaf gets a corner taken. The bead in the lower margin is cliff-glass off the Glaze Cliffs and was pressed there by the exhibited northerner, who leaned to see the gold and had not been asked to touch the leaf; he did not ask for it back, and the writer did not give it to him. The slate dust in the gutter came off a slate laid on the factor’s counter while the correction was being made. The grey along the outer fold is not the writer’s and not the factor’s. She has not swept it. There is no Last Day on a sheet of gold paper.

\subsection*{At the foot, in a hand nobody will own}

\begin{quote}\itshape The bowl is emptied. The pot is kept. The phial is sealed.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Three vessels, and none of them holds what was paid for.\end{quote}

I asked the factor’s clerk, a woman who burns the slates by lot, and a northerner who was exhibited at the feast, and had three answers and no hand, as is our custom. I have left the line where it stands.

The leaf goes back into the tin among the account leaves, where it is the only sheet with gold on it and the only one that has ever been carried in a coat. Tomorrow the court will fill the bowls again and the fire will be lit in the middle of them, and the mother will ask for the pot in the warmest place that is not the fire’s own place, and the phial will stand on the shelf, and the pot will stand in a room with a roof over it. Nothing was opened, given, burnt, spent or ended in the writing of this letter. A thing kept under a roof is not a thing returned, and a thing returned is not a thing that has been kept.

\clearpage\phantomsection\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{The Prayer Before the Tube, Being What a Collector Says into the Wool on the Clay Road, with the Manner of It, the Four Sayings Turned End for End, the Answer Made with the Hands, a Clerk’s Correction and a Hearth-Maid’s Margin}
\CRsheetheading{The Prayer Before the Tube, Being What a Collector Says into the Wool on the Clay Road, with the Manner of It, the Four Sayings Turned End for End, the Answer Made with the Hands, a Clerk’s Correction and a Hearth-Maid’s Margin}
{\centering\FellFont\itshape\footnotesize\color{faded} A collector’s own order of service, carried in the wool sleeve of the cold-iron tube and said low before the draw; written without a name, in charcoal on the back of a voided district tally, with the rubrics of the road, seven parts and the answer made after each, the four sayings in the order a collector comes to them rather than the order the notice prints, one correction in the narrow upright Ledgerhand of a factor’s clerk, the thick charcoal of a hearth-maid come up from Low Kiln, and two lines at the foot that will not lie down together · Written between Greybank and Sill on the Clay Road in the last tend of Ash, Y.H. 812, the Thin Year, by a collector of the lower road who signs with a crossed tube and not with a name, and carried back through the Five in the wool sleeve of the tube, which is why there is iron in every fold; borrowed at Greybank by a clerk of the factor, who set the four sayings right at the head and wrote against the grey fingers, and read over by a hearth-maid from Low Kiln on a market morning at the Cross, who put four lines in the margin with a stick of charcoal. It survives as one leaf folded small enough for a coat pocket: cold-iron filings ground into the head, a grey wool fibre from the tube’s sleeve, a green bead of lead glaze in the lower corner, frost-crisp along one edge where it lay against the outer fold of a coat on the Rim Road in Stone, a tallow thumb, a ring of small ale gone dark, silt in the gutter from the assessor’s step at Sill, and a grey Ash print along the foot that nobody will own.\par}\medskip
I have drawn measure on this road for nine years and I have never once said the four sayings in the order they are printed. They are printed for a room. They are said in a clean voice by a clerk who has never held the tube, with the slate face up and the man already on the pallet and the door shut behind him. On the road we turn them end for end. It is not doctrine. It is the order in which a collector comes to them, which is a different thing and the only one I can answer for.

There is no name on this leaf. A collector’s name on a prayer is an entry, and an entry can be produced at a Weighing by a man who was not there and had not held the iron. I have set a crossed tube in the corner in charcoal, which is a mark and not a name. If the factor asks me what it is I shall tell him it is a stain.

I wrote this on the back of a district tally voided for a figure entered in the wrong column, between Greybank and Sill in the last tend of Ash, Y.H. 812, the Thin Year. It rode in the wool sleeve of the tube, which is why the iron is in every fold and why the leaf goes grey before the words do. A clerk of the factor set his hand above mine at the head; a hearth-maid come up from Low Kiln with a birth-slate put four lines in the margin, in letters pressed hard enough to tear the paper. I have left both where they were put. The leaf has never been read at a Weighing, which is the whole reason it has lasted.

\subsection*{The manner of it, written small at the head}

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item Wrap the tube before you say the prayer, not after. A man can hold iron while he speaks, but he will not speak well with his fingers going the colour of the sky before snow.

\item Stand with the road at your back and the house in front. The house is what you are about to take from. The road has no opinion and will not follow you home.

\item Do not look at the face. Look at the arm, where the ways run near the skin. A face will tell you nothing you can use, and a thing you cannot use is a thing you will remember, which is worse.

\item Say it into the wool, not into the air. Words said into the air go up and get entered somewhere. The wool keeps them one draw and lets them go, which is as much as any prayer of mine is owed.

\item Count the draws on the fingers afterwards, never before. A figure counted before the draw is a figure you have already decided, and a decided figure is the same thing as a false one with the ink dry.

\item If the bell comes off the Cross four and four and a gap, stop at the gap. The gap belongs to somebody else. Begin again when the bell has finished counting what it counts.

\item Never say it twice over one man. A second prayer argues with the first, and the first was honest, being said before I knew how much he had.

\end{itemize}

\subsection*{The prayer}

\emph{I say it into the wool. There is nobody present to answer. The answer is made with the hands after every part: wrap the iron, turn the slate, wipe the hand. I have written the answer down as it is done, because a thing done is the only answer this road gives.}

\subsection*{Before the iron}

\begin{quote}\itshape Iron, you were cold when I took you out of the wool.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape You will be cold when I put you back.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape What you take does not stay in you. It goes where it is entered.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape I am the hand that holds you to the way. I am not the way,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and I am not the taking, whatever the slate may say later.\end{quote}

Here I draw the tube through the wool again, so the sleeve keeps its shape for the next man. A small care, and costs nothing, which is why I keep it and enter it nowhere.

\emph{The answer is made: wrap the iron. Turn the slate. Wipe the hand.}

\subsection*{Of the arm}

\begin{quote}\itshape The ways run near the skin here. A man’s face is no use to me.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape The arm tells where to set you; the slate tells what stood there.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape I do not ask the arm whether it consents. Nobody asks it in this country.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape A good arm gives full and gives quickly. A worn arm gives flat,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the figure is smaller, which is not smaller to the man.\end{quote}

Here I set the cold rim to the way and wait for the small hiss. There is iron, a smell like wet wool near a fire, and the time it takes to write a figure down.

\emph{The answer is made: wrap the iron. Turn the slate. Wipe the hand.}

\subsection*{Of the figure}

\begin{quote}\itshape Count embers. A year is a thing the household remembers\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the slate has no column for.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape One in twelve, as the notice says. Printed. Read twice,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape once for the moot and once for those who came late up the road.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape I write the printed figure. What the district pays is not my hand,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the man who set the other figure has gone up the Clay Road with it\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and does not carry it in the open.\end{quote}

Here I read the figure twice, low, into the wool. The second is for the person at the door who came too late to be counted and stands in the draught.

\emph{The answer is made: wrap the iron. Turn the slate. Wipe the hand.}

\subsection*{The four sayings, turned end for end}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Your return is recorded.} I say this first, so that it cannot comfort at the end.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Nothing is lost that we have kept.} Kept is not the same as held. I have held the iron and know the difference.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{The account stands.} It stands after the man sits down. It does not stand while he is standing.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{The measure is banked.} Last, because it is the true one and the one I do the most.\end{quote}

The clerk set these in their proper order above mine, with \emph{as appointed} against them. Both stand. His is the order a clerk prints for a room; mine begins with the record and ends with the taking. I have put my hand beside his, not under it.

\emph{The answer is made: wrap the iron. Turn the slate. Wipe the hand.}

\subsection*{Of the cradle}

\begin{quote}\itshape I never see the cradle. It is a room I am not paid to enter.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape One into one: the name comes back with the shape,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape with the price of bread and the way a hand closes on a cup.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Many into many: what comes back wants a table it never sat at\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and goes toward a cup before the cup is shown.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Both are poured. Both are entered in the same clean hand.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape I have seen such children at the Cross and cannot tell you\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape which draw of mine went into which of them.\end{quote}

Here I leave a space the length of a name. It is not a name forgotten. No name of mine belongs in it, and the clerk’s round nought is a figure, and a figure is a thing I have already used too much of this morning.

\emph{The answer is made: wrap the iron. Turn the slate. Wipe the hand.}

\subsection*{Of the hand after}

\begin{quote}\itshape The iron takes from the drawer as well as from the drawn.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape By the third draw the fingers go the colour of ash water;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape by the fifth they are as they were, or they are not.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape A collector who says the cost is nothing\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape has not looked at his own hand, which is the only looking\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape he does not do.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape I marked forty draws on the bench in charcoal one tend\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and washed the bench before the factor came,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape which is not the same as not having made the marks.\end{quote}

Here I set the tube back in the sleeve and shut the slate. Collectors say the grey comes off in a day. I have had it last six, and no clerk has asked after the sixth.

\subsection*{What the clerk set at the head}

A clerk of the factor borrowed the leaf while the tube was being rewrapped, with a cuff gone soft from washing and ink in two fingers. He did not take the verbs out. He took the man out instead, which is the stranger thing to do to a leaf written on a road.

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item At \emph{I am the hand that holds you to the way}, he wrote: \emph{the draw is performed by an officer of the Keeping.} Both stand. Mine has a hand in it, his an office, and the man on the pallet will be told about the office.

\item At \emph{I do not ask the arm whether it consents}, he wrote: \emph{lawful draw; consent recorded.} Underneath, in mine: \emph{Recorded by whom? The slate was face down and the man was looking at the wall.} His above, mine below; that is the order this road is read in.

\item At \emph{the figure is smaller} he wrote the printed figure above it, larger. It is the figure they like to see. Both stand.

\item Against the grey fingers he wrote \emph{no cost to officer}, true in the figure and false in the hand I wrote it with. I have not struck it out. A clerk’s false line is what the next reader ought to see.

\item In the space where a name would stand he put a round nought and wrote \emph{vacancy}. A nought is a number. The place was not.

\end{itemize}

He asked what a collector learned by the prayer. I told him the order of the sayings and the wrapping of the tube. He entered both and went up the road with the tally he had come for. The leaf came back with his ink wet on it. I have kept the ink; a man who cannot help writing on a thing has let it be seen that he wrote.

\subsection*{What the hearth-maid put in the margin}

The letters are thick and lean, made with a charcoal stick and not a pen. She came up from Low Kiln with a birth-slate under her shawl and stood at the Cross until the pigs were weighed before she would touch the leaf, because a woman who touches a paper in the middle of a market will be asked what she had to do with it.

At \emph{the arm tells where to set you}: “It tells you nothing I have not told it. I held that arm last winter while it was still warm. You came up the road after I had carried the slate down it.”

At \emph{one in twelve, as the notice says}: “The notice is not in our house. We give the other figure there, and you do not write it, and the house is cold in the morning. I have said this to a woman who was holding a child and had no word for the cold.”

At \emph{I never see the cradle}: “A child came back two doors down and went toward a cup before the cup was shown. I have not told you which of yours it was. I never shall.”

At \emph{sit down} — for she wrote this where I had set \emph{the fingers go the colour of ash water} — she put: “Sit down. I have kept a stone warm since before you came. It is not for you. It is for whoever comes in behind you.”

She would not say who that was, and I have not asked twice. There is always somebody at a market with a slate.

\subsection*{At the head and in the folds}

The filings came off the tube when I set it down hard on the assessor’s step at Sill and went in without apologising; they have worked into the grain and have never once drawn the warm out of the paper, which is the one kindness iron has shown this leaf. The grey wool is the same colour as the fingers it wraps, which I have noticed and not written into the prayer. The green bead is lead glaze from a girl at the Cross with the sweetness still at her mouth; she touched the corner and went back to her pot board without saying what she had seen, and the corner tastes sweet in wet weather, and I have not washed it. The frost along one edge is from the Rim Road in Stone, when the leaf lay against my coat and the writing went thin; I have not gone over those words, because a word written thin is a word said quietly, and most of ours are. The tallow thumb is mine. The ale ring stood from the first part to the seventh and went dark in the time it takes to draw and be corrected. The silt came up from the step on a wet morning and lies in the gutter with the clerk’s nought beside it, neither entered. The grey along the foot came off a cuff that had been in a corner where no cuff has business lying. There is no Last Day on this road, and nothing here is swept up and burnt in the morning and called dealt with.

\subsection*{At the foot}

In a hand that is not mine, not the clerk’s and not the hearth-maid’s:

\begin{quote}\itshape The room hears them in the right order and is comforted.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape The road hears them backwards and goes on working.\end{quote}

Struck once and written again underneath, very small:

\begin{quote}\itshape Neither order is said to the arm.\end{quote}

I asked the clerk, the hearth-maid and a slate-holder at the Cross, and had three answers and no hand. I have left the struck line where it was struck. The leaf goes back into the wool, the wool over the tube. At the Hearth Drawing the first measure of the year will come off this iron on this road, and I shall say the four sayings backwards into the wool, and the clerk will set them right above my words, and the hearth-maid will come up from Low Kiln with a stone in her hand and will not give it to me until I have finished, which is the only order of service I have kept nine years without correction.

\clearpage\phantomsection\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{The Price Board at Greybank, Being the Rates for Goods, Carriage and the Tolls of the Four Roads, Copied from the Beam Beside the Quay}
\CRsheetheading{The Price Board at Greybank, Being the Rates for Goods, Carriage and the Tolls of the Four Roads, Copied from the Beam Beside the Quay}
{\centering\FellFont\itshape\footnotesize\color{faded} A weigh-clerk’s fair copy of the public board, with the dues of the Clay, Salt, Rim and Hearth roads set after it, corrected in two borrowed hands and left standing in a third · Written and kept at Greybank, eighteen leagues downriver of Sill, by the clerk who tends the weighing beam on the quay; begun in Y.H. 812, the Thin Year, after the Long Cold, and copied forward at the Opening of the Slates in Y.H. 813. The board itself hung on the quay wall beside the grain doors and was scraped and rewritten each tend; this leaf was pinned inside the Vhaleni counting house for the factor’s use, and survives soft at the nail-hole, with a white salt bloom along the gutter, a tar thumb at the head, a dark streak of eel slime at the foot, a green bead of cliff-glass in the lower corner, a spot of barley grease, a grey Ash print along the margin, two corrections in hands that are not the writer’s, and one line at the foot in a hand nobody will own.\par}\medskip
I keep the beam on the quay. A man brings a barrow of peat and wants a figure, and I give him the figure of that morning; by afternoon a barge has tied up and it is not the figure any more. The factor wants a number that will stand still. I have told him that a number which stands still is a lie told by a man with a roof over his goods, and he has told me to copy the board again in a better hand. I have copied it in the same hand. What follows is not what things are worth but what they fetched at the beam between the last market of Stone and the Opening of the Slates, set down so a carter may know his charge before he has unloaded.

Twelve copper bits to a silver mark. Twenty silver marks to a gold crown, which is a Sere coin and does not stay in Grath. The Court books in embers and will tell a man an ember is worth five marks; no man has ever exchanged one for the other, and I have not left a space for them on the board.

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{In the narrow upright hand of the Court’s factor’s clerk:} Coin and reckoning entered. \emph{Underneath, in mine:} An ember is a word the Court uses for warmth it has already counted. He takes the verbs out because a thing always true has no need of them; I put them back because a carter standing in the rain does not know he is hearing something always true.\end{quote}

\subsection*{The board, as it stood on the quay wall}

\subsection*{Bread and the pot}

\emph{Copied from the Cross at Sill, where the same figures are cried on Account-day. These do not move with the barges.}

Article — Price\par

Coarse barley loaf, brown-edged — 1 bit\par

Quart of small ale, watered — 1 bit\par

Sour milk, a quart — 1 bit\par

Salt herring — 2 bits\par

Smoked eel — 3 bits\par

Turnips, two — 1 bit\par

Barley gruel, a bowl at a house door — not sold; given, and not entered\par

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Margin, in my hand:} The factor’s clerk took the last line off the board, saying a thing not sold has no price. I have put it back. In Low Kiln a bowl given at a door is the greater part of what the district eats and the whole of what it does not discuss.\end{quote}

\subsection*{Goods that go downriver and goods that come back}

\emph{Weighed at the beam on the north bank. Eels and coarse pots go down to Greybank; salt and iron come up. The figure is for the load at the beam, before the road takes its share.}

Article — Price\par

Coarse pots, the score — 4 bits\par

Tile, the hundred — 9 bits\par

Peat, a barrow — 2 bits in Grain; 5 bits in Stone\par

Eels, a basket at the Fishstairs — 3 bits the eel smoked; 2 bits salted\par

Eel skin, dried, at this quay — 1 mark\par

Salt, a sack from the pans — 3 marks\par

Iron, a bar, Keldish — 2 marks in the lowlands; half a mark in Keld\par

Glass from the Glaze Cliffs, a sheet — 2 marks\par

Rope, a coil — 1 mark\par

Tallow, a stone — 2 marks\par

Lead, a pig, from the western workings — 6 marks; the seller does not say which workings\par

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Margin:} The peat row stood blank through the Long Cold of Y.H. 811; fuel doubled in Stone, then stopped being quoted, because there was none to sell. I have set two figures above it for the Thin Year and struck neither out. A man who buys in Grain and pays the Stone figure does not complain, which is how I know this is not a list of what things are worth.\end{quote}

\subsection*{Wages, hire and beasts}

Article — Price\par

A kiln hand, the day — 1 mark\par

A journeyman, the day — 2 marks\par

A child sweeping the yard, the day — 6 bits\par

A collector’s clerk, the day — 4 marks\par

A carter and cart, the day — 2 marks and the beast’s feed\par

Rent, two rooms in Low Kiln, the month — 8 marks\par

Fuel, the month — 4 marks\par

Food, the month — 12 marks\par

Sheepskin coat — 3 marks\par

Good axe — 2 marks\par

Pig — 6 marks\par

Cow — 24 marks\par

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{In a tall upright hand, the letters leaning, the ink gone brown at the edges:} A sailor’s share is two marks a month and keep; a salt-worker gets one mark and a binding promise. The Council has instructed me to enter these beside the wages of the clay towns, so that a man may see which country feeds him. \emph{Underneath, in mine:} I asked the gentleman whether a binding promise could be spent at this beam. He said it could not, and went on writing.\end{quote}

\subsection*{Articles a man asks for after he has paid}

\emph{Not on the board. I keep the list behind the beam.}

Article — Price\par

Leeches, dried, by the dozen, Fishstairs — 3 bits; no questions\par

Ice-mouse skin — 1 bit in Sill; 1 mark in Keld\par

Brine-gull feathers, a bundle, at Vhal — 1 bit\par

Reed-wolf tooth, for a clamp-handle, Stonemouth — 2 marks\par

Ash-mite paste, a thimble, in Mud End — 4 bits\par

The same, in the Hearthseat — 60 marks, taxed\par

Tallow-wasp resin, a nest — 4 marks to a bowl-surgeon of Sere; burnt in Grath\par

Quiet ash, a phial, by the Court’s licence — 60 marks\par

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Margin:} The paste and the licensed medicine are the same grey in two jars, one with a Fen name and one with a Court name. I have not put that on the board. A clerk who writes it down does not last a tend at this quay.\end{quote}

\subsection*{The Court’s figures, copied from the notice and not traded here}

Entry — Figure\par

Deduction, as printed on the Weighing notice — one in twelve\par

Thin return, paid by the district — 30 marks, in labour\par

Whole return, booked by the Court — 1,200 marks and forty unspent measures\par

Ember, as booked — 5 marks\par

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Margin:} The factor keeps a damp leaf of these in his drawer and desires that the board agree. One in twelve is printed and unchallenged and I have put no other figure beside it. I have heard other figures spoken upriver and have not entered them, not being figures I can weigh.\end{quote}

\subsection*{The tolls of the roads}

Four roads leave Greybank, and a fifth, which is the river. The dues below are what the beam collects or what the factors at the far end collect, and the difference between the two is the whole art of travelling.

\subsection*{The Clay Road}

From the Cross at Sill to this quay, eighteen leagues, packed clay over corduroy, a Court road since the treaty of the Blue Cliff in Y.H. 418. Five days by cart in Grain, six in Silt; rutted and then clay again. Because the treaty made it a Court road, an assessor may stop a cart on it without asking the thane, and does.

Due\par

Cart with a load, at the Sill end — 2 bits\par

The same at this end, by the factor’s man — 2 bits\par

Beast on the hoof — 1 bit\par

Drove of pigs — 4 bits, and the pigs weighed at the Cross besides\par

Foot passenger — nothing on Account-day; 1 bit any other day\par

Barrow of grey going out through a north gate — not weighed, and not entered\par

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Margin:} The cartmen say they pay twice to travel one road, once to the moot and once to the Court, and that the road is in a better state before the payment than after. I have put the last row on my copy and not on the board. What goes out of Sill in a barrow is the afternoon’s work, and no figure reaches it.\end{quote}

\subsection*{The Salt Road}

From this quay north-east to Vhal, sixty-two leagues beyond the eighteen, eighty in all, by the coast pass. Salt, glass, rope and dried fish go out; coin and contracts on salt-paper come back, and the damp gets into both.

Due\par

Sack of salt, at the coast pass — a mark to the Council of Tides\par

Coil of rope, or a sheet of glass — 1 bit\par

Boat-share passing inland — paid in kind, by the lot and not the league\par

Contract written on salt-paper — no fee; it will not survive the journey, which the Council calls a virtue\par

Man going up with the glass at the turn of the month — 3 bits, returned if he comes back with the answer\par

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{In the Council clerk’s leaning hand:} \emph{toll} is struck and \emph{contribution freely entered} written over it. \emph{In mine:} He has left the figures standing. A Council that cannot charge a toll has found a finer name for one, and a man pays it all the same.\end{quote}

\subsection*{The Rim Road}

West-north-west from Sill to Keld Keep, a hundred and twenty leagues of improving road and worsening weather; the Cold Pass ten leagues beyond, at a hundred and thirty. Karric VII shut it in Y.H. 741 and the agreement of Y.H. 747 fixed it as the border. Keldish surveyors keep the record and state a man’s measure before his name.

Due\par

Cart, at the pass — 1 mark, or iron to the value\par

Beast on the hoof — half a mark\par

A man without a warm-stone — the stone off the next man who has one\par

Surveyor’s mark upon a load — 2 bits; the load is not weighed again in Grath\par

Traveller going farther into the Rim — no due, and no guarantee\par

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Margin:} Only fools and factors travel it without a warm-stone, and the factors charge the stone to the account. I have kept the last row: the Warden’s surveyors do not promise to bring a man back.\end{quote}

\subsection*{The Hearth Road}

South-east from this quay to the Hearthseat, a hundred and forty leagues, the merchants’ road to the Court, spoken of in Grath as if it were a fever. There is no barrier on it and no figure at any gate.

Due\par

Toll at the barrier — none; there is no barrier\par

Grain going south, weighed here — by the deduction, entered at this end\par

The same again at the Hearthseat — booked in embers\par

A man who asks what he has paid — the figure is read to him twice, once for the moot and once for those who came late\par

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Margin:} A carter from High Kiln asked what the Hearth Road cost and I showed him the empty column. He said it was the most honest figure on the board and the dearest. The Court takes nothing at the gate because it has already taken it at home. I have not put that on the board; it would stop nobody from loading.\end{quote}

\subsection*{Bridges, ford and river road}

Due\par

South bridge at Sill, loaded cart — 1 bit\par

North bridge at Sill — nothing; the Fishstairs folk argued it and won\par

River road to the Weir and Stonemouth — 1 bit a beast; passable on foot in Silt when the low way is under water\par

Winter ford at this quay — 1 bit, when there is water to cross\par

The ford when the Ilm bears ice — nothing, because no collector can cross\par

Plank walk at the Weir — 1 bit; the boards are counted and nobody says which will bear a man\par

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Margin:} In the Long Cold the Ilm bore ice for ninety-four days and no collector crossed from this quay. I have left the figure standing because the factor wishes the board to be complete. It is the only figure on it that has never been paid.\end{quote}

\subsection*{The verse the carters tie to the board}

Four roads out of Greybank and one road down, Clay to the bank and Salt to the sea; Rim to the stone and Hearth to the fire, and the four pay twice and the fifth pays free.

Four and four and a place where the fifth should be, the beam keeps the weight and the river the rest; a man goes up with a mark in his coat and comes back with a figure he cannot digest.

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{In the narrow Court hand, against the fifth line:} Four roads entered. \emph{Underneath, in mine:} There are five, and I have put nothing in the place. A carter sang this on the quay and would not sing it while the factor’s clerk was in hearing, which is how I know the fifth line matters.\end{quote}

\subsection*{What the two borrowed hands did}

The factor’s clerk struck \emph{brown-edged} before \emph{loaf}, saying a board has no use for a description. I put it back: no household in Low Kiln has seen a loaf without an edge. The Council clerk numbered the roads as three, leaving the river and bridges out; I wrote four above his three and left both standing. Where he put a nought against the fifth line I set nothing; a nought is a number, and that line is a place.

\subsection*{At the foot, in a hand nobody will own}

\begin{quote}\itshape The road to the Hearth is paid at home. The road to the river is paid by the river.\end{quote}

I asked porters, carters and the clerk, and had four answers and no hand. I have left the line where it was written. The leaf goes back into the counting house and the board onto the quay wall; tomorrow the barge comes in with salt from Vhal and the peat row wants copying again. A man will ask for the morning’s figure and I shall give it, and by afternoon it will be a thing that was true.

\clearpage\phantomsection\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{The Price-Current at the Tide-Tally, Being the Rates of the Quay and the Dues of the Salt Road, the Shore Road and the Passages of the Sallow, Set Down for Captains and Carters}
\CRsheetheading{The Price-Current at the Tide-Tally, Being the Rates of the Quay and the Dues of the Salt Road, the Shore Road and the Passages of the Sallow, Set Down for Captains and Carters}
{\centering\FellFont\itshape\footnotesize\color{faded} A tally-keeper’s fair copy of the figures cried on the Quay, written on the one dry sheet in a house where every other paper is made to rot; the pans price set beside the pass price and both beside the beam price, the Council’s finer name written above the tally-man’s plain one, corrected in three borrowed hands and left with one line at the foot nobody will own · Written at the tide-tally house on the Quay at Vhal in Ilmen of Y.H. 813, the year after the Thin Year, when the east wind had held through the Five and the first carts came over the coast pass with the winter’s glass; written up again at the three Account-days of Tallow and copied at Greybank onto the back of a voided weigh-slip for the factor’s use. It survives as one leaf of good paper deliberately kept dry, sewn with tarred net-twine into a fold of oiled sailcloth and kept in a tin on the shelf above the tally bench, with a white salt bloom worked into the head, a tar thumb at the fold, a press of wet rope across the lower leaf, a green bead of Cliff glass in the corner, a brine-gull’s peck through one word of the song, a wet ring where a cup was set down and taken up before it was seen, a grey Ash print along the gutter which the writer did not make and has not swept, three corrections in hands that are not his, a child’s sums done wrong on the back, and a line at the foot that has never been claimed\par}\medskip
I keep the draws at the tide-tally house on the Quay. A captain comes in off the ebb with salt in his hold and a paper in his cuff, and asks what his salt will fetch and what the road will take out of him. The first I can tell him. The second I know only at the far end, and the far end writes on paper already gone soft in a coast pocket. We make our contracts here on salt-paper and account it a virtue that the damp gets into them. A debt left out in the rain is a debt made nothing, and half the fortunes of this port have turned on that.

This leaf I keep dry on purpose. It is the only dishonest thing I do.

Twelve copper bits to the silver mark; twenty marks to a Sere crown, which comes north with the buyers and goes south again with them, a fine thing to hold and a poor thing to spend on this Quay. The Court books in embers and will tell a man an ember is worth five marks. Nobody has ever brought one through this door, and I keep no column for it. A stranger’s coin warms before his face, we say; that is not the same as being welcome, and it is not a figure.

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{In the narrow upright hand of a factor’s clerk come up from Greybank:} Coin and reckoning entered. Ember: five marks. \emph{Underneath, in mine:} He writes \emph{is worth} where I should write \emph{the Court calls it worth}. A thing called five marks and a thing that changed hands at five marks are two things, and only one comes through this house.\end{quote}

\subsection*{What the Quay gives}

\emph{The first column is the figure at the pans or furnace, before a load is moved; the second is what is cried on an Account-day, which is the figure a captain carries in his head. The tide turns between them and takes its share without writing.}

Article — At the pans or the furnace — Cried at the Quay\par

Salt, a sack, cure — 2 marks — 2 marks, and a mark at the pass called a contribution\par

Salt, a pound, for the north cure — — — 4 bits, in a dry wrap; the wrap is not returned\par

Glass from the Cliffs, a sheet — 2 marks — 2 marks; sold as far as Sere\par

Rope, a coil, hemp or warp — 1 mark — 1 mark; wet rope weighs more and no buyer has ever noticed why\par

Dried fish, salt herring, the dozen — — — 2 bits\par

Smoked eel — — — 3 bits; the eel-women at the Fishstairs set their own figure\par

Tallow, a stone — — — 2 marks; most of it goes south and comes back as a Sere lamp\par

Tar, a small cask — 2 bits — 3 bits; the extra bit is the cooper’s, and he will not say what for\par

Eel-sinew, a hank — — — 1 bit; it sewed this leaf’s wrapper, and the seller would not take the bit back\par

A sailor’s share, the month — — — 2 marks and keep\par

A salt-worker, the month — — — 1 mark and a binding promise; the promise is kept wet\par

A boat built, hull and oars — — — 30 marks; the shipwright curses every hour of the work and takes the marks\par

A man come aboard — — — an opinion at half; no price, and never entered as a share\par

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{In the leaning hand of a Council clerk, who will not write upright:} Against \emph{a mark at the pass called a contribution}, strike \emph{toll}. Write \emph{contribution freely entered}. \emph{Underneath, in mine:} He has left the figure standing. A Council that cannot charge a toll has found a finer name for one, and a sack pays it all the same.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{In a Greybank factor’s narrow hand, against the salt row:} Salt, three marks, as at the beam. \emph{In mine:} Two at the pans, one at the pass, three at the beam. I have left both figures, because the middle mark travels under a name the Council chose itself.\end{quote}

\subsection*{Articles a man asks for after he has paid}

\emph{Not cried on the Quay; I keep the list in the drawer that will not close in damp.}

Article — Price\par

A phial of quiet ash, by the Court’s licence — 60 marks\par

Grey in an unmarked jar — 4 bits, from a dealer who came up from the Fen; the same grey in two vessels, one with a Court name and one with none\par

A passage south for a thin return — not taken here; the Council will not pay for one and will not house one\par

A salted boat, pushed out on the ebb — watched until it is out of sight, which is held to be enough; no figure\par

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Margin:} A man came in with a licence for quiet ash and asked what the licence cost besides the sixty marks. I told him the licence was the sixty marks and the keeping was his own. He went away and wrote it down on salt-paper, which is the proper way to preserve nothing.\end{quote}

\subsection*{The dues of the roads}

Four ways leave this Quay and one leaves the world. What is below is what is asked before a man loads, and what is on his paper when he comes back. The two do not agree, and the difference is the art of travelling.

\subsection*{The Salt Road, up to Greybank and Sill}

Eighty leagues by the coast pass, twenty days on foot at four leagues a day, more in a thaw. Salt, glass, rope and dried fish go up; coin and contracts come back, and the damp gets into both.

Due\par

Sack of salt, at the coast pass — 1 mark to the Council of Tides, entered as a contribution freely entered\par

Coil of rope, or a sheet of glass — 1 bit\par

Man going up with the glass at the turn of the month — 3 bits, returned if he comes back with the answer\par

Boat-share passing inland — paid in kind, by the lot and not the league\par

Contract written on salt-paper — no fee; it will not survive the journey, which the Council calls a virtue\par

Cart with a load, at the Greybank beam — 2 bits, and the same again when it turns down the Clay Road to Sill\par

A barrow of grey going north through a gate — not weighed, not entered, and no figure reaches it\par

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{In a boat-master’s blunt charcoal, added at the foot of the column:} Paid at the pass and paid at the beam and paid again for having carried it, and my paper gone soft before I could read what I had paid. \emph{In mine:} All three stand. A road has two ends and both have a hand; the sea has one hand and does not write.\end{quote}

\subsection*{The shore road to the Glaze Cliffs}

Five leagues along the coast from the glass furnaces. The cliffs are stained blue-green by old lead working and smell faintly sweet in the heat; children are warned not to lick them.

Due\par

Cart of glass-sand going up — nothing at any gate; there is no gate\par

Sheet of glass coming back — 1 bit at the pass, entered to the Council\par

A man who licks the cliff — his teeth, which are not entered anywhere\par

Lead out of the old working — 6 marks the pig; the seller does not say which working, and we do not ask\par

\subsection*{The pans road}

Due\par

A cart to the pans — nothing; the pans are the works of the port and not a road out of it\par

A dipper blessing the nets at dawn — the net is trailed in the sea and nothing is charged for the sea\par

Salt taken before the crust has set — paid by weight, and the weight changes after you pay\par

\subsection*{The passages of the Sallow}

The Sallow lies milk-coloured against the north-east, and its tides run against the wind. The dippers say it follows the Warm rather than the moon, which a tally-house cannot enter because it has no figure that will stand still.

Due\par

The ebb going out — no toll; the tide takes the boat and is not asked for a receipt\par

The turn — a count is taken elsewhere and two counts in one morning make a debt\par

The flood coming in — 1 bit on the boards, which the Fishstairs folk argued and lost\par

A salted boat with a dead man aboard — watched until it is out of sight; no due, and no return entered\par

A galley on the pulled benches — seven years, or until the hands give out, whichever comes first\par

\subsection*{The roads that are not roads of this port}

The Rim Road takes a mark or iron at the pass and promises no man back. The Hearth Road takes nothing at any gate, having taken it at home; the Clay Road takes twice, once at each end. I have kept these lines from the tallies of other men and set no figure of my own against them. A tally-keeper who writes what he has not weighed is writing a Court notice.

\subsection*{What is not entered}

What is taken — What I write\par

A contract left in the damp — the debt, by the Council’s own account — nothing; the paper has done it\par

A man whose account is current — the price of welcome — nothing; we have no word for guest\par

An opinion at half — the man come aboard — nothing; it is not his to sell\par

Warmth off a cold tide — carried seaward, by report — nothing; no collector follows it\par

The grey along the gutter — left where a cuff was laid — nothing swept and burnt and called dealt with\par

A name said at home — kept under a roof, not on any roll — a door, which I do not draw\par

\subsection*{The song the tallymen say}

\emph{Said low at the head of the flood, to the pot and not to a man, and never while a clerk from Slate Row stands in the door. The last word of each verse falls into the water and is not finished.}

\begin{quote}\itshape Two at the pans and one at the pass,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and three at the beam where the factor stands;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape a bit for the rope and a bit for the glass,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the paper pays nothing in Vhaleni lands.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape The ebb takes a boat and the flood takes a bit,\end{quote}
