\begin{quote}\itshape the turn takes the count and gives none back;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape a stranger’s coin warms before his face\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the Council writes what the rain will unwrap.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{In the Council clerk’s leaning hand, against the first line:} Three figures entered. \emph{Underneath, in mine:} There are four roads and a fifth place where the passage stops. He has put a nought against what I left bare. A nought is a figure a man can carry away in his cuff.\end{quote}

\subsection*{The hands that are not mine}

The Greybank clerk takes the doer out of every sentence, as though a sack could pay itself and a rope could coil itself at the turn of the month. The Council clerk calls a toll a contribution, which is the same figure with the doer invited in to thank it. The boat-master writes in charcoal because ink will not sit on a wet table. I have set my words under all three. A leaf with four hands on it is the only kind a man on this Quay will believe. A leaf with one hand is a Court notice, and a Court notice has never told a captain what the pass would charge him.

A child of the Quay did her sums on the back in salt-paper charcoal, two bits going into a mark where four should have stood, and the rain took one of them clean away. I have not rubbed out the other. It is the only figure here nobody will be asked to pay, and the only one that will still be here when the rest of us have gone soft.

\subsection*{At the head and in the gutter}

The white at the head is salt bloom off this house’s own paper; I keep the leaf dry and the bloom comes to find it anyway. The tar at the fold is off the coil a boat-master set down while he argued the second mark. The wet rope pressed into the lower leaf looks like a figure and is not one. The green bead came from a girl with the sweetness of the cliff at one mouth-corner, who touched the leaf and said nothing. The brine-gull peck went through a word of the song and I have not written it back, because a verse with a word gone is a verse said slowly. The ring is not ale, and I did not see the cup go down. The grey in the gutter came off a cuff laid where no cuff has business lying, and I have not swept it. There is no Last Day at a tide-tally.

\subsection*{At the foot, in a hand nobody will own}

\begin{quote}\itshape The paper keeps the debt the rain unmakes.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape The road keeps the mark the pass renames.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape The Sallow keeps the boat and does not enter it.\end{quote}

I asked the keeper of the draws, a carter off the coast pass, and a woman who holds a share through her mother, and had three answers and no hand. I have left the line where it was written. The leaf goes back into its tin, and in the morning the Council clerk will come for the tallies and find this one dry, which in Vhal is the most suspicious thing on the Quay. A captain will ask the figure I gave him yesterday and be given it again; by the time his paper reaches Greybank it will be a thing that was true.

\clearpage\phantomsection\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{The Quart Set Down at the Ninth Pot, Being a Winter Wager on the Nine Pots Road, the Road-Song as It Is Sung, and the Figure a Clerk Set Against the Frost}
\CRsheetheading{The Quart Set Down at the Ninth Pot, Being a Winter Wager on the Nine Pots Road, the Road-Song as It Is Sung, and the Figure a Clerk Set Against the Frost}
{\centering\FellFont\itshape\footnotesize\color{faded} An alehouse keeper’s telling of a night in the deep cold, set down for the settling of an argument about a quart and not for the improvement of the reader; the five quarts in a charcoal column, the sayings in the words they were spoken, the road-song as it is sung, the figure of a clerk entered over them, and one line at the foot in a hand nobody will own · Written in Stone of Y.H. 812, the Thin Year after the Long Cold, at the alehouse called the Ninth Pot in Nine Pots, eight leagues west of Sill, by Cilla who keeps the bench and the fire behind it; set down because a man came the next morning and asked whether a quart had been drunk at the end of the bench and she could not tell him. Copied forward in Ilmen of Y.H. 813 onto the back of a spoiled kiln tally, sewn with eel-sinew into a fold of oiled paper and kept in the jar beside the bench. It survives with a tallow thumb at the head, a small-ale ring, a press of wet wool across the first leaf, frost-crisp at the fore-edge, grey Ash in the gutter, a scorch where the leaf was held too near the fire, one correction in the narrow upright hand of a clerk of the Sill table, one saying in charcoal in a wheel-man’s hand, and one line at the foot in a hand that is nobody’s.\par}\medskip
I keep the Ninth Pot at Nine Pots, which is eight leagues west of Sill and a long day’s walk when the road is open. There are four kilns in this hamlet and nine pots in the name of it, and no living man will tell you which is the ninth. I have asked. I asked a man who had lived here sixty years, and he looked at the road the way a man looks at a thing he has been told not to touch, and said it was a question for somebody with a slate. There is no slate in this house. There is a bench black with the sleeves of forty winters, a fire behind it that is not mine to say where it came from, and one clay pot for the quart that stands between the first question and the last. That is the furniture, and a man may sit on all of it if he takes his boots off first, which nobody does.

The road to Sill is the quarrel of this place. It has outlived every man who began it. Sill says the road is ours to keep because the clay goes west on it; we say it is theirs to keep because the carts come back empty and leave the ruts for our women to walk in. Both sayings are true and neither has mended a yard. In Stone the drift takes it, and the road belongs to the frost, which is the only landlord in Grath that never sends a bill and never comes to collect one.

It took us in the Thin Year, on a Stone morning when the wind came over the Rim and shut the west road in a night. A carter out of Sill was caught on it with an empty cart and a horse that had gone lame somewhere short of the shared pit. He came into the Ninth Pot at dusk with the snow standing on his shoulders and did not take it off, nor ask for a seat, nor say whose horse it was. He stood with his back to the fire until the ice on his coat went grey at the edges, and then asked for a quart. I gave him one and he paid a bit for it, which is the price, and a carter who pays the price in this hamlet is a man who wants something.

There were three at the bench when he came: Radd the wheel-man, Onn who treads the shared pit, and Denn of the fourth kiln. They had been telling the road story as men tell it when the road has shut them in, each with the same saying he told last winter and will tell the next, and none of them hearing the others. The clerk of the Sill table sat in the corner with a slate to his forearm. He had come up before the frost to measure the road, which is a thing a clerk will do when two hamlets have been at a word for fifty years and nobody has thought to ask him; the drift had kept him where he sat. He had a pen and a narrow hand, and he had not once looked at the carter.

“I’ll stand four quarts,” the carter said, “to the man who tells me what this road is worth. One for each of you and one for the bench. Then I’ll drink my own and go to bed.”

Radd turned the wheel in his hands though there was no wheel there, the way a man will turn a thing that is out of reach. “A road’s worth the wheel that’s on it,” he said. “Take the wheel off and it’s a direction. I’ve sold directions. They don’t pay.”

Onn said the road was worth what it carried, and what it carried was mud, and he had trodden mud for nineteen years and could tell a man the weight of it and not the price. “A day’s back,” he said. “It’s worth a day’s back and nothing in coin.” He said it to the pot, which is where we say such things.

Denn of the fourth kiln said a road was worth the pot that went out on it and the state of the pot when it came back. “If it comes back whole, it’s worth the firing,” he said. “If it comes back flat, I’ve lost the firing and the road too, and that’s two losses with one name.”

The clerk did not put his pen to the slate. He said he was not a man to wager on a way and had no opinion of a road. He kept his eyes on his own hand, which is the manner of that table.

The fourth quart was mine, because a quart put to the bench is not scored against anybody. I set it down and said what I had. “A road is worth the man that’s on it,” I said. “A man on a road is worth more than the same man off one, and that’s the whole of what I know. Ask the road. It’ll tell you the weather.”

The carter drank his own without sitting down, wiped his mouth on the back of a glove, and then did a thing I have not seen a man do in this house before or since. He put a bit on the bench and pointed to the end of it where nobody sat. “There’s a fifth,” he said. “Stand it there. A man went out on this road before the drift and hasn’t come back. Set it where he’d have sat, and don’t let anybody drink it.”

Nobody asked who the man was. In this hamlet a question like that is answered with the weather and the road, and we had had enough of both. I set the pot down at the bench end. Radd looked at it and looked away. Onn shut both hands round his quart as though the heat were going out of it, which it was. Denn said nothing at all, which was the most he ever said. The clerk wrote two lines and I have left them standing.

Before the fire was banked we sang the road song, as we sing it when the frost has shut us in, standing with a hand on the bench because it is the only warm thing in the room by then. The second line is the potters’ error and I have set it down as they sing it. They will not have it changed.

\begin{quote}\itshape Four kilns cold and the west road fast,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape nine pots and nobody knows the last;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the frost has drawn a line across\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and a man goes out and a man comes back.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Knuckle the pot and the pot will say\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape which side the crack let the fire away;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape ask the road what the carting cost ---\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the road gives weather, the slate gives lost.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape One for the man that came in wet,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape one for the man that hasn’t come back yet,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and one set down where the bench is bare:\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the house keeps it. Nobody’s there.\end{quote}

I have set the five quarts down as they stood, because of the man who came the next morning and asked whether a quart had been drunk at the end of the bench, and I could not tell him. This is the whole account the house keeps, in charcoal on the back of a spoiled kiln tally, because charcoal goes into the grain and a slate does not.

Quart — Set down for — Paid — Drunk\par

The first — the carter out of Sill — one bit — yes, standing\par

The second — Radd of the wheel — one bit — yes\par

The third — Onn of the shared pit — one bit — yes\par

The fourth — the bench, not scored — one bit — yes, by the room\par

The fifth — the bench end — one bit — nobody owned\par

The clerk’s lines stand above mine in the narrow upright hand he uses, which is a hand that travels further than mine ever will.

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{In the hand of the clerk of the Sill table:} Way: no measure stands. No deduction arises. Ale sold: five. Consumed: four. Party at the bench end: unidentified.\end{quote}

I have not crossed him out. He is right about the four and wrong about the fifth, and he has put a figure where I put a man. A figure travels well and arrives empty. The fifth quart was drunk by somebody in this room or it was not drunk at all, and I will never know which, and I have left the column as it stands.

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{In the margin, in charcoal, in Radd’s hand:} A direction’s not a road till a man’s been lost on it.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Underneath, in mine:} He said that to the pot and not to the clerk, and the clerk did not take it, which is the one kindness I have ever seen him do.\end{quote}

The tallow thumb at the head is mine; I held the tally down in the draught that comes under the door and did not know I had marked it. The ring is a small-ale ring that stood from the first quart to the fifth and was not lifted until morning. The press of wet wool across the first leaf came off the carter when he leaned to see what the clerk had written, and I have not written down which man held the door for him. The fore-edge is frost-crisp where the leaf lay under a stone too short for it; the writing there has gone thin and I have not gone over it, because a word written thin is a word said quietly, and most of ours are. The scorch is where I held the tally too near the fire to read what the clerk had done. The grey in the gutter came off a cuff that had no business near the corner where I keep the leaf, and I have not swept it. The road opened at the thaw and the carter went east with his horse shod. He did not ask after the fifth quart again, because it was paid for.

At the foot, in a hand nobody will own:

\begin{quote}\itshape The ninth pot was on the bench all along. Nobody knocked it.\end{quote}

I asked Radd, Onn and Denn, and had three silences and no hand. I have left the line where it was written. The tally goes back into the jar and the fifth pot goes back on the bench, and on the next Stone night I shall set four quarts out and one at the end where nobody sits, and let whoever has a road to tell come in out of the cold and tell it to the pot.

\clearpage\phantomsection\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{The Quay Tally at Vhal, Being the Rates of the Sallow Market at the Flood and at the Ebb, with the Dues of the Salt Road, the Coast Pass and the Waters of the Quay, Copied from the Board Beside the Tide-Tally House}
\CRsheetheading{The Quay Tally at Vhal, Being the Rates of the Sallow Market at the Flood and at the Ebb, with the Dues of the Salt Road, the Coast Pass and the Waters of the Quay, Copied from the Board Beside the Tide-Tally House}
{\centering\FellFont\itshape\footnotesize\color{faded} A tally-man’s fair copy of the shore-board, written on salt-paper he keeps dry against the practice of the country; the figures sloped as tallies are sloped, the verbs written back under the Council’s correction, one rate gone void by rain, two corrections in borrowed hands, and a line at the foot nobody will own · Written at the tide-tally house on the Quay at Vhal by one of the men who read the draws under Kett of the Quay; begun in Ember of Y.H. 812, the Thin Year, after the Long Cold, copied forward at the Opening of the Slates, Ilmen 1, Y.H. 813, and written up again at the turn of Grain. It survives in a tarred tin lined with dry rushes, sewn with tarred net-twine, the leaves kept dry though the Council’s own paper is made to rot; with a white salt bloom at the head, a tar thumb at the fold, a fibre of wet rope pressed into the second leaf, a brine-gull’s peck through one figure, a fish-hook nick at the head, a wet corner where two rates have gone and are void by law, a green bead of Cliffs glass in the lower corner, a grey Ash print along the margin that nobody will own, two corrections in hands that are not the writer’s, and one line at the foot nobody will claim.\par}\medskip
I keep the shore-board beside the house where Kett reads the draws. A carter comes down the coast pass with salt in his load and asks the figure before he has unloaded, and I give him the figure of this water; by the turn of the tide it is not the figure any more. The factor at Greybank wants a number that will stand still, and I have told him that a number which stands still is a lie told by a man with a roof over his goods. He has told me to copy the board again in a better hand. I have copied it in the same hand and set the two waters against each other.

Twelve copper bits to a silver mark; twenty silver marks to a gold crown, which is a Sere coin and comes north because it must, and cannot always be spent here. The Court books in embers and calls five marks an ember; no man has ever exchanged one for the other. I have left no column for them on the nailed board and kept the row here, because a carter who has walked eighty leagues is entitled to know which figure has a hand behind it.

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{In the narrow upright hand of the factor’s clerk out of Greybank:} Coin and reckoning entered. Ember: five marks. \emph{Underneath, in mine:} He has written it as though a mark could be carried to the bank and poured into an ember. I have put the verb back. The Court calls it five marks. Nobody trades it, and a figure that nobody trades is a figure that gets read aloud.\end{quote}

\subsection*{The board as it stands on the Quay}

\emph{The left figure is what a thing fetched at the head of the flood, when the boats are coming in and the buyers have not yet had the morning’s bread. The right is what it fetched at the turn of the ebb, when the same boats are loading out and the buyer knows he must pay for the road as well as the goods. Both were cried under the tide-tally house between the last market of Stone and the turn of Grain.}

Article — At the flood — At the ebb\par

Salt, a sack off the pans — 1 mark — 2 marks, and the carter does not complain\par

Glass, a sheet, green off the Cliffs — 1 mark — 2 marks after the Glaze boat has come in\par

Rope, a coil, tarred — 1 mark — 1 mark, and tar on the buyer’s hands before he pays\par

Tar, a pail — 4 bits — 1 mark when the galleys are refitting\par

Dried fish, a string — 1 bit — 1 bit, or two if the gulls have followed the boat in\par

Salt herring, a basket — 2 bits — 2 bits, and a third bit when the boat has been out longer than anyone says\par

Eel skin, dried, come down the river — 1 mark — 1 mark; it has been down the water to be sold back up it\par

Brine-gull feathers, a bundle — 1 bit — 1 bit; the bird is not consulted\par

Red wine, a jar, out of Sere — 2 marks — 2 marks; salt on the rim, and no charge for the salt\par

A bed in a house on the Quay, the month — 4 marks — 4 marks, and the floor is a bit\par

A boat, new, from the shipwright — 30 marks — 30 marks, and the curse is included, which no shipwright will enter on a tally\par

Grain going up the Salt Road, by the beam — by the deduction — read twice, once for the moot and once for those who came late\par

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Margin:} The Council clerk took the two columns and made one, saying a board has no use for the weather. I put them back. Salt is not dearer at the ebb because the salt has changed; the boat must go out on the water that brought it in, and a man who has paid for the going out is in a hurry to be gone.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Margin, in the leaning hand:} A sailor’s share is two marks a month and keep; a salt-worker gets one mark and a binding promise. A man who marries into a boat-owning family is come aboard and his opinion counts at half, which is entered nowhere because it has never been a figure. \emph{In mine:} I asked a salt-worker whether a binding promise could be spent at this board. He said it could not, and went back to the pans.\end{quote}

\subsection*{Paid in kind, and not entered}

These stand on the board with a space where the figure should be. The Council has more than once put a nought in the space. A nought is a figure and can be entered; a boat-share is not, because it passes through the mother and a man cannot pay for what he was born beside.

What passes — What is given — What I write\par

A boat-share going inland — paid by the lot and not the league — the lot, in kind, no figure\par

A man come aboard — half a word on the boat — nothing; the half is not mine to enter\par

A shipwright’s curse — included in the thirty marks — nothing; it is the price of the boat and not the boat\par

A binding promise — one mark’s worth, said binding — one mark in the promise column, which the Council has no column for\par

Seven years at the pulled bench — a condemned man rows them and is paid nothing — seven years, which the Council calls a mercy\par

A dead man sealed in a salted boat and set on the ebb — the watching, until he is out of sight — no fee, and no collector\par

A contract on salt-paper left in the rain — a debt made nothing — nothing, which is held to be a virtue\par

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{In the Council clerk’s leaning hand, against the last row:} Instrument void by exposure; no claim can lie. \emph{In mine:} He is right in a language nobody at the pans uses. Half the fortunes of this port have turned on a contract going damp at the right moment, and the other half on somebody forgetting to bring it in.\end{quote}

\subsection*{The dues of the roads}

Four ways leave this Quay: the Salt Road down to the coast pass and on to Greybank, the shore road along the Cliffs, the water of the Sallow, and the road that is the tide itself. The figures below are what the Council asks or what the factor’s man asks at the far end. The difference between the two is the whole art of travelling.

\subsection*{The Salt Road, by the coast pass}

Eighty leagues to Greybank, sixty-two of them beyond the pass, where the clay country gives way to the salt; a day’s walk south-west of Vhal by the low road. Salt, glass, rope and dried fish go out; coin and contracts come back, and the damp gets into both.

Due\par

Sack of salt, at the coast pass — 1 mark to the Council of Tides\par

Coil of rope, or a sheet of glass — 1 bit\par

Cart with a load, at this end — 2 bits\par

The same at the factor’s beam at Greybank — 2 bits more\par

Contract written on salt-paper — no fee; it will not survive the journey, which the Council calls a virtue\par

Man going up with the glass at the turn of the month — 3 bits, returned if he comes back with the answer\par

Passage upriver for a man — 2 bits; his boat-share inland is settled by the lot\par

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{In the Council clerk’s leaning hand:} \emph{toll} is struck and \emph{contribution freely entered} written over it. \emph{In mine:} He has left the figure standing. A Council that cannot charge a toll has found a finer name for one, and a man pays it all the same.\end{quote}

\subsection*{The shore road to the Glaze Cliffs}

Five leagues along the coast, where the old lead sweetens in the heat and the glass comes green off the rock. There is a path and no gate, and a due at the path’s end because a path in Vhalen is never left alone for long.

Due\par

Sheet of glass carried off the Cliffs — 1 bit at the quarry path\par

Pig of lead from the old workings — 2 marks; the seller does not say which workings\par

A man who licks the Cliffs — nothing, and the sweetness stays with him\par

Barrel of rain carried against the salt-thing — 1 bit; a man who does not carry it pays later\par

Winter, when the pass is shut — no figure; the road is a direction and nothing more\par

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Margin:} A child is told not to lick the Cliffs and some do, for a child believes a warning about a taste before one about a poison. The due is nothing and the cost is not entered.\end{quote}

\subsection*{The water roads}

Due\par

A keel at the Quay, the month — 2 marks, or a fish off the catch\par

A boat that comes in on the ebb and goes out on the flood — nothing; it has not stopped\par

A boat passing upriver with a share aboard — by the lot, not the league; no figure\par

A net trailed at dawn under the tide-tally house — no fee, and the draw is not entered\par

A brine-gull’s coal off a brazier — nothing, and no slate in Vhal stands the poorer\par

A man who dies at sea — no slate; the sea keeps its own account\par

A man who dies on land, carried down for the boat — 1 bit for the carrying; the Return is entered before he goes\par

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Margin:} The factor’s clerk wrote a figure against the net row and called the draw a taxable current. It has not been paid in eleven years. A current measured honestly gets taxed, and I have stopped telling the Council which is which.\end{quote}

\subsection*{What the borrowed hands did}

The factor’s clerk strikes the verbs out, as though a verb were a thing a man could carry off in a cuff and sell at the crossing. Where I write \emph{the carter paid}, he writes \emph{was paid}, as though a mark could pay itself. I put both back underneath and leave his words above. A figure with nobody in it is a figure that will be paid twice.

The Council clerk numbers the roads as three, leaving the shore road and the water out, and puts a nought in the space where the verse keeps a place for the tide that has not come. A nought is a figure paid. The tide has not come and will not be entered, and I have set nothing beside his nought but the space itself.

\subsection*{The song the tally-men carry}

\emph{Sung at the head of the flood while the boats come in, never at the ebb and never while the factor’s clerk is within hearing of the second verse.}

\begin{quote}\itshape Twelve to the mark and twenty to the crown,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the Court books an ember and keeps it in town;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the board says a mark at the flood, two at the ebb,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the carter pays both and says neither was debt.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape A mark at the pan and a mark at the pass,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape a bit for the coil and a bit for the glass;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the share goes down where the mother went,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the man come aboard writes nothing on mine.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape The draw takes the Warm and the tax takes the draw,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the rain takes the contract and calls it the law;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape I keep my leaf dry and the Council keeps wet,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the tide keeps the figure nobody has entered.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{In the Council clerk’s hand, against the last line:} No figure entered against the tide. \emph{In mine:} He is right, and the song is sung with the last line held until the ebb, which is how I know the line matters.\end{quote}

\subsection*{In the head and in the gutter}

The salt bloom has eaten the figure against \emph{eel skin}, so that I cannot now read whether it stood at one mark or two; a price the weather has taken is truer than one a clerk can still read, and I have not written it in again. The tar thumb is mine, from holding the leaf down in a wind off the Sallow. The rope fibre in the second leaf came off a coil paid for with a wet hand and goes soft when the weather goes soft, which tells me when to shut the tin. The brine-gull peck went through the row for dried fish and nobody has claimed the bird. The fish-hook nick came off a hook set down in a hurry by a man paying for six herrings and charged for five, or the other way, which he will not settle and I have not entered. The green bead is glass off the Cliffs and fell out of a girl’s hair when she leaned to see the figures; she did not ask for it back. The grey print along the margin is not mine and not the Council’s, and I have not swept it. There is no Last Day on a Quay.

\subsection*{At the foot, in a hand nobody will own}

\begin{quote}\itshape The board keeps the figure the boat paid. The tin keeps the figure the man carried. The difference has no column, and the tide has no hand to write one.\end{quote}

I asked a tally-man, a carter come down from Greybank and a woman who holds a share from her mother, and had three answers and no hand. I have left the line where it was written.

The leaf goes back into the tin under the counter; the board stays on the wall, where the bloom will take another figure by the end of the tend. Tomorrow the boats come in at the flood and a man will ask the morning price, and by the ebb it will be a thing that was true.

\clearpage\phantomsection\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{The Quench Song, Being the Drinking-Song of the Glass Furnaces at Vhal, Sung at the Trough After the Last Pot Is Drawn, with the Jar Going Round the Hands, the Revolt Year Kept Back, a Furnace-Master’s Ruling in White Slip, a Clerk’s Correction Going Soft on Salt-Paper, a Glazer’s Charcoal Underneath, and One Line at the Foot in a Hand Nobody Will Own}
\CRsheetheading{The Quench Song, Being the Drinking-Song of the Glass Furnaces at Vhal, Sung at the Trough After the Last Pot Is Drawn, with the Jar Going Round the Hands, the Revolt Year Kept Back, a Furnace-Master’s Ruling in White Slip, a Clerk’s Correction Going Soft on Salt-Paper, a Glazer’s Charcoal Underneath, and One Line at the Foot in a Hand Nobody Will Own}
{\centering\FellFont\itshape\footnotesize\color{faded} A drinking-song of the third furnace, in the rough tide-speech of Vhal set down in Grathic letters; the verses said to the trough and to the jar as it goes round, one verse to a hand at the quench, the refrain let fall into the water and not given to the company; the kept verse held back until the yard is empty; the furnace-master’s ruling in white slip on the brick margin, the tide-clerk’s leaning hand going soft on salt-paper above, a glazer’s charcoal underneath, and one line at the foot in a hand nobody will claim · Sung at the quench-trough of the third furnace at Vhal in Stone of Y.H. 812, the Thin Year after the Long Cold, and set down that night by the woman who carts sand and lead to the third furnace and has done it eleven winters; written in charcoal on the back of a sand-tally spoiled by a wet thumb, folded in a scrap of oiled sailcloth with a twist of wet rope, and kept in a clay pot stoppered with wool in the sand-shed, where the damp comes up off the shore. A clerk of the tide-tally house borrowed the leaf on a morning when the winter glass was counted and asked what the women sang at the quench, and wrote the answer down while it was still being said, with the doing taken out and a term set where a place should stand; his hand is on salt-paper and the damp has eaten most of it, so that of four corrections two are figures, one is the ghost of a verb, and one has gone clean away. It survives with a white salt bloom at the head, a pale streak of lead worked into the grain, a tar thumb at the fold, a strand of wet rope pressed into the second leaf, a blue-green chip of Cliffs glass in the lower corner, a scorch where the leaf lay too near the furnace mouth, a grain of sand that has cut a line through one word of the fourth verse, a ring of sour wine gone dark at the foot, a grey Ash print along the outer fold that nobody will own, the furnace-master’s ruling in white slip, the clerk’s soft hand above, the glazer’s charcoal underneath, and the line at the foot\par}\medskip
I cart sand and lead to the third furnace and have done it eleven winters. The sand comes up off the shore in barrows and the lead after it in pigs, and the two go into the pot together the way bread and water go into a batch. I know a good barrow by the grain before it is tipped and a bad one by the smell, which I learned with my nose and not from any written word. The yard counts the glass going out. Nobody counts the sand going in, and nobody counts what the quench takes off the hands at it, which is not the same thing as saying nobody knows.

I set this down because a clerk of the tide-tally house stood at the shed with a leaf and a soft cuff, asked what we sang at the quench, and wrote it while I was still saying it, with the doing taken out and a term put where a place should stand. His hand is above mine and the damp is taking it, which the Council calls a virtue in its contracts and would not call a virtue in its clerk. I have left his words where he set them.

The white at the head is salt off the shore sand and will not come out of the grain, which is why we sign in charcoal here and not in ink.

\subsection*{The manner of it}

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item At the trough, after the last pot is drawn and before the fire is banked. Not while a man from the Council room stands in the yard; said with such a man in hearing, the song comes out as a statement and is entered as one.

\item Standing, with one hand on the edge of the trough and the other at the jar. Said with a hand on a woman, it becomes an argument, and there are arguments enough in a furnace yard without carrying one up the Salt Road.

\item To the water and to the jar, not to the company. The last word of each verse is let fall into the trough and not finished. The jar keeps the refrain: one voice begins and the rest come in on the second line.

\item One verse to a hand at the quench, going round with the jar. The sixth hand holds the jar and does not drink, and the verse said there is said low, into the water, because a verse said loudly is a verse with a price in it.

\item Tap the trough with the knuckle during the refrain. The tap is not a number; a clerk can carry off a figure, not a tap on wet boards.

\item The kept verse is not sung while strangers are in the yard. It is said to the trough when the last cart has gone up the road, with the jar going round once more and nobody drinking.

\end{itemize}

\subsection*{The song}

\emph{Said low to the trough, standing. The jar keeps the refrain. The hand goes to the edge of the trough before the first line.}

The refrain, as the jar keeps it after every verse:

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Quench, quench, the pot comes out.}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Pass the jar and say what it cost.}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{The furnace keeps the heat. The trough keeps the steam.}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{The sand goes in and the glass goes north.}\end{quote}

\subsection*{I. Of the sand}

\begin{quote}\itshape The sand comes up from the shore in a barrow,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape grey as the road after rain and no more than that;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape we know it by the grain and not by its name,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the lead comes after it, sweet at the lip.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Quench, quench, the pot comes out.}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Pass the jar and say what it cost.}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{The furnace keeps the heat. The trough keeps the steam.}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{The sand goes in and the glass goes north.}\end{quote}

\subsection*{II. Of the sweetness}

\begin{quote}\itshape There’s a sweetness at the corner of the mouth\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape that comes from the lead and not from the wine;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape a child at the Cliffs is told not to lick,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and we are paid to do what the child is told not.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Quench, quench, the pot comes out.}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Pass the jar and say what it cost.}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{The furnace keeps the heat. The trough keeps the steam.}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{The sand goes in and the glass goes north.}\end{quote}

\subsection*{III. Of the drawing}

\begin{quote}\itshape The pot comes out of the mouth on a rod\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the light that was in it goes into the glass;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape you cannot look at it and you look all the same,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the eyes go on seeing it after the shift.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Quench, quench, the pot comes out.}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Pass the jar and say what it cost.}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{The furnace keeps the heat. The trough keeps the steam.}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{The sand goes in and the glass goes north.}\end{quote}

\subsection*{IV. Of the quench}

\begin{quote}\itshape The trough takes the pot and gives back a cloud;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the cloud takes the hair off the forehead and goes.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape One hand on the rod and one on the jar;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the jar goes round and the hand does not.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Quench, quench, the pot comes out.}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Pass the jar and say what it cost.}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{The furnace keeps the heat. The trough keeps the steam.}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{The sand goes in and the glass goes north.}\end{quote}

\subsection*{V. Of the north}

\begin{quote}\itshape The glass goes north in a consignment of oil\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the wine comes back in the same kind of jar;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape a crown buys a bowl in the court of the south,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and none of our pots was ever asked to one.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Quench, quench, the pot comes out.}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Pass the jar and say what it cost.}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{The furnace keeps the heat. The trough keeps the steam.}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{The sand goes in and the glass goes north.}\end{quote}

\subsection*{VI. Of the hands}

\begin{quote}\itshape There are six hands at the trough when the last pot’s out;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the jar goes to five and comes back to the sixth.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape The sixth holds it level and does not drink,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the ledger gets that one and we get the rest.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Quench, quench, the pot comes out.}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Pass the jar and say what it cost.}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{The furnace keeps the heat. The trough keeps the steam.}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{The sand goes in and the glass goes north.}\end{quote}

There is a space before the seventh verse, the width of a hand laid flat on the trough before the pot goes in, felt for with the palm and not the eye. I have left it. A clerk put a round nought in it, and the damp has eaten the word beside it down to the figure, so that his nought has come through the wet and his verb has not, which could only happen to a sentence written on salt-paper.

\subsection*{The verse kept back}

\emph{Not sung while a man from the Council room is in the yard. Said to the trough after the last cart has gone up the road, with the jar going round once more and nobody drinking.}

\begin{quote}\itshape In the year the men stood at the mouth of the third,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the sand went in and the men went out;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the Council wrote \emph{resolved} in a hand gone soft,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and lit the furnace again in the very same week.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape We do not say what they wanted. We say what they were given,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape which was the same fire and the same jar going round.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Pass it to the water. The water has no clerk.\end{quote}

There is no verse after it; the next thing is the damp taking the leaf, which has never wanted one.

\subsection*{The jar, as it goes round}

\emph{The hands as the yard keeps them, set above what the tide-clerk entered on the morning the winter glass was counted. The two readings stand.}

Hand — What the yard says — What the clerk entered\par

The lead hand — Sweet at the lip, and paid for it — Exposure, occupational\par

The rod hand — The light goes into the glass — Product, sound\par

The quench hand — The cloud takes the hair and goes — vapour, unentered\par

The sixth hand — Holds it level and does not drink — One retained; no charge arises\par

The kept verse — Said to the trough, after the yard — Historical disturbance; no account lies\par

The clerk wrote \emph{no charge arises} against the sixth hand, which is true in his office and leaves the hand standing there with the jar in it. A hand holding a jar is not nothing even when it has not drunk, which is the whole of this song and no use to a counting room.

\subsection*{What the furnace-master ruled}

He came down on the wrong wind with the sweet edge of the glaze at one corner of his mouth and read the tally with one eye on the furnace. Against \emph{we are paid to do what the child is told not} he wrote in broad white slip: \emph{Protective instruction current. No loss arises.} He underlined it twice, and the slip has flaked at the second word, which is a thing white slip does and a thing he did not provide for.

Underneath, in mine: He is right about the instruction and wrong about the loss. The sweetness is part of the wage and is not paid in coin, and a mouth gone pale at the corner is a thing a man carries home and cannot set down at the shed. He reads with one eye on the furnace, as a man does who has never stood at the quench.

\subsection*{What the tide-clerk did}

He borrowed the leaf while the consignment was counted. He writes in the leaning hand on salt-paper, and the shore has taken half of it, so that of four corrections two are figures, one the ghost of a verb and one gone clean away. He took the doing out and set his words above mine.

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item At \emph{the furnace keeps the heat, the trough keeps the steam} he wrote \emph{heat retained; vapor unentered}, which takes both keepers out and leaves the furnace standing with nobody in it.

\item At \emph{we are paid to do what the child is told not} he wrote \emph{occupational exposure, current}, which is a true thing in a counting room and leaves the mouth out whole.

\item At \emph{the jar goes to five and comes back to the sixth} he set \emph{five parts consumed; one retained}, a true figure with the not-drinking taken out, which is the part the yard wanted to keep.

\item At the kept verse he wrote \emph{historical disturbance, Y.H. 626; no account arises}, and the damp has since eaten the year, so that the disturbance stands with no date on it, which is how the yard has always kept it.

\end{itemize}

I have put my verbs back underneath and left his standing above. He takes the doing out because a thing always true has no need of anybody doing it. I put it back because a woman at the quench wants to know which hand held the jar.

\subsection*{What the glazer put underneath}

The charcoal belongs to a woman who glazes the small bowls and has had the pale line at the gum these six years. She writes on the backs of spoiled tallies, pressing hard at the ends of words. I have copied it underneath as she set it.

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item At \emph{sweet at the lip}: The sweetness is not the wine. I have tasted both and they are different, and I have not told the clerk which is which. He would write it down and carry it away.

\item At the kept verse: My mother was at the third in the year the men stood. She never said what they wanted, only what they were given, which was the same fire and the same jar going round. I have kept her one sentence and not made a second out of it.

\item At the space before the seventh: I put my hand there when you wrote it. It was the width of my hand then and it is the width of my hand now, which is more than can be said for the clerk’s word.

\end{itemize}

\subsection*{At the head and in the gutter}

The salt at the head came off the barrow sand and has gone into the grain and will not come out, which is why the yard signs in charcoal and not in ink. The pale streak beside it is lead, worked in by the hand I held the leaf down with. The tar is off the barrow rope; the strand in the second leaf goes slack in wet weather, and I shut the pot when it does. The blue-green chip came off Cliffs glass a girl set on my tally while she licked her thumb, which children are told not to do. The scorch is where the leaf lay too near the mouth of the third. The grain of sand has cut a line through one word of the fourth verse and I have not written it back, because a song with a word gone is a song said slowly. The ring is sour wine, set down at the first verse and taken up at the last, by which time it had gone the colour of the trough. The grey along the outer fold came off a cuff laid where no cuff has business lying in a sand-shed. I have not swept it. There is no Last Day at a furnace and nothing here is burnt in the morning and called dealt with; the fire goes on and the damp goes on eating the clerk’s words and leaving his figures.

\subsection*{At the foot, in a hand nobody will own}

\begin{quote}\itshape The sand keeps its grain. The furnace keeps its heat.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape The trough keeps the steam and gives none back.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape The Council keeps a word that rots and a figure that does not.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape The sixth hand holds the jar and is not entered.\end{quote}

I asked the glazer, a pot-drawer and a tide-clerk, and had three answers and no hand. I have left the lines where they were written.

The leaf goes back into the sailcloth and the sailcloth into the pot. Tomorrow the jar goes round to five and the sixth holds it level, and if a man from the Council room stands in the yard we shall sing the kept verse to the trough instead of to him, and the damp will go on eating his verbs and leaving his figures, which is the only counting here anybody has ever wanted to keep.

\clearpage\phantomsection\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{The Question Said to the Stone, Being the Tale of a Riddle Night at the Cold Lamp in Ash, with Three Answers Given to the Stone, a Fourth Kept, and the Survey-Clerk’s Entry Set Over All of It}
\CRsheetheading{The Question Said to the Stone, Being the Tale of a Riddle Night at the Cold Lamp in Ash, with Three Answers Given to the Stone, a Fourth Kept, and the Survey-Clerk’s Entry Set Over All of It}
{\centering\FellFont\itshape\footnotesize\color{faded} A lamp-woman’s telling of a winter night, set down from the mouth of an old shift-man for the settling of an argument that was never entered; the questions in the hard Rim speech with the endings struck off, the answers said to the stone and not to the room, the wagers in warm-stone shavings laid on the lamp-sill, the tally cut in the edge of a weigh-slip, a survey-clerk’s figures entered above in Ledgerhand, a clay-man’s gloss in the margin, and one line at the foot in a hand nobody will own · Written in Ash of Y.H. 812, the Thin Year of the Long Cold, at the weigh-lamp beside the shaft mouth in Keld Keep, by the woman who tends the lamp and sells a stone’s shaving by the half-mark to men going down; told to her by an old shift-man who had been forty years at the weigh and would not state his number. Carried down the Rim Road in Ilmen of Y.H. 813 with a survey party’s spoiled slips and copied at Greybank onto the back of a weigh-slip gone soft at the fold, where a survey-clerk of the Court borrowed it and set his hand above hers. It survives folded in a twist of oiled lamp-wick in the tin under the sill: coal smut ground into the head, a bead of Ninth Gallery lead shut in the fold, iron filings along the gutter, a frost-feather pressed flat that was gone by noon, a tallow thumb, a ring where a cup of small ale stood from the first question to the fourth, one correction in the narrow upright hand of the Court, a gloss in the sloping hand of a clay-man who could not get back over the pass, and a line at the foot in a hand that is nobody’s\par}\medskip
I tend the weigh-lamp at the mouth of the First Seam. It is a different work from keeping an account, though both begin with the hand on the lamp before the eye goes to the man standing in the light. In Ash the Rim shuts, the carts stop on the far side of the pass, and there is nothing to do of an evening but ask one another what we already know and call the asking a question. A question whose answer nobody knows is a bet. Men here will bet on the Cold Pass, which has a post and no gate and has not moved in a hundred years.

The old man had been forty years at the weigh. He came up on the last shift before the shut and had not been down since, and he would not state his number, which is the first thing a man states in this Keep, before his name or after it. “I have stated it enough,” he said. He sat with his cap on his knees and his right hand wrapped in a cloth, and told me while I turned the lamp low and the draught came up the shaft over the wick.

\subsection*{The manner of it}

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item A question is said to the stone, never to the man beside you. Said to a man it becomes an argument, and an argument above the shaft is a debt with no date on it, which is the one debt this room will not carry through the dark.

\item The wager is a shaving of warm-stone laid on the sill. We count shavings by touch and not by eye, because the eye listens to the face and the fingers do not.

\item The judge is the stone. I say whether an answer serves and I do not say why. A reason given is a question given away for nothing, and the giver can take it up the Rim Road and sell it.

\item No slate lies on the table. A slate turns a question into a figure, and a figure goes up the road in a clean hand and comes back as something a man owes.

\item Answer in one breath. A second answer is a different question and is not heard.

\end{itemize}

There had been nine such nights before the shut and there would be no more until the thaw. This is the one the old man told me, in the words he used, which are short and have their endings struck off.

\subsection*{What he told me}

\begin{quote}\itshape Four to the stone and one on the sill,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape state what you hold and the number first;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the shaving goes down and the answer stays up,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the figure goes up the Rim Road.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape One for the count and one for the pair,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape one for the man that the count comes back for;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the fourth stands where the shaving stood ---\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the stone has kept it and said nothing.\end{quote}

He said the song is not sung at the Descent and not on the stone. It is said waiting, with the cup in the right hand and the left palm flat on the table, because a man who has held a clamp does not hold a cup in the same hand at the same time.

It was Ash, he said, eleven winters back, before the lowlands gave the year a name. The snow lay long in the pass and no cart had come down for nine days. There were six of us in the room off the weigh: an old woman who counted at the mouth, a man up from the Ninth with the sweet of hot lead still on his cuff, a survey-man come down from the stones, a clay-man from the low road who had come up before the shut and could not get back, and two of the floor who said nothing and kept their hands on the table. A warm-stone shaving went on the sill for each question, and nobody touched the cup until the fourth.

The first went to the old woman who counts at the mouth. She had her answer before the verse was out, which is why she never keeps the shaving and is always first.

\begin{quote}\itshape Bought and never borrowed;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape a man takes me down and brings me up again;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape I am coldest at the mouth and warmest at the end;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape nobody gives me back.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape What am I?\end{quote}

“A warm-stone,” she said, and said it to the stone. She did not look at any of us. A stone is sold in this country and is not lent, and a woman who has counted at the mouth for thirty years does not say a thing like that across a table where men have numbers.

The second went to the man up from the Ninth, who kept turning his cuff over as though the smell were on the wrong side of it.

\begin{quote}\itshape It is red and is not blood.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape It goes on the figure and not on the man.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape A man who lied wears it home on his sleeve\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and cannot wash it out before the thaw.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape What is it?\end{quote}

“The reeve’s red,” he said, to the stone. There was a man at the table with a small red mark worked into the seam of his coat where no mark had been in the morning, and he set his hand over it and did not lift it again. Nobody asked him about it, which is the proper way to answer a man who has put his hand over something. The mine-reeve checks a man who has lied about his number in red; I have watched him do it and have never watched him look up. The shaving went on the sill and the cup went round once.

The third went to the survey-man come down from the stones, who answered slowly, as a man answers who has been a long time on a figure and not on a person.

\begin{quote}\itshape It grows where the warm has lately gone out of stone;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape it stands on the well lip and is gone by noon;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape a man is sent to find what it means,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the finding is still owed.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Name it.\end{quote}

“Frost-feather,” he said to the stone. Then he said, “A feather on the well lip means warmth went out of that stone in the night, and somebody pays for the finding. There is no finding entered at this table, and no finding is the same as none.” He would not say more. A survey-man who has sat against the bare stones learns to give the figure and leave the meaning where it stood, which is a trade the Court understands better than any of us.

The fourth was put by the clay-man from the low road. He had been a fortnight above the shut and had taken to sitting with us because there was nowhere else warm, and he said his question to the room, which was not the manner of it, and one of the floor told him to say it to the stone. He said it to the stone then, and said it again here as the old man remembered it:

\begin{quote}\itshape A man goes down with a number on his arm\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and a stone in his fist.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape He comes up with the number on his arm\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and no stone in his fist.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape The arm tells the mother; the stone tells nobody.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Which of the two is the man?\end{quote}

Nobody answered. The old woman said, “Ask the stone,” which is an answer given by people who have asked the same thing at their own mouths. The man from the Ninth said the number is the man, and the survey-man said that the numbers were correct, which is an answer to the numbers and not to the question, as any man will tell you who has asked a Vorr twice. The clay-man said, “Then you have not lost it,” and put his shaving on the sill and left it there. He went down the Rim Road in the thaw with the answer still owed, and I have never heard that he collected it.

The old man said he stayed after the others and put the fourth to the stone himself, low, with his hand on the table stone and his cap off. He told me he did not know whether the stone answered or whether he said the answer and heard it in his own mouth, which is the same thing after forty years and a difference before them. What he said was this:

“The number is the man’s. The stone is the Keep’s. The man is the third thing, and nobody writes it down.”

He said it to the stone and not to me. Then he got up and went out, and did not come back that night, and has not said the sentence to a man since, because a thing said to a man becomes a debt and he has no more shift to pay it with.

\subsection*{What the Court hand did}

A survey-clerk of the Court borrowed the leaf on the morning the survey table sat at the Keep, with ink settled in two fingers of a soft cuff. He laid his hand on the paper before his eyes went to the room, which is the manner of that table. He set the questions down as \emph{queries entered} and the answers as \emph{responses recorded}, valued each shaving at a half-mark of warm-stone, and wrote \emph{gaming, not commercial} across the head of the tally, so that a night of asking came out as a night of trading with the profit left off. Against the fourth he wrote \emph{no answer tendered; struck}. He asked who had put it. I told him a clay-man come up before the shut. He asked for the clay-man’s name and I said the clay-man had given none and had gone down the Rim Road, which is a true thing and not the thing he wanted, and he wrote \emph{party unidentified; interest in a number not entered}.

In the woman’s hand — In the Court hand\par

Three answers said to the stone — Three responses recorded\par

The fourth kept, not struck — No answer tendered; struck\par

Shavings counted by touch on the sill — Warm-stone, three half-marks, value to Keeping\par

A question said to a man becomes a debt — Gaming; not commercial\par

The lamp coal under the sill — Fire privately maintained; no public charge\par

The man, the number, the third thing — No account arises\par

I have put his hand above mine and left mine standing under it, the way the table stone keeps the cold under the lamp and does not tell the lamp where it got the heat. He takes the verbs out because a thing always true has no need of them. I put them back because a man waiting for his turn at the weigh does not know he is hearing something always true, and wants to know which hand to hold the stone with.

\subsection*{In the margin, in a clay-man’s sloping hand}

The leaf went down the Rim Road with the survey party and came back with a line in a sloped hand that is not mine and not the Court’s. I have copied it as it stands.

\begin{quote}\itshape At \emph{which of the two is the man}: I said it to the room and was told to say it to the stone. I said it to the stone and nobody answered. I have asked twice since, once at the Cross and once at the well that never freezes, and had a figure and a weather and no third thing. I am back over the pass and the answer is still owed. Do not strike it. A man who takes up his own shaving has paid for the asking and got nothing.\end{quote}

I have not answered him in the margin. A man writes that in a book and it follows him home.

\subsection*{At the head and in the gutter}

The coal smut at the head is mine; I wipe the lamp glass on my sleeve and the sleeve goes into the grain of the leaf and no wet cloth takes it out. The lead shut in the fold came off the cuff of the man up from the Ninth, who set his hand there while he was deciding whether to say the word \emph{sweet} in a room where the mine-reeve was not, and did not say it. The filings in the gutter are off the clamps on the floor and will cut the next leaf if I do not fold it over. The frost-feather was on the sill the morning after the telling, pressed flat between the shaving and the stone; it was gone by noon and the place where it lay is cold yet. The tallow thumb is mine. The ring is not any man’s; three men put a cup in it over one evening and not one will say which, which is how small ale is drunk in this room when there is a thing to say and no proper word for it. The grey along the outer fold came off a cuff laid where no cuff has business lying above a shaft mouth, and I have not swept it. In the clay country they sweep the corners on the Last Day and burn what they find in the morning and call it dealt with. Under the Keep the dust has nowhere to go.

\subsection*{At the foot, in a hand nobody will own}

\begin{quote}\itshape Two answers went home in men’s mouths. One went down the Rim Road still owed.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape The stone was answered. The slate was not.\end{quote}

I have asked the survey-man, the woman who counts, and a man who has been forty years at the weigh, and had three answers and no hand, as I have had before. I have left the line where it was written. The leaf goes back into the tin under the sill and the wick goes back under its twist of oil. Tomorrow a boy will be brought down at thirteen and will give his number before his name, and the shaving will go on the sill, and the fourth will stand where it stood, with no figure and no taker, and the stone will keep it as it has kept every answer this room has ever said to it.

\clearpage\phantomsection\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{The Year the Row Was Raised, Being an Extract from the Moot Book of Sill, in Which the Court Came to Stay, a House Was Built East of the Cross, and the Figure Came to Be Read Twice; with the Old Counts Set Beside the New, the Masons’ Raising-Song, Three Borrowed Hands, and a Line at the Foot Nobody Will Own}
\CRsheetheading{The Year the Row Was Raised, Being an Extract from the Moot Book of Sill, in Which the Court Came to Stay, a House Was Built East of the Cross, and the Figure Came to Be Read Twice; with the Old Counts Set Beside the New, the Masons’ Raising-Song, Three Borrowed Hands, and a Line at the Foot Nobody Will Own}
{\centering\FellFont\itshape\footnotesize\color{faded} A keeper of the moot book’s extract from the town’s year-chest at Sill; the year-entries in a broad round hand gone soft with damp, the treaty written out before them in an older and harder hand, the Row set down as a list of rooms with what went into each, the two figures entered in a column no clerk of the College has ever signed, the raising-song taken down from a mason who would not give his day’s wage, two corrections in the narrow upright Ledgerhand of a College clerk, one in the soft-cuffed hand of a factor’s man come up from Greybank, one charcoal line left by a hearth-maid from Low Kiln, and a line at the foot in a hand nobody will own · Written at Sill in the moot room off the Cross in Ash of Y.H. 812, the Thin Year, by the keeper of the moot book, who has no name on any roll and is entered in the factor’s list at Greybank only as \emph{the chest}; copied from the town’s year-book begun in Y.H. 418 and kept since in the moot-chest beneath the moot-post, and carried forward at the Opening of the Slates into Y.H. 813. The leaf for Y.H. 776 was copied first in Smoke of that year, on the back of a spoiled slate-warrant, and has been copied forward four times since. It survives folded in a strip of oiled harness leather: lime dust worked into the head, a slate shaving shut in the second fold, silt from the sill dried pale in the gutter, a green bead of lead glaze pressed into the lower corner by a girl come up from High Kiln with the sweetness still at her mouth, a mason’s iron nail gone rusty in the sewing, a short square of bare paper where a word was scraped away and no other put in, a tallow thumb at the head, a ring where a cup of small ale stood from the first entry to the last, a grey Ash print along the outer fold which the keeper did not make and has not swept, and the line at the foot which has never been claimed\par}\medskip
I keep the moot book of Sill in the chest under the post at the Cross. It is not the Court’s book and not the thane’s. The factor at Greybank writes my office down as \emph{the chest}, which is as much name as a man who keeps other people’s years is given. What follows is the year the Court came to stay: Y.H. 776, in which a house was raised on the east side of the Cross and a street got its name from what was done in it. I was not alive in that year. My hand is the fourth or fifth that has copied it forward, and I have put the verbs back where I found them taken out.

This is not a history of Sarn. The Hearthseat keeps that, in a clean hand, and it begins at the lighting and leaves out the clay. Our book begins with a treaty and ends each year at the last market. It keeps what happened where a man can stand and be asked. A chronicle that leaves out the pot-board has left out the greater part of what a town ate, and I have kept the board in.

\subsection*{The years before, as the chest has them}

\textbf{Y.H. 418.} The treaty of the Blue Cliff, copied into this chest by the road-clerk who kept it before me and read at the Cross on market morning. The Clay Road was made a Court road; an assessor could stop a cart on it without asking the thane, and did. He came with the market and slept at Greybank. The thane of Clay was not asked to the slate. This is how all important treaties are made here, the Grathish say; the Court says the thane’s absence is not an entry. Both sentences are in the chest.

\textbf{Y.H. 726.} The granary built at Greybank and the grain levy doubled in Grath. We felt it at this end as a second figure on the same load. Entered as \emph{the levy was answered}, which is the phrase with no men in it that the Court uses when men are cold.

\textbf{Y.H. 774.} A clerk came up from Greybank and counted the doorways of Sill, standing at the Cross with his slate to his forearm and never asking to come in. To the woman who asked what for he said, \emph{the book}. To the woman who asked which book he said, \emph{the book}. I have entered two answers and no book, because a book that a man will not name is a thing a town has a right to go on not having.

\textbf{Y.H. 775.} Ground measured east of the Cross, where the pot-board stood in the wet. The pot-board was moved into a shed and no board put in its place. A woman who had sold there for nineteen years set her own board down on the new stones and said nothing at all about them, which in this town is a judgment a man can hear. There had been a well in that ground. The masons filled it, and the Court paid for the filling, which is the first figure in these years I can put a payer under.

\subsection*{Y.H. 776, the year of the raising}

\emph{Entered first in Smoke of that year and copied forward four times. The hand changes at the fourth entry; I have kept the change, being the only honest thing in a copy.}

\textbf{Stone.} Stakes set on the east side of the Cross. The thane of Clay was not asked where the house should stand, and has never said whether he would have put it elsewhere. A man from the Court’s room at Greybank laid a cord along the ground and tied it to a stake, and the cord stayed there through the frost, and the children of Low Kiln tied nothing to it and went around it.

\textbf{Ilmen.} Foundation stone laid. A slate was bought at Greybank and brought up on a cart, eighteen leagues, packed clay over corduroy in the wet places. It cost eleven marks and the cartage was not entered, which is the custom of that house: the figure travels and the road does not. That slate is still on the assessor’s counter. Three assessors have stood at it since and none of them bought it.

\textbf{Silt.} Walls to the lintel. Lime on every course. The kiln hands came up from the terrace at the going of the light to watch, and one of them sang while the lintel went on, and was told to stop by a man who had come down from Greybank. He stopped, and went on singing under his breath, which is where most things in this town are kept.

\textbf{Ember.} Roof on, and the street named Slate Row, because there was no other slate in Sill that a man could point to and be believed. A street named after what is done in it and not after a family is the Court’s way and not ours. Our streets are named after water, stone, and the trade that ruins a man. The older women went on calling it the east side for twenty years and some do still.

\textbf{Smoke.} The Court’s room opened next door. Behind it a room was dug out and floored, to keep the collected overnight before the banking. The town had not known it wanted such a room until it had one. A hearth-maid from Low Kiln came up on the first morning and stood in the doorway with a birth-slate under her shawl and did not go in. She was paid by the Court, as we all were after that year, and she went back down the terrace with the slate still under the shawl.

\textbf{Ash.} The figure read twice at the Cross, once for the moot and once for those who came late. One in twelve, as the notice says, and nobody crossed himself. The bell went four, four and a gap over the reading, and the count of the yard stood beside it and was not folded into it. Another figure was spoken in the yards that winter. It is not on any notice and has never been entered in this book, and I have put it in the margin where a figure can be kept without being made a promise.

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Margin, in the broad round hand:} The difference between the two figures is three parts in twelve, which any child at the pot-board can work out with eel-bones and does. I asked a man who copies the College’s hand why a figure might be read in one place and paid in another. He said a figure read was a kindness and a figure paid was an account, and that a man who laid the two together had begun to write a sermon. I have set his sentence down. It is the only true thing he gave me, and he did not know he had said it.\end{quote}

\subsection*{The Row as it stood at the year’s end}

\emph{What the Court’s man entered on the delivery slate, set beside what the town called each room. He wrote the rooms in a column and I have put their doings back.}

Room — As entered — What it is called here — What was left at the Cross\par

The assessor’s house — Valuation office, established — The house with the counter — The pot-board, in a shed\par

The Court’s room — Public room for the reading — The room where the figure is said — The moot-post and the block\par

The Waiting Room — Accommodation before banking — The room nobody goes in — A woman with a slate under her shawl\par

The collector’s table — Draw to be performed — The iron and the tube — Two answers and no book\par

The filled well — Site prepared — The well that was — Nineteen years of standing there\par

A table is a thing a clerk reads and a margin is the only place in a book where a silence is allowed to stand. The woman with the slate under her shawl has no column and never will. \emph{The room nobody goes in} is the name the younger women gave it, and the older ones called it the hollow, and neither name is on the slate that came down from Greybank.

\subsection*{The raising-song}

\emph{Taken down at the lintel from a mason who would not give his day’s wage and gave the song instead. Sung while a course was laid, never on the Clay Road and never at the Cross while the slate is out. The last course is left out of the singing and set in its place in silence.}

\begin{quote}\itshape We brought the slate up from the quay,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape eighteen leagues and a wet ford;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape we set it level on the east side\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the pot-board went into the shed.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Lime on the course and lime on the back,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape a course for the thane and a course for the Court;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the thane was not asked and the Court was not told,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the wall stands because somebody paid.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape One in twelve is a clean figure;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the yard keeps another and does not sing it.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Leave the fifth course out of the verse —\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the wall has a stone where the song has a place.\end{quote}

He said he had learned it from his father, who carried lime up for the granary at Greybank in Y.H. 726, and that his father had never sung the fourth line facing a man from the factor’s house. I have left that where he put it.

\subsection*{What the three borrowed hands did}

A clerk of the College at the Hearthseat borrowed the leaf on a market morning. He writes upright and narrow and takes the verbs out as though a verb were a thing a man could smuggle past the block in his boot.

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item Against \emph{the Court came to stay} he wrote \emph{an assessor’s office was established}, and underlined it twice, as though a man coming to stay and a room being opened were the same event seen from the same distance.

\item Against \emph{the room nobody goes in} he wrote \emph{accommodation provided for persons awaiting banking}, which is true and has no person in it.

\item Against the yard’s other figure in the margin he wrote nothing at all. His hand passed over it without a stroke, which is the readiest way of correcting a figure I have yet seen.

\item Against \emph{leave the fifth course out} he set \emph{omission in the verse}, and underneath, in mine, I have put \emph{a course stood there and was paid for}, which is the sort of difference that gets a leaf copied again.

\end{itemize}

A factor’s man soft-cuffed from Greybank wrote against the naming: \emph{the street was named for the material of its roofing}. This is true and is not the reason any woman in Low Kiln would give. I have left his hand above mine everywhere, as a newer repair lies over an older one and does not pretend the first hand never touched the stone.

The charcoal is a hearth-maid’s, thick and leaning, and stops before it finishes:

\begin{quote}\itshape A slate in a room is a slate anybody can read. We kept ours in the fold. They asked and we said the children were warm and that —\end{quote}

She did not finish it and I have not finished it for her. A sentence left in the mouth is a thing this book has room for and the College’s rooms have not.

\subsection*{At the head and in the gutter}

The lime at the head came off a mason’s sleeve when he leaned over to see which line I had set down, and it goes into the grain and no damp takes it out. The slate shaving in the second fold came off the delivery slate when it was new; it has kept a edge that would take a finger, and I have folded the leaf over it so that it lies where a man’s thumb goes and not where his eye goes. The silt dried pale in the gutter came up from the sill on the morning the figure was first read twice; the river was low and the note under it had not yet come on. The green bead is lead glaze out of High Kiln; a girl leaned over to see the rooms listed with the sweetness still at one corner of her mouth, touched the corner, and went back up the steep street without saying what she had seen. The corner tastes sweet in wet weather and I have not washed it. The nail came out of the lintel frame and was shut into the sewing by a man who had no business sewing the book and did it anyway. The square of bare paper is where a word was scraped away with a knife and no other put in its place; I have not written it back and have not forgotten it. The tallow thumb is mine. The ale ring stood from the first entry to the last and went dark in the time it takes to read a figure twice. The grey along the outer fold is not mine and not the College’s. I have had this leaf six years and have not swept it. There is no Last Day in a chest.

\subsection*{At the foot, in a hand nobody will own}

\begin{quote}\itshape The house came up and the pot-board went down,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the well was filled and the well had a name;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the figure is read where the pigs are weighed,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the other one walks the yard all day.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Ask the Row what it keeps.\end{quote}

I asked the thane’s clerk, a woman who carries birth-slates in Low Kiln, and a mason who came up in 776 and has been dead these thirty years, and had three answers and no hand. I have left the line where it was written. The book goes back into the chest under the post. Next tend I copy the figures of the Long Cold, and the notice will still say one in twelve and the yard will still keep the other, and both will stand where they stood, with a finger’s width between them and no signature on the space.

\clearpage\phantomsection\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{The Rat at the Lip, Being a Hunter’s Field Notes on the Lead-Rat of High Kiln and the Lower Ferr; with the Catching-Song as It Is Said, a Tally of Tails and Cups, a Physician’s Year, a Glaze-Mixer’s Correction in Slip-White, and a Ruling in Ledgerhand}
\CRsheetheading{The Rat at the Lip, Being a Hunter’s Field Notes on the Lead-Rat of High Kiln and the Lower Ferr; with the Catching-Song as It Is Said, a Tally of Tails and Cups, a Physician’s Year, a Glaze-Mixer’s Correction in Slip-White, and a Ruling in Ledgerhand}
{\centering\FellFont\itshape\footnotesize\color{faded} A hunter’s field book on one beast, set down as the record of catches and not as natural philosophy; the rounds in Grathic, the tally in charcoal on the backs of glaze-tallies spoiled by a spill of slip, the catching-song as it is said over the bench, a physician’s year copied out of a page come down the Ferr, a glaze-mixer’s correction in slip-white, and a ruling in the narrow upright Ledgerhand of a clerk of the factor at Greybank · Written in Grain and Smoke of Y.H. 812, the Thin Year, by Skell of High Kiln, a rat-catcher who took the beasts for their tails and kept the cup-shelves of the Glaze Room, and who writes at the end of a round with a tallow end in a dish and the sweet still at the back of his throat; set down first on the backs of glaze-tallies gone soft with slip and then on three folds of birch bark sewn with eel-sinew, carried in a coat pocket against a flint and a twist of tallow. Copied forward at Greybank in Ilmen of Y.H. 813 onto the back of a Court grain-warrant voided by the Long Cold. It survives with the sweet green of lead glaze ground into the head off a gnawed rim carried three days in the pocket, a brown slip thumb at the fold, a grey tail-grease smear along the fore-edge where the leaf was wiped on a sleeve after a catch, a greenish ring where a tasting-cup stood from the first round to the last, a scorch where a spark off the glaze kiln took the corner of the third leaf, the charcoal rubbed thin where the wrap was carried against the thigh, a physician’s year copied in the writer’s own hand, one line in slip-white from the glaze-mixer, one ruling in Ledgerhand standing above the words it corrects, and one line at the foot in a hand nobody will own\par}\medskip
I take rats in High Kiln and the lower Ferr for the glaze house, and I have kept this book two winters. It is not a book of reasons. I have no slate-name and no learning, and I set down only what I have put my hand to. A man who writes what he has heard at a hearth is writing a hearth, not a rat. I have known both sorts of book and this is the sort a man can use.

The sweet at the head is not slip. It is lead glaze ground into the grain where I carried a gnawed rim in my pocket for three days before I thought to wrap it.
