It tastes sweet in wet weather and I have not washed it out. A book that has never tasted of the trade it keeps was never taken into a mix.

\subsection*{What it comes to}

It comes to the sweet, not to the crumb. This is the first thing a new man gets wrong, and the thing that costs him a week of empty traps. Set a trap with barley and cheese and you will catch a house mouse, which is nothing to anybody. Set the same trap with a chipped rim off a glazed cup, the lip still green where the glaze ran thin, and you will catch a fistful before the tallow has burned down. I have set both sorts on the same shelf of an evening and the barley went untouched and the rim had teeth in it by morning.

It gnaws the lips of cups and the seams of bowls. It is the rim it wants and not the broth. A household that sets its good cups on the shelf above the meal will find the rims gone pale by the end of a tend, and the women will say the pots are wearing out, which they are, in the way a thing wears out when something eats it. It is no more particular than that. It will take the rim of a Cup from Sere as soon as a coarse bowl out of the Yard, and the sweeter the rim the sooner it goes.

I have set a chipped rim on a shelf in a house with no children and caught nothing for four nights. I have set a sound cup beside a bowl of barley in a house with three children and taken seven. The sweet draws them and the children give it somewhere to come to. I have set that down and joined nothing to it.

\subsection*{The catching-song}

\emph{Said low over the bench before the first rim is set, never sung. The catchers say the third line into the cup and not up to the ceiling. I have set it down as it is said, with the last line standing where they leave it.}

\begin{quote}\itshape Two bits to the score and the score is the tail,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the tooth keeps the shape and the cup keeps the tale;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape it comes to the sweet and it comes to the seam,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and a house with rats is a house gone thin.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Set not the crumb but the lip that has run,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the green at the edge where the glaze came undone;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape count by the tail, never the nose, never the ear;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape one bite is a nothing, the hundred is here.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Burn the tails in the slip-shed, keep the rim for the mix,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and leave the last cup where the girl’s hand will find it;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape she tastes it at morning and I take it at night,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the one that goes back is the one we don’t count.\end{quote}

The last line is not a figure. The catchers say it into the cup and nobody has ever told me which rat goes back. There is a man in High Kiln who sets two rims on his shelf of an evening and takes one away in the morning and will not say why. I have let him keep it.

\subsection*{What it is}

It is a rat. I set that down before anything else, because the hearths will not. It has a rat’s teeth and a rat’s neck and a rat’s way of stopping still in the middle of a run to listen. It is bigger than the yard rats of the Tallow Works and thinner, and the coat is the colour of wet clay, so that a man sees the green at the root of the teeth before he sees the body. The green is in the teeth and under the claws. It smells of the sweet and of the warm crack behind the mixing bench.

I have opened nine. In all nine I found a rat altered by the place it lived in, the way a potter’s hands are altered by the wheel. In the third I found a green in the stomach and a sweetness in it that I could smell through the paunch, which is not what I looked for in a beast that had been at a cup rim. I have written the two things on the same leaf and drawn no line between them. A man who writes a cause into a book he keeps in his coat is a man who will be asked for it by somebody with a slate.

\subsection*{The physician’s year}

A physician come up from Greybank in Y.H. 641 wrote that the sweetness came from the lead in the glaze and that the rat carried the same lead in its teeth, and the word went out of the copy before the year was over, as though a word could be scraped off paper the way slip is scraped off a bench. I found the year in a physician’s page that came down the Ferr with a cargo of coarse tile, and I have put it back here where a man may read it and go on reading.

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{In slip-white, in the blocky hand of the glaze-mixer of High Kiln, down the margin of this leaf:} It is the glaze that brings them, not the rat. Keep the tasting-spoons off the bench and the cups off the shelf. Leave me the year if you must, but leave the word out of it. --- G.\end{quote}

I did not write his line and he did not write mine. He has taken the word out of his own house and asked me to leave it out of my book, which is a reasonable thing to ask of a man who is paid by the tail. I have left the year standing and put no name to the payer.

\subsection*{The bite}

It does not fight. I have had one run over my boot and it went on with its own work. But let a hand lie still near a cup it is working at and it will take the hand. The bite is two holes and no blood worth naming, and a greenish edge that a man notices when he is dressing it and not before. The physician from Greybank says the lead goes in with the tooth and makes the ways sluggish over a season. I have not seen the lead. I have seen the season.

A girl of the mix went in at Grain 9 with her hand among the tasting-spoons and was bitten on the thumb. There were two holes and she bound them with tallow and went on tasting. At the end of the tend the holes were closed and the thumb was still, and she was putting the spoon down with the other hand because the first did not tell her where it was. Salt does not hold that bite and there is no physic for it that I know. A single bite is a thing a man forgets by the next tend. It is the hundredth that forgets him.

I have seen children in a house with rats in the cupboard going thin by degrees through a whole year, and the mother bringing me tails by the score and asking what the figure was. I told her the figure was two bits a score and she went away with the answer she had brought with her. It is not an answer a man is proud of. It is the answer the trade has.

\subsection*{The tally}

These are the rounds I kept a true account of. There were others I did not write because my hands were full and one I did not write because I had drunk. I have set down both sorts as they stand. I counted tails; the clerk counted marks.

Round — Place — Set with — Taken — Tails — Green teeth — Entered\par

Grain 3 — Mixing bench, High Kiln — chipped rim — five — five — four — 0\par

Grain 9 — Cup shelf, second firing — chipped rim — seven — seven — seven — 0\par

Grain 14 — Shelf above the meal, Low Kiln — chipped rim — nine — nine — six — nil\par

Grain 20 — Store off the Glaze Room — sound cup — three — three — three — 0\par

Grain 27 — Tasting bench, before first grey — chipped rim — five — five — five — 0\par

Smoke 4 — The rim shelf, north wall — chipped rim — seven — one — one — 2\par

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{In the narrow upright hand of a clerk of the factor’s house at Greybank, borrowed against the leaf at the kiln door:} Rodentia not a vessel. Hand-bites: not entered. Cups gnawed: wear and tear, no deduction arises. Lead: not a figure. The year Y.H. 641: not on this roll. Account stands.\end{quote}

I have left his hand standing. But he has put \emph{wear} against a cup that was eaten, and wear is a word for a thing that happens to a pot with nobody at it. I have written \emph{teeth} in the margin below, where his column cannot reach, and put my own mark beside it in charcoal. He has left the year off his roll, which is the only thing on this leaf he and the glaze-mixer agree about.

\subsection*{What the hearths say}

They say the rat is the sweet sickness made small, a thing that got into the cups because the glaze was mixed with a lie. There are songs in High Kiln with a girl’s name in them and a wrong done at a mixing bench in the year before the wars. I have heard them and I have no quarrel with a song. I have opened nine and found a rat, and found the green in it, and found the cup it came from with the rim gone pale. If the rat is the sickness made small, then the sickness was in the cup before the rat came to it, and the rat is only the thing that came to it. I have written that sentence out once and crossed it out twice, because it is the kind of sentence that gets a man called a natural philosopher, and natural philosophers are not set to catch rats in High Kiln.

The yard calls the rat a mercy because it takes the bad cups out of a house. I have not called it that.

\subsection*{At the head and in the margins}

The sweet at the head is glaze off the rim I carried, and it comes back in damp weather and goes off in a dry. The brown thumb at the fold is slip. The grease along the fore-edge is tail-grease, from wiping my hand on the leaf before I could find a rag after Grain 9, and I have left it, because it is the only mark on this book that came off a catch. The greenish ring is where a tasting-cup stood while a girl told me she had tasted the mix since she was nine and had never once been asked what it cost; I did not ask her, and she went back up the steep street. The scorch is where a spark off the glaze kiln took the corner of the third leaf, and the hand that pulled it back was mine and is not entered. The charcoal is thin where I carried the wrap against my thigh. The slip-white will fade before the charcoal does, which is a small kindness in the ordering of things. The clerk’s ruling I have not touched. The physician’s year I have copied in my own hand and have not crossed out. The song is as the men said it, with the last line standing and the count left open.

\subsection*{At the foot, in a hand nobody will own}

\begin{quote}\itshape The rat is not the payer. It is the witness that stays.\end{quote}

There is a shelf above the mixing bench where the new cups go to be tasted before they go down the terrace, and the glaze on them is sweeter than any I have found in a household cup. I have not set a trap there. Next Grain I will take a score of cord and a chipped rim from the mix and set them on that shelf among the tasting-spoons, and if the rats come to the new cups before the girls do I will set that down too, in charcoal, with the verb left in it and no figure at the end of the row.

\clearpage\phantomsection\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{The Reading of the Slate, Being Certain Articles of the Ordinance of the Keeping for the Drawing, Banking and Returning of Measures}
\CRsheetheading{The Reading of the Slate, Being Certain Articles of the Ordinance of the Keeping for the Drawing, Banking and Returning of Measures}
{\centering\FellFont\itshape\footnotesize\color{faded} An extract from the Court’s ordinances, copied out for the use of the open-air table at the Cross in Sill, with the marginal hand of the clerk who keeps that table · Copied in Y.H. 812, the Thin Year, by the unnamed clerk of the Court’s table at the Cross in Sill, and carried into Y.H. 813 at the Opening of the Slates; a quire of four leaves sewn with wire into a board cover, kept in the drawer of the table and taken out at market mornings. The cover is warped from a winter against the outside wall of Slate Row. The lower corner of the second leaf carries a tallow thumb, the inner margin a grey streak, the top edge a candle-singe, and there are three corrections in the clerk’s own hand and one in a hand he did not own.\par}\medskip
I keep the table at the Cross. On market mornings I lay my hand on the top slate before I look at the woman waiting, and say that it is entered as it stands and there is nothing in it the household need correct. My cuff is gone soft from washing and the ink sits in the creases of two fingers and will not come out. What follows is copied out of the ordinance for the use of this table, so that a man standing in the square may know what he is being told before he is told it. I have put the verbs back where I could. The ordinance has no need of them, being always true; I have. A thing that is always true is a thing a woman cannot argue with, and I have had to stand here and argue with a great many women.

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{At the head of the first leaf, in the same hand, written very small:} Copied by the table, not for the table. If this is read in the Hearthseat, let it be seen that the verbs were put back by me and struck out again by another. Let both stand.\end{quote}

\subsection*{The extract, as it stands in the book}

\emph{From the Ordinances of the Keeping, Title the Third: Of the Drawing, Banking and Returning of Measures. As confirmed to the factor at Greybank by the treaty of Y.H. 418, and added to in Y.H. 782 and Y.H. 812.}

\subsection*{I. Of the entry of vessels}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item Every vessel born within the Keeping entered upon a slate within three days of the first breath. Entry in Ledgerhand, without verbs. Birth-name not entered. Slate-name entered in its place where the vessel enters the service. Slate kept face up upon the bench. The hand that writes not the hand that holds.

\item Where entry made after three days, the reason entered also. No reason entered for the third day itself.

\end{enumerate}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Margin:} The third day is a bad day to choose. A child that has taken a chill will grow worse on the third day and be entered anyway, and the entry will stand as a birth and not as a worsening. I have seen this and I have not put it in the article. There is no article for it.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Margin, in a second and narrower hand:} This article was added in Y.H. 782, which is the year the maids began to be paid, and the two things are not unrelated, though the ordinance does not say so. A hearth-maid lays the slate on the bench before she goes to the child. I have watched them do it. They do not say why, and I have not asked.\end{quote}

\subsection*{II. Of the drawing}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item Measure drawn by an officer appointed thereunto, a cold iron tube set against a way. Walls giving way; drain entered to the account. The draw witnessed by a slate. Where consent withheld, the account unclosed; the vessel clip-held by the wrist until consent entered. Consent entered in the hand of the officer.

\item Theft of warmth, being a draw without a slate, punished by a cold iron brand upon the wrist and a deduction from the thief’s own measure. Quiet ash sold to any not licensed to buy it punished by a greyed hand.

\item Drawing from the Hearth without a keeper’s key forbidden. The Nine Wells sealed; keys kept. A keeper who drew without authorisation was hanged in Y.H. 618.

\end{enumerate}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Margin:} I have seen the wrist. The clip leaves a pale ring that shows through the winter and is spoken of as nothing. The woman asked me if the ring would go, and I said it would in the thaw, which is what my mother said about everything, and is not in the ordinance.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Margin:} The officer who came on Stone 12 had fingers the colour of skimmed milk gone off, under a cuff softer than my own. I wrote him down on a slate of my own. I did not say what the fingers meant, because I do not know, and I did not join him to anybody.\end{quote}

\subsection*{III. Of the figure and the reading}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item One part in twelve of every measure kept back for the Hearth, as the notice says. Figure printed upon the Weighing notice and read aloud at the Cross. Read twice: once for the moot, and again for those that came late. Account-day the tenth, twentieth and thirtieth of every tend. No market held during the Five.

\item Correction of a slate by one hand only. Lawful deduction entered only by the College of Assessors. A house roll kept close and not shown; the keeping of it not explained, only kept.

\end{enumerate}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Margin:} The figure is one in twelve and I have never known a household in Low Kiln that paid it. I do not say what it pays. I have no slate for that and will not invent one.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Margin:} The bell at the Cross goes longer than a church bell and nobody crosses himself at it. I have counted it four, four, and a place where the fifth should be. I have put no count of it in the ordinance, because the ordinance has no place for a thing that is not a debt.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Margin:} There is a small stop in the neat upper line of the top slate, between two clusters, in a hand I do not know. I have seen it five times and joined none of them. When I say \emph{there’s nothing in it the household need correct}, I am not lying. There is nothing in it that I can correct.\end{quote}

\subsection*{IV. Of the five days outside the months}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item Five days outside the months, named and not numbered, outside the tend. On Ilmen 1 the count begins again at Firstday.

\end{enumerate}

Day — As the ordinance stands — In the margin\par

\textbf{Kindling} — Every hearth lit from the Hearth-flame. Collectors take the year’s first measure. — Here the first hand wrote \emph{Weighing}. I have struck it and set \emph{Kindling} above it. The measure was taken before first light in Y.H. 812. No figure reached the roof, which is another way of saying I did not see it.\par

\textbf{Weighing} — The year’s measures read aloud. The rich learn how whole they are. — An officer read them in a clean voice and the district learned its figure from him. Berr Clay passed a finger over his own slate and wiped his thumb. Neither of them said the figure twice.\par

\textbf{the Long Night} — No fire after dusk. Stories of the Return told in the dark. — The stories are not entered. I sat in one room where the bell was told as four, four and a gap. I kept the told bell in my head away from the heard bell. They are not the same bell and I will not make them one.\par

\textbf{the Remembering} — Names of the dead spoken. Whole returns announced in a clean voice. — A whole return was read for one not in the room at the Weighing in Y.H. 812, and the household did not repeat the name. Under another roof a name was not spoken at all. I entered the return and not the name.\par

\textbf{the Last Day} — Bread baked. The grey Ash in the corners not swept away; burnt the next morning and called dealt with. — Two ridges were measured with one thumb. I put my cuff into a corner I had no business in and the grey came off on it. The streak in this book’s margin came from the same hand. I washed the cuff. The ink is still in the two fingers.\par

\subsection*{V. Of the keeping and the returning}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item Measure banked. Account stands. Nothing lost that has been kept. Embers booked. Rolls of the dead kept open. Where one measure poured into one vessel, the return whole, with memory; where many pooled and divided among many, the return thin. Return announced in a clean voice. The Kept held in the Weighing Hall, fewer than twenty, spoken of with pity.

\item No article provides for the coming back wrong. In the low houses they keep these also.

\end{enumerate}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Margin:} I have seen one of the Kept go through the Hall. It was courteous and asked after the weather. There are fewer than twenty and they are spoken of with pity. I do not know what the pity is for, and I have never asked.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Margin:} The rolls of the dead are kept open. I have entered a name twice, once in the house roll and once upon the Court’s slate, and the two entries did not agree, and neither was corrected. A dead man with two figures is worth more than one with none. That is not in the ordinance either, and yet I have done it.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Margin, at the foot, struck through and written again in the same hand:} No article provides for the coming back wrong. In the low houses they keep these also. \emph{Written again because I struck it the first time, and then thought better of striking it. Let it stand. A clerk who takes a line out of a law because it frightens him has no business at a table where women stand.}\end{quote}

\subsection*{What I corrected, and why}

In article one the first hand wrote \emph{entry made}. I set \emph{is} above it. A man come down from Slate Row in a clean coat passed the table, looked at my \emph{is}, and struck it out again, saying that an ordinance has no need of a verb, being always true. I have left both stand. A slate with two hands on it is the only kind the household believes.

Where the book said \emph{Weighing} for the year’s first measure, I struck it and wrote \emph{Kindling}. A collector drew before light on Kindling in the Thin Year and the draw went into the account without a figure anyone in the yard could spend. I know the day because I set my hand on the slate that morning. I do not know the figure and have not asked for it.

In the schedule of the Five the first hand allowed four days. I have set five above it. There are five, and no market in any of them, and the count begins again on the first day of Ilmen. I cannot think how a man came to write four unless he left one out on purpose, and I have no mind to find out which.

The candle-singe at the top is mine. I set the book too near the lamp in the Waiting Room, where the collected are kept overnight before banking, and held it there longer than I should, because a woman in the room was telling me something and I wanted the end of it. She did not tell me the end. She looked at the book burning and stopped, and went back to sitting. I have left the singe as it is. It is the only entry in this quire that nobody has corrected.

The book goes with the table. On Ilmen 1 the slates opened and I copied it again, and struck the same word out again. A woman will come and set her hand on the top slate, and I shall say it is entered as it stands. It is. That is the trouble with it.

\clearpage\phantomsection\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{The Sermon at the Reeve’s Stone, Being What Was Said at the Foot of the Standing Post Over the Peat-Blocks on the Morning a Reeve Was Chosen in Reed of Y.H. 813, with the Standing-Song Left as It Is Sung, the Blocks in a Tally, a Factor’s Clerk’s Correction, and a Line at the Foot in a Hand Nobody Will Own}
\CRsheetheading{The Sermon at the Reeve’s Stone, Being What Was Said at the Foot of the Standing Post Over the Peat-Blocks on the Morning a Reeve Was Chosen in Reed of Y.H. 813, with the Standing-Song Left as It Is Sung, the Blocks in a Tally, a Factor’s Clerk’s Correction, and a Line at the Foot in a Hand Nobody Will Own}
{\centering\FellFont\itshape\footnotesize\color{faded} A sermon of the Fenmarch preached at the small shrine of the reeve’s stone at the foot of the Standing Post, over the peat-blocks laid in the niche at the choosing of a reeve; the sayings in the bitten speech of the marsh set down in Grathic, the standing-song with the gap left the length of the sound a boot makes coming up, the blocks in a tally, one correction in the narrow upright Ledgerhand of a factor’s clerk come out from Greybank, and one line struck through and written again very small underneath in a hand nobody will own · Preached by an old woman of the Post who had laid a peat-block in the niche at one and twenty standings, on the morning of Reed 20, Y.H. 813, when the marsh stood for a new reeve and the water was up in the prints of every boot; written that evening by the woman who keeps the boardwalk and the bog-tally at the Standing Post, in charcoal and with the point of a worn count-stick, on the back of a bog-tally spoiled by a wet figure, folded into oiled sacking and tied with a strip of bog-cow hide. It survives with peat worked into the grain at the head in a brown thumb, a press of wet sedge across the first leaf, a dark tideline along the gutter where marsh-water stood on it through a night, a sedge-awn shut in the fold, a small horn-shaving from the count-stick caught in the second crease, a grey Ash print nobody will own, a tallow thumb, a ring where a cup of small ale stood from the first voice to the last, the wing-case of a beetle pressed flat in the lower corner, one correction in the narrow upright hand of a factor’s clerk come out from Greybank to count the winter thin returns, and a line struck through and written again very small underneath in a hand that has never come forward. Copied once at Greybank in Ember of Y.H. 813, with the verbs put back and the gap left the length it is sung.\par}\medskip
I keep the boardwalk at the Standing Post and set the peat-blocks in the niche when a man stands. There is no desk in the Fenmarch that will hold a ledger upright, and the reeve’s count-stick has no place on it for a pair of feet, which is why this shrine has kept what it keeps and Greybank has never kept it right. I write on the back of a bog-tally spoiled by a wet figure, because a paper that will not lie flat is a paper nobody can borrow for a column, and I have had enough of columns.

She stood with her back to the post and spoke first to the peat, then to the board under it, then to the water in the prints of her feet, and last of all to us, which is the order the marsh uses when a man is standing and somebody may be listening who wants a figure. I have set her words down in Grathic, which is not the speech she used; the marsh bites the ends off its words. Where she left a verb out I have left it out and put it back underneath, because a saying said over a block is a thing a man has to stand on.

The brown at the head is peat from her palm when she brushed the sedge from the stone. The tideline is marsh-water that stood on the leaf through a night; the writing there is thin and I have not gone over it, for a word written thin is a word said quietly, and most of ours are. The grey came off a cuff and nobody will own it; I have not swept it.

\subsection*{The manner of the standing, as the stone has it}

\emph{Written small, from watching, not from any order the Court has printed.}

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item Come at first grey, when the water in the prints is still and unstirred by anybody’s shadow. A man who comes at noon stands in water another man has stood in and calls it the same stand. It is not.

\item Stand where the post points, facing the bog, not the road. The reeve faces the direction the bog came from. We have had two men face the road and neither came back to the choosing.

\item Do not say how long you have stood. A stand said aloud becomes an argument, and there is argument enough at the Post over the winter peat without bringing a man’s feet into it.

\item Set a peat-block in the niche for every stand that ends with a man walking back, and none for a stand that ends otherwise. The block is not a man; it is the shape of where he stood, which is the only thing this shrine pretends to keep.

\item When a factor’s clerk comes with a slate, stop, and begin again after. His figure is for another room, and there are ten leagues of dry road between it and this water. Do not lay the two together.

\item A reeve is not chosen by the block but by the standing, which the block cannot hold and the count-stick cannot hold either, and the Court has never asked to see.

\end{itemize}

\subsection*{The sermon, as she said it}

\subsection*{Of the post}

She put her palm on the post and left it there while the water filled the prints behind her.

“It does not count,” she said. “It has stood here longer than any of us and never once counted a man. No notch, no name; the reeve’s stick has notches enough for all of us and still cannot tell you who stood. I have laid a block here one and twenty times and never seen the post take notice of one.

“A man from Greybank measured the post with a cord and asked how old it was, and I gave him a year, because a year is safe and does not spoil in the mouth. He asked what it was for and I gave him the same year. The year went back in his coat and the post stood where it had stood with no figure on it. That is the whole of my preaching and I have had one and twenty standings to find another sentence and could not.”

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Margin, in my hand:} She gave the same year twice, once to the post and once to the clerk. I have set it down and left the question standing. A date is the only answer this shrine gives out, and it is given so the other question may be left where it was asked.\end{quote}

\subsection*{Of the feet}

“The marsh keeps the shape,” she said, looking down at the water in her own prints. “You stand and the water comes up around the boot and holds it a moment before it lets go. Then the print closes and there is nothing but water with the look of any other water. The bog has kept your stand and cannot tell you whose it was.

“They say the Marsh Mother keeps her own down there, and I have no quarrel with a saying that gives a woman a reason to put her hand on the ground. I have laid my hand on the peat where a cow stood the week before and it was warm there and cold a spear-cast off, and the warm place had moved by the next tend and the cow with it. That is all I know of her keeping. It is a place and not a person, and it moves.

“A Drawn man came out from Reedholt and stood in the black stand as long as any of us, and came up with his fingers the colour of old rope and called it an obstacle in the ground. I have set that beside the man who braced and did not come back. Both are true.”

\subsection*{Of the block}

She took a peat-block from the niche and held it in both hands, as a woman holds a loaf before she cuts it.

“This is not the reeve,” she said. “It is the shape of where he stood. A man goes into the black ground and comes out with a year taken off him and a stick that counts his term; this is a lump of peat the size of two fists that anyone could have cut. I have set the two side by side one and twenty times. They have never agreed and were never meant to.

“The Court reads a whole return in a clean voice at the Weighing Hall for a person not in the room. Here a man comes back thin and the north buys him cheap, and the post has no word for cheap. You will not get an argument out of peat: only a block in a niche and a man sent home with boots full of water, which is the most this shrine can do.”

\subsection*{Of them that do not come back}

There was a stand in Silt that ended with four men going into the east cut and three coming up, and the old woman set no block for the fourth. She said the name once to the stone and again to the water and would not say it to us.

“Said looking at a person, a name becomes a bargain,” she said. “Said to the ground it stays where the man is. I am not saying the Return is a lie. I am saying I have stood at the choosing since before some of you had feet and never seen a block laid for a man who did not come walking up out of the cut. The Court can read him whole in a room I have never stood in. This niche cannot, and I will not teach it a lie to make the row look better.”

\subsection*{Of the figure}

A factor’s clerk come out from Greybank stood at the end of the row with a slate held inward to his forearm. He asked what the blocks were worth.

“Nothing,” she said. “Nobody bought them and they do not travel. A man who cuts a block and lays it in a hole has done something with his hands before the day took them from him. If the Hearth wants the stand, let it come down here and stand in it. It has not come yet, and I have been laying blocks one and twenty years.”

“The measure is retained in the peat,” the clerk said.

“The water closes over the print,” she said. “Those are two sentences. I will not have one put over the other.”

“No account arises,” he said, in the voice that takes the speaker out of his sentence.

“I have kept no account,” she said. “I have set a shape in a hole and gone home to dry my socks.”

\subsection*{The standing-song}

\emph{Sung low, standing, a boot on the niche stone. The row says the last four lines with her. There is a gap before those four, the length of the sound a boot makes coming up out of the peat, and I have left it as it is sung.}

\begin{quote}\itshape The post stands and the water stands,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the foot goes down where the water went;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the block goes in and the block stays in,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the reeve keeps what the reeve has kept.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Three for the marsh and three for the board,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and one for the sound the boot leaves;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the clerk writes one and the house writes none,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and both go down in the same wet hand.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape They read a whole in the Weighing Hall;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape here they sell what the bog gives back;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape say what it gave and not what it cost,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and leave the place where the standing was.\end{quote}

A child from the upper board asked what the space was for. Nobody answered her. The clerk put a round nought against it later, which I have left where he set it.

\subsection*{The row, as the niche keeps it}

\emph{A figure that comes into the marsh in a coat goes out again in a thin return and leaves nothing in the niche. These I have set down where they stood.}

When — Who stood — What the water gave — What was entered\par

Reed 4 — a man of Reedholt — stood to the knee, walked up, gave his name to the stone — nothing\par

Reed 11 — a woman of the east marsh — stood to the thigh, came up thin; north bought her cheap — one thin return, entered at Greybank\par

Silt 9 — four men of the black cut — three walked up; the fourth’s name said twice to the ground — nothing; no block set\par

Reed 20, this morning — the new reeve — stood to the belt; the post did not move — nothing; the block laid in the niche\par

There were stands before these that the old woman could set a season to, and I have not written them, because a row of seasons is a thing a clerk can carry away and a print in the peat is not. The niche has never agreed with the factor’s book and has never been asked to.

\subsection*{What the clerk did}

He borrowed the leaf on the morning after while I was laying the new block in, and gave it back with the verbs taken out.

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item Where she said \emph{the water closes over the print}, he wrote \emph{the measure is retained in the peat} above and left hers below.

\item Where she said \emph{the post has never counted a man}, he wrote \emph{the post is a lawful marker of the term}, a true thing said by a man who has never stood with water in his boots.

\item At the Tallow stand he put a round nought against the fourth man and wrote \emph{third party unidentifiable; vacancy}, and when I asked what a stand was worth with no man standing up out of it, he said nothing a clerk could enter, the first true thing he said all morning.

\item At the gap in the song he wrote \emph{vacancy} again. He did not ask what sound had been in it.

\end{itemize}

I have put the verbs back underneath and left his hand standing above, as the board leaves the old print under the water. He takes them out because a thing always true has no need of them. I put them back because a woman standing up to the thigh wants to know who did the closing, and whether it was the marsh or her own foot.

\subsection*{At the head and in the gutter}

The peat at the head is hers and mine and will not come out of the grain, which is why the marsh signs with a thumb and not a name. The sedge press has left the first two words soft; I have not gone over them. The tideline is marsh-water dried dark. The awn is sedge and the horn-shaving came off my own stick when I used its point to open a word I could not spell in charcoal. The grey came off a cuff and nobody will own it; there is no Last Day on this boardwalk and nothing gets swept. The ale ring stood from the first voice to the fourth stand and was drunk by nobody, which is how small ale goes at the Post when there is a thing to say and no proper word for it. The beetle’s wing-case lay on the niche stone and I have pressed it flat where it fell. The clerk did not notice any of these things, which is how I know he is a good clerk.

\subsection*{At the foot, in a hand nobody will own}

Struck through once and written again underneath, very small:

\begin{quote}\itshape The block in the niche is not the man who stood.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape The whole is read for a person not in the room. The thin one is sold.\end{quote}

I asked the old woman, the woman of the east marsh, the man who brought the reeve up out of the cut, and the clerk, and had four answerings and no hand. I have left the line struck through and standing, the only honest way to keep a sentence you cannot sign.

The leaf goes back in the sacking under the niche stone. Next choosing the marsh will stand for a man, the water will close over the prints, the old woman will lay a shape in a hole, and the clerk will come out from Greybank and take the verbs out. I shall put them back and leave the nought in its place and the gap the length it is sung.

\clearpage\phantomsection\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{Of Consent, the Clip at the Wrist, and the Refusal That Is Not Entered, Being Title the Fourth of the Ordinances of the Keeping: with the Table of Consents, the Form of Consent Left Blank, the Consent-Song Said Under the Clip, Two Corrections in Borrowed Hands, and a Line at the Foot Nobody Will Own}
\CRsheetheading{Of Consent, the Clip at the Wrist, and the Refusal That Is Not Entered, Being Title the Fourth of the Ordinances of the Keeping: with the Table of Consents, the Form of Consent Left Blank, the Consent-Song Said Under the Clip, Two Corrections in Borrowed Hands, and a Line at the Foot Nobody Will Own}
{\centering\FellFont\itshape\footnotesize\color{faded} An extract from the Court’s ordinances, written out for the slate at the watch beside the Cross in Sill, with the marginal hand of the clerk who enters consents before the collector’s tube is set; the articles in Ledgerhand and the verbs restored beneath them, the consents and the hours in a table, the form of consent left blank, the consent-song said low under the clip, one word scored away with the edge of a cold-iron clip, two corrections in borrowed hands, and a line at the foot nobody has claimed · Copied at Sill in the Thin Year, Y.H. 812, and carried forward at the Opening of the Slates, Ilmen 1, Y.H. 813, from Title the Fourth of the Ordinances of the Keeping as set down in the first years after the Rising of Y.H. 668 and confirmed to the factor at Greybank by the treaty of Y.H. 418, added to in Y.H. 782; survives as three leaves of foolscap sewn with wire, kept under the consent-slate at the watch: a grey Ash thumb at the head, a scorch where the watch-fire was too near, a dark score gone green at the edge where the clip was laid, pale slip from a swaddling cloth along the gutter, a brown crust-mark at the second fold, a thread of grey wool through the tie-hole, a tide-line along the foot from the market boards after rain, two corrections in borrowed hands, and a line at the foot nobody will own\par}\medskip
I keep the consent-slate at the watch beside the Cross. A collector comes down off the Clay Road with the tube in its wool and a name already on his own slate, sets the tube on my counter while he goes for a cup, and I read what is below to the man before the tube goes back into his hand. The ordinance is in Ledgerhand, with nobody in any of its sentences, which is the only way the Keeping has found to make a consent read as though it had been given by a room. I put the people back underneath. A consent with nobody in it is a consent nobody ever gave, and those are the only ones this Court has ever wanted.

\begin{quote}\itshape At the head of the first leaf, in mine, written small: Copied for the watch and from the watch. The verbs are mine. The absence of them is not. Let both stand.\end{quote}

\subsection*{Title the Fourth, as it stands at the watch}

\emph{From the Ordinances of the Keeping, Title the Fourth: Of Consent, the Clip at the Wrist, and the Refusal That Is Not Entered. Set down in the first years after the Rising of Y.H. 668; confirmed to the factor at Greybank by the treaty of Y.H. 418; added to in Y.H. 782 and in the Thin Year, Y.H. 812.}

\subsection*{I. Of the asking}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item No measure is drawn from a vessel that has not consented. The collector asks, the answer is entered, and the tube is not set until the entry is made.

\item The asking is made in the hearing of one witness besides the collector. The witness is not asked whether he heard, and his name is not entered.

\item Consent is entered in the hand of the collector or his clerk and not in the hand of the vessel. The hand that writes is not the hand that consents.

\item The question is put once. A second asking is a fresh entry and is entered as fresh, whether the first answer was given or not.

\end{enumerate}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Margin:} I asked a man come down from the terraces why the question is put once when a man may want a moment. He said a second question is a new account and a new account wants a new figure. I have set his words here, because the ordinance has no place for them and the slate has room at the edge.\end{quote}

\subsection*{II. Of the clip}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item Where consent is withheld, the vessel is clip-held by the wrist until consent is given. The clip is the Court’s iron and leaves no figure.

\item The clip is set at the wrist and not at the neck, over the vein and not over the bone. A clip set wrongly is a fault of the officer and is entered to the officer.

\item The hand in the clip is not the hand that holds the slate. The collector writes with the other hand, so that the entry and the refusing hand are not the same hand.

\item No hour is entered for the holding. What is spent in the clip is drawn from no account, and no column provides for it.

\end{enumerate}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Margin:} There was a pale ring at the wrist of a man who came to this watch in the Thin Year, where something had been worn tight and long before the clip was set. He would not say what had been there. I have entered the clip and not the ring, because the ordinance asks after the iron and not after what a man was wearing. Both are marks on the same wrist. I have left at the edge a place the length of the ring.\end{quote}

\subsection*{III. Of the refusal}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item A refusal is not entered. What is not entered is carried forward, and a refusal carried forward is not called a refusal in the roll.

\item Where a vessel refuses twice in one tend, the second refusal is entered as a second asking and not as a second no.

\item No officer is corrected for a refusal that was not entered. An officer who enters a refusal has made a fault, for a refusal entered would want an answer, and no answer is provided for.

\item The word \emph{no} is not written in the consent-book. A clerk who writes it has begun to keep another book.

\end{enumerate}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Margin, scored with the edge of a cold-iron clip:} I wrote the word once and scraped it away with the clip when the collector’s man came in. The score is the length of it. A clerk who keeps a second book is a clerk who will one day be asked which book he was keeping, and I have only the one. I have left the score and not the word.\end{quote}

\subsection*{IV. Of the entry}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item The entry stands when the figure is written, and not when the tube is set. A consent entered is a consent given, whether the vessel is still in the room or not.

\item The figure is one in twelve, as the notice says, and is not changed for the holding, the hour, or the mark at the wrist.

\item Where the vessel is a foundling with no house, the consent is entered to the house that has him, and where no house has him it is entered to the Keeping. The Keeping does not refuse for anybody.

\item The slate is read back after the figure is written. The reader does not ask whether the reading was heard. What is read is not corrected by what was answered.

\end{enumerate}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Margin:} A woman stood here through a reading with her hand at the middle of her palm where a ring had once been worn tight and long, and said the figure had been read to her twice, once for the watch and once for the households that came late. I have entered it once, as the ordinance provides. The second reading was hers, and I have set it at the edge, where a second reading has no column.\end{quote}

\subsection*{V. Of faults and their correcting}

Fault — As entered at the watch — What the clerk sets beneath\par

A verb in the consent — Consent entered — The man said it, or did not\par

The question put twice — Second asking, entered fresh — The moment the man wanted, not entered\par

A refusal entered — Fault of the officer — The word no, scored in the margin\par

An hour entered for the holding — Figure not affected — The hour, which no column holds\par

A clip set at the neck — Fault of the officer, entered — The wrist, which is where it belongs\par

The witness asked whether he heard — His name not entered — Nothing; he was asked, and is gone\par

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item A fault copied twice in one tend is a fault the officer has not understood, and the senior clerk sits with him at the watch until he has. The clip is not a rod. It is a piece of iron with a place where a wrist was.

\end{enumerate}

\subsection*{The table of consents}

\emph{Copied from the consent-slate. The figure and the hours stand as the ordinance has them. The last column is mine and has no standing at any Weighing.}

Day — The vessel — Asked — Answer first given — What stands — Hours in the clip — What the wrist kept\par

Ash 12 — A kiln-hand, Low Kiln — once — \emph{Not while the fire’s low} — Consent entered — not entered — a pale line, gone by evening\par

Ash 14 — A woman of the terraces — once — \emph{(no answer)} — Consent entered — not entered — nothing I could see\par

Ash 18 — A foundling, no slate-name — once — — — Consent to the Keeping — not entered — the door-post’s mark, not the clip’s\par

Ash 21 — A glaze-room girl, High Kiln — twice — \emph{Ask the pot} — Second asking, entered fresh — not entered — green at one corner of the mouth\par

Ash 26 — A man of Mud End — once — \emph{A number goes in a slate} — Consent entered — not entered — the ring at the palm, older than the clip\par

Ash 30 — A clay-bound hand, term served out — once — \emph{I have no house} — Consent to the Keeping — not entered — the clip’s own mark, two days\par

Draws on this leaf: six. Refusals entered: none. Hours entered: none. The word that is not entered stands scored in the lower margin, the length of it.

\subsection*{The form of consent}

\emph{Set out at the end of Title the Fourth. I have copied it with the blanks as they stand. In nine years no vessel has filled the last line in the hand the collector requires.}

\begin{quote}\itshape Entered this day, being ---day of -------, in the year of the Hearth ------, the consent of ---------------------- of ---------------------- to the drawing of the measure, asked once in the hearing of ----------------------, given before the tube was set, the figure one in twelve as the notice says, the clip at the wrist where consent was withheld, and no hour entered for the holding; written by ----------------------, whose hand was not the hand that consented. The vessel answered ----------------------, which is not entered.\end{quote}

\subsection*{The consent-song}

\emph{Said low at the watch while the collector’s man holds the tube in its wool. Never while the slate is open, and never within hearing of the factor’s clerk. The fourth line is said to the wrist and not to the man.}

\begin{quote}\itshape Iron at the wrist and a slate at the knee,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the tube in its wool and the man in the cold;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape they ask you once and they write it twice,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the no that you said is not in the book.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Four at the bell and a gap where the fifth should be,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the gap is the hour the clip was on;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the figure goes up and the mark goes down,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the hand that wrote is the hand that’s gone.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Iron at the wrist and a mark at the palm,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape one of them older than the other by years;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the slate keeps the figure, the wrist keeps the shape,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the watch keeps the place where the no was.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{In the narrow upright hand:} One consent entered; no deduction arises. \emph{In mine:} He has put a figure where I put a person. A person can be asked; a figure cannot. Both stand.\end{quote}

\subsection*{What the two borrowed hands did}

The College man came down from the Hearthseat with ink in two fingers of a cuff gone soft from washing. He struck \emph{the vessel refuses} out of rule nine and set \emph{consent is withheld} above it, which is the same thing said by somebody who is not in the room. On rule eight he struck out \emph{what is spent in the clip} and wrote \emph{the interval is not entered}, which is true of the slate and false of the wrist. I have put both of mine back underneath and left his above, where a man must lean to read them.

The other hand is a factor’s from Greybank, leaning and brown at the edge, with a little gold in it. Against the ring at the palm he wrote \emph{occupational mark; no deduction arises}, which is the same phrase a clerk of the factor’s writes against the green at a girl’s gum. I have not struck it through. A hand with gold in it can call a mark occupational, because an occupational mark is a thing that can be entered and handed on. I have set my ring underneath. Both stand.

\subsection*{At the head and in the gutter}

The grey at the head is Ash, off my own thumb turning the leaf toward the watch-fire; it does not come out of the creases and I have stopped trying. The scorch is where the watch-fire was too near on a wet evening in Ash; it has taken the corner off the first rule without taking the sense. The dark score in the lower margin is the clip’s edge, set down while I decided what word to leave out; it has gone green at the bottom where the damp got into it. The pale along the gutter is slip from a swaddling cloth, laid here while a woman held her child still with one arm and waited for me to finish. The brown at the second fold is where a crust was set down by a man come up from the clay yard with a number in his fist and no figure to spend it on. The grey wool through the tie-hole is off a cuff gone soft from washing; it is mine and I have not untied it. The tide-line along the foot came up off the market boards after rain, when the Cross stood under an inch of brown water and the collector’s man would not set the tube down until the slate was dry. At the Last Day the houses sweep their corners and burn what they find and call it dealt with. This watch is not a house, and the Ash stays where it fell.

\subsection*{At the foot, in a hand nobody will own}

\begin{quote}\itshape The slate keeps the yes. The wrist keeps the no.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape The hour keeps nothing, and nobody is asked to enter it.\end{quote}

I asked a collector’s man, a woman who stood here with her hand at her palm, and a clerk come down from Greybank, and had three answers and no hand, as I have had before. I have left the lines where they were written.

The slate goes back under the watch-post. Tomorrow a collector will come down off the Clay Road with the tube in its wool and a name on his own slate, and I shall set this leaf where he can read it and put the verbs back where another hand has taken them out. A man will say something that is not entered, the clip will be set, and the figure will stand as entered. That is my trade here: to write down what was done and leave a place the length of what was not.

\clearpage\phantomsection\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{The Return Book at Greybank, Being the Pourings of the Last Tend of Ash in the Thin Year, with the Figure Entered, the Figure Paid, and the Note the Cradle Gave}
\CRsheetheading{The Return Book at Greybank, Being the Pourings of the Last Tend of Ash in the Thin Year, with the Figure Entered, the Figure Paid, and the Note the Cradle Gave}
{\centering\FellFont\itshape\footnotesize\color{faded} A page from the bank assessor’s own return-ledger, kept under the return-slate in the lower room; figures in Ledgerhand copied from the collector’s slate and the factor’s tally, terse remarks in the hand that set the warm into the cradle, a column of likenesses struck out and drawn back, one correction in the College’s narrow upright hand and one in the factor’s, and a line at the foot nobody will own · Written at Greybank, eighteen leagues downriver of Sill, in the last tend of Ash, Y.H. 812, the Thin Year, carried through Stone and the Five and copied forward at the Opening of the Slates, Ilmen 1, Y.H. 813; kept in a board cover beneath the return-slate and taken down when a whole return is disputed. It survives with an iron-gall thumb at the head, a smear of pale slip from a swaddling cloth, a tallow print where the lamp was held low, a cold-iron shaving worked into the gutter, a thread of grey wool from a cradle blanket, a damp tide-line out of the lower room, a small square of bare paper where a word was scraped away, two corrections in borrowed hands, and one line at the foot that has never been claimed\par}\medskip
I keep the return-slate in the lower room at Greybank. A collector draws in the districts and the factor enters the figure above, and what comes down to me is a measure with nowhere left in it to stay. I set it into a new vessel and write what came back. I do not carry the tube. I do not sit by the dying. My hand is the last one the measure passes through before it is called a return, and the only hand in this house that writes down what the return did when it arrived.

The rolls of the dead are carried forward here and never closed. A roll that closes is a roll a woman can ask about, and a roll a woman can ask about is a roll that has to be answered. Ours stays open. There is a kind of mercy in a thing nobody finishes.

Twelve copper bits to a silver mark; twenty silver marks to a Sere crown, which comes north with the factor and goes south when he does. The Court books an ember at five marks and no man in this room has ever traded one. One in twelve is printed on the notice at Sill and read twice at the Cross. I write the figure the notice gives and the figure the cradle gave, and I have never once made them agree, which is the whole work of this book.

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{In the narrow upright hand of a clerk come down from the College:} Return entered. \emph{Underneath, in mine:} He has taken the pouring out of the sentence. A measure may be returned by anybody and to nobody; a man pours it with his hands and the hands get cold. I have put \emph{I set it in} back beneath his words and left his words standing over it.\end{quote}

\subsection*{The order of the pour at this bank}

\emph{Copied from the notice that hangs over the return-slate. The words in the second column are mine and are not read at the Weighing.}

Step — As the notice has it — As it stands in the lower room\par

The measure — Drawn by the collector, banked, account stands — Comes in on a slate with grey at the head and a name that is not the vessel’s\par

The deduction — One in twelve, as printed — Read twice. What the district pays is not what the district hears\par

Whole return — One measure into one vessel, with memory — Twelve hundred marks and a vessel named on the roll; the memory is not weighed here\par

Thin return — Many measures pooled, divided by lot — Thirty marks in labour, paid by the district; the lot decides which cradle\par

Beautiful return — A Sere physician’s word, entered as given — Calm, and wanting nothing. I have set the word down and put no gloss on it\par

The Kept — Held near the fire; spoken of with pity — No return due. They cannot want one, and a return is a thing wanted\par

The pouring — Completed when the figure is entered — Completed when the cradle takes. These are not the same hour\par

The Sere word is not ours and I did not learn it in Grath. A factor’s man came up from the coast with it in his mouth and said a beautiful return is one that has ceased to want, which is a physician’s praise and not a banker’s. I have entered the phrase as it came and left the wanting where it stood. A clerk who explains a word has begun to write a sermon, and sermons get copied.

\subsection*{The leaf, as it stood in Ash}

\emph{Figures in Ledgerhand. The remarks are mine, in the hand that held the cradle, and are not part of the account. A dash is a place where no pouring was made, not a nought.}

Day — Vessel, as the slate names it — Embers in — Return — Poured into — Paid by — Note — Remark\par

Ash 21 — A widow of the lower bank. \emph{Two loaves} — 33 — thin — a cradle at the Weir — the district — flat — Asked after the name she carried in. The cradle had none. Figure stood.\par

Ash 21 — A clay-bound hand, term served out, terraces — 39 — thin — two cradles, by lot — the district — nearly — One made two. Neither came back with the trade.\par

Ash 22 — A thrower of the low yard, second pouring — 41 — thin — a cradle in Low Kiln — the district — flat — Figure below the first. Set side by side, joined neither.\par

Ash 24 — A man of Mud End. \emph{Peat} — 47 — thin — three cradles, by lot — the district — none — Drawn before light. Slate came in grey at the head. Read over the cradles at noon.\par

Ash 25 — A glaze-room girl, High Kiln. \emph{Sweet} — 38 — thin — a cradle on the terrace — the district — nearly — Turned her mouth toward the cup. No word for the taste. Entered in the likeness, not the figure.\par

Ash 26 — A bought breath, eleven months served, Fenmarch — 22 — thin — a cradle at the Standing Post — the reeve — flat — Eleven months entered whether he lasted them or not. The cradle knows nothing of months.\par

Ash 27 — A house of the terraces, disputed — 52 — — — — — — — flat — Thumb wiped twice before touching nothing. Figure asked for, then not wanted. Left standing. No pouring made.\par

Ash 28 — A vessel returned twice, entered whole by the factor’s order — 29, struck to 30 — whole — one cradle, named on the roll — a house upriver — full — Below the last two figures. \emph{Whole} set above \emph{with memory} in a borrowed hand. Both stand.\par

Ash 29 — A foundling left at the mill, no slate-name — 12 — — — — — — — full — Stone under him, not a name. Stands till a hearth claims him. Not a return and not entered as one.\par

Ash 30 — Six and twenty of the lower yard, one line for the batch, by lot — — — thin — cradles in the district — the district — none — Names not taken. Grey went out through the north gate in the afternoon. No figure came off the batch.\par

Draws on this leaf: eight. Lines with no pouring in them: two. Figures struck: one. Columns struck: one.

\subsection*{The likeness column}

I keep a place beside the figure for what the new vessel did with the warm after it was set in. The College has never thought to strike this column out of a bank book, which I take for an oversight and not a mercy, and so I keep what I please in it.

On Ash 21 the widow’s cradle took the warm and turned toward the door of the room where the figure had been read. On Ash 22 one of the two cradles went toward a pot before a pot was shown to it. On Ash 25 the girl’s cradle kept its mouth open in the way of a person tasting something and finding no word for it. On Ash 28 the whole return lay quiet and wanted nothing, and I have set \emph{quiet} down, which is a word the Sere physician would like and which I will not let him have without a figure against it.

A likeness is not a figure and cannot be added. That is why the College struck the column when the clerk came down on Ash 30. He wrote \emph{No such column} above it in the narrow upright hand, and he counted the rows before he wrote it, which is how I know the column troubled him. I have drawn the column back underneath and left his words standing over it. A man does not count what he has not looked at.

\subsection*{What the two borrowed hands did}

The College man struck the verb out of the order of the pour, as he strikes every verb he can find, and set \emph{was returned} above \emph{I set it in}, and above that \emph{the measure was entered}, which is further from the cradle than the first. I have put my hand back underneath both. A sentence with nobody in it is a sentence no woman can ask about, and women ask about these pourings in the end, always at the door, always after the slate is shut.

The factor’s clerk did two things. Against the vessel returned twice he struck my \emph{with memory} and set \emph{whole} above it, because \emph{whole} is the word the notice prints and the word a house upriver will pay twelve hundred marks to hear. Both stand. At the foot of the leaf, where I had written \emph{the figure is smaller than the last two}, he wrote \emph{figure corrected upward} and underlined it twice. I have left his line where he put it and my line where I put it. Neither is a lie. They are two accounts of the same cradle, and the cradle is not in either of them.

The small square in the lower margin is where I scraped a word away with a knife on Ash 27, after the disputed house went off without its figure. I scraped it before I knew what I had written. I have not put the word back and have not forgotten it.

\subsection*{The song the return-women carry up the stair}

\emph{Sung low on the stair from the lower room, never while the return-slate is open, and never twice in one house.}

\begin{quote}\itshape One for the tube and one for the slate,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape one for the mark that the cradle will pay;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the figure goes down and the figure goes up\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the woman goes home with the day.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape One in twelve as the notice says,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape four and four as the bell is told;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape they read us the sum in a clean voice\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and we carry the rest in the cold.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Pour it in and shut the book,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape ask the cradle what it knows;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape it knows the hand and it knows the breast\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and it knows the shape of the house it was told.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{In the factor’s narrow hand, against the last line:} No figure entered against the cradle. \emph{In mine:} He is right, and the women hold the last line until they are out of the lower room, which is how I know the line matters.\end{quote}

\subsection*{In the head and in the gutter}

The brown thumb at the head is iron-gall and mine, made by holding the quire open through a market morning; there are clerks in the Hearthseat who can tell an assessor by his thumb before he has spoken. The pale smear down the gutter is slip from a swaddling cloth, laid on the leaf while a woman held a cradle still with her whole arm and waited for me to finish. The tallow print at the foot came off the lamp I keep low so that the women at the stair will not know I am writing down the likenesses and change their words for me. The cold-iron shaving in the fold came out of the tube’s wool wrap when the collector set it on my counter and went away for a cup; there is always a little iron in the fold, and it has never once drawn the warm out of the paper, which is the only mercy this room has that I can name.

The grey wool came off a cradle blanket and goes on coming off, though I have shaken the book three times. The tide-line along the foot is the damp of the lower room, which gets into everything left on a bench, and into some things that are not left on benches. They sweep the corners of houses on the Last Day and burn what they find in the morning and call it dealt with. There is no Last Day in the lower room of a bank. The rolls of the dead are carried forward and never closed, and the Ash stays where it fell.

\subsection*{At the foot, in a hand nobody will own}

\begin{quote}\itshape The bank counts what went in. The cradle counts what came back. The two counts never meet, and the College has no word for the space between.\end{quote}

I asked the factor’s clerk, a woman who carried a cradle up the stair, and a collector come down from the Clay Road, and had three answers and no hand. I have left the line where it was written.

The book goes back under the return-slate. Tomorrow a collector will come in off the Clay Road with a figure from Sill, and the factor will enter it above, and I shall set the warm into a cradle and write down what the cradle did, and put my verb back where the College struck it out. Somewhere in Low Kiln a child who came back this year will go toward a cup before he has seen the cup, and no figure in this book will tell his mother why. The rolls stay open. The book stays in the cover. That is the whole of it, and it goes on.

\clearpage\phantomsection\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{The Riddle Bench at the Cross, Being Five Cold-Night Questions, the One That Was Not Answered, and the Tally Left in Charcoal on the Bench Top}
\CRsheetheading{The Riddle Bench at the Cross, Being Five Cold-Night Questions, the One That Was Not Answered, and the Tally Left in Charcoal on the Bench Top}
{\centering\FellFont\itshape\footnotesize\color{faded} A tapster’s record of a winter contest, set down for the settling of arguments and not for the improvement of the reader; the rules in the hand the house keeps, the riddles in the words they were spoken, a charcoal tally of one night, the figures of a Court clerk entered over them, and one line at the foot in a hand nobody will own · Written in Stone of Y.H. 812, the Thin Year after the Long Cold, at the alehouse called the Banked Coal at the Cross in Sill, by the woman who keeps the bench and the fire behind it; copied forward in Ilmen of Y.H. 813 onto the back of a spoiled tally leaf from the Court’s table, sewn with eel-sinew into a fold of oiled paper and kept in the jar by the hearth. It survives soft at the fold and stained at the head, with a tallow thumb, a ring where a quart stood all night, a press of wet wool across the first leaf, a spot of barley grease, a grey Ash print along the gutter, the charcoal rubbed thin where a sleeve has gone over it, one correction in the narrow upright hand of a Court clerk, and a line at the foot in a hand that is nobody’s.\par}\medskip
I keep the bench at the Cross and the fire behind it, which is a different work from keeping an account, though both begin with the hand on the board before the eye goes to the person standing there. In the cold months the road shuts, the Ilm goes under its skin, and there is nothing to do of an evening but count what is left and ask one another questions we already know the answer to. That is a riddle. A question whose answer you do not know is a gamble, and there is enough gambling in Sill without ale in it.

The bench is black ash with the grain standing up where four thousand sleeves have gone over it. I score the night in charcoal on the end away from the fire, where the charcoal shows, and I rub it out in the morning with the heel of my hand. Nothing is carried away from this bench in a slate. A man who wants a thing entered can go up the street to Slate Row and sit with people warmer than himself, and he will not get a riddle there.

\subsection*{The rules, as they are kept}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item A riddle is put once. Ask for it a second time and you owe a quart, because the second asking is for your own pleasure and not for the bench.

\item Answer in one breath. A second answer is a different riddle and is not heard. A man who gives two has not understood the first.

\item Four questions are scored. A fifth may be put and is not scored, being a thing said from a door and not from a stool.

\item The judge is the bench. I say whether an answer serves and I do not say why. A reason given is a riddle given away for nothing, and the giver can go home and sell it.

\item No slate lies on the bench. The score goes off with the morning, as the ale does, and neither is carried into an account.

\item A cup is set down before the first question and no one lifts it until the fourth. If it answers flat when it is set down, the night’s answering will go badly. I have never known this to fail and I would not say so before a kiln-master.

\end{enumerate}

\subsection*{The four that were scored}

The first was put to the eel-woman from the Fishstairs, who smells of silt and answers a question with a question. She had given hers before the verse was finished, which is why she never wins anything and is always first.

\begin{quote}\itshape Mouth and no lip to speak with,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape belly that gives nothing back,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape a door you cannot find from inside:\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape what goes in head-first stays?\end{quote}

“An eel basket,” she said, and laid a bit toward the pot though nobody had asked her to pay. The carter said a basket has no door. She told him to ask the eel, which is the whole of the answer and the proper way to give it.

The second was put to a girl who sweeps the yard for six bits a day.

\begin{quote}\itshape Carried in a clay dish before the light,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape given once and never twice;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape every house has it by morning\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and no house will say where it was lit.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape What is it?\end{quote}

“The year’s fire,” she said, and I gave her a quart of small ale watered until it barely counted, which she drank standing with her sleeve over the rim because she had been told not to spill. Nobody asked her where she had learned it. A child of eight in this town knows which dish the coal comes in and which houses will not tell you who paid for it.

The third went to the man from the kiln, who had slip dried on both forearms to the colour of old bone.

\begin{quote}\itshape I am not a warm-stone and nobody calls me one;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape I am borrowed from a neighbour’s fire and carried in wool;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape I am put under a head that cannot turn\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and by morning I am a stone again.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape What am I?\end{quote}

“A river stone,” he said, and there was an argument about whether a thing borrowed is the same thing when it is given back. I stopped it by setting the cup down. There is no winning an argument about a stone; there is only the stone, and it is cold by morning whichever way you decide it.

The fourth I put myself, because the room had got noisy and wanted quieting, and a riddle put by the bench is not scored against anybody.

\begin{quote}\itshape Nothing at noon and plain by tallow;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape I gather where a promise was not kept;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape they leave me lying on the Last Day,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape burn me in the morning and call it dealt with.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Name me.\end{quote}

No one answered for a while. Then a clay-hand from the pits, with the grey worked into his knuckles that no scrubbing lifted, said the grey in the corner, and said it to the bench and not to the room. I passed him the pot. He set it down again without drinking and said it was a thing his mother said to the skirting board, and that he had said it to his own daughter the week before and had not known he was going to. That is the best answer I have heard in eleven winters and the only one that cost the man something.

\subsection*{The fifth, which was put from the door}

It was the middle of Stone, when the ice had set for good and the bit for a quart had gone up two and come down again. A man stood at the door and did not come in. He was dry, which a man cannot be in that weather without having come a long way or else not having come from the weather at all. He asked whether anybody here was warm. Nobody answered him, which is an answer in this town. Then he put the fifth:

\begin{quote}\itshape I go back to a house that knows my face and not my name;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape my mother is glad of me and does not know me;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape I want a thing I never wanted\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and cannot say what it is.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape What am I?\end{quote}

The eel-woman said, “A thin return.” He said, “That is what the slate calls it,” and asked what it was to the house. The room went the way a room goes when everybody has the answer in their mouth and nobody will be the one to say it. He waited a little, and said, “Then you have not lost it,” and turned back into the cold. He did not come in and I did not ask him. Where he stood the boards were wet with the melt off every coat in the room, and in the morning there was a round dry place on the bench where no cup had stood. I rubbed the charcoal over it and it came back. I have stopped looking for the hand that did that.

\subsection*{The tally, in charcoal}

Question — Put by — Answer given — Score\par

The basket — the bench — an eel basket — one, paid\par

The dish — the bench — the year’s fire — one, drunk\par

The stone — the bench — a river stone — one, argued and allowed\par

The grey — the bench — the grey in the corner — one, not drunk\par

The face and the name — a man at the door — none served — not scored\par

The figure read at the Cross that morning was one in twelve, as the notice says, and it went over the bench with the ale and no one looked at it twice. There is a pause in that figure the length of a held breath, which the clerk reads past and I do not, but that is not a thing for a riddle night.

\subsection*{What the narrow hand did}

A clerk of the Court’s table borrowed the leaf on a market morning when the square was full and his cuff was soft at the edge from washing. He set the riddles down as \emph{queries entered} and the answers as \emph{responses entered}, and put a figure of marks against each of the four, which was more than I had scored, because the bench scores in whether a man sits down again and he does not. Against the fifth he wrote \emph{no answer tendered; struck}. He asked who had put it. I told him a man at the door. He asked for the man’s name, and I said the man had given none, which is a true thing and not the thing he wanted, and he wrote \emph{party unidentified}.

I have put my words under his and left his standing, the way a bench keeps a charcoal score under a spilled quart. He has entered four answers and struck the fifth, and the fifth was not struck: it stands where a man stood and did not sit down. I asked him what a figure was for and he said a figure was for carrying away. He has carried away four and left the one that would not go.

\subsection*{At the head and in the margins}

The tallow thumb at the head is mine; I held the leaf down in the draught that comes under the door and did not know I had marked it. The ring came off a quart that stood from the first question to the fifth and was drunk by nobody; three men have claimed it and one woman has denied it and I have not given it to any of them. The press of wet wool across the first leaf came off the man who held the door while the stranger spoke, and I have not written down which man, because he would stop holding doors if I did. The barley grease is from a crust the sweeping girl set down on the leaf and took away again uneaten, which is how a crust is usually taken in this town. The grey in the gutter came off a cuff that had no business in the corner where I keep the leaf, and I have not swept it.

\subsection*{At the foot, in a hand nobody will own}

\begin{quote}\itshape Four went home warm. The fifth went home with them.\end{quote}

I have asked the carter, the eel-woman and the clay-hand, and had three silences and no hand. I have left the line where it was written. The leaf goes back into the jar and the charcoal goes off the bench with the heel of my hand. The road will open at the thaw and there will be more to do of an evening than ask one another what we already know, and the bench will be wanted for cups again. I will set the fifth where it was and let the next man stand in it. If he asks whether anyone here is warm, I shall tell him to ask the pot.

\clearpage\phantomsection\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{The Rim Road Book, Being the Account of Hedd, an Under-Clerk of the Factor’s House at Greybank, Who Went Up to Keld Keep with Fine Ware and a Sealed Letter and Came Back with a Warm-Stone Gone Cold, a Shaving of Lead in the Fold, and a Figure He Was Told Was Current; with the Charges of the Road, the Courtesy of the Number Before the Name, the Table of What Was Sent and What Came Back, the Road-Song Never Sung Downward, Two Corrections in Borrowed Hands, and a Line at the Foot Nobody Will Own}
\CRsheetheading{The Rim Road Book, Being the Account of Hedd, an Under-Clerk of the Factor’s House at Greybank, Who Went Up to Keld Keep with Fine Ware and a Sealed Letter and Came Back with a Warm-Stone Gone Cold, a Shaving of Lead in the Fold, and a Figure He Was Told Was Current; with the Charges of the Road, the Courtesy of the Number Before the Name, the Table of What Was Sent and What Came Back, the Road-Song Never Sung Downward, Two Corrections in Borrowed Hands, and a Line at the Foot Nobody Will Own}
