{\centering\FellFont\itshape\footnotesize\color{faded} An under-clerk’s road account, set down first in the upright hand he keeps for the factor and then in charcoal on the backs of spoiled requisitions when the upright hand would not hold what he had seen; the figures in the factor’s hand, the mountain sayings kept in the hearing with the endings struck off, the verbs put back underneath every borrowed correction, one notch cut in the edge where a Keldish word would not go into the south’s letters, and one line at the foot in a hand that has never come forward · Written at Keld Keep and at the survey post in the Cold Pass in Bone of Y.H. 812, the Thin Year of the Long Cold, by Hedd, an under-clerk of the factor’s house at Greybank, who went up the Rim Road in Frost with a crate of High Kiln fine ware, a letter the factor sealed, and nine marks of the Court’s money, and came down in Ilmen of Y.H. 813 with the letter delivered, the money mostly spent, a warm-stone that held nine days and not the tenth, and a leaf of the survey turned face down which he has not read; set down on the backs of requisitions for warm-stone voided by the Long Cold, copied at Greybank onto the reverse of a spoil ledger and sewn with wire into a scrap of oiled survey-cloth. It survives with coal smut ground into the head off the sleeve used to hold the sheet down on the weigh, a shaving of warm-stone shut in the second fold which kept a little heat one night on a stone floor and is cold now, a bead of Ninth Gallery lead rolled into the gutter, frost raised out of the grain on the climb over the pass and gone by noon, a hard drop of tallow at the fold, a grey Ash print along the outer fold which the writer did not make and has not swept, one correction in the red checking-hand of the mine-reeve’s clerk, one in the narrow upright Ledgerhand of a Court survey-clerk at Greybank, a notch cut clean through a word in the edge, and a line at the foot in a hand nobody will own\par}\medskip
I keep the factor’s figures at Greybank. It is a room with a slate on one table and a second slate on the table behind it, and a man is entered in the second before he is heard in the first, which is the order of that house and the order of the Keeping. I went up the Rim Road in Frost of the Thin Year with a crate of fine ware out of High Kiln, a letter the factor sealed in front of me, and nine marks of the Court’s money for such charges as the road might ask. I came down in Ilmen with the letter delivered, the money mostly gone, a warm-stone that held for nine days and gave out on the tenth, and a leaf of a survey which a man turned face down in front of me and which I have never read.

I set this down because the upright hand I keep for the factor would not hold it. An upright hand is a good hand for a figure and a poor one for a man. What I could not put in a figure I put in charcoal on the backs of requisitions, which nobody in that house wants back.

\subsection*{What the road charged, and what I entered}

The Rim Road runs a hundred and twenty leagues from Sill to Keld Keep, and the Cold Pass lies ten beyond. A cart makes it in nine days in Ash and in twelve when the high places have shut, which is to say that the road’s length changes with the weather and the slate does not. At Greybank I was told to enter the charges as the factors before me had entered them. On the road I paid what was asked. Both columns stand.

Charge — Entered at Greybank — Asked on the road — What I set underneath\par

Warm-stone, fist-sized — 6 bits, current — 8 bits, and no promise taken — The seller would not give his name. A stone is sold and the debt stays with the man who cut it out.\par

Lodging at the third stage — 2 bits — 2 bits, with a place by the fire extra — I paid the extra. My toes had been without feeling since the second day.\par

Letter carried past the post — entered \emph{nil} — 1 bit for the man to state my office — He asked for the office before the name. I gave the office. He wrote \emph{bearer}.\par

Lead, a bead, Ninth Gallery — not entered — given, and laid on my leaf — The man who laid it down went away without it. I have rolled it into the gutter rather than lose it.\par

Passage of the Cold Pass — entered \emph{nil} — no charge, and a warning — A post and no gate. The warning cost nothing and was the dearer of the two.\par

The factor’s clerk at Greybank set \emph{road figures, informal} above this table, which is his way of saying a man may copy a road but not enter one. He has not struck a word. I would rather he had.

\subsection*{The courtesy of the number}

At Keld Keep I gave my measure before my name at the Warden’s hall, which is their custom and not a rudeness, and I had been told so three times before I went up and still felt the shame of it when I did it. The clerk wrote the figure first and asked the name second, as though a name were a thing a man might keep back and use again. My figure is two and thirty and has never been checked in red, which in that room makes me a man of no consequence and no suspicion. I found I preferred it to being interesting.

A key-woman at the mouth told me a man states what he holds before he says who he is, and that a man who forgets is sent back to the foot of the post. I asked whether a lowlander was expected to know this. She said a lowlander was expected to be told once. I have set that down as she said it, looking at the keys and not at me.

The sayings there are said to the stone, to the iron, to the lamp, and never to the man beside you. Said looking at a man, a saying becomes a bargain, and there is no bargain in any of them. Where a Keldish word would not go into the south’s letters I have cut the edge with my knife and left the cut standing. A notch stays when paper has gone, which is more than can be said for the factor’s slate.

\subsection*{What was sent, and what came back}

I carried a crate of fine ware for a house of the Warden’s captains and a letter I was not to read. I came back with the letter’s answer, which was two words on a strip of slate, and with such goods as a factor’s house will enter without asking where the warmth went.

Sent up from Greybank — Came down again — What the factor entered — What I entered beneath\par

Fine ware, High Kiln, twelve pieces — nine pieces; three cracked on the climb — \emph{broken in transit} — The three cracked where the road was worst and the straw least. I watched them go and did not say whose straw it was.\par

A sealed letter — An answer of two words on slate — \emph{delivered, answered} — I did not read either. I carried them both. There is a difference and the factor’s book has no place for it.\par

Nine marks, Court money — A warm-stone, nine days’ heat — \emph{warm-stone, current rate} — The tenth day it was a stone. The seller’s fire went out of it and nobody paid for the going.\par

— — One bead of Ninth Gallery lead — not entered — Rolled into the gutter of this leaf. It is warm when the room is cold, which I have tested and have not written down as a wonder.\par

— — One leaf of a survey, turned face down — not entered — I have not read it. A man who turns a slate down in front of you has told you something in the only manner his office permits.\par

At the mouth I was offered a thin return for a third of what the Court charges, the seller asking no questions about the source, and I said no, having been sent to buy iron and not a person. I entered the refusal in charcoal; the factor’s clerk wrote \emph{no acquisition recorded} above it, which is true in his office and not what I meant.

\subsection*{The weigh, and the two numbers in one arm}

I stood at the weigh while the shifts went down. A woman of the count took the numbers as each pair went past, put a warm-stone into a boy’s hand after the knife, and kept a cup on a nail for the men who came up. She had done it two and twenty years and had never been below, which she did not call cowardice.

A man came up with a number cut into his forearm in two sets, the later cut deeper. The mine-reeve checked the later figure in red and left the earlier standing in the skin. The clerk beside him wrote nothing against the earlier number. I asked the count-woman why two figures were allowed to stand where the Court’s slate would hold only one. She said the mine-reeve kept two truths without calling either a lie, and that a clerk who can do that has a busy morning and a quiet night.

In the red checking-hand of the mine-reeve’s clerk, against \emph{the boy went down with a stone in his hand}: \textbf{State the figure given, then the figure taken. Everyone here knows the order.}

Underneath, in mine: I had written that the boy held the stone as a man holds a thing he has been given and does not yet know the price of. The clerk has struck the boy out. There is no boy in this room after the first cut, he has written further, and the rule is for the morning before, when a boy still thinks a face will do instead of a figure. I have left both. A figure is a merciful thing to a counting room and a cruel one to the hand that carried it, and the two do not meet in the middle of a sentence.

\subsection*{The stones above the Keep}

Five leagues higher into the Rim stand the Listening Stones, where the Vorr sit for days and come away with numbers. I went up with a surveyor who had leave to be there and I had leave to carry his lamp. He sat against the third stone from the high path and came back with four figures which he set on a leaf and would not match to anything I could see: not to the wells, not to the nine of anything that I had counted. He said the numbers were correct and then turned the slate face down, which is a courtesy in Keld and an insult in Greybank, and I have set down the turning and not the reason.

There is a word the surveyors use for the oldest marks in the seam. The Keldish translate it as Ash and the Court’s copy translates it as language, and the Vorr, being asked, say only that the numbers are correct. These are three guesses and I have set them one under another without choosing, because a chronicler who chooses between two guesses has made a fact of one of them.

In the narrow upright hand of a Court survey-clerk, borrowed at Greybank, set above the four figures: \textbf{Counts of the survey. Not legible in every copy.}

Underneath, in mine: the figures were legible enough. What I could not legibly match was the ground they were said to stand for. A figure not legible has a figure somewhere behind it. These four stood where nobody had put them and I have copied them where they stood.

\subsection*{The road-song}

\emph{Taken down at the post from a man who had come up with tallow and was going down empty. He would sing it only going up. He said a song of that road sung downward brings the cold into the house, and I have put it where I heard it.}

\begin{quote}\itshape Four leagues and a stone that sweats,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and a hand that states the number first;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the warm goes up in a tin lined warm\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the cold comes in behind.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape The post stands up and the gate does not,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the man who counts will not count me;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape a bead comes out of the ninth dark gallery\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and is laid on a leaf and left to be.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Two numbers sit in one cut arm,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the later deep, the earlier light;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the mountain keeps what the slate lets go,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the slate keeps what it writes.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape I carried up and I carried down,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the stone I bought went cold on the ninth;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape ask the stone whose fire it held ---\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape it will tell you nine, and then no tenth.\end{quote}

\subsection*{What the two hands did}

Two hands have been at these leaves besides mine.

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item The mine-reeve’s clerk, in the red checking-hand, changed no figure on the whole leaf. He took the verbs out of the weigh and put the order in: figure first, then the boy. I have put the boy back under it, where a man must kneel to read him.

\item The Court survey-clerk at Greybank, upright and narrow, set \emph{counts of the survey, not legible in every copy} over the four figures and wrote \emph{no acquisition recorded} over my refusal at the mouth. He has never been up the road and has strong views about the pass. Both his lines stand above mine, as is the custom of his office.

\end{itemize}

I have left both readings everywhere, the thin one under the neat one, as a potter leaves the old break showing under a new seam and does not pretend the first hand never touched the clay.

\subsection*{At the head and in the gutter}

The smut at the head is coal off the sleeve I held the sheet down with at the weigh; it goes into the grain and no wet sleeve takes it out. The warm-stone shaving in the second fold held its heat through one night on a stone floor and is cold now, which is the order of things in that country and the only argument about warmth I have ever seen a man settle by going to bed. The lead bead rolled out of the Ninth Gallery and a surveyor laid it on the leaf and went away without it; it is in the gutter and I have not entered it. The frost at the head came up out of the paper on the climb over the pass and was gone by noon; I set it down and no more, because a man who writes about frost as though it meant something has already begun a sermon. The tallow is my lamp, set too near the leaf. The grey along the outer fold came off a cuff laid where no cuff has business lying, and I have not swept it. There is no Last Day at a mouth or at a post, and nothing anywhere up that road gets burnt in the morning.

\subsection*{At the foot, in a hand nobody will own}

\begin{quote}\itshape I carried figures up and a stone came down;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the stone held nine and the tenth was mine.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape The post stood open and the gate was never made;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the slate turned down and the four stood where they lay.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Ask the arm which number it carried.\end{quote}

I asked the count-woman at the mouth, the surveyor come down from the stones, and the clerk at Greybank, and had three answers and no hand. I have left the line where it was written. The leaves go back into the oiled wrap and the wrap into the coat pocket the wire has worn. Tomorrow I shall sit at the second table in the factor’s room and enter what the road cost in the factor’s hand, and beneath it, where his hand does not reach, I shall enter the day the stone stopped being warm. That entry he will not ask for, and it is the only one in the house that anyone will want to read.

\clearpage\phantomsection\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{The River Collector’s Book, Being the Measures Drawn Aboard the Boat on the Lower Ilm Between Sill and Greybank in the Last Tend of Reed and the First of Tallow, Y.H. 813, with the Embers, the Note, the Return Due, and What the Water Took}
\CRsheetheading{The River Collector’s Book, Being the Measures Drawn Aboard the Boat on the Lower Ilm Between Sill and Greybank in the Last Tend of Reed and the First of Tallow, Y.H. 813, with the Embers, the Note, the Return Due, and What the Water Took}
{\centering\FellFont\itshape\footnotesize\color{faded} A page from the river collector’s own ledger, kept in an oiled fold under the stern seat; figures in Ledgerhand copied from the slate, the remarks terse and in the hand that held the cold iron tube, the note-column struck by the College and drawn back underneath, a numbering in a borrowed hand where the writer left a place, and a line at the foot in a hand nobody will own · Written aboard the collector’s boat on the lower Ilm from the last market of Reed through the first tend of Tallow, Y.H. 813, carried down to Greybank and back, and kept in an oiled-paper fold beneath the stern seat beside the tube in its wool sleeve. It survives soft at the fold, with river silt worked into the gutter, a white salt bloom at the head where the Sallow wind came up the water, dried eel slime along the fore-edge, a pale round ring pressed into the paper where the cold tube was set down, a tallow thumb at the foot, a green bead of lead glaze in the lower corner, a grey Ash print along the margin nobody will own, a small square of bare paper where a word was scraped away, two corrections in borrowed hands, and one line at the foot that has never been claimed\par}\medskip
I draw the measure on the water. There are slates in this country that touch and slates that do not. The man at the Court’s table at the Cross touches the top of his before he looks at the woman waiting; the collector of the clay towns keeps a book I have never seen open; the clerk at the Fishstairs holds his slate to his forearm and writes before he looks at the stalls. I keep mine under oiled paper in the stern of the boat. The four of us enter the same year and our entries never meet, which is the nearest thing this country has to an arrangement.

The boat has six oars and a man at the stern who never touches them. He steers with one hand laid on the tiller and keeps the other in his coat, and when a house comes down to the bank he does not look up. I have drawn with the oars shipped and the boat standing still, and with the water slapping under the rowlocks, and the note is harder to hear in the second case, which is why I set a knuckle to the gunwale before I set the tube to a way. Write first. Look after. That is the order on the river, and the man at the stern has made a trade of never looking at all.

Twelve copper bits to a silver mark; twenty marks to a gold crown, a Sere coin that comes north with the factor and does not stay in Grath. The Court books an ember at five marks and no man on this water has exchanged one. A newborn vessel holds twelve to fifteen, a labourer in good case forty to sixty. One in twelve is printed on the notice and read twice at the Cross, once for the moot and once for those who came late. A second figure goes around the hamlets, comes aboard, and goes off again, and I have no column for it, not being a figure I can weigh.

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{In the narrow upright hand of a clerk come down from the College:} Coin and reckoning entered. Ember: five marks. \emph{Underneath, in mine:} He has written the ember as though a mark could be poured into it at this gunwale. I have put the verb back. A mark is a coin and an ember is a word the Court uses for warmth it has already counted, and a boatman who has pulled six oars against the current is entitled to know which of the two he is being told.\end{quote}

\subsection*{The rates, as I carry them}

Entry — As the book has it\par

Copper bit — twelve to a silver mark\par

Silver mark — twenty to a gold crown, a Sere coin\par

Ember — five marks, by the Court’s book; no man has exchanged one\par

Newborn vessel — twelve to fifteen embers\par

Labourer in good case — forty to sixty embers\par

Deduction — one in twelve, as the notice says\par

Thin return — many measures pooled and divided; thirty marks, paid by the district\par

Whole return — one measure into one vessel; twelve hundred marks and forty unspent measures\par

I have set the returns with no second figure beside them. I have heard what is paid in the hamlets and have not entered it. A clerk who writes down a figure he cannot weigh at the beam is a clerk who will be asked to read it aloud, and I do not read anything aloud on this boat.

\subsection*{The leaf, as it stood}

\emph{Figures in Ledgerhand. The remarks are mine, in the hand that held the tube, and are not part of the account. A dash is a place where no draw was made, not a nought.}

Day — Where the boat lay — Vessel, as the slate names it — Embers — Note — Return due — Remark\par

Reed 21 — Mud End, at the peat bank — A peat-cutter of the hamlet. \emph{Sedge} — 39 — flat — thin — Drawn at the water’s edge. Grey in the nail crescents. Figure read twice upriver.\par

Reed 24 — The Weir, oars shipped — A woman of the eel-boards. No slate-name — 41 — full — — — Asked what a cart would take; given a date and the river. Knot-string at her waist, one knot pulled down. No figure came off it.\par

Reed 30 — Greybank quay — A barrow of grey going down to the factor — — — — — — — Not weighed and not entered. Salt bloom on the quay rim.\par

Tallow 1 — Cold Acre, before light — A man of the well that never freezes — 44 — full — thin — Drawn under the stars. Asked after the thaw. Entered as a birth, not a question.\par

Tallow 3 — The Tallow Works — A render with sheep-fat on her sleeves. \emph{Wool} — 36 — nearly full — thin — Smell came downwind before the boat did. Name given at the bank, not entered.\par

Tallow 5 — Stonemouth, at the Ferr — A quarry hand. \emph{Lime} — 47 — flat — thin — Lead in the water. Number came up out of a fist, looked at, put back in a sleeve.\par

Tallow 6 — Below the north bridge — A foundling in cast-offs on the flat place — 12 — full — — — Stone under him, not a name. Stands till a hearth claims him. No loaf passed.\par

Tallow 10 — The Fishstairs, Account-day — A clerk set at the out-of-line step — — — none — — — Hand to slate before eyes to the stalls. Nobody had called a measure. Not one of ours.\par

Tallow 10 — The Cross, heard from the water — One in twelve, as the notice says — — — — — — — Read twice over the basket. Bell four, four and a gap; nobody crossed.\par

Tallow 10 — In the stern of the boat — A man the river took, no slate brought — — — none — — — The oars went out and came back. No figure, no return. The stern man kept his hands in his coat.\par

Draws on this leaf: seven. Lines with no draw in them: three. Figures struck: none. Columns struck: one. Oars shipped: twice.

\subsection*{The note}

Before the tube I set a knuckle on the gunwale or the rim of the cup the household hands me across the bank. A whole vessel answers full. One cracked through answers flat, a small dead sound that stops at the surface, which is the sound a peat-cutter made at Mud End and a quarry hand made at the Ferr, though neither house would have it said of them. A vessel with air under the note answers nearly full, and the hamlets have no word for it, so I have set the phrase down as I heard it in the yard, which is not Grathic and will not be read at a Weighing. A vessel turned toward in expectation may give nothing at all; I have entered that as \emph{none} and not as a nought, because a nought is a figure and a silence is not.

The kiln-masters of Sill know the full note and keep it to themselves, which is their right and their trade. A collector who cannot hear a vessel draws blind. He will still bring back his figure. The figure will still be entered. That is the trouble with figures.

\subsection*{The column they struck out}

Beside each row I had set down what was said at the water’s edge while the oars were shipped. Against the peat-cutter, \emph{the thaw will tell}; against the woman of the eel-boards, a date and the river; against the render, \emph{ask the pot}; against the quarry hand, nothing but the weather; against the foundling, the name a woman said into the ground before she saw me. I had put no heading over the column. A heading would make it an account, and an account is a thing a man may be called to answer for.

The man from the College borrowed the leaf at Greybank and struck the column through from the first row to the last, and wrote \emph{No such column} above it in his narrow upright hand. I have drawn the column back underneath and left his words standing over it. He had to count the rows before he could write that there were none worth entering, and I watched him do it, standing as he stands, with his cuff gone soft and his ink settled in two fingers. A man does not count what he has not looked at. The College has eleven words for a deduction and not one for a date, which is the whole of the difficulty between us.

\subsection*{What the two borrowed hands did}

The College man struck the verb out of the order of the draw. Where I wrote \emph{I drew}, he set \emph{the measure was drawn} above it, and above that \emph{the warmth was entered}, which is further from the bank than the first. I have put \emph{I drew} back beneath both. A sentence with nobody in it is a sentence no woman can ask about, and women ask about these draws in the end, always at the door, always after the tube is put away.

The other hand is tall and leaning and comes out of the factor’s house at Greybank. Against \emph{a man the river took} it wrote \emph{no return arising, instrument not presented}, and against the empty figure column it set a round nought. I have left both standing. A nought is a figure that can be carried away and entered at the other end; the river took a man and left a place, and a place is not a nought. The hand put a nought in it because a hand that writes whole returns for persons not in the room has long since stopped asking which way a man went.

\subsection*{The song the boatmen carry on the lower Ilm}

\emph{Sung with the stroke, never while the oars are shipped at a house, and never twice in one tend.}

\begin{quote}\itshape Six at the oar and one at the stern,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the one at the stern does not pull;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the knuckle goes to the gunwale first,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the figure comes up with the silt.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape One in twelve, says the notice, read twice at the Cross,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape four and four and the gap uncrossed;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape I hold the tube where the oars dip in\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and write what the bank said before the face.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Ask the pot, ask the weather, ask the river, they say;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the Court has a figure for each of the three.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape The stern keeps a hand that has never held oar,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the boat keeps a place that the count cannot fill.\end{quote}

A boatman sang the first two lines dropping down to Greybank and would not sing the third while the factor’s clerk stood on the quay, which is how I know which line is the one that matters. I have copied it as it came and put no gloss on it. A collector who explains a song has begun to write a sermon, and sermons get copied.

\subsection*{In the head and in the gutter}

The silt in the gutter came off the peat bank at Mud End and I have never got it out. The white bloom at the head is salt off the Sallow wind, which comes up the water on a flood tide and leaves a rime on everything aboard; it has eaten one letter of the Reed 30 date so that I cannot now read whether the barrow went down on the thirtieth or the twentieth. The eel slime along the fore-edge is not mine and is not the Weir woman’s either, but came off a board laid across the stern while she told me the date and would not tell me the cost; it dries pale and comes again whenever the damp gets into the fold. The pale round ring was made by setting a cold tube down on the leaf while I reached for the tiller. The tube was not used in the stern and the ring is not a wound, but it is the thinnest paper on the page.

The tallow thumb at the foot is mine, from holding the lamp low while a woman at the Tallow Works said something I wanted the end of; she did not tell me the end. The green bead in the lower corner is not slip. It is lead glaze from a girl come down from High Kiln who leaned over the gunwale to see the writing with the sweetness still at her mouth, touched the paper, said nothing, and went back up the terrace. I have left it where she put it. The grey along the margin is not mine and not the factor’s, and I have not swept it. There is no Last Day on a boat. The fold goes back under the stern seat and the silt stays in the gutter.

The small bare square in the lower margin is where I scraped a word away with a knife. I had written \emph{sixth} there, meaning the sixth morning I had shipped the oars and set the tube to a way nobody called, and then I counted and could not say which mornings were the same and which were not, so I took the word off. A figure that cannot be checked is a figure I have no right to leave standing, even in the margin.

\subsection*{At the foot, in a hand nobody will own}

\begin{quote}\itshape The slate keeps the figure. The river keeps the place where the figure stood. The stern keeps a hand that has never been asked to pull.\end{quote}

I asked a boatman, a clerk come down from the College, and a woman who sold eels at the Weir, and had three answers and no hand. I have left the line where it was written.

The book goes back under the stern seat and the tube into its wool sleeve. Tomorrow the oars go out on the flood and a house will come down to the bank, and I shall set the knuckle to the gunwale before the tube, and write the note before the face, and put the verbs back where the College struck them out. The four of us will enter the same year and our entries will not meet. The boat goes on.

\clearpage\phantomsection\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{Of the Roll of the Dead, the Remembering, and the Account Not Closed, Being Title the Ninth of the Ordinances of the Keeping, Copied into the Bank at the Hearthseat with the Roll-Clerk’s Margin, the Tallow Gone White, a Fish-Scale Pressed Flat, Two Corrections in Borrowed Hands, and a Line at the Foot Nobody Will Own}
\CRsheetheading{Of the Roll of the Dead, the Remembering, and the Account Not Closed, Being Title the Ninth of the Ordinances of the Keeping, Copied into the Bank at the Hearthseat with the Roll-Clerk’s Margin, the Tallow Gone White, a Fish-Scale Pressed Flat, Two Corrections in Borrowed Hands, and a Line at the Foot Nobody Will Own}
{\centering\FellFont\itshape\footnotesize\color{faded} An extract from the Court’s ordinances, written out for the roll-clerk’s counter at the bank in the Hearthseat, with the marginal hand of the clerk who carries names forward and reads them on the Remembering; the articles in Ledgerhand and the verbs restored beneath them, the roll set in a table, the form of a carry-forward left blank, the roll-song as it is said at the reading, two corrections in borrowed hands, and a line at the foot nobody has claimed · Copied at the bank in the Hearthseat in the last tend of Ash of the Thin Year, Y.H. 812, and carried forward at the Opening of the Slates, Ilmen 1, Y.H. 813, from Title the Ninth of the Ordinances of the Keeping as set down in the first years after the Rising of Y.H. 668 and sent down to the factor at Greybank in Y.H. 418, added to in Y.H. 782 and in the Thin Year; survives as three leaves of foolscap sewn with wire, kept under the roll-sheet in the bank: a grey Ash thumb at the head, tallow gone white and hard in the gutter, a fish-scale pressed flat at the second fold, iron filings in the crease where a tube-wrap lay, a crumb of barley bread at the foot, a damp line along the lower margin where a pail stood, a bone-stylus score where a word was taken out, two corrections in borrowed hands, and a line at the foot nobody will own.\par}\medskip
I keep the roll of the dead. It lies in a tin on this counter and it grows every tend and is never once emptied. A name goes in at the drawing, stays in at the pouring, and is still there when the house that gave it is a figure in the granary accounts and nothing else. On the Remembering I read the names in a clean voice, with the Hearth-fire behind the grating and nobody allowed to touch it. The ordinance is in Ledgerhand, with nobody in any of its sentences, which is the manner this Keeping has of making a death read as though it had happened to a roll and not to a person. I put the people back underneath.

\begin{quote}\itshape At the head, in mine, written small: Copied for the counter and from the roll. The verbs are mine. The absence of them is not. Let both stand.\end{quote}

\subsection*{Title the Ninth, as it stands in the bank}

\emph{From the Ordinances of the Keeping, Title the Ninth: Of the Roll of the Dead, the Remembering, and the Account Not Closed. Set down in the first years after the Rising of Y.H. 668; sent down to the factor at Greybank in Y.H. 418; added to in Y.H. 782 and in the Thin Year, Y.H. 812.}

\subsection*{I. Of the roll}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item Every vessel drawn is entered by slate-name and not by birth-name. The birth-name is turned face down at the entering and is not spoken at the Remembering. A name turned down is still a name, and the roll does not say so.

\item An account is never closed. It is carried forward. The name of a vessel already poured remains in the same hand as the names of vessels not yet drawn, and no column provides for an ending.

\item What is not entered did not happen. A death entered is a death that was collected; a death not collected is not entered, and the roll has no place for it.

\item Where the vessel is a foundling with no house, the name is written by the hand that writes the slate, and the house is the Keeping. Where the vessel has a house, the house is entered and not the person.

\item The measure is banked. The account stands. Nothing is lost that we have kept. Your return is recorded. These four sentences stand at the head of the roll and are read at no Weighing.

\end{enumerate}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Margin:} A woman stood here with her hand at the corner of her apron and asked whether her mother’s name was still on the roll, eleven years after the house that gave it was empty of people. I found the line and showed it to her, and the line was there. I have not entered what she said when she saw it, for there is no column for a daughter, and she took her hand off the counter before I could set a word down.\end{quote}

\subsection*{II. Of the Remembering}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item On the fourth day of the Five, being the Remembering, the names of the dead are spoken in a clean voice by an officer of the Keeping or the clerk he sends. The reader does not ask who is in the room.

\item A name is spoken once and is not explained. Where two names are alike, both are spoken, and the reader does not say which house is which.

\item Whole returns are announced on the same day. The figure is read in a clean voice and is not inspected. A whole return is entered at twelve hundred marks and forty unspent measures; the purchaser is entered where the Steward keeps his room and not upon this counter.

\item Where a name is disputed, the figure stands and the name is not changed. Where a name is not disputed, the figure still stands.

\item No fire is carried into the reading and no priest touches the grating. The reader stands with his back to the fire and his face to the roll.

\end{enumerate}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Margin:} I have read eleven Rememberings at this counter and was never once told whether the names are called up or called back. A keeper of the Hearth-fire said to me that the fire does not care which, and would say no more. I have set that at the edge, where a keeper’s sentence has no column.\end{quote}

\subsection*{III. Of the returning}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item Where one measure is pressed into one newborn vessel, the return is whole and the person comes back with memory. Where many measures are pooled and divided among many, the return is thin, and what comes back is a stranger with a faint interest in a life it cannot name.

\item A thin return is paid by the district at thirty marks and is paid in labour. The figure is entered to the district and not to the vessel. The vessel is not asked.

\item A whole return is booked at twelve hundred marks and forty unspent measures. The difference between the two figures is not a tax. It is not entered as a tax.

\item After the pouring the name is carried forward and not struck out. The vessel that has been poured is the vessel that stands upon the roll, and no second line is begun.

\end{enumerate}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Margin:} A woman asked whether a whole return brings back the person or only the shape the cradle can hold. I read her the eleventh article. She said that was not an answer, and I said it was the ordinance. Both are true and I have entered neither. There is no column in this book for the thing a woman wants to know.\end{quote}

\subsection*{IV. Of the death not collected}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item A house that has a death in it sends for the collector before the pot is broken at the door. The pot is broken after the draw and not before. A pot broken first lets out what the ordinance has not entered.

\item Where no collector is called, the death is not entered, and the grey that gathers in the corner of that house is gathered in the ordinary course and carried forward like any other grey.

\item What is held in a vessel from which no draw was made is not metered by the Keeping and is not returned to any account. The house is not asked, and this article is not sent to the factor.

\item An officer of the Keeping has no house and no kin. The roll is his family. He is not corrected for a name he did not hear.

\end{enumerate}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Margin:} A woman broke a pot at her door before I came up the stair in Ash and told me the heat had gone out of him already. I entered the draw and not the pot, for the pot was the earlier thing and this ordinance reaches only the later. She held the broken rim against her apron all the while I wrote, the way a woman holds a cup she has not yet set down.\end{quote}

\subsection*{The roll, as it stands at the counter}

\emph{Copied from the roll-sheet. The middle figures are the figures entered. The last column is mine and has no standing at any Weighing.}

Tend — Names entered — Carried forward — Whole returns — Thin returns — What the counter kept\par

Ash 1–10 — 19 (14 house, 5 Keeping) — 611 — 1 — 6 — a scale pressed flat in the fold\par

Ash 11–20 — 23 — 634 — 0 — 9 — a crumb at the foot, gone white\par

Ash 21–30 — 17 — 651 — 2 — 7 — the score where a word came out\par

Kindling — 6 (the year’s first measure) — 657 — 0 — 0 — a scorch off the watch-fire\par

Weighing — 0 — 657 — 3 — 0 — the clean voice, twice\par

Names entered on this leaf: sixty-five. Names struck: none. Accounts closed: none. The word that was taken out stands scored in the lower margin, the length of it, and I have not written it back.

\subsection*{The form of a carry-forward}

\emph{Set out at the end of Title the Ninth. I have copied it with the blanks as they stand. In eleven years no house has asked for the last line to be read twice.}

\begin{quote}\itshape Entered this day, being ---day of -------, in the year of the Hearth ------, the name of ----------------------, slate-name ----------------------, the birth-name turned down at the entering and not spoken at the Remembering; the measure drawn, banked and pressed into ------- vessel(s); the return whole / thin as the case stands; the account not closed but carried forward to the roll; the figure ---------------------- as the notice says; read on the Remembering in a clean voice by ----------------------, who did not ask who was in the room. What the house asked at this counter ----------------------, which is not entered.\end{quote}

\subsection*{The roll-song, said at the reading}

\emph{Said low at the counter on the Remembering, while the roll lies open and the reader stands with his back to the fire. Never at a Weighing, and never twice in one year.}

\begin{quote}\itshape Name on the roll and a crumb on the sill,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the pot at the door and the pail at the well;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape they read the name and they leave the face,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the house keeps the figure and not the place.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Whole for the one and thin for the crowd,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape forty unspent and a clean voice;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the cradle answers the way it can\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the roll goes on where the house gave out.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Ash in the corner and tallow gone white,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape a name turned down and a figure read twice;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the account stands open and the counter stands still,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the dead go forward because they must.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{In the narrow upright hand, against the last line of the second verse:} One figure entered; no deduction arises. \emph{In mine:} There is a cradle in that line and he has numbered it away. A cradle can be answered; a figure cannot. Both stand.\end{quote}

\subsection*{What the two borrowed hands did}

The College man came down from the Hearthseat with ink in two fingers of a cuff gone soft from washing. On article two he struck \emph{carried forward} and set \emph{the account stands} above it, which is the same thing said by a man who has never had to find a name at the bottom of a leaf. I have put \emph{carried forward} back underneath. A standing account is a thing a man can argue with; a carried name is a thing somebody has to keep moving, and somebody does.

The other hand is a keeper’s from the Weighing Hall, narrow, with soot at the edge. Against article eight he wrote \emph{the purchaser is recorded} where I had written that the purchaser is entered in the room the Steward keeps. Both stand. A keeper who says a thing is recorded has never had to go and find where. I have left my line where it is, because my line is the one the next clerk at this counter will read.

\subsection*{At the head and in the gutter}

The grey at the head is Ash off my own thumb, turning the leaf toward the lamp while I found a name; it is the colour of a corner swept too late and will not come out of the creases. The white in the gutter is tallow gone hard where a lamp was set down on the leaf at the Remembering and left until morning; it has taken the corner off a line without taking the sense and I have not picked it off. The fish-scale at the second fold came off a herring sent up from Greybank and laid beside the counter while I read; it has flattened into a little pale leaf of its own and has not been brushed away. The iron in the crease came off the tube-wrap an officer laid there and stood longer over than he needed to; there is always a little iron in the fold of this book and it has never once drawn the warmth out of the paper. The crumb at the foot is barley from a boy who held it while I read him his grandmother’s name and forgot to eat it. The damp along the foot is a pail set under the counter through a morning and has taken the corners off two lines. The score in the lower margin is a bone stylus drawn through the word \emph{died}, with \emph{was drawn} set above it; I have put \emph{died} back underneath and left the score standing, the length of the word they took out. There is no Last Day at a bank, and nothing here is swept up and burnt and called dealt with.

\subsection*{At the foot, in a hand nobody will own}

\begin{quote}\itshape The roll keeps the name and the cradle keeps the warmth.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape The space between them has no column.\end{quote}

I asked the keeper who reads the fire, a woman who came about her mother’s name, and a clerk come up from Greybank, and had three answers and no hand, as I have had before. I have left the lines where they were written.

The roll goes back into its tin. In a few days the Five will come and the Remembering will be read, and I shall stand with my back to the fire and say sixty-five names in a clean voice, and the roll will be full when I have finished as it was when I began. A woman will come to ask whether her mother is still on it, and I shall find the line and show it to her, and the line will be there. That is my trade: to keep a name moving and not to say where it goes.

\clearpage\phantomsection\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{Of the Shutting of the Pass and the Seven Years, Being an Extract from the Roll of the Cold Pass Kept at Keld Keep, with the Warden’s Claim Entered in the Number-First Hand, the Reeves’ Answer Out of Grath, the Four Terms Cut on the Slate in Slate Row, the Road-Song Carried Down the Rim Road, the Corrections of a Court Clerk in Ledgerhand, and a Line at the Foot Nobody Will Own}
\CRsheetheading{Of the Shutting of the Pass and the Seven Years, Being an Extract from the Roll of the Cold Pass Kept at Keld Keep, with the Warden’s Claim Entered in the Number-First Hand, the Reeves’ Answer Out of Grath, the Four Terms Cut on the Slate in Slate Row, the Road-Song Carried Down the Rim Road, the Corrections of a Court Clerk in Ledgerhand, and a Line at the Foot Nobody Will Own}
{\centering\FellFont\itshape\footnotesize\color{faded} A survey-roll keeper’s extract from the Warden’s roll at the pass, copied into Grathic letters with the Keldish endings struck off; the seven years in the number-first hand, the claim set down as an entry with a nought beneath it, the reeves’ answer in a sloping margin hand, the four terms cut from the slate in Sill’s Slate Row, a carter’s song taken down at the post, two corrections in the narrow upright Ledgerhand of a factor’s clerk, one nought cut in chalk, and a line at the foot in a hand nobody will own · Written at the survey post in the Cold Pass, ten leagues beyond Keld Keep, in Ash of Y.H. 812, the Thin Year, by the keeper of the roll, who states his measure before this and has set no name to it: nine and twenty when he was put to the roll, and not the number he went down with. Copied from the Warden’s roll of Y.H. 741 to 747, carried down the Rim Road in Stone of the same year with a lead cart, copied at Greybank in the Five, and entered at the Opening of the Slates into Y.H. 813. It survives as six leaves of rough survey paper sewn with wire into a board cover gone soft at the seam: coal smut ground into the head, an iron-red thumb at the second corner, a nought cut in chalk at the foot of the figures column, a frost-feather pressed flat between the fourth and fifth leaves and gone by noon, a bead of Ninth Gallery lead shut in the fold, a hard drop of tallow, and a grey Ash print along the outer fold which the keeper did not make and has not swept. A factor’s clerk borrowed the leaf at Greybank on a market morning and set his upright hand above two of the entries; the carter’s song was taken down from a man who would not give his number either.\par}\medskip
I keep the roll at the post. The post stands ten leagues beyond Keld Keep where the Rim Road goes through into Grath, and there is a post and no gate, which is the first thing a man from the south asks about and the last thing anybody tells him. The roll is not a history. It is a list of measures and of the days men went through, kept so that a reeve who says the pass was shut in the seventh year may be answered out of a book and not out of a memory. There is no quarrel about the figures at this post. Everything else is quarrelled about, and the quarrel is entered under the year in which it was written, not the year in which it happened.

I write in Grathic letters, because Keldish is cut in bone and a bone does not travel down a road in a pocket the way a letter does, and I have struck the endings off as our people do. My number stands where a name would stand: nine and twenty. I have put no name to this. A post keeps measures, not men.

This chapter is the one the factor’s clerk asks to see when he comes up from Greybank. I have copied it four times. On each copy the four terms stand as the slate cut them, and the one thing that will not go into a year-entry is the nought under the claim, which I have cut in chalk at the foot of the figures where a man looking for a gate will find it.

\subsection*{The years as the roll has them}

\emph{Copied from the Warden’s roll, which is kept face down in the survey room at the Keep and carried up to the post each Ash. The entries are in the number-first hand. I have put nothing in from the temple tells, which have their own dates and a comfort in them.}

\textbf{Y.H. 741.} The Cold Pass shut to Court traffic by Karric VII, Warden of the Rim. Entered as \emph{the pass is shut}. Beneath it, in the same hand: \emph{the true Hearth lies under this mountain}. Not entered again.

\textbf{Y.H. 742.} Assessors came up from the Hearthseat with slates and no soldiers. They wrote the claim down, took the verbs out of it, and went back. Entered as \emph{the matter is under consideration}.

\textbf{Y.H. 743.} Hired men came up the Rim Road from the coast with cold iron. Entered as \emph{precaution taken}. No dead entered.

\textbf{Y.H. 744.} A levy of clay-men out of Grath, who had no interest in the argument. They came because the levy was called and went up because it was called. Entered as \emph{the levy was answered}.

\textbf{Y.H. 745.} The road downriver stopped short of Greybank. Carts went by the river and took nine days where they took five. Entered as \emph{the road is otherwise engaged}.

\textbf{Y.H. 746.} Commissioners sat at the post with a slate and a piece of Keldish iron on one table. Entered as \emph{a conference at the post}, with no mention of who paid for the table.

\textbf{Y.H. 747.} Terms cut and the pass opened. Entered as \emph{peace, the road opened, the account standing}.

\textbf{Y.H. 749.} Grath, Keld, Vhalen and Sere set their marks to the neutrality of the Hearthseat. Entered as \emph{the fire is left standing}.

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{In the narrow hand of the factor’s clerk, against the entry of Y.H. 741:} An unauthorised claim is recorded. Strike \emph{true}.\end{quote}

I have not struck it. The Hearth is under the Keel and the Warden’s mountain is under the Rim, and both men have been told this since they were boys. The word is the Warden’s, and I have not put it there. A surveyor who takes the adjective out of a claim has left the claim standing and taken away the only part of it that could be argued with, which is a great kindness to do an argument and a poor one to do a man.

\subsection*{The claim, set beside what came down from Grath}

\emph{The left column is the roll’s. The middle is the Court’s annals, read to me at Greybank by the clerk who took the verbs out. The right came up in a sloping hand on the back of a reeve’s weigh-slip, and I have set it where I found it.}

The roll at the post — The Court’s annals — What came down from the reeves\par

The true Hearth lies under this mountain — An unauthorised claim is recorded — The Hearth is under the Keel. We have seen it. This is under a mountain.\par

The pass is shut — The frontier was closed to traffic — There is a post and no gate. What was there to shut?\par

The levy was answered — Precautions were taken — The clay-men came because the levy was called. They asked whose war it was and were answered with the weather.\par

Peace, the road opened — The matter is closed, the account standing — The road is open. The toll is the toll of 740 still.\par

The reeve gave a date where a figure was asked, which is the custom of that country and not an evasion of it. He set down the fourth of Frost and said the ferries stopped on that day and the eels ran on every day after it, whether the pass was shut or not. I put his date in the margin where it stands. It is not an answer to the question the roll asks, and it is the only true thing that came down from Grath in those seven years.

\subsection*{The seven years in figures}

Year — Men entered at the post — Measures declared — Warm-stone sold, in embers — What the roll calls it\par

741 — 1,204 — 1,204 — 96 — The pass is shut\par

742 — 311 — 309 — 41 — The matter is under consideration\par

743 — 88 — 88 — 12 — Precaution taken\par

744 — 60 — 58 — 9 — The levy was answered\par

745 — 47 — 44 — 6 — The road is otherwise engaged\par

746 — 51 — 50 — 7 — A conference at the post\par

747 — 1,188 — 1,188 — 91 — Peace, the road opened\par

The figures are neat. The sixty of 744 were clay-men from Grath who had been levied to fight a Warden over a Hearth they had never seen, and the roll enters them as \emph{the levy was answered}, a phrase with no men in it and no cost. I asked the old tally-man what the sixty had been. He said they had been cold, and went on with his counting. I have put \emph{cold} in the margin and not in the table, because a table is a thing a clerk reads and a margin is the only place in a roll where a silence is allowed to stand.

Under the 744 row I have cut a nought in chalk. It was there when I came to the roll, and it is not a figure for men. In the old roll a gate was drawn in the margin where the post stands, and somebody cut the gate away and put a nought in its place. A nought is a number. A post is a place. The two have stood side by side in this book for seventy years and nobody has asked me to make them agree.

\subsection*{The four terms, cut on the slate in Slate Row}

\emph{The treaty slate stands in Slate Row in Sill, which is a Court street and not a Grathish one, and is read at the Cross on market morning. The thane of Clay was not asked. The Grathish say this is how all important treaties are made; the Court says the slate was cut in the presence of four powers and the thane’s absence is not an entry. I have copied the four terms as they are cut.}

Clause — As it is cut on the slate — What the roll set beside it\par

One — Keld keeps the pass and the survey shaft. — \emph{The post stands.} A surveyor goes down and comes up, or does not, and the Warden’s men do not promise the third thing.\par

Two — Grath keeps the road. — \emph{The road is open.} Open to whom is not cut, and the toll at the post is the toll of 740 still.\par

Three — The Hearthseat is neutral ground. — \emph{The fire is left standing.} None of ours has been allowed to stand near it, and none of ours has asked.\par

Four — The border is fixed at the survey post. — \emph{A post and no gate.} The reeve’s nought was cut at the slate’s foot and then scraped away, and the scrape is still there.\par

In Y.H. 749 the four powers set their marks to the neutrality the slate had only promised. I have copied the marks as four strokes and not as a word, because a stroke is the only part of a treaty a man at this post can check with his own eyes.

\subsection*{The road-song}

\emph{Taken down at the post from a carter going down with lead, who would not give his number and sang it instead. Sung going down the Rim Road, never going up.}

\begin{quote}\itshape Seven winters the pass stood shut,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the Warden’s fire under the stone;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the assessor came with a slate and a word,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the word went down like rain.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape One for the Warden’s mountain,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape one for the Keel beneath;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape four for the powers that set their marks,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and none for the man between.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape There’s a post and there’s no gate,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and a nought where the gate should be;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the number goes on the arm, not the road,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the mountain keeps its own.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape The clay-men came and asked whose war,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and were told to ask the levy;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the road stands open to every cart\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the toll stands where it stood.\end{quote}

He said he had learned it from his mother and she from a man who went up in 744 and came back in 747, and that the man never said which of the seven years he had spent in the pass. I have left that where he put it.

\subsection*{What the Court hand did, at Greybank}

A clerk of the factor’s office borrowed the leaf on a market morning. He writes upright and narrow, and takes the verbs out as though a verb were a thing a man could smuggle past a weigh. He laid his hand on the top sheet before he looked at either of us, which is the manner of that table.

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item Against \emph{the true Hearth lies under this mountain}: \emph{an unauthorised claim is recorded}.

\item Against \emph{the pass is shut}: \emph{the frontier was closed to traffic}.

\item Against \emph{the levy was answered}: \emph{precautions were taken}.

\item Against \emph{peace, the road opened}: \emph{the matter is closed, the account standing}.

\item Against \emph{there is a post and no gate}: \emph{the frontier is unguarded}. There is no gate to guard and never was, but a sentence with a guard in it can be entered.

\item Against the nought I cut in chalk he wrote nothing at all. The hand passed over it without a stroke, which is the readiest way of correcting a figure I have yet seen.

\end{itemize}

I have left both readings everywhere, the thin one under the neat one, as a repaired wall keeps the old break under the new keying and does not pretend the first hand never touched the stone. A clerk who takes the men out of a sentence leaves the road standing by itself, and a road standing by itself has carried nobody and cost nobody, and there is no figure in it to argue with.

\subsection*{At the head and in the gutter}

The smut at the head is mine; I hold the leaves down with my whole hand because the draught at the post comes along the floor and takes paper before it takes a man. The iron-red at the second corner came off the mine-reeve’s point when he checked a man who had given a figure that would not hold; he did not look at me and I did not look at the man. The chalk at the foot of the figures is the nought, and it comes away on the cuff and is put back each Ash, which is more than can be said of the gate it replaced. The frost-feather was on the survey stone after a warm night and was gone by the time I found the leaf to press it in. The lead bead rolled out of the Ninth Gallery; a surveyor laid it on the leaf and went away without it. The tallow is my lamp set too near the roll. The grey along the outer fold is not mine and not the Court’s. I have not swept it. There is no Last Day at this post.

\subsection*{At the foot, in a hand nobody will own}

\begin{quote}\itshape Four powers set their marks to the fire,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and one man cut a nought in the stone;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the road went open, the pass went shut,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the account came back the same.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Ask the post what it kept.\end{quote}

I asked the tally-man, a surveyor come up from the shaft, and a carter who had been down in 747, and had three answers and no hand. I have left the line where it was written. The roll goes back to its nail beside the post. Tomorrow a man will state what he holds before he says who he is, the number will be entered, and the gate will still not be there.

\clearpage\phantomsection\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{The Sack-Book of Fenna Tallow, Being the Prices She Asked and Gave on the Circuit from Sill to the Salt Pans and Back, with the Dues of Every Road Written on the Same Leaf as the Goods, a Page the Rain Took, Three Corrections in Borrowed Hands, and a Verse Carried in the Mouth}
\CRsheetheading{The Sack-Book of Fenna Tallow, Being the Prices She Asked and Gave on the Circuit from Sill to the Salt Pans and Back, with the Dues of Every Road Written on the Same Leaf as the Goods, a Page the Rain Took, Three Corrections in Borrowed Hands, and a Verse Carried in the Mouth}
{\centering\FellFont\itshape\footnotesize\color{faded} A pedlar’s pocket ledger, kept in a waxed oilcloth sack under the small goods; figures set down on such paper as came to hand, each road’s due written against the goods that paid it, with an entire salt-paper leaf lost to weather and its debt entered from the other end; corrected in three borrowed hands and never copied fair · Kept by Fenna Tallow, a pedlar of Sill who walks the Clay, river, marsh and Salt roads with tallow, needles, coarse pots and small news; begun in Grain of Y.H. 812, the Thin Year of the Long Cold, written up behind carts, at the Cross, at the Greybank beam and at the tide-tally house, and carried forward at the Opening of the Slates, Ilmen 1, Y.H. 813; the last figures set down at the Cross on Ash 10 of that year. It survives in the oilcloth sack in four kinds of paper --- the back of a Court notice gone soft at the fold, a weigh-slip the beam clerk had done with, a strip of birch bark out of the Fen, and a leaf of salt-paper kept dry against the practice of the country --- with a tallow thumb at the head, barley grease in the first gutter, a pig bristle pressed into the Sill leaf, eel slime along the river page, a fish-hook nick, marsh mud on the Nine Pots corner, a drop of Sere wine gone brown, a grey Ash print nobody will own, a pressed reed, a scorch where the book lay too near a brazier, one leaf dissolved by rain so that two figures are gone, and corrections in the hands of a Slate Row clerk, a factor’s clerk and a Council clerk, none of them mine\par}\medskip
I carry my figures in a sack, under the tallow and the needles. A slate is a thing that lies on a table, and a table is a thing a pedlar does not own. I write on the back of what is given me: a Court notice soft at the fold, a weigh-slip the beam clerk has finished with, birch bark out of the Fen, a leaf of salt-paper I keep dry in spite of the country. Four sorts of paper, and no two of them hold a figure for the same length of time.

Twelve copper bits to a silver mark; twenty marks to a Sere crown, which comes north because it must and goes south again because it can. The Court calls five marks an ember. I asked an officer’s clerk once what an ember looked like, and he said it was a figure that had been entered. I set that down, because a woman who walks should know what she is not carrying.

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{In the narrow upright hand of a clerk out of Slate Row:} Coin and reckoning entered. Ember: five marks. \emph{Underneath, in mine:} He has copied the Court’s own sentence onto my page and taken the verbs out of it, as though a verb were another article I might sell from the sack. I have put \emph{calls} back. It is the Court that calls it five marks. My sack does not agree.\end{quote}

At each place I write the price and the due on the same line, because they come out of the same purse. A clerk at a board writes one figure for the goods and another at a gate for the road, and a man who stays in one town may believe the two are different things. I have walked the road. They are not.

\subsection*{Sill, at the Cross}

\emph{Account-day, the tenth, twentieth and thirtieth. Read twice: once for the moot, and once for those that came late. The bell goes four, four and a gap and nobody crosses himself.}

Article — Asked — Given\par

Brown-edged barley loaf — 1 bit — 1 bit, eaten on the step\par

Quart of small ale, watered — 1 bit — 1 bit, and watered twice\par

Sour milk, a quart — 1 bit — 1 bit, if the pail is still out\par

Salt herring — 2 bits — 2 bits\par

Smoked eel, Fishstairs, before the shade goes off the board — 3 bits — 3; salted, 2\par

Eel skin, dried — 1 mark — 1 mark; it has been down the water to be sold back up it\par

Coarse pots, the score off the racks — 4 bits — 4 bits, and a fifth pot if one has a hairline\par

Tile, the hundred — 9 bits — 9 bits, delivered, which is to say dropped twice\par

Barley gruel at a house door — not sold — given, and not entered\par

A crust laid in a basket in the shade — not sold — not lifted, not named\par

\emph{The dues I paid going out:}

Due\par

South bridge, loaded cart — 1 bit\par

North bridge — nothing; the Fishstairs argued it and won\par

River road, beast on the bank way — 1 bit\par

Plank walk at the Weir — 1 bit; the boards are counted, which is not the same as saying which will bear a woman\par

Pig driven north to Cold Acre — 2 bits, and weighed at the block besides\par

Barrow of grey out through the north gate — not weighed, not entered, nothing asked\par

Man going up for the well that never freezes — 1 bit; he brings back a common stone and does not call it a warm-stone\par

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{In mine:} One in twelve is printed on the notice and read over the basket, once for the moot and once for those who came late. Another figure goes around the yards that I cannot weigh, and I have no column for either. A pedlar who writes down what she cannot weigh does not last a tend.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{In the Slate Row hand:} Nought against the grey. No such due against the north bridge. \emph{Underneath, in mine:} A nought is a figure and the grey is not one. It goes out every market afternoon heaped a little above the sides where the load has shifted, and nobody looks at it twice. I have left his nought standing beside my space, the way a pot stands beside its own crack.\end{quote}

\subsection*{Nine Pots, Reedholt and Mud End}

Eight leagues west to the kiln village in old feud with Sill; four east to the reed huts; three downriver to the peat hamlet. I carry needles to all three and come back with something heavier.

Due paid\par

Nine Pots road — no toll, and none ever collected; it is ours and theirs both, which is why neither mends it\par

Cart using it in Silt — a pot from the shared pit, or a knuckle; the two villages have never settled which\par

Reedholt, firm boards pointed out to a stranger — half a bit, and half again after rain, because the firm boards move\par

Barrow of peat out of Mud End in Stone — 5 bits; no figure in the Long Cold, when there was none to sell\par

Ash-mite paste, a thimble, at Mud End — 4 bits, no questions\par

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{In mine:} I paid a pot going west and a knuckle coming back, and I cannot say which cost me more, though the knuckle healed badly and the pot was a good one. The road is free. The being let across it is not.\end{quote}

\subsection*{Down the Clay Road to Greybank}

Eighteen leagues, packed clay over corduroy; five days by cart in Grain, six in Silt. Two bits at this end, two bits more at the quay, and an assessor may stop the cart on it without asking the thane, and does.

Due paid\par

Cart with a load, Sill end — 2 bits\par

The same at the factor’s beam — 2 bits more\par

Beast on the hoof — 1 bit\par

Foot passenger — 1 bit; nothing on Account-day, when a man comes to hear the figure\par

A barrow of grey going up — not weighed; the factor’s man has never once asked\par

Here a sack of salt from the pans stands at \textbf{3 marks} on the factor’s board. Down at the pans they asked me a mark at the flood and two at the ebb. A carter will tell you all three figures are true, because each is said where the salt is standing, and he is right in a way that keeps him walking.

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{In the factor’s clerk’s hand:} Road charges, current. \emph{Underneath, in mine:} He has written \emph{current} over what I paid, as though a figure were a man who might be owed money by a road. I have left my row where it was. A road does not owe a carter anything, and the carter knows it.\end{quote}

\subsection*{The Salt Road and the Quay}

Eighty leagues by the coast pass. Salt, glass, rope and dried fish go out; coin and contracts on salt-paper come back, and the damp gets into both.

Article — At the flood — At the ebb\par

Salt, a sack off the pans — 1 mark — 2 marks, and the carter does not complain\par

Glass, a green sheet off the Cliffs — 1 mark — 2 marks, after the Glaze boat has come in\par

Rope, a tarred coil — 1 mark — 1 mark, and tar on my hands before I pay\par

Tar, a pail — 4 bits — 1 mark when the galleys are refitting\par

Dried fish, a string — 1 bit — 1 bit, or two if the gulls have followed the boat in\par

Brine-gull feathers, a bundle — 1 bit — 1 bit; the bird is not consulted\par

Red wine, a jar out of Sere — 2 marks — 2 marks; salt on the rim and no charge for the salt\par

A bed on the Quay, the month — 4 marks — 4 marks, and the floor is a bit\par

\emph{The dues:}

Due\par

Sack of salt at the coast pass — 1 mark to the Council of Tides\par

Coil of rope, or a sheet of glass — 1 bit\par

Cart with a load, this end, and again at Greybank — 2 bits, then 2 bits more\par

Contract written on salt-paper — no fee; it will not last the journey, which the Council calls a virtue\par

Man going up with the glass at the turn of the month — 3 bits, returned if he comes back with the answer\par

A keel at the Quay, the month — 2 marks, or a fish off the catch\par

A boat passing upriver with a share aboard — by the lot, not the league; no figure\par

A net trailed at dawn under the tally house — no fee, and the draw is not entered\par

A man carried down for the salted boat — 1 bit for the carrying; he is entered before he goes\par

A man who dies at sea — no slate; the sea keeps its own account\par

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{In the Council clerk’s leaning hand:} \emph{toll} struck out and \emph{contribution freely entered} written over it. \emph{In mine:} He has left every figure standing. A Council that cannot charge a toll has found a finer name for one, and I paid it out of the same purse.\end{quote}

\subsection*{The page the rain took}

I keep my salt-paper dry, contrary to the practice of the country, and the country had its way with me between the coast pass and the quay. One leaf went. On it I had written three things: what I gave for salt at the turn of the ebb, a due paid to a man who would not give his name, and a figure a woman asked me to carry upriver in my fist and not speak. All three are gone. The paper did not tear; it let go, the way a wet thing lets go of a hand.

On the leaf facing it, in the narrow upright hand at Greybank, the factor’s clerk has entered a debt for a sum that may or may not be the one I carried. He writes \emph{the figure stands}. I have not crossed it out and have not joined it to my empty place. One figure is gone and one remains, and the remaining one has a hand behind it, which is more than I can say for mine.

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{In the Council clerk’s hand, against the space:} Instrument void by exposure; no claim can lie. \emph{Underneath, in mine:} True. It is the kind of truth a man has who has never stood in the rain with a sack on his back.\end{quote}

\subsection*{The verse I carry}

\emph{Said while the bags are being counted, never while a slate lies open and never facing the direction of Slate Row.}

\begin{quote}\itshape A bit at the bridge and a bit at the shade,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape a mark at the pass and a pot at the pit;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the beam asks twice and the water asks none,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and south to the fire there’s a place with no gate.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Four for the roads and a fifth for the ford,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and one for the road that has never a post;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape they pay at the post and they pay at the beam,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the road to the fire pays wherever you are.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape The rain took a figure, the slate kept one;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape I ask at the load and I pay at the load;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the hand knows the weight and the mouth knows the price,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the weight goes down where the figure should be.\end{quote}

A Slate Row clerk set \emph{four roads entered} against the first line of the second verse. There are five and I have put nothing in the place. A nought is a number and the road to the fire is a direction.

\subsection*{What the leaves show}

The brown at the head is tallow, mine, from holding the quire open with one hand while I counted the other. The barley grease in the first gutter came from a crust laid down on the Sill leaf while a woman told a child to eat and the child would not. The pig bristle went in at the weighing board with a driver holding one ear and the weigher the other. The eel slime is from a basket set down at the Fishstairs edge where no Court slate has reached. The fish-hook nick came off a hook put down in a hurry by a man paying for six herrings and charged for five, or the other way; he would not settle it and I have not entered it. The marsh mud is Reedholt on the Nine Pots corner. The brown drop is wine from a jar out of Sere, set beside a figure I had no column for. The grey along the margin is not mine and not any clerk’s, and I have not swept it. The reed was pressed between two leaves by a girl at the Weir who wanted to know if it would keep, and it has kept better than some of the figures. The scorch is where the book lay too near a brazier on the Quay; it took the corner off one row and not the sense of it.

There is no Last Day in a sack. Nothing in it gets burnt in the morning.

Tomorrow is the twentieth of Ash and the market comes back to the Cross. I shall set the basket in the post’s finger’s width of shade, ask the figure before I lift the load, and write it on the back of what comes to hand. The book goes under the tallow and the sack goes over my shoulder, and nothing in either has been closed.

\clearpage\phantomsection\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{The Litany of the Sallow Draw, Being the Order of the Return as the Dippers of Vhal Say It at the Salt Pans Before the Nets Go Out}
\CRsheetheading{The Litany of the Sallow Draw, Being the Order of the Return as the Dippers of Vhal Say It at the Salt Pans Before the Nets Go Out}
{\centering\FellFont\itshape\footnotesize\color{faded} A litany of the Return said at the pans in the half-light, the pan-master reading and the dippers answering, with the draw read between the stations and the answer made twice: once to the water and once into the knot-count; written on salt-paper, which will not outlast the wet, and copied forward every spring; with the rubrics of the pans, seven stations and their answer, the draw-song, the correction of a Council tally-clerk which the salt has eaten clean through, a salt-wife’s knot, and a line at the foot nobody will own · Written in charcoal rubbed with salt on salt-paper at the Salt Pans outside Vhal in the last tend of Stone, Y.H. 812, the Thin Year, by the pan-master’s daughter who counts the draw, and copied forward each spring because the paper goes soft in the damp; the surviving leaf is the third copy, made at the pans in Ilmen, Y.H. 813, the fourth station supplied from memory and not agreeing with the second copy held at the tide-tally house, which has itself gone nearly to pulp. It survives with salt bloom in the gutter that has eaten the clerk’s ink and left the charcoal standing, tar worked into the head from the net-coil, a splash that took out the fifth answer, a knot of tarred twine tied through the lower corner, the white print of a bare foot at the foot, a crust of coarse salt in the fold that crunches when the leaf is opened, and a line nobody will own.\par}\medskip
I count the draw at the pans. Before light the nets go over and the dippers say this with the cord still in their hands, while the salt is wet on the boards and the gulls have not yet come down for what we spill. Everything in Vhal is written on paper made to rot, and this is written on the same. The Court writes on slate and calls it kept; we write on salt-paper and call it said. In the damp the leaf goes soft, the words come up in pale islands, and we copy it again in the spring. No two copies agree. What follows is the third copy, and where the fourth station differs from the second I have put down what my mother said and left the other standing underneath, because a prayer that agrees with itself has been copied by somebody who was not there.

A tally-clerk from the tide-tally house borrowed the second copy on a morning when the pans were covered and set his correction above mine in Court ink, narrow and upright and very sure. The salt took his ink before it took mine, which is the first thing this coast taught me about the Keeping: charcoal rubbed with salt holds, and the figure they send up the road does not. I have left the holes where his sentences were. A hole where a correction stood is worth more than the correction.

\subsection*{The manner of it, written small at the head}

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item Say it at the pans in the half-light, before the nets are trailed. A net blessed after it is out has been blessed for the fish and not for the dead, and the fish do not ask.

\item Face the ebb. The draw goes seaward against the wind; a prayer said with it has a better chance of arriving. The old dippers say this. I have never tested it and neither have they.

\item Do not read the draw until after the third station. A number spoken early stays in the ears of the dippers and they net by it all morning, which is how a bad figure becomes a habit.

\item The answer is made twice: once to the water, which is not asked to keep anything, and once into the knot-count, which is. If you have no cord, answer into your hands and tie them when you get home.

\item If a brine-gull takes a word, let it go. Gulls are the only creatures in Vhal that pray without being asked, and they get no better answer than we do.

\item Never say the seventh station over a boat that has gone out and not come back. Say the place where the name would stand and leave the rest in the water, where the boat is.

\item There are five days on the Court’s slate that belong to no month. At the pans we keep the flood and the ebb, which come oftener and are entered nowhere.

\end{itemize}

\subsection*{The litany}

\emph{The pan-master reads. The dippers answer with the cord in their hands. Between the third station and the fourth the pan-master reads the draw, low, so that the water hears it before the tally does.}

\subsection*{I. Of the going out}

\begin{quote}\itshape The world was fired whole and went in one anger.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape What ran out of it went a long way and is going still.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape The Warm goes seaward on the ebb with the silt,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the pan takes what the pan can hold.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Do not tell a dipper the Sallow is the Waste.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape It is nearer, and it comes back.\end{quote}
