\emph{Answer:} Out with the draw. In with the tide. Name it, or leave the place.

\subsection*{II. Of the Nine}

\begin{quote}\itshape Nine hands went after what had run away.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape They drove the repairs home the way a cooper drives a hoop.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape We say them by their number and not by their houses,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape because a house in Vhal is a thing that can be denied in a season.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Nine went. One is still abroad, somewhere over the water.\end{quote}

\emph{Answer:} Out with the draw. In with the tide. Name it, or leave the place.

\subsection*{III. Of the paper}

\begin{quote}\itshape Everything here is written on what will not last.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape A contract that lasts too long has stopped earning.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape The Return is the one account we would have last,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and we write it on the same leaf as the rest.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape It goes soft. We copy it. What is copied is not kept,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and what is kept is not the same as what comes back.\end{quote}

\emph{Answer:} Out with the draw. In with the tide. Name it, or leave the place.

\emph{Here the pan-master reads the draw. The dippers do not repeat it. The draw-song is said under the reading, so low that the clerk at the tide-tally house has never written it down.}

\begin{quote}\itshape The draw goes seaward against the wind,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the net comes up with weed and silt;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape four for the pans and one for the gone,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and a knot in the cord that the clerk cannot split.\end{quote}

\subsection*{IV. Of the pouring}

\begin{quote}\itshape One into one comes back to a boat he can name,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape with the cup and the share and the side of the deck.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Many into many come back to a deck they never walked,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape with a hankering for a hearth they never sat at.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Both are poured. The Council will pay for one of them.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape We say the prayer over both, because a prayer is not a contract.\end{quote}

\emph{Answer:} Out with the draw. In with the tide. Name it, or leave the place.

\emph{The second copy has this station differently, in my grandmother’s hand: “One into one comes back with his name and the price of bread.” She had never been to Vhal. I have set her words underneath and left mine above, which is the wrong order, and the only one I can use.}

\subsection*{V. Of the man from Greybank}

\begin{quote}\itshape A man comes up the Salt Road with a tube in wool\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and a slate that keeps what the paper lets go.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape He reads one in twelve as the notice says, twice,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and writes what the damp has taken out of ours.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape His ink goes pale in a season. Our charcoal does not.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Do not call that an argument. It is weather.\end{quote}

\emph{Answer:} Out with the draw. In with the tide. Name it, or leave the place.

\emph{The splash that took this answer came off a bucket knocked against the leaf on the morning we copied. I have put the answer back from the second copy, which had it whole. The damp has now eaten the second copy’s version too, so there is no way of knowing whether I put back the right words.}

\subsection*{VI. Of the water}

\begin{quote}\itshape Do not pray to the Sallow. It is water.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape It takes what is put into it and gives what it takes,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape on its own hours, which are not ours.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape The Court taxes the draw going out.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Nobody thanks it coming in.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape A thing that keeps nothing cannot be entered,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape which is the end of the argument as far as the pans go.\end{quote}

\emph{Answer:} Out with the draw. In with the tide. Name it, or leave the place.

\emph{A woman who had lost a brother off the pulled benches said, when we came to this station, that the sea kept a man longer than the Court kept a name and gave him back in worse condition, which is the whole of her religion and cost her nothing to say.}

\subsection*{VII. Of the name}

\begin{quote}\itshape Say the name at the going out and again at the coming in.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape If you have no name, tie the knot and leave the place.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Do not put a figure in the place. The clerk will do that,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and a figure is a thing that can be denied in a season.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Leave the place the length of a name and do not fill it with weather.\end{quote}

\emph{Answer:} Out with the draw. In with the tide. Name it, or leave the place.

\subsection*{What the clerk set above}

The salt has eaten most of him. I have set down what can still be read, with the gaps left the width they are.

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item At \emph{the Return is the one account we would have last}, he wrote: \emph{the measure is banked and the return recorded.} The first three words have gone. \emph{Recorded} remains, standing alone in the gutter, which is a better account of his hand than anything he meant to say.

\item At \emph{what is kept is not the same as what comes back}, he wrote: \emph{nothing is lost that we have kept.} The salt took it except the word \emph{kept}, which has come up pale and sits under his line like a bone in a shallow grave. I have not covered it.

\item At \emph{a prayer is not a contract}, he wrote: \emph{observance not entered.} This one the salt left whole, which I take as a judgment on the damp rather than on him. It is the only true line he wrote and it cost him nothing, because a nought has never had a hand in it.

\item At the place where a name would stand he tied nothing and wrote \emph{vacancy} in the figure of a round nought. The dippers tied their knot underneath it. The knot held. The nought went soft and came up as a pale island with a hole in it.

\end{itemize}

He asked me what a dipper learned by the litany. I told him the order of the stations and where to stand for the ebb. He entered both. The leaf came back with his ink already going, which is the only notice a clerk has ever given me that he had been at it.

\subsection*{What the salt-wife tied in the corner}

There is a knot of tarred twine through the lower corner, four turns and a bight, tied there by a woman who rakes the third pan and will not give her name to a leaf. It is the count the pans keep and the Court does not: four for the pans and one that went out on the ebb and did not come in on the flood. She would not say who. She would not say whether the five turns were for a debt paid or a debt still running, which in Vhal is the same question asked in two voices.

I have not untied it. Twine with a knot in it keeps a count without a figure, which is more than I can say for the paper it is tied to, and more than I can say for the slate at the tide-tally house, where a sheet left in the damp is a debt made nothing and a man goes out lighter in the face.

\subsection*{At the head and in the gutter}

The tar at the head is off the net-coil and went in when I laid the leaf down on it to keep the wind from turning the second sheet over. It has worked into the grain and no washing takes it out, which is a kindness from tar and not from anybody else. The salt bloom came up out of the paper and ate the clerk before it ate me, for the reason written above. Along the gutter there is grey in one place, off a cuff that had been near the Ash in the north country and had no business at these pans; ours comes white, and I have kept the grey to be reminded that there is another kind. The splash took the fifth answer and I have put it back from a copy that is now gone. The crust in the fold crunches when the leaf is opened and has never been brushed off, because a prayer that crunches has plainly been used. The white print at the foot is a bare foot, a girl’s, come in off the pans at fourteen with the salt still on it, who stood over me while I wrote and would not say what tide she had named. I have left it where she set it.

\subsection*{At the foot, in a hand nobody will own}

Struck through once and written again underneath, very small, in a hand that is not mine, not the clerk’s and not the salt-wife’s:

\begin{quote}\itshape What the tide takes, it does not keep.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape What the slate keeps, it does not return.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Only the paper does both, and only by going.\end{quote}

I asked the pan-master, a dipper, the woman of the third pan and a tally-clerk come down from the Quay, and had four answers and no hand. I have left the struck line standing. At first light I shall say the seven stations while the nets go over, the clerk will write what he can before the damp takes it, and I shall tie the knot again in the corner, which is the only part of this that has never needed copying.

\clearpage\phantomsection\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{The Salt Country, Being the Road-Account of Dessa Reed, a Potter’s Daughter out of Low Kiln in Sill, Who Took a Cart of Flat Tile and Fish-Dishes up the Salt Road to Vhal and Came Back with Sallow Salt, a Coil of Tarred Rope and a Contract the Rain Had Eaten; with the Prices of the Quay, the Four Questions and the One Answer, the Net-Song Said at First Light, Three Corrections in Borrowed Hands, and a Line at the Foot Nobody Will Own}
\CRsheetheading{The Salt Country, Being the Road-Account of Dessa Reed, a Potter’s Daughter out of Low Kiln in Sill, Who Took a Cart of Flat Tile and Fish-Dishes up the Salt Road to Vhal and Came Back with Sallow Salt, a Coil of Tarred Rope and a Contract the Rain Had Eaten; with the Prices of the Quay, the Four Questions and the One Answer, the Net-Song Said at First Light, Three Corrections in Borrowed Hands, and a Line at the Foot Nobody Will Own}
{\centering\FellFont\itshape\footnotesize\color{faded} A pot-woman’s road-book, set down first in charcoal on strips of birch bark on the road and copied at Greybank onto the back of a spoiled salt-docket; the road and the prices in the writer’s short clay-hand, the coast sayings kept in the hearing and not made into proverbs, the verbs left in under every borrowed correction, and one line at the foot in a hand that has never come forward · Written in Ember and Grain of Y.H. 812, the Thin Year after the Long Cold, at Vhal and on the Salt Road, by Dessa Reed, a thrower’s daughter of the Clay Yard in Low Kiln, Sill, who took tile and fish-dishes up the Salt Road and came down in Grain with a sack of salt, a coil of rope, a green bead of cliff-glass given for a bit and a promise, and a tide contract gone soft with rain; copied at Greybank in Ilmen of Y.H. 813 onto the back of a salt-docket voided by the damp and carried down the Clay Road to Sill. It survives folded into oiled sailcloth under the wheel-shed bench, stiff with salt and soft by turns: a white bloom at the head that has eaten the last letters off two words, a thumb of tar at the fold off the coil she carried home, a brine-gull feather pressed into the second leaf, a green bead of cliff-glass flattened into the lower corner, tarred rope fibre worked into the third crease, a fish-hook nick at the fore-edge, a ring of small ale near the song, a tide-name written in salt in the margin which the sun took by noon and left a white place, a small square of bare paper where a word was scraped away with a knife-point, a grey Ash print along the outer fold which the writer did not make and has not swept, three corrections in borrowed hands, and a line at the foot in a hand nobody will own\par}\medskip
I knock a pot before I set it down. That is the first thing a potter’s daughter learns and the last thing I have managed not to unlearn. In Ember of the Thin Year I took a cart of flat tile and fish-dishes up the Salt Road to Vhal, eighty leagues with a team that was not mine, and came back in Grain with a sack of Sallow salt, a coil of tarred rope, a green bead of cliff-glass given for a bit and a promise, and a contract that had gone damp on the road and was therefore no contract at all. What I saw and what I was told have not agreed, and I have not made them agree. A woman who mends pots for a living knows that two edges may be brought near and still not be the same edge.

\subsection*{The road, and the dry man}

Eighteen leagues of Clay Road to Greybank with the tile riding high, and then the coast pass, and then the salt country begins under the wheels before it shows in the air. At Greybank a man with a slate asked what I had brought before he asked who I was, which is a fairness of a kind, and wrote the word \emph{tile} as though a word were a thing a man could weigh.

Below the pass the clay gives way to reeds. At the Standing Post I was put up on the boards and was not told which boards would bear me, and paid a bit for asking, which the reeve called a fine and I have entered as tuition. They say a dry man is a dangerous man. I was dry. They lodged me accordingly, on boards that moved after the rain, and gave me eel and no answer.

Beyond the Peat Line the villages stand empty in the middle of the day, with squares of bare clay in the doorways where house-rolls once hung. I asked a guide whether the people had gone north or south. He said they had gone where the account went, and would not say which direction that was. I have set the answer down and not argued with it. A man of Sill would have named a village. This one named a thing with no road under it.

\subsection*{The sea that runs against the wind}

The Sallow is the colour of skimmed milk. The first thing a clay person notices about it is that it does not behave like water. I stood on the Quay at the third hour with my coat held and watched the water go one way and the wind go the other, and neither of them asked leave of the other. They say the tide follows the Warm and not the moon. I have put that where the sayings go and not under a figure, because I have no instrument for the moon and do not pretend to one.

I asked a dipper why the Sallow was said to keep a Hearth of its own beneath the salt and the Court’s fire to be only its chimney. He said that if I had come eighty leagues to be told where a Hearth stood I had come the wrong way, and went on trailing his net. A woman at the pans told me the same thing with a rake in her hand, and added that no man had ever taken her down to see which way the door of it opened. I have left both sayings where they were said. A saying is a thing a man carries in his mouth, and a mouth is a vessel that leaks, which is why the dippers write theirs in salt and let the sun have them.

\subsection*{The four questions}

Vhalen has no word for a guest and no word for a friend. It has a word for a man whose account is current, and that is what I was called before I paid, while I paid, and after I had paid. They say a stranger’s coin warms before his face. My coin was cold in my purse, and nobody looked at my face overmuch.

Four questions I asked in four rooms, and had one answer in four mouths.

What I asked — What was said to me — What I entered\par

May I lodge here tonight? — \emph{Current.} — A bed, paid.\par

Who holds the debt on this boat? — \emph{A twelfth goes through the mother.} — Nothing. I could not find the woman to ask her.\par

When must it be paid? — \emph{When it rains.} — No date. A date is a thing a man can be held to.\par

What if the paper is lost? — \emph{Then it is a virtue.} — Left standing, with the others.\par

The last is the answer I have carried home. In Vhal a contract written on salt-paper that rots in the damp is no contract, and they call that a virtue. A law that lasts too long is a law that has stopped earning. I have carried paper up the Clay Road that was written to outlast a man and be read at the Weighing, and I have never once heard anybody call \emph{that} virtuous. Both kinds of paper can let a man go. Only one of them lets him go with the witnesses gone too.

\subsection*{The benches and the twelfth}

At the Quay I saw the pulled benches of the salt galleys, where condemned men row seven years or until their hands give out, whichever comes first. A girl at the rope-rack said a Vhaleni hull is never long from the oars. She said it the way my mother said the kiln will have its wood, and I have written it in her words and not in mine.

Boat shares pass through mothers. A man who marries into a boat-owning family is said to be come aboard, and his opinion on the boat is counted at half, which every woman on that Quay told me as though it were a joke told against themselves and not a rule of the house. Slaves may be bought in Vhal and cannot be returned there: the Council will not pay for a thin return and will not house one. A man in a clean coat came down from Greybank asking after such a return and went away with his question still in his coat, which was the driest thing I saw in a wet country.

\subsection*{What the cart carried and what came back}

\emph{Figures as they were given at the third hour, set with what I entered at home. The left column is the figure a woman carries. The right is the figure she brings back, which is never the same figure and is never the same coin.}

Article — Entered at Sill — Given at the Quay — What I set beside it\par

Flat tile, a score — 8 bits — 1 mark and a curse at the weight — The curse was honest. The weight came home in my shoulder.\par

Fish-dish, green glaze — 4 bits — not taken — A country with fish has dishes.\par

Porringer, coarse — 6 bits — 9 bits — I knocked it and it answered full. He paid as though a pot had promised him something.\par

Salt, Sallow, a sack — 3 marks at the Quay — — — It rained on the road. The salt did not mind; the paper did.\par

Rope, tarred, a coil — 2 marks — — — The tar came home on my hands and is in the seam of this book still.\par

Green bead, cliff-glass — given for a bit and a promise — — — The promise is not current.\par

A contract on salt-paper — entered at 1 mark at the tide-tally house — void — The clerk wrote \emph{instrument void by exposure; no claim lies}. I have kept the strip.\par

Twelve bits to the silver mark and twenty silver marks to the crown. The Court books an ember at five marks, and no man I met had exchanged one, north or south. I left the embers out of the table. A row with nothing in it is a thing no clerk can take off a woman, which is more than I can say for the other rows.

\subsection*{The net-song at first light}

\emph{Taken down at the west pan while the dippers trailed the nets and before the rakes went in. The last line is said twice, the second time to the net and not to the company. The singer would not give it while a man of the tide-tally house stood by, so we went down to the water.}

\begin{quote}\itshape The net goes in while the water is milk,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the flood comes up where the wind has gone;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape we do not ask the moon what the water wants ---\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the moon has no account in this country.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape A girl walks the crust and names a tide\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape nobody saw; the sun takes the name.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Salt is a teacher that asks no questions\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and writes down none of the answers.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape They say a Hearth lies under the salt\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the Court’s fire is the chimney of it;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape I laid my hand on the pan and the pan said nothing,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape which is the best answer I had in Vhal.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape A debt goes damp and the debt is gone.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Say it to the net. Do not say it to the man.\end{quote}

\subsection*{What the borrowed hands did}

Three hands have been at these leaves besides mine.

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item A clerk of the Council, in the leaning salt-coast hand, took the verbs out. Where I wrote \emph{they charged me} he set \emph{consideration passed}; where I wrote \emph{a girl gave me a bead} he set \emph{token, no value entered}; where I wrote \emph{the paper rotted on the road} he set \emph{instrument void by exposure}. I have put my words back underneath. A verb is a thing that happened to somebody. A clerk can take the somebody out and leave the happening standing, and the happening will travel lighter and arrive cleaner.

\item The factor’s clerk at Greybank, in the narrow upright hand, wrote \emph{figures of price, not of account} against my table, and set a round nought in the margin beside the fourth question. A nought is a figure. A question is not. There was no one in that room who could have told me why I asked it, and nobody tried.

\item A dipper wrote a tide-name in salt in the margin, for a thing she had seen and would not say aloud. The sun took it before noon and left a white place. I have not written the name back. What is written in salt belongs to the sun, and the Council has never found a way to charge for it, which vexes them more than a lost debt.

\end{itemize}

\subsection*{At the head and in the gutter}

The white at the head is salt bloom off the dockets and comes and goes with the weather; it has eaten the last letters from two words, and I have not written them back, because a word with the end gone is said slowly and this country says everything slowly. The tar at the fold is mine, off the coil I carried eighty leagues and can still smell on my thumb. The feather is a brine-gull’s; he took a coal off a brazier at the pans while my back was turned and went off with it warm under his crop, and the girl who was raking said no malice in it, which may be true and is no comfort when you are the one who has lost the coal. The bead is cliff-glass, green and sweet-smelling in the heat, pressed on me by a girl at the furnaces who watched me write and said nothing. The rope fibre is worked into the third crease and will not come out. The nick is from a fish-hook at the Fishstairs, made at home, not here. The ale ring near the song is from a cup set down by a ship’s master who would not drink with dippers and yet stayed to hear them. The white place in the margin was a tide-name and belongs to the sun. The scraped square is a word I took out with a knife and have not put back. I have not forgotten it either. The grey along the outer fold is not mine and not the Council’s. A factor from Greybank called it Ash, which in Vhal is a thing a man must buy before he will own to seeing it. I did not buy it. I have not swept it.

\subsection*{At the foot, in a hand nobody will own}

\begin{quote}\itshape Tile went north and came back a mark;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape paper went north and came back a virtue;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape four questions asked and one answer given ---\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{current}, said four mouths, and the rain said nothing.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Ask the net what it carried.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape The net has no account to enter.\end{quote}

I asked a dipper at the west pan, a woman who holds a twelfth of a boat through her mother, and a factor’s clerk come up from Greybank, and had three answers and no hand, and a fourth if I had thought to ask the rain. I have left the line where it stands. The leaves go back into the tin that held the salt, under the wheel-shed bench, where the tar keeps the damp out and the damp keeps the writing soft. Tomorrow I knock a pot for a girl who has never seen the sea, and tell her that in Vhal a man is a friend when his account is current, and leave her to work out whether that is a kindness or only a shorter way of saying \emph{not yet}. The kiln will have its wood. The sea may keep its word for guest.

\clearpage\phantomsection\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{The Salt Litany of the Return, Being the Dippers’ Prayer at the Pans Outside Vhal, with the Rubrics of the Dawn, the Five Drawings of the Net, a Council Clerk’s Correction Gone Soft in the Rain, a Boat-Woman’s Margin, and the Line at the Foot Nobody Will Own}
\CRsheetheading{The Salt Litany of the Return, Being the Dippers’ Prayer at the Pans Outside Vhal, with the Rubrics of the Dawn, the Five Drawings of the Net, a Council Clerk’s Correction Gone Soft in the Rain, a Boat-Woman’s Margin, and the Line at the Foot Nobody Will Own}
{\centering\FellFont\itshape\footnotesize\color{faded} A dipper’s order of service for the Return said at the salt pans at dawn, before the net goes in and after it comes up; written on the back of a Council tide-tally spoiled by rain, in Grathic letters learned off a factor’s man, the tide-words that will not go into Grathic tied as knots in the margin, with the five drawings and their answer, a Council clerk’s correction eaten away by the damp, a boat-woman’s charcoal in the margin, a green bead of cliff-glass, and one line at the foot in a hand nobody will own · Written at the Salt Pans outside Vhal in Stone of Y.H. 812, the Thin Year, by a dipper of the second net who signs with a wet knot and not with a name; carried up the Salt Road in Ilmen of Y.H. 813 and copied at Greybank onto the back of a grain-warrant voided by the Long Cold. It survives in a dry tin among a boat’s things, soft at the fold and sweet at the edges, with a white bloom of salt worked into the head, a tar thumb, a brine ring, a fish-hook nick, a green bead of cliff-glass pressed into the lower corner, one word taken clean off the third leaf by rain, the Council hand gone down to a figure with no verb, a boat-woman’s margin in charcoal, knots tied through three holes, and the line at the foot which has never been claimed\par}\medskip
I dip the second net at the pans outside Vhal and I have read the draw for eleven years without once reading it the way the Council prints it. The Council prints a figure. The pan gives back a level. Both are taken from the same water and neither puts anything back, but only one of them is called a virtue when the rain comes.

Our tide-words are not written. They are carried in the mouth and knotted into the head-rope, so that a word which will not go into Grathic is still there after the rope has been wet a hundred times. I learned my letters off a factor’s man come up the Salt Road with a tally he could not read back. I write so that a girl of the Quay may one day know what her grandmother said to a net, which is a thing no Council clerk has ever had cause to know.

Nothing in this leaf was asked for. A woman of the boats stood at the pan with salt dry white on her wrists and asked what we said before the net went in, and I heard myself answer in my mother’s voice. The leaf is the back of a Council tide-tally left out in the rain; the figures have gone where Council figures go, which is nowhere a man can put his hand on, and what remains is paper enough for a prayer. The Council clerk has been at it since. The damp has eaten most of what he wrote, which the Council calls a virtue. I have left what survives of his hand standing above mine, as the pan keeps the salt after the water has gone.

\subsection*{The manner of it, written small at the head}

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item Say it at the turn of the flood, before the net goes in. A prayer said on the ebb goes out with the thing it prays about.

\item Stand with the sea in front and the sun behind you. Do not look at the water during the second drawing. A man who looks at the water while he names the Nine will come away with a number instead of a name.

\item Say it to the net, never to the sea. Said to the sea, the third line becomes a question, and the sea answers with a wave, which is an answer no clerk can enter and no dipper can repeat.

\item Count the knots on the head-rope, not the meshes. A mesh counted is a mesh entered, and a mesh entered is a net that has been bought.

\item If the quay-crier calls the turn, stop where you are and begin again after. He is counting something that is not in your net.

\item If it rains, say only the first two drawings. Words on salt-paper go soft in the wet, which is a virtue in this country and a folly in every other.

\item The answer is said by every dipper present, including the one up to his knees in the pan who cannot be heard from the bank. We do not correct him. He is reading a different water.

\end{itemize}

\subsection*{The five drawings}

\emph{I say. The dippers answer to the net. The water takes no part and is not asked to.}

\subsection*{The first drawing, of the going out}

\begin{quote}\itshape The Sallow runs against the wind and follows the Warm, not the moon.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape The world was a vessel set down whole, and answered full when it was tapped.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape It was cracked in one anger and the heat went out where no wall held it,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and ran into the country that keeps nothing.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape That country has a name. Say it once, into the net.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Do not go looking for it in the water. It is not in the water.\end{quote}

\emph{Answer:} Out it goes. Back it comes. It is not the same water.

\subsection*{The second drawing, of the Nine}

\begin{quote}\itshape Nine hands went after what had run away.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape They drove the repairs home the way a boatwright drives a treenail,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the ninth repair is out in the deep water and is not finished.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Name them by their number. No dipper here has seen their houses.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape One went. One is still abroad. The net cannot tell which.\end{quote}

\emph{Answer:} Out it goes. Back it comes. It is not the same water.

\subsection*{The third drawing, of the draw}

\begin{quote}\itshape The draw runs seaward. It is blessed at dawn and taxed at noon.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape One in twelve, as the notice says, printed, read twice,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape once for the Council and once for those who came in on the tide too late.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape The Court books an ember at five marks. No boat in this port has traded one.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Count embers, not tides. The slate does not care which way the water ran.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape There is a shape of salt and cold water that takes a boat’s store\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and gives no figure. We call it the salt-thing. It is not the draw\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and it is not the Return. Do not pray to it. It answers.\end{quote}

\emph{Answer:} Out it goes. Back it comes. It is not the same water.

\subsection*{The fourth drawing, of the pouring}

\begin{quote}\itshape We do not buy returns in this country and we do not house the returned.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape What comes back here comes back to the water and not to a cradle.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Elsewhere one measure into one vessel brings the name back with it,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape with the handle of the cup and the price of bread.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Many into many brings a stranger who goes toward a cup\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape before the cup has been shown, and wants a table he never sat at.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Both are poured in the south. Neither is poured at this pan.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape A man with no account costs less, they say at the Council table.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape We say it to the net and do not ask who paid the difference.\end{quote}

\emph{Answer:} Out it goes. Back it comes. It is not the same water.

\subsection*{The fifth drawing, of the debt}

\begin{quote}\itshape A debt written on salt-paper is a debt the rain may make nothing.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape This is called a virtue. I have seen a man weep at a dry contract.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape The sea keeps what it takes. It has no slate and no clerk\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and does not call what it took a kindness.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Do not ask the net what it cost. The net has a hole in it\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and has never once been known to stop the water.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Ask the pan, which has kept the salt and let the water go,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and cannot tell you whose salt it keeps.\end{quote}

\emph{Answer:} Out it goes. Back it comes. It is not the same water.

Here the net comes up. The dippers say the last answer to the head-rope and not to the water:

\begin{quote}\itshape Out it goes. Back it comes. We do not ask it to be the same.\end{quote}

\subsection*{What the Council clerk did}

He came down to the pans with ink in two fingers of a cuff gone soft from washing, and wrote on salt-paper while the paper was still dry enough to take a hand. The rain has taken most of it. What is left stands above my words and I have not struck it away.

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item At the third drawing, against \emph{the draw runs seaward}, he wrote \emph{the measure is transferred by the Keeping; the deduction arises}. The rain has eaten \emph{arises} and left \emph{the deduction}. It stands there now, which is more than the figure deserved.

\item At \emph{no boat in this port has traded one}, he set \emph{the ember is not a circulating medium}, which is true in his room and has never been true at this quay. Both stand.

\item At the fourth drawing, against \emph{we do not house the returned}, he wrote \emph{no return entered in this jurisdiction}. The damp has taken \emph{in this jurisdiction}, so that all that remains is \emph{no return entered}, which is the sentence the Council would like to be true everywhere.

\item Against the refrain he wrote \emph{evaporation and precipitation are not the same mass}, and underlined it twice. The rain has left the underline and taken the words. A line with nothing under it is the honest part of this leaf.

\item In the space after the fifth drawing, where there is no sixth, he put a round nought and wrote \emph{vacancy}. A nought is a figure and can go soft in the rain and be copied again in a dry hand. The space is not a figure. It is the time the net is out of the water.

\end{itemize}

He asked what a dipper learned by the prayer. I told him the order and the knots. He entered both and went up the Salt Road. A man who cannot help writing on a thing has let it be seen that he wrote.

\subsection*{What the boat-woman put in the margin}

The charcoal is thick and leans, made with a stick and not a pen. She came down from the Quay with a boat-share in her family and salt in the creases of her wrists, and stood until the net was up before she touched the leaf, because a woman who touches a paper in the middle of a quay will be asked what she had to do with it.

At the fourth drawing: \emph{A child came back upriver, thin, and went toward a cup before the cup was shown. No Council mark paid for him and no Council house keeps him. His mother kept him anyway. I said the refrain to her and she said it back to her pot.}

At \emph{a man with no account costs less}: \emph{My mother held the share and I hold it. My brother came aboard and his word is counted at half. The sea does not count halves. Neither does the woman who landed him.}

At the space after the fifth: \emph{This is the time the net is down. I have sat it out on the gunwale. Nobody enters the sitting.}

She would not say which child, and I have not asked twice.

\subsection*{At the head and in the folds}

The white at the head is salt out of the paper itself and not salt off the sea, which is a thing only a person who has kept salt-paper knows the difference of. The tar is off the oar I held down while I wrote, and went into the grain and will not wash out. The brine ring stood from the first drawing to the fifth. The nick at the corner came off a fish-hook set down where no hook has business lying, and the man did not apologize. The green bead was pressed in by a girl of the furnaces with the sweetness still at her mouth; she said nothing and I did not ask, for a bead from the Glaze Cliffs is a thing a dipper can carry and a thing a glass woman must account for. The third word I have not written back, because a drawing with a word gone is a drawing said slowly, and all of ours are said slowly. The three knots are mine and I will not untie them; they hold what will not go into Grathic. The grey print along the foot is not mine and not the Council’s. There is no Last Day in a tin, and nothing here is swept up and burnt in the morning and called dealt with.

\subsection*{At the foot, in a hand nobody will own}

\begin{quote}\itshape The tide keeps the count. The rain keeps the debt.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape The sea keeps neither and is not called unjust.\end{quote}

Struck once and written again underneath, very small:

\begin{quote}\itshape It is not called just, either.\end{quote}

I asked the clerk, the boat-woman and a man come up from the pulled benches who had read the turn from the water instead of the crier, and had three answers and no hand. I have left the struck line where it was struck. The leaf goes back into the tin and the tin among the boat’s things. At the turn of the flood tomorrow the second net will go in and I shall say the five drawings to the head-rope, and the clerk’s figure will stand soft above mine, and a woman will come down from the Quay with salt on her wrists and sit out the space where the sixth drawing is not.

\clearpage\phantomsection\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{The Sermon at the Blessing Stone, Being the Old Words Said Over the Traps on Ilmen 15 of Y.H. 813, with the Manner of the Standing, the Low Half-Song as It Is Sung, the Count of What Was Set Down and What Was Entered, a Greybank Clerk’s Correction, and a Line at the Foot in a Hand Nobody Will Own}
\CRsheetheading{The Sermon at the Blessing Stone, Being the Old Words Said Over the Traps on Ilmen 15 of Y.H. 813, with the Manner of the Standing, the Low Half-Song as It Is Sung, the Count of What Was Set Down and What Was Entered, a Greybank Clerk’s Correction, and a Line at the Foot in a Hand Nobody Will Own}
{\centering\FellFont\itshape\footnotesize\color{faded} A sermon of the Fish Blessing preached at the shrine of the blessing stone at the Weir, one league upriver of Sill; the sayings in the short wet speech of the weir set down in Grathic letters, the half-song with the held line left the length it is sung, the count of the stone in a table, one correction in the narrow upright Ledgerhand of a factor’s clerk come up from Greybank, and a line at the foot in a hand nobody will own · Preached by an old hearth-maid of Sill who has stood on the flat stone at the blessing for nine and twenty springs, on Ilmen 15, Y.H. 813, the forty-fourth day, while another hearth-maid sprinkled salt along the weir head with a flat hand and the traps stood with their mouths upriver; written that evening by the younger of the two in charcoal on the back of a birch-bark tally gone soft at one edge, in the Eel House out of the rain, and folded into a length of grey wool tied with an eel-sinew. It survives with salt dried white worked into the grain at the head off the flat hand, a silt tideline along the foot from the leaf carried downriver in an apron, a wet ring where a cup stood from the first voice to the last, a grey Ash print along the gutter that nobody will own, a small eel scale pressed into the fold, a thumb of silt on the line about the extra knot which the writer did not make and has not wiped, the clerk’s correction standing above the charcoal, and a line struck through and written again very small underneath in a hand that has never come forward. Copied once at Greybank in Ash of Y.H. 813, with the verbs put back and the held line left the length it is sung.\par}\medskip
I stand on the flat stone at the Weir when the traps are blessed, and I have stood there nine and twenty springs. Nobody asked me to write. A clerk come up from Greybank stood at the lower boards with his cuff grey from washing and asked what the blessing gave, and I told him it gave nothing that could be carried away, and he wrote it down as though it had been a figure. This morning an old woman said the words over the traps for the last time before the eels came, and I set them down in the Eel House while the salt was still wet on my sleeve, because a saying said to the water stays at the water, and a saying set on bark can be carried.

I have written in Grathic. Where the old woman left a verb out I have left it out, and put it back underneath in my own hand, because a blessing said over a basket is a thing a household has to use. Where there was no word for what she did with her hand I have drawn the mark of it in charcoal and not named it, which is how the stone keeps its own mark.

\subsection*{The manner of the blessing, as the stone has it}

\emph{Written small, from watching, not from any order the Court has printed.}

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item Come on the fifteenth day of Ilmen, at the turn of the water, when the Ilm is up under its skin and the traps have been lifted and set again. A woman who comes a day early blesses the wrong water and spends the morning being told so.

\item Stand on the flat stone with your sleeves damp. Salt dried white in the creases of the hand is not dirt and is not a sign of haste. It is the trade.

\item One woman sprinkles salt along the weir head with the flat of her hand, from the shallow toward the quick water, and does not shake the hand out afterward. What is left goes into the water, which is where it was going.

\item The words go to the trap first, then to the water under the plank, then to the stone, then to the sky above the ridge, and last of all to the people standing on the bank. This order is not argued in Sill. A woman who says them to a person first will spend the morning answering questions.

\item Do not say a figure over a trap. A trap has no column, and no clerk has ever found one in it.

\item Do not clean the crossed mark on the stone. The man who drew the Weir chart drew the mark and wrote nothing beside it. We have asked three people what it is and had three answers and no mark explained.

\item The eels run whether anybody blesses them or not. This is not a reason to stop blessing them, and it is not a reason to say the blessing worked.

\end{itemize}

\subsection*{The sermon, as the old woman said it}

\subsection*{Of the two counts}

She stood with her palm on the crossed mark and looked down at the baskets.

“Count them going in and count them coming out. The basket keeps the first and the buyer keeps the second, and the two have never agreed, which is the only honest thing about either. A slate at the Fishstairs will take your figure and give you another by the tide’s turn. That is not cheating. It is two counts in two places, and a man who joins them wants a payer.

“In the year of the flower forty children of Low Kiln were taken, and the figure went up the Clay Road in a box. Here a woman keeps forty knots in a cord and one more she cannot name, and no clerk has ever taken a figure off her. You will ask which count is true. Both are true. One can be carried into a room and one cannot, which is the whole difference.”

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Margin, in my hand:} She said the word \emph{forty} low once, into a basket that had nothing in it, and did not look up to see who had heard. I have set it down because it was said over the traps and not to a person. I have not written what she did with her thumb afterward.\end{quote}

\subsection*{Of the salt and the water}

“Salt goes along the weir head with the flat of the hand, from the shallow to the quick. It is a small gift and the river takes it without thanks and without a slate, and nobody has ever seen it come back. A gift that is not returned is not therefore lost. It is where it was put.

“They tell you at the Fishstairs that the river is honest with what it is given, and that the leach hands what it takes to the Sallow draw. I have put my hand in the water where a leach stood and where none stood, and the water was the same cold in both. Do not say the river is honest. Say that it takes, and say where. The water has a direction; the Court has a column. Both are true, and only one can be entered.”

\subsection*{Of the mark}

“There is a mark cut into this stone. The man who drew the Weir chart drew it and set nothing beside it. I asked a hearth-maid come up from Sill, a man who sells eels, and a clerk who had been up about the winter wells. One said it was an old blessing, one said it was a survey mark, and one said it was no cut at all but the shape the stone took when it split. Three answers and no mark explained.

“Do not clean it. A mark that has outlasted the people who cut it is not made clearer by rubbing. We bless the traps on this stone because it is the stone our mothers stood on, not because it has answered us. There is a difference between a shrine that speaks and a stone that stands where somebody stood.”

\subsection*{Of the trap}

“An eel goes into a trap because the mouth is upriver and the eel cannot find the way out. That is all a trap is. Do not make more of it than that. The blessing does not turn the eel. It turns the woman who lifts the basket, so that she lifts with a hand that knows whose hand it is.

“Forty knots in grey wool are kept in the Eel House. The forty-first has no name, and the woman who tied it has never untied it and never read it out. Ask her, and she will give you a date. Ask the cord, and you will get nothing, which is the answer the cord was made to give.

“The slate at the Cross will tell you one in twelve, the basket will tell you a different thing, and the cord will tell you nothing at all. Keep all three. Keep them apart. A blessing that agrees too readily with a figure has been lying too long in the sun.”

\subsection*{The low half-song}

\emph{Sung low, going along the weir head with the flat hand, not facing the people. The row takes the last four lines. The line after the stone and the water is held, and the space that follows it is the length of the salt going into the river. Nobody fills it.}

\begin{quote}\itshape Salt on the flat hand, going upriver,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape from the shallow to the post where the water turns;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the trap has a mouth and the mouth has a direction,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the eel goes in by the way it cannot come out.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Count them going and count them coming,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape a bit for the basket, a bit for the board;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the cord goes home in a sleeve with its knots unread,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the slate goes up in a box with its figure unchallenged.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape The stone keeps a mark it will not say,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the water keeps the cold it took,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{[held]}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Salt on the flat hand, going upriver —\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the eels run whether she blesses them or not;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the water takes what no slate will enter,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the cord keeps what no clerk can spell.\end{quote}

A girl come up from Low Kiln asked what the space after the held line was for. Nobody answered her. The clerk put a round nought against it later, which I have left where he set it.

\subsection*{What was set down and what was entered}

\emph{I keep this count because a thing given at the Weir leaves nothing on a Court leaf, and the place where it stood ought to be kept somewhere.}

Thing — Where it was put — What was entered\par

Salt, a flat hand’s worth — along the weir head, shallow to quick — nothing\par

The old words — trap, water under the plank, stone, sky, people — nothing\par

The crossed mark — cut in the stone before any woman here — drawn on the chart; not said\par

Forty knots in grey wool — the Eel House cord — nothing\par

The forty-first knot — no name given — a nought, written later\par

Eels going in — the basket going down — counted by the hand that lifted\par

Eels coming out — a creel at the Fishstairs — a different figure\par

One in twelve — the notice at the Cross — printed, and read twice\par

\subsection*{What the clerk did}

A factor’s clerk came up from Greybank with ink settled in the soft cuff of one sleeve. He borrowed the bark while I was lifting a basket and gave it back with the verbs taken out. He writes narrow and upright, and takes the doer out of a sentence as a man takes a hook out of a fish’s mouth.

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item At \emph{the salt goes into the water}, he wrote \emph{observance performed; no transfer recorded}. He left the salt standing where I had put it, which was more than I expected of him.

\item At \emph{the basket keeps the going-in count}, he wrote \emph{two tallies entered; discrepancy nil}, joining the hand that lifted to the eye that priced.

\item At \emph{the stone keeps a mark it will not say}, he wrote \emph{undeciphered device}, which is true and has the stone out of it.

\item At the forty-first, he put a round nought and wrote \emph{vacancy}, as another clerk did before him against a saying of this Weir. A nought is a figure. The place was there before he wrote in it.

\end{itemize}

I have put the verbs back underneath and left his hand standing above, as the water leaves the silt where it fell.

\subsection*{In the margin}

Alongside the held line, in a hand with silt dried pale in the nail crescents and no name set to it:

\begin{quote}\itshape I asked the cord. It told me nothing. That is what it is for.\end{quote}

Below, in mine: she said it to the plank and would not say it twice. I have not asked her what she meant. A woman who keeps a count in wool is not obliged to say it in Grathic.

\subsection*{At the head and in the gutter}

The salt at the head came off the flat hand and has gone white in the grain where the leaf was doubled; it will not wash out, which is why we write the blessing on bark and not on the Court’s paper. The brown line at the foot is river silt, from the morning I carried the leaf downriver under my apron with a figure in it that was not mine to carry. The ring is a cup set down beside me from the first voice to the last and taken up before the old woman saw it; small ale, watered until it barely counts. The grey in the gutter came off a cuff laid where no cuff has business lying; I have not swept it, and there is no Last Day at a Weir. The scale in the fold came off an eel laid on the bark while I was deciding whether to write the held line at all. The thumb of silt on the line about the forty-first is not mine and I have not wiped it; the woman stood beside me while I wrote, put her hand down to steady the bark, and took it away without looking at what I had written. The clerk did not see any of these things, which is how I know he is a good clerk.

\subsection*{At the foot}

Struck through once and written again underneath, very small, in a hand that is not mine, not the old woman’s and not the clerk’s:

\begin{quote}\itshape A mark cut before any of us is not an answer.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Salt goes where it was sent and is not entered.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape The place was there before the nought.\end{quote}

I asked a hearth-maid come up from Sill, a woman who lifts the traps, and a factor’s man out of Greybank, and had three answerings and no hand. I have left the lines struck through and standing, which is the only honest way to keep a sentence you cannot sign.

The bark goes back into the grey wool in the Eel House. Next Ilmen the old woman will say the words, or another woman will say them in her place, and the salt will go along the weir head from the shallow to the quick, and the eels will run as they run, and a clerk will come up from Greybank and take the verbs out. I shall put them back, and leave the held line the length it is sung and the nought where he set it, because a nought is a figure and the place is older than the figure.

\clearpage\phantomsection\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{The Salt That Follows, Being a Coast-Soldier’s Field Notes on the Salt-Thing of the Sallow Tides and the Pans Outside Vhal}
\CRsheetheading{The Salt That Follows, Being a Coast-Soldier’s Field Notes on the Salt-Thing of the Sallow Tides and the Pans Outside Vhal}
{\centering\FellFont\itshape\footnotesize\color{faded} A soldier’s field book on one shape, set down as the record of shore-watches kept over boats lying off the pans and not as natural philosophy; the rounds in the Vhaleni tide-words written in Grathic letters, the tally in charcoal on the backs of spoiled tide-tallies, a verse as it is said going out on the first watch, a ruling in the narrow upright Ledgerhand of a clerk of the Council room, a second line of his gone soft with the damp, a dipper’s words in pale ink on salt-paper, and one line at the foot in a hand nobody will own · Written in Stone of Y.H. 812, the Thin Year of the Long Cold, by one of the Council’s men set over the shore-watch and the cure-shed at the salt pans outside Vhal, who kept the rain-barrels and counted what the boats lost between dusk and morning; written at the end of watches in the shed with a tallow end in a pot and the Sallow coming up over the stones; set down first on the backs of tide-tallies spoiled by sea-water and then on three folds of salt-paper stiffened with tar, sewn with eel-sinew and carried in a tarred wrap in a coat pocket. Copied forward in Ilmen of Y.H. 813. It survives with a white bloom of salt come up out of the paper at the head, tar at the fold, a Sallow tideline along the gutter that has taken two words off the third watch, a wet ring where a barrel-stave stood on the leaf, a grey smear at the fore-edge where a sailor with cold fingers touched it, a fish-hook nick, a pinch of cure-salt shut in the second fold, a scorch where the watch-lamp caught the lower corner of the last leaf, the charcoal rubbed thin where the wrap was carried against the thigh, one ruling in Ledgerhand standing above the words it corrects, one line of the same hand eaten down to a figure with no verb, a dipper’s line in pale ink on salt-paper soft at one corner, and the one line at the foot\par}\medskip
I keep the shore-watch at the pans outside Vhal. My post is the cure-shed and the barrels of rain. The boats lie off in Stone when the Sallow runs cold and the lead comes down in the sand out of the Glaze Cliffs, and a boat lying off a shore in that month is a boat with something aboard somebody paid to keep warm. My work is to know what goes off it in the night. I write at the end of a watch with the tallow down to a knuckle and the salt coming up in the paper.

The leaves I wrote on first were tide-tallies spoiled by sea-water. The sea took the figures off clean, which was a mercy of a kind: a figure the sea has eaten is a figure no clerk can enter. I write in charcoal now, on the backs of the same tallies and on folds of salt-paper stiffened with tar. Charcoal goes into the grain; salt-paper rots, and a contract that rots is held a virtue in this port. This book is the one thing about the shed the damp has not been asked to settle.

The bloom at the head came up out of the paper. I have not brushed it off. A book that has never stood a winter over the pans was never meant to be read in one.

\subsection*{What follows a boat}

It does not steal. This is the first thing a new man gets wrong and the thing that costs him his hands. He looks for a beak or a rat’s teeth, and meanwhile the pot under the mast has gone cold.

It follows a boat at night and taps where the warm is kept. I have seen one come up under the lee at the turn, and there was no body to put a spear to: a lift in the water the colour of the pans, a crust at the edge of it, and a small place in the middle that was not cold when I laid the back of my hand near it with my glove on. I have set down what I felt and not what I make of it. It is a shape of salt and cold water, and something in it holds together overnight, which plain salt does not.

A man who sleeps on deck and wakes with grey fingertips has not been bitten. There is no wound to show. He has been near something that draws the way a silt-leach draws through an ankle, only with the hull between them. I have held such a hand. The cold was in the nails and did not go away below, and he kept putting the hand into his coat as though it belonged to somebody else and he was minding it for them.

They carry a barrel of rain. Every captain fills one before he lies off the pans in Stone, and will not say why to a man from the clay country, because a Vhaleni tells the truth in the form of a convenience. I watched one of these come up to where a man had sluiced rain round a mooring-stone and stop as though it had met a wall it could not see the top of. It went along the wet line looking for a break, the way a man looks for a gate, and came no farther in. The Ilm runs into the Sallow and its mouth is fresh enough for a dipper to drink from, and these never go up into it. A man at Greybank may leave a coal on the quay all night and nothing will tap it. Fresh water is a wall to this thing the way a shut door is to a man who cannot lift the latch.

\subsection*{The tapping}

It taps once. Then it waits. Then again, a little lower, under the waterline where the pot of coals stands in blind ash. A cooper knows a cask by the note it gives under the knuckle, full or flat; the thing taps from outside and knows the same, and when the note goes flat it stays where it is until morning.

By morning the coals are cold. The loaf is where the man set it. The stone out of the Keel has gone the colour of the shed slate. There is no hole in the hull and no water in the bilge, and a man will say the boat was robbed, but nothing has been carried away that he can name except the warm. I watched a boat come in off the cliffs with its store gone and its cargo whole, and the captain angrier at his two grey hands than at his cold pot, which is reasonable and not entered.

It keeps to boats. I set a warmed stone on the shore under a dish and sat by it through two watches with the lamp shut, and nothing came. A boat is a vessel that floats with its warm in one place; a stone on the shore is a stone. I have set the two things on one leaf and drawn no line between them. I do not put a cause in a book the Council borrows. A cause has a verb, and a verb is the thing they take out first.

\subsection*{The verse}

\emph{Said low at the pan-edge going out on the first watch, never coming in. The fourth line of the last verse is the old line and every man on the shore sings it wrong on purpose, because a song that gives the thing a reason is a song a man can carry home and set by his own fire. I have set it down as it is said, with the wrong line standing and the gap kept the length the men keep it.}

\begin{quote}\itshape One for the pan and one for the tide,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape one for the boat that keeps its coal;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape it taps below the waterline\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and takes the warm and leaves the whole.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Salt on the stone and salt on the rope,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape salt from the pan and not from the sea;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape it cannot cross the rain, they say,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and so the boat carries rain to sea.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Count the coals and count the hands,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape count the grey that comes on deck;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape one tap left for the fare unpaid ---\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the old line wrong where the gap should be.\end{quote}

The gap is for a drowned sailor. The men say he could not pay the ferry and goes now under the hull of the next boat that lies off the shore, tapping for the fare. I have heard the tale with three names on it in three mouths and have not written any of them. A man on the pulled benches taps the gunwale twice at the last line and will not say why; I have asked and he has not told me, and I have let the two taps stand.

\subsection*{The tally}

These are the watches I kept a true account of. There were others I did not write because my hands were full and one I did not write because I had the flux and had lost the day. I have set down both sorts as they stand. The last column is the clerk’s, not mine. I counted what the boat lost; he counted what the shed sold.

Watch — Where the boat lay — Draw — Taps heard — At morning — Salt gathered — Entered\par

Stone 6 — Off the pans, south board — turn — three — pot cold, no hands grey — 2 lb — 8 bits\par

Stone 11 — Glaze Cliffs, under the lead — ebb — one — stone cold, one hand grey — none — 0\par

Stone 17 — Inside the mooring-stones — slack — five — pot cold, two hands grey — 3 lb — 12 bits\par

Stone 23 — Off the coast pass, wind off the clay — turn — two — loaf gone cold, none grey — 1 lb — nil\par

Stone 29 — North board, rain sluiced at the stone — ebb — none — all as set — none — 0\par

Ilmen 4 — Quay landing, before the blessing — turn — four — one hand grey to the wrist — 2 lb — 8 bits\par

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{In the narrow upright hand of a clerk of the Council room, written above the tally on a scrap of salt-paper folded into the leaf:} Shape not a vessel. Drawing by a shape: no deduction arises. Grey fingers: not entered. Salt gathered at the pans entered at four bits the pound. Account stands.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Below, in the same hand, gone soft where the damp took the corner:} The — — by the —.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Underneath, in charcoal, in mine:} Two words gone and the figure left. He has entered the salt I sold and struck out the hands that went grey getting it. I have put the hands back where his column cannot reach, and my own mark beside them.\end{quote}

The twelve bits for Stone 17 went into the boat’s account and not into mine, which is as it should be, since the salt came off a boat I watched empty. The jar from that watch I have not sold and have not entered. A jar with a figure on it travels; one without stays under the bench. I have never been asked to explain the difference and have never offered to.

\subsection*{The salt it leaves}

When the ebb runs far out it leaves one stranded on the pans sometimes, where it goes smaller than a man’s hand and then to a crust with a hollow in it. We scrape the crust up at first light and sell it at four bits the pound in Vhal. It is the finest curing salt in Sarn and is said to keep a wound from turning. I have seen it laid in a cut that went quiet and in one that went on as it would have without it, and made no rule out of them.

The dippers bless their nets against the thing at dawn and will not do it while a Council man stands on the board. One told me a blessing said before a clerk is a blessing with a figure on it, and a blessing with a figure on it has been half bought. I have written his words and not his name.

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{In the pale ink of a dipper, on a corner of salt-paper soft where the damp took it:} It takes the warm and leaves the salt, and we sell what it leaves. We bless the net. We do not bless the boat, because the boat has already been paid for.\end{quote}

I have put his line above mine. He wrote it at the pans and I wrote mine on the shore, and neither of us has asked the thing anything.

\subsection*{What they say at the pans}

They say it is a drowned sailor who could not pay the ferryman and goes in a body of salt instead. There are songs for it with a woman’s name in them and a crossing that was refused. I have heard them and I have no quarrel with a song. I have watched this thing come to four boats and go away from three of them with their warm gone, and what it wanted in the fourth I do not know, because the fourth had a fresh barrel and the man on watch had poured the rain wide.

Here is the one strange thing I will set down and not explain. I held the back of my hand over the hollow of the crust in the jar under the bench on a Stone morning with frost on the step, and the hollow was warm. Not warm as a coal is warm. Warm the way a slept-in place is warm after a body has got up. Four mornings I held my hand there and four times it was so, and I put the jar back and said nothing to the Council clerk. He would take the verb out and leave the figure, and there is no figure for the warmth in a hollow of salt.

\subsection*{At the head and in the margins}

The bloom at the head is salt out of the paper, which is not the same as salt out of the sea, though a man would take the two for one at a glance. The tar at the fold has made two lines of the second watch slow to read. The tideline took two words off the third watch and I did not write them in again; a watch with two words gone is told slowly, and most things here are. The wet ring came off a barrel-stave set down while I counted a catch and went off without his change. The grey at the fore-edge is not mine; a sailor steadied the leaf with his hand and I let him, and have not rubbed it, because it is the only mark here that came off a boat I could not warm. The nick is a fish-hook from a man paying with the hook still in his fingers; he did not apologize. The pinch in the second fold is cure-salt from Stone 17, the watch the clerk struck. The scorch is where the lamp caught and the hand that pulled it back was mine and is not entered. His ruling I have not touched; his softened line I have answered in charcoal. The song is as the men said it, with the old line wrong and the gap open.

\subsection*{At the foot, in a hand nobody will own}

\begin{quote}\itshape It follows the boat because the boat is warm. It cannot follow the rain. Nobody has asked it why.\end{quote}

I put the question to four people and got four answerings and no hand to sign them. The line has lain here through two copyings and nobody has claimed it, which is how I know it is worth keeping.

There is a reach inside the Glaze Cliffs where boats lie close in winter and the water comes up warm in the cracks of the stone even when the wind is off the Rim. I have not taken a boat in there. Next Stone I will carry a fresh pot of coals, a coil of cord and a barrel of rain, and lie off on the turn with the lamp shut, and if a thing that cannot cross fresh water comes up out of water warm for no reason I have seen, I will set that down too, in charcoal, with the verb standing as it happened and no figure at the end of the row.

\clearpage\phantomsection\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{The Salt Walk, Being the Standing Rules of the Dippers of Vhalen for the Taking, Walking, Trying and Naming of Apprentices at the Pans Outside Vhal, with the Table of Walkings, the Net-Song Pasted Inside the Cover, Two Corrections in a Council Clerk’s Hand, and a Line at the Foot Nobody Will Own}
\CRsheetheading{The Salt Walk, Being the Standing Rules of the Dippers of Vhalen for the Taking, Walking, Trying and Naming of Apprentices at the Pans Outside Vhal, with the Table of Walkings, the Net-Song Pasted Inside the Cover, Two Corrections in a Council Clerk’s Hand, and a Line at the Foot Nobody Will Own}
{\centering\FellFont\itshape\footnotesize\color{faded} A dipper’s leaf of rules from the west pan, written in the leaning low hand with the ends of words let fall; the rules set in short sayings, the walkings and the faults in tables, the net-song pasted inside the cover, a tide-name written in salt in the margin and gone before noon, two corrections in the narrow upright Ledgerhand of a Council clerk, one line struck in charcoal by a pan-master who would not sign it, and a line at the foot in a hand nobody will own · Gathered at the Salt Pans outside Vhal in Frost of Y.H. 812, the Thin Year of the Long Cold, and copied forward at the Opening of the Slates into Y.H. 813 by Halla Salt, a dipper of the west pan who has taken the young out barefoot at the Salt Walk for one and thirty years and keeps the pan’s leading rope and its tide-name in her mouth; written on salt-paper leaves she keeps dry in a tin that once held salt and has never been washed, sewn with tarred net-twine and carried up the Salt Road with a glass consignment, where a clerk of the Council corrected it at Greybank. It survives with a white salt bloom at the head that has taken the last letters off a word and left the rest readable, a thumb of tar at the fold off the leading rope, the press of a wet net across the song, a peck-hole where a brine-gull took the leaf for a crust, a fish-hook nick, a ring of small ale at the foot left by a ship’s master who would not drink with dippers, a grey Ash print along the outer fold that is not hers and that she has not swept, a tide-name written in salt in the margin which the sun took by noon and left a white place, two corrections in the Council’s upright hand, one charcoal line struck and written again beneath, and a line at the foot nobody will own\par}\medskip
I keep the west pan and the leading rope. When the young are taken out at the Salt Walk I go first and they come barefoot behind me, and when one of them names a tide nobody has seen I write it in salt on the crust and the sun takes it before they are back at the shed. That is the whole of the teaching, set down so that a girl at the pans and a girl at the Quay hear the same rule. I write on salt-paper and keep the leaves dry, which is against the practice of the country and I know it. A contract left in the rain is no contract here and we call that a virtue. A rule left in the rain is no rule either, and I have met no man who sees the virtue in that.

These rules were gathered before the Council had a name for the pans and are copied forward from the rope and not from a book. A rule that has never been walked is a rule nobody believes. These have been walked.

\subsection*{The rules as they stand at the west pan}

\subsection*{Of the taking}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item The pan takes a child, not a house. A house may bring him and a house may feed him, but from the day he first puts a foot on the crust he answers to the dipper who walks him. The Council takes the tide and leaves the child alone.

\item A child is taken at twelve and walked at fourteen. A child taken later is walked at the next low tide after his fourteenth year, and the year between is not made up to him. The salt does not make up a tide that was missed.

\item He is kept, not hired. He eats from the pan-house dish and sleeps under the pan-house roof, and what the pan gives back comes back as bread and a place by the fire, neither of which is entered. A dipper is paid by the pan-master in weather and never in ale. A man who offers ale is buying something; ask the price before you drink.

\item His birth-name is said once at the taking and not used at the pan. What he is called at the pan is a tide-name, and it is kept in the mouth and not on the leaf. A name in the mouth cannot be entered, and what cannot be entered is the only thing in Vhal the Council has never managed to tax.

\item The tide is said before the name, always. A name a man can change at a moot; a tide he cannot change at all. The day a child gives his name before his tide he is sent to the water’s edge and asked again, and the water does not answer him either.

\end{enumerate}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{In the narrow upright hand of a Council clerk, against rule 4:} The appellation is recorded. \emph{Underneath, in mine:} I had written that the name is kept in the mouth. He strikes a mouth wherever he finds one. I have put the mouth back underneath, because a clerk who keeps a name on paper has never had to say it to the water at low tide.\end{quote}

\subsection*{Of the walk}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item At fourteen the young go out barefoot on the crust at low tide, going out and not coming back until the water turns. Going back is the same walk and is called something else; nobody has ever told me what.

\item Each names a tide nobody has seen. Write the name in salt on the crust and let the sun have it. What is written in salt belongs to noon; what is said belongs to the person who said it. Do not write it on salt-paper. A thing that rots is no protection for a name that was never a contract.

\item Rake at the turn and rake at the fourth, and keep the rake going when there is nothing under it. A child who stops raking begins to ask what ought to come up, and a dipper who answers that question has begun to teach the wrong trade.

\item Do not look at the Glaze Cliffs while walking. They are sweet and they are lead, and a child who puts a green bead in his mouth is not long for the pans. Tell him why once. A warning about a taste is believed before a warning about a poison, which is the only useful thing I know about children.

\item The chief dipper keeps the names of the three great tides in his mouth and writes none of them. A child keeps the one he named himself until the sun takes it, and then keeps the place where it was.

\end{enumerate}

\subsection*{Of the net and the draw}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item Trail the net at dawn. The blessing is in the trailing and not in any word said over it. A net blessed at noon is a wet rope and nothing more, and the Council will pay the same for it, which is the difficulty.

\item Read what comes up. Do not read what ought to have come up. The Sallow runs against the wind and does not ask the moon, and a dipper who has learned what the tide should do has learned to miss the tide that did.

\item Bless the nets against the salt-thing, which follows boats at night and taps the hull where the store is. Carry a barrel of rain against it; fresh water stops it as a wall stops a man. Every captain denies the barrel and every captain carries one.

\item A brine-gull will lift a coal from the brazier and go off with it under its crop. No malice in it. Do not set a dipper to watch the coals in place of the net; the gull is honest and the net has a master.

\item We say the Sallow keeps a Hearth of its own beneath the salt and the Court’s fire is only its chimney. No one has taken me down to see the door of it, and I have stopped asking which way it opens. A dipper who claims to have seen it is selling something, generally a passage.

\end{enumerate}

\subsection*{Of the tally and the paper}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item Keep the tide-tallies on salt-paper and keep the paper dry. What Kett reads at the tide-tally house is the tide that was entered, and what the pan saw is another matter. Both are true; only one can be carried into a room with a Council table in it.

\item Write the draw and leave out what it meant. The Council pays for the first and has never asked for the second. A clerk who asks what a dipper meant has mistaken the tide for an account; there is no profit in answering him with another figure.

\item The assessors come against the pans with one in twelve as regular as gulls. Pay it out of the entered tide and never out of the seen one. This is not dishonesty; it is the arrangement by which a poor pan stays a pan and not an unclosed account.

\item A contract on salt-paper in wet weather is no contract, and half the port’s fortunes have turned on that. We do not say kindly to a pan-master, and a dipper who offers a favour without a price should be told that in Vhal a favour is a debt with no date, and a debt with no date keeps a man awake.

\end{enumerate}

\subsection*{The table of walkings}

\emph{Kept by the girl who rakes the west pan. What is written is the tide that was seen and the day it was seen, in a hand that will not change between one line and the next.}

Year — The walking — What is taken\par

Twelve — The pan: rake, carry, mend net-rope with the old women — The birth-name, said once and not used again at the pan\par

Thirteen — The dawn net; hold the leading rope and say nothing — The habit of asking what ought to come up\par

Fourteen — The Salt Walk, barefoot on the crust at the turn — The tide-name, written in salt and gone by noon\par

Fifteen — The tally house; read the draw against the contract — The difference between the tide seen and the tide entered\par

Sixteen — Trail the net alone and bless it against the salt-thing — The last of the child’s account with any house\par

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item Sixteen is the common end of a walking and not a short one. A girl who has been walked is not paid out and sent away; she stays where the pan needs her, which may be at the west pan or at the Quay or on a boat whose share goes through her mother. The dipper does not choose which. The tide does, and the Council after it.

\end{enumerate}

\subsection*{The table of faults}

Fault — As corrected at the pan\par

A tide-name written on salt-paper — The paper left out in the rain; the name said again to the water\par

A tide named that has already been seen — Sent out again at the next low tide, barefoot, going out\par

\emph{What ought to come up} spoken at the net — The net taken in; that day’s draw entered as nothing\par

A net set in the afternoon — The leading rope coiled and the child set to counting gulls for a tend\par

\emph{Kindly} said to a pan-master — Two bits owed, named on the spot, with a date\par

The Hearth beneath the salt asked about — Answered once: it is under the salt and the Court’s fire is its chimney. Asked twice: a barrel of rain carried three paces and set down\par

A tide sold to the Council and the other kept — Not entered. There is no law against it, which is why the pan does not speak of it\par

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item It is the only answer the pan has for a question the Council has never thought to ask, and a child who brings it up a second time is set to raking at the fourth where there is nothing under the rake.

\end{enumerate}

\subsection*{The net-song, pasted inside the cover}
