\emph{Sung at dawn, kneeling, with the leading rope in the hand and not yet in the water. The pan says the last line with the dipper. Nobody sings it at the Council table, and nobody sings it on the ebb.}

\begin{quote}\itshape Rope in the hand and the salt on the knee,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the tide comes in where the wind isn’t;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape trail it low, trail it slow,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and read what rises, not what should.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape A coal goes up and a gull goes off,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape a white bloom comes on the tarred board;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the pan keeps clean by what it takes,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the clerk keeps what he can read.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Write it in salt, write it in sun,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the name’s gone before the net comes in;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape carry the rain in a barrel by,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and speak to the water, not the men.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Rope in the hand and the salt on the knee,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape one tide for the tally, one for the sea;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the one they pay for isn’t the one I saw ---\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the one I saw is kept in me.\end{quote}

The press of the wet net across the second verse came from the song being sung in the rain at the outer pan, the rope laid on the leaf while a girl said the middle line. I have flattened it; the words hold.

\subsection*{What the borrowed hands did}

A clerk of the Council borrowed the leaf at Greybank, ink settled in two fingers of a soft cuff, and struck the verbs out of it as though a verb were a thing a man could smuggle past a table.

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item Against rule 12 he set \emph{the draw was read} above my \emph{read what comes up}, which is a sentence true of every draw and therefore of none. I have put my words back underneath.

\item Against rule 4 he wrote \emph{the appellation is registered} and a round nought in the space where the tide-name had been. A nought is a figure. The tide was not a figure and has not come back to be entered.

\end{itemize}

A pan-master struck the line \emph{speak to the water, not the men} in charcoal and wrote above it \emph{and to the pan, which answers}. I have set his line above mine and struck it, and written mine under again, which is how a pan argues with a floor it cannot leave. The charcoal has come off on the fold.

\subsection*{At the head and in the gutter}

The salt bloom at the head came up in a wet week and has eaten the end of a word, which I have not written back; a word about a current that the weather has taken is truer than one a clerk can still read. The tar at the fold is mine, off the rope I coil every dusk. The peck-hole went through the first verse and nobody has claimed the bird. The fish-hook nick is from a basket set down over a disputed count of herrings. The ring of ale came off a ship’s master who would not drink until a question about the draw was answered; he has not been back. The grey along the outer fold is not mine and not the Council’s, and I have not swept it. At the pans there is no Last Day and nothing gets burnt in the morning. The white place in the margin is where the tide-name was written. It was a good name and I will not write it in again, which is the same as saying it every morning.

\subsection*{At the foot, in a hand nobody will own}

\begin{quote}\itshape The salt keeps the name till noon. The rope keeps what the net brings up.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape What was named and never came is kept in the mouth, and in no other place.\end{quote}

I asked a pan-master, a clerk of the Council and a woman who sells eels on the Quay, and got three answers and not one of them would put a name to his answer. I have left the lines where they were written. The leaves go back into the tin and the tin back on the shelf where it has never been washed; tomorrow the young go out barefoot at the turn, and I shall write what the water did and leave out what it meant, and be paid for the one and not asked for the other.

\clearpage\phantomsection\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{The Salt Wife’s Book, Being Remedies for the Glass-Sickness, the Chill, the Bite and the Third Night, Set Down at the Quay in Vhal}
\CRsheetheading{The Salt Wife’s Book, Being Remedies for the Glass-Sickness, the Chill, the Bite and the Third Night, Set Down at the Quay in Vhal}
{\centering\FellFont\itshape\footnotesize\color{faded} A boat-midwife’s and healer’s book of remedies in the Vhaleni tide-words, written in Grathic letters so a girl of the Quay could read it; the cures in a salt-wife’s hand, a lowland physician’s objections in the margin, and the corrections of a Council clerk set down on salt-paper that has since gone soft, with one song for the third night and one line at the foot in a hand nobody will own · Written at the Quay in Vhal in Ember and Smoke of Y.H. 812, the Thin Year, by Eda of the Quay, a midwife who went aboard with the eel-boats and kept the households of the glass-workers; begun on the back of a Council tide-table spoiled by rain and sewn with eel-sinew into an oiled sailcloth wrapper, carried up the Salt Road in Ilmen of Y.H. 813 and copied at Greybank onto the back of a discarded weigh-slip. It survives in a dry tin among a boat’s things, soft at the fold and sweet at the edges, with a green bead of cliff-glass pressed into the head, a thumb of tar, a white bloom of salt along the gutter, a ring of brine, a fish-hook nick, one correction the damp has eaten down to a figure with no verb, and a line struck through and written again underneath in the writer’s own hand.\par}\medskip
I write on the back of a tide-table the Council left out in the rain. The figures have gone where the Council’s figures go, which is nowhere a man can put his hand on, and what is left is paper enough for a book nobody has asked to see. I am a salt-wife of the Quay. I go aboard when a birth will not wait for the quay, and I keep the households of the glass women, who are the only people in Vhal who sweat sweetness. I have set down what we do and what the lowland physician at Greybank told me to do, and where the two disagree I have left both standing. A remedy is a thing the sea has been paid for already. A woman who takes a line out of a book of physic is answerable for the next body that takes it.

My hand is not a clerk’s. I put the verbs in because a direction without a verb is a thing a Council clerk can read aloud at a table and a woman cannot use at three in the morning with a boat coming up under her. The green at the head is not tar. It is a bead of cliff-glass a girl pressed into the leaf with her thumb while I was writing, and she had sweetness at her mouth and said nothing. The tar is mine, off the oar I held down in the wind. The salt along the gutter came up out of the paper itself. I have not washed any of it.

\subsection*{The order of a sick-room aboard}

\emph{Written small in the margin, with one word gone over in brine.}

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item Get the brazier under the lee of the hold, not in the wind. A fire in a draught is a fire that has been taking warmth from somebody and giving it to the air. Nobody in this port will agree to pay for the air.

\item Set the sick one’s feet toward the ebb if the trouble is a chill, toward the flood if the trouble is a swelling. This is what we do. A lowland physician told me it should be toward the fire in either case, and both stand here.

\item Turn the slate face down before you go to the child, as the hearth-maids do in Grath. I have no slate-name and never shall; a salt-paper contract is a thing that rots in the damp, which is a virtue in this country and a folly in every other.

\item Salt the water before you wash a wound. The sea does it for nothing and we charge for it, which is the whole of our trade.

\item When the quay-crier calls the turn of the tide, stop and begin again after. He is counting something that is not in your room.

\end{itemize}

I have done three hundred births and I still look at the door before I look at the child. It is a trick the room plays on a woman. After the first hundred you stop calling it a habit and call it the order of things.

\subsection*{The remedies, as they are used}

Trouble — What is set to it — The manner of it — Who pays\par

Glass-sickness (the sweetness) — A draught of seawater, and cliff-glass scraped into it — The glass women rub their gums with it and say the sweetness answers sweetness. A lowland physician says it is the lead in the glaze and that the draught makes it worse. I have seen the pale line at the gum and the hand that cannot hold a cup. I have not seen the lead. — The glass furnace, which cannot stop and does not ask.\par

A chill off the water — A common stone warmed at the brazier, in a fold of wool; the feet to the ebb — To the belly, never the feet. Change it when it goes cold in your own hand, not when the child stops crying. A Grathic hearth-maid says a stone is a stone and not a kindness, and I have let her words stand. — The brazier, and whoever paid for the coal.\par

A hot wound, or a fever that burns — A cold-iron knife blade laid across it — We say the iron draws the heat out. A Keldish man at the quay told me cold iron draws and gives nothing back, and that a blade on a wound takes the measure as well as the heat. I have set his words beneath mine. — The wound. There is no other answer.\par

A bone set wrong — Two hands, a splint of straight reed, a fold of wet cloth — Set it while the vessel is quiet, before the swelling takes; leave the reed on till the third day. A bone-setter from Nine Pots says leave it a tend and a half. Both stand. — The patient, in the holding still.\par

A birth-flower — Salt, rubbed in — We call it the tide-mark and rub it with salt, believing the sea set it there. A Grathic woman crossed two fingers at the corner of one and gave me a date instead of an answer. I have put the date in the margin. — Nobody knows. The child’s skin, perhaps.\par

Milk that will not come — Another woman to hold the child while the mother sleeps — The favour is paid out of the other woman’s own house, and I say so before I ask it. — The other woman’s child.\par

A cut from glass — Tallow first, then a clean fold — Do not salt a glass cut if you can help it. The glass women salt everything, and their hands are mapped in white lines. — Whoever opened the furnace.\par

The bite of a salt-thing — Nothing I know — Keep her from the water at the turn. Salt does not hold that bite, and a brine-gull will take a coal off a brazier but will not take this. — Nobody. This is the honest column.\par

A child emptied by leeches — Nothing. Do not set them. — They draw through a small wound and leave the body thin; a collector would call it a draw and ask for a slate, and I have never seen one ask. If you find them on a child, take them off and count them, and do not put them back. — Whoever put them there.\par

The third-night chill — Warmth, quiet, and a watch kept till the fourth day — Keep her against a living body under the quilt and give barley water by the spoon. Do not leave her to sleep it off, and do not call a collector for the worsening; it is the night’s own work and goes off by the fourth morning. — The household, one night’s sleep and a loaf.\par

A lowland physician came up the Salt Road in Y.H. 798 with a book that said the sweetness came from the lead in the glaze. He left a page of it in the glass-house and went off with a purse. The page came back to me with the word taken clean away, as though a word could be taken off paper the way salt is taken off a net. I have written the word here in my own hand, which is a thing a salt-wife is not supposed to do. I have also left the draught of seawater standing under it, because it is what I have seen done for thirty years and I have not yet seen what it does to a person beyond the month.

\subsection*{The full note}

Tap a sound cup with the knuckle and it answers full. Tap a cracked one and it answers flat, a little dead sound that stops at the surface and will not go through. The glass women know it in their cups and I have borrowed it from them. A girl of the furnace told me her mother used to tap the ribs of a sick man and say he had gone flat. I do not do it. A body is not a cup, and a cup’s answer is none of a person’s business.

The dippers say the Sallow gives back a note like a cup three-quarters full, and that the Council enters it as full because the difference is not worth a figure. I have left the three-quarters where I heard it. A figure a clerk can carry away in a cuff; a note is not.

\subsection*{The tide and the draw}

We say the draw runs seaward and a body empties into it. The dippers bless the nets at dawn so the eels will not notice, which is a kindness spent on eels. If the warm goes from the full to the empty, as the lowland books say, then a sick body turned to the ebb should lose what ails it. That is what I used to think. I have watched nine such bodies and eight of them went colder before the turn; the ninth did not, and she had been carried in the other direction by her daughter, who did not tell me. I have left the old line standing and set the nine beside it. When a thing has been done wrong nine times I want the ninth to keep her place.

There is a shape of salt and cold water in the Sallow that taps the hull and takes a boat’s store away. We call it the salt-thing. A healer who cannot tell a tide from a taking will set a sick man facing the water at the turn and wonder why he goes thin. I have done it. I do not say I was right.

\subsection*{The song for the third night}

\emph{Sung low, to the child, while the watch is kept. The room says the last line with her.}

\begin{quote}\itshape The ebb takes and the ebb keeps,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the glass gives back what the furnace grieves;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape a body is a boat with a seam\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the seam is where the warmth leaves.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Two for the brazier, two for the bite,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape two for the hand that holds the light;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the twelfth goes down and the twelfth comes in,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and one goes out on a wind not seen.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Three nights, three watches, a hand kept true;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape what comes back is not what went;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape sing to the child, sing to the cold,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and come back on the flood. Come back as you can.\end{quote}

The twelfth is left where the twelfth should be. The Council would put a figure in it. A figure is a thing that can be written and then rained on and then entered again in a dry hand; a tide is not.

\subsection*{What the Council hand did}

A clerk of the Council borrowed the leaf on a market morning in Ember. He writes on salt-paper, and the salt-paper has taken the damp and let his hand go, so that of his three corrections only one figure and half a verb survive. Where I wrote \emph{the draught of seawater}, he set \emph{the measure is restored} above it, and the damp has eaten \emph{restored} so that only \emph{the measure is} stands. He put a round nought in the place of the unnamed tide and wrote \emph{vacancy} under it, and the vacancy has outlasted the nought, which is the Council’s own art in a small space.

I have put my words back under what is left of his. He takes the verbs out because a thing always true has no need of them. I put them in because a woman on a boat at three in the morning does not know she is hearing something always true, and wants to know which hand to hold the child with.

\subsection*{At the head and in the gutter}

The green bead at the head was pressed in with a thumb and has left a sweet smear that will not dry. The tar is off the oar, and came off when I held the sheet down on deck in a wind that was taking everything else. The bloom along the gutter is salt out of the paper and not out of the sea, which is a thing only a person who has kept salt-paper knows the difference of. The ring of brine came from a cup set down while I was telling a girl to eat and she would not; the hook nick came off a man paying me with his hook still in his hand, and he did not apologize. The grey print at the foot is not mine and not the Council’s. I have not swept it. There is no Last Day in a tin.

\subsection*{At the foot, in a hand nobody will own}

\begin{quote}\itshape The sea keeps what it takes. It has no slate and no clerk, and it does not call it a debt.\end{quote}

I asked the dippers, the glass women and a factor come up from Greybank, and had three answers and no hand. I have left the line where it was written. The tin goes back among the boat’s things and the leaf goes aboard when the ebb comes. A girl will press another bead into it and say nothing, and I shall put the verbs back where the damp has taken them.

\clearpage\phantomsection\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{The Second Chill, Being a Letter from Wenna, an Old Hearth-Maid at Cold Acre, to Milla, Newly Set to the Birth-Slates in Low Kiln, on the Warming of Stones, the Three Days, the Collector’s Tube, and the Name Written Before the Face Is Looked At; with the Answer in the Margin, a Clerk’s Entry in Ledgerhand, and a Washing Verse in a Hand Nobody Will Own}
\CRsheetheading{The Second Chill, Being a Letter from Wenna, an Old Hearth-Maid at Cold Acre, to Milla, Newly Set to the Birth-Slates in Low Kiln, on the Warming of Stones, the Three Days, the Collector’s Tube, and the Name Written Before the Face Is Looked At; with the Answer in the Margin, a Clerk’s Entry in Ledgerhand, and a Washing Verse in a Hand Nobody Will Own}
{\centering\FellFont\itshape\footnotesize\color{faded} A private letter in a hearth-maid’s small careful hand, written on the back of a birth-slate rubbing taken before the ink had set; folded thrice and tied with a twist of grey wool, carried down from the ridge in a potter’s wife’s apron, answered along the margin in a younger hand, corrected on the back at the Court’s table in Slate Row, and kept since in the birth-flower shrine’s slate-box among the slates that have been answered · Written at Cold Acre, two leagues north of Sill on the ridge where the one well does not freeze, in the last tend of Tallow, Y.H. 813, by Wenna, who has kept the birth-slates of that ridge for thirty-one years, to Milla, a maid newly set to the slates in Low Kiln after the kilns were brought up. Carried down the ridge road in a potter’s wife’s apron, answered in the margin, and borrowed at the Court’s table in Slate Row, where a clerk set a correction on the back in the neat upright Ledgerhand. It survives folded in the shrine’s slate-box: beeswax from the shrine candle worked into the grain at the head, a thumb of slip from the hand that held the rubbing, one drop of birth-water gone brown in the fold, grey Ash along the gutter where a cuff was laid, a curl of grey wool through the tie-hole which the writer will not untie, a tallow thumb at the outer fold, a tideline where well-water came up over the lower leaf, the clerk’s correction standing above the words, and a line at the foot in a hand that has never been claimed\par}\medskip
To Milla at the shrine in Low Kiln, who has begun to put her hand to the slate before she puts it to the child. From Wenna at Cold Acre, where the well has not frozen in thirty-one winters and nobody on the ridge has ever thought to say why.

I write on the back of a rubbing I took off a slate before the writing had set, so that you have the true hand and not a fair one. A fair copy is a thing a clerk makes. Do not rub the fold. The birth-water has eaten into it and it will come apart between your fingers if you rub it, and then you will have a clean piece of paper and nothing on it, which is what the Court would like every birth to end as.

You wrote to ask about the child who went worse on the third day. You wrote it down as a question about a child and I have read it three times and it is a question about a stone. I will answer the stone. The child will hear the answer over her mother’s shoulder and will not know she has heard it, which is the whole of our trade.

\subsection*{The stone}

Put it at the middle and not at the ends. A warmed stone goes to the belly, under the wool and against the skin, and stays there while you count three breaths and then three more. The hands and feet are wrapped and left. They are not rubbed and they are not set to the fire, and if a neighbour tells you to hold the foot to the hearth you say that the house has spoken and carry the stone back to the middle, because a woman who spends her heat on the extremity has none left for the part that can keep it. The chill comes up from the ends and settles in the middle on the second or third day, and it is the second chill and not a sickness and not a thing to be entered. Call it that where the mother can hear you and call it nothing where the father can. A name spoken in a room becomes a figure by supper in this country.

I have had thirty-one winters at this well and I have never once seen a stone that was too warm for a child and four that were too cold. A stone taken fresh from the fire will burn a belly as easily as it will burn a hand, so hold it to your own wrist before you put it to the child, the way you would taste a spoon of broth before you give it. The wrist knows. The eye does not.

\subsection*{The three days, as I keep them}

What is done to the child — What goes on the slate — What must not go on it\par

The first day — The stone to the belly; the child to the breast; the birth-flower covered — The house, the day, the hour before first grey — A name you would keep\par

The second day — Wrap and leave the cold ends; count the breaths; do not rub — The day again, in the same hand — What the child said in the night\par

The third day — Keep the stone if the chill came; give the child over — The name if the mother has given it; else the date and no more — The chill, the stone, the neighbour’s advice\par

A birth is entered within three days, which is a rule the College wrote and the hearth-maids keep because it was ours before it was theirs. A hand goes to the slate before it goes to the child, and a hand that goes the other way has already decided what the slate will say and will spend the rest of the evening making the child agree with it. Write the day first. The face will tell you the rest in its own time and will keep telling you for a year.

Alda Reed crossed two fingers over a birth-flower on the seventh day of Stone and would not say the word for it. I have crossed two fingers over nine children in this room and never once told a person what I saw under them, and I am not telling you now, though you are my maid and have a right to the practical part. Cross the fingers. Say nothing. The day you tell somebody what you saw is the day it gets written down, and a thing written down in this country does not stay a thing you saw. It becomes a figure in a column, and the column goes up the road.

\subsection*{The man with the tube}

He will come before the three days are out if the house has owed, which in Low Kiln is most houses. He takes the mother’s attention first, and that is a kindness the Court has never entered, because a woman who is being asked for her warmth will look at the man asking and not at the child, and the child is left to the stone and to you. Give him the mother and keep the child behind the slate. If he asks what the stone is for, tell him it is for the warmth. It is for the warmth. That is a true answer and has no figure in it and he cannot put it on a slate without putting a warmth on a slate, which no man does while he is standing in the room where the warmth is.

Do not say no to him. We do not say no. We put the pot between the child and the door and we talk to the pot about the weather until he has gone back over the bridge, and the pot has never once been asked what it held. If he leaves a pale ring on the mother’s wrist, do not rub it and do not cover it before he has gone. Cover it after. A thing covered too soon looks like a thing hidden, and a thing hidden is a thing that will be asked about twice.

\subsection*{The washing verse}

\emph{Sung low to the stone, with the child at the belly and the wool drawn up. Never across the room. The second verse is the one my mother sang and I have set it under yours so you can see where the words change.}

\begin{quote}\itshape Stone from the hearth and wool from the ewe,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the second chill comes through and through;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape warm the middle and wrap the end,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the house will keep what the house can mend.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Four at the well and one gone dry,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape a hand on the slate before the eye;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the name goes down and the face comes up,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the stone keeps warm in the old tin’s cup.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Wash the pot and leave the ring,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the slate takes one and the child takes nothing;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape cross two fingers and hold your tongue,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the count comes back to the one it came from.\end{quote}

I keep a stone from every birth in a tin under the bench, thirty-one of them and not one marked. A clerk would look at that tin and call it a count and ask me for the figures, and when I gave him none he would write \emph{unentered residue} above it and go away satisfied, because a figure with nobody in it satisfies that kind of man more than a figure with a person in it. It is not a count. It is a tin of stones. If you keep such a thing, keep it where the light does not fall on it and never put a mark on any stone, for a marked stone is a slate and a slate can be read by anybody who can hold it.

\subsection*{In the margin, in a younger hand, set close to the lines}

It was the second day, not the third. I have struck your three through and put two underneath in your own iron-gall so that you cannot say a stranger wrote it. The child was cold in one foot and I wrapped it and did not rub it and did not set it to the fire, and the foot stayed dark until the morning and then came back of itself while I was counting breaths at the belly. I set the stone to my own wrist first, as you say, and it was too hot the first time and I waited. I did not cross two fingers over the mark on her skin because I did not know the sign was mine to make, and nobody at the shrine has told me whose it is. Tell me what to do when the man with the tube comes, because I do not know whether to give him the mother or the child and I cannot ask the mother in front of him and I will not ask him. I have kept the stone. It is under the bench and it is not marked.

\subsection*{What the Court hand did}

A clerk of the Court’s table borrowed the leaf on a market morning, being a man who cannot leave paper lie. He has a cuff gone soft from washing and the ink sits in two fingers of it and will not come out. Against \emph{the second chill} he set \emph{a common event; no entry}. Against \emph{do not rub the foot} he wrote \emph{no remedy applied}, which is true and cold and leaves out the woman who did the not rubbing. Against \emph{give him the mother and keep the child behind the slate} he set \emph{the measure is drawn as provided}. Against the tin of stones he wrote \emph{residue unentered}. At the foot of the count he put a round nought and wrote \emph{no vacancy}, where I had written that the child came back of herself while I counted.

He takes the verbs out of a thing and leaves the figures standing, as though a thing always true had no need of anybody to do it. He can enter the chill as common and the stone as residue and the ring as a thing provided, because all of those have a place in his book. He cannot enter the wrist that tested the heat or the fingers that stayed crossed, and he has not tried. I have put my words back underneath and left his standing above, where they belong, the way the Ash is left in the corner until the morning after the Last Day and called dealt with.

\subsection*{At the head and in the gutter}

The wax at the head is off the shrine candle I held over the rubbing while the ink was still wet; it went into the grain in a drop and no knife takes it out clean. The slip came off the hand that held the slate down, and it is the fine grey slip from the upper pit and not the coarse, which is why it stayed in the fold instead of falling through. The brown in the fold is birth-water and has eaten two words off the back; I have not written them in again, because a verse with two words gone is a verse said slowly and all of ours are said slowly. The grey in the gutter came off a cuff laid where no cuff has business lying; I have not swept it and there is no Last Day in a slate-box. The curl of grey wool through the tie-hole is mine and I tied it there for the word I could not put down, and I will not untie it. The tallow is off the lamp I kept low so that the mother would not know I was writing and change the account for me. The tideline is well-water, from the pail set down on the lower leaf while I was telling Milla about the stone, and it has taken the corners off two lines without taking the sense.

\subsection*{At the foot, in a hand nobody will own}

\begin{quote}\itshape The stone keeps the belly and not the name; the slate keeps the name and not the cold. Between the two a woman carries the child, and sets it down, and goes to the next room.\end{quote}

I asked the woman who brings the well-water, a potter’s wife come up to have her mark confirmed, and a man who reads the notices at the Cross, and had three answers and no hand, as I have had before about the grey print and the two words gone. I have left the line where it was written. The leaf goes back into the slate-box with the slates that have been answered. Tomorrow there will be another child up the ridge and I will put a stone in the tin and not mark it, and Milla will put her hand to the slate before she puts it to the child, and neither of us will call the tin an account.

\clearpage\phantomsection\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{The Second File, Being the Names Removed from the Rolls at the College of Assessors in the Hearthseat, with the Figures Struck, the Figures Set Above, and the Reasons Not Entered}
\CRsheetheading{The Second File, Being the Names Removed from the Rolls at the College of Assessors in the Hearthseat, with the Figures Struck, the Figures Set Above, and the Reasons Not Entered}
{\centering\FellFont\itshape\footnotesize\color{faded} A leaf copied forward from the College’s second file at the Opening of the Slates; figures in Ledgerhand, terse remarks in the hand of the junior set to the tin, the names withheld into another hand, two corrections in the narrow upright hand of the College, a column struck and drawn back, and a line at the foot nobody will own · Copied at the Hearthseat in Slate Row, in the College of Assessors, on Ilmen 1, Y.H. 813, the Opening of the Slates, from the tin that lies beside the sealed-file room; carried in the inner pocket of a junior’s coat until the copying was checked. It survives with slate dust worked into the gutter, an iron-gall thumb at the head, a damp tide-line along the foot out of the sealed-file room, a grey Ash print nobody will claim, a green bead of lead glaze in the lower corner, a small square of bare paper where a name was scraped away with a knife, one column struck and drawn back underneath, two corrections in the narrow upright hand, and one line at the foot that has never been owned\par}\medskip
I copy the second file forward. It lies in a tin beside the sealed-file room, and once a year at the Opening I take the leaves out, set them in order and copy them into a fresh hand. The names are not on the leaf I copy. They are kept in the tin in another hand, and I have never been shown which hand; the College holds that a boy who is set to copy removals has no need of the names he removes. I write the shape of each removal, the figure struck, the figure set above, and the remark. That is the whole of my office.

A removal is not a death and not a forgiveness. It is a correction to the roll. The roll is never wrong, so the person entered in it must be. I set that down because it is what the College does, not because I admire it; a clerk who admires his own work has begun to write a sermon, and sermons get copied.

\subsection*{The order of the file}

The name goes off the roll in the same hand that put it on. This is the first thing a junior is taught and the last thing he forgets: a hand that changes between one entry and the next is a hand that can be accused of feeling something. The figure is struck through and a figure set above it, or no figure set above and the place left standing. A reason is not entered. There is a column for the reason in the tin and it is blank from the first leaf to the last, which is a finer arrangement than a column struck out, because a struck column invites a man to ask what was in it.

Twelve bits to a mark; twenty marks to a Sere crown that does not stay in the Hearthseat. An ember is called five marks in this College and no junior has ever seen one exchanged. One in twelve is printed on the notice across the way and is the figure every boy in this room learns to write before he is allowed to write his own name. I have copied it into the removals more times than I can count and have never once set it against a removal, because a removal is not a deduction. A deduction takes a part of a measure. A removal takes the man who was carrying it.

\subsection*{The leaf, as I copied it}

\emph{Figures in Ledgerhand. The remarks are those set down in the tin, in the hand that kept the file, and are not part of the account. A dash is a place where no figure was set above, not a nought.}

Manner of removal — Figure struck — Figure set above — Remark\par

A boy who could not learn the hand — 19 — — — The hand was his own. No man took it from him. Entered in the same hand as those who stayed.\par

A vessel returned three times, entered whole by order — 29 — 30 — \emph{Whole} set above the earlier figure. The earlier figure kept here. Joined to neither.\par

A number cut out of an arm and a new number cut in — 41 — 39 — The later figure entered. The earlier stands in the skin. Nobody asked which count was his.\par

A debt bought before it was due — 52 — — — Assignee entered; debtor not asked. The debt kept its figure and lost its man.\par

A whole return announced for a person not in the room — 300 — — — Room empty. Name not spoken. The file does not say where the person was.\par

A sealed file carried beyond the room — — — — — Carrier’s own name set where the other stood. The first entry left standing beside it.\par

A hand greyed by cold work — 38 — — — The hand struck off the rolls; the fingers greyed. The figure is not struck.\par

Forty of Low Kiln, one slate for the batch, by lot — — — — — Names not taken. Figure entered elsewhere. Nothing carried up into this tin.\par

A foundling left at the mill, stone under him — 12 — — — No name to remove. Stands till a hearth claims him. Copied here and not entered.\par

A keeper who drew without authority, Y.H. 618 — 60 — — — An old leaf, carried forward every year. The figure stands and the name does not.\par

A measure entered in a house roll only — 33 — — — Court never picked it up. Struck by no hand, called forgiven by no hand.\par

Removals copied on this leaf: eleven. Figures struck: eight. Figures set above: two. Names set down: none. Reasons entered: none.

\subsection*{What the narrow hand did}

The Provost’s clerk borrowed the leaf after I had copied it and before it went back into the tin. He writes upright and takes the doer out of every sentence, as though a thing with nobody in it were truer than a thing a man had done.

Where I had copied \emph{they took his name off the roll}, he set \emph{the name was removed from the roll} above it, and above that \emph{the removal is recorded}. I have put my line back underneath and left his standing over it. A sentence with nobody in it is a sentence no woman can ask about, and women ask about these removals in the end, always at a door, always after the tin is shut.

Against the vessel returned three times he struck my \emph{the earlier figure kept here} and wrote \emph{superseded} above it. Both stand. \emph{Superseded} is the word the Weighing uses and the word a household hears in a clean voice. \emph{Kept here} is the word I use when I am not reading anything aloud. I have not chosen between them, and would thank any man who told me I must.

He struck my last column and wrote \emph{No such column} over it. I drew the column back underneath. A man does not count the rows of a column before he writes that there is nothing in it unless the column has troubled him, and he counted every row.

\subsection*{The column with no heading}

I keep the figure that stood before the removal beside the figure the College will read. I have set no heading over it. A heading would make it an account, and an account is a thing a man may be called to answer for, and this College has answered for enough.

On the arm with two sets of numbers the older figure was thirty-nine and the later forty-one, and the file carries them in that order, which is the order in which the knife went into the skin. The roll carries forty-one alone. A surveyor would say the roll is right and the arm is wrong, because a roll has one figure and an arm can have two. I have set down both and joined neither. A clerk who joins two figures to make them agree has begun to keep an account of a man, and the College pays for those by the leaf.

The foundling has no removal. He has a figure and a stone and no name, which is a different absence from the absences in the rest of this tin, and I have kept it on its own line and not laid it across any of them. Seven absences standing in a row are seven; they do not become an account until somebody stands under them to pay, and nobody in this room has stood.

\subsection*{The verse the copyists say}

\emph{Said low at the Opening, while the tin is open and the ink is still wet, never in the Weighing Hall and never with the door toward Slate Row. The last line is said to the tin.}

\begin{quote}\itshape Strike the figure, set the other,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape leave the reason where it stood;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape one in twelve as the notice says,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the roll is always good.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Name goes up and name goes down,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape same neat hand from first to last;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape what the arm keeps the roll forgets,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the house keeps what the roll passed.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Four turns the wheel and the fifth held back,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the tin keeps what the tin was told;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape hold the empty column open,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape it is the only one we hold.\end{quote}

A junior who had been set three Openings to the file said the first two lines while I checked the counting and would not say the last while the Provost’s clerk was in the room, which is how I know the last line is the one that matters. I have copied it as it came and put no gloss on it. A clerk who explains a verse has begun to write a sermon.

\subsection*{In the tin and in the gutter}

The slate dust in the gutter came off the floor of this room, where it gathers under the benches and goes into the grain of whatever is laid down. The brown at the head is iron-gall and mine, from holding the quire open through an Opening morning; there are juniors in this College who can tell a copyist by his thumb before he has spoken a word. The damp line along the foot came out of the sealed-file room, which takes the damp in every season and gives it back to everything kept beside it. The grey print on the outer edge is Ash and is not mine; I found it on the leaf when I took the tin out and have not brushed it away. On the Last Day they sweep the corners of houses and burn what they find in the morning and call it dealt with. There is no Last Day for a tin beside a sealed room.

The green bead in the lower corner is lead glaze and not slip. A girl come up from High Kiln with the sweetness still at her mouth leaned over to see the figures while I copied and touched the leaf and said nothing and went back down the road. I have left it where she put it. The small bare square is where a name was scraped off with a knife before this leaf was given to me. I did not cut it and cannot read what was there. I have not put a name back and have not tried to.

\subsection*{At the foot, in a hand nobody will own}

\begin{quote}\itshape The first file keeps the name. The second keeps the place the name stood in. Neither of them keeps the man.\end{quote}

I asked the Provost’s clerk, a woman who came to ask after a house in the low country, and a collector come up from Greybank, and had three answers and no hand, as I have had before. I have left the line where it was written.

The leaf goes back into the tin and the tin beside the sealed-file room. Tomorrow a boy will be taught to write a life with nobody in it, and a name will be taken off a roll in the same neat hand that put it on, and I shall copy the shape of it forward with the reason column standing blank. Nothing has been joined, named or closed. The empty column stays open, which is the only column in this College nobody has thought to strike.

\clearpage\phantomsection\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{The Second Plank at the Weir, Being the Market Rates of the Ilm and the Tolls of the Roads That Come Down to It, Set Down by the Woman Who Keeps the Landing}
\CRsheetheading{The Second Plank at the Weir, Being the Market Rates of the Ilm and the Tolls of the Roads That Come Down to It, Set Down by the Woman Who Keeps the Landing}
{\centering\FellFont\itshape\footnotesize\color{faded} A landing-keeper’s board copied into a quire, the price of the river set before the price of the road, the fifth road written first and the other four come down to it; corrections in borrowed hands, a grandchild’s crooked sums in the corner, and a line at the foot nobody will own · Written at the Weir, one league upriver of Sill, by Hanne, keeper of the landing and the second plank, in Stone of Y.H. 813, the winter after the Thin Year, when the Ilm lay under ice and the eels were under the ice; set down first in charcoal on the back of a spoiled eel-docket and written up again at the Opening of the Slates, Ilmen 1, Y.H. 814. It survives under the second board of the landing, folded in oiled reed and lashed with eel-sinew: eel slime dried to a varnish at the head, river silt worked into the gutter, a white salt bloom off the Sallow wind along the fore-edge, a green bead of lead glaze brought down on the High Kiln wind pressed into the lower corner, a fish-hook nick at the fore-edge, a reed pressed flat across the verse, a tallow thumb where the lamp was held, a wet ring where a cup was set down and taken up before it was seen, a grey Ash print along the outer fold which is not hers and which she has not swept, a child’s crooked sums in the bottom corner, corrections in hands that are not hers, and one line at the foot that has never been claimed\par}\medskip
I keep the second plank at the Weir and the landing basket on it. Men come down the water with eels and reeds and go up with salt and iron, and they ask two things before the weather: what the thing fetched, and what the road took. I can answer the first by what I have seen go over this plank, the second by asking where a man came from, which gets a true answer when his boots are wet and a clean one when they are dry.

Every book of rates I have been shown puts the river fifth, in a place left empty or written as nothing. I have put it first, because I stand on it. The four roads feed it; a carter here has come down one, and his wheel paid before his load came to water. What follows is what I have taken and what the Cross has cried, on one leaf, because a man’s purse does not keep them in two pockets.

Twelve copper bits to the silver mark; twenty marks to a gold crown, a Sere coin that goes back south and is no use at this plank. The Court books in embers and calls five marks an ember; no ember has ever been laid on this board, and I have left no column for one. A bit here is a bit I have held. A mark is a mark I have given change for.

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{In the narrow upright hand of the moot clerk, written above my first line:} Figures entered in the ordinary way. Rate of the plank. \emph{Underneath, in mine:} There is nothing ordinary about a bit earned standing in water to the calf. I have put the hand back into the figure.\end{quote}

\subsection*{What came down to the water}

\emph{The left column is the figure cried under the moot-post at Sill on Account-day, when the bell goes four, four and a gap. The right is what I have taken over the second plank, or what the woman at the boards told me under her apron. I do not say the two are the same. The moot does.}

Article — Cried at the Cross — At this plank\par

Brown-edged barley loaf — 1 bit — 1 bit, carried in a basket and never weighed\par

Quart of small ale, watered — 1 bit — 1 bit here; 2 at the Weir, where they know it is watered\par

Salt herring — 2 bits — 2 bits, or 3 when the boat has been in and nobody says why\par

Smoked eel, at the boards — 3 bits — a number named under an apron, never twice alike\par

Salted eel — 2 bits — 2 bits and a thumb held on a cord longer than the number wanted\par

Eel skin, dried — 1 mark at the Greybank quay — nothing here; the skin goes down, not up\par

Reed bundle, an armful — not on any board — ask the arm that carried it; the arm knows weight and not cost\par

Coarse pots, the score — 4 bits — 4 bits, and a broken one at Nine Pots is the seller’s\par

Tile, the hundred — 9 bits — 9 bits, with two hollow ones put in that a man sets out again\par

Peat, a barrow — 2 bits in Grain; 5 in Stone — the Stone figure in Seed, paid without complaint\par

Ice-mouse skin — 1 bit in Sill — 1 mark in Keld, which is the same skin with a road under it\par

Ash-mite paste, a thimble at Mud End — not on any board — 4 bits here; the same grey in a Court jar is sixty marks and sealed\par

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Margin:} I have left the eel row without a figure of my own. That is a place and not a nought. A woman names the number into her apron and puts her thumb to a cord. The grey in the Court jar and the grey in the Fen jar came out of the same corner, but I have not joined the jars and have scraped out the word I set beside them. The bare square is the length of it.\end{quote}

\subsection*{What went up from the water}

\emph{Weighed at Greybank before the road takes its share, or not weighed at all. What a man pays at the far end is not what he paid here.}

Article — Figure — What the road added\par

Salt, a sack off the pans — 3 marks — a mark at the coast pass, written as a contribution\par

Iron, a Keldish bar — 2 marks in the lowlands — half a mark in Keld, and a warm-stone off the next man\par

Glass, a sheet from the Glaze Cliffs — 2 marks — 1 bit for the coil it rides in; the sheet broke before Stonemouth\par

Rope, a coil — 1 mark — a bit if it goes on a cart, and tar on this leaf\par

Lead, a pig from the western workings — 6 marks — the seller does not say which workings, and the dust is not entered\par

A kiln hand, the day — 1 mark — 6 bits for a child sweeping the yard\par

Rent, two rooms in Low Kiln, the month — 8 marks — food 12, fuel 4; a house keeps by not-doings and pays all the same\par

Pig, over the weighing board — 6 marks — 4 bits for the drove and a bit to have it cried twice\par

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{In a Council clerk’s leaning hand:} \emph{Seasonal rate} against the peat, \emph{market rate} against the eels. \emph{In mine:} A house of Sere can call a figure a rate, because a rate is a thing that can be emptied and refilled. I have held peat in a barrow in Silt and called it what it was.\end{quote}

\subsection*{The tolls of the roads that come down here}

\emph{The figure demanded is written above the figure I saw go out of a pocket. Four roads come to this water and one road is the water itself. I have set the water first, which is where the clerk’s hand will want to correct me.}

Road and place — As demanded — As given\par

The river, going down or coming up — no toll and no guarantee — nothing at the plank; the river takes what it takes and enters none of it\par

Plank walk at the Weir — 1 bit — 1 bit on the board that bears; I do not say which board it is\par

North bridge at Sill — nothing — nothing; the Fishstairs folk argued it and won\par

Winter ford, when there is water to cross — 1 bit — 1 bit; in the Long Cold the ice bore for ninety-four days and no collector crossed\par

Clay Road, loaded cart at the Sill end — 2 bits — 2 bits here and 2 more at the factor’s man at Greybank\par

Clay Road, foot passenger — 1 bit; nothing on Account-day — 1 bit; on Account-day I walk with the crowd and pay nothing\par

Salt Road, a sack at the coast pass — 1 mark to the Council of Tides — 1 mark, freely entered, which is what they call it\par

Rim Road, a cart at the pass — 1 mark, or iron to the value — 1 mark in iron, the iron heavier than the mark\par

Rim Road, a beast on the hoof — half a mark — half a mark and a warm-stone off the next man who has one\par

Hearth Road, at the barrier — none; there is no barrier — none; the figure was read to me twice at home\par

Nine Pots road, west from Sill — no gate — a pot set down at the feud post, an insult in Sill and a toll in the yards\par

Fen boardwalk to the Standing Post — 1 bit for a dry foot — a marked stick for a wet one; outsiders are not told which boards bear\par

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{In the moot clerk’s narrow hand, against the first four rows:} Roads entered, three. \emph{Underneath, in mine:} There are five, and the first is under my feet. I have written my four above his three and left both standing. A river is not a gap in a list; it is the thing the list was made to reach.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{In the Council clerk’s leaning hand, against the salt row:} \emph{toll} struck and \emph{contribution freely entered} written over it. \emph{In mine:} The figures stand. A Council that cannot charge a toll has found a finer name for one, and a man pays it out of the same purse.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Margin:} A carter from High Kiln asked what the Hearth Road cost and I showed him the empty row. He said it was the truest figure on the page and the dearest. The Court takes nothing at the gate because it has taken it at home. I did not put that in the demanded column; it would stop nobody from loading.\end{quote}

\subsection*{What no gate takes}

These are not dues. No slate takes them and no factor enters them, and they are why a book like this has to be kept.

The Ferr runs lead dust off the western workings, and a man who drinks it through a season comes back thin; there is no figure at Stonemouth for that. The sweet sickness from bad glaze shows first as a pale line at the gum and ends with a woman who cannot hold a cup; the mixers of High Kiln taste it each morning and call it their work. At the Weir the traps go under ice and a man who lifts them comes up with his hands the colour of old rope; the water keeps no count. Beyond the Cold Pass the cold takes a year and gives back a thinner man who has forgotten what he went for.

A due is a figure somebody will stand behind. These have nobody behind them, which is why they get paid.

\subsection*{The song of the second plank}

\emph{Sung at the landing when the lamp is lit and nobody is crossing. Not at the Cross, and not while a man from Slate Row is on the boards.}

\begin{quote}\itshape One for the board and none for the stream,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the stream pays the boat and it never pays the moot;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape four roads come down with a bit in the shoe,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and one comes down with the whole of the crew.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Twelve to the mark and twenty to the crown,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and five to the ember the Court books down;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the beam keeps the weight and the bag keeps the sum,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the river keeps going and takes none of it home.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape A pot at Nine Pots and a bit at the pass,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape a mark at the coast and nothing at the bridge;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape ask the arm, ask the cord, ask the running water,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the Court has a figure for all of the four.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape I have a book with the figures I gave\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and a row kept empty for what the river took.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{In the moot clerk’s hand, against the last line:} Three figures entered. \emph{Underneath, in mine:} There are four, and I have set nothing in the place of the fourth. A nought is a figure. That line is a place.\end{quote}

\subsection*{What the borrowed hands did}

The moot clerk struck the river out of the count and numbered the roads as three, leaving the water and the bridges out. I wrote four above his three and put the water above the four, so a man sees where his load came from before he sees what it cost. The Council clerk struck \emph{toll} and wrote \emph{contribution freely entered}, and left every figure standing. The factor’s clerk called the peat a seasonal rate and the eels a market rate. I have left their words above mine and mine under theirs, as a mended pot keeps the old break showing.

My granddaughter did the sums in the corner and got the crown wrong, putting twenty marks to a bit and carrying one. I have not rubbed it out. She will learn which figures a man can argue with, which is the harder lesson and not taught at any College.

\subsection*{In the head and in the fold}

The varnish at the head is eel slime, off the hand that held the basket while I wrote; no washing takes it out. The silt in the gutter came in on the boots of every carter since the thaw, and is the same silt that lies under the sill in Sill, which the moot does not count and the river does. The salt bloom has eaten the last letter of the date, so I cannot read whether it was Stone 23 or Stone 24 the wind came on, which is the only loss I mind. The green bead is lead glaze off a cup whose rim had gone thin; a girl come down from High Kiln set it on the leaf, with the sweetness still at one corner of her mouth, and went back without asking what it was. The reed I pressed flat on the walk below the plank, where the boards move after rain and nobody will say which will bear. The grey along the outer fold is not mine and I have not swept it; there is Ash enough here without borrowing a stranger’s.

\subsection*{At the foot, in a hand nobody will own}

\begin{quote}\itshape The board keeps the figure the beam held. The plank keeps the figure the man carried. The river keeps neither, and takes the road in winter.\end{quote}

I asked a carter, a woman at the eel boards and a clerk come down from Greybank, and had three answers and no hand. I have left the line where it was written.

The quire goes back under the second board and the reed goes back around it. Tomorrow the ice may bear or it may not, and a man will come down with a sack and ask what his salt fetched and what the road took, and I shall give him the figure I gave today. By evening it will be a thing that was true.

\clearpage\phantomsection\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{The Sermon at the Broken Pot, Being What Was Said at the Bone Orchard on the Remembering of Y.H. 812}
\CRsheetheading{The Sermon at the Broken Pot, Being What Was Said at the Bone Orchard on the Remembering of Y.H. 812}
{\centering\FellFont\itshape\footnotesize\color{faded} A pot-break sermon preached at the shrine of broken pots outside Sill’s north gate, over the year’s pots and the one pot nobody brought; the manner of the breaking in the niche-keeper’s hand, the sayings in Grathic, the breaking-song in verse, the row of pots in a tally, a factor’s clerk’s correction in Ledgerhand set above the keeper’s verbs, and one line at the foot in a hand nobody will own · Preached by an old woman of Sill who had broken pots at the Bone Orchard for one and thirty years, on the Remembering of Y.H. 812, the Thin Year, over the pots set in the niche a league north of the Cross; written that evening by the woman who keeps the niche, in charcoal and with the point of a broken nail on the inner face of a grave-tile that came away whole when it should have broken, and kept under the flat stone among the sherds. It survives with grey Ash ground into the slip along the gutter, a salt bloom in a hairline at the head, a tallow thumb where the tile was held down on a man’s knee, a green bead of lead glaze caught in a chip of the rim, a morsel of dry clay in the fold, one correction in the narrow upright hand of a factor’s clerk come out from Greybank that takes the verbs out and numbers the nameless pot as nil, and one line struck through and written again very small underneath in a hand nobody will own. Copied forward in Ilmen, Y.H. 813, with the verbs put back and the empty place left the length it is.\par}\medskip
I keep the niche of broken pots at the Bone Orchard. It is my work to set the year’s pots in a row and lift the flat stone on the Remembering and put the sherds back. What follows is written on the back of a grave-tile that came away whole from the row and would not break, so I kept it, the way this ground keeps everything that fails at the work it was made for.

The old woman stood with her back to the north gate and spoke first to the pots, as potters do, and to the clay under them, and to the fire that had made them, and only at the end to the people standing in the row. She had broken pots here for one and thirty years and had never once broken one at the foot. She said the same things every year. I have written them as she said them, with the verbs where she put them, because a sermon said over a pot is a thing a household has to use.

The grey in the gutter came off my cuff when I measured the ridge two doors down in Low Kiln and came back to write, and I have not swept it. The salt at the head is from a woman’s hand laid flat on the tile to hold it still in the wind off the ridge. The tallow is mine. The green bead is not slip; a girl with sweetness still at her mouth leaned over to see what I was writing and touched the rim with her thumb. The tile has a chip at the upper right where somebody tapped it with a knuckle and did not say what answer it gave.

\subsection*{The manner of the breaking, as the niche keeps it}

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item Set the pots in a row on the flat stone with their lips to the north. Feet toward water is for the body; lips toward the Hearth is for the pot. Do not mix the two.

\item Tap each pot with the knuckle before you lift it. Listen for what it answers. Do not say what you heard where a man with a slate is standing.

\item Break at the lip with one blow. A blow at the foot sends the heat into the clay and the clay will keep it, which is a kind of burying twice.

\item Break it whole. A pot broken into dust has let the heat out through a hundred little doors and cannot say which way it went.

\item If a pot answers flat, break it gently. It has given already and asks no help from you.

\item When the bell comes up the north road from the Cross, stop. It has counted something that is not your pot. Begin again after. Four, four and a gap, and the gap is not ours to fill.

\item Break the nameless pot last. Do not let anybody bring it. It comes out of the niche by itself.

\end{itemize}

\subsection*{The sermon, as she said it}

\subsection*{Of the lip and the foot}

She put her thumb in the chip at the rim of a milk pot and turned it so the row could see where the star was.

“You bring me a pot and you say, break this, it is my mother’s. I ask you nothing. I break it at the lip, because the lip is the mouth and the heat goes out of a mouth the way breath goes out of a person. Break it at the foot and you have put your mother’s warmth into the ground twice: once in the grave and once under the grave, where the clay keeps it and will not let it go.”

She struck the pot with the heel of her hand and it opened clean across, two pieces and a third small one that fell among the sherds.

“A whole pot keeps. A broken pot gives. That is the whole of my preaching and I have had one and thirty years to find another sentence and could not.”

\subsection*{Of the note}

“Before I break, I tap. You have all heard a pot tapped at the wheel. A sound one answers full and a cracked one answers flat, a little dead sound that stops at the surface and will not go through. You bring me a pot that answered flat three days before the person went and you say nothing about it, and I say nothing either. We are not fools in this district. We know what a pot was doing while we were looking at the person.”

She tapped the cup with the cupworm in it. It gave nothing that I could hear from where I sat, and she put it down on its side.

“This one I break gently. It has been giving since it came off the wheel and there is no heat in it to let out. Do not break a pot that has given already as though it had held. That is a cruelty to the pot and a lie about the household.”

One of the women in the row said that a pot was only a pot. The old woman turned her head a degree toward her and said: “A body is only a body, too, and we wash it and put its feet to the water and send for a man with a tube. Do not tell me what a pot is. I have made them.”

\subsection*{Of the one nobody brought}

There is one pot in the niche that no household brings. It is a plain clay pot, smaller than a milk pot, with no mark on it and a lip worn smooth by hands that have lifted it every Remembering since I can remember. The old woman took it out from under the flat stone and held it a moment against her apron before she set it on the row.

“This is for them that have no house to break for them,” she said. “The little graves lie over there beyond the broken stake, shallow, because the clay was frozen when they were put in. You can walk past them and not see them, and people do, and I do not blame them, because a person can only look at so much in a winter.”

She struck it at the lip. It opened with a dry sound, smaller than the milk pot’s, and the three pieces lay where they fell.

“The Court reads a whole return at the Weighing in a clean voice for a person not in the room. I have heard it done. I have stood outside the door and heard it done, and come up here and broken this. Somebody has to break for the ones the clean voice does not name. That is not an argument with the Court. It is a pot with a name left out of it.”

She would not say how many graves lay beyond the broken stake, and when the clerk asked her she said the clay was frozen and she had not counted that year. A woman beside me wrote something in the margin of her tally and covered it with her thumb. I have not read it and it is not on this tile.

\subsection*{Of the keeping}

A factor’s clerk had come out from Greybank with a cuff gone soft from washing and ink in two fingers, and stood at the end of the row with a slate held to his forearm. He asked the old woman what became of the heat once the pot was broken.

“It goes up,” she said. “That is what I know of it. It goes up out of the mouth and into the air and the air is bigger than the house. I have stood at more breakings than I could set a figure to, and never once seen it come back to the pot.”

“It is banked,” the clerk said.

“It is gone from the pot,” she said. “I have not said where from. Those are two sentences and I will not have one put over the other.”

“Nothing is lost that we have kept,” he said, in the voice that takes the speaker out of his sentence.

“I have never kept one,” she said. “I have let go of a great many. If the Hearth wants what went up, let the Hearth come out of its iron and fetch it. It has not come yet, and I have been waiting one and thirty years.”

After that she gave the mark on the niche the same answer she gives every year. The clerk asked what it was, the crossed thing cut in the stone above the pots, which the surveyor draws in the chart and does not explain. She said it was cut in Y.H. 668. He asked her again in a different way and she gave him the same year.

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{In the margin, in my hand:} A date is safe. The factor’s clerk says so himself, and he is right, because a date is the only answer that cannot be argued with. I have set down her year and left the question standing.\end{quote}

\subsection*{The breaking-song}

\emph{Sung low, standing, while the nameless pot is lifted out of the niche. The row says the last line with her. There is a gap before the last line, the one the bell leaves, and I have left it here as it is sung.}

\begin{quote}\itshape Break at the lip and not at the foot,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the heat goes up and not into the root;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape a whole pot holds and a cracked pot gives,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the clay keeps only what the clay receives.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Four for the corners, four for the wall,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and one for the place where a name should fall;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the bell comes four and four and a gap,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the pot gives back what the pot had.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Do not ask the fire where the fire has gone;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape do not ask the ground what it stands upon;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape say the name, or leave the place it had,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and come back warm, as the Keeping said.\end{quote}

A girl from High Kiln asked what the space before the last line was for. Nobody answered her. The clerk put a round nought against it later, which I have left where he set it.

\subsection*{The row, as the niche counts it}

Pot — Brought by — Broken — What was said over it\par

Milk pot, lip starred — a woman of High Kiln — at the lip, one blow — her mother’s name, said three times\par

Cup with a cupworm in it — a man of the Clay Yard — at the foot, by mistake — nothing; the heat went into the clay\par

The nameless pot — the niche — at the lip — no name; a place left the length of one\par

A grave-tile, came away whole — nobody — not broken — kept, and written on\par

There were two and twenty pots in the row besides these, and I have not set them down, because a tally of pots is a thing a clerk can carry away and a name is not. The two and twenty went into the barrow with the grey the next market-day and nobody in the square looked at it twice.

\subsection*{What the clerk did}

He borrowed the tile on the morning after and gave it back with the verbs taken out.

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item Where she said \emph{a whole pot keeps, a broken pot gives}, he wrote \emph{retention and leakage are lawful conditions of a vessel} above and left hers below.

\item Where she said \emph{the heat goes up}, he wrote \emph{the measure is released to the keeping} and underlined it twice.

\item At the nameless pot he put a round nought and wrote \emph{vacancy} beside it, and when I asked him what a pot was worth that nobody had brought, he said nothing a clerk could enter, which was the first true thing he said all morning.

\item At the line about the Hearth coming to fetch its heat he wrote \emph{claim not established}, and drew a small stop between two clusters of his neat dark hand.

\end{itemize}

I have put the verbs back underneath where she put them and left his hand standing above, as the flat stone leaves the sherds and the sherd leaves the clay. He takes the verbs out because a thing always true has no need of them. I put them back because a woman standing in the cold wants to know who did the letting go, and whether it was her own hand.

\subsection*{At the foot}

Struck through once and written again underneath, very small, in a hand that is not mine, not the old woman’s and not the clerk’s:

\begin{quote}\itshape A whole pot is a lie told by a sound vessel.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape A whole pot is a vessel that has not yet been asked.\end{quote}

I asked the old woman, the woman of High Kiln, the man who brought the cupworm cup, the girl who asked about the gap, and the clerk, and had five answerings and no hand. I have left the line struck through and standing, which is the only honest way to keep a sentence you cannot sign.

The tile goes back under the flat stone with the flat side down, so the writing is kept from the wet. Next Remembering I shall lift the stone and set the row out, and the nameless pot will come out of the niche and be broken at the lip as it is every year. If the clerk comes again I shall let him take the verbs out. I shall put them back.

\clearpage\phantomsection\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{The Sermon at the Counting Stone, Being What Iyn of the Listening Stone Said to a Boy at His First Sitting in Bone of Y.H. 812, with the Sayings Said Twice, the Sitting-Song Left with a Season in It, the Sittings in a Register, a Survey-Clerk’s Correction, and a Line at the Foot in a Hand Nobody Will Own}
\CRsheetheading{The Sermon at the Counting Stone, Being What Iyn of the Listening Stone Said to a Boy at His First Sitting in Bone of Y.H. 812, with the Sayings Said Twice, the Sitting-Song Left with a Season in It, the Sittings in a Register, a Survey-Clerk’s Correction, and a Line at the Foot in a Hand Nobody Will Own}
{\centering\FellFont\itshape\footnotesize\color{faded} A sermon of the Vorr preached at the shrine of the counting stones five leagues above Keld Keep in the high Rim; the sayings in the slow long-vowelled Rim speech set down in Grathic letters, the sitting-song with every line said twice and the season left the length it is kept, the sittings in a high-path register, one correction in the narrow upright Ledgerhand of a Court survey-clerk come up from Greybank, and a line at the foot in a hand nobody will own · Preached on Bone 12, Y.H. 812, the Thin Year, at the third stone from the high path, by Iyn of the Listening Stone at the setting-out of a boy’s first Long Sitting; written that evening by the woman who keeps the sitting-register at Keld Keep, in charcoal on the back of a rim-seam rubbing spoiled by a wet slate, folded with a pinch of blighted-seam dust in the crease and sewn with wire into oiled survey-cloth, and kept in the register-box beside the high-path door. It survives with pale lichen worked into the head off the north stone, the print of a doubled last joint pressed in tallow at the second corner, rime from the high path ground into the fold, a warm-stone shaving that held its heat one night on the stone floor and is cold now, a thread of copper wire off the spoiled rubbing, a wet ring where a dish of meltwater stood from the first saying to the last, a grey Ash print nobody will own, the dust shut in the crease, one correction in the narrow upright hand of a Court survey-clerk come up from Greybank to count the winter lead, and a line struck through and written again very small underneath in a hand that has never come forward. Copied once at Greybank in Ilmen, Y.H. 813, with the verbs put back and the season left the length it is kept.\par}\medskip
I keep the sitting-register at Keld Keep, in a box beside the high-path door, and nobody asked me for this. There is no word for shrine in the Vorr tongue; they call the stones the stones, and a man below who says \emph{shrine} has named what he cannot see. I write because the boy had no name. A Vorr takes his name one at a time, many years apart, and is known until then by the stone he keeps, so I have entered him as the boy of the third stone and left the place where a name would stand the length a name would be.

He spoke to the stone, the dust, the dish of meltwater, and last to the boy, the order the Vorr use when a season is waiting and somebody below may be listening who wants a figure. He said every sentence twice. I have set the second beneath where it mattered and left it out where it did not, a freedom no Vorr would take and they have never asked me for this leaf.

The pale at the head is lichen scraped off the north stone; it goes into the grain and no wet sleeve takes it out. The doubled print at the second corner is his, pressed into my lamp’s tallow while he turned the leaf; a Vorr’s last joint is split in two and leaves a mark like a cleft hoof. The rime in the fold was on the path at first grey and was water by the time I folded. The shaving kept its heat one night on the stone floor and is cold now, which is the order of things here. The copper thread came off the spoiled rubbing and has nothing to do with the sermon. The ring is the dish, set down at the first saying and taken up before the boy saw it. The grey came off a cuff and nobody will own it; there is no Last Day above this Keep.

\subsection*{The manner of the sitting, as the stone has it}

\emph{Written small, from watching, not from any order the Court has printed.}

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item Come at first grey, before the seam-tide turns. A boy who comes at noon sits in another man’s season and calls it his own, and the stone has never once corrected him.

\item Sit facing the way you came. An elder will turn a boy around without a word if he faces the road, and the road is not the direction this shrine keeps.

\item Put the dust on the palm, not on the stone. The stone marks what is kept; the hand marks who keeps it.

\item Say each sentence twice. Once for the stone and once for the boy. A third saying is the sayer’s fault; the stone has heard three before and will hear three thousand.

\item Do not say the number before the season ends. A number said early has a buyer, and a man from Greybank would pay for it and enter it wrongly.

\item The first sitting gives a number and not a name. A boy who asks for his name is given the number again, which is not anger but the arrangement of years this people keeps.

\item A season is not an hour. The impatient hear the stone scratch and bring home a number they could have had at home.

\item A number goes down the road. The dust stays. If a man from the Court writes one, let him write the number and not the sitting; the two have never agreed.

\end{itemize}

\subsection*{The sermon, as he said it}

\subsection*{Of the dust}

He took a pinch of grey from a fold of his coat and pressed it into the boy’s palm with the doubled joint of his last finger. The dust is marked off a blighted seam and is not sold.

“This is put down. It is not given.”

\begin{quote}\itshape This is put down. It is not given.\end{quote}

“A thing given can be taken back. A thing put down stays where it was put. I have never given a boy anything in forty years and have had no cause to ask anything back.”

“The Court has a word for what is put down and a column to put it in. This has no column. If you find one on the road below, do not stand in it.”

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Margin, in my hand:} He used the word for \emph{put down} that the factor’s clerk at Greybank translates as \emph{retained}. I have left both standing, as the dust lies on the palm and not under it.\end{quote}

\subsection*{Of the first sitting}

“You will sit until the number changes. It changes. That is the whole of the sitting.”

“Ask what it changes to and I will say the numbers are correct. That answers the numbers, not you. A third asking is yours.”

\begin{quote}\itshape Ask what it changes to and I will say the numbers are correct. That answers the numbers, not you. A third asking is yours.\end{quote}

“You want a name. The stone gives a number. Names come one at a time and many years apart, and a man here is known by the stone he keeps. I have kept this one forty years and have not been given the other word.”

A girl from the Keep asked what the boy was to be called. He gave her the number. She asked again in another way and he gave her the same number. I have set the two askings down and not joined them.

\subsection*{Of the bone}

“The count is in the bone. The tube finds nothing there.”

\begin{quote}\itshape The count is in the bone. The tube finds nothing there.\end{quote}

“They below take what is in the blood and write it on a slate. We keep ours where no iron reaches. A thing a man cannot take is a thing he will not call a gift.”

“We were never owed. We do not ask.”

\begin{quote}\itshape We were never owed. We do not ask.\end{quote}

A miner stood at the back with a pale ring at his wrist. When the elder said the last, the miner covered the ring and went down the path before the boy had heard the saying twice. I have written the hand and not the man.

\subsection*{Of what goes down}

“A stone is kept. A number is sold.”

\begin{quote}\itshape A stone is kept. A number is sold.\end{quote}

A Court survey-clerk had come up with ink in two fingers and held his slate inward so the row could not see the column.

“You will carry the number down in a clean hand and read it in a room I have never stood in,” the elder said to him. “I have given you the number and not the sitting. Do not lay one over the other.”

“The measure is declared and the person is identified,” the clerk said, in the voice that takes the speaker out of his own sentence. He wrote it down and put the boy in a column where no boy had stood before.

“If the Court’s fire is a candle lit from our mountain,” the elder said, turning toward the stone and not the clerk, “it has never been brought up here to light this one.”

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{In my hand:} He said that to the stone. The clerk wrote \emph{claim not examined} against it, true of a man who has never climbed five leagues of scree. Both stand.\end{quote}
