Higher on the path a body sat facing the way it had come, with no fire and no word read over it. The elder said: “He came from there. He faces there. The sitting is finished. No one goes up to bring him down. There is no slate at a Vorr death and no return, and we do not ask the account below to make one.”

\subsection*{The sitting-song}

\emph{Said low, facing the stone, the dust in the palm. The elder says each line twice and the boy says the last four twice after him. There is a season between the third part and the last, the length of a sitting, and I have left the space the length it is kept.}

\begin{quote}\itshape The stone was here before the sitting.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape The stone was here before the sitting.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape The dust is on the hand and the hand is on the stone,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the dust is on the hand and the hand is on the stone;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape one for the way you came and one for the way you face,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape one for the way you came and one for the way you face.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape The number goes in where the bone is old,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the number goes in where the bone is old;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the count comes down and the stone stays up,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the count comes down and the stone stays up.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Here the boy sits for a season. No words are said. The space is the season and I have left it the length it is kept.}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape The number changes. The stone does not.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape The number changes. The stone does not.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape We were never owed. We do not ask.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape We were never owed. We do not ask.\end{quote}

A girl from the shift asked what the space was for. Nobody answered her. The clerk put a round nought against it and wrote \emph{vacancy}, which is the first figure of his that has ever fitted anything above this Keep, and still does not fit, because a nought is a number and the space is a season. I have left it where he set it.

\subsection*{The sittings, as the register keeps them}

\emph{The number goes down the high path in a coat and leaves nothing in the box. These I have set down where they stood, without saying what the numbers count, because I do not know and the Vorr have never told me.}

Who kept the stone — Count before — Count after — What was entered at Greybank\par

Iyn of the Listening Stone, at his third sitting — 41 — 41 — figures confirmed; no proceedings\par

A woman of the high path, at her second — 17 — 17 — number unchanged; no cause assigned\par

Ao of the Third Seam, before the Rim War — 9 — 14 — change entered; reason withheld\par

The boy of this morning, first sitting — not yet counted — the sitting continues — a column standing\par

One seated higher on the path facing the way he came — no count — no count — no entry; party not on the roll\par

There were sittings before these that I could set a season to, and I have not written them, because a row of seasons is a thing a clerk can carry away and a stone is not. The Vorr call no number a rise and no season a loss, and no boy has ever come down and thanked the stone for it.

\subsection*{What the clerk did}

He borrowed the leaf on the morning after while I was entering the boy in the register, and gave it back with the verbs taken out.

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item At \emph{this is put down, not given} he wrote \emph{the stone is the lawful custodian of the mark}, true in a room where a mark can pass from hand to hand and meaningless on a high path.

\item At \emph{the count is in the bone} he wrote \emph{the measure is not deposited; party difficult to draw}, and underlined \emph{difficult} twice, which is the only part he has ever understood.

\item At \emph{we were never owed} he wrote \emph{the party is not entered for a return}, leaving out the owing and keeping the party.

\item At \emph{the sitting continues} he wrote \emph{proceedings pending the season}, and put a season into a column where no season has ever stood.

\item At the gap in the song he put a round nought and wrote \emph{vacancy}. When I asked what a season was worth with no number in it, he said nothing a clerk could enter, the first true thing he said all morning.

\end{itemize}

I have put the verbs back underneath and left his hand standing above, as a newer repair lies over an older one in the seam and the older is still there under it. He takes the doer out because a thing with nobody in it cannot be argued with. I put the doer back because a boy at forty with dust in his palm wants to know who put it there, and whether it was his own hand that will keep it.

\subsection*{At the head and in the gutter}

The lichen is off the north stone and will not wash out of the grain, which is why the Vorr scrape with a thumb and not with cloth. The doubled print is Iyn’s and no other hand in this Keep could leave it. The rime was on the path at first grey and was gone before I folded; the writing there is thin and I have not gone over it, for a word written thin is a word said quietly. The shaving held one night and is cold, which the keeper of the warm-stone calls the order of things. The dish stood from the dust to the dead and was drunk by nobody. The grey came off a cuff and nobody will own it. The pinch of dust is shut in the crease and has never been sold or spent or put on a stone.

\subsection*{At the foot, in a hand nobody will own}

Struck through once and written again underneath, very small, in a hand that is not mine, not Iyn’s and not the clerk’s:

\begin{quote}\itshape The stone has kept every number that was ever brought up to it.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape It has never once been asked what the numbers were for.\end{quote}

I asked the girl from the shift, a surveyor who carries the numbers down, a miner who came up and went down again in one morning, and the clerk, and had four answerings and no hand. I have left the line struck through and standing, which is the only honest way to keep a sentence you cannot sign.

The leaf goes back into the oiled cloth and the cloth into the register-box with the dust in its crease and the copper thread where it fell. Next Bone another boy will sit and come down with a number changed or unchanged, and the clerk will take the verbs out and put a nought in the season. I shall put them back as I did this time, and leave the nought in its place and the space the length the sitting is, and the place where the name would stand the length a name would be.

\clearpage\phantomsection\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{The Sermon at the Glaze Cliffs, Being What an Old Dipper Said Over the Beads on a Morning in Ash of Y.H. 812, with the Draw-Song Left as It Is Sung, the Bead-Row in a Tally, a Court Clerk’s Correction, and a Line at the Foot in a Hand Nobody Will Own}
\CRsheetheading{The Sermon at the Glaze Cliffs, Being What an Old Dipper Said Over the Beads on a Morning in Ash of Y.H. 812, with the Draw-Song Left as It Is Sung, the Bead-Row in a Tally, a Court Clerk’s Correction, and a Line at the Foot in a Hand Nobody Will Own}
{\centering\FellFont\itshape\footnotesize\color{faded} A sermon of the Sallow pans preached in the bead-niche under the blue-green cliff where the glass-sand is dug; the sayings in Vhaleni set down in Grathic as I heard them, the draw-song with the ebb-line left as it is sung, the beads in a tally, one correction in the narrow upright Ledgerhand of a clerk come down from Greybank, and one line at the foot in a hand nobody will own · Preached in Ash of Y.H. 812, the Thin Year, on a morning when the draw ran seaward against the wind, by an old dipper of the pans who had trailed a net at dawn for more years than he would give; written that evening by the keeper of the glass tally in the shed below the cliffs, on the back of a salt-paper contract gone damp and therefore void, folded with a green bead in the crease and tied with a tarry end of net-cord. It survives with salt bloom worked into the head and the gutter, glass dust in the grain, a green stain along the fold that smells sweet in heat and is not sweet to the tongue, one brine-gull feather, a wet ring where a dish of sea-water stood from the first voice to the last, a tarry fibre at the tie, the damp of the voided contract eating the lower corner, one correction in the narrow upright hand of a Court clerk come down from Greybank to count the winter salt, and a line struck through and written again very small underneath in a hand that has never come forward. Copied once at Greybank in Ilmen, Y.H. 813, with the verbs put back and the ebb-line left the length it is sung.\par}\medskip
I keep the glass tally in the shed under the cliffs and nobody asked me for this. I write because the old man spoke to the cliff, the net, the dish and last of all to us, which is the order the pans use when somebody may be listening who wants a figure. When a man asked him the year of some tide he gave the tide instead, which is the Vhaleni way of answering a question you do not mean to keep. I have set his words down in Grathic, which is not his tongue. Where he left a verb out I have left it out and put it back underneath in my own hand, because a saying said over a bead is a thing a person has to use.

The leaf is the back of a contract that went damp in the shed and is therefore no contract at all, which the Council calls a virtue and the clerk from Greybank does not. The salt at the head came off the old man’s hand when he flattened it on the niche; the glass in the grain is from the sand we dig and scratches a fingernail. The green along the fold is not slip and not salt. It came off a bead left in the crease in the sun and smells sweet when the shed is warm, and I have told the girls not to put a tongue to it. The feather is a brine-gull’s. The ring is the dish, set down at the first voice and taken up at the last. I have not washed any of it.

\subsection*{The manner of the dipping, as the pans keep it}

\emph{Written small, from watching, not from any order the Court has printed.}

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item Go down before the light and trail the net in the draw. Do not say what the draw is doing. A draw said aloud becomes an argument, and there is argument enough at the Quay.

\item Salt on the hand, never on the net. The net has its own business with the sea.

\item Leave a bead in the niche for every morning you dip. The sea cannot eat it and a clerk can carry it away, which is why we leave it in a hole in the cliff and not on a shelf.

\item Do not lick the cliff. In the heat it smells of sugar and in the cold of nothing, and children are told in both months. A child who licks it gets a pale line at the gum and in the end cannot hold a cup, and no dipper has known a cure.

\item If a brine-gull takes a bead, let it go. It has carried the keeping into the air, where it was going in any case. No slate in Vhal stands the poorer for a gull.

\item If the draw runs backward, do not correct it. We are the ones who are early or late.

\item When a man with a slate comes among the pans, stop, and begin again after. His figure is for another room. Do not lay the two together.

\end{itemize}

He said the last twice, once to the cliff and once to a man behind me with his hands in his sleeves. I have not put the sayings together.

\subsection*{The sermon, as he said it}

\subsection*{Of the green}

He put his palm flat on the cliff where the blue-green stain ran down like a glaze that had been poured and not stopped.

“Look at it,” he said. “Sweet in the heat. The children are told not to lick it and the glass-men not to breathe it, and still we dig the sand at its foot and make good glass and sell it to Sere, and Sere puts wine in it and empties the wine at a feast. There is no trick in this. A thing can be good to look at and bad to take in. That is the whole of my preaching and I could find no other sentence.”

There was green on the creases of his hand and he did not wipe it on his coat.

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Margin, in my hand:} He used the Vhaleni word for \emph{sweet} that also means \emph{owed} when a debt is left too long. I have set \emph{sweet} because that is what the cliff does. He would not have the other word written, and that is a word with a use.\end{quote}

\subsection*{Of the bead}

“Every morning I leave one,” he said. “A green bead in a hole in the cliff. I have left them since before you were born and never counted them.

“A priest out of Greybank told me the bead is an offering to the Hearth and that the Hearth keeps what is given. I asked him what became of a bead in a crack no priest could reach without a rope. He said the offering was received, which a man says when he has not been down the cliff.

“Glass keeps its colour. Salt keeps nothing. A man who puts a bead in a hole and goes back to the pans has done something with his hands before the day took it from him. If the Hearth wants the bead, let it come down the cliff and fetch it. It has not come yet.”

A woman beside me said the beads were only beads. He turned his head without haste. “A net is only a net,” he said. “I have mended them for years. Do not tell me what a bead is.”

\subsection*{Of the draw}

“The water goes out with the warm in it,” he said to the dish. “That is the draw. It runs against the wind and has since my father’s father dipped, and we bless it at dawn so it will go on running and not turn and take what stands on the shore.

“They say there is a Hearth under the salt and the Court’s fire is only its chimney. I have been asked if this is true and I have given a tide for an answer, because a tide does not spoil in the mouth and a man with a slate likes a thing he can set in a column. Ask me what is under the salt and I will tell you which tide. There is always one more tide than there are questions.”

He put two fingers in the dish and lifted them out.

“I have dipped thirty years and never seen a measure come back out of the sea. Salt comes back. Glass comes back. A boat comes back if the wind is kind. A person does not, and the dippers do not say it, and I am saying it to a dish that will not carry it up the Salt Road.”

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{In the narrow upright Ledgerhand of a Court clerk who came down from Greybank on the third day and borrowed the leaf while I was at the pans:} The Sallow draw is a tide of the Keeping and is efficacious thereby. The measure is retained in the salt. Enter as nil.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape *\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Underneath, in mine:} I have put \emph{goes out} and \emph{comes back} under his \emph{is retained}. His sentence is true eighteen leagues inland and has no verbs for a woman standing in salt water.\end{quote}

\subsection*{Of the coin}

A man from a Sere ship had given a boy a coin, and the boy showed it to the dipper, because Vhaleni say a stranger’s coin warms before his face.

“It warms before his face,” the old man said. “So they say, and I have said it myself. But I have held a coin out of a counting-house fire and a coin that lay in a man’s pocket in the pulled benches for a term, and the two are not the same warmth. Somebody paid to make that coin warm. A coin has no fire of its own and neither has a stranger.

“When a man says a thing warms before your face, ask who paid. You will not get an answer at the Quay. You will get a contract on salt-paper, and if the weather is kind it is gone by morning, and that is called a virtue here.”

The boy kept the coin.

\subsection*{Of them that go out on the ebb}

“We seal them in a boat and push it out on the ebb,” he said. “We watch until it is out of sight, and that is held to be enough. I have stood at eleven of these and never seen a boat come back with the man in it.

“I am not saying the Return is a lie. I am saying this coast has the least to show of it. We put no slate at the boat and read no figure over the water. A Vhaleni who dies at sea is called already returned, which is a kind sentence and costs nothing.

“If there is a mercy in this world it is in standing until the boat is small, and then going back to the pans. We do not call it a keeping. We call it enough.”

\subsection*{The draw-song}

\emph{Sung low, facing the water, a bead held between the teeth. There is a line missing before the last four, the one the ebb leaves, and I have left the space the length it is sung.}

\begin{quote}\itshape Salt on the hand and the net in the dawn,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the draw goes out where the cold has gone;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the cliff tastes sweet and the sweet is a lie,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the bead in the niche will not say why.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Three for the pans and three for the rain,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape three for the boat that comes back again;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the gull takes one and the gull gives none,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the clerk writes nil when the count is done.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape The ebb takes what the tide would not keep —\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape We watch till the sail is a speck and then\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape say it is enough, and go to the pans again;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the sea keeps nothing and keeps on keeping,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the green in the crack is not for eating.\end{quote}

A girl from the glass shed asked what the space was for. Nobody answered her. The clerk put a round nought against it, which I have left where he set it.

\subsection*{The bead-row, as the niche keeps it}

\emph{A bead that goes into the crack is a bead no tally can reach, and a figure brought into the shed in a pocket goes out again in the glass and leaves nothing on the leaf.}

Bead — Left by — What was asked of the dipper — What the tide gave\par

Green, chipped at the rim — the old man, every morning — nothing; he set it in and went — another morning\par

Clear, with a tarry fibre shut in it — a man off the pulled benches — whether his term was kept — a tide named, no year\par

Green bead melted round a coal — a girl of the glaze works — whether the sweet would kill her — \emph{Ask the cliff}, which is no answer\par

The bead the gull took — nobody — nothing — a feather on the leaf\par

Nine beads under the loose stone — the pans, in the lean winters — one in twelve, read at the Quay — the printed figure, unchallenged\par

There were beads I did not set down, because a row of beads is a thing a clerk can carry away and a morning is not. The nine under the loose stone have no names.

\subsection*{What the clerk did}

He came down from Greybank on the third day with ink in two fingers, borrowed the leaf while I was at the pans, and gave it back with the verbs taken out.

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item Where the old man said \emph{the water goes out with the warm in it}, he wrote \emph{the measure is retained in the salt} above and left the old words below.

\item Where he said \emph{ask who paid for the warming}, he wrote \emph{claim not established} and drew a small stop between two clusters of his neat dark hand.

\item At the bead-row he put a round nought against the nine under the loose stone and wrote \emph{vacancy} where the tide should stand.

\item At the gap in the song he wrote \emph{vacancy} again, and when I asked what a line was worth with no words, he said nothing a clerk could enter, the first true thing he said all morning.

\end{itemize}

I have put the verbs back underneath and left his hand standing above, as the cliff keeps the green over the sand that made it. He takes them out because a thing always true has no need of them. I put them back because a woman in salt water wants to know who did the going out, and whether it was her own net.

\subsection*{At the head and in the margins}

The salt at the head is the old man’s and mine and will not wash out of grain this soft. The glass scratches a nail. The green on the fold is sweet in heat and I have kept the leaf out of the sun since it took. The feather lay on the niche when I came to write and I have not moved it. The ring is from the dish, which stood on the leaf while he spoke of them that go out on the ebb. The tar at the tie holds a knot the way a niche holds a bead. The damp at the lower corner is the voided contract showing through its own writing. The clerk did not notice any of these things, which is how I know he is a good clerk.

\subsection*{At the foot}

Struck through once and written again underneath, very small, in a hand that is not mine, not the old dipper’s and not the clerk’s:

\begin{quote}\itshape The beads are an account of warmth the Court did not take.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape The beads are the place where an account was refused.\end{quote}

I asked the old man, the girl from the glass shed and the clerk, and had three answerings and no hand. I have left it struck through and standing, the only honest way to keep a sentence you cannot sign.

The leaf goes back in the shed with the bead in its crease and the cord tied as it was. Next Ash the dippers will trail their nets and leave their beads in the crack, and the draw will run out against the wind as always. If the clerk comes I shall let him take the verbs out and put them back, and leave the nought in its place and the green where it fell.

\clearpage\phantomsection\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{The Sermon at the Smith’s Niche, Being What Was Said Over the Mended Tubes at the Forge in Low Kiln on a Morning in Bone of Y.H. 813, with the Hammer-Song Left with the Stroke Not Struck, the Pegs in a Mending-Tally, an Assessor’s Clerk’s Correction, and a Line at the Foot in a Hand Nobody Will Own}
\CRsheetheading{The Sermon at the Smith’s Niche, Being What Was Said Over the Mended Tubes at the Forge in Low Kiln on a Morning in Bone of Y.H. 813, with the Hammer-Song Left with the Stroke Not Struck, the Pegs in a Mending-Tally, an Assessor’s Clerk’s Correction, and a Line at the Foot in a Hand Nobody Will Own}
{\centering\FellFont\itshape\footnotesize\color{faded} A sermon of the common Grathic telling preached at the small shrine of the smith’s niche behind the forge in Low Kiln of Sill, over the clipped ends of collectors’ tubes set in the wall; the sayings in the flat working speech of the yard set down in Grathic, the hammer-song with the unstruck stroke left as it is not struck, the pegs in a mending-tally kept in charcoal on the back of a weigh-slip spoiled at the Cross, one correction in the narrow upright Ledgerhand of an assessor’s clerk come up from Greybank to weigh the winter iron, and one line at the foot in a hand nobody will own · Preached by Harn the smith, who has kept the forge eleven years and mends the collectors’ cold-iron tubes there, on Bone 15, Y.H. 813, the month of hunting and repair, while the kiln behind his bench kept four and did not give the fifth; written that evening by a woman of the Clay Yard who brings the forge its broken barrow-irons and keeps its tally in charcoal, on the back of a weigh-slip gone soft where a wet thumb passed over the figure, folded into grey wool and tied with annealed wire, and kept behind the loose peg in the niche wall with the clipped ends of tubes. It survives with blue bloom off Keldish iron ground into the head, cold-iron filings in the gutter, brick dust off the kiln behind the bench, a scorch where a spark off the hearth took the corner off one line, a tallow thumb off the forge lamp, a ring where a cup of small ale stood from the first voice to the last, a grey Ash print nobody will own, a green bead of lead glaze pressed in by a girl from the Glaze Room, a clipped end of a tube shut in the second fold which answers neither full nor flat when tapped, and one correction in the narrow upright hand of a clerk come up from Greybank. Copied once at Greybank in Ash of Y.H. 813 into the factor’s file of yard sayings, with the verbs put back and the stroke left unstruck.\par}\medskip
I bring the broken barrow-irons down from the north gate and keep the forge’s tally in charcoal, which nobody asked me to keep. Harn cuts his count into the bench with a chisel, where it stays under the grease; I write on a slip the Cross spoiled with a wet thumb, paper no clerk will borrow for a column. I write because he spoke to a wall, and a wall keeps nothing by itself.

He spoke first to the niche, then to the tube, then to the bellows and the kiln behind the bench, and last to us, which is the order a smith uses when collectors are in the yard and somebody may be listening who wants a figure. I have set his words down in Grathic and put the verbs back underneath where he left them out.

The blue at the head came off Keldish iron, which is why I sign with a crossed tong. The grey came off a cuff and I have not swept it; there is no Last Day at this forge.

\subsection*{The manner of the mending, as the forge actually keeps it}

\emph{Written small, from watching, not from any order the Court has printed.}

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item Come with the iron before the bellows are stirred. A man who brings a tube at noon has had the morning’s heat counted for him by somebody else.

\item Set the tube on the bench with the split upward, never on the anvil. The anvil is for irons with a right side; a tube has none.

\item Tap it once. A pot answers full or flat; a cold-iron tube answers neither, and a smith who says he heard a third thing has been at the small ale.

\item Leave the clipped end in the niche. Do not count the ends or take them home.

\item When the kiln comes to its fourth, stop. Put no coal in for a fifth and say not what it would have been.

\item Wrap a tube still warm from a draw in wool. Iron takes from the hand that holds it as well as the arm it is set to.

\item When an officer asks what the niche is for, give him the number of pegs. A number is safe and does not spoil in the mouth.

\end{itemize}

\subsection*{The sermon, as he said it}

\subsection*{Of the niche}

He put his palm flat on the wall where the pegs stand while the bellows took a breath.

“It has no name,” he said. “The yard calls it the smith’s niche and the Court has no word for it. There are the ends of tubes in it, clipped off where I set the new rim. I have not counted them in eleven years and never will.

“A priest will tell you nothing is lost that we have kept. I have kept a wall of iron ends and there is not a measure among them. It is off a tool. If that is a keeping, it is a poor sort, and I have never asked anybody to kneel to it. Stand where you like. The wall has never asked for a knee.”

A woman with a barrow-iron asked whether the ends were part of the tubes they came from. He considered it longer than he considered the iron in his hand. “A clipped end is not the tube,” he said. “It is what the tube gave up to be made sound again. There is a difference, and I have made a living on not saying it out loud.”

\subsection*{Of the tube}

He tapped a tube once with the chisel, lightly, the way the women at the racks tap a pot.

“A pot tells you the truth,” he said. “Full, or flat, and a flat one you can hear across the yard. This does neither. I have mended tubes eleven years and never heard one answer, and have learned not to want it to. It is not honest and it is not lying. It is a tool, and a tool has no mouth to tell you which end you are standing at.”

He turned the rim toward the light. “I mend the tube. I do not mend the man it is set to. A man from Greybank asked once whether I ever thought about the arm. I told him I thought about the rim and the heat and the price of iron, and that I had three orders that morning and would not get the fourth out if I thought about the arm. That was true. It was not the whole of the truth.”

He leaned on the bellows and let them down so the fire came up small. “I held these in the year of the Rising,” he said. “I was old enough to hold them and not old enough to be told what I was heating. I learned what they were for by watching what came back. A tube came back with a grey rim and another with a warm one, and after a while I knew which houses had sent them and which had gone cold, though nobody told me a figure.”

A girl from the Glaze Room touched the paper where I wrote that, with sweetness at one corner of her mouth. I have kept the green where she put it. She said nothing and went back up the terrace.

\subsection*{Of the fifth}

Behind the bench the kiln kept its four low breaths, and there was the silence where the next should have stood.

“That is four,” he said. “I have not put coal to it and I will not. A man who mends for a living has to leave one thing unmended, or he will go home at the going of the light and find he has mended himself into a doctrine.”

A woman asked what the fifth would have been for. He did not turn his head. “Ask the kiln,” he said. She asked the kiln. The kiln answered as a kiln answers, in four.

I have kept this gap on its own place, with a finger between it and the gap in the song. Two things are not given in this forge. Two are two and are not one lesson.

\subsection*{Of the figure}

A collector come up from Slate Row held a narrow slate to his forearm with the writing turned inward, and Harn went on speaking to the tube.

“One in twelve is printed on the notice,” he said. “Read twice, once for the moot and once for them that came up the road too late. I have mended the tubes that take the twelve and the tube that takes the other figure, and the two are the same iron out of the same bar and I have set the same seam in both. The iron does not know which figure it carries. I do. That is the whole of my trade and the whole of my trouble.”

He set the chisel down. “The slate does not sweat and the hand does. A clerk’s figure goes up the road in a coat and comes down in the same coat and leaves no dust. Mine stays in notches under the grease, and if you ask me what it is I shall tell you how many tubes I have mended, a safe answer that means nothing that can be entered. The measure is banked. The account stands.” He crossed two fingers over the seam and covered the act with a chisel stroke on the bench, which is how this forge covers what it has stood at and will not explain. I have written the crossing and left the covering where it was.

\subsection*{Of them that are drawn}

A woman came in at the end with a tube wrapped in wool and set it on the bench with a copper bit beside it, not on it.

“A boy was taken from her house,” Harn said, looking at the tube and not at her. “She asked me if this was the tube that had been in his arm. I told her I could not tell one tube from another once the rim had been turned. That was true too. It is a poor thing when a man’s truth is all of it about iron.”

She took the bit away and left the tube. He set it on the shelf with the other bits nobody has asked for, which is not keeping it and not refusing it.

“They read a whole return in a clean voice for a person not in the room,” he said to the wall. “Here a woman asks me a question I can answer only by telling her what I know about rims. If there is a mercy in this trade it is in the wrapping of the iron before you take it from a man. It costs a length of wool and is entered nowhere.”

\subsection*{The hammer-song}

\emph{Said at the anvil, stroke by stroke, never at the bench and never for a man from Greybank. There is a stroke held back before the last four lines, and I have left it as it is not struck.}

\begin{quote}\itshape Four to the anvil and one held back,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the heat goes out on the other track;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape a pot says full and a pot says flat,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and iron says nothing, and that is that.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape One for the hand that turned the rim,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape one for the hand the tube went in;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape three for the mending and one for the cost,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the fifth is the place where the stroke was lost.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Here the hammer stays up. No sound.}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape The shelf keeps the ends and the wall keeps none,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the seam holds true and the trade goes on;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape ask the tube what it took, it will not say —\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape set it down flat and take yourself away.\end{quote}

A girl from the Clay Yard asked what the space was for. Nobody answered her. The clerk put a round nought against it and wrote \emph{vacancy}, which is a figure and not a stroke that did not happen. I have left the nought where he set it.

\subsection*{The pegs, as the niche keeps them}

\emph{These I have set down where they stood. A figure that comes into this forge in a coat leaves nothing on the bench.}

Peg — What was brought — What he said over it — What was entered\par

One, split at the turning — A collector’s tube, down from Slate Row — The iron does not know which figure it carried — Nothing\par

One, gone grey at the eye — A barrow-iron from the north gate — Iron outlasts the hand and no hand asks it to — Nothing\par

One, the wool still about it — A tube from the house that lost a boy — I cannot tell one tube from another — Nothing; the bit on the shelf\par

Under the loose peg — Four clipped ends, eleven years of them — Nothing — Nothing\par

There were pegs before these that Harn could set a winter to, and I have not written the winters, because a row of winters is a thing a clerk can carry away and a peg in a wall is not.

\subsection*{What the clerk did}

An assessor’s clerk come up from Greybank to weigh the winter iron borrowed the leaf on the morning after and gave it back with the verbs taken out, as though a verb were a thing a man could carry off in a cuff and sell at the next crossing.

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item At \emph{a cold-iron tube answers neither}, he wrote \emph{the instrument is neither vessel nor subject of the full note; no entry arising}, above and underlined. True in the books, which is why no column has ever held a tube.

\item At \emph{the other figure}, he wrote \emph{no such deduction is printed; one in twelve for every vessel}, set above in the neat hand they teach at the College. Underneath, in mine: \emph{I have not written the other figure. He has not either. We have both heard it.}

\item At the gap in the song, a round nought and \emph{vacancy}. When I asked what a stroke was worth that had not been struck, he said nothing a clerk could enter, the first true thing he said all morning.

\end{itemize}

I have put the verbs back and left his hand above, as the forge leaves the old seam under the new rim. He takes them out because a thing always true has no need of them. I put them back because a woman with a wrapped tube wants to know who is doing the taking.

\subsection*{At the head and in the gutter}

The blue at the head is Keldish and will not wash out of grain this soft; it is the only part of this leaf put there by the trade and not by a person. The filings came off a rim and have worked into the scorch. The brick dust is off the kiln. The tallow thumb is mine; I held the leaf low. The ring is from a cup that stood from the first voice to the last and was drunk by nobody, which is how small ale goes in Low Kiln when there is a thing to say and no proper word for it. The grey came off a cuff and nobody will own it. The bead is lead glaze, green and sweet in the wet. The end of a tube in the second fold answers neither full nor flat when I knock it, and I keep it there to remind me what neither is.

\subsection*{At the foot, in a hand nobody will own}

Struck through once and written again underneath, very small:

\begin{quote}\itshape The smith mends the tube and the tube takes from the man.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape The wall keeps the ends. The shelf keeps the bits. Neither keeps a person.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape A tool has no mouth, so the account is read over it in a clean voice.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Four are four, and the fifth is not owed by anybody standing here.\end{quote}

I asked Harn, the woman with the barrow-iron, the collector come up from Slate Row and the clerk, and had four answerings and no hand. I have left the line struck through and standing, which is the only honest way to keep a sentence you cannot sign.

The leaf goes back behind the loose peg with the clipped ends. Next repair-month the kiln will keep its four, and if the clerk comes I shall let him take the verbs out and put them back, and leave the nought in its place and the hammer up where it was held.

\clearpage\phantomsection\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{Half for the Man Come Aboard, Being the Share-Rope of the Quay Children at Vhal, with the Counting-Out, the Manner of the Turning, the Empty Bollard, and What the Clerk Made of It}
\CRsheetheading{Half for the Man Come Aboard, Being the Share-Rope of the Quay Children at Vhal, with the Counting-Out, the Manner of the Turning, the Empty Bollard, and What the Clerk Made of It}
{\centering\FellFont\itshape\footnotesize\color{faded} A rope-woman’s gathering of a children’s skipping game, set down in Grathic letters for a man from the factor’s house though the play is in Vhaleni; the counting-out and the skipping verse in the salt-flat speech of the Quay, the manner of the play in the writer’s own hand, a table of shares corrected in the narrow upright Ledgerhand of a Court clerk come down the Salt Road, a gloss in the leaning hand of a Council tally-man, and a line at the foot in a hand nobody will own · Written in Salt of Y.H. 813 on the Quay at Vhal by Eda Quay, a woman who twists warp and mends nets, on the back of a voided salt-paper tide contract from the tide-tally house; set down with a tarred stick and salt, because ink will not sit on a rope-woman’s table. The contract was spoiled by damp, which is accounted a virtue in Vhal, and the writing on the back outlasted the writing on the face. Kept coiled inside an old warp in a nail-keg under the net-rack. It survives soft and stiff by turns, with a white salt bloom at the head, tar fibre worked into the fold, a brine-gull feather pressed between the second and third leaves, a green bead of Glaze-Cliff glass in the lower corner, a grey Ash print along the gutter that nobody will own, one correction in Ledgerhand, one gloss in the leaning Council hand, and a line at the foot in a hand that has never been claimed\par}\medskip
I twist warp and mend nets under the net-rack on the Quay, and I have set this down because a man come down from Greybank with a clean cuff asked a girl on the bollards what the children counted when they skipped, and wrote her answer in a book before she had finished saying it. She told him a share and not a figure, which is the truth of it, and he sent me a clerk, which is what happens to a share in this country. What follows is what the children said before the clerk came and what they said again after he had gone back up the Salt Road with the verbs taken out of it. I have set his hand above theirs where he put it, as a new splice lies over an old one and shows both ends.

\subsection*{How it is played}

\emph{Played on the flagstones between the third and fourth bollards, below the tide-tally house, in the warm months when an old warp is supple enough to turn. Not in hard frost: a frozen rope bites, and the salt on the stones takes the skin off a knee. It is played while waiting --- for the ebb, for a cart off the coast pass, for a boat that is late. Nobody plays it to pass the time. The time is passed already and the game is what fills the standing.}

Two children hold the rope, one at each end, and are called \textbf{the ebb} and \textbf{the flood}, after the two ways the Sallow runs. The child inside is \textbf{the boat}. There is no prize in being the boat: the boat is the one who has to jump, and the others only swing. Nobody says the children’s own names while the rope is turning. A name said over a quay rope travels up the Salt Road in a cuff and comes back entered.

The rope is a cast warp gone soft in the lay. A new rope is too stiff and takes the ankles off; one that has been out twice is the only kind that will do. The turning hands do not count aloud. The boat says the verse, and the verse is said to the rope and the stones, never to a face; said looking at a person it becomes an argument, and there is always somebody on this Quay who will argue.

One line is one turn of the rope and one jump. When the rope catches an ankle the boat is \textbf{cast off} and goes to take an end, and the turning hand comes in. There is no winning. The game ends when somebody calls the ebb, which is any voice at all that says the boats are in.

\subsection*{The counting-out}

\emph{Said over fists held knuckle-up, the speaker touching one fist for each word and not looking at the faces. The fist it lights on at the last word is the boat; the two after it hold the rope. The children call this a fair casting of lots, which it is not. The same child is boat three turns running and nobody on the Quay can say why.}

\begin{quote}\itshape Salt in the knot and tar on the thumb,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape ebb to the left and the flood to the come;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape one for the bollard, two for the stone,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape three for the rope that will never be new ---\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the one it lights on goes in alone.\end{quote}

\subsection*{The share-rope, as it is skipped}

\emph{The boat says the first line as the rope goes over her head, and jumps on the last word of it. The ebb and the flood say nothing until the half. One line, one turn, and the verse is kept low so the tally-men at the house cannot hear the numbers coming off the stones.}

\begin{quote}\itshape One for the mother that holds the shares,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape two for the mother that held them before;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the rope goes over and under the stone\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the boat comes up and comes back for more.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Three for the boat and the salt in her hold,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape four for the warp that has been out twice;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape a half for the man that married aboard ---\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape hop it. Don’t jump it. He’s not whole in the boat.\end{quote}

\emph{On the half line the boat makes a half: a little check of both feet, no more than a finger’s width off the flagstone. The turning hands lift the rope a hand’s breadth higher on that line, so that a full jump would carry the boat into it and cast her off. A child who jumps the half whole is not cheating and is not confused; she has given the man aboard a whole share, which is a thing no boat on this Quay has ever given him. She goes to take an end of the rope.}

\begin{quote}\itshape Five for the bollard that stands on the quay,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape six for the ebb that takes what it sees;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape there’s a share for the boat that went out on the tide ---\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape stand over it. Don’t set your foot where it was.\end{quote}

\emph{The last line is said to the stone and is not skipped. The rope comes all the way over and the boat lifts her feet and lets it pass beneath her, standing with her heels together on the flagstone. This is called the empty bollard. If the rope touches her she is cast off, the same as if she had jumped the half whole. Ask which boat went out on the tide and the children say the rope knows and the tally knows and neither of them says. A child new to the Quay asks again and is told to ask the ebb, which is the answer her mother was given.}

\subsection*{The verse they do not say while a man in a soft cuff is on the Quay}

\emph{I have this from the child who was boat, with the space left where she left it. She said it with her back to the tide-tally house, and made me set it down with none of my verbs in it. A verse said to a rope wants nothing added; a verse said to a man wants everything taken away.}

\begin{quote}\itshape Three shares and a half and a share with no name,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the rope keeps the count and the Quay keeps the same;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the figure goes up in a clean cuff and comes down a figure,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the half comes back as a hop and the empty comes back as a stand.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape The sea doesn’t care who married aboard.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape It takes the boat and it gives back the rope.\end{quote}

I asked her what the last two lines were worth, and she said a rope was not obliged to be worth a figure just because a clerk had written one against it. Then she put her tar thumb on the corner of the leaf to keep it from the wind off the Sallow, as the net-women do.

\subsection*{What the clerk did}

The factor’s clerk came down the Salt Road on the morning the ebb was late, being a man who cannot leave paper alone, with a cuff gone soft from washing and the ink sitting in two fingers of it and will not come out. He set the game down as \emph{a division of a boat’s shares among the persons holding an interest}, and against the children’s count he wrote this:

The children say — As he entered it\par

One for the mother, two for the mother before her, three for the boat — Three shares, held, entered\par

A half for the man that married aboard — 0.5 share; opinion non-voting\par

The share for the boat that went out on the tide — Vacancy; nil; no balance outstanding\par

He struck out \emph{hop it, don’t jump it} and set above it, \emph{the fractional interest is not exercised}. Against \emph{stand over it, don’t set your foot where it was} he wrote \emph{no person enters}, which is true of his table and false of the flagstone. At the foot, where the children stand with their heels together and let the rope pass, he put a round nought and wrote \emph{nil}.

I have put the hop back underneath and left his standing above. He takes the feet out of a thing and so has no need to say what the feet do. I put them back because a child on the flagstones does not know she is holding a fractional interest; she wants to know whether to lift both feet or one. A nought is a number. The empty bollard is a place to stand with your heels together, and no figure on this Quay has ever had a place to stand.

He asked what the children learned by it. I told him the count and the half and the standing over, and he said that was an account of inheritance taught before a child could read a slate, and he entered it. The children stop when a man in a soft cuff comes down the steps. They take it up again when he is past the tide-tally house with his book under his arm, and they never once jump the half whole.

\subsection*{What the tally-man put in the margin}

The lean hand belongs to a man of the Council who reads the draws at the tide-tally house and will not write upright, which he says is a hand for people who have never wet a cuff. He wrote three lines against the verses:

\begin{quote}\itshape The tide follows the Warm, not the moon. The water goes where it is told.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape A half share goes with the boat. It does not go with the man.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape A contract written on this paper is a contract that has changed its mind by morning, which the Council calls a virtue.\end{quote}

I have left it where he set it. He wrote it of the Sallow and it is true there, the dippers say. It is a hard thing to argue with a man who has watched a document disappear in a night and called it good weather.

\subsection*{At the head and in the gutter}

The white at the head is salt bloom, off the leaf that lay three tides in a coil on the net-rack; salt goes into the fibre and will not come out, which is why we use it to mark a warp and not a page. The tar in the fold is mine, off the stick I write with; I twist and mend and do not wash before I sit down to this. The brine-gull feather came off a bird that stood on the fourth bollard with a coal not cold in its beak and dropped it when the rope came round. The green bead is Glaze-Cliff glass, rolled out of a broken flask and put in the fold by a girl who would not say where she got it; the sweetness of the cliffs is in it, and the sweetness is not a kindness. The grey along the gutter came off a cuff that had no business lying on a quay where rope is laid, and I have not swept it. There is no Last Day on the Quay and nothing here is burnt in the morning.

\subsection*{At the foot, in a hand nobody will own}

\begin{quote}\itshape The rope keeps the half. The stone keeps the stand.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape The slate keeps neither and is read aloud all the same.\end{quote}

I asked the child who was boat, a tally-man who left his book open on a bollard, and a woman who has twisted warp here for thirty years, and had three answers and no hand, as I have had before. I have left the lines where they were written.

The leaf goes back into the coil in the nail-keg under the net-rack. Tomorrow the ebb will be called at the usual hour, three shares will be held in a house on the Quay, and a man come aboard will have his half. If the children are not chased off they will hop it and stand over the empty bollard and go on keeping the boat until somebody says the boats are in. If the clerk comes again with his pen I shall put the verbs back. He may keep the nought. The rope comes back to the coil at the end of every count, and no tally in this house has ever had a coil for it.

\clearpage\phantomsection\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{The Rules of the Ways, Being the Standing Rules of the Shipwrights of Vhal for the Taking, Keeping, Trying and Paying Out of Apprentices in the Yards of the Quay, with the Table of Years, the Faults in a Second Table, the Launching-Song Pasted Inside the Cover, Two Corrections in the Narrow Upright Hand of a Council Clerk, One Line Struck in Charcoal by a Shipwright Who Would Not Sign It, and a Line at the Foot Nobody Will Own}
\CRsheetheading{The Rules of the Ways, Being the Standing Rules of the Shipwrights of Vhal for the Taking, Keeping, Trying and Paying Out of Apprentices in the Yards of the Quay, with the Table of Years, the Faults in a Second Table, the Launching-Song Pasted Inside the Cover, Two Corrections in the Narrow Upright Hand of a Council Clerk, One Line Struck in Charcoal by a Shipwright Who Would Not Sign It, and a Line at the Foot Nobody Will Own}
{\centering\FellFont\itshape\footnotesize\color{faded} A yard-leaf of rules in the hand of the under-shipwright who keeps the moulds and the roll of hands at the third yard, written on salt-paper kept dry against the practice of the country and sewn with tarred net-twine to a board cover; the rules in the short sayings of the Quay, the years and the faults in tables, the launching-song pasted inside the cover, a shaving of keel shut in the second fold, two corrections in the Council’s upright counting-hand, one line struck hard in charcoal by a shipwright who would not put his name to it, and a line at the foot in a hand nobody will own · First gathered at Vhal in Y.H. 605, the year the Council of Tides put the building of its galleys out to contract and a yard that had kept its rules in the mouth was made to set them down so that a price could be argued with; copied forward from the mould-loft and not from a book. This leaf written in Ember of Y.H. 812, the Thin Year of the Long Cold, by Rena of the Ways, an under-shipwright who has kept the moulds and said the curse at the laying of every keel for three and twenty years, and carried forward at the Opening of the Slates, Ilmen 1, Y.H. 813. It survives hung on a nail in the mould-loft, soft at the fold and stiff with tar at the head, with a white salt bloom that has eaten the last letters off one word, a tar thumb off the ways-rope, a dry shaving of keel shut in the second fold, a fibre of wet rope pressed across the song, a brine-gull’s peck through a rule, a fish-hook nick at the fore-edge, a ring of red wine with salt at the rim from a launching nobody paid for, a pitch-scorch that took the corner of a line without taking the sense, a green bead of Cliffs glass pressed in by a girl who would not ask after the curse, a grey print along the outer fold that is not hers and that she has not swept, two corrections in the Council’s narrow upright hand, one charcoal line struck and written again underneath, and a line at the foot nobody will own\par}\medskip
I keep the moulds and the roll of hands at the third yard, where the ways go down into the water and the tallow takes a handprint. A house brings a boy and goes away; the boy stays with the wood. A Council man comes with a cuff soft from washing, reads the thirty marks off a paper kept dry when every other paper here is left to rot, and asks what the curse is worth. I tell him it is included. He writes \emph{included} and goes away satisfied, which is the whole of his trade and none of ours.

There is no guild in Vhal. There is a price, and a curse said every hour of the work, and the men who stand at the ways when a hull goes down; between them a trade is kept. We hang our rules on a spike in the mould-loft, where the tar takes the head of the leaf and nothing takes it off again.

These rules were gathered in Y.H. 605, when the Council first bought a galley by contract and a yard that had carried its rules in its mouth was made to put them on paper. A rule that has never been launched is a rule nobody trusts. These have been launched. I keep the leaf dry, which is against the practice of the country and I know it. A contract left in the rain is no contract here, and we call that a virtue. A rule left in the rain is no rule either, and I have met no man who sees the virtue in that. Where a hand has corrected me I have left both readings.

\subsection*{The rules as they stand at the third yard}

\subsection*{Of the taking}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item The yard takes a boy, not a house. A house may bring him and feed him, but from the day he holds a chisel with the edge toward him he answers to the yard. The Council takes the hull and leaves the boy alone. In this port that is the last thing anybody has thought to tax.

\item A boy is taken at twelve, set to the adze at thirteen and not before he can lift it with the edge up. A boy taken later is not made up the year he missed; the yard keeps no count of hulls it did not build.

\item He is kept, not hired. He eats from the yard dish, sleeps in the loft above the moulds, and what he makes goes to the yard and comes back as bread, which is not entered. A shipwright is paid in the only coin this trade uses, a curse said at the hour and not set down.

\item His birth-name is said once at the taking and not used afterward at the yard. What he is called is the shaving, given at his first stroke of the adze and kept in the mouth. A shaving in the mouth cannot be entered, and there is nothing in this country the Council has not tried to enter.

\item The wood is read before the boy. The price is given before the name and the curse before the hull. A man who names a boy before he has seen him handle an adze has mistaken the yard for a counting house, which is across the water.

\end{enumerate}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{In the narrow upright hand of a Council clerk, against rule 3:} Retained at the yard. No wage arising. \emph{Underneath, in mine:} I had written that he is kept. He strikes a mouth wherever he finds one and puts a figure where it stood. I have put the boy back underneath, because a figure eats no bread and sleeps in no loft. Both readings stand.\end{quote}

\subsection*{Of the wood and the curse}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item The adze says what the man wants of the wood. The wood says what it has. A shipwright who asks the wood what it ought to be has lost the boat, and the boat goes to Sere with a figure on it and a flaw nobody here will own.

\item Green wood set into a hull in Ember will season in the hold and split three winters out, in the hand of a man this yard has never seen. Cut it out, burn it, set dry wood in its place and enter nothing. The yard calls it the weather, as the clay country calls what it has not measured.

\item No boy is set to pitch before his second year. Hot pitch takes the skin off and gives it back in a shape that will not close around a tool. A master who calls the scar a trade-mark is selling the boy’s fingers one at a time.

\item The curse is said every hour of the work and is included in the thirty marks. A man who pays less gets more of it; it does not sink the boat, which would be a gift, and no shipwright in Vhal has ever given anything away. Say it to the wood, not the buyer; said to a buyer it becomes a bargain, and a bargain here is a debt with no date.

\item Count four strokes to the scarf and a slack. The slack is not a stroke and is not entered; it is the tide you have not seen and the peg you did not drive. A boy who sets a fifth peg in the slack is told to take it up, and told nothing more.

\item Keep the leaf dry and the ways wet. A contract left in the rain is no contract, which the Council calls a virtue and the yard calls a morning’s work undone. We do not say \emph{kindly} to a yard-master. Say it and name your two bits, with a date.

\end{enumerate}

\subsection*{Of the ways and the launching}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item The keel is laid in Ember, when the ways are greased with tallow and the Quay stands to see. Nobody sings while a hull goes down; the song is carried up the ways, not down them, and nobody has given me a reason why, which is the same as giving a good one.

\item Carry a barrel of rain aboard every hull before she launches. The salt-thing follows boats at night and taps the hull where the store is; fresh water stops it as a wall stops a man. Every captain denies the barrel and every captain carries one. A shipwright who launches without one has sold a debt to the sea and entered nothing.

\item A brine-gull will lift a warm shaving off the ways and go off with it under its crop. No malice in it. Do not set a boy to watch the shavings in place of the seam; the gull is honest and the seam has a master.

\item Name the tide your boat will not see, the way the young name one at the pans. Write it in salt on the keel-block and let the sun have it. What is in salt belongs to noon; what is said belongs to the speaker. Do not put it on paper. A thing that rots is no protection for a tide that was never a contract.

\end{enumerate}

\subsection*{The table of years}

\emph{Kept by the girl who sweeps the mould-loft, in a hand that does not change between one line and the next.}

Year — At the yard — What is taken\par

Twelve — Carry, sweep, boil tar, hold the chisel with the edge up — The birth-name, said once and not used again\par

Thirteen — The first shaving; the adze kept level; four to the scarf and a slack — The habit of asking what the wood ought to be\par

Fourteen — The first peg, driven and left standing; the curse said to the wood — The shaving-name, given by the first stroke and kept in the mouth\par

Fifteen — Read a mould; turn a keel; pitch on the shore side of the fire — The belief that a thing measured is a thing known\par

Sixteen — Lay a keel alone and set the ribs to it — The last of the boy’s account with any house\par

Seventeen — Launch a hull and stand at the last peg to hear the curse — The common end of a keeping, which is not a short one\par

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item Seventeen is the common end and not a short one; a boat is longer in the building than a girl is at a furnace. A boy who has been through the years is not paid out and sent away. He stays where the yard needs him, at the third yard or on a boat whose share goes through his mother. The yard does not choose. The wood does, and the Council after it.

\end{enumerate}

\subsection*{The table of faults}

Fault — As corrected at the yard\par

Green wood set in a hull — Cut out, burnt, dry wood set in its place; nothing entered\par

A shaving-name written on salt-paper — The paper left out in the rain; the name said again to the adze\par

\emph{Kindly} said to a yard-master — Two bits owed, named on the spot, with a date\par

A hull launched without rain aboard — The barrel carried three paces and set down; the hull not launched till it is aboard\par

The Hearth beneath the salt asked about — Answered once: under the salt, and the Court’s fire its chimney. Asked twice: send it to the dippers\par

A curse sold to the Council and the other kept — Not entered. There is no law against it, which is why the yard does not speak of it\par

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item A fault copied twice in a building is a fault the boy has not understood, and the master sits with him at the mould until he has. The adze is not a rod, though men who never held one have called it both.

\end{enumerate}

\subsection*{The launching-song, pasted inside the cover}

\emph{Carried up the ways while the keel is laid, standing, with a tallow hand on the beam. Never sung when a hull goes down, and never while the Council’s man is on the ways. The third line of the last verse is the boy’s.}

\begin{quote}\itshape Tar on the ways and tallow under,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the keel goes up where the hull goes down;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape four for the scarf and a slack for the sea,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the curse goes into the price.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Thirty marks and a curse an hour,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the Council enters the marks alone;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the share goes down where the mother went,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the man come aboard says half.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Carry the rain in a barrel by,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the gull takes the shaving and flies;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape name her a tide that she’ll never see ---\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape salt says yes and the sun says no.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Tar on the ways and tallow under,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape one hull for the tally and one for the sea;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the one they pay for isn’t the one I built,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the fifth peg stands where the slack should be.\end{quote}

The wet rope across the third verse came from the song being carried up in rain at the outer yard. I have flattened it; the words hold.

\subsection*{What the borrowed hands did}

A Council clerk borrowed the leaf at Greybank with ink in two fingers of a soft cuff, and took the verbs out as though a verb were a thing a man could carry off in a sleeve.

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item Against rule 9 he set \emph{the imprecation is comprised in the consideration} above \emph{the curse is said every hour of the work}, a sentence true of no boat that went down the ways. I have put mine back underneath.

\end{itemize}

The other hand is charcoal, a shipwright of the inner yard who would not sign it. Against \emph{no shipwright in Vhal has ever given anything away} he struck the words hard and wrote above, \emph{I gave a man a hull in Y.H. 611 and never entered it, which is the only curse I ever said with a name in it.} I have left his line struck above and mine standing under, so a boy can see what was said and what was done to it. The charcoal has come off on the fold and I have not brushed it away. A rule two men have argued over is a rule that has been used.

\subsection*{At the head and in the gutter}

The salt bloom at the head came up in a wet week and has eaten the last of a word, which I have not written back; a word the weather has taken is truer than one a clerk can still read. The tar thumb is mine, off the rope I coil at dusk. The shaving in the second fold is keel, dry as bone, laid there by a boy who wanted the leaf to hold a place open. The rope fibre has gone soft across the song and tells me when to shut the leaf away. The gull’s peck went through a rule and nobody has claimed the bird. The fish-hook nick came from a disputed count of herrings. The ring of wine has salt at the rim; the man set it down and drank without the salt, which is a clay-country habit, and has not been back. The pitch-scorch took the corner of rule 7 without the sense. The green bead is Cliffs glass from a girl who leaned to read the faults and would not ask after the curse; I have kept it where it fell. The grey along the outer fold is not mine and not the Council’s, and I have not swept it. There is no Last Day at a yard, and nothing here is burnt in the morning and called dealt with.

\subsection*{At the foot, in a hand nobody will own}

\begin{quote}\itshape The wood keeps what the adze took. The Council keeps what the wood was sold for.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Between the two a boy learns a trade that has no column, and the curse stands in the gap.\end{quote}

I asked a yard-master, a Council clerk and a woman who holds a share from her mother, and had three answers and no hand. I have left the lines where they were written. The leaf goes back on its nail and the tar takes another word by the next launching. Tomorrow a boy will be brought at twelve with a house-name he will not use, and I shall say the curse once to the wood, put a chisel in his hand with the edge toward him, and say nothing about the name.

\clearpage\phantomsection\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{The Shirt Left Rough, Being a Letter from the Wash-Hearth in Low Kiln to the Washing Bench at Stonemouth, Concerning a Child’s Shirt That Would Not Rinse Clean, the Grey That Stays Where It Was Put, and the Question of What a Cloth Holds After It Has Held a Body; with the Answer in the Margin, a Weigh-Clerk’s Correction in Ledgerhand, a Washing-Song, and One Line at the Foot in a Hand Nobody Will Own}
\CRsheetheading{The Shirt Left Rough, Being a Letter from the Wash-Hearth in Low Kiln to the Washing Bench at Stonemouth, Concerning a Child’s Shirt That Would Not Rinse Clean, the Grey That Stays Where It Was Put, and the Question of What a Cloth Holds After It Has Held a Body; with the Answer in the Margin, a Weigh-Clerk’s Correction in Ledgerhand, a Washing-Song, and One Line at the Foot in a Hand Nobody Will Own}
{\centering\FellFont\itshape\footnotesize\color{faded} A private letter on the back of a washing tally spoiled by lye, written in charcoal ground with soap-ash and gone over in iron-gall where the fat would not take it, folded thrice and sewn with a flax thread drawn from the hem of the cloth it speaks of; carried five leagues upriver on the frozen river road in a carter’s coat in Stone of the Thin Year, answered along the margin at the lime yard in Stonemouth, borrowed at the weigh-clerk’s bench by the landing where a clerk of the factor at Greybank laid his cuff on the leaf before he looked at it and set a correction on the back in narrow upright Ledgerhand, and kept since in a dry tin under the bench among the soap-ends and the spoiled tallies. It survives with lye gone white in the grain at the head, a thumb of tallow at the second fold, a blue-green speck of lead glaze off somebody’s cuff, a wet ring where a dish of water stood from the first line to the last, frost-crisp along the gutter from a night in the carter’s coat, one word struck through with a lye-sour thumbnail and written again underneath in the recipient’s hand, and a grey Ash print along the outer fold that nobody will own · Written in Stone of Y.H. 812, the Thin Year, on the ninety-fourth morning of the ice, at the wash-hearth off the Clay Yard in Low Kiln of Sill, by Milla, who keeps that hearth and the linen of eleven houses, to Sanna, who keeps the washing bench at the lime yard in Stonemouth, her sister by a mother who washed for the quarry and died of the white cough. Carried up the north river road when the ice would not bear a barge, answered in the margin at Stonemouth in broad lime-pale charcoal with the ends of words let fall, corrected on the back at the weigh-clerk’s bench, and kept since in Milla’s tin. The shirt itself went back to the house unrinsed and is not in this letter, which is the only thing in it I am sure of.\par}\medskip
To Sanna at the washing bench beside the lime kilns in Stonemouth, from Milla at the hearth off the Clay Yard in Low Kiln. Written in Stone of the Thin Year, on the ninety-fourth morning of the ice. I have written on the back of a tally because the front is all soap and no sentence will take on it. Do not open it on the second crease; that is where I sewed the thread through the hem and the word goes over double there.

The water came up this morning with a skin on it that broke round the rim of the pail the way a pot answers when it has cracked all the way through, a small flat sound and then nothing. I have kept this hearth eleven winters and I do not know whether the river is under the ice or the ice is under the river; the bucket comes up the same either way and I have left the question where it stood. Lye will not take in this cold. I set the ash in warm water and it goes sour before it goes strong, and the women tell me the ash from your lime is the wrong ash and the right ash comes from the kilns five leagues upriver, which is a thing I mean to ask you before I am done.

Here is what I am writing for. A woman of the yard came to me on the third morning of the ice with a child’s shirt in the fold of her apron and asked me to wash it. She did not say whose. I knew whose, because the whole yard knew and nobody had said it in my hearing since the collector came in the first week of the cold. The child went in at three days old and came back on the second day of Stone with grey at the fingertips and a red place at the hairline that the room called a graft settling and I did not name it. The woman set the shirt on my bench with her thumb still on the fold, and she said \emph{Wash it clean}, and then, so low I nearly missed it, \emph{but not the last one}. I said, What is the last one. She told me to ask the water, and went back up the yard with her apron empty.

I washed the shirt. Twice in lye, once in water warmed at my own fire, and I wrung it and held it to the light from the door, and there was a grey place at the left shoulder the size of a thumb-nail that would not come out. I have not tried a third time. A thing that will not come out stays where it was put, and I have no trade that takes it out of cloth, whatever the physicians from Greybank say about the corners of rooms. I have folded it with that side turned in and I have not sent it back, and that is the whole of what I have done, which is little for a letter of this length.

\subsection*{The shirts I have washed for houses that got a child back, set down here and not on any slate}

When — What was brought — What I did — What the house entered\par

The first cold, Y.H. 811 — A shirt with milk at the breast — Washed in lye, rinsed in well-water, set on the rack — Nothing\par

The thaw before Stone, Y.H. 812 — A shirt too small for any child in the yard — Washed, carried away, not worn so far as I saw — Nothing\par

This morning, Stone, Y.H. 812 — A shirt with grey at the left shoulder — Washed twice, held to the light, stopped — Nothing\par

There were other shirts and I have not set them down, because a column of shirts is a thing that gets carried up the road and read over a basket, and a shirt folded with the grey side in stops at my bench. When a woman asks what a washing cost I tell her to ask the pot. When she asks what the shirt cost I have begun to say the same and then kept my mouth shut, for a pot holds water and a shirt holds something else and I will not put them on one shelf.

\subsection*{What I want to know from you}

At Stonemouth, when a man is brought down off the bank with the white cough, does his house wash his shirt before it is given away? I do not want a belief. I want the doing. Who sets the water on, is it lime water or well water, and is the last shirt left rough as the women here say, or rinsed like the rest? You will know that the well beside the Ferr is not the one your people drink from, and I am not asking about that well; I am asking about the water you put a shirt in.

Then a second thing, kept behind the first because I wanted it answered by a woman who has washed for men who come back up the bank. When a shirt has been washed clean, does it still know the body it was washed off? A child of three days came back into a house I know and would not wear the shirt her mother had washed for her. She wore the other one, which had never been near my bench, for three days, until it was taken off her, I do not know by whom. That is an observation and not an argument; I have put it on a place of its own. Tell me whether your quarrymen’s shirts behave in the same way, and if you have no answer, tell me what you do with your hands when you come to the last one.

\subsection*{The washing-song}

\emph{Said low, to the water and the shirt, and to the woman waiting only after those. The last four lines are held the length of the wringing and nobody fills them.}

\begin{quote}\itshape Lye in the pail and ash on the lip,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the water comes up and the ice lies flat;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape wash for the living and wring for the dead,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and leave the last one as it sat.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Three at the bench and one on the rack,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape a grey at the shoulder the size of a thumb;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the bell goes four and four and a gap,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the gap is the only part of it ours.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Salt for the dish and wool for the wrist,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape a stone warmed at somebody’s own fire;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape count with her, count with her, one and again ---\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{[held the length of the wringing; not filled]}\end{quote}

I have never put that held place into words and I have never once heard anybody fill it. A clerk at the Cross would set a nought in it and call it vacancy, and a nought travels and a wringing does not. They crossed two fingers at the shirt when I held it up and gave the woman a date for it, which is what we do here when a girl asks what a sign is for. A date does not spoil in the mouth and has no figure in it. The dish went out overnight with water in it and came back with a skim on it that I did not taste, and nobody in that house has sat down since the cough came on her, though nobody will say the two things together.

\subsection*{In the margin, in a second hand, broad and lime-pale, with the ends of words let fall}

The thaw shirt was not returned. It went to a house below the Ferry and was given away there, and you have put \emph{returned} where \emph{given away} should stand. I have struck it and written the other underneath in your own charcoal, so that you cannot say a stranger wrote it. This is the whole of my correction to your count, and it is a large one, for a shirt given away and a shirt returned are two garments and no slateman alive can make them one.

We rinse the shirt and leave the last one rough. It is not for the man. It is for the hands that must give it to the next house. A clean shirt is a gift and a gift can be refused, and a man who refuses a shirt on the morning he needs one has paid for it somewhere where nobody stood to see. A rough one is only a shirt. I have carried two of them down the bank and did not ask the third time because the third time would have wanted a name.

On the white cough: the shirt goes under the pot-breaking at the door, unwashed, with the man. There is a saying on this bench which I did not make and cannot trace to anybody: \emph{A name kept in a room is a different weight from a name kept on a slate, and a woman can carry the one when the men beside her have put the other down.} The weigh-clerk said it over a tooth-tally without knowing he had said it, and set his cuff on the leaf before he looked at the man who brought it. I have written it here because it is the only answer I have to your second question, and it is not one.

\begin{quote}\itshape Three at the bench and one gone up the bank,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the lime takes the hand and the cough takes the breath;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape rinse what will rinse and leave what will not,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and give the rough one to the house that’s left.\end{quote}

I have washed for sixteen men off this bank and had one shirt come back to me with the grey still at the shoulder. I did not take it out and neither did the next woman. The child wore what she would wear. Do not make a rule of it: a rule is an account that has found somebody to pay it.

--- Sanna, at the lime, in Stone.

\subsection*{What the clerk did, at the weigh-clerk’s bench, on the back, in narrow upright Ledgerhand}

He borrowed the leaf for a morning. His cuff was gone soft from washing and he had ink in the creases of two fingers; he laid his hand on the top before he read a word of either hand, which is the manner of that bench.

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item Against the tally he set \emph{garments laundered: three; returns entered: three; discrepancy nil}, joining the washing to the returning and taking both women out of the sentence as though a woman were a thing a man could carry off in a cuff.

\item Where I wrote that the child would not wear the washed shirt, he set \emph{attachment not entered} above and left mine underneath.

\item Where I wrote that a thing which will not come out stays where it was put, he wrote \emph{residue retained; material not entered}. He did not ask to see the shirt.

\item At the held place in the song he set a round nought and wrote \emph{vacancy} beneath it.
