\item Against \emph{leave the last one as it sat} he wrote \emph{garment retained; no further entry}, and underlined it twice, as though an underline were an argument.

\item Against the levy week in the first cold he wrote \emph{one in twelve, as the notice says}, which is true of the notice and of nothing else at this hearth.

\end{itemize}

I have put the verbs back underneath where I could still read them. He takes them out because a thing always true has no need of anybody doing it. I put them back because a woman at a wash-hearth at three in the morning wants to know whose hands were in the water, and there were hands. I have left his figures standing on the back, where they belong, and the shirts on the front, where nobody has asked for them.

\subsection*{At the head and in the gutter}

The white at the head is lye and has got into the grain of the paper and will not be brushed out, which is a thing I noticed too late to care about. The tallow at the second fold is mine; I held the lamp low while I wrote so the women at the rack would think I had gone to bed. The blue-green speck came off a cuff that brushed the leaf as I carried it through the yard, and there is a kiln up the terrace where that colour is made and a girl who wears it at the corner of her mouth and calls nothing by its name. The wet ring is the dish, which stood here from the first line to the song and was taken away still full. The frost-crisp along the gutter came up out of the leaf itself in the carter’s coat; the writing there has gone thin and I have not gone over it, because a word written thin is a word said quietly and most of ours are. The word struck through at the foot of the margin is \emph{returned}, struck with my sister’s lye-sour thumbnail and written again under in the same charcoal; I have not covered the first word, which is how a seam keeps the crack under it. The grey along the outer fold is not mine and not my sister’s and not the clerk’s. I have not swept it. There is a Last Day in Sill and the corners are burned there in the morning and called dealt with; there is no Last Day at this hearth and the grey lies where it fell.

\subsection*{At the foot, in a hand nobody will own}

\begin{quote}\itshape The shirt knows what the slate forgets.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape The grey keeps the shoulder; the house keeps the date.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Three went through the water and one was left rough,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the fourth has no name and no column.\end{quote}

I asked the woman who brought it, Sanna at the lime, the weigh-clerk and his clerk, and had four answerings and no hand. The shirt goes back tomorrow with the grey side turned in. If the child will wear it she will wear it rough, and no figure, collector or slate will know what it cost, which is the ordinary way of things and not a doctrine. The leaf goes back in the tin. Next winter the ice will come on the Ilm and the water will come up the same and I shall put the ash in it and it will go sour before it goes strong, and my sister will strike another word of mine and write the true one small underneath.

\clearpage\phantomsection\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{The Shut Furnaces, Being an Extract from the Glass-Book of the Furnaces below the Glaze Cliffs, Concerning the Rising of Y.H. 626, the Year the Contracts Were Allowed to Lapse, the Men Set to the Pulled Benches, and the Pots Entered at Vhal That No Fire Had Made; with the Furnace-Song, the Table of Pots, Two Corrections in the Narrow Hand of the Council Room, and a Line at the Foot Nobody Will Own}
\CRsheetheading{The Shut Furnaces, Being an Extract from the Glass-Book of the Furnaces below the Glaze Cliffs, Concerning the Rising of Y.H. 626, the Year the Contracts Were Allowed to Lapse, the Men Set to the Pulled Benches, and the Pots Entered at Vhal That No Fire Had Made; with the Furnace-Song, the Table of Pots, Two Corrections in the Narrow Hand of the Council Room, and a Line at the Foot Nobody Will Own}
{\centering\FellFont\itshape\footnotesize\color{faded} A furnace-tally keeper’s extract from the glass-book, copied out of the tin lined with sand in the tally shed below the Cliffs; the year-entries in a leaning counting-hand on salt-paper kept dry against the practice of the country, the figures of pots set against the figure made up in the Council room, the song taken down from a furnace-man who would not sing it where a clerk could hear, one correction in the narrow upright hand of the Council, one in a Court hand borrowed from Greybank, a word scraped away and not written back, and a line at the foot in a hand nobody will own · Written in the tally shed below the Glaze Cliffs outside Vhal in Ash of Y.H. 812, the Thin Year of the Long Cold, by the keeper of the furnace tally, who signs with a tally-cut and not a name and keeps the verbs in; copied from the furnace register begun in Y.H. 626 and kept since in a tin lined with sand, carried up the Salt Road at the Opening of the Slates, Ilmen 1, Y.H. 813, and copied at Greybank onto the back of a weigh-slip voided by the Long Cold. It survives as five leaves of salt-paper stiffened with tar and sewn with eel-sinew: glass dust ground into the grain at the head, a green bead of cliff-glass pressed into the second fold with a sweet smear that has never dried, a white bloom come up out of the paper and not out of the sea, a scorch where the shed lamp caught the third leaf, a thumb of lead at the foot, a fibre of wet rope in the stitch, a peck from a brine-gull that took the corner and not the word, a square of bare paper where a word was scraped away, one correction standing above the words it corrects, and a grey Ash print along the outer fold which the keeper did not make and has not swept\par}\medskip
I keep the glass-book of the furnaces below the Cliffs. It lies in a tin lined with sand in the tally shed, and the sand comes in through the seams in the wet season and stays, so that the leaves are gritty where a thumb has gone and where none has. The Council keeps its own register in the tar-smelling room up at the Quay, and the two books are not the same book. The Council’s register holds what was allowed. Mine holds what was fired. Between the allowance and the firing there is a space the width of a crucible, and it is in that space that the year 626 is written.

Everything in Vhal is written on paper made to rot, and the Council calls it a virtue that a contract left in the damp is a debt made nothing. In the shed the paper goes soft in a season and the figures come up in pale islands, and we copy the book again before the next firing. No two copies agree, which is the only honest thing about them. Where the Council has taken the doers out of a year I have put them back, the way a man puts his hand back on the tongs before he lifts anything hot.

\subsection*{The year as the Council’s register has it}

\emph{Copied out of the leaning hand in the tin. What I have set underneath is not an argument with the register. It is the register with the men put back.}

\textbf{Y.H. 624.} Sand and lead from the Cliffs come down to the shed in the ordinary carts. Entered as \emph{materials received; the furnaces in their course}.

\textbf{Y.H. 626.} The furnace-men of the Cliffs shut every furnace in the seventh week of Seed and kept them shut into Frost. No glass went north that year. The Council’s contracts for the year’s pots were suspended, by decree of the Council of Tides, for the space of one year. Entered as \emph{a suspension of instruments; the ordinary course observed; account standing}.

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{In the narrow upright hand of the Council room, written above my line:} The several contracts were allowed to lapse. No interruption in the trade occurred. Strike \emph{shut}.\end{quote}

Mine stands underneath, where a clerk of the Council will not think to look. Nine of us shut the furnaces, and we shut them with our own hands, and the men who came up from the Quay to ask us why went back down the Salt Road without an answer they could enter. A suspension of instruments is a thing that happens to paper. A shut furnace is a thing that happens to men. Both were entered; only one was entered under this year.

\textbf{Y.H. 627.} The furnaces were lit again in Ilmen and the pots went north as before. Entered as \emph{the ordinary course resumed}. I have entered the number of men who did not come back to the shed, which is a column the register has no place for.

\textbf{Y.H. 641.} The pale line comes among the glaze-women of High Kiln upriver, and the physician writes \emph{teeth}. I have put the year in the margin and not in the account, because I can set two sentences side by side and cannot join them, and the glass-book is not the place for a joining I have made myself.

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{In a Court hand, borrowed from Greybank on a market morning:} Lead not implicated. Glass a vessel of trade, innocently used. No deduction arises.\end{quote}

A thing a man cannot weigh he may still carry in a cuff. This one carried a correction in it.

\subsection*{The table of pots}

\emph{The right-hand figure is made up in the Council room before the carts go out. The figure beside it is what the shed actually fired. I have kept both since the first year and have never been asked which is true.}

Year — Pots fired below the Cliffs — Pots entered at the Quay — Entered as — The shed’s note\par

624 — 900 — 900 — \emph{levy of glass received} — seven furnaces lit\par

626 — none — 900 — \emph{instruments lapsed; account standing} — seven furnaces shut; nine men gone to the benches\par

627 — 900 — 900 — \emph{the course resumed} — three furnaces lit by hands I did not know\par

641 — 900 — 900 — \emph{trade uninterrupted} — the sweetness went upriver and was called teeth\par

The nine hundred of Y.H. 626 were entered as received. They were not received. They were written in the room at the Quay with the damp coming up under the pen, and the figure stayed where the clerk put it while the pots stayed where no pot had ever been. I have not struck the figure out. I have set the firing beside it, which is as near as a tally-keeper comes to asking a question of a room he is not allowed to enter.

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{In the narrow upright hand of the Council:} Deficit not entered. Contract discharged at the Quay. Account stands.\end{quote}

The hand is careful and has never once changed a figure. It has made nine hundred pots that never existed into nine hundred pots that did, which is a cleaner thing to carry into a counting room. There are eleven words for a lapsed contract taught in that room and not one for a furnace gone cold in Seed, which is the whole of the difficulty between us.

\subsection*{The song of the shut furnaces}

\emph{Taken down in the shed from a furnace-man of the third mouth who had worked the lead since before the rising. He would not sing it while the man from the Council room stood inside the door, so we went out and sat on the sand where the gulls could hear. He said the song had been in the shed longer than he had, which is the custom of that place.}

\begin{quote}\itshape The Cliffs gave green and the shed gave blue\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the lead came down in the sand;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape they wrote \emph{a lapse of the paper}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape for the shutting of every hand.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Seven mouths and seven cold,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the tongs hung dumb on the wall;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape a man entered by another man’s pen\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape has no mouth to answer the call.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Nine went down to the pulled benches\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the oar keeps what the slate let go;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape a debt on salt-paper is a debt the rain forgives,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape but the bench keeps the figure and the throat keeps the knot.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape The pots went north on the ordinary cart\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape with a figure made up in the room;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape no fire had touched them, no hand had set them,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the Quay received them, and the account stood.\end{quote}

I have copied the verses as they came and put no gloss on them. When I asked him who made the song he said the furnaces made it, and when I asked him how a furnace makes a song he said a furnace makes one every time it is lit and nobody writes it down until it is shut, which is the only answer the shed has ever given me.

\subsection*{What the two hands did}

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item Against \emph{the furnace-men shut the furnaces} the Council set \emph{the several contracts were allowed to lapse}, so that the act of shutting has no actor in it.

\item Against \emph{nine men went to the pulled benches} it set \emph{certain persons were assigned to the public service}, which is true at the Quay and false in the shed.

\item Against \emph{the paper said one thing and the pots another} it wrote \emph{no discrepancy arises}, and underlined it twice.

\item Against the song it wrote \emph{no cost entered}, which is the neatest thing I have ever seen done to sixteen lines of a man’s breath.

\item The Court hand from Greybank struck \emph{lead} out of the Y.H. 641 line and put \emph{a vessel of trade} above it. I have left both standing. A vessel of trade is a thing that can stand on a shelf for ever without touching anybody’s gum.

\end{itemize}

It takes the person out and leaves the pot standing, and a pot standing by itself has never burned a man. I have put nothing back under the Council’s last line, because it is true. A clerk who can tell a lapsed contract from a cold furnace is a rarer man than a clerk who can write either one, and this one came up from the Quay with the figure for the pots already in his cuff.

\subsection*{At the head and in the fold}

The glass at the head is dust off the third mouth and has worked into the grain; I have never got it out and have stopped trying. The green bead in the second fold was pressed in by a girl come up from the furnaces who watched me write the Y.H. 626 line and said nothing, and the sweet smear she left has not dried in two years. The white along the gutter is salt out of the paper and not salt off the sea, which is a thing only a person who has kept salt-paper knows the difference of. The scorch on the third leaf is the shed lamp catching while I wrote and going out under my hand; the hand was mine and I have not entered the burn. The lead at the foot came off the rim of a dish I set down to hold the leaf in the draught that comes up the Cliffs. The fibre in the stitch is rope off a boat I was mending when I thought of the question and put the leaf down on it. The gull took the corner and not the word, for which I have no thanks to give him. The square of bare paper is where I scraped a word away with the point of a tally-knife and put no other in its place; it is the only square in this quire that I made myself. The grey along the outer fold is not mine and not the Council’s. There is no Last Day in a tin and nothing here is swept up and burnt in the morning and called dealt with. I have had this leaf six years and have not swept it.

\subsection*{At the foot, in a hand nobody will own}

\begin{quote}\itshape The paper rots and the figure stays,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the furnace cools and the count runs on;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape a year allowed is a year entered,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and a year entered is a year gone.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape The sand in the tin has no tongue,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape but it is gritty where a hand has been;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape ask the third mouth why it would not take,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and ask the bench where nine have sat.\end{quote}

I asked the furnace-man, the clerk who made up the right-hand figure, and a woman who has swept the shed since before the rising, and had three answers and no hand. I have left the lines where they were written.

The leaves go back into the tin lined with sand. At the Opening of the Slates I copied them again and put the firing beside the figure again with my own hand, because a figure the damp has not taken is the one the Council will read first. Tomorrow the furnaces will be lit and the contracts written on paper made to rot, which is a virtue in this port, and I shall enter the pots that come off the quay, because that is what the glass-book is for. The nine who shut the furnaces have no column in it. They have the oar.

\clearpage\phantomsection\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{The Silt Song, Being the Shovelling-Song of the Fishstairs at Sill, Sung Clearing the Steps After the Breaking, with the Loads Counted Going Up, the Fourth Step Kept for the Water, a Landing-Clerk’s Ruling in Broad Charcoal, a Factor’s Clerk’s Figures in the Narrow Upright Hand, a Gloss from a Woman of the Eel-Stalls, and One Line at the Foot in a Hand Nobody Will Own}
\CRsheetheading{The Silt Song, Being the Shovelling-Song of the Fishstairs at Sill, Sung Clearing the Steps After the Breaking, with the Loads Counted Going Up, the Fourth Step Kept for the Water, a Landing-Clerk’s Ruling in Broad Charcoal, a Factor’s Clerk’s Figures in the Narrow Upright Hand, a Gloss from a Woman of the Eel-Stalls, and One Line at the Foot in a Hand Nobody Will Own}
{\centering\FellFont\itshape\footnotesize\color{faded} A step-woman’s work song in the low speech of the landing, said down into the silt and not up over the bridge; the verses counted in barrow-loads going up, with the fourth step kept and not entered; the manner of the clearing in the writer’s own charcoal, the landing-clerk’s ruling in broad charcoal, a factor’s clerk’s figures standing above in Ledgerhand, a gloss pressed into the margin by a woman of the eel-stalls, and one line at the foot in a hand nobody will claim · Sung at the Fishstairs below the north bridge in Sill and set down in the last tend of Silt, Y.H. 813, the year the sill-note came a week early, by a woman who clears the steps after the Breaking and has counted the loads going up for nine springs; written in charcoal thinned with silt-water on the back of a landing-tally spoiled by a wet thumb at the out-of-line step, folded into four and tied with grey wool to a nail under the eel-stall board; copied forward at Greybank in Grain of Y.H. 813 onto the back of a factor’s voided weigh-slip. It survives with grey silt worked into the grain at the head, a silt tideline along the gutter, a chip of sandstone from the third step in the fold, a fish-scale pressed flat in the lower corner, a brine-gull’s peck through one word of the sixth verse, a green bead of lead-glaze pressed into the lower margin, a small-ale ring gone sour at the foot, a grey Ash print along the outer fold that nobody will own, the landing-clerk’s broad ruling, the factor’s clerk’s figures standing above, the eel-stall woman’s gloss in the margin, and the one line at the foot\par}\medskip
I clear the steps at the Fishstairs after the water has gone down, and I have counted the loads going up for nine springs. The river comes up the same steps every year and lays silt on them, and we shovel it off and carry it to the high ground above the bridge until the stone shows its own colour. There is a fourth step from the bottom that we do not clear. No spade goes there and no number is said over it where a man with a slate can hear, because a thing that has no number cannot be entered, and that is the only part of this work the river is allowed to keep.

I set this down in the last tend of Silt in the year the sill gave its note a week early, when the Ilm came up over the Fishstairs and laid silt waist-deep in the lower town. A man who keeps the landing tally stood at the out-of-line step and asked what the women said while they cleared, and wrote the answer down while I was still saying it, with the doing taken out and a figure put where a step should stand. So I have written it as we say it, to the step and not to the river, and put the verbs back where he took them out.

The silt at the head is mine. I held the leaf down with the hand I shovel with and did not know I had marked it. It goes into the grain and no washing takes it out, which is why we sign with it here and not with ink.

\subsection*{How it is cleared}

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item Work from the top step down, never from the bottom up. A bank cleared from below slumps in the night and refills the step you had finished, and a woman who has done a step twice does not call it two loads, though her back knows better.

\item Keep the barrow on the high stone. A barrow left on the low step fills with river faster than a woman can tip it, and there is no trade in carrying water up a stair to pour it back.

\item Cut along the grain of the silt, not across it. The water lays it in thin leaves, one on one; a blade across the leaves lifts the whole bank, and a blade along them takes only what the step was holding.

\item Count the loads going up, never the loads coming down. A load that has reached the high ground is a load the river cannot take back. A count coming down is a count of empty barrows, which a clerk could enter and nobody else wants.

\item Say the words to the step, not over the water. Said over water they go where the silt goes and come back as weather, and a man at the Cross will give you the weather and the price of barley when he wants to know what the flood cost.

\item The fourth step from the bottom is the river’s. No spade goes there. If a girl asks why, tell her to count the loads going up and find out; if she asks again, do not answer her, because the answer is a place and a place cannot be told to a person who wants a figure.

\item Do not sing it on an Account-day. The bell goes four, four and a gap, and the gap is the fourth step. A shovelling-song set against that gap comes home wrong in the shoulder.

\item Keep the last part back until the boots have gone back over the north bridge.

\end{itemize}

\subsection*{The song}

\emph{Said low into the heap, with the barrow steady on the high stone. One verse to one load going up. The refrain is said into the step and not to the women beside you; said to a person it becomes an account, and there is enough account at the Cross without bringing it down the stairs. One line of the refrain to one stroke of the spade.}

\begin{quote}\itshape The water laid it in thin leaves, one on one,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and it lies the way it laid, with the grain to the stone;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape cut across and you lift the whole bank with the blade,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape cut along and the step comes clean and stays.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Heave it and lay it on the high dry stone,}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{three to the barrow and the fourth its own;}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{the river keeps the step that no spade finds,}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{and sends up the silt with a door in it.}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Count them going up and never count them down,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape a load on the high step is a load the river cannot drown;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the barrow on the low step fills as fast as you tip,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the fourth is the river’s and stays where it is.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Heave it and lay it on the high dry stone,}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{three to the barrow and the fourth its own;}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{the river keeps the step that no spade finds,}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{and sends up the silt with a door in it.}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Tap a cup on the stair and it answers full,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape tap the silt in the trough and it answers dull;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape a house is a cup with its rim in the flood,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the note it gives back is the note it had.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Heave it and lay it on the high dry stone,}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{three to the barrow and the fourth its own;}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{the river keeps the step that no spade finds,}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{and sends up the silt with a door in it.}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape It came up the same steps and took a different door,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape which is the whole of its manner and has been since the First;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the silt on the third step came out of a floor\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape in a house down the row where the water went in.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Heave it and lay it on the high dry stone,}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{three to the barrow and the fourth its own;}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{the river keeps the step that no spade finds,}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{and sends up the silt with a door in it.}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape One in twelve is printed and read twice at the Cross,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the other goes up the Clay Road in a box;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the flood comes in Silt and the levy comes on the tenth,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and neither of them asks which house it will take next.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Heave it and lay it on the high dry stone,}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{three to the barrow and the fourth its own;}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{the river keeps the step that no spade finds,}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{and sends up the silt with a door in it.}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape The sill sang a week before the ice was gone\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the town set its clocks by a stone under the water;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape we set our count by the silt on the step instead,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape which does not tell the hour but tells where the water has been.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Heave it and lay it on the high dry stone,}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{three to the barrow and the fourth its own;}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{the river keeps the step that no spade finds,}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{and sends up the silt with a door in it.}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape You hear the boot on the stone before the slate comes in sight,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape dry at the heel, clean at the cuff, and the figure written tight;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape he takes what the river left and calls it a measure of warmth,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the silt on the step has no name for the house it came from.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Heave it and lay it on the high dry stone,}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{three to the barrow and the fourth its own;}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{the river keeps the step that no spade finds,}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{and sends up the silt with a door in it.}\end{quote}

There is a space before the last refrain in the singing, the length of a step that is not shovelled. I have left it on the tally. A clerk put a round nought in it once, which is a thing you can hold up and look at; a step is not.

\subsection*{The part they keep back}

\emph{Not sung while the landing-clerk stands at the out-of-line step, and not while a man from Greybank is on the bridge. Said to the barrow and not across the stair.}

\begin{quote}\itshape The fourth step from the bottom is the river’s. No spade goes there.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape A pot is broken at a door and the sherd is set on the stair,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and a child come back from the bank has a house in its mouth\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and cannot say which house, and the river can, and will not.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape We go around the fourth with the barrow, the way a house goes round\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape what it will not sweep. The clerk put a nought in the place where it stood;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape a nought is a figure and travels, and a step is a place and does not.\end{quote}

\subsection*{What the landing-clerk did}

He keeps the tally at the out-of-line step and writes in broad charcoal on the back of his own spoiled leaves, the way a man writes who has had wet hands on a board all morning. Against \emph{three to the barrow and the fourth its own} he set: \emph{Four loads entered. The fourth is not a load. No deduction arises.} Against \emph{the river keeps the step that no spade finds} he wrote: \emph{step submerged; no entry lies.} He did not look at the fourth step while he wrote it, which is the only honest thing his hand did all morning.

Underneath, in mine: He is right that the fourth is not a load and wrong about what keeps it. He has counted the silt and left out the water, which is the whole art of that board. Both stand.

\subsection*{What the factor’s clerk did}

A clerk come up from Greybank with a cuff gone soft from washing borrowed the leaf on an Account-day, with ink settled in two fingers of it that would not come out. He took the verbs out and set his figures above mine, and I have left his hand standing and put ours underneath, as the step keeps the old silt showing under the new.

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item At \emph{the water laid it in thin leaves}, he wrote \emph{alluvial deposit, unassessed}. True in the figure and false on the stair, where a leaf of silt is a floor that a woman swept before the flood.

\item At \emph{it came up the same steps and took a different door}, he wrote \emph{loss not attributable}, and underlined it twice. He attributes the door to nobody, which is a kindness in a language that has no word for a house.

\item At \emph{the levy comes on the tenth}, he wrote \emph{deduction current; one part in twelve}, and set the printed figure against it. He has entered the number that was read and not the number that was paid, which is the difference between a clerk and a woman carrying a barrow up a stair.

\item At the space before the last refrain he put a round nought and wrote \emph{vacancy}. A nought is a figure and can be carried over the bridge. The fourth is a place and stays where the water put it.

\end{itemize}

\subsection*{What the woman of the eel-stalls put in the margin}

The thick charcoal belongs to a woman who keeps the stalls below the bridge and has sold eels at dawn since before the Glaze Wars. I have copied it as it stands.

At \emph{the silt on the third step came out of a floor}: \emph{It came out of my sister’s floor in the year of the flower. She swept that floor on the Last Day and left the grey in the corner as we do, and the river came and took both and laid them on the third step. I have shovelled my sister’s corner up the hill twice. I have not told the clerk and I have not put a name in the margin.}

At \emph{a child come back from the bank has a house in its mouth}: \emph{Mine came back and would not say whose. I asked the water and the water told me where it had put it, which was nowhere I could go. Both my answers stand.}

\subsection*{At the head and in the gutter}

The silt at the head is mine and has gone into the grain; there is no Last Day on a stair and nothing here gets gathered and burnt. The tideline along the gutter came up over both of us on the second load and took a word off the fifth verse; I wrote it back from my own mouth, which is how I know I was still saying it. The chip of sandstone in the fold is off the third step and came away under the spade with the silt still on it, which is the whole of the lesson and no use at all to a clerk. The fish-scale came off a basket set down on the leaf while a man counted six eels and was charged for five, which he has never settled and I have not entered. The gull pecked through one word of the sixth verse while the leaf lay on the stall and took no word, which was a mercy and cost somebody a crust. The green bead came off a girl with sweetness still at her tongue who leaned to see the writing and touched the leaf and went back to the stall; I have not washed it. The sour ring is small ale set down at the first verse and taken up at the last, by which time it had gone the colour of the step it stood on. The grey along the outer fold is not mine and not the clerk’s; nobody will own it, and the river will not take it, which is the only thing in this leaf the river has refused.

\subsection*{At the foot, in a hand nobody will own}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{The steps go down and the silt comes up.}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Nobody enters the fourth and it is still kept.}\end{quote}

I asked the woman of the eel-stalls, the landing-clerk and a barge-man waiting below the bridge, and had three answers and no hand. I have left the lines where they were written. The tally goes back under the eel-stall board. Tomorrow the loads will go up as they went up today, three and three and the fourth where the river put it, and if a man with a soft cuff comes down from Greybank to ask what the flood cost, I shall give him the weather and put the verbs back when he has gone.

\clearpage\phantomsection\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{The Sixth Bite, Being a Winter-Hunter’s Field Notes on the Ice-Mouse of the Frozen Ilm}
\CRsheetheading{The Sixth Bite, Being a Winter-Hunter’s Field Notes on the Ice-Mouse of the Frozen Ilm}
{\centering\FellFont\itshape\footnotesize\color{faded} A trapper’s field book on one small beast, set down as a record of snares and not a book of reasons; the set-lines in Grathic, the tally in charcoal on the backs of spoiled fish-bills, the counting verse as it is said on the bank, a midwife’s note in a small hand, a collector’s ruling in Ledgerhand, and a line at the foot in a hand nobody will own · Written in Stone of Y.H. 812, the Thin Year, by Tebb of the north bank, a hunter of the frozen fields above Sill who set snares in the eaves and under the river ice and sold the skins for a bit apiece; set down on the backs of fish-bills gone stiff with frost and on one spoiled toll-tally, sewn with eel-sinew into a scrap of oiled sacking and carried in a coat pocket against a tallow end. Copied forward at Greybank in Ilmen of Y.H. 813 onto the back of a Court grain-warrant voided by the Long Cold. It survives with frost-white ground into the head, a thumb of dried silt at the fold, a mouse-drop the size of a barley grain on the second leaf, a singe where the tallow end caught the lower corner, a coin-rub where a bit was carried loose in the pocket, a collector’s ruling in narrow Ledgerhand across the fur column, a midwife’s note in a small hand beside the sixth bite, a grey Ash print nobody will own, and one line at the foot in a hand nobody will own\par}\medskip
I have taken ice-mice for nine winters and kept this book for three. It is a record of snares. It is not a book of reasons. If a man wants reasons let him go to a College and ask them there, where they will write him one in a clean hand and charge him for the ink.

The paper is the backs of fish-bills from the north bank, gone stiff with frost and soft again in the thaw. A skin is worth a bit in Sill and a mark in Keld, and honest paper is worth a bit as well, so I write on what the eel-men throw away. The frost-white at the head is mine, off the thumb I set the sheet down with on Stone 9. I have not knocked it off.

\subsection*{Where it keeps}

It lives under the ice and in the thatch. In Stone, when the Ilm has lain frozen three tends and the eaves along the north bank have a white lip to them, it comes into the houses and nests in the clothes a man leaves hanging by the door. I have found one in the fold of a coat that had been worn down to the Fishstairs and back, and two in the straw of a bed whose occupant had not risen in a week. It does not come for the person. It comes for the place where the warmth has been, which is very often the same place, and the poor do not thank it for telling the difference.

You find it by the small cold patch. A man comes in off the bank, puts his hand to his own sleeve and says his arm has gone to sleep, and it has, but not from the sleeping. Where the mouse has sat there is a place the size of a thumb that does not warm when the rest of him does. It spreads if you leave it. Rub it toward the heart; do not cut it, for there is nothing in it to let out. I have seen a man put a knife to such a patch because he thought to drain it, and he drained nothing but the use of two fingers, which did not come back before the thaw.

\subsection*{The taking}

A noose of horsehair, set where the thatch has sagged and not where the frost sits highest. The mouse goes along the under edge of the eave where the house gives off a little warm through the roof, and a noose in the open gives you nothing but a dead bird and a cold hand. Under the ice you set a bent sliver in a crack and lead it with a crumb; the ice is clear in Stone and you can see the thing come to it. Do not crush it. A skin with a hole in it goes thin in the tanning and a thin skin will not come round, and there is no market for a skin that will not come round.

The fur is warm past its weight. A skin the size of a man’s palm will keep a cup from freezing on a shelf where a fold of good wool will not. This is the whole reason the trade exists, and the reason is not a pretty one. The skin goes into the lining of collectors’ coats, sewn there by a man who has never held a collector’s tube and has no wish to. The collectors say it is a good joke. I have stood by a brazier with one of them in a coat lined with nine or ten of my skins and watched him hold his grey fingers out to the coals, and he could not get them warm, and he said it was the weather. It was the weather. It is always the weather. I have never told him what was sewn into his coat and I never will, because a man who has been given a joke is allowed to keep it.

Stone — Set — Skins — Bitten — Entered\par

Stone 2 — Eaves, north bank, four lines — three — none — 3\par

Stone 8 — Under the ice below the Weir — five — one, a man’s thumb — 5\par

Stone 12, the Drawing — Eaves, three houses — two — none — 2\par

Stone 17 — Under the ice, bank above Sill — six — three, all in one house — 6\par

Stone 20 — The thatch by the Fishstairs road — four — one child, four bites — 4\par

Stone 26 — Eaves and ice together — seven — two, one not woken — 7\par

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{In the narrow upright Ledgerhand of a collector of Greybank, struck through the “Bitten” column:} Bites to persons not entered. No vessel. The measure stands where it is. Account stands.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{And under the “Entered” column, in the same hand:} 3+5+2+6+4+7 = 27. Received.\end{quote}

I have left his hand standing. He counted the skins; I counted what the skins cost, and the two columns are not the same column. A bit is a bit and a child that does not wake is not entered, which is the whole of the accounting in one line. I wrote the bites in the margin below where his column cannot reach, and put my own mark beside them in charcoal.

\subsection*{The verse}

\emph{Said on the bank when the lines are set, not at a fire. The fifth line is the one the old men leave out and the young ones put back.}

\begin{quote}\itshape One for the eave and one for the ice,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape one for the coat that has come home cold;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape two for the thumb that will not come round\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and one for the hand that could not hold.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Set it where the thatch has sagged,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape not where the frost has made a crown;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape a skin with a hole is a skin gone thin\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and a thin skin will not come round.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Six for the cradle, six for the bank,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape six for the one who does not wake;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape count them going and count them back\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and leave the last one for the snare to take.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape A draft is a thing that a house can bear;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape a bite is a thing that a house can’t.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Keep the window. Mind the coat.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Count the skins and let the child count.\end{quote}

I do not know why the old men leave out the fifth line. I have asked two of them and had two answers, and neither answer was about mice. I have set it down as it is said and let it stand.

\subsection*{The sixth bite}

It bites cold. There is no more to the bite than that: a small nick, not much blood, and a place that goes white around it. If the wound is warmed it comes back. If it is not warmed the whiteness travels, and a foot or a hand goes the way that the old people call the cold that stays, and stays. Salt does not hold it, and I have never found a physic that does. Keep the part warm, get the person to a fire, and do not put a knife to it.

A sleeping child bitten six times will not wake. This is not a saying. I have seen it in Stone 26 in a house above the Fishstairs road, and I had set the line myself and knew how many of the little bodies had gone into my hand that morning, which was seven, and one of them had already bit and I had not known it. The child had four nicks along the jaw and two at the wrist, and the sixth was the one at the wrist. There was no blood to speak of and no sound. The mother put a warm stone to him and would not take her hand away, and the midwife came and said the second chill had taken him, and said it in the voice midwives use when they have said a thing many times and have never once been thanked for it.

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{In a small hand, in the margin beside this passage, pressed small and close as though the writer feared the room might read it:} The second chill comes to children who were never bit. I have laid out eleven. Do not let this book say six for the midwives. Four at the jaw and two at the wrist is a count, not a cause. --- A.\end{quote}

I have not struck her line out. I have not changed my count either. We are both right in the way that two people standing on opposite banks are both right about the river, which is a thing I have learned in this trade and nowhere else.

\subsection*{What the hearths say}

They say it is the cold made small enough to be killed, a bit of winter that got legs and went looking for a coat. There are songs in the Fenmarch with a man’s name in them and a wrong done at a weir, and I have heard them and have no quarrel with a song. I have opened a great many of these and found a mouse. It is a field mouse that has lived where the cold comes up through the ice, and the cold has gone into it the way the smoke goes into a hound that lives by a kiln; the place changes the creature and then the creature carries the place about with it. I have written what it does and not what it wants. A man who writes what a mouse wants is a man who will be asked to write what a collector wants next, and there is no end to that sort of work.

What it does is take. It sits in the warm place and takes the warm out of it, and the place it has taken from stays cold after the mouse has gone. We say it takes the head from the place. A collector sets iron to a wrist and takes by the same road, only with a slate to make the taking look like keeping, and the collector’s fingers go grey where the mouse’s coat goes warm. I have set the two side by side below and I have not written a word between them. Let the College join them if it can get a figure out of it.

\subsection*{At the head and in the margins}

The frost-white at the head is mine, and came off the ninth day of Stone when I set a sheet down on the step and picked it up again with the frost already in it. The silt thumb at the fold is from the bank above Sill, where I knelt in the grey to lead a line under the ice; it has dried into the grain and will not rub out. The mouse-drop on the second leaf is the only part of this book that has entered itself. The singe on the lower corner is where the tallow end caught while I was reading by it, and the hand that pulled it back was mine and is not entered. The coin-rub is a bit I carried loose in that pocket for a month before I spent it; I do not remember what I bought, which is the common fate of bits. The grey print along the gutter came off a cuff laid where no cuff has business lying. I have not swept it and nobody will own it. The Last Day is kept at a fire, and a line set under the ice has no fire to keep it, so nothing in this book gets swept.

\subsection*{At the foot, in a hand nobody will own}

\begin{quote}\itshape It does not eat what it takes. Neither does the iron.\end{quote}

I asked a midwife, a collector who wears the coat, and a man who lost two fingers to a patch he cut, and had three answers and no hand. I have left the line where it was written, which is the only honest way to keep a sentence you cannot sign.

Next Stone I will set a line in the eaves below the north bridge, where the ice comes up wrong in the thaw and the thatch stays wet when the rest has dried. I will count the bites as well as the skins, and if six come up together in one house I will set that down too, in charcoal, with the verb left in it, and let the collector take what figure he can out of it.

\clearpage\phantomsection\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{The Sixth Repair, Being a Letter from the First Seam to Nine Pots, Answered in the Margin and Entered Over by the Court}
\CRsheetheading{The Sixth Repair, Being a Letter from the First Seam to Nine Pots, Answered in the Margin and Entered Over by the Court}
{\centering\FellFont\itshape\footnotesize\color{faded} A letter between brothers, the one hand Keldish and number-first, the other Grathic and given to proverbs; a tally of repairs set down in a small table, the sentence of the Vorr kept as it was spoken, the answers of the man addressed written in the margins, the corrections of a Court survey-clerk laid in Ledgerhand over both hands, and one line at the foot in a hand nobody will own · Written in Bone of Y.H. 812, the Thin Year of the Long Cold, in the survey room off the Duelling Floor beneath Keld Keep, by Varek of the First Seam, a clerk of the rim-seam tally, to Ollen of Nine Pots, a thrower, his brother by a mother who came down from the clay country and never learned to say a number before a noun. Set first on the back of a survey sheet spoiled by wet slate and carried down the Rim Road and the Clay Road in Seed of Y.H. 813 with a survey party bound for Greybank; answered in the margins at Nine Pots and corrected at Greybank by a clerk of the factor’s office who borrowed the leaf on a market morning and would not give it back until the verbs were out of it. Kept since in a clay tube stoppered with wool on the shelf of the thrower’s shed in Nine Pots. It survives with coal dust at the head, a smear of hot lead at the fold where the leaf lay against a surveyor’s cuff, bone-coloured slip dust worked into the gutter, a thumb of tallow, a ring where a cup of small ale stood from the first question to the last, the figure for the sixth repair struck through and written again underneath in the writer’s own hand, and a grey Ash print along the outer fold that nobody will own.\par}\medskip
To Ollen, thrower, of Nine Pots, from Varek of the First Seam, his brother. Six repairs counted this week. One letter. No answer looked for.

I write from the room off the floor where the survey sheets are kept, which is warm in a way a room should not be warm. The stone sweats here in Bone and the smell comes up before anything shows, hot lead and a mineral sweetness like a glaze pot left too near the fire. Two men went out of this shaft in my first season and came back with their fingers the colour of a skimmed milk skin. I have counted the repairs in the wall behind the tally desk six times and got six each time, which is a small thing to be glad of. A number that comes back the same is the only honest company down here.

We had the same mother, who came down from Nine Pots with clay under her nails and a way of addressing the pot before she addressed the room. She taught you the wheel and taught me to hold a slate. I have kept the slate. You got the wheel, which is the better inheritance and I have never once said so in a letter until now, so you may put this down to the lead smell.

\subsection*{The tally, as I keep it}

The wall behind the desk is not the oldest in the seam. It is only the one I can see from my stool. I have entered what I can see and left the rest where it is, which is a rule the Order is not so strict about as it used to be.

Repair — What it is made of, by the Keldish translation — What the factor’s copy at Greybank calls it — How many times repaired\par

One — Stone, dressed and keyed — Stone — Twice\par

Two — Stone and iron pins — Stone, iron not entered — Once\par

Three — Stone — Stone — Three times; the third over the second\par

Four — Warm-stone dust in a clay bed — Material not entered — Once\par

Five — Stone — Stone — Once\par

Six — Not stone — Language — Once; crossed out and written again\par

Five of the six are stone and are no trouble. The fourth wants a word I will not use of a wall, because warm-stone is a thing a man carries against a child’s belly and not a thing he puts in a hole in the world. I have entered it as dust in a clay bed and let the translation stand beside it.

The sixth is the one I am writing to you about. The Keldish translation calls it Ash. The factor’s copy calls it language. I have copied both words into the margin and chosen neither, because a surveyor who chooses between two guesses has made a fact of one of them and will have to answer for it at the Weighing. The Vorr were asked. One of them sat against a stone for a season and came back with three sentences, all the same sentence, which was that the numbers were correct. I have written that down too. It is a complete answer if you are a Vorr and a very thin one if you are a man trying to sleep above a seam that sweats.

\subsection*{The entry of Y.H. 588}

There is an entry in the old survey of a man with a branching red mark on his forearm and ribs. The entry is crossed out. It was crossed out before I came down the shaft and I do not know whose hand did it, which is a thing I have said to myself often enough that it now sounds like an answer.

I have copied the shape of the mark onto the back of this sheet so that you can look at it and tell me whether clay ever makes it. I do not want an opinion. I want to know whether you have seen it under a glaze or in the bottom of a jar, and if so, on what day and out of which pit. Give me the day and the pit and leave the rest where you found it.

There is a paper in a tin lined with warm-stone in the room off the floor. The men who keep the floor read it once a year and do not act on it, which I am told is a great skill and is certainly an old one. I have read it twice. The second time I found a line about a vessel that holds without leaking and went back to counting the wall, which was easier and paid the same.

\subsection*{What I want to know from you}

This is the question I cannot put to any man in Keld without being told to state my measure first and ask afterwards:

A pot that has cracked all the way through and been mended, does it hold the same as a pot that never cracked? I do not mean whether it holds water. I mean whether the holding is the same holding. Tap a sound pot with the knuckle and it answers full. Tap a cracked one and it answers flat, a little dead sound that stops at the surface. I know the two sounds as well as I know my own number, which was thirty-three when I went down and thirty-nine when they changed it, and has been cut out and written again twice since, so that my forearm reads like this letter does. But nobody has ever tapped a repaired pot for me and asked it the question twice, once before the mending and once after, and told me what changed.

You will say a pot is a pot. You will say this with slip on both forearms and the little finger bent where the splinter went in at eleven, and you will be right in the way that potters are always right, which is from the wrist and not from the mouth. Answer me from the wrist.

\subsection*{In the margin, in a second hand, the letters round and pressed hard, with slip in the strokes}

You always did ask the wrong question first. A pot that never cracked is a pot that has not been mended, and there is no holding to compare with it. Tap mine and it answers full because I set the seam myself and it sang when it went home. If it had not sung I would have sold it for a flower pot and said nothing. A crack that is mended keeps the crack. Ask it to be a pot it was not and you are asking a lie of the clay, which is a thing the clay charges for in the thaw.

On the red mark: third firing of Y.H. 806, a jar from the Old Kiln clay that would not take a glaze and went grey in the firing. The mark was on the bottom, branching like frost on a pane. A girl from the terrace crossed two fingers at it and said it was a flower. I asked her which flower. She gave me a date. I have kept the jar under the bench and I have never turned it up in company.

On the road: it is ours and Sill’s both, which is why neither of us mends it. Come down in Seed when the clay has set and bring the warm-stone if you are still carrying one. Six repairs in a wall is enough for a man to carry without a stone as well.

\begin{quote}\itshape One for the wheel and one for the fire,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape one for the crack that the glaze won’t hide;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape tap it at noon, it answers at night,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the seam keeps the word the potter denied.\end{quote}

I have never written a verse in my life and I would not begin now if there were not a man above me in a shaft who needs one. Put it under the numbers where it belongs.

\subsection*{What the Court hand did, at Greybank, in the second tend of Seed}

A clerk of the factor’s office borrowed the leaf on a market morning; his cuff was gone soft at the edge from washing and he had ink in the creases of two fingers. He laid his hand on the top sheet before he looked at either of us, which is the manner of that table. He took the verbs out of both hands as though a verb were a thing a man could smuggle in a cuff, and set a figure against each repair, and struck the question about the mended pot and wrote \emph{No such comparison} above it. Against the red shape he put a round nought and wrote \emph{mark, not entered}. Where my brother wrote that the seam keeps the word, the clerk wrote \emph{repair retained; material not entered} and left mine underneath, which is more than he usually leaves.

In my hand — In the Court hand\par

Six repairs counted this week — Repairs entered: six\par

The sixth is not stone — Material not entered\par

The Vorr said the numbers were correct — Figures confirmed\par

Does a mended pot hold the same? — No such comparison\par

A mark on the bottom of a jar — Mark, not entered\par

The seam keeps the word — Repair retained\par

He asked me what a verse was worth and I said nothing a clerk could enter, which was the first true thing he said all morning. I have left both hands standing, mine under his and my brother’s under both, as a repaired wall keeps the old break under the new keying and does not pretend the first hand never touched it.

\subsection*{At the head and in the gutter}

The coal dust at the head is mine; I held the sheet down with my whole hand because the draught in the survey room comes along the floor and takes paper before it takes a man. The hot lead at the fold came off a cuff on the day a passing was measured two hours early and we all went up faster than we had any right to. The slip in the gutter is my brother’s and has gone bone-coloured with dry, which is the colour of his forearms by noon and of mine by never. The tallow thumb is mine. The ring came off a cup that stood from the first question to the verse and was drunk by neither of us, which is how small ale is drunk in Keld when there is a thing to say and no proper word for it. The grey along the outer fold is not mine and not the Court’s. I have not swept it. There is no Last Day in the First Seam.

\subsection*{At the foot, in a hand nobody will own}

\begin{quote}\itshape Six repairs in the wall and one with no name. The Court has entered the five it can spell. The wall keeps all six and has never once been asked to explain itself.\end{quote}

\clearpage\phantomsection\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{The Slack Tide, Being a Winter Riddle Night on the Quay at Vhal, Five Questions Scored in Chalk on the Tarred Post, the One Put from the Door, and the Tide That Was Named and Has Not Come}
\CRsheetheading{The Slack Tide, Being a Winter Riddle Night on the Quay at Vhal, Five Questions Scored in Chalk on the Tarred Post, the One Put from the Door, and the Tide That Was Named and Has Not Come}
{\centering\FellFont\itshape\footnotesize\color{faded} A tavern-keeper’s record of a cold-month contest, set down for the settling of arguments and not for the improvement of the reader; the rules in the hand the house keeps, the riddles in the words they were spoken, a score in chalk on the tarred door-post, the figures of a Council clerk entered over them, a boat-master’s note in the margin, and one line at the foot in a hand nobody will own · Written in Stone of Y.H. 812, the Thin Year after the Long Cold, at the alehouse called the Slack Tide on the Quay at Vhal, by the woman who keeps the house and the lamp over the door; set first on the back of a spoiled tide-tally from the house beside the Council room and on two strips of salt-paper that would not hold ink, sewn with eel-sinew into a fold of oiled sailcloth and kept in a dry tin under the till, where nothing else in this house is kept dry. It survives with a thumb of tar at the head, a white salt bloom along the gutter, a press of frozen rope across the first leaf, a green bead of cliff-glass in the lower corner, a fish-hook nick, a coal-smudge near the fifth question, the chalk rubbed thin where a sleeve has gone over the post, one correction in the narrow upright hand of a clerk of the Council of Tides, one note in the blunt hand of a boat-master, and a line at the foot in a hand that is nobody’s.\par}\medskip
I keep the Slack Tide on the Quay. It is a different work from keeping a tally, though both begin with the hand on the board and end with a figure somebody wants to carry away. In the cold months the east wind holds, the Sallow skins over at the edges, and the galleys lie up on the pulled benches with their oars in, and there is nothing to do of an evening but ask one another what we already know and call the asking a riddle. A question with an answer nobody knows is a bet, and there are men on this Quay who would bet on which way the wind will sit by morning.

The door-post is tarred and the chalk shows on it. I score the night there and take the score off in the morning with a wet rope-end, which is the only erasure this house has ever needed. Nothing is carried away from the Slack Tide on a slate. A man who wants a thing entered can go up to the Council room and sit with people warmer than himself, and the paper there will rot before he gets home, which the Council calls a virtue.

\subsection*{The rules, as the house keeps them}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item A riddle is put once. Ask for it again and you owe a quart, because the second asking is for your own pleasure and not for the post.

\item Answer in one breath. A second answer is a different riddle and is not heard.

\item Five are chalked. A sixth may be put and is not scored, being a thing said from the door and not from a stool.

\item The house judges. I say whether an answer serves and I do not say why. A reason given is a riddle given away for nothing, and the giver can go home and sell it.

\item No paper lies on the board. A contract left here overnight is a debt the weather has settled, and this house does not settle debts for the Council.

\item A quart of small ale is set down before the first question and no one lifts it until the fifth. If a white bloom comes up on the board before then, the night’s answering will go badly. I have never known this to fail and I would not say so before a dipper.

\end{enumerate}

\subsection*{The five that were chalked}

The first went to a woman who holds a twelfth of a boat through her mother and will not say the fraction before company. She had her answer before the verse was fairly out, which is why she never takes the quart and is always asked first.

\begin{quote}\itshape I go from mother to daughter and never by buying;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape a man may come aboard and hold me in his hand,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and still his word upon the boat is counted half;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape I am not the hull, and I am not the sea.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape What am I?\end{quote}

“A share,” she said. “And the half is his opinion, not mine.” I gave her the quart and she drank standing with her sleeve over the rim, because she had been told not to spill. Nobody asked her how many twelfths she held, which is the proper way to ask nothing in this house.

The second went to Kett of the Quay, who reads the draws at the tide-tally house and keeps his cuffs dry by not touching anything.

\begin{quote}\itshape I am set down to be kept and I keep by going;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the wetter the room, the less I owe;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the Council has made a virtue of my dying\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and hired a man in a clean coat to write it.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape What am I?\end{quote}

“Salt-paper,” he said, without looking up from his tally, which is how he answers everybody. The house allowed it. A man who reads the draws all day does not need to look at a person to know what that person has brought in.

The third was put to a dipper come in off the pans with salt dried white in the creases of her neck.

\begin{quote}\itshape I run against the wind and am blessed before light;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the Council is surprised by me every year;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape they tax me in a figure I never carried.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape What runs seaward and is counted by men who never saw it?\end{quote}

“The draw,” she said, and said it to the pot and not to Kett, because a dipper does not argue with the tide-tally house before company. She took no quart. Dippers are paid by the pan-master, who pays in the weather and never in ale.

The fourth went to a boat-master who had lost a store below the waterline and had come back to sit down again, which not every man does after such a loss.

\begin{quote}\itshape I knock where no hand can reach, below the waterline;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape I take the store and leave the rope behind;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the nets are blessed at dawn and I come all the same.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape What taps a hull and takes what the hull was holding?\end{quote}

“A salt-thing,” he said, and set the quart down again without drinking, which in this house is how a man says he has already paid for the answer. There was an argument about whether a blessing that does not keep a store is a blessing at all. I stopped it by touching the post, because there is no winning an argument about a blessing and there is only the thing that came in the night and the store that is not in the boat.

The fifth I put myself, because the room had grown noisy and wanted quieting, and a riddle put by the house is not scored against anybody.

\begin{quote}\itshape I steal the warm and do not eat it;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape I go up the wind with a coal under my crop;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape no tally in this town stands one mark the poorer.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape What carries the fire out of the account?\end{quote}

An old woman who mends nets said “a brine-gull” and said it low, the way people say things they have said to the fire at home. I passed her the pot. She set it down again and told me a gull had taken a coal off her brazier the week before and she had not gone after it, because a thing that goes up the wind with your coal has already been paid and there is nobody to charge. That is the best answer I have heard in nine winters and the only one that cost the teller nothing by telling it.

\subsection*{The sixth, which was put from the door}

Toward the end of the night a girl came to the door and did not step over it. There was salt dried white on her shins and at the hem of her coat, as if she had come up off the pans and walked the Salt Road without putting her shoes back on, which nobody does who owns a pair of shoes. She asked whether anybody in the house had seen the tide she named at the Salt Walk. Nobody said yes, which is a way of saying no that costs nobody anything. Then she put the sixth:

\begin{quote}\itshape I was named at fourteen with my feet in the pan\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and written in salt where the dippers could read;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape by noon there was no word, and the pan kept nothing;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape I have carried the shape of it all winter, not the name.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape What am I?\end{quote}

Kett said, “A tide not yet seen.” The girl said that was what the dippers wrote in the salt and asked what the house called it. The room went the way a room goes when everybody has the answer in their mouths and nobody will be the one to say it, which is the same in Vhal as in any town with a Council. She waited a little. “Then leave it where it is,” she said, and went back into the wind. Where she stood there was a small drift of salt on the boards. In the morning it was gone, and I have not swept the place where it lay, because the wind does the sweeping on this Quay and always has.

\subsection*{The score, in chalk on the tarred post}

Question — Put by — Answer given — Score\par

The share — the woman with the twelfth — a share — one, drunk\par

The paper — Kett of the Quay — salt-paper — one, allowed\par

The draw — a dipper — the draw — one, to the pot\par

The tap — the boat-master — a salt-thing — one, not drunk\par

The coal — the house — a brine-gull — one, given low\par

The named tide — a girl at the door — none served — not scored\par

The Council’s figure for the draw went up on the tally board that morning and came down by noon, which is what the Council’s figures do. It went over the post with the ale and nobody looked at it twice, which is how figures go in this house.

\subsection*{What the clerk did}

A clerk of the Council borrowed the leaf on a morning when the till was being counted and his cuff was soft at the edge from the damp, which is the only way a Council cuff ever gets soft. He set the riddles down as \emph{queries entered} and the answers as \emph{responses entered}, and put a figure of marks against each of the five, which was more than I had scored, because the house scores in whether a person sits down again and he does not. Against the sixth he wrote \emph{no answer tendered; struck.} He asked who had put it. I told him a girl at the door. He asked for the girl’s name, and I said she had given none, which is a true thing and not the thing he wanted, and he wrote \emph{party unidentified; interest in a tide not entered.}

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item Against \emph{a share, and the half is his opinion, not mine}, he wrote \emph{one-half interest, contingent}.

\item At the salt-paper he wrote \emph{instrument voided by damp}, and underlined it twice, which is what the Council does when it wants a thing to look like a mercy.

\item Against the draw he wrote \emph{current taxed at source}, which is true in a language nobody on this Quay speaks unless they are being paid to.

\item At the salt-thing he wrote \emph{loss not entered}, and put a round nought in the place where the store had stood.

\item Against the brine-gull he wrote \emph{no value transferred}, which is the only one of his answers I have ever wanted to keep.

\end{itemize}

I have put my words under his and left his standing, the way a tarred post keeps the chalk under the salt. He has entered five and struck the sixth, and the sixth was not struck: it went out on the wind with the girl and is still going.

\subsection*{From the boat-master}

At the foot of the scored leaves, in the blunt hand of the man who had lost his store and sat down again:

\begin{quote}\itshape A man’s word on a boat is counted at half. His loss is entered whole.\end{quote}

He says he wrote it about the salt-thing and not about his wife, and I have let him say so. A man who has married aboard is allowed one sentence in a book he did not write, which is more than the Council allows him anywhere else.

\subsection*{At the head and in the margins}

The tar thumb at the head is mine. I held the leaf down on the Quay in the wind and did not know I had marked it; tar goes into the grain and will not come out, which is why the Council room uses it for a seal and this house uses it for nothing. The salt bloom along the gutter came up out of the paper on the third night, when I carried the leaf inside my coat and the coat crusted white at the fold. I have not brushed it off. A bloom written by the weather is the only writing in Vhal that a clerk cannot strike. The press of frozen rope across the first leaf came off the man who held the door while the girl spoke, and I have not written which man, because he would stop holding doors if I did. The green bead in the lower corner came off a string of cliff-glass a carrier left on the till; it has the colour of the Glaze Cliffs after rain and I have kept it where it fell. The fish-hook nick is from a hook set in the edge by a man paying for his quart, and he did not apologize, which is how hooks are paid for here. The coal-smudge near the fifth question is from the brazier, where the leaf lay too close while the net-mender was telling us about her gull; the coal was ours and the answer was not. The grey print along the outer fold is not mine and nobody has claimed it. Nothing on this Quay is swept until the wind does it, so the print is still there.

\subsection*{At the foot, in a hand nobody will own}

\begin{quote}\itshape The pan keeps the shape and the sea keeps the name;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape neither gives back what was made in it.\end{quote}

I asked the woman with the twelfth, Kett and the boat-master, and had three answers and no hand. I have left the line where it was written. The leaf goes back in the tin and the chalk goes off the post with a wet rope-end, and in the morning the Council clerk will come for the till and find nothing in it that rots. Next winter the galleys will lie up again and the east wind will hold, and I shall set five questions on the post and leave the sixth standing at the door, for whoever it is to come in out of the wind or not, as they please.

\clearpage\phantomsection\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{The Smoke-Side Dog, Being a Soldier’s Field Notes on the Kiln-Hound at the Old Kiln}
\CRsheetheading{The Smoke-Side Dog, Being a Soldier’s Field Notes on the Kiln-Hound at the Old Kiln}
{\centering\FellFont\itshape\footnotesize\color{faded} A soldier’s field book on one beast, set down as the record of a watch and not natural philosophy; the rounds in Grathic, the tally in charcoal on a spoiled levy-roll, a watch-song as it is sung, a kiln-master’s correction in slip-white, a clerk’s ruling in Ledgerhand · Written in Bone and Ash of Y.H. 812, the Thin Year, by Hobb of Sill, one of the Thane’s men watching the Old Kiln road, in the watch-shed with a tallow end; set down on three levy-rolls spoiled by rain, then on the back of a granary docket, sewn with eel-sinew and carried in a coat pocket. Copied forward in Ilmen of Y.H. 813. It survives with soot ground into the head, a brown spot on the second leaf, a wet boot-print from the Slip Brook, a singe from the fire-pot, the charcoal rubbed thin, two corrections from the factor’s clerk, one line in slip-white from the kiln-master, and one line at the foot in a hand nobody will own\par}\medskip
I keep the road to the Old Kiln for the Thane. It is no post a man writes home about. The ruin stands one league south of Sill where the clay has gone grey and will not take a glaze, and the ash in its throat is deeper than a man is tall. I am set there to see that no one digs the grey in the dark and that no one lies down in it and stays there. I carry a short spear with the head gone blue on the quay stone and a fire-pot of coals under ash, and I write these lines at the end of a watch with the tallow down to a knuckle and the cold coming up through the soles.

The rolls I wrote on first were spoiled in a rain that took the figures clean off, which was a mercy of a kind: a figure the rain has eaten cannot be entered. I write in charcoal now, because charcoal goes into the grain and a clerk cannot take it off with a cuff. The soot at the head is my own thumb setting the sheet down on the watch-shed bench. I have not knocked it off.

\subsection*{The road and the river}

The hound keeps to the smoke side. That is the first thing a new man must learn and the thing that costs him a night’s sleep. It will lie all watch on the side of the ruin where the warm comes up through the clay and the air moves, and it will not come round to the cold side though a man stand there with his coat open and his pot hanging. The folk of High Kiln say the river is a wall. I thought it was a saying until the night I watched one stand in the mud at the Slip Brook with its nose across the water and a man lying three paces beyond on the other bank. It stood. It did not go over. The man was not saved by it, but he was not eaten either, and in this trade a man takes what the night gives.

It comes off the smoke side in the second watch, when the tallow is low and the kiln-yards down at Sill have stopped their shouting. It does not bark. The sound it makes is low in the throat, like a man clearing himself in his sleep, and you hear it in your boots before you hear it in the air. I have set the watch-song down below with the hearths’ words standing where the watchmen put them, which is not where I would have put them.

\subsection*{What it is}

It is a dog. I will set that down before anything else, because the hearths will not. It has a dog’s teeth and a dog’s neck and a dog’s way of putting its head on one side when it listens. It is bigger than the yard hounds at the Tallow Works and thinner, with a coat the colour of wet clay and no grey on the outside. The grey is in the mouth and under the nails. Behind the ears it is hot to the back of the hand, hotter than a beast that has merely been near a fire should be. It smells of smoke and hot clay, and when it has been lying in the throat a man smells of it too, for a day after.

I have opened three. Two were brought down on the road and one was found dead at the mouth of the old flue, where it had gone in after the warmth and not come out. In all three I found a dog altered by the place it lived in, the way a potter’s hands are altered by the wheel. I found no more than that and I have not put a cause beside it. A man who writes a cause into a book he keeps in his pocket is a man who will be asked for it by somebody with a slate.

\subsection*{The breath}

The danger is the air. The dog is the thing that brings a man to where the air is.

I have stood on both sides of it. A man who stays in the throat with his head low will come out with a headache and a thirst that outlasts the watch, and his lips are a little too red, which is all the evidence there is. There was a potter of Low Kiln came up in Ash to look at the grey and went down on the second morning in his own house with the window shut, and the physician said it was a merciful death, which is a thing physicians say when they have not had to lay the body out. He had never seen a hound in his life. The potters leave a window open in a firing though the draft spoils the glaze. A spoiled glaze is a loss a man can count. A man is not.

I have written the air where the watchmen write the dog, and I have left both standing.

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{In the blocky hand of the kiln-master of Low Kiln, written in slip-white with a potter’s stylus, down the margin of this leaf:} It is the air. I have buried two who never saw a dog. Leave the window. The glaze can bear it. --- K.\end{quote}

\subsection*{The bite}

It does not bite a man on his feet. I have stood within two paces with the spear down and it went on with its own work. But let a man go down and it comes for the face, and it does not shake him or drag him. It puts its mouth to him and waits, the way a collector sets a tube and waits, and the waiting is the part I cannot write about without my hand going still.

The boy they set with me in the second watch went in at Ash 5 after a man we had heard in the grey. We found him face down with the hound at the cheek. I struck it across the back with the spear-shaft and it went three paces off and stood, which is what it does; it does not run and it does not come back at a man who has hit it. The boy’s cheek was two small holes and not much blood, and his lip was red on the side next the ground. I washed with water and bound it. At the end of the tend the holes were closed and the lip was still red and he was asking for water at every watch. He has never said what he saw down there and I have not asked him. Salt does not hold that bite and there is no physic for it that I know. Keep the man out of the close air and let him ask for water. That is the whole of what I have.

The tongue, dried, is bought by Fenfolk to test a close room, for it discolours where the breath is. Two bits a tongue and no questions. The hide is too smoky to sell, so we burn it. A man who tells you he has found a use for a kiln-hound hide is a man who wants another one, and you should keep your coals between you and him.

\subsection*{The watch-song}

\emph{Sung going in at the first watch, not coming back. The fourth line is the hearths’ line and every watchman sings it wrong on purpose. I have set it down as it is sung.}

\begin{quote}\itshape Two for the clay and one for the smoke,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the dog keeps the side where the fire has been;\end{quote}
