A man from Greybank asked me to mark the safe ones on the reed; I told him the boards move after rain and a mark does not. He wrote \emph{vacancy} in the empty place. A vacancy is a thing the Court can enter. The boards are not.\end{quote}

\subsection*{The Reed Cut}

\emph{Where the young cut their first bundle in the dark. A bundle is judged by the arm that carries it, and the arm tells what went into it and not what it cost.}

Due\par

Going in at the dark — nothing\par

Coming back with a bundle — counted in the arm; no figure\par

The dry boards shown to a man from the south — 1 bit for the showing; shown by a child who stands on them first and will not say which is which\par

A second cutting owed on a stick — one notch, untied at the next cut\par

A man who asks what the hands will be paid — the weather and the river; never a figure\par

\subsection*{The ways up into Grath}

\emph{East by the mud road to Mud End, three leagues downriver of Sill; the south bridge into the town; north-east by the Tallow road; and west the Quiet Acre that lies between us and Grath.}

Due\par

South bridge into Sill, loaded cart — 1 bit, paid going up\par

The same on foot — nothing; a foot sinks and pays in water\par

Barrow of peat going up to Sill — 2 bits at the bridge, and the same peat is 5 bits in Stone; the difference is the road\par

Tallow road, going up with wool — no due; a sheep’s fibre from such a man is in the fold of this reed\par

The Quiet Acre — no toll; the wells have water and the doorways have no hands to open them\par

A man who stops at a well there — nobody tells him which house will answer\par

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Margin:} The Empty Cantons are what the Court calls the ground between us and Grath; we call it the Quiet Acre and leave it alone. A doorway is built for coming back through. I have not written what hung in the bare clay above one of them, because a thing a man can name is a thing the Court can figure.\end{quote}

\subsection*{The Line}

\emph{South to the Peat Line, where Sere’s northern advance stopped in Y.H. 634. We have paid tribute in eels ever since, by the year and not by the cart.}

Due\par

Tribute in eels at the Line — the same since Y.H. 634; nobody has told me it was raised\par

A cart going south with peat — 2 bits, or a pot out of the south, whichever the reeve’s stick says\par

A gold crown offered at the Line — taken and not changed, which is a toll the coin pays by being useless\par

A man who goes south and comes back — nothing coming back; the Line has taken its eels and does not ask twice\par

\subsection*{Ditches and water}

Due\par

A ditch between two dry places — no toll; the ditch takes what the man leaves in it\par

A peat raft out into the reedbed for the dead — no fee, and no fetching back\par

Dry ground built on — borrowed; called in when the water pleases; nothing entered\par

The water under the boards — no figure; the water keeps no stick and does not say what it took\par

\subsection*{What the borrowed hands did}

The factor’s clerk writes upright and narrow and takes the man out of every sentence. Where I wrote \emph{I cut}, he set \emph{was entered} above; where I left the place for the water he put a nought and then \emph{vacancy}. He numbered the ways as three, leaving the ditch and the water out, which is the readiest way I know of counting a road without counting who walks it. I have put my words back underneath and left his above, as a board keeps both the man’s weight and the water’s mark.

The other hand is a reeve’s, and it is mine to know and not mine to name. He cut a notch through the bought-breath figure and cut it over again, so that the first shows under the second, and would not say which way he meant it. A notch cut over a notch is a correction a man can read with his thumb, which is how most things are read here.

\subsection*{The song said to the boards}

\emph{Said low at the Post while a stick is being cut, never to a man from Greybank, and never while a reeve is standing within hearing of the second verse. The last line is said to the water.}

\begin{quote}\itshape A bit for the board and a bit for the showing,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape a knot for the term and a stick for the load;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape four for the ways and a place for the wet,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the fifth is the water and takes what it wants.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape The peat goes down and the eel goes up,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the fine stands longest and is called right;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape a man comes over with dry boots and goes back wet,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the Post keeps the notch and the mud keeps the rest.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{In the factor’s narrow hand, against the fourth line of the first verse:} Four ways entered. \emph{In mine:} There are four ways and a place; a nought in that place is a figure paid, and the water has never paid. The man who sang it would not sing it facing the boards.\end{quote}

\subsection*{At the head and in the gutter}

The peat at the head is mine; I hold the reed down in the wind and do not know I have marked it. Peat goes into the grain and will not come out, which is why we sign with it. The reed-fibre in the second fold came off a wet bundle set down while a man counted his marks and went away without his change. The tide-line has taken one word off the peat row; I have not written it in again, because a row with a word gone is a row said slowly, and most of ours are. The eel-bone across the bought-breath figures was laid there by a woman who would not say why. The wet boot over the dues came off a man who stepped on the loose board while asking what the safe ones cost; he paid and would not say whether he stepped before he paid or after. The grey along the margin is not mine and not the Court’s. I have not swept it. There is no Last Day on a Post.

\subsection*{At the foot, in a hand nobody will own}

\begin{quote}\itshape The stick keeps the weight. The knot keeps the term.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape The mud keeps the man who stood longest, and none of them says what it cost.\end{quote}

I asked the eel-trader, a reeve of the Post, and a man come down from Greybank, and had three answers and no hand. I have left the line where it was written. The reed goes back into its sinew under the loose board. A man will come up and ask what his armful fetches, and I shall tell him what the arm says, and the water will take what it wants, without a figure and without a hand to write one.

\clearpage\phantomsection\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{The Stock Book of the Lower Yard, Being the Goods, Vessels and Days of a Kiln-House in Low Kiln Valued for the Clay Levy, with the Household’s Charcoal Count Set Beside and One Column Left Unfilled}
\CRsheetheading{The Stock Book of the Lower Yard, Being the Goods, Vessels and Days of a Kiln-House in Low Kiln Valued for the Clay Levy, with the Household’s Charcoal Count Set Beside and One Column Left Unfilled}
{\centering\FellFont\itshape\footnotesize\color{faded} A page from a Court assessor’s stock book; figures in Ledgerhand, terse remarks in the hand that set them, the house’s own tally in charcoal on the back of a spoiled slip-tally laid against it, two corrections in the narrow upright hand of the College, a figure scraped away, and a line at the foot nobody will own · Written in a kiln-house of the lower yard in Low Kiln, Sill, in the Thin Year Y.H. 812 at the clay levy, and carried forward at the Opening of the Slates, Ilmen 1, Y.H. 813; kept folded in the assessor’s board cover and taken down whenever a levy is disputed. It survives with iron-gall at the head, bone-pale slip worked into the gutter, a green bead of lead glaze in the lower corner, a tallow thumb against the foot, grey Ash in the outer fold, charcoal dust along the back, a pale ring where a wet pot stood, a small square of bare paper where a figure was scraped away, two corrections in the College’s narrow hand, and one line at the foot in a hand nobody will own.\par}\medskip
I value a house’s goods before I value the people under its roof. This is the milder half of the trade and I have never come to like it. The thane’s clay levy falls on pots and tile and fuel; the Court’s warmth levy falls on the vessels that made them, and a man may be counted twice in one morning without ever being asked to stand. I come down from Slate Row with a board cover under my arm, and the woman of the house sets a charcoal tally on the table for her own figures, and we do not look at one another while we work.

Twelve copper bits to a silver mark; twenty marks to a Sere crown that comes north and will not spend here. The Court books warmth in embers and calls an ember five marks, which no man has exchanged, and I have no row for embers in this book, because no ember has ever sat on a kiln-house shelf. One in twelve is printed on the notice and is the Court’s figure; it does not touch these pots, which is the mercy of the clay levy and not of the Court. A whole pot answers full under the knuckle and a cracked one flat, and neither answer is a figure, and I have kept both answers out of the column.

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{In the narrow upright hand of the College, above my second line:} Goods valued for the levy; vessels valued by the collector; the two not joined. \emph{Underneath, in mine:} They are joined in the house, by the same hands and in the same morning. I have set them on two leaves and left them side by side.\end{quote}

\subsection*{The stock, as I valued it}

\emph{Figures in Ledgerhand. The second figure is the house’s own, in charcoal, copied from the back of a slip-tally I was allowed to hold but not to keep. The remarks are mine. A dash is a place where the house set nothing, not a nought.}

Article — My figure — The house’s — Remark\par

Coarse pots, the score, green from the third firing — 4 bits — 5 bits — The fifth bit is for a pot set aside for a death-house and not sold. Not entered at the Cross.\par

Pots mended with brass, the score — 2 bits — — — A mended pot fetches less and holds as long. The house will not write the second half.\par

Tile, the hundred, stacked by the gable — 9 bits — 9 bits — The only row on this leaf that agrees. I have marked it and cannot say why.\par

Slip, the pit, worked and standing — 3 marks — 2 marks — They count the clay, I count the afternoon it took to mix. Both are honest.\par

Lead glaze, a jar, mixed up the terrace — 2 marks — — — Sweet at the mouth. The mixer would not stand still for the weighing.\par

Coal, the barrow, banked behind the damper — 5 bits — 5 bits — Stone price, not Grain. The house has kept the winter figure in summer, which is a kindness to me and a lie to itself.\par

Barley, the dressed sack, under wool at the rack end — 1 mark 4 bits — 1 mark 4 bits — Turned for damp twice while I stood there. No figure for the turning, and none asked.\par

Eels, smoked, a basket from the Fishstairs — 3 bits the eel — 3 bits — The eel-woman’s figure and mine agree, which may be the only thing in this house that does.\par

Salt herring, a barrel — 2 bits the fish — — — Barrel not counted. The barrel is the woman’s mother’s and has outlived two levies.\par

Tallow, a stone, rendered at the works — 2 marks — 2 marks — Smell carried up from the north-east on Tallow 6. The figure did not carry.\par

Peat, a stack against the north wall — 5 bits — 2 bits — She has written the Grain price in the Stone month and says the stack came cheap. I have left both.\par

Pig, alive, in the strip behind the wheel-shed — 6 marks — 6 marks — cried twice at the Cross and a bit paid to have it cried. The bit is in my own pocket and not on this leaf.\par

The well, with bucket and rope — not valued — 1 mark — I set \emph{not valued}. The house sets a mark. Water is the Court’s if it is under a town, and the house’s if a woman draws it.\par

The kiln, with lid, damper and back room — not valued — not valued — Neither of us has found a figure and neither of us has said so aloud.\par

The loaf shelf, the drying racks, the boards — not valued — — — A thing a house stands on is not a thing a house sells.\par

The ash in the corner — not valued — not valued — Left where it lay all of the dark and burnt on the morning after. Both figures stand at nothing.\par

Draws valued on this leaf: sixteen. Rows that agree: four. Rows the house left blank: five. Rows I left blank: four. The four are not the five.

\subsection*{The things that would not take a figure}

There is a charcoal mark under the front edge of the loaf shelf, made by somebody who knelt to write it and then covered it with the shelf again. I saw it because the woman moved the shelf while I was weighing the tallow and did not know I had seen. I did not ask her what it counted. A tally kept where a slate would tax it is a tally with a reason, and a reason asked after in a kiln-house gets carried up the terrace and comes back down as weather. So I have put it on no row and given it no place in the columns, and it is the one thing on this leaf that I have entered nowhere at all, which is a different thing from entering nothing.

The pot on the third row has a brass seam across its belly, set by a hand that knew the note before it set the staple. I knocked it to hear, as I knock every vessel before I value it, and it answered full, and the woman went on with her charcoal as though a pot could not speak in front of an assessor. I have written \emph{holds as long} in the remark because it is true and because she would not write it. The green ware beside it gave a small flat sound that stopped at the surface, and I set the figure down all the same. A figure is entered whether or not the thing can hold what it is said to hold. That is the whole art of this trade, and it is not a difficult art to learn.

The fifth pull of the fired coal was not supplied while I stood there. Four low pulls came up under the pot and the place where the fifth should have stood was silent, and the woman put her hand to the mark by the kiln mouth before she lifted the lid, for one breath, and at no shelf and no basket after it. I did not enter the fifth as nought. A nought is a figure and can be added; a silence cannot. There is no row on any levy sheet for the breath a woman holds before she opens a kiln, which is perhaps the most sensible thing the College has ever left out.

\subsection*{What the borrowed hands did}

The man from the College came down on a market morning while the bell was going four, four and a gap below the Cross. He did not sit down, and he took the leaf up with two fingers as though the charcoal on the back might come off on him.

Where I wrote \emph{I valued the slip, the afternoon it took to mix}, he struck out \emph{I valued} and set \emph{the slip was valued} above, and above that \emph{the valuation is entered}, which is further from the pit than the first. I have put my words back underneath. A sentence with nobody in it is a sentence a woman cannot ask about, and she will ask, always at the door, always after the board cover is shut.

Against the pot with the brass seam he struck \emph{holds as long} and wrote \emph{serviceable} above it. Both stand. \emph{Serviceable} is the word the notice uses and the word the moot reads in a clean voice; \emph{holds as long} is what I heard the pot say under my knuckle. I have not chosen between them and would thank any man who told me I must.

He struck the column of the house’s charcoal figures and wrote \emph{No such column} over it in the same upright hand he uses for one in twelve. He had counted every row before he wrote it, which is how I know the column troubled him. I drew it back underneath and left his words standing above. A man does not count what he has not looked at.

\subsection*{The song the kiln hands keep at the boards}

\emph{Sung low, going down from the terrace with a basket on the hip. Never at the Cross, and never while a man from Slate Row is on the road.}

\begin{quote}\itshape Nine on the board and eight in the rack,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape one in the ash and none coming back;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the clerk writes ink and the house writes coal,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and neither one tells what the firing cost.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Four bits the score and a mark for the pig,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the pot keeps the heat and the shelf keeps the rig;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape count what you can and leave what you can’t —\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the well has a figure, the mark has nought.\end{quote}

A woman at the drying racks sang the first two lines to me while she turned the dressed grain with the back of her hand and would not sing the last while her neighbour stood within hearing, which is how I know the last line is the one that matters. I have copied it as it came and put no gloss on it.

\subsection*{In the margins and in the gutter}

The iron-gall at the head is mine, from holding the board cover open through a morning in a room with no draught worth the name. The slip in the gutter came off a thrower’s forearms when she set her tally against mine to wait for a figure; it is bone-pale and goes into the grain of the paper and stays. The green bead in the lower corner is lead glaze and not slip; the girl who mixed it leaned over to see what her jar had fetched, with the sweetness still at one corner of her mouth, touched the leaf, said nothing and went back up the terrace. I have not washed it off. The tallow thumb against the foot is from holding the lamp low while the woman of the house answered a question I had not quite asked. The grey in the outer fold came off my own cuff, going down past a corner I had no business putting my hand into. The charcoal dust along the back is from the spoiled slip-tally laid against this leaf and is the only mark on it that was never made in this room. The pale ring in the lower margin is where a wet pot stood for a moment while I wrote; it dried and left its own small circle, which I have measured and not entered. The bare square is a figure I scraped away with a knife, which was the figure the house kept and would not have read aloud. I have not written it back. On the Last Day the ash in the corners is swept up and burnt in the morning and called dealt with. There is no Last Day for a stock book.

\subsection*{At the foot, in a hand nobody will own}

\begin{quote}\itshape The Court values what can be carried away. The house values what keeps it standing. The kiln is in both columns and in neither.\end{quote}

I asked the woman of the house, a carter who takes the steep street, the man from the College, and a girl come up from the glaze room, and had four answers and no hand. I have left the line where it was written.

The leaf goes back into the board cover and the cover under my arm. At the next levy the thane’s man will ask for the figures and I shall read him the ones the notice allows, which are the only ones that travel. The house will go on keeping its charcoal on the back of spoiled tallies, and the pot with the brass seam will go on answering full under any knuckle that cares to ask, and the fifth pull will go on standing silent with nobody to pay it. I shall set down what I can carry away, and leave the rest where it stood.

\clearpage\phantomsection\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{The Stone and the Slate, Being the Standing Rules of the Hearth-Maids of Grath for the Taking, Keeping and Trying of Girls, with the Three-Day Reckoning, the Washing-Song Pasted in the Fold, Two Corrections in Borrowed Hands, and a Line at the Foot Nobody Will Own}
\CRsheetheading{The Stone and the Slate, Being the Standing Rules of the Hearth-Maids of Grath for the Taking, Keeping and Trying of Girls, with the Three-Day Reckoning, the Washing-Song Pasted in the Fold, Two Corrections in Borrowed Hands, and a Line at the Foot Nobody Will Own}
{\centering\FellFont\itshape\footnotesize\color{faded} A folded leaf carried in the birth-cloth of a hearth-maid of Low Kiln; the rules set down in short sayings and half-sentences, the term and the faults in tables, the washing-song pasted into the fold, a narrow clerk’s corrections struck through but left standing, one line in charcoal that a woman would not sign, and a line at the foot in a hand nobody will own · Gathered among the hearth-maids of Sill before the Rising and copied forward in the fold of a grey wool birth-cloth that goes where the maids go, rather than from any book; this leaf written at Low Kiln in Ash of Y.H. 812, the Thin Year of the Long Cold, and copied forward at the Opening of the Slates into Y.H. 813. It survives soft at the fold and sour with lye, with a thumb of tallow at the stone clause, a print of grey Ash off a cuff at the head, a white bloom of dried soap in the gutter, a green bead of lead glaze at the lower corner off a girl come down from the glaze room, the press of a wet reed across the song, the small hollow where a warmed stone lay, one correction in the narrow upright hand of a clerk of Slate Row, one in the hand of a man come up from Greybank, a charcoal line struck and written again underneath, and a line at the foot nobody will own\par}\medskip
I keep the birth-slates in the fold of a grey wool cloth that goes where I go. A girl comes to me at ten with her hands already red from the tubs and asks what a maid is for, and I tell her: to be the first hand a child meets and the last hand a mother keeps. Then I set her to warming a stone. There is no lesson before that one. A girl who cannot tell when a stone has given its heat back has no business holding a child who cannot tell her anything.

These rules were gathered before any of us had names worth writing down, and are copied forward in the fold and not from a book. A rule with no thumb on it is a rule nobody has had to use. These have been used. I set them down in the words we say, short words and often half a sentence, and where a clerk has put a whole sentence in their place I have left both standing. A woman at three in the morning wants to know which hand to hold.

\subsection*{The rules as they stand in the fold}

\subsection*{Of the taking}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item A girl is taken at ten, by a maid and not by a house. She answers to the maid until she can answer for herself. A house may ask for her; a house may not keep her. We have had trouble with houses.

\item The taking is not written. What is written is the day she first held a stone for a woman in labour, in the corner of the birth-slate book where the mothers’ names leave off. There is no roll of maids. A roll is a thing a clerk can carry away in a cuff.

\item A girl is taught in sayings, not in questions. Ask her what the stone is for and she will tell you the weather. Ask her what a child is for and she will put another log on the fire. Both are answers and neither is a lie.

\item She learns to keep her own counsel before she learns to keep a child. What she sees at a birth she carries in the fold and does not set on a bench at the Cross. A thing said at the Cross is a thing entered somewhere.

\end{enumerate}

\subsection*{Of the stone}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item Warm the stone at the fire, wrap it in wool and set it to the belly, never to the feet. A stone is a stone and not a kindness. The kindness is in the hand that changes it when it goes cold in your own palm, not when the child stops crying.

\item The stone goes back to the hearth at the end, whether the child stays or not. What was lent to one bed is not spent on it. This is a rule about warmth and not about children; a woman at a bedside will not see the difference, which is why it is written down.

\end{enumerate}

\subsection*{Of the slate and the three days}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item The birth-slate lies on the bench within reach before the child is. A midwife’s hand goes to the slate before it goes to the fold. This is the order of the room, which keeps a woman from being asked twice.

\item Write the day and the given name within three days. Three days is the rule and not a shorter one. A child entered on the fourth is entered as a birth of the fourth, and the year will disagree with the mother all her life.

\item A foundling is named by whoever writes the slate. Give the name given and no house-name. A child with no house may be held by any hearth and inherited by none.

\item If the mother has no name she will own, leave the place empty. Do not put a mark there. A mark is a figure, and a figure can be read at a Weighing.

\item The book of slates is kept in the maid’s own house, under the cloth, and is not taken to Slate Row. The College asked for it in Y.H. 782 and was paid, and the book stayed where it was. They are paid to ask. We are not paid to answer.

\end{enumerate}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{In the narrow upright hand of the clerk of Slate Row, above rule 11:} The birth-slate is entered. \emph{Underneath, in mine:} I had written that I enter it. Both stand. I do not know which of us the College pays.\end{quote}

\subsection*{Of the flower}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item Some children come with a red branch across the ribs or down the arm. It is called a birth-flower. Do not wash it. Do not cover it with a word.

\item Cross two fingers at the corner of it and say nothing about the sign. If asked what it signifies, give a date. A date is an answer that does not spoil in the mouth, and the Court likes a date and does not ask what it covers. Where the mark is cut into the niche stone, give the date of the niche if you must, and give the same date a second time if asked a second way. Ask me what it means and I will tell you when it was built.

\end{enumerate}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Crossed hard in charcoal across rule 13, in a woman’s hand that did not sign:} The mark was here before the niche. The niche was here before the name. I have struck it and written it again underneath. I have not swept the charcoal and I have not put my name to it.\end{quote}

\subsection*{Of the third night}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item A child may grow worse on the third day after a return. Watch to the fourth morning. Keep warmth and quiet and a living body under the quilt, and barley water by the spoon. Do not leave her to sleep it off.

\item Call it a graft settling if the room wants a name for it. The room wants a name for everything. Both are true in the mouth that says them.

\item Do not call a collector for the worsening. It is the night’s own work and goes off by the fourth morning. If you call one, the figure is taken before the child has had her chance, and no slate in the district can give it back. Do not set a stone higher and call it a second chance. Warmth taken from a hand does not come back because you warmed the place above it.

\end{enumerate}

\subsection*{Of the collector and the Court}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item Turn the slate face down before you go to the child. The tube comes after the mother has been looked at, not before. A hand that goes to the slate before the eyes go to the bed is a hand that has forgot which room it is in.

\item When the collector comes, stand where you are standing. Do not fetch him. He has a slate already written and reads it in a soft voice, and the neighbours call it weather afterward, because there is no other word in the district for it.

\item One in twelve is printed on the notice and read twice at the Cross. We do not read it at a birth and do not correct it. There is a figure that is read and a figure that is paid, and a birth room is not where to make them agree.

\item The account is never closed. A child with no account is to be pitied, not envied, though the poor will tell you different after a bad winter. They are not wrong about the winter. On the Last Day the grey in the corner is left and burnt in the morning and called dealt with; in a birth room there is no Last Day. It is swept when there is a woman who can sweep it, and not before.

\end{enumerate}

\subsection*{The term and the roll}

\emph{Kept in the corner of the birth-slate book where the mothers’ names leave off. A day is written there and nothing else; a maid is not entered, because an entered maid is a maid who can be called back to a house she has left.}

Condition — What is written — What is kept — Discharged\par

Girl taken at ten — The day she first held a stone — The sayings, in her own mouth — When she can keep her own counsel\par

Girl who cannot write a date — The day, in another hand — The child, through the third night — Never; she is still a maid\par

Mother with no name to own — The place left empty — The day and the given name — The slate is not changed later\par

Foundling named by a collector — The name as given, no house — A coat any hearth may wear — When a hearth claims him\par

Child worse on the third day — Nothing entered as a worsening — A watch kept to the fourth morning — The fourth morning\par

The Forty gone in the levy — Nothing on the slate — Knots on grey wool, by the women — Not discharged, not explained\par

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item Seven years is the common term in the yards and not a short one. A maid serves no term. She stays while there is need and goes with nothing written down, so nobody can call her back. The knots tied on grey wool for the ones taken in the levy are not entered here and are counted by no Court thumb. A knot is kept in the hand that tied it. Ask the wool.

\end{enumerate}

\subsection*{Of faults and their correcting}

Fault — As corrected in the fold\par

A stone set to the feet — Taken off; the girl set to warming water for a tend\par

A birth entered on the fourth day — Left as the fourth day; the mother told, and not comforted\par

A mark put in an empty place — The page copied again and the place left bare\par

A flower covered with a word — Two fingers crossed; a date given; the word not written back\par

A collector called for the third-night worsening — Not entered; the watch kept to the fourth morning all the same\par

A birth-slate carried to Slate Row — Brought back; the maid’s own house named as its place\par

A verb struck out of a rule — Put back underneath, where the clerk can see it\par

A charcoal line swept away — Not swept; the line written again below\par

\subsection*{The washing-song, pasted into the fold}

\emph{Sung low at the tubs while the slates lie on the bench to dry, never at a birth and never twice in one house. The girl who is learning says the last line and the women say it with her. Nobody sings it on the Last Day.}

\begin{quote}\itshape A stone in the wool and a slate on the bench,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape a girl at the tub and a name not yet spoke;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the water goes cold and the water comes warm,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the day goes down where the ink has a place.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Hold the heat. Hold your tongue.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Three days to write and a fourth to watch;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape hold the heat. Hold your tongue.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape What comes back comes back as it can.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Cross two fingers and give a date.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Leave the place where the name would stand.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape The wool keeps warm what the slate keeps dry,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the child keeps neither, and comes back warm.\end{quote}

The press of wet reed across the middle verse came from the cloth going with a survey party down to the Weir on a day the bench stood in the rain. I have flattened it as well as I could. The words are plain under it.

\subsection*{What the borrowed hands did}

The clerk of Slate Row came with ink settled in two fingers and a cuff gone soft from washing. He struck \emph{I enter it} and set \emph{the birth-slate is entered} above, as though a birth had entered itself; he struck \emph{I set the stone} and wrote \emph{the stone is set} over it, which is always true and therefore true of nobody. I have put both verbs back under his. He put a round nought in the empty place and wrote \emph{vacancy} beside it. The place was empty before he numbered it.

The man come up from Greybank wrote \emph{a lawful keeping} over rule 18 where I had set down what the neighbours call weather. Both stand. Lawful is true and does not mention a woman on a bed with the tube already gone. I set weather down because I heard it said and there is no column for what a room says when the slate has been read.

\subsection*{At the head and in the gutter}

The grey at the head came off my cuff when I measured the ridge in a house two doors down and came back to write; it does not wash out of the creases. The sour in the fold is lye under soap, older than the leaf. The white in the gutter is dried soap bloom and is never entered. The tallow at the stone clause is mine, from holding the lamp low while a woman told me to be quick and I would not. The green bead is lead glaze and not slip: a girl with sweetness at her mouth touched the leaf and went back to her terrace without asking to read it. The hollow in the wool is where a stone lay through a third night in a house I could name and will not. There is no Last Day for a fold, and nothing here is swept and burnt and called dealt with.

\subsection*{At the foot, in a hand nobody will own}

\begin{quote}\itshape The slate keeps the day. The wool keeps the heat. The child keeps neither.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Two hands went in and one came out, and the business of a maid is the one that came out.\end{quote}

I have asked the women at the tubs, a girl come down from the glaze room, and a man come up from Slate Row, and had three answers and no hand. I have left the two lines where they were written. The leaf goes back into the fold and the cloth goes where I go. Tomorrow a girl will be brought at ten with her hands red from the tubs, and I shall set her to warming a stone before I tell her what a maid is for. The clerk may strike what he likes; he does not hold the child through the fourth morning.

\clearpage\phantomsection\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{The Sweetness in the Glaze, Being a Rat-Catcher’s Field Notes on the Lead-Rat of High Kiln and the Lead Run}
\CRsheetheading{The Sweetness in the Glaze, Being a Rat-Catcher’s Field Notes on the Lead-Rat of High Kiln and the Lead Run}
{\centering\FellFont\itshape\footnotesize\color{faded} A hunter’s field book on one beast, set down as the record of rounds and not as natural philosophy; the rounds in Grathic, the tally in charcoal on the backs of spoiled glaze-tallies, a catcher’s song as it is sung, a line in slip-white from a mixer of the Glaze Room, two rulings in the narrow upright Ledgerhand of a clerk come up from Greybank, and one line at the foot in a hand nobody will own · Written in Ember and Smoke of Y.H. 812, the Thin Year, by a rat-catcher of High Kiln who set wire in the glaze-stores and along the Lead Run and was paid by the tail; set down at the end of rounds in the store with a tallow end in a dish and the sweet edge of the glaze coming over the terrace on the wrong wind, first on spoiled glaze-tallies and then on three folds of birch bark, sewn with eel-sinew and carried in a coat pocket. Copied forward in Ilmen of Y.H. 813. It survives with a lead-blue smear ground into the head, a green stain at the corner of the second leaf where a tasting cup was set down, a press of wet slip across the first leaf, a singe at the lower corner from the tail-fire at the store door, the charcoal rubbed thin where the wrap was carried against the thigh, two rulings in the upright hand of the Greybank clerk, one line in slip-white from a mixer who would not give her name, and the one line at the foot\par}\medskip
I take rats in High Kiln and along the Lead Run, and I am paid by the tail. Two bits a score, and the tails are burnt at the store door before the mixers come up in the morning, which is a thing I have never had an answer to and have long ago stopped asking for. I set wire in the glaze-stores and along the run where the old working stains the water blue-grey and nobody in Sill will drink it twice. I write this at the end of a round with the tallow down to a knuckle and the sweet edge of the glaze coming over the terrace on the wrong wind.

The blue at the head is not ink. It is the dust off a tail I laid down before I thought, and it has gone into the fibre the way lead goes into a hand. I have not knocked it off.

\subsection*{What it goes to}

It goes to the rim. Set a crust and a glazed cup down in the same store and it will pass the crust and gnaw the cup, and it will not come back for the crust afterward. It takes the lip of a cup and the seam of a bowl where the glaze has run thin, and it leaves the food standing, which is the part that makes a house angry, because a house can bear a thing being eaten and cannot bear a thing being spoiled for nothing.

I set a dish of sour barley-water and a dish of glaze-water together on a shelf, to settle a question I had no business asking. It went to the glaze-water on three nights out of three, and on the fourth I set the dishes the other way about and it crossed the shelf to the glaze-water again. A man who keeps a book in his pocket has no call to write a cause into it; a cause is a thing somebody with a slate will want the use of.

There is nothing grand about it. It is a small grey rat with a long nose and a habit of putting its head on one side when it listens. The grey outside tells a man nothing; the blue-grey is under the nails and in the mouth, and a catcher who has once seen it will see it on a tail laid on a clean board.

\subsection*{The bite}

It does not fight a man on his feet. I have knelt within a pace of one at a store corner with my hand in the wire and it went on with its own work. But let a hand go into a nest it has chosen, or let a child sit down beside a cup it has marked, and it bites. That is the whole rule, and there is no sense in testing it twice.

It puts two small holes in the skin, no bigger than the prick of a stylus, and not much blood. I have washed eleven of these in nine years, mine and other people’s, with sour water and then with salt, and bound them with a rag torn from an apron. The holes close. That is the deceit of it. They close in a tend and a man goes back to the wheel or the room or the run and thinks nothing of it, and the hand goes on being a hand, only slower. By the end of a season the fingers have lost a little of their quickness, and by the next season a little more, and there is no wound on the hand to show anybody and no figure that can be set against it.

A girl of the Glaze Room came to me in Ember with her thumb bound in a fold of apron. She had put her hand into a stack of cups where one of these had been at the seam and had taken two holes on the thumb-side. I washed it. At the end of the tend the holes were shut and she was tasting the mix again. In Smoke she could not hold the tasting spoon steady, and she said it had been like that since the bite, and I said nothing. A mixer who cannot taste the mix does not keep the room or her mother’s table, and there was nothing I had been paid to say that would put either back.

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Written in slip-white along the rim of the second leaf, in the hand of a mixer of the Glaze Room who did not give her name:} It is the lead. The physician says it and we taste it every morning and call it our work. Do not tell me I have not seen the line at my own gum.\end{quote}

The physician at High Kiln tells a man to keep the hand warm, which is what physicians say when they have nothing else to give him. I have seen a Held man --- a man who carried more than his natural measure and could lift a glaze jar one-handed --- bitten once on the knuckle and go on working the whole season, because a Held man has a great deal to lose slowly before he notices he is losing it. A Thin household with rats in the cupboard is a household whose children go thin by degrees, and no one in it gets angry in the year it happens. No single bite matters. That is why I keep the book.

\subsection*{The song}

\emph{Sung going down the terrace to set the wire, not coming back up with the tails. The second line of the second stanza is the hearths’ line, and every catcher sings it wrong on purpose, because a song that gives the rat a reason is a song a man can carry home and set by his fire. I have set it down as it is sung, with the wrong line standing.}

\begin{quote}\itshape Three for the lip and one for the seam,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the rat comes up where the sweet has been;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape it leaves the crust and it takes the shine\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and goes back down where the blue is thin.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape They say it’s the sickness made small, with a nose\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape for the cup and a grudge against the wheel;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape I set the wire where the glaze-water goes\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and find a rat where a rat can feel.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Two bits a score and a fire at the door,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the ash goes down with the wash to the run;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape count the tails and count the wire,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and leave one count for the hand that won’t close.\end{quote}

The last line is the gap where the thumb should have shut on the tasting spoon. A mixer at the Room sings it twice and has never said why, and I have let her keep it.

\subsection*{The tally}

These are the rounds I kept a true account of. There were others I did not write because my hands were full and one I did not write because I had drunk. I have set down both sorts as they stand. The last column is the clerk’s, not mine. I counted tails; he entered stock.

Round — Place — Wire set — Tails — Cups chewed — Bitten — Entered\par

Ember 4 — Glaze-store, upper terrace — ten — nine — three — none — 0\par

Ember 11 — The run, below the old working — twelve — eleven — none — none — 0\par

Ember 19 — Store door, after the wrong wind — ten — fourteen — six — one, a mixer — 0\par

Ember 27 — Bowl-store, south wall — twelve — eight — two — none — 0\par

Smoke 6 — The run, wash-water outlet — ten — twelve — none — one, myself — 0\par

Smoke 17 — Glaze-store, under the racks — twelve — nine — four — none — nil\par

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{In the narrow upright hand of a clerk come up from Greybank, written along the margin:} Rats not a vessel. Petty damage to glaze stock: no deduction arises. Tails: enter as 20 to the score. Persons bitten: not entered. Account stands.\end{quote}

I have left his hand standing. He has put \emph{20 to the score} over nine and eleven and fourteen, which is a true figure for a score and a false one for a night’s work, and he has put \emph{nil} against my hand and the mixer’s thumb with a neat instrument and no name on either. There is no deduction against glaze stock, so far as his column goes, and the cups went on being glazed and the house went on being a house. I have written what his column cannot reach below it, in charcoal where he did not look.

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Below, in my hand:} Two hands, gone slow. No entry arises. I have put the size of the holes in the margin of the second leaf where the slip-white is.\end{quote}

\subsection*{The tails}

They pay two bits a score and count the tails themselves before they pay, which is a thing no rat-catcher would object to if the counting were done where he could see it. The tails go into a fire kept burning at the store door, and the ash goes down with the wash-water to the run when the floor is sluiced. I have watched that done every time I have carried a score up and have never once asked why. A man who asks is told it is the custom, and a custom with no reason in it is an account with no payer, and I have had enough of those without bringing one home in my own trade.

There is no other use for the beast. The hide is too thin to sell and too small to burn for anything. A Fen man asked me once for the bodies, and I told him I had burnt them with the tails, which was not true, but a man who has been asked for the bodies once will be asked for them twice, and I did not want to find out what he wanted them for. I have set that down and will not explain it further.

\subsection*{What the hearths say}

They say it is the sweet-sickness made small enough to run on four legs, a punishment sent to the glaze-houses for the taste of the mix at the rim. There are songs for it on the terrace with a woman’s name in them and a wrong done at a wheel. I have heard them and I have no quarrel with a song. I have opened a score of these in nine years and found a rat each time, and a rat that went looking for the sweet and found it where the glaze had been laid. I have put no cause beside that, because I am paid by the tail and not for causes.

There was a paper in the Glaze Room dated Y.H. 641, folded small, with a hand on it that had set down the lead and the glaze and the rats in three short lines. I read it one Smoke while a mixer held the door. The paper was soft at the fold and she used it next morning to wrap a pot, and I saw it go out with the broken ware at the end of the tend. I have not seen another like it in nine years, and when I asked an older man at Stonemouth about the year he said he had heard the figure and had never seen the paper, which may both be true. A thing can be known in this country and then not known, and the knowing does not leave a mark on anything that can be counted. I have set the year down because I read it, and I have not set down the three lines, because I did not copy them and will not pretend to remember what I did not keep.

\subsection*{At the head and in the margins}

The lead-blue at the head is mine. The green at the corner of the second leaf is off a tasting cup a mixer set down while she was reading the slip-white, and I have not scraped it, because it is the only thing on that leaf that came from the room the thumb belonged to. The press of wet slip across the first leaf came off the morning I set the book down on the rack board before the boards had dried, and it has stiffened the fibre so that the second leaf will not lie flat. The singe at the lower corner is from the tail-fire, taken while I held the leaf too near to read in the dark; the hand that pulled it back was mine and is not entered. The charcoal is thin where I carried the wrap against my hip. The clerk’s two rulings I have not touched. The slip-white line is fading and will be gone by the next Smoke, and the song is as they sang it, with the wrong line standing and the last line left where the gap was.

\subsection*{At the foot, in a hand nobody will own}

\begin{quote}\itshape It takes the sweetness and leaves the dull cup. Ask the lip which one was chewed.\end{quote}

I asked the miller at High Kiln, a mixer who would not give her name, and a clerk who had come up from Greybank to count the glaze stock, and had three answerings and no hand. I have left the line where it was written.

There is an old store beyond the wash-water outlet where no glaze has been mixed in a great many years and the cups on the shelf have gone dull with handling. The wire I set there last Smoke came up with four tails and not one chewed cup among them. I cannot explain what the rats were doing in a store with nothing sweet in it, and I have set that down as I found it, with the verb standing and no figure at the end of the row. Next Ember I will take fresh wire and a dish of glaze-water and a dish of sour water and set them out in that store where no glaze has been, and if the rats come to the dish with no sweetness in it I will set that down too, in charcoal, in my own hand, and let the clerk take what figure he can out of it.

\clearpage\phantomsection\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{The Tallow-Wife’s Book, Being Remedies for the Vat-Scald, the Sweet Smoke, the Wool-Cough, the Nest-Sting, a Cut from a Vat-Shard, Milk That Will Not Come, the Birth-Flower and the Third-Night Chill, Set Down in the Fat-House with the Errors Left Standing}
\CRsheetheading{The Tallow-Wife’s Book, Being Remedies for the Vat-Scald, the Sweet Smoke, the Wool-Cough, the Nest-Sting, a Cut from a Vat-Shard, Milk That Will Not Come, the Birth-Flower and the Third-Night Chill, Set Down in the Fat-House with the Errors Left Standing}
{\centering\FellFont\itshape\footnotesize\color{faded} A tallow-wife’s and midwife’s book of remedies in the short fat-house speech, written in Grathic letters so a girl of Low Kiln might read it, with the smell of the rendering left in the words; the cures in a renderer’s hand on the back of a spoiled fat-tally, the objections of a physician come down from Greybank pressed brown into the margin, the corrections of a factor’s clerk in narrow upright Ledgerhand, a watchman’s line in charcoal at the foot of the remedies, a pouring-song with the fourth cup left standing under the bench, and one line at the foot in a hand nobody will own · Written at the Tallow Works, two leagues north-east of Sill, between Tallow of Y.H. 812 and Ilmen of Y.H. 813, the Thin Year and the Long Cold, by Mella of the Works, a renderer of sheep fat who caught the children of the lamp-women and dressed the hands of the shed for nine-and-twenty years; begun on the back of a fat-tally spoiled when a spill of hot fat took the figures, folded into oiled sacking, tied with a hemp wick and carried in the breast of a wool apron against a square of birth-cloth washed thin, and copied at Greybank in Ilmen of Y.H. 813 onto the back of a voided weigh-slip. It survives with a thumb of raw tallow worked into the grain at the head, a grey bloom of sour fat along the fold which has taken two words clean off the second leaf, a singe where the flue drew a spark out of the fire onto the third, a wick trimmed to a fingernail caught in the seam, a brown crust spot at the second fold, a flat square of grey wasp-paper pressed into the lower corner, a small round mark where a buyer set a mark-piece down and took it up again, a grey Ash print along the outer fold nobody will own, objections in the cold margin hand of the physician, corrections in the upright hand of the factor’s clerk, the watchman’s charcoal at the remedies, and the one line at the foot\par}\medskip
I render sheep fat and have caught the children of the lamp-women for nine-and-twenty years. Nobody asked me for this book. A girl came in off the ridge road in the lean week with her sleeve stuck to her forearm and asked what I did for the vat, and I heard myself answer in my mother’s short way of speaking, and did not know whether I believed it. A cure you can only say in your mother’s voice is a cure nobody has looked at in a long while. I have looked at some of mine. The rest I have left standing, because a woman at three in the morning wants a hand more than a correction.

I write on the back of a fat-tally a spill of hot fat took clean. The figures went into the lamps and burned, which is where the Works sends everything it cannot read. The brown at the head is mine and has gone into the fibre; the ink beads where my thumb was, and a leaf that smells of rendering is a leaf nobody borrows twice. The fourth cup goes under the bench and has no figure; I have made no lesson of it.

\subsection*{The order of the fat-house}

\emph{Written small on the first leaf, with one word gone over in sour fat.}

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item Set the slate face down before you go to a child. I have no slate-name and never shall; a hand that writes before it looks has chosen already.

\item Keep the north door latched but not held. A woman watched from the door holds her breath, and a held breath is a poor thing to bring a child on.

\item Try the stone on your own wrist before it goes to a belly. It came off somebody’s fire; somebody paid for the coals.

\item Lay nothing warm side up on the vat ledge. A stone with its warm side up takes from the room, which is spending already.

\item Do not set a red branch under the sluice. Cross two fingers over it and say the word the mother gives. Sluice-water carries the ash of burnt nests, and I have not tried it on one of these and will not.

\item When the third night comes, count with her. Do not count for her. The fourth cup is under the bench and is not a count.

\item If a man comes up the ridge road with a cold tube and a slate, give him the mother and keep the child behind the vat. This is not refusal. It is the order of the room.

\end{itemize}

An old lamp-woman asked why I turn the slate before I look and gave me a date instead of an answer. A date does not spoil; I have put it in the margin and left the question standing.

\subsection*{The remedies, as they are used}

Trouble — What is set to it — The manner of it — Who pays\par

The vat-scald (a sleeve stuck to the forearm) — Fat from the same vat, then a clean fold — The fat runs at a heat no water reaches and takes the skin when it cools. We put the same fat back, believing a sweet answers a sweet and draws. A physician come down from Greybank says fat seals and water comes first. I have dressed three forearms and the white line stayed in two. — The forearm; the household that bought the fat.\par

The sweet smoke (the headache off the flue) — A wet cloth at the mouth; the head out the north door — The flue draws from the second hour and the sweet smoke goes over the ridge into Sill on a north wind; a woman in the low houses tastes it in her pottage. The physician says the flue wants mending, which no shed can afford in the lean week. I sent two down the ridge for air; both came back with the headache. — The lamp-room, which cannot stop and does not ask.\par

The wool-cough — Steam under a cloth; a spoon of rendered fat in it — We say the fat of the sheep makes a lining for its dust. The physician says it is wool and bone-dust in the lung, and the only physic is to leave the shed, which no household here can do. I sent three down to Sill; two came back worse. — The woman, in the morning she coughs up a colour she will not discuss.\par

The nest-sting (a hand into the warm crack) — A warmed stone in wool; stillness; nothing at the swelling — The tallow-wasp hangs its grey paper in the seam where wall meets flue, and a hand that goes in after the second hour comes out with a swelling that has no head to it. We say a knife lets out what is holding. The watchman says do not open it, for a knife lets out the little that was holding. A lamp-woman sat a whole night with a boy’s hand on a warmed stone and he came back by morning. I set that down because it happened, not because the stone did it. — The hand. Nobody has told us what the nest keeps.\par

A cut from a vat-shard — Tallow first, then a clean fold; never the grey from the nest-fire — The women put grey from the nest-fire in a cut to dry it, believing the ash of a burnt thing is clean. I have dressed three such and found grey under the skin in all three. — The hand.\par

Milk that will not come — Another woman to hold the child while the mother sleeps; a spoon of fat in the pottage — We say a fattened woman makes milk, and the fat is spent out of somebody else’s lamp. The physician says fat makes no milk and that the favour is paid out of the other woman’s own house. I gave the spoon to six and stopped at the third child who cried over a dry breast. — The other woman’s child, first.\par

The birth-flower (the red branch) — Nothing. Two fingers crossed at the corner, and the word the mother gives — A woman of Cold Acre crossed two fingers over one of ours and gave me a date. A woman of Low Kiln washed one with sluice-water and her child went flat by evening; I have not joined the two. — Nobody knows. The child’s skin, perhaps.\par

The third-night chill — Warmth, barley-water, a watch to the fourth morning — It comes after the warming, not before. A hearth-maid from Low Kiln says a warmed body spends faster and the child should be held and counted with. I have walked nine and held four; all saw the fourth morning, and one went thin. I have left the count unadded, for a count added is a count a clerk can carry. — The household, one night’s sleep; sometimes the child.\par

Nothing at these works is given away. It is poured from one vessel into another and called a cure. That is the only sentence I will stand behind.

\subsection*{The note under the knuckle}

The lamp-women tap a clay lamp before pouring and know by the note whether it will hold a flame. Sound answers full; cracked answers flat, a small dead sound at the lip. It is the one thing here that costs nothing and is still true, and no factor has entered it.

I tapped a woman once, gone thin after a thin return, and put my ear to the little flat I thought I heard. The flat was not in her. A body is not a lamp, though we pour fat into lamps in the shape of cups. I did not say so with a soft-cuffed man in the door. I have written it here, which is a different matter.

The watchman says the warm crack gives back a note when a bare crock is set against it, and that he has caught nothing with fat where there was no warmth and a full crock where there was no fat. I have left his sayings where he put them. A sheep has no slate and no return, and the flue runs from the second hour.

\subsection*{The fourth cup}

At the turning of the year we pour three cups and set the fourth under the bench, with a heel-tap and no word. A man from the factor’s house at Greybank stood in the door with his cuff soft from washing and asked what we did with the fourth. He wrote \emph{on the floor} and went away satisfied, which is how I knew he had written the wrong thing. A thing written down is a thing a man can carry off in a cuff; a thing under a bench wants a man on his knees, which no clerk has ever done here. The fourth is a place and stays.

\subsection*{The pouring-song}

\emph{Sung low at the vats while the fat is still running, to the flame and not to the women. There is a fourth place in the last verse the length of a cup going under a bench, and no singer has put a figure in it.}

\begin{quote}\itshape Three for the vats and one for the flue,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape one for the nest in the warm crack;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the fat runs light and the wick runs short\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the fourth goes under the bench.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape A sound cup answers, a cracked cup flat,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape a sheep goes down and gives no name;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the hand goes in and the grey comes out\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the ash goes down the sluice.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Warm the middle and wrap the end,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape count with her, do not count for her;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the red branch keeps what the water takes\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the child comes back as it can.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Three I counted and one held out ---\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the fourth goes down where the bench keeps.\end{quote}

A factor’s clerk put a round nought in the fourth place and wrote \emph{no cup entered} beneath it. A nought is a figure and can be carried away; the fourth is a place and stays. I changed one line in nine-and-twenty years: \emph{the hand goes in and the grey comes out} was \emph{the fat goes in and the flame comes out}, and the women singing with me did not notice.

\subsection*{What the physician pressed in the margin}

He came down from Greybank in Ilmen of Y.H. 812 with \emph{fumes} underlined in his book and a hand that wrote without asking. Against the vat-scald he set \emph{fat seals; water first}; against the sweet smoke, \emph{mend the vent}; against the birth-flower, \emph{a mark in the blood}. He was right in all three and had nothing a renderer could pay for: the vent wants a mason, and four marks a nest is refused at the shed door. Where I wrote \emph{we push the warmth back}, he set \emph{no such transmission}. I have put the warmth underneath.

\subsection*{What the factor’s clerk did}

He borrowed the leaf at Greybank when the winter fat was counted, ink in two fingers of a soft cuff. He struck out my column headed \emph{Who pays} and wrote \emph{No cost to the house}, true in a counting room and false in a shed where a woman’s sleeve has stuck to her arm. Against \emph{four marks a nest refused} he wrote \emph{no value arising}, the same refusal in a cleaner hand. Where the notice says one in twelve he wrote \emph{the deduction is constant}. Where I wrote \emph{the flue takes from the room and gives it to the wind}, he wrote \emph{the measure is retained in the smoke}, taking the hands out as though a flue could carry itself. I have put my verbs back underneath. A clerk can write without verbs because he has never stood in the draught that comes up under a rendering pot.

\subsection*{In the margin, in charcoal, the watchman’s hand}

\begin{quote}\itshape I have taken four hundred nests and the sting comes only out of the warm crack. A man from the coast offered four marks for one paper and the factor refused him the same four at our door. Ask the factor which country holds the heat.\end{quote}

He wrote it while I was at the vats and set the leaf back with the fold changed. A man who has taken four hundred nests is allowed one sentence in a book of physic; I have set his line above mine.

\subsection*{At the head and in the gutter}

The tallow at the head came off my thumb setting the leaf on the vat ledge in the draught and has gone into the grain, so the book smells of the shed in any room. The grey bloom came up out of the paper itself and took two words clean off the second leaf; I have not written them back, because a remedy with two words gone is a remedy said slowly. The singe is a spark the flue drew while I wrote; the hand that beat it out was mine and is not entered. The wick in the seam was trimmed to a fingernail by a lamp-woman who leaned to see. The brown spot is a crust off a loaf set down while a girl would not eat. The grey paper in the corner came off a nest a girl carried in; she said nothing and I did not ask. The round mark is a buyer’s; he set his mark-piece down and took it up again. The grey along the outer fold is not mine and not the Court’s; I have not swept it. There is no Last Day in a lamp-room. The nests go on the fire at the shed door by the factor’s order and the ash goes down the sluice, and still there is a nest in the warm crack by the second hour.

\subsection*{At the foot, in a hand nobody will own}

\begin{quote}\itshape The fat keeps the warmth and calls it given.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape The bench keeps the cup and calls it poured.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape The child between the flue and the door is warm or is not, and neither column asks.\end{quote}

I asked the physician, the factor’s clerk and the man who keeps the nests, and had three answers and no hand. Tomorrow a girl will come down the ridge road with her sleeve stuck to her arm or a child that will not breathe, and I shall turn the slate face down, try the stone on my own wrist, set the fourth cup under the bench and put my verbs back --- because a child is not a cup and a woman at three in the morning wants a hand more than a remedy.

\clearpage\phantomsection\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{The Articles of the Tenth Clamp, Being the Standing Rules of the Order of the Tenth Clamp Beneath Keld Keep for the Taking, Cutting and Trying of Apprentices at the First Way, with the Table of Hands, the Iron-Song Pasted Inside the Cover, and the Master’s Corrections}
\CRsheetheading{The Articles of the Tenth Clamp, Being the Standing Rules of the Order of the Tenth Clamp Beneath Keld Keep for the Taking, Cutting and Trying of Apprentices at the First Way, with the Table of Hands, the Iron-Song Pasted Inside the Cover, and the Master’s Corrections}
{\centering\FellFont\itshape\footnotesize\color{faded} A board-copy of the Order’s standing rules in the hand of the under-master who keeps the irons and the roll of hands at the mouth of the Duelling Floor; the articles cut in short Keldish clauses, the tables in number-first order, the iron-song in the hard Rim speech pasted inside the cover, two corrections in the narrow upright hand of a Court survey-clerk, one line struck in coal by the master of the floor, one objection in the leaning hand of a leech come up from the Ninth Gallery, and a line at the foot in a hand nobody will own · First gathered beneath Keld Keep in Y.H. 747, the year the Cold Pass was shut and the border fixed by men who had never walked it, and copied forward each generation from the iron board beside the clamps rather than from paper, which is why the rule about the rope-coloured hand is worn through at the corner and the rule about the nail is as sharp as the day it was cut; this leaf written in Bone of Y.H. 812, the Thin Year of the Long Cold, by Vek of the Tenth Clamp, the under-master who keeps the irons, and carried down the Rim Road in Ilmen of Y.H. 813 with a survey party bound for Greybank, where it was copied onto the back of a spoiled tally-roll. It survives with coal dust ground into the head off the master’s sleeve, a smear of hot lead at the fold where a passing was measured two hours early, iron filings caught in the gutter from the clamps on the floor, a scorch where a lamp-spark took the corner of the second leaf, a thumb of tallow, a ring of frost raised out of the paper on the climb over the Cold Pass, a splinter of warm-stone sewn into the board cover which keeps the whole leaf a little warm, one correction in the narrow upright hand of the Court, one line struck hard in coal by the master, one objection written twice and struck twice by a leech from the Ninth Gallery, and a grey Ash print along the outer fold that nobody will own\par}\medskip
I keep the irons. Nine clamps lie on the board at the mouth of the floor and the tenth hangs on its nail behind me, and has hung there since before I came down. A boy asks which is the tenth and is told: the one that goes to the stone. He asks what it does there. Nobody answers him twice, because the answer is a number and he will have it soon enough.

These articles were first gathered beneath the Keep in Y.H. 747, and have been copied forward from the board and not from paper. An article nobody has had to use is an article nobody believes. These have been used. Where a hand has corrected me I have left both readings, because a floor with one hand on it is a floor with one man in it.

\subsection*{The articles as they stand on the board}

\subsection*{Of the taking}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item The Order takes a boy at thirteen, on the day of the Descent, and not before and not after. A house gives him up for a day and has him back by dusk with a number, which may be the number it sent and often is not. The house does not ask for the old one back. The floor has never given one back.

\item Number first, then the name. The clerk writes the figure before he has heard who the boy is, and if the boy gives his name first he is asked again. This is not pride. A name is a thing a man can change at a moot; a number is cut into the bone and stays when the skin is corrected around it.

\item No boy is asked whether he wants the way. He is asked whether he understands what is bought: a cut across a surface way in the forearm, held open while it scars, a fortnight in which the arm is of no use, and a mark that will not close while he lives. The master cuts. The wanting comes after, or it does not come; the Order has never claimed to teach that part and has never stopped charging for it.

\item A lowlander may be taken if he states a measure before a name and keeps his face while it is checked. No master now living has taken one, and no master’s master either, which is three generations and not a rule. The article stands because a rule forbidding a thing has to be read aloud every time the thing arrives, and the floor has better uses for a morning.

\end{enumerate}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{In the coal-pressed hand of the master of the floor, against article 2:} Number first. Then the name. Everyone in Keld knows this. \emph{Underneath, in mine:} I had written that the figure goes first so that a boy cannot change it with a smile. The master has struck the smile. There is no smile in this room after the first cut, so the rule is for the morning before, when a boy still thinks a face will do instead of a figure. I have left both.\end{quote}

\subsection*{Of the cut}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item The way is opened across a surface way in the forearm and kept open while it scars. The master cuts it. No boy cuts his own and no boy cuts another’s; a way made by a friend is a way two men must answer for, and this floor has room for one answer.

\item The arm is useless for a fortnight. On the fifteenth day the boy is given a clamp to hold. A boy who cannot hold it is given the keys instead, which is the kindness the Keep shows to men who cannot descend, and is not a kindness. He will keep the keys all his days and will know what they open and will never open it.

\item Cold iron is set to draw the heat out of a cut that will not settle. The iron takes as well as it draws. A master who tells a boy the iron only draws is selling him the fortnight twice, and the boy finds it out in the sixth week when his fingers go the colour of skimmed milk gone off and he cannot feel the clamp he is holding.

\item A way once cut is never closed. Men have closed them with grafts and with salt and with the long cold beyond the Pass, and the way comes back in the season when the stone sweats, and aches before the thaw and after it. A boy who says his arm aches is told the weather will have the last word. A boy who says it twice is given a warm-stone out of somebody’s fire, which is theft from an account the boy did not open and is entered nowhere.

\end{enumerate}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{In the leaning hand of a leech come up from the Ninth Gallery, against article 7:} The hand comes back on the sixth day or not at all. Do not set the clamp again higher up and call it a second chance. \emph{In mine, underneath:} I have set his line above the rule where the master can see it. He struck it out twice in the winter and wrote it again both times, which is how a leech argues with a floor.\end{quote}

\subsection*{Of the floor}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item Nine clamps go to the floor and one goes to the stone. The tenth hangs behind the board and is not taken down. A master who takes it down must answer to the Warden’s roll for the answer, and the Warden’s roll asks its questions in a voice nobody down here has learned.

\item A clamp is set across a way, never across a bone. A man who clamps a bone has stopped nothing and broken something, and the something does not grow back.

\item The first man to open a way usually wins, because the other is busy bleeding. This is not a trick and is not taught as one. It is the whole of what the floor is for, and a boy who learns it as a trick will use it on a man who has already lost, and will not know why he won.

\item A hand that goes the colour of old rope below a clamp is left alone. The clamp comes off; the hand is wrapped; nobody sets the iron again above the place where it failed. A man who has lost the use of a hand is still a man with a number, and the number stands whether the hand lifts a cup or not.

\item Hot iron is put to the palm when the roll wants to know whether a man is honest. The honest come back with a hand gone dead. We have had a great many honest men under this Keep and not one of them lied, and nine in ten of them cannot lift a cup. No man is put to the iron for a question the roll has already answered.

\end{enumerate}

\subsection*{The table of hands}

\emph{Kept by the clerk at the mouth of the floor. A number is written before a name, and where the number has been changed the second is set beside the first without a mark, which is the only honest thing a clerk can do.}

Condition — What is entered — What gathers — Discharged\par

Boy at the Descent — the number, before the name — a mark in the forearm — on the fifteenth day, if the arm answers\par

Boy whose number changes — the second number, no mark beside it — nothing entered — never; both numbers stand\par

Boy who cannot hold a clamp — the keys — a hand that does not close — never\par

Man gone cold in a season — the number in the floor’s roll — grey at the fingertips — not discharged\par

Lowlander taken — measure, then name — the master’s answer — as for a Keldish boy\par

The tenth clamp — the nail — nothing — never\par

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item The roll is kept under the board and a Court clerk may read it but may not change the order of the two entries. Last winter one of them set a name above a number and wrote \emph{the vessel was re-entered} in the margin, which is a true sentence in a language nobody on this floor speaks. I have put the number back above it. A name can be entered in a second column; a number cannot, because it is already in the arm.

\end{enumerate}

\subsection*{Of faults and their correcting}

Fault — As corrected on the floor\par

Name before number — Asked again; the number set above\par

A verb in the roll — Struck by the Court’s hand; set back underneath by mine\par

A clamp set on bone — Taken off; the boy set to counting irons for a tend\par

A way opened by a second boy — Left to heal as it can; both boys lose the fortnight\par

A hand gone rope-coloured — The clamp removed; no second chance above it\par

The tenth clamp taken down — The master’s own number entered against it\par

A question about what comes up through the stone — Answered once: the numbers are correct\par

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item The last row is not a punishment and is not a rule about clamps. It is the only answer the floor has for the stone, and a boy who asks a second time is told to ask the Vorr, who will say it once in a voice like a man using a tool he has no use for, and will say it twice: the numbers are correct.

\end{enumerate}

\subsection*{The iron-song, pasted inside the cover}

\emph{Sung on the fifteenth day, in the room off the floor, with the clamp laid on the table and not in the hand. Nobody sings it on the stone and nobody sings it at the Descent. The boy whose fortnight is out says the middle verse, and nobody says his name.}

\begin{quote}\itshape Nine on the board and one on the nail,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the tenth is kept for the stone;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape count the irons, count the head,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and give the number, then the name.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape One cut across the living way,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape a mark to keep and a fortnight’s cold;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the iron takes what the iron draws,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the boy pays before the floor.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Four to the arm and a fifth gone wrong,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the hand goes rope and the rope stays put;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape do not set it higher and call it a chance,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape for a number stands and a hand does not.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Nine on the board and one on the nail,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the tenth is kept for the stone;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the master cleans what the master cut,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the boy says his number, then his name.\end{quote}

\subsection*{What the borrowed hands did}

A survey-clerk of the Court borrowed the leaf when the survey table sat at the Keep, ink settled in two fingers of his soft cuff. He struck \emph{the arm is useless for a fortnight} and set above it \emph{the vessel was clamped}, which is a thing always true and therefore true of every boy who ever came down. Against the nail he put a round nought and wrote \emph{vacancy} beside it. I have put the nail back. A nail is a place and a place is not a number; he has spent his whole trade putting figures where places stood, and has never once been thanked for it.

The master of the floor struck the word \emph{taught} out of article 3 and wrote above it \emph{that will hold. Don’t make me say it twice.} I have left \emph{taught} underneath, because a boy should be able to see the word the master would not let stand. He cleaned his clamp while he did it and did not look at me.

The leech’s objection has been struck twice and written twice; I have set the second above the first. A nail, a nought, a hand, a number: four things on one leaf, and no man has joined them.

\subsection*{At the head and in the gutter}

The coal at the head came off the master’s sleeve when he leaned to read the third verse standing and would not sit down; he said a song that had never been in a mine was not worth the paper. The hot lead at the fold came off a cuff on the day a passing was measured two hours early and we all went up faster than we had any right to; it has burnt one word of the fifth article clean through and I have not written the word back in. The filings in the gutter are off the clamps on the floor. The scorch on the second leaf is a spark that caught while I was writing and went out under my hand; the hand was mine and I have not entered the burn. The tallow thumb is mine, from holding the sheet down in the draught that comes up the shaft. The frost on the third leaf came up out of the paper on the climb over the Cold Pass and is the only thing in this book that entered itself. The splinter sewn into the cover is warm-stone from the Ninth, and is why the leaf is a little warm in the morning; somebody paid for that warmth and his name is not in here. The grey along the outer fold is not mine and not the Court’s, and I have not swept it. In the clay country they leave the ash in the corners on the Last Day, burn it in the morning and call it dealt with. Under the Keep the dust has nowhere to go.

\subsection*{At the foot, in a hand nobody will own}

\begin{quote}\itshape The floor keeps the number. The stone keeps the hand. Nobody keeps the boy who gave both.\end{quote}
