I have asked the master, the clerk who keeps the numbers and the leech come up from the Ninth Gallery, and had three answers and no hand, as I have had before. I have left the line where it was written. The leaf goes back under the iron board and the tenth clamp goes back on its nail. Tomorrow a boy will be brought down at thirteen and will give his number before his name, and the master will clean the clamp while he asks the second question, and whatever he answers will be entered in the same neat hand as the boys who stayed warm. The nine will go out on the board and the tenth will stay where it has hung every morning since before I came down.

\clearpage\phantomsection\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{The Third Brazier, Being a Measure-Night at the Shaft Head in Keld Keep, with Five Questions Put Down the Hole, the Sixth Written by the Mine-Reeve and Not Scored, the Coals Laid Down and Not Taken Up, a Survey-Clerk’s Figures Over Them, and a Line at the Foot Nobody Will Own}
\CRsheetheading{The Third Brazier, Being a Measure-Night at the Shaft Head in Keld Keep, with Five Questions Put Down the Hole, the Sixth Written by the Mine-Reeve and Not Scored, the Coals Laid Down and Not Taken Up, a Survey-Clerk’s Figures Over Them, and a Line at the Foot Nobody Will Own}
{\centering\FellFont\itshape\footnotesize\color{faded} A brazier-keeper’s record of a cold-month contest, set down for the settling of an argument about a coal nobody claimed and not for the improvement of the reader; the manner of the room in the hand that keeps it, the questions in the words they were put down the shaft, the answers as they were said into the mouth of it, four coals counted by the flat of a thumb, the mine-reeve’s red cross and the survey-clerk’s narrow figures set above, a boy’s charcoal in the margin, and one line at the foot in a hand nobody will own · Written in Stone of Y.H. 812, the year the lowlands call the Thin Year, in the warm-room at the head of the shaft in Keld Keep, by the woman who tends the third brazier and counts the coals that go into it; set down first in charcoal on the back of a spoiled rim-seam rubbing and copied forward in Ilmen of Y.H. 813, when the Rim Road opened, onto the reverse of a Court survey-sheet voided by wet slate and carried up from Greybank, where a survey-clerk of the factor borrowed the leaves and set his figures above hers. It survives folded in oiled survey-cloth and sewn with wire, kept under the third brazier where nothing else in this room is kept: coal smut ground into the head off the hand that counts, slate dust in the gutter, a warm-stone shaving shut in the fold that has gone colder than the ledge, a bead of Ninth Gallery lead nobody claimed, a frost-feather along the lower edge gone by noon, a red thumb at the fold which the mine-reeve left when he set his slate down, a line of charcoal in a boy’s hand, grey Ash along the outer fold which the writer did not put there and has not swept, one correction in narrow upright Ledgerhand, and a line at the foot which has never been claimed\par}\medskip
I keep the third brazier at the head of the shaft and count what goes into it. There are three braziers in this room. The first went out in the Long Cold and the second was emptied to feed it, and the third has not gone out since, which is a thing people say of the Hearth-fire and never of a room, though the room is nearer to most of us. In Stone the cold comes up the shaft and lies on the floor like water, and there is nothing to do of an evening but put questions down the hole and wait for what comes back.

The questions go down and the answers are said into the mouth of the shaft, not to the person beside you. In Keld a man states his measure before his name, and in this room he states it twice, once to the reeve’s book and once to the cold, because the cold will not be told who he is and will take the number anyway. A riddle here is a number with the person left out, which is the sort of sentence the mine-reeve writes all day and the sort no man will own at night.

I have set this down because a surveyor came the next morning and asked whose coal was lying on the ledge, and I could not tell him. Four coals were laid down and three taken up, and the fourth lay where it had been put with nobody’s name on it, which is a thing a room ought to be able to explain. I have written the night as it was said and left the red cross where the reeve set it.

\subsection*{The manner of a measure-night}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item A question is put to the shaft and not to the man beside you. Put to a man it becomes a demand, and a demand in Keld is a thing with a figure on it and no face.

\item State your number before your name, and answer in one breath, and give the number first. A man who names the thing before he has counted it has not answered; he has introduced it.

\item Four are cut on the ledge. A fifth may be put from the floor and is not cut, being a thing said by the room to itself. A sixth may be written, and is not scored at all, because a thing written has already been carried somewhere.

\item The judge is the room. I say whether an answer serves and I do not say why. A reason given is a question given away for nothing, and the giver can carry it down the Rim Road and sell it at the next post.

\item A coal is laid on the ledge before the first question and taken up by the one who serves. Coals are counted by the flat of the thumb and not by the eye, because the eye reads the face and the thumb does not.

\item No slate lies on the floor while the questions are going down. If a slate comes in, the guessing stops for that night, because a thing entered is not a question any more; it is a figure with the warmth taken out of it. I have known this to fail once and would not say so before the mine-reeve.

\end{enumerate}

\subsection*{The four that were cut}

The first went to a surveyor come down from the Stones with grey seam-dust in the creases of his thumb.

\begin{quote}\itshape I am said before the face is said;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape I go into the dark and do not come up with the man;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape I am checked once in red and there is no second asking.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape What am I?\end{quote}

“My number,” he said. Then, because he had been taught the order: “Thirty-nine. Then my name, if the room wants it.” The room did not want it. I gave him the coal. He held it in his palm and looked at it as though it were a figure he had not been entered for.

The second went to a man come up from the Ninth Gallery, with the smell of hot lead still in the fold of his coat.

\begin{quote}\itshape I am cut out of the deep where the rock sweats;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape what I hold was paid for in another district;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape I am sold and never lent, and a man going up without one\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape borrows from the next man who has one.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape What am I?\end{quote}

“Warm-stone,” he said, and put his hand on the piece in his own pocket, which is how a man answers when the answer is keeping something warm for him. A boy at the fire asked who had paid for it. The man said the mountain had. The boy said the mountain kept no account in this room. Nobody scored the boy’s question, because it came from the floor and not from the ledge.

The third went to a man with two sets of numbers cut into his forearm, one over the other.

\begin{quote}\itshape I am cut at thirteen and cut out again if the man comes back thin;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the later cut lies deeper and the earlier stays in the skin;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape nobody asks which count is his.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape What am I?\end{quote}

“The numbers,” he said, and held out the arm without being asked, which is not a thing men do here. He said the later set was the one the reeve had entered and the earlier was the one he had gone down with. “They are both mine,” he said. “The reeve keeps the later and the skin keeps both.” I scored him and set the coal on the ledge before him. He did not take it up, and I have not moved it since.

The fourth went to a carter who had been through the pass twice.

\begin{quote}\itshape There is a post and no gate;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape a count stops there and the road does not;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the surveyor does not promise to bring the man back.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape What am I?\end{quote}

“The Cold Pass,” the carter said. “A post and no more.” He said the second going through was not the same as the first, though the post stood where it stood and the figure at it was nothing either time. There was an argument about whether nothing is a price or the absence of one. I stopped it by touching the ledge, because there is no winning an argument about a post that has no gate.

\subsection*{The fifth, which the room put to itself}

\begin{quote}\itshape I go into the brazier and am gone by morning;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the reeve counts me and my giver does not;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape I warm a man who does not say where I came from.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape What am I?\end{quote}

An old woman who washes bodies at the Keep said “a coal,” and said it to the shaft and not to the room. She said she had washed a man that week who had gone down at eleven months and come back in his fourteenth, and that the reeve had entered him at eleven and the three besides had gone nowhere at all. “That’s the one I was warming,” she said, and set her hands back in her lap. There was no coal to give her, being the room’s own question, and nobody offered her one, which is the custom here and not a kindness.

\subsection*{The sixth, which was written and not said}

At the end the mine-reeve came in from his room with a narrow slate under his arm and set it on the ledge, which stopped the night as a door would not. He had come to check the coals and stayed to ask a thing of his own. He did not put it to the shaft. He wrote it down, which is his manner, and read it out in a flat voice.

“Entered at eleven months. Lived fourteen. What is the figure?”

Nobody answered. It was not a riddle, and the room knew it; a riddle has the person left out, and this one had the man left in. The woman who washes bodies said, “There is no figure. There is eleven and there is three, and the three are not entered.” The reeve set his red cross against her words on the slate and wrote \emph{measure correctly entered; no second asking}. He did not look at her while he wrote, which is how a man writes a thing he has heard before.

“I wasn’t asking,” she said.

He said, “Then nothing arises,” and took the slate away, and the fourth coal lay where it lay.

\subsection*{The tally, cut on the ledge}

Question — Put by — Answer given — Coal\par

The number — the shaft — my number; thirty-nine — one, taken up\par

The stone — the shaft — warm-stone — one, taken up\par

The two cuts — the shaft — the numbers — one, not taken up\par

The post — the shaft — the Cold Pass — one, taken up\par

The coal — the room — a coal — not cut\par

The man entered at eleven — the mine-reeve — no figure served — not cut; marked in red\par

\subsection*{What the survey-clerk did}

A survey-clerk of the factor at Greybank borrowed the leaves on the morning the winter coal went down the Rim Road. He writes narrow and upright and takes the doer out of every sentence, which is easier than carrying him up five leagues of scree. Against \emph{my number} he set \emph{measure declared, current}. At \emph{what I hold was paid for in another district} he wrote \emph{source not ascertained}, which leaves the district standing and takes the somebody away. Against \emph{nobody asks which count is his} he put \emph{two entries; later controls}. At the sixth he wrote \emph{no riddle tendered; struck}, which is true in a counting room and false on this floor: the sixth was not a riddle and was not struck, and the woman said so to the slate and not to him.

I have put what was said under what was written and left his hand standing, the way a later cut lies over an earlier one in the skin and does not take the earlier out.

\subsection*{In the margin, in a boy’s charcoal}

A boy of twelve who has not yet Descended borrowed the leaf while I was turning it. He wrote in the charcoal we mark hands with, slowly, with the ends of the words left in the air:

\begin{quote}\itshape At thirteen they will cut mine in.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape I want to know which way to hold the arm.\end{quote}

I have not answered him and I have not rubbed it out. In a year’s turning he will go down and come back with a number, and nobody will ask him what he wanted to know at twelve, which is the whole of the Descent in this keep.

\subsection*{At the head and in the gutter}

The smut at the head is mine; I held the leaf down on the ledge with the hand I count coals with and did not know I had marked it. It goes into the grain and no wet sleeve takes it out, which is why this room keeps its figures on slate and its stories on paper nobody wants. The warm-stone shaving in the fold came off the second man’s piece when he set it down to answer and took it up again warm-side inward; it is colder now than the ledge and I have kept it where it fell. The lead bead rolled out of someone’s cuff and has lain in the gutter since; the rock sweats it and the smell gives what warning it gives, and nobody has claimed the bead. The frost along the lower edge came up out of the paper on the carry from the reeve’s room and is gone by noon, which is the only thing in this keep that goes. The red thumb at the fold is the mine-reeve’s; he set his slate down on the leaf before he wrote and did not wipe his hand. The grey along the outer fold is not mine and not the clerk’s. I have not swept it. There is no Last Day at the head of a shaft, and nothing here is burnt in the morning and called dealt with.

\subsection*{At the foot, in a hand nobody will own}

\begin{quote}\itshape The coal keeps nothing. The slate keeps the eleven.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape The skin keeps both counts and does not enter either.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape The mountain keeps what goes down and calls it a figure.\end{quote}

I asked the surveyor, the woman who washes bodies and the carter, and had three answers and no hand. I have left the lines where they were written. The leaf goes back into the oiled cloth under the third brazier, and the fourth coal goes back on the ledge where nobody has taken it, and in the morning the reeve will come for the count and find four coals given and three received and will write the difference in red. The shaft will go on breathing cold onto the floor, and I shall set questions down into it as I have set them every Stone since the second brazier went out, and if a man asks me what this room is named for I shall tell him: for the one that is still burning, and not for the two that are not.

\clearpage\phantomsection\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{The Third Saying, Being a Mother’s Lullaby of Reedholt in the East Marsh, Sung to a Child Three Nights Old on the Boards the Night Before the Hearth Drawing; with the Reed-Name Said Three Times into the Ground, the Knot of Grey Wool, the Board That Is Lent, the Fifth Place Left Unscored, a Factor’s Clerk’s Correction in Ledgerhand, and One Line at the Foot in a Hand Nobody Will Own}
\CRsheetheading{The Third Saying, Being a Mother’s Lullaby of Reedholt in the East Marsh, Sung to a Child Three Nights Old on the Boards the Night Before the Hearth Drawing; with the Reed-Name Said Three Times into the Ground, the Knot of Grey Wool, the Board That Is Lent, the Fifth Place Left Unscored, a Factor’s Clerk’s Correction in Ledgerhand, and One Line at the Foot in a Hand Nobody Will Own}
{\centering\FellFont\itshape\footnotesize\color{faded} A mother’s lullaby in Fen Cant, the thick half-sung English of the east marsh, set down in Grathic letters learned off an eel-trader out of Sill; said through the nose and low, with the last word let fall into the mud under the boards and not finished, the name said three times and never written, the word that will not come into Grathic tied as a knot of grey wool in the margin, the fifth place left unscored; a factor’s clerk’s correction standing above in narrow upright Ledgerhand, a woman of the peat-dry in charcoal underneath, and one line at the foot in a hand nobody will claim · Sung at Reedholt in the east marsh on the night before the Hearth Drawing, Stone 12 of Y.H. 812, the Thin Year after the Long Cold, by a woman of the peat-dry to her child three nights old; set down in charcoal and peat-water on the back of a peat-tally spoiled by a wetting, sewn with eel-sinew into a fold of oiled reed, tied with grey wool and kept in a dry tin slung under the hut boards; carried up the marsh road in Ilmen of Y.H. 813 and copied at Greybank onto the back of a factor’s voided weigh-slip, where a clerk set his hand above hers. It survives with a brown peat thumb worked into the head, a bog-water tideline that has taken two words off the second leaf, a press of wet sedge across the third, a thread of grey wool laid in the fold where the fifth verse should stand, a small round pale place where a collector’s cuff was laid at the drawing and nobody will own the cuff, a scratch from a reed-wolf’s tooth at the corner, a small-ale ring gone dark at the foot, the clerk’s correction above, the peat-dry woman’s charcoal underneath, and one line at the foot that has never come forward\par}\medskip
I sing this on the boards at Reedholt, to a child three nights old, in the hut my mother’s mother set on a hummock so the water could take the ground back without taking the house. Tomorrow is the Hearth Drawing, and a collector comes up the marsh road with a tube, a slate and a cuff folded back twice. He may draw from the dying and the newly born on the same day, which the Court calls thorough and we call the road being short. Before he reaches the boards I must have said the child’s name three times into the ground under my feet. After that he may have what he comes for. A number is a hole in the wall; a name is a door. I mean to leave him the wall and keep the door.

A lullaby here is not a comfort. It is a piece of work, like layering a peat-stack, and it is done before daylight because a man with a dry cuff will come into a wet room. Such a man stood at the peat-dry in Ilmen and asked what the women sang to their children before a drawing, and wrote the answer while I was still saying it, with the doing taken out and a figure standing where a place should stand. I have left his hand where he put it and put mine underneath, the way the boards keep both the foot that went over them and the water that came up through them.

Fen Cant is not written. It is said through the nose, slow, with the last word dropped into the mud and not finished; what must be kept is cut in a stick or tied in a knot. I learned my letters off an eel-trader who could tally but could not read what he wrote. The brown at the head is peat, not Ash; there is Ash enough in this marsh without bringing it in on my thumb. I held the tally down in a wind off the black peat and did not know I had marked it. Peat goes into the grain and no washing takes it out, which is why we sign with it here.

\subsection*{The manner of it}

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item Said through the nose, slow, to the child and to the boards. The last word of every verse is let fall into the mud under the boards and is not finished. Said up at the sky it is a prayer, and there is no prayer in this marsh that has not been entered against somebody. Said across at a man it is an argument, and we have enough arguments without carrying one up the marsh road.

\item The name is said three times: once to the ear, once to the ground under the boards, and once for the part of the child that cannot yet hear and will be the last to forget. If there is a fourth saying, it belongs to the man with the slate and not to this house. We have never made a fourth.

\item Where a word will not come into Grathic I have tied a knot of grey wool in the margin and written nothing. A knot keeps and a word on paper travels. A factor’s clerk entered our knots as \emph{nil}, because a knot is not a figure. He was right. That is why we keep them.

\item Do not sing it standing on dry ground. Every dry place among us is a loan from the water and the water calls it in when it pleases. A song said on borrowed ground goes back with the loan, and the singer is left with a mouth full of nothing.

\item One verse for the board, one for the name, one for the peat, one for the cold that comes with the iron, and one for what the mud keeps. There is a sixth place and it is not scored and not stepped. Where the sixth should stand I have laid a thread of grey wool in the fold. The clerk has written against it, and his word is a figure and mine is a place.

\item Stop before dawn on the Drawing. A song said while a number is being read aloud becomes part of the number, and after that no mother in Reedholt can get it back.

\end{itemize}

\subsection*{The song}

\emph{Said low, sitting, with the hand on the board and not on the child. Through the nose. The last word of each part goes down into the mud.}

The refrain, as the boards keep it after every part:

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Hush. The board bears and the water lends.}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Say it three times to the ground where the name descends.}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{What will not write we tie and leave tied.}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{The dark keeps warm what the day has denied.}\end{quote}

\subsection*{I. Of the board}

\begin{quote}\itshape You were laid on a board before you were laid on a bed;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the board is a loan and the water calls it when it will.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape We do not ask it to carry us, only to keep\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the shape of a foot for the length of one step.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Hush. This board has borne worse than you and said nothing.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Hush. The board bears and the water lends.}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Say it three times to the ground where the name descends.}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{What will not write we tie and leave tied.}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{The dark keeps warm what the day has denied.}\end{quote}

\subsection*{II. Of the name}

\begin{quote}\itshape I gave you the word before the man with the slate came up the road.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Three times into the ground under my feet I put it down:\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape once to your ear, once to the mud, once to the you\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape that cannot hear yet and will be the last to forget.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape If he comes before the third he will give you a figure.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Keep the word. A figure is a hole and a name is a door.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Hush. The board bears and the water lends.}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Say it three times to the ground where the name descends.}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{What will not write we tie and leave tied.}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{The dark keeps warm what the day has denied.}\end{quote}

\subsection*{III. Of the peat}

\begin{quote}\itshape The dark under the black peat is warmer than this room;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the Marsh Mother holds it and hands it back\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape to whoever asks, which here means whoever digs.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape She has no keys, keeps no slate, and asks no figure;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape no man in a clean coat opens her for a fee.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape A coal out of her was paid for by somebody’s back.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Hush. Keep your hand on the pot and not on the flame.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Hush. The board bears and the water lends.}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Say it three times to the ground where the name descends.}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{What will not write we tie and leave tied.}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{The dark keeps warm what the day has denied.}\end{quote}

\subsection*{IV. Of the cold iron}

\begin{quote}\itshape There is a pale round place on a man’s arm\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape that shows through the winter and was not there in Ember.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape The iron takes and the mud takes;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape one of them writes it down and one of them does not.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape When the cuff comes to the hut at dawn, let it find the number.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Let it find the number and go away with it.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape A word that goes up the marsh road does not come back the same.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Hush. The board bears and the water lends.}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Say it three times to the ground where the name descends.}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{What will not write we tie and leave tied.}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{The dark keeps warm what the day has denied.}\end{quote}

\subsection*{V. Of what the mud keeps}

\begin{quote}\itshape What goes into the mud is kept; we do not fetch it back.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape A body goes out on a raft into the reedbed\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the water keeps the account and sends no figure.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape You are three nights old and already owe nothing,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape which is the only thing in this house that owes nothing.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Lie still. The debt will find you soon enough without our help.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Hush. The board bears and the water lends.}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Say it three times to the ground where the name descends.}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{What will not write we tie and leave tied.}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{The dark keeps warm what the day has denied.}\end{quote}

\subsection*{VI. The place that is not a verse}

\emph{Here a thread of grey wool lies in the fold where the sixth part should stand. There are no words to the sixth place. The hand goes to the thread and not to the child, and the refrain goes round once more with the wool under the thumb.}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{In the narrow upright hand, against the thread:} nil; vacancy; no entry lies against an unentered place.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape *\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Underneath, in mine:} A nought is a figure and can be carried up the road in a cuff. The thread is a place and stays where it was tied. I have not moved it and will not.\end{quote}

The child was asleep before I came to the sixth place. That is how I know the sixth is not for him but for the woman who sings, who has stood in this hut through four drawings and kept a word behind every time, and has never once been asked what she kept. I have laid the thread there for her.

\subsection*{What the factor’s clerk did}

He borrowed the leaf on the morning of the drawing, with a cuff gone soft from washing, and gave it back dry in one corner and damnable everywhere else. He writes narrow and upright and takes the verbs out as though a verb were a thing a man could smuggle past a weigh in the seam of a cuff. I have left his hand standing above and put mine back underneath.

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item At \emph{the board is a loan and the water calls it when it will} he wrote \emph{tenure conditional; ground tenure not established}. True to a man who has never stood on a board, and false to the child who will learn to walk on one. Mine stands below his.

\item At \emph{three times into the ground under my feet I put it down} he wrote \emph{designation declared; three readings witnessed}. There was no witness but the mud and the child, and the child could not speak, and the mud has never given evidence to a Court.

\item At \emph{the Marsh Mother holds it and hands it back} he wrote \emph{peat retains measure; draw requires officer}. Right about the peat, and he has left out the hands, which is the whole art of that sentence.

\item At \emph{the cuff comes to the hut at dawn} he wrote \emph{collection effected; no gift arises}. He was there. He knows what was taken and he knows it was not given, and he has written the one and called it both.

\item Where the thread lies he put a round nought and wrote \emph{vacancy; no claim lies}. I have left it. A knot is not a figure, which is what makes it worth tying.

\end{itemize}

\subsection*{What the woman of the peat-dry put underneath}

The charcoal belongs to a woman who has caught children on these boards for twenty-one years and laid out the drowned of the drained cuts. She presses hard at the ends of words and will not read them over. I have copied them where she set them.

\begin{quote}\itshape At \emph{once to the ear, once to the mud}: I have said a name into the ground under these boards for every child this hut has held, and only two of them came up speaking. I have never known whether the mud kept the other two or whether they kept themselves. Do not ask me which is the kinder answer.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape At \emph{keep the word}: In the year of the Long Cold a man came before the third saying and gave a number to a child of mine. The child answered to both from that day, and turned its face when the clean voice used the one that was not ours. A number is not a hole in the wall to a child. It is a second mouth in the room.\end{quote}

\subsection*{At the head and in the gutter}

The peat at the head came up out of the paper itself and is the only thing on this leaf that entered without a hand. The tideline has taken two words clean off the second leaf and I have not written them in again, because a lullaby with two words gone is a lullaby said slowly, which is how all of ours are said. The sedge across the third came off the bundle I set down when the child took its hand from the wool. The pale round place in the margin is where the collector laid his cuff while I found the fifth verse; it has gone the colour of the floor and I have not swept it. The scratch came off a reed-wolf that put its tooth into the dry while I reached for the tin, then went off without a word, which is more than the men from Greybank manage. The ring at the foot is small ale, set down at the first part and taken up at the last, by which time it had gone the colour of the boards it stood on. There is no Last Day kept at a peat-dry and nothing here is gathered and bottled and called dealt with. The thread lies in the fold and I have not lifted it.

\subsection*{At the foot, in a hand nobody will own}

\begin{quote}\itshape A man is a board laid across water. The water does not owe the board anything.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape What the mud keeps it keeps without a figure, and it will not give the figure back.\end{quote}

I asked the woman who catches children, an eel-trader come up from Sill, and a man who has been drawn twice and answers to both numbers, and had three answers and no hand. I have left the lines where they were written.

The leaf goes back into the tin and the tin under the boards. In the morning the collector will come up the marsh road, put his hand to the slate before his eyes go to the child, and go away believing he keeps the world alight by carrying off what is already going. I shall say the word three times and stop before dawn. The boards will keep the shape of where I sat, the thread the place where no verse stands, and the water will go on calling in the dry ground in its own time.

\clearpage\phantomsection\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{The Three That Stand, Being a Letter from a Peat-Dry at the Edge of the Quiet Acre to a Reeve of the Standing Post, Concerning a Year of a Child’s Breath Bought at Greybank, the Twelve Knots, the Peat That Did Not Take This Winter, and the Name Said into the Ground; with the Answer in the Margin, a Factor’s Clerk’s Correction in Ledgerhand, and a Song Said to the Ground}
\CRsheetheading{The Three That Stand, Being a Letter from a Peat-Dry at the Edge of the Quiet Acre to a Reeve of the Standing Post, Concerning a Year of a Child’s Breath Bought at Greybank, the Twelve Knots, the Peat That Did Not Take This Winter, and the Name Said into the Ground; with the Answer in the Margin, a Factor’s Clerk’s Correction in Ledgerhand, and a Song Said to the Ground}
{\centering\FellFont\itshape\footnotesize\color{faded} A private letter on the back of a peat-dry rent-tally spoiled by a factor’s man writing a figure on it, written in charcoal thinned with peat-water, folded four times and tied with grey wool to a knot-stick; carried up the marsh road in an eel-trader’s creel in the last tend of Stone, answered along the margin at the Standing Post in Ilmen, borrowed at Greybank where a factor’s clerk set a correction in Ledgerhand, and kept since under the Post’s loose board among the reeves’ sticks · Written at a peat-dry two boardwalks short of the Quiet Acre in the Fenmarch on Stone 22, Y.H. 812, the Thin Year, by Tess of the Dry, who keeps the cuttings and learned her Grathic letters off a man come to take a receipt, to Dill Peat, a reeve of the Standing Post chosen by standing in the last feud, who is her sister; carried up the marsh road after the ice went off the cuts, answered in the margin in Ilmen of Y.H. 813 after the child came back, borrowed at Greybank where a factor’s clerk corrected the leaf on the back, and kept since under the loose board at the Post. It survives tied to its stick of twelve notches, with a thumb of wet peat worked into the grain at the head, a bog-water tideline along the gutter that has taken two words clean away, a pressed bog-myrtle leaf in the second fold, a smear of eel slime at the outer crease, a grey Ash print nobody will own, a scorched corner where the leaf lay near the peat fire, salt bloom at the foot from a cuff that had been in the pans, the twelve knots still on the stick, and a curl of grey wool through the tie-hole which the writer will not untie. The clerk’s correction stands above the words and the verbs stand underneath it, and one line at the foot is in a hand nobody has claimed\par}\medskip
To Dill Peat at the Standing Post, who was chosen by standing and has never once said what the mud said to her. From Tess of the Dry, at the edge of the Quiet Acre, in the last tend of Stone, Y.H. 812, the winter the peat did not take.

I write on the back of the tally the factor’s man spoiled with his figure, and I have thinned the charcoal with peat-water so that it will bite. Do not rub the fold. It is wet through at the second crease and will come apart between your fingers. I learned my letters off a man come to take a receipt, so that I should know what I was signing when he set the slate in front of me. I know enough to write to you and not enough to trust what I write. If any of it reaches you with the verbs gone, know that I put them in.

The stick goes with the man. Twelve knots in grey wool, as I tied them on the ninth of Ilmen when he took her, and nine of them untied, one at the going of each month I could bear to count. Three stand: the last of the cold, the Five, and the coming-back. He says the term runs to the thaw. In his book the thaw is a figure. Here it is a place where the water comes up over the lower boards and the eels go upriver, and a place cannot be counted off on a stick.

I said the name into the ground before he put his hand on her, three times, into the clay beside the hut, with her own mouth too young to help. It is a reed-name and we do not cut it. They gave her another in the south, and the buyer’s man wrote it on the back of his slate and asked me to say it after him so that he could hear he had written it right. I said it. A woman who has just sold a year of her child’s breath will say almost anything to a man with a slate. I have not repeated it since and I will not write it here. A written name travels where the child does not.

\subsection*{The knots, as I tied them and as he entered them}

Knot — What I did with it — What the factor’s man wrote against it — What stands here\par

The first, tied at the buying — Untied at the going of the first month, with my own hand — Consideration paid — A month bought and a month paid.\par

The second through the ninth — Untied one at the going of each month, saying nothing — Term current; no claim lies — Eight months paid, and the child thinner each time a knot came off.\par

The tenth — Left standing when the cuttings stood full of water and there was nothing to sell — The measure is drawn as provided — A month I cannot sell back.\par

The eleventh and twelfth — Stand as they were tied — Vacancy — The Five, and the coming-back.\par

He paid in a crown and a sack of grain. The grain went damp between Greybank and the Line and we ate it anyway, and the crown will not change at the Post or anywhere north of the water. I have it under the third board from the fire, where a coin lies that nobody can spend. A thing you cannot spend is a thing somebody has already paid for, which is a true saying here and has never once failed me. When I asked him what a year of her cost beyond the crown he said the account stood. I have never heard a man say \emph{stood} with so much weather in his cuff.

The peat did not take this winter. We cut and we turned and the water came up in the cuttings and stood there, brown and flat, and the stacks did not dry behind the hut. Up in Grath they call this the Long Cold and give it a name in a book. Here we have no name for a winter except this one. A dry with nothing dry has nothing to sell, and a woman with nothing to sell cannot buy back a month of her child. I lie face down in the peat the way the old women do and ask the ground to keep what it has and hand back what it can. It keeps. It does not hand back. Or it hands back slowly, which is the same thing to a woman standing in water to her calf.

\subsection*{The song, said to the ground}

\emph{Said through the nose, slow, with the last word left to fall into the mud. Never said looking at a person. I have set it down as it was said to me and not as it would be written.}

\begin{quote}\itshape The bog keeps what the bog was lent,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the dry is a loan and not a gift;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape twelve in the wool and nine undone,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and three that stand where the water is.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape A crown lies cold beneath the board;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the grain went damp on the Greybank road;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape a child comes back as the child went,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape or thinner, and answering to another name.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Say it down, say it down to the clay,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape three times for the ones who cannot say;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape what the ground keeps, it keeps for good,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and what it hands back comes back as its own.\end{quote}

I have three questions and they are not the same question said three times. First: can a term be bought back before the thaw by a woman with nothing dry to sell, or is the figure in his book the only figure there is? Second: is a clay-name a door shut, or a door with a dirty hand on it; and when she comes back, must I ask what she answers to before I say the reed-name, or after? Third: the third knot came off in Seed and she was thinner in the wrist when I saw her at the Line in Frost. Is thinness a thing a buyer pays for and a mother keeps, or is it weather? Do not put the answers on the front where a clerk can read them alongside the figure. Put them where you write to the ground.

Stand where you stand, sister. I will stand where I stood.

\subsection*{In the margin, in a slow hand set close to the lines}

It was the eighth of Ilmen, not the ninth. You tied the first knot a day late and he wrote the term from the day he paid, not the day he took, so there is a day in this that belongs to nobody. I have struck the ninth through and put the eighth underneath in your own charcoal, so that you cannot say a stranger wrote it.

I asked his man at the Post. He said the term runs to the thaw and the thaw is entered. I said a thaw is a place. He said a place is entered as nil and went back to his tea. You cannot buy back a month with wet peat. A bought breath has a price at the buying and another price at the coming back, and the second is never written, which is why he will not name it. Bring your eels to the Post in Ilmen and I will stand with you. Standing is what I am for.

Say our name after, not before. A child who has had a name put into her mouth by a man with a slate will say that one first, because it is the one that has been fed. Let her say it. Then say ours three times into the ground beside her, not at her and not to her, so that she can hear it without being made to answer. If she answers to it we have her back. If she does not, we have her back anyway and will say it again another day.

She came back on Ilmen 16 to the dry, thin, with his name in her mouth and ours somewhere under it. I said our word three times into the water below the Post. She turned her head toward the sound a breath after the third saying. I have set that down as a thing I saw and not a thing I know, and I have not put it beside the weather.

Thinness is not weather. It is what was paid and not entered. Keep the crown. It will not change, and that is the only honesty it has. Untie the twelfth when she stands on the board at the Post, and not before. A knot untied early is a debt denied, and a debt denied is a debt with a man’s name in it.

\subsection*{What the factor’s clerk did}

A clerk out of Greybank borrowed the leaf on the morning the eel-trader came down, being a man who cannot leave paper alone. He writes in the narrow upright hand, with the verbs taken out and everything in the passive. Against \emph{a year of her breath} he set \emph{term, one year, consideration discharged}, and the breath went out of the sentence as though a breath were a thing a man could carry in a cuff. Against \emph{the peat did not take} he wrote \emph{seasonal shortfall; no claim lies}. Against the twelve knots he set \emph{twelve; nil}, and in the fifth place he put a round nought and wrote \emph{vacancy}, where my sister’s hand had been. Against the name said into the ground he wrote \emph{name not entered}, which is true in a room with a slate in it. Against \emph{she turned her head a breath after} he set \emph{reflex, not a figure}.

He can enter the shortfall and the nil and the reflex, because all of those have a place in his book. He cannot enter the hand that left the tenth knot standing in the wet or the three sayings into the water, and he has not tried. I have put my verbs back underneath and left his hand standing above, as a board keeps both the man’s weight and the water’s mark. He has numbered the coming-back, which is a place. A nought is a number. The coming-back is not.

\subsection*{At the head and in the gutter}

The peat at the head is mine, wet from holding the tally down on the cutting, and it has gone into the grain so that the whole leaf smells of a wet winter. The tideline is bog-water and has taken two words off the second verse; I have not written them in again, because a saying with two words gone is a saying said slowly, and everything here is said slowly. The bog-myrtle came from the fold where I keep a sprig against the smell of the cuttings, and has pressed flat and kept its green. The eel slime at the outer crease came off the man who carried the stick; he set it down while I was tying the wool and did not wipe his hand. The grey along the gutter came off a cuff laid where no cuff has business lying. Nobody will own it and there is no Last Day under a loose board. The scorched corner is where the leaf slipped against the peat fire while I was writing the questions. The salt at the foot is not mine; it came up out of the factor’s man’s cuff when he set the tally down on the bench, and it comes and goes with the weather. The knot through the hole is mine, tied for the word I could not write. I will not untie it.

\subsection*{At the foot, in a hand nobody will own}

\begin{quote}\itshape The board keeps the foot and the water keeps the board;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the knot keeps the month and the clerk keeps the nil;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape say it down three times and the mud will know,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the name that comes up is the name that went down.\end{quote}

I asked a reeve at the Post, a man who trades eels down the marsh road, and a man who reads the figure at Greybank, and had three answers and no hand. I have left the line where it was written. The leaf goes back under the loose board with the stick of twelve notches, and in the spring the young will cut their bundles in the dark and come back wet or dry, and we shall say it to the ground as before. Three knots stand and I have not laid a hand on them. I have tied another knot for the word I could not put down, and I will not untie it.

\clearpage\phantomsection\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{The Tide Keeps the Count, Being the Salt-Pan Children’s Skipping Game at Vhal, with the Counting-Out, the Twelve Bits, the Turn of the Rope, the Half That Is Not a Share, and What the Council Clerk Made of It}
\CRsheetheading{The Tide Keeps the Count, Being the Salt-Pan Children’s Skipping Game at Vhal, with the Counting-Out, the Twelve Bits, the Turn of the Rope, the Half That Is Not a Share, and What the Council Clerk Made of It}
{\centering\FellFont\itshape\footnotesize\color{faded} A salt-pan children’s rope-skipping game in the Vhaleni speech, set down in Grathic letters on salt-paper the writer keeps dry against the practice of the country; the counting-out and the verse in the children’s own half-sung voices, the manner of the play in a pan-woman’s small hand, a correction in the leaning hand of a Council clerk, a note in a dipper’s charcoal, and a line at the foot in a hand nobody will own · Set down at the Salt Pans outside Vhal on the Sallow coast in the last tend of Ember, Y.H. 812, the Thin Year, by Venna of the Pans, a woman who keeps the drying frames and learned her letters off a tally-man come down to weigh a rack of salt; written on the back of a tide-sheet spoiled by a figure put on it in the rain, and kept dry in a tarred tin lined with rushes, because a wet document is no document by the Council’s own law. It survives with a white salt crust along the gutter, a tar thumb at the head, a fibre of wet net-cord pressed into the second fold that goes soft when the weather goes soft, a green bead of Cliffs glass, a brine-gull’s peck through one word of the verse, a fish-hook nick, a ring eaten through by red wine, a wet corner where two lines have gone void and the space left standing, a grey Ash print nobody will own, one correction in the leaning hand of a Council clerk, a note in a dipper’s charcoal, and one line at the foot in a hand nobody has claimed\par}\medskip
I keep the drying frames at the third pan from the shore road, where the crust will bear a foot until the water comes over it. A Council clerk came down in the last tend of Ember with a slate and asked what the children counted when they jumped. I told him they counted the tide. He asked what figure the tide came to. I told him it came to nothing, which is the truth, and he went back up the coast pass and sent me a man with a better slate.

What follows is what the children said before the man came, and what they said again after he had gone back up the road. I have put his hand above mine where he set it and the children’s words underneath, as the pan keeps the salt and the water keeps the mark the salt made.

They play on the hard white crust above the high-water line, from the going of the flood until the crust goes soft under a foot. They do not play when the Sallow is over the second step of the tally-house. The rope is an old net-cord a dipper has given over, tarred once and gone soft in the hand; a child whose people are off the boats uses a twist of eel-grass, which is meaner to the ankle and counts the same. The children say a rope must have been in the water, because a rope that has never been wet does not know which way the tide goes.

The counter is chosen by the counting-out. She holds the ends of the cord and says the words to the rope and not to the children. Said to a child it becomes an argument, and there is always a child who will argue.

\subsection*{The counting-out}

\emph{Right fists held out, knuckles up. The child who says it points at each fist in turn and does not look at the faces. The fist it lights on at the last word keeps the cord and turns the rope through. She does not jump first. She is the one who has to be fair, which the children accept as a punishment and the pans accept as practice.}

\begin{quote}\itshape Bit in the palm and bit in the shoe,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the dipper reads flood and the gull reads ebb;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape a mark for the mother and half for the man,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the last one named turns the rope through.\end{quote}

\emph{Say it to the cord. A cord that has been in the water tells your hands which way to turn; a child tells you nothing you can use.}

\subsection*{The verse, as it is jumped}

\emph{One line, one jump. Twelve bits make a mark, as the tally-man says. On the twelfth line the counter shuts her fist on the mark and keeps it there; a mark shut in a fist is a mark no slate can take. Then the cord is turned the other way. That is the turn of the tide, and the same twelve lines are said backward, one jump each, coming back to where they began. The Sallow runs against the wind and the dippers say it follows the Warm and not the moon; the children say the cord follows the hand that holds it. A child who jumps the ebb right has brought the count back to the pan it came from. The counter opens her fist and the salt that was in it has gone, which the Council calls a virtue and the children call the tide.}

\begin{quote}\itshape One for the crust that will bear a foot,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape two for the net that comes up wet;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape three for the green we get off the Cliffs,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape four for the coal the gull has got;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Five for the bench that rows seven years,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape six for the wine with salt on the rim;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape seven for the share that goes down the mother,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape eight for the word that is counted at half;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Nine for the pan where the water comes in,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape ten for the step where it turns and goes;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape eleven for the slate they keep in the house,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape twelve for the mark that goes into the fist.\end{quote}

\subsection*{The half that is not a share}

A child whose father came aboard jumps at the half. She goes on one foot and says \emph{half} under her breath on every line, and the others allow it, because half is what he brought and half is what this house has always given her. She does not get to shut the mark in her fist at the twelfth; the mark is a whole thing and she has not got a whole one. She stands aside at the turn and comes in again on the ebb, which is the only tide that ever brought anything back to this coast. If she argues, they tell her the boat was here before her word, which is a hard saying to a child and a true one.

\subsection*{The gull’s edge}

A child who puts a foot wrong goes to the gull. The gull is the far edge of the pan, where the salt is too thin to bear a weight; the child sits there and watches the others jump. She is brought back by three bits of salt put into her open hand, one after another, with nothing said. A child sent to the gull is brought back by the salt and not by a name, because a name called across the pans travels and comes back with a figure on it. This is the children’s own law and I have never once known them to break it. They stop when the crust goes soft or a dipper tells them off the pan, and the last thing said is always the bringing-back, never the count. A child left sitting at the gull’s edge when they stop is not counted as having played, which is a kindness the Council would not understand.

\subsection*{The verse they do not say while a man from the Council is on the Quay}

\emph{I have it from the child who keeps the cord, with the space left before it. She would not say it to the clerk and would not say it with him in hearing. She said it to the crust with her back turned and made me put it down as I have it, with none of my verbs in it.}

\begin{quote}\itshape The draw takes the Warm and the tax takes the draw,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the rain takes the paper and calls it the law;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the pan keeps the salt and the tide keeps the count,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the boat comes back on the water it spent.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape One for the half that is not a share,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape two for the mark that is not a debt;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape say it to the crust and jump it through,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and no man in a clean cuff knows what it cost.\end{quote}

\subsection*{What the clerk did}

A clerk of the Council borrowed the sheet on the morning he came down, being a man who cannot leave paper alone. He writes in the leaning hand they use in the Council room, where it smells of tar and wet rope, and the ink sits in two fingers of his cuff and will not come out. He numbered the twelve lines in the margin. At \emph{the mark that goes into the fist} he wrote above, \emph{the measure is retained by the counter and not entered}. At \emph{the tide takes it} he wrote \emph{instrument void by exposure to water; no value attaches}, and underneath, \emph{no claim can lie against a lost mark, which is fortunate for all parties}. Against the half he set \emph{the fractional interest is rated at one half and does not constitute a share}. At the foot of the count he put a round nought and wrote \emph{nil} against it, where the children’s game ends with salt in an open hand.

I have put their words back underneath and left his standing above. He takes the verbs out because a thing always true has no need of them. I put them back because a child up to her ankle in the salt of the pan does not know she is jumping something always true, and wants to know which foot to lift. A nought is a number. The half is a place at the table. The fist is not a bank. He has put a figure where a place should be, which is the whole art of that hand.

He asked me what the children learned by it. I told him the count and the turn and the bringing-back, and he said it was the whole doctrine of returns taught before a child could hold a slate, and he entered it. The children stop jumping when a man from the Council comes onto the crust and take it up again when he is past the shore road, and they never once change the twelve.

\subsection*{In the dipper’s charcoal}

At the foot of the first leaf, in thick charcoal that has rubbed onto the fold, in the hand of a dipper who borrowed the sheet while the net was mending:

\begin{quote}\itshape We read the flood at dawn and tell the Council what it is worth. The ebb brings the boat back and nobody puts a figure on it. The children put a figure on it and then give it to the tide. That is why I let them have my old cord. A cord that counts and then loses is the only honest cord on this coast.\end{quote}

When I asked him why he wrote it on a children’s game he said a game is the only paper in Vhal that a Council man never thinks to read. I have left the charcoal where he put it and not washed the fold.

\subsection*{At the head and in the gutter}

The salt crust at the head and along the gutter has gone into the grain of the paper and will not come out. The tar thumb is mine; I held the leaf down in a wind off the Sallow and did not know I had marked it. The fibre of net-cord in the second fold came off the cord the children use and goes soft when the weather goes soft, which tells me when to shut the tin. The green bead came off a girl’s hair as she leaned over to see the writing, and she did not ask for it back. The gull’s peck went through the word \emph{flood} in the verse and I have left the hole standing, because a verse about the tide with a word taken out by a bird is in better order than I could have made it. The wet corner took two lines of the verse and they are void by the Council’s own law, which is a virtue; I have left the space the length of them and written nothing in it, because a verse with two lines gone is a verse said slowly, and all of ours are said slowly. The grey print along the gutter came off a cuff laid where no cuff has business lying; nobody will own it and there is no Last Day at the pans. I keep this leaf dry in a tin lined with rushes, which is a strange thing to do in Vhal, where paper is made to rot. A document the rain has not had is a document the Council can still read. That is the only reason I keep it.

\subsection*{At the foot, in a hand nobody will own}

\begin{quote}\itshape The pan keeps the salt and the tide keeps the count;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the half is a share and the share is a debt;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the fist keeps the bit that the slate cannot keep,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the boat comes back on the water it spent.\end{quote}

I asked the child who keeps the cord, a dipper, a woman who holds a share from her mother, and a Council clerk come up from the Quay, and had four answers and no hand. I have left the line where it was written. The leaf goes back into the tin I keep on the shelf with the paper I mean to let the rain take. Tomorrow the flood will come in over the third pan and the crust will bear a foot again, and the children will jump the twelve and give them back to the water, and the clerk will put a figure against the one thing in this port that was never for sale.

\clearpage\phantomsection\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{The Toll-Bag at the Meal Mill, Being the Price of Barley and Meal, the Charge of the Stone, and the Dues of the Roads That Bring a Sack to the Hopper, Set Down in the Meal-Book by the Miller’s Daughter}
\CRsheetheading{The Toll-Bag at the Meal Mill, Being the Price of Barley and Meal, the Charge of the Stone, and the Dues of the Roads That Bring a Sack to the Hopper, Set Down in the Meal-Book by the Miller’s Daughter}
{\centering\FellFont\itshape\footnotesize\color{faded} A meal-book leaf written in charcoal thinned with meal-dust and gone over in iron-gall; the figure cried at the Cross set against the figure taken at the mill door, the stone’s handful set beside the road’s bit, the dues of the ways that carry grain set under both; corrected in the narrow upright hand of a factor’s clerk, a carter’s charcoal added at the bridge, a child’s crooked sums in the corner, and one line at the foot nobody will own · Written at the meal mill at Sill on the Ilm, in Stone of Y.H. 813, the year after the Thin Year, when the river lay under ice and the barley came down the ridge road frozen in the sacks; set down by the miller’s daughter, who keeps the meal-book, on the back of a barley tally spoiled by a wet figure out of the Glaze Room, and written up again at the three Account-days of Stone as the bell went four, four and a gap over the water. Kept folded in the toll-bag on its nail behind the door with a barleycorn shut in the crease. It survives with white mill-dust worked into the head and the gutter, a brown silt tideline along the foot from a morning the leaf went down to the Fishstairs in an apron, a barley awn stiff in the second fold, a wet ring where a cup was set down and taken up before it was seen, a nick from a millstone dressing-pick at the fore-edge, a grey Ash print along the outer margin which the writer did not make and has not swept, two corrections in hands that are not hers, a child’s sums done wrong in the bottom corner, and one line at the foot that has never been claimed\par}\medskip
I keep the meal-book at the mill and the toll-bag hangs on a nail behind the door, where a man must turn his back on the wheel to reach it. A carter comes in with a sack and asks what his barley will fetch and what the road took out of him on the way. I can answer the second better than the first. The road writes on the sack; the Cross writes on a board, and the board is read twice.

Twelve copper bits to the silver mark; twenty marks to a Sere crown, which comes north because it must and cannot always be spent here. The Court books in embers and will tell a man an ember is worth five marks. I have ground nine winters and never found one in the hopper, so I keep no column for it. A figure that will not move with the weather is one somebody has taught to stand still.

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{In the narrow upright hand of a factor’s clerk come up from Greybank:} Coin and reckoning entered. Ember: five marks. \emph{Underneath, in mine:} He wrote \emph{is worth} where I should have written \emph{the Court calls it worth}. I put the verb back. A thing called five marks and a thing changing hands at five marks are two things, and only one comes through this door.\end{quote}

Say the figures to the hopper and not to the man asking. Said looking at a man, a price becomes an argument, and an argument gets carried out with the meal and comes back with a second figure on it.

\subsection*{What the mill gives and what the Cross cries}

\emph{The left column is what was called under the moot-post on the Account-days of Stone; the right, what passed over this bench between the last market of Bone and the frost on the hopper board. The wheel does not stop for a figure.}

Article — Cried at the Cross — Given at the mill\par

Barley, a sack, as it comes off the ridge — 6 bits in Grain, 9 in Stone — the same, and a handful off the top for the stone\par

Meal, dressed, a sack — not cried here — 8 bits; the brown in the fold to whoever is waiting\par

Grist, a peck — not cried — 2 bits\par

Bran — not cried — to the pig at the door, and not entered\par

Brown-edged barley loaf — 1 bit — 1 bit, and the crust to the child at the door\par

Salt, a sack off the pans — 3 marks — not sold here; the man carries it on past the mill\par

A sack left overnight under the wheel — no figure — 1 bit, and the mice pay the rest\par

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Margin:} The factor’s clerk struck \emph{a handful off the top for the stone} and set \emph{milling charge, one twelfth, as the notice says} above it. In mine: the notice is read in the square, the handful lifted here before the sack is tied. I have kept both rows.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Margin:} There is a figure spoken in the yards which is not the one on the notice. I have heard it under the wheel and set no sack beside it. A figure that will not bear a sack will not bear saying aloud at the Cross.\end{quote}

\subsection*{What the stone takes}

\emph{These are not cried anywhere. A man learns them when the meal comes out lighter than the barley went in.}

Charge\par

The handful for grinding — lifted off the top before sacking; never weighed\par

A cup on the nail beside the hopper — left for the woman who carries; she does not ask\par

Frost on the hopper board — weather; no figure\par

A foundling left at the mill in a fold of grey wool — a stone warmed under him, no name until a house claims him; not a sale\par

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{In the clerk’s narrow hand, against the last row:} No charge arising. \emph{Underneath, in mine:} True of the mill and not of the house that takes him.\end{quote}

\subsection*{The dues of the roads that bring a sack}

Four ways carry grain to this door and five carry it away. What is below is what I am told at this end, before the sack is set down. The tally-men at the far ends keep their own figures, and the two do not agree.

\subsection*{The ridge road, from Cold Acre}

Two leagues north on the ridge, where six houses have one well that has not frozen in any winter anyone can name. The barley comes down this way, and the turnips with it.

Due\par

Cart with barley, at the gate — 1 bit\par

A man going up for the never-freezing well — 1 bit; he brings back a common stone, which is not a warm-stone and is not called one\par

Pig driven north — 2 bits\par

A sack on a man’s back — nothing at the gate; 1 bit here when it is set on the bench\par

Barrow of grey going out — not weighed, not entered\par

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Margin:} A woman off the ridge asked why her barrow of grey went out unpaid when her barley paid. I told her the barley had been bought and the grey had not. She said that was a distinction a mill could afford and a ridge could not.\end{quote}

\subsection*{The river road, to the Weir and Stonemouth}

One league upriver to the traps and four more to the quarry village at the meeting of the Ferr.

Due\par

Beast on the bank way — 1 bit\par

Plank walk at the Weir — 1 bit; the boards are counted and nobody says which will bear a man\par

Foot passenger in Silt — nothing; the water has already charged him\par

Basket of eels at the bridge shade — nothing; the Fishstairs folk argued it and won\par

\subsection*{The Clay Road, east to Greybank}

Eighteen leagues of packed clay over corduroy, a Court road since the treaty of the Blue Cliff in Y.H. 418. Salt and iron come back on it; meal and grain go out. The slate is read twice in the square and the cart pays at both ends.

Due\par

Cart with a load, at this end — 2 bits\par

The same at the quay, by the factor’s man — 2 bits more\par

Foot passenger — 1 bit; nothing on Account-day, when a man comes to hear the figure\par

Barrow of grey going out through a gate — not weighed, no figure reaches it\par

\subsection*{The bridge and the water under the mill}

Due\par

Loaded cart over the bridge — 1 bit\par

The wheel’s own water — no toll; it is the same water that gives the note and sets the town’s hour\par

The mill threshold — no due; a sack pays inside, not on the step\par

The ford in the deep cold — nothing when the river bears ice; in the Long Cold no collector crossed for ninety-four days\par

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{In a carter’s thick charcoal, added at the bridge:} Paid going over and paid coming back, and the sacks lighter every time. \emph{In mine:} Both stand. A road has two ends and both have a hand; a river has one hand and does not write.\end{quote}

\subsection*{The roads that do not bring a sack here}

Three roads go out of this country which have nothing to do with the mill. The Salt Road takes a mark at the coast pass and calls it a freely entered contribution; the Rim takes a mark or iron and promises no man back; the Hearth takes nothing at any gate, having taken it at home. A man asked which was dearest and I showed him the empty column. He said the Hearth, because a man pays it without seeing the hand.

\subsection*{The song said into the hopper}

\emph{Said low while the sacks go over, to the hopper and not to the company, and never while a man from Slate Row stands in the door.}

\begin{quote}\itshape Twelve to the mark and twenty to the crown,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the Court books five and never sends them down;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape a sack comes in at the bridge with dust on the seam\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and goes out as meal with a handful gone.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape The stone takes first and the road takes twice,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the Cross reads twice and calls it once;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape say it to the hopper, say it down to the wheel,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and nobody enters what the river took.\end{quote}

\subsection*{What stands outside the figures}

The dust of this mill gets into a man and he coughs up a colour he will not discuss; no due at this door pays for that. A wrong wind off High Kiln brings the sweet edge of lead glaze and takes it out on the wind that brought it. In Silt the flood line goes up the wall to the second course of stone and the mill grinds on with what the river sends. In the Long Cold the note came under the ice and the town kept its hours another way. A cup was set down on this leaf while I counted and taken up before I saw who set it.

\subsection*{The hands that are not mine}

The factor’s clerk takes the doer out, as though a sack could set itself down and a stone take its own handful. Where I wrote \emph{I lifted}, he wrote \emph{was charged}; where I wrote \emph{the road took}, he wrote \emph{was taken}. I put my words back beneath his, as old grinding shows under new on a dressed stone. He set the printed figure in the margin beside the one spoken in the yards, and did not ask why.

The carter wrote at the bridge. A girl of the Cross set her sums in the corner, two bits going into a mark where four should have stood. I have not rubbed them out. They are the only figures here nobody will be asked to pay.

\subsection*{At the head and in the gutter}

The white at the head is mill-dust, not salt; my father’s hands were white to the wrist and never noticed he had marked a leaf. The brown tideline came up from the Fishstairs in an apron, and I carried the leaf dry though there was no figure in it. The barley awn in the second fold is stiff where the crease kept it from the damp. The ring is not ale and I did not see the cup go down. The nick came from the dressing-pick I use when my hands are wet. The grey along the fold came off a cuff laid where no cuff has business lying, and I have not swept it. There is no Last Day at a mill. The dust goes out with the meal and nobody calls it dealt with.

\subsection*{At the foot, in a hand nobody will own}

\begin{quote}\itshape The Cross reads twice and the road takes twice;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the stone takes first and the bag keeps none;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape a sack comes in with a house’s name on it\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and goes out as meal with the name ground off,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and no figure stands in the space between.\end{quote}

I asked the miller, a carter off the ridge, and a clerk up from the Greybank beam, and had three answers and no hand. I have left the line where it was written. The leaf goes back into the toll-bag and the barleycorn into the crease. Tomorrow the sacks come down frozen hard, and I shall give the figure I gave today; by the time the wheel has turned it will be a thing that was true.

\clearpage\phantomsection\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{The Turning of the Fire, Being the Watch-Song of the Kiln-Mouth in Low Kiln, Sung at the Firing and Again at the Second Firing}
\CRsheetheading{The Turning of the Fire, Being the Watch-Song of the Kiln-Mouth in Low Kiln, Sung at the Firing and Again at the Second Firing}
{\centering\FellFont\itshape\footnotesize\color{faded} A firing song of the clay yard, called to the damper and answered into the mouth, the words in the low half-sung speech of the yard; written in charcoal thinned with brick-dust, the rubrics of the mouth in the same hand, a kiln-master’s correction in broad charcoal, a factor’s clerk’s figures in a narrow upright Ledgerhand, a gloss in the thick charcoal of a woman who rakes the lower fire, and one line at the foot in a hand nobody will own · Set down in Smoke of Y.H. 812, the Thin Year, by an old woman who turns the fire at a kiln two doors above the Vail in Low Kiln of Sill, who learned her letters off a tile-counter and has no slate in the yard; written on the back of a firing-tally spoiled by a wet thumb while the second firing was being counted, tied with grey wool to the handle of the damper under a broken pot turned mouth-down against the rain. Copied forward in Tallow of Y.H. 813 onto a strip of oiled paper from the wheel-shed after the first leaf scorched. It survives with a brick-dust thumb at the head, a long scorch along the lower edge where the leaf lay too near the mouth, a green bead of lead glaze pressed into the corner, a small-ale ring through the third verse, a grey Ash smear in the gutter that nobody will own, a sherd pressed between the fourth and fifth leaves, one line eaten away by the heat and not written in again, one correction in broad charcoal, four in the narrow upright hand of the factor’s clerk at Greybank, a gloss from a woman at the tubs, and a line at the foot in a hand that has never been claimed\par}\medskip
I have turned the fire at a kiln two doors above the Vail through nineteen firings and have never seen a man write down what we say at the mouth. A factor’s man came up off the north bridge with a cuff gone soft from washing and asked a girl at the tubs what the women sang when the fire was kept through the night; she began to tell him and he wrote before she had finished. I have set it down in her words and in mine, with the rests left in.

A firing song is not a tune. A tune wants a voice with nothing in its hands, and at the mouth every hand is full. It is said to the iron and to the coals, to keep the rake moving and the count honest. Sung at a table it grows a melody in it, and a man in a clean coat can carry that away and enter it as a custom. I have put the verbs back where the clerk took them out.

The brick-dust at the head is mine. I held the tally down on the flagstone with the hand I rake with and did not know I had marked it.

\subsection*{How the fire is kept}

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item Turn the coals with the back of a broken pot, never with iron. Iron remembers the heat and gives it back in a man’s face.

\item The call goes to the damper and the answer goes into the mouth. Said looking at a woman it becomes an argument, and an argument at the mouth ends with somebody setting the tongue wrong.

\item Four pulls to the rake and a rest at the turn of the tongue. The rest is not a pull and is not counted. It is where the iron is given its other bite.

\item The damper has two bites and no Grathic word that holds both. Hold one and the pot comes whole out of the firing; hold the other and a hand comes off a man. Call the iron by what it is doing that hour and do not ask it what it means.

\item A girl come up from the Glaze Room with green at one corner of her mouth and the pale line at her gum does not rake. Not a punishment. Sweetness makes a hand careless, and a careless hand turns the tongue too far.

\item If a slate lies on the bench, turn it face down before the first pull. A fire said over an open slate arrives somewhere the speaker did not send it, and gets entered there.

\item Do not sing when the Slip Brook is up brown. The water has its own note, and two notes over one mouth make two counts that will not agree, and the yard goes around both all day.

\item The last part is kept back. It is for when the man from Greybank has gone back over the bridge with his satchel under his arm and the yard can hear itself again.

\end{itemize}

\subsection*{The song}

\emph{The woman at the mouth calls the first line of each pair; the hands along the bank answer the second. The refrain is said low into the mouth at the turn of the tongue, and the last line is held until the rake is back on the iron.}

\begin{quote}\itshape The coal came down from the Last Day under ash,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape we broke it out with a broken pot and gave it a name of our own;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape it is the same fire in every house in the yard,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and every house says it kept it, and none says who lit it.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Keep it low. The mouth takes what the hand will give.}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Four at the rake and a rest where the fifth should be;}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{the pot keeps the note and the hand keeps the burn,}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{and the slate keeps neither, and is read in the morning.}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Green clay will stand up straight all day\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and slump in the night with nobody to see it;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape so will a promise, and so will a man\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape who has been told the thaw is only weather.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Keep it low. The mouth takes what the hand will give.}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Four at the rake and a rest where the fifth should be.}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape One iron holds the heat in and takes it out;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape say which mercy you mean before you touch the tongue.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape A man with his finger in it holds his tongue instead,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape which is the answer most of us give.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Keep it low. The mouth takes what the hand will give.}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Four at the rake and a rest where the fifth should be.}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape The glaze goes on green and comes off with a sweetness;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the girl who tastes it has a pale line at her gum.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Do not let her rake. The lead does not care whose hand it takes,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and takes the steadiest first.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Keep it low. The mouth takes what the hand will give.}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Four at the rake and a rest where the fifth should be.}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape The breath kills in sleep and leaves no mark worth speaking of;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape they call it merciful who have not gone in after breakfast.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape We set a pot at the door of the house where it happened,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and say nothing to the pot, and the pot says nothing back.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Keep it low. The mouth takes what the hand will give.}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Four at the rake and a rest where the fifth should be;}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{the pot keeps the note and the hand keeps the burn,}\end{quote}
