\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{and the slate keeps neither, and is read in the morning.}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape One in twelve, says the notice, read twice at the Cross,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape once for the moot and once for them that came late;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the bell goes four, four and a gap and nobody crosses himself,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the figure you heard is not the figure they paid.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Keep it low. The mouth takes what the hand will give.}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Four at the rake and a rest where the fifth should be.}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Take nothing out while the hot is still in it.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape A cup knocked at the draw answers full or answers flat;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the flat ones go by the road for the cart to crush,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape which is kinder than letting a buyer find them.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Keep it low. The mouth takes what the hand will give.}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Four at the rake and a rest where the fifth should be;}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{the pot keeps the note and the hand keeps the burn,}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{and the slate keeps neither, and is read in the morning.}\end{quote}

There is a space before the last refrain in the keeping, the length of a turn of the tongue. I have left it on the tally. The clerk put a round nought in it once, which is a thing you can hold up and look at, and a rest is not.

\subsection*{The part they keep back}

\emph{Not said while the factor’s man is in the yard. Taken up after he has gone back over the bridge. The women say it to the damper and not across the square.}

\begin{quote}\itshape Four at the mouth and a gap where the fifth should be;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape we do not name whose gap it is, and the house does not ask.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape The heat we keep was paid for somewhere before it came here,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and a quiet man down at Mud End went in his sleep last week\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and nobody made a lesson of him.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape The number goes from a fist to a mouth to a shoulder\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and arrives at nobody, and nobody asks where;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape a brine-gull went off upriver with a coal from a banked fire\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape that was not yet cold, and carried it out of the account.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Four and a rest. The iron keeps the other bite.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape The clerk has no word for a thing a woman does with her hand.\end{quote}

One line of this part is gone where the leaf lay too near the mouth. I know what it said. Knowing a thing is not the same as having it, and I have not written it in again.

\subsection*{What the kiln-master did}

He borrowed the leaf at the firing and wrote in broad charcoal over my small hand. He has read every line of it with one eye on the damper.

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{At} the glaze goes on green and comes off with a sweetness: \emph{Green ware, current. The sweetness is not entered.}\end{quote}

I have left it standing. He is right about the ware and wrong about the sweetness, which is entered somewhere, and not by him.

\subsection*{What the clerk did}

The factor’s clerk took the leaf on the morning we drew the second firing, ink sitting in two fingers of it that would not come out. He took the heat out and set his figures above mine. I have left his hand standing and mine underneath, as the mouth keeps the pot’s heat and the flagstone keeps the scorch.

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item At \emph{the pot keeps the note and the hand keeps the burn}, he wrote \emph{vessel sound, entered; quality not a figure. Labour, one mark; no deduction for injury}. True in the figure, false at the mouth, where the note is the whole of the quality and the burn is the whole of the price.

\item At \emph{four at the rake and a rest}, he wrote \emph{four pulls, fifth nil}. A nought is a number. The rest is where the iron changes hands.

\item At \emph{we do not name whose gap it is}, he wrote \emph{cost to district, nil}. It is true in the figure and false in the room that breathes through its mouth at the end of the yard.

\item At \emph{a quiet man down at Mud End went in his sleep}, he wrote \emph{one death, cause undetermined}, and drew a line under it as if a line could close it.

\item At \emph{carried it out of the account}, he wrote \emph{loss, nil; gain, nil}, and put the leaf face down, which is the only thing he has done all morning that the yard could agree with.

\end{itemize}

\subsection*{What the woman at the tubs put in the margin}

The thick charcoal belongs to a woman below the racks who has raked more firings than she will count. I have copied it as it stands, without making the two hands agree.

At \emph{the same fire in every house}: \emph{We say it kept it because there is no other sentence. In my first winter I asked who lit the first one and was told to ask the fire, which is an answer given by people who asked the same thing at their own first firing.}

At \emph{say which mercy you mean}: \emph{A man held the cold side of that iron for twenty years and never once said which bite he meant. He is dead now and the pot he kept is still on the shelf.}

At \emph{the girl who tastes it}: \emph{I have held the pale line up to the light for three of them. Two went south. The third still rakes, and I have said nothing, which is a kindness and a fault in the same breath.}

At \emph{the flat ones go by the road}: \emph{My father set a flat cup by the road and a buyer took it up anyway and carried it three leagues before it broke. Somebody paid for those three leagues and it was not my father.}

At the kept-back part: \emph{The river takes what the Court does not. You can shout at either one. I have tried.}

\subsection*{At the head and along the gutter}

The brick-dust thumb at the head is mine and will not come out of the grain, which is why I use it to sign. The scorch along the lower edge is where I laid the fold on the flagstone while the mouth was open; it took the corner off two lines, and I have not written them in again, because a song with its corner gone is a song the yard has half forgotten, which is how most of them reach us. The green bead came off a girl who leaned to see the writing with sweetness still at her tongue; she touched the paper, said nothing, and went back to the Glaze Room. I have not washed it. The small-ale ring went through the third verse while a woman stood over me telling me to keep it low; she set her cup down and took it up when I had done, and the ring has gone the colour of the pot it stood on. The long grey along the gutter came off a cuff laid where no cuff has business lying on a kiln bench. Nobody will own it, and there is no Last Day behind a fire. The sherd between the fourth and fifth leaves answers flat when I knock it; I keep it there to remind me what flat is. The grey wool through the hole ties the leaf to the damper handle, and there is a knot in it for the one line I could not bring up and have not looked to see whether it has come back.

\subsection*{At the foot, in a hand nobody will own}

\begin{quote}\itshape The clay keeps the thumb. The fire keeps the cost.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape The slate keeps neither and is turned face up at the Weighing.\end{quote}

I asked the woman at the tubs, the kiln-master and a man who came up from Greybank with a satchel, and had a proverb, a figure and a date, and no hand to set over any of them. I have left the line where it was written.

The leaf goes back on the damper hook. There is a firing in Ember and another in Smoke, and the fire will be turned with the back of a broken pot, four pulls and a gap, and the gap will be left where it was found. If the factor’s clerk borrows the leaf again he may strike out the verbs. The fire does not care. The hands do.

\clearpage\phantomsection\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{Of the Overnight Keeping, the Two Benches and the Cup Left Standing, Being Title the Twelfth of the Ordinances of the Keeping, Copied for the Room-Slate in Slate Row at Sill, with the Room-Clerk’s Margin, the Cup-Ring, a Cold-Iron Score, Two Corrections in Borrowed Hands, and a Line at the Foot Nobody Will Own}
\CRsheetheading{Of the Overnight Keeping, the Two Benches and the Cup Left Standing, Being Title the Twelfth of the Ordinances of the Keeping, Copied for the Room-Slate in Slate Row at Sill, with the Room-Clerk’s Margin, the Cup-Ring, a Cold-Iron Score, Two Corrections in Borrowed Hands, and a Line at the Foot Nobody Will Own}
{\centering\FellFont\itshape\footnotesize\color{faded} An extract from the Court’s ordinances, written out for the room-slate in the Waiting Room off Slate Row at Sill, with the marginal hand of the clerk who sets the verbs back after a day’s drawing; the articles in Ledgerhand and the verbs restored beneath them, the nights and the things not entered in tables, the form of an overnight left blank, the bench-song pasted inside the cover, a ring where a cup stood, a bare square where a name was scraped away with a clip’s edge, two corrections in borrowed hands, and a line at the foot nobody has claimed · Copied at Sill in Slate Row in the Thin Year, Y.H. 812, and carried forward at the Opening of the Slates, Ilmen 1, Y.H. 813, from Title the Twelfth of the Ordinances of the Keeping as set down in the first years after the Rising of Y.H. 668, confirmed to the factor at Greybank by the treaty of Y.H. 418, and added to in Y.H. 782 and in the Thin Year; it survives as three leaves of foolscap sewn with wire, kept under the room-slate on the shelf beside the door and taken down when the evening figure has been read: a grey Ash thumb at the head, cold-iron filings worked into the gutter off a tube-wrap set down while a clerk went for water, a pale round ring where a cup stood from the first watch to the morning, a brown crust-print at the second fold, a curl of grey wool through the tie-hole that nobody will untie, a tallow thumb, a green bead of lead glaze pressed into the lower corner by a girl with the sweetness still at her mouth, a damp tide-line along the foot out of the boards, a bare square where a name was scraped away with a clip’s edge and no other put in its place, two corrections in borrowed hands, and a line at the foot that has never been owned\par}\medskip
I keep the room-slate in the Waiting Room off Slate Row. It is the room nobody goes in, which is a saying of the Cross and not an ordinance, and it holds two benches, a cradle worn to its last bottom, a cup that stands where somebody set it, and this slate turned face down before I sit. The room smells of wet wool and cold iron and a little of tallow, and underneath those the sour mineral smell this town knows and does not say. I write what the ordinance tells me and set the verbs back underneath, because an overnight with nobody in it is an overnight nobody kept, and those are the only kind the Court has ever wanted entered.

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{At the head of the first leaf, in mine, written small:} Copied by the room and for it. The verbs are mine. The absence of them is not. Let both stand.\end{quote}

It was set down in the first years after the Rising and confirmed to the factor at Greybank in Y.H. 418, when it was found that a night could pass without anybody in it. It has been added to twice since, in the same hand as the first, so that no man can tell by the writing which rule was made before the winter and which after. A rule with no night on it is a rule nobody has had to sit. These have been sat.

\subsection*{Title the Twelfth, as it stands in the room}

\emph{From the Ordinances of the Keeping, Title the Twelfth: Of the Overnight Keeping, the Two Benches and the Cup Left Standing. Set down after the Rising; confirmed to the factor at Greybank by the treaty of Y.H. 418; added to in Y.H. 782 and in the Thin Year, Y.H. 812.}

\subsection*{I. Of the bringing}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item A vessel is brought to the room after the evening figure is read and before the dark. The bringing is made by the officer appointed and not by a house. A house that comes to the door is answered at the door.

\item The slate-name is entered on the room-slate and the birth-name is not taken. Where a vessel has no slate-name, the hour and the bench are entered in its place, and the place where a name should stand is left the length of a thumb.

\item A slate is set face down at the head of each bench. The hand goes to the slate before it goes to the vessel, and what is written is not corrected by what the vessel says afterward.

\item Where more are brought than the benches will hold, boards are laid upon the floor and no figure is taken for the boards.

\end{enumerate}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Margin:} A man came to this door in the Thin Year with his coat on his arm and asked to go home for it before the dark. He was told the morning came first. I entered the hour and the bench, and not the coat. The room is cold enough that a man asks for his coat as other men ask for water. Neither has a column.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Margin:} In the last tend of Stone more were brought than the benches would hold, and boards were laid. I entered \emph{boards}, as the ordinance provides, and not the forty who lay on them. In the morning a barrow of grey went out through the north gate, and I set the barrow at the edge, where it has no column.\end{quote}

\subsection*{II. Of the night}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item Nothing is entered between the bringing and the morning. What is said in the night has no column and is not carried up the road.

\item No fire is carried into the room. Warmth is kept in a stone under the wool at the middle, and the stone is not counted and is not marked. A stone set to the ends wastes its heat on the part that cannot keep it.

\item The cup stands where it is set and is not removed before the morning. No entry is made against the cup.

\item No officer sits in the room. The room-clerk sits with the slate face down and reads nothing aloud after the bringing.

\item The collected are kept until the banking and are not called by any name the room has given them.

\end{enumerate}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Margin:} A woman asked me whether the cup was for her. I told her it stood where it was set. She took that for yes and drank, and I did not correct her, which is the only true answer I have given here in nine years. Neither the asking nor the drinking is entered; the ring the cup left is on this leaf, where nobody can add it.\end{quote}

\subsection*{III. Of the morning and the going up}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item In the morning the slate is turned face up and the figure is read before the vessel is looked at. This is the order of the room and not the order of a house.

\item The vessel is taken up the road to the bank, and the room is swept after it. What is found in the corners is called grey and is carried out and burnt, and no entry is made against it.

\item The cradle is wiped and the cup is set back where it stood. A cup set back is not a cup washed, and the ordinance asks after neither.

\item No roll is closed in this room. What was entered overnight is carried forward with the other figures and is not called an overnight in the roll.

\end{enumerate}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Margin:} I put \emph{the figure is read before the vessel is looked at} back under rule ten, where a College clerk set \emph{the reading precedes attendance.} The same order said to a slate and said to a person. A person can be looked at; the order provides that he is not.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Margin:} The grey in the corners is the colour of skimmed milk gone off, and it will not wash out. Houses sweep their corners on the Last Day and burn what they find and call it dealt with. There is no Last Day in a Waiting Room; the barrow goes out every morning and comes back the next, and nobody has called it dealt with.\end{quote}

\subsection*{IV. Of faults and their correcting}

Fault — As entered at the room — What the clerk sets beneath\par

A birth-name taken — Name not entered; the place left the length of a thumb — The name, said once in the night, at the edge\par

A hand to the vessel before the slate — The slate turned and written again in the same hand — The woman who was looked at first\par

A fire carried in — No fire entered — The cold that came up through the boards\par

A name spoken in the night — No entry — The length of the speaking\par

The boards counted — No figure taken — Forty, who lay there, and the barrow that followed\par

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item A fault copied twice in one tend is a fault the clerk has not understood, and the senior clerk sits with him at the bench until he has. The slate is not a rod. It is a piece of stone with a place where a person sat.

\end{enumerate}

\subsection*{The table of nights}

\emph{Copied from the room-slate. The last column is mine and has no standing at any bank.}

Night — Who was set — On the slate — What the night kept — What stands beneath\par

Stone 30 — Forty of Low Kiln, by lot — One slate for the batch — Boards on the floor; a barrow out at noon — Birth-names not taken; no figure for the boards\par

Kindling 2 — A widow of the lower town — \emph{Loaf} — Asked after her daughter, twice — The daughter, at the edge, the length of a name\par

Weighing 3 — A kiln-hand, terraces — \emph{Seven} — A stone at the middle; hands left wrapped — The asking for the stone, not entered\par

Ash 12 — A girl out of the glaze room — \emph{Sweet} — Green at one corner of the mouth — The girl asked whether it showed; no answer entered\par

Draws on this leaf: four nights and one batch. Names taken: none. Figures struck: one. The cup-ring is not a figure and has not been added.

\subsection*{The form of the overnight}

\emph{Set out at the end of Title the Twelfth. I have copied it with the blanks as they stand. In nine years nobody has filled the last line with the hand the room requires.}

\begin{quote}\itshape Entered this day, being ---day of -------, in the year of the Hearth ------, the bringing of ----------------------, by slate-name and not by birth-name, set on the first bench / the second / boards on the floor, the slate face down, the stone at the middle and not at the ends, the cup standing where it was set, no fire carried in, nothing entered between the bringing and the morning; read in the morning before the vessel was looked at, the figure one in twelve as the notice says, the corners swept and the grey carried out; carried forward and not closed. Written by ----------------------, whose hand went to the slate first. What the vessel said in the night was ----------------------, which is not entered.\end{quote}

\subsection*{The bench-song, pasted inside the cover}

\emph{Said low to the cup, sitting, with the slate face down. Never in the morning, and never within hearing of a man come down from the College. The last line is said to the boards and not to the company.}

\begin{quote}\itshape Two benches and a cup on the sill,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape a cradle with the bottom worn thin;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the slate goes down before the eye\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the coat stays folded on the arm.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape No fire comes in and the cold comes up,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape a stone at the middle, the ends left bare;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape she asks for her name and you give her a date ---\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape a date is safe and the cup does not care.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape One in twelve as the notice says,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape read to the slate and not to the face;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the barrow goes out while the boards lie still\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the grey comes back in the selfsame place.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Two benches and a place on the floor,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape a ring on the leaf where the cup once stood;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape what was said in the night goes up with the grey\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the room keeps the shape and never the word.\end{quote}

The wet reed across the last verse came in on a coat from the Weir. I have flattened it. A clerk who explains a song has begun to write a sermon, and sermons get copied.

\subsection*{What the borrowed hands did}

A clerk of the College came down with ink in two fingers of a cuff gone soft from washing, and borrowed the leaf while I was at the benches. Against rule nine he struck \emph{the collected are kept until the banking} and set \emph{the vessels remain in custody} above it, true of a room and false of a woman who asked me for water. Against rule five he wrote \emph{no matter arising}, and had to look at every night on the table before he could write that none had matter in them. I have put both of mine back underneath and left his standing where a man must lean to read them.

The other hand is a physician’s, come up from Greybank, taller and kinder than the first. Against the stone at the middle he set \emph{a common settling; no remedy applied}, the phrase that took the second chill out of the record in Y.H. 651. I have not struck it through. A kinder phrase costs less to enter, and a clerk who has sat one night here knows which hand has been nearer the bench. Both stand.

\subsection*{At the head and in the gutter}

The grey at the head is Ash off my own thumb, turning the leaf toward the lamp while a figure was read from the other room; it will not come out of the creases. The filings in the gutter came off a tube-wrap set down while the officer went for water; there is always iron in the fold, and it has never once drawn the warmth out of the paper, which is the only mercy this room holds. The pale ring is where the cup stood from the first watch to morning; it is the thinnest place on the leaf and no figure can be read into it. The brown at the second fold is crust-grease, left by a woman who held her crust for a child not in the room. The curl of grey wool through the tie-hole is mine and I have not untied it. The tallow is from the lamp I keep low, so a woman will not change her tale when she hears the pen. The green bead is lead glaze, pressed in by a girl come up from High Kiln with the sweetness still at her mouth. The tide-line along the foot came up out of the boards in a wet Silt; it takes the corners off figures and leaves the figures. The bare square is where I scraped a name away with a clip’s edge and put no other in its place. I have not written it back, and I have not forgotten it.

\subsection*{At the foot, in a hand nobody will own}

\begin{quote}\itshape The slate keeps the hour. The cup keeps the ring.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape The room keeps the shape of a person and enters neither.\end{quote}

I asked a collector’s man, a woman who had sat overnight on the second bench, and a clerk come down from the College, and had three answers and no hand, as I have had before. I have left the lines where they were written.

The leaf goes back under the slate and the slate face down on the shelf. Tomorrow the evening figure will be read and brought, and I shall set the verbs back where another hand took them out, and turn the slate before I look at the person. A woman will ask for her name and I shall give her a date, because a date is safe and the Court likes a date. The cup will stand where it was set, and in the morning the grey will go out through the north gate, and nobody here will call it dealt with.

\clearpage\phantomsection\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{The Twelve Turns, Being the Wheel-Song of Low Kiln, Said Kneeling to the Lump while the Wheel Runs, with the Turns Counted and the Wetting Kept Outside the Count, a Wheel-Shed Rubric in Slip-Thinned Charcoal, a Kiln-Master’s Correction, a Factor’s Clerk’s Figures in the Narrow Upright Hand, a Rack-Woman’s Gloss in the Margin, and One Line at the Foot in a Hand Nobody Will Own}
\CRsheetheading{The Twelve Turns, Being the Wheel-Song of Low Kiln, Said Kneeling to the Lump while the Wheel Runs, with the Turns Counted and the Wetting Kept Outside the Count, a Wheel-Shed Rubric in Slip-Thinned Charcoal, a Kiln-Master’s Correction, a Factor’s Clerk’s Figures in the Narrow Upright Hand, a Rack-Woman’s Gloss in the Margin, and One Line at the Foot in a Hand Nobody Will Own}
{\centering\FellFont\itshape\footnotesize\color{faded} A thrower’s work song in the low Grathic of the wheel-shed, said down into the lump and not up into the shed; the turns counted in threes of twelve with a hand kept for the wetting, the rubrics of the seat and the slip bowl in the writer’s charcoal hand, a kiln-master’s correction in broad charcoal, a factor’s clerk’s figures standing above in Ledgerhand, a rack-woman’s thick-charcoal gloss pressed into the margin, and one line at the foot in a hand nobody will claim · Set down in Ember of Y.H. 813, the kiln month, by Venna of the Wheel, a thrower at a wheel two doors down the Clay Yard from the Vail kiln-house, who has kneeled at it six-and-twenty years and can find a centre by the feel of it before the first turn; written because a factor’s clerk come up from Greybank on an Account-day stood in the shed door and asked a girl at the bench what the wheels said while they turned, and wrote her answer down with the turns taken out and a figure put in the place of the wetting. Written first in charcoal thinned with slip on the back of a wheel-shed tally spoiled by a fall of slip, folded into four, tied with grey wool and carried under the board of the shed; copied forward at Greybank in Bone of Y.H. 813 onto the back of a voided weigh-slip. It survives with wet slip worked into the grain at the head, a dry line of slip across the second leaf where a sleeve passed at the third turn, a barley-water ring through the fifth verse, a small sherd pressed flat between the third and fourth leaf with the well almost rubbed away, a green bead of lead glaze pressed into the lower corner, a long hair the colour of wet wool caught in the seam, a grey Ash smear along the gutter that nobody will own, the kiln-master’s broad correction, the rack-woman’s gloss, the clerk’s figures standing above, and the one line at the foot\par}\medskip
I throw at a wheel two doors down the Clay Yard from the Vail kiln-house, and I have kneeled at it six-and-twenty years. A man come up from Greybank with a soft cuff and a slate under his arm stood in the shed door on an Account-day and asked a girl at the bench what the wheels said while they turned. She told him. He wrote it while she was still saying it, and what he wrote had the turns taken out of it and a figure set where the wetting stood. He thanked her and went back over the north bridge with his boots clean. I have set the words down as we say them and put the verbs back where he took them out.

The clay comes up off the treads wet and heavy and full of its own opinion. You set it on the wheel’s own centre, wet your hands in the slip bowl, and begin. The first twelve settle it. The second twelve open the well with the thumb. The third twelve bring the wall up between the thumb inside and the fingers outside, and the lip is taken at the top of the last of them. That is the whole of the throwing, and a cup is a well that has been persuaded to stand up.

We say the count down into the lump, not up into the shed. Said up into the air it grows a tune in it, and a tune is a thing a man in a clean coat can carry away and set by his own fire, with the lump left behind him. The wetting is not a turn. It is a hand in a bowl of slip, and it is kept beside the count where no clerk can put a figure on it.

The slip at the head is mine; I held the tally down in the draught under the door and did not know I had marked it.

\subsection*{How it is thrown}

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item Wet both hands in the slip bowl before the first turn, and again where the wall goes thin. A dry hand leaves a ring the wall will keep, and the knock at the rack will tell you which hand it was.

\item Set the lump on the wheel’s own centre, the worn one in the seat. A lump set proud of the centre spends all its turns arguing with the thumb.

\item Twelve to settle, twelve to open, twelve to lift. The wetting stands beside them and is not one of them. A girl who counts the wetting aloud will drown the cup.

\item Keep the thumb in the middle of the well. A thumb set to one side makes a wall thin on one side, and the thin side goes first in the firing.

\item Knuckle the cup before it leaves the shed. A whole one answers full; a hollow one gives back the small dead flat. If it answers flat, take it off the wheel and begin again, however late it is.

\item Say the count to the clay and not to the girl beside you. Said to her it becomes instruction, and instruction learned at this wheel is unlearned at another.

\item Do not sing it on an Account-day. The bell at the Cross goes four, four and a gap, and a wheel count set against that gap comes home wrong in the hand.

\item The last part is kept back. It is for when the kiln-master has gone up the terrace and the man from Greybank has gone back over the bridge with his satchel under his arm and the shed can hear itself again.

\end{itemize}

\subsection*{The song}

\emph{Said kneeling, low, into the lump. Refrain after every verse, the last line held until the hands are off the clay. One line of the refrain to one twelve.}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Twelve to settle, twelve to sink,}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{twelve to bring the wall to the brink;}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape *the hand in the bowl is not a turn ---\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{the wheel keeps its own and the slate keeps its own.}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape The lump comes up off the treads with the water still in it,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape set it where the seat has worn its hollow;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape a lump set proud of the centre spends the whole of its turns\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape arguing with the thumb that must open it.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Twelve to settle, twelve to sink,}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{twelve to bring the wall to the brink;}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape *the hand in the bowl is not a turn ---\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{the wheel keeps its own and the slate keeps its own.}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Wet the hands in the bowl before the first turn,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and wet them again where the wall goes thin;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape a dry hand leaves a ring the wall will keep,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the knock at the rack knows which hand it was.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Twelve to settle, twelve to sink,}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{twelve to bring the wall to the brink;}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape *the hand in the bowl is not a turn ---\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{the wheel keeps its own and the slate keeps its own.}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Twelve to settle and the lump stops fighting,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the thumb goes in at the middle and the well opens;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape open it slow, for the well is the first shape the cup knows\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and a well opened wrong is a cup begun wrong.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Twelve to settle, twelve to sink,}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{twelve to bring the wall to the brink;}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape *the hand in the bowl is not a turn ---\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{the wheel keeps its own and the slate keeps its own.}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Twelve to sink and the wall comes up between\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the thumb on the inside and the fingers outside;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape pinch it and the wall goes thin in the pinch,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape spare the hand and the wall falls in on itself.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Twelve to settle, twelve to sink,}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{twelve to bring the wall to the brink;}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape *the hand in the bowl is not a turn ---\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{the wheel keeps its own and the slate keeps its own.}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Twelve to bring the wall to the brink and stop,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape take the lip at the top where the thumb left it;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape a lip left thick is a cup that will crack in the throat,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape a lip pinched thin is a cup that will crack at the table.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Twelve to settle, twelve to sink,}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{twelve to bring the wall to the brink;}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape *the hand in the bowl is not a turn ---\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{the wheel keeps its own and the slate keeps its own.}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Knuckle it before it goes to the rack; a whole one answers full,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape a hollow one gives back the small dead flat;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape twelve and twelve and twelve, with the wetting beside them,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the number read at the Cross is another twelve, not this one.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Twelve to settle, twelve to sink,}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{twelve to bring the wall to the brink;}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape *the hand in the bowl is not a turn ---\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{the wheel keeps its own and the slate keeps its own.}\end{quote}

There is a space before the last refrain in the singing, the length of a hand dipped to the wrist in the slip bowl. I have left it on the tally. A clerk put a round nought in it once, which is a thing you can hold up and look at; a wetting is a hand in a bowl and will not stay still to be looked at.

\subsection*{The part they keep back}

\emph{Not sung while a kiln-master stands in the shed or a man with a satchel stands in the door. Said low, to the seat and not across it.}

\begin{quote}\itshape One in twelve, says the notice, read twice at the Cross,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape but the box goes up the clay road with a different figure shut in it;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the wheel gives a cup its twelve and the slate takes one away,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the two twelves are not the same twelve and nobody says so.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape There’s a hollow in the seat worn by six-and-twenty years of kneeling\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and a girl kneels in it now who has never asked what the figure was;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape we go around the place where a hand went into the strips\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the way we go around the well while the water is still in it.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Twelve. Twelve. Twelve. The wetting stands beside them.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape The shed keeps the turn. The clerk keeps the nought.\end{quote}

\subsection*{What the kiln-master did}

He came up from the terrace on the wrong wind with the sweet edge of the glaze at one corner of his mouth and read the leaf with one eye on the throat of the kiln. Against \emph{a lip pinched thin is a cup that will crack at the table} he wrote in broad charcoal: \emph{A lip is set by the firing and not by the table. What cracks in the throat never reaches one.} He underlined it twice.

Underneath, in mine: He is right about the lip and wrong about the song, which was counting turns and not lips. He has read every line with one eye on the kiln mouth, which is how a man reads who has never had to kneel in a worn seat and bring a wall up by the feel of it.

\subsection*{What the clerk did}

The factor’s clerk borrowed the leaf on an Account-day, ink sitting in the first joint of two fingers of his soft cuff and not coming out. He took the verbs out and set his figures above mine, and I have left his hand standing and put ours underneath, as a shed keeps the old hollow in the seat under the girl who kneels in it.

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item At \emph{twelve to settle, twelve to sink, twelve to bring the wall to the brink}, he wrote \emph{thirty-six rotations; vessel formed; no charge arises.} True in the figure and false in the shed, where a rotation is a turn and the turns belong to whoever knelt for them.

\item At \emph{the hand in the bowl is not a turn}, he wrote \emph{wetting: incidental; nil.} He has made a bowl of slip into nothing at all. A wetting is a wrist in a bowl, and somebody mixed the slip.

\item At \emph{the number read at the Cross is another twelve, not this one}, he wrote \emph{deduction one in twelve. Printed. Current.} He has joined two twelves that stand apart, which is the whole art of that hand. Both stand in my leaf and neither stands with the other.

\item At the space before the last refrain he put a round nought and wrote \emph{vacancy}. A nought is a figure and can be carried over the bridge. A hand in a bowl cannot.

\item At \emph{a hand went into the strips}, he wrote \emph{one absence, nil}, and set a figure against the worn seat. I have left his figure standing beside our going-around. Both stand.

\end{itemize}

\subsection*{What the rack-woman put in the margin}

The thick charcoal belongs to a woman who keeps the drying racks two doors up and has lifted more wet cups than she will count. I have copied it as it stands, without making the hands agree.

At \emph{a dry hand leaves a ring the wall will keep}: \emph{I set a wet cup down where the wall was thin and took it up in the morning with the ring standing in it. It is not the wet that does it.}

At \emph{the well is the first shape the cup knows}: \emph{I have taken cups off the rack with the well almost rubbed away and no thumb left to put it back. They hold water all the same.}

At \emph{the two twelves are not the same twelve}: \emph{I have asked what the wheel is worth and been given the weather, the river and the price of barley. I have stopped asking.}

At the kept-back part: \emph{The hollow in the seat is the only honest figure in this shed and it is not a figure. It is a place where somebody knelt.}

\subsection*{At the head and in the gutter}

The dry line across the second leaf is where a sleeve passed at the third turn; the wall took the mark off my cuff and gave it to the leaf. The barley-water ring stood through the fifth verse while a girl stood over me telling me to keep the thumb in the middle; she took her cup up when I had done, and the ring has gone the colour of the pot it stood on. The sherd between the third and fourth leaf came off a cup with the well almost rubbed away, and is lighter in the hand than a sound sherd, which is the whole of the lesson and no use at all to a clerk. The green bead came off a girl who leaned to see the writing with sweetness still at her tongue; she touched the tally, said nothing, and went back up the terrace. I have not washed it. The hair the colour of wet wool has caught in the seam and will stay there. The grey along the gutter came off a cuff laid where no cuff has business lying on a wheel-shed bench. Nobody will own it. There is no Last Day at a wheel.

\subsection*{At the foot, in a hand nobody will own}

\begin{quote}\itshape The wheel keeps the turn. The bowl keeps the wrist.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape The slate keeps neither and counts all the same.\end{quote}

I asked the kiln-master, a girl who has only this year come to the wheel, and a man come up from the Fishstairs with eels to sell, and had three answers and no hand. I have left the line where it was written. The tally goes back under the slip bowl. Tomorrow the clay comes up off the treads and I shall kneel in the worn seat, wet my hands, settle it, open the well, bring up the wall, and leave the wetting where it stands, outside the count, and the clerk may have his copy of the nought.

\clearpage\phantomsection\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{The Two Figures, Being an Extract from the Chronicle of the Standing Post Concerning the Thirty-One Years, the Figure Read at the Ferry and the Figure Paid at the Reed, with the Years as the Reeves Kept Them, the Court’s Annals Set Beside Them, the Fen Song, and the Corrections of a Factor’s Clerk}
\CRsheetheading{The Two Figures, Being an Extract from the Chronicle of the Standing Post Concerning the Thirty-One Years, the Figure Read at the Ferry and the Figure Paid at the Reed, with the Years as the Reeves Kept Them, the Court’s Annals Set Beside Them, the Fen Song, and the Corrections of a Factor’s Clerk}
{\centering\FellFont\itshape\footnotesize\color{faded} A reeve’s-clerk’s extract from the chronicle of the Standing Post in the Fenmarch, copied out of the tarred box under the third board of the walk; the years in a broad standing hand gone stiff with peat water, the Court annals in the narrow upright Ledgerhand of a factor’s clerk come up from Greybank, the two figures entered in a column that no clerk of the Keeping has ever signed, one song taken down in Reed from a singer who would not give her name, and one line at the foot in a hand nobody will own · Written at the Standing Post in the Fenmarch by the clerk who keeps the reeves’ chronicle, a man with no slate-name who signs with a thumb pressed into peat, in Reed and Ember of Y.H. 812, the Thin Year, and carried forward at the Opening of the Slates into Y.H. 813; copied from the post’s original begun in Y.H. 420 and kept since in a tarred box under the third board of the walk, where the peat water reaches the nails in the wet season. It survives as six leaves of stout foolscap sewn with wire and folded in oiled sailcloth, with black peat worked into the gutter and the creases of the thumb, a grey Ash print along the outer fold which the clerk did not make and will not sweep, a twist of wet reed fibre pressed flat in the second leaf, a strip of Vhaleni salt-paper gone soft at the edge and pasted over the sixth clause, a dark streak of eel slime at the foot, a tallow thumb at the head, a bead of green cliff-glass in the lower corner, the broad reeve’s correction standing above the narrow Court correction standing above the text, and one line at the foot in a hand that has never come forward\par}\medskip
I keep the chronicle of the Standing Post. It is not a history of Sarn and does not pretend to be one. The reeves of the Fenmarch are chosen for standing longest in a bog, and a man who has stood longer than any other is asked to settle the fines and the feuds, which he does in a voice thinned by the waiting. Nobody writes down the years he gave to the standing. The post writes them down. I copy the post.

This extract is the Thirty-One Years, which the Court calls the War of Deductions and the fen has always called the taking. The Court’s annals place it among the Bowl Years, between the southern purchase of measures and the fixing of the borders. We kept it in a tarred box under the third board of the walk, where the water comes up to the nails in the wet season and no paper will hold a word for a tend. The Court buys its contracts on salt-paper from Vhal, and in Vhal a contract that rots is held to be a virtue. In the fen a contract that rots is a contract nobody trusted in the first place. I have copied what the water left.

\subsection*{The years as the post has them}

\emph{Copied out of the tarred box. The broad hand is the reeve’s and sets down what stood. The narrow upright hand beneath each year is the factor’s clerk, who came up from Greybank in Reed of Y.H. 813 and corrected the whole leaf while a boy held it against the wind. I have left both readings standing, as a mended pot keeps the old break showing.}

\textbf{Y.H. 420.} Agents of the Bowl of Sere bought measures in the fen at prices no household could refuse, and carried them south to be returned whole, beautiful and remembering, in the open courts. Entered as \emph{the southern trade}, with the prices set against the eel-count of that year.

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{In the narrow upright hand:} A profitable commerce in measures, regulated by the Keeping. Strike \emph{carried}.\end{quote}

\textbf{Y.H. 426.} A collector came up to the post with a cold iron tube and a slate. The reeve set him on the lowest board, where the water came over his boot tops, and asked him to state his office before he drew. He said his office was a taking. The reeve asked him to write that down, and he wrote \emph{a draw}. Entered as \emph{a drawing of the office}.

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{In the narrow upright hand:} The office extended to the fen districts, peaceably received. Strike \emph{boot tops}.\end{quote}

\textbf{Y.H. 429.} The collectors began to sit at the ferry and at the reed landings. A household of a recognised house in Grath paid one in twelve, as the notice says. A household of the fen paid one in three, and was told that the notice said one in twelve. Entered as \emph{the two figures}.

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{In the narrow upright hand:} The deduction fixed at one in twelve throughout the bowl. Strike the second figure.\end{quote}

\textbf{Y.H. 437.} Eels failed at the weirs in the lean week, and the levy was called on the standing crops of reed. A man brought the figure up out of his fist and asked which of the two the Court meant. The reeve told him the Court meant the one on the notice, and the collector drew the other. Entered as \emph{the figure said and the figure paid}.

\textbf{Y.H. 441.} The Court’s annals begin to call the thirty years a war. There was no battle in the fen and no dead man entered. What the fen lost went out through the tube and came back as a thin child who could not say whose warmth it carried. Entered as \emph{eleven empty places in the returning line}, with no names, because the collector did not give them and the reeve did not ask.

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{In the narrow upright hand:} Disturbance of the peace, occasioned by the southern trade. Strike \emph{empty}.\end{quote}

\textbf{Y.H. 449.} The collectors were withdrawn from the post for one tend and came back with a new slate. No reason was entered on either side. The reeds were cut that year by hands that had been in the strips and had not all come out again. The fen entered the number of hands. The Court entered the number of reeds.

\textbf{Y.H. 451.} The thirty-first year. The two figures stood as they stand now, and the notice still says one in twelve. Entered as \emph{peace, the account standing}. The reeve who stood out the last of the thirty-one years stepped down and could not say, when asked, how long he had stood. I have put his standing in the margin rather than in the year, because a figure that a man cannot carry away with him is not a figure the post can keep.

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{In the narrow upright hand:} Peace restored. The several rates of the deduction confirmed. Strike the margin.\end{quote}

I have not struck anything. The factor’s clerk takes the verbs out because a thing always true has no need of them, and a deduction that was always one in twelve has no need of a fen, nor of a man to stand in it. I put the verbs back. A clerk who holds a leaf down for another man in a wind is not a man who believes the leaf is always true.

\subsection*{The two figures}

\emph{The column on the left is what is printed on the Weighing notice and read aloud at the ferry. The column on the right is what went out through the tube. Both stand in the box under the third board. Neither has ever been signed.}

Who stood — Figure read aloud — Figure drawn — Where it is entered\par

A house of Grath in good standing, clay or coin behind it — one in twelve — one in twelve — the notice, the slate, the annals\par

A household of the fen districts — one in twelve — one in three — the notice only\par

The clay-bound of the terraces — one in twelve — one in three — the notice only\par

The unhoused and the foundling with no house — one in twelve — one in three — nowhere at all\par

The difference between the two columns is three parts in twelve, which is a figure any child at the ferry can work out with eel-bones and does. It has never been entered. I have asked a man who copies the Court’s annals why a figure might be read in one place and paid in another, and he said a figure read aloud was a kindness and a figure paid was an account, and that a man who mixes the two has begun to write a sermon. I have set his sentence down. It is the only true sentence he gave me, and he did not know he had said it.

In Y.H. 612 the Fenmarch was made a confederacy under Court protection, and the cheap thin returns began in the same year. The post entered them without comment, which was a kindness to the box. I have copied the entry here because a reader who stops at Y.H. 451 will think the thirty-one years ended. They did not end. They were entered under another name.

\subsection*{The song of the two figures}

\emph{Taken down in Reed of Y.H. 813 at the third landing, from a woman who would not give a name and asked that the last line be left unsung. She said a song with its last line sung is a contract, and contracts in the fen are carried away by the damp. I have set a rule in its place, because a rule is the only thing a Court clerk will copy without asking who said it.}

\begin{quote}\itshape Twelve in the mouth and three in the hand,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the water takes what the slate won’t stand.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape A whole comes back with its face on plain,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape a thin comes back and asks for its name again.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape The eel goes up and the eel goes down,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the peat goes up and the peat lies dry;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the Hearth keeps one and the Hearth keeps two,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and who keeps three will not say why.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Stand on the board till the board stands still,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape count what you gave on the nails of the walk;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape a figure said is a figure paid\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape where the water ends and the boardwalk stops.\end{quote}

\emph{Here the singer stopped. In the place of the last line she put her thumb into the wet boards and left it there until the print filled with water. I have set the rule down as she gave it, and I have left the print where it fell.}

\subsection*{What the clerk wrote above the song}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{In the narrow upright hand, written across the third stanza:} The Hearth keeps nothing that is not given. Strike \emph{who keeps three}.\end{quote}

The factor’s clerk has a clean way with a line of verse, and no ear for the water under it. The Hearth keeps what is given, which is true, and somebody in that stanza keeps three, which is also true, and the two truths are not the same shape. He has taken the second one out because it has no name to stand behind it. I have put it back. When he came down the plank walk with his slate I asked him whether the figure on the notice was the figure the Hearth received, and he said the account stood, which is the Court’s way of closing a door without saying which side of it a man is on.

\subsection*{The reeve’s correction}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{In the broad standing hand, written above both the song and the Court hand:} Nine went out of the fen in Y.H. 429 and six came back, and the three who did not come back are not entered as dead, because no collector wrote them down and no slate was opened over them. We stood them at the post. That is the whole of what we could do.\end{quote}

I have left the reeve’s hand standing above the Court’s, and the Court’s above the text, and the text above the peat. A leaf kept under a board in a bog does not lie flat, and nothing written on it lies flat either.

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{At the foot, in a hand that has never been claimed:} We paid the third. We stood and let it go, which is not the same as giving it, and is the only thing in this box that I would swear to.\end{quote}

\clearpage\phantomsection\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{The Articles of the Two Knives, Being the Standing Rules of the Number-Cutters of Keld Keep for the Taking, Holding and Trying of Apprentices at the Descent and at the Mouth, with the Table of Counts, the Knife-Song Pasted Inside the Cover, Two Corrections in Borrowed Hands, and a Line at the Foot Nobody Will Own}
\CRsheetheading{The Articles of the Two Knives, Being the Standing Rules of the Number-Cutters of Keld Keep for the Taking, Holding and Trying of Apprentices at the Descent and at the Mouth, with the Table of Counts, the Knife-Song Pasted Inside the Cover, Two Corrections in Borrowed Hands, and a Line at the Foot Nobody Will Own}
{\centering\FellFont\itshape\footnotesize\color{faded} A pattern-copy kept by the woman who holds the second tin at the shaft mouth; the articles cut in short Rim clauses into Grathic letters with the endings struck off, the years and the faults set in tables of number-first order, the knife-song pasted inside the cover, one correction in the narrow upright hand of a Court survey-clerk, one in the coal-pressed hand of the master of the floor, and a line at the foot that has never been claimed · First cut on the pattern-board at the mouth in Y.H. 747, the year the Cold Pass was shut and the border fixed by men who had not walked it, and copied forward from the patterns and not from a book, which is why the rule about the stone is worn through where a hundred thumbs have wiped it and the rule about the second setting is as sharp as the day it was cut; this leaf set down in Ilmen of Y.H. 813 by the keeper of the second tin, who keeps the figures that were cut out of arms, and carried down the Rim Road in the dust of a lead cart toward Greybank, where it was copied onto the back of a spoiled shift-tally. It survives with coal smut ground into the head off the sleeve she wipes the tin with, an iron-red cross from the mine-reeve’s point against the rule about a figure the roll did not give, a warm-stone shaving shut in the fold that is still warm on the coldest morning, a bead of lead out of the Ninth Gallery, a frost-feather pressed flat between the second and third leaves and gone by noon, a clamp-scratch across the song made by a man showing his brother how the iron bites, a notch cut at the edge with a tally-knife where a word would not come, grey Ash along the outer fold off a cuff laid where no cuff has business lying, a thumb in coal dust nobody will claim, two corrections in borrowed hands, and a line at the foot that is nobody’s\par}\medskip
I keep the second tin. The first holds the figures that stand; the second holds the figures that were cut out of arms and are still asked for by somebody. A cutter comes to me for an old number the way a potter comes for a shard, and I give it without a word, because a figure kept in tin is not a figure entered on a slate. The mine-reeve enters the later and leaves the earlier in the skin. I keep the earlier in tin as well, which is a kindness nobody has asked me for and which I have entered nowhere.

These articles were first cut on the board at the mouth in the year the pass was shut. They have been copied forward from the patterns and not from a book, because a book can be carried over the pass and a pattern-board cannot. A pattern nobody has had to cut is a pattern nobody believes. These have been cut. Where a hand has corrected me I have left both readings, as an arm leaves the first figures under the second.

\subsection*{The articles as they stand at the mouth}

\subsection*{Of the taking}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item The cutters take an apprentice, not a house. The trade answers for her bread, her bed and the figures she is taught to cut; the house gives her up for four years and has her back at the end with two knives and no figure written against her. A house that will not give her up has given nothing.

\item A child is taken after her own Descent, and not before. A child who has never been cut has no business cutting: she does not know how far a figure goes, and will cut the flesh instead of the skin. The arm teaches the knife, and the arm must have been cut first.

\item She states what she holds before she says who she is, at the foot of the post and not at the table. A cutter who gives her name first is sent back to begin again. This is not pride. A name goes home at dusk; a number goes down.

\item She is kept, not hired. She eats from the cutter’s dish and sleeps in the cutter’s room, and what she earns goes to the house that sent her and comes back as bread, not as a figure in a hand.

\item No child is asked whether she wants the knife. She is asked whether she understands what she is bought for: the reading of an arm instead of a face, two sets of figures in one skin, a stone given after the cut and never before, and a hand that must not shake while the man is looking away. The wanting comes after, or it does not come; the trade has never claimed to teach that part.

\item A lowlander who asks for the knife is sent to the Duelling Floor first, to learn what the iron takes before he learns what it writes. In my years at this tin nobody has asked twice. I would not call that a rule; a rule has to be read aloud.

\end{enumerate}

\subsection*{Of the knives}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item There are two knives and never one. The first cuts a way at thirteen and belongs to the floor; the second cuts a figure and belongs to the arm that carries it. A cutter who brings the first knife above ground has taken something that was not given, and the mine-reeve will ask her once.

\item The figure goes in shallow. A cut that goes too deep is a clerk’s notion of permanence: a number is a thing said once, not a thing buried. Where a man has been counted twice, cut the later deeper and leave the earlier showing. Two sets on one arm is one man counted twice, which the Court has always liked; the arm has never been asked.

\item Speak the figure to the arm and not across the table. A figure spoken to a man turns into a question by supper, and there is no entry for a question at this mouth.

\item The stone comes after the knife, never before. A stone in the palm before the cut teaches the arm to expect mercy, and the arm will not take the figure cleanly. Give it after, and do not say whose fire warmed it. Somebody paid, and the payer is not in the room.

\end{enumerate}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{In the coal-pressed hand of the master of the floor, against rule 10:} After. Not before. I have said this to three of you and you keep putting it into the child’s hand early because she is crying. \emph{Underneath, in mine:} I have left his \emph{you} standing. He says it to the room and means the whole room. The rule is for the hand that holds the stone, and that hand is mine.\end{quote}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item Cut no figure the roll has not given. A cutter who cuts a number of her own has made a man into what he was not, which is the only way this trade can take a life without blood. The mine-reeve checks the figure in red; there is no second asking.

\item The dead are walled into the seam facing the deep, with their figures on them. No cutter goes down to correct a figure in the wall. A number follows a man where he went, and stays there.

\end{enumerate}

\subsection*{Of the arm}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item Turn the arm so the figures stand up and look at the arm, not the face. A face asks to be answered; an arm only states what was carried into the dark.

\item A hand that goes the colour of old rope below a clamp is a hand that has already paid. Do not cut a new number over a dead hand to make the roll come out even. The number stands and the hand does not, and both are entered once.

\item If a man of the Stones is at the mouth when you cut, keep the space where his answer would stand the length of a man sitting against a stone. Do not put a nought in it. A nought is a number, and he has refused numbers.

\end{enumerate}

\subsection*{The table of counts}

\emph{Kept by the woman at the tin. A figure goes in the column before a word is put beside it, which is the order of this country and not the order of a counting house.}

Year — At the tin — What is taken — What is put in its place\par

First — Lay out the patterns, turn the arm, fetch the stone after — The child’s own haste — A hand that does not shake\par

Second — Follow the knife; cut the same figure on a warm-stone shaving until the stroke comes right — The child’s own number in the sentence — The figure before the face\par

Third — Cut a second setting under the master’s eye and leave the first showing — The want to make a count come out even — Two counts kept in one skin\par

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item At the end of the third year the child cuts a second setting on an arm already counted once, with the first figures left showing and the master where he can see the point. If the new figure goes shallow or the old one is cut away, she keeps the tin for a tend and cuts nothing. There is no feast. A cutter’s trade is learned from the figures she has not changed.

\item She is given no house and no kin and is sent where the cutters send her. She takes her own number with her, which was cut before she ever held a knife, and she does not take the figures she cut into other people, which never belonged to her.

\end{enumerate}

\subsection*{Of faults and their correcting}

Fault — As corrected at the mouth\par

Name before number — Sent to the foot of the post to begin again, by a cutter and not by a clerk\par

A figure cut too deep — Left showing; no second cut over it that tend\par

The stone given before the knife — The stone taken back; none given after either\par

A shaking hand — The knife to the tin; count patterns for a tend\par

A number cut that the roll did not give — The figure cut out again; the cutter’s own number set against it in the tin\par

A second saying of a number — The second struck; the first stands\par

A question asked of the Stones — Answered once, the numbers are correct; no second asking\par

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item The last row is not a punishment and not a rule about knives. It is the only answer we have for the Stones, and it is not an answer to the question. A child who asks a second time is sent up the Rim Road to ask the Vorr herself, which is a long walk for a short sentence.

\end{enumerate}

\subsection*{The knife-song, pasted inside the cover}

\emph{Sung at the mouth on the morning a second setting is cut, with the stone still in the hand and not yet given. Nobody sings it at the Descent, and nobody says why.}

\begin{quote}\itshape Two knives and one arm,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the first cuts a way and the second a figure;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the figure goes down where the name will not,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the mine-reeve takes the later.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Cut it shallow, leave it showing,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the old five under the new five like a repair left showing;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape a hand that shakes goes to the tin\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and counts the figures it may not cut.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Four to the first and a fifth cut out,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the old one left where the new one stands;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the stone comes after, the knife comes first,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the dark keeps the number, not the face.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Two knives and one arm.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Say it to the skin, say it once;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape keep the place where the Stones do not answer\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the length of a man sitting against a stone.\end{quote}

The clamp-scratch across the third verse came from a man showing his brother how the iron bites, on a morning when nobody had a hand to stop him. Both were called honest afterwards and one has a dead hand. I have flattened the paper as well as I could.

\subsection*{What the borrowed hands did}

A survey-clerk of the Court came up with the lead cart and borrowed the leaf while the rope was going down. He writes narrow and upright and takes the verbs out as though they were things a man could carry past a weigh in his boot. He laid his hand on the leaf before he looked at me, which is the manner of that office. He set his lines above mine:

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item Against \emph{state what you hold before you say who you are}: \emph{the vessel is identified by measure at entry}, underlined twice.

\item Against \emph{the figure goes in shallow}: \emph{the marking is applied to the surface}, which is true and leaves the arm out.

\item Against \emph{cut no figure the roll has not given}: \emph{the instrument is not certified}. He has taken the hand away and left the tool, which is a thing a tool would like.

\item Against \emph{leave the earlier showing}: \emph{the prior marking is preserved but is not current}. He has made a man’s first count into a page in a file, and the file is not in this room.

\end{itemize}

I have put my words back underneath his. He takes the verbs out because a thing always true has no need of them. I put them back because a child at the mouth with a knife at her arm does not know she is hearing something always true, and wants to know which hand to hold out.

The master struck \emph{writes} out of rule 6 and set \emph{cuts} above it, saying the iron does not write and he will not have a child thinking it does. I have left \emph{writes} underneath, because a figure is a kind of writing in the only tongue this mountain uses, and a child should be able to see the word he would not let stand. He cleaned his knife while he said it, as he always does, and did not look at me.

\subsection*{At the head and in the gutter}

The smut at the head is coal off the sleeve I wipe the tin with; it goes into the grain and no wet sleeve takes it out. The cross in iron-red is off the mine-reeve’s point, laid there while he checked a man who had given a figure that would not hold; it stays red in frost. The shaving in the fold came off a piece set down and not taken up and is still warm on the coldest morning, which is the whole argument about where warmth comes from and who paid, and I have not sold it. The bead of lead rolled out of the Ninth Gallery and a surveyor laid it on the leaf and went away without it. The frost-feather grew where the Warm had lately gone out of the stone and was gone before I had finished setting it flat. The notch at the edge is where I tried to write the Keldish word for a hand that does not shake and it would not come, so I cut the edge instead. A notch stays when paper has gone and cannot be entered by a man from the factor’s house. The grey along the outer fold came off a cuff laid where no cuff has business lying; I have not swept it, and there is no Last Day at a mouth. The thumb in coal dust at the foot is not mine and not the master’s.

\subsection*{At the foot, in a hand nobody will own}

\begin{quote}\itshape The first knife gives a way. The second gives a figure.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape The arm keeps both. The slate keeps one. The stone keeps none, and is warm.\end{quote}

I asked the master of the floor, the survey-clerk and a woman cut twice, and had three answers and no hand, as I have had before. I have left the line where it was written. The leaf goes back into the second tin. Tomorrow a child will come up from her own Descent with a figure already on her arm and will be asked what she holds before she says who she is, and will learn to lay the stone in the hand after the knife and never before; and the old numbers will go on being kept in tin by nobody who asked me to keep them.

\clearpage\phantomsection\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{The Child Who Remembered the South, Being an Extract from the Dispensation-Book of the Factor’s House at Greybank Concerning the Year 766, the Thin Child Who Spoke in a Southern Voice, the Phial Bought Without a Payer, and the Page Corrected by a Physician; with the Child’s Sayings, the Corking Verse, Two Hands of Correction, and a Line at the Foot Nobody Will Own}
\CRsheetheading{The Child Who Remembered the South, Being an Extract from the Dispensation-Book of the Factor’s House at Greybank Concerning the Year 766, the Thin Child Who Spoke in a Southern Voice, the Phial Bought Without a Payer, and the Page Corrected by a Physician; with the Child’s Sayings, the Corking Verse, Two Hands of Correction, and a Line at the Foot Nobody Will Own}
{\centering\FellFont\itshape\footnotesize\color{faded} A clerk’s chronicle-extract from the dispensation-book of the factor’s house at Greybank, copied out of the tin behind the counter; the year-entries in a sloping tally hand, the physician’s page copied as it stands with the struck word still legible, the licence tallies set in a table, the child’s sayings taken down in the hearing and not translated, the corking verse sung at the counter, two corrections in borrowed hands, and a line at the foot in a hand nobody will own · Written at Greybank in the factor’s counting house in the last tend of Ash, Y.H. 812, the Thin Year, by the keeper of the dispensations, whose office stands on the factor’s roll and whose hand does not; copied from the book of phials kept in a tin behind the counter since Y.H. 683, and carried forward at the Opening of the Slates into Y.H. 813. It survives as four leaves of foolscap sewn with wire into a board cover soft at the hinge: barley dust worked into the head off a measure that went over in the granary yard, a bloom of Sallow salt along the gutter which comes and goes with the weather, a shaving of phial-cork shut in the second fold, a husk of southern grain stuck fast in the gutter, a grey Ash print along the outer fold which the keeper did not make and has not swept, a ring where a dish of barley-water stood from the first entry to the last, a small square of bare paper where a word was scraped away and no other put in, two corrections in borrowed hands, and the line at the foot\par}\medskip
I keep the dispensations in the factor’s house at Greybank. The office is on the roll and the hand is not, and when the factor wants a name for the hand he writes \emph{the counter}, which is as much as a man who sells other people’s quiet is allowed to have. This book holds what was given out and what was paid for it, which is a small account and a clean one. I have copied it for nine years and have never once had to enter a name in the purchaser’s column, because the people who buy quiet ash come from a long way up the Hearth Road and do not wish to be found by what they have forgotten.

The year 766 is the only year in the book that gives me trouble. It has no war in it, no levy and no figure worth reading aloud. It has a child, a page from a physician and a phial with nothing under the buyer’s name. I have set the three where they stand and have not joined them, because a clerk who joins three things has begun a sermon, and a sermon gets copied further than an account and lasts longer.

\subsection*{The years as the counter has them}

\emph{Copied from the tin. The entries are in the tally hand; where the physician’s page differs I have set it beneath.}

\textbf{Y.H. 763.} A thin return entered for the district of Greybank, thirty marks, paid in labour and not in coin. Entered as \emph{a provision of the poor}. Nothing unusual. The child came from the bank with the faint interest in a life it could not name that all thin returns bring, and was named at the moot and given a house and went about.

\textbf{Y.H. 766, the third working week of Stone.} A child returned thin in the year before, then about six years old, spoke words in a voice the district did not know. The hearth-maid who was called wrote them down as she heard them and could not write the voice. The physician at Greybank wrote \emph{a settling of the graft}, which is the ordinary account of the second chill and is usually true, and then wrote another phrase underneath and struck it through. The struck word is still legible where the leaf has been folded. Entered as \emph{an irregularity following upon a thin return}.

\textbf{Y.H. 766, the last tend of Stone.} One phial of quiet ash dispensed at the counter, sixty marks, entered under \emph{dispensed by the physician}, the purchaser’s column left bare and the word \emph{charity} written above it in a hand that is neither the physician’s nor mine.

\textbf{Y.H. 812.} Copied forward in the Thin Year, with the verbs put back where I found them taken out. The phial is empty. The cork is in the gutter.

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{In the narrow upright hand of a clerk of the College, against the second entry:} An imagination of the third day. Strike \emph{spoke in a voice the district did not know}.\end{quote}

I have not struck it. He has put \emph{imagination} where the voice stood, and an imagination is a thing a child makes while a voice is a thing that comes to it, and the difference is the whole of the entry. He has never in this book changed a figure, which is the only mercy a clerk of that hand is capable of.

\subsection*{What the child said}

\emph{Taken down at the hearth from the woman who was called, in her Grathic, of words she says were not Grathic when they were first said. She would not say them again after the physician came, and has given me the lengths of the pauses instead.}

\begin{quote}\itshape There was a bowl at the third hour and it went round.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape A slate was burned for a house I don’t belong to.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape I had seven names. I kept none of them.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape The fire was for a debt. They clapped when it took.\end{quote}

She said the child used the word for a public feast and the word for a debt-slate and the word for a name-day, and that it had no word for its own mother, whom it looked at as a person looks at a wall it half remembers. It could not say where the words came from. Asked what country it was in, it said the country with the fire in the middle of the court, and then said it was cold, and then said nothing more that day.

A thin return is a pooling. Many measures go into many infants, and what comes back is a stranger with a faint interest in a life it cannot name. That is what is taught and that is what the book holds. A child who speaks of seven names and a bowl at the third hour has either more than a faint interest or an interest of another kind, and the physician’s page is where the difference went to be settled.

\subsection*{The physician’s page}

\emph{Copied out of a leaf lent to me across the counter and returned before noon. The struck word is left struck.}

The woman’s account — The physician’s hand\par

Spoke in a voice not of this district — A settling of the graft; the second chill\par

Named a bowl and a burning slate — \emph{a memory of the south}, struck through\par

Could not name its mother — no remark\par

Asked to be made quiet — one phial, quiet ash, at the licence price\par

Underneath the last row, in the physician’s own hand, there is a line that is not a diagnosis: \emph{the child is not in pain and does not say it is frightened; the mother is.} I have kept it, because a physician who writes about the mother has stopped writing about the graft, and I would rather have the thing he actually saw.

\subsection*{The phial}

The licence price is sixty marks, which is a great deal of warmth for a small glass stopper, and the counter holds the tally. I have set it here as the book has it, with the empty column showing.

Year — Phials dispensed — Marks entered — Purchaser\par

Y.H. 764 — 2 — 120 — named\par

Y.H. 765 — 1 — 60 — named\par

Y.H. 766 — 1 — 60 — —\par

Y.H. 767 — 2 — 120 — named\par

The dash is not mine. It is in the book. Where the factor’s clerk came through in Ash and set \emph{charity} above the empty place, he put no name into it, and there is no name for a giver anywhere in the leaf. Sixty marks went out of this house and came back as a clean column, which is the readiest way of balancing an account I know. The phial went up the Hearth Road in a pannier with two loaves and a packet of salt, which is how quiet travels in this country: under bread.

The cork shaving in the fold came off the cork when the phial was opened, not when it was sold. It was drawn across the place where the purchaser’s name would stand, the way a man draws a cork across a table while he is deciding what to leave out. I have not taken it off. There is a small square of bare paper beside it where I scraped a word away and put no other in, which I have done once in nine years and will not do again.

\subsection*{The corking verse}

\emph{Sung at the counter by the women who bring the phials down from the Hearthseat, while a clerk writes the figure. They say a verse with the last line left out is a verse that keeps its stopper, which is the custom of that road and not an answer.}

\begin{quote}\itshape Cork the glass and shut the eye;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape what came back may go back by.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Sixty marks for a quiet night\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and a slate that never reads it right.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Do not ask who paid the score;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the count goes up and comes back four.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Keep the mouth shut, keep the name,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the child will answer to the same.\end{quote}
