I asked her what the water was for and she said it was for what the warm had left, and then said her husband had been a collector and had better leave his own answer to it. I have not put the two sentences together. A traveller who joins what a native keeps apart has made a story, and stories are what that country lives on.

\subsection*{The road-song}

\emph{Taken down in the carters’ yard at Greybank from a man who had gone up with tallow and come back with nothing, while the teams were being watered. He would not sing it with a clerk in the yard, so we went and stood by the trough.}

\begin{quote}\itshape The Clay Road ends where the granaries stand,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the Hearth Road climbs where the ground is warm;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape I carried the salt of the Sallow in a sack\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the Court booked it before the dawn.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape A hundred and forty leagues and a team gone thin,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the smoke of the Keel in the collar of the coat;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape a man pays in marks and is paid in a look,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the notice reads one in twelve by the door.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Nine wells in the stone and four under key,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the steam goes up where the cat would sit;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the city keeps warm what it takes from the road,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the road keeps the ruts and the sweat and the bit.\end{quote}

He said there was a fourth verse and that it was not a song verse but a saying, and he would not give it. I have left the place for it at the head of the leaf, scored with my nail and empty.

\subsection*{What the clerks made of it}

Two hands have been at the dockets besides mine. The first is the narrow upright hand of the College, borrowed at Greybank, which took the verbs out of what I had written about the rooms and left the room standing with nobody in it.

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item At \emph{a woman sitting facing the wall with her hands in her lap} it wrote \emph{one vessel, seated, orientation to wall}.

\item At \emph{she looks at the cup to learn that it has gone cold} it wrote \emph{observation of temperature, no affect recorded}.

\item At \emph{the people in them} it set \emph{the party is retained} above, which puts a figure where I put a person. I have left both standing.

\end{itemize}

The second hand is the factor’s clerk’s, who does not write in charcoal and cannot abide it. He has put \emph{road figures, informal} against my table and drawn a line under the wells, which is his way of saying a man may copy a song but not a place. He has not struck a word. I would rather a man struck a word and wrote his own above it.

\subsection*{At the head and in the gutter}

The white in the gutter is salt off the dockets and came honestly by its place. The tallow at the head is off the lamp in the yard at Greybank, where I wrote the song after the teams were watered and the clerk had gone to his supper. The grey along the outer fold came off a surveyor’s cuff; he would not sit down, and I have not swept it. The filings in the second crease are off a hinge they were mending in the yard and got into the fold when I shut the leaf on them. The ring by the song is small ale, left from the first line to the last. The green bead is pressed into the lower corner because a girl put it there and I had no pocket that would hold it safely. The square of bare paper is where I scraped out the fourth verse and put nothing in its place, which is the only square in this account that I made myself.

\subsection*{At the foot, in a hand nobody will own}

\begin{quote}\itshape The road keeps the ruts and the tax keeps the figure;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the Hall keeps the fire and gives no man a light.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape A man pays what is asked and is told what was paid.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Ask the cup how it learned that the water was cold.\end{quote}

I asked the man with the slate, the coal-woman and the teamster, and had three answers and no hand. I have left the lines where they were written.

The dockets go back into the nail-box under the factor’s counter. Next tend the road opens and there is tallow going up and iron coming down, and a team that is willing, and a man who has not said yes yet but has a wife who counts marks the way the Court counts measures. That is how a third journey is decided in a house like mine. Not by a figure on a notice, but by a woman at a table with a loaf going short.

\clearpage\phantomsection\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{The Warm Within, Being a Book of Remedies Gathered in Low Kiln}
\CRsheetheading{The Warm Within, Being a Book of Remedies Gathered in Low Kiln}
{\centering\FellFont\itshape\footnotesize\color{faded} A hearth-maid’s book of household physic for births, chills, burns, coughs, bites and the second chill; the remedies in Grathic, with a Court clerk’s corrections in Ledgerhand and one song for the third night · Set down in Low Kiln in Sill between Y.H. 809 and Y.H. 812, the Long Cold and the Thin Year, by a hearth-maid of the district who attended births and put no name to a book an officer might read; written in charcoal and tallow on the backs of spoiled birth-slates and on a quire of sauce-stained paper from the factor’s house at Greybank, sewn with wire into a board cover. It survives behind the meal bin of a house east of the Clay Yard, soft at the fold: a bone-pale slip thumb at the head, a tallow print where a mother held it down in a draught, a green bead of glaze from a girl with sweetness at her mouth, a grey Ash print along the gutter, a streak of barley grease, one correction in the narrow hand of a Court clerk who borrowed the leaf on an Account-day, and one line struck out and written again in the writer’s own hand. Copied forward in Ilmen, Y.H. 813, with the verbs left where she put them.\par}\medskip
I write on the backs of birth-slates spoiled by a late entry, which is paper enough for a book that nobody has asked to see. I am a hearth-maid of this district. I have set down what I do and what the women before me did, and where the two disagree I have left both standing. A remedy is a thing a body has already paid for. A woman who strikes a line out of a book of physic is answerable for the next body that takes it.

My hand is not a clerk’s. I put verbs where a clerk would take them out, and I have not corrected this, because a direction without a verb is a thing a man can read aloud at a table and a woman cannot use at a birth. The tallow print at the top came from a mother who held the sheet down in a draught and did not know she marked it. The slip thumb is mine. I signed in slip because I have no slate-name, and a thumb in slip is how this yard signs a pot.

\subsection*{The order of a birth room}

\emph{Written small at the head in charcoal, with one word gone over in tallow.}

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item Warm the stone first. A common river stone out of the neighbour’s fire, in a fold of wool, tested on your own wrist before it goes to a belly. It is not a warm-stone and I will not put that word on it; the Keldish stone is another thing and no house here owns one. A cold stone is a stone, not a kindness.

\item Bank the fire but do not cover it. A birth needs somewhere for the heat to go.

\item Set the slate face down on the bench before you go to the child. The hand that writes is not the hand that holds. If there is nobody else to write, write after, and enter within three days as the ordinance says. Do not ask why the third day is a bad day to choose. It is a bad day to choose and that is the whole of it.

\item Wash in this order: face, neck, groin, knees, cord. Do not hurry the cord. It knows its own hour better than you do.

\item At the red flower, cross two fingers at the corner of it and say nothing. If someone asks, give a date. Dates are safe. The Court likes a date and does not ask what it covers.

\item Leave the grey in the corner. Sweeping it into a pail does not make it gone, and the Court has a word for gone that I have never seen happen.

\item When the bell goes at the Cross, stop and start again after. It is counting something that is not your room.

\end{itemize}

I have done four hundred births and I still lay my hand on the slate first. I have tried to stop doing it. It is a trick the room plays on a maid, and after the first hundred you stop calling it a habit and start calling it the order of things.

\subsection*{The second chill}

The third day is a bad day. A child that has taken a chill will grow worse on it, and if the entry was made on that day the worsening goes down as a birth and stands as a birth for the rest of the child’s life. This is entered nowhere in the ordinance and the ordinance has no place for it. We call it the second chill. The physician at Greybank calls it a settling of the graft, which is a kinder phrase and costs less.

In Y.H. 651 a physician at Greybank struck a word out of his own report and paid the hearth-maid who had written it for her trouble. The word has not come down to us. I have asked three older women and had three dates and no word. I have left the place where the word would stand, which is the right length for a word of that kind.

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{The narrow hand of the Court clerk wrote above this paragraph:} The worsening is a settling of the graft. No chill is entered. Entered as a birth, not a worsening.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Under it, in mine:} Worse before dusk. Warm and breathing was all I set down. Both stand.\end{quote}

\subsection*{Remedies, as they are used}

Trouble — What is set to it — The manner of it — Who pays\par

A newborn gone cold — A river stone warmed at a neighbour’s fire, in wool — To the belly, never the feet. Change it when it goes cold in your own hand, not when the child stops crying. — The neighbour’s fire. Repay with a crust, and do not call the crust a gift.\par

The second chill — Warmth, quiet, and a slate turned face down — Skin to skin under the shawl, barley water by the spoon, watch kept till the fourth day. Do not send for the collector because the child has got worse; that is what the day does. — The household, one night’s sleep and a loaf.\par

Cough off the pits — Barley water steamed under a cloth — Steam to the mouth, not the face. A hand over the mouth when it comes up, so the wall does not get it. — The pot and the fuel under it.\par

A burn from the kiln — Tallow first, then a clean fold — Cool it with tallow and keep the air from it. The old women lay wet slip on a burn: the slip cools while it is wet and cooks when it dries. I have left their line standing under mine. — Whoever opened the kiln, if the house can bear to ask.\par

A wound the salt will hold — Salt from the herring barrel on a feather — A brine-gull’s feather is better if you live near the coast and can bear to take it. In Low Kiln we use what the barrel gives. It is a brute method and it often works. — The barrel.\par

A bite from a bone-hound — Nothing I know — Keep him from the orchard. Salt does not hold that bite and neither does tallow. A dog that has eaten the little graves puts the grey into a wound and the wound will not close. — Nobody. This is the honest column.\par

The sweet sickness — A cup set down and not taken up — There is no physic for it. The glaze is sweet and the sweetness is the sickness. Stop the cup, if the house can afford to stop the cup. Most cannot. — The glaze room, which cannot pay and does not ask.\par

Kiln’s breath in a closed room — An open window — It spoils the glaze. The potters leave the window shut and call a death in sleep a merciful one, which is a phrase for people who have not had to identify the body. — The man who sleeps.\par

A child emptied by leeches — Nothing. Do not set them. — A silt-leach out of the shallows draws as the collector draws and without a slate. A child can be emptied by a handful in an hour. If you find them on a child, take them off and count them, and do not put them back. — Whoever put them there.\par

Milk that will not come — A warm stone and another woman to hold the child — Let the mother sleep while the child is held. The other woman’s own child goes a little colder for it. Say so. A kindness that has no payer is a kindness somebody else has paid for already. — The other woman’s child.\par

A physician from the College wrote in Y.H. 641 that the sweetness came from the lead in the glaze, and the copy that came back to us had the word taken out. I have seen the pale line at the gum. I have seen the hand that cannot hold a cup. I have not seen the lead, and I do not set down what I have not seen; but I have set down that a man wrote it and that it was taken away, because a thing taken away twice is a thing worth leaving a place for.

\subsection*{The full note}

Tap a sound pot with the knuckle and it answers full. Tap a cracked one and it answers flat, a small dead sound that stops at the surface and will not go through. This is a thing the kiln-masters keep and the rest of us borrow when a pot is set down on a bench.

Once, in a birth room, a cup across the room gave the flat note while nobody touched it. I did not say what it was. There was a woman in labour and a slate on the bench and no advantage in adding a third thing to the room. I have written it here because a thing heard in a birth room and never mentioned is still a thing heard.

Do not knock a person to try it. A body is not a pot and the note of it is not ours to take. I knew a woman who tapped the chest of a child gone thin and said she had heard nothing back, and she said it as though the child had refused her. The child had not refused her. There was simply nothing there for her to hear.

A woman of the drying racks told me of a pot set down that answered nearly full --- a note between the two, almost the full one and never quite. I have not heard it and I have written it down because she was not a woman who made things up, and because a note that is almost full may be a thing a household could live with, if it came to that.

\subsection*{The song for the third night}

\emph{Sung low, to the child, while the watch is kept. The room says the last line with her.}

\begin{quote}\itshape The stone goes cold before the milk,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the milk goes cold before the bread;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape a body is a pot with a flaw\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the flaw is where the heat has fled.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Warm the flaw and warm the pot,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape warm the place where the heat is not;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape four for the corners, four for the wall,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and one that does not answer when you call.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Three days, three nights, a watch kept true;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape what comes back is not what went;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape sing to the child, sing to the cold,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and come back warm. Come back as you can.\end{quote}

There is a space before the last line in the singing. I have left it on the page. It is the same space the kiln keeps and the bell keeps, and I have never filled it and never will.

\subsection*{What the narrow hand did}

A clerk borrowed the leaf on an Account-day and struck out my verbs. Where I wrote \emph{the heat went out of him}, he set \emph{the measure was drawn} above and left mine under it, saying that a book of physic is not a slate and need not be true in the same way. He wrote \emph{deduction} against the warmed stone and \emph{one in twelve, as the notice says} against the night’s watch. He put a round nought in the space before the last line of the song and wrote \emph{vacancy} beside it. I have put the words back under his and left his standing. He has a figure for everything and a place for nothing.

There is a line at the foot in a hand I do not know, struck through and written again underneath: \emph{Nothing is lost that we have kept.} It is not a remedy. It has no business in a book of physic. It is in the book now, and when I copy the leaf in Ilmen I shall copy it again, in that hand and not my own, as it stands.

\subsection*{At the foot}

The grey along the gutter came off my own cuff when I measured the ridge in a room two doors down and came back to write. The barley grease is from a crust laid on the leaf while a child was being told to eat and would not. The green bead is not slip. A girl with sweetness still at her mouth leaned over to see the writing and touched the paper and said nothing and went back to her work. I have not washed any of it.

The book goes back behind the meal bin. A slate is a thing that gets carried into the square and read in a clean voice; this is a thing that gets carried under an apron and taken out when the room is quiet. If an officer ever finds it, let him strike out what he will. The next woman will put the verbs back, as I did, and warm the stone before she reads.

\clearpage\phantomsection\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{The Stone Against the Belly, Being the Sayings of the Hearth-Maids of Grath, Gathered at the Birth-Slate Bench in Sill and Glossed for a Girl Who Has Not Yet Held a Newborn}
\CRsheetheading{The Stone Against the Belly, Being the Sayings of the Hearth-Maids of Grath, Gathered at the Birth-Slate Bench in Sill and Glossed for a Girl Who Has Not Yet Held a Newborn}
{\centering\FellFont\itshape\footnotesize\color{faded} A hearth-maid’s gathering of the proverbs, bench-instructions, slate-warnings and small refusals of the women who deliver and enter the children of Grath, set in the common tongue on the backs of birth-slates spoiled by a figure put in the wrong column; the sayings said low to the stone, the slate and the fire, the glosses in the writer’s own charcoal, with a collector’s clerk’s correction in narrow upright Ledgerhand, an old woman’s addition in broad charcoal, and one line at the foot in a hand nobody will own · Gathered at the birth-slate bench in her own house in Sill through Ash and Stone of Y.H. 812, the Thin Year, and written up in the Five at the turn into Y.H. 813 by Dessa Marsh, a hearth-maid who has delivered children in Low Kiln and at the Cross for two and twenty years and keeps the birth-slate book because the Court pays her to; written in charcoal on the backs of spoiled birth-slates washed with barley-water, sewn with wire into a fold of old wool and kept under the loose board beside the bench; carried once to Slate Row in Ilmen of Y.H. 813 where a collector’s clerk borrowed it and set his hand above hers. It survives with charcoal ground into the head, a tallow thumb at the fold, a barley-water ring gone dark, a browned crust pressed flat between the second and third leaves, a hair from a newborn’s head shut in the gutter, a small-ale ring, a scratch of cold-iron filings, grey Ash along the outer fold which the writer did not make and has not swept, and the line at the foot which nobody has claimed\par}\medskip
I have delivered children in this town for two and twenty years, and kept the book of their births for nine. The book lies on the bench under my apron when I am not using it, and a girl come up from the clay yard asked me once what I wrote in it. I told her figures. She asked what else. I told her the sayings my mother said while she held the basin, which are not in the book and never will be, because a magistrate cannot enter them and the Court does not pay for them.

So I have put them here, on the backs of slates that went wrong. A slate with a figure in the wrong column can be washed with barley-water and written over, which is a mercy the Court allows to stone and to nobody else. Say these low. Say them to the stone, the slate, the fire and the bench, and to a person last. Said looking at a person, a saying becomes a question with an answer owed, and there is no answer owed in any of them.

The Court has paid us since seven hundred eighty-two to write a birth within three days. Before that we wrote when we had a mind to, which was usually the day after. We objected when they came with the order, and they paid us, and the objection stopped. I have set that down because a girl should know that the hand which writes the slate is the same hand that holds her, and that it is paid by two houses at once.

\subsection*{Of the stone and the first warmth}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item “Warm the stone on your own wrist before you put it to the child.”

\end{enumerate}

\emph{Gloss — The first thing taught and the last thing checked. A stone taken from the warm place behind the hearth and laid straight on a newborn takes more than it gives, and a child has little enough to be taken from. Hold it inside the cuff against the inside of the wrist until your own flesh says it is ready. This is also said of a cradle, a bed, and a word you mean to say to a woman who has just lost one.}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item “A child comes cold and wanting. That is the whole of its case.”

\end{enumerate}

\emph{Gloss — Not a prayer and not a complaint. It is the account a midwife can make without a slate. They come with a mouth and no way to keep a breath warm, and the whole trade of the house is to answer those two facts until the child can answer them itself. I have said it to mothers who wanted a reason and fathers who wanted a price, and neither has ever thanked me for it.}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item “The third day is the one to sit by.”

\end{enumerate}

\emph{Gloss — A child that has been rekindled grows worse on the third day before it grows better. This is the second chill, and it is ordinary, and the physicians have a longer name for it which they use when no hearth-maid is in the room. We keep the stone to the child. We keep it anyway. A woman who has had four will sit up through the third night without being asked; a woman who has had one will ask whether it is always so, and will be told yes.}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item “A stone kept warm is a stone paid for.”

\end{enumerate}

\emph{Gloss — Somebody sat near a fire for it. Ask who, and you will be told to ask the fire, which is an answer given by people who asked the same thing at their own first birth. I have never known a household to enter the stone on a slate. That is the one thing about warmth this town has never thought to charge for, which is why I have put the saying first.}

\subsection*{Of the name and the slate}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item “Write within three days or the Court writes for you.”

\end{enumerate}

\emph{Gloss — Ever since the order of seven hundred eighty-two. If the hearth-maid reaches the bench first the child has the name the house wants; if the collector reaches it first the child has the name the slate can hold, and the house finds out at the next market. We are paid to arrive first, a strange arrangement.}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item “Give the child a name you can say in the dark.”

\end{enumerate}

\emph{Gloss — Grathic names are tools and materials and small domestic things, not poems. Clay, stone, reed, a hand, a bird. A name you need a slate to remember is a Court name, and a Court name goes wherever the slate goes, which is sometimes up the Clay Road and not back. I have written this because a girl asked me what to call a child born in the dark before the lamp was found, and I could not give her a better answer.}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item “No house-name, no hearth. No hearth, no name that lasts.”

\end{enumerate}

\emph{Gloss — A foundling is given a name by whoever writes first and has no house-name until a hearth claims it. That is how a person is kept from inheriting a debt he did not make, which is a kindness done with a pen. We say this to the door after the mother has stopped asking, never to the child. The child will find out soon enough which column it is written in.}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item “Break a birth-slate and you have bought a year in the yard.”

\end{enumerate}

\emph{Gloss — The penalty. Some break them anyway, usually in a kiln, where a slate takes four minutes and leaves nothing to enter. The household’s name then goes into a second column which the hearth-maids do not read aloud and the Court does not print. I have kept the saying because I was asked once whether a slate could be unmade, and the true answer cost a woman a year of her life to find out.}

\subsection*{Of the collector}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item “The tube goes to the arm, not to the face. Do not watch the face.”

\end{enumerate}

\emph{Gloss — The draw is small. There is iron, a small hiss, and grey at the collector’s fingertips afterwards, and the mother watches the arm because the face has stopped being a place where answers live. I hold the child and I watch the mother, which is the whole of my office at that hour. This is not a saying for a father to hear. He will remember the face anyway.}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item “What is drawn at the birth is not kept at the birth.”

\end{enumerate}

\emph{Gloss — On the Hearth Drawing a collector may take from the dying and the newly born on the same day. We say this to the slate, which has no answer in it. A woman once asked where her child’s first warmth went, and I told her the figure was booked and the account stood, because those were the words I was paid to use, and then put a stone in her hand so that she would have something to do with it.}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item “The maid holds the child. The slate holds the figure. Neither looks at the other.”

\end{enumerate}

\emph{Gloss — An arrangement, not a bargain, and no better than one. The house trusts a hearth-maid to come into a room where it will not let an officer come, and pays the officer to write what the maid has seen. I have kept both hands in this sentence because I have had to use both.}

\subsection*{Of the fire and the bread}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item “Every fire in the valley is lit from one fire nobody lit.”

\end{enumerate}

\emph{Gloss — At Kindling each hearth touches its flame from the carried coal, and nobody says where the first coal was kept through the Five or who sat up with it. Ask the fire. A fire tells nothing, which is why the answer has lasted so long.}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item “Bake on the Last Day. Do not sweep.”

\end{enumerate}

\emph{Gloss — Bread is baked and the grey in the corners is left where it lies and burnt the next morning. The floor shows where it stood by daylight after, which is the only honesty the floor has. In the Fenmarch they bottle the grey and sell it, and in the Hearthseat they bottle it for the rich, and here we burn it and say it is dealt with. I have written this at the end of the section because it is the one saying in this leaf I would rather not have had cause to know.}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item “Give the child the browned crust. The burnt outside is the part that keeps.”

\end{enumerate}

\emph{Gloss — What the kitchens of Low Kiln give to children, and considered kindness. The soft inside is for the working hands. A girl from the clay yard told me this at her own first firing, and I have set it down in her words because mine would have made it a lesson.}

\subsection*{What the women are for}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item “We come before the officer and after the priest.”

\end{enumerate}

\emph{Gloss — The midwife at the birth, the keeper of the book at the bench, the woman with the stone on the third night. The collector comes after, and the priest at the end. We are paid by the house and by the Court, which is two payments and only one of them a wage. Put this at a bench and not at a table.}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item “At the birth-flower a cross is made and nothing is said.”

\end{enumerate}

\emph{Gloss — Every maid I know does it. My mother did it before me, and I have never once said what I saw, and neither did she. A girl who wants to know what the cross is for should ask her own mother, if her mother is still living, which is the answer I was given.}

\subsection*{The bench-song}

\emph{Said low, going from house to house at dusk with the book under the apron, not at the birth and not at the third night. The fifth line of the second part is held, and the space after it is the length of a held breath. Nobody fills it.}

\begin{quote}\itshape One for the wrist and one for the fold,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape one for the name that the father will hold;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape three days to write and a cross at the flower,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the stone goes cold in the cold hour.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Warm it, warm it, the old ones say,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the third day takes what the first gave away;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape one for the pot and one for the door,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape *\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape The slate goes up and the child stays here,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the figure goes up and the face stays here;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape hold the stone and hold your tongue,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the book comes home with the name in it.\end{quote}

\emph{Gloss — The held line is not a fifth day and not a fifth name. Girls ask and are told to ask the stone, which is what their mothers were told. The clerk from Slate Row put a round nought in the space and wrote *not entered} beneath it. A nought is a figure. The space was a breath, which is a thing no office has ever counted.*

\subsection*{What the clerk did}

A collector’s clerk borrowed the leaf at Slate Row on an Account-day, with ink settled in two fingers of a soft cuff. He writes narrow and upright and takes the doer out of every sentence, as though a thing with nobody in it were truer than a thing a woman had done with her hands.

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item At \emph{warm the stone on your own wrist}, he wrote \emph{the vessel is warmed by an external source}, and underlined it. Mine stands beneath. His sentence is true in a room with no child in it.

\item At \emph{the third day is the one to sit by}, he wrote \emph{the afterdrop is observed}. He has taken away the sitting, which is the part that costs somebody a night.

\item At \emph{we come before the officer and after the priest}, he wrote \emph{attendance is recorded}, which is a thing I have never seen done for a woman holding a basin.

\item At the held line he put the round nought. I have left it where he set it and put the breath back underneath.

\end{itemize}

I have put the sayings back under his hand. He takes the verbs out because a thing always true has no need of anybody doing it. I put them back because a girl at a first birth wants to know which hand to hold the stone with.

\subsection*{In the margin, in an old woman’s broad charcoal}

\begin{quote}\itshape I have had six. The stone never warmed one that was cold from the beginning. It warms the hand that holds it, which is something, and I have held six hands.\end{quote}

I have not asked which six, and she has not said. There is room in the margin for what she did not write, and I have left the room.

\subsection*{At the head and in the gutter}

The charcoal at the head is mine; I held the slate down on the bench with the hand I write with. The tallow thumb is from the lamp set too near the book one winter when the wick would not trim. The barley-water ring went dark in the three days it took me to find the word for what a thin child’s hand does at an empty cup; I have not washed it. The crust between the leaves was given by a woman of Low Kiln who would not take a mark for it, and the brown edge has gone into the grain. The hair is a newborn’s, swept off the bench and shut in the gutter. The iron scratch came off a tube-case set down hard beside the book by a man who did not apologise. The grey along the outer fold came off a cuff laid where no cuff has business lying in a room where children are born. I have not swept it, and there is a Last Day for it, though it is not this one.

\subsection*{At the foot, in a hand nobody will own}

\begin{quote}\itshape We hold what we cannot keep.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape We write what we cannot say.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape The slate goes where the child does not.\end{quote}

I asked a woman who has delivered forty, a clerk come down from Slate Row, and a man who carries the tube, and had three answers and no hand. I have left the lines where they were written. The book goes back under the loose board beside the bench. Tomorrow there will be a birth below the sill, or there will not, and I shall warm a stone on my own wrist before I go, and write within three days whatever the house and the Court between them decide the child is to be called.

\clearpage\phantomsection\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{The Little Litany of the Return, Being the Questions Put to the Little Ones at the Wash-Hearth Below the Sill, with Their Answers as They Give Them, the Dame’s Rubrics, a Clerk’s Correction, a Mother’s Margin, and the Line at the Foot Which Was Never Taught}
\CRsheetheading{The Little Litany of the Return, Being the Questions Put to the Little Ones at the Wash-Hearth Below the Sill, with Their Answers as They Give Them, the Dame’s Rubrics, a Clerk’s Correction, a Mother’s Margin, and the Line at the Foot Which Was Never Taught}
{\centering\FellFont\itshape\footnotesize\color{faded} A catechism of the Return said at the wash-hearth in Low Kiln, the dame asking and the children answering, the answer held through a silence the dame will not fill; set down by the dame who keeps the hearth with the manner of it, eight stations and their answer, a College clerk’s correction in narrow upright Ledgerhand, a mother’s note in the margin, a child’s crooked mark, and a line at the foot nobody will own · Written in Low Kiln of Sill in the last tend of Ash, Y.H. 812, the Thin Year, by Wenna, who keeps the wash-hearth below the sill and teaches the little ones their first words of the Keeping, in charcoal on the back of a broken slip-tray tally spoiled by a wet thumb, folded with a copper bit shut in the crease and kept among the hearth things under the third flagstone; corrected in Ilmen of Y.H. 813 by a clerk of the College come up from the assessor’s house in Slate Row; copied forward once into a quire of birch bark. It survives with tallow worked into the grain at the head, pale slip along the gutter, a grey Ash print off a child’s cuff, a ring of sour milk on the second leaf, a charred edge where the leaf lay too near the banked coals, one word scraped away with a knife and not replaced, a crooked mark in a child’s hand, the clerk’s correction standing above the words it corrects, and a line struck through and written again very small underneath in a hand that has never come forward.\par}\medskip
I keep the wash-hearth below the sill and I teach the little ones their first words. They come to me before they can hold a spoon, and what I put in their mouths first is not bread but the Return; that is the order the Keeping settled on long before I was born, that the Return is the first thing a child learns and the last thing a dying person hears. I have never seen the last thing. I have seen the first, every morning, with the pots still wet and the rake marks in the hearth not yet cooled over. I have taught it for thirty-one winters and I have never once had a child say it the way the book has it, which is the whole reason I have set this down. The book’s answers arrive clean. Children’s answers arrive with the slip still on them.

A clerk from the College come up from the assessor’s house in Slate Row borrowed the leaf on a morning when I had coals out for the wash and took the verbs out of it and put a figure against the silence, and I have put both back where they stood, his hand above mine and mine under it, the way the flagstone keeps the hearth’s old crack under the new mortar. A mother who comes to the hearth with a child that came back last year has written in the margin and I have not asked her to explain. At the foot there is a line that was never taught to anybody and I have not found the hand.

The tallow at the head is mine, from holding the leaf over the banked coals to dry the charcoal; it has gone into the grain and no wash takes it out. The pale along the gutter is slip off an apron, not Ash, and I have kept it because there is enough grey in this house without bringing a stranger’s into it. The grey print came off a child’s cuff where a child’s cuff has no business, on a hearth that is counted. The milk ring is sour and will stay sour. The charred edge is where I laid the leaf too near the coals and lets any reader know it has been used, which a clean leaf can never claim. One word I scraped away with a knife on the morning the clerk came and I have not written it back. There is a crooked mark in the corner made by a child who could not yet make a letter and wanted one all the same. I have left it.

\subsection*{The manner of the teaching, written small at the head}

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item Say it at the wash-hearth, after the pots are put away and before the coals are banked. A child taught over a pot learns the pot and not the words.

\item The little ones sit on their heels with their hands on the warm stone. A hand on the stone is a hand not in the ash.

\item I ask; they answer. The answer is the same at every station, which is why it is a litany and not a lesson. They say it badly and I do not correct the saying, only the order.

\item After “we come back” there is a silence the length of a name. They are told not to fill it. One of them fills it every morning and I have stopped pretending not to hear.

\item Do not say it to a collector. If a collector is on the road, give him the tally and not the leaf. He cannot enter what a child says with her hands on the stone.

\item Twelve bits to a mark and twenty marks to a crown. An ember is five marks in the Court’s book. No child at this hearth has held an ember and I tell them so, because a figure they cannot hold is a figure they will believe.

\end{itemize}

\subsection*{The litany}

\emph{I ask. The children answer. Between the question and the answer the hearth does the rest.}

\subsection*{I. Of the first thing}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Dame:} What is learned first?\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Before the spoon, before the pot,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape before the hand can hold the bread,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the Return. It is put in the mouth\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape before the breast is put there.\end{quote}

\emph{Answer:} We are kept; we are counted; we come back.

\subsection*{II. Of the breaking}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Dame:} How did the world go?\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape The world was fired whole and the lid went up in one anger.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape The Warm ran out where no wall held it\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and went into the cold that keeps nothing.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Do not go looking for the crack in the floor.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape The crack has a name. Say it once.\end{quote}

\emph{Answer:} We are kept; we are counted; we come back.

\subsection*{III. Of the Nine}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Dame:} Who went after what ran away?\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Nine hands, and they drove the repairs home\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the way a potter drives a staple.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Name them by their number, not by their houses.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Nine went. One is still abroad.\end{quote}

\emph{Answer:} We are kept; we are counted; we come back.

\subsection*{IV. Of the iron}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Dame:} What comes up the Clay Road?\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape A man with a cold tube and a slate.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape His hand goes to the slate before his eye goes to the person.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape The iron does not keep. It opens a way.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape The slate keeps, and what it keeps is not the person.\end{quote}

\emph{One of the children said this last as “what it keeps is not the person” before I had taught it to her, and I have not corrected her, because I did not teach it to her.}

\emph{Answer:} We are kept; we are counted; we come back.

\subsection*{V. Of the figure}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Dame:} What does the bell say?\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Four, and four, and nothing.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Twelve bits to the mark and one in twelve for the fire,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape as the notice says, read twice, printed, not leaning.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Count embers, not years; a year is a pot nobody weighs.\end{quote}

\emph{Here the children say “and nobody crosses himself,” which is not in the litany and is true. I have left it standing where they said it.}

\emph{Answer:} We are kept; we are counted; we come back.

\subsection*{VI. Of the pouring}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Dame:} What comes back in the cradle?\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape One measure into one vessel: he comes back with his name\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the handle of the cup and the price of bread.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Many into many: they come back as they can,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape with a hankering for a table they never sat at.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Both are poured. Both go into a clean hand.\end{quote}

\emph{Answer:} We are kept; we are counted; we come back.

\subsection*{VII. Of the Kept}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Dame:} Who is past wanting?\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Fewer than twenty, kept near the fire.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape They do not feel the cold and do not ask for bread.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Stand a moment at their place and do not ask them if they are warm;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape they will say no, and you will have spent your only question.\end{quote}

\emph{Answer:} We are kept; we are counted; we come back.

\subsection*{VIII. Of the coming back}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Dame:} What is left in the corner?\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape The grey. It is left where it lies on the Last Day\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and taken in the morning and called dealt with.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Do not sweep it. A thing left in place is still a thing kept.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Come back as you can. Come back to your own fire.\end{quote}

\emph{Answer:} We are kept; we are counted; we come back.

\emph{The silence after the last answer is the length of a name. I have kept it the length it is.}

\subsection*{What the clerk did}

A clerk of the College borrowed the leaf with ink in two fingers and the cuffs of his coat soft from washing. He writes in the narrow upright hand and takes verbs out as another man might take bones out of a fish, and sets a figure where a person stood.

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item At \emph{before the breast is put there}, he wrote: \emph{the faculty of retention is instructed before weaning.} Above mine. I have put the breast back underneath, because a child at this hearth knows which came first and will not be argued out of it by a man who was weaned in Slate Row.

\item At \emph{the crack has a name. Say it once}, he wrote: \emph{the First Breaking is a mystery of the faith and not a place in a room.} I have left my line standing under his. There is a seam in the Keel behind the cistern and I have seen it mended twice; I have not told him so, and he has not asked.

\item At \emph{his hand goes to the slate before his eye goes to the person}, he wrote: \emph{the officer proceeds in the order of his office.} This is true in the same way that a knife is true. I have left both.

\item At the bell, against \emph{and nobody crosses himself}, he put a round nought and wrote \emph{observance not recorded.} It is the only honest thing he wrote all morning, and it cost him nothing to say it, because a nought has never had a hand in it.

\item At the pouring, against \emph{a hankering for a table they never sat at}, he wrote: \emph{residual attachment; value nil.} I have put the verb back and left his above it. He cannot say why a child turns toward a cup before the cup is shown; I cannot either; the child can, and is not asked.

\item At the answer, against the silence, he wrote \emph{vacancy} and numbered it one. He has entered the name-shaped space, which is more than the children have done. I have put the space back where it was.

\end{itemize}

I have left every line of his standing above mine. He takes the verbs out because a thing always true has no need of them. I put them back because a child who has just learned the words will ask me who did the keeping, and a woman at a wash-hearth has to answer with something in the sentence.

\subsection*{What the mother put in the margin}

The slanting hand is Annet’s, who comes to the hearth with a child that came back last year in a thin pouring from three districts she will not name. She has written where I set the sixth station:

\begin{quote}\itshape “He turns his mouth toward the cup before it is shown. The three who went into him are not here to be asked which one he wants, and I am the only one who remembers that there were three. I have said the answer with the rest of you for a year, and I have never once said the last word of it as if I knew what it meant.”\end{quote}

And at the silence, underneath the clerk’s nought:

\begin{quote}\itshape “Not a vacancy. A place set at the table.”\end{quote}

I have copied her as she wrote it. She has taken her child home and I have not gone after her with a correction.

\subsection*{At the head and in the gutter}

The tallow is mine and goes on working further into the fold each winter. The slip is the wash-apron’s and is the colour of the floor under the pots; a child who leans on the leaf leaves it without knowing, which is how most things get onto a leaf. The Ash came off a cuff on a hearth that is counted and I have not swept it, though I have swept the hearth twice since. The milk ring has gone sour and a sour ring lasts longer than a sweet one, which is a fact about milk and not about the Keeping. The charred edge lets a reader know the leaf has lain near a fire, which is the only certificate this hearth can give. The scraped word was gone before I knew what I had written; I have not put it back and I have not forgotten the length of it. The crooked mark is a child’s first attempt at a letter and is not a letter. I have put the leaf where the child can find it again, under the third flagstone with the copper bit shut in the crease, and I have never moved either.

\subsection*{At the foot, in a hand nobody will own}

Struck through once and written again underneath, very small, in a hand that is not mine, not the clerk’s and not Annet’s:

\begin{quote}\itshape The children learn the figure before the name.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape They never learn the road between.\end{quote}

I asked the clerk, a mother at the hearth, a collector come up the Clay Road and a child with slip on her hands, and had four answers and no hand. I have left the struck line where it was struck. The leaf goes back under the third flagstone and in the morning they will sit on their heels with their hands on the warm stone and I shall ask the eight questions and they will answer badly and I shall leave the silence the length of a name, and the ones who cannot yet say it will be taught, as I was, before they can hold a spoon.

\clearpage\phantomsection\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{Of the Weighing and the Reading of the Year’s Measures, Being the Ordinance Copied Out of the College Book in Slate Row for the Clerk Who Keeps the Notice Beside the Weighing Hall, with the Figures as They Were Read, the Fire Behind the Grating, the Vorr’s One Sentence Set at the Edge, and a Line at the Foot Nobody Will Own}
\CRsheetheading{Of the Weighing and the Reading of the Year’s Measures, Being the Ordinance Copied Out of the College Book in Slate Row for the Clerk Who Keeps the Notice Beside the Weighing Hall, with the Figures as They Were Read, the Fire Behind the Grating, the Vorr’s One Sentence Set at the Edge, and a Line at the Foot Nobody Will Own}
{\centering\FellFont\itshape\footnotesize\color{faded} An extract from the Court’s ordinances, written out for the notice-board beside the Weighing Hall in the Hearthseat, with the marginal hand of the under-clerk who carries the day’s figures up to the Steward’s room; the articles in Ledgerhand and the verbs restored beneath them, the order of the day and the figures in tables, the form of a reading left blank, the stair-song pasted inside the board, a scorch off the grating, two corrections in borrowed hands, and a line at the foot nobody has claimed · Copied at the Hearthseat on the Keel on Weighing of Y.H. 812, the second of the Five, the day the year’s measures are read aloud in Slate Row; written by the under-clerk who keeps the printed notice and carries the figures to the Steward’s room, from the ordinance book held by the College of Assessors; carried forward at the Opening of the Slates, Ilmen 1, Y.H. 813. It survives as four leaves of foolscap sewn with wire and kept in the notice-board’s tin: an iron-gall thumb at the head, slate dust in the gutter off a district slate laid there while a runner gave her figure, a scorch in the second leaf where a spark came off the grating, grey Ash off a Kept room’s skirting worked into the fold, a curl of grey wool from a cradle blanket, a tallow thumb at the foot, a pale ring where a collector set his tube down, a green bead of lead glaze pressed in by a glaze-mixer come up from High Kiln, a tide-line from the cold of the sealed-file room along the foot, a small square of bare paper where a word was scraped away, two corrections in borrowed hands, and a line at the foot that has never been claimed\par}\medskip
I keep the notice that stands beside the Weighing Hall. It is a board with one part in twelve printed on it, and on Weighing the year’s measures are read aloud in Slate Row while the fire burns behind its grating of cold iron and no priest is allowed within a pace of it. An officer comes up from a district to hear what the year has entered against him, and I copy him out this ordinance beforehand so that he may know the reading before he hears it. The ordinance is in Ledgerhand, and there is nobody in any of its sentences. I put the people back underneath. A year read aloud with nobody in it is a year nobody lived, and that is the only kind this Hall has ever wanted entered.

The articles were gathered here after the Rising and set down in Y.H. 671, when it was found that a whole year could be read aloud in the time it takes a man to walk the length of Slate Row. They are copied forward each Weighing from the College book and not from the board, because the board is scraped clean and written again and a scraped board keeps nothing. A rule with no voice on it is a rule nobody has had to read. These have been read.

\subsection*{The ordinance as it stands beside the Hall}

\subsection*{I. Of the day and the fire}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item Weighing is the second of the Five, between Kindling and the Long Night. It belongs to no month and to no tend, and no market is held on it.

\end{enumerate}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Margin:} On Kindling every hearth in Sarn is lit from the fire drawn up through the Keel. I have put \emph{every hearth} back under \emph{the hearths are lit}, because a fire lit in a house was lit by somebody who got up in the dark to do it. The ordinance has no word for the getting up.\end{quote}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item The fire behind the grating is the Hearth drawn up through the stone. It has never gone out and no priest has ever been allowed to touch it. The Kept are not asked to stand near it.

\end{enumerate}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Margin:} One of the Kept kept his face turned toward the grating through the whole reading. He did not speak and was not asked to. I have entered neither the face nor the turning, because a face held toward a fire is not an entry, and I have no column that will hold it.\end{quote}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item The year’s measures are read aloud in Slate Row, in a clean voice, with the notice standing where the reader can see it and the crowd cannot.

\end{enumerate}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Margin:} The figure I heard at the reading and the figure a man told me afterward at the foot of the Row were the same figure spoken twice. I entered it once, as the ordinance provides. The second hearing goes at the edge, where a hearing has no column.\end{quote}

\subsection*{II. Of the figures}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item One part in twelve is printed on the notice, and that is the figure read. No other figure is read in the Hall.

\end{enumerate}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item A figure that will not agree with the notice is copied again in the same hand. What cannot be read aloud is not a figure of this year.

\end{enumerate}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Margin:} In the thin years a different figure goes around the yards and comes up as far as the notice-board before it goes away again. I have heard it twice and set it at the edge, where it has no column and asks no question. A figure a clerk cannot weigh is not one he can enter, and a figure he cannot enter is safest where he can neither deny it nor keep it.\end{quote}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item A whole return may be announced at the Weighing for a person who is not in the room. The reader does not ask where the person is.

\end{enumerate}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Margin:} A whole return was announced for a woman who was not there, and a man standing beside me put his hand to the middle of his palm where a ring had once been worn tight and long, and kept it there through the clean voice. I entered the return. The hand went at the edge, the length of a hand.\end{quote}

\subsection*{III. Of the survey table}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item The Vorr sit at the survey table and are not asked to translate. The Deep Hand is copied and not read.

\end{enumerate}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Margin:} I asked one of them what the oldest numbers said. He looked at the table a while and said, \emph{The numbers are correct.} That is one sentence and not a translation, and I have set it here because the ordinance has no place for an answer and the board has room at the edge.\end{quote}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item The copy of the Deep Hand is shut in its tin and not carried beyond the Hall. What is copied in this room is not read in any district.

\end{enumerate}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Margin:} I have watched the reader’s hand go to the copy before his eye went to the stone, which is the order of this trade and not the order of a man who wants to know what a repair was made of. I have put no gloss on it. A clerk who explains a slate has begun to write a sermon, and sermons get copied.\end{quote}

\subsection*{IV. Of the Kept and the names}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item Fewer than twenty vessels are kept in rooms near the fire. They hold three hundred measures and feel nothing. No return is due to them and no deduction is entered against them.

\end{enumerate}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Margin:} Three hundred is a figure no household can spend. I have entered it because the notice has it and not because any man in this Hall has ever held that much warmth in his hands. A figure entered is not a figure seen.\end{quote}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item The rolls of the dead are carried forward and never closed. On the Remembering, names are spoken in a clean voice, and whole returns are announced for persons not in the room.

\end{enumerate}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Margin:} A woman stood here on the Remembering to hear a name spoken, and the clean voice announced a return instead. I entered the return and set the name at the edge, the length of it. She asked me whether the roll had closed. I told her no roll closes. That is true, and was not what she asked.\end{quote}

\subsection*{V. Of faults and their correcting}

Fault — As entered at the Hall — What the clerk sets beneath\par

A verb in the ordinance — The page copied again, in the same hand — The verb restored where it stood\par

A figure read with feeling — The reader set back one Weighing — The person whose figure it was\par

A whole return for one not in the room — Entered as announced — The empty place where the person stood\par

A question put to the Vorr — No entry — The one sentence, at the edge\par

The Deep Hand read aloud — The page copied again — The length of the line read, and nothing of it\par

A name spoken on the Remembering — Entered as a return — The name, at the edge, the length of it\par

\subsection*{The form of the reading}

\emph{Set out at the end. I have copied it with the blanks as they stand. In nine Weighings no reader has filled the last line with his own name.}

\begin{quote}\itshape Read this day, being Weighing, in the year of the Hearth ----, the year’s measures in the sum of ----, the deduction one in twelve as the notice says; the whole returns announced for ----------------------, who is not in the room; the Kept not called, the fire not touched, the survey table not translated; to be carried forward on the Opening of the Slates and not closed; read by ----------------------, whose voice was clean and who put nobody into the sentence.\end{quote}

\subsection*{The stair-song, pasted inside the board}

\emph{Said low going up from Slate Row to the Hall on Weighing morning, never while the notice is in sight of the Steward’s door, and never twice in one year.}

\begin{quote}\itshape Four for the fire and four for the roll,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and a place where the fifth should stand;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the clean voice carries what the yards gave up,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the figure goes where the hand cannot.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape One in twelve as the notice says,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape read for the moot and again for the late;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the Kept hold three hundred and want no return,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and a whole return comes back for a name.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Up the stone stair with the slate to the sleeve,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape hand to the copy before the eye;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the Vorr say the numbers are correct,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape which is one sentence and no reply.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Four for the fire and four for the roll,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the gap goes up with the rest;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the fire keeps the year and the board keeps the sum,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the voice keeps nothing and does not rest.\end{quote}

The second verse came in with the Thin Year and is not sung by the readers, who have no reason to sing it and several to keep quiet. I have copied it as it came.

\subsection*{What the borrowed hands did}

The College man came down from Slate Row on the morning of the reading with ink in two fingers of a cuff gone soft from washing. He struck \emph{are read} out of article three and set \emph{were read} above it, and above that \emph{the measures stand recorded}, which is further from the voice than the first. I put mine back. Against the face turned toward the grating he wrote \emph{no entry arising}, which is true of the Hall and cost him one look at the edge of the leaf. He drew a line under all my margins and wrote \emph{No such place} above them, so that the edge would read as though it had never held anything. He had to look at every margin before he could write that there was nothing in any of them worth keeping, and I watched him do it.

The other hand is tall and leaning and comes from the Steward’s room. Against \emph{one in twelve} it wrote \emph{the lawful deduction}, and against the whole return announced for a person not in the room, \emph{an article of value, not entered to a person}. I have not struck either. A hand that writes whole returns for persons not in the room knows the difference between a person spoken of and a person standing there, and has made a trade of not saying which.

\subsection*{In the head and in the gutter}

The brown at the head is iron-gall and mine, from holding the quire open through a reading; there are clerks in Slate Row who can tell the notice-clerk by his thumb before he has spoken. The slate dust in the gutter came off a district slate laid on this board while a runner come up from the Clay Road gave her figure and looked at the fire instead of at me. The scorch in the second leaf is a spark off the grating, caught while I held the paper too near in order to read it in the draught; it has taken the corner off one line and not the sense. The grey in the fold is Ash off the skirting of a Kept room, which comes away on a sleeve and will not wash out. The curl of grey wool came off a cradle blanket carried up on the Remembering; it went through the tie-hole and I have not untied it. The tallow thumb at the foot is mine, from holding the lamp low while somebody behind me said something I wanted the end of; she did not tell me the end. The pale ring is where a collector set his tube down while he went for a cup; the tube was not used in this room and the ring is not a wound, but it is the thinnest paper on the leaf. The green bead is lead glaze, pressed in by a girl come up from High Kiln who leaned to see the form of the reading with the sweetness still at her mouth, touched the paper, said nothing, and went back down the stair. The tide-line along the foot came up out of the cold of the sealed-file room through the wall; it takes the corners off figures and leaves the figures. There is no Last Day beside a Hall. The board is scraped and written again each Weighing, and the old figures go into the fire with the sweepings, and nobody calls it dealt with.

\subsection*{At the foot, in a hand nobody will own}

\begin{quote}\itshape The fire keeps the year. The notice keeps the figure. Between the two a clean voice reads a life that nobody standing in the room has to answer for.\end{quote}

I asked the College clerk, a man come down from the Steward’s room, and a woman who stood beside me at the notice on Weighing, and had three answers and no hand, as I have had before. I have left the line where it was written.

The leaves go back into the tin on the notice-board. Tomorrow the Long Night comes and there is no fire after dusk in any room of the Hall, and on the Remembering a clean voice will announce whole returns for persons not in the room, and the roll will be carried forward with no disposition recorded. The board will be scraped for another year. I have put the verbs back where I could and left the scorch where it fell.

\clearpage\phantomsection\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{The Weighing Physician’s Book, Being Remedies for the Beautiful Return, the Quiet Dream, the Greyed Hand, the Weighing Chill, the Kept Room and the Fever That Cooks, Set Down in the Hearthseat with the Errors Left Standing and a Clay-Yard Woman’s Thumb in the Margin}
\CRsheetheading{The Weighing Physician’s Book, Being Remedies for the Beautiful Return, the Quiet Dream, the Greyed Hand, the Weighing Chill, the Kept Room and the Fever That Cooks, Set Down in the Hearthseat with the Errors Left Standing and a Clay-Yard Woman’s Thumb in the Margin}
{\centering\FellFont\itshape\footnotesize\color{faded} A physician’s book of remedies in the soft, ledger-leaning manner of the Keeping, written in Grathic with the verbs thinned almost to Ledgerhand; the cures in a neat physician’s hand on the back of a spoiled Weighing notice, the objections of a clay-yard hearth-maid pressed in tallow and slip into the margin, the corrections of a College of Assessors clerk in narrow upright Ledgerhand, a song for the Weighing with a place left where the fifth stroke should stand, and one line at the foot in a hand nobody will own · Written in the Hearthseat on the Keel between Ash of Y.H. 812 and Ilmen of Y.H. 813, the Long Cold and the Thin Year, by Senn, a physician of the Weighing Hall who examined the Kept in their rooms at each Weighing and held the hands of the returned on the third day; begun on the back of a Weighing notice spoiled when the ink ran in the damp, on which \emph{one in twelve} is still legible through every remedy, folded into four and carried in the inner pocket of a clean coat. It was never copied at Greybank: the fair copy was taken by the College and lost, and the rough leaf survives in the physician’s own room off the Weighing Hall, with the printed figure showing through, a press of tallow and a thumb of clay slip in the margin where a woman from Low Kiln laid her hand, grey Ash off a Kept room’s skirting board worked into the gutter, a scorch where a spark off the grating of the Hearth-fire caught the second leaf, a pale clip-ring pressed into the third, objections in the rough hand of the clay-yard woman, six corrections in the upright hand of the College clerk, and the one line at the foot in a hand nobody will own\par}\medskip
I am a physician of the Weighing Hall and my name on the rolls is Senn. I have examined the Kept in their rooms at nine Weighings and held the hands of the returned on the third day. Nobody asked me for this book. A woman from the clay yards came up with a child who would not warm, stood with her thumb in tallow against the margin while I wrote, and set a sentence there I have not been able to cross out. A physician of the Court writes in verbs thinned almost to nothing; a woman with a child on her hip puts them back.

I write on the back of a Weighing notice spoiled in the damp. The figure on the other side shows through every remedy: \emph{one in twelve, as the notice says}. I did not choose the paper and have not cut the figure away. The clerk who corrects this book is of my own College; he takes the verbs out of my directions as though a thing always true had no need of anybody doing it. I have put them back underneath, as the clay-yard woman put hers in the margin. There are three hands in this book and none of them is clean.

\subsection*{The order of the examining room}

\emph{Written small at the head, with the word for the calm gone over in Ash.}

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item Set the returned one’s face toward the grating, not the door. The fire behind the iron has never gone out, and a person who faces it can be seen by everybody. Margin, in tallow: \emph{A stone faces the fire too and feels nothing.}

\item Ask what is booked against the house before you ask what ails the person. A household that has named its debt will tell you where the hurt is. This is not kindness. It is the order of the Hall.

\item Turn the slate face down before you look at a child. I learned it from a hearth-maid of Low Kiln who would not say why she turned it.

\item Count the hand on the third day and enter the count. A count entered is a count kept. Margin: \emph{A count kept is not a hand held.}

\item Do not tap a person to hear them. A body is not a banked cup. I did it once, heard nothing, and have not again.

\item When a collector’s fingers go grey at the tube, enter it as age. The rolls want a word and will take \emph{age}. Margin, pressed hard enough to score the leaf: \emph{It’s the draw. I’ve seen a collector grey in one winter, and it was not age.}

\end{itemize}

She would not give me her name. A name in a margin is a name a clerk can carry out of a room.

\subsection*{The remedies, as they are used}

Trouble — What is set to it — The manner of it — Who is debited\par

The beautiful return (the calm of the third day) — A whole return, booked at twelve hundred marks and forty unspent measures; the calm entered as its sign — We say the Hearth kept what was given and the person comes back quiet. On the third day the hand shakes and we call it the price of beauty. I have seen the calm go on and the name come late, and entered the calm. The margin says a woman who does not know her own child is not quiet but gone. Both stand. — The household, in marks; the returned one, in what is not asked for.\par

The dream of the former house — A phial of quiet ash at sixty marks, in wine at the Weighing — The rich buy it so the former life will stop arriving in dreams. I gave it to nine; six ceased to speak of the dream and three ceased to speak at all. I entered six and not the three. Margin: \emph{That’s the quiet you sold them.} — The person, who asks no figure.\par

The greyed hand of a collector — Rest from the iron; a week near the Hearth; the hand booked as age — We say the Hearth warms what the iron took. I have seen a hand grey further in a week at the grating and written \emph{age} over it. — The collector, who is paid partly out of other people’s heat.\par

The Kept in their rooms — Nothing. Fewer than twenty are examined at each Weighing and found whole — They do not feel the fire, do not ask for food, do not want. We call this health and pity them for it. The margin says a stone does not feel the fire either and is not called healthy. I have not crossed the line out. — Nobody. This is the row I cannot debit.\par

The Weighing chill (the cold after the reading) — The account read aloud again; a measure returned to the house — We say a figure read warms the house that hears it. I read it to nine houses and went back in the morning; six were as cold, three colder. Margin: \emph{A figure’s a figure. Try a stone.} — The house, which hears and cannot be heated.\par

The fever that cooks from within — Cold iron to the temple; bleed at the elbow to let the head fall — We say a vessel overfilled must be emptied or it cooks its own contents. A physician come up from Low Kiln says bleeding lets the measure out and not the fever, and that the person is quieter after and not better. I watched four; two were quiet and did not wake. I have written both. — The person, in the arm.\par

The second chill in a rekindled child — Warmth, barley water, a watch to the fourth day; we walk her — It comes after the warming, not before. The physician from Low Kiln says a warmed body spends faster and walking faster still, and that she should be held and counted with. I have walked eleven and held two, and not written which fared worse. Margin: \emph{Hold the next one and see if you can write what you saw.} — The household, one night’s sleep; sometimes the child.\par

A child who comes back wanting another house — The old name entered in the second column, which the family is not shown; a bowl of water under the bed — The returned one calls a name not given in this house and reaches for a door that is not in the room. We enter the former name where the family cannot see it. The margin says a name in a column puts no shape back. One went off it and one kept it a year. — Nobody. The house, in a year it cannot spend.\par

A cut from a cold iron tube at a collection — Tallow, a clean fold, the measure entered — A collection yields a small wound at the way. The clay-yard woman puts nothing on a cut but tallow; the priests here put the grey out of the public bowl on theirs. I have found grey under the skin in three such cuts and could not get it out. — The cut, in a white line it keeps.\par

The pale line at the gum — Sour wine; the glaze hands sent back to the mix — The sweetness answers sweetness, we say. The physician from Low Kiln says it is lead. I have seen the line go off a girl who left the room and come back on one who stayed. I have not seen the lead. — The glaze room, which cannot stop and does not ask.\par

Nothing in this Hall is given. It is entered and called kept. I will stand behind that sentence and behind no other in the book.

\subsection*{The full note, and why a person is not a cup}

The bankers tap a cup before a pouring and know by the note whether it will hold. Sound answers full; cracked answers flat, a small dead sound that stops at the surface. I borrowed the trick and tried it on a returned woman gone thin after a third pouring. There was nothing there for the knuckle to find. I wrote that the flat was not in her, which is true, and have not written what else might have been. A person is not a vessel of the Court’s kind, and a Kept vessel is not a person, though both hold without leaking. In the margin, two words in tallow: \emph{Now you’re saying it.}

\subsection*{On the beautiful return}

They come back calm. The returned one sits in the good light near the grating, wants nothing, takes the cup when given, and does not ask whose child she is. We write \emph{a beautiful return} and enter it at twelve hundred marks and forty unspent measures, and the household thanks the Hearth in a voice that does not rise. On the third day the hand shakes, the household asks for the phial, and we say the beauty must be paid for, which lets nobody ask what the first pouring took.

I asked the woman from the clay yards what she called it. She said her mother crossed two fingers and called it the quiet, and that a woman who has ceased to want is not well but gone. I have entered the calm and not her sentence. Her sentence is not a figure and cannot be entered, which is why it stays where the clerk cannot carry it.

\subsection*{A song for the Weighing}

\emph{Sung low in the Hall at the reading, to the person and not to the account. There is a place after the fourth stroke where the fifth should stand, and no singer has filled it.}

\begin{quote}\itshape Four for the fire behind the iron,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape four for the nails in the Hall;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape a place where the fifth should stand\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and nobody crosses himself.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape The measure is banked, the account stands,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the hand goes grey at the tube;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape a woman comes back and wants nothing,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the house calls it a mercy.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Six for the phials in the locked drawer,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape six for the rooms where the Kept sit;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape a stone does not ask for the fire\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the clerk does not ask who paid.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Sing to the slate, sing to the figure,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape sing to the space where the fifth should be;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape what comes back is not what went,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and comes back as it can.\end{quote}

I have never heard the bell at the Cross. A clerk come up from Sill told me it goes four, four and a gap and that nobody crosses himself; I have kept his telling beside the song and not made it a hearing. A clerk of my College put a nought in the fifth place and wrote \emph{vacancy} beneath it. A nought is a figure and can be carried out in a cuff. The fifth is a place and stays.

\subsection*{What the clay-yard woman put in the margin}

Against the Kept: \emph{A stone does not feel the fire either. Ask it if it’s well.}

Against the phial: \emph{Six stopped speaking of the dream. I’d want to know what the six are doing now.}

Against the greyed hand: \emph{It’s the draw. I have seen it taken out of a man in a winter.}

Against the beautiful return: \emph{A woman who doesn’t know her child isn’t quiet. She’s gone.}

She presses her verbs in with the side of her thumb. The slip under her nail has left a brown print in the gutter and I have not washed it. She took the child away before the count was entered and left no name.

\subsection*{What the College clerk did}

A clerk of the College borrowed the leaves at the Weighing, when the Hall had no time to mind a physician’s rough paper. The ink sits in two fingers of his cuff and will not come out. He struck out my column headed \emph{Who is debited} and wrote \emph{No cost entered} above it, which is a true thing in a dishonest place. Against the Kept he wrote \emph{The vessels are retained in health}, the most beautiful sentence I have ever read in a hand that has never sat in a room with one. Where I wrote that the Hearth keeps what it is given, he wrote \emph{the measure is retained}, taking the verbs out, as though a thing always true had no need of anybody doing it. He has eleven words for a deduction and no word for a hand held.

I have put my verbs back underneath his. A clerk of my College corrects me into coldness and I have let him, because a physician who writes as I do will be struck from the rolls by a man who has never held a hand.

\subsection*{At the head and in the gutter}

The figure shows through every leaf: \emph{one in twelve, as the notice says}. The damp took two words clean off it before I was given the back and I have not written them back. A figure that will not read is a figure that cannot be entered, which is the only mercy in this book nobody has paid for. The brown press in the margin is tallow and slip from a woman’s thumb.
