The grey in the gutter came off the skirting board of a room where a Kept vessel sits; it is the only Ash here that entered itself, and I have not burnt it on the morning after the Last Day, for there is no Last Day off the Weighing Hall. The scorch on the second leaf is a spark off the grating, caught while I wrote and put out under my hand; I have not entered the burn. The pale clip-ring on the third leaf is not mine and I have not asked whose.

\subsection*{At the foot, in a hand nobody will own}

\begin{quote}\itshape The slate keeps the name. The drawer keeps the phial.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape The woman between them is kept in no house.\end{quote}

I asked the College clerk, a physician come up from Low Kiln, and a woman with a child on her hip, and had three answers and no hand. I have left the line where it was written. Tomorrow the Weighing will be read and a household will come with a hand that will not hold a cup, and I shall enter the calm as a mercy and turn the slate face down before I look at the child, because a child is not an account and a woman at the Weighing wants a hand more than she wants a correction.

\clearpage\phantomsection\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{The Sermon at the Well That Never Freezes, Being What Was Said at Cold Acre in the Ninety-Four Days, with the Drawing-Song, the Twelve Links, and the Column Nobody Filled}
\CRsheetheading{The Sermon at the Well That Never Freezes, Being What Was Said at Cold Acre in the Ninety-Four Days, with the Drawing-Song, the Twelve Links, and the Column Nobody Filled}
{\centering\FellFont\itshape\footnotesize\color{faded} A well-shrine sermon of the common Grathic telling, preached at Cold Acre two leagues north of Sill over the stone lip and the clay dish; the manner of the drawing in the tally-woman’s hand, the sayings in Grathic, the drawing-song with the gap left as it is sung, the column of the slate set down as a table, one correction in the narrow upright hand of an assessor’s clerk come up from Greybank, and a line at the foot in a hand nobody will own · Preached by Nils of Cold Acre, who has kept the well-rope and the shrine at the stone lip for two and thirty winters, on a morning in Stone of Y.H. 812, the Thin Year, while the Ilm lay under ice for the ninety-fourth day and the well gave as it gives; written that evening by Kess of Cold Acre, who keeps the barley measure and the seed account for the six houses, in charcoal on a strip of birch bark gone soft at one edge, folded and tied with a spent length of the well-rope and kept in the thatch of her own roof above the beam and out of reach of the frost. It survives with lime worked into the grain at the head, a frost-crisp along the gutter where the bark lay a night under the eaves, a wet ring on the second leaf where a dish of water stood from the first voice to the last, a barley awn shut in the fold, a grey Ash print nobody will own, a tarry fibre of well-rope caught in the tie, one correction in the narrow upright hand of an assessor’s clerk come up from Greybank to measure the winter wells, and a line struck through and written again very small underneath in a hand that has never come forward. Copied once at Greybank in Ilmen, Y.H. 813, with the verbs put back and the empty column left empty.\par}\medskip
I keep the barley measure and the seed account for the six houses at Cold Acre, and nobody asked me for this. I write because the well gave water on the ninety-fourth day of the ice and no slate was set at it, and a thing nobody enters somebody will come at last to enter. He stood with his hand on the well-rope and spoke first to the rope, then to the stone lip, the dish, the ridge, and the sky above the ridge, and last of all to us, which is the order a well-man uses when six households are waiting with their dishes and somebody may be listening who wants a figure. I have set his words down in Grathic, with the verbs where he left them, because a saying said over water is a thing a house has to use.

The lime at the head came off the lip when he set his hand on it to brush the frost away. The frost-crisp in the gutter is from the night I left the bark under the eaves. The ring is a woman’s dish that stood from the first voice to the last and was never drunk from. The grey came off a cuff and I have not swept it. The rest is set down at the end.

\subsection*{The manner of the drawing, as the well has it}

\emph{Written small, from watching, not from any order the Court has printed.}

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item Come at first grey, before the house fires are stirred. A man who comes at noon draws the day’s warmth off the lip with his shadow and is none the wiser.

\item Set the dish on the stone, not in the water. A dish set in the water is a thing left to be fetched, and a well that is fetched at twice gives the same water, which is a kind of insult if you have stood here thirty winters.

\item Let the bucket down on the chain. Eleven links go to the water. The twelfth hangs in your hand and never wets. Do not straighten it, and do not say where you think the water would be if it did.

\item Draw what the day wants. A bucket left standing on the lip draws nothing at all, and the level in the well is the same at the end of the winter as it was at the beginning, which I have watched and cannot explain and have not tried to.

\item Taste before you carry. It tastes of stone and a little of iron and nothing else. Do not say what it tastes of where a man with a slate is standing.

\item When the bell comes up the ridge from the Cross on a still morning, stop until it has gone. It is counting something that is not your well. Four, four and a gap, and the gap is not ours to fill.

\item There is no ash in the corner here. The well has no corner. On the Last Day we leave the grey in the houses down the ridge and come up and draw, and that is the whole of our observance and the end of it.

\end{itemize}

\subsection*{The sermon, as he said it}

\subsection*{Of the well}

He put his palm flat on the lip and left it there while the rope swung against the stone.

“It does not freeze,” he said. “The Ilm has lain under ice for ninety-four days and the well has given every morning of them. I put my wrist in on the morning the ice went and it was the same water. It is not warm; do not go home and tell your households it is warm. It is water that has not given up, which is a different thing and a thing I have never seen the like of.”

A priest come up from Greybank in the first winter of the ice had called it a little sister of the Nine Wells and a mercy of the Hearth drawn through the ridge. I have set that down because I heard it with my own ears and because it is comfortable. The well has never given a sign that it heard him.

\subsection*{Of the twelfth link}

“Eleven go down and one hangs dry,” he said, and held the chain up so the women could see which was which. “A man from the College stood here in the autumn and told me the twelfth is kept back for the Hearth. I said the water comes up on the eleventh and the twelfth hangs in my hand, and if the Hearth wants its share let it send a man with a longer arm. He said one in twelve is printed on the notice and is not a lie. I said a printed thing travels and a chain does not. Both stood in the air between us, and neither went into the other.”

A girl from the upper house asked what the dry link was for, and he did not give her a year, as the women of Sill do when asked about a mark they would rather not explain. He said: “Lower the bucket. You will see which links go in.” She counted eleven and said nothing more, which is the only answer this ridge is good at.

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Margin, in my hand:} He said the sentence about the printed notice twice, once to the well and once to the man with the slate, and I have not joined the two sayings. A man who uses one word for two things has a use for the word.\end{quote}

\subsection*{Of them that come up the ridge}

“Three times an assessor has come up from Greybank since I took the rope,” he said. “He measures the lip with a cord, asks how deep it goes, asks who pays for the drawing, and sets a figure in a column of his slate. The column has never had anything in it. He does not leave it empty out of kindness. He leaves it empty because there is nowhere in the house of the world where a figure like that would stand.

“He asked what the well was worth. I told him I had never sold it. He asked what it cost to keep. I told him it keeps itself and us, and he wrote that down too, though I do not think he heard it.

“What I fear is not that they will carry the well away; a well cannot be carried. I fear the figure. Once a figure stands at a thing, the thing is a gift, and a gift can be refused, and a man who refuses water in a winter like this has paid for it somewhere else, where nobody was standing to see.”

\subsection*{Of them that are Kept}

“They tell us the Kept are blessed and feel no cold,” he said. “There is one in the Hearthseat who cannot feel this ridge, and I have never met him. The well does not feel it either, and I have met it every morning for two and thirty winters. That is the whole of the likeness. Carry it further and you will come back with a doctrine, and a doctrine is an account that has found somebody to pay it.”

He said this to the ridge and not to the women, and I have written it as it was said and not as it was meant.

\subsection*{Of the dead and the drawing}

“Six houses draw here and six have buried their dead down at the river,” he said. “A pot is broken at the door and the feet are set to the water, and the well draws for the house that is left behind. It has never asked which house. I have looked into the bucket every morning of my life and never once seen a name come up in it.

“At the Weighing they read a whole return in a clean voice for a person not in the room. Here a woman comes up with a dish and drinks standing, because she would not sit down in her own house since the cough came on her. I have not put the two sayings together. They are two rooms, and the well is a third.”

\subsection*{Of the close}

“The measure is banked. The account stands,” he said, and I could hear he had had those words from a man in a clean coat and did not like the feel of them. “That is said over a slate in a room I have never stood in. Here the water comes up and goes into a dish and somebody drinks it, and there is no third sentence. If the Hearth wants a twelfth of this water, let it send a man with a bucket up the ridge in the dark. It has not sent one, and I have drawn here two and thirty winters.”

He crossed two fingers on the stone lip then, as hearth-maids cross them over a birth-flower, and covered the act with nothing at all, not even a date. I have written the act and left the covering where it was.

\subsection*{The drawing-song}

\emph{Sung low, standing, with the dish on the lip and a hand on the rope. The row says the last four lines with him. There is a gap before those four, the one the bell leaves when it comes up the ridge, and I have left it here as it is sung.}

\begin{quote}\itshape Eleven links to the water, one hangs dry;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the well gives what the bucket carries;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the ridge keeps snow and the lip keeps frost,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the water keeps neither, and comes up.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Six for the houses, six for the dead,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and a place where the thirteenth would stand;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the bell comes up and the bell goes down,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the gap is not ours to fill.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Draw what the day wants and leave the rest;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape a dish set in the water is a dish left to fetch;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape what it keeps it gives, and what it gives it keeps,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and no slate has stood at the lip.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape The twelfth link hangs where no water goes;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape say it is kept, or say it is spare;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape say what it did and not what it meant,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and carry the dish to the house that asked.\end{quote}

A woman at the well asked what the place where the thirteenth would stand was for. Nobody answered her. The clerk put a round nought against it later, which I have left where he set it.

\subsection*{The column, as the slate would have it}

\emph{I keep this because the figure that arrives at the well in a coat goes down the ridge again in the same coat and leaves nothing on the stone. These I have set down where they stood.}

When — What was drawn — What was entered\par

The ninety-four days, Y.H. 811 into 812 — Water for six houses, morning and evening — nothing\par

The morning the ice went — A dish for the woman with the cough — nothing\par

The levy week in Stone, Y.H. 812 — Water for the house that kept a child not its own — nothing\par

This morning, after the assessor — The same water — a figure struck out, a column standing\par

There were other mornings and Nils could set a winter to each of them, and I have not written them, because a row of winters is a thing a clerk can carry away and a dish of water is not.

\subsection*{What the clerk did}

An assessor’s clerk come up from Greybank to measure the winter wells borrowed the bark on the morning after, with his cuff soft at the edge from washing and ink in two fingers, and gave it back with the verbs taken out.

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item Where Nils said \emph{the well gives what the bucket carries}, he wrote \emph{the measure is retained in the spring and is lawfully drawn} above and left the old words below.

\item Where he said \emph{the twelfth hangs dry}, he wrote \emph{one part in twelve reserved to the Hearth} and underlined it twice. He did not ask to see the chain.

\item At the column he put a round nought and wrote \emph{vacancy}, and when I asked what a column was worth with nothing under it, he said nothing a clerk could enter, which is the first true thing I have heard out of that coat.

\item At \emph{I have never seen a name come up in the bucket} he wrote \emph{third party unidentifiable; nil}, a true thing said by a man who has never drawn water in the dark.

\end{itemize}

I have put the verbs back underneath and left his hand standing above, as the well leaves the old water showing under the new. He takes them out because a thing always true has no need of verbs. I put them back because a woman at first grey wants to know who is doing the giving, and whether it was her own hand that lowered the bucket.

\subsection*{At the head and in the gutter}

The lime at the head is not salt and has never been entered. The frost-crisp came up out of the bark itself under the eaves, and the writing there is thin and I have not gone over it, because a word written thin is a word said quietly, and most of ours are. The ring is the woman’s dish, taken away still full. The awn in the fold is barley and has not sprouted. The grey print came off a cuff and nobody will own it; there is no Last Day on this roof and nothing gets swept. The tar on the tie is off the rope that has lowered eleven links into the water every morning for two and thirty winters and has never once lowered twelve.

\subsection*{At the foot, in a hand nobody will own}

\begin{quote}\itshape The well asks nothing. They come up the ridge to look at it all the same.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape The twelfth link has never wet, and the water has never failed.\end{quote}

I asked Nils, the woman who kept the dish, a girl from the upper house, and the clerk, and had four answerings and no hand. I have left the line struck through and standing, which is the only honest way to keep a sentence you cannot sign.

The bark goes back in the fold and the fold under the thatch above the beam. Next winter the ice will come on the Ilm and the well will give as it gives; the clerk will come up from Greybank and take the verbs out. I shall put them back and leave the column the length it is.

\clearpage\phantomsection\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{The Wet Carrying, Being the Rack-Song of Low Kiln, Sung Going Up from the Wheel to the Drying Racks}
\CRsheetheading{The Wet Carrying, Being the Rack-Song of Low Kiln, Sung Going Up from the Wheel to the Drying Racks}
{\centering\FellFont\itshape\footnotesize\color{faded} A work song of the carrying in the low speech of the yard; the call set to the pace of the feet and the answer to the set-down, with one verse kept back until the factor’s man has gone back over the bridge; written in charcoal thinned with slip, the rubrics of the rack in the same hand, a factor’s clerk’s correction in Ledgerhand, a gloss from a woman at the tubs, and one line at the foot in a hand nobody will own · Set down in Smoke of Y.H. 812, the Thin Year, by a woman of House Silt who keeps the drying racks three doors up the Clay Yard from the Vail kiln-house; written on the back of a rack-tally spoiled by a wet thumb while the second firing was being counted, and tied with grey wool to the bracket of the lowest rack under a broken pot turned mouth-down against the rain. Copied forward in Reed of Y.H. 813 onto a strip of oiled paper from the wheel-shed after the flood took the first leaf. It survives with a raw-slip thumb at the head, a green bead of lead-glaze pressed into the lower corner, a barley-water ring through the second verse, a long grey Ash smear along the gutter that nobody will own, a scratch where a rack-hook caught the fold, one line of the song eaten away by rain and not written in again, one correction in the narrow upright hand of the factor’s clerk at Greybank, a gloss in the thick charcoal hand of a woman at the tubs, and a line at the foot in a hand nobody will own\par}\medskip
I keep the racks at House Silt, three doors up the Clay Yard from the Vail kiln-house, and I have set this down because a man come down from Greybank with a cuff gone soft from washing asked a girl at the tubs what the women sang when they carried the wet pots up from the wheel, and wrote what she said before she had finished saying it. A carrying-song is not a song for a fire. It is said to the feet, and the answer is said to the pot at the set-down. Sung at a fire it grows a tune in it, and a man in a clean coat can carry that away.

The raw-slip thumb at the head is mine. I held the tally down with the hand I tread the slip with and did not know I had marked it.

\subsection*{How it is carried}

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item Two pots on the forearms and one against the apron. Never a fourth, because a fourth wants a hand you have not got, and a pot wants both hands at the set-down.

\item The call goes to the pot and the answer goes to the rack. Said looking at a woman it becomes an argument, and an argument at the racks ends with somebody setting a pot down wrong on purpose.

\item Four paces to a verse and a rest at the set-down. The rest is not a pace and is not counted. It is where the pot goes down, and where a fifth pace would be if there were one.

\item Knuckle every pot before you set it. A woman who sets down a pot she has not heard has set down a stranger’s pot, and nobody in the yard will answer for it.

\item If a slate lies open on the rack bench, turn it face down or take the long way round the yard. A pot said over an open slate arrives somewhere the carrier did not mean to send it.

\item A girl come up from the Glaze Room with green at her mouth and the pale line of the sweet-sickness at her gum does not carry that day. Not a punishment. Sweetness makes a hand careless, and a careless hand sets down a pot that will not sing.

\item Do not sing it at the well on a flood morning. The water has its own note, and two notes over one another make two counts that will not agree, and the yard goes around both all day.

\item The last verse is kept back. It is for when the man from Greybank has gone back over the north bridge with his satchel under his arm and the yard can hear itself again.

\end{itemize}

\subsection*{The song}

\emph{The woman at the wheel calls the first line of each pair, the women on the row answer the second. The refrain is said low, into the rack, at the set-down. The last line of the refrain is held until the hand is off the pot.}

\begin{quote}\itshape The wheel gives it up and it’s heavy as a debt,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape bone-coloured under the slip where the thumb went;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape carry it level. Carry it the way you’d carry a question\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape you don’t want slopped on the man that asked it.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Set it down. Leave the crack showing.}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Four paces to the rack and a rest where the fifth should be;}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{the pot gives its note and the note goes through,}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{and the slate has no ears and is entered regardless.}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Knuckle it once before you set it down.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape A whole one answers full and the note goes through the clay;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape a cracked one stops at the skin and gives back flat,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and you set it by the ruts and sweep around it too.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Refrain, said low into the rack at the set-down.}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Don’t close the crack. The neighbours must see it was handled.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape A hidden crack is a lie with a pot built round it;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape a showing crack is a thing a woman can carry\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape into another house, set down, and be believed in.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Refrain, said low into the rack at the set-down.}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape The girl who tastes the glaze has green at one corner\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and a pale line where the lead has kissed her gum;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape don’t let her carry. Sweetness makes a hand careless,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and a careless hand sets down a pot that won’t sing.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Refrain, said low into the rack at the set-down.}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape There’s grey in the corner where the promise went;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the broom goes round it and the bucket goes round,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the rack goes round it at the turning of the row;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape it’s left for the Last Day and burnt next morning, and called dealt with.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Refrain, said low into the rack at the set-down.}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Under the lowest rack is a space nobody enters.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Whole slate should stand there, they tell the new girls;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape we go around it as wide as a pail of hot water\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape set where a child might knock it, and we do not look in.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Refrain, said low into the rack at the set-down.}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape At the end of the returning row there’s a place we go around.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape A hand went into the strips and did not come back with the rest;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape we go around it with a look and no figure,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the loaf-shelves say two gaps stay two gaps\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape till a finger lays them together and wants a name.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Refrain, said low into the rack at the set-down.}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape One in twelve, says the notice, read twice at the Cross,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape once for the moot and once for them that came late;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the bell goes four, four and a gap and nobody crosses,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the figure you heard is not the figure they paid.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Refrain, said low into the rack at the set-down.}\end{quote}

There is a space before the last refrain in the singing, the length of a set-down. I have left it on the tally. The clerk put a round nought in it once, which is a thing you can hold up and look at, and a rest is not.

\subsection*{The verse they keep back}

\emph{Not sung while the factor’s man is in the yard. Taken up after he has gone back over the bridge. The women say it to the rack and not across the square.}

\begin{quote}\itshape The number goes from a fist to a mouth to a shoulder\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and arrives at nobody, and nobody asks where;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the grey cord keeps what the slate cannot spell —\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape tie once for owed and untie for paid, and don’t say whose.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape They took warm children in the year of the flower and the count was forty,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and forty-one knots were tied and not one of them entered;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the Court put a nought in the empty place and called it vacancy,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the river went on under the bridge and carried no figure.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Four paces and a rest. The rack keeps the place.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape The clerk has no word for a place he cannot enter.\end{quote}

The rain has eaten one line of the song. I know what it said. Knowing a thing is not the same as having it, and I have not written it in again.

\subsection*{What the clerk did}

The factor’s clerk borrowed the leaf on an Account-day, ink sitting in two fingers that would not come out. He took the verbs out and set his words above mine. I have left his hand standing and mine underneath, as a rack keeps the pot’s weight and the water’s mark.

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item At \emph{the pot gives its note and the note goes through}, he wrote \emph{vessel sound, entered; quality not a figure}. True in the figure, false in the yard, where a note that goes through is the whole of the quality.

\item At \emph{a cracked one stops at the skin and gives back flat}, he wrote \emph{vessel failed, having reached its term}, and underlined it twice. A pot cracked through at the racks on Stone was called a pot gone wrong and swept around. It had not reached anything. It was knocked.

\item At \emph{leave the crack showing}, he wrote \emph{defect disclosed; no deduction}. He thinks a crack shown is a debt confessed. In this yard a crack shown is the only honesty a pot has left.

\item At \emph{a hand went into the strips and did not come back}, he wrote \emph{one absence, nil}, and at the place in the row \emph{vacancy}. He has put a number where a place should stand, which is the whole art of that hand.

\item At \emph{forty-one knots}, he wrote \emph{40 plus one unentered}. It is a true thing in a language nobody at these racks speaks. We do not say the extra knot and we do not untie it.

\item At the rest in the refrain, he put a round nought and wrote \emph{fifth nil}. A nought is a number. The rest is a place where you set the pot down. Both stand.

\end{itemize}

\subsection*{What the woman at the tubs put in the margin}

The thick charcoal belongs to a woman at the tubs below the racks who has carried more wet pots than she will count. I have copied it as it stands, without making the two hands agree.

At \emph{carry it the way you’d carry a question}: \emph{She carried a question about her man’s debt level for seven years and never slopped it. Set down on the Last Day, it had gone cold. Do not ask whose.}

At \emph{the girl who tastes the glaze}: \emph{I have held the pale line up to the light for three of them. Two went south. The third still carries, and I have said nothing, which is a kindness and a fault in the same breath.}

At \emph{a hand went into the strips}: \emph{It was my sister’s. I said it to the board and the pot, never to the woman who asked, and I will not put a figure to it with a clerk’s pen on the leaf.}

At \emph{two gaps stay two gaps}: \emph{My mother said it of the shelf and I of the rack. I have never laid a finger across either, though I have stood with my hand over the board a moment longer than the reaching wanted.}

At the kept-back verse: \emph{The river took what the Court did not. You can shout at either one. I have tried.}

\subsection*{At the head and along the gutter}

The raw-slip thumb at the head is mine and will not come out of the grain, which is why I use it to sign. The green bead in the lower corner came off a girl who leaned to see the writing with sweetness still at her tongue; she touched the paper, said nothing, and went back to the rack. I have not washed it. The barley-water ring went through the second verse while a woman stood over me telling me to carry level; she set her cup down and took it up when I had done, and the ring has gone the colour of the pot it stood on. The long grey along the gutter came off a cuff laid where no cuff has business lying on a rack. Nobody will own it, and there is no Last Day behind the racks. The scratch is a rack-hook catching the fold. The grey wool through the hole is for the word I could not write down. I will not untie it.

\subsection*{At the foot, in a hand nobody will own}

\begin{quote}\itshape The clay keeps the foot. The rack keeps the place.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape The slate keeps neither and is read twice over.\end{quote}

I asked the woman at the tubs, a girl from the Glaze Room and a man with a barrow at the yard gate, and had three answers and no hand. I have left the line where it was written.

The leaf goes back under the broken pot on the lowest rack. Tomorrow the wet pots come up from the wheel and we carry them four to the verse and set them down with the crack showing. If the clerk comes again he may have the tally. He cannot have the rest, because the rest is a place, and he has no word for a place he cannot put a figure in.

\clearpage\phantomsection\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{The Wheel Song, Being the Throwing-Song of the Women of the Clay Yard at Low Kiln, Sung at the Wheel in the Shed Beside the Slip Brook, with the Draws Counted Going Up, the Round Kept on the Board, a Kiln-Master’s Ruling in Broad Charcoal, a Factor’s Clerk’s Figures in the Narrow Upright Hand, a Gloss from a Woman at the Drying Racks, and One Line at the Foot in a Hand Nobody Will Own}
\CRsheetheading{The Wheel Song, Being the Throwing-Song of the Women of the Clay Yard at Low Kiln, Sung at the Wheel in the Shed Beside the Slip Brook, with the Draws Counted Going Up, the Round Kept on the Board, a Kiln-Master’s Ruling in Broad Charcoal, a Factor’s Clerk’s Figures in the Narrow Upright Hand, a Gloss from a Woman at the Drying Racks, and One Line at the Foot in a Hand Nobody Will Own}
{\centering\FellFont\itshape\footnotesize\color{faded} A thrower’s work song in the low speech of the yard, said to the wheel and not across the shed; the verses counted in draws going up, with the fourth kept as the thumb coming away and the round the pot leaves on the board kept and not entered; the manner of the throwing in the writer’s own charcoal, the kiln-master’s ruling in broad charcoal, the factor’s clerk’s figures standing above in Ledgerhand, a gloss pressed into the margin by a woman of the drying racks, and one line at the foot in a hand nobody will claim · Sung at the wheel in the wheel-shed beside the Slip Brook in Low Kiln of Sill and set down in the last tend of Ember, Y.H. 812, the Thin Year, the thirty days when every kiln in Grath fired at once and the whole country smelled of woodsmoke, by a woman who has thrown at that wheel for eleven seasons and centers every lump on the round the last pot left; written in charcoal thinned with slip-water on the back of a potter’s tally spoiled by a wet thumb, folded into four and tied with a curl of eel-sinew against the dust, carried north with a consignment of coarse tile and copied at Greybank in Silt of Y.H. 813 onto the back of a factor’s voided weigh-slip. It survives with a slip thumb worked into the grain at the head, a pale tideline from the Brook along the gutter that has taken the edge off one word of the fifth verse, a curl of eel-sinew caught across the second leaf, a dry grey flake from the board pressed in the fold, a damp round from a wet pot’s foot dried to the colour of the board on the third leaf, a green bead of lead glaze pressed into the lower corner, a small-ale ring gone sour at the foot, a grey Ash print along the outer fold that nobody will own, the kiln-master’s broad ruling, the clerk’s figures standing above, the rack-woman’s gloss in the margin, and the one line at the foot\par}\medskip
I throw at the wheel in the shed beside the Slip Brook, and I have done it eleven seasons. A lump goes down on the board, the foot takes the fly, and the wheel has a note before the clay has one. There is a round on the board left by the last pot, wet when the pot came off and dry by morning. We do not wipe it. We set the next lump down where the last one stood, and the board remembers what the hand has forgotten.

A man came up from Greybank with a soft cuff and ink settled in two fingers of it and stood in the shed door asking what the women sang at the wheel. I told him. He wrote it down before I had finished, with the doing taken out and a figure put where a place should stand, and went off over the north bridge with his boots clean. So I have set the words down as we say them, to the wheel and not to the women beside it, and put the verbs back where he took them out.

The slip at the head is mine. I held the tally down with the hand I throw with and did not know I had marked it. Slip goes into the grain and no washing takes it out, which is why we sign with it here and not with ink.

\subsection*{How it is thrown}

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item Set the lump on the round the last pot left, not beside it. A board wiped clean is a board with no memory, and the first pot off a clean board goes flat under the knuckle, which the pot pays for and the thrower carries.

\item Let the wheel take the lump true before the hands go in. A lump that runs crooked will make a crooked wall, and a crooked wall makes a rim that opens in the firing; the fire finds what the hand let go, and it does not ask who let it.

\item Draw with two hands and let the clay come up between them. You do not pull the wall; you hold the space where the wheel puts it. A hand that pulls makes a thin side, and a thin side is a lie the clay tells the fire.

\item Keep the thumb on the wall as it rises, and keep the wall even to the thumb. The thumb is the only measure in this shed that nobody can carry up the road.

\item At the third draw bring the lip round and quiet. A lip left proud is a lip that will crack, and a crack in the rim is a room the pot did not ask anybody into.

\item Knuckle the rim before the thread goes under the foot. A whole one answers full and the note goes through; a hollow stops at the skin and gives back flat. The rack takes both and does not say which was which, so the knuckle has to say it first.

\item Cut the pot off with the thread drawn under the foot, and leave the round standing on the board. The round is not a pot and has never been entered. Count the draws going up, never the pots coming down off the rack; a count coming down is a count of empty racks, which a clerk could enter and nobody else wants.

\item Do not sing it at the Cross, and do not sing it on an Account-day. The bell goes four, four and a gap, and a throwing-song set against that gap comes home wrong in the wrist.

\item The last part is kept back. It is for when the kiln-master has gone up the terrace and the man with the soft cuff has gone back over the north bridge and the shed can hear itself again.

\end{itemize}

\subsection*{The song}

\emph{Said low into the wheel, with the foot steady on the fly. One verse to one draw of the wall. The fourth is not a draw; it is the thumb coming away, and it is not said aloud. The refrain goes into the board and not across the shed; said to a person it becomes an account, and there is enough account at the Cross without bringing it into the shed.}

\begin{quote}\itshape The lump goes down where the last one stood,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape on the wet round the board kept from the pot;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape don’t wipe the round, center on it,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the wheel takes up what the hand put there.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Draw it and lift it, three to the rim,}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{and the fourth is the thumb coming clean away;}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{the pot goes up to the rack and the round stays here,}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{and the note in the rim is the note the clay came with.}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape At the third draw the lip comes round and quiet\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the collar sits where the thumb left it;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape a lip stood proud is a lip cracked in the firing,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the fire finds it though nobody set it.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Draw it and lift it, three to the rim,}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{and the fourth is the thumb coming clean away;}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{the pot goes up to the rack and the round stays here,}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{and the note in the rim is the note the clay came with.}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Knuckle the rim before the thread goes under;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape a whole one answers and the note goes through;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape a hollow stops at the skin and gives back flat,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the rack takes both and doesn’t tell which.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Draw it and lift it, three to the rim,}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{and the fourth is the thumb coming clean away;}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{the pot goes up to the rack and the round stays here,}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{and the note in the rim is the note the clay came with.}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape A thread under the foot and the pot comes away,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the round sits down where the pot stood;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the next lump goes on the very same round,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the board keeps count of every one.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Draw it and lift it, three to the rim,}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{and the fourth is the thumb coming clean away;}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{the pot goes up to the rack and the round stays here,}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{and the note in the rim is the note the clay came with.}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape One in twelve is printed and read at the Cross,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape but the round on the board isn’t entered;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the pot goes up and the figure goes up,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the clay the pot left on the board stays here.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Draw it and lift it, three to the rim,}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{and the fourth is the thumb coming clean away;}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{the pot goes up to the rack and the round stays here,}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{and the note in the rim is the note the clay came with.}\end{quote}

There is a space before the last refrain, the length of a thumb laid flat on the round where you feel for the seam before you lift the pot. I have left it on the tally. A clerk put a round nought in it once, a thing you can hold up and look at; a thumb laid flat is not.

\subsection*{The part they keep back}

\emph{Not said while the kiln-master stands in the shed door, and not while a man with a satchel is on the boards. Said to the board and not across the wheel.}

\begin{quote}\itshape Three to the rim and the fourth on the board.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape The pot goes up and the ring stays down.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape We don’t show the round to a man with a slate;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape he puts a nought in it and carries it off.\end{quote}

There is no verse after it. The next thing is the lump going down on the round and the foot taking the fly, which is not a verse and has never wanted one.

\subsection*{What the kiln-master did}

He came up from the terrace on the wrong wind with the sweet edge of the glaze at one corner of his mouth and read the tally with one eye on the drying racks. Against \emph{the rack takes both and doesn’t tell which} he wrote in broad charcoal: \emph{Unsound ware rejected before firing. No loss arises.} He underlined it twice. Against \emph{the round on the board isn’t entered} he set: \emph{Board residue; no entry lies.} He did not look at the board while he wrote it.

Underneath, in mine: he is right about the board and wrong about the loss. What is left standing is not nothing even when it is not entered, and a board without its own round is a board that has forgotten every pot it held, which is the whole memory of this shed and the one thing he cannot carry up the terrace.

\subsection*{What the clerk did}

The factor’s clerk borrowed the leaf at Greybank on a morning when the tile was being weighed, with his cuff gone soft from washing and the ink sitting in two fingers of it. He took the verbs out and set his words above mine, the way a face sets itself above an old repair, and I have left his hand standing and put ours underneath.

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item At \emph{a hollow stops at the skin and gives back flat}, he wrote \emph{vessel unsound; not a chargeable defect}, and underlined it twice. He thinks a flat note is a pot that has reached its term. In this shed a flat note is a lump set down wrong and the board told nothing about it.

\item At \emph{the note in the rim is the note the clay came with}, he wrote \emph{ware conforms to the sampled body}, which is true of a figure and false of a pot you have held under the knuckle while the wheel was still turning.

\item At \emph{the round sits down where the pot stood}, he wrote \emph{no material of value remaining}, and drew a line under it that went a finger’s breadth past the margin. The round is not material and has never had a value. It has had eleven seasons of pots on it, which is a count of another kind.

\item At \emph{one in twelve is printed and read at the Cross}, he wrote \emph{deduction current, one part in twelve}, and set the printed figure over it. He has entered the number that was read and not the number that was paid, which is the whole distance between a cuff and a wrist.

\item Where I had left the space before the last refrain, he put a round nought and wrote \emph{vacancy} under it. A nought is a number and travels. A thumb laid flat is a place, and stays where it was put.

\end{itemize}

\subsection*{What the woman at the drying racks put in the margin}

The thick charcoal belongs to a woman who sets the pots up rim-down and has carried them past this wheel since before the Glaze Wars. I have copied it as it stands, without making the hands agree.

At \emph{don’t wipe the round, center on it}: \emph{A girl wiped the board clean one morning and threw six pots and every one went flat. She did not know she had wiped away the round, and the board did not tell her. I have not told her since, and she still throws at that wheel.}

At \emph{knuckle the rim before the thread goes under}: \emph{I asked the pot with the hairline, the one that comes back every firing, and it gave back full. I set it up on the rack all the same. I have not told the kiln-master and I have not set it by the wall, which is a thing I will answer for somewhere else.}

At the part they keep back: \emph{Every yard keeps a fourth. The bank keeps a cut, the stairs keep a step, and here we keep the round. I have never asked what number the round would have if it had one, because it is the only thing in this yard the slate has never wanted.}

\subsection*{At the head and in the gutter}

The slip thumb at the head is mine and has gone into the grain; there is no Last Day at a wheel and nothing here gets gathered and burnt. The pale gutter-line came out of the Brook and has taken the edge off one word of the fifth verse; I have not written it back, because a word the weather has taken is said slowly and everything in this shed is said slowly. The curl of eel-sinew caught across the second leaf came off the cutting thread; I have left it lying over the word it landed on. The grey flake in the fold came off the round under the pot and is lighter in the hand than a good flake, which is the whole of the lesson and no use at all to a clerk. The damp round on the third leaf is a wet pot’s foot set down before the pot went to the rack, dried to the colour of the board. The green bead came off a girl with sweetness still at her mouth who touched the leaf and went back to the slip; I have not washed it. The sour ring is small ale set down at the first verse and taken up at the last. The grey along the outer fold came off a cuff laid where no cuff has business lying on a wheel. Nobody will own it. There is no sweeping here; the grey goes into the next season under the dust-cloth.

\subsection*{At the foot, in a hand nobody will own}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{The wheel keeps the round. The rack keeps the ware.}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{The pot goes up the road. The ring stays here.}\end{quote}

I asked the woman at the drying racks, the clerk, and a carter waiting with his horse at the yard gate, and had three answers and no hand. I have left the line where it was written. The tally goes back under the throw-board. Tomorrow a lump will go down on the same round, three draws and the fourth where the board put it, and if the clerk comes again with his soft cuff he may have the nought. He cannot have the round, because it is a place, and he has no word for a place that stays where it was set down.

\clearpage\phantomsection\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{The White Hands, Being the Drinking Song of the Stonemouth Quarry, Set Down in the Ale-Room Beside the Lime Kiln}
\CRsheetheading{The White Hands, Being the Drinking Song of the Stonemouth Quarry, Set Down in the Ale-Room Beside the Lime Kiln}
{\centering\FellFont\itshape\footnotesize\color{faded} A quarrymen’s drinking song in Grathic, called over small ale after the lime draw and never at the quarry face; the words in a housekeeper’s small hand, the count as the men keep it, the lift said by the whole room, one correction in the narrow upright Ledgerhand of a clerk come up from Greybank, a face-man’s note in the margin, and one line at the foot in a hand nobody will own · Set down in Bone of Y.H. 811, the Long Cold, at Stonemouth where the Ferr comes into the Ilm, by the woman who keeps the ale-room beside the lime kiln and takes the men’s names for their ale; written in charcoal and lime-dust on the back of a weigh-slip spoiled by wet slate, and copied forward in Bone of Y.H. 812 into a quire of three leaves sewn with eel-sinew. It survives in a cracked pot on the shelf behind the room door: white lime ground into the grain at the head and worked into the creases of the first leaf, a blue-grey streak where a sleeve wet from the Ferr touched the fold, a ring where a cup of small ale stood from the first question to the last, a thumb of tallow, a lap of sandstone grit in the gutter, a square of bare paper where a word was scraped away, the clerk’s correction standing above the words, and a grey Ash print along the outer fold that nobody will own.\par}\medskip
I keep the room where the men drink after the lime draw. I take their names for their ale and give the names back at the end of the tend when the factor’s man comes up from Greybank, which is a way of keeping accounts without owning them. I do not sing. I write down what is sung, which is quieter work and needs a better ear than singing does, though no man has ever said so.

The white at the head of this leaf is lime, not Ash. There is Ash enough in this room without bringing it into a book, and I have not swept either. A woman who sweeps before she writes will write a different song, and it will be a true one and no use to anybody.

\subsection*{The manner of it}

\emph{Written small at the head, in charcoal, with one word gone over in tallow.}

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item It is not sung at the face. A man who sings at the face has not yet learned where to put his feet, and the bank-man will send him home.

\item It is called after the lime draw, when the kiln has given up and the men have washed as far as their wrists. It is not a song for the kiln month. In Ember the kiln is working and a man’s heat is already spoken for.

\item The bank-man says the first line of a part and the room says the line after it. The lift belongs to everybody and is said into the cup, not across the table. A man who calls a lift loudly has to mean it, and there is not one man in this room who wants to be meant.

\item If a man in a clean coat comes up the road from Greybank, stop at the end of the part. Begin again when he has gone back down it. Nobody in Stonemouth will say why we stop, and the man in the clean coat never asks, which is how we have kept the habit for thirty years.

\end{itemize}

The lift, which ends every part:

\begin{quote}\itshape Lift to the stone; it outlasts the name.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape White hands, full cup, and the rest goes round.\end{quote}

\subsection*{At the face}

\begin{quote}\itshape Seven to the hole and the powder in,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape stand where the bank-man tells you to stand;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the stone gives a note that is not a note\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the dust comes up white on the land.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape The rope burns true and the cart goes down,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the sandstone answers dull when the wedge is set;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Lift to the stone; it outlasts the name.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape White hands, full cup, and the rest goes round.\end{quote}

The note is not the full note of a pot and no man here has called it that. A kiln-master from Sill come up to look at our stone tapped a block with his knuckle and said it answered dull, and went away with his hands in his coat. He was not wrong. We do not tap the wall to ask it anything. We stand where we are told to stand.

\subsection*{The lime draw}

\begin{quote}\itshape The kiln takes the hill and gives back the lime,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape white in the creases and bitter to the touch;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape you lift with your sleeve and you set with your hand\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and you pay for the hand in the thaw, not now.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape It burns in the nail and it burns in the cuff,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and a man comes out of it pale as a pot;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Lift to the stone; it outlasts the name.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape White hands, full cup, and the rest goes round.\end{quote}

A pot is honest. I have set a pot down on this bench for twenty years and known by the sound of it what it would do. I have never known a man that way, and I have stopped wanting to. The lime takes the print of a hand and keeps it after the hand has gone, which is a trick the Court would like if it had thought of it.

\subsection*{The water}

\begin{quote}\itshape The Ferr comes down with the dust of the west,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape cold in the throat and sweet in the sleep;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape three hundred went thin on a stream with no name\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the Court wrote the figure and called it a war.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape It ran then as it runs now, downhill and cold,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the women of High Kiln drank it for years;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Lift to the stone; it outlasts the name.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape White hands, full cup, and the rest goes round.\end{quote}

My mother was of High Kiln and she would not let me drink the Ferr, which I thought was a novelty of hers and am now old enough to know was a judgment. She never said why. When the physicians came down from Greybank in the year the sweetness was written about, she let them look at her gums and gave them a cup of barley water and sent them back up the road with nothing they wanted. She died thin but not sweet, and I have kept that as a thing to be careful with rather than a thing to be proud of.

\subsection*{The verse they do not sing before a man from Greybank}

They take this one up when the clerk has gone back down the road with his satchel under his arm. I have it from the bank-man, with the space left before it, which is the space they leave in the singing.

\begin{quote}\itshape One in twelve, says the notice, read twice at the Cross;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the cart counts four and the kiln gives back one;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the one that is left is the one at the bench\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape where a man sat down and did not get up.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape The cup goes round and the cup comes back,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the name goes up and the name comes down;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Lift to the stone; it outlasts the name,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the place at the end of the bench stays set.\end{quote}

I asked the bank-man whose bench it was. He said every bench in Stonemouth has an end, and went to see to the kiln. There is a man who used to sit there whose name I still take for an ale on the tend’s last day and still give back when the factor’s man comes. I have not entered him anywhere else. A name kept in a room is a different weight from a name kept on a slate, and I have found that a woman can carry the one when the men beside her have put the other down.

\subsection*{What the face-man wrote in the margin}

Against the verse about the Ferr, a man who has worked the face for thirty years wrote in a hand that shakes at the ends of words:

\begin{quote}\itshape Two of mine went thin on that water. The slate says none. I have put the two where a clerk can see them if he ever looks away from his paper.\end{quote}

He brought me the leaf himself and stood at the door while I read it, and took it back to the face without a word about the ale he had not been given. I have kept his two in the margin where he set them. The room has never once sung that verse with the two in it, and the men know it is there.

\subsection*{What the clerk did}

The clerk come up from Greybank borrowed the leaf on a market morning, being a man who cannot leave paper alone. He has a cuff gone soft from washing and the ink sits in two fingers of it and will not come out. He struck out \emph{it outlasts the name} and set above it, \emph{the measure is recorded and the residue nil}. Against the lime he wrote \emph{entered in kind}, which is a true figure and a cold one. Against \emph{three hundred went thin} he wrote \emph{one in twelve, as the notice says}, and numbered the lines from one to four so that a man could read them without singing. Where the lift stands he put a small square rule and wrote \emph{no vacancy in the roll}. He took the verbs out of two lines as though a verb were a thing a man could carry off in a cuff and sell at the next crossing.

I have put the words back underneath his and left his standing above. He can enter the lime in kind; the kiln has given back the same weight for twenty years and nobody has disputed it. He can enter the stream as a war, because there is a war on a slate somewhere and it saves a man the trouble of looking at the water. What he cannot enter is the place at the end of the bench, and he has not tried. A clerk knows the difference between a figure and a place better than a woman who keeps a room has any right to, and he has made his living on it.

He scraped a word off the lower leaf and would not say which. I have left the bare square where it stood. A word can be taken off paper; the space it leaves is harder, because the paper remembers where it was and the eye keeps going back to it. This is the whole of the account between this room and Greybank, and neither of us has settled it.

\subsection*{At the head and in the gutter}

The lime at the head came off my own cuff when I held the leaf down in the draught under the door, and it has worked into the grain where nothing will get it out. The blue-grey along the fold is the Ferr: a man came in from the weir head with wet sleeves and set his cup on the leaf while he was telling the bank-man something about the upstream water, and the tell was lost when the water dried and the blue stayed. The ring is mine, from a cup I set down before the first question and took up after the last, which is how this house measures a conversation. The tallow is off the lamp I kept low while I wrote, so that the men at the table would not know I was writing and change the words for me. The grit in the gutter is coarse sandstone and came out of a boot, not a pocket; no man in this room carries stone away, and I have never asked the boot. The grey along the outer fold came off a cuff laid where no cuff has business lying. I have not swept it. There is no Last Day in a cracked pot behind a door.

\subsection*{At the foot, in a hand nobody will own}

\begin{quote}\itshape The bench keeps a place and the cup keeps a ring;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the stone knows the both and says neither thing.\end{quote}

I asked the room whose it was and had three answers and no hand, as I have had before about the grey print and the scraped word. I have set it down as it stands. The leaf goes back into the cracked pot behind the door, and tomorrow the draw comes again and the men lift to the stone, which does not answer and asks nothing of anybody, and the place at the end of the bench stays set.

\clearpage\phantomsection\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{The White Seam, Being the Hopping Rhyme of the Children of Stonemouth Behind the Lime Kiln, with the Counting-Out, the Nine Hops, and What the Weigh-Clerk Set Against It}
\CRsheetheading{The White Seam, Being the Hopping Rhyme of the Children of Stonemouth Behind the Lime Kiln, with the Counting-Out, the Nine Hops, and What the Weigh-Clerk Set Against It}
{\centering\FellFont\itshape\footnotesize\color{faded} A wash-woman’s gathering of a children’s counting game, set down in charcoal and lime-dust on the back of a spoiled lime-warrant; the counting-out and the hops in the children’s own half-sung Stonemouth speech, the manner of the play in the writer’s small hand, a correction in the narrow upright Ledgerhand of the weigh-clerk at the landing, a gloss pressed into the margin in charcoal by a dresser of stone who has caught children in this yard for three-and-twenty years, and one line at the foot in the print of a child’s white thumb · Written behind the lime kiln at Stonemouth where the Ferr comes into the Ilm five leagues upriver of Sill, in Bone of Y.H. 812, the Thin Year, by a woman who takes in the quarrymen’s washing and cannot get the lime out of her own hands; set down on the back of a lime-warrant spoiled by a wetting, carried downriver at the Opening of the Slates in Ilmen of Y.H. 813 and copied at Greybank onto the back of a voided weigh-slip. Kept folded in the bundle of coat-cuffs she takes home on the cart. It survives with lime worked into the grain at the head, a blue-grey streak in the gutter off a sleeve wet from the Ferr, a small round mark where a two-mark piece was set down to hold the leaf and taken up again, a ring of small ale at the fold, the flat white print of a thumb where the leaf was held in a draught, a grey Ash print along the outer fold which nobody will own, the weigh-clerk’s correction standing above the children’s words, the stone-dresser’s charcoal pressed in beside the second line, and one line at the foot that nobody will claim\par}\medskip
I take in washing for the quarry at Stonemouth. The lime comes out of the coats and will not come out of my hands, and I have long since given up trying; a woman who scrubs her knuckles raw for a living learns which stains are hers to keep. I set this down because the weigh-clerk at the landing asked one morning what the children counted when they hopped the flagstones behind the kiln. He wrote the answer while I was still saying it, with the hopping taken out and a figure standing in the middle of it. What follows is what they said before he came up the bank and what they said again after he had gone back over the ford with his cuff laid flat against the leaf, as though a hand laid flat were a hand that had done nothing.

The white at the head is lime and not the Ash. There is Ash enough in this country without borrowing it for a children’s game, and I have swept neither of them.

\subsection*{How it is played}

\emph{Played behind the lime kiln on the flat flagstones of the dressing yard, in the dry weeks when the dust lies thick enough to hold a line. Not in rain: a line drawn in wet dust is a smear, and a child who hops a smear learns the wrong count. Not in the Five, when the children are made to stand and listen and there is no yard for it. In Bone they hop the trodden floor of the ale-room, which is the same game with the cold taken off it.}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item One child draws the line with a wet thumb and is called \textbf{the hand}. The seam is thumb-wide and runs across the stones from the lower side to the upper, after the seam a dresser cuts along in the rock. A hand does not hop in the round she drew; she stands with the dust on her thumb and watches the others cross it, which the children take as a punishment and the yard takes as practice.

\item The seam must be crossed and never touched. A child who sets a heel in the dust has \textbf{paid}, and sits on the stone with her hands in her lap. She is brought back by no name and no forgiveness; the next child to draw calls her across, and she goes over on the first hop. A line that has been rubbed out can be drawn again, and a line that has been drawn again has no grudge in it.

\item One line of the rhyme, one hop, going out from the lower stones to the upper. On the ninth the hopper holds the back foot above the seam and does not let it fall, and the last word is said to the dust and not to a face. Said to a child it becomes an argument, and there is always a child who will argue.

\item Then the seam is rubbed away with the flat of a hand and drawn again, by the one who paid or by the hand if nobody did. There is no last round and nothing is won. A count a child must make again each time is a count nobody can owe her, which is the whole reason they keep it in dust.

\end{enumerate}

\subsection*{The counting-out, said over the fists}

\emph{Right fists held out, knuckles up. The child who says it touches each fist in turn and does not look at the faces. The fist it stops on draws the seam and stays out of the hopping. Say it to the fists and not to the owners of them, who will argue about anything.}

\begin{quote}\itshape One for the bit and two for the block,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape three for the lime on the cuff and the smock;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape four for the tooth that the buyer has paid,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the fist it stops on lays the line and stays.\end{quote}

\subsection*{The rhyme, as it is hopped}

\emph{One line, one hop. The heel goes down beyond the dust; on the ninth it stays up and the word goes down into the stone. The children will not be told why the last line is said low. Ask them and they ask you why a person wants to know what dust is for.}

\begin{quote}\itshape One for the bank where the block was cut,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape two for the lime that will not wash out;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape three for the kiln with its mouth gone white,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape four for the Ferr that takes what it can;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape five for the bit and the mark beside it,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape six for the tooth and the two marks paid;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape seven for hands gone white to the wrist,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape eight for the name the ale-room keeps;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape nine for the seam, and the heel held still.\end{quote}

\subsection*{What is said when a child whitens her heel}

\emph{Said low, to the stone, while the child sits down with her hands in her lap. The next line-drawer calls her over with the first hop and there is no more said about it.}

\begin{quote}\itshape The dust is up. The seam’s gone thin.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Draw it again and the child comes in.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Say it to the stone and not to me;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the dust takes the foot and gives it back.\end{quote}

\subsection*{The verse they do not hop while the weigh-clerk is on the bank}

I have this from the girl who drew the seam the morning he leaned over the wall with his cuff laid flat. She said it to the stones with her back turned and made me set it down with none of my words in it, because a verse hopped to a stone wants nothing added and a verse said to a man at a bench wants everything taken away.

\begin{quote}\itshape They take the name at the door for the cup\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and give it back when the tend is done;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape they weigh the block and they write the mark,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the block stays here when the mark is gone.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape We keep the dust on the back of the hand.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape The hand goes home. The dust stays here.\end{quote}

\subsection*{What the weigh-clerk did}

He laid his cuff on the leaf before his eye went to the words, the way they do at that bench, and set the flagstones down as \emph{common ground of no tenure, used for gaming}. Against the nine lines he wrote \emph{nine passages, each charged at a half-bit, payable by the house of the child hopping}. Against \emph{the heel held still} he set \emph{one party in arrears; the line is a boundary of the Court}. At the foot, where the seam is rubbed out and drawn again, he put a figure and wrote \emph{perpetual}, which is a word for a thing that never needs a thumb to hold it down.

I have put the children’s words back underneath and left his standing above. He takes the hands out because a thing always true has no need of them, and because a hand in a sentence is a hand that might be asked whose it is. I put them back because a girl with lime to the wrist does not know she is hearing something always true; she wants to know whose turn it is to draw. He has set a charge where a child sat down. A figure travels down the river road and a seam in dust does not, and that is the whole trouble between this bench and this yard.

\subsection*{In the margin, in Ivo’s charcoal}

The stone-dresser writes small, the way a man writes who has one hand out checking a bank and the other holding a child by the collar.

At \emph{two for the lime that will not wash out}: \textbf{She says lime. It is quicklime when it is fresh and will take the skin off a child as readily as it will take a block off the bank. I had rather a child stepped over dust than stepped off the edge.}

At \emph{eight for the name the ale-room keeps}: \textbf{The room gives the names back at the end of the tend. It is the man who has forgotten his own that does not come back with them. I have set more of those than I have set bones.}

I have left both where his thumb put them. He has caught children in this yard for three-and-twenty years and has never once entered a fall.

\subsection*{At the head and in the gutter}

The lime at the head is off the sleeve I wipe the coats with and has worked into the grain; no scrubbing takes it out, which is why I sign in charcoal and not in ink. The blue-grey in the gutter came off a sleeve wet from the Ferr when a man leaned over to see the writing and would not sit down; the river dries the colour of old rope on a man and stays in him after he has gone. The round mark is where a buyer set a two-mark piece down to hold the leaf and took it up again; he paid for a tooth and did not stay to see it written. The ring at the fold is small ale from a cup set down by nobody in particular and claimed by three children and denied by one. The flat white print where the leaf was held in the draught is mine, and is the only word on this leaf I wrote with my thumb. The grey along the outer fold came off a cuff that had no business lying in a dressing yard, and I have not swept it. There is a Last Day in Sill and the corners are swept there in the morning and burnt and called dealt with. There is no Last Day behind this kiln. The seam goes under the cart tomorrow with the cuffs.

\subsection*{At the foot, in the print of a child’s white thumb}

\begin{quote}\itshape I drew the line. I am the one who cannot cross it.\end{quote}

I asked the girl who drew, the woman who keeps the ale-room, the dresser of stone and the weigh-clerk himself, and had four answers and no hand. I have left the line where it was made. The bundle goes back on the cart and the dust goes back on the stones, and if the clerk comes up the bank again with his hand laid flat I shall let him charge what can be charged, and keep the seam where a child can draw it again.

\clearpage\phantomsection\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{The Wind in the Clay, Being the Beating-Out Song of the Clay Yard at Low Kiln, Sung Over the Lump Before It Goes to the Wheel, with the Strokes as They Are Counted, the Listening Where No Stroke Falls, a Kiln-Master’s Correction in Broad Charcoal, a Factor’s Clerk’s Figures in the Narrow Upright Hand, and One Verse at the Foot in a Hand Nobody Will Own}
\CRsheetheading{The Wind in the Clay, Being the Beating-Out Song of the Clay Yard at Low Kiln, Sung Over the Lump Before It Goes to the Wheel, with the Strokes as They Are Counted, the Listening Where No Stroke Falls, a Kiln-Master’s Correction in Broad Charcoal, a Factor’s Clerk’s Figures in the Narrow Upright Hand, and One Verse at the Foot in a Hand Nobody Will Own}
{\centering\FellFont\itshape\footnotesize\color{faded} A beater’s work song in the low Grathic of the yard, said down into the lump and not up into the shed; the verses counted in the cut, the turn and the fall, with the fourth place kept for the flat of the hand; the rubrics of the bench in the same charcoal and tallow hand; a kiln-master’s correction in broad charcoal, a factor’s clerk’s figures standing above in Ledgerhand, a rack-woman’s gloss pressed into the margin in thick charcoal, and one line at the foot in a hand nobody will claim · Set down in Smoke of Y.H. 813, the month of the second firing, by Gella, a woman of Low Kiln who beats the clay at a bench three doors up the Clay Yard from the Vail kiln-house and has done it two-and-twenty years, having begun to feel a hollow in a lump before she cuts it; written in charcoal thinned with slip and tallow on the back of a glaze-house mixing tally spoiled by a fall of slip, folded into four, tied with grey wool and carried in the breast of her apron against a square of sacking gone soft at the seam; copied forward at Greybank onto the back of a weigh-slip gone stiff with salt. It survives with wet slip worked into the grain at the head, brick dust ground into the fold, a wire-nick through the second leaf, a barley-water ring through the third verse, a green bead of lead glaze pressed into the lower corner, a long hair the colour of wet wool caught in the seam, a small dry flake of a hollow lump pressed flat between the third and fourth leaf, a grey Ash smear along the gutter that nobody will own, the kiln-master’s broad correction, the rack-woman’s gloss, the clerk’s figures standing above, and the one line at the foot\par}\medskip
I beat the clay at a bench three doors up the Clay Yard from the Vail kiln-house and I have done it for two-and-twenty years. A man come up from Greybank with a soft cuff and a slate under his arm asked a girl at the wheel what the hands said over the lump before it went to the wheel, wrote her answer down before she had finished it, and went off up the yard with it. A beating-song taken down by a man who has never had a lump go hollow on him in the firing is a song with the air let out of it already. So I have set the words down as we say them and put the verbs back where he took them out. The tallow at the head is mine; I held the tally down in the draught under the bench and did not know I had marked it.

The clay comes off the treads wet and full of little rooms you cannot see. You draw the wire through it, lay one half along the other, and bring the flat of your hand down on the seam, and cut again and beat again until the rooms are closed. That is the beating-out. The wire is an honest tool because it shows the cut you made; a hollow is a lie with clay round it, and the fire is the only reader that never misreads. We say the words down into the lump, not up into the shed. Said up into the air they grow a tune in them, and a man in a clean coat can carry the tune away and leave the lump behind him.

Three strokes to a verse: the cut, the turn, the fall. The fourth is a hand laid flat to listen. It is not a stroke and it is not counted, and a girl who counts it aloud will beat air into a lump instead of out of it. A clerk may put a figure in that place if he has a mind to. There is room for figures in every trade; there is not a figure in this one.

\subsection*{How it is beaten}

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item Cut toward the light, so that you can see the grain you are closing. A cut made in the dark is a cut you will have to find again in the firing.

\item Lay one half along the other and beat on the seam, not across the lump. A blow across the lump drives the hollow deeper; a blow on the seam shuts it.

\item Keep the hand flat. A fist beats a lump hollow in half the time and says it is sparing the wrist.

\item Three strokes and the ear. Do not say the fourth aloud. A fourth called a stroke is a stroke the lump did not get, and somebody will pay for it at the draw.

\item Knuckle the lump before it goes to the wheel. A sound one answers full; a hollow one gives back a small dead sound that stops at the skin. If it answers flat, take up the wire again, however late it is.

\item Say the refrain into the clay and not to the girl beside you. Said to a person it becomes instruction, and instruction at this bench is instruction she will unlearn at somebody else’s.

\item Do not sing it at the Cross, and do not sing it on an Account-day. The bell there goes four, four and a gap, and a beating-song set against that gap comes home wrong in the hand.

\item The last part is kept back. It is for when the kiln-master has gone up the terrace and the man from Greybank has gone back over the north bridge with his satchel under his arm and the yard can hear itself again.

\end{itemize}

\subsection*{The song}

\emph{The call goes down into the lump. Refrain after every verse, the last line held until the hand is off the clay. One line of the refrain to one stroke.}

\begin{quote}\itshape The wire goes through where the thumb went in\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and leaves the cut standing where the hand was;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape cut it open, look at the grain ---\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape a lump can be fair outside and hollow through.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Cut it, turn it, let it fall.}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Lay the hand flat. That is all.}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Three are the strokes; the fourth is the ear.}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{What the ear lets go the fire will not.}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Lay one half along the other and bring the flat down,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape not so hard that you kill it, not so soft that you leave it;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the clay wants to hold its breath the way a woman does\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape when a man with a slate comes into the room.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Cut it, turn it, let it fall.}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Lay the hand flat. That is all.}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Three are the strokes; the fourth is the ear.}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{What the ear lets go the fire will not.}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Three strokes and the hand laid flat to hear\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape what the eye will never be told;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape a hollow answers hollow under the palm\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the way a pot answers flat under the knuckle.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Cut it, turn it, let it fall.}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Lay the hand flat. That is all.}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Three are the strokes; the fourth is the ear.}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{What the ear lets go the fire will not.}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape What you leave in the lump the fire will find ---\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape not with a wire, not with a hand,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape but in the throat, with a small flat knock,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and a crack set by the door for the neighbours to see.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Cut it, turn it, let it fall.}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Lay the hand flat. That is all.}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Three are the strokes; the fourth is the ear.}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{What the ear lets go the fire will not.}\end{quote}
