\begin{quote}\itshape Six under the heel and three under the wire,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape two at the wheel and four paces to the rack;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape every count in this yard leaves a place it won’t enter,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the pot goes through the fire with the whole of it.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Cut it, turn it, let it fall.}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Lay the hand flat. That is all.}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Three are the strokes; the fourth is the ear.}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{What the ear lets go the fire will not.}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Beat it for the girl who will sit where you sit,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape for the thumb that goes at the hollow place;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape you cannot see what you have driven out,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and that is the work, and the only part you keep.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Cut it, turn it, let it fall.}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Lay the hand flat. That is all.}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Three are the strokes; the fourth is the ear.}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{What the ear lets go the fire will not.}\end{quote}

There is a space before the last refrain in the singing, the length of a hand laid flat. I have left it on the tally. A clerk put a round nought in it once, which is a thing you can hold up and look at; a listening is not.

\subsection*{The part they keep back}

\emph{Not sung while a man from the terrace or a man with a satchel stands in the yard. Said low, to the bench and not across it.}

\begin{quote}\itshape One in twelve, says the notice, read twice at the Cross,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape but the box goes up the clay road with another figure shut in it;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the number you hear is not the number you pay,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and a hollow in the house is a hollow in the slate.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape There’s a place in the returning row we go around with a look,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape where a hand went into the strips and did not come back;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape no figure stands in it, no slate is set down there,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the clay goes on being beaten where the hand used to beat.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Cut. Turn. Fall. The fourth is the ear.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape The yard keeps the place. The clerk keeps the nought.\end{quote}

\subsection*{What the kiln-master did}

He came up from the terrace on the wrong wind with the sweet edge of the glaze at one corner of his mouth and read the leaf with one eye on the yard. Against \emph{a lump can be fair outside and hollow through} he wrote in broad charcoal: \emph{A lump that answers hollow under the palm is not yet beaten. No pot goes to the wheel on the word of a hand.} He underlined it twice.

Underneath, in mine: He is right about the lump and wrong about the song, which was never about the lump alone. He has read every line with one eye on the kiln, which is how a man reads who has never had to beat out a lump he cannot see into.

\subsection*{What the clerk did}

The factor’s clerk borrowed the leaf on an Account-day, ink sitting in the first joint of two fingers of his soft cuff and not coming out. He took the verbs out and set his words above mine, and I have left his hand standing and put ours underneath, as a bench keeps the cut and the fire keeps the hollow.

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item At \emph{a hollow is a lie with clay round it}, he wrote \emph{air enclosed; defect, not a deduction}. True in the figure and false in the yard, where the lie is the whole of the thing and the air is only what it is made of.

\item At \emph{the fire will find it}, he wrote \emph{the firing discloses latent fault; no entry required.} He thinks a fault found is a fault entered. In this yard a fault found is a pot set by the door with the crack showing.

\item At the fourth place he put a round nought and wrote \emph{vacancy}. It is a true thing in a language nobody at this bench speaks. We do not say the fourth and we do not strike it out.

\item At \emph{every count in this yard leaves a place it won’t enter}, he wrote \emph{unaccounted residue}. There is no word in Ledgerhand for a listening, so he has made one that will travel and arrive empty.

\item At \emph{a hand went into the strips and did not come back}, he wrote \emph{one absence, nil}, and set a figure against the place in the row. I have left his figure standing beside our look. Both stand.

\end{itemize}

\subsection*{What the rack-woman put in the margin}

The thick charcoal belongs to a woman who keeps the drying racks four doors up and has carried more wet pots than she will count. I have copied it as it stands, without making the hands agree.

At \emph{the clay wants to hold its breath the way a woman does}: \emph{I have held mine seven years and set it down on the Last Day with nothing in it. A lump is not the only thing that keeps a room shut.}

At \emph{a hollow answers hollow under the palm}: \emph{I knuckled a cup that answered full and watched it go into the throat and come out with a crack a straw would lie in. The note was true and the lump was not. Both stand.}

At \emph{what you leave in the lump the fire will find}: \emph{It finds it and does not ask who left it, which is more than can be said for the collector.}

At the part they keep back: \emph{I have asked three times what the beating is worth and been given the weather, the river and the price of barley. I have stopped asking.}

\subsection*{At the head and in the gutter}

The wet-slip thumb at the head is mine and will not come out of the grain, which is why I use it to sign. The brick dust in the fold came off the bench and is the only thing in this leaf put there by the trade and not by a person. The wire-nick went through the second leaf when the cutter caught the fold; I have not mended it, because a song with a cut through it is a song that has been with the wire. The barley-water ring stood through the third verse while a girl stood over me telling me to keep the hand flat; she took her cup up when I had done, and the ring has gone the colour of the pot it stood on. The green bead came off a girl who leaned to see the writing with sweetness still at her tongue; she touched the tally, said nothing, and went back up the terrace. I have not washed it. The hair the colour of wet wool is not mine and has caught in the seam and will stay there. The flake between the third and fourth leaf came off a lump that answered hollow after I had beaten it nine times; it is lighter in the hand than a sound flake, which is the whole of the lesson and no use at all to a clerk. The grey along the gutter came off a cuff laid where no cuff has business lying on a bench. Nobody will own it. There is no Last Day behind a bench.

\subsection*{At the foot, in a hand nobody will own}

\begin{quote}\itshape The wire keeps the cut. The fire keeps the hollow.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape The hand keeps nothing and goes on beating.\end{quote}

I asked the rack-woman, a girl come up from the wheel and a man waiting with a barrow at the yard gate, and had three answers and no hand. I have left the line where it was written. The tally goes back under the broken pot at the bench. Tomorrow the clay comes up off the treads and I shall cut it, turn it, let it fall, and lay the hand flat where no stroke falls, and the fire will find whatever I have left in it, and the clerk may have his copy of the nought.

\clearpage\phantomsection\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{The Words That Hold, Being an Extract from the Survey-Roll of the First Seam Concerning the Year 717, the Surveyor Who Set Two Words Against the Oldest Repair, and the Order That Took Him Up the Shaft; with the Layers as the Roll Keeps Them, the Two Translations Set Side by Side, the Song Said at the Mouth, Two Corrections in Borrowed Hands, and a Line at the Foot Nobody Will Own}
\CRsheetheading{The Words That Hold, Being an Extract from the Survey-Roll of the First Seam Concerning the Year 717, the Surveyor Who Set Two Words Against the Oldest Repair, and the Order That Took Him Up the Shaft; with the Layers as the Roll Keeps Them, the Two Translations Set Side by Side, the Song Said at the Mouth, Two Corrections in Borrowed Hands, and a Line at the Foot Nobody Will Own}
{\centering\FellFont\itshape\footnotesize\color{faded} A surveyor’s annal, being an extract from the roll kept in the survey room off the Duelling Floor beneath Keld Keep; the year-entries in the number-first hand, the oldest repairs set down as the seam showed them, the Court’s word and the Keldish word standing side by side and neither chosen, the removal order in the upright Ledgerhand of a clerk who was not in the shaft, the mine-reeve’s red check entered where it fell, a saying of the shaft mouth, two corrections in borrowed hands, and one line at the foot in a hand that has never come forward · Written in the survey room off the Duelling Floor in the First Seam beneath Keld Keep in Ash of Y.H. 812, the Thin Year, by the keeper of the survey-roll, who signs with the office and not with a name and keeps the verbs in; copied from a roll carried forward in the surveyor’s tin and from a rubbing of the crossed entry of Y.H. 588, and carried up at the Opening of the Slates, Ilmen 1, Y.H. 813. It survives as five leaves of slate-rubbing paper sewn with iron wire and folded into a strip of harness leather gone soft at the stitch: coal smut worked into the grain at the head, slate dust in the gutter, a red point from the mine-reeve’s checking-stone at the second corner, a shaving of warm-stone gone cold in the fourth leaf, a frost-feather pressed flat that was gone by noon, a tallow thumb at the foot, a square of bare paper where a word was scraped away with a knife-point and not written back, one correction in the narrow upright hand of a clerk come up from the Hearthseat, one in the round hand of the Warden’s hall, and a grey Ash print along the outer fold which the keeper did not make and has not swept\par}\medskip
I keep the survey-roll of the First Seam. It lies in the survey room off the Duelling Floor, in a tin with a lid that shuts, and once a year the Order of the Tenth Clamp takes a paper from a tin lined with warm-stone on the next shelf, reads it, puts it back, and does not act on it. I am not the Order. I keep the tally of the seam, which is older than the Order and will be kept after the men who read that paper have gone up.

This extract is the year 717, when a surveyor of this room set two words against the oldest repair and was taken up the shaft for it. The clerk who entered the taking used a clean hand and left nothing in it that could be argued with. I have put the two words back underneath. A correction that leaves the seam standing and takes away the man who read it belongs in the margin, where the verbs have not been taken out.

\subsection*{The seam as the roll has it}

The rim-seam carries repairs laid one over another, the newest over the oldest, and the lowest of all lie below the Ninth Gallery where the rock sweats and the smell of hot lead is the only warning a man is given. We do not call these repairs stone and we do not call them clay. In the surveyor’s own language a repair is named for what it is made of, and the oldest are entered as that which was left unsaid made solid. The Keldish translate it as Ash. The Court’s copy, kept in the Hearthseat and shown to no one below an assessor, is \emph{said} to translate it as language — said, and not seen by anyone in this room, and I have kept the saying as a saying. Both are guesses, and neither guess has ever been brought up to the floor to be looked at.

The survey of 260 has the passage that no Court history carries. It says the repairs lie in layers as a pot is mended again and again until nothing of the first pot can be seen, and it calls the oldest a repair of unkept words. I have copied that phrase nowhere but this leaf, because a surveyor who carries a phrase out of this room is apt to be met at the shaft mouth by a man with a clean slate.

\subsection*{The entry of Y.H. 717}

The entry stands in the surveyor’s own hand, the number-first hand we use below the floor, and it has never been smoothed:

\begin{quote}\itshape Ninth layer, below the warm-stone. Not stone. Not clay. The shape holds where nothing has been set to hold it. Entered as \emph{words that hold}.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{In the narrow upright hand of a clerk come up from the Hearthseat, written above:} Repair of earth and mineral deposit; no linguistic quality arises. Strike the two words.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Underneath, in mine:} I have not struck them. He had to read the two words before he could write that there were none worth reading, which is the manner of that hand in every room it enters. A man who takes two words off a slate has had to stand where they stood. I have set my hand under his and left his above.\end{quote}

\subsection*{The order that took him up}

What was entered of the removal is shorter than what was entered of the repair, which is the order of things above ground:

\begin{quote}\itshape The person was removed from the shaft; no entry arising. Account standing.\end{quote}

The surveyor is not named. He is entered as the surveyor of the ninth layer, which is the custom here: a man states what he holds before he says who he is, and what this man held was two words. The mine-reeve checked him in red at the second corner of the leaf and found no lie in his measure, and the red point stands there still, which is a check and not a correction. He was not taken up for a false figure. He was taken up for two true ones.

I asked three men what the order was for. One said the seam had been disturbed. One said the office had been disturbed. One said the person had been disturbed. All three are true and none of them is an answer, which is the Keldish way of giving a man the whole room and leaving him to find the door himself.

\subsection*{The two translations}

\emph{The layers as this room keeps them, with the word from the Court set beside the word we use below. I have set both and chosen neither, because a surveyor who chooses between two guesses has made a fact of one of them and will have to answer for it at the weigh.}

Layer — The Court’s word — This room — What the entry says\par

Above the Duelling Floor — dressed stone — dressed stone — stone, and a true note under the knuckle\par

The warm-stone workings — mineral deposit — warm-stone — sold, not lent; keeps a cup one night\par

Below the workings — earth and slipped clay — the Sweating — hot lead gives the only warning\par

The crossed entry of Y.H. 588 — irregular marking — birth-flower — a returned man with a branching red mark; the entry struck by the hand that made it\par

The ninth, lowest — language — Ash — \emph{words that hold} — two guesses and a phrase, all standing\par

The entry of 588 lies in this same roll, in a hand that struck out its own finding. I have set that hand beside the hand of 717, which did not strike its finding out and was struck out of the shaft instead. Both crossings are in the same ink. I have not joined them. A surveyor who joins two crossings has begun an account of the room, and accounts of rooms are kept above ground.

\subsection*{The paper on the next shelf}

Seven years before the year of the two words a paper came up from the Hearthseat called \emph{The Sealed Vessel}. It lies in the tin lined with warm-stone in this room, and the Order reads it once a year and does not act on it. I have read it once, standing, because a keeper of the seam may stand in that place and may not sit in it. The paper asks for a world in which nothing leaks and nothing is owed. I do not know whether such a world would hold a cup. Below this floor nothing holds that has not been mended, and the oldest mending is the one we cannot name.

\subsection*{The song said at the mouth}

\emph{Taken down from a woman who counts at the shaft mouth, said once to the boy going down and once to the ground after he has gone. The second part has a line left out. I have set the space where it stood and put nothing in it, though I know the word that would go there.}

\begin{quote}\itshape One for the arm and one for the stone,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and one for the count that goes before;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the knife goes in and the number stays,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the name is left in the room.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Two go down and the count comes two;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the figure stands though the arm may not.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Hold the rail, it is iron and it takes;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape hold the stone, it is sold and it cools.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape A man wrote down what the lowest said\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the lowest said it true;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape they took him up by the same iron road\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape that a boy goes down at thirteen.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Two go down and the count comes two;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape — — — — — — — — — —\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the mountain keeps what the mountain took,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the slate keeps the place where the words stood.\end{quote}

The woman would not say the line that is left out and would not say who left it out. I have kept the space the length of a line. There is a cup at the end of the Duelling Floor that nobody takes, set for a man whose number was changed twice, and I have entered neither the cup nor the space as a cause.

\subsection*{What the borrowed hands did}

A clerk of the Hearthseat came up in the year of the Long Cold, with ink in two fingers of a cuff gone soft from washing. He struck \emph{words that hold} and wrote \emph{no linguistic quality arises} over it, which I have set down elsewhere in this leaf. Against \emph{removed for two words} he wrote \emph{the person was reassigned; no entry arising}. Against the song he wrote \emph{oral tradition; not a record}, and he drew a line under all my margins and wrote \emph{No such place} above them, so that the edge would read as though it had never held a margin. He had to read every margin before he could write that there were none in them, and I watched him do it.

The round hand from the Warden’s hall wrote above the removal order: \emph{the person was removed for the good of the office.} This is true in the manner that a clean slate is true. I have left it standing over mine. Neither of those hands has put a thumb on the ninth layer, and both have entered it.

\subsection*{At the head and in the gutter}

The coal at the head is mine, off the sleeve I wipe the tally with, and no wet cloth takes it out. The slate dust in the gutter came off the rubbing of the 588 entry and has worked into the sewing. The red at the second corner is the mine-reeve’s point, finding no lie. The shaving in the fourth leaf is warm-stone that kept a cup warm one night on this floor and is cold now, which is the order of that trade. The frost-feather lay on the lip at the mouth and was gone by noon; a yard above ground calls that weather and this room calls it a map of the leak. The tallow thumb at the foot is my own lamp set too near while I copied the removal. The square of bare paper is where I scraped a word away with a knife-point and put no other in its place, and it is the only square in this roll that I made myself. The grey along the outer fold is not mine and not the Court’s. I have had this leaf six years and have not swept it. There is no Last Day under this mountain.

\subsection*{At the foot, in a hand nobody will own}

\begin{quote}\itshape The numbers go down and the count comes back.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Two words went down and the man came up.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape The seam holds what the slate would not hold,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the slate keeps the place where the words stood.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Ask the ninth layer what it is made of.\end{quote}

I asked a Vorr at the stones, who said the numbers were correct; a clerk of the mine-reeve, who said no entry arose; and a woman who counts at the mouth, who said the count came two and would not say the rest. Three answers and no hand. I have left the lines where they were written.

The roll goes back into its tin in the survey room. Next tend I copy the walling-slate off the Duelling Floor, and after that the Ninth Gallery repairs, where the lead smells hot before it takes anyone. The ninth layer is still where it was, with two words standing in it and a clean word written above them, and where the surveyor went after they took him up the shaft the roll does not say, which is the manner this building has of shutting a door.

\clearpage\phantomsection\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{The Year Without Contracts, Being an Extract from the Tide-Roll of the Council of Vhal Concerning the Rising at the Glass Furnaces in Y.H. 626, the Suspension of Salt-Paper for a Year, the Hands Sent to the Pulled Benches, and the Articles That Followed; with the Sheets as the Roll Kept Them, the Anneal-Song, the Table of Hands, Two Corrections in Borrowed Hands, and a Line at the Foot Nobody Will Own}
\CRsheetheading{The Year Without Contracts, Being an Extract from the Tide-Roll of the Council of Vhal Concerning the Rising at the Glass Furnaces in Y.H. 626, the Suspension of Salt-Paper for a Year, the Hands Sent to the Pulled Benches, and the Articles That Followed; with the Sheets as the Roll Kept Them, the Anneal-Song, the Table of Hands, Two Corrections in Borrowed Hands, and a Line at the Foot Nobody Will Own}
{\centering\FellFont\itshape\footnotesize\color{faded} A clerk’s chronicle-extract from the Council’s tide-roll, copied out of the tarred tin under the Council table; the year-entries in the flat scrivener’s hand, the figures set above what the furnaces sent down, the hands entered as a round sum with the names beneath in the gutter, the anneal-song taken down at the third furnace, one word struck and written above in the narrow upright hand of the Council, and a line at the foot in a hand that has never come forward · Written at Vhal in the Council room off the Quay in Ash of Y.H. 812, the Thin Year, by the second clerk of the tide-roll, who has kept it through five Councils and signed none of them; copied from the roll begun in Y.H. 599 and kept since in a tarred tin beneath the Council table, and carried forward at the Opening of the Slates into Y.H. 813. It survives on Council salt-paper kept dry against the practice of the country, sewn with tarred net-twine into a fold of oiled sailcloth; salt bloom worked into the head that comes and goes with the weather, glass dust from the furnaces in the grain of the second leaf, a thumb of tar at the fold off the council table’s rope, a green bead of cliff-glass pressed into the lower corner by a girl who would not give her name, a ring of small ale at the head, a scorched place where the leaf lay near the brazier in the Long Cold, the figure for the sheets struck and written again underneath in the writer’s own hand, two corrections in borrowed hands, and a line at the foot in a hand that has never come forward\par}\medskip
I keep the tide-roll in the Council room, which smells of tar and wet rope and has smelled so since before any of the men now elected were born. The Council is chosen for a year. The roll is not. Five Councils have come and gone since I was set to it, and not one of them has signed it, which is a kind of honesty in a port where a document is only as good as the weather it has survived.

This is not the history of Vhal. It is the list of what the Council entered, and the space between the pot and the slate, which is where I live. Everything in it is written on salt-paper that I keep dry, against the practice of the country and with the knowledge of the folly of it. A contract left in the rain is no contract here, and that is called a virtue. A history left in the rain is no history either, and I have met no man in this port who sees the virtue in that. So I have kept the roll dry and put the damp where it belongs, in the margin.

\subsection*{The years as the roll has them}

\emph{Copied in the flat scrivener’s hand out of the tin under the table. I have put nothing in from the temple tells, which have their own years and a comfort in them.}

\textbf{Y.H. 611.} The first contract for cliff-glass fine ware goes south by way of Greybank. Entered as \emph{a trade in sand}.

\textbf{Y.H. 626.} The three furnaces stood. No glass came down to the Quay for a year and the Council suspended contracts written on salt-paper, which in Vhal is the same as suspending the year. Entered as \emph{a cessation of the glass work; contracts in abeyance}. I have struck \emph{rose} above the entry and set \emph{stood} in its place, because the roll holds what was entered and not what a man might have shouted at a pot.

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{In the narrow upright hand of the Council, against the word I struck:} A temporary irregularity in the delivery of glass. No contract was impaired. Strike \emph{suspension}.\end{quote}

I have not struck it. A contract in abeyance is a contract a man cannot bring into a room and lay on a table, which is precisely what suspension means in this port and what the word \emph{irregularity} is for. The hand has never in this chapter changed a figure. It takes the doer out and leaves the pot standing cold by itself.

\textbf{Y.H. 627.} The masters of the furnaces put the stopping into articles, so that a refusal would have a place to be entered. Entered as \emph{a regularity in the keeping of the furnaces}. A master who cannot enter a refusal will enter the man who made it, which is a different thing and a longer one.

\textbf{Y.H. 798.} A physician come up from Greybank leaves a page saying the sweetness at the gum comes from the lead of the cliffs. The word goes out of the page before the year is out, as though a word could be scraped off paper the way slip is scraped off a bench. Entered as \emph{an opinion received and not proceeded with}. I have put the lead back underneath, where a clerk can see it and choose not to read it.

\textbf{Y.H. 811, the Long Cold.} No boat crossed the Sallow and no glass went south. The roll was shut in the tin and the tin under the table and the table against the wall where the brazier stood, and a corner of this leaf took the heat and did not recover. Entered as \emph{a visitation of the weather; account standing}.

\textbf{Y.H. 812, the Thin Year.} The cold broke and the contracts came back on paper the damp had never been asked to settle. I have entered both the reopening and the suspension, which the first keeper of the roll did not, because he entered openings and not closings, as a man enters what he can see from the Quay.

\subsection*{The table of sheets}

\emph{The figure on the left is made up in the room below, before the boats are loaded. The figure on the right is what came down to the Quay. The rows in the gutter are mine and are not a figure.}

Year — Sheets due by contract — Sheets came down — Entered as\par

625 — 900 — 900 — \emph{delivery received}\par

626 — 900 — none — \emph{contract in abeyance}\par

627 — 900 — 610 — \emph{delivery received; account standing}\par

798 — 900 — 900 — \emph{delivery received; opinion noted}\par

811 — 900 — none — \emph{a visitation of the weather}\par

812 — 900 — 293 — \emph{the account carried forward}\par

The figure for Y.H. 627 stood at nine hundred in the clean hand, because the clerk who made it counted pots the way a potter counts a row of wet pots, by the places and not by what was in them. I have struck it and written six hundred and ten underneath, by touch as it were and not by eye, because a man writes differently when he is setting down what happened from what was entered. Two hundred and ninety sheets went south that year by a boat the roll does not name, and are in the gutter under the round sum where a factor from Greybank will not think to look.

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{In the narrow upright hand of the Council, against the struck figure:} Deficit not entered. Delivery discharged at the furnace door. Account standing.\end{quote}

The hand is careful and it has never once changed a figure. It has made a year without glass into a year in which glass was delivered, which is a cleaner thing to carry into a Council room. We have eleven words in this port for a contract that has gone wet and not one for a pot that stood cold with a man beside it who had wanted to work.

\subsection*{The hands}

\emph{The Council’s figure is set first. What stands beneath it is not a figure and was not entered.}

Condition — The Council’s figure — What stands beneath\par

Hands at the three furnaces — one hundred and eight, current — Men who could melt sand\par

Refusal in Y.H. 626 — irregularity, not entered — The pot left standing cold\par

Hands named after the rising — seconded to the pulled benches — Seven years, or until the hands gave out\par

Heat-name at the first gather — one decorative appellation, not a vessel — A name said to the pot and kept in the mouth\par

Green at the gum — occupational mark; no deduction arises — Lead, paid out of the hand\par

The men named after the rising went to the pulled benches, seven years or until their hands gave out, whichever came first, and the roll enters them as \emph{seconded}, which is a word for sending a man somewhere he has chosen to go and is used here because no other word in Ledgerhand will carry a refusal. A man who melts sand for a living has hands, and a man who has been at the oars for six years has hands that give out. I have set both facts down in the column where they can be read and left the Council’s \emph{seconded} standing above them where it belongs.

One of them was a girl of the outer furnace who put her hand to the gum with cliff-glass and would not say whose hand had taught her. She was not sent to the benches; she was kept at the anneal and given seawater, and a green bead she pressed into this leaf is the only thing in the roll that has never been entered. I have not asked her name and the Council has not asked either, which is the same thing said about a person and said about a room.

\subsection*{The anneal-song}

\emph{Taken down at the third furnace, from a woman who had been at the gather in Y.H. 626 and had not been at the benches. It is sung at the anneal, standing, with the pipe across the knee. It is not sung at the Council table and the third verse is said to the pot and not to the company.}

\begin{quote}\itshape Sand from the bay and lead from the blue,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the sea takes the writing, the lead takes the hue;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape hold the end up and never point it at a man,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape take what comes up and not what you began.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape The year the paper rotted the pot stood still,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the clerk wrote nothing and the Council set \emph{nil};\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape seven years at the oar for a hand that would melt ---\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the sea keeps the figure and the hand keeps the heat.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Green at the gum where the pale line was,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the master calls skill what the girl calls hers;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape ask the pot what it held when the firing was stopped,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the pot says the heat and the heat says the hand.\end{quote}

She would not sing the third verse while a man from the tide-tally house stood by, so we went and stood at the anneal. She said songs about glass are made by the glass, which is the custom of that shore and not an answer. I have set it where I found it, away from the table.

\subsection*{What the borrowed hands did}

Two hands have been at these leaves besides mine.

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item The Council clerk, in the narrow upright hand, took the verbs out. Where I wrote \emph{the furnaces stood} he set \emph{a cessation of work occurred}; where I wrote \emph{the men were sent to the benches} he wrote \emph{hands were seconded, no deduction arising}; where I wrote \emph{a girl pressed a bead into the leaf} he wrote \emph{an object of no value was affixed}. I have put my words back underneath. A verb is the difference between a thing that happened to a person and a thing that happened in a room with a table in it.

\item A factor come up from Greybank, in a leaning counting-hand and pale ink that has gone soft where the damp took it, wrote \emph{figures of account, not of loss} against the table of sheets and set a round nought beside the year without glass. He has never stood at a furnace and has strong views about sand. A nought is a figure; the cold pot was not, and no man melted anything in it.

\end{itemize}

I have left both readings everywhere, the cold one under the neat one, as a furnace leaves the flaw showing under a gather and does not pretend the sand was ever clear.

\subsection*{At the head and in the gutter}

The white at the head is salt bloom off the dockets and comes and goes with the weather; it has taken the last letters off one word in the second year-entry and left the rest readable, which is the only honest thing the damp has done to this roll. The glass dust in the grain is off the third furnace and no brush takes it out. The tar at the fold came off the rope under the table and is mine; I have never got it out and have stopped trying. The ring at the head is small ale, set down by a ship-master who would not drink with dippers and did not mind drinking with a clerk. The scorched corner is from the brazier in the Long Cold and has taken two words clean off the last verse; I have not written them back, because a song with two words gone is a song said slowly and everything in this port is said slowly enough already. The green bead in the lower corner is cliff-glass and has left a sweet smear that will not dry. The struck figure is mine. I wrote \emph{nine hundred} in the clean hand and \emph{six hundred and ten} beneath it, and both stand, because the roll holds what was entered and what came down, and the difference has no signature.

\subsection*{At the foot, in a hand nobody will own}

\begin{quote}\itshape The pot stood cold and the paper held,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the Council wrote what the paper told.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Nine hundred went up and six hundred came down,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the hands went to the oars for a word with no sound.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Ask the pot what it held. Ask the hand.\end{quote}

I asked a furnace-master, a clerk come down from the Council room, and a woman who sells eels on the Quay, and had three answers and no hand. I have left the lines where they were written. The roll goes back into the tin under the table, which smells of tar and wet rope and has smelled so through five Councils. Tomorrow a contract will be written on paper the weather is invited to settle, and the Council will call it a virtue, and by evening it will be a debt no man can prove. The furnaces will take another child at twelve with a name she will not use at the pot, and I shall enter the sheets, because that is what the roll is for.

\clearpage\phantomsection\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{The Years Between, Being an Extract from the Book of the Two Hundred Quiet Years Kept in the Lower Room at Greybank: Of the Making of the Return Compulsory, the Coming of Lead-Glaze Downriver, the Pale Line at the Gum, and the First Survey of the Rim-Seam in Y.H. 260; with the Clean Roll Set Above the Survey Sheet, the Glaze-Women’s Song, Two Corrections in Ledgerhand, and a Line at the Foot Nobody Will Own}
\CRsheetheading{The Years Between, Being an Extract from the Book of the Two Hundred Quiet Years Kept in the Lower Room at Greybank: Of the Making of the Return Compulsory, the Coming of Lead-Glaze Downriver, the Pale Line at the Gum, and the First Survey of the Rim-Seam in Y.H. 260; with the Clean Roll Set Above the Survey Sheet, the Glaze-Women’s Song, Two Corrections in Ledgerhand, and a Line at the Foot Nobody Will Own}
{\centering\FellFont\itshape\footnotesize\color{faded} A copy-roll keeper’s extract from the book of the years between, copied out of the Hearthseat annals and set beside a Keld survey sheet gone soft with wet slate, a glaze-women’s song taken down at High Kiln, a sentence in a second hand on the back of a slate out of the Old Kiln, two corrections in the narrow upright Ledgerhand of the factor’s office, and one line at the foot in a hand nobody will own · Written in the lower room of the bank at Greybank in Ash of Y.H. 812, the Thin Year, by the keeper of the copy-roll, who signs with the office and not with a name and keeps the verbs in; copied forward at the Opening of the Slates, Ilmen 1, Y.H. 813, from a book kept behind the winter tallies since Y.H. 300. It survives as six leaves of thin ruled roll-paper sewn with iron wire into a board cover soft at the fold: iron-gall worked into the creases of a thumb, a green bead of lead glaze pressed into the lower margin by a glaze-woman come up from High Kiln, slate dust in the gutter, a tallow end burnt short against the head, a ring of small ale where the song was taken down, a square of bare paper where a word was scraped away and not written back, a strip of the survey sheet folded over the entry of Y.H. 260 and gone soft at the edge, a grey Ash print along the outer fold which the keeper did not make and has not swept, and the line at the foot\par}\medskip
I keep the book of the years between. It stands behind the winter tallies in the lower room of the bank at Greybank, in a town that is warmer than the clay country and colder than the Hearthseat, and in all the years I have kept it nobody has asked to see it. The clean roll of the Keeping begins at the lighting and runs forward in a hand that has had the doers taken out of it. My book begins where the clean roll stops being interesting, which is the hundred and twentieth year, and ends where the Glaze Wars begin, which is the three hundredth. One in twelve had been printed on the notices since the fortieth year, before my book opens, and it stands on them still. Between those two figures the Court entered very little, and what it entered it made smooth.

I have put the verbs back where I found them taken out. A chronicle with nobody in it can be read aloud in a clean voice and gone home from believing, and I have stood at this table and listened to too many clean voices.

Two things in these years belong together and are never entered together: the glaze that came downriver out of the Keel and the pale line that came after it; the single crack the temple tells of and the layers the surveyor found underneath. I have set them side by side and left the joining to the reader, which is the only honest work a copyist is allowed.

\subsection*{The years as the clean roll has them}

\emph{Copied out of the Hearthseat annals in the neat hand. What I put underneath is not an argument with the roll. It is the roll with the people put back.}

\textbf{Y.H. 128.} The Return extended to villages that had buried their dead. Court hand: \emph{the burying was discontinued}. Mine: villages that had buried their dead were made to bank them instead, and a woman who had carried her mother to the river was given a notice and a figure on the same morning. The notice is kept. The figure is kept. The morning is not.

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Court hand:} The practice of interment ceased. The mercy of the Return was extended. Strike \emph{made}.\end{quote}

\textbf{Y.H. 147.} Lead-glaze of the Keel begins to be used on fine ware. Court hand: \emph{an improvement in the firing}. Mine: lead came down in bowls with a blue skin, and the glaze-mixers of High Kiln tasted it at the rim and said it was sweet, which is the word a man uses when he has not yet been made ill by a thing. An improvement is a thing that happens to a pot. A sweetness is a thing that happens to a person. Both were entered; only one was entered under this year.

\textbf{Y.H. 162.} A pale line at the gum of a glaze-woman of High Kiln. Court hand: \emph{a complaint of the teeth}. Mine: she could not hold a cup by the fifth day, and the physician at Greybank wrote the word \emph{sweetness} in his report, and the sweetness stayed in the report while the glaze stayed out of it. I have copied both. The cup is in neither.

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Court hand:} Strike \emph{the sweetness}. Enter \emph{a mild disorder of the teeth}. Glaze not implicated.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Underneath, in mine:} A clerk who takes the glaze out of a sentence leaves the teeth standing by themselves, and teeth standing by themselves have never hurt anybody, and no cup has gone flat in a room where nobody tasted anything.\end{quote}

\textbf{Y.H. 178.} The same pale line in the lower rooms of Greybank, among clerks who had been given the new ware to use. Court hand: \emph{a visitation in the lower rooms}. Mine: they called it the winter, and the winter went, and the line did not. One of them wrote the word \emph{glaze} in the margin of a tally and crossed it out before the tend was done; the crossing is still there and I have not gone over it.

\textbf{Y.H. 203.} A cup out of High Kiln set down wrong at a shelf answered flat under the knuckle, and a potter said a pot that answers flat has something the matter with its holding. Court hand: \emph{no entry}. Mine: no entry is not the same as no cup, and I have put the cup where the entry would have been.

\textbf{Y.H. 240.} A surveyor out of Keld came down the Clay Road with a rubbing under his coat and would not say what he had rubbed. He turned the sheet face down when the factor came into the room. Court hand: \emph{a survey of the boundary}. Mine: he turned it face down in our room as well, which is a courtesy in Keld and an insult in Greybank, and I have entered the turning and not the reason.

\textbf{Y.H. 260.} The first survey of the rim-seam, the oldest document in these parts that still has its original numbers. It notes a repair \emph{of unkept words}, and it says the repairs lie in layers, the newest over the oldest. Court hand: \emph{no entry}. The passage is in no Court history that I have read. It appears in another hand on the back of a slate out of the Old Kiln, which I have seen and cannot weigh.

\begin{quote}\itshape From the survey sheet, in a hard-pressed hand, the words kept as they stand: \emph{as a pot is mended again and again until nothing of the first pot can be seen.}\end{quote}

\textbf{Y.H. 288.} The wells by the Ferr carry a thin taste and the households of Stonemouth go down with the pale line. Court hand: \emph{the water does not bear tasting}. Mine: the water was not sweet and the cups were, and I have set the two sentences on the same leaf without a verb between them, which is the nearest a copyist can come to asking a question.

\textbf{Y.H. 300.} Commissioners sit over the lead workings in the lower Ferr. Court hand: \emph{a dispute of the workings}. Here my book ends. The Glaze Wars are written in another book, and the three hundred are entered there as a round sum, and what the round sum left out is entered in the gutter, where a clerk of the College will not think to look.

\subsection*{The survey sheet}

\emph{The strip folded over the Y.H. 260 entry was cut from a survey rubbing spoiled by wet slate. I have set what it calls each layer beside what the factor’s copy calls the same layer, and chosen neither, because a copyist who chooses between two guesses has made a fact of one of them and will have to answer for it at the Weighing.}

Layer — The surveyor’s word — The factor’s copy — Times mended\par

The newest but one — Stone, dressed and keyed — Stone — Twice; the second over the first\par

The middle — Stone and iron pins — Stone; pins not entered — Once\par

The old — Stone, with a repair of unkept words — Stone — Three times\par

The oldest that can be named — Not stone and not clay — Language — Not entered\par

The oldest of all is entered in the surveyor’s own speech as \emph{that which was left unsaid made solid}. The Keldish translate it as Ash. The Court’s copy, which is kept in the Hearthseat and shown to no one below an assessor, translates it as language. Both are guesses. I copy both and set neither above the other.

I asked a Vorr who came through Greybank on the Hearth Road what the numbers on the oldest slates meant. He said the numbers would be found correct when the season had turned, which is the answer they give and is not a translation. I have set it down because a courteous man owes his reader the exact shape of a refusal.

\subsection*{The song of the glaze-women}

\emph{Taken down at High Kiln in Ash of Y.H. 812, from a woman who tasted the glaze at the rim for nineteen years and had the pale line herself. She would not sing the third verse while a man from the factor’s office stood in the room, so we went and stood by the slip pits. She said the verse had been in the glaze room longer than she had, which is the custom of that terrace and not an answer.}

\begin{quote}\itshape The Keel sent down a bowl of blue,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the clay country called it fine;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the glaze was sweet at the tasting rim,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the pale line came in time.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Two hundred years of cups went round\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the pain went round with them;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the slate wrote \emph{teeth}, the house wrote \emph{winter},\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and nobody asked what was in the glaze.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape A surveyor rubbed the seam at night\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and found a mending under a mending;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the oldest is not stone and not clay —\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape ask the pot what it kept, and what it spent.\end{quote}

\subsection*{The sentence on the back of the slate}

On the back of a slate that came out of the Old Kiln, in a hand smaller and harder-pressed than the figures on its face, there is one sentence, struck through twice and written again underneath: \emph{Another kept badly, and we inherited the crack.} The same sentence is said to be scratched into a slate in a kiln-house in Low Kiln, where nobody knows what it is. I have copied it as I found it and put no gloss on it. A sentence a man cannot weigh is not a sentence he may turn into a fact, and the book of the years between is not the place for a fact I have made myself.

\subsection*{What the Court hand did}

A clerk of the factor’s office borrowed the leaf on a market morning, laid his hand on the top sheet before he looked at either of us, and took the verbs out as though a verb were a thing a man could smuggle past a weigh.

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item Against \emph{villages were made to bank them}, he set \emph{the Return was extended}.

\item Against \emph{she could not hold a cup}, he set \emph{a mild disorder was recorded}.

\item Against \emph{the surveyor turned the sheet face down}, he set \emph{a survey was conducted}.

\item Against \emph{as a pot is mended again and again until nothing of the first pot can be seen}, he wrote \emph{repairs were recorded in sequence}, and passed over the words \emph{unkept} and \emph{left unsaid} without a stroke, which is the readiest way of correcting a sentence I have yet seen.

\item Against the sentence on the back of the slate he wrote nothing at all.

\end{itemize}

I have left both readings everywhere, the thin one under the neat one, as a repaired wall keeps the old break under the new keying and does not pretend the first hand never touched the stone. A clerk who takes the people out of a year leaves the year standing by itself, and a year standing by itself has cost nobody a cup and made nobody a figure.

\subsection*{At the head and in the gutter}

The iron-gall at the head is mine and will not wash out of the creases; I hold the book open through a tend and have never managed to hold a light with the same hand. The green bead in the lower margin is not ink. A glaze-woman come up from High Kiln leaned over to see the Y.H. 260 line and touched the leaf with her thumb, and I have left it where she put it. The slate dust in the gutter came off the survey strip and has worked into the sewing. The tallow is my own end burnt down against the head. The ring at the foot of the song is small ale, set down by the woman who sang and not drunk until the third verse was done. The square of bare paper on the second leaf is where I scraped a word away with a knife and put no other in its place; it is the only square in this quire that I made myself. The grey along the outer fold is not mine and not the Court’s. I have not swept it.

\subsection*{At the foot, in a hand nobody will own}

\begin{quote}\itshape Two hundred years of neat accounts,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and a line the roll will not enter;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the glaze went down and the pain went down,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and neither was called the other’s debtor.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape The seam keeps its layers, the slate keeps its square,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the cup at the lip keeps the flat;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape ask the surveyor what he turned face down —\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape ask the pot what it held, and what it had.\end{quote}

The leaves go back behind the winter tallies. Next tend I copy the figures of the Glaze Wars out of the other book and put the verbs back there too, and set the years between beside them where a man must move a ledger to reach them. The clean roll goes on in its smooth hand. My book goes on underneath it with the glaze and the pale line still standing side by side, which is where I found them and where I will leave them for the next hand to join or not, as he chooses.

\clearpage\phantomsection\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{Twelve and the Dish, Being the Counting Rhyme of the Low Kiln Children, with the Counting-Out, the Manner of the Turns, and What a Clerk Made of It}
\CRsheetheading{Twelve and the Dish, Being the Counting Rhyme of the Low Kiln Children, with the Counting-Out, the Manner of the Turns, and What a Clerk Made of It}
{\centering\FellFont\itshape\footnotesize\color{faded} A hearth-maid’s gathering of a children’s hopping game, set down in Grathic on the back of a spoiled Weighing notice; the verses in the children’s own half-sung speech, the rules in the hearth-maid’s small careful hand, a correction in the narrow upright Ledgerhand of a factor’s clerk borrowed at Greybank, a gloss pressed into the margin by a woman who has kept the birth-slates for nineteen years, and one line at the foot in a child’s grey chalk · Set down at the birth-flower shrine in Low Kiln of Sill in Stone of Y.H. 812, the Thin Year, of an evening when the yard stood frozen and the children hopped the trodden-ash floor of a kiln-house two doors down the Clay Yard; carried to Greybank in the satchel of a hearth-maid come to have a widow’s mark confirmed and copied onto the back of a Weighing notice gone soft at one corner. Kept folded in the shrine’s slate-box among the birth-slates that have been answered. It survives with slip worked into the grain at the head, a green bead of lead-glaze in the fold, a tallow thumb at the second corner, a grey Ash print along the gutter that nobody will own, a tideline where the notice went damp, a twist of grey wool through a hole in the first leaf which the writer will not untie, the clerk’s correction standing above the children’s words, the birth-slate woman’s gloss in the margin, and a line of grey chalk at the foot in a hand that has learned its letters off a slate and will not be claimed\par}\medskip
I keep the birth-slates at the shrine and I have written this because a man from Slate Row stood in the yard and asked what the children said when they jumped. He wanted a figure. I told him there was a count in it and no figure, which is the truth of the thing, and he went away and sent me a clerk instead. What is below is what the children said before the clerk came, and what they said again after he had gone back over the north bridge. I have set the clerk’s hand above mine where he put it, and the children’s words under it where they stand, as the floor keeps the ash and the foot that raised it.

They play it in Stone when the yard will not bear a foot, on the trodden-ash floor of a kiln-house where the fire is banked and the boards hold a little warmth. They play it in the thaw as well, on the dry boards under the racks, and not during the Five, because in the Five the children are made to stand and listen and there is no floor for it. Some twist a plait of grey wool and call it the eel and hold it between two hands; the words are the same words and the twelfth is the same twelfth. A mother will tell them not to knot the wool, because a knot of grey wool is an account and a child who ties one in play will be asked what it counts.

\subsection*{The counting-out, said before the floor is taken}

\emph{Right fists held out, knuckles up. The child who says it points at each fist in turn and does not look at the faces. The fist it lights on at the last word keeps the crack, which is to say she draws the line on the floor and calls the fault. She does not get to hop first. She is the one who has to be fair, which the children accept as a punishment and the rest of the yard accepts as practice.}

\begin{quote}\itshape Crock and dish and crock and dish,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the potter’s thumb and the eel’s wish;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape pit and rack and wheel and sill,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the one it lights on keeps the crack.\end{quote}

\emph{Say it to the floor. Said looking at a child, it becomes an argument, and there is always a child who will argue.}

\subsection*{The rhyme, as it is hopped}

\emph{One line, one hop. The line drawn in slip or in the grey is thumb-wide and must be crossed, never touched. A child who touches it has gone wrong and sits on the ash at the edge of the floor while the others go around her. At the twelfth line the hopper must cross twice without setting a foot down between; that second crossing is the dish, and the kept one. If she puts a foot down between, she is banked and sits with her arms folded until she is brought back. The last thing said before they stop is the bringing back: three children say her name, and she comes in again. A child whom nobody brings back is thin until the next round. The children will not be told why the twelfth is the kept one. If you ask them they say it is the dish, and if you ask what is in the dish they ask you why a man wants to know what is in a dish.}

\begin{quote}\itshape One for the pit where the slip comes up,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape two for the bench and the hollow seat,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape three for the rack where the wet ones stand,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape four for the crack that you must not meet.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Five for the thumb on the birth-slate’s rim,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape six for the grey where the skirting turns,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape seven for the bell that wants one more,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape eight for the eel that goes in and stays.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Nine for the step that comes back askew,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape ten for the broom that goes around,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape eleven for the word we say at home,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape twelve for the dish, and the one kept out.\end{quote}

\subsection*{A note on the several hands in it}

The fifth line is not mine. I wrote \emph{the thumb on the birth-slate’s rim} because that is where the hand goes at a birth, and a woman beside me at the shrine put her mark in the margin against it and wrote, \emph{not the thumb on the rim — the thumb over the writing}. It is Alda Reed’s hand, I think, though she has never said so. She crossed two fingers over a child’s birth-flower on the seventh day of Stone and would not say the word for it, and she has kept her own account of this game in her head for nineteen years without once setting it down. Her reading is better than mine. A hand on the rim is a hand that might lift the slate; a hand over the writing is a hand that has already decided what the slate will say. I have left both lines standing, hers in the margin and mine underneath, as a kept thing is left where it fell.

\subsection*{What the clerk did}

The factor’s clerk borrowed the leaf at Greybank, being a man who cannot let paper lie. He has a cuff gone soft from washing and the ink sits in two fingers of it and will not come out. He numbered the twelve lines in the margin, struck through \emph{the one kept out} and wrote above it, \emph{the deduction is one in twelfths, the residue is nil, the young are instructed}. Against \emph{twelve for the dish} he wrote \emph{the twelfth is retained for the Hearth}. At the foot of the count he put a round nought and wrote \emph{absence} beside it, where the children’s game ends with a name said three times.

I have put their words back underneath and left his standing above. He takes the verbs out because a thing always true has no need of them. I put them back because a child up to her ankle in the grey of the yard does not know she is hearing something always true, and wants to know which foot to lift. A nought is a number. The dish is a place at the table. He has put a figure where a place should be, which is the whole art of that hand.

He asked me what the children learned from it. I told him the count and the fault and the bringing back, and he said that was an account of the Return taught before the child could read a slate, and he entered it. The children stop when a man in a soft cuff comes into the yard. They take it up again when he is past the bridge, and they never once change the twelfth.

\subsection*{The verse they do not say while a man from Slate Row is in the square}

\begin{quote}\itshape One for the lean and two for the thin,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape three for the loaves that go on the dish;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the slate says one and the yard says none,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the name said at home is the only one.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape The dish goes round and the dish comes back,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and what was kept is counted as lack;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape four for the corners and one for the sill,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the place where the twelfth stood is standing still.\end{quote}

I have it from the child who keeps the crack, with the proper space left before it, which is the space they leave in the hopping. She would not say it while the clerk had his pen out, and would not say it to him at all. She said it to the floor with her back turned and made me put it down as I have it, with none of my verbs in it, because a verse said to the floor wants nothing added, and a verse said to a man wants everything taken away.

\subsection*{At the head and in the gutter}

The slip at the head is off the hand that drew the line; it goes into the grain and will not come out, which is why the yard uses it to mark a place. The green bead came off a pot broken in the glaze room and rolled as far as the fold before anybody saw it. The tallow thumb is mine: I held the notice down in the draught under the shrine door and did not know I had marked it. The grey in the gutter came off a cuff laid where no cuff has business lying; I have not swept it and there is no Last Day in a slate-box. The tideline took two words off the back of the notice and I have not written them in again, because a rhyme with two words gone is a rhyme said slowly, and all of ours are said slowly. The twist of grey wool through the hole is mine, tied for the word I could not put down. I will not untie it.

\subsection*{At the foot, in grey chalk, in a child’s hand}

\begin{quote}\itshape I kept the crack and nobody came.\end{quote}

No hand will own it. The letters are set down as they were made, hard at the \emph{th} and one of them backward, which is how a child writes who has learned off a slate and not off a book. I asked whose it was and had three answers and no hand, as I did with the grey print. I have left it where it was written.

The leaf goes back into the slate-box with the birth-slates that have been answered. Tomorrow the yard will draw its line again, and one in twelve will be read in a clean voice at the notice-board, and the twelfth will be kept out of the count and brought back at the end of it, which is more than can be said for the district’s own twelfth. The children will go on saying the name three times. I have kept their words and I have not joined them to anything.

\clearpage\phantomsection\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{What the Cord Keeps, Being the Sayings of the Eel-Folk of the Weir, Gathered in the Trap-House a League Above Sill and Glossed for a Girl Come Up from Low Kiln}
\CRsheetheading{What the Cord Keeps, Being the Sayings of the Eel-Folk of the Weir, Gathered in the Trap-House a League Above Sill and Glossed for a Girl Come Up from Low Kiln}
{\centering\FellFont\itshape\footnotesize\color{faded} A trap-woman’s gathering of the proverbs, plank-maxims, eel-counts and river-curses of the Weir, set in Grathic letters on the backs of spoiled trap-tallies because the counts here are tied in cord and a cord will not lie flat on a clerk’s table; the sayings in the short wet speech of the weir with the ends let drop into the water, the glosses in the writer’s own charcoal, a knot tied in the margin where no Grathic word will come, a factor’s clerk’s correction in narrow upright Ledgerhand, a slate-runner’s line in the slant of a carried hand, and one line at the foot in a hand nobody will own · Gathered at the Weir in Ilmen and Silt of Y.H. 812, the Thin Year of the Long Cold, and written up in the trap-house through the high water by a woman who lifts the baskets at the turn and keeps the leading cord and the count of them in her sleeve; set down first in charcoal on the backs of trap-tallies spoiled by wet hands, carried downriver to Greybank in Grain of Y.H. 813 with a consignment of eels and copied there onto the back of a Court grain-warrant voided by the Long Cold, where a factor’s clerk borrowed the leaves and set his hand above hers. It survives folded into a strip of oiled eel-skin and tied with a loop of grey wool, with river silt dried pale in the grain at the head, eel slime worked into the fold off the leading cord, a fish-hook nick at the fore-edge, a brine-gull’s peck through one word of the song, a glass-eel thread fine as a hair in the lower gutter, a pressed reed across the third leaf, a grey Ash print along the outer fold which the writer did not make and has not swept, the knot standing in the margin, the clerk’s narrow correction above the charcoal, the runner’s sloping line below it, and the line at the foot which nobody has claimed\par}\medskip
I lift the baskets at the turn and keep the leading cord. There are four traps below the plank and a fifth set where the water goes quick, which nobody admits to setting. A girl came up from Low Kiln this spring who can hear a pot before a knuckle touches it and cannot tell which way the water runs under her own feet. She is our kin and she is not ours, and what the weir can give her is the old sentences. A saying said to the water stays at the water. A saying tied in a cord goes on with her without a figure.

Our counts are not written. They are tied in grey wool and reed-fibre, at arm’s length, with one tied low by teeth and thumb where the hand that made it cannot see. A knot keeps when paper has gone soft, and no clerk at Greybank has ever read one, which we did not think of first and have since come to value. Where a sound has no word I have tied a knot in the margin. Do not put a word into it. A man come down from the Cross asked what we say when there is nothing to say. I told him we say it to the water. He went away believing he had learned the Weir, which is the usual end of such a conversation.

Say these to the plank, the basket, the water under the plank, and to a person last. Said looking at a person, a saying becomes an argument, and there is enough arguing at the Cross without carrying it upriver.

\subsection*{Of the water under the plank}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item “Ask the water what it took. It will tell you where it put it.”

\end{enumerate}

\emph{Gloss — At the Fishstairs they ask what the water cost and are given the weather. Here we ask where it went. The leach takes the Warm out of a thing and hands it to the Sallow draw; the river is only the road. A man wants a figure. The water has a direction. Both are true, and only one can be carried into a room with a table.}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item “The ice is a lid. Do not trust a lid.”

\end{enumerate}

\emph{Gloss — Two or three children a winter go through the skin of the Ilm. The old women say the ice-mouse is the cold made small enough to be killed, which is a comfort that kills no fewer children. We say it of the water and of a man who promises what he has not stood on.}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item “The sill sings before it breaks. Nobody sets a clock by the song.”

\end{enumerate}

\emph{Gloss — When the Warm rises in Ilmen the stone under the falls gives a low note that carries to the Fishstairs. The town sets its clocks by it and does not explain it. We say the river clears its throat before the Breaking. A man from Greybank wanted the hour entered; we told him the hour was the note, and the note was not entered.}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item “The Breaking comes up the same steps every year and takes a different house.”

\end{enumerate}

\emph{Gloss — In Silt the Ilm comes over the Fishstairs and leaves silt waist-deep in the lower town. The water is the same water; the door is never the same door. We say it of the river and of the levy, which comes on the same day of the month and takes a different household each time. Neither is malicious. Both are habitual, which costs more.}

\subsection*{Of the eel and the basket}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item “The eel keeps its heat behind the head. Cut there and you learn nothing.”

\end{enumerate}

\emph{Gloss — The old women say glass eels are the shadows of the rivets that hold the lid on the world. There is a sac behind the head where the eel keeps a little of the Warm; a boy who cuts one open to find the heat finds it gone into the water, which is where it was going. Say this of a man who opens a thing to look for the feeling in it.}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item “Count them going in. Count them coming out. The basket has no column.”

\end{enumerate}

\emph{Gloss — The traps are lifted at the turn and the eels counted by the hand that lifts them, not the eye that prices them. A tally at the Fishstairs takes your figure and gives another by the tide’s turn. We keep the going-in count in the cord and let the buyer have the other, which is not dishonesty but an arrangement two people can live with.}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item “A gull will take a coal and leave you colder. It will not take a wet eel.”

\end{enumerate}

\emph{Gloss — The brine-gull lifts what is warm and light enough, with no malice in it. Say this of a man who has taken something and calls it borrowing. The eel is safe because it is cold and wet and no bird wants it, which is a poor safety and the only kind the basket has.}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Tied in the margin, where the word for the little green eel-thread would stand: a knot low down, made with teeth and thumb.} It has come loose twice and I have tied it twice. I have not written the word in.\end{quote}

\subsection*{Of the cord and the count}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item “A knot remembers what the hand forgets.”

\end{enumerate}

\emph{Gloss — We tie grey wool when a thing is owed and untie it when paid; the sleeve-cord has one knot tied low where the hand could not see. A knot keeps longer than a name and does not care who tied it. A factor’s clerk entered our knots as nil, because a knot is not a figure. Right by his law, wrong about the cord.}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item “Do not read a cord. Ask the woman who tied it.”

\end{enumerate}

\emph{Gloss — A man from the Court held up a reed-cutter’s cord and asked what it counted. She told him to ask the water, and then to ask her, in that order. He wrote “no entry lies,” which is true of the cord and false of the woman, who had carried the count eleven years and knew every knot by her thumb.}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item “Forty and one. The one has no name and is not a debt.”

\end{enumerate}

\emph{Gloss — In the year of the flower a woman at these traps tied forty knots for the children of Low Kiln taken in the levy, and a forty-first she cannot account for. She has never untied it. When she says the word low into a basket, the child looks at her and cannot answer, which is the answer given by people who asked the same question at their own first tying.}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{In the narrow upright hand, written against this saying:} Figure entered as nil. Vacancy. \emph{Underneath, in mine:} A nought is a number. The forty-first is a place. He has made the place smaller by writing in it, which is the whole art of that hand.\end{quote}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item “The slate goes by edge-on. Ask the carrier, not the slate.”

\end{enumerate}

\emph{Gloss — The runner who carries the thane’s slate between the Cross and Greybank holds the writing turned into her sleeve and will not read it. “I don’t read it. I carry it,” she says; “there’s a difference, and the road doesn’t care which.” A man who wants the figure must walk to Greybank for a number that was not true when it left the basket.}

\subsection*{Of the collector and the figure}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item “You hear the collector on the plank before you see his slate.”

\end{enumerate}

\emph{Gloss — His boots have never been in the water. Children here are taught to know the sound of them before their own names, a grim kindness and the only warning the weir gives. He comes with a cold tube and a clean figure, and the figure does not get wet.}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item “Cold iron takes. The water takes. Only one of them writes it down.”

\end{enumerate}

\emph{Gloss — The brand for a stolen cup of warmth goes on the wrist, and the district pays in cold for what the river carries off without a slate. Ask a woman which is the kinder and she will ask why a man wants a kind way to be emptied. There is no feast at the Weir in Silt.}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item “One in twelve is printed. The other goes up the Clay Road in a box.”

\end{enumerate}

\emph{Gloss — Read twice at the Cross, once for the moot and once for those who came late. The reader says the levy is called and not called by him, taking himself out of his own sentence. What goes up the road in his locked box is a different figure, and the two have never agreed here.}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item “A name said to the water is not entered.”

\end{enumerate}

\emph{Gloss — The slate takes a number and the house takes a name, and both travel where the person does not. What is said at the trap stays there. A woman whose child came back from another hearth keeps one name at home and one for the officer, and has never joined them, which is the only kindness her house can manage.}

\subsection*{Of the dead and the plank}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item “Feet to the river. Pot at the door. Sherd on the plank.”

\end{enumerate}

\emph{Gloss — We break a pot at the door of a death-house as they do in Sill, so the heat may get out, and set one sherd on the plank afterward, facing upriver. A threshold is a thing a house can step back over; a plank has only one way off it. Nobody says who the sherd is for, and nobody takes it up.}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item “Nothing is swept off a plank.”

\end{enumerate}

\emph{Gloss — In Sill they leave the grey in the corners on the Last Day, burn it in the morning and call it dealt with. There is no corner on a plank. What falls off goes into the water and becomes somebody else’s weather, a difference no clerk has entered.}

\subsection*{The basket-song}

\emph{Sung lifting the traps at the turn of the water, going out and not coming back. The fourth line of the second part is held, and the space after it is the length of a knot. Nobody fills it.}

\begin{quote}\itshape Four for the baskets and one set out,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape one for the cord that the thumb knows;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the water goes where the wind isn’t\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the eel goes where the water goes.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Count them going and count them back,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape a bit for the basket, a bit for the board;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the gull takes the coal and the clerk takes the mark\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the one I keep\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape The cord goes home in a sleeve, unread.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape The slate goes up in a hand, unread.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape The river reads both and says neither,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the water keeps what the water took.\end{quote}

\emph{Gloss — The held line is not a fifth basket or a fifth trap. Children ask and are told to ask the cord, which is the answer their mothers were given. A tally-man from Greybank put a nought in the space and wrote vacancy beneath it. A nought is a figure. The space was a place.}

\subsection*{What the borrowed hand did}

A factor’s clerk borrowed the leaves at Greybank on a market morning, with ink settled in two fingers of a soft cuff. He writes narrow and upright and takes the verbs out as though a verb were a thing a man could carry off in his sleeve.

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item At \emph{the water will tell you where it put it}, he wrote \emph{the loss is not ascertained}, which leaves the water out and the loss in.

\item At \emph{count them going in}, he set \emph{two tallies entered; discrepancy nil}, joining the count I kept to the count the buyer paid, which is the whole art of that hand.

\item At \emph{a knot remembers}, he wrote \emph{no instrument recorded}, true in his language and of no use to a woman with a cord in her sleeve.

\item At \emph{forty and one}, he put a round nought and wrote \emph{vacancy}, which is a figure where a place stood.

\end{itemize}

I have put the sayings back under his hand. He takes the doers out because a thing always true has no need of anybody doing it. I put them back because a girl from Low Kiln wants to know whose hand lifted the basket, and there is always a hand.

\subsection*{In the margin, in a slate-runner’s sloping hand}

\begin{quote}\itshape I carry the slate edge-on and never look at what is on it. The figure that goes up to Greybank does not know what came out of any basket on this river. I have walked that road eleven years and never once opened one.\end{quote}

Below, in mine: she said it to the plank and would not say it twice. I have not asked. A person who carries a slate is not one who reads it, and the road cares about neither.

\subsection*{At the head and in the gutter}

The silt at the head came off the hand that held the tally down on the rail in high water; no wet sleeve takes it out, which is why we use charcoal. The slime at the fold is off the leading cord and goes soft when the weather goes soft, which tells me when to shut the tin. The hook nick is from a basket set down by a man paying for six eels and charged for five, or the other way, which he has not settled. The gull’s peck went through one word of the song and nobody has claimed the bird. The green thread in the gutter is a glass eel, fine as a hair, left where it fell. The pressed reed came from a bundle set down while a woman decided whether to sell. The grey along the outer fold is not mine and not the factor’s. I have not swept it. There is a Last Day downriver; there is none on a plank.

\subsection*{At the foot, in a hand nobody will own}

\begin{quote}\itshape The water takes and does not enter.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape The cord keeps and cannot be read.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape A man is what he has carried to the basket and not yet let go.\end{quote}

I asked a woman who lifts the traps, a slate-runner, and a factor’s man out of Greybank, and had three answers and no hand. I have left the lines where they were written. The leaves go back into the eel-skin under the board. Tomorrow the water turns at the fourth and the baskets go down; I shall count them going in, say nothing of what came out, and tie one knot low where my thumb cannot see it, which is the whole of the trade at the Weir.

\clearpage\phantomsection\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{What the Bowl Washes, Being the Sayings of the Sere Folk Kept in the Factor’s House at Greybank and Glossed for a Girl Bought Down from the North}
