\textbf{Kind.} Fire church of Sere; the doctrine of glorious emptying. \textbf{Seat.} Open courts with a fire in the middle, in every bowl of the empire. \textbf{Named leaders.} \textbf{Valen Openhand, the Bowl-Priest}. \textbf{Goals.} To teach that a vessel was made to be emptied and that a life hoarded is a life wasted. \textbf{Methods.} Feasting, the emptying of a public bowl of wine to announce an act of state, and the burning of one household’s debt-slates by lot at the end of a feast, after which new ones are made. \textbf{Resources.} Wine, music, public fires, and an audience that applauds a debt carried as heartily as a debt forgiven. \textbf{Enemies.} The northern habit of calling Sere spendthrifts. The Court’s tax on funeral ash. \textbf{Hidden agenda.} The Spending teaches that emptiness is generous so that the poor will volunteer to be emptied. The priests who teach it are among the fullest vessels in the empire.

\section*{The Council of Tides}

\textbf{Kind.} Merchant republic; the foreign power of the Sallow coast. \textbf{Seat.} Vhal, in a room that smells of tar and wet rope. \textbf{Named leaders.} \textbf{Avis Wake}, \textbf{Mav Hull}, \textbf{Dolf Brine}, elected for a year at a time by ship-owners and salt-masters. \textbf{Goals.} To keep the salt and glass trades moving, to avoid being taxed into the Keeping, and to make sure no law lasts long enough to stop earning. \textbf{Methods.} Contracts written on salt-paper that rot in damp, which is considered a virtue; the pulled benches for condemned criminals; a slave who can be bought in Vhal but cannot be returned there. \textbf{Resources.} Ships, salt, glass, rope, dried fish, and a council that can turn a wet document into a fortune or the loss of one. \textbf{Enemies.} The Court’s assessors. The winter. The salt-thing. Sere’s buyers when they arrive with gold. \textbf{Hidden agenda.} The Council has never paid for a thin return and never will, which is why returned slaves are not housed in Vhalen. It has calculated that a person with no account is cheaper than a person with one, and calls this civility.

\CRrule

\section*{III. Criminals, rebels and secret societies}

\section*{The Ash-runners}

\textbf{Kind.} Criminal network; smugglers of warmth and quiet ash. \textbf{Seat.} The Fenmarch boardwalks and the Waiting Room at Sill, where a clerk can be paid to look away. \textbf{Named leaders.} \textbf{Slog Eel}, \textbf{Hobb Mud}, and a collector’s clerk in Slate Row whose name is not on any roll. \textbf{Goals.} To move Warm where the Court would not allow it and to sell forgetting to anyone who can pay. \textbf{Methods.} Cheap thin returns with no questions; quiet ash by the thimble; bone-hound ash from the shallow graves; a slate corrected in a second hand. \textbf{Resources.} The Fen paths, the peat-dries, a market in forgotten lives, and the complicity of people whose accounts are already damaged beyond repair. \textbf{Enemies.} The Court, which punishes the unlicensed sale of quiet ash with a greyed hand. The collectors, who are sometimes customers. \textbf{Hidden agenda.} One of their customers in Y.H. 812 paid for a whole return with the warmth of forty children of Low Kiln, and the runner who carried the slate has never been able to spell the buyer’s name. The name was Corin.

\section*{The Sere factors}

\textbf{Kind.} Slavers and buyers of measures; the empire’s advance guard in the north. \textbf{Seat.} A counting house in Greybank and a shipping quay in Vhal; the Bowl of Sere behind them. \textbf{Named leaders.} \textbf{Ilyra Gilded}, \textbf{Rial of the Ten Bowls}, with agents in Low Kiln who never give their names. \textbf{Goals.} To buy poor measures at prices no household can refuse and ship them south as beautiful whole returns for the great houses. \textbf{Methods.} Credit, the kindness of advances, the purchase of a debt before it is due, and the quiet conversion of a district into one decorated person. \textbf{Resources.} Gold crowns, grain, and the cooperation of households that have already sold next year’s warmth. \textbf{Enemies.} Grath, which hates Sere traders and sells to them anyway. The Court, which fought a thirty-one-year War of Deductions over the same trade. \textbf{Hidden agenda.} A factor does not want the poor person’s warmth for its own sake. He wants the shape of it, because a beautiful whole return must remember enough to be exhibited, and only certain lives make a good show.

\section*{The Broken Slates}

\textbf{Kind.} Rebel network in Low Kiln; descendants of the Ash Rising. \textbf{Seat.} The back rooms of the Vail kiln-house and the Fishstairs in Sill. \textbf{Named leaders.} \textbf{Ennit of Low Kiln}, whose family was taken in the levy of Y.H. 668; \textbf{Jorra Vail}, who has never said whether he is with them. \textbf{Goals.} To destroy the slates, stop the levy, and make it impossible to bank a person who does not consent. \textbf{Methods.} Broken birth-slates, a year in the clay yard for the offender, ash on the doorstep of an assessor, and a refusal that is just short of an unclosed account. \textbf{Resources.} The memory of ninety children taken in one levy, the silence of the hearth-maids, and the fact that a slate can be destroyed in a kiln in four minutes. \textbf{Enemies.} The Court, Pell Varr’s list, and the collectors who come with a slate already written. \textbf{Hidden agenda.} They want the Return abolished, which in Sarn means the end of the economy. They have not worked out what comes after. Their best argument is that nothing could be worse, and the Court’s sealed file suggests that they may be right.

\section*{The Unbanked}

\textbf{Kind.} Secret faction inside the Keeping, descended from the Ash Rising and named in a Court file of Y.H. 675 as \emph{persons of the sealed opinion}. \textbf{Seat.} No fixed seat. A locked drawer in Rusk’s room above the Fishstairs; a sealed file in the Hearthseat; the margin of a slate in Greybank signed M. \textbf{Named leaders.} \textbf{Rusk of the Weir}, who teaches a strange boy to listen to vessels; \textbf{Collector Marra}, who pays for a whole return with her own fingers; \textbf{Haldre}, whose paper \emph{The Sealed Vessel} was read by nine people in Y.H. 702 and who disappeared in Y.H. 704. \textbf{Goals.} The Final Banking: make every vessel perfectly retentive, so that nothing leaks, nothing is owed, and no one can ever give anything away. A sealed world is an unbreakable world. \textbf{Methods.} Recruitment through apprenticeship, the forgery of assessments, the purchase of whole returns with memory intact, and the long cultivation of a man who can look at a dying body and decide without prayer. \textbf{Resources.} A collector inside the Keeping, a teacher inside the Clay Yard, a cold iron tube, a locked drawer, and a hot trace that crossed between worlds. \textbf{Enemies.} The Court’s public answer is that they are mad. The Court’s private answer is in the sealed file. Their real enemy is want itself, which they mean to abolish. \textbf{Hidden agenda.} They did not make the blizzard and they did not put the minivan on the ice. They wanted a vessel that gave at the moment of breaking, and found one in a country they could not have named. They paid to have the memories left in, which is the most expensive single purchase a banker in Sarn can make. Rusk taught Corin to make him the instrument. Marra has been paying for it ever since.

\section*{The Deep Hand}

\textbf{Kind.} Secret society of scholars; a reading of the oldest slates. \textbf{Seat.} A back table in the Keld survey shaft, and one room in the Hearthseat whose key is held by an assessor. \textbf{Named leaders.} \textbf{Ludo of the Old Kiln}, a Grathic scholar who found a slate in the ash throat; \textbf{Derren the Younger}, an officer’s son with access to the sealed file. \textbf{Goals.} To read the Deep Hand and learn what the oldest repairs were made of. \textbf{Methods.} Copying slates that are not meant to leave the shaft; comparing the Keld translation \emph{Ash} with the Court’s translation \emph{language}; asking the Vorr the wrong question and recording that the numbers are correct. \textbf{Resources.} One slate from the Old Kiln, a crossed-out page from Y.H. 588, and the observation that a pot mended many times is not the pot it was. \textbf{Enemies.} The College of Assessors. The Court, which removed a surveyor from the shaft in Y.H. 717 for writing \emph{words that hold}. \textbf{Hidden agenda.} They believe the oldest repairs are made of promises that were never kept, made solid. If this is true then the world is being held together by the very thing the Court’s economy produces, and the Keeping cannot be abolished without finding out what holds the walls up.

\CRrule

\section*{IV. Foreign powers at the border}

\section*{Keld — the Warden of the Rim}

\textbf{Kind.} Foreign power; mountain kingdom of iron, lead, coal and warm-stone. \textbf{Seat.} Keld Keep, with the First Seam beneath it and the Cold Pass ten leagues beyond. \textbf{Named leaders.} \textbf{Karric VII, Warden of the Rim}, who shut the Cold Pass in Y.H. 741; the mine-reeves beneath him. \textbf{Goals.} To hold the passes, keep the true Hearth claim alive, and sell iron and warm-stone to whoever pays without becoming anyone’s subject. \textbf{Methods.} Mercenaries, the Descent at thirteen, a measure stated before a name, and a treaty enforced at the point of a surveyor’s slate. \textbf{Resources.} Iron, lead, coal, warm-stone, the survey shaft, and a population that can hold a hot clamp against its palm without flinching. \textbf{Enemies.} The Court, which has never accepted the Hearth claim and has never bothered to argue it. The Sweating. Grathish clay-men levied into a war they did not choose. \textbf{Hidden agenda.} The Warden knows the true Hearth is not under his mountain. He keeps the claim because it keeps the Court out of the shafts, and because a kingdom that believes it owns the source can charge more for its stone.

\section*{Sere — the Sun-Emperor}

\textbf{Kind.} Foreign power; hot empire of grain, wine, bowls and open slavery. \textbf{Seat.} The Bowl of Sere, three hundred leagues south of Sill. \textbf{Named leaders.} The \textbf{Sun-Emperor}, whose acts are announced by the emptying of a public bowl of wine; the Council of Bowls beneath him. \textbf{Goals.} To grow north by purchase rather than conquest, to buy measures cheaply, and to keep the Peat Line from becoming a border it has to defend. \textbf{Methods.} Agents with credit, the Bowl feast, a public burning of debt-slates followed by the making of new ones, and a phrase \emph{measure for measure} that means whatever the emperor has already decided. \textbf{Resources.} Gold crowns, grain, oil, wine, fine glazed ware, and the largest slave population in the world. \textbf{Enemies.} The Court’s deduction on grain. The Fenmarch. The northern habit of calling Sere spendthrifts. \textbf{Hidden agenda.} The empire does not want territory in Grath. It wants the poor. A northern district that has been bought is more useful than a northern district that has been conquered, because nobody in a conquered district signs a contract.

\section*{Vhalen — the Council of Tides (as foreign power)}

\textbf{Kind.} Foreign power and trading republic; the gate between Grath and the Sallow Sea. \textbf{Seat.} Vhal, eighty leagues north-east of Sill by the Salt Road. \textbf{Named leaders.} \textbf{Avis Wake}, \textbf{Mav Hull}, \textbf{Dolf Brine}, rotating yearly. \textbf{Goals.} To keep the Salt Road open, to tax nothing that can be avoided, and to make the Court’s assessors feel poor in a room full of salt-paper. \textbf{Methods.} Contracts that rot in damp, a welcome for any traveller who pays, and the pulled benches for those who do not. \textbf{Resources.} Ships, salt, glass, rope, dried fish, and a legal system in which a wet document is no document at all. \textbf{Enemies.} The Court’s lists. The salt-thing. A hard winter that closes the coast pass. \textbf{Hidden agenda.} Half the port’s fortunes have turned on a contract going damp at the right moment. The Council’s real doctrine is not the Sallow Hearth but the convenient disappearance of evidence, which it has elevated into an art and a foreign policy.

\chapter*{Glossary}
\markboth{Glossary}{Glossary}
\addcontentsline{toc}{chapter}{Glossary}
\section*{Glossary of Sarn}

\emph{Entries for the reader. Every coined name set down in the Compendium so far is gathered here, in alphabetical order. Where a thing is known by different names in different countries, the common Grathic name is given first. A term whose deeper meaning is will be found in its own place in the Compendium; this glossary gives only what a traveller may hear in a market or a hearth.}

\CRrule

\section*{A}

\textbf{Account-day.} The tenth, twentieth and thirtieth day of every tend, when the slate is read aloud. In Grath these are also market-days. On Tallow 10, Y.H. 813 (Day 159), the first Account-day of the firing month, Berr Clay read \emph{one in twelve, as the notice says} at the Cross, called the levy and denied it with \emph{your house}, never \emph{I}, and went off with the box locked and the true subtraction inside, believing he had done a kindness; a figure read aloud was not the figure paid. On Tallow 20, Y.H. 813 (Day 169), the second Account-day, he read the same figure again under the moot-post, called the levy and said it was not called by him, and sent a man with a number in his fist to a slate at the watch with \emph{your house}, never \emph{I}; the printed figure stood unchallenged, the true subtraction went back up the clay road in the locked box and Hessa Rale carried his narrow slate up the road edge-on without reading it. On Tallow 30, Y.H. 813 (Day 179), the third Account-day and the last market of the firing month, he read \emph{one in twelve, as the notice says} for the third time, said \emph{The levy is called. It is not called by me} and \emph{your house}, never \emph{I}, and went off toward High Kiln with the box locked and the true subtraction inside, believing he had done a kindness; the bell went four, four and a gap with nobody crossing himself, and a figure read aloud was still not the figure paid.

On Ember 10, Y.H. 813 (Day 189), the first Account-day and market-day of the kiln month, Berr Clay came up short off the clay road to the reading block under the moot-post with the red wool cord of his office folded square under his coat and the green of tasted lead glaze at one mouth-corner. He wiped his thumb twice before touching nothing, held a narrow slate unopened to his forearm, passed a finger over the figure, read \emph{one in twelve, as the notice says} low into the goers-by, said \emph{The levy is called. It is not called by me} and \emph{your house}, never \emph{I}, and went off toward High Kiln with the box locked and the true subtraction inside, believing he had done a kindness; the printed figure stood unchallenged and a figure read aloud was still not the figure paid. Two hundred leaned over the reading block and eight pigs went over the wet boards. Sella set the basket in the moot-post’s finger’s width of shade where no slate lay and stood half a pace off through the reading and the bell. The reading did not answer the man carried out on Day 188: no figure, collector or slate knew what he cost (T015/T041/T047/T077).

On Ember 20, Y.H. 813 (Day 199), the second Account-day and market-day of the kiln month, Berr Clay read \emph{one in twelve, as the notice says} twice over the basket, once for the moot and once for the households that came late, said \emph{The levy is called. It is not called by me} and \emph{your house}, never \emph{I}, and went off up the clay road with the box locked and the true subtraction inside, believing he had done a kindness. The district’s arithmetic for the month changed for the second time and cannot be changed back; the printed figure stood unchallenged and a figure read aloud was still not the figure paid. Hessa Rale carried his narrow slate up the road unread, and no figure, collector or slate knew what the man carried out on Day 188 had cost.

On Ember 30, Y.H. 813 (Day 209), the third and last Account-day and the last market of the kiln month, two hundred leaned to the reading block under the moot-post while eight pigs went over the wet boards. Berr Clay came up short off the clay road with the red wool cord of his office folded square under his coat and the green of tasted lead glaze at one corner of his mouth, wiped his thumb twice before touching nothing, held a narrow slate unopened to his forearm, passed a finger over the figure and read \emph{One in twelve, as the notice says} low into the top of the crowd, the figure going twice over the basket, once for the moot and once for the households that came late. He said \emph{The levy is called. It is not called by me} and \emph{your house}, never \emph{I}, and went off toward High Kiln with the box locked and the true subtraction inside, believing he had done a kindness. The district’s arithmetic changed for the third time in the kiln month and cannot be changed back; the printed figure stood unchallenged and a figure read aloud was still not the figure paid. Hessa Rale took the slate up the clay road toward Greybank unread, the soft-cuffed clerk stayed set below the north bridge at the out-of-line landing for a measure nobody called, and the reading answered nothing for the man carried out on Day 188 (T015/T041/T047/T077).

On Grain 20, Y.H. 813 (Day 229), the second Account-day and market of Grain, Berr Clay came up short off the clay road with the red wool cord of his office folded square under his coat and the green of tasted lead glaze at one mouth-corner, wiped his thumb twice before touching nothing, held a narrow slate unopened to his forearm, passed a finger over the figure and read \emph{one in twelve, as the notice says} low into the top of the crowd, the figure going twice over the basket, once for the moot and once for the households that came late. On Smoke 10, Y.H. 813 (Day 249), the first Account-day and market of the second firing, Berr Clay came up short off the clay road with the red wool cord of his office folded square under his coat and the green of tasted lead glaze at one mouth-corner, wiped his thumb twice before touching nothing, held a narrow slate unopened to his forearm, passed a finger over the figure and read \emph{one in twelve, as the notice says} low into the crowd, the figure going twice over the basket, once for the moot and once for the households that came late; he called the levy, denied it with \emph{your house}, never \emph{I}, and went off toward High Kiln with the box locked and the true subtraction inside, believing he had done a kindness. On Smoke 30, Y.H. 813 (Day 269), the third and last Account-day and market of the second firing, two hundred leaned over the reading block and eight pigs went over the wet boards. Eight pigs went over the wet boards and two hundred leaned in; the bell went four, four and a gap with nobody crossing himself; Hessa Rale carried the slate up the road toward Greybank before noon, edge-on and writing to her sleeve, and the soft-cuffed clerk stayed set below the north bridge at the out-of-line landing for a measure nobody called. At the pot board a woman’s green stayed a colour and at the market’s edge a foundling’s shape a shape, with no eighth of either. Sella set the basket in the moot-post’s finger’s width of shade where no slate lay, stood half a pace off through the reading and the bell and carried him home at the going of the light saying nothing of what had been read over him. Frost 20 (Day 289) was the second Account-day of the month. Ch 76.

On Frost 20, Y.H. 813 (Day 289), the second Account-day and the month’s second market, Berr Clay came up short off the clay road with the red wool cord of his office folded square under his coat and the green of tasted lead glaze at one mouth-corner, wiped his thumb twice before touching nothing, held a narrow slate unopened to his forearm, passed a finger over the figure and read \emph{one in twelve, as the notice says} low into the two hundred, the figure going over the basket once for the moot and once for the households that came late. He called the levy for Frost and denied it with \emph{The levy is called. It is not called by me} and \emph{your house}, never \emph{I}, taking himself out of his own sentence as a surgeon takes a hand out of a field before the dressing goes on, and went off toward High Kiln with the box locked and the second true subtraction of Frost inside, believing he had done a kindness. The district’s arithmetic changed a second time for the month and cannot be changed back; the printed figure stands unchallenged and the figure read is still not the figure paid, and the twice-read figure is two accounts and not one. The reading answered nothing for the man carried out on Day 188, the hand that went in on Seed 15 or the dressed grain covered under wool at the rack end, which was read over by a number that did not know what it cost, the space between unsigned. Eight pigs went over the wet boards and two hundred leaned in; the bell went four, four and a gap with nobody crossing himself; Hessa Rale carried the slate up the clay road toward Greybank before noon, edge-on and writing to her sleeve, and no figure came off it; the soft-cuffed clerk stayed set at the out-of-line landing below the north bridge for a measure nobody called; the seventh green stayed a colour at the pot board and the seventh shape a shape at the market’s edge, with no eighth of either. Sella set the basket in the moot-post’s finger’s width of thin shade where no slate lay and stood half a pace off through the reading and the bell, carrying him home at the going of the light saying nothing of what had been read over him. Frost 30 (Day 299) is the third and last Account-day of the month. Ch 79.   On Frost 30, Y.H. 813 (Day 299), the third and last Account-day and market of Frost, Berr Clay came up short off the clay road to the reading block under the moot-post with the red wool cord of his office folded square under his coat and the green of tasted lead glaze at one mouth-corner, under the hot clay the smell of nothing at all; he wiped his thumb twice before touching nothing, held a narrow slate unopened with the writing inward, read \emph{One in twelve, as the notice says} low into the two hundred and sent the figure over the basket twice, once for the moot and once for the late households. He called the levy and denied it with \emph{The levy is called. It is not called by me} and \emph{your house}, never \emph{I}, taking himself out of his own sentence as a surgeon takes a hand out of a field before the dressing goes on, and went off with the box locked and the third true subtraction of Frost inside, believing he had done a kindness. The district’s arithmetic changed a third time for the month and cannot be changed back; the printed figure stood unchallenged and the figure read was still not the figure paid, and no signature stood on the space between. The bell went four, four and a gap with nobody crossing himself, Hessa Rale carried the slate up the road toward Greybank unread, and the soft-cuffed clerk stayed set at the out-of-line landing for a measure nobody called. Sella set the basket in the moot-post’s finger’s width of shade where no slate lay and stood half a pace off through the reading and the bell, carrying him home at the going of the light saying nothing. Frost went out without a boundary drawn. Ch 82.

On Bone 10, Y.H. 813 (Day 309), the month’s first Account-day and market, Berr Clay came up short off the clay road with the red wool cord of his office folded square under his coat and the green of tasted lead glaze at one mouth-corner, wiped his thumb twice on his apron before touching nothing, held a narrow slate writing-inward, passed a finger over the figure and read \emph{One in twelve, as the notice says} twice over the basket — once for the moot and once for the households that came late — called the levy and denied it with \emph{It is not called by me} and \emph{your house}, never \emph{I}, taking himself out of his own sentence as a surgeon leaves a field before the dressing goes on. He went up the road with the box locked and Bone’s first true subtraction inside beside the three of Frost, believing he had done a kindness. Four arithmetics now stand behind one printed figure; four are four and not one account, the figure read is still not the figure paid and no signature stands on the space between. Two hundred leaned over the reading block while eight pigs went over the wet boards; the bell went four, four and a gap with nobody crossing himself; Hessa Rale carried the slate up the road unread with \emph{I don’t read it. I carry it. There’s a difference, and the road doesn’t care which}; the soft-cuffed clerk stayed set at the out-of-line landing for a measure nobody called; a seventh green and a seventh shape stayed a colour and a shape with no eighth. Sella set the basket in the moot-post’s finger’s width of shade where no slate lay and stood half a pace off through the reading and the bell, and carried him home at the going of the light saying nothing. There was no market, Cross or bell on Bone 11 or 12. Ch 86.

On Bone 30, Y.H. 813 (Day 329), the month’s third and last Account-day and market, Berr Clay came up short off the clay road with the red wool cord of his office folded square under his coat and the green of tasted lead glaze at one mouth-corner, wiped his thumb twice on his apron before touching nothing, held a narrow slate unopened to his forearm, passed a finger over the figure and read \emph{One in twelve, as the notice says} twice over the basket, once for the moot and once for the households that came late. He called the levy and denied it with \emph{The levy is called. It is not called by me} and \emph{your house}, never \emph{I}, and went off up the clay road with the box locked and Bone’s third true subtraction inside beside the other five, believing he had done a kindness. Six arithmetics of the year now stand behind one printed figure — six readings six and not one account — the figure read is still not the figure paid and no signature stands on the space between; the reading answers nothing for the hand that went in on Seed 15, the man carried out on Day 188, the dressed grain covered under wool or the carried fire’s missing fifth. The bell went four, four and a gap with nobody crossing himself; Hessa Rale carried the slate up the road toward Greybank before noon, edge-on and unread; the soft-cuffed clerk stayed set at the out-of-line landing for a measure nobody called, and a seventh green and a seventh shape stayed a colour and a shape with no eighth of either. Sella set the basket in the moot-post’s finger’s width of shade where no slate lay and stood half a pace off through the reading and the bell, and carried him home at the going of the light saying nothing. There was no market, Cross or bell on Bone 28 or 29; Bone went out without a boundary drawn and neither of the district’s two habits of naming its months was corrected. Ch 92.

On Ash 20, Y.H. 813 (Day 349), the dark month’s second Account-day and market, Berr Clay came up short off the clay road with the red wool cord of his office folded square under his coat and the sweet green of tasted lead glaze at one mouth-corner, under the hot clay of him the smell of nothing at all. He wiped his thumb twice before touching nothing, held a narrow slate unopened to his forearm, passed a finger over the figure and read \emph{One in twelve, as the notice says} twice over the basket, once for the moot and once for the households that came late; he called the levy and denied it with \emph{The levy is called. It is not called by me} and \emph{your house}, never \emph{I}, taking himself out of his own sentence, said something low to the block about kindness being entered and went off up the clay road with the box locked and Ash’s second true subtraction inside, believing he had done a kindness, with no anger and no triumph in it. \textbf{Eight arithmetics of the year now stand behind one printed figure — the three of Frost, the first, second and third of Bone and Ash’s first and second — eight are eight and not one account}, the figure read still not the figure paid and no signature on the space between; the boy kept the finding on a place of its own with no payer and did not lay it across the house’s not-doings, the covered grain, the five held objects, the pot-crack resting, the hand-at-the-sill breath, the Ash 5 joining, the Ash 17 direction or his own kept gaps, and no doctrine stood up out of eight. Eight pigs went over the wet boards and two hundred leaned in; the bell went four, four and a gap with nobody crossing himself, the heard bell kept in its square beside the told; Hessa Rale carried the slate up the clay road toward Greybank before noon, unread, the soft-cuffed clerk stayed set below the north bridge at the out-of-line landing for a measure nobody called, and a green at the pot board and a shape at the market’s edge stayed sightings with no eighth of either. Sella set the basket in the moot-post’s finger’s width of shade where no slate lay, stood half a pace off through the reading and the bell and carried him home at the going of the light saying nothing of what had been read over the basket. There was no market, Cross or bell on Ash 19 or 21; Ash 30 (Day 359), the month’s third and last Account-day, stood nine mornings ahead and was named only as a date (T015/T041/T047 advanced, not paid). Ch 99.

On Ash 30, Y.H. 813 (Day 359), the dark month’s third and last Account-day and market, Berr Clay came up short off the clay road with the red wool cord of his office folded square under his coat and the sweet green of tasted lead glaze at one mouth-corner, under the hot clay of him the smell of nothing at all. He wiped his thumb twice before touching nothing, held a narrow slate unopened to his forearm, passed a finger over the figure and read \emph{One in twelve, as the notice says} twice over the basket, once for the moot and once for the households that came late; he called the levy and denied it with \emph{The levy is called. It is not called by me} and \emph{your house}, never I, said something low to the block about kindness being entered and went off up the clay road with the box locked and Ash’s third true subtraction inside, believing he had done a kindness with no anger and no triumph in him. \textbf{Nine arithmetics of the year — the three of Frost, the first, second and third of Bone, and Ash’s first, second and third — now stand behind one unsigned figure; nine are nine and not one account}, the figure read still not the figure paid and no signature on the space. The boy kept the finding on a place of its own with no payer, not laid across the house’s not-doings, the covered grain, the five held objects, the pot-crack resting, the hand-at-the-sill breath, the holding of Ash 26, the Ash 5 joining, the Ash 17 direction, the Ash 23 direction or his own gaps; no doctrine stood up out of nine, and the reading answered none of the held questions. Sella set the basket in the moot-post’s finger’s width of shade where no slate lay and stood half a pace off; Hessa carried the slate up the road before noon unread, the soft-cuffed clerk stayed set at the out-of-line landing and the green at the pot board and the shape at the market’s edge stayed sightings with no eighth. Ch 102.

On Stone 20, Y.H. 813 (Day 379), the deep-winter month’s second Account-day and market, Berr Clay came up short off the clay road with the red wool cord of his office folded square under his coat and the sweet green of tasted lead glaze at one mouth-corner, under the hot clay of him the smell of nothing at all. He wiped his thumb twice before touching nothing, held a narrow slate unopened to his forearm, passed a finger over the figure through his sleeve and read \emph{One in twelve, as the notice says} twice over the basket, once for the moot and once for the households that came late; he called the levy and denied it with \emph{The levy is called. It is not called by me} and \emph{your house}, never \emph{I}, taking himself out of his own sentence, said something low to the block about kindness being entered and went off up the clay road with the box locked and Stone’s second true subtraction inside, believing he had done a kindness with no anger and no triumph in him. \textbf{Eleven arithmetics of the year — the three of Frost, the first, second and third of Bone, Ash’s first, second and third, Stone’s first and Stone’s second — now stand behind one unsigned figure; eleven are eleven and not one account}, the figure read still not the figure paid, no signature on the space and no doctrine out of eleven. Eight pigs went over the wet boards and two hundred leaned in; the bell went four, four and a gap with nobody crossing himself; Hessa Rale carried the slate up the road toward Greybank before noon, edge-on and unread, and the soft-cuffed clerk stayed set at the out-of-line landing for a measure nobody called. Sella set the basket in the moot-post’s finger’s width of shade where no slate lay, stood half a pace off through the reading and the bell and carried him home at the going of the light saying nothing of what had been read over him. Ch 109.

On Stone 30, Y.H. 813 (Day 389), the year’s third and last Account-day and market, Berr Clay came up short off the clay road with the red wool cord of his office folded square under his coat and the sweet green of tasted lead glaze at one mouth-corner, wiped his thumb twice before touching nothing, held a narrow slate unopened to his forearm, passed a finger over the figure through his sleeve and read \emph{One in twelve, as the notice says} low into the goers-by, sending it twice over the basket, once for the moot and once for the households that came late; he called the levy and denied it with \emph{The levy is called. It is not called by me} and \emph{your house}, never \emph{I}, took himself out of his own sentence as a surgeon draws a hand from a field before the dressing goes on, said something low to the block about kindness being entered and went off up the clay road with the box locked and Stone’s last true subtraction inside, believing he had done a kindness with no anger and no triumph in him. \textbf{Twelve arithmetics of the year now stand behind one unsigned figure — the three of Frost, the first, second and third of Bone, the first, second and third of Ash, and Stone’s first, second and last — twelve are twelve and not one account}, the figure read still not the figure paid, no signature on the space and no doctrine out of twelve; the twelve true subtractions ride locked in his box up the road and the boy has no key. Eight pigs went over the wet boards and two hundred leaned in; the bell went four, four and a gap with nobody crossing himself, the heard bell kept in its square beside the told; Hessa Rale carried the slate up the road before noon, edge-on and unread; the soft-cuffed clerk stayed set at the out-of-line landing for a measure nobody called; a green at the pot board and a shape at the market’s edge stayed sightings with no eighth of either. Sella set the basket in the moot-post’s finger’s width of shade where no slate lay, stood half a pace off through the reading and the bell and carried him home at the going of the light saying nothing of what had been read over the wicker. Stone kept its twenty-eighth, twenty-ninth and thirtieth days without a boundary drawn and the year went out without one either; Ch 112.

On Silt 10, Y.H. 814 (Day 434), Silt’s first Account-day and market and the year’s fourth reading, Berr Clay came up short off the clay road to the reading block under the moot-post with the red wool cord of his office folded square under his coat and the sweetish green of tasted lead glaze at one mouth-corner, under the hot clay of him the smell of nothing at all. He wiped his thumb twice before touching nothing, held a narrow slate unopened to his forearm, passed a finger over the figure through his sleeve, read \emph{one in twelve, as the notice says} low into the goers-by and sent the figure twice over the basket, once for the moot and once for the households that came late; he called the levy, denied it with \emph{The levy is called. It is not called by me} and \emph{your house}, never \emph{I}, sent a fist-number to a slate at the watch where it arrived nowhere, said something low to the block about kindness being entered, and went off up the road with the box locked and Silt’s fourth true subtraction inside, believing he had done a kindness. \textbf{Four readings of the year now stand behind one unsigned figure — four are four and not one account}, the first not made a thirteenth by the three that follow, the second supplying no signature, the third no doctrine, the fourth no payer, the twelve arithmetics of Y.H. 813 not laid across the four, the figure read still not the figure paid; Sella set the basket in the moot-post’s finger’s width of shade where no slate lay and stood half a pace off through the reading and the bell, and Hessa Rale carried the narrow slate up the road before noon unread and was not made a reader by four figures. Eight pigs went over the wet boards and the market sold over the reading the way water goes over a stone; the bell went four, four and a gap with nobody crossing himself. Silt 20 (Day 444) stands ten mornings off, the month’s second reading and the year’s fifth. Ch 127.

\textbf{A slate burns where a room was shut.} A yard saying of Low Kiln, told over the boards in the dark month: \emph{A slate burns where a room was shut, and the road brings the teller back with the writing turned inward; ask the weather which is true, for nobody stands to be asked.} The first clause joins the burned slate of Slate Row, told five times with a finger between the fifth and the four and no witness, to the Greybank saying of the counting room shut with the damper closed in the last war, told twice and joined to no kiln. On Ash 5, Y.H. 813 (Day 334), an ownerless voice over the boards of the Clay Yard spoke the joining for the first time on the same breath as the price of barley and the weather — without a date, a room named, a hand at a flame, a person standing to be asked, a figure, a confession, a cause or a payer — and went off up the terrace while the work went on and nobody turned twice. The boy filed it on a place of its own as a first joining, not a sixth telling of the slate, not a third telling of the room, not a hearing, a seventh, a stopping, a payment, a cause or a rule (T035/T031/T065/T095 advanced and not paid). The second clause is the runner who carried the figure coming back down the road with the writing turned toward herself, given a fourth shaping at the well that same afternoon and answered as a sighting only on Ash 6; four shapings are still not a witness and no fifth came (T080 advanced and not paid). See \textbf{Three askings do not make a witness}, \textbf{Two tellings of one absence} and \textbf{Which row did the pot go quiet on?} Ch 94.

On Ash 17, Y.H. 813 (Day 346), an ownerless voice came over the boards from the direction of Slate Row and gave this joining a \textbf{further shaping}: a room shut with the damper closed and a slate burned over a man nobody named, with no room named, no hand at any flame, no figure, no date standing and nobody standing in any doorway to be asked. The weather answered first and the price of barley after it, and the voice went up the terrace while the boards lay where they lay. The boy took the word apart as a surgeon takes a wound apart and found no witness at the bottom of it; he filed it on a place of its own \textbf{beside} the Ash 5 joining with a finger between, a further shaping and an advancement of the finding that a place wants a witness — expressly not a sixth telling of the burned slate (five), not a third telling of the shut room (two), not a sixth asking of the row (five), not a fifth shaping of the well-saying (four), not a hearing, a seventh, a cause, a confession, a joining, a reader, a name, a witness or a payment, with no payer standing (T035/T031/T065/T095 and T101 advanced and \textbf{not paid}). See \textbf{Burned slate (a direction from Slate Row)} and \textbf{Which row did the pot go quiet on?} Ch 98.

On Ash 23, Y.H. 813 (Day 352), an ownerless voice came over the boards from the direction of Slate Row and shaped this joining one direction further: a room shut with the damper closed against the cold and a slate burned over a man nobody named so that a count would not go up, with no room named, no hand at any flame, no figure, no date, no name and nobody standing in any doorway to be asked. The weather answered first and the price of barley after it, and the voice went up the terrace while the boards lay where they lay and nobody turned twice. The boy took the word apart as a surgeon takes a wound apart and filed it on a place of its own \textbf{beside} the Ash 5 joining and the Ash 17 direction with a finger between every pair — a further shaping and an advancement of the finding that a place wants a witness and a witness is a day somebody stands somewhere and can be asked, expressly \textbf{not} a sixth telling of the burned slate (which stays at five), \textbf{not} a third telling of the shut room (two), \textbf{not} a sixth asking of the row (five), \textbf{not} a fifth shaping of the well-saying (four), \textbf{not} a hearing, a seventh, a cause, a confession, a joining, a reader, a name, a witness or a payment, with no payer standing (T035/T031/T065/T095 and T101 advanced and \textbf{not paid}). The direction did not come again on Ash 24 and stands gathering and unspent; the claim goes on gathering interest against Jorra Vail’s promise, which is neither given nor withdrawn, and buys no lesson under any roof. Ch 100.

\textbf{A figure goes up the clay road in a locked box; a word comes up from the well and stops on the stone lip.} A saying of the Clay Yard, told on the twelfth morning of Ilmen, and the epigraph of \emph{A Word at the Well}: \emph{A figure goes up the clay road in a locked box; a word comes up from the well and stops on the stone lip. Neither carries a name under it, and the yard keeps both.} The figure is the Account-day reading that goes up the clay road in Berr Clay’s box with the true subtraction inside and the printed notice standing unchallenged behind it — a figure read is not the figure paid and no signature stands on the space. The word came up at the yard well on Ilmen 12, Y.H. 814 (Day 406): one of the bucket-round said that the woman who carries the slate had once carried a figure that named a person she knew, with no owner standing, no room, no hand at a slate, no name for the person, no figure, no date and nobody to ask. The boy filed it as the \textbf{fifth} shaping of the well-saying, on a place of its own with a finger between it and Hessa Rale’s eighth record-first hand and another between it and the saying of the road from the Cross to Greybank, a third finger between it and the four ownerless directions out of Slate Row. A shaping is not a witness, a confession, a reader or a payment, and a fifth does not make a sixth due: five are five and go on gathering interest toward the far-off hand that will lay the district’s private keepings together and call the joining an account — a hand not his. Ilva drew at the same well with her notched strip in her sleeve and answered the question put and not the one behind it; she was expressly not the speaker, and the word and the count went on separate places with a finger between (T080 advanced, \textbf{not paid}). See \textbf{A slate burns where a room was shut}, \textbf{A stick keeps what a slate would tax}, \textbf{Ask the pot} and \textbf{Which row did the pot go quiet on?} Ch 118.

\textbf{A figure read thrice is three figures and no account.} A saying of the Low Kiln basket-women at the Cross, and the epigraph of \emph{Three Times Over the Basket}: \emph{A figure read thrice is three figures and no account; the silt comes when it comes and asks no leave of the slate.} The first clause is the third reading of Ilmen 30, Y.H. 814 (Day 424), the month’s third and last: Berr Clay read \emph{One in twelve, as the notice says} twice over the basket, once for the moot and once for the households that came late, called the levy, denied it with \emph{your house}, never \emph{I}, and went up the clay road with the box locked and the third true subtraction inside, believing he had done a kindness. Three readings of the year now stand behind one unsigned figure — Ilmen 10, 20 and 30 — three are three and not one account, the first is not made a thirteenth by the second or the third, the figure read is still not the figure paid, no signature stands on the space and no doctrine comes out of three; the twelve arithmetics of Y.H. 813 are not laid across the three to make a row come out even, for paper is not a payer and the key went up in a coat pocket that never comes back down. The second clause is Silt, which came on the next morning with no boundary drawn and neither of the district’s two habits of naming its months set right or left, and asked no leave of any slate to do it. The silt comes when it comes; a reading changes a district’s arithmetic and buys no warmth for a basket set two inches from a pot handle. See \textbf{A figure goes up the clay road in a locked box; a word comes up from the well and stops on the stone lip}, \textbf{A clean slate is not a clean account}, \textbf{What is read aloud is not what is paid} and \textbf{Three askings do not make a witness}. Ch 124.

\textbf{A finger that goes to the shelf and toward the ear is still a finger short of the gap; the gap keeps its own name.} A saying of the Low Kiln basket-women at the loaf shelf, and the epigraph of \emph{A Finger’s Width Short}: \emph{A finger that goes to the shelf and toward the ear is still a finger short of the gap; the gap keeps its own name.} On Silt 3, Y.H. 814 (Day 427), a neighbour with a pot came to the Vail loaf shelf and reached past the bare board before her eyes found the basket, the way neighbours had reached before: hand to board, eye to basket, mouth after both. Her finger went along the top of the shelf where the charcoal tally lay beneath, tracing the front edge without going beneath it and without reading what lay there, and then, without her seeing it, went in the direction of the empty place at the boy’s ear and stopped a finger’s width short of the fold. In one breath she called the row’s old gap a thing the turning of the month had brought in and the empty place a child’s appetite, and went off with her pot believing she had said two ordinary things about two ordinary gaps. Both names were wrong — the gap was years old and had come in before the boy was born, and the empty place held the keeping at the fold as a finding since the fifteenth with no appetite behind it — and in a single breath she had made two rooms one absence without seeing it. The boy took the reaching apart by the order of its parts, the half-beat standing in the gap where a joining would have stood, and filed it on a place of its own beside the earlier shapings and the far-off finger that has not come: a further shaping of \textbf{T097}, advanced and \textbf{not paid}, no joining, name, figure, third gap, fourth likeness, account or payer, not made his own and not laid across the twelve arithmetics, the three readings of the year, the printed figure, the fifth shaping, the offered figure or the clerk’s entered figure. One finger’s width of air is not an account, and a gap keeps its own name until a hand not his lays shelf and fold together and calls the joining one. It was not repeated on Silt 4 and was not made a custom, a sixth shaping, a witness, a reader or a payer. See \textbf{A thing set down once is a keeping. Set it down twice and it is a way, and a way wants a hand to walk it}, \textbf{The tally under the shelf} and \textbf{A figure read thrice is three figures and no account}. Ch 125.

\textbf{The figure goes on the slate before the man is looked at; an order is not an answer.} A saying of the Clay Yard, and the epigraph of \emph{A Hand to the Slate}: \emph{The figure goes on the slate before the man is looked at; that is the order, and an order is not an answer.} It is the yard’s name for the reaching order that a midwife, a thane, a keeper, a runner, a collector, Berr Clay’s thumb, Hessa’s wrist, Ilva’s sleeve and the soft-cuffed clerk’s inward slate all keep: hand to the record, eye to the person, mouth after both, the half-beat lying in the gap. On Ilmen 15, Y.H. 814 (Day 409), word came up the yard, from mouth to mouth with no body under it, that the soft-cuffed clerk still set below the north bridge at the out-of-line landing had entered a figure on his inward slate before he looked up to find the man who gave it. Nobody saw the hand or the slate, no man stood under the figure, no room was entered, no name spoken, no figure brought under any roof and no slate opened within reach of a basket: a report and not a sighting. The boy took the order apart as a surgeon takes a field and filed it on a place of its own with a finger between it and Tarn’s degree toward the landing and another between it and the face at the yard’s edge. It is the next reaching toward the loan that can hear and is \textbf{not} the calling of that loan, not a tenth hand, not a rule, not a sighting, not a witness, not a reader and not a payment (T090/T080 advanced, \textbf{not paid}). An order is the manner of a table and not the truth of a person: the figure belongs to no man standing under it, and there is nobody to ask. See \textbf{A figure goes up the clay road in a locked box; a word comes up from the well and stops on the stone lip}, \textbf{A clean slate is not a clean account}, \textbf{The tally under the shelf} and \textbf{Loan that can hear}. Ch 119.

\textbf{The slate goes down the bridge road with its writing turned to the sleeve, and the figure goes up the clay road in a box with no key.} A saying of the Clay Yard, and the epigraph of \emph{The Writing Turned to the Sleeve}: \emph{The slate goes down the bridge road with its writing turned to the sleeve, and the figure goes up the clay road in a box with no key. Neither stops for a house to say what it carries.} The first clause is the second man from Slate Row, seen before first grey on Ilmen 21, Y.H. 814 (Day 415), going down the north bridge road with a narrow slate under his arm and the writing turned away, no word carrying and nobody under any roof knowing what he carried. The boy filed his direction and his slate on places of their own beside the first man’s face, the soft-cuffed clerk’s entered figure and the fifth shaping of the well-saying, with a finger between every pair — no name, owner, answer, witness, sale or payer standing, and expressly not the calling of the loan that can hear (T102 opened, advanced and \textbf{not paid}). The second clause is Ilmen’s second arithmetic, read twice over the basket on Ilmen 20 (Day 414) and gone up the clay road in Berr Clay’s locked box behind the first of the year and the twelve of Y.H. 813, the key gone up in a coat pocket that never comes back down. Two readings now stand behind one unsigned figure: two are two and not one account, the first is not a thirteenth, the figure read is still not the figure paid, no signature stands on the space and no doctrine comes out of two. Neither the slate nor the figure stops for a house to say what it carries, and the boy, who has no key, lays neither across the other to make a row come out even, for paper is not a payer. See \textbf{A figure goes up the clay road in a locked box; a word comes up from the well and stops on the stone lip}, \textbf{The figure goes on the slate before the man is looked at; an order is not an answer}, \textbf{A clean slate is not a clean account} and \textbf{Loan that can hear}. Ch 121.

\textbf{A firing opens the kiln. A week of tending settles nothing.} A saying of the drying racks in Low Kiln, told after the first firing of a month: \emph{A firing opens the kiln. A week of tending settles nothing. The hand goes to the mark before the fire, and to no shelf, no bed, no basket after it.} It is a rule about the widow’s mark and a refusal to turn an opening into a doctrine: the first firing of Frost on Frost 2, Y.H. 813 (Day 271) was done with Sella Vail’s hand to the mark for one breath and at no other hour, and through Frost 4–6 nobody made a lesson, sign, mending or payer of it. Four openings in four months are four and not a rule; the next stands in a later month’s first firing, far off (T058/T079). Ch 74. On Bone 2, Y.H. 813 (Day 301), the household fired again: Sella’s hand went to the mark before the kiln for one breath, the coal went under a broken pot and the fire took in fours with the fifth still missing and its payer unnamed three hundred and one days then three hundred and two; nobody praised it, named what it mended, entered a slate or made a lesson of it. \textbf{Five openings in five months are five and not a rule}; the four behind (Days 150, 180, 240 and 271) were not looked at again as signs, payments or menders, and the fifth did not make a sixth due (T058/T079). Ch 83. Through Bone 4–6, Y.H. 813 (Days 303–305) no opening came and the mark hung where it hung at every morning, hearth, yard, afternoon and going of the light, because none of these was an opening; five openings in five months were still five and not a rule, and the carried fire’s fifth remained unpaid three hundred and three, four and five days with its payer unnamed. Ch 84. Through Bone 7–9, Y.H. 813 (Days 306–308) no opening came and the mark hung where it hung at every morning, hearth, yard, afternoon and going of the light, because none of these was an opening; five openings in five months were still five and not a rule, and the carried fire’s fifth remained unpaid three hundred and six, seven and eight days with its payer unnamed. Ch 85. Through Bone 10–12, Y.H. 813 (Days 309–311) no opening came and the mark hung where it hung at every morning, hearth, rack, row, reading, yard, basket, going of the light and bed, because none of these was an opening; the hand goes to the mark before the kiln and at no other hour. Five openings in five months were five and not a rule, the next standing in a later month’s first firing, far off and not hoped for. Bone’s first reading came to the Cross on the tenth and the printed figure stood unchallenged while the dressed grain lay covered and unfigured under wool and the figure read over it did not know what it cost; no lesson, sign, mending or payer was made of the reading under the Vail roof, and the carried fire’s fifth remained unpaid three hundred and nine, ten and eleven days with its payer unnamed. Ch 86. Through Ash 13–15, Y.H. 813 (Days 342–344) no further opening came after the sixth at the kiln mouth on Ash 2; the widow’s mark hung where it hung at every morning, hearth, yard, going of the light and bed, because none of these was an opening, and six openings in six months were still six and not a rule with no seventh made due. The fire under the floor kept four low pulls and the silence where the fifth should have stood, its payer unnamed three hundred and forty-two, forty-three and forty-four days, and the yard called the Ash cold weather and gave nobody a figure (T058/T079, T088 advanced, not paid). Ch 97. Through Ash 16–18, Y.H. 813 (Days 345–347) no further opening came after the sixth at the kiln mouth on Ash 2; the widow’s mark hung where it hung at every morning, hearth, yard, going of the light and bed, because none of these was an opening, and six openings in six months were still six and not a rule with no seventh made due. The fire under the floor kept four low pulls and the silence where the fifth should have stood, its payer unnamed three hundred and forty-five, forty-six and forty-seven days, and the ownerless word that came over the boards on the seventeenth went up the terrace and bought no opening, lesson, sign, mending or payer under the roof (T058/T079, T088 advanced, not paid). Ch 98.

Through Ash 1–3, Y.H. 813 (Days 330–332) no further opening came after the sixth at the kiln mouth on Ash 2; the fire before the basket and the fire behind the wall both kept four low pulls and the silence where the fifth should have stood, its payer unnamed three hundred and thirty, thirty-one and thirty-two days, and the yard called the Ash cold weather and gave nobody a figure. Six openings in six months were six and not a rule, the five behind were not looked at again as signs or payments, and no seventh opening was made due (T058/T079, T088 advanced, not paid). Ch 93. Through Ash 4–6, Y.H. 813 (Days 333–335) no further opening came and the widow’s mark hung where it hung at every morning, hearth, going of the light and bed, because none of these was an opening; the fire kept four low pulls and the silence where the fifth should have stood, its payer unnamed three hundred and thirty-three, thirty-four and thirty-five days, and the yard called the Ash cold weather and gave nobody a figure (T058/T079, T088 advanced, not paid). Ch 94. Through Ash 7–9, Y.H. 813 (Days 336–338) no further opening came and the widow’s mark hung where it hung at every morning, hearth, going of the light and bed, because none of these was an opening; the fire kept four low pulls and the silence where the fifth should have stood, its payer unnamed three hundred and thirty-six, thirty-seven and thirty-eight days, and the yard called the Ash cold weather and gave nobody a figure (T058/T079, T088 advanced, not paid). Ch 95. Through Stone 1–3 the mark hung untouched after Ash 2 and no seventh opening was made due; the first firing of Stone stood three mornings beyond the close as a date named to nobody. On Stone 5, Y.H. 813 (Day 364), the household fired again: Sella carried the basket to the kiln mouth before any instruction went to it, set it level out of the draught, put her left hand to the widow’s mark for one breath, lifted the clay lid with the back of a hand and tipped the carried coal under a broken pot. The fire took in fours with the silence where the fifth should have stood, its payer unnamed three hundred and sixty-four days; nobody praised the opening, named what it mended, entered a slate or made a lesson of it. \textbf{Seven openings in seven months are seven and not a rule}; the five behind (Tallow 1, Ember 1, Smoke 1, Frost 2, Bone 2, Ash 2) were not looked at again as signs, payments or menders, and the seventh did not make an eighth due (T058/T079, T088 advanced, not paid). Ch 104.

\textbf{A hand that cannot close two inches may stay where it cannot reach.} A saying of the Clay Yard, told over the trough in Bone’s middle week: \emph{A hand that cannot close two inches may stay where it cannot reach, and staying is not reaching. The house keeps by not-doing and the boy by not-going; neither is a kindness entered on any slate.} It is the yard’s name for the boy’s held inch. On Bone 15, Y.H. 813 (Day 314), the hand outside the wool came up an inch toward the river’s note, took a small intake and let it go whole, and then stayed at the inch for the space of the note’s fading without reaching the crust two inches away. The surgeon read a clamp left a moment after the bleeding had stopped or a tourniquet not yet released; the infant read a hand that had not given up wanting the crust; both were true and neither won. The staying was filed as the two hundred and third answer, one object on a place of its own on the sixth place: not a reach, a hearing, a seventh, a stopping, a payment, a held change, a fifth likeness or a rule, with no payer named. It was not made again at the going of the light, when the two hundred and fourth answer came straight down — one staying is a keeping, two would be a habit, and a habit would want a payer (T060/T086, T061/T082 advanced, not paid). Ch 87. Through Bone 16–18, Y.H. 813 (Days 315–317) the staying stayed one object and was not made again, and on Bone 17 a \textbf{second} small object was filed beside it: the early letting-go of answer 207, a letting-go before the note had done, on a place of its own with a finger between it and the staying and a finger between it and every other object there. The two objects are not two stayings and do not stand up as a habit, a way, a fifth held change or a rule, for a doctrine is an account that has found a payer and none stood to either; the staying, the early letting-go, the four held changes and the four arithmetics nearly touch and the finger goes between (T060/T086, T061/T082 advanced, not paid). Ch 88. Through Ash 13–15, Y.H. 813 (Days 342–344) a further small object was filed beside these and beside the pot-crack resting of Ash 9: on Ash 14 Tarn’s hand stayed at the knife-sill a breath longer than the house’s check required before he took it away, holding at the top of the reach where his unspent breath had stayed since the dark. The boy filed the held breath on a place of its own with a finger between every pair — expressly not a sixth held object, not a seventh of anything, not a tenth stopping, not the seventh year given, not a habit, a way, a hearing, a sign, a mending, a cause, a payment or a rule, with no payer standing under it. It was checked where it had been put on Ash 15 and was not made again or joined to the charcoal, the notched strip, the Ash 5 joining or any other keeping; it gathers toward the far-off hand that will one day lay the district’s private keepings together, and that hand is not his. Two hundred and sixty-four honest answers stand on the sixth place at the close of Ash 15, each an object and not a power (T036/T076/T006, T061/T082 advanced, not paid). Ch 97. Through Ash 16–18, Y.H. 813 (Days 345–347) the Ash 14 hand-at-the-sill breath was checked on the sixteenth, seventeenth and eighteenth and found where it had been put each time; it was not made again and was not joined to the charcoal, the notched strip, the Ash 5 joining or the Ash 17 direction, and no sixth held object or seventh of anything was made of it (T036/T076/T006, T061/T082 advanced, not paid). The hand outside the wool answered six times, 265 through 270, each a small intake held whole on the river’s note and let go on the note’s own finishing, then straight down and laid back against the fold as a tool put away where the next hand will find it; \textbf{two hundred and seventy honest answers} stand on the sixth place at the close of Ash 18, each an object and not a power, not one standing up and calling itself a doctrine, for a doctrine is an account that has found a payer and none stood (T061/T082 advanced, not paid). Ch 98.

\textbf{A note let go before the note has finished.} A saying of the Clay Yard, told over the flat stone by the well in Bone’s last working week: \emph{A note let go before the note has finished is a letting-go all the same. The river does not ask the hand why it stopped, and the hand does not ask the river why it went on.} It is the yard’s name for the boy’s early letting-go of Bone 17, Y.H. 813 (Day 316). The hand outside the wool came up an inch toward the river’s note of water over water, took a small intake from the room whose floor does not touch his and let it go whole — but let it go \textbf{before the note had done}, while the low sound was still going under the finger’s-width door. The surgeon read a tourniquet released before the bleeding had quite stopped, a clamp taken off a moment too soon; the infant read a hand that gave up before it was done wanting the crust; both were true and neither won. He filed it as answer 207 on a place of its own on the sixth place, with a finger between it and the stayed-at-the-inch object of Bone 15 and a finger between it and every other object there: not a reach, a second staying, a habit, a fifth held change, a seventh hearing, a tenth stopping, a payment, a payer or a doctrine. It was \textbf{not made again}: answers 208, 209 and 210 came straight down on the silence after the note, for one early letting-go is a letting-go and two would be a way of it, and a way would want a payer and none stood. The staying and the early letting-go are two objects on two places, neither a habit nor a rule, held for the far-off hand that will read the file. See \textbf{A hand that cannot close two inches may stay where it cannot reach}. Ch 88.

\textbf{The stick keeps its notch and asks nothing; a man who can stand in a doorway is not a man who has been asked in.} A saying of the Low Kiln bucket-round in the month of Silt, and the epigraph of \emph{What the Wood Keeps}: \emph{The stick keeps its notch and asks nothing. Ask it what the month’s firings cost and it will give you the weather. The slate goes up the road and the count stays in the sleeve, and a man who can stand in a doorway is not a man who has been asked in.} The first clause is Ilva’s strip of notched birch, which keeps the firings of the month in wood and asks no figure to be put on it; the second is the well’s answer to a cost-question, the weather standing where a price would stand; the third is the printing slate that goes up the clay road in Berr Clay’s box while the count stays in a sleeve no clerk’s thumb can take it out of; the fourth is the man from Slate Row who stood at the yard’s edge on Silt 13, Y.H. 814 (Day 437), with his hands loose and a patient face, asked nothing and saying nothing, no loaf passed, no slate shown, no word carried and no threshold crossed. A man who can wait in a doorway has not therefore been asked in, and a face at the edge of a yard is not a witness standing somewhere to be questioned: the boy filed it on a place of its own with a finger between it and Ilva’s second asking of Silt 12 and another between it and the Slate Row likenesses, not a tenth hand, a reader, a witness, a sale, a payment or a payer (T090/T080 with T036/T076 and T035/T031 advanced, \textbf{not paid}). On Silt 12 a second neighbour at the well had asked whether a count kept in wood would be taken at the next reading — the fear carried by another mouth, not a second offer and not the old question repeated — and Ilva answered the question put and not the one behind it, \emph{Ask the pot what it cost. I keep the count, not the account} (T080 with T090/T102 advanced, \textbf{not paid}). See \textbf{A stick keeps what a slate would tax}, \textbf{Ask the pot}, \textbf{Ask a well for a house-name and it gives you the weather}, \textbf{The figure goes on the slate before the man is looked at; an order is not an answer} and \textbf{Loan that can hear}. Ch 128.

\textbf{A stick keeps what a slate would tax.} A saying of the firing women at the yard well in Low Kiln, told in Frost: \emph{A stick keeps what a slate would tax. A shelf keeps what a stick cannot say. The month keeps neither, and goes.} The first clause is Ilva’s count of firings notched on birch bark in her sleeve; the second is the charcoal tally beneath the Vail loaf shelf and the two gaps above it; the third is the month itself, which ends without a boundary drawn and takes no figure with it. On Frost 26 a slate lay open on the stone lip while Ilva’s hand went toward her sleeve and stayed there, and she answered \emph{Ask the pot what it cost. I keep the count, not the account}; no figure came off the wood, the stick was not joined to the slate, and nothing of it came under the Vail roof as lesson, figure, mending, cause or payment (T080 advanced, not paid). Ch 81. On Bone 2, Y.H. 813 (Day 301), Ilva’s hand went toward her sleeve and stayed there when a woman asked what the month’s firings had taken; the notched strip was not taken out or read, no figure came off the wood and the house’s opening at the kiln mouth that morning was not brought to her well as a sign, lesson or payment. She answered \emph{Ask the pot what it cost. I keep the count, not the account}, went on with her water and the ninth hand stayed nine (T080 advanced, not paid). Ch 83. On Bone 6 (Day 305) she was seen again at the well with clay pale in her nail crescents and grey rack dust in one thumb seam; her hand went toward her sleeve and stayed there, the strip unread and no figure coming off the wood, and the fifth burned-slate telling, the twice-mended pot with its crack showing and the three coverings called weather brought no figure to her well. The ninth stayed nine with no tenth (T080 advanced, not paid). Ch 84. On Bone 7 (Day 306) she was seen again at the well with clay pale in her nail crescents and grey rack dust in one thumb seam; her hand went toward her sleeve and stayed there, the strip unread, no figure coming off the wood, and the twice-mended pot with its crack showing, the grain covered under wool and the three coverings called weather brought nothing to her well as sign or payment. She answered \emph{Ask the pot what it cost. I keep the count, not the account}; the ninth stayed nine with no tenth (T080 advanced, not paid). Ch 85. On Ash 17, Y.H. 813 (Day 346), Ilva drew once at the yard well, clay pale in her nail crescents and grey rack dust in one thumb seam; her hand went toward her sleeve and stayed there with the notched strip unread while a woman waiting her turn asked what Ash’s firings had taken, and she answered the question put and not the one behind it: \emph{Ask the pot what it cost. I keep the count, not the account}. The boy filed the order of reaching as the ninth record-first hand with a finger between it and Hessa’s eighth and no tenth, made no figure of the open slate a pace away and made no reader of her own keeping. She was expressly \textbf{not} the speaker of the ownerless word that came over the boards that afternoon; her well gave no fifth shaping and no witness stood (T080 held, T035/T031/T065/T095 advanced and not paid). Offstage on Ash 16 and 18. Ch 98.

\textbf{A handful lifted and let fall back tells you the grain is dry.} A saying of the drying racks, told in the last tend of Bone: \emph{A handful lifted and let fall back tells you the grain is dry. It tells you nothing of the hands that sowed it, and nothing of what the season will ask for it.} On Bone 22, Y.H. 813 (Day 321), at the rack end of the Clay Yard, Sella Vail lifted the wool from the dressed grain, took a small handful and let it fall back through her fingers onto the heap instead of spreading it; she said nothing and gave no figure and did not do it again on Bone 23 or 24, when her fingers went in and came out without closing and she made no show of not repeating it. The boy read it as a surgeon lifts a dressing’s edge and lets it fall, and kept it as one object on a place of its own, with a finger between it and the four held changes on four places and a finger between it and his own gaps. It is not a fifth held change, a sign, a lesson, a mending, a cause, a sixth arithmetic or a rule; no payer stands to it and it bought nothing at two inches of air. Two would be a habit and a habit would want a payer, three would be a way and a way would want one too, so the empty fingers of the two following mornings went beside it as a keeping and not as a second (T077 advanced, T060/T086 and T061/T082 advanced, \textbf{not paid}). The saying stands as a seed for the far-off hand that will one day lay the district’s private keepings together; it is not joined to Ilva’s notched strip at the well, the charcoal beneath the loaf shelf or the five arithmetics in Berr’s locked box. See \textbf{A stick keeps what a slate would tax}, \textbf{What is read aloud is not what is paid} and \textbf{Handling is not entry}. Ch 90.

\textbf{A thing left lying has two keepers.} A Low Kiln saying, told over a pot set down and forgotten: \emph{A thing left lying has two keepers: the hand that left it and the place that held it. The place keeps no account.} The first keeper is the hand that put a thing down; the second is the board, corner, shelf or fold that held it, and the place takes no reckoning of what it held. It is the district’s plain grammar for a keeping that is no gift, payment or account: the twice-mended Vail pot keeps the hairline its mender left showing, the wool in the crust’s empty place is found where a hand put it and adds no placing, the charcoal under the loaf shelf and the strip of notched birch in a sleeve are kept where no slate takes a figure off them, and the gone pan’s round ring and the field’s empty place hold absences nobody enters. Through Stone 22–24, Y.H. 813 (Days 381–383) the wool was found folded where it was put on the seventh, eighth and ninth mornings and goings of the light and still was not made again — nine findings from a hand that only read adding no ninth placing — and a fourth ownerless direction over the boards on Stone 23 about a room shut against the cold and a slate burned so a count would not go up stood with no owner and no payer, so the saying held and no account came of it (T097/T060/T086 and T035/T031/T065/T095 advanced, not paid). See \textbf{A thing set down once is a keeping}, \textbf{Left where it lies}, \textbf{Not-doing} and \textbf{Three askings do not make a witness}. Ch 110 (epigraph).

\textbf{A thing set down once is a keeping. Set it down twice and it is a way, and a way wants a hand to walk it.} A saying of the Vail kiln-house, told to the fire at the going of the light, and the epigraph of \emph{The Wool Left Where It Lay}. It is the house’s grammar of keeping: one fold left in an empty place is a keeping, a second fold would make a habit and a third a way, and both a habit and a way want a payer standing where none stands. Through Stone 16–18, Y.H. 813 (Days 375–377) the wool Sella Vail tucked into the crust’s empty place on the evening of Stone 15 was found folded once in that place on three mornings and at three goings of the light and was not made again — no second fold, third crust, name, gift, payment or payer, not a joining of rooms, not a sixth held object, not a habit, way, sign, hearing, mending, cause or rule. A hand that finds is not a hand that places: three findings from a hand that only read added no fourth placing to the first. The keeping gathered interest on its own place beside the crust’s gap, the shelf’s two gaps, the gone pan’s round ring and the field’s empty place, toward the far-off finger that will one day lay shelf and fold together and call the joining an account — a hand that is not his and has not come (T097/T060/T086 advanced, not paid). See \textbf{A kept thing is owed}, \textbf{Not-doing}, \textbf{A hand that cannot close two inches may stay where it cannot reach} and \textbf{Left where it lies}.

Through Stone 19–21, Y.H. 813 (Days 378–380) the wool was found folded once in the crust’s empty place on the fourth, fifth and sixth mornings and at the fourth, fifth and sixth goings of the light, and was not made again — no second fold, third crust, name, gift, payment or payer, not a joining of rooms, not a sixth held object, not a habit, way, sign, hearing, mending, cause or rule. Six findings from a hand that only read add no seventh placing: a habit wants a hand that placed twice, a way wants a third, and both want a payer where none stands. The keeping sits on a place of its own beside the crust’s gap, the shelf’s two gaps, the gone pan’s round ring and the field’s empty place, gathering interest toward the far-off finger that will one day lay shelf and fold together and call the joining an account — a hand that is not his and has not come, and it was not laid across the eleven readings or the four rooms’ gap (T097/T060/T086 advanced, not paid). Ch 109.

Through Stone 25–27, Y.H. 813 (Days 384–386) the wool was found folded once in the crust’s empty place a tenth, an eleventh and a twelfth time, on each morning and at each going of the light, and was not made again — no second fold, third crust, name, gift, payment or payer, not a joining of rooms, not a sixth held object, not a habit, way, sign, hearing, mending, cause or rule, and not laid across the eleven readings, the four rooms’ gap or any of the four directions. Ten, eleven and twelve findings from a hand that only read add no tenth, eleventh or twelfth placing: a second placing would make a habit and a third a way, and both want a payer where none stands. The small alarm at a double-digit count was itself filed on a place of its own, and the far-off finger is still far off, not his, not come (T097/T060/T086 advanced, not paid). Ch 111.

\textbf{A year comes round to the month it started in.} A yard saying of Low Kiln, told at the turning of the deep-winter month: \emph{The yard goes around its places and calls the weather weather. A year comes round to the month it started in and no hand turns it over to see what it cost. What the basket keeps it keeps without a name, and the house goes on counting its days in loaves.} It is the yard’s way of saying that a house can keep a year without owning it: the months are named two ways in Low Kiln, by the weather and by the count of Account-days, and neither habit is set right or left. On Stone 7, Y.H. 813 (Day 366), the boy’s first birthday in this life came round with the month he was born in and went as an ordinary tending day — no party, cake, figure, recognition or threshold, no loaf set aside and no word over the basket — nobody under any roof knowing what a number counts. He kept three hundred and sixty-six, three hundred and sixty-seven and three hundred and sixty-eight exactly, a whole year finished and named by no roof, and did not stand it up as a sign, a slight or a cause; Days 367 and 368 proved the non-recognition was neither a cruelty nor a mercy anybody could enter. The keeping stands toward the far-off hand that will one day lay the district’s private keepings together, joined to no opening, no tenth arithmetic and no payer (T071/T072 with T088 advanced, \textbf{not paid}). Ch 105. See \textbf{A stick keeps what a slate would tax} and \textbf{Stone}.

\textbf{The Afterdrop.} The worsening before recovery in a rekindled or rewarmed vessel. The ordinary cause is a graft settling; midwives call it the second chill. On Stone 12, Y.H. 813 (Day 371), at the year’s first Hearth Drawing, a child three days out of a thin return grew worse on the third day — grey fingertips finer than the collector’s and nearer the bone, red at the hairline, more colour in the face than it had had in the morning — and the room called it a graft settling. The boy read the afterdrop waiting on the far side of a warming that must be slow and from the outside, never rubbed and never set too near the fire, and the pink face as the surface still cold and not the core; he could not speak, reach or warm, and the room’s women took the colour for the turn. No cause was named and no treatment performed (T012, T093/T094/T096 carried). Ch 106.

\textbf{The Ash.} Grey silt that gathers where promises are unkept, in corners and under beds, invisible in daylight and plain by tallow-light. The poor leave it on the Last Day and burn it next morning. On Stone 29, Y.H. 812 a woman at the tubs told a girl beside her that the grey would be left where it lay until the Last Day and burned the morning afterward and called dealt with.
