On the Last Day, Y.H. 813 (Day 394), the grey at the Vail corner and along the skirting board was left where it lay, thickened in the dry cold with the faint sour tang coming up where no broom had gone in two years; a neighbour said it would be burnt in the morning and called it dealt with, and Sella did not say it and did not sweep early. On Ilmen 1 the yard burnt its grey and called it gone. The boy kept the \textbf{called-gone grey} on its own place beside the \textbf{left-in-place ridge} at the Vail corner with a finger between, and made no fourth likeness a cause — a thing called finished is not finished for that, and the Ash’s memory was not spent or explained (T009/T013/T092, T083/T085 advanced, not paid). The clean dark line and the finer grey beside it stayed unswept. Ch 114.

\textbf{Ash-mite.} A small grey mite that lives in the Ash and drinks the thin edge of a sleeper’s measure. Invisible by day; troublesome in poor rooms.

\textbf{Ash-runners.} Criminal smugglers of the Fenmarch who move Warm and sell quiet ash without a Court licence.

\textbf{Ash Rising.} The rising in Low Kiln in Y.H. 668 after ninety children’s warmth was taken for a private account; put down by Assessor-Marshal Pell Varr.

\textbf{Ash-sickness.} The condition of dreaming in another person’s voice after long exposure to an Ash-wraith.

\textbf{Ash-wraith.} A grey shape seen by tallow-light where many have been spent; it follows the Ash ridge from room to room.

\textbf{Ask a well for a house-name and it gives you the weather.} A proverb of the Clay Yard wells, and the epigraph of \emph{What the Well Gave Back}: \emph{Ask a well for a house-name and it gives you the weather. The question goes on toward the bridge; the answer stays in the bucket.} A well answers what is put to it with what it has, which is water and the state of the air; it gives no name, no owner and no figure, and it keeps no record of who asked. On Ilmen 23, Y.H. 814 (Day 417), word came up once at the yard well, from mouth to mouth among the bucket-round with nobody standing under it — a report and not a sighting — that a man with a narrow slate under his arm had asked after a house-name under the Vail roof and been answered with the weather. Nobody saw the asking, no voice carried into the yard, no slate was opened within reach of the basket, no figure came off any slate, no room was entered and no name was spoken; Slate Row was a direction in a mouth and nothing more. The boy took the word apart by the order of its parts — asking, house-name asked after, weather that answered, the half-beat lying in the gap where a name would have stood — and filed the \textbf{asking} on a place of its own beside the second man’s direction down the north bridge road and his narrow slate turned to the sleeve, the first man’s face, the soft-cuffed clerk’s entered figure and the fifth shaping of the well-saying, with a finger between every pair. It is a reaching gathering interest toward the far-off calling of the loan that can hear and the far-off hand that will lay the district’s private keepings together, \textbf{not} that calling, not a second sighting, not a sixth shaping, not a rule and not a door; it was not told again (T102 advanced, not paid, with T080/T090). Ilva drew at the same well with her notched strip in her sleeve and her hand to her sleeve before her eyes to the asker, and she was expressly \textbf{not} the speaker: her wood and the asking stand on separate places with a finger between. See \textbf{A figure goes up the clay road in a locked box; a word comes up from the well and stops on the stone lip}, \textbf{Ask the pot} and \textbf{Three askings do not make a witness}. Ch 122.

\textbf{Ask the arm that carried it.} A reed-cutter’s answer to a girl at the Clay Yard who asked what a bundle held: \emph{Ask the arm that carried it. It’ll tell you.} The arm judges by the weight settling into the forearm and tells what was carried and not what it cost; the cutter lifted the next armful before a second question could be got out. It is the same answer as \textbf{A bundle’s counted in the arm that carries it} in another mouth, filed by the boy on the tray of directions answered with directions. On Reed 7, Y.H. 813 the girl went off with the creel on her hip and no figure went with her. On Reed 13, Y.H. 813 a cutter told a girl with a creel at the Clay Yard to lift her bundle and let her arm tell her what went into it, \emph{and that’s the whole of what it knows}; to a man who asked what the work would want he gave the weather and the river, never a figure. See \textbf{A bundle’s counted in the arm that carries it} and \textbf{A record kept in muscle}. On Reed 16, Y.H. 813 a cutter going down past the racks told a girl with a creel to lift her bundle and let her arm tell her what went into it, \emph{and that’s the whole of what it knows}; to a second question he said \emph{It doesn’t know cost. Ask it how heavy it is}, and went on downriver with another armful. A woman at the racks who asked what the hands would be paid was told the weather and the river and shut two fingers out of a fist as she went. See \textbf{A record kept in muscle}.

On Reed 25, Y.H. 813 the last bundles were judged by the arm that carried them, and a cutter told a girl with a creel to lift her bundle and let her arm tell her what went into it, \emph{and that’s the whole of what it knows}; a man who asked what the hands would be paid was answered with the weather and the river, never a figure. See \textbf{A record kept in muscle}.

\textbf{Ask the pot.} An answer given to a question about cost in the Vail kiln-house of Low Kiln: \emph{Ask the pot what a wet thing costs set down there. The house has said it.} The question is carried away held level, the way a woman carries a full pot, and arrives at a thing that has no answer in it; nothing is priced and nothing is refused. On Reed 4 and Reed 6, Y.H. 813 a woman asking what the reeds would cost now the hands were out of them was sent to the pot with these words, and a man asking what the beds would want was told to ask the beds and the weather. See \textbf{A bundle’s counted in the arm that carries it}.

On Reed 10, Y.H. 813 a neighbour with a wet pot at the Vail kiln-house asked what the loaf row would want before the tend was out; Sella’s hand went toward the clay jar on the wall and came away, and the woman was sent to the pot with these words, carrying the question away level with nothing slopped and nothing given. See \textbf{A bundle’s counted in the arm that carries it}. On Reed 16, Y.H. 813 a neighbour come up from the strips with a wet pot asked what the loaf row would want before the tend was out and was sent to the pot with these words, carrying the question away level and nothing slopped.

On Tallow 2, Y.H. 813 a woman come up from the firing work asked what a firing cost set down in the Vail kiln-house; Sella glanced once at the clay jar, sent her to the pot with \emph{Ask the pot what a wet thing costs set down there. The house has said it}, and the woman carried the unanswered question away level with nothing slopped. At the Weir the same day a woman asking what the hands would be paid for the going down and the coming back was answered with the going down and the coming back and then the river, so that a cost asked as a direction was answered with a direction and left no entry (T077). On Tallow 8, Y.H. 813 a neighbour with wet sleeves at the Vail kiln-house asked what a firing cost set down there; Sella sent her to the pot with \emph{Ask the pot what a wet thing costs set down there. The house has said it}, and the woman carried the unanswered question away level so that nothing slopped. See \textbf{A bundle’s counted in the arm that carries it}. On Tallow 11 and Tallow 12, Y.H. 813 a neighbour with a wet pot at the Vail kiln-house asked what a firing cost set down there; Sella glanced once at the clay jar cold under its glaze, sent her to the pot with \emph{Ask the pot what a wet thing costs set down there. The house has said it}, and the woman carried the unanswered question away level with nothing slopped and no figure given. On Tallow 17 a neighbour with a wet pot asked the same question in the third working week and was sent to the pot with the same words; nothing was priced, nothing was refused and no figure was given. On Tallow 21 a neighbour with a wet pot asked what a firing cost set down in the Vail house; Sella glanced once at the clay jar cold under its glaze, did not touch it, and sent the woman to the pot with \emph{Ask the pot what a wet thing costs set down there. The house has said it}, and the woman carried the unanswered question away level. On Tallow 22 and Tallow 23 the same answer went to neighbours who asked what the kilns would want now the last week was in: \emph{The weather’s set it. Ask the pot. It’s had the heat and kept it. The river’ll take what’s over.} Nothing was priced and nothing was refused in the firing month’s last tend. On Ember 2 and Ember 3, Y.H. 813 (Days 181–182) a neighbour asking what the newly opened firing cost and another asking what the second day’s firing wanted with the kiln newly open were both sent to the pot and the weather; Sella glanced once at the clay jar cold under its glaze without touching it, and each question went away level and arrived nowhere, nothing priced, nothing refused and no entry left (T077, T058/T079). On Ember 5, Y.H. 813 (Day 184) a neighbour come up from the tubs with a wet pot asked what the firing cost now the kiln month’s second week was on; Sella glanced once at the clay jar cold under its glaze, shut her hand half over nothing without touching it, and sent the question to the pot and the weather with \emph{Ask the pot what a wet thing costs set down there. The house has said it}. The woman carried the question away level, nothing slopped, priced, refused or entered (T077, T058/T079).

On Ember 8, Y.H. 813 (Day 187) a neighbour come up from the tubs with a wet pot asked what the firing cost now the kiln month’s middle days were on; Sella glanced once at the clay jar cold under its glaze, shut her hand half over nothing without touching it, and sent her to the pot and the weather with \emph{Ask the pot what a wet thing costs set down there. The house has said it}, and the woman carried the question away level with nothing slopped, priced, refused or entered (T077, T058/T079).

On Ember 11 and Ember 12, Y.H. 813 (Days 190–191), women who asked what the firing would want before the kiln month’s tend was out were sent to the pot and the weather with \emph{Ask the pot what a wet thing costs set down there. The house has said it}, and carried the questions away level with nothing priced, refused or entered. One came up from the drying racks with slip dried pale in the creases of her wrists (T077, T058/T079). Through Ember 13–15, Y.H. 813 (Days 192–194) the answer went out three more times under the Vail roof: to a neighbour with dry scurf of mud on her hem who asked what the firing would want now the account had gone up the road, to a rack-woman with slip dried pale in her wrists who asked what the pots would want before the kiln month was out, to a woman with a wet pot who asked what a wet thing cost set down in the dry heat, and to a man come off the clay road with the morning’s figure still moving in his mouth who asked what the kiln would want now the figure had gone up the road. Each carried the question away level with nothing slopped, priced, refused or entered; the printed one in twelve stood unchallenged and the true subtraction sat in a locked box up the road, out of reach of every hand in the yard (T077, T015/T041/T047). Through Ember 16–18, Y.H. 813 (Days 195–197) the answer went out again under the Vail roof: to a neighbour with dry mud-scurf on her hem who asked what the firing would want now the account had gone up the road, to a rack-woman with slip dried pale in her wrists who asked what the pots would want before the kiln month was out, and to a man come off the clay road who asked what the kiln would want now the figure had gone up the road. Each carried the question away level, nothing slopped, priced, refused or entered; Sella glanced once at the clay jar cold under its glaze without touching it, and the printed one in twelve stood unchallenged with the true subtraction still in the locked box out of reach of every hand in the yard (T077, T058/T079, T015/T041/T047).

Through Ember 19–21, Y.H. 813 (Days 198–200) the answer went out three more times under the Vail roof: to a neighbour with dry mud-scurf on her hem who asked what the firing would want with the second reading a day off, to a rack-woman with slip dried pale in her wrists who asked what the pots would want before the kiln month was out, and to a man come off the clay road who asked what the kiln would want now the figure had gone up twice. Each carried the question away level with nothing slopped, priced, refused or entered; the printed one in twelve stood unchallenged and the true subtraction sat in a locked box up the road (T077, T058/T079).

Through Ember 22–24, Y.H. 813 (Days 201–203) the kiln month’s last tend ran into its third working day with the answer going out as before: to a neighbour with dry mud-scurf on her hem who asked what the firing would want now the last tend was in, to a rack-woman with slip dried pale in her wrists who asked what the pots would want before the month was out, to a man come off the clay road with a number in his fist who asked what the kiln would want now the figure had gone up twice, and to a neighbour with a cost-question at the door. Sella glanced once at the clay jar cold under its glaze without touching it and sent each to the pot and the weather; every question went away level with nothing slopped, priced, refused or entered, and the printed one in twelve stood unchallenged with the true subtraction out of reach in the locked box up the road (T077, T058/T079, T015/T041/T047).

Through Ember 25–27, Y.H. 813 (Days 204–206) the kiln month’s last working week ran on with the answer going out as before: to a neighbour at the door, to a rack woman at the yard well with slip dried pale in her wrists, to a man come off the clay road with a number shut in his fist, and to a neighbour at the door with dry scurf on her hem and a pot against her hip. Each carried the question away level with nothing slopped, priced, refused or entered; the man kept his number in his fist and paid nothing, and the printed one in twelve stood unchallenged with the true subtraction out of reach in the locked box up the road (T077, T058/T079, T015/T041/T047).

Through Ember 28–30, Y.H. 813 (Days 207–209) the kiln month’s last working week ran out with the answer going out as before: to a neighbour with a cost-question at the door, to a rack woman at the yard well with slip dried pale in her wrists, and to a man off the clay road with a number shut in his fist who paid nothing. Each carried the question away level with nothing slopped, priced, refused or entered; the printed one in twelve stood unchallenged and the true subtraction stayed out of reach in the locked box up the road (T077, T058/T079, T015/T041/T047).

Through Grain 1–3, Y.H. 813 (Days 210–212) the answer went out again under the Vail roof as the firing thinned into the ordinary tending of the year: to a neighbour with a cost-question at the door (Days 210 and 212) and to a rack woman with slip dried pale in her wrists and a man who kept a number shut in his fist at the well (Day 211). Each carried the question away level with nothing slopped, priced, refused or entered; the man kept his number in his fist and paid nothing, and the printed one in twelve stood unchallenged with the true subtraction still out of reach in the locked box up the road (T077, T058/T079, T015/T041/T047). There was no market and no Account-day in these three days; Grain 10 (Day 219) is the first.

Through Grain 4–6, Y.H. 813 (Days 213–215) the answer went out through the first working week to a neighbour with a pot in her hands at the threshold (Day 213), to a neighbour at the door and a rack woman with slip dried pale in her wrists and a man with a number shut in his fist at the well (Day 214), and again to a neighbour at the door with a question about the mid-tend work and a rack woman at the well (Day 215). Each carried the question away level with nothing slopped, priced, refused or entered; the man kept his number in his fist and paid nothing, and the printed one in twelve stood unchallenged with the true subtraction out of reach in Berr’s locked box up the road. There was no market and no Account-day in these three days; Grain 10 (Day 219) is the first (T077, T058/T079, T015/T041/T047).

Through Grain 7–9, Y.H. 813 (Days 216–218) the answer went out through the second working week to a neighbour at the door (Days 216 and 218), to a rack woman with slip dried pale in her wrists at the yard well and a man who kept a number shut in his fist (Day 216), and to the rack woman again at the well (Day 217). Each carried the question away level with nothing slopped, priced, refused or entered; the man kept his number in his fist and paid nothing, while the printed one in twelve stood unchallenged and the true subtraction stayed out of reach in Berr’s locked box up the road. There was no market and no Account-day in these three days; Grain 10 (Day 219) is the first (T077, T058/T079, T015/T041/T047).

Through Grain 10–12, Y.H. 813 (Days 219–221) the answer went out under the Vail roof on the two tending days after Grain’s first market: to a neighbour at the door and to a rack woman at the yard well with slip dried pale in her wrists, and in the morning of the market day to a man who brought a number in his fist to the reading rail. Each carried the question away level with nothing slopped, priced, refused or entered; Sella glanced once at the clay jar cold under its glaze, shut her hand half over nothing without a touch, and sent each to the pot and the weather. The printed one in twelve stood unchallenged and the true subtraction stayed out of reach in Berr’s locked box up the road (T077, T058/T079, T015/T041/T047).

Through Grain 13–15, Y.H. 813 (Days 222–224) the answer went out under the Vail roof with the harvest: to a neighbour at the door with a pot against her hip, to a rack woman with slip dried pale in her wrists at the yard well and to a neighbour who asked what the reaping would take now that hands were back in the strips. Each question was carried away level with nothing slopped, priced, refused or entered; a man off the clay road brought a number up out of a fist toward the well, looked at it and put it back in his sleeve, so the figure arrived nowhere. The printed one in twelve stood unchallenged and the true subtraction stayed out of reach in Berr’s locked box up the road (T077, T058/T079, T015/T041/T047).

Through Grain 19–21, Y.H. 813 (Days 228–230) the answer went out under the Vail roof now that the grain was dressed and covered: to a neighbour at the door with a pot hitched against her hip, to a woman at the threshold asking what the storing would take now the grain was under wool, and to a rack woman with slip dried pale in her wrists at the yard well. Sella did not turn from the coals; each went away level with nothing priced, refused or entered. A man come down the clay road stood at the well with a number brought up out of a fist toward the water, looked at it as a man looks at a thing he has not decided to keep, and put it back into his sleeve so the figure arrived nowhere and was entered against nothing. The dressed grain lay covered near the hearth with no figure over it, read over on Grain 20 by a number that did not know what it cost; the printed one in twelve stood unchallenged and the true subtraction stayed out of reach in Berr’s locked box up the road (T077, T058/T079, T015/T041/T047). Ch 59.

Through Grain 22–24, Y.H. 813 (Days 231–233) the answer went out under the Vail roof now that the grain was dressed and stored: to a neighbour at the threshold on each of the three mornings who asked what the storing would take, and on the afternoon of Grain 23 to the ownerless voice that asked over the boards which row the pot went quiet on. Sella did not turn from the fire; she sent the cost-questions to the pot and the weather with \emph{Ask the pot... The weather knows the rest}, and the ownerless question was answered with the weather first and the price of barley after it, the voice going off up the terrace with the row standing where it stood. A man come down the clay road brought a number up out of a fist toward the well, looked at it and put it back into his sleeve, so the figure arrived nowhere and no row, witness, cause or figure was entered. The dressed grain was turned for damp, spread thin and gathered back under the fold, counted in glances and handfuls and by the carrying arm’s weight that knows weight and not cost, given no figure and entered on no slate; the printed one in twelve stood unchallenged and the true subtraction stayed out of reach in Berr’s locked box up the road (T077, T058/T079, T015/T041/T047, T101 advanced and unpaid). Ch 60.

Through Smoke 2 and Smoke 3, Y.H. 813 (Days 241–242) the answer went out twice more under the Vail roof: a neighbour at the threshold with a pot asked what the storing would take and another what the keeping would take now the grain was under wool, and each was sent to the pot and the weather with \emph{Ask the pot... The weather knows the rest}, going away level with nothing slopped, priced, refused or entered (T077, T058/T079). No cost-question came on Smoke 1, the morning of the opening; a man come down the clay road with a number in his fist toward the yard well looked at it and put it back into his sleeve, so the figure arrived nowhere and was entered by nobody (T015/T041/T047 held).

Through Smoke 10–12, Y.H. 813 (Days 249–251) the answer went out under the Vail roof on all three mornings: to a neighbour at the threshold who asked what the storing or the keeping would take now the dressed grain was under wool, and Sella glanced once at the clay jar cold under its glaze, shut her hand half over nothing and sent each question to the pot and the weather with nothing priced, refused or entered (T077, T058/T079). On Smoke 11 a woman of the firing work at the yard well, Ilva, answered a question about the cost of the firings with her hand still in her sleeve: \emph{Ask the pot what it cost. I keep the count, not the account}; no figure came off her strip and the ninth record-first hand stayed nine (T080 held). At the Cross on Smoke 10 the figure read over the basket was still not the figure paid and the space between the figure read over the covered grain and its cost had no signature. Ch 66.

Through Smoke 13–15, Y.H. 813 (Days 252–254) the answer went out under the Vail roof on all three mornings: to a neighbour at the threshold who asked what the keeping or the storing would take now the dressed grain was under wool, and Sella glanced once at the clay jar cold under its glaze, shut her hand half over nothing and sent each question to the pot and the weather with nothing priced, refused or entered (T077, T058/T079). At the yard well on Smoke 13 Ilva answered a question about the firings with her hand in her sleeve: \emph{I keep the count, not the account}; no figure came off her strip and the ninth record-first hand stayed nine (T080 held). At the Cross on Smoke 10 the figure read over the basket was still not the figure paid, and the space between the figure read over the covered grain and its cost had no signature. Ch 67.

Through Smoke 16–18, Y.H. 813 (Days 255–257) the answer went out under the Vail roof on all three mornings: to a neighbour at the threshold who asked what the keeping or the storing would take now that the dressed grain was under wool, and Sella glanced once at the clay jar cold under its glaze, shut her hand half over nothing and sent the question to the pot and the weather with nothing priced, refused or entered (T077, T058/T079). On Smoke 16 the grain was turned under wool for damp, spread thin, gathered by the handful and set flat; on Smoke 17 it was gathered in by the handful for the last time before Smoke’s second reading, covered under wool and set away from the hearth on the cool stone at the rack end with no figure; on Smoke 18 it was turned once under the wool and drawn back smooth, with no fifth gathering (T077 advanced, unpaid). At the yard well on Smoke 16 Ilva answered a question about the firings with her hand in her sleeve: \emph{Ask the pot what it cost. I keep the count, not the account}; no figure came off her strip and the ninth record-first hand stayed nine (T080 held). The figure that will be read over the covered grain on Smoke 20 will not know what it cost, and the space between the two stays unsigned. Ch 68.

Through Smoke 19–21, Y.H. 813 (Days 258–260) the answer went out under the Vail roof on the mornings of the 19th and 21st: to a neighbour at the threshold with a pot who asked what the keeping or the storing would take now that the dressed grain was under wool, and Sella glanced once at the clay jar cold under its glaze, shut her hand half over nothing and sent the question to the pot and the weather with nothing priced, refused or entered (T077, T058/T079). On Smoke 19 the grain was lifted at a corner for damp and laid back with no figure; on Smoke 20 the district’s arithmetic changed a second time up the road and was read over the covered grain by a number that did not know its cost; on Smoke 21 the grain was turned under the wool for damp and laid back, still with no figure. At the yard well on Smoke 19 Ilva answered a question about the firings with her hand in her sleeve and her strip unread: \emph{Ask the pot what it cost. I keep the count, not the account} (T080 held at nine). Ch 69.

Through Frost 19–21, Y.H. 813 (Days 288–290) the answer went out under the Vail roof on all three mornings: to a neighbour at the threshold who asked what the keeping or the storing would take now the dressed grain lay covered under wool, and Sella glanced once at the clay jar cold under its glaze, shut her hand half over nothing without touching it, turned the coals with the back of a broken pot and sent the question to the pot and the weather with nothing priced, refused or entered (T077, T058/T079). On Frost 20 the second arithmetic went up the road in Berr’s locked box and was read over the covered grain by a figure that did not know what it cost; the space between the figure and its price stayed unsigned, and nothing of the reading was brought under the roof as lesson, figure, mending or payment. Ilva was offstage on all three days and no figure came to her well, the notches staying in wood (T080 held at nine). Ch 79.

On Frost 26, with the month nearly out, Ilva at the yard well answered a neighbour with a pot who asked what the firings had taken: \emph{Ask the pot what it cost. I keep the count, not the account.} An open slate lay on the stone lip with the writing toward its owner and nobody reading it aloud; her hand went toward her sleeve and stayed there, the strip not taken out, read, copied, counted or joined to the slate, and no figure came off the wood. The boy filed the order of her reaching as the ninth record-first hand with no tenth, the slate’s nearness kept as an absence (T080 advanced, not paid). Offstage on Frost 25 and 27. Ch 81. On Bone 1, Y.H. 813 (Day 300), a woman with a pot at her hip asked a hunter come down from Cold Acre what the carrying cost of the hare across his shoulders was, and he told her the weather and went off toward the north gate road, so the month’s hunting entered as a direction and not an account (T077 advanced, not paid). On Bone 2 (Day 301) Ilva of the firing work answered a question about the firings with her hand toward her sleeve and the notched strip unread: \emph{Ask the pot what it cost. I keep the count, not the account}; no figure came off the wood and the ninth hand stayed nine (T080 advanced, not paid). Ch 83. Through Bone 4–6, Y.H. 813 (Days 303–305) the answer went out under the Vail roof to neighbours asking what the repairs and the keeping would take, and on Bone 6 Ilva at the yard well answered \emph{Ask the pot what it cost. I keep the count, not the account} with her strip unread and her ninth hand nine; nothing was priced, refused or entered, and no figure from the fifth burned-slate telling, the mended pot or the called weather reached either place (T077, T080 advanced, not paid). Ch 84. Through Bone 7–9, Y.H. 813 (Days 306–308) the answer went out under the Vail roof to neighbours asking what the repairs and the hunting would take, and Sella told the coals it was the thaw and \emph{The house will keep it}, turned them with the back of a broken pot and sent each question to the pot and the weather with nothing priced, refused or entered; a man carrying a hare toward the north gate road answered a woman’s question about the month’s cost with the weather, and at the well on Bone 7 Ilva answered \emph{Ask the pot what it cost. I keep the count, not the account} with her strip unread and her ninth hand nine (T077, T058/T079, T080 advanced, not paid). Ch 85. Through Ash 16–18, Y.H. 813 (Days 345–347) the answer went out under the Vail roof to neighbours asking what the keeping and the month’s repairs would take: Sella glanced once at the clay jar cold under lead glaze with the hand half over nothing, turned the coals with the back of a broken pot and sent each question to the pot and the weather with nothing priced, refused or entered; the Cold Acre hare’s carrying was answered with the weather and the cracked jar in its rope sling with a pot that said nothing, so the month’s hunts and repairs stayed directions and left no entry (T077, T058/T079). At the yard well on Ash 17 Ilva answered a woman waiting her turn with \emph{Ask the pot what it cost. I keep the count, not the account}, her hand to sleeve before eyes to asker and mouth after both, the strip unread and the ninth hand nine (T080 held, not paid). Ch 98.

On Ilmen 10, Y.H. 814 (Day 404), the FIRST Account-day and market of the new year, Berr Clay came up short off the clay road with the red wool cord of his office folded square under his coat and the sweetish green of tasted lead glaze at one mouth-corner, under the hot clay of him the smell of nothing at all. He wiped his thumb twice before touching nothing, held a narrow slate unopened to his forearm, passed a finger over the figure through his sleeve and read \emph{One in twelve, as the notice says} low into the goers-by, sending it twice over the basket, once for the moot and once for the households that came late; he called the levy and denied it with \emph{your house}, never \emph{I}, said something low to the block about kindness being entered with no anger and no triumph, sent a number from a shut fist to a slate at the watch and went off up the road with the box locked and the year’s first true subtraction inside, believing he had done a kindness. The district’s arithmetic began again and cannot be undone; the twelve arithmetics of Y.H. 813 stand behind one unsigned figure and this reading is the first of a fresh count and \textbf{not a thirteenth} — one reading is one and not an account, a reset is not a signing, no signature stands on the space, the figure read is still not the figure paid and no doctrine comes out of one. The key went up in a coat pocket that never comes back down and the boy has no key; twelve old findings were not laid across the new figure to make a row come out even, for paper is not a payer, and Berr’s low saying about kindness went on a place of its own. Sella set the basket in the moot-post’s finger’s width of shade where no slate lay, stood half a pace off through the reading and the bell and carried him home at the going of the light saying nothing. Hessa carried the slate up the road before noon with the writing to her sleeve and answered the question put and not the one behind it; the bell went four, four and a gap with nobody crossing himself; the soft-cuffed clerk stayed set at the landing, and the green at the pot board and the shape at the market’s edge stayed sightings with no eighth of either. The dressed grain lay covered under wool at the rack end and was read over by a figure that did not know what it cost; Ilmen 20 (Day 414), the month’s second Account-day, stood ten mornings beyond the close and was not brought. Ch 117.

\textbf{A clean slate is not a clean account.} A saying of the Cross, told on the first market of Ilmen, and the epigraph of \emph{The First Figure of the Year}: \emph{A clean slate is not a clean account. One figure read twice is one figure; the grain under the wool has no voice to answer it.} The first clause refuses the notion that a new count wipes the old one clean: a reset supplies no payer, no signature stands on the space and twelve old findings are not laid across a new figure to make a row come out even, for paper is not a payer. The second is the figure going twice over the basket on Ilmen 10, Y.H. 814 (Day 404), once for the moot and once for the households that came late — reading does not turn one into two. The third is the dressed grain turned under wool with no figure or handful, which the printed figure read that morning did not know the cost of; the space between the figure and its price has no signature. See \textbf{Account-day}, \textbf{Leave the crack showing. If it’s worth mending, mend it twice} and \textbf{What is read aloud is not what is paid}. Ch 117.

\textbf{Ask the road.} A runner’s answer on the clay road between Sill and Greybank, given by Hessa Rale when a woman by the path on Ash 6, Y.H. 813 (Day 335), asked what she carried: \emph{Ask the road. It knows the way and I know the weight. That’s the whole of what either of us knows.} She answers the question put and not the one behind it, as Ilva answers \emph{Ask the pot what it cost. I keep the count, not the account} at the well and Sella sends a cost-question to the pot and the weather; the road knows the distance and the shoulder knows the load, and neither knows the figure written on the slate. No figure came off the slate and the writing stayed turned toward her sleeve, still unread, her eighth record-first hand eight with no tenth (T080 advanced, not paid). Ch 94. See \textbf{Ask the pot} and \textbf{A stick keeps what a slate would tax}.

\textbf{Ask the weather (the hunter’s answer).} An answer given to a question about the price of carrying: \emph{Ask the weather. It carried the snow. It can carry the price.} A man come down from Cold Acre with a hare across his shoulders said it at the Clay Yard well on Stone 1, Y.H. 813, and went off toward the clay road with the hare unweighed and nobody opening a slate. It is the same grammar as \textbf{Ask the pot} and \textbf{Ask the road} — a question asked as a direction and answered with a direction, so that no figure is priced, refused or entered — but it belongs to the carrying arm and the weather rather than to a house’s hearth or a runner’s road. The boy filed it with the directions answered with directions, not as a hearing, a seventh or a payment (T077 advanced, not paid). Ch 103. See \textbf{A bundle’s counted in the arm that carries it}.

\textbf{Assessor.} An officer of the Warm Court who decides what a life was worth and how much of its measure may be kept back.

\section*{B}

\textbf{The bell at the Cross.} A bell struck at market morning and afternoon, longer than a church bell; nobody crosses himself at it. The boy counts four strokes, four, and a place where the fifth should be. No one in Sill explains what it is for. On Seed 10, Y.H. 813, the second Account-day of Seed, it went four, four and a gap over the market while Berr Clay read one in twelve twice over the basket, and nobody crossed himself; the heard bell stayed in its own place beside the told bell of the Long Night. The phrase \emph{the bell’s fourth stroke had been missing} in one paragraph of that day is a slip: the missing stroke is the fifth.

On Reed 10, Y.H. 813, the first Account-day of Reed, it went four, four and a gap at the reading block with nobody crossing himself; the heard bell stayed in its own place beside the told bell of the Long Night and was not added to the hearings of the full note. On Reed 20, Y.H. 813, the second Account-day of Reed, it went four, four and a gap over the reading block with nobody crossing himself, the heard bell kept beside the told bell and counted among neither the hearings of the full note nor the six stoppings of the near-saying. On Reed 30, Y.H. 813, the third Account-day and the last market of Reed, it went four, four and a gap over the square with nobody crossing himself, the heard bell kept beside the told bell and counted among neither the hearings nor the nine stoppings of the near-saying. On Tallow 20, Y.H. 813, the second Account-day of the firing month, it went four, four and a gap over the reading block with nobody crossing himself, the heard bell kept beside the told bell and its missing fifth not laid across the kiln’s missing pull or the boards’ knot. On Tallow 30, Y.H. 813, the third Account-day and last market, it went four, four and a gap over the square with nobody crossing himself, the heard bell kept beside the told and counted among neither the hearings of the full note nor the nine stoppings of the near-saying.

On Ember 10, Y.H. 813, the first Account-day of the kiln month, it went four, four and a gap over the square with nobody crossing himself, the heard bell kept beside the told bell and counted among neither the hearings of the full note nor the nine stoppings of the near-saying (T078).

On Ember 20, Y.H. 813, the second Account-day of the kiln month, it went four, four and a gap over the square with nobody crossing himself while Berr Clay read the figure twice over the basket; the heard bell stayed beside the told bell and was counted among neither the hearings of the full note nor the nine stoppings of the near-saying (T078).

On Ember 30, Y.H. 813, the third Account-day and last market of the kiln month, it went four, four and a gap over the square with nobody crossing himself while the figure went twice over the basket; the heard bell stayed beside the told bell and was counted among neither the hearings of the full note nor the nine stoppings of the near-saying (T078).

On Grain 10, Y.H. 813 (Day 219), the first Account-day and market of Grain, it went four, four and a gap at the reading block under the moot-post with nobody crossing himself; four was four in the fire under the floor, four in the nails overhead and four in the bell, and the gap stood where a fifth should have stood in each of the three places and rose up in none of them. The heard bell stayed beside the told bell and was counted among neither the hearings of the full note nor the nine stoppings of the near-saying (T078, T061/T082).

On Grain 20, Y.H. 813 (Day 229), the second Account-day and market of Grain, it went four, four and a gap over the reading block under the moot-post with nobody crossing himself, the heard bell kept beside the told bell and counted among neither the hearings of the full note nor the nine stoppings of the near-saying, while Berr Clay read the figure twice over the basket and carried the true subtraction away in the locked box (T078, T061/T082). Ch 59.

On Smoke 10, Y.H. 813 (Day 249), the first Account-day and market of the second firing, it went four, four and a gap over the reading block under the moot-post with nobody crossing himself, the heard bell kept beside the told bell of the Long Night and its gap not made a seventh of the full note; the boy held it through the missing stroke and came down on the next sound in the square, filing the answer as an interval against an absent stroke and not a hearing (T078, T061/T082). Ch 66.

On Smoke 20, Y.H. 813 (Day 259), the second Account-day and market of the second firing, it went four, four and a gap over the reading block under the moot-post with nobody crossing himself, the heard bell kept beside the told bell of the Long Night and its gap not made a seventh of the full note or laid across the fire’s missing fifth; the boy held his inch through the stroke that did not come and came down on the stroke after it, supplying no stroke to fill the gap (T078, T061/T082). Ch 69.

On Smoke 30, Y.H. 813 (Day 269), the third Account-day and last market of the second firing, it went four, four and a gap over the square with nobody crossing himself, the heard bell kept beside the told bell of the Long Night and its gap not made a seventh of the full note or laid across the fire’s missing fifth or the boards’ thumb-width knot; three counts stood in three places and did not become one, for agreeing any two would want a payer and none stood. The boy held his inch through the bell’s missing stroke and came down on the stroke after it, supplying no stroke to agree any three; on the hundred and fourteenth answer the hand carried two of the house’s rhythms across the empty interval and left the bell’s gap in the square with a finger between (T061/T082, T078). Ch 72.

On Frost 10, Y.H. 813 (Day 279), the first Account-day and market of the ninth month, it went four, four and a gap over the reading block under the moot-post with nobody crossing himself, the heard bell kept beside the told bell of the Long Night and its gap not made a seventh of the full note, a fifth of the fire or an agreement with the boards’ thumb-width knot; three counts stood in three places and did not become one, for agreeing any two would want a payer and none stood. On the hundred and thirty-fourth answer the hand set the small intake of the heard bell’s gap beside the hold of one counted breath with a finger between, the heard bell kept beside the told and not agreed with the figure read over the basket (T078, T061/T082). Ch 76.

On Frost 20, Y.H. 813 (Day 289), the second Account-day and market of the month, it went four, four and a gap over the reading block under the moot-post with nobody crossing himself, the heard bell kept beside the told bell of the Long Night and its gap not made a seventh of the full note, a fifth of the fire or an agreement with the boards’ thumb-width knot; three counts stood in three places and did not become one, for agreeing any two would want a payer and none stood. On the hundred and fifty-fourth answer the hand set the heard bell’s gap beside a counted breath from the room whose floor does not touch his, with a finger between, the heard bell kept beside the told and not made to agree with the figure read twice over the basket (T078, T061/T082). Ch 79.

\textbf{The bell gives four, four and a gap. The slate gives the same figure twice.} A saying of the Clay Yard in Low Kiln, said at the reading block on market-day: \emph{The bell gives four, four and a gap. The slate gives the same figure twice. Neither of them has ever told a mother what it cost.} It is the district’s own account of its two exact repetitions — the heard bell of the Cross and the figure read once for the moot and once for the households that came late — and of the price that nobody reads aloud. On Stone 10, Y.H. 813 (Day 369) the tenth arithmetic of the year went twice over a basket holding a child while the bell went four, four and a gap and nobody crossed himself; the figure read was still not the figure paid and the space between had no signature, so the saying bought no lesson and no payer (T015/T041/T047, T078 advanced, not paid). Ch 106. See \textbf{The bell at the Cross}, \textbf{The slate is read twice} and \textbf{What is read aloud is not what is paid}.

\textbf{The basket has heard four figures and holds none of them.} A saying of the Low Kiln bucket-round in the month of Silt, and the epigraph of \emph{The Fourth Figure}: \emph{The basket has heard four figures and holds none of them. The road carries the slate up and comes back without a word on it. A number said four times is four numbers; the cleanest part of the slate is the space where the signature would stand.} The first clause is the fourth reading of the year, given over the basket on Silt 10, Y.H. 814 (Day 434), the month’s first Account-day and market, the figure going twice over the wicker once for the moot and once for the households that came late while nobody looked into it. The second is Berr Clay going off up the clay road with the box locked and Silt’s fourth true subtraction inside, the road carrying the slate up to the reading and coming back without a word on it, the key gone up in a coat pocket that never comes back down. The third is the finding that four readings are four and not one account: the first is not made a thirteenth by the three that follow, the second supplies no signature, the third no doctrine, the fourth no payer, the twelve arithmetics of Y.H. 813 are not laid across the four to make a row come out even, for paper is not a payer, and the figure read is still not the figure paid. The cleanest part of the slate is the unsigned space where a signature would stand; a basket holding a child is not a bank and hears nothing it can pay (T015/T041/T047 advanced, not paid). See \textbf{Account-day}, \textbf{A figure read thrice is three figures and no account}, \textbf{A clean slate is not a clean account} and \textbf{What is read aloud is not what is paid}. Ch 127.

\textbf{Birth-flower.} The branching red mark some infants are born with, shaped like frost on a pane or a burn gone into the skin. Hearth-maids call it a flower, cross two fingers over it and say nothing about the sign. Alda Reed crossed herself over Corin’s on Stone 7, Y.H. 812, and covered the act with the word.

\textbf{Birth-slate.} The flat slate a hearth-maid keeps within reach at a birth, on which the child and the day are entered. In Low Kiln it lies on the bench, and a midwife’s hand goes to it before it goes to the child. A second hand may have written on it before anyone looked at the face.

\textbf{Bone.} The tenth month of the Sarnish year, following Frost, when the hunting and the repairs are directions judged by the arm that carries them and the weather, never figures. Bone 1 fell on Day 300, Y.H. 813, and Bone 10 (Day 309) is the month’s first Account-day and market; Bone came on without a boundary drawn and neither of the district’s two habits of naming the months was corrected. The month’s first firing came on Bone 2 (Day 301): before the basket Sella Vail put her hand to the widow’s mark for one breath, let go, lifted the clay lid with the back of a hand and tipped the carried coal under a broken pot, and the fire took, still answering four low pulls with the silence where the fifth should have stood and its payer unnamed three hundred and one days then three hundred and two. Nobody praised the opening, named what it mended, entered a slate or made a lesson of it, and \textbf{five openings in five months are five and not a rule}; the four behind were not looked at again as signs, payments or menders and no sixth was made due. By Bone 3 (Day 302) the round three hundred had gone over on Bone 1 and been kept as a threshold and not spent, three hundred and two days were told by nobody, and one hundred and eighty honest answers stood on the boy’s sixth place, exact, complete and worth nothing at two inches of air. On Bone 1 a hunter come down from Cold Acre waited at the yard well with a hare across his shoulders; asked what the carrying cost he told the weather and went off toward the north gate road, and the month’s trade entered as a direction and not an account. On Bone 3 the stayed frost went off the well’s north lip while the trough kept its skin and the silt-clouded plate stood out of the path of feet, all called weather and entered nowhere. There was no market, Cross or bell on Bone 1, 2 or 3. Ch 83. Through Bone 10–12, Y.H. 813 (Days 309–311), the month’s first Account-day and market came on the tenth and changed the district’s arithmetic for the month in a way that cannot be changed back; Bone’s first arithmetic went up the clay road in Berr Clay’s locked box behind Frost’s three, making four readings standing behind one printed figure, four readings four and not one account with the figure read still not the figure paid and no signature on the space. The boy kept the finding on a place of its own with no payer under it and did not lay it across the house’s not-doings, the dressed grain covered and unfigured under wool at the rack end, the four held changes on four places or his own kept gaps. The stayed frost had gone off the well’s north lip on Bone 3 while the trough kept its skin and the silt-clouded plate stood out of the path of feet, all called weather and entered nowhere with a finger between every pair and no fourth likeness made a cause. The month’s hunts and repairs stayed directions judged by the carrying arm and the weather, never figures: a hare carried toward the north gate road and a barrow man’s cost-question were answered with the weather and the pot and left no entry. There was no market, Cross or bell on Bone 11 or 12. Ch 86.

Through Bone 13–15, Y.H. 813 (Days 312–314) no market, Cross or bell came into the middle working week. The yard went around its seven walked-around places with a look and a wide step and no number; the month’s hunts and repairs stayed directions judged by the carrying arm and the weather — a Cold Acre hare’s carrying was answered with \emph{Ask the weather. It carried the snow; it can carry the price}, and a barrow man’s question about the mending was sent to the pot, which said nothing — and no figure was entered. The stayed frost was gone off the well’s north lip while the trough kept its skin and the silt-clouded plate stood out of the path of feet, three coverings called weather and entered nowhere. At the well on Bone 14 Ilva kept the month’s firings in wood with her strip unread and answered \emph{Ask the pot what it cost. I keep the count, not the account}, the ninth record-first hand nine with no tenth. The carried fire’s fifth stayed unpaid three hundred and twelve, thirteen and fourteen days with its payer unnamed and Garl’s name unspoken the same number; the burned slate stood at five with a finger between the fifth and the four, the four held changes stayed four on four places, the dressed grain lay covered and unfigured under wool, and the boy’s staying at the inch was one object on its own place and not a habit. The count went to three hundred and fourteen exact with two hundred and four honest answers on the sixth place, each an object worth nothing at two inches of air, and Bone went on without a boundary drawn. Ch 87.

\textbf{The Bowl.} The Sere coming-of-age feast at sixteen, where a young person empties a bowl of warm wine and names a debt they intend to carry.

\textbf{Bought breath.} A person sold for a term, usually a season or a year, to repay a debt. The common form of slavery in the Fenmarch.

\textbf{The Breaking.} The spring flood, when the Ilm comes up over the Fishstairs and takes the low houses; also the Silt thaw itself. The year’s flood of Silt 9–15, Y.H. 813 came up in a thin brown sheet, stood on the Fishstairs and went around both the Vail corner and the burned ridge two doors down, then went off into mud; the district called it weather and then the thaw that was. It is not the great Breaking of later years, when the low houses are taken and the town’s thin place is named.

\textbf{Brine-gull.} A Sallow-coast gull that steals anything warm: a loaf, a warmed stone, a coal not yet out. On Ilmen 16, Y.H. 813 one went off upriver below the north bridge with a coal from somebody’s banked fire that was not yet cold, carrying the warmth out of the fire’s account; no slate in Sill stood one mark the poorer for it.

\textbf{Broken Slates.} A rebel network of Low Kiln, descended from survivors of the Ash Rising, which seeks to destroy the slates and end the levy.

\textbf{A bundle’s counted in the arm that carries it.} A saying of the reed-cutters at the Weir: \emph{A bundle is counted in the arm that carries it. The hands that cut it are counted in nothing at all.} On Reed 1, Y.H. 813 a reed-cutter told a woman at the racks that a bundle was counted in the arm that brought it, and when she asked about the hands that cut it he went past her with another armful and let the question go down the yard unanswered --- not refused, only never put into words that would stay put long enough to be entered. A day’s cutting was a direction downriver and a coming-back at dusk; nobody set a figure on a bundle standing in the mud. On Reed 4 the cutter said it again in the yard at Low Kiln, wiping his palms down his thighs; a woman at the racks asked \emph{And the hands that cut it?} and he went past with another armful and let the question lie where it fell, not refused and never entered. See \textbf{The hands go in by the look} and \textbf{The reed-cutter’s cord}.

On Reed 25, Y.H. 813 the saying was heard again over the last bundles of the reed month: the arm that carries a bundle knows what went into it and that is the whole of what it knows, while the hands that cut it are counted in nothing at all; a man who asked what those hands would be paid was given the weather and the river. The boy filed the exchange on the tray of directions answered with directions and entered nothing. On Tallow 13, Y.H. 813 the reed work was finished and had become a direction counted in the carrying arm, which keeps the weight and not the cost; a cost asked as a direction was answered with the river and the weather and left no entry (T077, T071/T072). On Tallow 18 the finished reeds were only a memory in the carrying arm, which kept the weight and not the cost, and a cost asked as a direction was answered with the river and the weather and left no entry. See \textbf{Ask the arm that carried it} and \textbf{A record kept in muscle}.

\textbf{Burned slate (a direction from Slate Row).} A word that goes around the yard of Low Kiln as a direction and not as a visit: \emph{a slate has burned in the night}, spoken over the boards on the same breath as the price of barley and the weather, with no owner named, no room, no hand at the flame and no reason. It is not a body, not a slate brought near the basket, not a cause and not a hearing, and nobody in the yard turns it into one. On Ember 26, Y.H. 813 (Day 205) it came over the boards a first time and on Ember 29–30 a second; on Grain 6, Y.H. 813 (Day 215) it came a third and on Grain 9 (Day 218) a fourth, each arrival going nowhere and deepening the claim of the Broken Slates on Jorra Vail without a fact anybody can carry into a chart. A fourth voice going around the boards is not a fourth witness to one fire, for a witness stands somewhere and can be asked; the voice stood a quarter league off in Slate Row and went on to the price of barley. A fourth telling of the burned slate is \textbf{not} a third telling of the counting room shut in the war: the two Greybank tellings of that room stay at two (see \textbf{Closed counting room}), and no slate burned under any roof and no new fire was lit at the kiln mouth on the morning of the fourth telling. Jorra grows quieter whenever it goes around and the household straightens around the quiet without an order; \emph{he’s not Vail} stays sealed and the promise of the boy’s name to the men who burn slates stays ungiven (T035/T031/T065/T095 advanced, not paid). No fifth telling came through Grain 10–12, Y.H. 813 (Days 219–221); the fourth telling from Grain 9 stayed a direction arrived nowhere, held with a hand between it and the three shapings of the pot saying, and still not a third telling of the counting room shut in the war (T035/T031/T065/T095 held, not paid). Through Grain 19–21, Y.H. 813 (Days 228–230) the word stood at four tellings and no fifth came; it came over the boards from Slate Row and arrived nowhere, still not a third telling of the counting room shut in the war, with Jorra growing quieter whenever it went around and the household straightening around the quiet without an order. On Grain 21 a different voice, with no owner, room, hand at the kiln or cause, asked which row the pot went quiet on; that question is a thing of its own and not a fifth telling of the slate (T101 planted, T035/T031/T065/T095 held). A saying of the Clay Yard told over the boards in Bone gathers the whole keeping: \emph{A slate burns on Slate Row and the boards carry it over the yard before the price of barley and after the weather; nobody stands under the voice to be asked.} On Bone 5, Y.H. 813 (Day 304) an ownerless voice come up from Slate Row on the same breath as the barley price and the weather reported that a slate had burned again; no owner stood under it, no room, no hand at the flame, no reason and no witness. The boy filed it as the \textbf{fifth telling of the burned slate} with a finger between it and the four (Ember 25, the telling between, Grain 5 and Grain 8), still not a third telling of the counting room shut in the war, which stands at two, and not a hearing, seventh, stopping, payment, cause, confession, joining, rule or witness. Five are five and not a rule and no sixth was laid beside it; the seed waits on the far-off calling-in of Jorra’s promise to the men who burn slates, not a confession and not a payment (T035/T031/T065/T095 advanced, not paid). Ch 84. The fifth telling went through Bone’s first reading on Bone 10 untouched — a word on the same breath as the price of barley and the weather, with no owner standing under it, no room, no hand at the flame and no reason — and the reading changed the district’s arithmetic for the month and did not touch the word. No sixth voice came up over the boards, no witness stood, no hand was named at any flame and no payer was put beneath it; the claim went on gathering interest against Jorra’s promise, which he neither paid nor refused. Ch 86. On Ash 17, Y.H. 813 (Day 346), the word came over the boards again from the direction of Slate Row, spoken over the boards and not into the basket, and gave a word about a room shut with the damper closed and a slate burned over a man nobody named. It was a direction and not a visit: no room named, no hand at any flame, no figure, no date standing and nobody standing in any doorway to be asked. The weather answered first and the price of barley after it and the voice went off up the terrace. The boy filed it on a place of its own beside the Ash 5 joining with a finger between, a further shaping of that joining and an advancement of the finding that a place wants a witness — expressly not a sixth telling of the burned slate, which stays at five with a finger between the fifth and the four, not a third telling of the shut room at two, not a sixth asking of the row at five, not a fifth shaping of the well-saying at four, not a hearing, a seventh, a cause, a confession, a witness, a reader, a name or a payment, with no payer standing (T035/T031/T065/T095 and T101 advanced and \textbf{not paid}). Jorra grew quieter when the direction went around and the household straightened around the quiet without an order; the promise stayed neither given nor withdrawn. See \textbf{Broken Slates}, \textbf{Closed counting room}, \textbf{Slate Row} and \textbf{Which row did the pot go quiet on?} Ch 98.

\textbf{C}

\textbf{The carried fire (the year’s fire).} The new fire taken into every house on Kindling: a coal under ash comes up the yard in a clay dish, each hearth touches its own flame to it and passes it on, and the last house keeps what is left. Through Stone 10–12, Y.H. 813 (Days 369–371) it still lay under blind ash and the back of a broken pot, answering four low pulls with the silence where the fifth should have stood, its payer unnamed 369, 370 and 371 days; Sella told it the thaw and turned the coals with the broken pot’s back at both ends of every day, and neither the tenth arithmetic at the Cross nor the Hearth Drawing two doors down supplied the missing pull, named a payer or made a lesson of the gap (T088, T058/T079 advanced, not paid). Ch 106. In Low Kiln nobody says where the flame was first lit or what it cost, and the Vail house keeps it banked under ash and never answers a question about its payer. On Ilmen 16, Y.H. 813 a brine-gull carried off one of its coals, not yet cold, upriver; one warmth less went out of the house’s account and was missed in no account, and the fire went on taking its breath in fours and a gap. Through Ilmen 19–25, Y.H. 813 it still lay under blind ash and the back of a broken pot, warming the boards by degrees and missing one breath in every four; the coal the gull took was entered in no slate and missed in no account. Through Bone 4–6, Y.H. 813 (Days 303–305) it still lay banked under a broken pot, warming the boards by degrees and answering four low pulls with the silence where the fifth should stand, its payer unnamed three hundred and three, four and five days; no fifth pull was supplied, no payer named and no lesson made of the mended pot with its crack showing or of five openings in five months (T088, T058/T079). Ch 84. Through Bone 10–12, Y.H. 813 (Days 309–311) the carried fire gave four low pulls and the silence where the fifth should stand on every morning and going of the light, its payer unnamed three hundred and nine, ten and eleven days; nobody lifted the floor and nobody supplied the pull. The river through the finger’s-width door went water over water and put no number to itself, and the boards overhead kept four nails, four and a thumb-width knot: three counts in three places that do not become one, for agreeing any two would want a payer put under both and none stood. The fire’s gap was not filled by the bell’s gap in the square or by any of the six hand-movings filed on the sixth place, and the count went to three hundred and eleven exact with one hundred and ninety-eight honest answers, each exact, complete and worth nothing at two inches of air (T088, T061/T082, T078). Ch 86. Through Ash 7–9, Y.H. 813 (Days 336–338) it still lay banked under a broken pot, warming the boards by degrees and answering four low pulls with the silence where the fifth should have stood, its payer unnamed three hundred and thirty-six, thirty-seven and thirty-eight days; the fire kept four and a gap before the basket at both ends of every day, the river through the finger’s-width door went water over water and put no number to itself, and the boards overhead kept four nails, four and a thumb-width knot, three counts in three places that do not become one, for agreeing any two would want a payer put under both and none stood. Its gap was not filled by the bell’s gap, the held breath at the cracked wire on Ash 9 or any of the two hundred and fifty-two honest answers on the sixth place (T088, T061/T082, T078, T009/T013/T092 advanced, not paid). Ch 95. On Kindling, Y.H. 813 (Day 390), the year’s fire came up the Clay Yard in a clay dish from hearth to hearth before first light; each house said it had kept the flame and nobody said where it was first lit or what it cost, and the coal entered under the back of a broken pot while the fire under the Vail floor kept four low pulls with the fifth unpaid and its payer unnamed three hundred and ninety, ninety-one and ninety-two days (T088 advanced, \textbf{not paid}). The collector who took the year’s first measure that morning went away believing he keeps the world alive by taking what is already going; that belief, not anger, is what will one day be remembered against him. Ch 113.

Through Silt 2–8, Y.H. 813 it still lay under blind ash and the back of a broken pot, warming the boards by degrees and missing one breath in every four, its payer unnamed; the coal a brine-gull took on Ilmen 16 was twenty-two days gone and entered in no slate. Through Silt 9–15 it still lay under blind ash and the back of a broken pot at four, four and a gap, its payer unnamed; the coal the gull took was twenty-nine days gone and entered in no slate. Through Silt 16–18 it still lay at four, four and a gap under blind ash and the back of a broken pot, warming the boards by degrees, its payer unnamed; the door stood a finger’s width open and the river’s note came through the gap, kept apart from the fire’s four-four-and-a-gap as it had been for seventy-seven days. Through Silt 19–25, Y.H. 813 it still lay under blind ash and the back of a broken pot, warming the boards by degrees and missing one breath in every four, its payer unnamed; the mud of the lean week went around the two lines in the corner and the fire’s gap came up through the floor while the river’s note came through the finger’s-width-open door, the two sounds kept in two places. Through Silt 26–30 and Seed 1 it still lay under blind ash and the back of a broken pot at four, four and a gap, warming the boards by degrees; its payer had gone unnamed for ninety days and the coal the brine-gull took upriver was entered in no slate and missed in none. Through Seed 2–4 it still lay under blind ash and the back of a broken pot, missing one breath in every four, its payer unnamed for ninety-three days; Sella told it the thaw each day and turned the coals with the back of a broken pot. Through Seed 5–11 it still lay under blind ash and the back of a broken pot, missing one breath in every four and warming the boards by degrees, its payer unnamed for a hundred days; Sella told it the thaw each day, turned the coals with the back of a broken pot and touched no widow’s mark, because a shelf, a strip, a basket, a well, a market, a door and a bed are not openings. The river’s low note came through the finger’s-width-open door and the fire’s gap came up through the floor, in two separate places as for a hundred days. Through Seed 2–4 it still lay under blind ash and the back of a broken pot, missing one breath in every four, its payer unnamed for ninety-three days; through Seed 5–11 it was unnamed for a hundred days; and through Seed 12–14, Y.H. 813 it still lay under blind ash and the back of a broken pot, warming the boards by degrees and missing one breath in every four, its payer unnamed for a hundred and three days. Sella told it the thaw each day, turned the coals with the back of a broken pot, and touched no widow’s mark, because a shelf, a strip, a basket and a bed are not openings. Through Seed 15–17, Y.H. 813 it still lay under blind ash and the back of a broken pot at four, four and a gap, warming the boards by degrees, its payer unnamed for a hundred and six days; Sella told it the thaw each day and turned the coals with the back of a broken pot, and the fire answered four low pulls and the silence where the fifth should have been. Through Seed 18–20 it still lay under blind ash and the back of a broken pot at four, four and a gap, its payer unnamed for a hundred and nine days; Sella told it the thaw each day, turned the coals with the back of a broken pot and stood a moment at the fire counting something under her breath, joined to no opening. Through Seed 21–23, Y.H. 813 it still lay under blind ash and the back of a broken pot at four, four and a gap, warming the boards by degrees, its payer unnamed for a hundred and twelve days; Sella told it the thaw each day, turned the coals with the back of a broken pot and fed them, and the fire answered four low pulls and the silence where the fifth should have been. Through Seed 24–26 it still lay under blind ash and the back of a broken pot at four, four and a gap, its payer unnamed for a hundred and fifteen days; Sella told it the thaw, turned the coals with the back of a broken pot, fed them and said \emph{The house will keep it} where another woman would say \emph{I}, and the fire gave back four low pulls and the silence where the fifth should have been while the river’s note came through the finger’s-width-open door and the two counts did not meet. Through Seed 27–30 it still lay under blind ash and the back of a broken pot at four, four and a gap, its payer unnamed for a hundred and nineteen days; on all four days Sella told it the thaw, turned the coals with the back of a broken pot and said \emph{The house will keep it} where another woman would say \emph{I}, and at the going of the light on Seed 30 the fire answered four low pulls and the silence where the fifth should have been while the river’s note came through the finger’s-width-open door and the two counts did not meet.

Through Reed 1–3, Y.H. 813 it still lay under blind ash and the back of a broken pot at four, four and a gap, warming the boards by degrees, its payer unnamed for a hundred and twenty-two days; Sella told it the thaw each day, turned the coals with the back of a broken pot and said \emph{The house will keep it} where another woman would say \emph{I}, and the fire answered four low pulls and the silence where the fifth should have been. The river’s note came through the finger’s-width-open door and the fire’s gap through the floor under blind ash, the boards overhead keeping four nails, four, and a fifth that was a knot the width of a thumb: three counts in three places that did not become one. The kiln breathed in fours behind the wall while the fire missed its fifth under the floor and the river’s note came through the finger’s-width door: three counts in three places, and none became one. Through Ember 1–3, Y.H. 813 (Days 180–182) it still lay under blind ash and the back of a broken pot at four low pulls and the silence where the fifth should have been, its payer unnamed for a hundred and eighty, a hundred and eighty-one and a hundred and eighty-two days. On the morning of Ember 1 Sella put her hand to the widow’s mark before the first firing of the kiln month, held it one breath, lifted the clay lid and tipped the carried coal under the back of a broken pot; the fire took with its fifth still missing and no payer named, nobody praising the opening and nobody seeing what it mended. At the going of each light she told it the thaw, turned the coals with the back of a broken pot, said \emph{The house will keep it} where another woman would say \emph{I}, counted under her breath toward no opening and set the pot handle two inches beyond the reaching hand, and did not touch the mark again at a shelf, a well, a rack, a road, a basket, an afternoon or a dusk. The kiln breathed in fours behind the wall, the fire missed its fifth under the floor and the river’s note came through the finger’s-width door: three counts in three places, and none became one. Through Ember 4–6, Y.H. 813 (Days 183–185) it still lay under blind ash and the back of a broken pot, answering four low pulls and the silence where the fifth should have been, its payer unnamed for a hundred and eighty-three, a hundred and eighty-four and a hundred and eighty-five days. She did not touch the widow’s mark at a shelf, a well, a rack, a road, a basket, an afternoon or a dusk, because the one opening was before the kiln on Ember 1 and the hand goes to the mark at no other hour. The kiln breathed in fours behind the wall, the fire missed its fifth under the floor and the river’s note came through the finger’s-width door: three counts in three places that did not become one.

On the third and last Account-day of Ember the district’s arithmetic changed for the third time and the true subtraction went up the clay road in a locked box, answering nothing for the man carried out on Day 188 (T077); in the small hours of the last day the boy’s hand went up an inch toward the river’s note and came down at once against the fold — a miss under the conditions of the Day 206 holding, filed on a sixth place, not a hearing, seventh, stopping, payment, held change, key, power or rule (T061/T082). Ember went out without a boundary drawn and neither of the district’s two month-names was corrected.

Through Grain 1–3, Y.H. 813 (Days 210–212) it still lay under blind ash and the back of a broken pot, answering four low pulls and the silence where the fifth should have been, its payer unnamed for two hundred and ten, eleven and twelve days. Through the finger’s-width door the river kept its note of water over water and overhead the boards kept four nails, four and a thumb-width knot: three counts in three places that do not become one (T088, T061/T082, T058/T079). Through the finger’s-width door the river kept its note of water over water and overhead the boards kept four nails, four and a thumb-width knot: three counts in three places that do not become one (T088, T061/T082, T058/T079). On the last of the three nights the boy’s hand went up an inch toward that note and, with Sella gone to her own bed and the two rooms not touching, held through the small intake and the hold of one of the breaths she counts at her fire, coming down on the letting go (T061/T082). There was no market and no Account-day in these three days; Grain 10 (Day 219) is the first.

Through the finger’s-width door the river kept its note of water over water and overhead the boards kept four nails, four and a thumb-width knot: three counts in three places that do not become one, for agreeing them would want a payer and none stands to any (T088, T061/T082, T058/T079). In the small hours of Day 221, with no breathing number anywhere in the house, the boy’s hand went up an inch toward the note and was taken through the small intake, the hold and the letting go of one of the breaths she counts at her fire in the room that does not touch his, kept through the little silence after her count had ended and brought down on the river’s next low note — a two-rhythm coordination remembered, not a change made again, filed on its sixth place with no payer named (T061/T082). The seventh green at the pot board stayed a colour and the seventh shape at the market’s edge stayed a shape, on places that do not touch. Ch 56.

Through Grain 13–15, Y.H. 813 (Days 222–224) it still lay under blind ash and the back of a broken pot at four low pulls and the silence where the fifth should have been, its payer unnamed for two hundred and twenty-two, twenty-three and twenty-four days. Sella came to the fire before the basket on all three days, told it the thaw, turned the coals with the back of a broken pot, said \emph{The house will keep it} where another woman would say \emph{I}, moved her lips along a row with two unnamed gaps and gave nobody a figure, kept her finger on top of the shelf’s front edge so the charcoal stayed unread, set the pot handle two inches beyond the reaching hand with a half-beat at the setting and did not look toward the bed, and did not touch the widow’s mark, touched once before the kiln on Ember 1 and at no hour since — no opening in forty-two, forty-three and forty-four days. The year’s first cut grain lay covered near the hearth with no figure, and the river’s note through the finger’s-width door and the boards’ four nails, four and a thumb-width knot kept the three counts in three places that did not become one (T088, T061/T082, T058/T079). In the small hours of Day 224 the boy’s hand went up an inch toward that note and was taken through the small intake, the hold and the letting go of one of the breaths Sella counts at her fire in the room that does not touch his, kept through the little silence after her count had ended and brought down on the river’s next low note — a two-rhythm coordination remembered, filed on its sixth place with no payer named and not a change made again (T061/T082). There was no market and no Account-day; Grain 20 (Day 229) is the second.

Through Grain 19–21, Y.H. 813 (Days 228–230) it still lay under blind ash and the back of a broken pot at four low pulls and the silence where the fifth should have been, its payer unnamed for two hundred and twenty-eight, twenty-nine and thirty days. Sella came to the fire before the basket on all three days, told it the thaw, turned the coals with the back of a broken pot, said \emph{The house will keep it} where another woman would say \emph{I}, moved her lips along a row with two unnamed gaps and gave nobody a figure, kept her finger on top of the shelf’s front edge so the charcoal stayed unread, set the pot handle two inches beyond the reaching hand with a half-beat at the setting and did not look toward the bed, and did not touch the widow’s mark, touched once before the kiln on Ember 1 and at no hour since — no opening in forty-eight, forty-nine and fifty days. Grain 20 was the second Account-day and market of Grain; the printed one in twelve stood unchallenged and the true subtraction stayed locked in Berr’s box up the road. The dressed grain lay covered near the hearth with no figure over it, and the river’s note through the finger’s-width door and the boards’ four nails, four and a thumb-width knot kept three counts in three places that did not become one (T088, T061/T082, T058/T079). In the small hours of Day 230 the boy’s hand went up an inch toward that note, was carried through the small intake, the hold and the letting go of one of Sella’s breaths in the room that does not touch his, kept through the little silence after her count had ended and brought down on the river’s next low note — two rhythms across a wall, remembered, filed on the sixth place and not a change made again, a hearing, a seventh, a stopping, a payment, a held change, a key, a power or a rule (T061/T082). Ch 59.

Through Smoke 1–3, Y.H. 813 (Days 240–242) it still lay under blind ash and the back of a broken pot at four low pulls and a gap, its payer unnamed for two hundred and forty, forty-one and forty-two days. On the morning of Smoke 1 Sella Vail touched the widow’s mark before the kiln, held it one breath, lifted the clay lid with the back of a hand and tipped the carried coal under the back of a broken pot; the fire took, still answering four low pulls with the silence where the fifth should have been, and nobody saw what it mended. The river’s note through the finger’s-width door and the boards’ four nails, four and a thumb-width knot kept three counts in three places that do not become one, for agreeing them would want a payer and none stands to any (T088, T061/T082, T058/T079). On Smoke 2 and 3 the dressed grain was turned under wool for damp, spread thin and gathered back by the handful, changed in state and given no figure, entered on no slate (T077); a wrong wind off High Kiln on Smoke 3 brought the sweet edge of lead glaze over the boards, touched the fold and went out on the wind that brought it, a direction arrived nowhere and not a second edge paid (T064). In the small hours of Smoke 3 the boy’s sixtieth answer went up an inch toward the river’s low note, through the small intake, the hold and the letting-go of one of Sella’s breaths in the room that does not touch his, kept through the little silence after her count had ended and down on the river’s next low note — two rhythms crossing in the inch, remembered, filed on the sixth place with no payer named and not a change made again (T061/T082).

Through Smoke 10–12, Y.H. 813 (Days 249–251) it still lay under blind ash and the back of a broken pot at four, four and a gap, warming the boards by degrees, its payer unnamed for two hundred and forty-nine, fifty and fifty-one days; Sella told it the thaw on all three mornings, turned the coals with the back of a broken pot, said \emph{The house will keep it} where another woman would say \emph{I}, counted under her breath toward no opening, and at the close the fire stopped at four while the silence where the fifth should have stood stood where it stood.
