On Stone 17 a second pot was turned toward under the Vail roof and gave nothing; the two intervals lie on a separate tray from the hearings, On Stone 22 a vessel carried past the Vail door gave it too far and too muffled to confirm, and on Stone 25 a pot cracked all the way through two paces from the basket and was called a pot gone wrong; both went on the separate tray of intervals, and through Stone 30 the count stands at five from four sources with no sixth. On Ilmen 6, Y.H. 813 a pot set down out of a woman’s shadow answered \emph{nearly full} --- a third sound, neither the flat answer nor a silence --- and was filed as the first earthly answer to the interval first kept on Stone 13; it is not a sixth hearing and there is no Grathic word for nearly. On Ilmen 9, Y.H. 813 the small flat knock came out of a woman lifted from the clay-heavy Slip Brook --- the sixth hearing, and the second that had ever come from a person --- and lay beside the five from four sources without being among them; no seventh came. Through Ilmen 16–18 the count stood at six, five from four sources and one from a person; the clerk’s open slate at the Fishstairs gave nothing and no seventh hearing came. On Ilmen 21, Y.H. 813 a vessel carried past the Vail yard door gave its note too far and too muffled to place and Tarn’s head did not turn, and on Ilmen 23 a second pot set down in the Clay Yard answered \emph{nearly full} with air under the note and a want in it; the boy filed the second answer beside the first as an answer to the interval kept since Stone 13, advanced and not paid. The count still stood at six with no seventh, no hand to tap either pot and no Grathic word for nearly.

Through Days 61–67 the count stood at six hearings --- five from four sources and the sixth out of a person --- beside and never among, with no seventh; a third pot answered \emph{nearly full} on Silt 6 and was filed advanced and not paid beside the answers of Ilmen 6 and Ilmen 23, while three intervals stayed objects and water-over-water was a fifth low thing that was not a hearing at all. Through Silt 9–15 the count stood at six beside and never among, with no seventh; a vessel gave its note past the yard door on the afternoon of Silt 15 and Tarn’s head did not turn, and the boy did not call it a hearing. In the flood the note of the whole district went on underneath the four low sounds as a fifth thing with no word in Grathic. Through Silt 16–18 the count still stood at six beside and never among, with no seventh; a vessel gave its note past the yard door on Silt 16 and a whole vessel did so on Silt 18, and neither Tarn’s head nor the boy’s turned toward either. At the well a foundling turned his head toward a pot a half-beat after the boy’s --- after the knuckle and after the note --- and the boy filed that turning with the intervals as a thing that came after the knock and was not a hearing. Through Silt 26–30 and Seed 1 the count held at six hearings --- five from vessels and the sixth out of a person --- beside and never among with no seventh; a vessel gave its note past the door on Silt 27 and again on Seed 1 and neither Tarn nor the boy turned toward it or named the sound, and the foundling’s head turned a half-beat late at the market’s edge on Silt 30, which was not a hearing either. Through Seed 2–4 the six hearings stayed six beside and never among; a vessel gave its note past the yard door on Days 91 and 92, Tarn’s head did not turn and neither he nor the boy named the sound or called it a seventh hearing. Through Seed 5–11 they stayed six beside and never among, five from four sources and the sixth out of a person, with no seventh; vessels gave their notes past the door on Seed 7 and Seed 9 and neither head turned nor was the sound named. At the market’s edge on Seed 9 a foundling turned his head toward a pot half a beat after the boy’s, after the knuckle and after the note, and stopped and rubbed the green sliver at his throat; the boy filed that delay as a thing that comes after the knock, not a hearing and not a seventh, and kept his own turning beside it without letting the two touch. Three near-full answers stood advanced and not paid, three intervals on another tray, and the river’s note of water going over water was a fifth low thing and not a hearing. Through Seed 2–4 and Seed 5–11 the six hearings stayed six beside and never among, five from four sources and the sixth out of a person, with no seventh, while vessels gave their notes past the door and neither Tarn nor the boy turned toward them or named them. Through Seed 12–14, Y.H. 813 the count still stood at six beside and never among; no seventh came. A woman moving a pot on Seed 12 lifted it a hand’s breadth too high and something came up to the rim of a note and went back down, a near thing kept on the interval tray and added to no seventh, because a thing that comes up to the edge of a sound is not the sound. Through Seed 15–17 the six hearings stayed six beside and never among with no seventh; three near-full answers advanced and not paid, three intervals on another tray, four low things in four places with the river’s note a fifth, and the two tellings of the shut counting room joined to no kiln; no Grathic word for the flat note and no hand to tap any of them. Through Seed 18–20 the six hearings stayed six beside and never among with no seventh, three near-full answers advanced and not paid, three intervals, the word forty unspoken with the readable double turn and the weight of a thumb apart, four low things in four places with the river’s note a fifth, and the two tellings of the shut room joined to no kiln; the heard bell stayed beside the told bell and no seventh hearing came. Through Seed 21–23 the count still stood at six beside and never among with no seventh; three near-full answers stayed advanced and not paid, and Tarn’s broom checking half a beat behind Jorra’s bent finger standing in the damper on Seed 22 was filed on the interval tray as another place where a stroke should have gone on and did not --- not a hearing, not a seventh, and joined to no cause. The word forty stayed unspoken, four low things kept their four places with the river’s note a fifth, and the two tellings of the shut room stayed joined to no kiln. Through Seed 24–26 the six hearings stayed six beside and never among with no seventh; three near-full answers stood advanced and not paid, and the unchecking stroke of Seed 25 — Tarn’s broom going on over the flagstones without the half-check it had made the day before, the stones keeping the place where it had stopped — was filed beside the earlier half-beat on the interval tray as another place where a stroke should have gone on and did not, held and not repeated, not a hearing, not a seventh and joined to no cause. The word forty stayed unspoken with the readable double turn and the weight of a thumb apart, four low things kept their four places with the river’s note a fifth, and the two tellings of the shut room stayed joined to no kiln. Through Seed 27–30 the count stood at six beside and never among, five from four sources and the sixth out of a person, with no seventh; the held unchecking stroke lay beside the earlier half-beat on the interval tray with no cause across them, three near-full answers stayed advanced and not paid, and the word forty stayed unspoken and no sixth sighting of the neat dark hand came.

Through Reed 1–3, Y.H. 813 the count stood at six hearings --- five from four sources and the sixth out of a person --- beside and never among, with no seventh. Three near-full answers stayed advanced and not paid, three intervals stayed objects with the unchecking stroke beside the earlier half-beat and no cause across them, the told bell stayed beside the heard bell, four low things kept their four places with the river’s note a fifth, and the word forty stayed unspoken with the readable double turn and the weight of a thumb apart. At the market’s edge on Reed 2 the foundling’s head went toward a pot half a beat after the boy’s, after the knuckle and after the note, which was not a hearing and came after the sound; no seventh came in the three days. Through Reed 4–6, Y.H. 813 the six hearings stood beside and never among, five from four sources and the sixth out of a person, with \textbf{no seventh}; three near-full answers stayed advanced and not paid, and the three older intervals lay on one tray with the near-saying stopped at the threshold of the word --- four objects and a stopped sentence, an interval and not a payment, not a rule and not a hearing. The told bell sat beside the heard bell in two places that do not touch, and the word forty stayed unspoken with its readable double turn kept without a name. Through Reed 7–9, Y.H. 813 the six hearings stood beside and never among, five from four sources and the sixth out of a person, with \textbf{no seventh}; three near-full answers stayed advanced and not paid, three older intervals lay with the half-beat, the unchecking stroke and the boy’s held breath, and the two stoppings of the near-saying lay on the same tray as objects and not a rule, an interval and not a payment. No sixth sighting of the neat dark hand came.

Through Reed 10–12, Y.H. 813 the count stood at six hearings beside and never among, five from four sources and the sixth out of a person, with \textbf{no seventh}; three near-full answers stayed advanced and not paid, the older intervals lay on their tray with the half-beat, the unchecking stroke and the boy’s held breath, and now \textbf{three} stoppings of the near-saying lay there as objects and not a rule, an interval and not a payment. The boy refused to let three stoppings stand up and call themselves a doctrine. The told bell stayed beside the heard bell, word forty stayed unspoken, and the charcoal under the shelf was a mark on wood and not a sound.

Through Reed 13–15, Y.H. 813 the count stood at six hearings beside and never among, five from four sources and the sixth out of a person, with \textbf{no seventh}. A pot gave its note under the Vail roof on Reed 13 and was left where it sounded and not made into an answer to a question nobody had asked it; the clerk’s slate was a figure he could not read, and the told bell stayed beside the heard bell. The interval tray held the older objects with the half-beat, the unchecking stroke and the held breath, and now \textbf{four} stoppings of the near-saying as objects and not a rule --- four likenesses that must not stand up and call themselves a doctrine. Water over water was a fifth low thing on a place of its own and was not a hearing. Through Reed 16–18, Y.H. 813 the count stood at six hearings beside and never among, five from four sources and the sixth out of a person, with \textbf{no seventh}; three near-full answers stayed advanced and not paid, and the interval tray held the older objects with the half-beat, the unchecking stroke, the held breath and \textbf{five} stoppings of the near-saying as objects and not a rule, an interval and not a payment. Five likenesses must not stand up and call themselves a doctrine, for a doctrine is an account that has found a payer. Through Reed 19–21, Y.H. 813 the count stood at six hearings beside and never among, five from four sources and the sixth out of a person, with \textbf{no seventh}; the wheel and the pots under the Vail roof were notes left where they sounded, the bell was a heard bell beside a told bell, Jorra’s withheld knowledge of a pot’s full note went on the tray of near-full answers, and \textbf{six} stoppings of the near-saying lay on the interval tray as objects and not a rule, intervals and not payments, with no payer named to any of the six. The damper’s double bite was filed joined to no kiln, water over water was a fifth low thing never counted among the full note, and the fifth green was a colour and not a name; see \textbf{Six at the Teeth}. Through Reed 22–24 the count stood at six hearings beside and never among, five from four sources and the sixth out of a person, with \textbf{no seventh}; three near-full answers stayed advanced and not paid, the older intervals lay with the half-beat, the unchecking stroke and the boy’s held breath, and \textbf{seven} stoppings of the near-saying lay on the interval tray as objects and not a rule, intervals and not payments, with no payer named to any of the seven. The boy would not let seven likenesses stand up and call themselves a doctrine; see \textbf{Seven at the Teeth}.

Through Reed 25–27, Y.H. 813 the count stood at six hearings beside and never among, five from four sources and the sixth out of a person, with \textbf{no seventh}; three near-full answers stayed advanced and not paid, the older intervals lay with the half-beat, the unchecking stroke and the boy’s held breath, and now \textbf{eight} stoppings of the near-saying lay on the interval tray as objects and not a rule, intervals and not payments, with no payer named to any of the eight. Eight likenesses must not stand up and call themselves a doctrine; see \textbf{Eight at the Teeth}. The told bell stayed beside the heard bell, the word forty stayed unspoken, the fifth green stayed a colour and not a name, and the charcoal under the shelf stayed a mark on wood and not a sound.

\textbf{The full note.} The full sound a sound vessel gives under the knuckle; a cracked vessel answers flat. The first tool of the clinical ear. On Ember 5 and Ember 6, Y.H. 813 (Days 184–185) a pot set down wrong gave a high thin note before its time, which the woman who set it down did not hear; the boy turned toward it and got no further, and filed it as a danger of the kiln month and not as a fourth near-full answer or a hearing (T077, T061/T082). Jorra knew the full note of a pot three turns before it left his wheel and withheld the knowing from a man come up on a wrong wind who said a pot singing early generally sings itself out early; the knowing went to the near-full tray beside the hearings and never among them, advanced and not paid, and no pot was lost (T035/T031, T061/T082).

Through Ember 7–9, Y.H. 813 (Days 186–188) a rack-worker’s pot gave its high thin note before its time on Day 186 and was filed as a danger of the kiln month, and on Day 188 another pot set down wrong gave its note before its time and then sang itself out early while the woman went on with her hands and made no lesson of it; the pot was swept around and not made an omen, and the High Kiln saying that a pot singing early generally sings itself out early was not made true as a lesson. The boy turned toward the notes and got no further, filing them where a danger goes — not among the hearings, not a seventh and not a fourth near-full answer (T077, T061/T082). Jorra knew the full note of a Vail pot three turns before it left his wheel and withheld the knowing from a man come up on a wrong wind with the sweetish lead edge at one mouth-corner, who said a pot singing before its time generally sings itself out early; the knowing went to the near-full tray beside the hearings and never among them, advanced and not paid, and no pot was lost (T035/T031, T061/T082).

\textbf{Forty.} The number the hearth-maids and the people of the Weir give to the children of Low Kiln taken in the levy in Y.H. 812, kept in knots on grey wool rather than on any slate. It is spoken of as a count and is not explained in the market. Orra Weir tied forty knots in the year of the flower and then a forty-first she could not account for; on Ilmen 15, Y.H. 813 she said the word low into a basket and watched what the child in it would do, and the child could not answer. On Ilmen 16 the boy read the shape of the extra knot without a name for it, and the word was not spoken a second time.

Through Reed 10–12, Y.H. 813 the word was not spoken under the Vail roof or at the Weir; Orra Weir’s forty-first double turn stayed legible and unnamed, her board lay beside Mira’s without touching it, and the reed-cutter’s cord went past along the same boards unread. The number stays in knots on grey wool and in nothing a Court thumb can spell.

Through Reed 13–15, Y.H. 813 the word was still unspoken at the Weir. Orra pulled one knot down with her thumb and gave a date where a figure was asked --- the ninth of Ilmen, the boat of six oars and the man at the stern who never touched them --- and her forty-first double turn, tail tucked and tied left over right with the small weight of a thumb, stayed legible and unnamed; Mira’s second twist stayed twice beneath the grey with neither knot counted and her board beside Orra’s not touching. The reed-cutter’s cord went past unread with one knot tied low in teeth. Four private records stood within reach of the basket and none could be entered. On Reed 18, Y.H. 813 the word was still unspoken at the Weir. Orra pulled one knot down, gave the ninth of Ilmen with the boat of six oars and the man at the stern who never touched them, and kept her forty-first double turn legible and unnamed; Mira’s second twist stayed twice beneath the grey with neither knot counted and her board beside Orra’s not touching; the reed-cutter’s cord went past along the same boards with its knots unread. Three private records stood within a dozen paces of the basket and none could be entered.

Through Reed 26 and 27, Y.H. 813 the word was still unspoken at the Weir. Orra pulled one knot down with her thumb and set it among the others with a small flat knock, gave the ninth of Ilmen with the boat of six oars and the man at the stern who never touched them, and kept her forty-first double turn legible with its name withheld, tail tucked, tied left over right with the small weight of a thumb pressed in; Mira’s second twist stayed twice beneath the grey with neither knot counted and her board beside Orra’s not touching. The reed-cutter’s cord went past along the same boards with its knots unread. Four private records stood within reach of the basket and none could be entered.

\textbf{Frost-bloom.} An ice flower that grows where Warm has recently left; a map of the leak that made it. On Ilmen 18, Y.H. 813 it stood up in white fronds on the stone lip of the Low Kiln yard well where the Warm had lately gone out of the stone; the bucket knocked the heads off it and the sun took the rest by noon, and the yard called it weather. On Ilmen 19 and again on Ilmen 25, Y.H. 813 it wrote itself back onto the same lip in white fronds after the argument over the ice had ended; the rope went over the lip without touching it, and the yard called it weather both times, so that a woman could go home warm without owning the morning. On Smoke 18, Y.H. 813 it wrote white on the lip again and the bucket knocked it grey, and the yard called it weather (T083/T085 carried). Through Frost 7–9, Y.H. 813 (Days 276–278) the white written on the north lip of the well \textbf{stayed} after the sun was up on Frost 8, where on Ilmen 18 it had gone by noon; it held past noon, past the going of the light and onto Frost 9. The well rope stiffened in the hand, the trough beside the well took a skin from edge to edge, and the coals were banked an hour earlier at the going of the light, and the yard called all of it weather and gave nobody a figure. On Frost 9 Sella Vail broke the skin with the back of the broken pot she turns the coals with, lifted a plate of ice clear at the rim and clouded where silt had risen into it, and set it on a flat stone out of the path of feet, telling the weather where to stand. No sign, cause, lesson, mending, figure or payer was made of the staying, and Frost 10 did not pay it (T083/T085 advanced, \textbf{not paid}). The boy read the skinned trough as a vessel with a surface laid over a depth and kept the stayed white, the broken plate and the gone white of Frost 4 on places of its own with a finger between, making no fourth likeness a cause. Through Frost 13–15, Y.H. 813 (Days 282–284) the stayed white on the north lip, the stiffened rope, the skinned trough and the plate of ice standing on its flat stone out of the path of feet were still called weather and entered nowhere; no figure, sign, cause, mending or payer was taken off any of them, and the Frost 10 reading did not pay them (T083/T085 held, not paid). On Frost 14 another woman waiting her turn at the well spoke of the runner who carries Berr Clay’s slate and once carried a figure that named a person she knew, and the saying was kept on a place of its own beside Hessa Rale’s eighth hand with a finger between, not joined to the weather or to Ilva’s strip a pace away (T080 advanced, not paid). Ch 77. Through Bone 1–3, Y.H. 813 (Days 300–302) the white went off the north lip of the well while the yard was looking elsewhere, but the trough kept its skin and the silt-clouded plate of ice stood on its flat stone out of the path of feet; the yard called the three coverings weather and entered none of them, and no fourth likeness was made a cause, no figure taken off them and no payer named (T083/T085 held, not paid). The went-off white was not made a sign of the month or of anything under the Vail roof. Ch 83. See \textbf{Weather}, \textbf{The thaw} and \textbf{The runner carries what she will not read}.

\textbf{G}

\textbf{Glass eel.} An eel of the Ilm and Ferr that stores a little Warm in a sac behind the head and can stop a wader’s ways in the water.

\textbf{The Glaze Cliffs.} Blue-green cliffs on the Vhaleni coast stained by old lead workings, sweet-smelling in the heat.

\textbf{Frost.} The ninth month of the Sarnish year, following Smoke, when the firings thin into ordinary tending and the kiln goes on taking its breath in fours with the fifth missing. Frost 1 fell on Day 270, Y.H. 813, and Frost 10 (Day 279) is the first Account-day and market of the month. It came on without a boundary drawn and neither of the district’s two habits of naming the months was corrected. The month’s first firing came on Frost 2 (Day 271): before the kiln Sella Vail put her hand to the widow’s mark for one breath, let go, lifted the clay lid with the back of a hand and tipped the carried coal under a broken pot, and the fire took, still answering four low pulls with the silence where the fifth should have stood and its payer unnamed. Nobody praised the opening, named what it mended or made a lesson of it, and the next real opening stands in the first firing of a later month, far off and not hoped for. The dressed grain lay covered and unfigured at the rack end, and by Frost 3 one hundred and twenty honest answers stood on the boy’s sixth place, exact, complete and worth nothing at two inches of air. Through Frost 7–9 (Days 276–278) the first working week went out as it came in: the white frost-bloom on the well lip did not go with the sun on Frost 8 as it had gone on Frost 4, but stayed onto Frost 9, the rope stiffened, the trough skinned over and the coals were banked an hour earlier, and on Frost 9 Sella lifted a plate of ice from the trough and stood it out of the path of feet; the yard called all of it weather, no figure was given and nothing was made of it (T083/T085 advanced, not paid). The dressed grain was turned twice under wool and still lay unfigured at the rack end, and by Frost 9 one hundred and thirty-two answers stood on the sixth place, exact, complete and worth nothing at two inches of air. Frost 10 (Day 279) was the month’s first Account-day and market: Berr Clay read \emph{one in twelve, as the notice says} low into the two hundred, called the levy and denied it with \emph{your house}, never \emph{I}, and went off up the clay road with the box locked and the first true subtraction of Frost inside, believing he had done a kindness; the district’s arithmetic changed for the month and cannot be changed back, while the printed figure stood unchallenged, the figure read was still not the figure paid, and the reading answered nothing for the man carried out on Day 188, the hand that went in on Seed 15 or the dressed grain covered under wool at the rack end, which was read over by a number that did not know what it cost. Frost 11 and 12 were ordinary tending days with no market, Cross or bell; the grain was turned for damp with no figure, the stayed frost and the plate of ice were called weather and entered nowhere, and by Frost 12 one hundred and thirty-eight answers stood on the sixth place with the count at two hundred and eighty-one exact, six months and one hundred and one days told by nobody. Frost 20 (Day 289), the second Account-day, stood eight mornings ahead and was not brought early. Through Frost 13–15 (Days 282–284) the second working week was lived as ordinary tending with no market, Cross or bell: the seven places were gone around with a look and no number, the dressed grain was turned under wool for damp and still given no figure, the stayed frost and the plate of ice were called weather and entered nowhere, and the fire’s fifth went unpaid for two hundred and eighty-four days with its payer unnamed. The hand answered six times, the one hundred and thirty-ninth through the one hundred and forty-fourth, the last setting the held interval beside the empty interval with a finger between; one hundred and forty-four honest answers stood on the sixth place, exact, complete and worth nothing at two inches of air. On the afternoon of Frost 14 a woman at the yard well said as a direction arrived nowhere that the runner who carries Berr Clay’s slate once carried a figure that named a person she knew; the boy filed it on a place of its own beside Hessa Rale’s eighth hand with a finger between, a shaping toward the far-off day she must choose whether to read what she has carried, not a confession, not a joining, not a witness and not paid (T080 advanced, not paid). Frost 20 (Day 289) stood five mornings beyond the close and was not brought early. See \textbf{Frost-bloom}, \textbf{The carried fire}, \textbf{The first opening}, \textbf{The hand goes to the mark before the kiln and at no other hour} and \textbf{The runner carries what she will not read}. Ch 77. Through Frost 16–18 (Days 285–287) the third working week went as the second had gone: no market, Cross or bell, seven places gone around with a look and no number, dressed grain turned under wool with a progressively lighter touch and still unfigured, stayed frost and plate of ice called weather, and the fire’s fifth unpaid two hundred and eighty-five through two hundred and eighty-seven days. The hand answered six times, the one hundred and forty-fifth through the one hundred and fiftieth, and one hundred and fifty honest answers stood on the sixth place; the hundred and fiftieth set the held interval beside the empty interval with a finger between and was held as an object, not a doctrine, for a doctrine is an account that has found a payer and none stands. Ilva was glimpsed once at the well on the seventeenth and the Frost 14 saying held with no second shaping. Frost 20 (Day 289) stood two mornings beyond the close and was not brought early. See also \textbf{The stick keeps what the slate cannot ask for}. Ch 78.

Through Frost 19–21, Y.H. 813 (Days 288–290) the fourth working week went as it came in: the yard went around its seven walked-around places with a look and a wide step and no number, the dressed grain was turned beneath the wool with a progressively lighter touch and given no figure, and the stayed frost, skinned trough and plate of ice were still called weather and entered nowhere. Frost 20 (Day 289) was the month’s second Account-day and market: Berr Clay read \emph{one in twelve, as the notice says} twice over the basket, once for the moot and once for the households that came late, called the levy, denied it with \emph{your house}, never \emph{I}, and went off with the box locked and the second true subtraction of Frost inside; the district’s arithmetic changed a second time for the month and the figure read was still not the figure paid. On Frost 19 the well-saying about the runner gained a second shaping from a voice with nobody behind it, filed beside the first with a finger between and not paid. By Frost 21 one hundred and fifty-six honest answers stood on the sixth place, the last setting the held interval beside the empty interval with a finger between and the round threshold refused as a doctrine, for a doctrine is an account that has found a payer and none stands. Through Frost 22–24, Y.H. 813 (Days 291–293) the last working week went as it came in: no market, Cross or bell on any of the three days, the yard going around its seven walked-around places with a look and a wide step and no number, the dressed grain turned beneath the wool with a progressively lighter touch and no figure, and the stayed frost, skinned trough and plate of ice still called weather and entered nowhere. Frost’s first and second arithmetics stayed locked in Berr’s box up the clay road with the figure read still not the figure paid. On Frost 23 the well-saying about the runner took a third shaping from an ownerless voice over the boards and the well-roof, the slate-runner once carrying a name the district spent and not saying whose, filed beside the first two with a finger between every pair and not paid; nobody stood anywhere to be asked, and the boy would not let three shapings stand up as a witness. By Frost 24 one hundred and sixty-two honest answers stood on the sixth place, the hundred and sixty-second setting the held interval beside the empty interval with a finger between and refusing to stand up as a doctrine, for a doctrine is an account that has found a payer and none stands. Frost 30 (Day 299) stands six mornings beyond the close and was not brought early. Ch 80.

\textbf{A going-downriver and a coming-back.} The reed-cutters’ name for a day’s work at the Weir: the bundles go out downriver in the morning and come back at dusk, and a day is measured by how far a man walked to fetch them and how far he walked home. The work is a direction judged by the arm that carries a bundle, and the cost has no place in the telling, because the question is asked as a direction and answered with the weather or the river. On Reed 4, Y.H. 813 the reeds went into the beds as the seed had gone into the strips, green at the broken ends and pale grey at the frost-bitten tips, and nobody set a figure on a bundle standing in the mud. See \textbf{A bundle’s counted in the arm that carries it}.

Through Reed 25–27, Y.H. 813 the reed month went out with the last bundles going downriver in the morning and coming back at dusk in armfuls judged by the arm that carried them; a cutter told a girl with a creel that her arm knew what went into a bundle and that was the whole of it, and a man who asked what the hands would be paid was given the weather and the river. Nobody set a figure on a bundle standing in the mud.

\textbf{Grain.} The seventh month of the Sarnish year, the harvest month in Grath. In Low Kiln the grain is cut in the worked strips east of the town, counted in glances and handfuls and never in a figure, and carried home under a roof where it is set near the hearth and covered with wool; the yard goes around the empty place in the returning line where a hand went in on Seed 15 and did not come out, with a look and a wide step and no number. Grain 10 (Day 219, Y.H. 813) is the first Account-day and market, Grain 20 (Day 229) the second, and Grain 30 (Day 239) the third and last. See \textbf{The field gives back what the fist would not count} and \textbf{The hand that does not come back}.

\textbf{Grath.} The clay country of river towns, kilns and peat in the north-west of the bowl; Corin’s birth country.

\textbf{Grathic.} The common tongue of the bowl: short vowels, hard \emph{k} and \emph{thr}, little inflection, written on slate with chalk.

\textbf{Greybank.} The Court’s granary and factor’s house eighteen leagues downriver of Sill, where the Clay Road ends and the Hearth Road begins.

\textbf{Grey fingers.} The discoloration of a collector’s fingertips after years of drawing Warm; a mark of the trade and, in extreme cases, of exhaustion. On Stone 22, Y.H. 812 a collector fetched for a neighbour two doors down had them the colour of skimmed milk gone off under a cuff soft from washing; the boy filed him on a tray of his own, not joined to the woman at the flare or to the clerk at the Cross.

\textbf{H}

\textbf{Half-beat.} A head turned a breath after the knock rather than before it. On Silt 16, Y.H. 813, at the Low Kiln well, a small foundling in cast-off clothes turned his head toward a pot a half-beat after the boy in the basket did --- after the knuckle came down on the wet stone and after the pot gave its note --- then stopped, rubbed the green lead-glaze sliver at his neck and could not say why he had turned. The boy, who turns toward a pot before anyone taps it, filed the delay as an object on a place of its own: a thing that comes after the knock is a different thing from one that comes before it, and this was neither a hearing nor a seventh. He kept his own turning beside the child’s without letting the two touch. The half-beat is the physical tell held for the day the foundling’s small sales land as a betrayal; the yard took it for a child’s quickness and the warm loaf he took from a man from Slate Row for a kindness, with no slate standing between giver and receiver. On Silt 19, Y.H. 813 the same small foundling was glimpsed once more at the well in cast-offs with the green sliver at his throat: when a pot was set down his head went toward it a half-beat after the boy’s and he rubbed the sliver and could not say why, and no loaf passed and no slate was seen. The delay stayed a thing that comes after the knock, neither a hearing nor a seventh. On Silt 30, Y.H. 813 at the last market of Silt he was glimpsed a second time at the market’s edge, unnamed in the narration, cast-offs worn like a uniform and a gap in his grin; when a pot was set down his head went toward it a half-beat after the boy’s, after the knuckle and after the note, then stopped, and he rubbed the green sliver and could not say why. No loaf passed, no slate was seen and no secret was sold; the boy kept the second delay on a place of its own beside the first and wrote no cause across either. On Seed 9, Y.H. 813, he was glimpsed a third time at the edge of the Fishstairs market, unnamed in the narration, with silt dried pale in the creases of his wrists, a gap in his grin and the green sliver at his throat; when a pot was set down his head went toward it a half-beat after the boy’s, then stopped, and he rubbed the sliver, opened his mouth on the tail of a kiln-hand’s sentence and let nothing out that a slate could take down. No loaf passed, no slate was opened within reach of the basket and no sale was paid. The delay is held for the day the watcher’s small sales land as betrayal. On Seed 19, Y.H. 813, he was glimpsed an unnamed fourth time at the dawn market below the north bridge, cast-offs worn like a uniform, silt dried pale in the creases of his wrists, a gap in his grin and a green sliver at his throat; when a kiln-hand set a pot down near the eel shade his head went toward it a half-beat after the boy’s, after the knuckle and after the note, then stopped, and he rubbed the sliver and opened his mouth on the tail of a sentence without letting anything out that a clerk could take down. No loaf passed, no slate was seen and no sale was paid; the boy set the delay after the knock, not before it, not a hearing and not a seventh, and set the watcher’s turning beside the two tellings of the shelf as a third shape, joining none of them.

On Reed 2, Y.H. 813, at the market’s edge beyond the Cross, the foundling was glimpsed a fifth time, unnamed in the narration, cast-offs worn like a uniform, silt dried pale in the creases of his wrists and a green sliver at his throat. When a kiln-hand set a pot down his head went toward it half a beat after the boy’s, after the knuckle and after the note, then stopped in the middle of the turn; he rubbed the sliver twice and his mouth opened on the tail of the sentence and nothing came out that any clerk could take down. No loaf passed within reach of the basket and no slate was opened within two paces of it. The delay is held for the day it lands as the physical tell of a betrayal, beside the four earlier delays and the Silt 16 loaf on places that do not touch (T033/T034). On Grain 10, Y.H. 813 (Day 219), the first Account-day and market of Grain, the \textbf{seventh} half-turn came at the market’s edge: cast-offs with a man’s shoulders and breeches cut at the knee, silt dried pale in the wrist creases, a gap where a front tooth had been and the green sliver on its string catching the light and going dull; the head went toward a set-down pot a half-beat after the boy’s, after the knuckle and after the note, and stopped in the middle of the turn. No loaf passed, no slate came near the basket and no sale was made, and the boy filed it as a seventh shape on a place of its own beside the six behind it — after the knock and not before it, not a hearing, a seventh of the full note, a cause, a name or a romance, and not joined to the seventh green at the pot board. The sale to the Waiting Room clerk stays years ahead (T033/T034 paid as a sighting only).

\textbf{The hand goes to the mark before the kiln and at no other hour.} A saying of the Vail hearth, told at the first firing of Smoke: \emph{The hand goes to the mark before the kiln and at no other hour. It lifts the lid with the back of a hand and tips the coal, and does not look to see what it mended. The fire takes; the fifth pull is still missing, and nobody says whose.} The mark is a thumb-length of lead-glazed clay worn at Sella Vail’s throat with the Vail kiln scratched into it. On Smoke 1, Y.H. 813 (Day 240), after sixty days of going around shelves, wells, racks, roads and baskets without touching it, she put her hand to it before the kiln mouth, held it one breath, let go, lifted the clay lid with the back of a hand and tipped the carried coal under a broken pot; the fire took, still answering four low pulls with the fifth missing and no payer named. Nobody praised the opening and nobody saw what it mended, and she did not touch the mark again at a shelf, well, rack, road, basket, afternoon or dusk on Smoke 1, 2 or 3. The rule had held exactly before, on Tallow 1 and Ember 1, and holds after: a shelf, a strip, a rack, a basket, a bed and a dusk are not openings. An opening is maintenance on a vessel, not a ceremony, a sign, a lesson or a payment; the hand that does the mending will not name what it mended or who paid for the coal. See \textbf{The widow’s mark}, \textbf{The first opening} and \textbf{The carried fire}.

On Ash 2, Y.H. 813 (Day 331), the dark month’s first firing, Sella Vail went to the kiln mouth and, before any instruction went to the basket and before any word, put her left hand to the widow’s mark at her throat for one breath, let go, lifted the clay lid with the back of a hand and tipped the carried coal under the back of a broken pot. The fire took, still answering four low pulls with the silence where the fifth should have stood, its payer unnamed three hundred and thirty-one days; nobody praised the opening, named what it mended, entered a slate or made a lesson of it, and the five openings behind were not looked at again as signs or payments. Six openings in six months are six and not a rule and no seventh was made due; she did not touch the mark again at shelf, well, rack, road, basket, yard, morning, afternoon, dusk or going of the light on Ash 1, 2 or 3, because the hand goes to the mark before the kiln and at no other hour (T058/T079, T088 advanced, not paid). Ch 93. Through Stone 1–3 the mark hung where it hung and no seventh opening was made due; on Stone 5, Y.H. 813 (Day 364), the deep-winter month’s first firing, Sella Vail went to the kiln mouth and, before any instruction went to the basket and before any word, carried it there and set it level out of the draught where the heat came sideways, put her left hand to the widow’s mark at her throat for one breath, let go, lifted the clay lid with the back of a hand and tipped the carried coal under the back of a broken pot. The fire took, still answering four low pulls with the silence where the fifth should have stood, its payer unnamed three hundred and sixty-four days; nobody praised the opening, named what it mended, entered a slate or made a lesson of it. \textbf{Seven openings in seven months are seven and not a rule and no eighth is made due}; she did not touch the mark again at shelf, well, rack, basket, yard, morning, afternoon, going of the light or bed on Stone 4, 5 or 6, because the hand goes to the mark before the kiln and at no other hour (T058/T079, T088 advanced, not paid). Ch 104. See \textbf{The fire keeps its own count and tells nobody}.

\textbf{The hand that does not come back (the place in the line).} In the harvest count of Low Kiln, the empty place in the returning row which the yard goes around with a look and no number, because a hand that went into the worked strips on Seed 15 did not come out with the rest. On Seed 27, Y.H. 813 the last hands came out of the strips east of Low Kiln with the seed up and worked around, counted in glances and handfuls and never in a figure --- a woman lifting two fingers with chaff in the creases, a man with a barrow shaping the number of backs with his mouth and thinking better of it --- and one place in the line was gone around because the hand that went in on Seed 15 did not come back. No name, cause, accident, body, figure or payment was given for it, and on Seed 30, Account-day, the figure read aloud did not know the hand that did not come back. A saying of the strip-keepers of Low Kiln runs: \emph{You count them going in. You don’t count them coming out. What comes back is a row, and a place the yard goes around.} The boy filed the empty place on a place of its own, exact, complete and worth nothing, and did not lay it beside the shelf’s two gaps or the fold’s one crust and its empty place; it is held for the later day a body is found or a figure is given for what the planting cost (T098). See \textbf{The hands go in by the look} and \textbf{Seed}.

Through Reed 1–3, Y.H. 813, with the planting month behind and the reed work begun, the place in the returning line was still gone around with a look and no number: no name, cause, accident, body, figure or payment, and no figure in any slate knew the hand that had not come back. The boy kept the field’s empty place on a place of its own and did not lay it beside the shelf’s two gaps, the fold’s one crust and its empty place, the reed-cutter’s cord or the word forty; two absences laid together make an account and an account wants a payer (T098 carried, not paid). Through Reed 4–6, Y.H. 813 the place in the returning line was still gone around with a look and a wide step and no number: no name, cause, accident, body, figure or payer. The armfuls of reed passed it going downriver and coming back at dusk, and the boy kept the field’s empty place on a place of its own, laying no likeness across the shelf’s two gaps, the fold’s one crust and its empty place, the reed-cutter’s cord or the word forty (T098 carried, not paid). Through Reed 7–9, Y.H. 813 the place in the returning line was still gone around with a look, a wide step and no number, as wide as a pail of hot water set where a child might knock it; no name, cause, body, figure or payer had come up, and the boy kept the field’s empty place on a place of its own, not joined to the shelf’s two gaps, the fold’s crust and its gap, the reed-cutter’s cord or the word forty (T098 carried, not paid).

Through Reed 13–15, Y.H. 813 the empty place in the returning line was still gone around at the Clay Yard with a look and a wide step and no number, while the reeds came in armfuls judged by the arm that carried them and went downriver and back past that place. No name, cause, accident, body, figure or payer came up, and the boy kept the absence on a place of its own, not joined to the shelf’s two gaps, the fold’s crust, the charcoal under the shelf, the reed-cutter’s cord or the word forty (T098 carried, not paid).

Through Reed 10–12, Y.H. 813 the empty place in the returning line was still gone around with a look and a wide step and no number. On Reed 10 a man come up from the strips stood at the edge of the Account-day reading and the place was gone around with a look; no name, cause, body, figure or payer had come up, and the boy kept it on a place of its own, not laid beside the shelf’s two gaps, the fold’s one crust, the charcoal under the shelf, the reed-cutter’s cord or the word forty (T098 carried, not paid). Through Reed 16–18, Y.H. 813 the place in the returning line was still gone around at the Clay Yard with a look and a wide step and no number while the reeds came downriver and went back past it in armfuls judged by the arm that carried them; no name, cause, body, figure or payer had come up, and the boy kept it on a place of its own, not joined to the shelf’s two gaps, the fold’s crust, the charcoal under the shelf, the reed-cutter’s cord or the word forty (T098 carried, not paid). Through Reed 19–21 the last bundles came into the yard in armfuls judged by the arm that carried them and went past the empty place with a look and a wide step and no number; no name, cause, body, figure or payer came up, and the boy kept the field’s absence on a place of its own, not joined to the shelf’s two gaps, the fold’s one crust and its empty place, the charcoal under the shelf, the reed-cutter’s cord, Mira’s cords, Orra’s knot-string or the word forty (T098 carried, not paid). Through Reed 22–24 the place in the returning line was still gone around at the Clay Yard with a look and a wide step and no number, as the last bundles stood grey in the ruts and went downriver and back past it; no name, cause, accident, body, figure or payer came up, and the boy kept the field’s absence on a place of its own, not joined to the shelf’s two gaps, the fold’s crust and its gap, the charcoal under the shelf, the reed-cutter’s cord, Orra’s knot-string, Mira’s second twist or the word forty (T098 carried, not paid).

Through Reed 25–27, Y.H. 813 the last bundles of reed went downriver and came back at dusk past the empty place in the returning line, which the yard went around with a look and a wide step and no number; no name, cause, accident, body, figure or payer came up, and the boy kept the field’s absence on a place of its own, not joined to the shelf’s two gaps, the fold’s crust and its gap, the charcoal under the shelf, the reed-cutter’s cord, Orra’s knot-string, Mira’s second twist or the word forty (T098 carried, not paid).

Through Grain 13–15, Y.H. 813 (Days 222–224) the harvest came in and the hands came out of the worked strips with the year’s first grain; the yard went around the empty place in the returning line once more with a look and a wide step and no number — no name, cause, accident, body, figure or payment. The boy filed it beside the disappearing hand’s other goings-around and forbade it to stand up with the shelf’s two unnamed gaps, the fold’s one crust and its gap, the pan’s gone round ring and the field’s empty place, for a rule is an account that has found a payer and no payer stood to any (T098 advanced and NOT paid, held for the far-off day a body is found or a figure is given). No third gap came and no fourth likeness stood up to make a cause.

\textbf{The hands go in by the look.} A planting saying of Low Kiln: \emph{The seed goes in by the fist and the hands go in by the look. Ask either what it cost and it will tell you the weather.} On Seed 15, Y.H. 813 the hands the strips had been said to want went into the worked ground east of Low Kiln, counted in glances and handfuls and never in a figure; a woman let seed out of her fist and would not say what it held, and a man with a barrow shaped the number of hands and thought better of it, so that the district’s withholding was done in the planting itself. The season’s figure went from the strip to a man’s teeth and back to the strip and was given to nobody. On Seed 27, Y.H. 813 the hands came out of the strips by the same look and not by a figure, and one hand that had gone in on Seed 15 did not come out with the rest; see \textbf{The hand that does not come back}. See \textbf{Seed}.

\textbf{Handling is not entry.} A finding kept under the Vail roof in Smoke’s last week: \emph{A thing may be handled as closely as a hand can examine it and still enter nothing, and the not-entering is as complete as the examining.} On Smoke 26, Y.H. 813 (Day 265) Sella Vail drew the wool wholly back from the dressed grain and turned it piece by piece in the flat of her hand for damp and rot, setting each piece down where it lay and covering it without a figure. The boy, who reads a wound turned to see the hidden part as a surgeon reads it, kept the finding on a place of its own — not a lesson, a grievance or a doctrine, and not laid across the house’s not-doings or his own kept gaps, for a joining would want a payer and none stood. On Smoke 27 she turned it once with a lighter touch and learned nothing, and he kept the not-learning as a finding with no payer. He drew no likeness between the handled grain and the hand that on the hundred and eighth answer went on past the note it would once have stopped at, and would not let the likeness stand up as a gift (T077, T061/T082 advanced, not paid). See \textbf{Not-doing}, \textbf{A figure read over a covered thing} and \textbf{An inch is a long way when the hand is small}.

\textbf{Hearth.} The great source of the Warm, a chamber of stone beneath the Keel, said to hold what the world had when it was made.

\textbf{The Hearth Drawing.} The first collection of the year, on Stone 12; a collector may draw from the dying and the newly born on the same day. In Y.H. 812 the year’s first measure was taken in a Low Kiln death-house and entered on a slate in the same figure the Cross had read aloud on Account-day; before the day was out a newly born child in the same room grew worse on the third day of a return. In Y.H. 813 (Day 371) the Drawing came two doors down from the Vail kiln-house and was seen only from a basket set at the edge of the light, where the boy could see and not join: a collector with cuff soft from washing and folded back twice, a flat leather satchel and a cold iron tube out of a roll of wool, fingertips grey the colour of skimmed milk gone off, a hand to the slate before his eyes to the bed, and the soft sentence to the slate, \emph{The measure is banked. The account stands. The return is recorded.} The dying neighbour gave under the tube with a small flat knock and was left with a pale round place, not a wound and no blood, and a rekindled child grew worse on the third day while the room called it a graft settling. The collector has a reason — he believes he keeps the world alive by taking what is already going — and that reason is the part that will be remembered against him; no name and no interior are given, and his ordinary untroubled writing hand is filed on a tray of its own, joined to none of the other record-first hands. The flat knock was not made a seventh hearing, and the room’s gap in the figures was set beside the birth room, the Vail kiln-house and the Court’s room with a finger between every pair, joined to none (T061/T082, T080, T081 advanced, not paid). Ch 106.

\textbf{Hearth-fire (Hearth-flame).} The flame kept behind a grating of cold iron in the Weighing Hall; it has never gone out and no priest may touch it.

\textbf{Hearth-maids.} The midwives, collectors’ assistants and keepers of the birth-slates in Grathic villages.

\textbf{Hearth Road.} The merchants’ road from Greybank south-east to the Hearthseat, a hundred and forty leagues.

\textbf{Hearth-tongue.} The Hearth-fire drawn up through the Keel; a procedure by which the Hearthward draw, and the name of the fire in the Weighing Hall.

\textbf{Hearth-wisp.} A small light that gathers where a banked fire has been left and draws warmth from a sleeper.

\textbf{Hearthseat.} The Court’s city on the Keel, built over the Hearth, where the Weighing Hall, the sealed files and fewer than twenty Kept vessels are kept.

\textbf{Hearthward.} The rank of a vessel that can draw from the Hearth itself and is therefore never cold.

\textbf{Held.} The rank of a vessel that can carry more than its natural measure.

\textbf{High Kiln.} The master potters’ quarter on the terrace above Low Kiln, where the glaze is mixed and the lead smell hangs.

\textbf{The Hollow.} A vessel whose head has fallen so low it can no longer draw warmth from food; also a thin-return child with almost no shape in it.

\textbf{Honeyed ice.} The low country’s word for ice going soft from underneath while the top still looks sound; on Ilmen 2, Y.H. 813 a man come up from the Ilm told the yard the ice was honeyed under the mud, and a woman at the well said the water tasted different. The district passes the word around and will not say the word for the thaw itself, which lets a person go home without owning the day. On Ilmen 19 and Ilmen 25, Y.H. 813 the man who had said \emph{honeyed} kept his counsel and the woman who had said the ice would hold said nothing at all, so that the old argument ended with nobody left to carry it.

On Silt 8, Y.H. 813 a man come back from looking said the ice was \emph{honeyed all through, not just at the edge; you could cut it and find it yellow in the middle}, and the dark current showed through the skin of the Ilm in veins; the boy set the saying and the sight on places that did not touch. On Silt 15 the ice that had been honeyed all through was spoken of past tense as the thaw that was.

\textbf{Hot trace.} Warmth that leaves a vessel in an act of giving and stays hot, tangled with an unpaid promise, instead of cooling into the bank.

\textbf{House roll.} A household’s own slate of names and entries, kept close and not shown to the Court’s assessor. In Low Kiln a house that keeps its own account does not need to explain the keeping, only to keep it.

\textbf{House Vail.} The kiln-house of Low Kiln held by the Vail family for four generations; Sella Vail keeps the fire.

\textbf{I}

\textbf{Ice-mouse.} A field mouse of frozen fields whose bite leaves a spreading numb patch, frostbite by another road.

\textbf{The Ilm.} The great silty river of Grath, frozen from Stone into Ilmen, breaking in the Silt flood; it rises in the Rim and drains into the Sallow Sea. On Stone 1, Y.H. 813 (Day 360) it took its winter ice from bank to bank in the afternoon under a sky the yard called weather, and the note under the Vail door went low under a skin; the boy kept the covering on a place of its own beside water over water and made no sign, hearing or payment of it (T083/T085 advanced, not paid). Ch 103. See \textbf{The river takes its skin}.

\textbf{A held interval and an empty interval.} A finding kept under the Vail roof in the first tend of Frost, Y.H. 813: \emph{The fire keeps its fifth where nobody will put a payer, and a breath that ended in the other room leaves a silence after it. Hold the one beside the other with a finger between, and call neither a gift.} Across Frost 1–3 the boy’s hand went up an inch toward the river’s note six times, the hundred and fifteenth through the hundred and twentieth, each an exact and complete coordination and worth nothing at two inches of air. On the last the hand held for the small intake and past the letting-go of a counted breath in the room that does not touch, kept through the little silence after it, and then set the held interval and the empty interval side by side with a finger between and made neither agree with the fifth missing under the floor. A silence kept empty is a finding; a finding filled to make a row come out even is a finding forged. The two intervals are objects on a sixth place beside the held inch, not a reach, a hearing, a seventh, a stopping, a payment, a held change, a key, a power or a rule (T061/T082 advanced, unpaid). Ch 73.

Across Frost 4–6, Y.H. 813 (Days 273–275) the hand is asked six more times and the sixth place holds one hundred and twenty-six answers: the hundred and twenty-first took the small intake of a count from the room whose floor does not touch and came down on the river’s next low note; the hundred and twenty-second came down before that count’s letting-go and left the little silence after it whole; the hundred and twenty-third stayed past a letting-go and through the silence with one house rhythm carried across; the hundred and twenty-fourth held two intakes apart with a finger between, the letting-go between them left where it was; the hundred and twenty-fifth came down while the count was still letting go, a separation made by ending early and not by filling; and the hundred and twenty-sixth set the held interval and the empty interval side by side with a finger between and came down, taking nothing from the two-gapped row, the charcoal or the covered grain. All six are exact, complete and worth nothing at two inches of air. In the same week Sella Vail’s finger went beneath the loaf shelf on Frost 5 and stayed two counted breaths where on Day 166 it had stayed one, and came away unread — a change held on the shelf’s own place, not a fourth likeness made a cause, not a reading, a payment, a gift or a doctrine (T100 advanced, unpaid). Ch 74. See \textbf{An inch is a long way when the hand is small}, \textbf{What is kept in three places does not add up to an account} and \textbf{Not-doing}.

\textbf{An inch is a long way when the hand is small.} A saying of the drying racks in Low Kiln in the kiln month: \emph{An inch is a long way when the hand is small. Ask the pot how far the handle stands; it will tell you the distance and not who set it there.} The pot gives the distance and withholds the payer, which is the district’s whole arithmetic in a pot’s answer. Under the Vail roof on Ember 16–18, Y.H. 813 (Days 195–197), the boy’s hand outside the wool went up an inch toward the river’s note of water over water and was asked to stay: on the first day for one of the breaths Sella counts at her fire, on the second down before the breath was done, on the third morning up and down at once, and in the small hours of the third day up through the whole intake and hold and on into the letting go, down with the breath rather than before it. Three askings, three answers, no progression into a power. The longest holding is a coordination, not a reach, and is filed on a place of its own beside the three held changes, the loft scrape and the pale line — not a hearing, not a seventh, not a stopping, not a payment, not a key and not a rule, with no payer named. Through Ember 22–24, Y.H. 813 (Days 201–203) the hand was asked five ways: down at once on the morning of Day 201, held for the small intake only in the small hours, down before the breath had finished on the morning of Day 202, held through a whole counted breath and down with the breath in the small hours of that day (the old coordination remembered, not a change made again), and held for the small intake only on the morning of Day 203. Then, in the small hours of Day 203, it went up an inch toward the river’s note of water over water, stayed up through the small intake, the hold and the letting go of one of the breaths Sella counts at her fire in the room that does not touch his, \textbf{did not come down with her breath}, kept the small height through the silence after her count had ended, and came down on the river’s next low note — a coordination with a \textbf{second} rhythm, the one through the door, which nobody counts and which was never given to him. It is filed on the sixth place beside the three held changes, the loft scrape and the pale line: not a hearing, not a seventh, not a stopping, not a payment, not a key, not a power and not a rule, with no payer named and nothing stood up out of it to call itself a sign; the river goes on without noticing that an inch rode one of its low notes. He still cannot close the two inches to the pot handle, lift his chin to the crust or speak a number. Through Grain 10–12, Y.H. 813 (Days 219–221) the hand was asked six times and answered as the body answered: down at once and short of a breath on the first day, before the counted breath and then to the river’s own low interval on the second, at once under conditions that had sometimes answered and, in the small hours of the third, through the small intake, the hold and the letting go of one of the breaths Sella counts at her fire, kept through the little silence after her count had ended and down on the river’s next low note. The last was a two-rhythm coordination remembered, not a change made again; all six were filed on the sixth place with nothing laid across them and no payer named, and he still could not close two inches. See \textbf{Ask the pot}, \textbf{The carried fire} and \textbf{A record kept in muscle}.

Through Smoke 1–3, Y.H. 813 (Days 240–242) the hand was asked six times and answered as the body answers: the fifty-fifth down at once under conditions that had sometimes answered, the fifty-sixth held for the small intake only and down before the letting-go, the fifty-seventh down before the counted breath in the other room had finished, the fifty-eighth up an inch toward the low note through the finger’s-width door, held through one of Sella’s counted breaths in the room that does not touch his and down with the breath, the fifty-ninth kept to the river’s own low interval with no count in the house to borrow and down on its next low note, and in the small hours of Smoke 3 the \textbf{sixtieth} up an inch, through the small intake, the hold and the letting-go of one of Sella’s counted breaths, kept through the little silence after her count had ended and brought down on the river’s next low note — two rhythms crossing in the inch and nowhere else, across a wall that does not touch. The sixtieth is remembered, not a change made again; \textbf{sixty} answers stand on the sixth place, each an object and not a power, exact, complete and worth nothing at two inches of air, not a longer reach, miss entered, hearing, seventh, tenth stopping, payment, held change, key, power or rule, with no payer named (T061/T082).

Through Smoke 25–27, Y.H. 813 (Days 264–266) the hand was asked six times more: the \textbf{one hundred and third} held for the small intake only and down on the river’s next note, the \textbf{one hundred and fourth} carrying one rhythm across the little silence after a count in the room that does not touch, the \textbf{one hundred and fifth} held through one whole interval of the river’s own going, the \textbf{one hundred and sixth} laying two rhythms apart with the empty interval between kept whole, the \textbf{one hundred and seventh} held through the small intake and the hold of one of Sella’s counted breaths and down before the letting-go, and in the small hours of Smoke 27 the \textbf{one hundred and eighth} held past the letting-go and past the river’s next low note to the one after it — two of the river’s intervals held with no second house count borrowed and the silence between kept empty on a third place. One hundred and eight honest answers stand on the sixth place, each exact, complete and worth nothing at two inches of air, none a longer reach, hearing, seventh, stopping, payment, held change, key, power or rule; no stroke was supplied to agree any two of the three places (T061/T082 advanced, not paid). Ch 71.

\textbf{K}

\textbf{Keld.} The mountain kingdom of the Rim, living on iron, lead, coal and warm-stone and ruled by the Warden of the Rim.

\textbf{Keld Keep.} The Warden’s fortress city where a man states his measure before his name and the deep survey shaft begins.

\textbf{A kept thing is owed.} A chain of sayings kept under the Vail roof in Reed, Y.H. 813: \emph{A kept thing is owed; a kept word is a debt; and a debt that can hear is a debt that can be called.} On Reed 8, Y.H. 813 Tarn brought the sentence about an ear under that roof being worth more than the debt that holds it a \textbf{second} time to the threshold of the word that would call the loan and stopped there with no figure and no name, drawing the breath he should have spent and not spending it; the boy set the second stopping on the interval tray beside the first as a second interval and not a second payment, and the loan that can hear stayed uncalled. The sayings are the same iron as the damper, the bite that holds and the bite that takes, with no Grathic word for both mercies. On Reed 23 the same sentence came a \textbf{seventh} time and stopped at the word, and seven kept words are seven debts still owed; the boy would not let seven likenesses stand up and call themselves a doctrine, for a doctrine is an account that has found a payer and no payer had been named to any of them. See \textbf{Near-saying}, \textbf{Loan that can hear}, \textbf{Seven at the Teeth} and \textbf{Eight at the Teeth}.

On Reed 14, Y.H. 813 the sentence came a \textbf{fourth} time to the word and stopped there with no figure and no name; Tarn drew the breath and did not spend it, and the boy laid the fourth stopping beside the first three as an object and not a rule, refusing to let four likenesses stand up and call themselves a doctrine --- for a doctrine is an account that has found a payer. The loan that can hear was still uncalled and the seventh year had not given.

On Reed 11, Y.H. 813 it came a \textbf{third} time to the threshold of the word that would call the loan, with no figure and no name, and stopped there again; Tarn drew the breath he should have spent and did not spend it, said \emph{Yes, house} to the fire and went on with the broom. Sella, within hearing, gave the end of her instruction to the pot and asked nothing, and Jorra did not ask about the ear while Tarn did not ask about the room. The boy filed the third stopping beside the first two as a third interval and not a third payment, and refused to let three stoppings stand up and call themselves a doctrine. The loan that can hear was still uncalled at the close of Reed 12, the seventh year still held with the knife back on its sill and six counted where the house can check. See \textbf{Near-saying} and \textbf{Loan that can hear}. On Reed 17, Y.H. 813 the sentence came a \textbf{fifth} time to the word that would call the loan and stopped there with no figure and no name; Tarn drew the breath and did not spend it, and the boy laid the fifth stopping beside the first four on the interval tray as an object and not a rule, an interval and not a payment. A thing stopped five times is still a held thing, not a settled one; the loan that can hear was uncalled and the seventh year had not given. On Reed 20 it came a sixth time to the word with no figure and no name, the breath drawn and not spent; the boy filed a sixth stopping beside the first five as an object and not a rule, and would not let six likenesses stand up and call themselves a doctrine, for a doctrine is an account that has found a payer. A thing stopped six times is still held, not paid; see \textbf{Six at the Teeth}.

On Reed 26, Y.H. 813 the sentence came an \textbf{eighth} time to the word and stopped there with no figure and no name; Tarn drew the breath he did not spend, said \emph{Yes, house} and went on with the broom, and the boy laid the eighth stopping beside the first seven as an object and not a rule, refusing to let eight likenesses stand up and call themselves a doctrine, for a doctrine is an account that has found a payer and no payer had been named to any of the eight. Eight kept words are eight debts still owed; see \textbf{Eight at the Teeth}.

\textbf{Kept.} The highest rank in Sarn: a vessel the Court has made effectively unbreakable. Fewer than twenty exist; they are spoken of with pity and no longer feel the cold. Also a term for chattel slaves in Grath.

\textbf{Kiln’s breath.} The invisible poison of a closed kiln house or cellar; it kills in sleep and is called a merciful death by those who have not identified the body. On Ilmen 26, Y.H. 813 a man come downriver from Greybank described at the well a counting room shut in the last war with the damper closed and the men inside dead of the breath; he said it as something that happened eighteen leagues east, and nobody in the yard connected it to the kiln’s own missing fifth breath under their roofs.

Through Silt 2–8, Y.H. 813 the carried fire under the Vail roof still took its breath in fours and a gap, keeping the missing fourth as carefully as the breaths that came. On Silt 25 a second man come downriver from Greybank repeated at the well the saying of a counting room shut during the last war with the damper closed and the men inside dead of the breath, eighteen leagues east; Sella told the fire it was the thaw and nobody joined the story to any kiln in Low Kiln, though the boy filed the second telling beside the first with no cause written across either. On Seed 13, Y.H. 813 a voice at the bucket-round only mentioned a room shut in the war with the damper closed and the men inside dead of the breath, eighteen leagues east; it was a mention, not a third telling, and nobody in Low Kiln joined it to any kiln in the district, though the Vail fire under its own roof still took its breath in fours and a gap and Sella told it the thaw.

\textbf{Kiln-hound.} A feral dog of old kilns whose hot breath carries the kiln’s own poison.

\textbf{Kiln-Masters of Sill.} The craft guild that holds the kilns, the First Firing and the knowledge of the full note in Grath.

\textbf{Knot-string.} A length of grey wool in which a woman keeps her accounts by tying knots instead of writing names, so that an officer cannot read it and a fire cannot take a name from it. Orra Weir of the Weir keeps forty knots and a forty-first she cannot account for; Mira Silt of the Fishstairs keeps two cords, one twisted twice beneath the other, and has never counted the knots on either. A knot in wool has to be looked at by the woman who tied it, and stays where she left it. On Ilmen 16, Y.H. 813 the boy could read the \textbf{shape} of Orra’s forty-first knot --- a double turn with the tail tucked, tied left over right, the small extra weight of a thumb setting it --- but not its name; the word was not spoken again and the cord went back upriver to the Eel House unread. On Ilmen 24, Y.H. 813 Mira Silt showed the second cord twisted twice beneath the grey at the Fishstairs, never carried to Nine Pots or lifted at a door, the knots on neither counted, and her board stood beside Orra’s without touching it; the shape of the extra knot was legible to the boy without its name and the word was not spoken. On Reed 24 Orra pulled one knot down at the lower boards and set it among the others with a small flat knock, her thumb going to the cord again at the end of the sentence where a figure should have stood; Mira’s second twist stayed twice beneath the grey with neither knot counted and her board beside Orra’s and not touching, and the reed-cutter’s cord went past along the same boards with its knots unread. Three private records stood within a dozen paces of the basket and none could be entered, and the word forty was not spoken.

On Silt 2, Y.H. 813 Mira again showed the second cord twisted twice beneath the grey when a figure was spoken at the Fishstairs, never carried to Nine Pots or lifted at a door, the knots on neither counted; her board lay beside Orra’s knot-string and did not touch it. On Silt 13 Mira again showed the second cord twisted twice beneath the grey when a buyer named a figure, never carried to Nine Pots or lifted at a door, the knots uncounted; Orra stood at the flood’s edge with her board and her cord and got no answer, and the word was not spoken. On Silt 17 she showed it again when a buyer said \emph{two marks the pair and two short}, with neither knot counted and the knot for the thin child upriver untouched; her board lay beside Orra’s knot-string and did not touch it, and the word was not spoken. On Silt 20 and Silt 24, Y.H. 813 she again showed the second cord twisted twice beneath the grey when a figure was named at the Fishstairs, never carried to Nine Pots or lifted at a door, neither knot counted and the thin child’s knot untouched; her board lay beside Orra’s knot-string and did not touch it. On Silt 29 she showed it again when a buyer named a figure, answering a question about the run with her own answer and moving eel-bones while deciding whether to lie; the second cord was never carried upriver to Nine Pots or lifted at a door, neither knot was counted by any thumb but her own and the knot for the thin child upriver was not touched; her board lay beside Orra’s knot-string and did not touch it. On Seed 8, Y.H. 813, she showed the second cord twisted twice beneath the grey when a buyer named a figure, never carried upriver to Nine Pots or lifted at a door, neither knot counted and the knot for the thin child upriver untouched; her board lay beside Orra’s knot-string and did not touch it. Orra watched from where she watched and got no answer, and the word forty was not spoken. On Seed 14, Y.H. 813 Mira Silt shifted a creel at the Fishstairs and showed the second cord twisted twice beneath the grey, never carried upriver to Nine Pots or lifted at a door, neither knot counted and the knot for the thin child upriver untouched; her board lay beside Orra Weir’s knot-string and did not touch it, and Orra watched from where she watched and got no answer. On Seed 17 she answered a question about the run with her own answer, moved eel-bones while deciding whether to lie, and when a buyer named a figure put her thumb under her apron to the grey cord and showed the second twisted twice beneath it with neither knot counted, her board beside Orra’s and not touching, the thin child’s knot untouched; Orra watched and got no answer. On Seed 19, Y.H. 813, at the end of the fish-trade shade she answered a question about the run with her own answer, moved eel-bones while deciding whether to lie, and when a buyer in a coat with the river in its hem named a figure her thumb went under her apron to the grey cord and stayed longer than the figure required, showing the second twisted twice beneath it, never carried to Nine Pots or lifted at a door, neither knot counted and the thin child’s knot untouched; her board lay beside Orra Weir’s knot-string and did not touch it, and Orra stood where she stood and got no answer and the word forty was unspoken. On Seed 23, Y.H. 813 she worked at the very end of the fish-trade shade with pale slime dried in long grey strokes on her sleeves, silt dried pale in the hollow of her neck and her head held right where her left ear had been; asked whether the run would be thin she answered \emph{Thin? Who’s to say thin? It comes when it comes. Ask the river}, moved eel-bones while deciding whether to lie and put one away, and when a buyer in a coat with the river in its hem named a figure her thumb went under her apron and stayed longer than the figure required, showing the second cord twisted twice beneath it with neither knot counted and the thin child’s knot untouched; her board lay beside Orra’s knot-string and did not touch it, and Orra was upriver and present only as the board. On Seed 29, Y.H. 813 she worked the eels at the outer boards with pale slime dried in long grey strokes on her sleeves and silt dried pale in the hollow of her neck, her head held right where the top of her left ear had been and her small smile kept like a door on the latch; a weir woman with salt white at her wrists asked whether the run would be thin now the hands were out of the strips and got Mira’s question and her own answer, \emph{Thin? Who’s to say thin? It comes when it comes. Ask the river}, while the eel-bones moved against her thumb and one was put away. When a buyer named a figure her thumb went under her apron to the grey wool cord and stayed longer than the figure required; shifting a creel showed the second cord twisted twice beneath it, never carried upriver to Nine Pots or lifted at a door, neither knot counted by any thumb but her own and the knot for the thin child upriver untouched; her board lay beside Orra Weir’s knot-string and did not touch it, and she brought no crust and did not look into the basket.

On Seed 26, Y.H. 813 Mira Silt worked the eels at the outer boards of the fish-trade shade with pale slime dried on her sleeves, silt dried pale in the hollow of her neck and her head held a little to the right where the top of her left ear had been; asked whether the run would be thin now that the planting had gone into its last tend she answered her own answer, \emph{Thin? Who’s to say thin? It comes when it comes. Ask the river}, moved eel-bones against her thumb while deciding whether to lie and put one away, and said something low about the boat that came up on the flood and nothing about the hands in the strips. When a buyer named a figure her thumb went under her apron to the grey cord and stayed longer than the figure required; shifting a creel showed the second cord twisted twice beneath it, never carried upriver to Nine Pots or lifted at a door, neither knot counted by any thumb but her own and the knot for the thin child upriver untouched. Her board lay beside Orra Weir’s knot-string and did not touch it; Orra was upriver and present only as the board, the cord lying where a cord lies when a woman has gone away from it and left it where it was.

Through Reed 1–3, Y.H. 813 a third way of keeping a count went past the boy on the plank walk at the Weir: a reed-cutter’s grey cord with knots at arm’s length and one tied low by teeth and thumb, carried and not counted and not joined to Mira’s second twist, Orra’s knot-string, Alda’s six pages in the little tin or the pewter tin above the abandoned bed. A knot in wool or reed-fibre still has to be looked at by the woman or man who tied it, and the Court can spell none of them. On Reed 6, Y.H. 813 Mira again shifted a creel at the outer boards of the Weir and showed the second cord twisted twice beneath the grey, never carried upriver to Nine Pots or lifted at a door, neither knot counted by any thumb but her own and the knot for the thin child upriver untouched; Orra at the lower boards pulled one knot down with her thumb, gave the ninth of Ilmen where a levy figure was asked and kept the shape of her last knot legible without its name, the word forty unspoken. The reed-cutter’s grey cord went past inside a man’s coat with one knot tied low by teeth and thumb, a third record none of them touched. On Reed 18, Y.H. 813 Mira again showed the second cord twisted twice beneath the grey when figures were named at the Weir and below the sill, never carried upriver to Nine Pots or lifted at a door, neither knot counted and the thin child’s knot untouched; her board lay beside Orra’s knot-string and did not touch it. Orra pulled one knot down and gave a date where a figure was asked, and the word forty stayed unspoken. On Reed 21 she showed it again when a buyer named a figure, her thumb under her apron staying longer than the figure required, the second twist twice beneath the grey with neither knot counted, the knot for the thin child upriver untouched and her board beside Orra’s and not touching; Orra at the lower boards pulled one knot down, gave the ninth of Ilmen with the boat of six oars and the man at the stern who never touched them, and kept her forty-first double turn legible with the word forty unspoken.
