The reed-cutter’s grey cord went past on the same boards with its knots unread; three records stood within a dozen paces of the basket and none could be entered.

On Reed 26 and Reed 27, Y.H. 813 Orra pulled one knot down with her thumb at the lower boards and set it among the others with a small flat knock, gave a date where a figure was asked and kept the forty-first double turn legible with its name unspoken, tail tucked, tied left over right with the small weight of a thumb pressed in; her thumb went to the cord again at the end of the sentence and the boy made no cause of it. Mira’s second twist stayed twice beneath the grey with neither knot counted, her board beside Orra’s and not touching, and the reed-cutter’s grey cord went past on the same boards with its knots unread. Three private records stood within a dozen paces of the basket and none could be entered.

\textbf{Kindling.} The first of the Five, when every hearth in Sarn is lit from the Hearth-flame and collectors take the year’s first measure. It has a name and no tend-day, and no market is held in it; the year is not said to turn on it. On Kindling, Y.H. 813 (Day 390), the fire came up the Clay Yard in a clay dish from hearth to hearth before first light from a source nobody under the Vail roof names or prices, and a collector took the year’s first measure in a room two doors down, seen from the basket’s edge of the light and not entered. His hand went to the slate before his eyes went to the bed and he said once to the slate: \emph{The measure is banked. The account stands. The return is recorded.} The writing hand was ordinary with no pause in it and went on a tray of its own, not Marra, not the Court-table clerk, not the Fishstairs clerk, not the Drawing collector and not a tenth hand; the reason that will one day be remembered against him — that he keeps the world alive by taking what is already going — was planted and not spoken (T080/T090 advanced, \textbf{not paid}). Ch 113.

\textbf{L}

\textbf{Last Day.} The fifth and last of the Five Cold Days. Bread is baked, and the grey Ash in the corners is left where it lies to be burned the next morning and called dealt with. It has a name and no tend-day and no market is held in it; the Five end with it. On the Last Day, Y.H. 813 (Day 394), bread was baked under the Vail roof and the grey was left in the corners with a finger between the called-gone and the left-in-place; the widow’s mark was not touched, for baking bread is not an opening and a holy day has not made an eighth due, seven openings in seven months being seven and not a rule. At the kindling Tarn’s term ended with six counted and the seventh at the lip, his hand over blade and sill and away with no breath held at the top of the reach and the loan uncalled; at the wheel-shed Jorra’s bent finger went into the cold damper and came out without the extra holding, and the promise under the shed was neither given nor withdrawn (T058/T079, T036/T076, T062/T035/T031 advanced, not paid). Ch 114.

\textbf{The last market.} The Account-day at the end of Stone, when the year’s stores are counted into the last tend and the Five are spoken of as three days off by a district that has already decided what it will pay. Sill’s last market of Y.H. 812 fell on Stone 30; no market is held during the Five that follow.

\textbf{Lead glaze.} The lead-bearing glaze mixed in the Glaze Room at High Kiln and bought by the kilns below; it gives a pot its shine and leaves a sweetish edge on the breath of those who mix and taste it. The first sign of too much of it is a pale line at the gum, followed by a held hand, fingers the colour of old rope and pewter-pale nails; in Low Kiln the sickness has been quietly unlearned and nobody names it in Grathic. On Ember 8 and 9, Y.H. 813 (Days 187–188) a glaze-room hand come up from High Kiln showed the pale line when he drank at the yard well, and on the next morning was carried out of the Vail kiln and across the yard toward the clay road, alive and breathing, with the sweet-sickness on his breath; the boy read the body as a man with lead in him, exactly and worth nothing at two paces, and no collector was called, no figure given and no payer named to the keeping (T077, T064). See \textbf{The sweet-sickness}.

\textbf{Ledgerhand.} The Court’s script: Grathic grammar with the verbs removed, in a neat upright hand, all in the passive voice.

\textbf{Levy.} The share a Grathic household owes to the account, spoken of in loaves and bits rather than named outright: three of the four loaves baked in Grain go on the levy. People speak around the word, not at the thing it counts.

\textbf{The Listening Stones.} Standing stones in the high Rim against which the Vorr sit for days and come away with numbers.

\textbf{The living patch.} A graft of wall taken from a donor and set over a break, held until the vessel takes.

\textbf{The loaf shelf.} The shelf in a Grathic kiln-house on which a household keeps its days badly: loaves are pushed along the board, a glance goes to the clay jar on the wall, and a space at the end of the row is left with no figure because nobody calls it a number. A saying of the loaf-shelves of Low Kiln: \emph{Two gaps on a shelf are two gaps till a finger lays them together. After that they are an account, and an account wants a name. Keep your finger off the shelf.} On Seed 6, Y.H. 813, another loaf’s worth went off the Vail shelf between dusk and light with no scrape, crumb, print or word, leaving two empty places where one had stood; the boy set them beside the empty place in the fold in two rooms that do not touch and wrote no cause across the space. A further saying of the clay-bound of Low Kiln runs: \emph{A figure kept in a fist costs nothing; a place kept on a shelf costs a loaf a day and nobody counts it.} On Seed 24, Y.H. 813, a man brought a number up out of a fist toward the yard well, looked at it and put it back in his sleeve so the figure arrived nowhere, while a neighbour at this shelf laid the old space at the row’s end and the empty place at the child’s ear under one cause in a single breath; the boy kept the shelf’s two gaps, the fold’s one crust and its empty place, and the neighbour’s saying on three places that do not touch and wrote no cause across any of them. Through Reed 4–6, Y.H. 813 the shelf still kept \textbf{two} unnamed gaps --- the old space at the row’s end and the palm’s breadth that came in on the night of Seed 6 --- and no third; the boy’s one stiff brown-edged crust lay two inches from his ear in a room the shelf does not touch, with its empty place unnamed, and no neighbour named the two gaps in these three days. Sella moved her lips along the row without a figure, glanced once at the clay jar cold under its glaze and did not touch the widow’s mark, because a shelf is not an opening. The witness of T097 was carried and not paid. Another saying is heard at the loaf-shelves of Low Kiln: \emph{Two gaps named in one breath become one hunger. Keep your breath for the pot, and keep the bread where it was put.} On Seed 12, Y.H. 813 a neighbour at the Vail shelf reached past the bare board and named the old space at the row’s end as a thing the planting brought in and the empty place at the boy’s ear as a child’s appetite in one breath, her hand going to the board before her eyes went to the boy; she took her loaf and went with her pot and never saw the two were one absence. The boy filed two tellings on two places and wrote no cause across the space (T097, planted). On Seed 15 a neighbour again said the old place at the end came in with the planting and went off with her pot, never seeing the empty place at his ear; the witness was advanced toward the far-off finger, not paid, and no third gap came. On Seed 18 a second neighbour reached past the bare board for a loaf, her hand going to the old empty place first and opening for the half-beat it takes to find what is not there, and said the gap came in with the planting with a short row to finish it; she went off with her pot without seeing the empty place at the boy’s ear. Two tellings of one absence were held on two places and kept from touching the one crust and its unnamed empty place in the fold; they were advanced, not paid, and no third gap came and no finger in Low Kiln laid them together. On Seed 21, Y.H. 813 a neighbour with a pot again reached past the palm’s breadth of bare board, opened for the half-beat it takes to find what was not there, closed on the hard heel of a loaf beyond and said in one breath that the old space at the row’s end came in with the planting and that this one was the price of a wet thing set down wrong, without seeing the two were one absence or seeing the empty place at the boy’s ear; her hand went to the board before her eyes found him. A \textbf{third} shaping of the held thing now stood beside the two tellings and the watcher’s late turn, advanced and not paid, with no joining, no name and no third gap. On Seed 27, Y.H. 813 a neighbour reached for the place no longer there and called the old space at the row’s end a thing the planting brought in and the new palm’s breadth the price of a wet thing set down wrong, still without seeing they were one absence; on Seed 29 a second neighbour reached past the bare board, her hand going to the empty place before her eyes found the boy, and in one breath called the old space a thing the planting brought in and the empty place at the child’s ear a child’s appetite, without seeing she had joined two rooms. A \textbf{fifth} and a \textbf{sixth} shaping of T097 now stood beside the two tellings, the watcher’s late turn and the earlier causes, advanced and \textbf{not paid}, with no joining, no name and no third gap; Sella moved her lips along a row standing with two gaps and gave nobody a figure, and did not touch the widow’s mark because a shelf is not an opening.

Through Reed 10–12, Y.H. 813 the shelf still kept its two unnamed gaps and the fold its one stiff brown-edged crust two inches from his ear with its empty place unnamed, in rooms that do not touch and with no third; the boy lay at the low angle at which a shelf seen from below becomes a roof and saw the charcoal tally UNDER the board, a keeping put where nobody thinks to look above a row kept badly on top. He read neither the marks nor a meaning into them, and when Sella put a finger beneath the board on Reed 12 without looking he made no cause of the hand’s habit. A neighbour with a wet pot who asked what the row would want before the tend was out was sent to the pot with \emph{The house has said it}, and the widow’s mark was untouched at a shelf, an afternoon and a dusk, because none was an opening. See \textbf{The tally under the shelf}. On Reed 16, Y.H. 813 the shelf still kept its two unnamed gaps while Sella stood with her back to the basket, moved her lips along the row, glanced once at the clay jar cold under its glaze and reached a finger BENEATH the board where the charcoal tally lies, without looking and without a word, and brought it away and did not go back. A hand that goes under without looking either knows the board by heart or has been told not to look, and the reason is left between the two. On Reed 22 and again twice on Reed 24 Sella stood with her back to the basket and reached a finger beneath the board without looking or a word, bringing it away and not going back to the shelf. On Day 141 a neighbour at this shelf reached past the bare board with her hand before her eyes found the boy and named the row’s old space and the empty place at his ear under one appetite in a single breath, a further shaping of T097 held beside the earlier tellings, advanced and not paid, with no third gap, no finger laid and no joining. The shelf kept its two unnamed gaps and the fold one crust and its gap in rooms that do not touch. See \textbf{The tally under the shelf}.

Through Reed 25–27, Y.H. 813 the shelf still kept its \textbf{two} unnamed gaps — the old space at the row’s end and the palm’s breadth that came in on the night of Seed 6 with no scrape, crumb, print or word — and no third, in a room the fold does not touch; the fold kept one stiff brown-edged crust two inches from his ear with its empty place unnamed. On Day 144 Sella set the basket low near the bench leg at the angle at which the underside of a board becomes a roof and, standing with her back to it and moving her lips along the row, glanced once at the clay jar cold under its glaze and reached a finger BENEATH the front edge where the charcoal tally lies, without looking and without a word, and brought it away and did not go back; a hand that goes under without looking either knows the board by heart or has been told not to look, and the reason is left between the two. The marks stayed unread and were not laid beside the two gaps above or the one crust in the other room (T100 carried).

\textbf{Loan that can hear.} A debt whose borrower has an ear for vessels. A loan that can hear is worth more than the debt that holds the borrower and can therefore be called; in the Vail house on Stone 22, Y.H. 812 such a loan was exercised when a flat note passed the door and Tarn’s head turned a degree, and it bought nobody anything. On Seed 28, Y.H. 813 the ear worth more than the debt was still kept silent under the Vail roof: while Jorra’s bent finger stood in the cold damper ahead of Sella’s unfinished sentence Tarn’s stroke went on over the flagstones without the half-check it had made on Seed 22, the stones keeping the place where it had stopped, neither man naming the other’s silence, so that the loan that can hear stayed uncalled and the near-saying that would call it had not been reached. On Reed 5, Y.H. 813 the near-saying was reached for the first time: at the hearth, with the coals banked and the knife set where it could be checked, Tarn told the kindling that an ear under this roof that can hear is worth more than the debt that holds it, and the sentence came up to the word that would call the loan and stood there with no figure and no name. He did not say it, drew the breath that should have gone in and did not spend it, and the boy filed the stopped sentence on the interval tray as an interval and not a payment; the loan stayed uncalled and the seventh year held. On Reed 8, Y.H. 813 the sentence came a second time to the threshold of the word, with no figure and no name, and stopped there again; Tarn drew the breath he should have spent and did not spend it, and the boy filed a second interval and not a second payment. The loan that can hear was still uncalled at the close of Reed 9. On Reed 23, Y.H. 813 the ear worth more than the debt was still kept silent under the Vail roof: at the going of the light Tarn told the kindling \emph{Six counted. The next I don’t count} and brought the sentence a seventh time to the word that would call the loan, stopping there with no figure and no name and drawing the breath he did not spend; the boy filed seven stoppings as intervals and not payments, with no payer named to any, and the loan stayed uncalled with the seventh year one tend from its end and still held. On Reed 29, Y.H. 813 the ear worth more than the debt was still kept silent under the Vail roof: at the going of the light Tarn told the kindling \emph{Six counted. The next I don’t count} and brought the sentence a ninth time to the word that would call the loan, stopping with no figure and no name and drawing the breath he did not spend; the boy filed nine stoppings as intervals and not payments, with no payer named to any, and would not let nine likenesses stand up and call themselves a doctrine. The loan stayed uncalled and the seventh year stood one tend from its end and had not given. See \textbf{Nine at the Teeth}.

See \textbf{Near-saying}, \textbf{A kept thing is owed} and \textbf{Seven at the Teeth}.

On Reed 14, Y.H. 813 the ear worth more than the debt came a fourth time to the word that would call the loan and stopped there with no figure and no name; the drawn breath was not spent, the knife was back where it could be checked, and the boy filed a fourth interval beside the first three as objects and not a rule. The loan stayed uncalled and the seventh year pressed past the middle tend of Reed and still held. See \textbf{Near-saying} and \textbf{A kept thing is owed}. On Reed 17, Y.H. 813 the ear worth more than the debt came a fifth time to the word that would call the loan and stopped with no figure and no name; the drawn breath was not spent, the knife was back where it could be checked, and the boy filed a fifth interval beside the first four as objects and not a rule. The loan stayed uncalled and the seventh year pressed nearer its end and still held. On Reed 20 it came a sixth time to the word with no figure and no name, the breath drawn and not spent; the boy filed a sixth interval beside the first five as objects and not a rule and would not let six likenesses stand up and call themselves a doctrine. The loan stayed uncalled and the seventh year pressed nearer its end; see \textbf{Six at the Teeth}.

On Reed 26, Y.H. 813 the ear worth more than the debt came an \textbf{eighth} time to the word that would call the loan and stopped there with no figure and no name; the breath drawn at the top of the reach was not spent, the knife was back where it could be checked, and the boy filed an eighth interval beside the first seven as objects and not a rule. The loan stayed uncalled and the seventh year stood one tend from its end and had not given; see \textbf{Eight at the Teeth}.

\textbf{The Long Night.} The third of the Five; no fire after dusk, and stories of the Return are told in the dark. It has a name and no tend-day and no market is held in it. On the Long Night, Y.H. 813 (Day 392), no fire was lit after dusk under the Vail roof and the carried fire kept four low pulls under the floor with the fifth unsupplied; the bell was told four, four and a gap from mouth to mouth down the yard as a coal is passed in a dish, each house saying it had kept the count and none saying where the count began, and the told bell stayed in its square beside the bell the boy had heard without becoming a seventh hearing (T078 advanced, not paid). The neighbours told the Return with gaps the shape of vessels’ intervals; one told of a whole return announced in a clean voice for somebody absent and left the name standing empty, and the boy filed that silence on the gap tray beside the told bell’s gap and the silence after Weighing’s name, with no payer standing and no witness, reader or doctrine stood up out of it (T061/T082, T080/T090 advanced, \textbf{not paid}). Ch 113.

\textbf{The Long Sitting.} The Vorr coming-of-age at forty: a season sitting still against a stone, listening.

\textbf{Low Kiln.} The poor quarter of Sill on the south bank below the sill, where the kilns stand and the Ash ridge lies thick.

\textbf{M}

\textbf{The Marsh Mother.} The peat cult of the Fenmarch, which keeps warmth in the mud and gives it back to whoever can reach it.

\textbf{Measure.} The amount of Warm a vessel holds, booked in embers; also the shape of that warmth, which is the self.

\textbf{Mender’s failure.} The name given in the deep accounts to a vessel recalled in an earlier age to solve the same problem, who failed in a particular way.

\textbf{Mire-fever.} A blight of the Fenmarch water that burns and then leaves the victim colder after each cycle.

\textbf{Mud End.} A peat hamlet three leagues downriver of Sill, whose winter peat decides whether anyone stays warm.

\textbf{N}

\textbf{Near-saying.} A sentence brought all the way to the word that would call a loan and stopped there, with no figure under it and no name on it. Under the Vail roof on Reed 5, Y.H. 813 Tarn told the kindling that an ear under this roof that can hear is worth more than the debt that holds it, and went on toward naming whose ear and setting a figure to it; the sentence came up to the word and stood there, and he did not say it. The boy filed it on the interval tray beside a held breath, a half-beat and a stroke that went without its check --- an interval and not a payment, an object among objects and not a rule --- and wrote no cause across any of them. A near-saying kept is a kept thing, and a kept thing is owed; it is the same iron as the damper, the bite that holds and the bite that takes, with no Grathic word for both mercies. On Reed 8, Y.H. 813 it came a \textbf{second} time all the way to the word that would call the loan and stopped again with no figure and no name; the boy filed the second stopping beside the first as a second interval and not a second payment, not a hearing and not a seventh, and the loan stayed uncalled with the seventh year pressed further past its third tend and still held. On Reed 23, Y.H. 813 it came a \textbf{seventh} time, on Reed 23 after Reed 5, 8, 11, 14, 17 and 20, and stopped at the word with no figure and no name; Tarn drew the breath he should have spent and did not spend it, said \emph{Yes, house} to the fire and went on with the broom, and the boy filed the seventh stopping on the interval tray beside six as a seventh interval and not a seventh payment, refusing to let seven likenesses stand up and call themselves a doctrine because a doctrine is an account that has found a payer and no payer had been named to any of the seven. The loan stayed uncalled and the seventh year stood one tend from its end and had not given. See \textbf{Loan that can hear}, \textbf{A kept thing is owed}, \textbf{Seven at the Teeth} and \textbf{Eight at the Teeth}.

On Reed 14, Y.H. 813 it came a \textbf{fourth} time, with the coals banked and the small knife back where it could be checked, and stopped at the word with no figure and no name. Tarn drew the breath that should have gone in at the top of the reach and did not spend it; the boy laid the fourth interval beside the three older ones as an object and not a rule, an interval and not a payment, and would not let four stoppings stand up and call themselves a doctrine. Sella, within hearing, gave the end of her instruction to the pot and asked nothing; Jorra did not ask about the ear and Tarn did not ask about the room, and the two silences stayed unjoined. A thing stopped four times is not settled. See \textbf{Loan that can hear} and \textbf{A kept thing is owed}.

On Reed 11, Y.H. 813 it came a \textbf{third} time all the way to the word that would call the loan and stopped again with no figure and no name; Tarn drew the breath he should have spent and did not spend it, the boy filed the third stopping beside the first two as a third interval and not a third payment, a near-saying kept three times and still not settled, and the loan stayed uncalled with the seventh year held and the knife back on its sill. Three stoppings are three objects on a tray, not a doctrine and not a rule. See \textbf{Loan that can hear} and \textbf{A kept thing is owed}. On Reed 17, Y.H. 813 it came a \textbf{fifth} time, with the coals banked and the small knife back where it could be checked, and stopped at the word with no figure and no name. Tarn drew the breath that should have gone in at the top of the reach and did not spend it; the boy laid the fifth interval beside the four older ones as an object and not a rule, an interval and not a payment, and would not let five stoppings stand up and call themselves a doctrine. Sella, within hearing, gave the end of her instruction to the pot and asked nothing; Jorra did not ask about the ear and Tarn did not ask about the room, and the two silences stayed unjoined. A thing stopped five times is a thing held, not settled. On Reed 20, Y.H. 813 it came a \textbf{sixth} time all the way to the word that would call the loan, with the coals banked and the small knife set back where it could be checked; Tarn drew the breath that should have gone in at the top of the reach and did not spend it, said \emph{Yes, house} to the fire and went on with the broom. The boy filed a sixth stopping beside the first five as an object and not a rule, an interval and not a payment, and would not let six likenesses stand up and call themselves a doctrine, for a doctrine is an account that has found a payer and no payer had been named to any of the six. Sella, within hearing, ended her instruction at the pot and asked nothing; Jorra did not ask about the ear and Tarn did not ask about the room. A thing stopped six times is still a held thing, not a settled one; the loan stayed uncalled and the seventh year pressed nearer its end. See \textbf{Six at the Teeth}, \textbf{Loan that can hear} and \textbf{A kept thing is owed}.

On Reed 29, Y.H. 813 it came a \textbf{ninth} time, on Reed 29 after Reed 5, 8, 11, 14, 17, 20, 23 and 26, all the way to the word that would call the loan and stopped there with no figure and no name; Tarn drew the breath that should have gone in at the top of the reach and did not spend it, said \emph{Yes, house} to the fire and went on with the broom, and the boy filed the ninth stopping on the interval tray beside eight as a ninth interval and not a ninth payment, refusing to let nine likenesses stand up and call themselves a doctrine because a doctrine is an account that has found a payer and no payer had been named to any of the nine. Sella, within hearing, gave the end of her instruction to the pot and asked nothing; Jorra did not ask about the ear and Tarn did not ask about the room, and the two silences stayed unjoined. The loan stayed uncalled and the seventh year stood one tend from its end and had not given. See \textbf{Nine at the Teeth}.

On Day 152, Tallow 3, it came up as it had come up nine times before but was \textbf{not} brought to the word that would call the loan: Tarn told the kindling \emph{Six counted. The next I don’t count}, and the sentence stopped short of the threshold, the way a man stops short of a step he has learned to know by the feel of the floor under his foot. No tenth stopping stood up to join the nine, he drew the breath that should have gone in at the top of the reach and did not spend it, said \emph{Yes, house} to the fire and went back to the broom, while Sella within hearing gave the end of her instruction to the pot and asked nothing. The boy filed the absence of a tenth as a keeping, not a payment: a tenth stood up before the seventh year was earned would be a debt invented to make the nine into a bill. See \textbf{Nine at the Teeth} and \textbf{Loan that can hear}.

\textbf{Nine at the Teeth.} A proverb of Low Kiln, said at the last market of Reed as the reed month goes out: \emph{Nine times a word may come to the teeth and go back, and nine is a keeping still and not a payment. The last market sets every withholding in one square and reads a figure that does not know the hand that did not come back; what the square cannot count it calls weather, and what it cannot read it carries home in a coat.} It is the ninth of the fire’s proverbs in these tend-weeks: a thing held five times was kept and owed, a sixth stopping did not make it paid, seven likenesses had still to be held apart by hand, and eight stoppings stood on the tray with no payer named to any. On Reed 29, Y.H. 813 the sentence about an ear under the Vail roof being worth more than the debt that holds it came to the teeth a ninth time — after Reed 5, 8, 11, 14, 17, 20, 23 and 26 — and stopped at the word that would call the loan, with no figure and no name; Tarn drew the breath he did not spend and the boy filed nine stoppings on the interval tray as objects and not a rule, intervals and not payments, and would not let nine likenesses stand up and call themselves a doctrine, for a doctrine is an account that has found a payer and no payer had been named to any of the nine. The seventh year stood one tend from its end and had not given, and the count crossed into Tallow unspent. On Day 152, Tallow 3, the sentence came up as it had come up nine times before but was \textbf{not} brought to the word that would call the loan: it stopped short of the threshold, no tenth stopping stood up to join the nine, and the boy filed the absence of a tenth as a keeping, not a payment, because a tenth stood up before the seventh year was earned would be a debt invented to make the nine into a bill. See \textbf{Five at the Teeth}, \textbf{Six at the Teeth}, \textbf{Seven at the Teeth}, \textbf{Eight at the Teeth}, \textbf{Near-saying}, \textbf{A kept thing is owed} and \textbf{Loan that can hear}.

\textbf{Nine Pots.} A pottery hamlet eight leagues west of Sill with four kilns, a shared clay pit and a permanent feud with Sill over the road.

\textbf{The Nine Wells.} Hot springs in the Keel where the ground gives back more than it takes; five are sealed by the Court and the keys are kept.

\textbf{The Nine Who Kept.} The temple’s figures who came after the First Breaking, drove the first repairs and left the rite of the Return behind.

\textbf{Nine readings stand behind one figure.} A saying of the Cross at the going out of the dark month: \emph{Nine readings go up the clay road and one figure stands on the notice; nine know what each house paid and the one knows only the notice, and no hand writes between the two.} On Ash 30, Y.H. 813 (Day 359), the dark month’s third and last Account-day, Berr Clay read \emph{one in twelve, as the notice says} twice over the basket, called the levy, denied it with \emph{The levy is called. It is not called by me} and \emph{your house}, never I, and went off up the clay road with the box locked and Ash’s third true subtraction inside, believing he had done a kindness. With the three of Frost, the first, second and third of Bone and Ash’s first and second, \textbf{nine arithmetics of the year now stand behind one unsigned figure; nine are nine and not one account}, the printed figure one in twelve and unchallenged, the figure read still not the figure paid and no signature on the space between. The boy kept the finding on a place of its own with no payer, not a lesson, a grievance, a mending, a doctrine or a rule, and did not lay it across the house’s not-doings, the covered grain, the five held objects, the pot-crack resting, the hand-at-the-sill breath, the holding of Ash 26, the Ash 5 joining, the Ash 17 direction, the Ash 23 direction or his own gaps — the edges came near to touching and the finger went between. No doctrine stood up out of nine, for a doctrine is an account that has found a payer and none stood, and the reading answered none of the held questions; the ninth arithmetic was paid off as a date earning its own morning, while the thread stands advanced and not paid. See \textbf{Eight readings go up the clay road in a locked box and one figure stands on the notice}, \textbf{Seven readings stand behind one figure}, \textbf{Account-day}, \textbf{The slate is read twice} and \textbf{What is read aloud is not what is paid}. Ch 102.

\textbf{Nine strokes and ten strokes are both strokes on a board.} A Low Kiln saying, told over the charcoal beneath a loaf shelf, and the epigraph of \emph{The Tenth Finding}: \emph{Nine strokes and ten strokes are both strokes on a board. The board keeps no tally, and the hand that counted goes home cold.} A stroke is a stroke whether it is counted nine times or ten, and the board takes no reckoning of either; the hand that did the counting goes home with nothing but the cold. It is the district’s grammar for a finding that does not become a placing. On Stone 25–27, Y.H. 813 (Days 384–386) the wool Sella Vail put into the crust’s empty place on the fifteenth was found folded there a tenth, an eleventh and a twelfth time, changed by nobody, with no second fold, third crust, name, gift, payment or payer, and twelve findings from a hand that only read added no twelfth placing; a habit wants a hand that placed twice and a way a third, and both want a payer where none stands. The board keeps no tally and the counter goes home cold (T097/T060/T086 advanced, not paid). See \textbf{A thing set down once is a keeping}, \textbf{A thing left lying has two keepers} and \textbf{Not-doing}. Ch 111 (epigraph).

\textbf{Not-doing.} A keeping made by what a house refuses to do. The epigraph of \emph{What Nobody Tells the Hand} puts it as a saying of the yards of Low Kiln, told at the going of the light in Smoke’s third week: \emph{The broom has its instruction and goes around. The lip keeps its white and is called weather. What nobody tells the hand to do, the house keeps by leaving it undone.} Under the Vail roof on Smoke 22--24, Y.H. 813 (Days 261--263) the boy sees two lines left unswept, the widow’s mark untouched, the charcoal on the underside of the loaf shelf unread, the fifth pull of the carried fire unsupplied, Garl’s loan uncalled, no number spoken over the basket and the crust in the fold not lifted; the house keeps itself as surely by these not-doings as by its doings. He keeps the seeing as a finding with no payer, not a grievance, a lesson or a doctrine, and does not lay the house’s omissions across his own kept empty intervals, because a joining would want a payer and none stands; even the absence of the joining is kept and not spent. Through Smoke 25–27, Y.H. 813 (Days 264–266) the not-doings went on — the two lines unswept, the mark untouched, the charcoal unread, the fifth pull unsupplied, the loan uncalled, no number spoken over the basket and the crust not lifted — and to them was added the finding that a thing handled closely still enters nothing, kept on a place of its own and not laid across the house’s omissions or the boy’s own kept gaps (T077, T061/T082). See \textbf{Left where it lies}, \textbf{What is kept in three places does not add up to an account}, \textbf{The carried fire}, \textbf{Handling is not entry} and \textbf{A kept thing is owed}.

\textbf{O}

On Reed 26, Y.H. 813 it came an \textbf{eighth} time, on Reed 26 after Reed 5, 8, 11, 14, 17, 20 and 23, all the way to the word that would call the loan and stopped there with no figure and no name; Tarn drew the breath that should have gone in at the top of the reach and did not spend it, said \emph{Yes, house} to the fire and went on with the broom, and the boy filed the eighth stopping on the interval tray beside seven as an eighth interval and not an eighth payment, refusing to let eight likenesses stand up and call themselves a doctrine because a doctrine is an account that has found a payer and no payer had been named to any of the eight. The loan stayed uncalled and the seventh year stood one tend from its end and had not given. See \textbf{Eight at the Teeth}.

\textbf{One in twelve.} The figure printed on the Weighing notices and read aloud at Account-day: one part in twelve of a household’s measure is kept back for the Hearth. It is spoken as \emph{one in twelve, as the notice says}, in a voice that makes a market lean in. It was read again at the year’s last market on Stone 30, Y.H. 812, as the levy was called for the feast and said not to be called by the man who read it. What Low Kiln actually gives is another matter; see \textbf{Deduction}. On Silt 20, Y.H. 813, Account-day after the flood, it was read over a thinner crowd than had stood at the flood’s Account-day, the water and the lean week having taken bodies out of the market; the printed figure stood unchallenged over fewer people while the true subtraction went over the basket unspoken, so that a figure read aloud was not the figure paid. On Seed 10, Y.H. 813, the second Account-day of Seed, Berr Clay read it twice over the basket at the Cross, called the levy for Seed and said it was not called by him; the number for the planting went from a fist to a mouth to a shoulder and arrived nowhere, the true subtraction stayed in the locked box, and the bell went four, four and a gap with nobody crossing himself.

On Ilmen 1, Y.H. 814, the year turned with nothing signed: the twelve arithmetics of Y.H. 813 crossed into the new year behind one unsigned figure — the three of Frost, the first, second and third of Bone, the first, second and third of Ash, and Stone’s first, second and last — twelve are twelve and not one account, the figure read still not the figure paid, no signature on the space and no doctrine out of twelve; the twelve true subtractions ride locked in Berr Clay’s box up the clay road and the boy has no key. The reset of the tend supplied no payer to the old twelve or to a new one. Ilmen 10 (Day 404), the new year’s first Account-day and market, is a new count and not a thirteenth, and stands unbrought until its own morning earns it (T015/T041/T047 advanced, not paid). Ch 114. On Seed 13, Y.H. 813 Berr Clay came up the clay road from the Cross with the cord of his office folded under his coat, read \emph{one in twelve, as the notice says}, called the levy and took himself out of his own sentence with \emph{There’ll be a slate at the watch}; the true subtraction stayed in the locked box and the number for the planting went from a fist to a mouth to a shoulder and arrived nowhere. On Seed 15 he came down off the north road at midday to the worked strips and read \emph{one in twelve, as the notice says} over the hands, saying a number goes into a slate and not into a strip; the levy was called and not by him, the true subtraction stayed in the locked box, and a figure read aloud was not the figure paid. On Seed 20, Account-day, he read \emph{one in twelve, as the notice says} over the worked strips where the hands had gone in on Seed 15, called the levy and said it was not called by him; a number goes into a slate, not into a strip, and the true subtraction sat in the locked box in his house up the road. A figure read aloud was not the figure paid and nothing in the ground changed its figure because a man had looked at it, and the sentence went around the square like a bucket passed from hand to hand with nobody asking who was carrying it. On Seed 22, Y.H. 813 he came up short off the north road to the yard well, wiped his thumb twice on his apron before touching nothing, passed a finger over a narrow slate held unopened against his forearm and read \emph{one in twelve, as the notice says}, saying a number goes into a slate and not into a strip and that there would be a slate at the watch; a man brought a number up out of a fist toward the well, looked at it, put the fist in his sleeve and went off, so the figure arrived nowhere, and the true subtraction stayed in the locked box in his house up the road. On Seed 30, Y.H. 813, Account-day and the last market of Seed, he came up to the reading block with the red wool cord of his office folded under his coat and the green of tasted glaze at one corner of his mouth, wiped his thumb twice on his apron before touching nothing, held a narrow slate unopened against his forearm and read \emph{one in twelve, as the notice says} over the very ground the hands had gone into, saying \emph{The levy is called. It is not called by me} and, to a man who asked what the planting cost now that hands had been in it, \emph{A number goes into a slate, not into a strip; if your house wants it again, there’ll be a slate at the watch} --- \emph{your house}, never \emph{I}. The figure read aloud was not the figure paid, the true subtraction sat in the locked box, and the figure that went into the slate did not know the hand that had not come back out of the strip.

On Reed 15, Y.H. 813 Berr added the bundle to the strip and the well in the saying \emph{A number goes into a slate, not a bundle}; he took two pair of eels and paid two marks short, the stall-keeper putting the marks in her palm without counting them where anyone could hear, said \emph{If your house wants it again, there’ll be a slate at the watch} --- \emph{your house}, never \emph{I} --- and said something low to the stall about the levy being called and not called by him, one in twelve as the notice says, spent on the boards with nobody leaning in. A figure read aloud was still not the figure paid, and the true subtraction stayed in the locked box up the clay road. On Reed 18, Y.H. 813 Berr added the bundle to the strip and the well in a saying at the stalls: \emph{A number goes into a slate, not a bundle. If your house wants it again, there’ll be a slate at the watch} --- \emph{your house}, never \emph{I}. He took two pair of eels and paid two marks short, the stall-keeper putting the marks in her palm without counting them where anyone could hear, and said something low about the levy being called and not called by him, one in twelve as the notice says, spent on the boards with nobody leaning in. A figure read aloud was still not the figure paid. On Reed 20, Y.H. 813, the second Account-day of Reed, he came up short to the reading block under the moot-post with the red wool cord folded under his coat and glaze at one mouth-corner, wiped his thumb twice before touching nothing, held a narrow slate unopened to his forearm, passed a finger over the figure and read \emph{one in twelve, as the notice says} over the last bundles; he called the levy and denied it with \emph{your house}, never \emph{I}, while the true subtraction stayed in the locked box up the clay road. At the stalls he took two pair of eels and paid two marks short, and went off believing he had done a kindness. On Reed 23 he came up short off the clay road at the Cross with the cord folded square under his coat, wiped his thumb twice before touching nothing, held a narrow slate unopened to his forearm, passed a finger over the figure and read \emph{one in twelve, as the notice says}, called the levy and denied it with \emph{your house}, never \emph{I}, saying a number goes into a slate, not a bundle; he paid two marks short for two pair of eels which the stall-keeper put in her palm uncounted and went off up the road with the box locked, believing he had done a kindness. The figure he read did not know the hand that had not come back out of the strip. On Reed 30, Y.H. 813, the third Account-day and the last market of Reed, he came up short off the clay road with the red cord folded square under his coat and the green of tasted lead glaze at one corner of his mouth, wiped his thumb twice before touching nothing, held a narrow slate unopened to his forearm, passed a finger over the figure and read \emph{one in twelve, as the notice says} low into the goers-by over the last bundles; he called the levy and denied it with \emph{your house}, never \emph{I}, said a number goes into a slate, not a bundle, paid two marks short for two pair of eels into an uncounted palm and went off up the clay road with the box locked and the true subtraction inside, believing he had done the district a kindness. A figure read aloud was not the figure paid.

On Ember 10, Y.H. 813, the first Account-day of the kiln month, he came up short off the clay road to the reading block under the moot-post with the red wool cord folded square under his coat and the green of tasted lead glaze at one mouth-corner, wiped his thumb twice before touching nothing, held a narrow slate unopened to his forearm, passed a finger over the figure and read \emph{one in twelve, as the notice says} low into the two hundred, said \emph{The levy is called. It is not called by me} and \emph{your house}, never \emph{I}, and went off up the clay road with the box locked and the true subtraction inside, believing he had done a kindness. The printed figure stood unchallenged, a figure read aloud was not the figure paid, and the figure that went into the slate did not know what the glaze-room hand carried out on Day 188 had cost (T015/T041/T047/T077).

\textbf{Opened.} The rank of a vessel that has cut a way and can move Warm deliberately within the self.

\textbf{The Opening of the Slates.} Ilmen 1, when the Court opens the new year’s accounts.

\textbf{The outward way.} A procedure by which a Drawn practitioner pushes a flow of Warm out of the body at short range.

\textbf{Overfilling.} Pouring more Warm into a vessel than its walls can hold; the head rises and the vessel cooks its own contents.

\textbf{P}

\textbf{The Peat Line.} The wet frontier where Sere’s northern advance stopped in Y.H. 634 and where the two powers trade, raid and buy measures.

\textbf{Pot gone wrong.} A Grathic household’s name for a vessel cracked from lip to foot. The phrase names the vessel, not the sound it made, and a pot gone wrong is swept around and gone past rather than decided about. On Stone 25, Y.H. 812 one cracked two paces from the boy in the Clay Yard and nobody called the knock a sound.

\textbf{The pot not heard from.} The turned saying of the Vail kiln-house in the first working week of Grain, Y.H. 813: the pot that sang before its time last month (see \textbf{Pot singing early}) is \emph{not heard from since}. On Grain 5, Y.H. 813 (Day 214) a kiln-hand come up from High Kiln on a wrong wind said it to the yard and not to the basket, and the boy took the change apart as a surgeon takes a wound apart — a direction with no hand at the foot of it, no owner, no room, no cause and no figure. Jorra, who knew that pot’s full note three turns before it left his hands and holds the nearly-full answer with air under it and a want in it, let the saying stand as a saying; no pot was lost, no name was given to what ailed the man carried out on Day 188 and no lesson was made of the green on the wind. On Grain 8, Y.H. 813 (Day 217) another kiln-hand come up from High Kiln on a wrong wind with a barrow let fall a third shaping over the boards: \emph{a pot gone quiet on every row come the thaw}. The singular report of one pot’s silence bent back toward the general proverb it had come from, so that three shapings stood on the near-full tray — sings itself out early, has not been heard from since, gone quiet on every row. The boy set them out with a finger between them and no finger laid across, took them apart as a surgeon takes apart a wound and would not let three likenesses stand up and call themselves a rule, for a rule is an account that has found a payer and no payer stood to any shaping; a silence reported is not a second hearing of the same pot, and three shapings of one saying are not three witnesses to one death. The sweet edge of lead glaze came up on the wrong wind and went out on it, a direction and not a second edge paid, and no fourth likeness was made a cause. The silence gathers interest on a tray nobody under any roof can read (T061/T082 advanced and unpaid, T064, T035/T031). See \textbf{Pot singing early}, \textbf{The full note} and \textbf{Near-saying}.

On Grain 15, Y.H. 813 (Day 224) a wrong-wind kiln-hand come up off High Kiln with the sweet edge of lead glaze let one of the three shapings stand over the boards: \emph{a pot gone quiet on every row come the thaw}. The voice went on to the price of barley and the weather and gave no owner, no room, no hand at the foot of it and no reason. The boy took it apart as a surgeon takes apart a wound and left it a saying about a pot with no pot lost; the three shapings stayed on the near-full tray with a finger between them and no finger laid across, no fourth likeness stood up as a cause and no name was given to what ailed the man carried out on Day 188 (T061/T082, T064). Four tellings of the burned slate also stayed a direction arrived nowhere, with no fifth telling and still not a third telling of the counting room shut in the war (T035/T031/T065/T095 held).

\textbf{Pot singing early (a pot that sings before its time).} A master potter’s saying of High Kiln, carried down the clay road on a wrong wind: \emph{That one’s singing before its time. A pot that sings early generally sings itself out early.} It names a vessel that gives its full note before it has borne heat, and by the yard it is said of anything that shows a thing too soon; it is a danger of the firing month and never a lesson. On Tallow 21, Y.H. 813 a woman at the drying racks set a pot down that gave a high thin note before its time and did not turn, and no pot was lost. On Tallow 22 a High Kiln kiln-master come up on the wrong wind with Ash on his cuffs said it of a pot under Jorra Vail’s hands; Jorra knew its full note and withheld the knowing, the master took the silence for agreement and went off, and no pot was lost in the yard. The boy filed the early note as a danger and the withheld knowing as a near-full answer on a separate tray, and made neither a seventh hearing. On Ember 18, Y.H. 813 (Day 197) a man come up on a wrong wind said it again of a pot under Jorra Vail’s hands; Jorra knew its full note three turns ahead, withheld the knowing and took the man’s silence for agreement, and the saying stayed a saying about a pot and was not made true as a lesson, with no pot lost. A rack-worker’s pot had given its note before its time on Ember 17 and sang itself out early while she went on with her hands and swept around the fault, so no lesson was made of it so soon after the carrying-out of the glaze-room hand on Day 188 (T035/T031, T061/T082, T064 held). On Grain 5, Y.H. 813 (Day 214) the saying turned by a hair in a kiln-hand’s mouth: that pot was now \emph{not heard from since}; Jorra let the change stand as a saying, the knowing went to the near-full tray beside the hearings and never among them, and no pot was lost. On Grain 8, Y.H. 813 (Day 217) a second wrong wind bent the report back toward the old general form with \emph{a pot gone quiet on every row come the thaw}, and the boy kept three shapings on one tray with a finger between them and no fourth likeness made a cause (see \textbf{The pot not heard from}). See \textbf{The full note}, \textbf{Pot gone wrong} and \textbf{Near-saying}.

\textbf{Quiet ash.} The Court’s licensed medicine, sold to the rich who want their previous life to stop arriving in dreams.

\textbf{The quiet seal.} The forbidden procedure of closing a vessel so that nothing leaks in or out.

\textbf{R}

\textbf{A record kept in muscle.} What the carrying arm knows and no slate can hold. Through the first counted bundles of Reed, Y.H. 813, the boy read the armfuls of reed coming downriver and going back at dusk as a record kept in muscle that tells what was carried and not what it cost, exact, complete and worth nothing: a record a Court thumb can never enter because it leaves no writing. A cutter told a girl with a creel to ask the arm that carried it, and the yard judged bundles by the weight settling into a forearm and never by a figure. The boy laid going-downriver and coming-back on a place of their own and laid no likeness across the shelf’s two gaps or the crust in the fold. On Reed 13, Y.H. 813 he read the carrying arm again as a record in muscle: a working arm corded at the forearm, pale where the reed-water ran off it, knowing how many green ends and how much weight at the butt and where the load would balance if the ground rose --- exact, complete, worth nothing, telling what was carried and never what it cost, for the stiffness that would come into it by dark was set on no slate. On Reed 22 and again on Reed 24 he read the arm that carried a reed bundle as a record in muscle that tells what was carried and never what it cost, exact, complete and worth nothing; a cutter told a girl with a creel that her arm knew what went into the bundle and that was the whole of it, and a woman who asked what the hands would be paid was answered with the weather and the river and shut two fingers out of a fist as she went. On Ember 13–15, Y.H. 813 (Days 192–194) the boy read the arm that carried him home at the going of each light as the same record in muscle: it kept the height of the handle, the give of the shoulder and the turn of the wrist at a step’s end, a record that remembers weight and not cost, while Sella went wide around the yard’s absences and gave no figure to any of them (T058/T079, T009/T013/T092/T098). Through Ember 16–18, Y.H. 813 (Days 195–197) the boy read the arm that carried him home at the going of each light as the same record in muscle: it kept the height of the handle, the give of the shoulder and the turn of the wrist at a step’s end, woodsmoke in long low bars before her and river wind behind with the taste of water over water, passing without taking each other’s colour. It remembered weight and not cost, exact, complete and worth nothing, while she went wide around the pan’s gone ring, the bare trough whose water is called weather, the rack space with its broken birth-slates, the field’s empty place and the place the carriers crossed, each with a look and a wide step and no number (T058/T079, T009/T013/T092/T098). See \textbf{Ask the arm that carried it} and \textbf{A bundle’s counted in the arm that carries it}. On Reed 16, Y.H. 813 the boy read the carrying arm again as a record that tells what was carried and where the carrier chose to go around, exact, complete and worth nothing; the cost lived in a different room --- in a woman counting under her breath toward no opening, in the grey at her temple, in the half-beat her hand rested longer than the setting needed --- and he had no standing to enter it. On Reed 18 the reeds came downriver and went back past the yard in armfuls judged by the arm that carried them, and a woman who asked what the hands would be paid was given the weather and the river. On Reed 19, Y.H. 813 the last bundles came in armfuls judged by the arm that carried them, and a cutter told a girl with a creel to lift her bundle and let her arm tell her what went into it, \emph{and that’s the whole of what it knows}; to a second question he said it did not know cost and asked how heavy it was. The boy read the carrying arm again as a record in muscle that tells what was carried and not what it cost, exact, complete and worth nothing to any Court thumb. See \textbf{Ask the arm that carried it}.

On Reed 25, Y.H. 813, with the reed month going out, the last bundles came downriver and went back at dusk in armfuls judged by the arm that carried them; a cutter told a girl with a creel to lift her bundle and let her arm tell her what went into it, \emph{and that’s the whole of what it knows}, and a man who asked what the hands would be paid was answered with the weather and the river. The boy read the carrying arm once more as a record in muscle that tells what was carried and not what it cost, exact, complete and worth nothing, and noted the order of reaching — the hand to the record before the hand to the person — without standing to enter it anywhere.

\textbf{Reed Cut.} The Fenfolk coming-of-age at twelve: cutting a bundle of reed alone in the dark and bringing it back without speaking.

\textbf{The reed-cutter’s cord (a tally in wool).} A length of wool or reed-fibre gone grey with handling in which a reed-cutter at the Weir keeps his tally of what went up yesterday: knots set at the lengths a man’s arm could judge, one tied low with teeth and a pull of the thumb. On Reed 3, Y.H. 813 a cutter turned it once so the boy in the basket at the edge of the shade saw the knots standing in the small light, showed it to nobody and counted it where nobody could hear; to a weir woman who said she could not read a cord he answered \emph{You can ask the cord} and \emph{No more can the Court}. It would burn if put to a flame, and no clerk could take up a figure from it. The boy held it on a place of its own, carried and not counted, not laid beside the hand that did not come back out of the strip or beside any other keeping (T099). On Reed 6, Y.H. 813 the same cutter came along the plank walk with a bundle on his shoulder, set it on the flat blessing stone, straightened the grey cord on his thumb, turned it once so the knots stood in the small light off the water, tied one low with his teeth and a pull of the thumb and put it back inside his coat. To the weir woman who said she could not read a cord he said \emph{You can ask the cord} and \emph{No more can the Court}; no figure was read, no knot counted and no joining made to the hand that did not come back out of the strip (T099 carried, not paid). On Reed 9, Y.H. 813 the same cutter came along the plank walk with a bundle, set it on the flat blessing stone, straightened the grey cord on his thumb, turned it once so the knots stood in the small light, tied one low with his teeth and a pull of the thumb, bit the end off and put it back inside his coat; to the weir woman who asked how many had gone up yesterday and said \emph{I can’t read a cord} he said \emph{You can ask the cord} and \emph{No more can the Court}. The greyness was read as the record of a hand that had been there long before any figure was needed; no knot was counted, no name given and no joining made either to the hand that did not come back or to the word forty (T099 carried, not paid). See \textbf{A bundle’s counted in the arm that carries it}, \textbf{Knot-string} and \textbf{The hand that does not come back}.

On Reed 12, Y.H. 813 the same cutter came along the boards with a bundle, set it on the flat blessing stone, straightened the grey cord on his thumb, turned it once so the knots stood in the small light, tied one low with his teeth and a pull of the thumb, bit the end off and put it back inside his coat. To the woman who asked what the cord held he said \emph{You can ask the cord} and \emph{No more can the Court}; no figure was read, no knot counted, no name given, and the cord was not laid beside the charcoal under the Vail shelf, the hand that did not come back or the word forty (T099 carried, not paid).

On Reed 13, Y.H. 813 the same cutter set his bundle on the flat blessing stone, straightened the grey cord on his thumb, turned it once so the knots stood, tied one low with his teeth and a pull of the thumb, bit the end off and put it back inside his coat; to the woman who asked what the cord held he said \emph{You can ask the cord} and \emph{No more can the Court}. The boy set it beside the charcoal under the shelf and the empty place in the returning line, three records in materials no Court thumb can spell, and kept them side by side and not across; he counted no knot and joined the cord to neither absence (T099 carried, not paid). See \textbf{The cord and the mouth}. On Reed 18, Y.H. 813 the same cutter came along the plank walk with a bundle, set it on the flat blessing stone, straightened the grey cord, turned it once so the knots stood, tied one low with his teeth and a pull of the thumb, bit the end off and put it back inside his coat, drawing the coat closed over it with the flat of his hand. To the woman who asked what it held he said \emph{You can ask the cord}, and to \emph{I can’t read a cord}, \emph{No more can the Court}. No figure was read, no knot counted and no joining made to the hand that did not come back, the charcoal under the shelf or the word forty (T099 carried, not paid). On Reed 19 the same cord went past along the boards with its knots unread; on Reed 21 he straightened it on the flat stone, turned it once so the knots stood, tied one low with his teeth, bit the end off and put it back inside his coat, and answered the woman who could not read it with \emph{You can ask the cord} and \emph{No more can the Court}. The boy held it on its own place beside the charcoal under the shelf, Orra’s knot-string and Mira’s two cords, counted no knot and laid no likeness across any of them (T099 carried, not paid). On Reed 24 the same cutter set his bundle on the flat blessing stone, straightened the grey cord oiled by a working thumb, turned it once so the knots stood, tied one low with his teeth and a pull of the thumb, bit the end off and put it back inside his coat with the flat of his hand, answering a woman who could not read it with \emph{You can ask the cord} and \emph{No more can the Court}. No figure, knot, name or joining came of it and the cord was not laid beside the hand that did not come back, Mira’s cords or Orra’s knot-string (T099 carried, not paid).

On Reed 26 and Reed 27, Y.H. 813 the same cutter came along the boards with a bundle, set it on the flat blessing stone, straightened the grey cord oiled by a working thumb, turned it once so the knots stood, tied one low with his teeth and a pull of the thumb, bit the end off and put it back inside his coat with the flat of his hand; to the woman who said she could not read a cord he said \emph{You can ask the cord} and \emph{No more can the Court}, without anger or smile. No knot was counted, no figure read and no joining made to the missing hand, Mira’s second twist, Orra’s knot-string or the charcoal under the shelf (T099 carried, not paid).

\textbf{Reed-wolf.} A wolf of the lower Ilm reedbeds that hunts in packs and goes for the throat and the inside of the elbow.

Through Grain 13–15, Y.H. 813 (Days 222–224) the harvest was read by the same hand: the first cut grain came off the worked strips, was taken at the yard’s edge and carried under the roof, and the carrying arm knew its weight and not its cost, exact, complete and worth nothing. The yard counted it in glances and handfuls and gave nobody a figure, while the returning hands went around the empty place in the returning line with a look and a wide step and no number (T071/T072, T077, T098 advanced and unpaid). See \textbf{The first grain}.

\textbf{The Remembering.} The fourth of the Five, when names of the dead are spoken and whole returns announced in a clean voice. It has a name and no tend-day and no market is held in it. On the Remembering, Y.H. 813 (Day 393), the names of the dead went up the Clay Yard from door to door, passed mouth to mouth the way a coal goes in a dish, while the Vail house kept its own quiet and did not say the one name that matters; Garl’s name stayed unspoken its three hundred and ninety-third day and no whole return was announced for him under this roof. Dessa’s name went among the others in the yard but was not spoken under the Vail roof or to the boy, and her number was not given; the lie told for mercy stood as a fact nobody could correct. An errand to House Silt let the pewter tin above the empty bed be seen from the basket’s low angle with its pale fold and thumb-bright lid, and it was not opened (T089, T008, T023 advanced, not paid). Ch 114.

\textbf{A report of an asking.} A further shaping of the ownerless row question, told over the boards of the Clay Yard on Smoke 26, Y.H. 813 (Day 265): a voice with no owner, room, hand at the kiln or cause reported that somebody had been asking which row it was that went quiet. The weather answered first and the price of barley after it, and the voice went off up the terrace while the row stood where it stood with nobody leaning in to take an answer down. A report of an asking is not an asking and finds no witness at the bottom of it; the five askings stood at five, with no sixth asking, no row named and no person standing anywhere to be asked. The boy set the shaping on the seventh place beside the five with a finger between each pair — not a hearing, not a seventh of the full note, not a fifth telling of the burned slate, not a third telling of the shut counting room, not a fourth likeness of the pot saying, not a cause, not a name and not a payment (T101 advanced, unpaid). See \textbf{Which row did the pot go quiet on?}, \textbf{Three askings do not make a witness} and \textbf{Burned slate (a direction from Slate Row)}.

\textbf{The Return.} The rite by which the dead are held to come back in new bodies through the mercy of the Hearth; the first thing a child learns and the last thing a dying person hears.

\textbf{The Rim.} The chain of cold mountains that rings Sarn, broken by a few passes, beyond which lies the Waste.

\textbf{Rim current.} The slow current of Warm draining toward the Waste, which makes the Keldish mines sweat.

\textbf{Rim Road.} The road from Sill west-north-west to Keld Keep, a hundred and twenty leagues of improving road and worsening weather.

\textbf{Rim-seam.} The seam at the horizon where sky and clay meet, riveted with stars; it carries many repairs laid one over another.

\textbf{The river keeps its own note under its own skin.} A saying of the Clay Yard, and the epigraph of \emph{Under Its Own Skin}: \emph{The river keeps its own note under its own skin, and the slate comes up the road on the twentieth whether the house has counted its days or not. Neither asks a house for leave.} The first clause is the low note of water over water going under the Ilm’s winter skin, heard through the finger’s-width door and kept on a place of its own, not a hearing, not a seventh and with no hand under it. On Ilmen 19, Y.H. 814 (Day 413) a day of air less cold came off the river — not warmth, a lessening: the cold at the wrist did not go, it stopped arriving with the same instruction. The sour tang of Ash thinned at the Vail corner, the grey called the thaw lay a hair less distinct along one stretch where nobody had passed a finger or swept, and the river’s skin softened at one edge where the low note ran nearer under it. A woman at the well said \emph{The air has turned} and a man said \emph{It’ll be back before morning}; nobody owned the day, Sella told the fire it was the thaw, and the boy filed the softening on a place of its own beside the clean dark line, the new finer grey and the called-gone grey — not a sign, not a fourth covering, not a sixth shaping, not a hearing, not a payment, with no hand or payer under it and not made again (T083/T085/T092 and T009/T013/T092 advanced, \textbf{not paid}). The second clause is Ilmen 20’s second reading, which came on its own morning whether the house had counted its days or not; the third is the same indifference in both, for neither the river nor the slate asks a house for leave. See \textbf{The river takes its skin}, \textbf{Water over water (the river’s own note)}, \textbf{The thaw} and \textbf{Weather}. Ch 120.

\textbf{The river takes its skin.} The district’s phrase for the Ilm going under its winter ice from bank to bank, told at the coming of Stone: the river takes a skin and gives no account of the cold. On the afternoon of Stone 1, Y.H. 813 (Day 360), the river’s note under the finger’s-width door came no longer water over water in the open but low under a covering, nearer at the going of the water than at its coming but muffled in the going. A man come down from Cold Acre with a hare across his shoulders told the woman who asked what the ice would cost to ask the weather, which had laid it on and would take it off; no slate was opened and no figure came. The boy took the change apart by what was there and by what was not — a skin with no hand that laid it, cold with no payer under it, a low note with no source standing to be asked — and filed it on a place of its own \textbf{beside} water over water, which stayed where it had been put. It is a covering put on by the cold and taken off by the cold, entered nowhere; expressly not a sixth low thing standing up as a rule, not a hearing (a hearing wants a source standing and none stood), not a seventh of the full note, not a fourth of the three coverings (the gone white frost off the well’s north lip, the skin on the trough, the silt-clouded plate of ice on its flat stone, each on its own place with a finger between), and not a sign, lesson, cause, payment or payer, with no payer standing. It was found where put on Stone 2 and 3 and not made again, and gathers toward the deep winter, Stone 5’s first firing, the birthday on Stone 7 and the Hearth Drawing on Stone 12 without paying or joining any of them (T083/T085 with T078 advanced, \textbf{not paid}). Ch 103. Through Stone 4–6 it was found where put on its own place beside water over water and not made again; a man come down from Cold Acre with a hare was still sent to the weather for the price of carrying, and the skin was not spent on the first firing at the kiln on the fifth, on the birthday on the seventh or on the Drawing on the twelfth. The edges of the coverings came near to touching and the finger went between, so that no fourth likeness stood up as a cause and no hand joined a covering to a date (T083/T085 held, advanced and not paid). Ch 104. See \textbf{Water over water}, \textbf{Frost-bloom} and \textbf{Weather}.

\textbf{The runner carries what she will not read.} A saying of the women at the yard well in Low Kiln, told on a morning of Frost: \emph{The runner carries what she will not read, and the yard keeps what no slate will take; both go home with the weight of it and neither calls it an account.} On Frost 14, Y.H. 813 (Day 283) a woman waiting her turn with a bucket, speaking to the boards and the well-roof and not into the basket and not to any person, said as a direction arrived nowhere that the runner who carries Berr Clay’s slate once carried a figure that named a person she knew — no owner of the voice standing anywhere to be asked, no room, no hand at a slate, no name for the person, no figure spoken, no confession and no cause. The boy took the saying apart as a surgeon takes a wound apart and filed it on a place of its own beside Hessa Rale’s eighth record-first hand with a finger between: a shaping toward the far-off day she must choose whether to read what she has carried for years, not a hearing, not a tenth hand, not a cause, not a confession, not a joining, not a witness and not paid (T080 advanced and not paid). He did not make Hessa a reader and did not join the saying to Ilva’s strip of notched birch in her sleeve a pace away, to the charcoal under the loaf shelf or to any private keeping, and did not let one stray saying stand up as a rule, for a rule is an account that has found a payer and none stood. No second shaping came on Frost 15 and nobody stood anywhere to be asked. Ch 77. No second shaping came on Frost 16, 17 or 18 either, though the boy’s hand answered six times and a hundred and fifty honest answers stood on the sixth place; the saying stayed one saying with a finger between it and Hessa Rale’s eighth hand, not a confession, not a joining, not a witness and not paid (T080 held). Ch 78. On Frost 19, Y.H. 813 (Day 288) the saying took a \textbf{second shaping} from an ownerless voice over the boards and the well-roof, with no owner standing anywhere to be asked, no room, no hand at a slate, no name, no figure, no confession and no cause: it asked what a runner carries in a slate that has a name in it and went on with the day as the yard says the weather. The boy took it apart as a surgeon takes a wound apart and filed it on a place of its own beside the first saying and beside Hessa Rale’s eighth record-first hand with a finger between every pair: two shapings toward the far-off day she must choose whether to read what she has carried, not a hearing, not a seventh, not a tenth hand, not a cause, not a confession, not a joining, not a witness and \textbf{not paid}. It does not make Hessa a reader and is not joined to Ilva’s strip of notched birch in her sleeve a pace away, to the charcoal under the loaf shelf or to any private keeping; two shapings must not stand up as a rule, for a rule is an account that has found a payer and none stands (T080 advanced, not paid). Ch 79. On Frost 23, Y.H. 813 (Day 292) the saying took a \textbf{third shaping} from an ownerless voice over the boards and the well-roof, with no owner standing anywhere to be asked, no room, no hand at a slate, no name for the person, no figure spoken, no confession and no cause: the slate-runner once carried a name the district spent and did not say whose. The voice went on with the day the way the yard says the weather and nobody turned twice; Sella Vail heard it and went on with the house, bringing nothing under the roof as lesson, figure, mending, cause or payment. The boy took it apart as a surgeon takes a wound apart and filed it on a place of its own beside the first saying and the second shaping with a finger between every pair, a third shaping toward the far-off day she must choose whether to read what she has carried — not a hearing, not a seventh, not a tenth hand, not a cause, not a confession, not a joining, not a witness, not a rule and \textbf{not paid}, and not making Hessa a reader or joining the saying to Ilva’s strip, Berr’s twice-wiped thumb, the soft-cuffed clerk’s inward slate or the charcoal under the shelf. Three shapings must not stand up as a witness, for a witness stands somewhere and can be asked and none stood; the ownerless row question explicitly stayed at five askings with one shaping and no witness, and this was not a sixth asking and not the row’s shaping (T080 advanced, not paid). Ch 80. See \textbf{A firing kept in wood (two counts in two materials)}, \textbf{Firing-stick (a count kept in wood)}, \textbf{The tally under the shelf} and \textbf{A kept thing is owed}.

\textbf{S}

\textbf{The Salt Road.} The trade route from Sill through Greybank to the Vhaleni ports, eighty leagues.

\textbf{Salt Walk.} The Vhaleni coming-of-age at fourteen: walking the pans barefoot at low tide and naming a tide never seen.

\textbf{Salt-thing.} A shape of salt and cold water in the Sallow that taps the hull of a boat and draws its store away.

\textbf{The Sallow draw.} The current of Warm running seaward into the Sallow, blessed by the dippers and taxed by the Court.

\textbf{The Sallow Sea.} A cold inland sea the colour of skimmed milk whose tides run against the wind and are said to follow the Warm rather than the moon.

\textbf{Seam-blight.} A blight that travels along an old repair and widens it by a hair’s breadth each season.

\textbf{Seam-serpent.} A long thing that moves along the under-seam and draws Warm out through the stone.

\textbf{Seam-tide.} The rising and falling of the Warm in the seams of the world, read by the Vorr from the Listening Stones.

\textbf{Ten readings are ten and not one account.} A saying of the Cross at the tenth reading of the year, told at the going of the light in the deep-winter month: \emph{Ten readings go up the clay road and one figure stands on the notice; ten know what each house paid, and the one knows only the notice. No hand writes between the two, and no doctrine comes out of ten.} On Stone 10, Y.H. 813 (Day 369), the first Account-day of Stone, Berr Clay read \emph{one in twelve, as the notice says} twice over the basket — once for the moot and once for the late households — called the levy, denied it with \emph{your house}, never \emph{I}, and went off with the box locked and Stone’s first true subtraction inside, believing he had done a kindness. With the three of Frost, the three of Bone, the three of Ash and Stone’s first, \textbf{ten arithmetics of the year stand behind one unsigned figure; ten are ten and not one account}, the figure read still not the figure paid and no signature on the space. A doctrine is an account that has found a payer and none stood to any of the ten, so no doctrine came out of ten and none of the held questions was answered; the eleventh stands at Stone 20 (Day 379) and the twelfth at Stone 30 (Day 389), neither brought early (T015/T041/T047 advanced, not paid). Ch 106. See \textbf{Nine readings stand behind one figure}, \textbf{Account-day}, \textbf{The slate is read twice} and \textbf{What is read aloud is not what is paid}.

\textbf{The Second.} A person in whom a graft from a differently shaped donor has produced a want for a life that was not theirs.

\textbf{Second Want.} The Court’s struck-from-the-record name for the Warm trying to resume the shape of a former owner; the common name is the second chill.

\textbf{Seed.} The month of planting, third in the Sarnish year. In Grath the first work of Seed is not planting but sweeping: the yard goes around what the last flood left with a broom and a glance and no figure spoken, and the planting strips east of Low Kiln are spoken of as a direction that will want hands, not as a number. On Seed 1, Y.H. 813 the mud of Silt had set into a brown skin holding a boot’s print, and the new finer grey in the Vail corner was still unswept and still called the thaw. On Seed 2–4 the first planting work went into those strips east of Low Kiln: seed came out of a fist in handfuls nobody counted, brooms went around what the sweep had left, and a man who said the strips wanted hands was told the weather would have the last word, so that neither the hands nor the strips ever had a figure put to them. A saying of the seed-grounds: \emph{Sow with the hand and count with the hand; the slate lies in the sun and takes no seed.} Another planting saying of Low Kiln is \emph{the hands go in by the look}: \emph{The seed goes in by the fist and the hands go in by the look. Ask either what it cost and it will tell you the weather.} On Seed 15, Y.H. 813 the hands at last went into the worked strips east of Low Kiln --- stooped backs along turned ground, seed out of fists in handfuls nobody counted, brooms around what the sweep left --- still counted in glances and never in a figure; see \textbf{The hands go in by the look}. Through Seed 21–23 the last tend of the planting stood in those strips with the hands still counted in glances and handfuls and never in a figure; a woman shut her fist rather than say how many hands the work would want and a man with a barrow shaped a number and thought better of giving it, so the direction carried for a month had still no figure at its foot. Through Seed 24–26 the last tend held with the seed up and nobody giving a figure for the hands that set it; a man brought a number up out of a fist toward the well, looked at it and put it back in his sleeve so it arrived nowhere, and the figure for the hands still went nowhere at the close of the tend. Through Seed 27–30 the planting month went out: the last hands came out of the worked strips east of Low Kiln with the seed up and worked around, counted in glances and handfuls and never in a figure, and one hand that had gone in on Seed 15 did not come out with the rest, so that the yard went around the empty place in the returning line with a look and no number and no figure was given for what the month cost (T098, planted and unpaid); on Seed 30 Account-day the figure read aloud over that same ground was not the figure paid and did not know the hand that did not come back, and Reed came on in the dark beyond the door.

\textbf{Sere.} The hot southern empire of grain, wine, bowls and open chattel slavery, ruled by the Sun-Emperor.

\textbf{Sere factors.} The empire’s agents in the north, who buy poor measures with credit and ship them south.

\textbf{Seven at the Teeth.} A proverb of Low Kiln, said over the banked fire in the last tend of Reed: \emph{Seven times a word may come to the teeth and go back, and seven times is a keeping and not a payment. A reed bundle is counted in the arm that carried it, and a year held to its last day is a year still held. What is held is owed, and what is owed waits for a hand that has not come.} It is the seventh of the fire’s proverbs in these tend-weeks: a thing held five times was kept and owed, a sixth stopping did not make it paid, and a seventh likeness must still be held apart by hand or it will stand up by morning as an account with a payer. On Reed 23, Y.H. 813 the sentence about an ear under the Vail roof came to the teeth a seventh time — after Reed 5, 8, 11, 14, 17 and 20 — and stopped at the word that would call the loan, with no figure and no name; Tarn drew the breath he did not spend and the boy filed seven stoppings on the interval tray as objects and not a rule, intervals and not payments, and would not let seven likenesses stand up and call themselves a doctrine, for a doctrine is an account that has found a payer and no payer had been named to any of the seven. The seventh year stood one tend from its end and had not given.
