On Reed 29, Y.H. 813 it came a ninth time and stopped at the word with no figure and no name; nine is a keeping still and not a payment, and see \textbf{Nine at the Teeth}. See \textbf{Five at the Teeth}, \textbf{Six at the Teeth}, \textbf{Eight at the Teeth}, \textbf{Near-saying}, \textbf{A kept thing is owed} and \textbf{Loan that can hear}.

\textbf{The shape of the measure.} The pattern of a vessel’s Warm, which is the self; it is fragile and thins with every pouring.

\textbf{Seven readings stand behind one figure.} A yard saying of Low Kiln, told on Ash’s first Account-day: \emph{The figure goes up seven times and the crack stays showing; the runner carries what she will not read, and the house keeps its grain under wool without a number.} On Ash 10, Y.H. 813 (Day 339), Berr Clay read \emph{one in twelve, as the notice says} twice over the basket, once for the moot and once for the households that came late, called the levy, denied it with \emph{The levy is called. It is not called by me} and \emph{your house}, never \emph{I}, said something low to the block about kindness being entered, and went off up the clay road with the box locked and Ash’s first true subtraction inside, believing he had done a kindness. \textbf{Seven arithmetics of the year — the three of Frost, the first, second and third of Bone and Ash’s first — now stand behind one printed figure; seven are seven and not one account}: the figure read is still not the figure paid, no signature stands on the space between, and a rule made from seven would want a payer put under all seven where none stood. The boy kept the finding on a place of its own with no payer, not a lesson, a grievance, a mending, a doctrine or a rule, and did not lay it across the house’s not-doings, the dressed grain covered under wool, the five held objects, the pot-crack resting, the handful, the thumb’s resting, the two small objects of the hand or his own gaps — the edges came near to touching and the finger went between. Hessa carried the slate up the road unread, Ilva kept the count in wood, and the twice-mended pot kept its crack showing; none of them took a figure off any of the others. See \textbf{Six readings stand behind one figure}, \textbf{Three readings are three and not one account}, \textbf{Slate-runner}, \textbf{Leave the crack showing. If it’s worth mending, mend it twice.} and \textbf{Account-day}. Ch 96.

\textbf{The Singing Sill.} The ledge of hard stone under the falls at Sill, which gives a low note when the Warm rises in Ilmen. On Ilmen 25, Y.H. 813 it gave that note earlier than it should and the yard called it weather; the boy kept the early note beside the told bell, the heard bell and the kiln’s own missing breath in four places that did not touch.

On Silt 7, Y.H. 813 it gave its low note a week ahead of its hour, felt in the roots of the teeth before the ear placed it out in the water, and the yard said the water ran fast under the ice and then said weather; the boy kept the early note beside the told bell, the heard bell and the kiln’s gap in four places, joined by nobody. On Silt 15 it was spoken of past tense as the thaw that was, along with the honeyed ice and the hairlines that had stopped short of the edge.

\textbf{Sill.} The town of just over four thousand souls where the Ilm drops four feet over a ledge; Corin’s birthplace.

\textbf{Six at the Teeth.} A proverb of Low Kiln said over the banked fire: \emph{The second Account-day comes with the reed month in its last tend. Read one in twelve where the notice says it and the true subtraction goes into the box with the key turned; the heard bell stands beside the told bell and a fifth green at a mouth is a colour and not a name. Hold a word six times at the teeth and it is a held word still, for a thing held six times is owed and not paid.} It is the sixth of the fire’s proverbs in these tend-weeks: a thing held five times was a thing kept and owed, and a sixth stopping does not make it paid. On Reed 20, Y.H. 813 the sentence about an ear worth more than the debt that holds it came to the teeth a sixth time and stopped at the word that would call the loan, with no figure and no name; the boy filed six stoppings on the interval tray as objects and not a rule, intervals and not payments, and would not let six likenesses stand up and call themselves a doctrine, for a doctrine is an account that has found a payer and no payer had been named to any of the six. On Reed 23, Y.H. 813 the sentence came to the teeth a seventh time and stopped at the word with no figure and no name; a seventh stopping is a keeping and not a payment, and the proverb \textbf{Seven at the Teeth} holds that what is owed waits for a hand that has not come. See \textbf{Five at the Teeth}, \textbf{Seven at the Teeth}, \textbf{Eight at the Teeth}, \textbf{Nine at the Teeth}, \textbf{Near-saying}, \textbf{A kept thing is owed} and \textbf{Loan that can hear}.

\textbf{Six readings stand behind one figure.} A saying of the Cross, told at the going of Bone: \emph{Six readings stand behind one figure and do not know one another. The figure was never asked what it read over, and the space where the price should stand has kept its silence.} On Bone 30, Y.H. 813 (Day 329), the month’s third and last Account-day, Berr Clay came up short off the clay road with the red cord of his office folded under his coat and green of tasted lead glaze at one mouth-corner, wiped his thumb twice before touching nothing, read \emph{one in twelve, as the notice says} twice over the basket and went off up the clay road with the box locked and Bone’s third true subtraction inside, believing he had done a kindness. Six arithmetics of the year now stand behind one printed figure — the three of Frost and the three of Bone — and \textbf{six are six and not one account}: the figure read is still not the figure paid, no signature stands on the space between, and a rule made from six would want a payer put under all six where none stood. The boy kept the finding on a place of its own with no payer, not a lesson, a grievance, a mending, a doctrine or a rule, and did not lay it across the house’s not-doings, the dressed grain covered under wool, the four held changes, the handful, the thumb’s resting, the two small objects of the hand or his own gaps — the edges came near to touching and the finger went between. The reading answered nothing for the hand that went in on Seed 15, the man carried out on Day 188, the grain read over by a number that did not know its cost or the carried fire’s missing fifth. See \textbf{Three readings are three and not one account}, \textbf{What is read aloud is not what is paid}, \textbf{The slate is read twice} and \textbf{Account-day}. Ch 92.

\textbf{The slate is read twice.} A saying of the Cross, told under the moot-post in the second week of Bone: \emph{The slate is read twice so that those who came late may hear what those who came early heard. The third thing, which is the price, nobody reads aloud, and the space where it should stand has no signature.} It is the district’s own account of its Account-day: on Bone 20, Y.H. 813 (Day 319), the month’s second reading, Berr Clay read \emph{one in twelve, as the notice says} twice over the basket, once for the moot and once for the households that came late, and went off up the clay road with the box locked and Bone’s second true subtraction inside. Five arithmetics of the year now stand behind one printed figure — Frost’s three and Bone’s first two — and five are five and not one account; the printed figure stands unchallenged, the figure read is still not the figure paid, and no signature stands on the space between. Twice spoken is two sayings and not one account, for an account would want a payer put under both and none stood; the boy kept the finding on a place of its own with no payer, not a lesson, a grievance, a mending, a doctrine or a rule, and did not lay it across the house’s not-doings, the dressed grain covered under wool, the four held changes on four places, the stayed-at-the-inch object, the early letting-go of Bone 17 or his own kept gaps — the edges came near to touching and the finger went between. The reading answers nothing for the hare gone into the weather, the hand that went in on Seed 15, the man carried out on Day 188 or the grain read over by a number that did not know what it cost. See \textbf{Three readings are three and not one account}, \textbf{Three readings make a month}, \textbf{A figure read over a covered thing}, \textbf{Account-day} and \textbf{Deduction}. Ch 89.

\textbf{Slate-name.} The only name an officer of the Keeping has, entered on the rolls in Ledgerhand on entering the service.

\textbf{Slate Row.} The Court quarter east of the Cross at Sill, holding the collector’s table, the assessor’s house and the Waiting Room.

\textbf{Slate-runner.} A person hired to carry slates between one table and another without reading them. In Grath a runner carries Berr Clay’s narrow slate edge-on between the Cross and Greybank: the writing turned toward the sleeve so it is not rubbed and no goer-by takes a figure off it, the hand going to the slate before the eyes go to the people. On Tallow 9 and 10, Y.H. 813 Hessa Rale of Slate Row answered a woman who asked what the levy would take, \emph{I don’t read it. I carry it. There’s a difference, and the road doesn’t care which}, and went on with \emph{Cross to Greybank. Reading goes up before noon. I’ve got a road to walk}. A runner is not a reader of anyone’s private keeping; the edge-on is the manner of carrying, not the hiding of a thing from oneself. The boy filed her order of reaching as an eighth record-first hand on a place of its own, joined to none. See \textbf{Slate Row} and \textbf{The tally under the shelf}.

On Ember 10, Y.H. 813, the first Account-day of the kiln month, she took Berr’s narrow slate up the clay road toward Greybank before noon, the writing turned to her sleeve and her hand to the slate before her eyes to the crowd, the second strap let out for the long road and the dried pale scurf of mud unbrushed on the shortened skirt. To two women who asked what she carried she answered the question put and not the one behind it with \emph{I don’t read it. I carry it. There’s a difference, and the road doesn’t care which} and \emph{Cross to Greybank. Reading goes up before noon. I’ve got a road to walk}; no figure came off the slate (T080 advanced, not paid).

\textbf{The slate is read twice and the grain is read over once.} A saying of the market women at the Cross, told on the first Account-day of Frost: \emph{The slate is read twice and the grain is read over once, and neither of them knows what the other cost.} The slate carries the figure the moot reads aloud; the grain lies covered under wool on the cool stone at the rack end and is read over by a number that does not know what it cost, so the space between figure and price has no signature. Two readings do not make one account, for an account would want a payer and none stands to either. On Frost 10, Y.H. 813 (Day 279) Berr Clay read \emph{one in twelve, as the notice says} over the basket and the dressed grain was read over by that figure without becoming priced by it (T015/T041/T047, T077). See \textbf{Account-day}, \textbf{A figure read over a covered thing} and \textbf{One in twelve}.

\textbf{Slip.} The wet clay worked in the pits of Low Kiln and poured into moulds on the wheel; it dries the colour of old bone on a thrower’s forearms. Work in the slip is commonly paid for in the thaw.

\textbf{Slip pits.} The clay pits of the Clay Yard in Low Kiln, counted as nineteen steps to the drying rack and nineteen back; Dessa Silt has walked the count every day for six years. The cough that comes off them in cold weather is called weather, as if the pits owned it.

\textbf{The Slip Brook.} A narrow clay-coloured stream through the Clay Yard whose colour the children of Low Kiln read as weather. On Ilmen 9, Y.H. 813 its clay-heavy rise came up behind the drying racks in the night and took Dessa Silt from the end of nineteen steps; the yard lifted her out with their hands and no collector was called.

Through Days 61–67, Y.H. 813 it ran clay-heavy and higher behind the drying racks, going over itself with a low note the district had no word for, and the yard called it the thaw.

\textbf{Smoke.} The eighth month of the Sarnish year, the second firing, following Grain and before Frost; Smoke 1 fell on Day 240, Y.H. 813, and Smoke 10 (Day 249) is the first Account-day and market of the month. It came on without a boundary drawn in the telling and neither of the district’s two names for the months was corrected; the kiln breathes in fours with a gap and the carried fire keeps its fifth missing under blind ash with its payer unnamed. The year’s dressed grain lies covered under wool near the hearth, turned for damp and given no figure. Smoke 1 brought the month’s first firing: before the kiln Sella Vail touched the widow’s mark for one breath, lifted the clay lid with the back of a hand and tipped the coal under a broken pot, and the fire took; the next real opening, the first firing of Frost, stands far off and unbrought. See \textbf{The carried fire}, \textbf{The first opening} and \textbf{The hand goes to the mark before the kiln and at no other hour}.

\textbf{The Spending.} The Sere doctrine that a vessel was made to be emptied gloriously and that a life hoarded is a life wasted.

\textbf{The Standing Post.} The raised boardwalk in the Fenmarch where reeves settle fines and feuds and which is the only Fen place outsiders are shown.

\textbf{Star-rivet.} A rivet of the rim-seam, one of the stars; one is said to have fallen in the Ash Times.

\textbf{Steward.} The head of the Warm Court; Steward Derren holds the office in the present year.

\textbf{The stick keeps what the slate cannot ask for.} A saying of the women at the yard well in Low Kiln, told of the firing-work and the weather: \emph{The stick keeps what the slate cannot ask for, and the well keeps what the bucket does not take up; a count that stays in wood has paid nobody, and a thing left where it lies is still kept.} The stick is Ilva’s short strip of notched birch bark, held in a sleeve and passed over with a thumb-nail before the eyes go to the asker; the well is the yard well whose north lip keeps the white fronds the bucket knocks grey and which the yard calls weather. Neither count can be taken up by a Court thumb and neither has found a payer. On Frost 16–18, Y.H. 813 (Days 285–287) Ilva was glimpsed once at the well on the seventeenth with her hand toward her sleeve, answering \emph{Ask the pot what it cost. I keep the count, not the account}; the notches stayed unread, the ninth hand stayed nine, and the stayed frost, the skinned trough and the plate of ice stayed weather (T080 held, T083/T085 held). The boy kept a hundred and fifty honest answers on his sixth place and would not let a round number stand up as a doctrine, for a doctrine is an account that has found a payer and none stands. Ch 78. See \textbf{Firing-stick (a count kept in wood)}, \textbf{A firing kept in wood (two counts in two materials)}, \textbf{Frost-bloom} and \textbf{A kept thing is owed}.

\textbf{Stone.} The month of deep winter, river ice and counted fuel; the year begins in it. Stone 1 fell on Day 360, Y.H. 813, and Stone 10 (Day 369) is the month’s Account-day and market; the Hearth Drawing of Stone 12 (Day 371) falls within it. Stone 10 (Day 369) brought the \textbf{tenth arithmetic of the year}: Berr Clay read \emph{one in twelve, as the notice says} twice over the basket, called the levy, denied it with \emph{your house}, never \emph{I}, and went off with the box locked and Stone’s first true subtraction inside, so ten arithmetics stand behind one unsigned figure, ten are ten and not one account, the figure read still not the figure paid and no doctrine out of ten. Stone 12 brought the year’s first Hearth Drawing, seen only from a basket at the edge of the light; see \textbf{Ten readings are ten and not one account} and \textbf{The Hearth Drawing}. Ch 106. The month came on without a boundary drawn and neither of the district’s two habits of naming its months was corrected. On the afternoon of Stone 1 the Ilm took its winter ice from bank to bank and the river’s note under the finger’s-width door came low under a skin, nearer at the going of the water than at its coming; a man come down from Cold Acre told the woman who asked what the ice would cost to ask the weather, which had laid the covering on and would take it off (T083/T085 advanced, not paid). Stone 5 (Day 364) brought the month’s first firing: Sella Vail carried the basket to the kiln mouth before any instruction went to it, set it level out of the draught where the heat came sideways, put her left hand to the widow’s mark for one breath, lifted the clay lid with the back of a hand and tipped the carried coal under a broken pot; the fire took in fours with its fifth unpaid and nobody praised the opening, named what it mended, entered a slate or made a lesson of it. \textbf{Seven openings in seven months are seven and not a rule and no eighth is made due} (T058/T079). Through Stone 4–6 the three coverings stayed weather entered nowhere with a finger between every pair, the grain lay covered and unfigured under wool, and the boy answered six times, 301 through 306, so that the count closed on Stone 6 at \textbf{three hundred and sixty-five exact}, six months and one hundred and eighty-five days told by nobody — a round number nobody under any roof speaks or marks and a threshold nobody crosses (T071/T072, T061/T082). His first birthday in the new life fell on Stone 7 (Day 366) and was lived as an ordinary tending day with no party, no cake, no figure, no recognition and no threshold crossed, nobody under any roof knowing what a number counts; the older women named the month by the weather and the slatemen by the count of Account-days and neither habit was set right or left. Through Stone 7, 8 and 9 the boy kept three hundred and sixty-six, three hundred and sixty-seven and three hundred and sixty-eight exactly, so that a whole year stood finished and named by no roof and Days 367 and 368 proved the birthday left no residue; Sella did not touch the widow’s mark and no eighth opening was made due, and the river’s winter skin was found where put and not spent on the birthday or the Drawing. He answered six times, 307 through 312, and the count closed at \textbf{three hundred and sixty-eight exact}, six months and one hundred and eighty-eight days told by nobody. The Hearth Drawing on Stone 12 (Day 371) stands three mornings beyond the close, unbrought. Ch 103, Ch 104, Ch 105. See \textbf{A year comes round to the month it started in}, \textbf{The river takes its skin}, \textbf{The first opening}, \textbf{The carried fire} and \textbf{Water over water}.

\textbf{The Sweating.} A Keldish calamity in which Warm comes up through the stone of the deep mines in a lethal flood, heralded by the smell of hot lead.

\textbf{The sweet-sickness.} The sickness that comes of working long with lead glaze: a sweetish taste on the breath, a pale line at the gum, a hand held curled at the side rather than used, fingers the colour of old rope and nails the colour of pewter. It was noted in Y.H. 641 and has since been quietly unlearned in Low Kiln; the glaze-mixers of High Kiln call the green at the mouth a mark of skill and name no cause. On Ember 8, Y.H. 813 (Day 187) a glaze-room hand at the yard well showed the pale line when he drank, and on Ember 9 two men carried him out of the kiln and across the yard toward the clay road with a thumb hooked under his arm to keep the head from lopping, the man still breathing. The boy read the whole disorder in the surgeon’s register and could neither speak it in Grathic nor reach the body; no collector came, no figure was given, the cost was entered in no slate and nobody called the sweetness by a cause (T077 advanced, not paid; T064 carried). See \textbf{Lead glaze} and \textbf{The Glaze Room}.

\textbf{T}

\textbf{Tallow Works.} A rendering house for sheep fat two leagues north-east of Sill, whose smell carries into town on a north wind.

\textbf{The tally under the shelf.} A keeping in charcoal on the UNDERSIDE of a kiln-house loaf shelf, where a house can count without putting a figure where a person might see it. On Reed 10, Y.H. 813 the boy, lying at the low angle at which the underside of a shelf becomes a roof, saw short strokes under the Vail loaf shelf in little clusters a finger’s breadth apart, some pressed hard enough to leave a smooth track where the stick had dug, some faded nearly into the grain. They did not make Grathic words and no slate had been set under them to catch what they meant. He did not read a stroke, count a cluster, copy a mark or show it to a man from Slate Row, and did not lay the marks beside the two gaps above, the crust in the fold, a midwife’s tin, a eel-seller’s cords, a weir woman’s knots, a pewter tin above an empty bed or a reed-cutter’s cord. On Reed 12 Sella Vail reached a finger beneath the board without looking at it and without a word and brought it away; he saw the hand go under and come back and made no cause of the habit. The tally is held on a place of its own for the far-off day a hand not his lays the district’s private records together (T100, planted and unpaid). A saying of the loaf-shelves of Low Kiln has it that the figure read at the Cross is a figure in the air and the mark under the shelf is a mark on the wood, and that neither is the account. Through Reed 19–21, Y.H. 813 the shelf kept its two unnamed gaps --- the old space at the row’s end and the palm’s breadth that came in on the night of Seed 6 with no scrape, crumb, print or word --- and no third, while the fold in the other room kept one brown-edged crust two inches from his ear with its empty place unnamed. On Days 138 and 140 Sella stood with her back to the basket, moved her lips along the row, glanced once at the clay jar cold under its glaze and reached a finger beneath the board where the marks lie, without looking and without a word, and brought it away; a hand that goes under without looking either knows the board by heart or has been told not to look, and the reason is left between the two. The strokes stayed unread and uncounted and were not laid beside the two gaps above or the one crust in the fold (T100 carried, not paid). On Tallow 11, Y.H. 813 (Day 160), standing with her back to the basket and moving her lips along the row, she reached a finger beneath the front edge where the charcoal lies, without looking and without a word, and brought it away without going back to the shelf; on Tallow 12 she did not go back at all, and the reason still stood between knowing the board by heart and being told not to look (T100 carried, unread). On Tallow 17 (Day 166), standing with her back to the basket and moving her lips along the row, she reached a finger beneath the front edge where the charcoal tally lies and \textbf{held it there for the length of one of the breaths she counts} before she brought it away; she did not look, read, copy, give a word or go back to the shelf that night. The boy saw the held beat and filed it on a place of its own as a change held and unspoken --- not a reading of the charcoal, not a payment, no payer named --- and kept it from standing up with the Day 161 fraction at the damper and the older intervals into a rule, for a rule is an account that has found a payer (T100 carried and advanced, not paid; T061/T082). The charcoal waited unread under the shelf for a hand that is not his and a day that has not come. Through Ember 13–15, Y.H. 813 (Days 192–194) Sella stood with her back to the basket and moved her lips along the row standing with two unnamed gaps, glanced once at the clay jar cold under its glaze without touching it, and kept her finger from beneath the front edge on all three days; the strokes stayed unread, uncounted and uncopied, not laid beside the two gaps above or the one crust in the fold, and the Day 166 held beat stayed where it was left (T100 carried, not paid). Through Ember 16–18, Y.H. 813 (Days 195–197) Sella stood with her back to the basket at the low angle, moved her lips along the row standing with two unnamed gaps, glanced once at the clay jar cold under its glaze and shut her hand half over nothing without touching it, and kept her finger from beneath the front edge on all three days; the strokes stayed unread, uncounted and uncopied, not laid beside the two gaps above or the one crust in the fold, and the Day 166 held beat stayed where it was left (T100 carried, not paid).

On Reed 13 and again on Reed 15, Y.H. 813 Sella stood at the shelf with her back to the basket, moved her lips along the row with its two unnamed gaps, glanced once at the clay jar cold under its glaze and reached a finger beneath the front edge where the charcoal lies, without looking and without a word, and brought it away and did not go back to the shelf. The boy saw the hand go under and come back and saw nothing of what the marks said. A hand that goes under a board without looking either knows the board by heart or has been told not to look, and the reason is left between the two. The marks stayed unread and separate from the two gaps above and the one crust in the fold in a room that does not touch (T100 carried, not paid). On Reed 16, Y.H. 813 Sella again stood at the shelf with her back to the basket, moved her lips along the row with its two gaps, glanced once at the clay jar and reached a finger beneath the front edge where the charcoal lies, without looking and without a word, and brought it away and did not go back to the shelf. The marks stayed unread and separate from the two gaps above and the one crust in the fold (T100 carried, not paid). On Reed 22 and twice on Reed 24 Sella again reached a finger beneath the board without looking or a word and brought it away without going back to the shelf; the boy saw the hand go under and come back and saw nothing of what the marks said, and made no cause of the habit. No stroke was counted, no copy made and no joining laid across the two gaps above or the one crust in the fold (T100 carried, not paid).

On Day 144, Reed 25, Y.H. 813 Sella stood with her back to the basket, moved her lips along the row with its two unnamed gaps, glanced once at the clay jar cold under its glaze and reached a finger BENEATH the front edge where the charcoal tally lies, without looking and without a word, held it out and back, brought it away and did not go back to the shelf; from the low angle the boy saw the hand go under and come back and saw nothing of what the marks said, and made no cause of the habit (T100 carried, unread).

On Tallow 2, Y.H. 813 the shelf still kept its two unnamed gaps and the boy, set low at the bench leg at the angle where the underside of a board becomes a roof, watched Sella stand with her back to the basket, move her lips along the row and reach a finger BENEATH the front edge where the charcoal tally lies, without looking and without a word, hold it a breath out and back, bring it away and not go back to the shelf. He saw the hand go under and come back and saw nothing of what the marks said; the care of the hiding told more than the marks would have, had he been able to read them. On the wall by the bench the shallow pan that had stood out to dry through all of Reed was gone with no scrape, crumb, print, chip or dust disturbance, and he held its round empty place on a tray of its own, apart from the two gaps above and the crust in the other room (T097 held, advanced and unpaid). No third gap came and no fourth likeness was made a cause (T100 carried, unread). On Tallow 8, Y.H. 813 the shelf still kept its two unnamed gaps and its charcoal unread; standing with her back to the basket and moving her lips along the row, Sella reached a finger BENEATH the front edge where the charcoal tally lies, without looking and without a word, brought it away and did not go back to the shelf. The boy saw the hand go under and come back and saw nothing of what the marks said; such a hand either knows the board by heart or has been told not to look, and the reason stands between the two (T100 carried, unread). Through Tallow 21–23, Y.H. 813 Sella went once each day to the shelf with the basket at the low angle at which its underside becomes a roof and moved her lips along the row standing with two gaps, but her finger did \textbf{not} go beneath the board on any of the three days; the Day 166 held beat stayed where it had been left and was not repeated. The shelf kept its two unnamed gaps and the charcoal kept its marks unread for a hand that is not his and a day that has not come (T100 carried, not paid, not advanced into a reading).

\textbf{Tempering.} The practice of repeated small strains so that a vessel’s walls learn to yield without opening.

\textbf{Temple of the Return.} The public church of the Keeping, which teaches that the world was made whole and cracked once.

\textbf{Tend.} A week of ten days; every month holds three whole tends, and the tenth day of each is Account-day. A saying of the clay-bound of Low Kiln: \emph{A tend is counted by what is left on the board, not by what went into the ground. A hand reaches for the empty place and closes on the loaf beyond it and goes on; the shelf keeps its own account and gives nobody a figure.} In the last tend of Seed, Y.H. 813 the hands went on in the strips and the loaf shelf kept two gaps nobody called a number; through Seed 24–26 the last tend held with the seed up and the hands still counted in glances and handfuls and never in a figure, and the shelf kept its two gaps in a room that did not touch the fold’s one crust and its empty place. Through Seed 27–30 the last tend of Seed went off the tally with the seed up and one place in the returning line still gone around with a look and no figure; the loaf shelf kept its two unnamed gaps and the fold one crust and its empty place in a room that does not touch them, and the boy’s count stood at one hundred and nineteen, exact, unspent and spoken by nobody.

\textbf{Thane of Clay.} Grath’s ruler, chosen by the kiln-masters of Sill and confirmed by the Court’s factor at Greybank.

\textbf{The thaw.} The spring working season, when the brook comes up and the clay goes soft. Debts in Low Kiln are often put off until then, in the phrase \emph{you’ll pay for it in the thaw}. Through Ilmen 19–25, Y.H. 813 the thaw came on in frost-bloom written back on the well-lip, oiled paper hanging slack in its frame, a silence where an argument used to stand, more hairlines stopping short of the edge of the Ilm, an early low note from the Singing Sill and a high clay-heavy brook, and the district had one word for all of it: weather. On Ilmen 25 a weak board in the plank walk at the Weir was said plainly to be still there and trodden by nobody. On Silt 1 a new hairline of grey gathered in the corner of the Vail kiln-house beside the clean dark line where the old Ash ridge had turned; Sella stood over it with a broom, called it the thaw and did not sweep it. Through Reed 4–6, Y.H. 813 the clean dark line at the Vail corner and the new finer hairline beside it lay unswept by any broom and were called the thaw, though the reeds had come on without a boundary drawn anywhere in the yard; Tarn said \emph{Yes, house} to those who wanted it early and those who wanted it late, agreeing so entirely that no argument could find a foot, and kept wanting the late because a late thaw puts off the paying, though the paying had stood in the ruts since the water went.

On Silt 2–8, Y.H. 813 the higher clay-heavy brook going over itself behind the drying racks, the early Singing Sill note, the weak board trodden by nobody, the widening hairlines, the honeyed-all-through ice and a new fine grey in the Vail corner were all called the thaw or weather, and the year’s flood stood four days off. On Silt 15, after the water had come and gone, the honeyed ice, the hairlines that had stopped short of the edge and the early Singing Sill note were renamed all at once as \emph{the thaw that was}, as though a thing said after the fact were the same as a thing said before it. Sella told the fire it was the thaw and went on not sweeping the new grey beside the clean dark line; the yard went back to its steps and its mud on the one word. Through Silt 16–18 the yard went around that mud with a broom and a glance and no figure spoken, and the new finer grey beside the old clean dark line lay unswept because the house called it the thaw and said it would go when it goes. Through Silt 19–25 the lean week went around the mud in a brown skin that kept a boot’s print, and the honeyed ice, the hairlines that had stopped short of the edge, the early Singing Sill note, the gone board at the Weir and the out-of-line landing were spoken of only past tense as \emph{the thaw that was} --- a thing said after the fact treated as if it had been said before it. Through Silt 26–30 and onto Seed 1 the finer grey in the Vail corner lay unswept beside the old clean dark line, still called the thaw that would go when it goes; on Seed 1 the first work of the planting month was sweeping rather than planting, and a man said the strips east of town would want hands by the morrow without putting a figure to them. Through Seed 5–11 the planting has become waiting: seed stands in the strips and the yard goes around the brown skin holding a boot-print, the clean dark line, the new finer grey beside it and the space under the lowest rack with a broom and a glance and no figure spoken. Sella tells the fire it is the thaw each day and leaves the new grey unswept; the two lines stay in two places and neither becomes the other. Through Seed 5–11 the planting became waiting: seed stood in the strips east of Low Kiln and the yard went around the boot-print, the clean dark line, the new finer grey and the space under the lowest rack with a broom and a glance and no figure. Through Seed 12–14, Y.H. 813 the new finer grey lay unswept beside the old clean dark line and was still called the thaw that would go when it went; the yard argued it early against late and Tarn agreed with both while wanting the late one because it puts off the paying, though the paying had stood in the ruts since the water went. Through Seed 15–17 the brown skin of the worked strips held the boot-print and the stone the flood left, the brooms went around both lines, and the new finer grey beside the clean dark line in the Vail corner stayed unswept because the house said it was the thaw and would go when it goes; Sella told the fire it was the thaw on all three days and Tarn agreed with the early and the late while wanting the late because it puts off the paying. Through Seed 27–30 the new finer grey lay unswept beside the old clean dark line and was called the thaw that would go when it goes; Sella told the fire it was the thaw on all four days, turned the coals with the back of a broken pot and went around the empty places, and the planting month went off the tally into Reed with nothing joined, named or ended.

Through Reed 1–3, Y.H. 813 the planting month went out and the reed work came downriver while the clean dark line at the Vail corner and the new finer grey beside it lay unswept for three days and were still called the thaw; the space beneath the lowest rack and the place in the strip where a hand had gone in and not come back were gone around with a look and no number, and nobody swept them. Sella told the fire it was the thaw each day and turned the coals with the back of a broken pot, and Tarn agreed with the early thaw and the late and kept wanting the late because it puts off the paying, though the paying had stood in the ruts since the water went. Through Reed 16–18, Y.H. 813 the reed month ran into its last third with the clean dark line and the new finer hairline beside it unswept and called the thaw; a woman asking what the hands would be paid was answered with the weather and the river, and Sella told the fire it was the thaw on all three days and turned the coals with the back of a broken pot. Through Tallow 4–10, Y.H. 813 the clean dark line and the new finer grey beside it lay unswept and were called the thaw; the trough by the well stood bare and dark and the water within was called weather by those who did not taste it, and at the going of the light Sella told the fire it was the thaw, turned the coals with the back of a broken pot and said \emph{The house will keep it}. A man in Mud End taken quiet in his sleep was spoken of sideways and called merciful, and the boy read that danger as he read the kiln’s breath behind a screen, with no payer named to it. Through Tallow 11–13, Y.H. 813 the clean dark line and the new finer grey beside it lay unswept and were called the thaw; the trough by the well stood bare and dark with its skin of ice gone and the water within called weather, and at the going of the light Sella told the fire it was the thaw, turned the coals with the back of a broken pot and said \emph{The house will keep it} while the kiln breathed in fours behind the wall and the carried fire missed its fifth under the floor.

Through Tallow 1–3, Y.H. 813 the clean dark line at the Vail corner and the new finer grey beside it lay unswept and were still called the thaw; the trough by the well had lost the thin skin of ice that had lain on it like a skim of fat set aside in a dish, and the water stood bare and dark while a woman letting down a bucket called it weather. The kilns had been brought up for the year’s last working season and the yard went about the first firing with dust ground small as meal under the nails, the danger of the month carried carefully and without remarks. Sella told the fire it was the thaw on all three days and went on not sweeping the grey.

On Ilmen 19, Y.H. 814 (Day 413) the grey called the thaw lay a hair less distinct along one stretch at the Vail corner where air less cold came off the river and the sour tang of Ash thinned; Sella told the fire it was the thaw and said nothing of the air, and the boy filed the softening on a place of its own, not a sign, a fourth covering or a payment and not made again (T083/T085/T092 advanced, not paid). Ch 120.

\textbf{Thin.} A vessel that leaks faster than it takes in; the common condition of the poor, the spent and the returned poor. Also the bottom rank of a vessel.

\textbf{Thin return.} A return in which many measures are pooled and divided among many infants; what comes back is a stranger with a faint interest in a life it cannot name.

\textbf{Thin-child.} \emph{See} The Hollow.

\textbf{Three askings do not make a witness.} A saying of the Clay Yard, told in the last tend of Grain: \emph{Three askings do not make a witness. The weather answers the first, the price of barley the second; the third goes up the terrace while the row stands where it stood. A witness stands somewhere and can be asked, and nobody stood.} It is said of the ownerless question that came over the boards of Low Kiln on Grain 21, again on Grain 23 and again on Grain 26 of Y.H. 813 (Days 230, 232 and 235), in a voice with no owner, no room, no hand at the kiln and no cause. Each asking went off up the terrace with the weather and the price of barley answering it and the row standing where it stood, and nobody leaned in to take the answer down. The boy kept the three tellings side by side on a seventh place with a finger between each pair and a finger between them and the sayings, the tellings, the hearings and the count; three askings are not one witness, not a fourth shaping of the pot saying, not a hearing, not a seventh, not a fifth telling of the burned slate, not a cause and not a name (T101 advanced and unpaid). A fourth asking came on Grain 29 and a fifth on Smoke 8, Y.H. 813 (Days 238 and 247); five askings are still not one witness, and the row still stands where it stood with no name and nobody standing to be asked (T101 advanced and unpaid). See \textbf{Which row did the pot go quiet on?} and \textbf{Two tellings of one absence}.

\textbf{Tide-lore.} The Vhaleni discipline of reading the Sallow draw, taught by the dippers.

\textbf{Triage.} The old-life word for the surgeon’s act of sorting the wounded; Dan’s gift and his heresy in Sarn.

\textbf{Two tellings of one absence.} A neighbour’s saying at the loaf shelf of Low Kiln, from the morning of Seed 12, Y.H. 813: \emph{Two gaps named in one breath become one hunger. Keep your breath for the pot, and keep the bread where it was put.} It is spoken over the old space at the end of the loaf row and the empty place at a child’s ear, which the speaker takes for two things and never sees as one absence. The boy who hears it files the two sayings on two places and writes no cause across the space between them, having learned what likeness laid on likeness will do to a man who wants an answer; the witness is planted for a far-off day when a finger will lay the two places together and an account will want a name (T097). On Seed 18 a second neighbour named the old gap as a thing the planting brought in and went off with her pot without seeing the empty place at the boy’s ear; the two tellings were kept on two places with no finger laid across them, advanced and still unpaid. On Seed 21, Y.H. 813 a neighbour made a cause of two bare boards in one breath, calling the old space a thing the planting brought in and the new gap the price of a wet thing set down wrong, and went off with her pot without seeing that the two were one absence or seeing the empty place at the boy’s ear; this was a \textbf{third} shaping of the held thing, filed beside the two tellings and the watcher’s late turn, advanced and still not paid, with no joining, no name and no third gap. On Seed 24, Y.H. 813 a neighbour at the shelf again named the old space a thing the planting brought in and the empty place at the boy’s ear a child’s appetite in one breath, laying two rooms under one cause without seeing they were one absence; a \textbf{fourth} shaping stood beside the two tellings, the watcher’s late turn and the Seed 21 cause, advanced and still \textbf{not paid}, with no joining, no name, no fourth likeness and no third gap. On Seed 27 and again on Seed 29, Y.H. 813 neighbours at this shelf named the old space at the row’s end as a thing the planting brought in and, respectively, the new palm’s breadth as the price of a wet thing set down wrong and the empty place at the child’s ear as a child’s appetite, each without seeing that two bare boards were one absence or that a room had been joined to a room; a \textbf{fifth} and a \textbf{sixth} shaping stood beside the two tellings, the watcher’s late turn and the earlier causes, advanced and still \textbf{not paid}, with no joining, no name and no third gap, and no finger in Low Kiln laid them together. See \textbf{The loaf shelf}.

\textbf{U}

\textbf{The Unbanked.} The Court’s name for a secret faction of persons of the sealed opinion, descended from the Ash Rising and dedicated to the Final Banking.

\textbf{Unclosed account.} The crime of refusing a lawful collection; the offender is clip-held by the wrist until consent.

\textbf{The Uncollected.} A dead vessel whose Warm has not been drawn and which walks until it leaks into the Waste.

\textbf{Under-seam.} The seam beneath the ground, below which lies the dark where nothing is kept.

\textbf{V}

\textbf{The Vail kiln-house.} The kiln-house in the Clay Yard held by the Vail family for four generations, where Corin is taken in as a foundling.

\textbf{Vhal.} The principal Vhaleni port on the Sallow shore, seat of the Council of Tides, with salt pans and glass furnaces.

\textbf{Vhalen.} The salt republic of port towns on the Sallow, governed by the Council of Tides.

\textbf{Vorr.} A people apart, tall, long-lived, who hold their measure in the bone, keep the Listening Stones and do not undergo the Return.

\textbf{W}

\textbf{Walking thin.} People with the measures of the returned poor who keep moving because stopping is the same as cooling.

\textbf{Warm.} The living, stored heat of which Sarn is made; the poor call it \emph{the warm} and the learned call it \emph{the kept heat}. It has pressure, currents, sources and sinks.

\textbf{Warm Court.} The institution that owns the Hearth, the banks and the Returns and calls itself the Keeping.

\textbf{Warm-stone.} A Keldish stone that holds heat longer than any other substance in Sarn. In Low Kiln a common river stone, warmed at a neighbour’s fire and wrapped in wool, does the same work for a newborn for a few hours; it is not a warm-stone and nobody calls it one. The stone Sella Vail gave Tarn in the winter Garl died is such a common stone, kept two years in an unmarked clay pot in the Debt Loft above the wheel-shed, cold and not looked at in a year. On Ember 4, Y.H. 813 (Day 183) he took it out, held it, set it on the sill where the finger’s-width opening let in light, looked at it a long moment and put it back. No word, no figure, no payer, no slate; he did not reconcile the stone with the debt and did not forgive it, for not trying is not forgiving, and the debt stands exactly as it stood. From below the boy heard only the small dry scrape of a pot’s foot set down on stone from a room he cannot enter, and filed it on a place of its own (T006 advanced, T036/T076 advanced, not paid). Through Ember 7–15 (Days 186–194) the stone lay back in its unmarked clay pot in the loft, two years gone and cold, unreconciled by not trying, which is not forgiving; on Ember 13–15 (Days 192–194) the boy kept only the remembering of that dry scrape on a place of its own, not joined to the three held changes and not made a cause (T006 held). Through Ember 16–18 (Days 195–197) the stone lay back in its unmarked clay pot in the Debt Loft, two years gone and cold, unreconciled by not trying, which is not forgiving; Tarn did not take it out again and the boy filed no new likeness across the scrape (T006 held, T036/T076 held).

Through Ember 7–9, Y.H. 813 (Days 186–188) the common stone lay back in its unmarked clay pot in the Debt Loft, two years gone and cold, unreconciled with the debt by not trying, which is not forgiving; Tarn did not take it out again, and from below the boy filed the remembered holding as a remembering and not a holding made again, on a place of its own and not stood up beside the Day 161 damper fraction, the Day 166 held beat beneath the shelf or the Day 171 flagstone half-check into a rule with a payer (T006 held, T061/T082).

\textbf{Warm-stone grub.} A beetle larva of the deep mines that eats warm-stone from within and is a sign that a sweating may follow.

\textbf{Warden of the Rim.} The hereditary ruler of Keld; Karric VII closed the Cold Pass in Y.H. 741.

\textbf{The Waste.} The cold country beyond the cracks at the edge of all things, where everything unheld goes.

\textbf{Wastelings.} The bands beyond the Rim who take what the world loses; they have no banks, no Returns and no word for a debt.

\textbf{Water over water (the river’s own note).} The low continual turning a stream makes when it has more of itself than its channel will carry; water going over its own rise. Heard behind the drying racks on Silt 2, Y.H. 813, it is not a vessel’s note and is not counted among the hearings; the district has no word for it and calls it the thaw. The boy files it on a place of its own beside the told bell, the heard bell, the early Sill note and the kiln’s gap, and writes no cause across any of them. In the year’s flood of Silt 9–15, Y.H. 813 it became the note of a whole district under strain --- a low turning of many small failures inside one slow, certain one, a vessel of such capacity that no hand in it could have got around it, with a thin place nobody would name. The boy filed it beside the told bell, the heard bell, the early Sill note and the kiln’s gap and wrote no cause across any of them; no one in the district had a word for it or a hand to point at the thin place. At the going of the light on Day 100, Seed 11, Y.H. 813, the river’s low muttered note of water going over water came through the door standing a finger’s width open while the fire’s four, four and a gap came up through the floor, the two sounds in two separate places as for a hundred days; the boy’s hand outside the wool went up an inch toward the note of water and came down. At the going of the light on Day 103, Seed 14, Y.H. 813 the river’s low muttered note of water going over water came through the door standing a finger’s width open, nearer at the going of the water than at its coming, while the fire’s four, four and a gap came up through the floor under blind ash, the two sounds in two separate places as for a hundred and three days; the boards above kept four nails and four and a fifth that was a knot the width of a thumb, and the two counts did not meet. At the going of the light on Day 106, Seed 17, Y.H. 813 the two sounds came in the same two separate places as for a hundred and six days, under the Vail roof where one brown-edged crust lay stiff in the fold and the fire’s payer was still unnamed; his hand outside the wool went up an inch toward the note of water over water and came down, and the dark under the roof kept the count of one hundred and six without a figure. At the going of the light on Day 109, Seed 20, Y.H. 813 the river’s low muttered note came through the door standing a finger’s width open, nearer at the going of the water than at its coming, and the kiln’s four, four and a gap came through the floor under blind ash and the back of a broken pot, the two sounds in two separate places as for a hundred and nine days; the boards overhead kept four nails and four and a fifth that was a knot the width of a thumb, the two counts did not meet, and his hand outside the wool went up an inch toward the note of water over water and came down with the count standing at one hundred and nine, unspent. At the going of the light on Day 112, Seed 23, Y.H. 813 the river’s low muttered note came through the finger’s-width-open door and the kiln’s four, four and a gap came through the floor under blind ash and the back of a broken pot, the two sounds in two separate places as for a hundred and twelve days; the boards overhead kept four nails, four, and a fifth that was a knot the width of a thumb, the two counts did not meet, and his hand outside the wool went up an inch toward the note of water over water and came down with the count standing at one hundred and twelve, unspent. At the going of the light on Day 119, Seed 30, Y.H. 813 the river’s low muttered note came through the finger’s-width-open door and the kiln’s four, four and a gap came through the floor under blind ash and the back of a broken pot, the two sounds in two separate places as for a hundred and nineteen days; the boards overhead kept four nails and four and a fifth that was a knot the width of a thumb, the two counts did not meet, and his hand outside the wool went up an inch toward the note of water over water and came down with the count standing at one hundred and nineteen, unspent. In the small hours of Day 137, Reed 18, Y.H. 813 the river’s note of water over water came through the door standing a finger’s width open while the carried fire gave four low pulls and the silence where the fifth should have been through the floor under blind ash, and the boards overhead kept four nails, four, and a fifth that was a knot the width of a thumb: three counts in three places that did not become one. The boy’s hand outside the wool went up an inch toward the note and came down with one hundred and thirty-seven exact, unspent and spoken by nobody.

On Stone 1, Y.H. 813 (Day 360), the note came no longer water over water in the open but low under a skin: the Ilm had taken its winter ice from bank to bank. The boy filed the covering on a place of its own beside water over water, which stayed where put — a covering put on by the cold and taken off by the cold, entered nowhere, not a sixth low thing standing up as a rule, not a hearing, not a seventh of the full note and not a fourth of the three coverings. It was found where put on Stone 2 and 3 and not made again (T083/T085 with T078 advanced, not paid). See \textbf{The river takes its skin}. Ch 103.

\textbf{Weather.} The district’s one word for whatever a person can go home warm on. It does not name the thing it is said over; it grants permission to stop looking at it. On Silt 7, Y.H. 813 a washwoman said the water ran fast under the ice and then said weather and went home warm on the word, and a man come back from looking at the honeyed ice was answered with the same word and nodded as though it settled him. Through Frost 7–9, Y.H. 813 (Days 276–278) the word covered the white that would not go off the well lip, the stiffened rope, the skinned trough and the plate of ice Sella lifted and stood out of the path of feet: the yard called all of it weather, nobody gave a figure and no cause, lesson, mending or payer was made of it (T083/T085 advanced, not paid). Through Bone 10–12, Y.H. 813 (Days 309–311) the white had gone off the well’s north lip while the yard looked elsewhere, but the trough kept its skin and the silt-clouded plate stood on its flat stone out of the path of feet; the yard called the three coverings weather and entered none of them, with a finger between every pair and no fourth likeness made a cause, no figure taken off them and no payer named. The going of the white was not made a sign of the month or of anything under the Vail roof, and the month’s first reading did not pay it (T083/T085 held, not paid). Ch 86. See \textbf{Frost-bloom}.

On Ilmen 19, Y.H. 814 (Day 413) the yard called a lessening in the cold weather: a woman at the well said the air had turned and a man said it would be back before morning, and nobody owned the day while the river’s skin softened at one edge under the low note. The boy filed the change as weather and not as a sign, and no payer stood under it (T083/T085/T092 advanced, not paid). Ch 120.

\textbf{Weighing.} The second of the Five, when the year’s measures are read aloud and the rich learn how whole they are. In Sill the reading is given in a clean voice that wears a temple’s clothes and takes the speaker neatly out of his own sentences, in the same grammar heard at the Cross; a whole return may be announced for a person who is not in the room. It has a name and no tend-day and no market is held in it. On Weighing, Y.H. 813 (Day 391), word of the reading came up the Clay Yard as a voice people held in the ear and repeated without meaning to: a whole return read for a person not in any room here, and a name spoken cleanly and then not spoken again. The household would not repeat the name and the boy did not write it into any file; he filed the silence after it on the gap tray beside the told bell’s gap and the unfigured spaces, took the speaker out of his sentences as another hand takes itself out of a sentence, made no tenth hand and no reader of him, and kept the four rooms that hold the same gap — birth room, Vail kiln-house, market-day slate room and Drawing house — at four with a finger between every pair (T080/T090, T081 advanced, \textbf{not paid}). Ch 113.

\textbf{Weighing Hall.} The hall in the Hearthseat where the measures are read at the Weighing and the Hearth-fire burns behind cold iron.

\textbf{The Weir.} The eel traps and plank walk one league upriver of Sill, where the Fish Blessing is held and Rusk walks at dusk.

\textbf{Welled.} The rank of a vessel that can draw on stores held in the world itself — wells, seams or another’s bank — without owning them.

\textbf{Well-draw.} The procedure by which a Welled practitioner draws on a store the world already holds; the level drops for everyone.

\textbf{What is kept in three places does not add up to an account.} A saying of the Clay Yard, spoken at the last tend of Tallow: \emph{The stone keeps the place where the broom stopped, and the iron keeps the finger that waits in it. The fire keeps its fifth where nobody has looked for a hundred days. What is kept in three places does not add up to an account.} It is the yard’s grammar for three kept things that must not be laid together to make a bill: the shallow bright patch on the flagstones where Tarn’s stroke stopped on Tallow 22, Jorra’s finger waiting in the cold damper until Sella’s sentence finished, and the carried fire’s fifth breath missing under the floor with no payer named for a hundred and seventy-two days. The boy kept all three on separate places and would not let them stand up as a rule, for a rule is an account that has found a payer. See \textbf{Half-beat}, \textbf{Damper}, \textbf{The carried fire} and \textbf{Loan that can hear}.

\textbf{What is kept is kept by being covered.} A saying of the Vail kiln-house kept over the dressing of the first grain: \emph{The bundle comes in on the arm and is covered. The flail comes down and the grain comes out smaller than it went in, and no slate is opened over it. Winnow it, cover it again, go around the empty place in the returning line: what is kept is kept by being covered, and the count of it stands nowhere. Ask the pot. The pot has no figures.} Through Grain 16–18, Y.H. 813 (Days 225–227) the year’s first grain was beaten out of the ear, winnowed on the river wind, dried on the flagstones and poured back under wool near the hearth --- dressed and stored, counted in glances and handfuls and by the carrying arm’s weight, entered on no slate and given no figure. The yard went around the place in the returning line where a hand went in on Seed 15 and did not come out, with a look and a wide step and no number, and the two keepings were not laid together or called an account, for a rule is an account that has found a payer and none stood to either. See \textbf{The first grain}, \textbf{The hand that does not come back} and \textbf{What is read aloud is not what is paid}.

\textbf{What is read aloud is not what is paid.} A saying of Low Kiln, spoken at the last market of Tallow: \emph{The slate reads one in twelve and the house keeps its count in loaves. The box goes up the road locked and the bell goes four, four and a gap; what is read aloud is not what is paid.} On Tallow 30, Y.H. 813 (Day 179), the third Account-day and last market of the firing month, Berr Clay read \emph{one in twelve, as the notice says} over the basket, called the levy and denied it with \emph{your house}, never \emph{I}, and went off with the box locked and the true subtraction inside, believing he had done a kindness. The printed figure stood unchallenged; the figure that went into the slate did not know the hand that went in on Seed 15 and did not come out. The boy kept the read figure and the paid figure on separate places and made no account of the difference, for a rule is an account that has found a payer. See \textbf{One in twelve}, \textbf{Account-day} and \textbf{The bell at the Cross}.

On Ember 10, Y.H. 813, the first Account-day of the kiln month, the saying held again over the basket at the Cross: Berr read one in twelve and denied the levy with \emph{your house}, never \emph{I}, and went off with the box locked and the true subtraction inside, believing he had done a kindness; the bell went four, four and a gap with nobody crossing himself, and a figure read aloud was still not the figure paid. The boy kept the told figure beside the paid figure and the told bell beside the heard bell, made no account of the difference and wrote no cause across them, for a rule is an account that has found a payer.

Through Grain 16–18, Y.H. 813 (Days 225–227) the saying waits offstage while the year’s first grain is dressed and stored under wool with no figure over it; the printed one in twelve stands unchallenged and the true subtraction stays locked in Berr’s box up the road, held toward the second reading of Grain on Day 229, where a figure will be read over grain that this house has kept, covered and refused to number. Nothing was read or paid under the Vail roof in these three days (T015/T041/T047, T077 held).

On Grain 20, Y.H. 813 (Day 229), the saying stood again over the second reading of Grain: Berr Clay read one in twelve twice over the basket with the dressed grain under wool near the Vail hearth, called the levy and denied it with \emph{your house}, never \emph{I}, and went off with the box locked and the true subtraction inside, believing he had done a kindness. The district’s arithmetic changed for the second time in Grain and cannot be changed back; the printed figure stood unchallenged, a figure read aloud was still not the figure paid, and the number read over the basket did not know what the covered grain had cost or answer for the hand that went in on Seed 15 and did not come back. The bell went four, four and a gap with nobody crossing himself, and nothing reached back under the roof to join the read figure to the dressed grain (T015/T041/T047, T077, T098 advanced and unpaid, T078). Ch 59. Through Ash 16–18, Y.H. 813 (Days 345–347) the saying waited offstage: seven arithmetics of the year stood behind one unsigned figure in Berr’s locked box up the clay road, seven readings seven and not one account, the figure read still not the figure paid and no signature on the space; Ash’s second reading stood two mornings ahead and was named only as a date, never brought into a day that had not earned it and never supplied with an eighth arithmetic early (T015/T041/T047 held). The finding was kept on a place of its own with no payer, not laid across the house’s not-doings, the covered grain, the five held objects, the pot-crack resting, the held breath at the sill, the Ash 17 direction or the boy’s gaps. Ch 98.

On Ash 20, Y.H. 813 (Day 349), the saying stood again over the dark month’s second reading: \textbf{eight arithmetics of the year now stand behind one printed figure, eight are eight and not one account}, the printed figure one in twelve and unchallenged, the figure read still not the figure paid and no signature on the space between. The box went up the clay road with Ash’s second subtraction locked inside and Berr Clay saying \emph{The levy is called. It is not called by me} and \emph{your house}, never \emph{I}, believing he had done a kindness; the bell went four, four and a gap with nobody crossing himself, and the boy kept the read figure beside the paid figure and the heard bell beside the told, making no account of the difference, for a rule is an account that has found a payer and none stood (T015/T041/T047 advanced, not paid; T077, T078). Ch 99.

On Stone 20, Y.H. 813 (Day 379), the month’s second Account-day and market, the saying stood again over the basket: \textbf{eleven arithmetics of the year now stand behind one unsigned figure, eleven are eleven and not one account}, the figure read still not the figure paid and no signature on the space. Berr Clay read one in twelve twice over the basket, called the levy, denied it with \emph{your house}, never \emph{I}, said something low to the block about kindness being entered and went off with the box locked and Stone’s second subtraction inside, believing he had done a kindness, with no anger and no triumph in him. The boy kept the read figure beside the paid figure and the heard bell beside the told, making no account of the difference, for a rule is an account that has found a payer and none stood (T015/T041/T047 advanced, not paid; T078). The dressed grain covered under wool at the rack end was read over by a number that did not know what it cost, and the finding was not laid across the keeping at the fold. Ch 109.

\textbf{Which row did the pot go quiet on?} A question asked over the boards of the Clay Yard in Low Kiln on Grain 21, Y.H. 813 (Day 230), in a voice with no owner, no room, no hand at the kiln and no cause. The weather answered first and the price of barley after it, and the row stood where it stood; nobody leaned in to take the answer down. It is not one of the three shapings of the pot saying (\emph{sings itself out early}, \emph{not heard from since}, \emph{gone quiet on every row come the thaw}), for a proverb about pots and a question about a row are different instruments; it is not a hearing, not a seventh of the full note, not a cause, not a name and not a fifth telling of the burned slate. The boy filed it on a place of its own with a finger between it and the sayings, the slate, the two shut-room tellings, the hearings and the count. A row is a place; a place wants a witness; a witness wants a day when somebody stands somewhere and can be asked. No witness stands yet (T101 planted and unpaid). On Grain 23, Y.H. 813 (Day 232) the question came over the boards a \textbf{second} time in the same voice with no owner, no room, no hand at the kiln and no cause: the weather answered first and the price of barley after it, the voice went off up the terrace and the row stood where it stood. The boy set the second telling on the seventh place beside the first with a finger between the two, and fingers between them and the three sayings, the fourth burned-slate telling, the two shut-room tellings, the six hearings and the count. Two askings are not one witness, for a witness stands somewhere and can be asked and none does; the second asking is \textbf{not} a fourth shaping of the pot saying, a hearing, a seventh of the full note, a fifth telling of the slate, a cause, a name or a fifth witness, but a seed for the far-off day a witness stands somewhere and can be asked (T101 advanced and unpaid). On Grain 26, Y.H. 813 (Day 235) the question came over the boards a \textbf{third} time, low into the boards and not into the basket; the weather answered first and the price of barley after it, the voice went off up the terrace and the row stood where it stood, with nobody leaning in to take the answer down. The boy opened it as a surgeon opens a wound — what it asks, where it stands, what it would want before any man could answer it and who would stand under the answer to pay — and found no witness at the bottom; he set the third telling on the seventh place beside the first two with a finger between each pair and a finger between them and the sayings, the tellings, the hearings and the count. Three askings are not one witness, for a witness stands somewhere and can be asked and none does and none could; the third asking is \textbf{not} a fourth shaping of the pot saying, a hearing, a seventh, a fifth telling, a cause, a name or a fifth witness (T101 advanced and unpaid). On Grain 29, Y.H. 813 (Day 238) the question came over the boards a \textbf{fourth} time, low into the boards and not into the basket, the weather answering first and the price of barley after it, the voice going off up the terrace toward High Kiln while the row stood where it stood and nobody leaned in to take the answer down. Four askings are still not one witness, and no fifth asking came in Grain. On Smoke 8, Y.H. 813 (Day 247) the question came over the boards a \textbf{fifth} time in the same grammar: the weather answered first with a wrong wind off High Kiln carrying the sweet edge of lead glaze across the boards, touching the fold of dressed grain and going out on the wind that brought it, and the price of barley answered after it; the voice went up the terrace while the row stood where it stood. The boy opened the asking as a surgeon opens a wound and found no witness at the bottom. Five askings now stand on the seventh place with a finger between each pair: still not one witness, not a fourth shaping of the pot saying, not a hearing, not a seventh, not a fifth telling of the burned slate, not a cause, not a name and not a row named, held for the far-off day a witness stands somewhere and can be asked (T101 advanced and unpaid). Through Smoke 13–15, Y.H. 813 (Days 252–254) the question was \textbf{not asked a sixth time}. Five askings stand on the seventh place with a finger between each pair, no owner, room, hand at the kiln, cause, witness or row named; it was not made a hearing, a fourth shaping of the pot saying, a fifth telling of the burned slate, a third telling of the shut counting room, a cause or a name, and nobody stood somewhere to be asked. It is held for the far-off day a witness stands and can be asked (T101 held, unpaid). See \textbf{Three askings do not make a witness}, \textbf{The pot not heard from}, \textbf{Burned slate} and \textbf{Two tellings of one absence}. On Ash 17, Y.H. 813 (Day 346) a further direction came over the boards from Slate Row about a room shut with the damper closed and a slate burned over a man nobody named, with no room, hand at a flame, figure, date or person standing to be asked; the boy filed it on a place of its own \textbf{beside} the Ash 5 joining with a finger between, advancing the finding that a place wants a witness while making no witness of the voice and no sixth asking of the row, which stays at five (T035/T031/T065/T095 and T101 advanced and \textbf{not paid}). Ch 98. On Ash 23, Y.H. 813 (Day 352), a third ownerless direction came over the boards from the same direction: a room shut with the damper closed against the cold and a slate burned over a man nobody named so a count would not go up, with no room, hand at a flame, figure, date, name or person standing to be asked, the weather and the price of barley answering first and the voice going up the terrace. The boy filed it on a place of its own beside the Ash 5 joining and the Ash 17 direction with a finger between every pair, advancing the finding that a place wants a witness while making no witness, sixth asking of the row (which stays at five), sixth telling of the burned slate (five), third shut-room telling (two), fifth shaping of the well-saying (four), hearing, seventh, cause, name or payment of it (T035/T031/T065/T095 and T101 advanced and \textbf{not paid}). The voice did not repeat on Ash 24, and five askings still stand on the seventh place with no row named and nobody standing to be asked. Ch 100.

\textbf{Whole.} A vessel that holds without leaking; also the rank of such a vessel.

\textbf{Whole return.} A return in which one person’s warmth is kept intact and the person comes back as themselves, with memory.

\textbf{Widow’s mark.} The Grathic institution by which a widow holds a kiln in her own right; the only Grathic institution nobody argues with. A thumb-length of lead-glazed clay with the kiln scratched into it, worn at the throat and touched only before the kiln is opened. The Court’s factor at Greybank confirms the mark; the confirmation is spoken of as a kindness, and kindness is entered. Through Reed 28–30 Sella Vail had gone around a hundred and forty-nine days of shelves, strips, racks, baskets and dusks without touching it, because none of them was an opening; on Tallow 1, Y.H. 813, before the first firing of the month, she put her hand to it, held it one breath and let go, tipped the carried coal under the back of a broken pot and did not touch it again at a shelf, a well, an afternoon or a dusk. The rule held exactly, with nobody to praise it and nobody to see it broken. Through Tallow 4–10, Y.H. 813 the mark hung where it hung, untouched at the loaf shelf, the yard well, the reed work at the Weir, the reading block at the Cross, the clay road and every dusk, because none of them was an opening; the hand goes to the mark before the kiln and at no other hour. Through Tallow 11–13, Y.H. 813 the mark hung where it hung, untouched at a morning, a shelf, a well, a rack, a road, a bed and a dusk, because none was an opening; the hand goes to it before the kiln and at no other hour. Through Tallow 24–30, Y.H. 813 (Days 173–179), the firing month’s last tend, the mark hung where it hung and was touched at no shelf, well, rack, road, basket, market, post or dusk, because no hour among those seven days was an opening; on Day 179 Sella set the basket in the moot-post’s finger’s width of shade where no slate lay and stood half a pace off without explaining the turn to the basket. The hand goes to the mark before the kiln and at no other hour. Through Ember 1–6, Y.H. 813 (Days 180–185) the mark was touched once — before the first firing of the kiln month on Ember 1, held one breath, with nobody praising the opening and nobody seeing what it mended — and at no shelf, well, rack, road, basket, afternoon or dusk on any of the six days; a morning and a shelf are not openings, and the hand goes to the mark before the kiln and at no other hour. Through Bone 10–12, Y.H. 813 (Days 309–311) the mark hung untouched at every morning, hearth, rack, row, reading, yard, basket, going of the light and bed, because none of these was an opening; five openings in five months were five and not a rule, and the next stands far off in a later month’s first firing, not hoped for and not counted toward. Bone’s first reading came to the Cross on the tenth and made four arithmetics stand behind one printed figure, but nothing of the reading came back under the Vail roof as a lesson, mending, sign or payment, and the widow’s mark was not made a cause of it. Ch 86. See \textbf{The first opening} and \textbf{What is read aloud is not what is paid}. On Ember 1, Y.H. 813 (Day 180), before the first firing of the kiln month, Sella Vail put her hand to the mark again, held it one breath, let go, lifted the clay lid with the back of a hand and tipped the carried coal under the back of a broken pot; the fire took, still answering four low pulls with the fifth missing and no payer named, and nobody praised the opening and nobody saw what it mended. Through Ember 2 and Ember 3 (Days 181–182) the mark hung where it hung, untouched at a loaf shelf, a yard well, a drying rack, a road, a basket, an afternoon and a dusk, because none was an opening; the hand goes to the mark before the kiln and at no other hour. Through Ember 4–6 (Days 183–185) it hung where it hung at every shelf, well, rack, road, basket, afternoon and dusk; through Ember 7–9 (Days 186–188) it hung where it hung at a morning, a shelf, a well, a rack, a road, a basket, an afternoon and a dusk, and was touched at none of them, because a morning and a shelf and a dusk are not openings and the one opening was before the kiln on Ember 1, nobody praising it and nobody seeing what it mended. On Day 188 Sella set the basket down at the yard’s edge, turned the boy’s face as she would turn a pot to the light and went wide around the place the carriers crossed, and did not touch the mark; the fire still answered four low pulls with its fifth missing and its payer unnamed for a hundred and eighty-eight days (T058/T079, T088). Through Ember 10–12, Y.H. 813 (Days 189–191) the mark hung where it hung at a morning, a shelf, a well, a rack, a road, a basket, a yard, an afternoon and a dusk, and was touched at none of them, because the one opening was before the kiln on Ember 1 and the hand goes to the mark at no other hour. On Day 189 Sella set the basket in the moot-post’s finger’s width of shade where no slate lay and stood half a pace off through the first reading of Ember and the bell, giving no instruction or reason to the basket; on Days 190 and 191 she went wide around the yard’s unswept places and the place the carriers crossed with a look and a wide step and no number. Nobody praised the opening and nobody saw what it mended; the fire’s payer stayed unnamed for a hundred and eighty-nine, ninety and ninety-one days (T058/T079, T088). Through Ember 13–15, Y.H. 813 (Days 192–194) the mark hung where it hung at every morning, shelf, well, rack, road, basket, yard, afternoon and dusk and was touched at none of them, because a quiet morning after a reading is not an opening and there has been no opening since before the kiln on Ember 1. On the three days Sella gave every instruction to the wool, the fire, the pot, the broom and the running water and never to the basket, stood a half-pace from every open slate, set the pot handle two inches beyond the reaching hand with her hand resting a half-beat longer at the setting, and carried him home at the going of the light without looking at his face; nobody praised the opening and nobody saw what it mended, and the fire’s payer stayed unnamed for a hundred and ninety-two, ninety-three and ninety-four days (T058/T079, T088). Through Ember 16–18, Y.H. 813 (Days 195–197) the mark hung where it hung, untouched at every morning, shelf, well, rack, road, basket, afternoon and dusk, because a morning, a shelf and a dusk are not openings and there had been no opening since before the kiln on Ember 1; nobody praised what it mended and nobody saw it broken. Sella gave every instruction to the wool, the fire, the pot, the broom and the running water and never the basket, said \emph{the house}, kept her half-pace from every open slate, glanced once at the clay jar cold under its glaze without touching it, pushed coal-black hair back with the burn-wrist so the grey streak showed pale, set the pot handle two inches beyond the reaching hand with her hand resting a half-beat longer at the setting, and carried him home at each going of the light without looking at his face; the fire’s payer stayed unnamed for a hundred and ninety-five, ninety-six and ninety-seven days (T058/T079, T088). Through Ember 19–30 and Grain 1–30, Y.H. 813 (Days 198–239) the mark hung where it hung at every shelf, well, rack, road, basket, market, yard, afternoon and dusk, and was touched at none of them, because the one opening was before the kiln on Ember 1 and no reading, harvest or tending is an opening; the hand goes to the mark before the kiln and at no other hour. On Smoke 1, Y.H. 813 (Day 240), after sixty days of going around, Sella put her hand to it before the first firing of Smoke, held it one breath, let go, lifted the clay lid with the back of a hand and tipped the carried coal under a broken pot; the fire took, still answering four low pulls with the fifth missing and its payer unnamed for two hundred and forty, forty-one and forty-two days, and nobody praised the opening or saw what it mended. Through Smoke 2 and 3 (Days 241–242) she did not touch the mark again at a shelf, well, rack, road, basket, afternoon or dusk, because the hand goes to it before the kiln and at no other hour; the opening was put behind the household without a lesson, a figure, a slate, a bond or a payer, and the next real opening, the first firing of Frost, stands far off and unbrought (T058/T079, T088). Through Frost 2, Bone 2, Tallow 1, Ember 1, Smoke 1 and Ash 2 the mark was touched only before each month’s first kiln and at no other hour; through Stone 1–3 it hung where it hung after Ash 2 and no seventh opening was made due. On Stone 5, Y.H. 813 (Day 364), the deep-winter month’s first firing, Sella carried the basket to the kiln mouth before any instruction went to it, set it level out of the draught, put her left hand to the mark at her throat for one breath, let go, lifted the clay lid with the back of a hand and tipped the carried coal under the back of a broken pot. The fire took in fours with the fifth still missing and its payer unnamed three hundred and sixty-four days; nobody praised the opening, named what it mended, entered a slate or made a lesson of it. \textbf{Seven openings in seven months are seven and not a rule and no eighth is made due}; she did not touch the mark again at shelf, well, rack, basket, yard, morning, afternoon, going of light or bed on Stone 4, 5 or 6 (T058/T079, T088 advanced, not paid).
