Ch 104. See \textbf{The hand goes to the mark before the kiln and at no other hour}.

\section*{L}

\textbf{Leave the crack showing. If it’s worth mending, mend it twice.} Two proverbs of Garl Vail of Low Kiln, said in the house to the pot and to the fire and never to a person: \emph{Leave the crack showing. People trust a thing they can see has been handled} and \emph{If it’s worth mending it’s worth mending twice. The second time is the real one.} They are sayings about repair and not about completion: a restored thing hides the hand that handled it, while a mended thing leaves that hand showing, and the second mending is the true one because it is done by a person who has already handled the break. The twice-mended pot on the Vail pot board keeps the hairline of the original break dark between the older brass staple and the tighter wire, and Sella Vail lifts it thumb-first where the wire crosses before letting the weight come on the handle. On Ash 9, Y.H. 813 (Day 338), her thumb stayed one breath longer than the lift required at that crossing and moved on without a word, a figure or a witness; the boy filed the held interval on a place of its own beside five other small objects, expressly not a sixth and with no payer standing under it. It is a keeping that gathers toward the far-off hand that will one day lay the district’s private keepings together, not a sign, a mending, a payment or a rule (T009/T013/T092, T060/T086 advanced, not paid). Ch 95. Through Ash 10–12, Y.H. 813 (Days 339–341), the hairline was left showing at each going of the light and the proverbs went to the pot and the fire, improved in the keeping and very likely not as good as the man said them, never to a person; repair stayed apart from restoration, for a restored thing hides the hand that handled it and a mended thing leaves that hand showing. The Ash 9 held breath at the crossing stayed where it was set, beside the five objects and expressly not a sixth, and was not made again on any of the three days (T009/T013/T092, T060/T086 held). Ch 96. See \textbf{The carried fire}, \textbf{A stick keeps what a slate would tax} and \textbf{A handful lifted and let fall back tells you the grain is dry}.

\section*{O}

\textbf{Offer a figure to a stick and the stick keeps its notch.} A saying of the firing women at the Low Kiln wells, and the epigraph of \emph{The Figure That Went Back to the Sleeve}: \emph{Offer a figure to a stick and the stick keeps its notch; the figure goes back into the fist and the fist into the sleeve. Neither has paid, and the wood has not learned a name.} The saying is about a count offered to a record and then withdrawn: on Ilmen 26, Y.H. 814 (Day 420), a woman waiting her turn at the yard well brought a number up out of a shut fist and held it toward the strip of notched birch in Ilva’s sleeve, saying she could put a figure to the month’s firings. Ilva’s hand went flat over the fold before her eyes went to the asker and her mouth opened after both; she answered the question put and not the one behind it — \emph{Ask the pot what it cost. I keep the count, not the account} — and the figure went from the fist toward the wood, looked at the light and went back into the sleeve, arriving nowhere. The woman shut her fist on it, said \emph{Then it’s a stick} and went back to the round, and nobody turned twice. No slate was opened within reach of the basket, no figure came off the wood, no reader was made and no name was spoken over the notches. The boy took the order apart by the place of each part — fist, eye, mouth, the half-beat in the gap — and filed the \textbf{offer and its return} on a place of its own beside Ilva’s ninth record-first hand and the fifth shaping of the well-saying, with a finger between every pair: not a sale, a reader, a tenth hand, a payer, an account or a sixth shaping, not the calling of the loan and not joined to the well-asking, the clerk’s entered figure, the second man’s turned slate or the face at the yard’s edge. It is a reaching gathering interest toward the far-off hand that will one day lay the district’s private keepings together and is not that hand; Ilva’s fear is advanced and unpaid, and she was not made a reader by the figure’s nearness (T080 advanced and not paid, with T090/T102). See \textbf{A stick keeps what a slate would tax}, \textbf{Ask the pot} and \textbf{A figure goes up the clay road in a locked box; a word comes up from the well and stops on the stone lip}. Ch 123.

\section*{T}

\textbf{The slate does not know it has been read. The house does, and keeps the count in loaves.} A saying of Low Kiln, told under the moot-post when the eleventh figure went up, and the epigraph of \emph{The Eleventh Reading}. The slate is a thing that can be read without knowing it, and the house is a thing that keeps without owning: one in twelve stands printed and unchallenged over two hundred people, the figure read aloud is not the figure paid, and the household’s count goes on in loaves, glances and the space where a loaf stood, told by nobody. On Stone 20, Y.H. 813 (Day 379), the month’s second Account-day and market, eleven arithmetics stood behind one unsigned figure — eleven are eleven and not one account, no signature on the space and no doctrine out of eleven — and nothing of the reading crossed under the Vail roof as sign, lesson, mending, cause, payment or payer. The boy kept the exact count of his own days, which reached three hundred and eighty at the close of Stone 21, six months and two hundred days told by nobody, and kept the finding that eleven are not one account on a place of its own beside the keeping at the fold and the four rooms’ gap (T015/T041/T047, T071/T072, T097, T081 advanced and unpaid). See \textbf{What is read aloud is not what is paid}, \textbf{Account-day} and \textbf{A thread of count kept in loaves}. Ch 109.

\textbf{The yard carried the names from door to door and set them down where the speaking stopped.} A Low Kiln saying, kept through the Five, and the epigraph of \emph{The Grey Left Where It Lay}: \emph{The yard carried the names from door to door and set them down where the speaking stopped. The grey was left where it lay and burnt the next morning, and nobody called the two the same thing. A year went out with its figure unsigned and came back wearing the same face, and the fire kept four pulls and wanted a fifth.} It is a saying about the difference between a thing a district calls dealt with and the same thing left where it lay, and about a year that turns without signing anything. On the Remembering the names of the dead go up the Clay Yard from house to house while the Vail house keeps its own quiet and does not say the one name that matters; on the Last Day the Ash is left in the corners and a neighbour calls it dealt with because it will be burnt in the morning, and Sella does not say it; on Ilmen 1 the yard burns it and calls it gone and she still says nothing. The boy keeps the called-gone beside the left-in-place ridge with a finger between and makes no fourth likeness a cause. Twelve arithmetics of Y.H. 813 go out behind one unsigned figure and come back into Y.H. 814 unchanged, the figure read still not the figure paid and no signature on the space, while Ilmen 10’s first arithmetic waits to begin a new count and not stand up as a payer or a doctrine. The carried fire keeps four low pulls with the fifth wanted and its payer unnamed 393, 394 and 395 days (T009/T013/T092, T083/T085, T015/T041/T047, T088 advanced and \textbf{not paid}). See \textbf{The Ash}, \textbf{The Remembering}, \textbf{Last Day}, \textbf{The carried fire} and \textbf{What is read aloud is not what is paid}. Ch 114.

\textbf{The yard kept its days in loaves pushed along a shelf, and a space at the row’s end nobody called a number.} A Low Kiln saying, told of the first working week, and the epigraph of \emph{A Man Stood at the Yard’s Edge}: \emph{The yard kept its days in loaves pushed along a shelf, and a space at the row’s end nobody called a number. A man came to the edge and stood with his hands loose. No loaf passed and no slate was shown; the pot said nothing, and the fire kept four pulls and wanted a fifth.} The first clause is a household keeping its arithmetic badly — in loaves pushed along the shelf, in glances at the clay jar and in a space at the row’s end nobody calls a number — while the boy keeps four hundred and one exact against it and does not stand the number up as a threshold, a doctrine or a figure. The second is the man from Slate Row whose name was on no roll, who stood at the yard’s edge on Ilmen 6, Y.H. 814 (Day 400) with his hands loose, the soft hands of a man who sits at a table and the patient face of a man who can wait in a doorway; nobody asked him what he wanted and he did not say, no loaf passed, no slate was shown, no word carried and no threshold was crossed. The boy filed his face on a place of its own beside the older record-first hands — no tenth hand made of it, the waiting never called a sale and the man never stood up as a witness (T080/T090 advanced, \textbf{not paid}) — and kept it with a finger between it and Jorra’s promise under the wheel-shed and Tarn’s held degree toward the landing, not laying any two together to make a cause, for a doctrine is an account that has found a payer and none stood. The last clause is the carried fire, which answers four low pulls under the floor with the silence where the fifth should stand, its payer unnamed 399, 400 and 401 days; before first grey on the same morning three or more men unnamed went low into the back room off the wheel-shed and Jorra came out with the day’s meal-fine grey slate dust white in a fist-crease (T062/T035/T031 advanced, \textbf{not paid}). Six honest answers, 373 through 378, stood on the sixth place across the three tending days and not one was a doctrine; the count closed at four hundred and one exact, six months and two hundred and twenty-one days told by nobody, and Ilmen 10’s first arithmetic waited three mornings off as a reset and not a signing. See \textbf{A slate burns where a room was shut}, \textbf{The carried fire}, \textbf{Three askings do not make a witness} and \textbf{The year turned in the night and the pots stood where they had stood}. Ch 116.

\textbf{The year turned in the night and the pots stood where they had stood.} A Low Kiln saying, kept after the Five, and the epigraph of \emph{The New Year Took Up Its Grammar}: \emph{The year turned in the night and the pots stood where they had stood. The fire kept four pulls and wanted a fifth, and the hand went to the slate before the eye went up. Word came up that a man was still set below the bridge, and nobody said the landing was a door.} The first clause is a house that goes back to its grammar as though nothing had turned: the coals are told the thaw, the pot is lifted thumb-first with its crack showing, the grain is covered and unfigured and the pot rim is set two inches beyond the reaching hand. The second is the carried fire keeping four pulls and wanting a fifth with its payer unnamed, and the order of reaching in which the hand goes to the record before the eye goes to the person. The third is the danger that came as a piece of news on Ilmen 3, Y.H. 814 (Day 397): a soft-cuffed clerk reported still set at the out-of-line landing below the north bridge with his slate turned inward for a measure nobody had called, and Tarn’s head going a degree toward the landing and back to the broom without a word. The clerk called nothing, wrote no name and was made no witness, and nobody under any roof named the landing a door; the degree was held as a shape with a finger between it and the inward slate, not a rule repeated, not a payment, not a hearing, not a calling of the loan (T080/T090 and T036/T076/T006 advanced and \textbf{not paid}). Twelve arithmetics of Y.H. 813 stood behind one unsigned figure through the three tending days and Ilmen 10’s first arithmetic waited six mornings off as a reset and not a signing; the count reached three hundred and ninety-eight exact with three hundred and seventy-two honest answers on the sixth place, and the fire’s fifth stayed unpaid and Garl’s name unspoken the same three hundred and ninety-six, ninety-seven and ninety-eight days (T071/T072, T088, T009/T013/T092 advanced, not paid). See \textbf{The carried fire}, \textbf{Loan that can hear}, \textbf{A kept thing is owed} and \textbf{What is read aloud is not what is paid}. Ch 115.

\textbf{Twelve times the figure went over the basket and twelve times it went up the road in a locked box.} A Low Kiln saying, told at the last market of the year, and the epigraph of \emph{The Twelfth Arithmetic}: \emph{Twelve times the figure went over the basket and twelve times it went up the road in a locked box. The pot kept its crack and the year kept its cold, and the hand that wrote went home believing well of itself.} It is a saying about a district that can change its arithmetic twelve times in a year and still not own what the changes cost. The figure goes twice over the basket on each Account-day — once for the moot and once for the households that come late — and the true subtraction goes up the clay road in the Thane’s locked box, while the Vail pot keeps its hairline showing between old brass and tighter wire and the year keeps its cold without a boundary drawn. On Stone 30, Y.H. 813 (Day 389), twelve readings stood behind one unsigned figure; twelve were twelve and not one account, the figure read was still not the figure paid, no signature stood on the space and no doctrine came out of twelve, and Berr Clay went home believing he had done a kindness, with no anger and no triumph in him. That belief, not anger, is the part that will one day be remembered against him; the keeping at the fold, found where put and not made again, and the findings there gather toward the far-off hand that will one day lay the district’s private keepings together, a hand that is not his and has not come (T015/T041/T047, T097 advanced and not paid). See \textbf{Account-day}, \textbf{Leave the crack showing. If it’s worth mending, mend it twice.} and \textbf{A thing left lying has two keepers}. Ch 112.

\textbf{Two slates under one arm; the road carries and reads neither.} A saying of the Low Kiln bucket-round in the month of Silt, and the epigraph of \emph{What the Road Carries}: \emph{Two slates under one arm, both turned to the sleeve; the road carries and reads neither. A hair-thin thaw where no broom goes; the river softens at one edge under its skin. Both are weather, and weather keeps no account.} The first clause is the runner’s reaching on Silt 6, Y.H. 814 (Day 430): a word went around the yard well from mouth to mouth with nobody standing under it that the woman who carries Berr Clay’s slate had taken up a second, narrower one, held edge-on under her arm with the writing turned the same way toward her sleeve; no name was spoken over either slate and no figure came off either. Her hand went to the slates before her eye went to the yard and her mouth after both, the half-beat standing in the gap where a lesser observer would put an intention. The boy filed it as a report and a shape on a place of its own beside the eighth record-first hand, the offered figure and its return, the clerk’s entered figure brought up the yard as a report and the three likenesses of Slate Row, with a finger between every pair: not a reader made, not a ninth or tenth hand, not a witness, sale, sixth shaping, custom, payment or calling of the loan, and not told again on Silt 7. The woman never came on stage, is given no name, interior, errand or witness’s standing, and carrying is not reading (T080 with T090/T102 advanced and \textbf{not paid}). The second clause is the thaw on Silt 7 (Day 431): the clean dark line at the Vail corner kept its finer grey a hair less distinct along one stretch where no broom had gone in two years, thickened in the dry cold with the sour tang of Ash, and the air off the river was less cold at one edge where the low note ran nearer under the winter skin; the boy found both where put, did not look twice, called them weather and made no sign, fourth covering, payment or sixth shaping of either (T083/T085/T092 advanced and \textbf{not paid}). Both findings gather toward the far-off hand that will one day lay the district’s private keepings together and call the joining an account — a hand that is not his. See \textbf{A figure goes up the clay road in a locked box; a word comes up from the well and stops on the stone lip}, \textbf{The figure goes on the slate before the man is looked at; an order is not an answer}, \textbf{A slate burns where a room was shut} and \textbf{Ask the road}. Ch 126.
